## CHAPTER III.

### On the wondrous craftsmanship of the Sun: also on the causes and effects of solar spots and torches.

<margin>Utility derived from the motion of the Sun.</margin>
<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'C' containing a scene of a person, possibly an astronomer, seated in a landscape and holding a tool, appearing to perform observations or measurements.</image-desc>
SINCE there is an incredible and almost divine power of the Sun in the world—for from the Sun comes all movement, life, preservation, and the adornment of both celestial and terrestrial things—so much so that the more closely you contemplate it, the more miracles you find in it, I think it befits a philosopher to search all the treasures of nature to bring forth teachings worthy of such a great miracle.

Let it be fixed and settled, then, that if the Sun were stationary, the governance of this earthly world would be far different; namely, the state of things would be most turbulent. The globe of the earth would not be habitable everywhere, nor would the arrangement of the Atmosphere be the same as we now experience it, on account of the absence of the Sun's benefit, which gives life to and preserves all things. From these things the generous goodness of divine providence shines forth, because it gave to this star <note>In the 17th century, the Sun was often categorized as a "star" or "wandering star" (planet) in the broader sense of a celestial body.</note> both a daily motion in longitude and an annual motion in latitude, and an eccentric one at that. By the diversity of such movement, the atmosphere is distributed into a steady moderation and a temperature suited to human uses. For by this we have the changes of the seasons—winter, summer, autumn, and spring; by this we pass through the cycles of years, months, weeks, and indeed days, the variety of which the one and same Sun effects by its presence and absence. Therefore, the power of the Sun is given to the earthly globe by divine providence through daily and annual local motion, which acts as the conveyor of its hidden powers and faculties. 

But lest the earth always be struck by the same solar rays, or lest the other part of the solar body turned toward the stars appear to be idle, divine wisdom gave to the body of the Sun its own motions, distinct from all others, <margin>Admirable things about the Sun's motion.</margin> by which individual motions (as is established from irrefutable experiments) in twenty-

<column-break/>

-ty at the demand of nature? See the figure placed here, in which the radiant light CBA strikes both the earth and the moon, and the remaining stars; this light, reflected onto the shaded opposite part of the earth, acts as a substitute for the absent Sun with moderate heat and light, and there produces various effects according to the varying mixture of the power communicated.

-seven days, it completes one revolution around its own center. By the benefit of this rotation, whatever power it contains, it successively pours out most abundantly upon the earth as well as the entire Heaven, and thus upon each individual star. 

And that this circulation of the Sun was granted by the Creator for the sake of the earth is evident from the fact that it does not revolve by a simple motion, but by an annual circling of a movable axis around which the first motion is described. By this it happens that the Sun inclines toward the earth around the northern peak and the southern depression, and "nods" <note>original: "nutet"; Kircher is describing the Sun's axial tilt or obliquity relative to the Earth's orbit</note> over a period of six months, and deviates by that same alternating appearance of the poles and movable axes above the solar horizon and concealment below it. This dizzying oscillation <term>librationem; a term for a slow rocking or swaying motion, often used to describe the Moon's wobble, here applied to the Sun</term> must not be doubted to have been made for the benefit of the earth also. For from this it happens that through the thirteen rotations <note>original: "lustrationes"; literally "purifications" or "surveying journeys," referring here to the roughly 13.5 rotations the Sun makes in a year</note> by which it surveys the whole Universe, just as the earth is always cherished by different light, so it is undoubtedly imbued with different solar power. 

This variety of influences is wonderfully promoted by that perpetual mutual conjunction, separation, departure, and return of "spots" <term>maculae; sunspots</term> and "torches" <term>faculae; bright, hot spots on the Sun's surface</term>. For <margin>Reasoning concerning the spots of the Sun.</margin> if the shadow of the Moon in a solar eclipse alters the earth so much, how much alteration do we believe the Sun will cause in higher things—the Sun which repeatedly suffers "eclipses" of 50 or 60 spots and shadows of such great size that they seem to equal the surface of the Moon or the Earth? Therefore, since the Sun now proceeds as if mourning in a sort of spotted trail of shadows; and now, having cast off its mournful veil, it appears entirely serene, bright, peaceful, and smiling, at one moment seeming to vomit flames, and soon after black soot; certainly reason teaches that these things act upon the earth in different ways and produce dissimilar effects, since by this alternation they vary, hinder, promote, increase, and diminish the light of the Sun itself.

which, when changed, necessarily causes the solar influence upon the Earth and sublunary things <note>Things "under the moon," referring to the changing, earthly realm in the Aristotelian worldview.</note> to change accordingly. Almost all the astronomical records of the ages prove that this is the case. <margin>Various histories.</margin>
Indeed, Suetonius records that at the time Julius Caesar was being murdered, a certain thick and sooty matter was seen around the Sun for a long time. Also, in the time of the Emperor Justinian, for an entire year the Sun was so obscured, as if covered by a veil, that it shone so little and so dimly that it seemed to have been turned into the Moon. See Aldrovandus’s book *On Prodigies*. <note>Ulisse Aldrovandi (1522–1605) was a celebrated Italian naturalist.</note> The Arabs observed a similar solar prodigy in the 64th year of the Hegira, as Haël <note>Likely referring to the Arab astrologer Haly Abenragel.</note> records in his *Astrology*; a great desolation of things followed it. We read in Paul the Deacon that in the year 790, for a space of 17 days, even while the sky was most serene and clear, the Sun shone so dimly that it cast almost total darkness over the world. A massive comet also followed this obscurity. Cornelius Gemma, in his *Cosmocritica*, records that in the year 1569, the Sun’s disk appeared to all of Europe as if suffused with a bloody color for many days; this phenomenon was followed by both a comet and civil unrest. Finally, in the year 1625, shortly before the Swedish War, throughout the entire course of the year, the solar

<column-break/>

disk was covered by a massive boiling of spots, observed both by me in Germany and by our fellow Jesuit Scheiner in Rome. <note>Christopher Scheiner was a famous astronomer who debated Galileo over the nature of sunspots.</note> If astronomers were to note all these things diligently, perhaps from such phenomena compared with sublunary effects, a "New Astrology" could be established—one much more certain than that common planetary astrology. In the Moon, our friend Cysatus <note>Jean-Baptiste Cysat, a Swiss Jesuit mathematician and astronomer.</note> also noted an atmosphere, or an exhalation of vapors, during the solar eclipse of 1628, on the very day of the Lord’s birth. I do not doubt that the same happens in the other planetary globes, which, as centers distinct from the center of the universe, also establish various spheres of exhalations. From these, if I am not mistaken, the origin of comets—ignited both above and below the Moon—and the birth of "New Stars" <note>Supernovae.</note> is clearly revealed.
<margin>Origin of comets.</margin>
I could bring forward many things in this place regarding the manner in which the Sun and the other planets pour out their spheres of exhalations, and how comets can be born from them. However, since it is not always the mark of a prudent man to babble on rashly about all the ways these particular reasons for such unusual effects can vary, I only wished here to suggest the cause of these phenomena generally <note>original Greek: κατ' ὅλον (kat' holon)</note> for others to comment upon; but perhaps elsewhere we will open our opinion more fully on these matters, once we understand that these discussions of ours have not been displeasing. You see, therefore, what a great harvest of secrets in philosophy, what a fertile field, is opened by this new phenomenon discovered in the most recent times. But lest we seem to have said these things only in passing, it remains for us to discuss the nature and efficiency—the logic by which all these things happen through heat.

# CHAPTER IV.
->On the light of the Moon and of the other Stars.<-

In order that a greater variety of things and effects might shine forth in this mundane craftsmanship, divine providence wished to establish several bodies in this world, each imbued with various and different qualities. These, being "impregnated" by the fertile rays of the Sun, might strive toward new combinations of things to be generated on Earth, carried there by the reflected rays of solar light, acting as a mixture of seeds. To make this more convenient, He willed the Moon to revolve around the Earth and the planets around the Sun as their center, so that they might more conveniently pour the rays received from the Sun onto the Earth. Since, however, the said

<column-break/>

bodies drink in the Sun’s brightness not only on their surface but deep into their very marrow, and tint it with their own native properties, it happens that the Sun’s "seminal virtues" <note>The inherent powers or "seeds" of life believed to be carried by light.</note> are propagated into those bodies through light rays. There, they are mixed with the seminal virtue peculiar to each of the planets and other stars. Then, acting both through the reflected ray onto the Earth and through the direct and refracted ray into the atmosphere, they produce diverse and innumerable effects according to the disposition and capacity of the Earth—which is similarly filled with a certain "universal mixture of seeds." <note>original Greek: πανοσπερμίᾳ (panospermia)</note> That this "tinting" occurs is evident from their very different colored lights: such as the leaden light of Saturn, the fiery light of Mars, the silvery light of Venus, and the clear, serene light of Jupiter. # The Illumination of Celestial Bodies

That the variety of colors does not originate from the light of the Sun is proven by this: if they proceeded from the Sun, all planets would be imbued with a similar color at the same time, and if one changed, they would all change. It is also evident that color does not come from the medium <note>The "medium" refers to the space or ether between celestial bodies.</note> through which light travels, because individual planets preserve their own tints in every place, position, and time. Therefore, it must be firmly concluded that the incoming light of the Sun is stained by the inherent colors of the planets themselves. From there, the light is reflected back toward the Earth together with the planets' specific qualities—in accordance with Proposition 3—and thus the light is ultimately stained in various ways. This is no different than how solar rays passing through differently colored glass cause different colors of light to appear on the surfaces upon which they fall. Furthermore, this influence upon the Earth varies based on the planets' approach toward or retreat from both the Sun and the Earth, as well as their various positions in respect to the heavens and the terrestrial horizon. No one should doubt that various modifications of these qualities are caused by the refraction of the rays as they fall through the humid medium <note>Meaning the Earth's atmosphere.</note> and proceed proportionally.

<margin>An ethereal Earth?</margin>
Hence, lest the Earth be dissolved by the excessive intensity of the heat from the solar rays, the Creator placed the Moon—which I shall call an "Ethereal Earth," following Plutarch <note>Plutarch (c. 46–120 AD) was a Greek philosopher who wrote "On the Face Which Appears in the Orb of the Moon," suggesting the Moon was a solid, earth-like world.</note>—opposite the Sun. He created it as a kind of watery body endowed with innumerable virtues, so that the solar rays might be refracted and tempered by its cooling effect. Thus, the rays are communicated to our land along with their own fertile "seeds," so that they might encourage new offspring and fruit. These two bodies—our Earth and that ethereal lunar Earth—possess a great similarity to one another, by which one fosters the other. They favor each other with mutual influences, by which they and their respective parts live, are preserved, and are altered. Indeed, that our seas 

<column-break/>

are moved in various ways according to the phases of the Moon requires no testimony, as nothing is more common knowledge. All these things could not happen unless the greatest sympathy existed between the Moon and our own world. This sympathy consists of a great harmony of both powers and actions. Harmony of powers, in turn, consists only in a similarity of essence, since powers reside in a thing according to its essence and proceed from it; and it is necessary that actions be produced according to the nature of those powers. Since the Moon is a rough body, entirely similar to our Earth, being dense and opaque, <margin>The nature of the Moon's body</margin> it not only perfectly drinks in the solar rays, but reflects those absorbed rays back to us through a mutual communication of powers. Yet, so that this influence would not always be the same, the most wise Architect fashioned the Moon with such skill that it would face the Earth with an unequal appearance over the space of a month. Thus, from its different positions, it strikes the Earth with varying intensities of action, thereby promoting the generation of things according to the needs of nature. We have said the Moon is a rough body and entirely similar to the Earth because, from various observations made by the Lincean philosophers <note>The "Lyncei" or Academy of the Lincei was one of the first scientific societies, famous for its member Galileo Galilei and their use of the telescope.</note>, a certain mountainous and shallow quality has been noted on the Moon, just as the following experiment will teach you.

# Book I. Part I.

The wondrous face of the Moon.
</margin>
...just as we said of the Sun in the preceding pages: with this single difference, that the "little torches" <note>original: *faculæ*</note> and spots in the Sun are constantly changing; in the Moon, however, they are always consistent and motionless. You would say you were looking upon a certain sea washing over immense tracts of land. Here, in the midst of the light, you can see islands scattered far and wide as if in an ocean; elsewhere, you can see shadowy depressions <note>original: *lacunas*; referring to the lunar maria or craters.</note> from whose center very bright rays spread out. You will also notice at the very edge of the Lunar disk a certain tremulousness—one might call it a smoky exhalation—which many of the Linceans <note>The *Lyncei* or Academy of the Lincei was the first modern scientific society, of which Galileo was a member.</note> therefore call the "atmosphere of the celestial earth." On this same edge, you will observe with no small wonder—especially when the Moon is 

<column-break/>

halved <note>original: *dichotoma*; the quarter-moon phase.</note>—what look like steep cliffs and chains of mountain ranges. We present these features in this figure, just as a certain Neapolitan artist and I myself here in Rome have observed them on more than one occasion through excellent telescopes <note>original: *tubis*; literally "tubes."</note>. From these observations, when properly compared with one another, we can infer nothing else but that the Moon is entirely similar to our own Earth: a body, evidently, composed of water and celestial earth, endowed with countless powers of hidden "seeds" <note>Kircher uses "seeds" (*semina*) to describe the inherent potential for generating life or physical effects.</note>. These powers, mixed with the rays of the Sun, produce that multitude of things on Earth which we indeed marvel at every day; yet no one can easily grasp the logic of this mixing.

Furthermore, we believe that those intense lights diffused into rays are nothing other than the highly polished surfaces of the more elevated lunar regions, reflecting the rays of the Sun more powerfully than other parts. If we were on the Lunar body, I would certainly say that the inaccessible peaks of the highest mountains—such as the Alps, the Pyrenees, the Andes, or the Caucasus—covered in perpetual snow and ice, would reflect a similar light back to us looking from the Lunar globe. For it can hardly be said how intense a light of this kind they reflect; I remember observing this with pleasure in the year 1638 while I was surveying Mount Etna from the mountains of Calabria and the neighboring islands. That these are elevated parts of the Lunar body is sufficiently declared by the surrounding shadow. But these are our conjectures; if anyone brings forward something

<column-break/>

better, I promise we will subscribe to his view without hesitation. However, since we have discussed these and similar matters in our *Magnetic World* <note>Kircher's *Magnes; sive de Arte Magnetica* (1641).</note> regarding this kind of magnetism of the Sun, Moon, and Earth, and are treating them specifically in our *Subterranean World* <note>Kircher's *Mundus Subterraneus* (1665).</note>, we refer the curious reader there.

Furthermore, the remaining planets also modify the solar rays they receive according to the condition of their own nature, and by reflecting them, they impart their own virtues to the earthly body. For they owe almost all the light they send back to the Earth to the Sun—not as clean and polished mirrors, but as the Moon, Venus, Jupiter, Saturn, and other cratered <note>original: *lacunosa*; literally "pitted" or "full of hollows."</note> bodies illuminated by the Sun. I said "cratered bodies" because the experience of the Linceans has shown that the bodies of the planets are by no means polished, but exceedingly rough, divided, and rugged, marred by various spots and shadows...

From this phenomenon, it clearly appears that the bodies of the stars are not perfectly spherical, nor luminous of themselves, but rough, unequal, and rugged—much like other "celestial earths." As they soak up the light of the Sun, they strike that same light back toward us, imbued with various powers, for certain ends intended by the Author of Nature. And so it is clear that all celestial light bestowed upon the earthly globe from the whole universe, in whatever way, is Solar—whether it comes immediately from the Sun itself through a direct or refracted ray, or mediately through the stars by a reflected ray. While this light is much weaker in terms of luminosity than the former, it is almost certain that, in terms of active power, it carries something unique from the specific property of the star. Thus, one may recognize here a source of celestial influences. For it is known by long experience that the Sun rising with Arcturus <note>A bright star in the constellation Boötes.</note> brings storms; with Aquila <note>The Eagle constellation.</note> it brings snow; with Andromeda a period of turbulence; with the Aselli <note>Two stars in the constellation Cancer.</note> sudden disturbances of the air, rain, and thunder; with the Dog Star <note>Sirius, the brightest star in the sky.</note> serenity

<column-break/>

and heat; with Hercules winds; with the Hyades rains; and with others, it moves other qualities impressed upon the air. Since we see this happen at fixed times of the year, the cause should certainly not be attributed solely to the wandering planets, which obtain different modifications of their powers in different locations. <margin>The sole cause of certain effects is the Sun's motion around its own axis.</margin> Therefore, as the Sun is rotated on its own axis by its annual motion, a star is opposed to it by a certain similarity of nature with that solar part facing it. Hence it is no wonder that an infinite variety of influences—which can in no way be grasped by the human mind—is brought down to these lower regions, as will be clear to anyone combining the parts of the stars with the parts of the Sun imbued with various powers. Thus, no one should doubt that planets possess one power when at their perigee <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note>, another at their apogee <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Earth.</note>, another at middle longitudes, and others when positioned in different parts of the Zodiac. We shall declare this more fully in our *Sacred-Physical Astrology* <note>original: *Astrologia hierophysica*; Kircher's term for a study of the heavens that combines physical observation with theological and symbolic interpretation.</note>.

# CHAPTER V.
## Concerning Fire, night-shining bodies, and the production of heat in the world.

<margin>There are various kinds and species of fire: one is charcoal; another is flame; another is light; and each of them is truly fire. <note>original Greek: ἔςι δὲ γένη καὶ εἴδη τοῦ πυρός· ὁ μὲν ἄνθραξ· τὸ δὲ φλὸξ, τὸ δὲ φῶς, ἔκασα αὐτῶν πῦρ ὂν. From Aristotle’s *Topics*, Book 5.</note> There is not just one species of fire: for charcoal, flame, and light are different in their specific nature, yet each exists as fire.</margin>
Having now examined celestial light, let us descend to earthly light—namely, Fire—and see what it might be. In the fifth book of his *Topics*, Aristotle established three species of it in these words: "There is not just one species of fire," etc. Before Aristotle, Plato confirmed these three species of fire in his *Timaeus*, and after him, his disciple Theophrastus did the same; however, these species cannot in any way apply to sublunary fire <note>The "sublunary" region refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, everything below the sphere of the Moon.</note>. For if the element of fire were Charcoal, it would be ignited; if ignited, it would shine; if it shone, it would illuminate the lower and upper regions simultaneously; and along with this illumination, it would always heat the air—all of which contradicts our experience. It is therefore clear that sublunary fire is not charcoal. Nor can it be Flame: for if flame were the element of fire, it would provide heat; if it heated, it would set things on fire; if it set things on fire, it would consume and destroy; but none of these things apply to our elemental fire. Therefore, it is not flame. Neither can it be called Light; for if it gave off light, it would produce a glow and illuminate us—indeed, it would show itself most clearly at night when the Sun is absent. But all these things are contrary to our senses. Therefore, under the hollow of the Moon <note>The region where the ancient Greeks believed a pure "sphere of fire" existed.</note>, there is no fire of the condition described by Aristotle; rather, it seems he calls the most subtle part of the air "fire" only out of custom. Regarding this elemental fire, therefore—since it is not a visible, luminous body—we shall not treat it here. Instead, we speak of our "culinary" or household fire, which Aristotle calls the <term>boiling of hot breath <gloss>original Greek: πνεύματος θερμοῦ ζέσιν</gloss></term>, or the ignition of dry wind, and others call "burning smoke." If it is smoke, then it comes from moisture; if it comes from moisture and heat, it is a mixture; therefore, it is by no means a simple element, and consequently cannot be a primary element. Another kind of fire must therefore be identified in the nature of things, which we have hinted at previously and will explain more fully in our section on the Subterranean World. Our common fire, then, is nothing other than air ignited by the violent collision of two bodies, whose heat catches a fuel of combustible matter and turns it into flame; and this flame, with its light, illuminates everything in all directions. This is that luminous, fiery sublunary body—the sole comfort for those dwelling in darkness, our "Domestic Sun,"

<column-break/>

the illuminator of nights and shadows, the substitute for the Sun and Moon. It is no less necessary than the other types of fire described, and its light is of the same nature as celestial light, possessing the same qualities.

How it exists in nature, how it is produced, and how it perishes, must now be discussed.

It must first be said that air, when drawn into a state of extreme thinness, eventually turns into fire. It is made thin by motion, and this motion is caused by the collision of two bodies, or by the struggle of opposites, which is called <term>antiperistasis <gloss>The compression or intensification of a quality—like heat—when surrounded by its opposite, like cold.</gloss></term>. In the first way, fire is drawn from flints, or the axles of wheels catch fire and burn when they grow hot from violent and continuous motion. By this same art, certain peoples of America use two pieces of warm, dry wood, one of which is rotated within a notch in the other until it catches flame. Aside from this, they know no other way of producing fire, having been taught by experience—if I am not mistaken—by observing the aforementioned burning of wheels.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration titled "The Fire-Making Machine of the Americans." It depicts a mechanical frame made of wooden beams. A vertical wooden spindle is held in place by a horizontal crossbar. A cord is wrapped around the spindle, which, when pulled back and forth, would spin the drill rapidly against a base plate to generate fire through friction.</image-desc>

Pliny testifies that this same fire is excited by the rubbing together of laurel and ivy wood. However, it is also ignited by *antiperistasis*, and thus we see many fiery phenomena occur in the air. From this come the omens of the "foolish fire" <note>original: *ignis fatuus*; also known as will-o'-the-wisps.</note>, "leaping goats," falling stars, "Castor and Pollux" <note>St. Elmo’s Fire, often seen on the masts of ships during storms.</note>, and similar things, about which one should consult the Meteorologists. Furthermore, the air is more easily ignited the subtler it is. Hence, in the Andes mountains of Peru and Chile—the highest in the whole world—the air is so thin that almost no one passes through them without suffering or a loss of breath. The air there is so disposed toward ignition that it may be set aflame by even a slight motion or breath. You may see

<margin>Marvelous things concerning meteors in the mountains of Peru and Chile.</margin>

# Illumination of Celestial Bodies

<margin>How heat and fire are produced by the friction of wood.</margin>
Indeed, travelers in these mountains not infrequently appear entirely fiery, their horses and beasts of burden also seemingly vomiting flames from their mouths and nostrils. These things might deservedly seem like paradoxes to some, were they not confirmed to me by Father Alonso de Ovalle <note>original: "Alphonso Dualle"</note>, Procurator of the Chilean Province of the Society of Jesus. He was an eyewitness who had traveled that route through the Andes several times, and he confirmed this to me in person even as I was writing these words. Truly, there is no other reason for this than that from the fatty and viscous breath and the very subtle sweat of both men and beasts—combined with the thin mountain air and thinned out through movement and friction—an ignition and inflammation easily follows. This is not unlike what we see in the highest region of the air, where fiery impressions are made by the impulse and agitation of the winds. Truly, we treat the marvelous nature and properties of these mountains more fully in our work, *The Subterranean World* <note>original: *Mundo nostro subterraneo*, Kircher’s 1665 masterpiece on geology and the earth's interior.</note>. However, one difficulty here torments us greatly: by what reasoning is heat produced by the friction of wood or stones? Some wish it to be produced by a "virtual heat" <note>A scholastic term referring to a power or capacity latent in a substance that is not yet active.</note> lurking within the mixture; but this cannot be said, since heat is sometimes produced from a mixture that is extremely cold, and that virtual heat—being an accident—cannot reach the level of substance to create fire. Some argue for rarity <note>term: rarity/rarefaction: the thinning of matter to become less dense.</note> alone, which motion causes in the rubbed body; for we see that the more solid a body is compared to others, the greater the heat it gives off—as steel does more than wood, and stones are more suited to producing fire the harder they are. This happens for no other reason than that the air between them is more rubbed and made rarer. This does not happen through simple compression (by which it is only made subtler and condensed), but through a violent impulse, by which one part is vehemently propelled and another is condensed; then, the propelled part, due to the "shunning of the vacuum" <note>term: *horror vacui*: the Aristotelian belief that nature abhors a vacuum and will immediately move matter to fill any empty space.</note>, attracts another part with such force that it heats it. Furthermore, fire is more easily drawn out from corners than from the middle of a stone, because the strike is more certain and more focused, or because it rarefies more easily, or because a smaller portion of the material is interposed. Yet, because it is difficult to conceive how friction (which is a local motion) positively produces heat, or how the rarity following the heat effectively causes the heat—for it is not enough to say that heat has a connection and proportion with rarity, since heat is found in the heavens without rarity (according to some) and is an effect of heat in sublunary things—this opinion does not seem sufficient. There are those who wish local motion to cause heat because by that means the less hot and dry parts are pulled apart, leaving behind the hotter and drier parts, in which a more intense heat is then detected and produced, and through

<column-break/>

which it is transmitted into the adjacent body. For whenever two solid bodies encounter each other through motion, the more they approach, the more the intercepted air is rubbed—that is, its thicker and foreign parts (namely earth and water) are more segregated and expelled. These foreign impressions, being more dense, impede the meeting of those bodies and are more strongly impelled and thrust away by them, leaving behind the purer and more refined parts of the air. In these parts, heat flourishes, being nearly at its highest by its own nature; and if any heat was taken away by external impressions, once those are removed, the parts return to their original state from their own form through natural emanation. Thus, with the impediments removed, heat will be intensely perceived in these purer parts. In the moving bodies themselves, a similar heat, and sometimes fire, is produced. But leaving these opinions behind, we say first: fire is not produced from the parts of the air, but from the substance of the stone or the dry wood. Consequently, the "efficient cause" <note>term: efficient cause: the primary source of change or rest; in this context, the "trigger" for fire.</note> of the fire is not nature, but either the Author of Nature immediately, or celestial light—with local motion, the friction of parts, elongation, and rarity concurring as "dispositional factors." For we see on one hand that through the friction of a hard stone, fire is generated as its substance is reduced to very thin parts; on the other hand, there is no sufficient, proximate, and principal cause of such generation. It is not the air, as is clear from what was said; it is not the rubbed body, otherwise it would be seeking its own destruction and would produce something substantially unlike itself (which is repugnant to a determined sublunary cause); and finally, it is not local motion, rarity, or density, since it was shown just before that these only concur dispositionally. Therefore, it is through celestial light. The "disposition" happens in this way: first, by local motion and the impulse of those rubbed bodies, the substance is thinned. Then, by this thinning, the form is either entirely corrupted—because it cannot be preserved with such small, thin, and subtle matter—or it is so weakened that it can no longer preserve its own qualities in its being. <margin>The manner of the production of heat.</margin> Finally, that matter—either stripped of its form or with a form already weakened—by reason of its dryness and the heat remaining from the predominance of fire, has a greater disposition toward fire than toward anything else. Therefore, placed in such a disposition, the "form of fire" is introduced by the light of the celestial bodies. Although it could also be said that friction causes heat through the greater distance between the parts of either the air or another body, by the negation of "indistancy" <note>A philosophical way of saying the parts are no longer touching or packed together.</note> between the parts of the containing body that are more distant from each other, and according to its requirement, by God or by the light of the celestial bodies in

<sig>B 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: the same (eodem)</meta>

<summary>Kircher discusses the physical production of heat and fire through friction, using reports from the Andes mountains to illustrate atmospheric ignition, and argues that friction is merely a preparation for "celestial light" or God to introduce the actual form of fire.</summary>

# Book I. Part I.

...directly through the same air, and through that medium, rarity is produced. Sometimes, however, it is also produced by the air itself; namely, when the air first becomes thin and first conceives heat, such as when a shot arrow conceives heat and catches fire from the air, which acts as an instrumental cause. It is clear, therefore, that friction produces heat in no other way than because, out of a natural connection with heat and dryness, it moves toward that requirement or proximate natural cause—if such is found—or light. However, rarity (assuming it is a quality) cannot produce heat by itself. For a secondary quality resulting from a mixture of primary qualities cannot produce those primary ones; rather, it naturally follows the produced heat. But perhaps we have discussed these matters more extensively than was necessary. Therefore, let us return to our fire: if we consider it a little more attentively, we will surely find in it many things
<margin>Properties of fire.</margin>
worthy of the greatest admiration. For first, turning into a flame, it performs a deputy service for the Sun by dispelling all shadows with its light. Second, a flame is not a permanent thing, but a merely "successive being." At almost every moment, for the use of this sublunary world, it is renewed so that it may perish; it perishes as it moves, and no differently than a river (according to the testimony of Aristotle), it is perpetually born and 
<margin>Flame is perpetually successive.</margin>
dies, being always the same yet always different. Hence, light also, since it depends on the parts of the flame for its becoming and its preservation, is successive and perpetually vanishes. Even smoke itself—for example, from wax candles—shows this to be so; since smoke takes its origin from the flame, as the smoke flies away, the matter of the flame must also fly away. Since the flame remains almost the same size, if something flies away from it on one side, it must be replaced by resolution from elsewhere: thus, it succeeds itself perpetually.

### Corollaries on Flame.

It is clear from what has been said that heat alone is sufficient for the production of flame; however, experience teaches us that nothing can be resolved into flame which is not also resolvable into vapors and exhalations. Since the parts of a flame perpetually succeed one another, that which is resolved into flame must be of such a nature that its parts can always follow one another and restore the lost parts of the flame. However, that which cannot be resolved into vapors and exhalations cannot have its parts fly upward, nor occupy the place of the perishing parts of the flame; hence gold and other metals, because of their dryness,
<column-break/>
do not serve the production of flame. Therefore, for things to be inflamed, they must possess humidity—and not just any humidity, but a fatty, oily, and viscous kind, such as is found in certain oils and "quintessences" <note>In alchemy, a quintessence is the purest concentrated essence of a substance.</note>. Heat is also necessary for the 
<margin>There is no such thing as cold flame.</margin>
production of flame, since without it there is no rarefaction <note>The process of a substance becoming less dense; thinning out.</note>, without rarefaction there is no lightness of the body, and without lightness, no upward ascent of flame is possible. Thus, those who ridiculously assert that a "cold flame" can exist are to be laughed at.
<margin>Flame is only an accidental change.</margin>
It is clear, secondly, that the conversion of a thing into flame is not a "substantial" change but only an "accidental" one <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, a substantial change creates a new kind of thing, while an accidental change only alters the qualities of the same thing (like water turning to ice).</note>, since this matter relates to flame in exactly the same way as water relates to ice; though they appear different, there is only one essence of water, varied by accident. The same must be said of oil, sulfur, wax, tallow, and other combustibles. But you will say the reasoning is unequal: for ice can be resolved back into water, but flame cannot be resolved back into its inflammable matter.
<margin>Flame.</margin>
But I deny this premise; for the fact that flame can be reduced back into wax or something similar is taught by the irrefragable experiments of the Chemists. They can reduce <term>Tutia</term> <note>original: "Tutiam"; zinc oxide or "philosopher's wool" collected from the chimneys of smelting furnaces.</note> back into the metal from which it came; they can reduce escaping Mercury, or <term>white lead</term> <note>original: "cerussam"</note> and <term>red lead</term> <note>original: "minium"</note> back into the lead from which they originated. 
<margin>The Author's secret.</margin>
I myself know an admirable secret by which the ash left behind from the combustion of an inflamed thing may be restored to itself. Thus, by the chemical art, vegetables can be restored from the ashes of vegetables. I mention this in my work *The Magnetic Art* <note>original: *Arte Magnetica*, Kircher's 1641 book on magnetism and "alliances" in nature.</note>, and through many experiments—both in *The Magic of Light and Shadow* and in our *Subterranean World*—we demonstrate that salt extracted from plants, when sown, allows the plant from which the salt was produced to be reproduced by that same "sowing." Therefore, the argument is clear.

It is clear, thirdly, that the extinction of a flame (whether it happens by pouring over it its contrary, water; or by a blast or the force of winds; or by suffocation or other means) is nothing other than the cessation of the production of fire through a medium. For light is like a species of heat, which can occupy the eyes in a thousand ways according to the diversity of the compositions of things. Unless this is granted, no reason can be devised as to why light should change color if it shines through a saturated medium, or why colors should change light if they are confounded, or why colored glass should tint it. For the reason of these things to be assigned, light and heat must be placed under the same proximate genus, about which we will speak more fully in the following. But let us now turn our attention to the nature of luminous animals.

<summary>Kircher defines flame as a "successive being" that requires oily humidity and heat to exist, comparing its constant renewal to a flowing river. He argues that combustion is an accidental change rather than a substantial one, citing alchemical examples and his own method for restoring plants from their ashes.</summary>

# CHAPTER VI.

## On the Illumination of Animals.

->Or<-

### On the light created within Animals.

## §. I. On the Light of Glow-worms.

<margin>Description of the Glow-worm.</margin>
The Glow-worm, called *pyrolampis* <note>original: "πυρολαμπὶς"</note> or *lampyris* <note>original: "λαμπυρὶς"</note> by the Greeks—meaning a winged animal shining in the darkness—is referred to by Hesychius as a *cantharis* <note>original: "κανθαρίς," a type of beetle</note> that shines at night. Because of this, many have judged it to belong to the beetle family. Varrinus, in his Lexicon, calls them "household lamps" <note>original: "λαμπτήρες"</note> that appear throughout the home. The Latins call it sometimes *Cincindela*, sometimes *nitedula* (little shiner), *nitela*, and occasionally *lucula* or *luciola*. It is an insect that shines at night and is of two kinds: the *pteron* <note>Greek: "πτερόν"</note> (winged) and the *apteron* <note>Greek: "ἄπτερον"</note> (wingless). Its head is entirely covered from the top by a sort of hood, shaped like an inverted and overhanging shield, of a dark color like a sheath. Its small head is pitch black and arranged into two small bumps, like eyes colored like jet. It has a ringed belly divided into many segments, at the end of which are two translucent droplets like fire, though their color tends from a fiery brightness toward green or bluish-gray—a color never found in the flame of burning sulfur. They are seen most clearly when the belly is compressed and that transparent fluid moves toward the end of the abdomen. When lying on its back with its chest or rather its belly raised, it shines like fire. Pliny, and those who agree with him, seem not to have considered this carefully enough, believing that the glow-worm shines only when its wings open and is shaded when they are closed. While I was living in Malta <note>original: "Melitæ"</note> and encountered a huge multitude of them shining at night, I collected a great number of them to observe their nature and to search more deeply into the origin of this living light. I noted that the little creature, by a voluntary motion (so to speak), now retracts and now ejects that shining matter, according as it perceives the presence of a friend or an enemy. For when it was pinched or provoked, it retracted the matter, and after a little time, it brought the retracted matter forth again. This happened especially when several glow-worms (or lamps) were placed together; as if exulting in an ambitious glory of light, it would show off the proud ornaments of its shining fluid to the utmost. You would say it was competing to be looked at.

<column-break/>

Nor should Nature be thought idle in such a wonderful projection of light. First, it indicates to the country folk the time for the ripening of barley and the final sowing season, when millet and panic grass are usually planted. Concerning these, Pliny says quite beautifully in his usual manner: <margin>Nature is by no means idle in such glow-worms.</margin> *Already,* he says, *Nature had created the Pleiades <note>original: "Vergilias"</note> as notable clusters in the sky; yet not content with these, she made others on earth, as if crying out: "Why do you look to the sky, farmer? Why do you seek the stars, peasant? Already the nights press upon you with shorter sleep. Behold, I scatter for you peculiar stars among your grasses, and I show them to you in the evening as you unyoke from your work, and I ensure you cannot pass them by through a troubling miracle. Do you see how the brightness, similar to fire, is covered by the closing of the wings, and carries light and night within itself?"* <note>original: Pliny the Elder, Natural History, Book 18</note> Baptista Mantuanus also sings of them:

> At last, with these studies we passed that winter,
> Spring has returned, now the woods are green, now the vineyard is in leaf,
> Now the grain is in ear, now the reaper thinks of the barley:
> Now the glow-worms fly at night with their little shining wings.

<margin>Why they are endowed with light.</margin>
Furthermore, since this creature is sought as food by many animals, and nature has provided the defenseless little insect with no other protection, it seems she equipped it with this light. For with this fiery torch—hateful to some—it wards off enemies as if holding up a shield; while they think it is actual fire, they are frightened away from the hunt. Yet, so that it is not betrayed by its own light to the ambushes of certain animals seeking it for food, it eludes these snares by no other weapon than the voluntary withdrawal of its light. Thus, it is both a lamp for itself in the darkness, by which it may run with unhindered feet, and a breastplate against enemies. A certain distinguished poet of our time described this quite aptly in these verses:

> So small a bird flying at night flashes in the air,
> Just like a glowing spark; which as a boy, long ago,
> I feared to touch among my peers, lest it
> Should burn me—for that weak age is ignorant of things.
> Because it shines at night, it has earned its name:
> Either it glows because it is lit like a fiery lamp;
> Though the cause is one, the name is not just one.
> Now seeking the heights, it flashes with moved wings,
> Again, with wings drawn in, it hides its golden, tawny glory,
> And fleeing far, it flickers lightly with burning fire.

The author also cites classical and contemporary poetry to illustrate the insect's role as a seasonal indicator for farmers and its "miraculous" nature.</summary>

> And wherever it flies, it carries its own lights with it,
> Lights which ward off the darkness, and which despise the winds:
> Now, like a submissive thing, it flies toward those watching, and
> Becomes more and more sparkling as it draws near, and before
> One's face it is like tiny morsels of glowing iron,
> From which Proserpina was snatched by Stygian Jove <note>A poetic name for Pluto, god of the Underworld.</note>; for
> She <note>The glow-worm.</note> was one of her companions; changed from her ancient form,
> She still seeks the traces of her mistress, surveying all things.

<margin>What the light of the glow-worm is.</margin>
The question is asked, therefore: what is that splendor, what is that light, and how is it implanted in these tiny creatures? Aristotle, in his short work *On Wild Animals*, as Philatheus <note>Likely referring to a commentator on Aristotle.</note> writes, asserts that polished and smooth bodies composed of air and water are fit for producing a glare, but not for emitting light; thus, night-shining animals are highly polished, and while they fly, they rub against the air and glow. He argues that gems and polished transparent things are likewise fit for such a glare. We, setting aside opinions of this sort, say that the night-shining Glow-worms possess this intrinsic and innate light—by which they both see and are seen—from provident Nature for the aforementioned purposes. This is no different than the light seen in rotting wood or the scales of fish; they possess that inborn light from a form of fire. For since these little animals are bloodless <note>term: *exsanguia*; ancient biology classified insects as "bloodless" because they lack red hemoglobin.</note> and very cold, the fiery parts—or the heat concentrated by nature around the site of digestion—acquire there the power of shining necessary for the animal. We see the same thing

<margin>Why fish shine when they move.</margin>
happen in Fish. To those living in the cold element of water, Nature provides very hard, viscous scales, where the earthy parts prevail with a certain fiery power to strengthen and preserve the natural heat. In rotting wood, however, the fiery heat is collected at the extremities along with airy moisture. Experience teaches that many fish—but most especially the Pike, the Goby, the Anglerfish <note>original: *Rana piscatrix*, literally "the fishing frog."</note>, as well as oysters, crustaceans, and the rest of the sea's offspring—possess

<margin>Oyster-light.</margin>
the power of shining in the dark. Oysters, when placed in an obscure place and allowed to decay, occasionally pour forth so much light from themselves that they might rightly seem like portents to those ignorant of the causes of things. There are also the *Dactyli* <note>term: *Dactyli*; the Pholad or "Date-shell" mollusk, famous in antiquity for its bioluminescence.</note>, a type of shellfish, which, even when rubbed in the hands, scatter light from themselves like sparks; I remember observing this myself on the shores of Malta, Sicily, Calabria, and the Ligurian Sea. But concerning the wonders that can be performed by the benefit of this light, consult my *Magic of Light and Shadow* <note>original: *Magia lucis et umbrae*; Kircher's own landmark work.</note>, where we derive marvels from these things as a professional study.

<margin>The American night-shining caterpillar.</margin>
Herrera <note>Antonio de Herrera y Tordesillas, a Spanish historian of the Americas.</note> writes that in New Spain, in the mountains of Guatemala, a certain kind of Caterpillar is found which no one may touch with impunity due to the virulence of its poison; wherefore, with a light born in its belly like a lamp, it warns travelers to avoid it with "all oars and sails" <note>An idiom meaning "with all possible speed."</note>, because it flashes with such a deadly light.

<column-break/>

### Experiments on the liquid of Glow-worms.

BUT I cannot omit in this place those miracles regarding the liquids of Glow-worms which many promise themselves. There are those who use this liquid mixed with others for writing letters that no one can read except at night and in the darkness; they also paint images on walls which they claim are hidden at the rising of the sun but appear at its setting. Some prepare the night-shining humor in this way: they take rotting willow wood and a Glow-worm, mixing them all together with the white of eggs, and use that mixture. Others think the liquid of "fire-shiners" <note>original: *πυρολαμπῶν* (pyrolampōn)</note> can be made from

<margin>Luminous liquid.</margin>
all putrefying things that consist of the greatest whiteness, light, and transparency. Giambattista della Porta <note>A famous Neapolitan polymath and alchemist.</note> stores the luminous matter of the Glow-worm, separated and ground on a porphyry stone, enclosed in glass under horse dung for fifteen days; then, adding a little mercury, he distills an essence through an alembic, which he believes, when enclosed in a glass vial, can illuminate an entire house. This is the nonsense of nonsenses <note>original: *Nugae nugarum*.</note>. For I do not see how that humor—after being changed so many times, coagulated, fixed, circulated, putrefied, distilled, and mixed with that most devouring Mercury—could be preserved in its original purity.

These are the boastings of empty quacks and marketplace charlatans. To uncover the truth of the matter, I certainly tested each one, making the attempt with the greatest diligence; but I could not express even one tiny drop of humor from fifty insects. Indeed, I found that this meager humor, as soon as it is separated from the little animal, dies along with it, leaving behind scarcely any trace of its light. I also observed that the humor offers traces of light only in that place where Nature hid it for certain ends; outside of its natural place, it perishes completely. If, therefore, that simple separated humor can scarcely provide the effect of any light, how much less an effect do we believe it will provide when corrupted by so many mixtures and twisted by so many alterations from its primeval nature? Therefore, all the things that Wecker <note>Johann Jacob Wecker, a Swiss physician and author of a book on "secrets."</note> trifles about catching fish at night by the benefit of a shining liquid are false; and false are the things that Porta fakes regarding the illuminating of houses, which go against the principles of nature. For since light of this kind, as experience has taught us, depends on the voluntary movement of the animal, it is certainly necessary that when the animal fails, the humor also fails. However, we judge differently regarding the scales of fish and the rotting fragments of crabs and oysters; for these can provide a material suitable for producing wonders, as will be seen in the *Magic of Light and Shadow*.

<header>Bioluminescence of Aquatic Creatures.</header>

# CHAPTER VII.
## On the Bioluminescence of Aquatic Creatures.
### Or
### Concerning the miraculous light of certain things born in the waters.

<margin>A wonderful experiment with shining fluid.</margin>
The Piddocks and Razor-clams <note>original: "Pholades & Solenes"</note>, offspring of the sea from the shellfish family—which some call "Fingers" <note>original: "Dactylos"</note>, some "Long-caps," and others "Channels"—live within porous rocks, drawing their life from the salty moisture. Nature has bestowed upon them a fluid so luminous that, as I have often discovered through experience, they glow in the dark exactly like fire. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist of the 1st century AD.</note> mentions them in these words:
> *Nature has granted Razor-clams the ability to shine with a distinct glare in the dark when light is removed; and when this fluid is agitated, it shines in the mouths of those eating them, it shines on the hands, and even on the floor and on clothing when drops fall; so that it is clear beyond doubt that this is the nature of the juice which we marvel at even within the body.* 
Certainly, one who has not seen the thing can hardly be led to believe that what is told is true. I have found the experiment to be most true: indeed, when the fluid is scattered into the dark air with a sprayer, it immediately displays a kind of fiery rain, and it renders the hands, clothes, and whatever is stained by the glue of the shining fluid no less shimmering than sparks and flames. If anyone has ever seen falling drops of lit fat <note>original: "laridi," likely referring to tallow or lard used in lamps.</note>, they will easily be able to imagine these little lights. Furthermore, Rondeletius <note>Guillaume Rondelet, a 16th-century French physician and naturalist famous for his study of fish.</note> ascribes the cause of this splendor to the sticky juice of the Razor-clam; we say more truly that the cause of this light is a transparent, sticky fluid, luminous by its own nature, bestowed by nature upon these animals for certain purposes. It is much the same way that we see many things that are tenacious and as if compacted by glue—smooth, even, and polished—and for that reason reflecting light, as we said concerning the glow-worms. For this fluid seems to be given to them for no other reason than to seek the necessities of life, as will be seen in the following section.

<column-break/>

### Section I. *On the Bioluminescence of the Sea-Lung.*
Another marvel of the sea occurs here, which, although it is nearly the lowliest and most despicable of all bloodless creatures <note>term: *exsanguia*; ancient biology classified invertebrates as "bloodless" because they lack red hemoglobin.</note>, yet acquires no small nobility from its innate light. Some call it the "Sea-Lung" <note>term: *Pulmonem marinum*; likely the *Rhizostoma pulmo*, a large species of jellyfish.</note>, and others the "Nettle," because it affects the private parts and hands in a wonderful way with a certain hidden burning sensation. I have found the fluid of this animal, or <term>Zoophyte</term> <note>A term used by early naturalists for organisms like corals or jellyfish that seemed to be part animal and part plant.</note>, to be so similar to the fluid existing in the "Fingers" <note>Piddocks</note> that there is almost no effect shown by that one which cannot also be shown by this one. It is marvelous, however, that the fluid of this Sea-Lung, when smeared on black rods or any other things, makes them appear shimmering in the dark just like fire. I first discovered the experiment for this at the Waters of Mars <note>near Marseille, specifically the town of Martigues</note>, and later I remembered that Belon <note>Pierre Belon, a 16th-century French explorer and naturalist.</note> had observed the same thing; for he says that rods and sticks smeared with it vibrate with light in the manner of lit torches at night. From this, I gathered that there are traces of this fluid, shimmering with its own congenital light, in almost all fish, and especially in the soft crustaceans and shellfish.

<margin>Why nature endowed marine animals with light.</margin>
As to why nature wished to imbue these animals with that light, I judge the cause to be this: since they mostly dwell at the bottom of the sea and cling to rocks, and the bottom of the sea is extremely dark—so much so that divers <note>original: "Urinatores"</note> affirm that in many places it can in no way be reached by the sun's rays—nature gave them this viscous fluid imbued with a feigned light. She did this so that the animals, dwelling in perpetual darkness, would not seem to be equipped with eyes by nature in vain. By the benefit of this fluid, as if by a lamp born within them, they might both seek food and more easily elude the snares of enemies by the voluntary emission of light and darkness, and thus not be left wanting for their needs.

<header>Book I. Part I.</header>

# CHAPTER VIII.
## On the Luminescence of Stones.
### On the Phengite Stone, or Mineral Phosphorus.

<margin>Signs of the luminous stone.</margin>
Not long ago, a certain mineral <note>original: "fossile," referring to something dug from the earth</note> was discovered in the territory of Bologna which, when prepared by a specific method and exposed to light, drinks it in and incorporates it so tenaciously that if it is taken out of its case in a dark place, it pours out the captured and preserved light just like glowing coals, much to the wonder of those watching. And although the distinguished Fortunio Liceti <note>A 17th-century Italian physician and philosopher who wrote a famous treatise on this stone.</note>, in his booklet on the *Lithophosphorus* <note>original: "Lithophosphoro," meaning "stone that brings light."</note>, says it is found only in the territory of Bologna, I have nevertheless found clear signs of this same mineral at Tolfa, in the place where they are accustomed to dig for alum stones (commonly called *Alume di Rocca* <note>Rock Alum, a mineral salt used in dyeing and medicine.</note>); this mineral is entirely similar in qualities to the Bolognese one. For this kind of mineral is a certain mass of selenitic sulfurous gypsum mixed with much Arsenic, Antimony, and Vitriol <note>original: "Chalcanti," a term for metallic sulfates.</note>. That it is indeed a gypsum is shown by the lime into which it is very easily reduced; its caustic and depilatory <note>original: "psilotrica," meaning hair-removing.</note> power demonstrates the arsenic; its ability to induce vomiting shows the antimony; and finally, its sharp acidity demonstrates the vitriol. These effects are also found to be present in the Bolognese stone.

<margin>Its preparation for absorbing light.</margin>
It is prepared to drink in the light in this manner. The stone—either whole, if it is pure and of the better sort, or reduced to a very fine powder if it is impure and contains mixed parts—is calcined <note>heated to a high temperature in a furnace to drive off impurities.</note> in a small furnace built for this purpose. It is then formed into a single mass using egg white, or even common water, or by some with linseed oil. If it does not capture light after the first calcination, the process must be repeated until you achieve the desired effect. This success is signaled by certain efflorescences <note>powdery crusts that form on the surface of a mineral.</note> resembling tiny grains of dew, which the stone seems to sweat toward the surface; it is in these grains specifically that the power of capturing light resides, without the interference of any other substance.

<margin>How it should be enclosed.</margin>
The stone, prepared in this way, is placed in certain boxes or small chests made for the purpose. If you wish to show the beauty of the borrowed light to friends, you must expose the stone in its case to the brilliance of the Sun during the day, or if the Sun is not shining, to daylight or even twilight. If at night, you may expose it to a strong fire and lit torches. (From all

<column-break/>

<margin>How long they must be exposed to light.</margin>
<margin>They pour out the captured light in the dark.</margin>
of these, it can attract light and draw it into itself, though in proportion to the source: the more eminent the light, the more abundant and effective the light with which the stone will shimmer in the dark.) Once the stones have been exposed to light for a little while—say, a quarter of an hour—to more perfectly and intimately conceive the "offspring" of light within themselves, you then carry them, closed in their case, into a dark place. Upon opening the box, you will see them diffuse light from themselves just like burning coals. However, this does not last forever; depending on the quality of the stone or the abundance of the captured light, it lasts sometimes more, sometimes less. This duration, however, never tends to exceed an hour unless they are exposed to light again. Gradually, as the power weakens, the light is extinguished; yet experience shows that the captured light is preserved longer if the box is kept closed in the darkness. Note also that this light-capturing power does not remain in the stone forever; like a magnet whose power dies away, it becomes "exhausted" over time once the power itself has breathed its last through the subtle, fiery qualities mixed into the lime.

<margin>Various opinions of different people regarding this light.</margin>
Just as the spectacle of this prodigious stone excited the greatest admiration among Philosophers, it also vehemently inflamed the minds of many with its wonderful light to inquire with all zeal into the cause of such a rare effect. From this, as usually happens with new and rare things, various opinions emerged from various people. Some, seeing that this light was carried in a closed box to a dark place and preserved there without any dependence on a luminous body, thought that light is a physical body—contrary to what the common School of Philosophers believes. They thought the stone attracts light in the same way that Naphtha attracts fire and a Magnet attracts iron. Others wanted the light in this stone to be a quality of celestial and fiery substance, glowing in the dark just like all other "night-shiners" <note>original: "Noctiluca," referring to naturally bioluminescent things.</note>. Some believe the stone is ignited by the surrounding light according to atomic particles, into which they claim it is constantly being resolved; others mix in different theories.

But that all these cited reasons and causes are frivolous, deceptive, and rest on no foundation of truth will be clear from what follows. Against the first opinion, I conclude thus: if this light were a body for the reason that it is conserved in a place separate from a luminous body...

He details the furnace "calcination" process and discusses contemporary theories about whether light is a physical substance or a celestial quality.</summary>

He now begins a philosophical investigation into whether this light is a physical "body" or a "quality," and how it compares to magnetism and bioluminescence.</meta>

<page-num>19</page-num>
<header>The Lighting of Stones.</header>

...could be preserved; there would be no reason why the same should not be said of light and heat in glowing iron. Just as the light in our stone is preserved in the absence of the Sun, so too could heat and light in glowing iron be preserved for some time after the cause is gone—that is, after the fire is extinguished. Yet, no philosopher until now has called the heat and light produced in iron by fire "bodies" <note>In 17th-century physics, a "body" refers to a physical substance or matter, as opposed to a "quality" like color or heat.</note>. Therefore, that opinion is false. It is not an essential property of light—especially secondary light, which our light here is—to depend so strictly on a luminous body that it must die out instantly when the luminous body is removed. This would be against manifest experience. For we note that by looking at snow or the Sun, we "imbibe" light in such a way that upon entering a shaded place, we are rendered blind because of the images of light <note>original: "species luminis," referring to what we now call afterimages.</note> impressed upon the eye. Secondly, it would follow that even magnetic force is a body, since it can be transferred from a magnet into iron and remain there even after the magnet (the cause producing the quality) is destroyed. Consequently, all qualities would be bodies; who does not see how absurd this is?

<margin>It does not pull light as naphtha pulls fire.</margin>
Regarding the other part of the opinion, I deny that this stone "pulls" light in the same way a magnet pulls iron or naphtha <note>A flammable liquid hydrocarbon, similar to petroleum or kerosene.</note> pulls fire. No "attraction" takes place in this operation. For a magnet, besides altering the iron by producing a quality in it so that it may join itself to its own perfecting good, also positions it in a certain way; none of this happens in this communication of light. The stone is not moved to a different location by receiving this light, nor does it acquire any certain position in relation to anything else; rather, it remains merely passive in receiving the light. Therefore, there is no reason to say that this stone "pulls" light as naphtha pulls fire, since the reasoning for each is different. In fact, naphtha does not properly "pull" fire;

<margin>How naphtha is said to pull fire.</margin>
rather, when fire touches that vaporous sphere which naphtha pours out through its continuous, oily, and flammable exhalation, the fire ignites that entire bituminous vapor—as a medium most suitable for inflammation—almost in a moment, and thus it *seems* to pull the fire. Therefore, the naphtha does not pull the fire, nor the fire the naphtha, as the common people think; rather, the fire "runs" toward the naphtha as if toward a most welcome fuel, propagating itself as much as it can. It is no different than if, after a candle is extinguished, we bring another lit candle near the exhaling smoke (no matter how far from the wick), and we immediately see that ignited smoke propagate itself bit by bit and relight the extinguished candle. In this way, lightning and most ignited meteors—such as the "rods" which the common people call falling stars—are usually ignited, even though they lack magnetism. Indeed, this operation is also beautifully demonstrated by an experiment we proposed elsewhere, involving the display of lightning through the ignited vapor of the quintessence of wine <note>original: "quintae essentiae vini," meaning highly concentrated alcohol or ethanol.</note>. It is clear, therefore, that no magnetic action proper to our stone intervenes in the conception of light. 

<column-break/>

Now it remains for us to see how the light imbibed in this stone is preserved, or what the true reason for this prodigy might be. And first, I deny that this light is a quality derived from some celestial substance into the stone. Since this descending quality is incorruptible by nature, how could it produce a light in our stone that lasts only a very short time? Or how could it be resolved into "atomic" particles continuously without the greatest inconvenience and conflict with natural forces? I cannot see how this would work. I would gladly show all of this more extensively here, had it not been excellently and most eruditely performed by Fortunio Liceti in his *Lithophosphorus*, whom I cited above.

<margin>The light of the stone differs from bioluminescence.</margin>
I say, therefore, that the light produced in our stone is not of the same nature as the light shining in night-shining things <note>original: "Noctilucis," referring to bioluminescent organisms.</note>, as many philosophers wrongly believe. For the light in night-shining things—such as in rotting oak, fireflies, the eyes of cats, the heads of certain fish, rotting oysters, the mold on ships, and similar things—is not produced by a luminous body. Rather, all these things have their own light, just as carbuncles <note>A term for red gemstones, like garnets or rubies, once thought to glow in the dark.</note> and other precious stones have a light implanted by nature for certain ends, by which they shine in the dark. This can in no way be said of the light of our stone, which is only communicated to it from the outside. Furthermore, the light in night-shining things lasts as long as the subject it inhabits; it is otherwise for our stone's light, which as soon as it is acquired, is extinguished bit by bit not long after and falls back into its chaos. To give the genuine reason for this light, I suppose: First, that air illuminated by the Sun is filled with a most subtle vapor, highly suited for receiving light. Second, that our stone is so purified by <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to remove impurities and change its structure.</note> and baking from the mixture of earthly filth that its substance is thinned and rarefied. By the opening of its pores, it is made into a body most fit for receiving those vapors suffused with whatever light with which the air teems when a luminous body, fire, or the full Sun is present. These things being supposed: since its pores are opened by calcination, our stone—by its "thirsty" dryness—naturally seeks that vaporous offspring pregnant with light. Just as a sponge seeks nearby moisture...

<meta>The catchword "morem" (manner/way) at the bottom indicates the next page will likely complete the sponge analogy: "in the manner of a sponge."</meta>

<summary>Kircher argues that the Bologna Stone does not "pull" light through magnetism but acts as a porous sponge that physically "soaks up" light-bearing vapors from the air after being purified by fire. He distinguishes this from bioluminescence (like fireflies or rotting wood), which he views as an innate, internal light.</summary>

<page-num>20</page-num>

### CHAPTER IX.
#### *On the Properties of Light.* <note>original Greek: "περὶ φάου" (peri phaou)</note>

---

<image-desc>Decorative initial T containing a landscape scene with a building and trees.</image-desc>
I find the nature of light to be so abstruse and hidden that the further I feel myself progress in it, the more I see myself involved in greater darkness. Nevertheless, like the night-owl <note>original: "Nycticorax"; a bird of the night often used as a metaphor for the intellect struggling with divine or natural mysteries</note>, I open my eyes so that, as much as fits a fragile intellect, I may sustain at least some ray of light. It must be noted, therefore, that light can be considered in various ways: first, as it exists in a luminous body; second, as it is diffused from it; next, as it is received in a medium <note>the space light travels through, such as air or water</note>; and finally, as it is viewed in the thing acted upon, or the final boundary.

<margin>The wonderful power of light.</margin>
Thus, the first property of light is that it is intimate to the luminous body, so much so that nothing can be more joined to it. Since it is its property and its form, light makes the subject pleasing, beautiful, useful, and most worthy of praise—indeed, even of admiration. It provides the body with such power that it can also illuminate other things. Hence, light is the purest and most effective of all qualities, polluted by no filth of bodies, rich in everything and in need of nothing. In its power, it contains all colors, smells, tastes, and even the four primary qualities <note>Heat, cold, moisture, and dryness</note>. It is invincible and untamed, for there is no darkness that it does not overcome by its diffusion, nor is there any created agent that could destroy it; nor does it have a "contrary" in the strict sense. Therefore, it most easily dominates transparent bodies everywhere,

<column-break/>

mony and saltpeter, which have no place in other substances. This, indeed, is my opinion regarding the nature of the said stone.

##### Corollary.

<margin>Wonders which can be shown with the help of this luminous stone.</margin>
From what has been said, it follows how many spectacles—and those most worthy of admiration—can be exhibited in the darkness with the help of this mineral. Due to their rarity, these hold no small place among the "sacraments" of natural magic. For example: Christ the Lord shining with his wounds, or the glory of Paradise (with the lime arranged according to the rules of Sciography <note>The art of projecting shadows or architectural perspective</note>), or the glowing eyes of animals. Thus, things invisible in the dark are suddenly rendered visible, along with innumerable other things which anyone, according to the sagacity of their own wit, will be able to devise. Concerning the use of this stone, see the "Magic of Light and Shadow."

exercising its empire through all the regions of the world.
Furthermore, as light is considered externally, it communicates itself to things without any diminution of itself, diffusing itself in a moment—not in a twisted or winding ray, but in a straight and shortest line, ordained by nature to reach its effect more quickly. Indeed, all natural agents seem to emulate this mode of action, as will be seen later. Moreover, the further down it descends, the more rays it emits; its cone is in the light itself as if at the forehead, while its base is in the medium or the illustrated object. Thus, rays are diffused in every direction, just as the center, or a point, or the center of a circle is diffused into the entire circumference by innumerable lines in a "uniformly difform" illumination, as will be explained later.
Truly, as light is received in a medium, it is certain that it illustrates all the particles of that medium and, as it were, animates the formless things. In the medium, it is also subsequently either reflected or refracted, about which you will find extensive discussion in the *Art of Reflection* <note>original: "Arte Anacamptica"</note> and the *Art of Refraction* <note>original: "Anaclastica"</note>. But as it is viewed at its terminus, it has this property: that it renders bodies (however opaque or even partially transparent) clear. It frees them from darkness by scattering the gloom and manifests all colors, which experience teaches us can in no way be emitted without light. Indeed, it reveals not only colors, but also the magnitude, figure, number, motion, and rest...

...reveals rest, unity, roughness, smoothness, sharpness, equality, inequality, similarity, dissimilarity, extension, proximity, distance, position, division, beauty, ugliness, opacity, and transparency, as well as the timing of actions and passions. Among its other properties, however, its diffusion through a medium is so wonderful that it seems endowed with a kind of sense: for when it falls upon transparent <note>original: "diaphana"</note> bodies, it insinuates itself joyfully as if through kindred things, and both penetrates and permeates them in every direction, filling them with its own cheerfulness and fecundity as if it were animating them. Opaque objects, however, it turns away from as if with a certain indignation, as though they were contrary to its nature; and as if it regretted having even touched them, it recoils from them immediately, seeks out its own kind, and chooses rather to be broken <note>referring to refraction or scattering</note> than to be joined in a hostile and disparate partnership. If, however, a hole should occur anywhere in an opaque body, light rushes through it to escape, and as if exulting in this flight, it shows itself more broadly and grandly on the opposite side than the hole itself, appearing to mock the kingdom of darkness. In a word, light is possessed by such a desire to amplify itself that it does so in whatever way it can; indeed, it does not disdain to gather itself into the narrowest of holes, provided that through them it may pour itself out more widely. For it does not think it beneath itself to pass through any holes, of whatever size or quality, and to show itself more grandly and broadly beyond them than within the hole 

<column-break/>

itself, yet it disdains to remain there. If anyone, by blocking the hole, should strive to commit it to a prison, he would find that light is a thing impatient of every prison and bolt. But if one acts honorably and offers a passage through any hole, then by kindly insinuating itself into the narrow opening, light magnificently expands itself into that most perfect of all shapes—the circular—clearly showing with what love of perfection it is possessed. Nor is it constricted or thickened in any passage through a hole, even if it appears brighter there; and even if it is far removed from the hole and dilated more thinly, it indicates by this very fact that its powers are stronger when closer to their source. For the closer it is to the hole, the more vividly it illuminates, even if more narrowly; but with a greater divergence, it illuminates more broadly, though more feebly. It is as if it assumes strength and vigor while squeezed and compressed within the narrow straits of cracks and holes, but once dilated or going off in different directions, it becomes weaker as its virtue is spread out and disunited. It becomes more rarefied the further it departs from its source, so that at last, as if forgetting its own splendor, it enters into a marriage with shadow, and finally yields its place to the contrary children of darkness. Having thus seen the nature <note>original Greek: "φυσις" (physis)</note> of light and its wondrous play in the universe of things, let us now turn our pen to explaining its specific gifts.
