# CHAPTER X.

## A scholastic inquiry into the nature and efficiency of Light in the sublunary world, and its causalities.

### §. I. On the necessity of Light.

It is the common opinion of the wise that light must necessarily exist, given the nature of things, and that it is not among that class of beings which have a merely contingent existence; this is proven by the following inductions. Among visible things, colored bodies hold the greatest place, yet they cannot be seen except through the generation of their images <note>original: "species"; in scholastic philosophy, these are the 'forms' of objects that travel through the air to the eye</note> in a medium, and the transmission of those same images to the eyes. For these images exist in the medium like an act in a subject, or a certain form in its matter. Since the acts of active things do not occur except in a disposed subject, and forms are not produced except in matter specifically

<column-break/>

appropriated to them, it follows that the images of colors and colored things require a certain immediate disposition in the medium in which they exist and occur. This final form and disposition—which draws out the images and forms of visible things into actuality—will be nothing other than light. Light, therefore, is so necessary to the world that the world cannot consist without it. This is especially true because the stars do not act upon these lower regions except through heat-bearing light; and since the generation of all things is perfected by that fertile heat, communicated to lower things by the flood of celestial rays, it is clear that the world cannot exist without light. Therefore, Light is necessary to the world.

### §. II. On the Final Cause of Light.

The final cause <note>The "final cause" is the purpose or goal for which a thing exists.</note> of Light is divided into the common and the proper. The common cause is threefold: God, the World, and Mankind. God is the one to whom all things are coordinated as the ultimate end; it is for His sake that all things which act according to nature perform their actions. The World is the second, for light was established by nature for its adornment and perfection; without it, the world could neither be called an "ordered whole" <note>original Greek: "κόσμος" (kosmos), meaning order or the world-system</note> nor enjoy the perfection due to it. Finally, there is Mankind, who, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> testifies, is the end of all things. Man must also be called the end of light, for his natural desire is to understand and know all things. Since these things cannot be grasped without the senses—especially without the service of sight—light was absolutely necessary for perceiving the many differences between things and for knowing them intimately.

The proper final cause is also threefold: Heat, Color, and Light. Heat is the author of all generation; light seems to have been established for the sole purpose of producing it. Thus the Philosopher rightly "called the sun the principle of life" <note>original Greek: "ἥλιον ἀρχὴν ζωῆς εἶπεν"</note>; he calls the Sun the generative principle and believed that the various generations of sublunary things <note>Things on Earth, beneath the moon.</note> occur only through the heats reaching us from the heat of the Sun. Regarding Color, light was given by nature solely for the production of the visible form of color, as was demonstrated a little while ago. Finally, there is light itself, or the lucid body, for the sake of seeing which light acts as a representative species <note>A "species" in this context is a philosophical term for the sensory image or likeness of an object that travels to the eye.</note>; light serves as a kind of instrument for producing heat in lower things.

### §. III. On the Material Cause of Light.

<margin>The two types of transparency.</margin>
Plato maintained that the material cause of light was "the whole world and all the bodies of the world as the subject of light" <note>original Greek: "τοῦ φωτὸς ὑποκείμενον πάντα τὸν κόσμον, καὶ πάντα τὰ τοῦ κόσμου σώματα"</note>. Aristotle, however, held that "the material cause of light is the transparent insofar as it is transparent" <note>original Greek: "φωτὸς αἰτίαν ὑλικὴν εἶναι διάφανον καθ᾽ ὃ διάφανον"</note>. To understand both views, however, it must be noted: there are two kinds of transparent things. First, the indeterminate transparent, such as all diaphanous <note>Clear or see-through.</note> substances; second, the terminate transparent, which includes all opaque and colored bodies. The former admits transparency through all its parts, both outer and inner; the latter admits transparency only on its outermost surface. Light is the "act" or fulfillment of both the inner and outer transparency. Therefore, the proximate matter of lights is the transparent body. Within this category, the primary example <note>original: "praecipuum analogatum," a logical term for the most perfect representative of a category.</note> is the diaphanous transparent—such as air, water, glass, and the like—which admits light internally. The secondary example

<column-break/>

is the "non-transparent" <note>original Greek: "ἀδιάφανον" (adiaphanon)</note> such as the Moon, the earth, mixed or colored bodies, and others that receive light only on their surface. On that surface, they possess a transparency generated by the external diaphanous medium, since every nature is the procreator of an essence like unto itself, as Aristotle wisely teaches in the third book of his *Physics*.

### §. IV. On the Formal Cause of Light.

Since substances differ from accidents <note><term>Accident</term>: In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that exists only within a substance, like the color of an apple or the heat of water, rather than being an independent thing itself.</note> in that substances are defined by their essence, while accidents are defined by the addition of their subject, it follows that the "genus" (which designates the matter in the definition of substances) designates the "form" in the definition of accidents. Since accidents are the acts and forms of their subject, and specifically light is the act and form of a transparent body, one might object that we are placing "form upon form." To prevent this, we state that all accidents (which are forms of parts) are called the "proper forms of the whole" by the Schools <note>The Scholastic philosophers.</note>, and these are their generic causes. Thus, to seek the formal cause of an accident is nothing other than to seek the "genus" to which it is reduced as a species; light is form by its very genus, and it has no other physical formal cause than itself. Since the supreme categories of all things are reduced to Substance and Accident, we shall make it clear through these arguments that light is not a substance, but an accident, and therefore a physical form:

I. Everything that arises formally from a light or a lucid body, just as whiteness arises from a white thing, is an accident. But light is formally produced by a source of light; therefore, light is not a substance, but an accident. For if a substance were produced by light, it would be acting beyond its powers by creating something more perfect than itself, which is absurd. Therefore, light is an accident, not a substance.

II. That which is present or absent without the destruction of the subject is an accident. Light is present in or absent from the air and the transparent without destroying them. Therefore, light is an image of the source and a visible species of the lucid thing. But an image representing an object to the cognitive faculty is not a substance, but an accident. Therefore.

III. That which can be diminished or intensified is an accident. Light can be intensified and diminished based on the condensation or rarefaction of the transparent subject, the proximity or distance of the light source, and the greater or lesser perfection of the opaque body in relation to the transparent body. Therefore.

IV. That which is added to a being that is already "in act" <note>Already fully formed and existing.</note> is an accident, not a substantial form. Light is added to the ether, the air, and other transparent bodies which are already beings in act. Therefore.

V. The end...

V. The goal and limit of an alteration that occurs while the subject remains the same is not a substantial form, but an accident <term>Accident: In Aristotelian philosophy, a property or quality (like color or temperature) that can change without the object itself turning into something else.</term>. Light <note>original Latin: "lumen"</note> is the goal of illumination, which is an alteration occurring between darkness and light while the transparent subject remains the same; therefore, [light is an accident]. Since light is neither a quantity, nor a relation, nor an action, it must necessarily be classified under the category of quality, specifically within the third kind of quality; and it is among those "passible" <note>Capable of being felt or suffered.</note> qualities that produce a sensation in the senses. We have therefore assigned the formal cause of light: that by its very nature, it is an accident and a physical form. If we were discussing the metaphysical formal cause, we would say it is that which holds the place of the "difference" in the metaphysical definition of light.

### §. V. On the Efficient Cause of Light. <term>Efficient Cause: The primary agent or force that brings an effect into existence—for example, a carpenter is the efficient cause of a table.</term>

Therefore, the chief, total, and adequate cause of light—the principle that generates light <note>original: "lumen"</note> in a transparent medium—is the luminous body in an absolute sense. By its simple presence, it pours forth light from itself and generates it through a simple action in the transparent medium, of whatever kind that medium may be. The partial, effecting cause of light, and the principle by which a luminous body first produces light in a transparent medium, is the "source-light" <note>original: "lux"</note>; that is, the form that constitutes the luminous body as something "luminous." This form is followed by the "radiant-light" <note>original: "lumen"</note> in the transparent medium, just as the visible image of colors follows in a medium, or as a shadow in light follows the opacity of a body. By no different logic does a fire burning on a pyre produce heat in the air; that heat of the air then generates a similar heat in those standing nearby, who are nevertheless said to be heated not by the air, but by the fire as the primary principle of the heating.

<margin>How a luminous body produces light in a transparent medium.</margin> Therefore, just as heat generates an image of itself in the air that affects people, so a luminous body produces a likeness and image of its source-light—namely, visible light—in the transparent medium, like the face of a man produces his image in a mirror; or like a colored body pours an image of its color into an illuminated transparent medium. Just as a colored body pours its image into the medium not from a single point only, but from its entire surface, so the light, as an image of the luminous body, is diffused not from a single point or from the center alone, but from its entire luminous surface. Therefore, the adequate effective cause of light is the luminous body as such; its primary "source-light" [lux] is a quality, of which the radiant light [lumen] produced in the transparent medium is the genuine image and likeness.

### First Corollary.

<margin>Light is not drawn out from the potentiality of matter.</margin> From this it is clear that light, in its generation, is not "drawn out" from the potentiality of the perfected transparent matter by the luminous body, but rather comes to it from the out-

<column-break/>

side from a perfected source-light. I demonstrate this as follows: <margin>What it means to be "drawn out" from the potentiality of matter.</margin> For a form to be drawn out from the potentiality of the underlying matter is properly nothing other than for a form to arise from a generator through the transformation of the underlying matter which already contains some "rudiment" of that form. But there is no way this can apply to light; rather, it must come to the transparent medium from the outside. This is because light is produced from the luminous body into the Transparent Medium just as images <note>original: "species"</note> are produced in the air. Sensible images, like the likenesses of objects, are generated by those objects in the medium and in the sense organs, not by drawing them out from the power of the receiving matter, but rather they are induced into the matter by the object. Therefore, light is not drawn out from the power of matter. Reason also confirms this: in the same medium, contrary forms (like black and white) are generated by contrary objects; yet the same subject cannot be simultaneously disposed toward contrary forms. Forms that are drawn out from the potentiality of matter require contrary dispositions for contrary forms; therefore, [light is not one of them]. Furthermore, a form that is born immediately upon the presence of its efficient cause, and dies immediately upon its absence, is not drawn out from the power of matter; light is such a form; therefore, [light is not drawn out from matter]. Finally, just as the image of our face is not drawn out from the potentiality of the mirror in which it is formed when we are present, so it is with light. Therefore, light is not drawn out from the power of matter. This was the point to be proved. It can be further confirmed by the fact that "intentional species" <note>The invisible forms or images that travel from an object to the eye.</note> are said to be more spiritual than other accidents, and less material.

### Second Corollary.

<margin>Light is not a simple emanation, but a true production.</margin> From this it also follows that the origin of light in a transparent medium is not a simple emanation, but a true production resting on the action of the source-light; light is not produced by an idle efficient cause that does nothing. Just as "risibility" <note>The capacity for laughter.</note> in a human follows the essence of the rational soul without the soul doing extra work, and as size in a natural body follows the nature of the matter without the matter acting, [so some think light follows the source]. But light is truly and really produced by a luminous body that is actively operating. For whatever flows from something by simple emanation depends on it as qualities or passions depend on a formal or material cause; but it was demonstrated previously that a luminous body is neither a formal nor a material cause, but an efficient cause. Therefore, light cannot arise by simple emanation; it must be through a real production of an agent resting on a real operation. Furthermore, things that occur through simple emanation from something are, for the most part, different in kind [heterogeneous]; but light is the image of the source-light, and is similar to it and of the same kind [homogeneous];

### Third Corollary.

<margin>Definition of light.</margin> It is clear, therefore, that light <note>original: "lumen"</note> is nothing other than a sensible quality physically produced by a luminous body present in a transparent body, which assists in the creation of heat,

<column-break/>

# C H A P T E R XI.
->On the wondrous powers of light in producing the miracles of sublunary nature.<- <term>Sublunary: Literally "under the moon"; referring to the Earthly realm where things are subject to change and decay.</term>

The great fertility and power of light to act is nowhere more evident than in the wonderful miracles it paints and fashions in the air.
The question is asked, therefore: by what power does it perform these things? For this to happen, it must be noted that light always strives to create something similar to itself in all things. In this, it is like a "univocal agent" <term>Univocal agent: A cause that produces an effect of the exact same nature as itself, such as a fire starting another fire.</term> which seeks to produce something of its own kind. Experience clearly teaches that light is indeed generated from light everywhere. First, the light of rays generates other light in the surrounding air; if anyone were to deny this, they would by the same effort have to deny that the air is dark <note>The author argues that if light didn't reproduce itself in the air, we would only see the sun and nothing else would be illuminated.</note>. Since that is absurd and contradicts experience, it must be said that light necessarily generates another like itself. Furthermore, it is well known that light produces more light when it is reflected from an opaque, polished body, as well as

<column-break/>

when it is refracted in a denser medium. This light receives various names according to the variety of the material and the diversity of the primary source. Concerning these, consider the following experiments.

### First Experiment.
#### On the color of various Flames.

If you mix the color of copper-rust <note>original: "ærugineum"; verdigris</note> into a small dish of "water of life" <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; high-proof distilled alcohol</note> or some other distilled liquor, and then light the prepared liquid, you will see—not without wonder—a flame of an intense green color. If, however, you mix cinnabar <note>A bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide.</note> with the said liquid, the ignited fluid will show you a flame of the most intense red. If you further mix sulfur into it, you will have a blue flame. It is the same flame, but tinted in different ways according to the diversity of the material from which it draws its nourishment.

#### On apparent color.

...the rays of the Sun terminating, and you will see at point D an extremely intense redness; but when the angle is changed, you will see that color clearly varied from red into a crimson <note>original: "puniceum"</note> mixed with yellow. At point K, the same likeness of red color will also appear, although much weaker than at D. There is no other reason for this than the varying refraction in a denser medium; just as light, failing through various degrees, passes into different colors. For color appearing in red bodies of this kind is nothing other than light varied by different refractions. Thus, the light of the Sun falling on point B of the sphere, being refracted in the denser medium, falls on C; from here it is reflected back to D, and then from D, being refracted once more, it finally seeks the eye at E. Since the light is refracted twice here, and once reflected within the uniform medium, it finally reaches H; it necessarily reaches the eye having been weakened in various ways from its native clarity, degenerating as if into a certain shadowy light. That such multiple refraction is the cause of colors is evident from the fact that the redness at K varies greatly from the redness at D, in that it verges toward crimson. Since this color is further removed from the white color which the light reflects at point D, it must also undergo more refractions. For the ray of the Sun F, falling on G, is refracted to H, then to I, and from I to K, and finally from there into the eye E. You see, therefore, that a color becomes more "shadowy" the more refractions it undergoes within a circular body or a transparent polyhedron. But since we deal with these and similar matters specifically in our *Catoptric Magic* <note>Referring to the study of mirrors and reflected light</note>, we refer the reader there. It is enough for us that all apparent colors are nothing other than the light of the Sun in a denser medium, affected in different ways by reflection and refraction; it departs further from the native color of light the more it is weakened and rendered shadowy through various refractions, as if passing through the multiple surfaces of a body. But we shall discuss these things more fully in what follows.

Since, therefore, the light of incidence generates light, as do the reflections on the surface of a mirror (or a bounded transparent body), and the refractions in a second, denser transparent medium;

<column-break/>

this second light is called by the names of "glitter" <note>original: "fulgoris"</note> and "brightness" <note>original: "splendoris"</note>. Furthermore, since from this second light a third light is generated outside the point of reflection and outside the material of refraction in the transparent medium—I mean reflected and refracted light—it happens that the light, being variously modified, acquires the various properties of colors. Thus, from the rays of the Sun refracted in the morning vapors of the horizons, there arises a certain intense redness 
<margin>The colors of the dawn.</margin>
in the sky, which we call the beginning of the dawn <note>original: "aurora"</note>. It is nothing other than the light of the Sun refracted variously and more deeply in the medium; this redness approaches the essence of light more closely as the Sun comes nearer and nearer to the horizon, and as a greater part of the atmosphere is illuminated. The same must be said of the Sun's rays refracted in the vapor of the western horizon, which constitute the evening twilight <note>original: "crepusculum"</note>. There, it is clearly seen how the light defines itself: from the bright, clear, and serene light of the Sun touching the horizon, it turns into yellow and saffron, then into red, from red into blue, and from there into dark shadow. This diversity of colors draws its origin from the varying reflection of the borders of light and shadow in the thinner medium.

Furthermore, even during the peak of day, when these same rays are refracted in a dewy cloud opposite the Sun, the colored and variegated light of the rainbow is produced,
<margin>The color of the rainbow.</margin>
concerning which we treat in our *Catoptric Magic*. From these same solar rays in a cloud positioned below the Sun, <term>parhelia</term> <note>original: "παρήλια"; also known as "sun dogs," these are bright spots that appear on either side of the sun.</note> occur, or a light is generated of a doubled or tripled Sun. From these same refracted rays, all the colors of clouds, "rods," "halos," "chasms," and other meteorological impressions are born. The phenomena of the heavens and of comets also draw their origin from this. Thus, light as a "univocal agent" <note>In philosophy, a "univocal agent" is something that produces an effect of the same nature as itself—here, light producing more light.</note> generates in a clear or transparent medium a new light, either of the same kind—such as the second light reflected from the air outside the rays, or from a mirror outside the direct path of the light source, or refracted by a second transparent medium that does not change the appearance of the rays—or of a somewhat different appearance but of the same general category, such as the second light refracted in a cloud or vapor under the appearance of a rainbow, or rods, or sun dogs, or others of that kind.

## CHAPTER XII.
->*How Light Generates the Visible Forms of Colors in a Medium.*<-

I assume first, in opposition to certain thinkers who believed that light efficiently produces colors within colored bodies themselves, that light is neither the instrumental cause nor the total cause of producing visible forms <note>original: "species visibiles." In Scholastic science, a "species" was an immaterial likeness or image of an object that traveled through the air to the eye.</note>. It is not the former, because in such a production, light would act as a "habit" <note>original: "habitus," a stable quality or disposition</note>; however, a habit cannot function as an instrumental cause. It is not the latter, because colors themselves are the primary actors in that production, while light merely cooperates. Indeed, light by itself cannot produce any images of colors in a transparent medium <note>original: "perspicuo," referring to any clear substance like air or water</note>. Since light relates to all parts of a transparent medium indifferently, there would be no reason why it should generate red, white, or any other color in one part rather than another. Therefore, the entire and sole efficiency of light provides this: it "elevates" all colors so that, without the direct service of the matter to which they are bound, each color can create its own visible image in the transparent medium. Light, then, acts in the efficiency of colors as a "principle by which" <note>original: "principium quo"</note> or as a primary partial agent. It does not act as the "form" of the color—since color already possesses its own true likeness for production—but rather as an agent that lifts colors above the condition of their underlying matter, allowing them to produce a somewhat immaterial

<column-break/>

likeness of themselves. For since color is a form "submerged" in matter, while light is removed from all "contagion" of matter, a material form is naturally unfit to act on its own and cannot rise above its material state. It necessarily requires an immaterial principle that is elevated above the conditions of matter to produce something independent of the underlying subject. This principle is nothing other than light. When joined to color, light enables that color to form a visible representation in the transparent medium, acting as a kind of likeness removed from all subject matter. It produces this image in the medium in exactly the same way that the **active intellect** <note>original: "intellectus agens." An Aristotelian concept describing the part of the mind that transforms sensory images into abstract thoughts.</note> enables **phantasms** <note>original: "phantasmata," or mental images</note>—which dwell in the material organ of the imagination under individual and material conditions—to produce a completely immaterial image of themselves in the "possible mind," without the material organ or any individual conditions cooperating with the phantasms themselves. Therefore, the fact that a color's representation is immaterial comes from the immateriality of light; however, the fact that it represents a specific color comes not from the light (which is indifferent to all colors) but from the specific color from which it is produced. We shall see more on these matters in the following sections.

## CHAPTER XIII.
->*How Heat is Generated by Light in the Earth, in the Air, or in the Atmosphere.*<-

I assume first that light is an **equivocal agent** <term>equivocal agent: a cause that produces an effect different in kind from itself, such as the sun (light) producing heat</term> in the production of heat. If our fire heats things, it does so "formally" and as a **univocal agent** <term>univocal agent: a cause that produces an effect of the same nature as itself (e.g., fire producing fire)</term>; it does not heat insofar as it is bright. In its brightness, it is an equivocal agent. For it is characteristic of univocal agents to produce things like themselves, just as it is for equivocal agents to produce things unlike themselves. If fire heated things simply because it is bright, then certainly the flame of a candle or of very dry straw would produce a much more intense heat than a glowing coal or a red-hot iron, which contradicts experience. Therefore, fire does not heat univocally, but equivocally. I assume secondly that light does not produce heat

<column-break/>

everywhere, but only in matter suited for heat. It does not produce heat in the "ether" because of the thinness of that expanded body, nor in water immediately (as will be seen later), nor in the depths of the earth, because the opacity and thickness of the mass act as an obstruction.

It remains, therefore, that heat is produced by light only on the surfaces of worldly bodies.

<margin>When heat is produced.</margin>
How this happens must now be explained. It should be noted that air is naturally warm and moist, but both qualities are very weak <note>original: "remissas," meaning diluted or not intense</note>. Because of its thinness, air is easily changeable into fire.

<margin>What the refining edge of heat, dryness, is.</margin>
Experience teaches us that the "refining edge" of heat is dryness; for heat is greatly sharpened when moisture is beaten back and diminished. Since, furthermore, moisture...

## CHAPTER XIV.
### How Heat produces cold, dryness, and moisture in the sublunary world.

It may indeed seem new to someone how from the same efficient cause in the same matter, different and contrary effects of heat and cold, moisture and dryness, can be produced. But to explain it <unclear>more accurately</unclear> <note>original: "ἀκριβέστερον" (akribesteron), meaning more precisely or strictly.</note>; Note that we are not dealing here with that coldness which happens to the earth because of the "bluntness" of the rays falling upon it, since that defect of heat is by no means on the part of the Sun, but on the part of the earth being unable to receive the Sun's light conveniently. Nor is it a matter here of the nightly cold following the absence of the Sun, for this is a cause of cold by accident; but of that coldness which the Sun, Moon, and other stars bring upon the earth, by a certain power appropriate to them, instilled by the Author of Nature to temper the Sun's heat. 
<margin>The cold Moon.</margin>
Among the other stars, however, the Moon excels in this cooling power, which it communicates to the earth in the following way. Since the Moon has a body of a cold and moist <term>complexion <note>In ancient and medieval science, "complexion" refers to the balance of the four primary qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note></term>, and is as if another earth composed of moisture and terrestrial parts, it happens that the Sun's rays, mixed with the Moon's coldness, are no longer hot, but imbued with lunar power as they are reflected back to the earth. For as that great Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval polymath who wrote extensively on the natural sciences.</note> rightly says: 
<margin>Lunar force mixed with Solar power.</margin>
*The light of the Sun received from the stars is received into the depth of the stars, and thus incorporated into the stars, it brings in the power of the stars, and causes an effect of various qualities, according to how the stars in which it is incorporated are diversified.* For as Averroës <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an influential Andalusian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle.</note> also rightly teaches, the Moon has the light of the same Sun tempered with the cold and the moist, so that from the light of the Sun it has a moving heat, and from the tempered cold it receives a temperament; and the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle.</note> says: 
<margin>Comparison of the Moon's monthly motion to the solar year.</margin>
Just as the Sun throughout the whole course of the year, by its approach and recession from us, produces summer and winter; so also the Moon in its monthly span, tending toward the fullness of its light;

<column-break/>

in the full moon, however, tending toward <term>syzygy <note>original: "syzygiam." The alignment of three celestial bodies, such as the Sun, Earth, and Moon.</note></term> with the Sun with light diminishing daily, it takes on, as it were, the character of a certain winter. Now, the Moon would produce winter by no means, unless one said that the Moon is the producer of cold among us. To understand these things better, Note secondly, that there is a double cause of lunar coldness: privative and positive. The former we can not incongruously call the thinness of heat, or its absence in the lack of light; thus, being full of light, it produces a lunar summer. 
<margin>Why we feel greater cold at the time of the full moon than at the time of the new moon.</margin>
But why we usually feel greater cold at the time of the full moon than at the time of the <term>interlunium <note>The "between-moons" period when the moon is not visible; the new moon.</note></term>: we establish this cause, that the lunar rays—thinning and rarefying the thicker material of dewy vapors with their previously generated warmth—when the air is cut and refined by them, some warmth necessarily arises from such a cutting of the air. By this, the pores being loosened, the surrounding cold, penetrating to the internal recesses of the human body, begins to strike the sensitive parts with a more troublesome cold; hence it is a positive cold with respect to us. This, however, does not happen at the time of the interlunium, since then the vapors, penetrated by no light and retaining their native thickness, are unfit to penetrate the narrower pores of the body. Therefore, by their native coldness, they strike only the outermost surface of the part, further passage being denied. 
<margin>Why full moons are felt more constantly cold.</margin>
Why also full moons are felt to be colder in summer than in winter, the cause is that the middle compared to one extreme has the character of the other extreme: so the summer nights of the full moon, compared to the heat of the dog days <note>The hottest days of summer, traditionally associated with the rising of the Star Sirius (the Dog Star).</note>, are tempered cold, just as in a bath lukewarm water is felt as cold because of the efficacy of the greater surrounding heat. It is added that on full moon nights, the thinner aqueous vapors made to hang suspended in the infused air penetrate more easily through the pores of the skin to the inner parts of the human body, which, possessing a more exquisite sense, feel the slightest cold.

<margin>How the Moon produces dryness.</margin>
I come now to the other quality, namely the one contrary to moisture, which is dryness; it must now be explained how this can be produced by the humid Moon. Just as heat necessarily follows when moisture is consumed by the rays of the Sun, and dryness follows heat: so it is entirely probable that both occur from the light of the Moon drawing moisture out of bodies, leading to dryness. <column-break/>

Truly, as the lunar light increases day by day and reaches its peak of fullness, just as it generated a maximum accumulation of humors in worldly bodies, so, once the finer parts of that moisture are consumed through evaporation, it brings about dryness through the induction of rot; for things that are rotting first become wet, and then dry. Therefore, the Moon, by means of the light she borrows from the Sun, most greatly corrupts meat exposed at night by rot, causing their native moisture to flow out, and thus, as we have said, she brings about dryness by accident. Hence, astrologers call the third and fourth quarters of the Moon dry and cold; and maniacs—or "lunatics"—because of the predominance of melancholy (or black bile) as the moisture of the brain turns toward dryness, are accustomed to exercise their furies most intensely, according to that passage of Nonnus in the *Dionysiaca* <note>Nonnus of Panopolis was a 5th-century Greek poet; his *Dionysiaca* is an epic poem about the god Dionysus.</note>, where the Moon says this of herself:

<margin>The night moon leads meat to rot.</margin>

# CHAPTER XV.
## The wonders of Solar and Lunar light in plants and animals.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'C' featuring a face within the crescent moon, surrounded by solar rays and stars.</image-desc>
It is certain that in the Sun, Moon, and Stars, besides light, heat, and the other primary qualities, there are yet other qualities present, as their paradoxical effects demonstrate. These certainly can be ascribed to no other cause than a hidden miracle of power <note>original: "latenti virtutis miraculo," referring to 'occult' or unseen properties that were not yet explained by 17th-century physics.</note>. For if these effects were performed by the help of the primary qualities, they would necessarily be impressed upon all things that possess said primary qualities; yet this is not found to be the case. For example, if a Magnet <note>A naturally magnetized piece of the mineral magnetite.</note> attracts iron because it is cold and dry, and similar to itself in temperament, there is certainly no reason why it should not attract all cold and dry things by the same logic. Therefore, that attractive effect of the Magnet is by no means to be attributed to the primary qualities, but to a force or a certain peculiar quality flowing immediately from the abyss of the Magnetic essence. Likewise, if the Sun and Moon had a certain sympathy with stones, plants, and animals because they themselves were dry, hot, cold, or humid, they would certainly produce similar effects in all

<column-break/>

bodies of such a complexion; yet this is contrary to experience. There should be no doubt, then, that they perform this by another quality. For it is well known that there are certain stones, called "selenite" <note>From the Greek 'selene' (moon); traditionally believed to wax and wane with the moon.</note> for this reason, which are accustomed to follow the motion of the Moon in all things; Proclus <note>A 5th-century Greek Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> also mentions in his first book *On Sacrifice and Magic* that he possessed such a stone, which underwent all the Moon's changes, increases, and decreases.

<margin>The selenite stone follows the motion of the Moon.</margin>
<margin>Wonders concerning a certain lunar stone.</margin>
Mizaldus <note>Antoine Mizauld (1510–1578), a French physician and astrologer known for his collections of "secrets" and natural wonders.</note> reports wonders concerning a stone of this kind from the Indies. The stone was spherical, the size of a pigeon's egg, and pitch-colored; it expressed the increases and decreases of the lunar light through a certain glowing spot, which grew as the Moon waxed and shrank as it waned, so that at the time of the new moon it appeared like a millet seed, but at the full moon it reached the size of a pea. Nor did it only imitate the Moon's phases, but it even followed its motions. And lest this should seem an imposture, Mizaldus adds that he took up an experiment of this matter for one entire month in the presence of that celebrated Royal Mathematician, Orontius Fineus <note>Oronce Finé (1494–1555), a significant French mathematician and cartographer.</note>; and the stone was approved by everyone as a purely natural thing and as a greatest miracle of nature.

Yet what I say is certain; you will find the natural explanation for it given in our *Magnetic World*, on page 756.

Cardano <note>Girolamo Cardano (1501–1576), an influential Italian polymath.</note> reports in his book *On Astrological Judgments* that Pope Clement VII possessed a solar gem called the *Helites* <note>original: "Helitem," likely referring to a "sun-stone" or a variety of feldspar.</note>, which had a golden spot that turned around every day with the Sun, rising and setting with it. You may read of similar things regarding a statue of the Sun fashioned by Boethius at Ravenna, which turned itself perpetually with the Sun, as recorded by Hieronymus Rubius in his *Antiquities of Ravenna*. We shall show the true reasons for all these things through irrefutable experiments in our *Magic of Light and Shadow*, where the reader will find many remarkable and curious things. I will not speak here of the experiments concerning the effects of silver, iron, mercury, and other minerals, as we have expressly reserved this material for our *Subterranean World*; only he who has been made certain of these effects by experiments himself knows how these minerals maintain a certain wonderful harmony with the Sun, Moon, and Stars. <margin>Solar and lunar plants.</margin> But I come also to plants, in which the greatest abundance of "luminous offspring" presents itself: they are joined with the lights of the Sun, Moon, and Stars by such great bonds of friendship that they seem in no way able to be separated from them. # CHAPTER XVI.
### *How celestial light, through its natural heat, may determine the longevity of animal life: and herein is revealed the true foundation of judicial Astrology concerning the life of man.*

---

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap for the letter 'E', featuring multiple figures in a scene that appears to be a gathering of scholars or deities in a classical setting.</image-desc>
It was shown from Aristotle in the preceding sections how the approach and withdrawal of a luminous body is the principle of light born among us, and that by the mediation of light, it produces the heat that generates and preserves animals in life. Now, however, it must be seen whether the circuit of our life depends on the circuits of the stars. Many Philosophers have asserted this; Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a prolific Dominican friar and philosopher who sought to reconcile Aristotelian science with Christian faith.</note> declares it expressly in these words: *"Therefore, all time which exists in a physical body, and every life that lives, has its number in the celestial circuit, and is bounded by that same celestial circle; for from that circle one considers how far the power of the generator extends in bringing a thing into being, before it brings about the perfect corruption of the thing; for the order of all lower causes depends on the order of the higher; and all time that a thing exists in duration, and every life, is measured by a period: yet not all are measured by the same period; but some have a greater, some a smaller, according as they more greatly receive and retain the powers flowed down to them from the celestial circle."* These are the words of Albertus. The Philosopher <note>Aristotle is often referred to simply as "The Philosopher."</note> confirms this, as if by his own calculation, in Book 4 of *On the Generation of Animals*, Chapter 10. There he says expressly that the times for carrying a fetus in the womb are for each animal largely proportional to their lifespan; and the times of all pregnancies, births, and lives demand to receive their dimension from the celestial circuits. In order that all these things may be understood:

<margin>The four times of the fetus in the womb.</margin>
It must be noted first that there are four periods of an animal's stay in the womb: **conception**; **perfect formation** (or organization); **complexion** <note>In this context, the "temperament" or physical constitution.</note>, which is the acquisition of its proper temperament through the pouring of parenchyma <note>The functional tissue of an organ.</note> between the fibers of the limbs; and **growth** to a suitable body size. To these correspond just as many periods of duration for animals outside the womb, which maintain an exact proportion

<column-break/>

with the times of generation in the womb. Therefore, experience teaches that the more long-lived a certain animal is, the longer it remains in the womb, and that the generation of larger animals is of longer duration than the generation of smaller ones. To provide a reason for this:

<margin>The dual temperament.</margin>
It must be noted second that an animal has a double temperament: one is **essential**, which it acquires while it is situated within the womb, from the causes promoting its nature or generation; the other is **accidental**, which the animal acquires from the surrounding air when it is brought out of the womb at birth into the open air. Since the air by its nature is hot and moist, it can alter the naturally hot and moist constitution of the newborn animal. It is certain that such an alteration can be easily impressed by the air upon the human body because of its softness, tenderness, the thinness of the skin, and the porous nature of its substance. In other animals, however, whose substance is harder and whose natural hide covering the body is thicker, either no affection or a very small one arises from the mild heat and moisture of the air. Added to this is the celestial heat communicated to the air through the light of the stars; by altering the temperament of the fetus situated in the womb, and by affecting the blood and seed (the two principles of animal generation), this heat can bring about the essential temperament. Since, therefore, because of the tenderness and softness of the female womb, it is more easily altered by the surrounding air and celestial heat than an animal fetus, the human fetus alone—for the reasons stated—can acquire both an accidental and essential hot or moist temperament (in which the reason for life alone consists), and consequently a maximum vitality. Other things, however, can receive their dimension of length or brevity according to the ratio of their stay in the womb, following the circuits—that is, the movements of the stars, especially those wandering in the Zodiac. This is not necessarily by reason of the motions of the entire celestial spheres specifically, since those motions...

if they [the celestial bodies] were uniform, they would be unfit for promoting the greatest diversity and variety of dimensions regarding the length and circuit of the times of pregnancies, births, and the lives of all living beings. Instead, through the circuits of the stars' logic, they apply now more, now less light to the Atmosphere. From this variety of light, different degrees of heat arise, which are naturally suited to promote various generations and lives according to their length or brevity. Such are the circuits of the Sun and Moon; for lunar light is the principle of generations and changes in the Atmosphere because of the light it receives from the Sun. As we said above, the Moon reflects this light strongly into our Atmosphere, and through this reception and reflection of solar light, the Moon becomes a rival to the Sun and its partner, promoting changes itself—sometimes toward generation, sometimes toward destruction. For as Aristotle rightly says: <gloss>when the circular order fails</gloss> <note>original Greek: "ὅτε ὁ ἐν κύκλῳ τάξις ἀπολείπει" — a reference to the cycle of coming-to-be and passing-away.</note>. Just as that great Sun, approaching its Northern <note>original: "Boreale"</note> dominion, strikes the surface of the earth at acute angles and thins the air by the multiplication of its rays—and once thinned, heats it, and once heated, prepares it for a vigorous warmth that is the procreator of all living things in spring and their preserver in summer—so too when it returns to its Southern <note>original: "Australe"</note> dominion of the hemisphere. When it strikes our earth at <margin>The Moon is a rival to the Sun in producing things.</margin> obtuse angles, due to the lack of ray-multiplication and the resulting deficiency of weak heat, it is necessary for things to verge toward their end. Likewise, the Moon, acting as the Sun's substitute, promotes generations to a wonderful degree during the 14-day space of its increasing light, as if a spring and summer quarter had passed. But when its light fails during the other fourteen days, it fails to promote the generation of things, as if through the course of an autumn and winter quarter. For as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle was often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> rightly says, the Moon brings heats and coolings upon things throughout the circuit of the entire monthly year. Indeed, excessive heat, by consuming all the native moisture, destroys the nature of living things; rather, it corrupts living beings by moving them. Hence, the Creator so tempered the hot and the moist in the two luminaries [Sun and Moon] that heats—moderately tempered by the moist lunar cold—might produce generations (with moderate heat acting as the primary cause, and moderate cold as a

<column-break/>

contributing cause tempering the excess of heat), whereas without such moderation, they would cause corruption.

Since, therefore, all living things are generated first either in the air or in the water, and once brought forth, <margin>On what the longevity of human life depends.</margin> they live in the same place (for all things brought forth reflect the nature of their origins, and most especially retain the conditions of their birthplace, which has the greatest power over those things that are born and dwell within it); and since all composite bodies consist of a temperament of air and water, or heat and moisture; and since the body of the seed, the principle of living things, has a foamy consistency fashioned from air and water and swelling with spirits; and since, furthermore, air and water are most affected according to the logic of the Sun, Moon, and stars, it follows that the similar nature of animals, being subject to the same periods, is affected in an equal manner. For that which is the cause of a cause is necessarily the cause of the thing caused. Indeed, it is consistent with reason that less important things change in a similar way to the change of more principal things, since both depend upon them. Reason dictates that the cycles of less important things follow the cycles of the more principal things upon which they depend. For less important things in the world are governed by the more principal; that is, since the motions of the celestial stars govern all things, and changes occur in our Atmosphere—namely in the primary elements of air and water—according to the circuits of the Sun and Moon, it is much more necessary that similar and proportional changes occur in the less principal parts of the world, such as living beings, which are like certain fruits, outcomes, or experiences of those same solar and lunar periods.

### Corollary.

Hence it is clear that just as the Solar year is divided into four seasons by the two Equinoxes and Solstices—Spring, which is hot and moist; Summer, which is hot and dry; Autumn, which is cold and dry; and finally Winter, which is cold and moist—so too is the Lunar month divided into four quarters. These quarters correspond to the seasons of the Solar year in a wonderful way, such that the two solar solstices exactly match the conjunction [New Moon] and opposition [Full Moon] of the Moon, while the Equinoxes match the two <term>dichotomies</term> <note>original Greek: "διχοτομίας" — refers to the first and last quarter moons, where the moon appears cut in half.</note> of the same, both waxing and waning. All of these things are seen beautifully expressed in the following figure.

### CHAPTER XVII.

->While the Sun and Moon, by their light, carry the heat and other qualities of the stars onto the earth as if by a vehicle, they bring about the generation of all things in the earthly realm <note>original: "sublunarium," literally "sublunary" or "under the moon"—the traditional term for the Earth and its atmosphere.</note>, mixed from the seeds proper to each thing.<-

the Sun and the Moon, and their movements. It is an order characterized by such discordant harmony, such harmonious dissonance <note>original: "discordi concordia, tam consona dissonantia"—this is a classic rhetorical device used to describe how the universe's conflicting elements (hot, cold, wet, dry) balance each other perfectly.</note>, so absolute and for all...

The Philosopher <note>Aristotle is frequently referred to simply as "The Philosopher."</note> rightly says: *Motion produces generation unceasingly, because it brings in and draws away the generative principle.* <note>Original Greek: "φορὰ ποιεῖ τὴν γένεσιν ἐνδελεχῶς, ἐπειδὴ εἰσάγει τὸ ὑπὸ τὴν αἰγλῶν ἥσσω κλει" (Note: the OCR contains some Greek errors, but the Latin text clarifies the meaning). For while the Sun, approaching us, generates a more vigorous heat with its more vigorous light, the stalks sprout, and young plants as well as animals of every kind are stimulated into fertile movements for the procreation of new offspring. In the Autumnal season, however, as the Sun in turn departs from us and revisits the southern signs <note>The zodiac signs of the southern hemisphere, specifically starting with Libra or Scorpio in this context.</note>, our earth—struck by the remote and weak light, as if by an infertile ray—is destroyed by a lack of heat in generated things. The leaves of trees fall away as if from a certain scaly old age; animals hide themselves in caves and dens as if mourning; the earth itself, stripped of all its decorative furnishings and bearing with difficulty the absence of its "marrying light," lies gloomy and shriveled, as if dressed in a mournful garment.

<margin>The wondrous workmanship of the Moon.</margin>
Hence, lest the sublunary world suffer the loss of its functions through the excessive absence of the Sun, the Moon was established by the Author of Nature with such skill that she completes in a monthly space the circle which the Sun completes in a year. Thus, joined twelve times to the Sun as if to a Husband, she conceives new seeds for things to be generated. By Divine disposition, it was also brought about that the light which the Sun, positioned in a low place in the southern signs, could not conveniently communicate to the lands subject to the North, might be supplied by the Moon. Positioned in the opposite signs, she acts like a certain small Sun, or a substitute for the Sun, making up for every defect of this light. Thus, when the Sun is positioned in low Capricorn, the Moon occupies high Cancer at the greatest increase of her light. Conversely, when the Sun occupies the high point of Cancer, the Moon enters the low region of Capricorn at her greatest increase. Thus it happens that the winter light of the Sun, failing in Capricorn, is supplemented by the summer Lunar light in Cancer; and the light of the Sun in Cancer, which possesses excessive heat, is tempered by the winter light of the Moon in Capricorn, which possesses a duller heat. And so, through the course of the entire year, the excesses and defects of Solar heat correspond in a wondrous proportion to the reciprocal excesses and defects of Lunar heat.

<margin>The course of the Moon corresponds to the seasons of the year.</margin>
For the first quarter, or age, which corresponds to childhood, is moist; then, as the heat gradually draws out the moisture, it becomes dry and hot, which corresponds to the second age. Thirdly, as the heat fails while the moisture departs (since moisture was the proper object

<column-break/>

of heat), such is the third age. Namely, as the cold increases, an extreme moisture is introduced—not one that nourishes or increases, but an external wetting which is "phlegmatic" moisture; and such is the final age, as is clear in the preceding figure. Between the annual Solar summer and the monthly Lunar summer, there is this difference: that the Sun in its summer promotes a hot and dry constitution for the year; <margin>The Moon rules over generations in its own time.</margin> but the Moon, in the peak of its increasing strength (that is, in its "summer"), introduces a milder warmth with its light, by which solid things flow into humors, and the moist multiplication of vapors swells at the time of the full moon. This mild heat, or gentle warmth acting upon moisture, procreates moist vapors from them; unable to consume them, it leaves them in their original matter, whence moist things grow and are filled, as if impregnated by the "marrying light." From this it is further evident that Lunar warmth—which is constituted from her innate moisture mixed with the heating power of the Sun communicated to her through light—is the cause of the generation of things. You will find all these matters treated at length in our *Magnetic World* <note>Kircher's *Mundus Magneticus* (1641).</note>, Part 3, on the Magnetism of the Sun and Moon. <margin>The anomaly of planetary motion contributes much to the variety of effects in the lower world.</margin> For the same reason, the rest of the Planets have been assigned various positions and relationships relative to the Earth and the Sun, and a various anomaly of motions; so that by their approach to and retreat from the Sun, Moon, and Earth, they may cause various effects in the lower things through a diverse mixture of light and qualities. See what we write more extensively on these things in the *Physico-Astrological Gnomonica*, as also in our *Subterranean World* <note>Kircher's *Mundus Subterraneus* (1665).</note>.

<margin>The foundation of judicial astrology.</margin>
From this it is clearly evident that these periods of the stars and their various motions in the Zodiac, promoting different "aspects" of light among themselves, are the cause of changes in the air, waters, and winds, as well as the generation, life, and death of living creatures. Consequently, this is the unique foundation of Astrological judgments <note><term>Judicial Astrology</term>: The practice of predicting future events or human character based on the positions of celestial bodies. Here, Kircher argues it is based on physical, natural laws of light and heat.</note> regarding the events of storms and the accidents of life in the sublunary world. Thus, the lives of animals, intercepted between birth and death, are numbered and measured by the numbers of the periods of the Sun and Moon. Hence it is also clear that a skilled astronomer can very well predict the life and death of those born; indeed, he can count the days of the lifespan of any living thing whose moment of birth he knows. For all these things depend on a natural cause: namely, on the "temperament" <note>In historical medicine, "temperament" refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) or qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) imprinted on a person at birth.</note> instilled in the fetus by the surrounding environment. However, it can also succumb to the opposite and more powerful temperament of the surrounding environment, which specific configurations of those same stars in the heavens will be able to produce in the air at certain times to come. Because of the great regularity of the celestial periods, these coming configurations of the stars can be known in advance by skilled Astronomers—as has been said—even at the time of generation and birth. Consequently, they can predict the duration of any life, even if not exactly, due to the indefiniteness of matter. For the matter of living things is not, by its own nature, defined to be ruled and governed solely by the stars and their light and heat generated in the environment; rather, it is indefinite, undergoing all changes and suffering from any causes whatsoever. Indeed, it is often flowing from diseased parents and is so poorly disposed that it is not fit to perceive the forces of the heavens exactly or to be perfected by the aid of the stars. For the well-constituted matter of a newborn will be affected in one way by the same alignment of stars, and diseased matter in another; because, clearly, through many accidents, matter is disposed differently than it might be moved by the celestial circle. Therefore, men die in various ways, sooner or later than they are naturally destined to as mortals, and similarly other animals. In this way also are the ages of all things; because when the planets, positioned in their periodic circle, are stronger, they give more years of life; when they are weaker, they give fewer. See what we have handed down more extensively on these matters in our *Physical-Astrological Gnomonics* <note>The author refers to his own work, likely a treatise on sun-dials or the measurement of time through light and its relation to astrology.</note>. If anyone, therefore, knew the powers of the signs and stars in their periodic circle at the moment something is born, he himself could probably predict the entire life of the generated thing. I said *probably*, because that final natural limit of life, appointed to each by God, is for the most part interrupted by the various excesses of accidents, passions, anger, love, revenge, grief, pleasure, and intemperance, which render life shorter than it was established by nature. You see therefore, Reader, how all worldly things depend on the beneficial heat of lights, and how to one skilled in the science of light, nothing in the nature of things can remain hidden.

It is concluded, therefore, that this world of ours is both visible and beautiful through the participation in light; and the bodies that are in the world are more perfect the more they participate in light. Thus, light in this universal world is, as it were, in the temple of God Most High, a kind of visible Divinity and an image of God. For it communicates itself most easily and happily to all by its own goodness; it bestows itself on all things, and spreads itself everywhere through all things, and is the cause for all things to be enlightened, warmed, formed, generated, nourished, excited, and preserved. For while it penetrates all things with its warmth, it nourishes all within, and makes all fertile both inside and out. Therefore, by the participation of light all things are brought forth, and all things run their circles. And it is just like a certain mind

## CHAPTER XVIII.

### Can any foundation for Natal Astrology be established from the aforesaid? And can the interior powers be the subject of influences?

<margin>The Astrologer can predict not certainly and infallibly, but only probably.</margin>
We are not speaking here of necessary things having a connection with the celestial bodies, such as the humors <term>Humors: In ancient medicine, the four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—whose balance determined health and personality.</term> of animals and vegetables; likewise the rivers and seas. For no one of sound philosophy will deny that these are the proper subject of celestial influences, and it has been made more than sufficiently clear from what was said before. But we are speaking of the interior powers <note>The "interior powers" refer to the human mind, will, and intellect.</note>, whether they, as all Astrologers wish, are in truth capable of some influence. To settle this dispute, it must first be noted that the influence of the heavens upon free will can be considered in two ways: direct or indirect. The first is that by which it concurs immediately either toward the perfection of a power or toward active production; II. by which it concurs mediately into something external, or the body itself: hence each is twofold. For Direct influence either tends toward the will by imprinting some quality there by which it moves it to act, or it acts simultaneously with the will itself. Indirect influence either changes some internal object, from which a change in the will follows; or it imprints certain qualities upon the human body, by which—by reason of the natural conjunction of spiritual and material operations—the will is enticed to act. This also happens in two ways: First, by either increasing or relaxing the four humors; for when "choler" <note>Yellow bile, associated with heat and aggression.</note> is increased, men are provoked to anger. Second, by disturbing health and the dispositions of the body. Since, according to Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; his theory that the soul’s inclinations follow the body’s physical makeup was a major philosophical challenge to the concept of free will.</note>, the soul follows the temperament [of the body]...

[the state of] the body follows; once the state of the body is changed, the affections of the soul are also changed, whether this change hinders the use of freedom or removes it [entirely], as can be seen in those who are <term>Maniacs</term> <note>Historically, this referred to those suffering from fits of insanity or extreme behavioral changes.</note> and <term>Lunatics</term> <note>The author uses this term literally: those whose mental states were believed to be affected by the cycles of the moon.</note>. Next, a difficulty arises regarding indirect influence: whether by reason of this it can somehow be said that the Heavens reach, incline, entice, move, and draw the will.

These things having been established, I state first, that celestial bodies reach the will or the intellect of a thing by no direct influence, whether mediated or immediate: because the material does not reach the immaterial as a proximate principal cause. Second, because the will is a free cause, while the Heaven is determined to a specific course. Third, because the order of nature in the Universe and its perfection requires that the nobler things not be subject to the less noble: however, the rational soul is always nobler than the heaven. Nor does it work against us that demons, which are spiritual substances, are sometimes moved by physical things, such as herbs, <term>rue</term>, <term>St. John’s Wort</term>, and fumigations; or that the same [celestial influence] has more power over Lunatics at the time of the full moon than at any other time. For this happens not at all because demons are subject to celestial influences or are moved by material things, but either to deceive men and ensnare them in this superstition, or because they find better dispositions in brains overwhelmed by humors to exercise their power over men. As for the fact that Mages choose a certain time, that happens from a pact entered into with a demon. That herbs which put demons to flight (<term>demonifuges</term>) are found, which are contrary to the demon—this does not happen because they act formally upon demons by impressing on them a quality contrary to their nature, but because they have qualities opposed to the active principles applied by demons; hence, such things are sometimes lawfully used by the Catholic Church in exorcisms.

I state secondly, that by no reasoning do celestial bodies reach spiritual powers, even mediately

<column-break/>

and indirectly, in such a way that the will is intrinsically inclined or moved to necessarily produce such an action. This is against the Astrologers, who all feel that the will is not indeed forced, but is drawn by enticement. This is both because it is clearly gathered from what has been said, and because the influence of celestial bodies is likened to the passions of the senses: but those do not incline [the will] intrinsically, because an intrinsic inclination is only from something impressed into the thing: but passions impress nothing intrinsic upon the will; therefore, even granted any influence whatsoever and any presentation of an object, the will is able to act and not to act. At most, therefore, the intellect can be moved insofar as a material <term>phantasm</term> <note>In Aristotelian thought, a "phantasm" is a mental image or sensory impression from which the intellect derives abstract concepts.</note> determines the <term>agent intellect</term> toward the production of <term>intelligible species</term>; yet alongside this stands the choice of the will to determine the intellect, or not to determine it: for who shall prevent it from either suspending its assent, or from not judging, or from turning toward some [other] object? Then, given the motion of the intellect, the will nonetheless remains in a state of <term>indifference</term> <note>original: "ἀδιαφόρῳ" (adiaphoro), meaning a state of neutrality or lack of bias.</note>.

I state thirdly: celestial influences flow indirectly into the will, insofar as they either disturb the humors, or alter the <term>complexion</term> <note>In medieval medicine, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that determines a person’s temperament.</note>, or change it intrinsically. This is proved first: because the reasoning for the complexion is the same whether it is received from God, from nature, or received through the mediation of the stars: but the natural complexion indirectly moves the will: therefore [so do the stars]. Second, because the mode of acting follows the mode of being, just as the mode of being of the rational soul in man is like the mode of a form giving being to matter, and depending—not indeed in its intrinsic perfection, but in its extrinsic—upon matter as its partner by which it is perfected; therefore it also [depends] upon the causes of such motions, namely upon the celestial body, which communicates such a complexion or hidden quality.

# Effects of Illuminations

The astrologer is kept in the dark, and the length of time an infant remains in the mother's womb—or any other method of investigating the moment of conception—provides him with very little help. This is because the infant's duration in the womb is disrupted by various external factors, such as the mother’s physical labor, the foods she eats, the physical temperament of the woman, illnesses, or other daily occurrences. Furthermore, the astrologer does not actually know which star truly rules over the infant.

<margin>The Uncertainty of Astrology</margin>
Therefore, unless all concurring causes are known, an effect that depends on multiple causes cannot be known with certainty. Since an infant’s <term>temperament</term> <note>In pre-modern medicine, "temperament" or "complexion" referred to the balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—which determined a person's health and character.</note> and natural inclinations depend on many factors, it rightly follows that nothing certain can be divined about them. Indeed, if even one cause is absent or unknown, the entire judgment must necessarily be corrupted. In this way, an astrologer would falsely judge that different crops of wheat, sown in different fields of the same town under the same star, would have an equal yield. For although the celestial cause is the same, and consequently the same effect should follow in respect to it, the other concurring causes are different—such as the quality of the wheat and the seed, the fertility of the field, the diligence of the farmer, and the use of fertilizer; thus, a different result will occur. 

One must judge that the same happens in the birth of an infant. Since the temperament of the body depends on the formative power of the seed, the warmer or cooler physical makeup of the parents, the food with which the mother is nourished, the quality of the air, the intense imagination of the spouses, and the time of conception, it is in vain to divine the nature of the child through the stars unless these other factors are known. Let us suppose, for example, that at the same moment in time, two infants are conceived: one by a noble father who is well-nourished and of a strong nature, and a mother of excellent health who was raised on delicate foods; the other by a peasant who is sickly and "cold," and a mother of poor health nourished on coarse foods. Certainly, the temperament of each infant will be vastly different, and consequently, their habits and character will also differ. 

Therefore, if one person or another excels with a greater spark of talent, it arises not so much from a dominant <term>Mercury</term> <note>In astrology, Mercury is the planet associated with the intellect, communication, and wit.</note> or other planets, but from these other partial causes, as will be discussed in the following book: namely, from the physical makeup of the parents, from the imagination and disposition of the father at the time of conception, and from the foods the father ate eight days before procreation. Since a greater or lesser degree of talent depends solely on the greater or lesser arrangement of the <term>organs</term> <note>The author refers to the physical structures of the brain and body that facilitate the soul's expression.</note>, and the arrangement of the organs depends on the balance of the primary qualities, and that balance depends primarily on the blood and seed, and secondarily on the elements—and the quality of the seed depends on the foods used by the parent at the time of conception, as has been said—it necessarily follows that the excellence of talent comes not just from the stars, but from these stated factors.

<column-break/>

For this reason, <term>Galen</term> <note>A famous Greek physician (129–c. 216 AD) whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years.</note> quite appropriately advises parents who wish to procreate talented children that they can achieve their desire through imagination, choosing specific foods for that purpose, and selecting the right time; the aspects of the stars, however unlucky or hostile to talent they may be, will not stand in the way. Furthermore, the fact that astrologers attribute so much to Mercury—thinking that the power of communicating talent lies with him alone—is sheer vanity. Any skilled astronomers who have ever observed the star of Mercury anywhere will agree with me: Mercury's power is so dulled and weakened—both because of its extremely small body (forty times smaller than the Earth) and because it is almost perpetually hidden by the Sun's rays—that it possesses scarcely any influence over these lower realms. Indeed, in relation to the Sun's rays, it behaves in the same way as a drop of wine dispersed into a barrel full of water. 

What more can I say? Not even those things pertaining to Medicine, Agriculture, and Navigation—where divination is permitted—can be predicted from the inspection of the stars alone without a comparison made to the Earth. Indeed, the constitution of different horizons is so varied that I think it is nearly <note>original: "ἀδύνατον" (adynaton)</note> impossible for the same position of the stars to produce an equal and similar effect in different horizons, even with an equal influence. We see that some parts of even a single climate are more prone to rain, and others to clear skies; in some it rarely rains, in others frequently and almost always. In some neighboring areas, perpetual winds rage; in others, there is a humidity hostile to bodies. All these local symptoms have their origin not from the Heaven, but from the particular nature of the places and the arrangement of the mountains. Thus, in Avignon, rains were once more frequent; today, due to the draining of a nearby lake beyond the Rhone, almost all rain seems to have been banished. 

Added to this is the fact that light in a <term>Celestial Theme</term> <note>An astrological chart or horoscope.</note> behaves differently with respect to different horizons; so much so that I would dare to say we can scarcely travel 15 leagues without the celestial light varying and producing different effects in the <term>celestial houses</term> <note>The twelve divisions of an astrological chart representing different areas of life.</note>. First, under a <term>right sphere</term> <note>The sky as seen from the Earth's equator.</note>, the celestial houses—without which you can accomplish nothing in <term>judicial astrology</term> <note>The branch of astrology used to predict future events or a person's fate.</note>—receive far different effects of light than under an <term>oblique sphere</term> <note>The sky as seen from mid-latitudes.</note>. Those under an oblique sphere are entirely different from those under a <term>parallel sphere</term> <note>The sky as seen from the North or South Pole.</note>, where, besides the fact that all celestial houses vanish and the Sun moves perpetually above or below the horizon, influence can have no power at all by reason of the <term>cardinals</term>, angles, or <term>cusps</term>. But more on these and similar matters elsewhere. Therefore, the things they babble about regarding the "Terms of the Egyptians," or about "bright," "dark," and "pitted" degrees, are nothing but nonsense from the Egyp-
