## CHAPTER I.
### *On the origin and definition of Shadow.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'U' depicting a figure playing a lyre in a landscape setting.</image-desc>
<margin>Description of light and shadow.</margin>
The Shadow is the companion of light, the second mimic of the Sun and Moon, and the Mistress of the lower world,
> *A rival to the gods, and prior to the gods, she would be a goddess herself,*
> *Had she not been damned to perpetual and opaque darkness.*
<note>The author is quoting a poetic personification of Shadow as an ancient, divine force.</note>

We proceed to explain this admirable work of light—the shadow, I say—which if you look at its antiquity, it is most noble; if its nature, most sharp; if its power, most strong; if its glory, most honored. It prevails in such antiquity that it seems to be junior only to the Creator; for before the first existence of all things, it played in that "nothingness"; then, in that Chaos and the <term>Tohu and Bohu</term> <note>Hebrew: "formless and empty," describing the state of the universe before creation in Genesis 1:2.</note> of the mundane body, it cast certain first principles of its essence, as it were. And finally, brought forth from the very womb of birthing nature, it did not reach maturity through certain stages of infancy and childhood, but immediately embracing this whole Universe, it covered it with its dark-red mantle.

And on the day it was brought forth, it was great. And it shall remain as long as the machine of the world

<column-break/>

stands, perpetually constant to itself and similar, removed from every contagion of corruption, the restraint of worldly heat, the mirror of worldly beauty, the unique tempering of things, without which neither would the world be perceptible, nor would the composition of things obtain the balance due to them.

Concerning this, therefore, it is now asked: what is it? Vitellio <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1285), a friar and physicist who wrote a massive, influential treatise on optics.</note> in his 3rd and 4th Postulate, maintains that shadow is created in the absence of light, and conversely, that shadow fails upon the introduction of light. And elsewhere, he says that shadow is the privation of a certain light while the actual presence of another light exists in a dark place. Others say it is the privation of primary light and the lessening of secondary light, according to that saying of Lucretius <note>Titus Lucretius Carus (c. 99–55 BC), Roman poet and philosopher.</note>:

> *For it can be nothing else but air devoid of light,*
> *that which we are accustomed to call shadow.*
<note>original: "Nam nihil esse potest aliud, nisi lumine cassus / Aër, id quod nos umbram perhibere solemus."</note>

<margin>What a shadow properly is. | Shadow is not a purely privative being.</margin>
Whatever it may be, Aristotle testifies—and it is most evident to everyone—that darkness is the contrary to light, and obscurity is properly called its opposite. But what kind of opposition is this between light and darkness? Is it purely <term>privative</term> <note>In philosophy, a "privative" state is the absence of a quality that should normally be present (like blindness being the privation of sight), rather than a positive thing in its own right.</note>...

<summary>This page marks the transition from a critique of traditional astrology to a scientific and philosophical study of shadows, which the author personifies as an ancient, essential element of the natural world. He begins by exploring various definitions of shadow from historical figures like Vitellio, Lucretius, and Aristotle.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from the previous page, the author moves from a critique of traditional astrology into a physical and philosophical investigation of light and shadow, which he calls "Sciognomia" or the knowledge of identifying shadows. He begins by debating whether darkness is merely an absence of light or a physical substance in its own right.</meta>

<page-num>47</page-num>
# Sciognomia
# <note>The Knowledge of Shadows</note>

...it must be discussed whether this is a privative <note>In philosophy, a "privation" is the lack of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness is the privation of sight.</note> or in some way a positive resistance, and whether anything else is opposed to light besides darkness. It is well known from Aristotle that light is opposed to darkness, just as a "habit" <note>A "habit" (habitus) refers to the presence of a quality or state of being.</note> is opposed to its own privation. Yet, although you may find in the entity of darkness the greatest privation of light, I cannot be led to believe that obscurity and darkness are a pure and simple privation of light, separated from all positive existence. For first, darkness so contracts the vision that, besides the pain it brings to the eyes, it even occasionally causes blindness if it lasts too long; but real and positive operations like contraction and blinding cannot come from a naked and mere privation as an efficient cause (unless we wish to say that a privation produces a positive effect beyond its own powers). Again, contraries that mutually break one another by blunting and dulling possess a nature that is in some way positive: such are light and darkness. Therefore, just as a flame is not fire itself, but a body mixed with a great predominance of fire, so too darkness is not a pure privation, but possesses a visible nature joined from a privative and a positive entity. If, therefore, darkness and obscurity are not pure privation, then shadow is certainly not; although it can also be said to be opposed to light in some way.

<margin>Two types of obscurity.</margin>
Thus, two types of obscurity can be considered in this place: the first, consisting of a privative nature, is opposed to light as a "habit," and is called by the name of **darkness**; the other, obtaining a more positive essence, resists light as a contrary quality, and this is called **shadow**, which is a highly positive entity because it moves the sense of sight most intensely.

<margin>Definition of shadow.</margin>
We, therefore, setting aside the definitions of others, say that **shadow** is nothing other than the absence of the principal rays of the Sun, caused by the interposition of an opaque body that is immediately illuminated. I said "principal rays of the Sun" to exclude reflected rays, which are nothing other than a kind of offspring of shadows; and "by the interposition of an immediately illuminated body" to exclude the obscurity and darkness of underground caverns and other places impenetrable to the Sun.

<margin>What are ray, light, splendor, and sheen.</margin>
These things being established, we say that luminous bodies are indeed contrary to opaque bodies, but not entirely in a privative way, but a positive one: for the former emit light, while the latter emit darkness. From light and darkness, certain "offspring" are born, which, like their mothers, are diffused through the <term>transparent medium</term> <note>original: "diaphano." The substance, like air or glass, through which light travels.</note>. From a luminous body, **rays** first flash out; from rays comes **light**; from light comes **splendor**; from splendor comes **sheen** <note>original: "nitor."</note>. Splendor is indeed light diminished by the thickness of the transparent medium; sheen is a certain light, but one corrupted by a shadowy mixture. From

<column-break/>

the contrary opaque body, it produces another offspring of its own propagation; first indeed, **darkness** flashes from it, which is opposed to the rays of light; from darkness comes **darkening** <note>original: "obscuratio."</note> opposed to light; from darkening comes **shadow** <note>original: "umbra."</note> opposed to splendor; from shadow, **shading** <note>original: "umbratio."</note> takes its origin, opposed to sheen; and from sheen and shading itself comes **adumbration** <note>original: "adumbratio," meaning the sketching or graduation of shadow.</note>. All of these have a manifest action upon the transparent medium; for they fill it with themselves no less than that numerous offspring of light mentioned a little earlier, and they propagate themselves further through it, contract themselves into a shorter space, and make things darker or clearer; they drive light from one place, and are driven by light from another; they take away sight from many animals. No one endowed with sight and mind will deny that all these are actions of opacity. For action and passion <note>In the classical sense, "passion" means being acted upon or receiving an impression.</note> come from the powers of acting and being acted upon: all powers are procreated from an essence proper to themselves, exist in that essence, are founded in it, and flow from it. Therefore, obscurity, shadow, and shading are not simple privations of light and brightness, but are true beings, of the kind called "positive." Furthermore, both shadow and flashes differ by a greater or lesser degree of whiteness or blackness, according as they are nearer to the source of light or darkness, or further receded from the source, in which both light and obscurity are at their peak.

<margin>What are shadow, darkening, and darkness?</margin>
From this it is clear that the further flashes recede from the light, the more blackness they acquire; and the further shadows recede from darkness—with blackness diminished—the more whiteness they acquire, all of which the sight can judge. For an opaque body admits no light and no whiteness, while light admits no blackness. Hence, through darkness, only light and shining whiteness are perceived without any colors; but through the obscure, both light and whiteness and even colors are perfected to some extent, though all are fainter. In shadow, both the presence and distance of colored things are discerned; but **shading** <margin>The process of light to darkness and darkness to light.</margin> <margin>or likeness <note>original Greek: "οἵωσις" (oiōsis). In this context, it refers to the shading used to create the likeness of a 3D form.</note></margin> represents all things more clearly.

In **adumbration**, where sheen is mixed with shading, all things are seen in a middle way, as it were. These differences do not arise from anywhere else except from the mixture of light and opacity and those things which are procreated by them. From these things shown at length, it is clear that the image of an opaque object—as it is a certain "third visible thing" formally distinct from a colored or a luminous body—is nothing other than the shadow; it is the proper visible species and image of the opaque body, insofar as it is opaque. We have decided to confirm this by these reasons: First, light creates shadow beyond the opaque body in the genus of visible things, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle was commonly referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in medieval and Renaissance texts.</note> testifies; but according to the same Author, light creates nothing except the representative species <note>The "species" was thought to be a tiny image or likeness of an object that traveled through the air to the eye.</note> of visible objects: therefore, shadow is the image of some...

<summary>The author argues that darkness and shadows are not merely the absence of light (privation) but are positive physical entities with their own "offspring" and effects on the eye. Book I. Part II.

...of that visible object; since a visible object is not, a shadow is also not the image of light, nor of a colored body lacking very vivid light, but is the image of an opaque body turned away from the light source, born to be seen in a secondary, weak, and relaxed light. Therefore, a shadow is the image of an <margin>A shadow is the image of an opaque body turned away from a bright body.</margin> opaque body. Again, an opaque body is a specific visible thing in light, naturally suited to emit a shadow from itself into a transparent <term>diaphano: a medium that allows light to pass through, like air or water</term> medium; yet visible objects in an illuminated transparent medium cannot formally emit anything from themselves except their own image and visible species <term>species: in medieval and early modern optics, this refers to the "form" or "likeness" of an object that travels through the air to the eye</term> representing them. Therefore, a shadow is nothing other than a likeness representative to the sight of an opaque body, from which it flows into the clear medium. Thirdly, an opaque body has its own visible species distinct from the visible species of a bright body and a colored body in the transparent medium; because light is the image of the brightness (or the bright body) from which it proceeds, and besides the species of colored things emanating from themselves, no third thing proceeds from an opaque body except the shadow. Therefore, the shadow is the image and species born to represent the opaque body to the sight.

# CHAPTER II.
### How light cooperates to produce a shadow.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' containing a circular emblem with a floral or sunburst design, surrounded by leafy scrollwork.</image-desc> SINCE the species of any object placed beneath a light source is generated by that object governed by the present light, it happens that light concurs in the origin of a shadow as a partial cause cooperating with the opaque body. For since an opaque body is represented by its visible species, and thus a shadow is something more material <note>The author uses "material" here to suggest that the shadow is a lower or less "spiritual" form of transmission than pure light</note>, it cannot act beyond its own powers, producing from itself something more excellent than it is. Hence, a material agent, unless governed by something immaterial and elevated above the condition of its own matter, can never produce an effect more immaterial than itself. Therefore, the opaque body cannot by itself produce a shadow, which is less material than it; thus, in total darkness, an opaque object emits no shadow. The opaque body therefore requires the benefit of light—namely, an immaterial form—to produce a shadow as its visible species. And since the opaque body and the colored body are usually the same thing—just as the body of a firefly <note>original: "cincindela"</note> appears as light without color [at night], but by day appears as colored rather than light—in the same way, an opaque body is both opaque and colored. On the side where it is illuminated, it moves the sight by virtue of being colored; but on the side turned away from the Sun—namely, the part illustrated by a smaller, weak, and faint light—it moves the sight by virtue of being opaque.

### Corollary.

And from these things it is clear that darkness does not differ from light in the function of vision, as it seems the <column-break/> Psalmist <note>The author of the Psalms, usually referring to King David</note> looked to this very point when he said:
> As is its darkness, so too is its light. <note>original: "Uti tenebræ ejus, ita & lumen ejus." (Psalm 139:12)</note>
What? Shall darkness then also be light? Or at least not without a mixture of light? Truly, it is so. For <margin>Darkness always contains something of light.</margin> they always have that light admitted, and even if they did not, they are themselves light, but at the minimum. For it is confessed in the nature of things that if one of a pair of contraries is found, the other must necessarily be found as well. All men feel that heat, moisture, softness, and rarity <note>In the sense of being "thin" or "diffuse" like air</note> exist in nature; they feel likewise that their contraries—cold, dryness, hardness, and density—also exist. Those things are said to be contraries which are the extremes of the same genus. Therefore, in the genus of visible things, there will also be two extremes, and these contrary to each other: the maximum and the minimum, which exist in all types of things. In the genus of visible things, we find the maximum visible thing, which is the light of the Sun, and the minimum visible thing contrary to light, which is the blackness or opacity of the earth. Thus, the contrary to the greatest light is the minimum light. Since, therefore, darkness belongs to the genus of lights, and both light and darkness hold the entire globe of the earth both inside and out, it was true to assert that all things lie in light, whether it be minimal or maximal. But this very thing becomes manifest by another reasoning: for all opaque bodies are imbued with some color. Now, every color—as will be seen later—is <margin>All things participate in something of light.</margin> "shadowed light." <note>original: "lux opacata"</note> Since color clothes all things, and every color is the offspring of light and illumination, all things that lie in colors will also lie in light.

## CHAPTER III.
### On the weakening and intensification of shadow.

Since shadow is the absence of light, a greater absence of light will result in a greater shadow, a smaller absence in a smaller shadow, and the total absence of almost all light results in the greatest shadow. For we see that the thickest darkness is not immediately driven away by a tiny lamp, but a very great light is needed for that task. Therefore, there is a certain range not only in light, but also in shadows themselves, which are capable of intensification and weakening <note>The author uses the Scholastic terms *intensio* and *remissio* to describe how qualities like heat, light, or shadow increase or decrease in strength.</note>. Hence, we quite properly call darker shadows "dense"; for when parts within the same subject increase, they are enlarged by the addition of quantity, just as several bodies crowded into a narrow space are "densified." From this variety of increase and decrease, different degrees of obscurity arise. Indeed, "shadow" and "darkness" are distinguished only by the inequality of their intensity and weakness. A "shadow" is the least of all obscurities, while the greatest of all is "darkness" <note>original: *tenebrae*</note>. If these are viewed in comparison to the sun's light, a shadow is the absence of a smaller light, but "darkness" signifies that level of obscurity which interrupts human handiwork and takes away the use of sight. Between darkness and the shadow of the Sun lies that "twilight light" <note>original: *crepera lux*</note>, which immediately precedes the rising of the Sun and follows its setting. Whether this is shadow or darkness is a matter of doubt; we categorize it among the shadows, as we teach in our *Photosciatheric Cosmography* <note>The author refers to his own work, likely a treatise on the measurement of light and shadows, from the Greek *phōs* (light) and *skia* (shadow).</note>, and as will appear shortly.

<margin>Various degrees of shadow.</margin>
Furthermore, each of these differences in obscurity is assigned various degrees according to "more" or "less." For a second shadow is darker than the first, and a third darker than the second, and so on. Thus, when the Sun is positioned on the horizon, there is light without shadow; but as the Sun sets,

<column-break/>

it creates a shadow that is the least obscure of all. From then on, the shadow becomes continually darker the deeper the Sun descends below the earth, so that at midnight, at certain times, it can be called the "thickest darkness." From these points, it is first evident that just as light is increased by the addition of another light, so a shadow becomes darker by the addition of another shadow. For if two lights are set out and an opaque body is placed before them (not in the same straight line as the lights), it is clear that the opaque body casts as many shadows as there are lights. <margin>Experience.</margin> Experience also teaches us that a darker shadow exists right next to the opaque body for no other reason than that this spot is deprived of the glow of both lights, while the rest of the area is deprived of only one. This is truly nothing other than that spot nearest the opaque body being darkened by a "doubled shadow." 

Secondly, it is clear from these facts that light, having traveled further from its first source, continuously weakens. The illumination of huge pyramids teaches this: their shadow weakens so gradually that you can hardly distinguish the furthest and thinnest portion from the surrounding light; yet near the base, you will find the tightest shadow for the reasons stated. Therefore, just as light is diffused from a bright body into a medium "uniformly-varied" <note>original: *uniformiter difformiter*. This is a technical term from medieval physics meaning a rate of change that is constant, like a steady gradient or linear acceleration.</note>, so it is with the shadows of opaque bodies. Thirdly, it is clear that the more rays of light an opaque body intercepts, the larger the shadow it projects. Since shadow is in some way the opposite of light, it is necessary that the same things that happen to light also happen to shadow. Therefore, just as light is greater when it contains more rays and the object is more intensely illuminated, so a shadow is greater when it contains more "shadowy rays"—and it contains as many shadowy rays as the opaque body blocks luminous ones. Therefore [the conclusion follows].

# Book I. Part II.

...surrounding light, and by their obstruction they produce shadow. Hence all opaque things are in themselves dark, and they cast shadows, obscurities, and darkness upon others.

<margin>The wondrous craftsmanship of the earth regarding shadow and light.</margin>
The Creator willed the Earth—the mother of darkness and of all opaque things—to be spherical, so that it might better receive the alternations of light and shadow. Hence we see the surface of the earth illuminated by the light of the Sun, and also covered by darkness in cycles—not of centuries, nor of years, nor of months, but of days and hours. For while the Sun revolves from its rising through its setting and back to its rising again in the space of twenty-four hours, it illuminates the entire surface of the earth with its luminous and shadowy rays alike; for as rays approach some part of it, darkness is driven away from there, and where darkness follows, light is driven away, so that they always, in a certain perpetual alternation, both flee and put each other to flight. When we are in the light, we call it day; and while in darkness, we call it night. And the Author of nature assigned the day to the labors and occupations of men, but the night to their rest.

<margin>The benefits of the shadow of the Earthly globe.</margin>
Most wisely, therefore, has the shadow been arranged. First, so that the parts of the earth most effectively struck and heated by the rays of light might be tempered by the nightly shadow. Second, so that the air, dissipated by the excessive thinning <note>The author refers to the classical idea that heat "rarefies" or thins the air, while cold "condenses" it.</note> caused by the light, might be condensed again by the cold of the nightly shadow and refresh the parched earth with a kindly sprinkling of its moisture. Third, so that these "light-shadow" <note>original: *lucumbres* — a wordplay combining *lux* (light) and *umbra* (shadow)</note> radiations might serve as markers for hours, days, nights, and years, acting as the starting points and boundaries of time's definition. Fourth, so that the magnificence of the Creator might be shown in that greatest adornment of the constellations—the Moon, the Planets, and the fixed stars—all of which, without shadow, would lie hidden in the light of the Sun itself as if covered by perpetual darkness. For who could ever have reached the knowledge of so many secrets of nature—which we now observe with the greatest awe every night by its aid—unless God had drawn this shadow over us? For we contemplate that admirable beauty, efficacy, and variety of the lights and stars. You see, therefore, how many benefits flow to us from the single shadow of the earthly cor-

<column-break/>

-poreal body. These are surely so great that I do not know whether light or shadow benefits us more. Lest the inhabitants of the earthly globe should be able to complain about the Creator's providence, days and nights are so aptly distributed around the earth throughout the entire year and in all places that neither light overcomes darkness nor darkness light at any moment of time anywhere. 

<margin>All regions of the world share equally in light and darkness.</margin>
For if all the hours of both light and darkness were collected into one single period, no place on earth would be found that has not seen exactly six full months of darkness and six full months of light <note>The author is describing the astronomical fact that over a full year, every point on Earth receives the same total duration of daylight and nighttime.</note>.

<margin>Why the earth always has more light than darkness.</margin>
However, because light, by its inherent nobility, is the primary quality and the preserver of all things in the lower world, the necessity of nature also willed that the earthly body should obtain more light than darkness, lest shadow—which is a kind of deprivation of such a great good—should bring harm to things. Therefore, the Author of nature first established the atmosphere, so that the rays of the Sun refracted within it might show the Sun above the horizon sooner than it actually is. <term>Refraction: the bending of light as it passes through the atmosphere, which makes the sun appear to rise earlier and set later than its physical position would suggest.</term> Added to these is that admirable variety of twilights, by which the harmful density of darkness is tempered for a while, bringing enormous benefits to the world: for to those situated near the pole, it brings a perpetual, almost "twilight" <note>original: *creperam* — meaning "obscure" or "doubtful" light</note> or "doubtful" light, having driven away the darkness. He also appointed the Moon and stars as deputies of the Sun, so that in its absence they might mitigate the horror of the darkness. Hence it happens that the Moon, the Mistress of the night, performs her duty more effectively the longer the Sun is away: for experience teaches that in the winter time, when the darkness is greater, the Moon shines longer and more effectively upon the earth; and for those at the pole, the Moon compensates for the Sun's six-month absence with its own six-month illumination—that is, by being continually present through six whole signs <note>Referring to the six zodiacal signs that comprise the half of the Moon's orbit visible above the polar horizon.</note>. Lest that perpetual presence of the Moon should harm the earth with its excessive humidity <note>In ancient and medieval science, the Moon was believed to govern the quality of "moisture" in the natural world.</note>, nature decided to defend shadow with shadow; while the shadowy part of the lunar body is turned toward us, it diverts the light of the Moon for a time, and thus serves the earth equally with both light and shadow. All these things are the greatest proofs of divine wisdom.

# CHAPTER V.
## On the Art of Sciognomics.
### Concerning the wondrous nature of shadows, compared to trees, plants, and metallic locations, and their Sciognomics.

<margin>The shadow of trees granted for refreshment.</margin>
If nature had ordained shadow for no other reason than to temper the heat of the Sun, it would have been enough even for the beasts. Who does not know how pleasing, how delightful, and how useful these retreats of shadow are—not only to men, but even to the beasts themselves—when, with bodies dissolved by the heat, nothing is more welcome than to linger in shady places to restore one's strength?

> When the ash tree begins to spread its summer shadows,
> and the slender pines nod with their lofty tops,
> the berry-bearing laurel extends its arms with branches,
> and the gentle Etesian winds <note>The Etesian winds are annual Mediterranean summer winds, known for providing relief from the heat.</note>, and a breeze softer than sleep,
> graze the echoing forests with a sharp murmur.

<margin>The shadow of a plane tree held an entire army.</margin>
These shadows have occasionally been so welcome to entire armies that ancient authors record that divine honors were given to them. But to follow the benefits of shadows more extensively, let us first speak of their quality; we observe that they are mostly somewhat chilly, sometimes health-giving, and occasionally even harmful to men and animals. And indeed, it might seem marvelous to someone how a shadow, consisting of a "privative" <note>In philosophy, a "privative" nature means something defined by what it lacks—in this case, shadow is defined by the absence of light rather than being a "thing" itself.</note> nature, can produce such various effects of alteration in the bodies of humans and beasts?

> To such an extent that they often cause pains of the head,
> if anyone has lain prostrate in the grass beneath them.

In order for paradoxes of this kind to be explained:
It must be noted that air has been allotted this nature: as soon as it is struck by solar light, it goes off into a very thin substance, as if scattered. Conversely, as soon as it is deprived of those rarefying rays by the interposition of an opaque body, it thickens from that thinness into a denser body. Just as it is the property of cold to condense and constrict.
<margin>Why there is always a soft and somewhat chilly breeze in shady places.</margin>
From this it happens that in shadows, for the most part, we enjoy that somewhat chilly breeze, which is most welcome to bodies that are weary and dissolved by heat. For since the condensation of air necessarily follows the dissipation of shadow,

<column-break/>

and its contraction into a narrower space, it happens that the packed air—so that a vacuum is not left anywhere—violently attracts other air situated everywhere outside the shadow. From this violent attraction, an agitation of the air follows, and from that agitation, a chilly breeze must necessarily result. And this is the genuine reason why a very thin and most pleasant wind usually occupies shady air. Now, however, it must also be explained by what means a shadow spreads abroad qualities that are sometimes health-giving and sometimes harmful.

->*Shadows are said to be sometimes health-giving, sometimes harmful.*<-

Just as there are those among the common philosophers who think wrongly that shadow is something purely "positive" <note>A "positive" entity is something that has its own independent existence or substance, like a rock or water, rather than just being an absence of something else.</note> because shadows are found to be imbued with various qualities that sometimes help and sometimes hinder; so too among the more learned, not a few are hallucinating when they pronounce absolutely that shadow is the pure and simple privation of light. For since shadows enjoy a fellowship of both entities—that is, they consist of a privative entity and a positive one alike, as we have shown in the preceding pages—it follows that the shadow concurs as a specific cause in the production of the qualities impressed within those shadows. How this can happen, I now reveal.

<margin>Two types of shadow: accessible and inaccessible.</margin>
It should be known, therefore, that shadow can be considered in two ways. One is found in places inaccessible to the Sun, such as shadows within domestic walls, like those of bedrooms and chambers. The other is caused in the midst of light by the interposition of some opaque object. Of the opaque things causing shadows, there is again an almost infinite multitude and variety, such as the shadows of walls, fortifications, houses, temples, and the most diverse trees.

We shall speak here only of the shadows of trees; for under these especially is found the greatest collection of the aforementioned qualities. For there are different trees endowed with different qualities, as is well known, which the shadows participate in, for the reason that follows.

### The Foundation of the Sciognomic Art.

When trees are struck and heated by the most burning rays of the Sun, it happens that the moisture existing in the more delicate parts of the trees—namely the leaves—is dilated by this heat and exhales into subtle vapors. For this reason, in the summer time, we see the leaves of trees mostly flaccid and appearing as if dried out. However, this vapor, being imbued with the natural quality of the trees, infects the air similar to itself with that same quality. This vapor is mixed with the "shadowy air," which acts as a thicker subject; the vapor naturally seeks this air as if it were cold for its own preservation, lest it vanish, dissipated by the excessive heat of the Sun. When this air enters the pores of the bodies of humans and animals, which have been loosened by the heat, it brings either benefit or harm to them by the contagion of its own substance, according to the nature of the diffused quality. And this is the foundation upon which we rely to subjoin here the remaining rules of the Sciognomic Art for the benefit of Physicists <note>In this context, "Physicists" refers to students of natural philosophy and medicine.</note>, so that it may be known which tree shadows are to be kept and which are to be avoided.

### First Rule.

<margin>The shadow of trees is health-giving.</margin>
The shadows of all those trees consisting of a certain "airy" nature are health-giving to the human body: Pear, Apple, Quince, Almond, and all kinds of Oranges and Citrons; and they are indeed healthier the less hairiness their fruits possess. For these trees exhale vapors very similar to the vapors of [human] nature—that is, to the spirits <note>In early modern medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids that circulated in the body to maintain life and transmit sensation.</note>. Thus, by these shadows, a feverish spirit is tempered and comforted, and human limbs are wonderfully restored. 
<margin>The ancient Egyptians.</margin>
Hence it was the custom of the Egyptians to cure all those diseases whose power lay in the disturbance of the spirits—such as frenzy, melancholy, scotoma <note>A blurring or dimming of vision.</note>, vertigo, and sadness—by applying music within the pleasant shadows of trees possessing a certain dissipative faculty. Among those trees which the Greeks call *skiapous* <note>original: *σκιάπους*, literally "shadow-footed," referring to trees with broad foliage providing much shade.</note>—the Linden, the Plane, the Poplar, the Elm, and the Ash—nature itself seems to have produced them for no other end than for pleasure and the promotion of the unique relaxation of minds through their shadow. Indeed, the shadows of these individual trees affect bodies with the same quality of which they themselves consist. Thus, the Arab Albucasis <note>Albucasis (936–1013) was a famous Arab physician and surgeon from Al-Andalus.</note> writes that the shadow of citron trees is wonderfully beneficial to a burning heart. Columella <note>A Roman writer on agriculture (4–70 AD).</note> also records that the shadows of honey-apples are prescribed for the "Tabid" <note>Those suffering from "tabes," a wasting disease or consumption.</note> because of the humidity they exhale, which is pleasing to the lungs; and so it is with others.

### Second Rule.

Shady places planted with health-giving herbs—Roses, Thyme, Wild Marjoram, Hyssop, Mint,

<column-break/>

<margin>Plants that exist under trees have medicinal power.</margin>
Nard, and other species of healthy plants—have been found to wonderfully comfort the human body when they are dissolved by the heat and infect the shadowy air with their healthy and "vapid" <note>Used here in the sense of "full of vapors" or essences.</note> breaths. Indeed, they affect individual limbs with that quality which they naturally desire to be imbued with: thus, in the shadow of "Cardiac" plants, the breaths benefit the heart; "Pulmonary" plants benefit the lungs and chest; "Hepatic" plants the liver; "Aphrodisiac" plants the sexual organs; and others benefit other limbs, when their qualities are impressed into the shadowy air and the medium of the vapor. Hence we see the animals themselves rejoice around the time of twilight—when herbs are most accustomed to evaporate their powers—just as they do in the fragrance of the shadows of meadows. 
<margin>A marvelous example concerning a certain young man.</margin>
This same point is confirmed by an example of a certain young man, which Henricus Corvinus, a famous Botanist in Rome, related to me by word of mouth and as an <term>autoptes</term> <note>original: *αὐτόπτης*, an eyewitness.</note> (eyewitness) of the matter. For the said young man, as often as he visited a certain place in his garden, notable no less for its greenery than for the pleasantness of its shadows, was driven by such violent stings of lust that, agitated by an unusual itching affection of the body, he seemed to have contracted "satyriasis" <note>A medical term for excessive or uncontrollable sexual desire in men.</note>. It happened, however, that while a friend was dealing with the said Corvinus (a noble perfumer/druggist), he revealed his passion to him. Corvinus, suspecting what it was, asked to be shown the place. Once this was done, he found the entire place filled with a certain kind of *Satyrium* <note>A genus of orchid traditionally associated with satyrs and believed to be a powerful aphrodisiac.</note>, the name of which we deliberately keep silent. Once found, nothing was easier for the skilled Botanist than to assign the cause of such a violent symptom. He also reported that this herb excites venereal motions so powerfully that even by holding it in the hand, one exposes oneself to the manifest danger of a "satyric" commotion. Therefore, it is no wonder that he was so powerfully agitated by Venus, who had so frequently trodden upon the genuine offspring of the same herb with his weight.

### Third Rule.

<margin>Foul-smelling trees cause headaches.</margin>
The shadows of all trees breathing out a foul-smelling odor are harmful to the head, such as all species of pitch-trees: the Pine, the Larch, the Fir, the Turpentine tree, the Cypress, and the Elder. For the excessive violence of the "vapid" exhalation offends the head and the brain, and causes headaches, as those who unadvisedly catch their shadows for too long know, and as will be made clear by examples. Hence, we see that those who have slept under the shadows of such trees, or have lingered there too long, mostly contract a great heaviness of the head and pain.

...produce the greatest symptoms there. I have seen some who, while sleeping under larch, pines, and firs, were so burdened by this odor that they contracted a fever from it and remained confined to their beds for many months. <margin>The marvelous property of the American Larch.</margin> Carolus Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a foundational Flemish botanist.</note> also records in his *Exotics* that there is a type of Larch in America under whose shadow those sleeping are seized by such a powerful delirium that, upon waking, they are driven out of their minds and assume strange behaviors. Some act as Prophets, some as soldiers, others as merchants; each person acts out whatever their natural inclination incites them to at that time. This occurs solely through the efficacy of that potent, exhaling bituminous virtue and the shadow exerting itself more powerfully. Giambattista della Porta <note>An Italian scholar and polymath known for his work on natural magic and optics.</note> records that in a shady place planted with Mandrakes, Nightshade, Thorn-apple, and other sleep-inducing herbs, one is seized by the deepest sleep, from which they cannot be awakened except by the most powerful remedies. And we have seen an example of Thorn-apple <note>original: "Stramonio." Likely *Datura stramonium*, known for its hallucinogenic and toxic properties.</note> being used by a soldier, who used to invite travelers to drink wine mixed with the juice of the said herb. He would drive them so mad that they fell into a lethargy, losing both their lives and their goods to the robber; some did not return to their senses for a long time, and even then, they found themselves stripped of all their possessions.

<margin>
The death-bringing shadows of poisonous trees.
</margin>

## Rule Four.

The shadows of all trees that spread a poisonous quality must be avoided as death-bringing and destructive; such are the clustered Monkshood, Thorn-apple, a certain kind of Spurge, and other species of Aconite. For no one rests in the shadow of these without punishment. When the poison has been spread and drawn into the pores of animals (which are loosened by heat), it brings upon them symptoms so violent—if not sudden death—that unless they are treated early, they rarely escape with their lives. According to the testimony of Pliny, the shadow of the Yew tree is also so destructive that it kills even those taking food beneath it; hence, perhaps not inappropriately, the word for poison (*Toxicum*) earned its name from the Yew (*Taxus*). Botanists offer us almost innumerable examples of this, though we shall taste only a few from the many. <margin>An example of the death-bringing shadow of Monkshood.</margin> There is a certain mountain here, by far the most prominent of all those surrounding the Roman plains, looming over the Tiburtine field, named Januarius, commonly called Monte Gennaro. <margin>Mount Januarius.</margin> On the summit of this mountain, not long ago, two goatherds were found dead under a certain tree within a short span of time. While doctors inspected them to examine the cause of death and found them lacking any blow or wound, the livid color of their faces finally provided a clear sign of some hidden poison. But while no one recognized the nature of the poison, they investigated the cause more anxiously, fixed in wonder. Finally, having consulted the peasants who

<column-break/>

knew the nature of the mountain well, they discovered the cause of death was clustered Monkshood (*Napellus racemosus*), a shrub of most virulent poison not uncommon in this mountain wilderness. The herders, sweltering in the heat, had prostrated themselves under its shadow and, filled with the virulent evaporation, had fallen asleep—and at the same time, fallen into eternal sleep. Warned by this example, the remaining shepherds began to flee the shadow of such shrubs as if they were the Lerna <note>A reference to the Lake of Lerna, home of the mythical Hydra; a metaphor for a place of deadly danger.</note>. Herrera <note>Antonio de Herrera y Tordesillas (1549–1625), a Spanish historian of the Americas.</note> relates similar examples concerning New Spain, where he says trees are found that are so virulent that no one can approach their shadow without punishment and manifest danger to their life. <margin>Animals themselves flee death-bringing shadows.</margin> Indeed, he says the animals themselves, by natural instinct, withdraw from them as much as they can. All the herbs growing beneath them are also poisonous and possess a lethal faculty. Mattioli <note>Pietro Andrea Mattioli (1501–1577), a renowned Italian physician and botanist.</note> also records in his *History of Aconites* that many people were killed in shady places where a great force of Aconite was growing. <margin>The marvelous power of the Aquapun tree.</margin> Herrera narrates in his *History of America* that in the New Kingdom of Granada <note>Modern-day Colombia and parts of Venezuela.</note>, there is a tree called *Aquapun* of such potent virulence that the Spaniards, initially ignorant of its destructive power, would sleep under its shadow and become distended with an immoderate swelling of all their limbs, like those suffering from dropsy. He asserts that the naked barbarians <note>A colonial term for the indigenous inhabitants.</note>, or those fallen asleep from drunkenness, staying too long under it, die everywhere in a miserable kind of death, their skin bursting from the excessive swelling of all their intestines. No one who has more deeply scrutinized our Sciognomic foundation should doubt that the reasons for this must be attributed to the virulent vapor of the tree and its pestilential breath, which possesses a swelling power.

<margin>
Shady places harmful to miners.
</margin>

## Rule Five.

It is very well known that shady valleys filled with metallic exhalations in various places induce various symptoms in humans staying there. Hence, in fields teeming with Arsenic and mercurial spirits, no one stays during summer nights without danger to their life. Indeed, exhalations from Antimony and sulfur, caught in the night air, enter the pores of the human body and remove a man from this world without any hope of safety. From this, the cause is clear why certain places are so hostile to human health, and why many sleeping in fields and mountains under the open sky are seized by paralysis, tremors of the whole body, and convulsions of all limbs—for no other reason than the metallic spirits lurking there. In the Andes of Peru, vomiting and other exotic symptoms happen to many, solely because of the abundance of Antimony and Saltpeter infecting the brain and stomach; and this is why sleeping in the Roman fields is so dangerous, especially in the summertime, because of the nocturnal...

# Book I, Part II.

<margin>Why the night and summer air of Rome are so harmful.</margin>
...ssessions; because, clearly, the summer Sun extracts a great abundance of exhalations from the malignant qualities of the earth’s cavernous bowels. These exhalations are condensed by the somewhat chilly night air and returned to their natural state within the shadowy air. When they enter the pores of those who are sleeping, they infect and corrupt the blood through the contagion of their own substance. Malignant fevers follow this corruption of the blood, leading to the dissolution of the native heat <note>A concept in early medicine referring to the vital internal warmth believed to sustain life.</note> and, finally, death.

### On the Sympathy and Antipathy of Shadows.

It is certain that the shadows of things also vary according to their sympathy or antipathy. Some shadows are friendly to certain animals, while others are hostile. The shadow of the Ash tree is friendly to the sheep kind, but it is so hostile to serpents—according to the testimony of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist.</note>—that they would sooner pass through fire than through its shadow. While the former is certainly true, we have discovered the latter to be false through actual experimentation. Both quadrupeds <margin>Why the Nightingale loves the Ash.</margin> and birds recognize this power that is hostile to serpents, and they all live safely under the shadow of this tree. For this reason, the Nightingale also loves it most of all; since there is a great antipathy between it and serpents, it lives safe and secure within its shady branches as if in a most fortified citadel against its enemy. Hence, there is no shadow that is not sought after by some animals, and yet avoided by others. For the shadow of the Ash, as Pliny testifies, is friendly to all animals but hostile to almost all venomous ones. <margin>Monkshood.</margin> The Yew <note>original: *Taxus*</note>, however—which the Arabs mistakenly call "mouse-monkshood" <note>original: *Napellum muris*</note> because they do not grasp the difference in Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> between *mis* and *mys* <note>original Greek: *μὶς* and *μῦς*</note>, the first of which signifies a mouse and the second a fly—is different. We have restored the name to "fly-monkshood"; for to this day, candidates of the secret medical arts provide an antidote for those infected by poison made from the flies born from the roots of this shrub, reduced to a powder. The shadow of this tree is friendly to serpents, toads, and venomous insects, inasmuch as their poison is strengthened there, but it is hostile to all other living creatures.

<margin>Cacao.</margin> Cacao is a shrub of New Spain <note>Modern-day Mexico and Central America.</note> from whose fruits that most celebrated drink, commonly called Chocolate, is made. This plant is so enamored with the shadow of the Ebony tree that without it, it perishes as if in indignation; it cannot grow to maturity except under its shadow. Hence, almost no shrub of this plant is found (according to Francisco Ximenes, Herrera, and Laetus) that does not have an Ebony shrub joined to it, shading it and defending it against the trees of the Sun.

<column-break/>

<margin>The Arum genus of herbs.</margin>
The aforementioned authors also mention a certain species of Cuckoo-pint <note>original: *Arum*</note> whose fruit protrudes in the shape of a cylinder. Since it cannot endure the Sun, nature has clothed it with a very long leaf, curved at the top like a parasol, so that it is inaccessible to the Sun's rays. 

<image-desc>A botanical woodcut of an Arum plant. It depicts a large, broad leaf with prominent veining alongside a reproductive structure consisting of a tall, thick spadix protected by a large, hood-like spathe that curves over the top.</image-desc>

For it is shielded against the rising, midday, and setting Sun in such a way that the solar rays cannot touch it from any side; however, toward the North, it catches the free breeze with its open leaf. Our own Cuckoo-pint seems to have something similar, as will be evident to anyone examining the matter. There are also herbs that vehemently love the specific shadow of certain trees; thus, Polypody and Hart’s-tongue fern are inseparable from the Oak; Maidenhair and Ivy-leaved Toadflax from the shady walls of springs; and Thapsia, Cuckoo-flower, and Pennywort from the shadows of spruce trees; while all kinds of Monkshood are friendly to the shadows of Yews. There are also shadows contrary to other shadows; <margin>Marvels of the Walnut's contrariety with the Linden.</margin> thus, it has been proven by the experience of Schenck <note>Johann Georg Schenck von Grafenberg (1560–1620), a German physician.</note> and others that a headache which someone contracted in the shadow of a Walnut tree is, by some wonderful reason, mitigated as soon as they reach the shadow of a Linden tree. <margin>Marvels concerning the bite of a mad dog.</margin> Experience has also taught that if someone who has contracted Rabies <note>original: *Hydrophobiam*</note> from the bite of a mad dog is cured and then enters the shadow of a Cornel tree, they fall back into it irremediably. This strange power was first observed in a certain man from Lyon in the year 1636, as the author of the *Medici-Philosophical Pentagon* relates.

<header>The Art of Shadow-Knowledge.</header>

<margin>The shadows of Tora and Antora.</margin>
...he relates. Again, whoever sleeps under a shadow where the Tora plant <note>original: "Tora." Likely referring to *Aconitum pardalianches*, also known as Leopard's Bane or Wolfsbane, traditionally considered highly poisonous.</note> grows abundantly and breathes in its poisonous vapor, will be healed immediately if they move to the shadow where the Antora plant <note>original: "Antora." Likely *Aconitum anthora*, known as Healing Wolfsbane, which was historically believed to be an antidote to the poisonous Tora.</note> grows, as the poisonous breath is expelled. From this, a rule can be formed:

<margin>A universal rule of the Art of Shadow-Knowledge.</margin>
The harmful quality of herbs that grow under the shadow of a particular tree is expelled and dissipated by the shadow of another "antidote" herb. For just as the power of one herb taken internally acts against the power of another which it overcomes, so too the vapor or breath of one is overcome by the vapor of another, specifically by one that possesses an opposite nature <note>original: "antipathico." The theory of sympathy and antipathy was central to Renaissance natural magic and medicine.</note>.

<column-break/>

And these are the things we thought necessary to say regarding the physical efficiency of shadows, so that the importance of the shadow of any given thing might be clear from the histories we have recounted. Through this, everyone may see how the great mysteries of nature lie hidden beneath the "shadowy covering" of nature itself. If all these things were observed with precision, I believe no one who weighs these matters correctly could doubt that they would offer physiologists a great opportunity for new observations never seen before. But now, let us turn from this physical dissertation on shadows to the subject of colors.

# PART THREE
## ON THE COLORATIONS OF NATURAL THINGS,
### OR
## ON COLOR,
## THE OFFSPRING OF LIGHT AND SHADOW,
### WHICH IS ALSO CALLED THE CHROMATIC ART.
### PREFACE.

---

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut drop cap 'C' showing a river landscape with a tower and buildings under a cloudy sky.</image-desc>
It is certain that no body is found within the boundaries of this sublunary world <note>The region below the moon, which in Aristotelian physics was the realm of change and decay.</note> so transparent <term>diaphanous: allowing light to pass through</term> that it does not have some degree of opacity joined to it. Consequently, if there were no opaque body in this world, there would be no reflection of light, nor any refraction of that light in different mediums. It is also certain that no color would be visible in the world except for that original color created within light itself. If color were removed, all vision in the world would necessarily perish, since everything visible is seen only through a colored surface. Indeed, not even the shining body of the Sun could be seen unless it were opaque and stopped our sight. From this, it is consequently clear that neither light can exist in any way without shadow, nor shadow without light; and the beauty of the entire

<column-break/>

world <note>original: "κόσμος" (kosmos). The Greek term implies both the world and the concept of order and beauty.</note> is so constituted from light and shadow that if you were to withdraw one or the other, the world could not be called "ordered," nor could that admirable beauty of nature fall under our sight in any way. Therefore, whatever is able to be seen in this world is only visible through "shadowy light" or "lucid shadow." Since color is a certain affection of an opaque body—or, as I might say with some others, a kind of "opacified light"—it is the genuine offspring of light and shadow. We have decided to treat it in this place so that the highest ornament of worldly beauty, and the wonders that can be performed in nature by its help, may become known to the curious reader. However, since in all good philosophy one must have a precise knowledge of a subject before reasoning soundly about it and its qualities, we shall fulfill the philosopher’s precept and begin our Study of Color <term>Chromatologiam: the systematic study or logic of color</term> with a definition of color.

Book I. Part III.

### CHAPTER I.
->What is color?<-

<margin>Various definitions of color.</margin>
The PYTHAGOREANS <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras, known for blending mathematics, music, and mysticism.</note> believed that color was nothing other than <term>ἐπιφάνειαν <note>original: "epiphaneian"</note></term>, that is, the surface of a body. They defended this view as follows: Color and surface relate to each other as "one and being" <note>A philosophical concept where two things are essentially the same thing under different names.</note>; since these are the same, just as they arise through a single birth, so they are destroyed by the same corruption. All of this applies to both color and surface; for if color is removed, the surface is removed, and vice versa. Therefore, they are the same. PLATO, however, wished for a certain kind of color to be light in an absolute sense; he defined it as a kind of little flame and glow flashing out from individual bodies, having parts adapted for the sense of sight to perceive. ALBERT <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who sought to reconcile Aristotelian philosophy with Christian thought.</note> thought that if light were removed, a certain quality remained in bodies arising from the "primary qualities," which serves as the "matter" of color, while light is its "form" and its active state. He confirms his opinion with these arguments: because colors—when they are observed in the clouds at the rising of the dawn, or in the feathers of peacocks—have no cause other than light; therefore, they do not differ from light. Certainly, these thinkers would have spoken well if they could have demonstrated that these colors were not "true" and real, but purely apparent and ghostly, having no proper causes of their own. Again, when light is absent, all bodies are hidden; therefore, no color exists as visible before the arrival of light; thus, color is the same as light. To this we respond: when light is absent, colors are indeed hidden and snatched from our eyes, but not from the things themselves; for they are visible by their own nature, even if they are not bathed in light. <margin>The Aristotelian definition.</margin> A better

<column-break/>

definition is therefore the Aristotelian one, which says color is nothing other than <term>κινητικὸν τοῦ κατ' ἐνέργειαν διαφανοῦς. καὶ τοῦτ' ἔστιν αὐτοῦ ἡ φύσις <note>original Greek: "kinētikon tou kat' energeian diaphanous. kai tout' estin autou hē physis"</note></term>, that is, "that which moves that which is actually transparent, and this is its nature." Color, therefore, moves the transparent medium <note>Such as air or water.</note> which is already actually illuminated by light. Color is distinguished from light in this way: light, while it moves the transparent medium, makes it "clear" or see-through; but color requires the medium to be already illuminated in order to move it. It is not that the medium is illuminated earlier in time than it is moved by color; rather, at one and the same time that it is "stained" by color, it is also illuminated by light—by that light, I say, which is sent back to the sight from a body visible by its color, carrying with it the image and form of the color. Elsewhere, the same Philosopher <note>Aristotle was often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in academic texts.</note> is cited saying color is <term>τὸ χρῶμα ὁ ὁρισμὸς τοῦ διαφανοῦς ἐν τῷ σώματι ὁριστῷ <note>original Greek: "to chrōma ho horismos tou diaphanous en tō sōmati horistō"</note></term>, the "limit of the transparent in a defined or bounded body." This "limit" or surface should not be taken in an absolute sense, as the Pythagoreans took it, but insofar as it is visible. For only visible color dwells in the boundary of a body; although the colors of "mixed things" <note>Physical compounds or substances.</note> thoroughly pervade the entire substance of a thing, they cannot fall under the senses unless they are radiating from the outermost surface. If, occasionally, colors are also seen deep within gemstones and other solid masses—such as flies, gnats, ants, and other families of insects committed to a perpetual tomb inside amber—this happens because such bodies are not entirely opaque, but are partially transparent. Hence, it is no wonder that the colors of those things emerge from the depths and become visible. Therefore, although color is not strictly light, it is found to have a great kinship with it in all things: for just as light does, so too color produces something like itself and spreads it far and wide through the transparent medium, as will be seen later.

<margin>The difference between color and light.</margin>
This power belongs to nothing else. Therefore, the only difference between light and color is that light travels through its sphere of power by itself, whereas color does so only by the benefit of light. Light is visible by itself and always in an active state; color is visible only in potential, and becomes active only upon the arrival of light.

->On the multiple variety of colors.<-

<margin>The division of colors.</margin>
PHILOSOPHERS have generally categorized all colors into "true" and "apparent." Among the true colors, I find there are two extremes, three middle colors, and likewise three composed from these; and that the entire offspring of the remaining colors has its origin

<column-break/>

from these. <margin>The extreme colors.</margin> In the first category are white and black, opposites to one another, and thus, as they say, separated by the "whole diameter" <note>Meaning they are as far apart as possible, like opposite points on a circle.</note>. From these, whiteness—being most similar to light—is nobler than black, which is closer to darkness. Hence, the whiter a thing is, the closer it becomes to light; and as much as

<margin>The color white.</margin>
Furthermore, besides these middle colors, according to the testimony of the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle.</note> himself, no other species of color is pleasant in itself: whatever colors remain result from these eight—the three simple and three composite colors we have mentioned. The two extremes <note>White and black.</note> allow for easy mixing with the middle colors, which they do not so much change as they intensify or diminish. White elevates the others; black depresses them by darkening: hence, black is to white as darkness is to light. Yellow, red, and blue relate to white as a shadow relates to light when it is deprived of a greater or lesser amount of illumination.

<margin>Yellow.</margin>
Yellow, the color closest to light, shines out in saffron that has been heavily diluted with water; in <margin>True colors.</margin> "apparent" colors <note>Refractive colors like rainbows or prisms.</note>, it is produced from intense light and a very small transparent part of the air. In "true" colors <note>Pigments or the inherent colors of objects.</note>, however, it arises from a body approaching the nature of transparency, as will be said later; it contains beneath it a numerous family descending from it, <margin>Various kinds of colors.</margin> such as: pale yellow, lemon-yellow, reddish-yellow, weasel-colored, rust-colored, dusky, roan, tawny, royal-yellow, and lion-colored.

<margin>Red.</margin>
The color red, being equidistant from the extremes, participates equally in shadow and light; it has beneath it: red, rosy, glowing-red, ruddy,

<column-break/>

<margin>Blue.</margin>
flashing, blood-red, pale-yellow, date-brown, fiery, and flaming. Blue follows red; it relates to black just as yellow relates to white, or as shadow relates to darkness; it has beneath it: blue-gray, lead-colored, and sea-blue. The composite colors also have their own accidental differences.

<margin>Colors belonging to the golden color.</margin>
Under golden, yellow, and red are included orange, saffron-colored, and tawny. <margin>Those under green.</margin> Under green: copper-rust, herbaceous, leek-green, and sea-green. <margin>Purple.</margin> Under purple are rose-colored, pale ruby, amethyst, Phoenician purple, violet, and dyer's purple. And there are others and others, which, since they are innumerable—just as the names by which they are called are lacking—we deliberately leave them in their own "chaos." Let it suffice for us, as far as the weakness of human intellect allows, to assign the reasons for some of the more obvious ones in this treatise. Furthermore, the figure attached here sufficiently declares all other things regarding lights and colors; it will be clear to anyone who correctly compares one with another that all things have a certain analogy to lights and colors.

## CHAPTER III.

### Aerial Coloration,

->Or<-

### On the apparent colors in air and water, and their causes, effects, and use in our Art of Light and Shadow.

<margin>The colors of clouds.</margin>
Among the apparent or "phantastic" colors are numbered the colors in the clouds and those shining in the air at dawn; these should not be thought so phantastic that they do not possess true causes and reasons for their appearance.
<margin>What the cause of such diverse color in clouds may be.</margin>
Since they exist in a physical body—namely, in the <term>exhalation <note>In 17th-century science, "exhalations" were dry, earthy fumes, while "vapors" were moist and watery.</note></term> which, mixed with vapor, shines through along with the light—they appear differently according to the density of the medium, not phantastically, but truly and realistically. For if the exhalation is subtle and of the thinnest substance, the cloud will turn yellow; if it is thick and <gloss>denser <note>original: "παχυτέρᾳ"</note></gloss>, it will turn red. If it is watery, it will present itself to be seen dressed in a blue veil; finally, if it is earthy, it will be foul with a mournful pall. You see, therefore, that according to the quality of the cloud, the mixed color of the light is varied. Moreover, since a cloud is a body, it must necessarily be colored as well: not phantastically, but realistically.
<margin>The colors of the dawn.</margin>
We shall teach below that the colors shining forth during the dawn are created by the various mixtures of light and shadow in the air (as if in a denser medium) through refraction. For when the Sun is positioned below the boundary of the dawn, the air is seen as dark; but when it is 18 degrees from the horizon, because of the deeper shadows of the air, it reveals the first traces of light, reflecting a certain bluishness. Near the middle of the dawn, it turns red due to an equal participation of light and shadow; but near the end of the twilight, it turns yellow due to the thin shadow of the air mixed with the light, which is followed shortly after by the light itself—concerning which we shall speak more at length in what follows. It

<column-break/>

blue, sometimes dark and as if opaque, and others imbued with different colors. To this category also belong the colors appearing in the rainbow and in halos, and the various colors shining forth on the surface of the sea. Then there is that brilliant color seen in the feathers of birds through the radiation of the Sun. Thirdly, the color which the Sun produces on a wall when passing through stained glass, according to the diversity of the colors of the glass. Fourthly, the colors resulting from the various refraction of light in polyhedral glasses <note>Prisms or multi-faceted glass jewels.</note>: about all and each of these we must speak, so that the wonderful effects of light and shadow may be more clearly revealed.

<margin>Experience. An analogy.</margin>
happens to clouds, therefore, in the same way as the staining of waters: for if you tint water with a little saffron, you will produce yellow; if the tincture is more abundant, red; but if a little earth is sprinkled into the water, it becomes ash-gray; if a great deal, it acquires a dark face. The same things happen to the transparent air as happen to a glass ball filled with water.
<margin>The colors of the sea.</margin>
Again, the sea is seen as sometimes white, sometimes blue, and sometimes greenish when the Sun falls upon it. The reason for this thing is indeed varied: first, the different depth of the sea and the color of the bottom. Thus, a sea consisting of a green bottom turns entirely green, like the various tracts of the Mediterranean Sea which they commonly call *le Prateriè* <note>The Meadows; likely referring to seagrass beds.</note>. A sea that consists of a red bottom reflects red waves, such as the <term>Erythræum <note>The Red Sea.</note></term>; but the deepest sea is seen imbued with a black color, such as the <term>Euxine <note>The Black Sea.</note></term>, which is for that reason called "Black."
<margin>Colors of the sea and their causes.</margin>
Therefore, the sea acquires its color according to the color of the bottom, which nevertheless is not situated in the water itself, but in the underlying floor.
And this is one reason why the sea appears imbued with different colors. The second reason is the light itself brought through the air, which, variously refracted, reflects various colors. It happens occasionally that the sea reverberates such colors to us as the clouds themselves resting upon it are imbued with. Therefore, the cause of the sea's colors is varied. Hence, when the sea is viewed from a distance with the Sun's ray opposite, it turns purple; for then red is mixed with blue, which shines through from the exhalation mixed into the air. For this reason, the sea, especially at the time of sunset...

<margin>On the blue color of the air.</margin>
But as to why the air, and the most distant places to which the ray of sight cannot fully reach, appear blue for the most part: although various thinkers have assigned various causes to this, none seems to have hit upon the genuine one. Some believe the cause lies in the base of the <term>retina <note>The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye.</note></term> being imbued with a blue color; some in the will of the Creator; others in the very nature of the air. We shall manifest our own feelings on the matter in a few words.

### Why Does the Sky Appear Blue?

<margin>The author's opinion on the color of the Sky.</margin>
It must be understood, therefore, that our sight can see nothing unless it is imbued with color. However, since the sight is not always directed at opaque bodies or surfaces bounded by colors, but is instead carried into the transparent lack of opacity of infinite aerial and celestial space—as when we look at a clear sky or the most remote peaks of the highest mountains—nature required a certain color for that immense transparent space. This was so that the sight would not be frustrated by lacking its necessary terminus, nor vanish into darkness and nothingness. Yet this color could not be white, yellow, or red, since these colors, being closer to light, require the presence of a physical object to be seen. (For just as things that are near are likened to light, so things that are most remote are likened to darkness. Hence, bright colors, since they are only perceived within a determined space, approach shadows and darkness the more they are removed from the light or the power of sight.)
<margin>Why the sky is seen as blue.</margin>
Therefore, when the sight is carried into those immense ethereal spaces, it ought to be terminated there; yet, because of the infinite distance and the infinite multiplication of the layers of air, it could only be terminated by darkness. Nevertheless, since such a color [black] would be unsuitable both for the eyes and for the world, it was brought about by the most wise counsel of nature that the sight should be terminated in a certain "mean" or middle color—such as blue—consisting of an unequal mixture of light and darkness, like a most pleasing shadow. This ensures the sight is not too scattered by bright colors, nor constricted by dark ones, nor inflamed by red. Nature, in her providence, bestowed this blue color upon the world—being the closest color to black or darkness—so that those most pleasant celestial spaces might be contemplated with unoffended sight. Furthermore, the color of water most closely emulates this blue color of the air. Just as black is the color of the central Earth, so a yellowish-orange color—like that of clay—is found near the outer surface of the earth, appearing purer to those digging deep underground in almost any location.
<margin>The blue color of water</margin>
From this, the thicker waters turn green from a mixture of yellow and blue, namely when the parts are joined not by chance,

<column-break/>

but by a certain natural fellowship. Hence plants also are green at the beginning, but later, when they pass beyond maturity and their moisture is consumed, they turn yellow again like the earth, returning to the ground from whence they were taken. Indeed, watery moisture, coagulated by <term>concoction <note>A process of "ripening" or "cooking" by natural heat, thought to transform substances in nature.</note></term>, breaks out for the most part into plants, even under the waters themselves, as is evident in seaweed; thus, moisture alone, without any other mixture of seed, can be fit for producing small plants. I confirm the truth of this matter by a certain admirable miracle of nature, which Andreas Libavius reports in Volume 4 of his *Chemistry* as a thing surveyed and examined with his own eyes.

### A Wondrous Experiment of Vegetable Nature in Distilled Liquid.

In the place cited above, Andreas Libavius tells of a marvelous plant which grew in water distilled and purified of all dregs of seed; it was, as is likely, born from the fertility of the moisture alone. But since the matter is worthy of examination by philosophers, I provide the letter itself from Jeremiah Corner, Chief Physician of Brandenburg, given to Libavius, in which he describes the miracle of nature in these words: *"Accept this picture of a little plant born to me in the distilled water of Trifalatina (which is in Meissen, by the 'Three Firs' not far from the city of Zwickau). You have the picture now, I say, but I wish you could have had the living*
