# The Great Art, Book I, Part III.

...it seemed to be fused together like glass, or to cling to a thread, and in this way it spread small branches to the sides. These were full of little leaves, which were not wide considering the size of the whole, but oblong. They were a pleasant green, like the tender leaves of a primrose or a young rosemary plant—oblong and delicate, like sharp grass—with a color of <term>citrine-green <note>A yellowish-green color, from the Latin "citrinus" (lemon-colored).</note></term> that was not quite a deep green. I do not doubt that it could have risen higher and grown further, since it remained firm and upright without any trembling motion even when the glass was shaken slightly. But, lamentably, due to an unexpected frost during the feast of the Nativity of the Lord <note>Christmas</note>, the water froze during the night (as did other things) in the cold <term>Museum <note>In the 17th century, a "museum" was a scholar’s study or a room for scientific curiosities and experiments.</note></term>, which was not heated at that time. Consequently, after the plant was found to have been thawed by heat, it was damaged by the force of the cold and torn from the bottom. Thus, it now floats in the water; although its color is intact, it appears diminished in size, with a certain viscosity gathering around it. This occurred in the year 1608. The distilled water was prepared in the month of June by Martin Gallus, a pharmacist; the "painting" <note>Referring to the chemical formation resembling a plant.</note> formed on the 12th of December; and the herb was first observed in November. These details are from Cornerius, as cited by Libavius.

From these accounts, it is clearly evident that water—along with some portion, however imperceptible, of <term>feminine dregs <note>In alchemy, the "feminine" principle often refers to the passive, material, or receptive component of a substance.</note></term> which always remains in water even after much distillation—can grow a vegetable body. This humor, passing from potentiality into act, first degenerates into a certain green substance. See the wonders we have handed down concerning these portentous plants in our work *The Subterranean World*. But let us return to the color of the air.

<margin>The air possesses a certain opacity.</margin>
The sky, therefore, appears blue because of the interposition of many parts of air and their mutual penetration, which take on the role of a certain opacity. For the air has this specific property: over a long distance, it covers up even colored things that are perfectly visible in bright light—even to a healthy and sharp sight—so that they are not seen at all, and the air itself appears darker, namely, blue. Both of these qualities belong to an opaque body, not a transparent one. Therefore, the many parts of air interposed between the object and the sight, although they are all equally illuminated by light, take on a kind of density from the multitude of intervening surfaces. And thus, in a clear body, acting against its own nature to create a certain opacity, they reflect that blue and ashen color, which is very close to darkness. All transparent things confirm this:

<margin>Opaque Selenite.</margin>
For if one places two pieces of glass, or crystals, or <term>selenite <note>A transparent variety of the mineral gypsum, often used in experiments on light.</note></term> one on top of the other, both will become more opaque. The doubling of layers hinders the penetration of light more than a single layer, and tripling more than doubling, and so on to infinity. Selenite demonstrates all of this almost to the eye; when it is dug out of the earth, it looks like nothing but stone or opaque earth,

<column-break/>

gleaming and mirror-like only on the surface. But when you have split it into the tiniest thin sheets, you will find nothing more transparent. <margin>An experiment performed on selenite.</margin> From a mass of this "mirror stone," the length of a palm, the width of half a palm, and the thickness of two barleycorns, I remember that I once cut 120 thin sheets. Each one was so clear and transparent that no glass or crystal could be compared to it; when exposed to the air, it became almost invisible because of the extreme thinness of its substance, and it cast no shadow when held in the sun. Yet all those sheets joined together so multiplied the shadows by the addition of parts that you would have called it an almost opaque body, ending in a shadow close to darkness. Thus, this single experiment provides a <term>demonstration <note>original: "ἀποδείξιν" (apodeixin), a Greek term for a logical proof or clear manifestation.</note></term> for the cause of the celestial color—I mean, the blue. For the parts of a transparent body joined to other transparent parts become more opaque the more you stack them, until finally they deny passage to light, sight, and color. Therefore, what we see in transparent glass must also be believed to happen in fluids. So it is with the seas, as I have heard from the excellent divers <note>original: "urinatoribus"</note>—Turkish slaves in Malta—who had spent many years seeking pearls and coral in the Red Sea. <margin>The Sun's rays do not penetrate to the bottom of the deeper sea.</margin> They say that the sun's rays only illuminate the bottom to a certain depth. Where the sea is deeper, the bottom is left in perpetual darkness without any trace of light. There is no other reason for this than the compaction of the sea's surfaces. All of this is established by daily experience. Indeed, water in a small glass vessel allows light a much freer passage than if the vessel were larger, which brings on a total shadow. In lakes and rivers as well, even if they are very clear, the depths appear black, while the shallow bottom does not. <margin>An objection.</margin> But you will object: "Then the air would be visible by itself; but no transparent body is visible by itself." I respond: no transparent body, insofar as it is transparent, is visible by itself, but rather insofar as it has some opacity joined to it. Thus, since the air takes on a degree of opacity through that infinite compaction of surfaces, it is visible not by its own nature, but by "accident"—namely, by reason of its compacted parts. All glass things are visible by their own nature because of their solidity, for since they come from the earth, they necessarily take on some opacity; but transparent water is numbered among the invisible things. Therefore, transparent things become opaque according to certain degrees: the <term>ether <note>The highest, purest part of the atmosphere or space.</note></term> least of all, the air less so, water more so, and crystalline things even more, while precious stones are the most opaque of all. Through this diversity of opacity, they produce and show colors and appearances in the light, as we shall now discuss.

# On the Coloring of Natural Things.

## Experiment.
### On the various colorations of water.

The colors with which waters are tinted are either thick and dreg-like—being not at all translucent—or they are clear and transparent in the manner of glass. If the color is of the first kind, floating as a suspension in the water, it is obvious that when viewed against the light, it appears black and dark. This is because the thickness of the material intercepts the ray of light and repels it back toward its source. This will become known through this experiment: if you place a glass <term>ampulla <note>A flask or bottle with a globular body and two handles, common in historical laboratories.</note></term> full of tinted water before a ray of light. Indeed, that same color, if the glass is viewed from the side that receives the light ray, exhibits its proper appearance and form, which the reflected light ray brings back to the eyes of the beholder. 

But if the color inherent in the water is exceptionally clear, when viewed against the light, it represents its own image—and all the more vividly as the light is more excellent. Yet, when viewed from the same side from which the light falls, it appears dark; it is even blacker the more saturated it is, and clearer the more diluted it is. For since the luminous ray penetrates directly through the substance of the water 

<column-break/>

and the color simultaneously, with nothing standing in its way and no part being repelled back to the sight, certainly neither the water nor the color will be seen; instead, it will exhibit the appearance of a black opacity. For that which is not seen presents a certain likeness to darkness. It is clear, therefore, that waters stained with a transparent color appear dark when viewed from the place where the light originates.

One may see something similar in the sea, when the waves are still and it shows a level surface, specifically near sunset. If we look at the seawater while turned toward the East, we perceive a certain opaque depth in it. Since the brightness of the sun, falling obliquely upon the highest level of the water, increases the shadow beneath it, and is then thrown back toward the opposite side—namely, the East—it allows the sight a greater penetration. Thus it happens that the water appears darker on that side. On the contrary, if we look at the sea facing the Sun, its brilliance so floods the surface of the waters that no path into the depths is open to the sight. This same brilliance, rebounding from the smoothness of the water, so strikes the sharpness of the eyes that, however much one wishes, one can see nothing perfectly.

## CHAPTER IV.
### Anaclastic Coloring

### On colors in polyhedral glasses.

<image-desc>A decorative historiated drop-cap 'P' featuring a scholar seated in a study with books and architectural motifs.</image-desc>When a certain Philosopher had more attentively considered the hidden nature of colors, it is read that he broke out into these words for good reason: *As the eyes of bats are to the light of day, so is the intellect of our soul to those things which are most manifest of all.* <note>original: "Sicut veſpertilionum oculi..." This is a famous quote from Aristotle's Metaphysics, Book II, Chapter 1, often used to humble human reason before the mysteries of nature.</note> In my judgment, nothing is truer. For as many as I have read who, up to this point, have written especially about the colors of the Rainbow, they bring forward some reasons for such a manifold offspring of colors; yet they fluctuate so much in all things that, carried away by a certain tide, though they seem to say everything, they say nothing. When I looked upon this calamity, I thought the matter should be attempted through experiences, as much as is possible for human industry. Driven by the heat of a striving mind, I left nothing untried to find the true causes of such a rare effect shining forth in glasses. In this, I seem to have achieved the goal of finding certain general reasons for individual colors.

<column-break/>

<margin>The nature of colors is inscrutable.</margin> However, as to the manner of measurement in which individual colors are mixed with one another, even if someone knew it, it would not be the mark of a prudent man to tell of it. This is especially true since he could in no way bring forward a necessary or even likely reason for these things, as they are deeper than the weakness of human genius can in any way reach—being reserved, as I might speak with the <term>Rabbis <note>The author refers to a Jewish tradition that unresolved doubts and scientific mysteries will be explained when the prophet Elijah returns.</note></term>, for the times of Elijah. Here I laugh at the efforts of the Metaphysicians—the useless attempts at speculation by certain men who, when they cannot comprehend light and colors (things which are the most manifest of all, and than which nothing is more obvious or comes more into human use), presume that they can attain the natures, entities, properties, and affections of the highest beings, which are far removed from all stain of bodily contagion. They err, they err! For if they wish to be commended for the praise of their genius, let them labor in elucidating this darkness which is most manifest of all. Let them assign to us some reason for this which might in some way satisfy the acclaimed effort of the Philosophers, and we will gladly subscribe to them.

...not waste their life and strength in vain on those things placed beyond every goal of our intellect, about which we are only permitted to know as much as if they had never existed in the nature of things. But having said these things in passing, let us return to our purpose. The question is: what are those colors? Of what mixture of things do they consist? But since these things cannot be understood without experiment, we will first set forth our experiments so that, having examined them, we may proceed more safely in the scrutiny of causes.

### Various Experiments regarding the Mixture of Colors.

First, we took care to have glasses prepared for us tinted with every kind of color: White, Yellow, Red, Blue, and Black; and we observed that the mixture of light in these glasses is the same as in the mixture of material colors <note>Kircher is noting that mixing colored light or looking through layered colored glass follows similar rules to mixing physical paints.</note>.
<margin>Beautiful experiments.</margin>
This can become known in three ways: first by a direct ray, then by a refracted ray, and finally by a reflected ray. Thus, let two pieces of glass be placed, yellow and red, one over the other, and you will see that objects seen through them immediately shine with a certain golden color. The same will happen if you catch a reflected ray, passing directly through the glasses, on a white paper: for both will tint the transparent medium with that mixture of color which the glasses themselves compose. If you join yellow and blue again, and examine them by the triple ray, you will find the medium tinted by them, and the whole object-paper, luxuriating in a most pleasant green. Finally, if you try with red and blue, there will be born for you a medium and a surface shining with proud purple. White and black, however, produce something ashen. White with yellow will produce a reddish color; and with another similar one placed on top, it will make an intense red; blue with green will generate a <term>peacock color <note>A shimmering blue-green or iridescent hue.</note></term>. Thus, not without the greatest pleasure of the mind, you will see various colors born from the combination of colored glasses.

<margin>The reflected ray is tinted by the color of the mirror from which it is reflected.</margin>
Where it is most worthy of admiration, even the reflected ray, though not passing through the glass, nevertheless assumes the mixture of color and strikes it back onto the wall. Again, if anyone looks intensely at the Sun and then turns away toward dark objects, he will first see everything as white, soon yellow, then red, afterwards green, and finally blue, until his sight is restored to its proper state; he will perceive this through a vision degenerating from light through the said colors into black by a natural proportion <note>Kircher is describing the phenomenon of "after-images," where the eye's receptors are overstimulated by bright light.</note>.

Second, take a triangular glass, or

<column-break/>

one cast into the form of a prism, or any angular glass body, through which—whether by a visual, reflected, or direct ray—you observe objects in the Sun: you will certainly find them tinted with the same fourfold kind of colors. Again, in all glass vials around the boundary of water and air, you will notice the same colors. These experiments being established;
<margin>What those colors appearing in the glass are.</margin>
I say first, that these colors are nothing other than diminished and fouled light, and thus are a middle ground between darkness and light. So that these things may be understood, it must be noted that whole and perfect light cannot be made except with the greatest strength of color in the greatest thinness or rarity. Therefore, if light is diminished by color or exists in a non-pure thinness, it recedes from its natural perfection as much as the color is diminished, or as much as the medium is more dense or rare; consequently, light that is diminished and weak due to insufficient color must be called impure and fouled by reason of a denser transparent medium. For it was proven above that this light is more effective and strikes the visual power more vehemently when it has a greater <term>concentration <note>original: "constipationem"; here meaning the crowding or density of light rays.</note></term> of rays, and consequently a greater color from the union of parts; but it acts more feebly on the eyes when it has a greater dissipation of rays, and consequently a lesser color from the dissolved union. Hence, since there are almost infinite degrees between darkness and light, heat and cold, diverse flames or lights are also made according to the diverse thinness and rarity occurring in the medium. White, yellow, red, blue, golden, purple, green—and indeed the proper color of light is white, which is usually seen in the Sun in the clearest air, and in a camphor flame: this, mixed with a denser transparent medium, is fouled and driven toward black and darkness. If, therefore, the color is intense in the thinnest medium of luminous bodies, the color will be most bright; if it consists of minimal color in the thickest medium, the color will be most shadowy, and barely visible against neighboring darkness; which the experiments declared above beautifully teach. The remaining intermediate colors, according to the degree of color and density and thinness of the medium, approach now light, now darkness. Hence colors that suffer less from opacity are closer to white, but more remote when they suffer more from the opacity of the medium. Since, therefore, there is a varying constitution of the transparent medium in angular glass, and it has one or another concentration of parts, the light falling upon it and being refracted must necessarily be tinted and fouled according to the greater concentration of parts. Therefore, colors arise from a transparent medium of a denser sort—not just any, but that which lacks natural thinness, such as dewy...

But if they are carried through an unequal transparent medium of denser air, the more deeply they penetrate,

Let **RTS VXY** be a prism: and let the Sun be **Ce-l. n.** and the eye **D H M K**. In this, a twofold position of things is seen: one through a reflected ray, which changes things neither in shape nor color, but shows them inverted; this occurs when things penetrate the glass perpendicularly. The other is through a <term>refracted ray <note>Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one medium, like air, into another, like glass.</note></term>, and here it shows things neither in their natural position nor color, but now curved, now circular, and adorned with every kind of color. Therefore, refraction alone causes these various distinctions of colors in this case, and not reflection; for reflection passing through the glass perpendicularly shows things no differently than they are—just as houses, buildings, and trees on the bank of a river appear inverted. But when a ray of the Sun falls obliquely upon any side of the prism, it is refracted twice before returning to the eye, and by this refraction, it recedes much from its pristine vigor; since the medium is also of unequal density. Hence the refracted light, weakened and stained by varying refraction at varying depths of the transparent medium, renders colors now more, now less approaching white and black. Furthermore, three primary colors are noted in the prism: red, yellow, and blue. Yellow for the most part mediates between the red and blue ends; while green,

### Corollary I.

<margin>The cause of the colors of the rainbow.</margin>
First, it is evident from this that the colors of the Rainbow <note>original: "Iridis"</note> have no other origin than that which we have stated regarding the glass prism. For all colors are generated from the same order of rays, but reflecting from different depths of the cloud. Where the rays first enter the cloud, a most brilliant and crimson <note>original: "puniceus"</note> color is spread over the entire surface of the cloud and vapor where the rays of the pyramid of illumination reach. But they are not seen because the reflection of the ray is diverted elsewhere than to the eye of the spectator. Where the ray has penetrated a little deeper, it is weakened, and returns toward the eye through the interior surface of the cloud, entangled by much opacity and the shadows of the drops. Thirdly, driven even further into the depth with light that is still thinner and dark, the peacock-color and blue emerge through the interior and lowest curvature of the arc. Where you will see, by a straight ray penetrating the transparent medium, it produces an arc very similar to white from the dewy waters: toward the earth, however, the realm of shadows produces a blue color close to darkness due to the depth of the medium and the weakness of the light declining from the straight ray: but toward the sky, the border of light produces a reddish color from the border of the black cloud, fouled more than the middle, yet less than the lowest arc.

### Corollary II.

<margin>Angular transparent bodies cause colors.</margin>
Hence it is clear that wherever light falling on angular transparent bodies causes re-

<column-break/>

fraction, all the colors of the Rainbow appear there, as is shown most extensively in our *Catoptric Magic*, where we shall represent innumerable spectacles of this kind and Rainbows, to which we refer the reader. Hence water dispersed into dew between the eyes and the Sun immediately reflects the Rainbow with every difference of color, as is well known.

### Corollary III.

<margin>The lunar rainbow.</margin>
From this it is also clear that solar light alone is sufficient to represent these colors; other lights indeed reflect them only dimly; nor is the light of the Moon sufficient to form a colored image from it, as I remember having observed most diligently in a lunar Rainbow, which it happened for me to see here in Rome in the year 1640, on the day before the Kalends of October <note>September 30th</note> at the time of the full moon, with the greatest admiration; which, however, was imbued with no color at all, but like a white band or zone, it gripped half the sky (a wonder to see). From which it became known to me thereafter, almost uniquely, that for producing the colors of clouds, the dawn, and the Rainbow, a most robust light is needed, namely that of the sun.

### Experiment.

->*On a certain remarkable wood staining water into every kind of color.*<-

<margin>Description of the tree.</margin>
In this place we have thought it by no means to be omitted to mention a certain kind of white Mexican wood, which the natives call <term>Coatl</term> and <term>Tlapazatli</term> <note>Likely *Lignum Nephriticum*, famous in the 17th century for its fluorescent properties</note>. Although experience up to now has taught that it stains water only with a blue color, we have nevertheless found through continuous experience that it transforms water into every kind of color; which might rightly seem a paradox. The shrub of the wood is large, as they say, and not infrequently grows into the bulk of a tree; its trunk is thick, knotless, like a pear tree; the leaves are not unlike the leaves of the chickpea or rue; the flowers are small, oblong, yellow, and arranged in spikes: it is a cold and humid plant, although it departs little from a temperate middle. Thus, the wood of this described tree, fashioned into a cup, first stains water poured into it into an intensely blue water, the color of the Bugloss flower <note>A plant with vibrant blue petals</note>; and the longer it stands in it, the more intense a color it will acquire. Therefore, if you pour this water into a glass sphere and expose it to the light, not even a trace of blue color will appear, but like pure, clear spring water, it will show itself limpid and clear to those looking at it. Furthermore, if you direct this glass vial toward a more shaded place, the whole liquid will reflect a most pleasing green; if in still more shaded places, red, and so according to the objects...

...condition of its powers <note>original: "potentiarum"; referring to the inherent qualities of the wood</note>, it will change color, remarkable to say. Yet, it should not be seen as a "real" color either, since when exposed to light, no such dye is seen in it, and it only exerts itself in different kinds of colors when exposed to different objects.

## CHAPTER V.

### Metallic or Mineral Coloration.

<margin>How something can be both transparent and colored at the same time.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter 'C' depicting a figure in a landscape with trees and clouds.</image-desc>
Color is seen in gems in two ways: either transparent <note>original: "diaphanus"</note> or opaque. Opaque color is that which receives light but does not transmit it; transparent color is that which transmits it. Each either exists even when light is absent, or does not exist when light is absent but is produced from a composition of light and shadow, as was said in the preceding sections. However, how the same thing can be both colored and transparent seems difficult to investigate; for in a transparent object, sight or light ought not to be terminated. Every color, however, "terminates" <note>defines the limit or surface of</note> the view; and yet color is perceived by the senses in transparent objects, diffused throughout their entire material, which seems absurd.

Therefore, it must be said that color properly terminates sight in opaque bodies, when it is present continuously and in a fluid state <note>original: "in fluore"</note>. When, however, it is united and its material parts do not have a surface, it does not absolutely terminate the transparent medium itself, but only partially and imperfectly, insofar as it is in some way opaque. Thus, the transparency remains despite such color, though imperfectly; the light is affected and altered by some opacity in the color, and it is terminated in the opaque body not by its own color, but by a foreign one. A perfect and absolute transparent medium is one that lacks all color and transmits the color of light exactly as it received it, in straight lines. I say "in straight lines" so as not to exclude the rainbow <note>original: "iridem"</note>, a gem, or a hexagonal crystal...

<column-break/>

<margin>Uses of this wood and its water for Kidney Disease.</margin>
...trained by various experiments, I finally found the cause of this, which we shall reveal in the following sections. This wood is called *Nephriticum* <note>original: "Lignum Nephriticum"; likely the Mexican Kidneywood, *Eysenhardtia polystachya*</note>, because it is a most proven remedy for ailments of the kidneys and bladder. The locals <note>original: "Barbari"; literally "Barbarians," a common period term for non-European indigenous peoples</note> prepare it thus: they soak the wood, cut into small chips and shavings, in the best and clearest spring water. They use this water constantly and dilute their wine with it, experiencing wonderful effects without any disturbance of the humors; no other dietary regime is needed beyond a temperate one. Indeed, the taste of the water is no more changed by the immersion of the wood than if nothing had been soaked in it at all. It is said to be hot and dry in the first degree <note>A classification from Galenic medicine regarding the "temperament" of a substance</note>. It has been observed, however, that after the wood has been soaked in water for fifteen days, its virtue is entirely exhausted, and it no longer stains the water with color.

---

...which, even if they are absolutely transparent because they receive light in straight lines and transmit it the same way, can nevertheless—through the refraction of light upon multiple surfaces—either transmit various colors (which they neither have nor received) onto a neighboring body, or render them visible within themselves, showing different colors from different positions of the eyes.

An imperfect transparent medium is of two types: it is either stained with a color by which the passing light is terminated, or it is stained in some part with a transparent color that varies that same color (when light is added and refracted through several surfaces), as happens in the Opal gem. In this, the color is truly transparent, and yet that same color is altered and changed by the refraction of light, and from a different viewpoint or eye position, it offers itself to the sight as something else in the same spot. Leaving aside the "apparent" colors in transparent things, let us turn our pen to the causes of "real" colors in gems. Some think these various colors are induced in gems by metallic and mineral exhalations or spirits, because metals and minerals seem to have various kinds of colors within them potentially, which are brought into action by some moving force.
<margin>Various experiments.</margin>
Indeed, we see that from lead <note>original: "plumbo"</note>, the greatest whiteness is produced by vinegar alone, and the greatest blackness by oil; from the same burning, yellow, vermilion <note>original: "miniatus"</note>, hyacinth-color, green, and red are drawn out. From vitriol <note>iron or copper sulfates</note> also come red, white, green, black, blue, and yellow, so that there is almost no mineral that does not contain innumerable colors within itself.

### Great Art of Light and Shadow, Book I, Part III.

<margin>Sal Ammoniac contains the seeds of all types of colors within itself.</margin>
...it possesses in potential, and finally brings it forth. Others seek a more immediate cause of color: they claim that Sal Ammoniac <note>original: "Sal Ammoniacum"; here referring not just to the chemical ammonium chloride, but to a "universal salt" or spiritual principle in alchemy believed to be the source of all color and life</note>, which is found in the greatest abundance in minerals, metals, and the earth, produces those various colors—not only in those substances, but also in plants, their flowers, and every part of an animal; and for that reason, it also generates colors in gems, stones, and all other things. Furthermore, they call this the "Sal Ammoniac of Nature," a certain life-giving spiritual Salt which, when joined with sublimated wine <note>distilled alcohol or spirits</note>, rises up before it. It is thought by them to be the "prime mover" in the generation of any thing, and no less a preserver—acting like a balsam—and an ornamenter of all things with various colors. The reason for this opinion is that it is found in all things and can be extracted from them. Furthermore, once collected and distilled, it displays every kind of color by itself, because it is of a fiery nature and almost incorruptible; even with the slightest heat, it dissolves into the air like an exhalation, which is most suitable for dyeing anything, and it tints glass with various colors. This is the view of Josephus Quercetanus <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a French physician and chemist</note> according to Anshelmus Boëtius <note>Anselmus de Boodt (1550–1632), a Flemish mineralogist and physician</note>. Some others believe colors are produced by the varying mixture of the elements and their "concoction" <note>the process of ripening or maturing through heat</note>. Most derive them from the primary qualities <note>the Aristotelian qualities: Hot, Cold, Wet, and Dry</note> passed into matter. We, leaving aside these various opinions, shall bind ourselves to one certain truth.

We do not deny, first of all, that colors can indeed have their origin from the primary qualities; for just as there are various juices in the human body, which all have their duties in the "Microcosmic Republic" <note>the human body viewed as a miniature version of the universe</note>—there are white, black, yellow, and red flows <note>original: "fluores"; referring to the bodily humors</note>—so nature has established various flows in the earth. These, penetrating all the winding paths of the earth, tint the ground they fall upon. 
<margin>The cause of different colors in stones.</margin>
Then, coagulated here by a "peach-like juice" <note>original: "succo persico"; likely referring to a specific mineralizing fluid or thick consistency</note>, it produces stones of different colors according to the variety of the mixture. Such stones are Marbles, Alabasters, and Jaspers, which have their origin from the "flow" created within the earth, just as the various streaks and irregular channels—now white, now black, as in Alabasters; now white and black, as in Jasper; now green with brown and yellow—sufficiently demonstrate. We have treated these matters specifically in our work *The Subterranean World* <note>original: "Mundo subterraneo"; Kircher's massive 1665 encyclopedia of geology</note>. Furthermore, there are certain "seedbeds" <note>original: "seminaria"</note> established in individual things by provident nature, from which each is assigned its own natural color, by which it might be distinguished from any other.
<margin>Why are colors bestowed upon things?</margin>
For just as the <term>shaping power</term> <note>original: "vis plastica"; the inherent force in nature that gives matter its form and shape</note> lurking in the seed grants to each thing its own form and figure suitable for its natural operations, so too in the seed of every thing there lurks a <term>chromatic power</term> <note>original: "vis chromatica"; the "coloring force"</note> by which each thing might be adorned with a suitable color. For if nature had not produced this diversity of colors in things,

<column-break/>

<margin>Certain colors owed to things are contained within the shaping power.</margin>
there would have been no distinction of individuality within the nature of things as far as sight is concerned. For we generally recognize a thing by its colored surface; and this is most clearly seen in gems and stones. Hence, stones and gems that have a peculiar and proper shape—such as <term>tongue-stones</term> <note>glossopetra; fossilized shark teeth</note>, star-stones <note>asteria</note>, coral, <term>Jewish stone</term> <note>lapis Judaicus; fossilized sea urchin spines used in medicine</note>, and the <term>cat's eye</term> <note>Aelurophtalmus</note>—usually possess the seedbed and principle of color in the nature from which they are formed. However, those which have no determined shape are usually tinted by an "exhalation" as a more remote cause, or by a "metallic spirit" and "Sal Ammoniac" as a more immediate cause. All colors, however, draw their origin either from light and darkness, or from heat and cold, or finally from transparency and opacity, as was said a little while ago. Here it must also be noted that all intermediate colors can be transparent; yet white and black are incapable of any transparency. 
<margin>No gems are perfectly white or black.</margin>
Hence, no gems are perfectly white or black. They are not white because the multitude of surfaces of which the matter is composed prevents the sight from passing through; just as crystal, when ground into powder, turns white, though its parts were previously transparent when united. In the same way, the whitest snow, when dissolved into water, is restored to its original transparency; and transparency always decreases in white bodies as much as whiteness increases, and vice-versa. Since transparent things consist of no color of their own, nature willed that when crushed they should assume no other color than white, as it is neighbor to the light. But if someone should object that the Ruby, Sapphire, and Emerald are transparent gems, and yet do not turn white when crushed? I respond that as much whiteness is added to these crushed gems as there is transparency in them. Hence it happens that colored gems reduced to powder no longer show that full color, but a "sub-white" <note>whitish or pale</note> one, since that tiny portion of color is much more brilliant by the benefit of light within the transparent medium than when "smothered" in the disconnected parts of the dust. Truly black gems cannot be transparent, since black most effectively terminates the sight, being the proper quality of opaque bodies. 
<margin>Intermediate colors are transparent.</margin>
All intermediate colors can be transparent, and are therefore capable of any color. Even a crystal, when a color is placed beneath it and viewed from the opposite side, appears entirely stained. For the color, transmitted by the refracted rays through the density of the crystal, seems to cling in it for a while and play about like something floating, until it reaches the desired point. Then, that flat surface of the crystal which is diametrically opposite the underlying color catches the rays of color raised upward from its internal or hollow part, and sends them back to the lowest surface of the crystal, which then...

# On the Colorations of Natural Things.

...they return again to the eyes, mixed with the first rays, they show a saturation of color through the density of the crystal more than they do in the surrounding air: thus it happens that the entire crystal appears to be tinted.

### *Experiment*
### *Deceptions in the Tinting of Gemstones.*

<margin>The Joining of Crystal.</margin>
Fragments of crystal are carved into the shape of a native gemstone. A silver foil, remarkably polished and dyed with a specific color, is placed underneath in its setting as tightly as possible so it doesn't fall out; thus, the crystal appears to be a natural gemstone. To make them even closer to an imitation of true gems, they carve two pieces of crystal so that when joined together they reflect the form of a single stone. It is necessary, however, for those surfaces where they are joined to be exactly flat. Furthermore, they join these together with a "tear" <note>referring to a drop of clear resin</note> of the purest sort, in which a specific color has been ground and perfectly mixed. For Mastic <note>A resin from the mastic tree, *Pistacia lentiscus*, used as a high-quality adhesive and varnish</note>, melting by fire and hardening by cold, binds the parts of the crystal into one body like a solder; the color, however, when viewed from the front through the density and depth of the crystal, will shine through. Because of the various reflections from every side, it imbues the stone with a much deeper tint than if only a dyed silver foil had been placed beneath it. Others also insert a glass tile dyed with a similar color between two fragments of crystal (such as selenite), coated with pure mastic. But see more concerning fake gems in our *Subterranean World* <note>Kircher's encyclopedic work *Mundus Subterraneus* (1665)</note> and in chapter 5 of our *Horographic Magic*.

### *Experiments*
### *Concerning the Wonderful Coloration of Minerals, Proven by the Author.*

<margin>A wonderful variety of colors in quicksilver.</margin>
We must explain a triple Chromatism <term>Chromatism: here used to mean the process by which a substance acquires or changes its color</term> here. The first occurs through the tinting of the entire mass by "projections" <note>an alchemical term for casting a powder into a melt</note> and absorptions. The second occurs through degrees of fire and cold. The third through washings, rinsings, and boilings. First, if you heat quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>—which has been frozen by the vapor of lead—in a bronze spoon over lit coals, behold! Soon such a great variety of colors will appear to you in the melted material that no greater variety could be imagined in the world. They are so bright that none of those called "apparent colors" <note>colors created by light refraction, like a rainbow, rather than by pigment</note> can be compared to them. From this experiment, which I have observed quite frequently, it became brilliantly clear that quicksilver is the seed of all metals, containing the potential and power of all their colors within itself, which are brought into action by heat.

<column-break/>

<margin>How copper is made white.</margin>
Secondly, if you wish to make white copper <note>a silver-colored alloy, often called "white brass" or "paktong"</note>, you can achieve this not only with calcined talc and tin, or by melting and boiling it with silver; but also by the "projection" of a powder made from the white lime of mercury sublimate nourished with oil of Tartar <note>a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</note>. You may also perform this whitening another way: take a powder made from lime of Tartar, Alum, and white Arsenic—diluted with a lye of lime and dried—and cast it into melted copper, and you will have what you seek. Sometimes we have played with a "water" made from mercury sublimate with Sal Ammoniac through deliquescence; copper or iron quenched in this is gifted with a silver color. <margin>The "Physical Egg," a great secret of nature.</margin> If someone wishes to put in the labor and repeat the sublimation again and again, then dissolve the sublimated materials in *aqua regia* <note>original: "aqua regia"; a highly corrosive mixture of acids capable of dissolving gold</note> and digest the solution; he will possess a great secret in nature: namely, the "Physical Egg," whose yolk in the middle is red, while the surrounding water acts as the white, which is tinted by the yolk just as the white is tinted by red.

<margin>The conversion of black lead into white.</margin>
Thirdly, you shall convert black lead into white by this art. Let a powder be made from white arsenic, lime of Tartar, rock salt, and Sal Ammoniac, which you shall soak in vinegar for seven days. After soaking, boil it until dry. Its dust, cast upon melted lead, will provide a great aid in fashioning silver-like vessels.

<margin>How Borax may become blue.</margin>
<margin>Which juices are suitable for dyeing.</margin>
Fourthly, the white Borax of the goldsmiths will be turned blue if it is ground, kneaded with urine, and dyed with Woad <note>original: "Glafto"; a plant used to produce blue dye</note>; or it becomes purple if it is dyed more intensely. By a similar art, you can dye crystalline sugar with colors that are not at all harmful. Also salts of every kind indiscriminately. Glassmakers also use it in tinting glass. The dyeing juices are those of black grapes, bloody Amaranth, pomegranate blossoms, "berry-bearing" knotgrass <note>likely *Polygonum*, used for red dyes</note>, and the seeds of the three-grained Heliotrope, which at first touch gives a green color, but soon turns blue and purple, most suitable for tinting papers. Also the leaves of Cyperus or Henna <note>original: "Alcanna"</note>, with whose juice the Arabs are accustomed to dye the manes and tails of horses and the feathers of ostriches red and yellow. Also American Cochineal, the "Dyer's Grain" <note>original: "Coccus Baphicus"</note>, and our own Kermes produce a purple dye. Alder leaves, Madder, and Woad dye in various ways, about which see *The Subterranean World*.

<margin>Another way of tinting things.</margin>
The second method is through degrees of fire, by the same reasoning through which we excited an infinite variety of colors from quicksilver earlier; just as others are also accustomed to excite most perfect colors of ineffable variety from Bismuth (or "Indian lead"). Therefore, not without reason, the Chemists <note>Alchemists</note> have called this the "Peacock's Tail" <note>original: "Caudam Pavonum"; a stage in the alchemical process where a rainbow of colors appears</note> and the "Iris" (the Rainbow). <margin>Other experiences concerning metallic colors.</margin> Therefore, by the power of fire, red ochre is made in new pots smeared with clay and burned; and the same material, once made white-hot and quenched in vinegar, will give a purple color. Truly, White Lead <note>original: "Ceruffa"</note> is made from lead and vinegar; this again...

# The Great Art, Book I, Part III.

<margin>Various experiments.</margin>
...burned again it becomes Minium <term>Minium: Red lead, a bright orange-red pigment often used in manuscripts</term>; copper burned with sulfur degenerates into Cinnabar <note>original: "Cinnabarim"; likely referring here to a copper sulfide compound that resembles mercury-based cinnabar</note>. Spirit of vitriol <term>Spirit of vitriol: Sulfuric acid</term> tints iron into copper; Sal Ammoniac <term>Sal Ammoniac: Ammonium chloride, used by alchemists as a flux and cleansing agent</term> turns lead into tin. The colors of individual substances, if they are smeared with another species, acquire another appearance through "cooking" <note>concoctio: a process of heating or ripening</note>, just as types of vitriol do. For heat affects the matter of colors; indeed, it can make dull colors illustrious. If you mix water with pottery clay and scales of copper smoothed upon a porphyry stone, the mixture appears stained with a reddish color like copper; yet when exposed to the fire of a furnace, it is made green. The color prepared from the scales of iron is "Melinus" <note>A yellowish-white or quince-colored pigment mentioned by Pliny</note>. Raw Zaffre <term>Zaffara: A cobalt ore used to produce deep blue glass and glazes</term> tints pottery, but when thoroughly cooked in a dark fire, it is changed into a most excellent blue. Caesalpinus <note>Andrea Cesalpino (1524–1603), an influential Italian physician and botanist</note> says there is a stone that tints glass blue, and if a little more is added, black; from ash-colored it tends toward a very dense, brittle purple, which does not melt by itself, but when nitre <note>Saltpeter or sodium carbonate</note> is added, it flows like water. However, since I have not yet performed an experiment on its practice, I would not wish to affirm it.

<column-break/>

<margin>Through washing and boiling.</margin>
The third method is through elutions <note>elutiones: the process of washing or extracting a material</note> and boiling, by this industrious method: metallic things that can be diluted and dissolved in water, such as salts and alums, are purged of filth by dissolving them in pure water, filtering, and coagulating them. This work is repeated as long and as many times as necessary until a pure and splendid color is achieved. Thus salts, whether mined or boiled down, and those extracted by art from ashes, are white, shining with a snowy brilliance; some are even transparent, such as saltpeter and alum. Litharge <term>Litharge: Lead oxide, usually yellow or reddish</term> is not only thinned by washings but is even rendered snowy white. I could hand down innumerable experiments in this place, but since we have reserved them for our *Subterranean World* <note>Kircher's massive 1665 work, *Mundus Subterraneus*, which deals with geology and chemistry</note>, I have thought it superfluous to repeat them here. From all of these things it is clearly evident that the cause and reason for the composition of colors is entirely diverse and cannot be bound to a single cause. All of these, however, depend on the precepts handed down just a little while ago.

# CHAPTER VI.
## Botanical Chromatism.
->OR<-
### On the colors shining forth in herbs.

---

<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'I' featuring ornate leaf patterns and scrollwork.</image-desc>
In herbs, flowers, and fruits, the fact that nature plays with a remarkable variety of colors is more than sufficiently testified by the various distinctions of Tulips, Lilies, and Anemones. For that the flowers of the Iris have such a harmonious series of colors, that Tulips now redden from black into yellow, now turn purple from white into blue, and now luxuriate into every kind of color from a multicolored base—this should by no means be granted to the primary qualities alone. Rather, as was said in the preceding sections, it is due to the "chromatic virtue" <term>chromatic virtue: The specific innate power within a living thing to produce its colors</term> contained in the "spermatic faculty" <term>spermatic faculty: The reproductive or formative essence of a seed</term>. Just as the "plastic virtue" <term>plastic virtue: From the Greek 'plastikos', the formative force that shapes an organism according to its kind</term>, which each plant contains, 
<margin>From where does color in flowers come?</margin>
enriches the plant with the proper and fitting shape of its leaves, flowers, and fruits; so also the chromatic virtue—with the primary qualities and the "sal ammoniac" existing in each thing serving as a vehicle for the colors—bestows a convenient color upon individual plants, flowers, and fruits, whether for ornament or for the knowledge of its interior character, as if it were an interpreter of its own virtues. How nature bears itself in such a diverse production of colors must now be explained.

<column-break/>

<margin>Why plants are green,</margin>
It is asked first, then, why individual plants are green as soon as they emerge from the earth, then become earthy, and finally are imbued with one color or another in their flowers and fruits. I respond: since every variety of colors in herbs proceeds from "concoction" <note>the process of ripening or chemical refinement through heat</note>, which is nothing other than a perfection emanating from natural heat, the earthy moisture will be, as it were, the matter of the plants and simultaneously their nourishment when they are born. The Sun, however, is like the father and the cook, so that the nature of plants is similar to stagnant waters thickened with green and saffron-yellow. Just as colors are produced in water by the action of the Sun, so it is in plants. Moreover, the more the moisture is dried out, the more they approach yellowness and green. Hence in Autumn we see most trees turn yellow. Why the 
<margin>Why the root of plants is white.</margin>
root is mostly white is because, being implanted in the earth, it can neither be reached by the solar rays nor consequently be dried out, whence it remains in its original state; but as soon as the seed, excited by heat, has gone out of the earth, the moisture begins to be cooked by the Sun and the efficiency of the surrounding air, and consequently tends from natural moisture toward dryness; not otherwise than...

# On the Colorations of Natural Things.

...and we have spoken about the greening water, to which the moisture of plants in all things is likened. Therefore, all moisture, through the action of the Sun, obtains a green nature. However, when a stalk has been thoroughly dried out from an abundance of moisture, it seems to take on an earthy nature; the moisture then bursts out into the leaves. When the leaves no longer grow, nature—using the generative power <note>original: "spermatica vi"; the life-force responsible for reproduction and growth</note> within—first paints the flowers with the remaining sap, according to the seminal reasons <note>original: "seminales rationes"; a philosophical concept referring to the internal "blueprints" or "seeds" of design within a species</note> of each plant.

<margin>How colors are changed in plants.</margin>
In the center of the flowers, where the moisture is concentrated by the action of the Sun, the matter is gradually "cooked" <note>concoctio: the process of ripening, often likened to digestion or chemical refinement</note> into fruit as nature requires. Sal ammoniac <term>Sal ammoniac: Ammonium chloride; alchemists believed this salt was invisibly present in plants to help produce color</term>, invisibly admitted into the fruit, provides it a color proportioned to its seminal reason. Thus, the "radical moisture" of a plant is the material cause of colors, holding the potential for all types of colors of which any plant is capable. The efficient cause is the Sun, through the heat of the surrounding air, which performs the cooking and ripening; by this, the colors proper to individual plants are brought from potential into reality. All of this is clearly seen in the Cherry: first, from the green, it produces white flowers decorated inside with golden threads. In the center of these, the earlier moisture, as yet "undigested," turns into a green ball, then into a reddish one, then purple, and finally into a black edible fruit, following certain degrees of cooking and ripening as nature demands, until it achieves its perfection and serves the needs of man, for whose sake it was produced. From this, it is clear why green buds produce flowers that are sometimes white (as in most Apples, Pears, and Cherries) or sometimes a reddish-flesh color (as in Almonds). The fruits, meanwhile, are sometimes green (like Peaches), sometimes yellow-orange (like Melons), occasionally reddish (like Apples), sometimes deep purple (like Plums), and in many cases black (like Mulberries). This is because the stages of ripening take on colors according to the plant's natural temperament and its seminal reasons, as has been frequently emphasized.

<margin>Why black and green flowers are not found.</margin>
It is also clear why black and green flowers are rarely found. This is because leaves occupy the first stage of growth, and flowers the second. Since green is appropriate for the first stage of production, it cannot belong to the flowers—except very rarely or when induced by art, as will be seen later. Nor can they be black, because the color black denotes perfect cooking, ripening, drying, and the final stage of perfection, which cannot occur in flowers. But you might say many flowers have spots, like the Poppy. I respond that these spots are not a sign of ripening, but the work of the generative faculty intended by nature as an ornament for the flower, as the striped patterns in Beans, Peonies, and all others clearly show.

<column-break/>

## Experiments.

->By what art and method given colors may be induced into flowers.<-

<margin>Flowers are not colored by metallic juices.</margin>
Truly, those "Paeologists" <note>likely referring to botanical theorists or those specializing in the Peony (Paeonia)</note> are greatly deluded who think color can be induced in flowers by metallic juices. Since metallic juices are mostly corrosive and endowed with a certain "gnawing" faculty, they are far from helping flowers; rather, they destroy them completely, being composed of a foreign nature. Thus, Porta <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), an influential Italian scientist famous for his work on "Natural Magic"</note> is mistaken in thinking that plant roots watered with the juice of Cinnabar <note>original: "Cinnabaris succo"; mercury sulfide, a bright red pigment</note> will flourish into intensely red flowers. All those are deceived who believe that flowers darkened with Ochre, Sandarac <note>original: "Sandaraca"; here referring to a red arsenic mineral</note>, or Orpiment <note>original: "Auripigmento"; a yellow arsenic mineral</note> will change into a tawny or yellowish color. They err who hope to produce an intense color by first miserably torturing bulbs in vinegar for several days and then adding some mineral juice. These are the various persuasions of inexperienced men: nature seeks what is "homogeneous" [of the same kind] and is impatient of anything "heterogeneous" or of a dissimilar nature. Therefore, anyone who desires to produce new "monsters" <note>monstra: in the sense of marvelous or extraordinary botanical variations</note> of flowers must do so with juices of the same kind—that is, herbaceous ones. And not just any herbaceous juices, but those that are "sympathetic" to the nature of the flower being tinted. It should also be known that any color which nature spontaneously avoids cannot be introduced by any art, such as the color black.

<margin>Flowers cannot be imbued with black color by art.</margin>
Therefore, those who want mourning flowers to emerge in a blackish dress by watering plant roots with the juice of the Cuttlefish <note>original: "Loliginis succo"; squid or cuttlefish ink</note> are wandering far from the truth. In vain does one give what nature denies. Anyone who yearns to perform the miracles of nature must observe nature’s rule exactly; if he does otherwise, he will sooner "wash an Ethiopian" <note>A common classical idiom for attempting the impossible</note> than force nature to obey him. Indeed, I say further, led and taught by long experience, that no juice—even one born of plants—can properly and naturally tint flowers. This is because all tinting proceeds from the plant's own internal "radical moisture," and because external heat cannot overcome the internal natural color hidden in the generative mass without a change in its very essence. Eventually, the tint will be forced to submit to the plant’s own nature. The plant's "chromatic power" will struggle to transform any incoming color into its own nature, much like red wine that is drunk is usually tinted by the kidneys and bladder into the natural color of the limbs. If this were not so, in places with red earth, all plants would burst into red flowers, just as in chalky places they would have to be white—yet experience shows the opposite. Therefore, let no one trust Porta,

<margin>By grafting, plants acquire various different colors.</margin>
Regarding the "impostures" of Alessio Piemontese and Johann Wecker <note>popular authors of "books of secrets" containing recipes for alchemy and household magic</note>, no one is better taught in certain methods and dyes for flowers than our friend Ferrarius in his *Culture of Flowers*, as instructed by the philosopher Faber the Lyncean <note>Joannes Faber, a member of the Accademia dei Lincei, the same prestigious scientific society as Galileo</note>; I could only wish that this "Lynx-eyed" observer had seen more clearly in such a manifest matter. Nature, therefore, has taught us another way by which we can tint flowers, and this is done through the art of "emphyteutics," or grafting. Experience teaches that a Peach grafted onto a Mulberry produces fruit that is entirely red with a blood-like color; there is no doubt about this, as it is nearly common knowledge. It is similarly well-known that an Almond grafted onto a Pear assumes the colors of the pear blossoms while it is in bloom. By this art, therefore, the seeds of different plants can be so joined together that they obtain a shared nature, as it were, and a reciprocal use of color. Thus, if the bulb of a white flower is grafted into a red Parsnip or a "Blood-Beet," it will no longer shine with white, but with a blood-red color; if, however, you graft the same plant into the root of Alkanet <note>original: "Anchusa"; a plant whose roots are used to produce a red dye</note>, through this clever and conciliatory grafting, it will deviate from white and shine with the reddish-purple color of the Alkanet.

<column-break/>

<margin>Various examples of grafting.</margin>
If, however, you desire a bicolor offspring for a plant, a white Rose grafted onto a red one will produce a rose sharing both colors. Likewise, Carnation flowers grafted into various bulbs will yield a mixture of whatever colors the flowers were. Some even lead Roses and Jasmine to bloom with a conspicuous golden beauty by grafting them onto Broom <note>original: "Genista"; a shrub known for its bright yellow flowers</note>. And this is the true method of tinting flowers that conforms to nature; I have no doubt that whoever observes it will perform miracles in the intentional transformation of flowers. Truly, he who desires to know more of this sort should consult our *Magnetic World* <note>Kircher's book "Magnes, sive de Arte Magnetica"</note>, where we have discussed this "phytomagnetism" at length. As for the wonderful secret of nature by which the shapes of any things whatever can be induced into plants and flowers themselves by a certain magical and hitherto unheard-of craftsmanship; since that is not of this forum, we have reserved it for our *Subterranean World* <note>Kircher's massive work "Mundus Subterraneus"</note>.

### On the colors in Animals.

The class of Quadrupeds allows for a smaller variety of colors, yet among them, the Horse is notable above the rest. Its most common colors are white, black, and red, from the mixture of which yellow, chestnut, and ash-gray arise; each of these has different causes. # On the Coloration of Natural Things.

Quadrupeds <note>four-legged mammals</note> rarely take on green, gold, or blue colors, as these colors are naturally incompatible with their temperament; the aforementioned colors are the work of a watery nature and, consequently, are proper to plants. But because they also have their origin from the waters: 
<margin>Why birds are capable of every kind of color.</margin>
Birds, however, draw their origin partly from water and partly from air; hence birds are capable of all the colors of which herbs and plants are also capable.
<margin>Why insects receive all types of colors.</margin>
Insects, however, since they consist of a mixed nature from earth, air, and water, also enjoy all colors—not indeed by certain natural intentions, but according to the disposition of the decaying matter from which they are mostly born <note>This refers to the historical theory of "spontaneous generation," where insects were thought to arise from rotting material</note>; or from imagination, by which they are transformed into various colors; or finally, by natural metamorphosis, which a diversity of colors necessarily follows. Therefore, four-legged animals, which abound in earthy moisture more than other land creatures, are incapable of the color green, both for the stated reason and also because of the mucous sluggishness and the waste product from which the skin is nourished. For the waste products that nourish the skin are either blood or phlegm <note>original: "pituita"; one of the four bodily humors in ancient medicine</note>, the waste of neither of which is green, herbaceous, leek-colored, or purple; but these colors are taken on by those things born from bile, which blood and phlegm cannot nourish.
<margin>Why perfect quadrupeds are not imbued with a golden color.</margin>
Furthermore, as to why quadrupeds—unlike birds—are incapable of those shining colors like gold, sky-blue, and purple, I assign this reason: since the hair of animals is very thin and one does not stick to another, it cannot reflect the light of the Sun mixed with color. But in feathers this does not happen, since they adhere to each other in such a way that they form one continuous surface, as it were; and therefore, by refracting the shining rays, they can better reflect colors of this sort. Thus, the primary cause of color...

<column-break/>

<margin>The cause of color in living creatures.</margin>
...in animals, insofar as it depends on temperament, is moisture variously affected by heat. As for the fact that many animals are now seen spotted with black and white, or white and red, we say the cause of this change is the work resulting from the imagination of the animals during mating <note>This refers to the "maternal imagination" theory, where it was believed that what an animal saw or thought during conception could influence the offspring's appearance</note>, as we shall say later. Again, as for the fact that certain birds shine with a marvelous order and arrangement of colors, we assert this is the work of a "Chromatic faculty" latent in the seed, intended ultimately for the adornment of the living creature and the pleasure of human sight. Of this sort are Peacocks, Kingfishers, Hoopoes, and countless other birds that have become known in the New World, in whose feathers the will and choice of a "Painter-Architect" <note>A metaphor for God or the organizing intelligence of Nature</note> is clearly perceived. For when a single small feather of a Peacock, which we call the "mirror" <note>original: "speculum"; the "eye" of the peacock feather</note>, is arranged with such artistry and such a variety of colors in the most exquisite order, we can certainly assign no other cause to this work than reason and an architectural intellect. For physical qualities act on matter in a blind way and observe no specific shape; yet in the peacock's "mirrors," a shape is observed in the colors, along with a boundary for where such-and-such a color ought to be. This is no different than what Nature usually does when she builds a human; for she observes a shape in everything and, by the benefit of a "plastic faculty" <note>the formative power in nature that gives things their shape</note>, establishes a boundary in the matter for how far it ought to proceed.

### The Great Art, Book I, Part III

...and has rough, bony edges that are lightly serrated. Its eyes are very large, set in deep hollows, and match the color of its body; the pupil itself does not move, but the animal looks around by moving the entire eye, always keeping its mouth gaping open. It has a long tongue, similar to an earthworm, at the end of which is a certain spongy and sticky bulb; with this, it draws in the flies, gnats, and mosquitoes on which it lives, as if they were caught in birdlime <note>A sticky substance historically used to trap small birds</note>. I have personally tested this: when a fly was held out, the chameleon snatched it with its palm-length tongue and immediately pulled it into its belly without any movement of its lips. Therefore, those who assert that this animal lives on air or dew alone are wonderfully mistaken; for why would nature have granted it a belly and a tongue if it were deprived of the ability to eat? Its front feet were very different from the hind ones; the former had three toes on the inside and two on the outside, while the latter had three on the outside and two on the inside. It is an animal of a cold temperament, as can be gathered from the sluggish motion it adopts. Having described its form, it now remains for us to see into which colors it turns itself. Most authors report that it turns into all colors except white and red. However, experience has taught me otherwise. For this chameleon, when placed on a green cloth, turned so green that it could hardly be distinguished from the cloth beneath it; but when wrapped in a very white handkerchief, it grew so white that it could not even be told apart from the handkerchief itself. Indeed, some people, barely able to see the animal when it had transformed into the whiteness of the cloth, thought they had lost it. So—

<margin>The cause of the colors.</margin>
—it immediately assimilates whatever colors it touches. Various authors assign various causes for this. Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman grammarian and compiler</note> says it reflects colors it encounters like a mirror, due to the reflection of its leathery skin. Others attribute the cause to the animal's fear and its food, which they believe is air alone. Let us reveal what we think. First, it must be known that just as this animal is extremely cold, it is also extremely timid. It is also very slow-moving, so that it can in no way escape the danger of those lying in wait for it, except by this single gift of nature: that it transforms itself into the color of the thing it sits upon so perfectly that it cannot be seen, and thus eludes the eyes of its predators. Nature therefore granted it a skin—which I have observed with the greatest curiosity—consisting of a somewhat dilated, translucent moisture <note>original: "humore pellustri"</note> that is highly suited for taking on colors. Thus, when it is placed on a green leaf, the animal's imagination <note>original: "phantasia"; early modern science often attributed physical changes to the power of an animal's "imagination" or internal sensory processing</note>, as if dancing at a most pleasing object, dilates the skin and makes it ready to absorb colors. This dilated skin receives the "species" <note>The visual qualities or "forms" of an object</note> of the color within the translucent moisture of the skin, much like light is received in our Phengite stone <note>A type of transparent or translucent crystal, possibly selenite, used by ancients for windows</note>, or in "Phosphorus" <note>likely referring to bioluminescent minerals or the "Bolognian Stone" rather than the chemical element</note> when ex-

<column-break/>

-posed to light. Since the moisture of the skin is uniform and continuous, it happens that the greenness of the leaf beneath it, drawn into itself, reflects the entire body back to the eyes of observers. The same thing happens if it is placed on white cloth or paper.

<margin>What is the effective principle of color in the Chameleon.</margin>
The effective principle of color <note>The "active cause" in Aristotelian terms</note>—the *material* cause—is the animal's skin with its flowing, translucent moisture. But the *formal* cause—the "how"—is the animal's imagination itself. By perceiving a colored body, the animal dilates its skin, making it ready to absorb the color. For a dead chameleon is moved by no color; this is a clear sign that there is an internal principle by which it transforms itself into the target color through voluntary motion. This is not unlike how we see a human face turn red from shame or pale when struck by fear. For a similar reason, it is well known that the Polyp <note>an Octopus</note> changes according to the color of the rock to which it clings. This is my opinion on the "Chromatism" <note>The process of coloring</note> of the chameleon; however, if someone teaches me a better one, I promise I will not be unwilling to support them.

### Experiment on the Coloration of Animals.

This "Chromatism" has been discussed at length in our *Art* <note>Referring to his previous works or the general discipline</note>. Therefore, I thought it should be briefly repeated here. It should be noted that the great variety of colors shining forth in animals has its origin in the imagination—either of the animals during mating, or of birds sitting on their eggs. For whatever color they imagine at that time, they will pass that same color on to their offspring. Sacred Scripture itself teaches this "Chromatic Magic" in Genesis 30 <note>The text says Gen 27, but the story of the rods is Gen 30</note>, where Jacob, by placing variegated and spotted rods before the mating flocks, produced spotted offspring. By this art, dogs and horses will produce offspring of the same color as the blankets under which they were kept while mating. If these are spotted like tigers, or marked with white and red, white and red animals will be born. Likewise, birds will hatch chicks of the same color as the curtains within which they sat while brooding over their eggs. Such is the power of the imaginative faculty. Hence, Ravens and Bears in the Arctic regions turn to a snowy color due to the perpetual sight of the snow, through the power of the imaginative faculty. Hence, domestic birds are transformed into all kinds of colors by the variety of objects around them. From these briefly suggested points, the reason is clear by which a "Mage of Light and Shadow" <note>original: "Magus Luc-umbris"</note> can perform wonders in the coloration of animals through the benefit of light and shadow. But for those who want more on these matters, as I have said, let them consult *The Magnetic World* <note>Kircher's own work, *Mundus Magneticus* (1641)</note>, which treats these things more extensively.

# CHAPTER VIII.

### The Art of Chromocritics, or on the Judgment and Divination of Colors.

<image-desc>A decorative historiated initial 'C' containing a figure, likely a scholar or philosopher, surrounded by ornate leafy vine-work.</image-desc>
SINCE the colors of natural objects provide the clearest indications of their internal light or shadow, heat or cold, and moisture or dryness—and since heat, cold, moisture, and dryness are the primary elements of all mixed bodies—I believe no one can doubt that a wise <term>physiologist</term> <note>In this context, a "physiologist" is a natural philosopher who studies the inner workings and "physics" of nature.</note> can produce many insights into the nature of anything, or form probable judgments about it, based on the external "tint" or color with which it is clothed. Therefore, having investigated the colors of individual things, along with their causes and origins, to the best of our ability in the preceding chapters, it remains for us to apply this <term>Chromotosophia</term> <note>From the Greek "chroma" (color) and "sophia" (wisdom): the wisdom or deep knowledge of color.</note> to our Art of light and shadow, and to turn the study of these matters toward some human use. However, we shall proceed here only according to universal principles. For I am well aware that countless causes contribute to the "complexion" (the physical and temperamental makeup) of men, just as infinite mixtures of colors can be created; thus, there are as many diverse inclinations in a person as there are diverse faces and countenances. Consequently, nothing can be determined with absolute certainty or "apodictic" proof in this matter—which is not our intention here anyway. Rather, we are investigating only the universal principles of color in humans in order to draw certain conjectures.

### §. I. Chromocritics of the Weather.

IT is well known, not only to sailors and farmers but to anyone who pays any heed to the time, that changes in the weather are detected by no truer signs than the various tints of the clouds and the sky. Most of these manifest themselves through the "light-shadowed" <note>original: "lucumbri," a blend of light and shadow</note> color of various clouds mixed with light. Furthermore, because the production of rain clouds depends mostly on the rising and setting of the Sun, the Moon, and the fixed stars, one must especially observe their "Chronica," "Cosmica," and "Heliacal" <note>These refer to different timings of a star's appearance in relation to the sun: rising at sunset, rising with the sun, etc.</note> disappearances and appearances. Therefore, the most characteristic signs of the weather are taken first from the light of the Sun and the Moon as they are variously affected. For since the Moon is like a "second Sun" at night, and for the same reason—due to a lack of light—the beginnings of the months until the diagram of the <term>dichotomous</term> <note>original: "διχοτόμου," meaning "cut in half," referring to the half-moon or first quarter phase.</note> Moon are colder; and thereafter, as the light gradually prevails, the heat intensifies. One must especially watch the points of the "dichotomous" Moon, and by their logic, consider the year, the day, and the months. The Pleiades

<column-break/>

<margin>The rising of the Pleiades.</margin>
undergo a "dichotomous" year both in their rising and their setting, as do the Solstices and the Equinoxes. For whatever the state of the air happens to be at the setting of the Pleiades, or at the point of the Solstice or Equinox, the air itself usually retains that same state until the next Solstice or Equinox; if a change is to occur, it happens after the Solstice. But if no change occurs then, the air will remain in its state until the Equinox, and likewise from there until the rising of the Pleiades. As unshakeable experience has taught, the Moon acts upon these lower regions as the "monkey of the Sun" through a certain parallel <term>photismus</term> <note>Illumination or light-pattern.</note>. Indeed, the rays of the full and the middle Moon bisect the month (starting from the new moon) in such a way that a change usually happens on the fourth day, or at least the seventh; and if no change occurs by that time, it will certainly happen at the full moon. Likewise, one should track from the full moon to the seventh day of the waning month, from the seventh to the fourth, and from there back to the <term>Neomenia</term> <note>The New Moon or the start of the lunar month.</note> and the "silent" Moon. This same pattern of change usually takes place within a natural day; for the morning sunrise, noon, evening, and sunset—like different degrees of light—correspond to the parts of the night as if they were parallel degrees of shadow, and they hold equal power in the changes of the weather. But for all these matters, you may consult what was treated more extensively in the preceding sections. Therefore, setting aside general signs, let us descend to particulars. Let this be:

->The First Rule.<-

WHENEVER the sky turns purple before sunrise amidst darker clusters of clouds, it certainly portends either rain later that day or a change in the weather. If this happens in the evening, it portends fair weather, according to that common saying:

> A red sky in the morning indicates coming rains:
> A red sky late in the day indicates it will be serene.
<note>This is a version of the famous "Red sky at night, sailors' delight; Red sky in morning, sailors take warning."</note>

<margin>Why does a red sky in the morning portend rain, but in the evening fair weather?</margin>
But one might rightly wonder here: why does the same appearance of red in the morning and evening Sun produce different weather effects? I answer: purple clouds in the morning portend rain because the rising Sun, with its vehement heat, soon distills into water the nocturnal vapors and clouds heavy with moisture that have been raised, as they are already predisposed toward rain. However, the evening vapors—not dissolved by the daytime Sun—are coagulated and condensed by the cold of the night. Thus, pressed by the weight of their own inherent gravity, they are restored to the earth from which they came by "postliminy" <note>A legal term used metaphorically here to mean "returning to one's original state or right."</note>, leaving the state of the air purified of all dregs of exhalations. Furthermore, if the rising Sun proceeds from a black veil, it portends both rain and winds; for the blackish color of the clouds denotes both a packing together of vapors and, consequently, the most suitable material for winds; winds, if the clouds...
