## §. II. The Color-Diagnosis of Stones, Plants, and Animals.

### *§. I. On the opinions of certain authors regarding colors in plants.*

<margin>Plants of the same color are not always of the same nature, but have different qualities.</margin>
<margin>Why the eyes of children are white.</margin>
We are dealing here with a slippery business, and I have no doubt it will seem reckless to those who judge things only by their outermost surface. I am well aware that one and the same plant can have various colors. For some show a white root, a green stalk, and on this <note>original: "πανταχρώμους"</note> multicolored flowers. However, the colors white, black, red, yellow, and blue have different causes for their mixtures, as has been said. Hence, in two plants of the most diverse natures, we still find the same color. Thus, Leopard's Bane <note>Aconitum genus, known for being highly toxic.</note> produces a perfectly golden flower, and we see the Sow-thistle produce the same; yet experience has taught that the former is lethal to those who take it, while the latter is extremely healthy for those who eat it. From this, something other than color is required for us to perfectly know the character lying hidden beneath the plant's color. For this to become known, we must first investigate where the color in plants comes from and what it consists of. There are, therefore, various colors in plants: white, yellow, red, gold, crimson, blue, and a dark hue verging on black. From the mixture of these, innumerable others arise, acting as intermediates. Our inquiry begins with white. Aristotle says that whiteness comes from weakness; and for this reason, it is seen in the eyes of children, for newly born offspring are weak; but later, they change into their own colors implanted by nature. We subscribe to this opinion all the more willingly because we see great arguments for its truth. For I see that almost all living creatures are white, whether they are produced that way because of weakness or some blind defect of nature. Theophrastus supports this opinion: all things are white before they are black, being weaker and more fragile, both in animals and in

<column-break/>

a blue shadow of the luminous sphere, fashioning a sort of rudimentary rainbow. Whenever this happens, you may certainly divine that southern rains are imminent. Hence, the phenomena of <term>parhelia</term> <note>Also known as "sundogs," these are bright spots that appear on either side of the sun due to ice crystals in the atmosphere.</note> and halos, by common judgment, promise heavy rains for the same reason. Thus, the colors of the heavenly lights approaching dark tints promise rain; those approaching redness promise winds; and those approaching white, gold, and rose most often promise a "laughing" sky.
> *A pale Moon rains, a red one blows, a white one clears.*
But leaving these things aside as commonly known, let us turn ourselves to the other secrets of our <term>Chromocritice</term> <note>The art of judging or divining through colors.</note>.

Since they arise from superfluous moisture, they do not have a firm substance; that they are weak is evidenced by roses and the leaves and fruit of the pomegranate, which are white at the beginning, but finally, through the <term>concoction</term> <note>A term from Galenic medicine and alchemy referring to the "ripening" or "cooking" of internal fluids by heat.</note> of the juice, they change into a crimson or <note>original: "halurgum"</note> sea-purple color. The parts of the leaves near the root always turn white, since moisture abounds there from the supply of nourishment; on the other hand, the tips of the leaves are usually more colored, since there is less moisture and more "concoction" there. Whiteness in plants, therefore, occurs from the admission of watery parts with earthy ones, and signifies a moist and cold <term>complexion</term> <note>The physical temperament or balance of humors.</note>; in humans, however, brightness from the mixing of earthy parts with air denotes a balanced temperament of color. It should also be noted that when transparency is present with whiteness in a watery moisture, it denotes that little "earth" is in it, except as much as suffices for the boundary of the transparent moisture; but where there is opacity, there is more earth. Hence the Gourd, Chickweed, Water-lily, Knotgrass, the white flowers of pear trees, and white Roses are of a cold and moist temperament. White animals also follow this, such as the Goose, the Swan, the Ostrich, the white Rabbit, and similar creatures, which are full of moist and cold excrements. The lemon-yellow or saffron color in plants, just as it is midway between white and red, also obtains a middle temperament between the said colors, always observing the nature of the place they enjoy. For just as the yellow flower of the Buttercup <note>original: *Ranunculus*</note>, which delights in water, is warm in the first degree, so the flower of St. John's Wort <note>original: *Hypericon*</note>, which delights in mountains, is warm in the third degree and yellower than the Buttercup. For flowers also have degrees of intensity and remission in their colors, which he who intends to practice Phytomancy <note>the art of diagnosing the nature or future of plants, or using plants for diagnosis</note> must observe. For just as the bright colors, white and yellow, relate to the dark ones—red, blue, and black—so too the temperament of plants, which the colors indicate, relates to the [general] temperament. For since every temperament is composed of hot, cold, moist, and dry, and these qualities originally arise from various mixtures of light, certainly he who knows how to combine everything rightly will easily come to the knowledge of plants through this parallel comparison. But having briefly sampled these things, let us now establish some rules by whose benefit we may be more easily aided in discerning the nature of plants.

## §. III. Rules for the Color-Diagnosis of Stones, Plants, and Animals.

<margin>Various powers in plants.</margin>
First, it must be noted that our purpose here is by no means to speak of the hidden or specific virtues of plants, but of those that emanate from the primary qualities. For the hidden powers of things do not depend on the natural temperament in any way, but have their own origins, which only he is fit to assign who has penetrated with a sagacious mind those secret seedbeds of hatred and love, concord and discord, among natural things <note>This refers to the "sympathies and antipathies" common in Renaissance natural magic</note>. Indeed, to investigate the powers of these plants more deeply, I planted plants of rare faculty gathered from everywhere in our domestic garden, so that from the combination of colors, juices, flowers, fruits, and leaves, I might arrive at a true knowledge of their qualities; hence I have thought nothing should be said here which experience itself has not made me certain of.

Second, it must be noted that a triple virtue can be considered in plants: either manifest, emanating from the primary qualities; or specific and occult, flowing from the form of the thing; or a middle one resulting from both, which again constitutes a plant fit for use and health-bringing, or poisonous, or of a middle quality, an Antidote <note>original: *Alexiteria*</note>. Regarding each of these, these rules may be formed.

### First Rule.

<margin>Rule.</margin>
Whenever, therefore, herbs of the same color occur which nevertheless produce different effects, persuade yourself that this is a manifest sign of some added latent virtue having no commerce with the primary qualities.

### Second Rule.

<margin>Herbs resembling bile are useful for increasing or expelling bile.</margin>
All other herbs which, by their flowers or juice, resemble one of the four humors—namely blood, yellow bile, phlegm, and black bile—contribute for the most part to either increasing or expelling that same humor.

### Third Rule.

The saffron colors of edible plants, and those which swell with a tawny and golden juice, increase bile when taken in continuous use, provided they have their origin from the primary qualities. <margin>Which are the bile-expelling herbs?</margin> Of this kind are Orache <note>original: *Atriplex*</note>, which according to Pythagoras causes the "royal disease" <note>jaundice</note> and paleness; Musk-melons, honey, saffron, and tawny turnips. The juice of the Coconut <note>original: *indicæ nucis*</note>, and all plants which, besides their color, are imbued with a sweet taste, increase yellow bile in a wondrous way. Some things cause jaundice <note>original: *Ictericos*</note> even without being eaten, as Philes <note>Manuel Philes, a 14th-century Byzantine poet who wrote on the properties of animals</note> reports concerning the yellow frog, which douses those looking at it too intently with a jaundiced color. Authors report the same of the saffron-colored Lizard <note>original: *Stellione*</note>. Truly, saffron-colored herbs, whether in flower or juice, which among the edible...

Consequently, the former will move bile more, while the latter will move phlegm. I have decided to indicate these things briefly, lest we seem to have asserted anything "too universally" <note>original Greek: *καθολικωτέρως* (katholikoteros)</note> in such a difficult business.

### Rule Four.

<margin>Black-colored herbs.</margin>
Whatever plants are rough with a black color show themselves to be children of black bile by this very mournful clothing. Therefore, by a certain similarity, some will increase black bile (the melancholic humor), while others will even evacuate that which has increased. Know for certain, then, that whichever herbs are sad with a black color, or show themselves fierce with a yellow, brownish, or spotted mantle, portend something contrary and detrimental to human nature. Pythagoras, in his precepts, said that black things pertain to death. Macrobius, citing the testimony of Veranius in his book *On Pontifical Words*, pronounced that black trees were "unhappy" and white ones "happy";

<column-break/>

for which reason they were committed to the protection of the lower deities (the gods of the Underworld), about which we have treated at length in our *Oedipus Hieroglyphicus*. Dream-interpreters also, as seen in Artemidorus, signify the commotion of black bile and all things ill-fated through "black dreams." Herbs of a black or ashen color, or others declining toward black, are:

<margin>The noxious power of Henbane.</margin>
Henbane <note>original: *Hyosciamus*</note>, whose seeds when devoured strike not only men but all animals with vertigo and drive them mad; Bindweed <note>original: *Smilax*</note>, Mandrake, and several kinds of Celery, Nightshade, and Poppy. These herbs consist of flowers that are partly black, partly yellow and ashen, or spotted with a spreading paleness. All these foul and formidable things, by the increase of black bile, not only excite "scotomia" <note>dizziness with dimness of sight</note>, vertigo, and epilepsy, but also occasionally kill men through lethargy.

<margin>Monkshood resembles a dead man's head in its flower.</margin>
The Monkshood <note>original: *Napellus*</note> demonstrates how formidable it is by its very flower, which expresses the skull of a dead man.

<margin>Properties of the Bean.</margin>
It was not without reason that Pythagoras wanted his disciples to abstain from the Bean <note>original: *Faba*</note>, a plant of a pale nature. To those who eat it frequently, it brings delusion and a stupor of the mind with significant disturbance. Indeed, by its flatulent breath of vapor and its "satyric" effects <note>referring to sexual arousal or lust</note>, it so convulses the person that it renders students of wisdom incapable of performing the actions of the mind with dignity. Nature demonstrates this through a certain hidden "characterism" impressed upon it: for if it is soaked in water, after a day it shows an open vulva by its gaping. Furthermore, the humor in which it was soaked is tinted with a certain black soot, which declares "in the pattern" <note>original Greek: *ἐν τῷ τύπῳ* (en toi typoi)</note> what it plots within the vital humor. Hence, among the Egyptians and the Roman Priests of Jupiter <note>original: *Flamines Diales*</note>, it was held in such abomination that they considered it unsafe not only to eat them, but even to be present among them when flowering, or to rest or sleep near them.

<margin>Black animals move black bile.</margin>
Furthermore, all those black animals are usually counted among these children of black bile; most physicians feel that their flesh, by frequent use, moves the melancholic humor, induces quartan fevers, and causes cancers. For this reason, the buffalo—with its black skin and hair and its foul, formidable appearance—is forbidden as food. Black-colored cats are also a cause of epilepsy and other lethal symptoms, as they obstruct the passages of the brain with a certain poisonous and deadly quality; their fur causes consumption <note>original: *phthisim*</note>. For this same reason, they judge that one must abstain from eating nocturnal birds—the owl, the black swallow, and others—and Columella explains this in these verses:

> Hence Chiron, son of Amythaon, taught many things:

> To wail their funereal songs from the high rooftops.

# The Art of Judging by Color.

...they do not only move the humors, but once moved, they attract them to themselves, and once attracted, they draw them away through whatever gate is provided. Of this kind are White Hellebore, Black Hellebore, and Mandrake. I shall say nothing here of the eating of black meats—such as those of the Wolf, the Buffalo, the Peacock, the Duck, and other animals—which, because they consist of the worst juices <note>original: *pessimi succi*; in humoral theory, this refers to fluids that create "bad blood" or melancholy</note>, are condemned by Physicians. And from these few examples, unless I am mistaken, the nature of the black color in natural things sufficiently appears, and it is clear what it portends.

<margin>Why black aromatics are healthy, while black animals are harmful.</margin>
But perhaps someone will object at this point that Pepper, Bezoar, Balsam, Juniper Berries, and countless other similar things are also black; yet these are so far from being harmful that, by their aromatic power, they instead greatly strengthen the heart and the vital spirits. I respond that the blackness of those things comes from a very different temperament. For they consist of a certain fiery and solar virtue, and a temperament that is hot, dry, and scorched <note>original: *adusti*</note>, of which the said blackness is a kind of indicator. Besides these, they are endowed by nature with a certain specific gift by which, like almost all aromatics, they strengthen the heart, the fountain of life. But those plants and animals of a deadly appearance that I mentioned consist of a cold-moist or cold-dry temperament and a thick, smoky juice. Furthermore, their own heavy odor reveals a malignant nature, as they smell of something virulent. Certainly, in these and similar things, I believe one must stand by the judgment not only of the eyes, but also of the scent. But having indicated these things briefly, let us now hasten to the rest.

### Rule Five.

<margin>White things that move phlegm.</margin>
All those plants with white flowers or endowed with a thicker juice, which also mostly have their origins in marshy places, increase the humor they resemble by a certain similarity and proportion they have to phlegm or pituita <note>original: *pituitam*; the cold, moist humor associated with winter and the lungs</note>. But others of a drier temperament correct and purge that same humor. Truly milky plants, such as Spurge <note>original: *Titymallus*</note>, Milkwort, Sow-thistle, and the Egyptian plant *Beitalzar*, multiply milk in nursing mothers; and so it goes for the rest.

### Rule Six.

<margin>Red plants move and increase the blood.</margin>
Indeed, some plants of a red color increase the blood and, by a similarity of nature, easily unite with it; thus the Red Beet, Red Wine, and the juice of the Mulberry are believed to turn entirely into blood. Some cleanse and purge the blood when it is corrupted, such as Roses, Lesser Centaury, and things similar to these. Certain things also benefit those suffering from hemorrhoids and dysentery because of the similarity of color: thus the Corn Poppy <note>original: *Papaver Rhæas*</note>, Pomegranate flowers, dried Roses, Pomegranates, Sumac, Peony, Amaranth, and Coral—all from the blood-red 

<column-break/>

lineage of plants. From minerals, we have Red Lead <note>original: *Minium*</note> and Cinnabar powder; from animals, goat's blood. These obtain a very great power—both for stopping any kind of bleeding and for the consolidation of wounds—by the "character" or signature they display.

### Rule Seven.

<margin>Herbs of mixed color have mixed power.</margin>
The mixed colors of plants, since they consist of different temperaments, also obtain different effects; for color results from different degrees of "concoction" <note>the process by which the body's heat matures the humors</note>. I say, therefore, that *dichromous* <note>original: *διхρώμους*; two-colored</note> or bicolored plants consist of a dual power: thus white and saffron-colored flowers purge both phlegm and bile at the same time, as Chamomile does according to Galen. Also Feverfew, Elderberry, and Danewort <note>original: *Ebulus*</note>, according to Aelius. By the same reasoning, *leucomelane* <note>original: *Leucomelanæ*; white-black</note> roots, being made of black and white, are found to purge both phlegm and melancholy. In this way, different colors cure different humors in the human body: thus Sea Starwort <note>original: *Tripolium*</note>, All-heal <note>original: *Panaceæ*</note>, and *Triphera* <note>a traditional medicine composed of three parts</note> benefit all humors.

<margin>Multicolored snakes possess a diverse power of harming.</margin>
Arnaldus <note>likely the medieval physician Arnaldus de Villa Nova</note> asserts that a *polychromous* <note>original: *πολυхρώμον*; many-colored</note> snake, marked with many and various spots, has as many ways of harming as it has distinct colors. There is a proverb: "The bite of a Salamander needs as many doctors as it has spots." It is also commonly said that the Opal has as many virtues as it has colors.

## §. IV. Color-judgment to be established regarding complexions and various human characters.

Now we proceed to investigate the characters of men by the benefit of color—a task altogether difficult and perhaps reckless. For since there is a very great variety in the human complexion, arising as it does for the most part from an infinite chain of causes, certainly anyone who promised to bring forth something absolutely certain <note>original: *apodictice*</note> in so varied a business should be considered insane. For just as there is hardly any man who agrees with another in everything regarding his face, gait, voice, and other features of the body, so also does one differ from another in natural inclination. Yet, because all men consist of some predominating humor out of only four humors, and these shine forth most in color, we shall discuss the indications of colors based on probability and only according to certain universal principles. While we do this, we shall first discuss what color is, how it is fourfold in man, where it takes its origin, and how some belong to men and others to women. Finally, we shall see which ones are peculiar to each Region.

<margin>What color is in the human body.</margin>
Color, therefore, is nothing other in the human body than the extremity of a transparent body actually existing in...

# Great Art, Book I, Part III.

A surface is the determined boundary of a body; it is called "colored" when a determined transparency is found within it and is seen once it has received action from an external light. For every composite thing is either transparent <note>original: *diaphanum*; refers to the ability of light to pass through a substance</note> or formed from transparent parts, since everything consists of the four elements, three of which are transparent. Therefore, when the surface is acted upon by external light through the transparency present there, it is called "color," and a surface of this kind is called "colored." Since colors are the extremities of a composite body, and because the body is composed in various ways, various colors arise from this.

However, since we are dealing with the colors of men, who consist of the four humors <note>In ancient and medieval medicine, the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—were believed to determine a person's health and temperament</note> endowed with various colors, it is necessary that various colors be found on the human skin due to the internal mixing of these humors. Therefore, we believe that a man's color is determined by the mixture of the four humors as established by the forming principle in the mother's womb.

There are three colors found naturally in man: two extremes, white and black (the latter belongs properly to the Ethiopians and the Torrid Zone <note>The "Torrid Zone" refers to the tropical regions near the equator</note>); the other belongs to the peoples of the cold intermediate Zone, and is a mixture of white and red, each of which has its own range. Toward white, there is pale, yellow, and sallow; toward black, there is dark and ghastly; toward rosy, there is crimson, red, and purple. In regions where men are naturally white or rosy, the woman is usually fairer than the man; where they are black, the woman’s blackness is more luminous than the man’s. Naturally, more watery humor and less melancholy <note>original: *melancholici*; referring to the "black bile" humor associated with earth and heaviness</note> is usually found in a woman than in a man; for this reason, the man is also more robust than the woman and prompter for action.

<margin>Different climates produce men of different colors.</margin>
Thus, under different climates, men of different colors are produced. In the Torrid Zone, just as there is the greatest variety of all things, so too is there a remarkable diversity of plants, animals, and men, both because of the efficacy of the Sun constantly bearing down upon it, and because of the natural constitution of the earth and the arrangement of mountains and seas. Many of these people differ so much in their manners and inclinations within even a small tract of the sky that you would think them born in climates entirely different from one another. And just as their temperament is varied, so do histories record them as being more prone to vice than other nations. Nevertheless, almost all possess a color that is either black, like the Ethiopians, or a brownish-chestnut closely approaching it, or a yellowish-black, such as is found among the Abyssinians, Egyptians, Indians, and the peoples of New Spain <note>Modern-day Mexico</note>, Granada <note>Likely New Granada, modern-day Colombia</note>, and Peru. However, you will find it very difficult to guess their character from their color, since the sky, the power of the earth, natural constitution, the character of parents, and the habit of living

<column-break/>

must be considered above all when investigating the nature of barbarian nations. Concerning these people who are so far removed from us, since little remains for us to say, let us prepare ourselves to examine the manners of men living under the Temperate Zone; especially those who dwell from the 30th degree of latitude to the 55th degree.

<margin>The Temperate Zone is the most excellent of all.</margin>
For we find that under this Zone of the earth, all Empires had their beginning, owing to the excellent moderation of the air which also overflows into their bodies. Under this Zone, we see the emergence of men who are both distinguished by the splendor of Empire and Dominion, and admirable in their science, knowledge, and invention of various things—the greatest men of the entire world.

<margin>The manners of Europe.</margin>
In Europe, therefore, the figures of men are quite diverse, as are their bodies. Some have a white and rosy color, tawny or reddish hair, tall bodies, fleshy and robust, with fierce and suspicious minds, capable of enduring cold and labor. Others are endowed with mostly the same color but with brownish hair and agile limbs; these seem to have a restless, vehement mind, given to disputes, prone to anger, mocking, and playful. Some others, since they approach more toward the temperament of black bile, are dark in color with black hair, of medium body, with a robust, constant, bold, and proud mind—difficult to tolerate in prosperous fortune, but humble in adversity. There are also those who have black hair and a scorched <note>original: *adustam*; often used to describe skin darkened by sun or "burnt" humors</note> face: just as the color of the countenance is diverse, so too are diverse manners indicated.

<margin>The physiognomic principle.</margin>
Hence, that physiognomic principle is for the most part false and should by no means be admitted: "To every man in whom there exist physical qualities that usually exist in the bodies of men of such-and-such a region, there also belong the manners, habits, and inclinations of the soul proper to those regions." For from this it would follow that all Italians would have the same complexion <note>In this context, "complexion" refers to the internal balance of humors, not just skin tone</note> according to the nature of their climate, as would the Germans, French, and Spanish each according to their own, and different from the others—which experience itself teaches to be false. For in each of these regions are found men who are learned, prudent, holy, and lovers of wisdom; and in all of them are found those who are vicious, luxurious, heretical, perverse, unruly, and endowed with depraved manners.

<margin>Every nation has its own illustrious men.</margin>
Italy has produced men conspicuous for their intellectual subtlety and the founders of illustrious Orders, Saint Benedict and Saint Francis. Spain also produced Saint Dominic and Ignatius; France too has her own, Bernard and William; Germany has Norbert and Bruno; Africa has Augustine; Egypt has Anthony; and finally Greece has Basil, the Father and Teacher of all, from whom as if from certain...

# The Art of Color Analysis

From the seedbeds of every age, men illustrious for their holiness have come forth. Italy has its distinguished theologians, as does Spain; France boasts its own men like Hilary <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a leading Latin theologian</note> and Irenaeus; Germany triumphs with its Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), the "Universal Doctor" and teacher of Thomas Aquinas</note>, that peak of intellects, just as chilly Scotland does with its most subtle Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), known as the "Subtle Doctor" for his complex metaphysics</note>; Africa has its Cyprian, Egypt its Athanasius, and finally Greece its various Gregorys. The same must be felt regarding the other talents of grace and nature granted to each nation, as well as the vices peculiar to each people. Therefore, in the opinion of all, he would be foolish and insane who argued thus: "He is German, therefore a drunkard; he is Italian, therefore lustful; French, therefore fickle, vain, and of a headstrong mind; Spanish, therefore proud and cruel." The vices of the Italians, Spaniards, and French are found in Germany; and in France, those of Italy, Spain, and Germany. In all and in each, vices and virtues are found indiscriminately. That some nations indeed seem more inclined toward this or that vice should be attributed not so much to nature as to the customs of the fatherland—customs which obtain a certain natural force over their people. Germans take on the vices of Italians, and Italians those of Germans; both take on those of the French and Germans if, with the reins loosened, they follow the corrupt customs of the people while in those respective lands. But let us return to our purpose.

There are various causes for the colors shining forth in the human body, all of which are very far removed from mere light and darkness. The first and principal cause is the varying temperament of the humors <note>The "temperament" refers to the specific balance or mixture of the four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile</note>, especially of the white and the black—namely, phlegm and melancholy. Since colors are caused by the mutual relationship of the primary qualities <note>The primary qualities are hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>—or rather of bodies, because the logic of color is situated in this relationship of the dry and the moist among themselves—these qualities are introduced through "passion." That is to say, they arise from the reciprocal action the primary qualities exert upon one another. Thus, color can be called nothing other than a quality of a mixed body arising from the mutual relationship of the primary qualities with light in a transparent body. Experience also teaches us this: for if a dry cloth is moistened, it changes color; if a purple cloth is soaked in water, it loses its color; if that same cloth is dried, it either returns to its original color or acquires a different one. This is also evident in humans and other living things: according to whether they become more or less dry or moist, they take on various differences in color. We have said this arises from the relationship between the passive principles; for the fire that is within things sustains two roles: either as the principle of heat or of light. Insofar as it is the principle and source of heat, it produces smells and tastes; but insofar as it is fit by its nature to produce light,

<column-break/>

it causes colors. The light and heat of the Sun greatly promote this varying condition of the humors according to different climates. <margin>*Color under the Torrid Zone.*</margin> For where the heat is vehement and the Solar rays continually strike the earth perpendicularly—as under the Torrid Zone <note>The tropical regions near the equator</note>—the "burnt" humors constitute the black color of the men, their curly hair, and their lean bodies. The affections of the mind necessarily follow this constitution of the humors, as will be seen shortly. Those, however, who participate less in the Sun's heat and rays—because the rays strike the earth at an oblique angle—their humors are also less "burnt" by the Sun's heat. Hence, from the dry and the moist, the hot and the cold, tempered humors constitute a better physical complexion <note>term: complexion; in this context, it refers to the internal "mixing" of humors which manifests as skin tone and temperament</note> in their bodies. <margin>*The character of the Temperate Zone.*</margin> From this, they always approach white and rosy tones more closely the further they are removed from the Torrid Zone; a better complexion is followed by a better wit and a better disposition. Such are the Europeans and a large part of the Asians who inhabit the Temperate Zone. <margin>*The character of the Frigid Zone.*</margin> But those who receive the Sun's rays at the most oblique angle—such as the peoples subject to the Frigid Zone, condemned to perpetual frost—sort out a nature contrary to those under the Torrid Zone due to a lack of heat. Since they swell with excessive moisture, the power of the intellect (which consists in moderate heat) is so blunted that they seem scarcely in control of their reason. Hence they are also perpetually foul with a pale or leaden color, unfit for studies and for performing great deeds; they are those to whom the soul, as the saying goes, seems to have been given merely as a substitute for salt <note>A common ancient idiom (from Aristotle or Pliny) suggesting the soul only serves to keep the body from rotting, implying a lack of higher intelligence</note>. Following this universal logic of Solar influence is the annual influence. For just as the Sun, by the abundance or scarcity of its light upon the earth, establishes a dry or moist complexion in the bodies of different peoples, so the Sun by its annual motion provides the same in particular places. In summer, being higher with heat and rays, it thins the humors by inducing dryness, whereby the color is also forced to undergo variation; in winter, however, due to the lack of heat, bodies are filled with moisture, resulting in a more vigorous color that approaches white. Therefore, the body—according as it suffers from more or less heat and light, and as the humor is separated from the dry and is "burnt"—becomes more moist or dry, hot or cold. <margin>*The nature and quality of regions change color.*</margin> Furthermore, the nature and quality of regions also contribute greatly to causing different inclinations: for one region is distinguished from another by the diversity of the relationship that the Sun and stars have with the earth. One of these relationships is universal, of which we have spoken; the other is particular, born from the nature of the land and the place. For under the same latitude, it happens that some inhabit flat plains open on all sides, while others inhabit the highest peaks of mountains—stony, sterile, and destitute of moisture; while others...

# The Great Art, Book I, Part III

...inhabiting lakes, marshes, wooded areas, and lands entirely sheltered from the winds. Just as these places have various colors, they also produce various <term>temperaments</term> <note>The "temperament" was a Renaissance concept that a person's personality and health were determined by the balance of four bodily fluids or "humors": blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile.</note> and inclinations. These facts are too well known to need repeating. Since different locations produce different air, and this inhaled air—as the material part for the generation of spirits—reaches the heart, it may weaken, strengthen, or alter the heart's balance. Furthermore, because different places produce different fruits and have different waters which people use, and since it is certain that different foods alter and change the blood, it is clear that food and drink, along with the air, have the greatest power to affect our bodies. Thus, the diversity of inclinations is evident. The Sun, then, is the active principle of colors; the humors are the passive principle; and the warming light of the Sun is the formal principle, affecting the humors in various ways depending on the disposition of the earth receiving it. From this varied affection, different temperaments and colors are born among peoples. Hence, different peoples obtain distinct differences in color. Thus, one who has acquired a <term>bilious temperament</term> <note>Characterized by yellow bile, historically associated with an ambitious or hot-tempered nature.</note> under the dominance of blood has certain inclinations; another, who is <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>Associated with excess phlegm, historically making one calm or sluggish.</note> under the dominance of <term>melancholy</term> <note>Associated with black bile, historically making one pensive or introspective.</note>, has others; the latter is humble in obeying, while the former is proud in commanding.

<margin>Education and morals.</margin>
Another cause for the diversity of character among peoples can be attributed to education, habit, and training. Indeed, to be accustomed to things from a tender age is so powerful that habit and education can correct, overcome, change, and pull temperament and its inclinations in the opposite direction. This has great strength, especially in man. For man primarily approaches a perfect temperament, which, being in balance, is easily turned toward opposite sides. From this it is clear how it can be deduced from a man's temperament that he is "placed in the hand of his own counsel" <note>A reference to the biblical idea of free will; man is not a slave to his biology.</note> and is the master of his own actions, so that he can do or not do those things suggested to him by his temperament, his emotions, or any other cause.

<margin>Society.</margin>
The third cause is society, just as this relates to education. For it is certain that we are such as those with whom we are familiar, or those with whom we share a great necessity.

<margin>Age.</margin>
The fourth reason is age; for experience teaches that various ages are held by various passions. Studies follow age, and these are so powerful that, according to the common saying, we call them a "way of life"—the exercise and work which each person undertakes by his own choice, by chance, or by the will of his family, whether in the Military, Scholarship, Medicine, or Theology. Hence, those following a military way of life—

<column-break/>

**Right Column:**
—adopt military character; those embracing religious life, through continual meditation and <term>maceration</term> <note>The spiritual practice of fasting or mortification to subdue the physical body.</note> of the flesh, are usually so accustomed to changing their temperament that you might say they were almost different people. Consequently, certain regions occupied by a specific type of learning entice others to handle similar things through use and habit. Thus, certain peoples accustomed to Empires are mostly held by the ambition for honors and the appetite for ruling; other nations would be tempted by this as well, if they were not deprived of the opportunity to reach it. In a word, use, habit, and the moderation of the mind are so powerful that there is nothing one nation can do that another could not also do, if it willed it effectively; nor is there any vice of one nation that could not draw other peoples to the same through use and habit.

<margin>Invective against certain authors.</margin>
A certain perverse affection has possessed the minds of some writers so much that, without any judgment or reason, they are carried away with never-ending praise for only that nation toward which their own affection and particular love incites them. Regarding others, however, out of a certain ill-advised, hasty, and perverse judgment, they rashly blurt out everything other than what pertains to praiseworthy actions. This is the worst kind of writers, hateful to all those who are accustomed to scrutinizing details more precisely according to the ruler of prudence and discretion. But these are <term>digressions</term> <note>original: πάρεργα (*parerga*), meaning side-matters or secondary works.</note>. Let us return to our purpose and resolve our art into its first principles. We say, therefore, that every mixed body—whether it is transparent or opaque (that is, participating in both)—consists of four elements. The elements, in themselves, are simple bodies; of the simple bodies, some are transparent, others are <term>opaque</term> <note>original: ἀδιάφανα (*adiaphana*), literally "not-transparent" or light-terminating.</note> or bound the transparent. One is called Earth, the others Water, Air, and Fire. Of these four, two are passive principles and two are active. Earth is dry, and therefore bounded; water is moist, and therefore "boundable," though in itself unbounded; and these two are passive. Therefore, they dominate in things according to their mass: earth in more perfect things, water in less perfect ones. Furthermore, the two active ones are Air and Fire, of which the latter is hotter and the former less so; both are luminous. But air is more transparent, while fire is more luminous. Both of these elements dominate in animals according to their power. Therefore, white comes from the dry; thus, earth is white or yellowish. If water is mixed with this, a black color arises, as is clear in moistened clods of earth, and as has often been shown when we discussed the color of the elements. For the material cause of all blackness is water, just as cold is the efficient cause. If a small amount of air is added, with enough heat that these two elements are properly mixed together, greenness will be produced; for in plants, the first <term>concoction</term> <note>The process of "ripening" or "cooking" through internal heat.</note> of moisture produces greenness. If fire is joined to a greater amount of air, it produces the color red, because—

...since there is greater light in this than in green; if a great amount of fire enters the mixture, <term>purple</term> <note>original: "purpureus" — in this context, it often refers to a deep, rich red like arterial blood.</note> will be born. However, a greater fire, by drying out that which consists of the dry and the moist, obscures the light, as we see in wood that is burned. Next, therefore, comes the color blue, followed by black, which is the offspring of watery earth scorched by intense heat. These, then, are the simple colors which are born from the mixture of elemental qualities and the elements themselves. Hence, dryness and moisture seem to affect the matter, insofar as dryness and moisture are found in the passive elements; while heat and cold, insofar as they are active, provide the form. However, for the passive elements to form colors or contribute to their constitution, they do so not merely as they are dry or moist, but insofar as they are <term>diaphanous</term> <note>meaning transparent or translucent</note> or non-diaphanous; likewise, the active elements act not merely as they are hot, but insofar as they are luminous or non-luminous. If someone should say that the air is not bright and the earth is not white, it must be understood that the elements and principles are not such in *actuality*; for if they were such in actuality, they would already exist in a perfect state and not as a beginning, and they would not be principles but rather things originated and composed. They are, therefore, such in an incomplete and potential state, but not in actuality or in a complete and perfect state. Furthermore, the <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note> from which a perfect animal is constituted, although they correspond to the four elements of the world, all tend toward redness and a purple color when they are arranged according to nature. For we have said that this is the color of perfect animals—the color of those humors which exist in the vessels—just as greenness is the color of plants. For almost every plant that is drawn from the earth has its own greenness; the leaves are green, and the branches are green, and although some plants emit a milky, yellow, or red juice at the first break, the final fluid always ends in green.

<margin>Every perfect animal born from mating possesses a bloody fluid.</margin>
Similarly, in every perfect animal born from mating—not only the <term>viviparous</term> <note>giving birth to live young</note> but also the <term>oviparous</term> <note>egg-laying</note>—if it breathes and has lungs, the natural fluid drawn out is purple and approaches a red color, though it is not simple. For diluted purple indicates <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita"</note> (that is, blood); bright and shining indicates <term>yellow bile</term>; and a saturated color approaching crimson, which has become more spread out, expresses to us the natural <term>melancholy</term> <note>or "black bile"</note>. But if, contrary to nature, one or another humor is individually affected by heat or cold, they will produce blackness, lividity, paleness, yellowness, whiteness, and many other colors, which you may see discussed among the Physicians. On the surface of the human body, however, generally no more than two colors are found according to nature: namely white and black, under which, as if they were general categories,

<column-break/>

others can in a way be contained, which usually appear in the human face and skin. But let us come to the particular precepts of our <term>Chromocritices</term> <note>The Art of Color-Judging.</note>.

### Rule I.

#### Concerning the signs of a black or brownish color in the human face.

<margin>Black Ethiopians are timid.</margin>
Those who are very black, such as the <term>Ethiopians</term> <note>A general historical term for people from sub-Saharan Africa.</note>, are timid, weak, prone to hasty counsel, and inconstant. This is because when much internal heat is drawn out by great external heat, the internal parts become cold, deprived of their natural heat, and then subsequently grow warm with accidental heat; and when the external moisture is drawn to the skin and scorched by that heat, they turn black. This is how they become black. Therefore, for one whose exterior is black, the moisture has been drawn out with the heat to the exterior parts, and there it is scorched by the external environment. Therefore, whoever this happens to, his internal parts are cold; and for him whose internal parts are cold, fear occurs. Thus, one whose face is black or dark, with small eyes and curly black hair, is consequently timid, malicious, deceitful, and one whom you could never trust; he is also prone to the greatest and most vehement anger, which seethes in secret while he waits for a place and time to do harm. Because these kinds of men fear even when all is safe and hold everything in suspicion, distrust is born from fear, deceitful plotting from distrust, and finally, from this come monstrous crimes, such as those described by <term>Leo Africanus</term> <note>A 16th-century Moorish diplomat and author famous for his "Description of Africa."</note> regarding the people who inhabit Numidia, Libya, and Guinea.

<margin>The nature of a black and scorched man, an Ethiopian.</margin>
But since this color is very rare among Europeans, we have thought it best to discuss it only briefly. If, however, someone of this constitution is born in Europe, it is due to a defect—either of the <term>mother's imagination</term> <note>The historical belief that a mother's intense thoughts or sights during pregnancy could physically alter the fetus.</note>, or the paternal seed, or the maternal womb, which, being hotter than is right, draws the natural moisture and heat of the embryo to the outer parts and scorches the moisture in that place around the skin, thus tinting the fetus and making it dark. From this, there subsequently arises a propensity for slavish fear because the internal parts are cold.

### Rule II.

#### Concerning the signs of a white, yellowish, or ashen color in the human face.

Since the color white, according to what has been said, is proper to women—and women are extremely timid because they have little blood around the heart but much around the womb—it follows that everyone who is white by nature is also timid...

<margin>What whiteness in a person signifies.</margin>
[They] are timid because of a great excess of phlegm <note>original: "pituita"—one of the four humors, associated with water, cold, and moisture</note>. Since phlegm is moist and cold, fear necessarily follows it; indeed, all moist and cold things are timid, as is most apparent in fish and insects. But someone might object: the English, French, and Germans are fair and white; therefore, they should be of a timid nature. Yet the heroic deeds of their wars sufficiently declare that these nations yield to no other in audacity and magnanimity. However, audacity, fortitude, and magnanimity cannot be born except from great heat of the heart—in which they abound—while we say that white people are naturally destitute of it; therefore, the rule is false. I respond that just as great blackness is not the cause of fear (in terms of the excess of blackness), but is a sign of a natural disposition that could define a man, so great whiteness is a sign of the other extreme. All extremes, as such, are flawed; therefore, he who wishes to maintain the name of a "man" should be neither [purely] white like a woman, nor black like an Ethiopian. When we speak of whiteness here, we speak only of an intense, pale whiteness, such as that with which the inhabitants of the Cold Zones are imbued.

<margin>What the rosy color of the French and Germans portends.</margin>
However, the Germans, French, and English, for the most part, possess not only whiteness, but are also endowed with a certain rosy color, or a yellow and honey-toned hue mixed with purple. Since this color is proof of much blood and heat, they should not be numbered among the timid.

Whenever a color appears like that of ash—since this is the effect of black bile <note>melancholy</note> under the dominance of phlegm, and black bile is not naturally hot, though it can become moderately warm—you would not call such a person brave, but rather humane and temperate, and not one who craves the possessions of others. He who is properly honey-colored, reflecting the color of honey, has too much yellow bile <note>choler</note> in him. He who has acquired a quince-like color <note>original: "cydonitem"—a golden-yellow hue</note>, which leans more toward a dark, lion-like tawny color and shows a ruggedness <note>original: "squalorem"</note>, is formed from much black bile heating up, along with much yellow bile mixed with parts of phlegm and blood. Men imbued with this color

<margin>Melancholic-Cholerics.</margin>
are for the most part strong and magnanimous. Because they consist of black and yellow bile, the former (reflecting the earth) provides constancy, strength, and solidity, while the latter (being similar to fire) provides vehemence, speed, and promptness in actions.

### Rule III.

*Concerning the reddish or fox-like color in man, and its significance in the hair and face of the human body.*

There is a double redness: one is saturated and lacks luster, leaning toward black with a little 

<column-break/>

paleness, such as we almost always find in red copper; the other is brilliant, purple, or rosy, greatly gladdening the eyes. Bright red or glowing redness is also twofold: one is flesh-colored, the other is scarlet, which we see in Cinnabar <note>a bright red mineral pigment</note>. Since this latter is not natural to man, we are speaking of the first. This reddish-yellowish color, because it consists of much burnt black bile joined with yellow bile, means that if these two humors are scorched by corrupt heat, they incline the man to nothing noble, nothing worthy of a great spirit or heart. Instead, partly because of the earthy quality which is cold, it will agitate him with constant fear and suspicions. As for dryness, it will make it difficult for him to bond with others, hence they are <term>solitary</term> <note>original: <term>μονωτικοὶ</term> (monotikoi)—meaning those who prefer to be alone or isolated</note>. What he takes up, he retains for a long time; what he rejects, he does not easily receive back. But the heat of the bile, reflecting the heat of fire, strives for restless agitation and inquiry, from which comes cunning. However, the portion of black bile is much greater than the yellow, which is why fear dominates. If fear did not dominate, he would be bold, but instead, he is a timid animal, like the fox. Therefore, since the temperament of the cunning is made of much black bile joined with yellow bile (both being natural to them but moderately heated), the quality of their skin and hair will result in a "fox-like" color from this mixture. Most Cretans are said to be of this color, hence they are cunning, and according to the common Greek proverb: <term>The three K's are the worst</term> <note>original: <term>Τρία κάππα κάκιστα</term> (Tria kappa kakista)—an ancient slur referring to the Cappadocians, Cretans, and Cilicians, all regarded as untrustworthy in antiquity</note>. Anyone can easily gather the vices that arise from cunning—

<margin>Signs of the fox-colored person.</margin>

->Signs of the yellowish color.<-

A yellowish color, such as is seen in honey, consists of phlegm and yellow bile. Those who abound in much phlegm and yellow bile tempered with black bile turn out (even in the judgment of Aristotle) to be lukewarm, lazy, slow, and frequently irresolute and unfit for great actions due to diminished digestion. And since it is characteristic of the cold to crave more than it can digest, such people will also show signs of gluttony and intemperance. Being provoked by yellow bile will also move them to anger, which fear (due to the mixed-in cold) will render ineffective. However, they will turn to blasphemy and threats against those who are absent; hence they are devoted to grumbling and detraction.

# The Art of Judging by Color

[The complexion] with natural yellow bile and thin phlegm <note>original: "pituita"—the cold, moist humor</note>, which young people exhibit when heated by vigorous movement, is properly called purple. For those imbued with this temperament—the bilious and the sanguine—abound in natural heat and, consequently, swell with subtle spirits. They cannot lack sharpness of wit; they are, therefore, acute. This sharpness of wit renders them well-suited for handling the liberal arts <note>the traditional academic subjects of a free citizen, such as grammar, logic, and rhetoric</note>, even if the excessive fervor of their choler <note>yellow bile</note> and blood makes them more mobile than is balanced, and even unstable. What vices follow this complexion, I leave to the reader to examine.

<margin>The flame-like color in a human face.</margin>
But a flame-like color, since it argues for a certain unknown internal inflammation, will incline those imbued with it toward mania and frenzy—the worst and most dangerous of all natures. You will see their eyes are flaming, perpetually breathing out fire, always ready to harm and hurt; there is no moderation in their words, no humanity in their eyes, no kindness in their manners, and no grace in their dealings. They live for brawls and contentions, intolerable to themselves and others. For they catch fire with choler at any word, and while they please only themselves and applaud only themselves, esteeming themselves alone above all others, they are despised by most others as insolent. Let everyone beware of such a person; let no one dispute with them, or contend even for the slightest cause. For if, in a dispute, their spirit grows a little hotter, they are easily driven into mania and frenzy and become so wild that, in the violence of their foaming heat, they not only break out into insults but are soon not ashamed to lay violent hands upon you.

### Rule V.
#### On the signs of colors in the eyes.

<margin>Why man alone enjoys diverse eye colors.</margin>
The bodies often follow the color of the eyes; hence we see that white bodies for the most part have blue-gray eyes <note>original: "caesios oculos"—often referring to light blue, grey, or "owl-colored" eyes</note>, and black bodies have black eyes; regarding which, see Simon Portius <note>Simone Porzio (1496–1554), an Italian philosopher who wrote a famous treatise on eye color</note> on the color of the eyes. At this point, we must only discuss why man alone has such a great variety of eyes. For as Aristotle rightly professed, every species of animal has its own specific eye color; for instance, Oxen have one; Goats and Donkeys have one, and so it is for the other species. This is not found in humans; for among men, some are endowed with blue-gray eyes, some with black, some with greenish, and others with another color. Therefore, the cause of this variety is sought. Some attribute it to light and brightness; others to the scarcity or abundance

<column-break/>

of the aqueous humor <note>the clear fluid inside the eye</note>. Astrologers, with their usual rashness, ascribe it to the different aspects of the planets; others devise other explanations. We say that he who knows the cause of why men are so diverse from one another—such that hardly anyone can be found whose face does not differ from another's—will certainly also be able to assign the cause for the variety of eyes. Just as this variety cannot fall solely upon the mixture of the humors, so it is a matter of deeper consideration, to be ascribed solely to the plastic power of the seed <note>term: "vis plastica"—the "formative" or "sculpting" force believed in early modern science to build the body from the embryo</note>.

<margin>Why humans have such diverse faces.</margin>
We therefore assert that this variety occurs because when a man and woman know each other <note>a biblical/archaic euphemism for sexual intercourse</note>, they are of a wandering mind; and just as the fantasies <note>original: "phantasmata"</note> of both are various and diverse, so too are the conceptions formed and figured under those imaginations. For although it occasionally happens from the mixture of humors, it most often has its origin in the imagination of the parents at the time of coitus, and from the plastic power. You will find this treated more extensively in our *Magnetic Art*, in the chapter on the magnetism of the imagination.

<margin>The eyes are an incitement for lovers.</margin>
Furthermore, no part of the body pleases lovers so much as the eyes; nothing presents itself so readily to those wishing to know a person as the said eyes. Because of the various imaginations of both spouses, and especially of pregnant women when they turn their eyes toward various sights and "cook" them in their minds, no one will doubt that a varied temperament is induced in the child's eyes by this fixed and intent imagination. It is clear that colors are induced in the eyes by the plastic power according to the constitution of the natural humor or the imagination of the pregnant woman. This is evident because the colors of the pupils and the iris do not come from the temperament of the humors alone; rather, to determine this pattern of circles, there is a need for a "chromatic power" subordinate to the plastic power. Just as it forms the eye, so it joins the proper colors to them along with the proper shape.

<margin>The judgment of eye color is difficult.</margin>
Hence, a very difficult judgment is given regarding the color of the eyes in the business of divination, since they are frequently not born from the temperament of the four humors alone, but, as has been said, they obtain the specific causes of their origin.

### Rule VI.
#### On the color of the Hair.

It is likewise a slippery business to pass judgment on the variety of colors shining forth in the hair, due to the various causes they have. Sometimes they vary due to the abundance or lack of nourishment, as in children; or due to the "concoction" <note>digestion or "ripening" of fluids by heat</note> or rawness of the food by which they are nourished. Thus, the native heat—the primary architect of concoction—varies the hair when it is changed either by disease or by age. For the color of hair is one thing in infancy, another in youth, and another in old age; which we also see in plants...

...we see this occur. Hair also frequently assumes color from excess humors through a process similar to dyeing; that is, the vapors of bilious, phlegmatic, or melancholic humors, when mixed with the material of the hair, impart their own color to it. In this way, black hair arises from the dreg-like waste of black bile <note>original: "atra bilis"</note>; yellow hair from yellow bile; white from phlegm <note>original: "pituita"</note>; and red from a mixture of bile and phlegm. Thus, these can be taken as signs of a person’s internal inclination and the temperament of the brain.

<margin>Different regions produce different hair colors.</margin>
The external air also has a great power to impress color upon the hair. It is certain that in different regions, hair changes not so much because of the brain’s temperament, but because of the condition of the surrounding air. Indeed, in scorched regions, the external heat affects the body, burning the nourishment of the hair and consequently inducing a black color. Conversely, those who live in the North <note>original: "sub Aquilone," referring to the North Wind</note> have hair that is soft and grows luxuriously, because their blood and "sweet flavors" <note>referring to the pleasant balance of humors</note> provide grace and strength; hence, the color is also more cheerful. This is likewise evident in the fur of animals, which frequent experience teaches us undergoes changes in color according to the conditions of the sky. Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger, a famous Renaissance scholar</note> reports that in Wozkam, a region of Sarmatia <note>an ancient name for the vast lands of Eastern Europe and Russia</note>, any animals that either migrate there or are brought from elsewhere turn white. In Canada, or New France, animals change their color twice every single year; these facts certainly demonstrate the great power of the air in changing hair and fur.

<margin>Certain waters change the color of hair.</margin>
There is also a property in certain waters that dyes animals with various colors: in some places they are white, in others black, solely by the power of the water they drink. On this subject, see our work *The Subterranean World* <note>original: "Mundum nostrum subterraneum," Kircher’s 1664 encyclopedic work on the Earth</note> regarding the varied nature of waters. Consequently, because of these and similar factors, it can be difficult to establish a judgment of a person's internal character based on color alone.

### §. V. Rules

#### On the color of Urine, and its signs.

Hippocrates rightly and wisely said that in acute diseases, nothing declares the state of the sick person so much as the colors of the urine. Since these colors exist in a nearly infinite variety, a very serious question arises among physicians: what is the cause of this chromatic diversity in urine? Some have thought that since urine is generated from the liquid that is consumed and is a purely watery, thin waste-product of the "first concoction" <note>the first stage of digestion in the stomach</note>, it behaves toward colors just as water does toward dyes. Just as water has no color of its own by nature, but acquires it from external things that stain or dye it, so too do they believe urine's colors are caused by the mixture of some substance dyeing it. Others wish for it to be rendered

<column-break/>

<margin>The true science of the coloration of urine.</margin>
colored because it receives different colors according to the various mixtures of yellow bile. Neither opinion can hold up. The first fails because in a healthy person, traces of such a mixture ought to appear, yet experience does not show this. The second fails because in many diseases, urine is black or intensely red, a tint that cannot be produced by yellow bile by any means.

We say, therefore, that urine is not rendered colored by the mixture of some humor, but by natural heat through a process of alteration and "concoction" <note>the internal "cooking" or processing of fluids by the body's heat</note>. Just as water heating up over a fire departs from its natural color, so too does urine when heated and scorched by natural heat. For it is the property of fire, or heat, to transmute mixtures into various types of color, as we have shown in our experiments with minerals.

Urine relates to natural heat in the same way that natural water relates to light; but water is variously altered by light and heat. We frequently see stagnant water degenerate into green, then into yellow, and finally we experience it turning black.

Thus, when natural heat is in its most balanced state, it renders the urine citron-colored, or the color of straw, which is the sign of the best and most perfect urine. But when the native heat is more intense than is natural, it also intensifies the color of the urine; hence, in tertian fevers <note>malaria-like fevers that spike every three days</note>, we see the urine become intensely red.

<margin>The crisis of urine.</margin>
But when the natural heat is too greatly weakened, the urine appears either white or ash-colored due to a defect in concoction. Where the force of indigestion is greatest, as in those suffering from lientery <note>a form of diarrhea where food is passed undigested</note>, the urine is rendered clear, limpid, and entirely watery. In cases of mania and frenzy, however, the urine is rendered scorched and black because of a violent excess of heat. Thus, natural heat is the "remote" <note>underlying</note> cause of the color of urine, while the mixture of bile is the "proximate" <note>immediate</note> cause.

<margin>Experience.</margin>
For heat acts immediately upon the bile, and through the mediation of the bile, it acts upon the urine. Experiment proves the matter: if you place any colored water over a fire and make it boil, it will produce different colors according to the different degrees of heat. For instance, water tinted with saffron will degenerate from yellow into intense red, then into purple, and finally into a black color. The same can be seen in all colored waters.

However, I do not deny that there can be other causes that color the urine, as will be seen shortly. For example, a white color in urine can be caused by a lack of native heat, a hidden fault of "rawness" <note>undigested matter</note>, or a poor quality of the blood (namely if it is watery, serous, or poorly colored). It can also be caused by an obstruction or a blockage of the vital parts by thick and melancholic humors, or even by an abundance of drink, as happens in drunkards. Finally, it may be caused by the mixing of some substance that dyes it white, as in phlegmatic or purulent conditions, and...

# The Art of Color-Judgment

<margin>Red urine.</margin>
...is evident in those suffering from hemorrhages. I say this because red urine can have various causes for its tint. First, from the force and effectiveness of heat: for if the heat is in its natural state, the urine will be rendered a yellow-citrine color; if the heat is increased, it will become red; if it is most intense, it will turn black due to the excessive burning <note>original: "adustionem," a term in humoral medicine for when a substance is "overcooked" by internal heat</note> of the blood. If the heat is extremely intense and combined with a virulent humor, the urine will turn green; if the heat is near extinction, it will turn blue. However, it can occasionally be tinted a red or bloody color by accident, without any excess or lack of natural heat—as happens in the ulceration of the kidneys and bladder, or due to the nature of a color that is accidentally added to the urine, or even from things eaten or drunk that tint the urine. Therefore, there can be innumerable causes for the color of urine, not only in the sick but also in those who are perfectly healthy. The color of urine is one thing before a meal and another after; one thing in the evening and another in the morning; it differs in children, in adolescents, and in the elderly; it differs in choleric, phlegmatic, and sanguine temperaments, and finally, it is different in melancholic ones. Yet, in healthy people of any age and at any time, the urine always leans toward a yellowish hue; the difference in the color shining forth in the healthy can easily be identified simply by the intensity or lightness of that yellowness. In the diseased, however, almost all colors of urine are <term>preternatural</term> <note>meaning "beyond natural," or abnormal</note>. It is now time for us to briefly declare what these signify. And since not long ago I happened upon the records of the Arabian physicians and found a subtle judgment regarding the colors of urine, it seemed right to add it here, translated from the Arabic, for the sake of students of medicine, so that we omit nothing that seems to pertain in any way to this art of ours.

# § VI. Rules of Color-Judgment
## On the state of the sick based on the colors of urine, taken from the records of the Arabs and translated into Latin by the Author.

### Signs of the color white in urine.

When the color white is in the urine, it is either due to an obstruction (as in the elderly), or because of the weakness of the natural heat and a lack of strength, or because of the dissolving of moisture; from this, you shall form these six rules:
I. Very clear urine signifies an obstruction of the spleen, paleness of the face, and a heavy constitution of the whole body.
II. White urine with a leaden-colored circle denotes a blockage of the brain and the beginnings of the <term>falling sickness</term> <note>original: "comitialis morbi," an old term for epilepsy</note>.
III. White and dreggy urine indicates an abundance of thick and undigested humor.
IV. Ash-colored and purulent urine indicates an ulcer of the kidneys or the urinary tracts.
V. White mixed with lead-color indicates a stone in the kidneys or bladder.
VI. White, thick, and fatty urine signifies <term>consumption</term> <note>original: "phthisim," a wasting disease usually associated with tuberculosis</note>.

#### Signs of the color black.
Since a black color in the urine arises either because of the burning of the natural heat, or due to a mixture of "black" matter, or finally because of the total extinction of heat; you shall form these rules:
I. Black urine along with a sediment of matter of the same color during a fever notes headaches and a disturbance of the mind.
II. Foul-smelling black urine notes <term>pneumonia</term> <note>original: "peripneumoniam"</note>, or a violent inflammation of the lungs, and usually signifies that death is near.

<column-break/>

III. Urine that is first green and then black denotes death, because it shows an excess of cold that is suffocating the natural heat.
IV. Black urine passed drop by drop denotes death; however, if it persists until the seventh day, it offers hope of recovery.
V. Black urine during a "quartan" fever <note>a fever that recurs every four days, often associated with malaria</note> is a sign of health.
VI. Black urine accompanied by a burning fever and sweat on the forehead designates imminent death.

#### Signs of the pale color in urine.
Since a leaden paleness <note>original: "livor"</note> of the urine signifies the "ultimate cooling," as physicians say, you shall form these rules from it:
I. Leaden-colored urine is a sign of death.
II. Urine that is pale in its upper part shows an extremely poor condition of the head.
III. A leaden color continuously remaining in the urine denotes <term>dropsy</term> <note>original: "hydropisim," a swelling caused by excess fluid</note> and the suffocation of the natural heat.
IV. A pale or leaden color with small grains and bubbles at the bottom signifies an ulcer of the lung and consumption.
V. A thin leaden color with a fattiness like oil portends the loss of natural moisture.
VI. A leaden color in those suffering from <term>phrensy</term> <note>original: "phreneticis," referring to a state of delirium or brain inflammation</note> marks death.

### *Signs of the green color.*

Since a green hue in urine most often reeks of a venom <note>original: "virus," here referring to a poisonous or foul quality</note> hidden within the corruption of the humors, you shall form these rules from it.
I. A green color during a great fever portends death.
II. A green color in a child indicates a spasm and an abundance of cold humors in the nerves.
III. A green color with a small cloud <note>original: "nubecula," referring to suspended sediment</note> at the bottom, and accompanied by stomach pain, is a sign that poison has been consumed.
IV. A green color with a green circle appearing in those suffering from frenzy <note>original: "phreneticis," referring to inflammation of the brain</note> portends death.

### *Signs of the red color.*

When, finally, redness of the urine arises—either from an obstruction formed between the gallbladder and the intestines, or from an unnatural inflammation—

<column-break/>

nature [is revealed], as in all fevers; you shall observe these rules regarding the tint.
I. Red urine most often denotes an excess of heat.
II. Red urine in those with kidney disease <term>nephriticis: those suffering from kidney ailments or stones</term> is a sign of a hidden ulcer.
III. Red and turbid urine indicates an ulcer of the liver.
IV. Urine of an oily color, when it is scanty and foul-smelling, portends death; for the stench signifies a boiling and corruption of the humors, the scantiness signifies a weakness of the vital power, and the oily quality signifies the dissolution of the body's parts.
V. A red color degenerating into a leaden hue indicates ulcers of the chest and consumption <term>phtisim: a wasting disease, usually pulmonary tuberculosis</term>.
VI. Red mixed with black indicates an inflammation of the liver.
VII. Red or fiery-colored urine indicates a one-day fever <note>original: "febrim ephémeram," a fever lasting only a single day</note>.
VIII. Fiery-colored urine that is thick and mixed with saffron-yellow indicates jaundice <note>original: "icteritiam"</note>.

#### toward which, as the primary Idea, the operations of all nature are directed.
# CHAPTER I.

->*All the powers of natural things emulate the path of diffused light.*<-

<margin>All things emulate the Creator.</margin>
Since the Nature of things ought to have represented God the Creator—to the extent that each thing was able by the condition of its own essence—and since the Creator found nothing better, more adorned, or more excellent than Himself; it followed that while He revolved this corporeal world in His mind, He destined for it a form as similar to Himself as possible. From this arose the whole genus of quantities, and within it the distinctions of the curved and the straight, and that most excellent of all things: the spherical surface. For in the sphere, the most Wise Creator played with the image of His own sacred Trinity <note>original: "sacræ suę Triadis." Kircher uses the geometry of the sphere—center, radius, and surface—as a mathematical metaphor for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>. Hence, the central point is a certain image of the sphere; the surface is the image of the innermost point; and the path to finding it—which is understood to be produced by an infinite extension of the point from itself until it reaches a certain equality of all departures—results in the point communicating itself into this amplitude. Thus, the point and the surface are equal in proportion, with density communicated alongside amplitude. Hence, there is on every side, between the point and the sur-

<column-break/>

face, a most absolute equality, a most tight union, a most beautiful conspiracy <note>In the Latin sense of "conspiratio," meaning a breathing together or harmonious agreement.</note>, a connection, relation, proportion, and symmetry. And although there are clearly three things—the center, the surface, and the intervening space—they are yet so much one that none can be absent, even in thought, without the whole being destroyed.

This, therefore, is the genuine and most fit image of the corporeal world, which is looked up to—either simply or with a certain respect—by whatever aspires to the highest perfection among corporeal creatures. Therefore, although bodies themselves are contained by the boundaries of their own surfaces and cannot multiply themselves into a sphere, they were endowed with various powers <term>virtutibus: "virtues" or "powers," referring here to the active forces or emanations a physical object exerts on its surroundings</term>. These powers, while nesting in the bodies, are in truth a little more free than the bodies themselves and lack corporeal matter; yet, consisting of their own kind of matter that <margin>All things emulate Light.</margin> admits Geometric dimensions, they go forth and affect a sphere. What wonder is it, then, if that principle of all ornament in the world—Light, I mean, the most excellent thing in the entire corporeal world and the mother of all faculties—[is the link] of the corporeal and spiritual world...
