# CHAPTER II.
## On the radiation of light and visible species.

<note>The term "visible species" refers to the 17th-century concept of "intentional species"—the formal images or "likenesses" that objects were thought to emit so they could be perceived by the eye.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'S' (replacing the Latin 'C') at the beginning of the chapter, featuring a figure within an ornamental rectangular frame.</image-desc>

SINCE light had to be communicated to individual bodies, its outflow, ejaculation, or radiation had to be suitable to its origin in a distant place. But since light is capable of obeying geometric laws, that communication could in no way happen without a conjunction of dimensions. It will be communicated, therefore, either by the approach of its source to the objects (which is absurd, since no substance can be, as the Philosopher <note>The "Philosopher" is a standard reference to Aristotle.</note> testifies, the immediate principle of its own operations, unless we wish to admit action at a distance without a medium, which is equally absurd); nor can it be by some other hidden power. Therefore, it must be communicated to worldly bodies by nothing else than this radiant flowing-forth of light, which is like a certain local departure and outflow from its own body. And this <term>actinobolia</term> <note>original: ἀκτινοβολία, meaning "the throwing of rays" or radiation.</note>, or radiation, is what we intend to discuss here. Since its true geometric genesis consists in the equality of the gaps through which a central point is spread onto a surface, surely the evolution of a sphere could not happen except through straight lines, according to the third pronouncement of the preceding section. For if it used curved lines running back into themselves, there would be no equality in the spreading, nor diffusion in the propagation of power.

<margin>The movement of things.</margin>
To better understand these things, it should be noted that when nature, in its works, affects either the unity of parts or their separation, both occur through movement along a straight line. For the shorter the distance between things, the more united they are understood to be; but straight lines are the shortest of all lines between the same points. Therefore, every unifying movement of things—such as that of weights toward the earth or steel toward a magnet—must necessarily occur in a straight line. If it were otherwise, nature would strive with no efficiency, contrary to the sixth Pronouncement; for all parts of the movement would not tend toward the same end, but somewhere in the middle of the journey, that which was to be united to another would deflect from this urge for union. The same must be understood regarding the continuous movement of separation, which in natural things is called "violent"; for a straight path is only contrary to another straight path. Indeed, among all worldly bod-

<column-break/>

<margin>The nature of light.</margin>
-ies, just as the Sun is the first, so by its action or "actinobolism" <note>Kircher's term for the active emission of rays.</note> it outshines all others. And this miraculous offspring of light originates from its source, yet is not torn away from it; it is diffused from there, but never "poured out" and lost. For it always adheres to its root and mother, propagating shoots and branches from the root, which have their origin from it, and are propagated, nourished, increased, and preserved by it. That primary light is unique and one, and moves in a circle; this secondary light is manifold, spread out into innumerable branches and lines, and these are not only long, but also somewhat wide, narrowing to a point and ending in a cone. These are joined only at their origin, but in their progress they are separated by an interval, first smaller, then larger. And this was the reason why the Opticians <margin>Definition of a ray.</margin> defined a "ray" as a luminous line, or illumination through a straight line. For the Latins invented the term "rays" (*radios*), which the Greeks called <term>aktinas</term> <note>original: ἀκτίνας.</note>, and the extension and projection of such lines they called <term>actinobolia</term>. Hence we also distinguish "light" from a "ray" just as one distinguishes a third light from a second. For a ray is a second light leaping out from the first in a straight and sharp manner, projecting not only in a line but also in a cone. However, the propagation of light is not conceived as being done by lines *around* the rays; rather, it revolves and fills every place between rays that are always becoming more distant. Light can exist without rays being actively present (as is clear at dawn); however, rays cannot exist without light, as they are the source from which rays emanate.

<margin>The manner of flowing light.</margin>
Having seen the flowing-forth, let us now see how it flows—whether from individual points of the shining body, or from the entire surface of the Sun. For this to be understood, it must first be known that we consider these shining lines not as mathematical lines, but as physical ones endowed with width. Consequently, we infer that the radiant flowing of light happens from all and individual physical points, and even from the entire width of the Sun, by a perpetual and lasting emanation (not a successive one), which is interrupted only by the obstacles of opaque bodies. When these are removed, the rays penetrate spaces in a moment, favoring no one part more than another.

<summary>Kircher explains that light radiates in straight lines because they are the most efficient and geometric path for natural forces. He distinguishes between "primary light" (the source), "rays" (directional lines), and "light" (the general illumination that fills space), using gravity and magnetism as parallels for this linear movement.</summary>

<page-num>81</page-num>
<header>On the Radiations <note>original: "Actinobolismis," a term derived from Greek meaning the emission or shooting forth of rays</note> of natural things.</header>

into which they incline toward one side rather than another, they are twisted into none; but like the straightest lines, they are ejaculated in a straight path from their source through the immense spaces of the heavens and the elementary atmosphere all the way into the earth itself. This occurs by a flow that is indeed uniformly difform <note>A Scholastic physics term meaning a quality that changes at a constant rate, such as light growing dimmer the further it travels from its source</note>, yet perpetually immobile in that same place. They are not driven from that place by any force, whether their own or another’s; they do not push against the place, nor are they moved from it. When light is moved, however, they either follow it or are drawn by it; when light departs, they also depart. When the transparent medium <term>diaphanum</term> through which they pass is moved, they do not follow it; even when an illuminated opaque object in that place is moved, they remain. 

# CHAPTER III.
## On the entity of rays: whether they are accidents, or substance, or bodies?

The miraculous powers of the rays described just before have appeared so obscure to all philosophers until now, that there has hardly been anyone who dared to assert anything certain about such a hidden nature. Will they be substances, then, or only species <note>The "species" or "intentional species" were thought to be the images or forms sent out by objects to the eye</note> and images of the primary light—things that are, as they say, "intentional"? Certainly, since rays shine by themselves, emit light, and produce heat, they should be listed among real entities rather than "intentional" ones. Nor do they seem able to be "accidents" according to some, since it is characteristic of accidents to be present or absent from a subject without the destruction of that subject <note>In Scholastic philosophy, an "accident" is a property like "redness" or "warmth" that must exist within a "substance" like an apple or water</note>. Rays do not seem to happen <note>A play on the Latin "accidere," which means both "to happen" and "to be an accident of"</note> to any foreign thing, nor can they be absent from their source and then return to it; for they never depart from the Sun and light, but are always present to it. Therefore, they cannot be called accidents in respect to the Sun. 

Since these same rays are perpetually present in the ethereal or celestial world, illuminating it, and can never be absent from it; 
<margin>Solar rays are not accidents.</margin> 
therefore they cannot be accidents to it either, and consequently should by no means be called accidents of the ether. But perhaps they can be accidents to the air: for it is well known that air is dark without rays, and becomes luminous when those accidents are present. Therefore, rays can be present or absent from the air without its destruction; thus they would be accidents, which we see happening in all material transparent things. But to explain what kind of accidents those might be—"here is Rhodes, here is the leap" <note>original: "hic Rhodus, hic saltus," a Latin proverb meaning "prove it here and now"</note>. Perhaps as qualities? As colors? So says Aristotle. But these ideas cannot be reconciled: for the colors of mixed bodies, as well as their own qualities, are so inherent in their subjects that they cannot be taken away without the destruction of the subject. Yet it has already been seen that rays are now absent, now present in the air, while the subject remains unharmed and uncorrupted.

<column-break/>

Into whatever transparent medium they fall, whether thin like air, fluid like water, or solid like crystal, they penetrate, illuminate, and fill it in the same moment. This happens in various ways: if in air or the ether, they penetrate in a straight line; if in a denser medium, such as water and vapors, they become refracted and reflected—becoming as much shadowier as the medium is denser. Thus, we can say that these luminous rays are the causes of every color appearing in clouds, waters, and stars, just as was said in the preceding book and will be said more extensively in those following.

Therefore, rays do not have the character of colors or qualities proper to things in their entity. Furthermore, rays are not affected or corrupted by the air, water, or other transparent media, whether they are present or absent; nor do we see them corrupt the water or air themselves, since these are not the proper subjects of the rays. Therefore, they cannot be called a quality or color of transparent bodies. Neither are they their quality, nor relation, nor action, nor passion, 
<margin>What kind of accident a ray might be.</margin> 
nor time, nor place, nor position; they do not possess these things themselves, nor are they possessed by them. Therefore, rays are accidents to transparent things in no category. 

We are not speaking here of just any kind of accident, but of that which is proper and natural to some object—namely, whether the ray requires a support and prop for its existence, which, if removed, would cause the ray itself to perish. Certainly, if we consider things more deeply, it seems that rays require no such support to exist. For if they needed any, they would need one akin to themselves rather than something foreign. And if this were so, they would need an aerial one, and not a watery one. Why then do they descend into both air and water—not their proper subjects—if they are sustained in the ether alone? Yet they are in these things daily, and they are in them by no help from the media; rather, they are in them by themselves, and consist in them by their own powers. Therefore, air, water, and watery things are not the objects of rays: therefore they lack a subject; therefore they exist by themselves far from the Sun and light: therefore they exist as a substance. Certainly, our reasoning seems to demonstrate this for certain; but of what kind of substance? Material, or formal? Or composed of both? Not the former, since we will later call rays "immaterial"; nor the latter, since rays—being long, wide, and deep, and always affecting a conical shape—take on a triple dimension...

will be assigned, and referring the radiant flow of light not to the category of qualities, but to the first Category <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "First Category" is Substance. Hence, in so difficult a matter, I would not easily determine anything, lest by thrusting a "New Philosophy" upon the world, I seem to contradict what was asserted in the previous book. Therefore, withdrawing from the most obscure darkness of this light, let us turn to those things which are both better known to us and can better help us understand the light that follows.

# CHAPTER IV.

->All visible objects radiate in a sphere <note>original: "in orbem," literally "in a circle," but here implying a three-dimensional spread</note> according to the pattern of light.<-

Experiment itself proves this proposition. For since one and the same visible thing is seen by many people at once, it follows that from every point of the visible object, every point of the medium <term>medium</term> <note>The substance, such as air or water, through which light travels</note> between which a straight line can be drawn, is irradiated. From this it follows that all points of the visible object, and its entire "species" <note>The "intentional species" were the images or forms thought to be emitted by objects so they could be perceived by the eye</note>, flow together and terminate in every point of the medium that can be connected by straight lines; thus the entire medium is filled and crowded with visible species. There are as many "views" in the medium as there are points in the medium, and each one, by a certain and proper radiation of the visible thing, will see one and the same species. From this it happens that, according to the rule of light, a visible thing radiates with rays that are sometimes parallel, sometimes converging, and intersecting each other in many ways. All of this Vitello <note>Witelo, a 13th-century friar and scientist whose work on optics was a standard text</note> demonstrates extensively from Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham, the medieval Arab polymath often called the "father of modern optics"</note>: namely, that the species of any visible point occupies and fills its surface, and at any point on the surface of the eye, the entire species of the visible object is gathered. By the same reasoning, any point of a mirror radiates, and the entire species of the visible object is in every point of the mirror, and the species of any visible point is in the entire surface of the mirror. Thus, a visible point situated in the open air would unfold its radiation into a complete sphere, such as almost all the stars produce; but in opaque bodies or surfaces, it unfolds into a hemisphere. Yet a straight line cannot be connected from that same visible point to every point of an object, even if

<column-break/>

no other opaque thing stands in the way; and therefore, not every point of a visible object can radiate. For let there be a visible Sphere AB, and let the concave part of its periphery HCFLD be facing point A. I say that from point A, straight lines cannot be drawn to every point of the periphery LDH; for the straight line LH, touching the periphery of Sphere AB at point A, cuts the opposing periphery at points H and L. It is clear, therefore, that no straight line can be drawn from point A to the points of the periphery HDL, and for that same reason, point A can radiate to none of the said parts of the arc, but only to the part of the arc HCEL. These things are also clearly shown in the spherical figures A and the flat figure B; and indeed, in the Sphere, a point of light from point C cannot radiate beyond the tangent of the sphere, just as it cannot radiate beyond the plane B.

If, however, point A were placed in the hollow of some glass sphere, as is clear in figure B of the previous figu-

<meta>This page transitions from the philosophical debate on the nature of light rays to the practical geometry of optics. While the previous page pondered whether rays were a "third kind of being," Kircher now begins to demonstrate their mathematical behavior in space, utilizing classical authorities like Lucretius and medieval opticians like Witelo.</meta>

<page-num>83</page-num>
<header>The Radiation of Light.</header>

It is clearly evident; it could radiate into the entire circumference. In a word, every point—whether it be luminous or visible—radiates to all those points of the medium to which a straight line can be drawn. Lucretius describes this radiation quite elegantly in his usual way, when he sings:

> *I shall begin to explain what strongly pertains to these matters,*
> *the existence of those things we call the "images" of things:*
> *which, like membranes stripped from the outermost body of things,*
> *fly hither and thither through the air.*
> <note>original: "simulacra." Lucretius was an Epicurean philosopher who believed objects shed thin "skins" or films that travel to our eyes to create sight.</note>
>
> And elsewhere: *Now those things which I call the "images" of things are carried*
> *everywhere, and are cast abroad into all parts;*
> *so much so, that from all things matter is also carried in a*
> *flow, and is sent out everywhere into all parts.*

It is commonly known that this radiation occurs according to an optical figure. For since every point of a visible object radiates, it follows that the entire width of the visible object forms a pyramid at any point in the visible medium, having as many sides as the base has angles. If, therefore, the radiating visible object is a circle, and the point of the medium is in a ray flowing normally from the center of the circle, the entire radiation will constitute a perfect cone. If, however, the point is on an oblique central line, it will form an oblique cone. If the visible object is a square, the radiation will constitute a four-sided pyramid; if a pentagon, a five-sided pyramid, and so on to infinity. For as Vitellio <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1285), a famous medieval natural philosopher and mathematician known for his work on optics.</note> correctly demonstrates, innumerable optical figures or pyramids are formed between the radiator and the radiated object, with their bases and vertices illuminated mutually. However, so that we may proceed more solidly in this subject, we have decided to confirm those things said concerning <gloss>the casting of rays</gloss> <note>original: "ἀκτινοβολίας" (aktinobolias)</note> or radiation through brief and very easy propositions.

### Proposition I.

->*Whenever the Sun, having entered a circular opening, falls upon a plane parallel to the opening, it projects a circular light upon it.*<-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a light source point A on the left projecting rays through a circular aperture labeled B and C. The rays continue to form a larger elliptical/circular projection on an inclined plane labeled DE, with point D at the top and E at the bottom.</image-desc>

<column-break/>

Let the luminous body be A, and the opening BC, through which the radiant flow of light passes onto a plane parallel to it, which is DE. I say that this luminous projection is a circle. For, as is said in the study of conics, if a cone is cut by a plane parallel to its base, the section becomes a circle. Therefore, since BC is a circle, it is necessary that the section DE, being parallel to BC itself, is also a circle. The same must be said of a shadow: for if BC were a solid circle, the projection of the shadow onto the plane DE would be a circle.

### Proposition II.

->*Whenever a luminous body passes through a three-sided opening onto a plane parallel to it, it will project a light that is indeed larger, but exactly similar in shape to the opening.*<-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of light projection through a triangle. A point source A on the right projects rays through a triangular aperture BCD in the center onto a larger triangular projection EFG on a parallel plane on the left. Lines connect point A to each vertex of the aperture and its corresponding vertex on the projection plane.</image-desc>

Let the luminous body be A; let BCD be the triangular opening; and let EFG be the plane. I say that the projected light EFG is similar to the shape of the opening BCD, even though it is larger. For once the three rays ABF, ACE, and ADG have been extended, it will be clear through the 16th proposition of the 11th book and the 2nd proposition of the 6th book of Euclid's *Elements* <note>Euclid's *Elements* was the standard textbook for geometry for two millennia.</note> that what is proposed is true. If, however, BCD were opaque, the shadow FEG would be similar to the shape of the opaque body BCD.

### Corollary I.

From this it is clear that it can happen that light entering through an opening that is not equilateral may nevertheless form an equilateral light on the opposite wall. Suppose there is a radiant pyramid ABCD in the preceding figure, whose base is BCD, and let the pyramid itself be cut by a plane oblique to the base, which is EFG; this triangle will now not be equilateral. If, therefore, the luminous body A is understood to radiate through the triangle EFG, the base of the <term>actinobolism<note>The casting or radiation of rays.</note></term> BCD will clearly be an equilateral triangle. The same must be said of a shadow.

### Corollary II.

From this it is also clear that it is possible for an equilateral <note>In this context, a shape with equal sides, such as a perfect circle or square.</note> light to be projected through any other non-equilateral figure.

### Corollary III.

From this it is also clear how, given an elliptical aperture, a circle can be projected onto the opposite plane; or, given an elliptical opaque object, a circular shadow can be projected.

### Proposition III.

*The less the peripheries of two circles and of similar, similarly-positioned figures are removed from one another, the more they converge into the likeness of a single circle and a single figure.*

Let there be two circles, ABCE and AFCA, intersecting each other at points A and C. I say that the less the peripheries ABC and AFC are distant from each other, the more the composite figure ABCA, joined from the periphery 

<image-desc>A geometric construction consisting of a large outer circle labeled A, E, B, F. Inside are two intersecting arcs that form a lens-shaped area in the center labeled A and C. Within the figure are inscribed several smaller circles and labeled points including D, E, F, and C.</image-desc>

of both circles, will approach the likeness of a single circle. Alternatively, the same must be said of triangles DEF and FBC, and any other polygons: for the less the sides DE and BF of the said triangles are distant from one another, the more they will fall into the likeness of a single triangle. Now, the peripheries of two similar and similarly-placed circles can approach each other so closely that the difference is scarcely perceptible, and thus both are considered to be one circle, and both one figure. Since this is evident to the eye, it requires no further demonstration. Therefore, "The less the peripheries of two circles," etc., which was to be shown.

### Proposition IV.

*Rays that proceed from the extremities of a luminous body through the opposite extremities of an aperture*

<column-break/>

*intersect each other between the aperture and the luminous body.*

Let there be a light source AB, exposed to an aperture CD. Let the rays AC and BD proceed from the extremities of the luminous body A and B, crossing through the opposite edges of the hole, C and D.

<image-desc>A vertical optical diagram showing three light sources of different sizes (labeled ST, CD, CN) at the top. Rays from these sources pass through a single circular aperture labeled B. The rays cross at a common intersection point E located between the source and the aperture. Below the aperture, the rays diverge to project circular images of varying sizes (labeled HG, EF, and IK) onto a flat plane. The diagram illustrates how source size relative to aperture size affects projection size.</image-desc>

I say that their common intersection E falls between the aperture and the luminous body. For the rays AC and BD, along with the diameters of the aperture (DC) and the luminous body (AB), constitute two triangles, AEB and CED, facing each other at their points <note>original: "mucronibus." This refers to the apexes of the triangles meeting at a single point.</note>. Since their bases AB and CD are at a maximum distance, it is necessary that their vertices exist in the middle between them. Furthermore, the intersection E of the rays AC and BD is the common vertex of both triangles. Therefore, it falls between the aperture and the luminous body, which was to be demonstrated.

### First Corollary.

From this it is clear that if the diameters of the luminous body and the aperture (AB and CD) are equal, the vertex E of the triangles will be exactly in the middle between them. If, therefore, the solar rays passing through an aperture were to travel a distance as great as the distance of the Sun from the aperture, the light projected on the opposite side would be equal to the size of the Sun's surface. If, however, the light projected beyond the aperture exceeds that equality, it will be larger; if it is less than the halfway point, it will always be smaller the closer it approaches the aperture.

### Second Corollary

It is also clear that if the luminous body is equal to the aperture, the light projected onto the opposite plane will be equal to the luminous body. If the source is larger, the projected light will be smaller; if the source is smaller, the projected light will be larger. All these things are clearly evident in the figure, in the three circles ST, CD, and CN. Where the light CD is equal to aperture B, it projects a light circle EF equal to CD. The luminous body ST, being larger than aperture B, projects HG, a light circle smaller than the body ST. Finally, CN, a luminous body smaller than aperture B, projects a light circle IK, which is larger than the luminous body CN.

### *Third Corollary.*

It is also evident that shapes projected through an aperture appear inverted, and that they appear sometimes equal to the original objects, and at other times larger or smaller.

### **Proposition V.**

->*The Sun, shining through many-sided openings, does not form a shape with straight lines, but closely mimics a circle.*<-

One can see a very clear example of this in wicker lattices; when the rays of the Sun pass through their corners onto a target wall, they describe a circle more accurately than a triangle. This matter was once discussed by the Philosopher <note>Kircher refers to Aristotle, who famously asked in his *Problems* why the sun produces a round image through a square hole.</note> and his followers, and has also been much debated by Modern thinkers <note>The *Neoterici*, or "Moderns," likely refers to recent astronomers like Johannes Kepler or Christoph Scheiner.</note>; yet it has been fully understood by few. The Philosopher attributes the cause of this phenomenon to the radiant cone. In this, he does indeed touch upon the cause of the phenomenon, but not the whole cause; for rays extending from a point of a luminous body in every direction join themselves not only to a circular body, but to a body of any shape. Thus, rays do not gather into an orb regardless of what they strike; rather, they do so in one way at one time, and differently at another. Furthermore, when light from the entire luminous body falls upon a single point, the light does not always take on the shape of a cone <note>original: *turbinis*, literally a "whirl" or "spinning top" shape, used here to describe a conical beam of light.</note>, but rather the varying shape provided by the luminous body. Nor does he assign a reason in the latter part of the problem: for it is not enough that the Sun's shape is circular and that the light is carried in straight

<column-break/>

lines, unless it is also shown how light passing through quadrangular apertures is "blunted" <note>By "blunted," Kircher means the sharp corners of the aperture's shape are softened or lost in the projection.</note> and withdraws itself from the protruding angles, thus favoring the shape of the luminous body rather than the aperture, even when the shape of the lattice resists it. But so that such a remarkable phenomenon might be explained more fully, the rarity of the effect seems to claim this right for itself.

Let the solar body, therefore, be AB, and the aperture be a small slit of any shape, such as CD, through which the splendor of the Sun flows to illuminate the opposite plane FE. Now, from the infinite

Consequently, their two peripheries together are larger, and thus they approach the likeness of a single circle more closely according to the third Proposition. 

And although from the extension of the rays, not only the aforementioned diameters of the illuminations increase, but also their differences FK and HE, these differences increase by no sensible amount compared to the diameters. This arises because angle FCH is greater than angle FBK (according to the 16th Proposition of the 1st Book of Euclid's *Elements* <note>Euclid's Elements 1.16 states that an exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either of the opposite interior angles.</note>), and thus the legs FC and HC diverge more than the legs FB and KB. Therefore, if they are extended, FH grows much more as it becomes MN than FK does as it becomes MO. In the same way, KE grows more as it becomes OL than HE does as it becomes NL. 

Hence, their peripheries will finally seem to merge into the shape of a single orb. Moreover, they will result in roundness much more clearly if other circles were projected through the holes CD from points other than A and B. Consequently, since the boundary of a bright circle is made of infinite bright points, and all describe their own circles, it is clearly evident that from the infinite circles caused by *actinobolism* <term>actinobolism: from the Greek *aktinobolismos*, meaning the emission or shooting out of rays</term>, one circle will finally be seen.

### First Corollary.

From this it follows that when the Sun shines through any hole whatsoever, the further the light recedes from the hole, the more the projected light approaches the form of that same circle (parallel to the plane of the circle which is the boundary of the radiant surface). Finally, with the sense of sight being deceived, it appears perfectly circular, since every hole that allows the passage of a Solar ray is of an infinitesimal size in relation to the Sun's magnitude and distance.

### Second Corollary.

Finally, you see how the pyramids or cones of light, which fall from individual points of the Solar body through quadrilateral or any polygonal holes, are arranged into an orb. For their axes, having crossed near the holes, touch the vertices on one side and the centers of the bases on the other; wherefore they complete the circle on both sides, one of which occupies the Solar orb, and the other that place on the plane which only the axes of the pyramids reach. Furthermore, the protruding portions of the bases surround this circle on all sides:

<column-break/>

from which it surely happens that all the light received by the plane appears to emulate a circle. But let us finally prove all these things with experiments, so that the truth may appear more clearly.

### Third Corollary.

Finally, if the luminous body were of any polygonal shape projected through any

### Experiment I.

Therefore, let two or three very small holes be made near each other in some window, through which the same number of illuminations may be transferred to a piece of paper placed opposite. These, when the paper is moved close to the hole, will appear small and overlapping each other very little, and thus will not present a single circle. However, the further the paper is removed, the larger they become and the more they overlap each other, and for that reason, they coalesce into almost one circle. Yet they never reach geometric roundness, even though they present it to the sense of sight. The reason for this is that, as said above, rays are not mathematical lines, but are endowed with some width, and consequently, the points from which they consist are not mathematical, but physical; and an infinity of these never produces a mathematical or geometric circle.

<margin>A remarkable experiment.</margin>

If, however, you set up a triangular piece of wood or board, and the [square] hole...

<margin>Other experiments.</margin>

### Corollary

<margin>The utility of these experiments.</margin>

**H**ence, almost all phenomena of observations in a dark place <note>Kircher is referring to the *camera obscura*, literally "dark room."</note> are made clear. For what can be said of the Sun can also be said of any other luminous body; thus, an eclipsed Sun, as well as the Moon, likewise produce an eclipsed and inverted illumination. This also explains why the appearances of things are shown inside exactly as they appear outside; all of which we shall treat in the following sections. Indeed, this single experiment has taught astronomers to measure with a compass the magnitudes of Solar eclipses, the proportions of the diameters of the Sun and Moon, and the inclinations of the circle passing through the centers of the luminaries relative to the vertical—all without damage to the eyes and without the error that is usually committed by mere estimation. But here we cannot omit to reveal a certain notable fallacy in this matter, which is that all

<column-break/>

eclipses detected by this art have occurred much larger in the heavens than they appeared in the projected beam, with all of them showing the diameter of the Moon in the heavens to be much larger than in the beam. Because Tycho Brahe <note>A famous Danish nobleman and astronomer (1546–1601) known for his accurate celestial observations.</note> did not foresee this, he was led—not without wonder—to pronounce the diameter of the Moon to be always a fifth part smaller in conjunctions <note>When the Moon is between the Earth and Sun (New Moon).</note> than it appeared in oppositions <note>When the Moon is opposite the Sun (Full Moon).</note>, even though both are equally distant from us. There are also other causes for this diminution, which we shall reveal elsewhere, if it pleases the Divine Power. But all these things will be better learned in the following experiment.

<margin>The fallacy in the observations made by Tycho Brahe.</margin>

### Experiment III.

-> Remote distance converts an angular luminous body into a spherical one. <-

**I**t happens for the most part that when we are far away from a luminous body of any shape, we nevertheless see it as round. Thus,

<image-desc>An optical diagram illustrating how different light sources (Sun, Moon, Venus, a flame) are perceived by the human eye through an aperture, showing the transition from their true shapes to circular projections over distance.</image-desc>

in the diagram placed here, the eye **A**, under the rays **AB** and **AC**, gazes upon Venus **BC** as spherical; yet, when in perigee, it is horned like the Moon, as has become known in these recent times to the Lyncean Academy <note>The *Accademia dei Lincei*, the scientific society to which Galileo belonged. Likewise, when the part of the horn of the six-day-old Moon **CD** rises above the horizon, it appears so round that it has sometimes moved the unskilled to suspect a new star has arisen. Also, the luminous edge **IG** of the six-day-old Moon appears more prominent than the shadowed part. The same must be said of the flame **T**, which we perceive as a pyramid shape when present, but when remote, we judge to be endowed with a round figure.

In this way, lamps of a conical shape reflect their flames when nearby, but in distant places, such as long hallways, they are seen as shining little spheres, larger than usual; all of which are nothing other than illusions of the eyes. For nothing can be conceived either in the luminous bodies themselves, or in the transparent medium <note>original: "diaphano medio," the air or material the light passes through</note>, that could cause this effect; therefore, it exists in the eye alone. This is also evident from the following: if you cover the horn of the Moon, or any angular luminous body, with your hand, the same round appearance will always remain.

<margin>Stars are smaller than they appear.</margin>
It is clear from these points that twinkling stars are not actually as large as the common crowd of astronomers think, since their diameter is dilated by the surrounding light; and consequently, nothing certain can be defined regarding the magnitude of the stars.

### Experiment IV.
#### On the twinkling of the stars.

<margin>What the twinkling of stars is.</margin>
The twinkling <note>original: "scintillatio"</note> of the stars is a frequent experience, even if few have reached its genuine cause. For we all experience that stars do indeed twinkle, but in different ways: fixed stars twinkle more, wandering stars [planets] less; they twinkle more when near the horizon and less when elevated above it; more in the arctic than in the antarctic; more in rainy weather than in clear skies; more today than yesterday. Those endowed with weak light twinkle more than those with intense light; Saturn less than Jupiter; Venus at its farthest and nearest points less than Mercury. We assign the cause of all these things not to the stars' own rotation; not to a "feverish paroxysm," as some have ridiculously asserted; not to the solar rays (which we previously stated are unmoved); not to a trembling vibration from the primary and secondary motions; not to a restless ejaculation of rays from the stars; not to a tremor of the sight; nor to a trembling of the [visual] power caused by the effort of seeing. Rather, we assert that the twinkling of stars is nothing other than a single and sole interruption of the "species" <note>The "species" refers to the visual image or form of the object traveling through the air to the eye.</note> falling from them into the eye, caused by the restless running-to-and-fro of vapors affected in various ways. For these vapors, partly by their running-between, make the received image more brilliant through refraction; and thus, at the moment of their passage, they offer a certain light more effective than usual. Partly by their distinct running-between—which had almost choked the ray of the star—they open a free path for the optical cone to the eye at rapid intervals through purely transparent gaps. For when the turbulent vapors are divided, and some have slipped away haphazardly while others are configured differently, some rays are entirely hidden, others are weakened, and others are refracted. From this it happens that one part of the star seems to be pulled upward, another downward, and to be twisted in

<column-break/>

different directions; indeed, this restless agitation of vapors is found most especially in stars situated near the horizon and in the vaporous Southern region. The following demonstrates the truth of the experiment: for if, in an open field, you look at the gilded globe of some tower <margin>A beautiful observation.</margin> illuminated by the Sun when the vapors are still, you will gaze upon it without any agitation; but when vapors raised by the solar rays intervene, you will see the image of the globe brought to the eye wavering in every direction, even to the point that the globe seems to dance in every direction. Therefore, what the vapors do and are capable of doing to a globe, they do the same to the stars. Anyone who has looked at a furrow in the fields during springtime when the Sun is hotter will discover the said agitation of vapors and a certain wondrous trembling of the air by a truly remarkable experiment. Moreover, the agitation of the vapors derives its origin from nowhere else but the condensation, rarefaction, and continuous alteration of water and air.

### Proposition VI.
#### The rays of the Sun, and of any luminous bodies, do not mix.

<margin>A wondrous property of rays.</margin>
This nature and property of rays is also a wondrous thing: that in "actinobolism" <term>actinoboliſmo</term> <note>From the Greek "aktinobolismos," meaning the emission or radiation of rays.</note>, rays are by no means mixed with other rays, nor are they broken, nor do they go off in different directions; but each one is poured out for itself in a straight path. Take this experiment as proof.

### Experiment I.

Let there be three luminous bodies A, B, and C, which pour light through a hole D onto an opposite

table E; they will all indeed run together

<meta>This page continues Kircher’s exploration of the behavior of light. Previously, he discussed how light appears to the eye and the nature of twinkling. Now, he moves into the geometry of light rays passing through an aperture, specifically arguing that rays of light do not "mix" or interfere with one another even when passing through the same point, a principle fundamental to the operation of the camera obscura.</meta>

<page-num>89</page-num>
<header>The Radiation of Light.</header>

...all the lights at once in the opening of the hole D, in such a way, however, that as experience has proven, they are by no means mixed together. Instead, each proceeds along its own path and in a straight line: from A to F; from B [to G]; and finally from C to H. This is not unlike <term>Angelic spirits</term> <note>Kircher uses a theological analogy here: just as multiple angels can occupy the same space without physically colliding, light rays occupy the same aperture without interfering with one another.</note> when they meet in some common place. For this reason, if the light source A is removed, the light at F ceases; if B is covered, its light at G is taken away; and if C is blocked, the light that had been at H is extinguished without any harm or diminution to the remaining lights. If, however, an opaque body is placed at position D, then F will be the shadow of light source A, G the shadow of light source B, and H the shadow of body C. Therefore, when the three lights meet at D, they are not confused in a tumultuous way or without order; rather, each one, having preserved its own integrity, takes its own path and proceeds in a straight line. If they were not transmitted in a confused state through straight lines, then either the ray from luminous body A would be carried to H, or to G. But this is absurd in optics, since it is impossible for a luminous body to illuminate anything with its direct ray except through a straight line, as <term>Alhazen</term> <note>Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), the "father of modern optics."</note> demonstrates at length in Book 1 of his *Optics*, along with <term>Vitello</term> <note>Erazmus Ciołek Witelo (c. 1230–1280s), a Polish friar and physicist whose work on optics was a standard text in the Renaissance.</note>. Furthermore, very strong reasons support this experiment. First, indeed: since lights are carried in straight lines, it is impossible for them to be mixed; for in order to be mixed, it is necessary that they invade one another. This, however, cannot happen unless they deflect from their straight path; otherwise, each would remain in its own place and could not occupy the seat of another, and therefore could not be mixed. Next, the rays which leap forth from every part of a luminous body in all directions are by no means mixed, but each distinct ray holds its own straight journey, as can be gathered from the preceding experiments. Therefore, the lights that proceed from distinct light sources are not mixed among themselves, but each proceeds on its own path to where the force of the light source impels it. Nor does it stand in the way that many lights meet in the same medium, as some object. For there are many lights in the same place (for example, at G) in the same way that two angels might penetrate one another, or just as color and heat meet while they are in the same subject. Nor does it stand in the way, as others object, that in the same medium, one light cannot be assigned here and another there; for this is true of those lights which are not carried through the same medium, but it is false in the convergence of many lights.

### Practical Demonstrations Resulting from What Has Been Said.

From these things it follows how someone might more easily and distinctly represent in the dark all those things which we said could be done in the previous experi-

<column-break/>

ments—and what is more, according to a straight <term>species</term> <note>original: "speciem," referring to the visible image or "form" emitted by an object.</note>—at night, using only candles, in the following way.

<image-desc>A technical diagram of a camera obscura setup. On the left (illuminated side), there is an upright drawing of a face. These rays cross at the hole and project onto the back wall of a darkened room on the right, where the image appears upside down (inverted). Labels M, N, L, O, and Z mark the boundaries of the image and the projection area.</image-desc>

<margin>Representation of things in the dark.</margin> Take any image, subtly painted in any color on thin paper, and dip it in oil. Once dry, enclose it within the sides of the window MONL. I say that if you place any number of candles in positions L and O before the image, passing through the hole S (which must be made in the wall lying between the illuminated room and the dark one), the <term>species</term> of the image which you wish to show will be represented on the walls or on white paper placed opposite it, with all its shading. They will be inverted if you place the image M, N, L, O upright, and upright if you place it inverted. For since any point of the image transmits its own <term>species</term> to the opposite wall of the dark room according to what was said previously, and since we have shown that light rays are diffused along straight lines, it happens: first, that those parts which are at the bottom of the painted image become the top in the likeness of the image, and vice versa; second, that the image, perfectly illuminated by the candles placed before it, uniformly casts its own <term>species</term> with all its shadows into the opposite part of the dark room, as is clear in the example provided.

<margin>They manifest the hidden concepts of the mind in a closed place.</margin> From this it also follows how someone can manifest the hidden concepts of their mind to another person staying in a dark place, and describe whatever things they wish on the wall, solely by the aid of transmitted <term>species</term>.

The likeness will also appear imbued with the same color as the painted image: if yellow, yellow; if green, green; and so on for the rest. For light mixed with any matter assumes that color with which the matter itself has been im-

# The Great Art, Book II. Part I.
<page-num>90</page-num>

...as has been shown at length in the preceding sections, which will become even clearer in the following experiment.

<margin>Another experiment.</margin>
Let there be a transparent glass lamp, perhaps green, whose oil is also imbued with a green color along with a green wick; if this is lit, it shows everything in green, including the faces of those looking on. If you desire to see everything as black, you will achieve this by adding the <term>ink of cuttlefish</term> <note>original: *saepiis atramento*; this refers to the dark pigment harvested from the sepia or cuttlefish, commonly used as ink and here used as a coloring agent for fuel.</note>; for when moved near the lamps, if it is ignited, it will cast forth a black flame. Thus <term>Anaxilaus</term> <note>A Pythagorean philosopher and physician from the 1st century BCE who was said to perform "magical" feats using natural science.</note> is said to have played such tricks, as recorded by <term>Philostratus</term>, where he made the bystanders appear like <term>Ethiopians</term> <note>In the historical context of the 17th century, this term was used to describe people with very dark skin.</note> using cuttlefish ink. Furthermore, you will see everything as yellow if you mix <term>orpiment</term> <note>A deep orange-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used as a pigment.</note>, saffron, and the husks of lupin beans with the oil, and light it with a yellow cord in a yellow lamp. <term>Simeon Sethi</term> <note>An 11th-century Byzantine Jewish scholar known for his works on the properties of foods and medicines.</note> also relates that if someone dips a wick—that is, the flax of the lamp—into cuttlefish ink and the rust of copper, the surrounding people will appear partly waxen and partly black due to the sprinkling of the mixed substances. As for what <term>Giambattista della Porta</term> <note>An Italian polymath and playwright known for his work *Magia Naturalis* (Natural Magic). Kircher often cites him but here expresses skepticism of his more "miraculous" claims.</note> presumes to do—namely, making the heads of bystanders appear as those of horses or donkeys—I consider that to have more boastfulness than truth. However, I would dare to affirm as an eyewitness that it is true one can make a room appear full of grapes. Truly, concerning these matters, see the more extensive treatise in *The Magic of Light and Shadow*.

And thus far we have spoken of the direct projection of images. It remains for us to say something also regarding their reflected projection. Just as

<margin>Representation by a reflected ray.</margin>
the surfaces of polished bodies describe their own lights, colors, and forms from any of their points into an opposite dark place by a direct ray, as has been said; so too light, received upon a wall together with color, can be reflected according to the straightness of the lines. For according to Proposition 1 of this work, the form of light is always diffused from a luminous body in a straight line into every body opposite to it, and similarly for a colored form having the action of light. Therefore, when these fall upon a mirror or another third body, a reflection of light, color, and forms always occurs because of the opacity of such a body, which is proven by the following experiment.

### Experiment II.
#### *How the images of things are to be represented inside a certain house.*

<margin>Experiment on the reflected ray.</margin>
Let a ray of the Sun descend into a house through a hole onto a colored object, and let a mirror be placed in opposition to it. Again, let a concave vessel, like a cup, white on the inside, be placed against the mirror and adjusted so that the reflected light falls upon that white body. Thus, the color of that body upon which the light first fell will appear upon the surface of the white body.

<column-break/>

<margin>How inverted images may appear upright in various ways.</margin>
Color is therefore reflected together with light; thus it also falls upon a polished body together with the light. If that body is dense and hard, the color is totally reflected from it with the light, such that it colors the polished body. If, however, the polished body is rare and transparent in its nature, such as water, glass, and similar things, then the colors will be reflected from it while the lights penetrate it. This is evident from the fact that the form of reflection from these bodies consists of weaker light and color than from other, denser bodies. It now remains for us to teach by what means those images which appear inverted in a dark place may appear upright. This can be done in two ways: either by the inversion of external things (if their condition allows for it), or by the aid of a <term>lenticular glass</term> <note>A convex lens, shaped like a lentil.</note> or a mirror. The former can be done without difficulty; the latter in the following manner. In a dark place, set a mirror opposite the opening—not one that scatters and dissipates light, but one that unites it by gathering it. Move it back and forth until you recognize the true image in its proper size by its proximity to the center. If you look closely, you will see the colored clothes of men, their faces, gestures, and movements; the sky scattered with clouds in a deep blue color, and birds flying. What is wonderful is that everything near the center of the mirror will be reversed; but if you move them further from the center, you will see them larger and upright as they truly are. But of these things, we speak more fully in our *Catoptric Magic* <note>Kircher's term for the study of mirrors and reflection.</note>.

### *Corollary I.*

It is clear from this to philosophers and physicians in what place vision occurs in the eyes: for the <term>visual image</term> <note>original: *idolum*; in early modern optics, this referred to the "phantom" or likeness of an object that travels to the eye.</note> is admitted through the pupil like a window, and the back portion of the eye's sphere, being situated there, performs the role of a small mirror.

### *Corollary II.*

It is clear that every reflection weakens light, colors, and generally all forms. For since continuous light is stronger than scattered light (according to the 1st Postulate), and since we see that light is weaker the further it is from its origin, it is clear that light proceeding from a point of some luminous body toward the surface of a polished body or mirror in the shape of a pyramid undergoes a greater weakening—both because of the light's distance from its source and because of its scattering—the further it is from that point. Reflected light from a mirror is even weaker, both because of its distance from the point of reflection and because of the scattering and the reflection itself. Since colors are the "apes of light," they likewise fade and are always seen to be weaker and less perceptible as they are further removed from the movement of light, whether direct or reflected, as shown in the preceding sections.

# The Irradiation of Light

...it will appear clearly to anyone making a trial through experiments, as is established by the following experiment.

### Experiment III.

### On the Weakening of Reflected Light.

<margin>A reflected ray always displays weaker forms than a direct one.</margin>
If a colored, transparent body is placed in the path of a ray striking a mirror, so that the ray passes through it and falls upon the mirror, you will perceive that when the light hits the mirror and is reflected onto a white wall, this reflected light is much weaker than the original. In the same way, a reflected color is weaker than the color from which the reflection originates. It is therefore evident that all reflection weakens both light and color; however, it weakens colors more than light, because colors strike the surface more weakly than light does, and thus they are more easily diminished during reflection. For when a weak color reaches the mirror, it is mixed with the inherent color of the mirror itself, and because of this mixture, it is changed and "muddled," so to speak. Thus, the reflected color appears weak, somewhat obscure, and dim. Furthermore, the distance of the reflected form from the point of reflection increases this weakness. What was proposed is therefore clear.

### Corollary

It is clear that reflected light and color are weaker than the primary light and color; however, they are stronger than <term>secondary</term> <note>Kircher refers here to "secondary" or scattered light that has not been concentrated by a reflection or direct beam.</note> light and color when they are at an equal distance from the same source. Someone might perhaps object here that the weakness of forms in reflection is due only to their distance from their origin; but that this is false will be clear from the following experiment: for even if direct and reflected light are moved an equal distance from their source, the reflected light will always be found to be weaker.

### Experiment IV.

### On the Weakening of Reflected Light.

<margin>Another representation by which the weakening of reflected light is shown.</margin>
Let a ray of the sun enter a darkened room through a hole. Let a <term>steel mirror</term> <note>original: *speculum chalybeum*; in the 17th century, mirrors were frequently made of highly polished metal rather than silvered glass.</note> (which should be smaller than the hole) be placed opposite the hole, so that the remaining light from the hole falls upon the ground on a piece of clean paper, while the light reflected from the mirror is cast onto another white body held aloft. Ensure that the distance from the hole to the elevated body is the same as the distance to the paper on the ground. Once this is done, you will perceive that the light reflected onto the surface of the elevated body is much weaker than that which appears on the surface of the paper lying on the ground. No reason can be assigned for this lessening of light except for the reflection itself. For as was said in the preceding Corollary, the direct light is muddled when mixed with the color of the mirror,

<column-break/>

falling away from its original perfection. It is then carried to the target imbued with this muddiness. If, however, a mirror could be provided that possessed the same clarity as light itself, the reflected light—being without the mixture of an obscure color—would undoubtedly be of the same quality as the direct light. The same shall be said for reflected light and secondary light. Likewise for true colors and <term>intentional</term> <note>original: *intentionalibus*; in the science of the time, "intentional" colors were those produced by light and medium (like a rainbow) rather than being inherent in a solid object.</note> or secondary colors. For if secondary light falls on a body placed at the same distance from the source but outside the point of reflection, you will find this secondary light to be much weaker than reflected light. The reason is the same as the previous ones; therefore, what was proposed at the beginning is clear.

# The Great Art, Book II. Part I.

### Experiment VI.
#### On Light.

Take a hollow cylinder, in whose curved surface there are three openings, A, B, and C. Opposite these, let three lit torches be placed so that their light, passing through the openings, shines together upon a single spot on the interior surface, ED. The light at ED will then be three times the intensity of the light which each of the radiant cones—DIA, IBK, and EKC—possesses on its own. For just as 3 relates to 1, so the light DIE (composed of the three radiant cones) relates to the single cone KFC or DIA. And just as 2 relates to 1, so the light LKE or DLI relates to DIA or EKC, which is a simple segment of a cone. Again, as 3 relates to 2, so the light DLE

<margin>The wonderful proportion of mixed light.</margin>

relates to the segments DLI or ELK. The first proportion is triple, the second is double, and the third is <term>sesquialter</term> <note>A ratio of 1.5 to 1, or 3:2.</note>. Therefore, the light is intensified according to the number of torches, provided that each is placed at an equal distance from the openings; and when

<column-break/>

cones of equal intensity are positioned, the common convergence of all the light will relate to any one of them as the total number of cones relates to one. If, however, the point of common convergence is perforated so that the cones gradually diverge from each other again, and each light falls upon the opposite wall MN, then MOP and QNR will be a <term>lunula</term> <note>A crescent-shaped area of light.</note> relating to the segment PO or QR (which is curved on both sides) in a 1 to 2 ratio; and each of these relates to the segment PR, which is common to all, in a 2 to 3 ratio.

### First Corollary.

<margin>Images are formal, not virtual.</margin>
From this it is clearly evident that the <term>images</term> <note>Kircher uses the word "species," which in 17th-century science referred to the physical forms or "likenesses" that objects emit so they can be seen.</note> of things are formal, not virtual. For if they were virtual, they would spread themselves out equally in every direction after they joined together.

### Second Corollary.

<margin>Whether images are divisible.</margin>
It is clear from this that just as the object is divisible, so too are the radiant cones, since any one ray differs in reality from another, just as one cone differs from another. I would not, however, easily grant the reverse of this proposition—that just as the image is divisible, so the object must be. For regarding what is seen at the convergence of all the rays of a cone, we assert that it is not the image itself, but the <term>vertex</term> (the tip) of the images. Visible images have size; they are not indivisible points, except when they flow together into a single point, which is the vertex of the radiant cone. Should anyone stubbornly insist that the images exist within that point of convergence, we respond that they are indeed there, but not in a way suited to move the sense of sight, since nothing can be moved "under" a point. Therefore, they lie hidden there by their own power <note>original: "virtute"</note> potentially, like a tree in a seed, which is eventually brought into reality through <term>reflection</term> <note>original Greek: ἀντινοβολισμὸν (*antinobolismon*), referring to the rebounding or interaction of rays.</note>. For since that point relates to the scattered rays and the rays collected back to itself as the center of a circle relates to its radii—and since it pours out all those rays—it is divisible not in actuality, but only in potential. It is divisible not in itself, but in its rays. One could even say it is divided by degree, not by quantity. Furthermore, the wonderful things that result from experiments of this kind will be made clear in our section on the "Magic of Light and Shadow," where we shall describe the use of these experiments more extensively.

***

## CHAPTER V.
### On Irradiation, or the radiation of color.

Experience has made it almost common knowledge that light illuminating colors is reflected in every direction, and that these illuminated colors radiate in a circle, not unlike light itself, though somewhat more weakly. Furthermore, the surfaces of bodies of any shape transmit the lights, colors, and forms of opposite things from any of their points into a dark place, following the path of straight lines. To explain this proposition in a few words:

<column-break/>

Note first, that there is a two-fold nature to this pro-

# The Irradiation of Light.

<margin>
*The nature of light.*
</margin>

...part of the proposition. The first part considers the nature of light and colors; the second considers the manner in which forms are reflected along their own lines. Regarding the first point: note secondly that it is the nature of light that whatever color it touches, it is immediately tinted by it. It is then no longer propagated as pure light, but as light affected by that color, diffused far and wide through a transparent medium <note>original: "medium diaphanum"</note>. For since every body that either shines with its own brilliance or is imbued with some color must necessarily be opaque—as is learnedly demonstrated by Aquilonius <note>François d'Aguilon (1567–1617), a Jesuit mathematician and physicist whose work on optics was a primary source for Kircher.</note> in Book 1 of his *Optics*, proposition 31—and since nothing among sublunary <note>Objects existing below the moon, i.e., on Earth, subject to change and decay.</note> things is perfectly transparent, nor is there any opaque object <note>original: "ἀδιάφονον" (adiaphonon), used here to mean non-transparent or opaque.</note> that is not visible by light or color, it follows that a certain reciprocity occurs between the light, the colored object, and the opacity. Thus, color becomes mixed with light as if it were a specific quality of it. Consequently, many different types of light arise from this mixture. Indeed, unless every light were affected by some color, nothing would remain by which one could be distinguished from another, since light is a quality without which nothing in the world would be visible. It is therefore necessary to demonstrate what was proposed: that the native color of an object coalesces with light into a single appearance and a single sight. From this concrete joining and tempering, according to the

<margin>
*Why the lights of the planets are of different colors.*
</margin>

diversity of colors, a diverse difference in light is also produced. Hence, the light of the Sun is observed everywhere as golden, that of the Moon as silvery, that of Mars as reddish, the light of a sulfurous flame as blue, and the light of burning copper <note>original: "æruginis," referring to the green film or "verdigris" on weathered copper.</note> as green. Nor does it contradict this that Aristotle says in his book *On Colors*, chapter 1: "The light of fire is its color." For no other color of fire is found besides this, and for that reason, it alone exists as a visible thing, since other visible things become so through its benefit; and we can attribute the sight of fire to nothing else but light. These things are rightly said by Aristotle, since neither the color of fire can be seen without light, nor can light be seen unless it is affected by color. Hence Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous 15th-century Italian scholar who translated Plotinus.</note>, in his commentary on Book 1 of Plotinus’s second *Ennead*, attributes every variety of colors that we discern in different lights to the rarity or density of matter. He says in the cited passage: "We know that light is more brilliant the purer it is; on the contrary, it turns red in thick matter,

<column-break/>

pale in medium matter, but shines brightly in the thinnest matter." And he applied this to the celestial stars as well, which he said shine with various colors for the same reason that the color of saffron <note>original: "croci"</note> appears red when gathered together, pale when diffused, and finally brilliant when most widely spread. Truly, however, the greater or lesser thinning of matter can only achieve this: that the color becomes more diluted; it cannot actually change the species of the color. Therefore, it will never happen that the color of saffron becomes blue, no matter how much the matter is thinned or compressed. From where, then, do the flames of certain things appear golden, others reddish, others purple, others

<margin>
*Why flames are of different colors.*
</margin>

blue, and finally others green? Surely it is from the specific color of the flammable material, which, mixed with the light, shines and gleams as one. Thus, the light which is primarily within a lucid body is imbued with the color of that body; but the light which emanates from the lucid body, although it is much weaker and of a thinner essence, nevertheless perpetually retains the same color it received from its source. The only change is that here, too, the color is thinned, and it fades gradually just as the light does, always more so the further it recedes from its origin. Indeed, unless we say that light is affected by color in this way, no probable reason will exist by which we can show that one light differs from another, as has been said, when it is nonetheless certain that one is white, another yellow, another reddish, or affected by another color. Just as the lucid body itself is seen through the light that falls from it, so the proper color of the lucid body is perceived through its own image by means of the color of the light. Furthermore, light does not only borrow colors from the specific material from which it flows, but also from the very bodies upon which it strikes: for it is stained by the color of whatever it is reflected from. Thus, the color cast off <note>original: "decisus color"</note> is carried through the transparent medium with the light, and it penetrates wherever the light itself goes. These "shards" or "skins" <note>original: "exuviæ," referring to the thin outer layer or "husks" of color that detach from an object.</note> of colors are of a much thinner essence than the colors themselves, and they differ no less from true colors than direct light differs from reflected light—that is, the first from the second. I wish to record a most clear experiment of this matter, from which the spectator will also receive no small pleasure.

# The Great Art [of Light and Shadow], Book II, Part I.

...by the transmission of solar rays. Once these things are properly prepared, a white paper should be placed behind the glass inside, at that distance where the solar rays are naturally meant to converge into a single point. For here, whatever things are outside will be seen depicted in their own colors on the paper, not without a certain allure for the sight and delight for the mind; and the image will differ in no way from the thing itself, except only in size and position. For the position will necessarily be inverted, and the size will always be smaller as the object is further from the glass.

<margin>Why colors are not poured forth without the benefit of light.</margin>
But someone might ask here: what are these colors, why are they not poured out without the help of light, and finally, why are they only represented in darkness? To the first, I reply: these colors are none other than those which, being reflected from true objects, are carried along with light through a transparent medium <note>original: "medium diaphanum"</note>. For these, being refracted by the density of the glass itself, glide through the narrow opening onto the target paper, where they then appear visible; otherwise, they could in no way be seen in an open medium because of the thinness of their essence.

<margin>Intentional colors.</margin>
For these colors are only intentional <term>intentional: In Aristotelian and Scholastic physics, an 'intentional species' is the non-material form or image of an object that travels through the air to the eye or a surface.</term>, not corporeal; they are of exactly the same nature as those reflected from colored objects with light onto nearby walls. However, since these colors are by no means diffused without the assistance of light, the cause is that light is, as it were, the form and soul of colors, without which they lie hidden under a dark power. When light arrives, they are led out into action and visibility, and as if animated, they represent the living images of the things from which they emanated. Furthermore, the reason why they are not represented except in darkness is this: because the light by which they are sustained as if by a foundation <note>original: "hypostasi"</note>

<image-desc>
An elaborate optical diagram illustrating the principles of the camera obscura and projection. 
1. At the top, a demonic-looking figure with horns and a tail stands on a pedestal outside a room. Optical rays originate from its head and body, converging through an aperture in a wall. Inside the darkened space, these rays pass through a convex lens and project an inverted image of the figure onto a vertical screen. 
2. Below this, a simpler diagram shows light passing through an aperture 'A' to project the image of a cross 'B' onto a surface.
3. At the bottom left, a circular horological or optical instrument resembling a sundial is depicted, with a gnomon casting a shadow and markings for hours 6 through 2.
4. At the bottom right, a second circular diagram features radial divisions numbered 1 through 12, likely representing a projection scale or coordinate system.
</image-desc>

<column-break/>

is so very thin that it is easily overcome by a greater light. When that greater light is removed, the "intentions" of the colors similarly hide. For the same power is not present in colors as in the solar star; for the sun pours out so much light from itself that even its second, third, and fourth [reflections] are effective in stirring our sight. But colors are so weak that the first intention—that is, the one cut off nearest to the primary color—is overwhelmed by the smallest light, nor can it endure any greater light than that which bodies, having repelled it, send to our sight. For just as secondary light (or a reflected ray in the dark) relates to the primary light that is the origin of its essence, so do secondary or "intentional" colors relate to the nearest true colors from which they flowed. Indeed, color is a kind of *Ape of Light* <note>original: "Simia quaedam lucis"</note>, which mimics light in all things, although it can never reach its perfection. And hence it is that it can never represent mixed images <note>original: "species"</note> except by secondary light alone, and that in the dark, as has been said. Finally, why the images appear inverted will be shown below.

### First Corollary.
### On parastasis <term>parastasis: A Greek term used here to mean the formal representation, exhibition, or "setting before" of an object.</term>, or the representation of things.

From what has been said, it can be gathered by what skill playful representations—such as hunts, battles, and even appearances of terrifying forms—can be demonstrated in any dark place. I certainly remember that I once saw the crucifixion of our Lord Christ accurately represented in a dark place by this method.

<margin>A representation made for Emperor Rudolph.</margin>
By this method, as I learned from a man of great name who was present at the spectacle, all the Roman Caesar predecessors from Julius Caesar even unto Maurice were represented in their correct appearance <note>original: "recta specie"</note> to the Emperor Rudolph II by a distinguished mathematician. This was done so vividly that all who were present thought it was done by magical art or necromantic conjuration.

<margin>A playful representation.</margin>

### Second Corollary.

From these things it is clear that whatever has been said so far regarding the **radiation of light** <term>actinobolismus: From the Greek 'aktis' (ray) and 'ballo' (to throw), referring to the way light radiates or 'shoots' out.</term> is also to be understood regarding the radiation of colors. For just as rays are projected unmixed into a dark place during the outpouring of light, so too are the images of colors. Thus, even if the images of all colors flow together at a common point of intersection, they are in no way confounded there; rather, every radiating point of a surface is propagated in a straight path onto a dark wall without any mixture or confusion of images occurring at the point of intersection.

### Third Corollary.

<margin>The medium is always full of the images of innumerable things.</margin>
Hence it is also clear that any transparent medium is full of infinite images of visible and colored things, which nevertheless penetrate each other without any confusion. Thus, the images of towers, houses, windows, men, and animals, radiating in a circle, produce an infinite multitude of images; yet only he who has skillfully enclosed them within a dark space will be able to see them. I say that the said image of the cross is multiplied infinitely within the pyramid CB, so that as many images of the cross can be conceived within C and B, or CA, as there are sections allowed by the said pyramid.
