# THE GREAT ART, BOOK II. PART I.

## CHAPTER VI.

### On Actinobolism <note>From the Greek 'aktinobolismos', meaning the emission of rays or radiation.</note>, or the radiation of sound, and its parallel comparison to light: likewise on the nature, medium, and subject of sound.

<margin>Sound imitates light.</margin>
We have stated in the preceding pages that all things in nature strive for the character of light in their radiation. Having seen, therefore, the Actinobolism of light and color—which are the objects of sight—let us now see by what radiation the object of hearing performs its operations. For it is certain, as daily experience teaches, that sound creates a sphere of power within which alone it may be perceived, and outside of which it cannot. But this sphere cannot be formed unless it is established through straight lines diffused in every direction from the sounding subject through the medium, as if from a center. Therefore, the radiation of sound closely emulates the flow of light, and there is no other difference in their radiation <note>original: "ἀκτινοβολίας"</note> except that light is propagated with instantaneous motion, while sound travels through the air with successive <note>meaning step-by-step or taking time</note> motion.

Indeed, the poet Virgil himself seems to imply that light and sound are in some way the same thing when he says:
> *Then the fire is heard more clearly.* <note>original: "Tum clarior ignis auditur" — Virgil, Aeneid, Book II.</note>
> As also in Book 6:
> *And dogs were seen to bark through the shadow.* <note>original: "Visæque canes latrare per umbram" — Virgil, Aeneid, Book VI.</note>

For nothing can encounter the eyes that cannot also present itself to the ears under the same logic. Just as it is the property of light to represent the different colors of bodies according to the different directions of the rays—now falling <note>incident</note>, now reflected—upon surfaces, and from there to the eyes; so it is the property of sounds to represent the different qualities of bodies by means of the moved air hitting and striking their surfaces. Thus, we might not incongruously say that colors are nothing other than the different immersion and reflection of rays in a medium, just as sounds are nothing other than the different motions of the air. For if anyone could see the most subtle motions of the air while some musical instrument was sounding, they would surely see nothing else than a painting shadowed with a remarkable variety of colors, by which the diverse qualities of the sounding bodies would present themselves to the eyes, as has been said. Furthermore, just as light considered in itself is invisible, so is sound. For we can see nothing in this world except colored surfaces representing, as much as they can, the Sun and other luminous bodies. Moreover, concave mirrors show well enough that light is invisible,

<column-break/>

for they leave no trace of rays except at the point where the rays meet, provided an opaque reflecting body is applied. Indeed, to speak more strictly, I say that no <term>accident</term> <note>In philosophy, an 'accident' is a quality or attribute (like color or sound) that cannot exist on its own but must exist within a substance or body.</note> is sensible in itself, except through the bodies by which it is sustained, or through the quantity that gives them extension, without which it would vanish into a point—into nothingness. Therefore, just as light is invisible, so is sound; yet while it makes the air sensible to us, it manifests many qualities of bodies which we would not know how to recognize without the help of sounds. And if anyone looks a little more deeply into the nature of light, they will find it to be nothing other than a certain motion of the air, as it were, which carries with it the image of the first mover—namely, the luminous body—to present it to the eyes under the name and appearance of color or light. So sound is nothing other than a motion of the same air, which carries with it the different qualities of its cause—namely, the bodies moving it. From this, it presents an image to us under the name and appearance of sound. For the sensible form—for instance, of some ringing bell—presents itself to the eyes of a deaf person under exactly the same logic as it happens to the ears of a blind person. Furthermore, just as light cannot be preserved without the actual influence of the body from which it flows, so also sound cannot exist without the motion of the air. (Those people are therefore to be laughed at who think that sound can be preserved for a long time shut up in a tube, as will be discussed more fully in our *Catoptric Magic*; indeed, experience teaches us better, showing that we are affected with greater pleasure when we read a history or a vivid description of something, or hear it sketched out by a distinguished orator with various figures of words and sentences as if with certain colors, than if we were looking at it with our eyes.) Just as the <term>species</term> <note>An 'intentional species' was thought to be a likeness or 'image-entity' that travels from an object to the sense organs.</note> of objects affect the eye and the optic nerve in a hidden way to produce a similar image by means of the <term>spirits</term> <note>Referring to 'animal spirits,' which early scientists believed traveled through the nerves to transmit sensations.</note>, so also the image of a sounding body carried by the air affects the "implanted air" <note>An early anatomical theory that air was trapped inside the ear to facilitate hearing.</note> and the acoustic and auricular nerve to represent the image of the sounding body. From these things, if I am not mistaken, the immense similarity between optical and acoustic bodies is clearly shown in their manner of acting and producing both sight and hearing in humans.

<margin>Refraction and reflection of sound.</margin>
Finally, just as sight is refracted in a denser medium, so is sound, as will be shown extensively hereafter.

# The Radiation of Sound.

...be given. For what else is sound when received in a very porous and soft body, if not a kind of shadow of sound, casting an obstacle so that it might not extend any further?

### Corollary

<margin>By how much sound is deeper within water than the same sound outside of water.</margin>
From this follows a certain method for determining how much deeper a sound made within water is compared to the sound of the same body made outside of water, and consequently, how much thinner air is than water. For it was discovered not long ago by the experience of an eminent Mathematician that the sound of a certain bell, which was (for example) of the second degree outside of water, was of the fifth degree inside water, and consequently was deeper by one minor harmonic tenth <note>In musical theory, a tenth is an octave plus a third; Kircher is describing a significant drop in pitch due to the medium's density.</note>; the cause of which thing is none other than the rarity and density of the different media. For water resists the form <note>original: "speciei"</note> of a sounding body more within the water than outside of it; from this resistance is born a slowness of motion in the medium, and a deeper sound follows this slowness. For just as one medium relates to another medium, so do vibrations made in one medium relate to vibrations made in the other; and as vibrations relate to vibrations, so sound relates to sound. If, therefore, as in the proposed example, it were as 5 to 2, the motion of air to the motion of water will hold the same proportion: from which the rarity of air to the density of water will hold as 125 to 8 <note>Kircher is using a cubic relationship (5 cubed is 125, 2 cubed is 8) to compare the volumes or densities based on the linear pitch intervals.</note>. Truly, concerning these matters, consult our *Musica Curiosa*, where we treat these and similar things professionally. These things having been so considered, let us now proceed to a further inquiry into sound.

<margin>What sound is.</margin>
Sound, therefore, is nothing other than a sensible quality that can be perceived by hearing. It is not motion, as some believe, of bodies colliding with each other; nevertheless, sound follows the motion of colliding bodies—not immediately, but by means of the breaking of the intermediate air. Hence, bodies that possess more air and smoothness obtain the greatest power of sounding, because air is broken more in smooth and airy bodies than in non-airy and thick ones. Thus, two solid bodies colliding are not always necessary for sound; rather, the impulse of air and water is most fit for producing sound, as pipes, the roaring of the sea, and thunder clearly teach. Therefore, when air is broken by the collision of any bodies whatsoever, sound is made, which is diffused from the point of collision, radiating into a sphere no differently than the forms <note>original: "species"</note> of colors. For just as colors emit their forms everywhere through radiation as representatives of the object, so too does sound emit its form.
<margin>The collision of two solid bodies is not always necessary for sound.</margin>

<margin>Water is a subject of sound.</margin>
Furthermore, the medium of sound, by which its forms are carried to the hearing, is not the subject of sounds; but air and water are. Regarding air there is no doubt; concerning water, experience

<column-break/>

also makes us more certain: for Pliny reports that fish are accustomed to be gathered by a certain sound; the same Pliny reports that fish, being called by name, have been known to appear; indeed, they even fear thunder vehemently, which would not happen unless they heard beneath the waves. Divers <note>original: "Urinatores"</note> also assert that they perceive more intense sounds beneath the water, and all the more easily the less they are distant from the surface of the water. This is a manifest sign that sound penetrates through the air into porous bodies—of which kind are water, wood, and walls—to the power of hearing. Water, therefore, is a medium for sound, even if sounds are translated much more fluidly and easily through air than through water.
<margin>Comparison of the direct and reflected ray to sound in air and in water.</margin>
For just as a ray of light relates to a denser medium in which it is refracted and dimmed, so the sounding ray is also refracted in a denser medium. Therefore, the sounding forms are dimmed and blunted by the thickness of the water, just as visible forms are in a denser medium.
<margin>Why sound is not so clear in a hall decorated with tapestries.</margin>
Hence, in rainy weather and vaporous air, we hear less than when the air is clear. Also, in halls draped with tapestries, the voice is perceived with more difficulty, being blunted and absorbed, than when the walls are stripped of tapestries. From this also the reason is deduced why music languishes in a place full of people: because it loses its power when absorbed within the hollow mouths <note>or "cavities"</note> of human bodies. Likewise, a hall strewn with wool or straw so blunts sound that it is scarcely perceived. Concerning which, more will be said in the following pages.

<margin>How sound is propagated through a medium, whether through real being or intentional being.</margin>
But it remains to be explained in this place by what means sound is propagated through a medium: whether through real being, or through intentional being <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "intentional being" refers to the way an object's form exists in the mind or the air as a "species" or image, rather than its physical matter moving.</note>, or "species"? Certainly, it seems more consistent with reason that it is propagated through species, since in all things it acts just like visible species. But visible species were established by nature for no other reason than that they might present a material object—otherwise disproportionate to the power of the sense—through themselves, as if through a representative of the object. Therefore, by the same reasoning, sound transfers the sounding object to the power of hearing through intentional being, or the representative species of the sounding object. Although I do not doubt that, to some extent, sound is also propagated really and physically according to its being, since sound takes its greatest strength from the continuous agitation of the air, without which it could not be propagated in any way. Nor can any reason be given to prove that a sounding quality of this kind diffuses its whole self *really* in every direction, since for their perception it suffices for species to be emitted from them to the workshops of the senses—lest, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> testifies, that be done through many things which can be done through fewer.

But you will argue to the contrary: Light diffuses itself into the medium according to its real being, therefore so does sound. I respond that the reasoning for sound is not the same as for light in all things, as is evident from the following: for

## CHAPTER VII.
### The Art of Reflected Sound, or Echology.
#### Definitions.

---

I. **Phonocamptics** <note>From the Greek *phōne* (sound) and *kamptikos* (curving/reflecting). Original: "Φωνοκαμπτική"</note> is nothing other than the reflection of the voice, which people commonly call an Echo; hence we call **Phonocamptics**, or **Echology**, that faculty which teaches the methods of constructing multi-form Echoes. Regarding this art, we have seen fit in this chapter to treat it according to the standard of light, to the best of our ability.

II. A **sound line** is that through which the voice goes and returns.

III. A **straight sound line** is that line which returns to the source of the sound by the same path it traveled.

IV. An **oblique sound line** is one which reflects obliquely toward the opposite side.

<margin>The Phonocamptic Medium.</margin>
V. We call the **Phonocamptic Medium** the air or water through which the form of the sound is propagated.

VI. We call the **Phonocamptic Object** that thing which the voice strikes and is reflected from.

VII. The **line of action** refers to the entire sounding length of the line within which the sound is perceptible.

<margin>The Phonoclastic Medium.</margin>
VIII. We call a **Phonoclastic body** <note>From the Greek *phōne* (sound) and *klastos* (broken/refracted). Original: "Phonoclasticum"</note> that within which sound is refracted.

Just as the visible form of light falling upon a smooth and polished body is reverberated in a mirror at the same angle at which it is seen toward the power of sight; so too is the sounding form beaten back toward the power of hearing at the same angle at which the sound flows in. This is made clear from that wonderful repercussion of the voice hitting harder bodies, which they call an Echo: so much so, that an Echo is nothing other than an articulate voice, or a modulated,

<column-break/>

reflected sound, radiating in every direction by the motion of the air, meeting an object that is a direct, flat, hollow, and sufficiently smooth body, and returning from there to the sound-maker and the speaker like a bouncing ball. We call the straight line along which the voice is propagated directly a **sound line**, just as we call that which is propagated from light a **light ray**. For according to this line, in open and free air, it is diffused straight in every direction just like light, nature always striving for a shortcut, which is achieved through the straightest lines. I said *in free and open air*; for if the voice finds an obstacle, it propagates itself according to it. For example, if a building is concave and circular, it is carried along this surface in a circular flow, as happens in vaults and arches, as will be revealed in what follows where we shall untie the causes of each. Furthermore, just as in the radiation of light one ray is straight and another oblique, so it is in the propagation of sounds; their angles of incidence are always equal to the angles of reflection, just as in light, as we have demonstrated in the **Anacamptic Art** <note>Anacamptics is the study of reflected light (catoptrics).</note>. But let us explain all these things in a few propositions.

### Proposition I.

> *A voice radiating in a circle, when it finds a Phonocamptic body—that is, a hard reflecting body—as if terrified by the unpleasant encounter, radiates back in a circle.*

<margin>What an Echo is.</margin>
Let **A** be the radiating voice, whose forms are carried normally <note>In a straight line perpendicular to the surface.</note> toward the objects or rocky places **B, C, E, D, I**. I say that the reflected voice at points **B, C, E**, and even the bottom of the well **I**, will return to point **A** through the lines **IA, BA, CA, EA, DA**. For since, by hypothesis, the voice [is carried] into the said points...

...striking solid bodies, it reflects at right angles; however, it is certain that a straight ray is reflected back upon itself. All sound rays at point A will be reverberated more slowly or more quickly according to the proportion of the distance of the sounding body and the body reflecting the voice—also known as the **Phonocamptic** <note>From the Greek words for "sound" and "curving." This refers to any surface, like a cliff or wall, that causes an echo.</note> object.

### Corollary.

From these principles, it is plain and clearly established why, for those standing on mountains, the voice is sometimes reverberated to us from the bottom of the valley: namely, because the sound ray returns to point A at a right angle <note>original: "normalis"</note> from the cliff C. The reason why an Echo is also sometimes perceived in springs and deeper wells is that the voice at A, having been reflected off the surface of the water at D, returns to the place from which it had set out. It is also clear why an Echo is not returned in the angles of steep valleys: because the voice radiating from F to G is reflected upward from there to point A. If someone were therefore standing in the opposite location, A, he would undoubtedly perceive the reflected voice.

### Proposition II.

#### A voice striking a wall obliquely is reflected obliquely.

Suppose there is a wall, A, and a voice, B, which strikes it obliquely at point C; it will be reflected from there to point D. Since the angle of incidence, BCE, is equal to the angle of reflection, FCD, in 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing the reflection of a sound ray off a vertical wall labeled L. A point source B projects a ray to point C on the wall, which then reflects to point D. Various auxiliary lines and arcs labeled A, E, F, S, and T demonstrate the mathematical proof that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The ground plane is indicated with hatched tiling.</image-desc>

point C, the voice will therefore return unharmed to D. Thus, if an ear is placed there, it will perceive the voice radiating from B to D. If the voice were to return not to D, but to S (which is impossible): since there-

<column-break/>

-fore the angle FCS contains the angle FCD, it would certainly be larger than it; and thus also larger than the angle of incidence, ECB, which we assume to be equal to the angle of reflection, ECD. Therefore, the angle of incidence would be equal to the angle of reflection and yet not be equal; the voice would also be heard at S and yet not be heard, which are absurdities. Therefore, it will not be reverberated at S, but at D, under the same angle at which it had flowed from B—which was to be demonstrated.

### Deduction.

It is clear from this that a voice radiating obliquely is not reflected back to the speaker, but is diverted elsewhere. This is because oblique sound behaves toward its reflected forms <note>original: "species"; in 17th-century physics, this refers to the sensory "image" or information carried by a wave.</note> in the same way as a visible object behaves toward the images reflected from a mirror viewed obliquely. These are not seen except at the same angle at which they struck—namely, an oblique one. The same is true for sound. Therefore, the sound reflected from B to C will be heard at D. From this, it is clear by what reasoning a sound can be so arranged that the place from which it originates cannot be known by any means. We shall discuss these deceptions later.

### Proposition III.

#### At what distance a multi-syllable reflection occurs.

Since sounding lines are not mathematical abstractions but physical ones, endowed with a certain width, it is impossible to determine the distance of a single-syllable reflection with total exactness. Blancanus <note>Giuseppe Biancani (1566–1624), a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who wrote "Echometria," a study of the measurement of echoes.</note> in his *Echometria* sets this distance at 24 feet; I have sometimes found it to be 30, sometimes 36, or even 40 feet with the same intensity of voice. I attribute this variation, first, to the reflecting body; for I have found that the harder the reflecting body is, the more swiftly and further the "form" of the sound is carried, just as a ball behaves when struck against a very hard floor. Second, I attribute it to the medium <note>In this case, the air.</note>, which is sometimes thicker and sometimes thinner; all these things greatly delay the carrying of the voice, which is why the Echo attains different strengths at different times.

<margin>What the line of action is.</margin>
For in cloudy, impure air, agitated by various motions, sound responds more weakly than in pure, clear, and quiet air. For this reason, I estimate that summer times are better than winter, just as clear and quiet nights are more suited for phonocamptics <note>the study of reflected sound</note> than the daytime. Nevertheless, by diligent observation, a monosyllabic reflection occurs between 24 and 40 paces from the phonocamptic object; for below 24 paces, you can hardly perceive anything distinct from the original voice; but from 40 paces, the first syllable of the voice is returned clearly and distinctly. Indeed, we say the maximum distance is as great as half the "line of action": we call the line of action that distance within which the sound remains perceptible, such as line B V. I say the line C S is the maximum distance within which the sound reflected from C can be heard; and this distance is equal to B C, which is half of B V. The reason is that sound continued from point C to V without reflection is propagated with as much

intensity as it is reflected to S when an obstacle is found at C; for the voice changes nothing in the intensity of its species <note>In 17th-century physics, "species" refers to the formal qualities or "image" of the sound traveling through the air</note> due to reflection. If C were an opening, the voice would be heard at the exact same moment and with the same syllables in different places V and S. The minimum and maximum distances having been determined, it is certain

between all of it, a polysyllabic Echo is completed. For let the maximum distance of the sound-source from the phonocamptic object be 46 paces, and the minimum be 24 paces; experience has taught that a monosyllabic Echo is returned at a distance of 36 paces, a trisyllabic at 42, a tetrasyllabic at 45 paces, and finally it vanishes into nothing. These things must be understood when the space between the <term>phonocamptic</term> <note>original: φωνοκαμπτικὸν; the reflecting surface</note> object and the sounding body is the middle of the line of action. For it can happen otherwise, that the reflected line of the voice is longer than the straight sounding line—namely when the sounder is closer to some wall and the voice is more intense—for then the voice is heard reverberated behind the sounder, concerning which we give these rules:

<margin>Rules for measuring Echoes.</margin>
Either the reflecting body is at the halfway point of the line of action, and then the direct and reflected lines are equal; or the straight sounding line is less than half the line of action, and thus the line of reflection will be greater; or finally, the straight line will be greater than half, and thus the reflected one will be smaller; whether the <term>phonodromia</term> <note>original: φωνοδορωία; literally "the running of sound," or the path it travels</note>, that is, the path of the voice, be straight or oblique. You see, therefore, that just as a line of action of light is given, always equal to the straight and reflected lines taken together, so it is in sound: so that we may easily know the nature of sound from the nature of light itself.

If someone possesses a parabolic mirror, they will be able to converse with another person on any subject in a lowered voice with the help of this mirror. Let AB be the parabolic mirror and E be the focus of the parabola—that is, the common point where all rays meet. Let C be the sounding or vocal source, and let the friend's ear be applied at point E. I say that voices, however softly spoken from C and directed toward the mirror opposite, will all be reflected from there into point E. The mirror, however, must be large and spacious. See my discussion on the mystery of this mirror in the location cited above.

Therefore, a sound originating from A and radiating toward B, when it encounters a denser medium standing in its way, does not travel in a straight line from A through B to F, but is redirected to C. Thus, if an ear were positioned at F, on the seabed, I say it would not perceive the voice; but an ear placed at C would. For the same principle applies to the spreading of the forms of sound as it does to light; just as an eye at F would not see object A because of refraction, but would see it if positioned at C, the same logic holds for sound. Truly, concerning these and similar matters, see the very extensive treatise in our *Anaclastica* <note>The study of refracted light or sound bending through different mediums.</note>.

### Corollary.

From these points, it follows that the denser the medium, the weaker the voice will be. However, the clearer and thinner the medium, the stronger and more intact the voice remains, just as has been said concerning light. This is why we hear less in vaporous, cloudy, or thick air than in that which is limpid, serene, and thin. Likewise, we hear less in marshy places than in mountainous and high-altitude regions. Again, we hear less in meadows and grassy places than in rocky, alpine ones, because in the latter, the voice—though reflected in various ways—is not absorbed as it is in the former. In churches full of people, we hear less than in empty ones; finally, beneath the water, we perceive the forms of sound

<column-break/>

very weakly, and indeed the more weakly the deeper we listen.
<margin>The Deaf Rock in Scotland.</margin> George Buchanan <note>A famous 16th-century Scottish historian and scholar.</note> relates in his *History of Scotland* that in the province they call Fife, a huge rock is found, commonly called "The Deaf Rock" by the inhabitants. This is because when any noise is made on the opposite side of the rock—even if a military cannon is fired—those hiding beneath it become so deaf to it that they do not perceive even a trace of the sound. If this is true, the cause of the matter could certainly be, firstly, the extreme solidity of the stone, which no sound ray can penetrate; and secondly, the position and arrangement of the rock, which allows no ray of the sonic form to reach the ears. Given these factors, those hiding beneath it would necessarily be deaf to even the most violent sound. These are the things we deemed necessary to say briefly concerning the radiation of sounds. Whoever desires more concerning the nature of sound and its effects in stirring the souls of men should consult our *Magnetic World* in the chapter on the *Magnetism of Music*, our *Catoptric Magic*, and our *Curious Music*; there he will find everything pertaining to this business treated with precision. It now follows that we should say something concerning *Phonocritica* or *Phonognomia*.

# CHAPTER VIII.
## PHONOGNOMIA,
->OR<-
### *On the divination regarding the temperament of any given body to be performed from its sound and voice.*

---

Just as in the preceding sections we established the art of *Chrimocritica* <note>Judging the nature of a thing by its color.</note> by inspecting the colors implanted in each thing, so in this place we have decided to establish *Phonocritica*, or *Phonognomia*, by a certain parallel reasoning, so that the immense riches of light and shadow might lie more clearly open to the curious reader.
<margin>Two types of sound.</margin> It must be noted, therefore, that we can consider two types of sound here: animated and inanimate. Animated sound is again either rational or irrational. Rational sound is nothing other than the voice brought forth from a living being by the help of the windpipe, the larynx, and the epiglottis, with the intention of signifying something. By this last phrase, we distinguish the human voice from the sounds of brutes and inanimate objects, and those sounds which occur without intention. Irrational animated sound is the cry of brutes, established to signify the passions of the soul. Inanimate sound, however, is the collision of any non-living bodies, such as 

<column-break/>

thunder, the explosions of cannons, and the clashing of wood, metals, and other bodies. When, therefore, the sound of one body is higher <note>original: "acutior" - sharper or higher in pitch</note> than the sound of another body equal to it in size, then it is necessarily concluded that the body with the higher sound consists of a thinner substance, indicating a predominance of air or fire. But, so that you may proceed more safely in this art, take this experiment.

### Phonocritic Experiment.
#### *On investigating the nature of different kinds of woods, bones, and minerals through sound.*

Let blocks <note>original: "parallelopipeda"</note> or cylinders be made from every kind of wood—previously properly dried—all equal in size. Strike these with a pick while they are suspended by a thread, and you will perceive the most diverse species of sounds. For some will sound a semitone, others a whole tone, a major third <note>original: "ditonum"</note>, or an augmented fourth <note>original: "tritonum"</note>; others a fourth <note>original: "diatessaron"</note>, a fifth <note>original: "diapente"</note>, or even an octave <note>original: "diapason"</note>...

you will find they sound differently; and by observing the proportions of their harmonies, you will easily judge the natural construction of bodies—namely, how much more compact one is than another, or how much more rare and porous. Since the density of any body arises from the greatest packing together of earthy and watery parts, one will be denser than another to the degree that its parts are more tightly packed. The more packed a body is, the heavier it will be; the heavier it is, the more slowly it will be moved; and finally, the more slowly it is moved, the lower <note>original: "gravius," which in Latin means both "heavier" and "lower in musical pitch."</note> it will sound.

<margin>The weight of sound is twofold. From whence come depth and sharpness.</margin>
The depth of sound in bodies is of two kinds: for some have a low sound that is forceful; others a low sound that is muffled <note>original: "obtusus," meaning blunt or dull.</note>. The former offers signs of an earthy and dry temperament; the latter of a watery, moist, and poorly compacted one. "Rarity" <note>In this context, rarity is the opposite of density—being thin or spread out.</note>, however, since it originates from a highly porous substance and can contain much air, makes bodies rarer the more porous they are; and the lighter they are, the more quickly they will be moved, and consequently, they will sound higher and sharper in pitch. Note, however, that we are not speaking here of soft and liquid bodies, such as wool, feathers, liquids, and similar things that do not consist of a compact or solid substance (of which we shall speak later); but of solid and hard bodies. Some of these will also have a sharp, forceful, and penetrating sound; others a sharp sound, but muffled and weak. Just as the former provides evidence of porosity and lightness, so the latter provides evidence of porosity but of a flabbier substance. The same must be said of bones and metallic bodies—gold, silver, copper, iron, and lead. You will find all these things explained most extensively in our *New and Curious Musurgy* <note>Referring to Kircher’s famous 1650 work on music theory and acoustics, *Musurgia Universalis*.</note>. From these principles, rightly considered, we form the following Phonocritic Canons <note>Rules for judging by sound.</note>.

### Phonocritic Canon 1: On solid bodies.

<margin>How the predominance of qualities in bodies can be known through sound.</margin>
If the sound of any solid body, compared to the sound of another body of equal size, is low and muffled, it gives clear evidence of a watery predominance—as seen in lead, due to the abundance of mercurial moisture. If, however, it has a sound that is low but forceful, then you may certainly judge it to be of an earthy, smooth, and well-compacted temperament, as can be seen in iron and steel. Furthermore, if the sound of a solid body is sharp and thin, it gives signs of an airy temperament and a porous but flabbier substance, as seen in tin. Finally, if the sound is sharp, forceful, and penetrating, then you may certainly conclude the body is of a fiery temperament, or of a thin and extremely light substance, as seen in bronze <note>original: "aëreis," here likely referring to "aes," copper or bronze alloys used for bells.</note>.

<column-break/>

## Phonocritic Experiment II.
### On the temperament of liquids.

<margin>Different liquids have different sounds.</margin>
Take three, four, or five glass chalices, all equal in shape and size, which you will fill with different liquids—water, wine, and other distilled waters—yet in such a way that they all have an equal level of fullness. This done, rub the rim or edge of the chalice with a moistened finger for a long time until you perceive a sound; this sound will indeed be different according to the variety of the liquids. For the subtler a liquid is, the higher it will sound, and the thicker it is, the lower. Hence oil, since it is more compact and sluggish, will also sound much lower; water will sound lower than "water of life" <note>original: "aqua vitæ," or brandy/concentrated alcohol.</note>, and this in turn sounds lower than spirits or quintessences <note>highly distilled or refined substances.</note>. Note, meanwhile, that oily liquids, although they are much subtler in substance than elementary water (being of an airy nature), their sluggishness and viscous substance cause a somewhat greater depth of sound. In other liquids lacking this sluggishness, you will easily judge the elemental predominance, for which these are the rules.

### Phonocritic Canon 2: On liquids.

<margin>How the temperament of liquids can be discerned through sound.</margin>
If the sound of the chalice is low and muffled, you may conclude a watery temperament of the infused liquid, as in spring water—which, however, sounds higher than marsh water, as the latter is of an earthy and dreg-filled temperament. If the sound is sharp and thin, you have a sign of an airy temperament, as in all distilled waters, which always have a sharper sound than any elementary water. Finally, if the sound is very sharp, subtle, and penetrating, it will provide evidence of a fiery temperament, as appears in spirits and quintessences; these, in the same quantity in equal glass chalices, cause a sharper sound than in other liquids. Truly, how much subtler one liquid is than another, the sound itself will indicate. For if one of them sounds an octave <note>original: "diapason."</note> above another, it is certain that it is twice as subtle as the other. But concerning these matters, consult our *Curious Musurgy*, which treats all things most extensively.

### Phonocritic Canon 3: On the voices of animals.

Voice was granted by nature to brute animals for this purpose: that through it they might signify their passions, either to humans or to those of their own kind. For it is established by experience that birds, dogs, cats, and oxen form one kind of voice when they are moved by choler <note>anger</note>, and another when by melancholy, or...

<margin>How the temperament of animals may be known from the sound of their voice.</margin>
...[influenced by] phlegm; they produce one sound while they love and flatter, another while they desire mating and are afraid, or when they vehemently long for something. For when they are moved by <term>cholera<note>Yellow bile, the humor associated with fire, heat, and a quick temper.</note></term>, it is certain they emit a sharper sound than when they are driven by hunger. Thus, <term>cholera</term>, being rare, subtle, and thin, sharpens the voice, whereas <term>melancholy<note>Black bile, the humor associated with earth, coldness, and sluggishness.</note></term> and phlegm lower it due to the sluggishness of the humor; the boiling of the blood, however, renders it temperate. If, therefore, the passion is choleric, the voice is more agitated and sharp, as can be seen in dogs and cats driven by rabies; when they desire mating, they emit a sharp and moaning voice, a sign of fermenting blood. Thus, moved by various humors, they emit various voices. From this knowledge, a science could be formed by which one might understand the voice and language of animals, just as we read concerning Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century Greek philosopher often credited in legendary accounts with the ability to understand the speech of birds and animals.</note>; and we explain the language of these animals most extensively <margin>The book called The Tower of Babel.</margin> in our work which we entitle *The Tower of Babel*, where, in its own time, the curious reader will find many rare and new things hitherto unseen.

### Canon 4. The Phonocritic of the human voice.

<margin>The temperament of men, which can be known through the voice.</margin>
Although the variety and multitude of voices in men is no less than the variety of human faces, the affections of the inner man can perhaps be more easily and certainly tracked through the voice than through color. Hence we read that Plato was accustomed to say, in order to know someone's nature: "Speak, that I may see you." By this, he seemed to imply nothing else but the manner in which he could know the internal nature of the soul through the voice. The sacred pages also testify that Isaac knew the difference between the brothers not by touch, but by voice <note>A reference to the Biblical story in Genesis where Isaac, though blind, identifies his sons Jacob and Esau by their voices.</note>. Galen also knew the capacity of the chest through the voice when he said that those who have a strong voice, which they can continue without interruption, have a large chest. But here Galen speaks only of the strong voice, the cause of which is a wide and vast chest with large, ample lungs and strong muscles of the larynx and epiglottis. There are, however, other differences of voices which take their origin not so much from the chest, lungs, and epiglottis as from the temperament: such as a voice that is slow, fast, sweet, harsh, distinct, confused, shrill, sharp, heavy and bass, moderate and temperate, or ridiculous. All these differences of voices are signs of different temperaments, and they can easily be combined with colors, as follows.

### §. I.

->On the intense and deep voice, which corresponds to the color black.<-

Those who cry out loudly with a deep voice are, according to Aristotle, compared to

<column-break/>

<margin>Conjecture from the voice of the Donkey.</margin>
donkeys, and consequently they are injurious, abusive, petulant, and given to insults. That donkeys are insulting and petulant is sufficiently shown by their nature, which is petulant, injurious, and abusive when well-fed. Whence Aristotle concludes: The donkey has a very large and deep voice, and the donkey is indiscreet, petulant, and abusive; therefore, those whose voice is large and deep are petulant, indiscreet, and abusive. But it remains for us to see the reasons for this. We see that a large voice is present in those animals that have a large <term>windpipe<note>original: "asperam arteriam," literally the "rough artery," the historical term for the trachea.</note></term> and emit much air from it; they have a deep voice who slowly drive much air out of the windpipe. Therefore, those animals which are large have a large voice, because they possess large instruments. Consequently, such men are necessarily the same. <margin>The reason for the assertion.</margin> Those who have a large voice also have a broad chest, a large windpipe, and a thick neck; therefore, the element of earth dominates in them according to their bulk. If, however, we perceive a depth joined with a large voice—which the slowness born of cold produces—it indicates a cold and dry temperament, that is, an earthy one. He who has such a temperament is indeed greedy and timid, but also indiscreet and vile; those who in prosperity are intolerable in their insolence, and in adversity are more timid than a little hare: a nature which Cornelius Tacitus noted in Caligula <note>The Roman Emperor known for his erratic and cruel behavior.</note>.

### §. II.

->On the voice that is deep at the beginning and fails into sharpness, which corresponds to the blue color.<-

Those who begin with a deep voice and end in a sharp one, we number among the complainers, the wrathful, and the mournful, like the Oxen, whose nature it is. Let us explain the reason for this in a few words. It is certain that in those suppressed by mourning and grief, heat is gathered from the circumference to the center around the heart along with the spirits; consequently, the upper limbs are left in cold, destitute of heat. Because of the cold <margin>Conjecture from the bovine voice.</margin> predominating in that place, the voice is slow and deep, just as the abundant heat around the heart requires abundant air. Whence the mournful draw in much air, which, returning slowly, moves much external air; thus, a thick and deep voice emerges at the beginning. And since by speaking and complaining—to use the words of the Poet—

> Grief is poured out by tears, and poured out by speech;

It happens that from complaining talkativeness, the heat moved and released from around the heart exits and moves the air with great speed, which motion must necessarily be followed by a sharp sound.

## §. III.
### *Concerning the sharp, soft, and broken voice, which corresponds to the color white.*

Whosoever, while speaking, emits a voice that is sharp, soft, and fractured, we say those men are soft and effeminate. By "soft voice" here, we mean a voice that is both slow and relaxed, moving very little air—the kind we hear in women and in children when they are coaxing, or when speakers falter in the middle of their words. The <term>Poet<note>A common reference to the Roman poet Virgil.</note></term> testifies that this is a sign of a great movement occurring in the heart with this verse:

> She begins to speak, and stops in the middle of her utterance. <note>original: "Incipit effari, me diaque in voce resistit." from Virgil’s Aeneid, describing Dido’s hesitation.</note>

I would believe the cause of this thing to be a lack of heat and an excess of waste humor: for when heat is lacking, it moves the voice in such a soft and interrupted way; it fails when compared to the excessive moisture by which it is nearly overwhelmed. Therefore, let us reason thus: A sharp, soft, and interrupted voice teaches us that moisture dominates over heat; the temperament in which this occurs is effeminate and soft, and it reveals inclinations toward weakness and dejection of the soul. Therefore, a voice of this kind does not cause, but rather indicates, a softness of soul and a womanly nature.

## §. IV.
### *Concerning the deep and tangled voice, which corresponds to the red or fiery color.*

Whosoever, while speaking, has a voice that is deep, loud, and tangled, they—according to the testimony of the <term>Philosopher<note>A standard reference to Aristotle, whose works on physiognomy and ethics were central to this period's science.</note></term>—are bold, brave, and ready of hand. We call a voice "tangled" when the words are confused and inarticulate among themselves due to the excessive speed of the speaker; they are uttered from the mouth so hurriedly that one syllable, overtaking another, confuses the listener. This is how those people usually speak who, being naturally bold and struck by a great commotion of the soul, seem to make noise rather than to speak.

<margin>The reason why men of deep and tangled voices are bold.</margin>
We give this cause for the matter: Since a brave person has a temperament that is vehemently hot and dry, the "earthy" and dry qualities produce a deep voice; because the heat moves a great deal of air, it is necessary for the voice to emerge loud and tangled. While the vehement heat moves the air, because the air is somewhat disproportionate to the heat's power and vigor, the heat impels it more forcefully than is proper; the voice propelled from behind overtakes the preceding one, and is almost mixed with it, thus rendering the voice "tangled." Whosoever, therefore, shall have a voice of this—

<column-break/>

—kind, we shall say that he is bold, headstrong, and vehement, having attained no small amount of bodily strength.

## §. V.
### *Concerning the soft voice without strain, which corresponds to a yellowish color.*

Those who possess a soft voice without strain are the opposite of the preceding group; for they are mild-mannered and are compared to sheep, according to the Philosopher. You will perceive this in children and maidens when they are cheerful without disturbance and disposed according to nature; from this, we form the following reasoning.

<margin>The reason for the soft voice.</margin>
Whosoever, while speaking naturally and without affectation, has a small, soft, and relaxed voice, they are mild and of a somewhat timid nature, just like sheep, which have a voice of this kind and are likewise mild and timid. Those who naturally endure injuries, are only moderately angered, and do not rise up for revenge, usually enjoy this sort of sheep-like voice. Therefore, they are of a moist and cold temperament, to which both the habits of the soul and the voice accommodate themselves.

## §. VI.
### *Concerning the sharp and intense voice, which corresponds to an intensely red color.*

Whosoever, while emitting a voice, is sharp and intense, they are prone to anger, petulant, lustful, and are compared to <term>Typhon<note>In mythology, a monstrous giant associated with volcanic heat and chaos; here used to describe a volatile, "stormy" personality.</note></term> and goats. For the goat is an animal of a hot temperament verging toward dryness, and has <term>melancholy<note>Black bile, the humor associated with earth and coldness.</note></term> mixed with <term>phlegm<note>The humor associated with water and coldness.</note></term>; since these do not harmonize well, they indicate a certain corruption of moisture within the dryness, and the heavy, rank odor they exhale declares this sufficiently.

<margin>The reason for the sharp voice.</margin>
Thus, whosoever shall have this nature will also have a voice similar to goats and the same impulsive inclinations. But let no one think we take "inclination" here to be so violent that it cannot be tamed by the opposing acts of virtue; for no one is so malicious and perverse that he cannot be capable of virtue. I conclude, therefore, with the Poet:

> The envious, the angry, the lazy, the wine-drinker, the lover, 
> No one is so wild that he cannot become mild, 
> If only he lends a patient ear to cultivation. <note>original: "Invidus, iracundus, iners, vinosus, amator, / Nemo adeò ferus est, qui non mitescere possit, / Si modo culturæ patientem accommodat aurem." from Horace, Epistles 1.1.38.</note>

But leaving these things aside, let us turn our pen to investigate the <term>actinobolisms<note>From the Greek 'aktinobolismos,' meaning the emission of rays or radiations; here referring to the hidden influences or "beams" emitted by objects.</note></term> of the remaining things.

### CHAPTER IX.

->Concerning the **radiation** <note>original: "ἀκτινοβολίᾳ"</note> of the remaining senses: smell, touch, and taste.<-

->Concerning Osmetic or Odorous Radiation.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop-cap letter 'C' depicting a figure (possibly a saint or scholar) at a desk within an ornate circular frame and floral scrollwork.</image-desc>

<margin>**Osmetic radiation** <note>original: "ἀκτινοβολισμὸς ofmeticus"</note>.</margin>
<margin>Odor is diffused spherically.</margin>
SINCE odor is a quality resulting from the mixture of primary qualities—with the dry and the hot dominating—it acts as a stimulus for the sense of smell; certainly, this quality cannot be perceived by the sensory organ except through **osmetic radiation**, or a radiation diffused spherically from the subject through the medium. If we illustrate this through an experiment: if a globe made of musk is suspended from the ceiling by a silver thread, experience teaches that the scent of the musk is perceived from every part of the surrounding space. This would not happen unless it poured itself forth from the scented body through the medium in imitation of light. However, it differs from the radiation of light in that the transit of odor through a medium is successive <note>moving step-by-step over time</note>, whereas the transit of light is instantaneous. Furthermore, the "sphere of power" of an odor is material, while that of light is separated from all association with matter. A doubt finally arises here: how is this **osmetic radiation** carried through the medium? Does it travel by its **real being** <term>esse reale; the physical presence of particles or substance</term>, or by its **intentional being** <term>esse intentionale; the sensory image or "species" of the object that the mind perceives</term>? All those who believe that odor is a smoky breath, or a steamy evaporation—and consequently a substance rather than a quality—support the first part of the question. Many others leave the second part in doubt. We must now reveal what we think about both. We say that the odor which things themselves emit through the medium is not "breath" <note>vapor</note> formally, but subjectively. That is, the odor we perceive should by no means be thought of as that smoky exhalation diffusing evaporatively from the fragrant body into the medium; rather, the odor exists *within* that breath as its subject, and is carried by it through the medium as if by a vehicle. This is how we understand those who call a smoky exhalation an "odor." Indeed, as has been said, odor results from the thickening of primary qualities in mixed bodies, with dryness dominating and heat cooking away and drying out the moisture. That dryness and heat predominate in odor is proven by the fact that fragrant things lose their scent if they are soaked too much. Furthermore, fragrant things only originate in regions subject to the most burning Sun. The predominance of dryness in odor is also proven by the nature of the **osmetic organ** <note>the nose/olfactory system</note>: when the organ is filled with moisture and phlegm, it loses its power of smelling, as we experience in ourselves when afflicted by a cold catarrh. Experience also teaches that heat—at least a temperate heat—is required for odor. Plants and flowers growing in marshy and swampy places breathe out
<margin>Experiment.</margin>
<margin>How osmetic radiation is carried through a medium.</margin>
<margin>Odor exists in a smoky exhalation subjectively, not formally.</margin>
<margin>The source of odor.</margin>

<column-break/>

no scent, or at least a very dull one, for no other reason than a lack of heat suppressed by excessive moisture. Likewise, fragrant waters and dried balsam exhibit the most intense odor. I said "at least temperate heat" because if fragrant things are reduced to ash by fire, they not only do not smell but lose all their power. Therefore [to return to our purpose], radiation occurs through the medium for some distance by its **real being**, but also reaches more remote places by its **intentional being**, just as we taught concerning the transmission of the species of sound. The reason for the former is this: since the medium is "affected" by sound and odor, according to the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle</note>; and for the medium to be affected by odor is nothing other than for the air to be so affected by the scented thing that it smells of it; and since nothing can smell of something unless the odor is present in its **real being** (just as a thing must have whiteness to be white), we rightly say that real odor is received in the air, and consequently carried through the air according to its **real being** in a **uniformly-difform** manner <note>original: "uniformiter difformiter," a scholastic term for a quality that changes or fades consistently across a distance</note>. However, one must not think that odor is spread according to its real being across the entire distance in which it is perceived, since it is unlikely that it possesses such power as to communicate itself perfectly to the entire sphere. Therefore, it requires a "deputy" of the object, which is nothing other than the **species** <note>the sensory form or image</note> of the odor. Thus, odor is carried not only by its **real being** for some distance, but also to more remote places by its **intentional being**. If a carcass is exposed in a field, you will immediately see eagles and crows, stirred by its foul smell, flying from even the most remote places. Yet it is probable they are not stirred by the *real* odor of the carrion, since it is inconceivable that a smoky breath could radiate to a distance of many miles. Therefore, they are stirred by the **intentional odor**, ordained by nature through a singular providence for animals so they would not fail in their necessities. Thus, air and water are subjects for odor, just as they are for light and sound. Regarding air, there is no doubt. Regarding water, many doubt; but I have found through manifold experience that fragrant things radiate even in waters. There should be no doubt that fish are lured by things imbued with a heavy odor. Some will object here that fish run to bait because they are stirred by the sight of the object or by some "occult quality." This is wrong: for if only the sight of the thing moved the fish, then no fish would be caught at night. Yet experience teaches that no time is more suitable for catching fish than the night. Therefore, they are stirred by the odor of the baits, which I learned by this experiment.

<margin>Whether water can be a subject of osmetic power?</margin>

### Experiment.
### On the radiation of odor within the medium of water.

<margin>An experiment performed on an octopus.</margin>
Take earthworms toasted over a fire and, having fixed them to a hook, lower them into a deep pool; immediately, the fish, stirred by the scent of the toasted worms, will rush together in schools to the great profit of the fisherman. But if you infect that same mass of worms with the juice of **Asafoetida** <note>original: "Assæ fœtidæ," a pungent dried latex from certain herbs, often called "stinking gum"</note>, you will not only fail to entice the fish, but you will drive them all away with the foul odor of this herb. I performed a similar experiment at **Civitavecchia** <note>original: "Centumcellis," a port city near Rome</note> in the year 1639. When the sailors at that time discovered a huge **Octopus** <note>original: "Polypum"</note> attached to a certain rock in the harbor, and there was no way to tear it away while it was entangled in so many tentacles, I advised them to rub it with the juice of **Fleabane** <note>original: "Publicariæ," likely *Pulicaria*, an herb used to repel insects</note>, as I had learned that the odor of this plant was extremely offensive to it. No sooner said than done; for they had scarcely touched the octopus with the said herb when, behold, its tentacles relaxed, and seeking its own safety in flight from the hostile odor, it finally fell into the wicker traps and allowed itself to be captured. I add that fish recognize other fish, whether friends or enemies, by no other means than by smell. It is so certain that they are stirred to the desire for procreation and lust by smell alone—just like land animals—that anyone who denies it would seem to contradict undeniable experience. Who does not know that the **Pike** <note>original: "Lucius"</note> is greatly attracted by the smell of latrines, **Whales** by aromatic musk, **Anchovies** by seaweed, and **Barbels** by duckweed? And so it goes for the others, which would take a long time to re-

<column-break/>

cite. However, I would not deny that the sense of smell is duller in aquatic animals than in land animals, and that the radiation of odor in water relates to the radiation of odor outside of water just as **refracted radiation** relates to **direct radiation**. For just as a ray of light is broken and dulled in a denser medium, so too is the ray of odor. But let these remarks on odor suffice. The remaining senses, Taste and Touch, since they are not moved unless the object is present, consequently do not claim a radiation as proper to themselves as odorous things do; nevertheless, they possess some radiation within the sensory organ itself. However, since these depart furthest from the analogy of light, we have decided they should be omitted.

### Corollary.

From this **actinobolia** <note>original: "ἀκτινοβολίᾳ," the emission or throwing out of rays</note> of odorous things, it is clearly evident that there is no stone, plant, tree, or animal that does not radiate in a circle through its material effluvium of scent, which acts as a kind of vehicle. No "mixed body" <note>an early scientific term for a complex substance or organism</note> can be identified that entirely lacks all odor. If, therefore, all things possess some odor, then they shall radiate; and since they radiate uniformly, it follows that the limit of the radiation's activity will produce a shape identical to that of the radiating body. For example, if a piece of musk is round, the boundary of its poured-forth "sphere of virtue" will be a circle; if it is square, the boundary will be square, and you may reason similarly for others. Let these remarks on sensible radiation suffice; hereafter, we must speak of that other radiation of **sympathetic power** implanted in things.

## CHAPTER X.
## On **actinobolism** <note>original: "ἀκτινοβολισμῷ"</note>, or the radiation of the **plastic power**, or the formative power within the seed.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'R' set within a square woodcut border featuring stylized floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>
We now approach a difficult task and a work full of risk as we probe the very "kernel" of nature. This is that **plastic power** <note>the "formative force" or "virtus plastica" believed to be the invisible architect that organizes matter into a living organism</note> which fashions a body from the seed of any plant or animal. It can hardly be said how much this has exercised the wits of most physicians and philosophers, driving many to despair and all to wonder. For within it lies hidden the **Divine Craftsman** <note>original: "divinus Opifex"</note>, who works in the deepest recesses of the body without any tools and without commotion, producing a work worthy of admiration, filled with such a variety and elegance of dissimilar parts—and this from raw and unformed matter in which no dissimilarity, no variety, and finally no distinction of parts is apparent to the senses. For we see in a seed—though without any visible 

<column-break/>

trace—the whole tree lying hidden with its root, trunk, branches, leaves, and fruits. From a grain of barley proceeds the root, the stalk, the ear, and the grains. In the egg of a female bird lies the bird with each and every limb, and with all the differences of colors. In the seed of animals lies the body with all its members: the heart, brain, lungs, liver, spleen, bladder, stomach, kidneys, nerves, veins, and tendons, each of which is endowed with its own certain shape, color, and properties. Who, then, separates things so varied and disparate when they are hidden in a uniform body? Who solidifies uniform matter now into bones, now scatters it into liquid, now pushes it into soft flesh, and now extends it into nerves and cartilages? Surely no one else but that **plastic power**, the master form implanted in each thing that propagates by generation through the power of Almighty God. This power [assigns] to each member its due...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on how odors and other invisible forces radiate through space. Having previously examined the behavior of scents in water, the author now explores the "plastic power"—the formative force in nature—and compares its action in the womb to the way light projects an image through a pinhole.</meta>

<page-num>109</page-num>
<header>The Ray-Casting of the Plastic Power.</header>
<sig>O 3</sig>

assigns position, color, figure, proportion, and quality: by its truly miraculous craftsmanship, the body is hollowed out into so many tubes, canals, passages, and small vessels. In what manner it does these things, no one, as far as I know, has correctly explained. We shall attempt something according to the small measure of our own talent.

<margin>The wondrous power of the seed is whole in the whole and whole in every part.</margin>
To touch briefly upon each point: we suppose that this **plastic power** <note>The "virtus plastica" was a traditional concept of an internal force that shapes and organizes a living being from a seed.</note> diffuses itself equally throughout the entire mass of the seed; that is, it is "whole in the whole, and whole in any part of the seed." The reason for this is that sometimes individual offspring, and sometimes several, arise from one source, and a fetus is completed no less from some single part than from the whole. Finally, no confusion or disturbance of parts occurs, except very rarely; yet this would necessarily happen if the power related itself unevenly to the subject. For if a part of the seed were cut away, the portion of the fetus subject to that specific power would necessarily perish when that portion of the seed was missing, and thus a confusion of the figure would be introduced by a transposition of parts. Even if the seed, to our senses, does not seem to have different parts, it does have them when considered in itself, since it is not entirely simple but composed of many things. Indeed, that portion of the power which formed the brain will by no means produce the heart or the liver; and that which gave shape to the bones will by no means stretch out the membranes or wind the coils of the intestines, as that most learned and <term>polymathic <note>original Greek: $\pi o \lambda \upsilon \mu \alpha \theta \eta \varsigma$</note></term> Doctor Marcus Marci demonstrates in his ingenious work, *On Operative Ideas*. The only difficulty is how a power so mingled together does not act in a confused way, but rather in a most <term>orderly <note>original Greek: $\epsilon \upsilon \tau \alpha \kappa \tau \omega \varsigma$</note></term> and regulated fashion. To explain this, the experiment previously mentioned in the first chapter of this book must be repeated here.

<margin>Experiment.</margin>
Let the figure of a man, with each and every limb, be painted on some object exposed to the rays of the Sun. This being done in a darkened room—according to the experiment shown in this book regarding "Chromatic Illumination"—let the image-form of the man depicted a moment ago be introduced through a very tiny pinhole onto a paper displayed in the darkened chamber. Experience will teach you that the image-form is represented inside together with the color of every limb. If, however, you apply the paper directly to the hole, the entire diffusion of the forms will be disturbed, and nothing will appear except a bright circle. But the further you move the board away from the hole, the more the image-forms will unfold, until they have reached their natural perfection. Here it is certain that rays from every point of the limbs of the image radiate through the medium and are united without confusion in the pinhole. Although to the senses this appears to be a simple radiation of light, once it is unfolded even a little, you will find it is not a simple image, but one marked by an infinite 

<column-break/>

variety of colors, with each part distinct, and you will see with wonder that the individual limbs radiate together in an <term>orderly fashion <note>original Greek: $\epsilon \upsilon \tau \alpha \kappa \tau \omega \varsigma$</note></term> without any confusion, and that the colors of the individual limbs also differ along with the images. If any thing in the nature of things explains that incomprehensible and simple variety of the plastic power, this surely explains it. I say, therefore, that the plastic power, or the craftsman of form, is contained in the sperm in exactly the same way as the forms of colors are contained in the air. For the seed—falling from each and every part by the movement of passion and the spermatic <term>actinobolism <note>original: "$\alpha \kappa \tau \iota \nu o \beta o \lambda \iota \sigma \mu \tilde{\omega}$," meaning the casting or emission of rays</note></term> into the woman’s womb, which is the natural place for prolific radiation—is there poured out as a material that is simple and uniform to the senses. However, as the natural heat of the vessel promotes it, it begins to unfold by its radiation. Through these "spermatic ideas" and "reasons," the parts begin to differ, and soon the limbs are distinguished and separated from one another. Just as all visible forms are contained by power in a single point of a pinhole, yet when unfolded they distinguish the figure, position, and colors of individual limbs, so exactly is the plastic power in the seed. For some rays, being longer, reach the outermost surface; others end suddenly at their origin; some are terminated in a spherical surface, others in a flat one, and others in different ways; from which all variety results in the fetus, as is clear in the figure. # Great Art, Book II: Part I.

Then, carefully inspect the yolk with a **small microscope** <note>original: "smicroscopio"; an early term for the microscope, which was a relatively new invention in the 17th century</note>, and there will appear in it a manifest likeness of a heart, thickened like a living drop of blood, and agitating itself in a certain wonderful manner with bloody fibers. From this center, fibers are drawn out in all directions, just as rays are drawn from light or streams from a fountain. And although the vital motion of the heart and arteries appears immediately after three days, you will find that none of the remaining limbs appear yet, until after four more days the spinal column—drawn down from the brain like a certain rough draft or cloudy substance—appears. Then, successively, the remaining limbs appear according to the perfection of each, in which the individual organs are sculpted to be suitable for their functions; colors proper to each are painted on them; and each is endowed with a taste and smell proper to its own nature, until they grow into the perfect mass of a finished structure. If someone were to observe one egg broken every day from the first incubation, he could undoubtedly, by the stated method, easily recognize the order and process of the limbs in the generation of each; just as in man, since the principle of the limbs in an animal is the same as in man. <margin>The development of parts in man is not simultaneous.</margin> It is clear from these things, therefore, that the unfolding of species into individual limbs is by no means **simultaneous** <note>original: "σύγχρονον" (synchronon)</note>; but rather, according to the perfection of the parts, the unfolding happens sometimes earlier, sometimes later. All these things are also evident from the display of colored images, which—unless you display them at a precise distance from a pinhole—you will perceive as nothing other than a crude sketching of shapes. <margin>The analogy of man's limbs with the parts of the world.</margin> Just as individual images radiate from a center into a sphere by their own rays without confusion, so too does the image of the **formative power** <note>original: "plastica virtutis"; the internal force believed to organize matter into living bodies</note> radiate from the center to the circumference. It is no different than how the mind of the World-Maker evolved all the species of the world-machine from the center of the earth into the most diverse members—into elements and celestial spheres. First, He gathered the Sun into a sort of heart for the **macrocosm** <note>original: "megacosmi"; the "great world" or universe</note>; He fashioned the Firmament into the brain, Saturn into the spleen of the world, Mars into the liver, Mercury into the lungs, Jupiter into the spirits and blood, Venus into the seed of heaven, and finally the Moon into the **upper abdomen** <note>original: "Hypochondria"</note>. He fashioned all these into a "Great Man" by a good covenant. Likewise, in the "Small Man" <note>the human being, seen as a miniature version of the universe</note>, there should be no doubt that an unfolding of forms occurs, along with color, taste, and other properties.

The only difficulty arises from this: if the formative power unfolded the forms of the limbs latent in the seed with infallible proportion, it would follow that all men would be similar in the outline of their bodies and other qualities. Yet they are so far from being so, that among millions of people, not two are found to be similar in all things. In man, who does not marvel

<column-break/>

<margin>The variety of faces in humans.</margin> at the variety of faces? Who would not be stunned by the differences in gait and gesture in individuals, along with such great diversity of natural inclinations? I say, therefore, that this great variety of things is not to be attributed to the formative power alone; but rather to the imaginations, affections, and the perpetual motion of the versatile human wit flourishing in the parents while they know one another. These, reaching the prepared matter as if by their own radiation, imprint upon it that variety which we have mentioned. Since this wandering motion of the soul ceases in animals, it is no wonder that individuals are for the most part found to be so similar that they can hardly be distinguished, except by spots of color. However, as for the manner in which parents imprint upon their children the forms of things vehemently agitated in the mind, we have spoken at length in *The Magnetic Art*, in the chapter on the **Magnetism of the Imagination**, to which we refer the reader.

### Corollary.
#### On the Radiation of the Imagination.

<margin>The wondrous power of the imagination is declared in certain observed examples.</margin> The power of the imagination sufficiently declares that all things in the world happen through mutual co-radiation. The rays of the imagination have such power that they seem to transform a person into the very thing they are vehemently agitating in their mind. What is more ridiculous than those who, deluded by the power of the radiating imagination, reach the point where one, believing himself turned into a shell or glass, yielded to those he met lest he be shattered; another, excited by the crowing of roosters and believing himself turned into one, is read to have run about with the flapping of arms and a ridiculous voice, emulating the shaking of wings and other behaviors proper to roosters. Not a few have thought themselves deprived of a head. Read in Schenck’s *Medical Observations* about those who were turned into various animals, such as wolves, bears, dogs, and stags conspicuous with branching antlers. <margin>The cause of such wonderful effects.</margin> From where does this wondrous power come? I answer that the efficient cause is the material radiation of the **phantasy** <note>the faculty of the mind that produces mental images</note> apprehending external things with vehement imagination. The formal and exemplary cause is the **melancholic humor** <note>one of the four bodily fluids or "humors" in ancient medicine, associated here with a heavy, mirror-like quality</note> received in the cells of the brain. Because of a corrupt and preternatural disposition and an immovable tenacity, this humor—acting as a sort of mirror—receives the forms apprehended from outside, with the phantasy as the principal agent and the spirit as the carrier. These forms are then reflected and move the phantasy, determining it toward that which they represent. This is no different from how the forms of colors radiating through a medium only appear when they have been collected in a dark place, as if in a mirror.
