# The Radiation of the Power of Imagination

...transmitted through the [senses]; they acquire nothing but an **intentional existence** <note>original: "esse intentionale"; a Scholastic term referring to the way an object exists in the mind as a representation rather than as physical matter</note>. Thus, external things—through chance and through a vehement apprehension by the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"</note>, acting as a kind of sense organ—are transmitted into the cloudy and vaporous medium of the brain. There, struck by reflected rays, they move the imagination toward that which they represent. 

<margin>The cause of dreamers and melancholics is the same.</margin>
The same must be thought regarding the images seen by those who dream. For there is no difference between dreamers and **melancholics** <note>In the 17th century, "melancholy" referred not just to sadness, but to a state of clinical delusion or "madness" caused by an imbalance of humors</note>, except that for the former, while sleeping, images of things are exhibited to the imagination in a natural mirror of vapor; whereas for the latter, while awake, they are exhibited in a preternatural mirror. This **humor** <note>A bodily fluid or vapor</note> sometimes draws its origin from the vapors of the stomach (as in dreamers), sometimes from the liver, sometimes from the midriff and spleen (as in hypochondriacs), and even from the smoky exhalations in menstruating women. 

We have said that this humor is most fit for the representation of images. This humor is stirred up by the apprehension of some most vehement object, or by some violent passion of the soul—such as anger, love, revenge, or fear—or cooked by the long-lasting meditation of a fervent mind. Once raised into the brain and sticking there persistently, it acts like a certain mirror, reverberating the things brought to the imagination by a kind of reflected ray (while the intellect and the domain of reason are meanwhile bound by the turbulence and thickness of the spirits).

<margin>The cure of Melancholics.</margin>
Experience teaches that this is indeed the case; for when the imagination is changed, the madness ceases. Thus, for a certain man who imagined that stag horns had grown on him, a certain Physician cut off real stag horns from a child's head, and then, while the man was watching, threw them away; this was enough to immediately free the man from his madness. 

<margin>The cure of a ridiculous imagination.</margin>
Another was freed by a similar means who imagined that he carried his nose like an elephant's trunk. By cutting a long **sausage** <note>original: "farcimine"</note> that had been tied to the child's <note>The text likely means a mock-up or a hidden attachment on the patient, or perhaps a servant acting as an "infant" or "proxy"</note> nose, which he believed to be his true nose, that madness vanished along with the imagination. So too, he who believed he was deprived of his head was freed from his insane imagination by the imposition of a leaden hat, by whose weight he finally persuaded himself he had recovered his head.

<margin>The cure of those afflicted by phantasms.</margin>
They are freed by apprehension alone, in the following manner. Since all these people are affected by a great dread arising from the extreme distress of the thing they perceive, it is certain that this melancholic humor is greatly increased by the sorrow of the mind. Therefore, once this dark **soot** <note>original: "fuligo"; a term for the dark, smoky vapors thought to cause depression and madness</note> of the brain is dissipated, the man soon returns to his former state. But this soot cannot be dissipated in melancholics except by immense joy, such as would occur if they were freed by the removal of the object they so loathe and fear. If, therefore, a skilled Physician, with singular industry, were to "amputate" that vain apprehension of (for example) stag horns in a feigned way, so that the imagination truly believed they were cut off,

<column-break/>

it would undoubtedly happen that the heart, dilated by this immense joy with the help of the suppressed spirits, would cause the spirits (which were congealed by sorrow) to become thin and diffuse into the brain. They would soften that humor and lead it into a state of thinness. Once this thinness is introduced, the vain images and fantastic shadows would consequently be dissipated. With these dissipated, they would undoubtedly be restored to the former serene light of the mind.

<margin>An example declaring the power of the imagination.</margin>
I will clarify the matter with an example. If someone were to paint on a mirror's surface the horns of a stag, the head of an elephant, a man without a head, or something similar, using transparent colors—that is, tinctures of various salts, about which I have written in my *Magic of Light and Shadow*—and then, in a dark place, let the sun's rays fall upon the said mirror; it is certain that the light reflected onto the opposite wall, along with the colors, would exhibit the figure we had painted on the mirror. Therefore, the stag horns will appear depicted on the wall for as long as the painting remains on the mirror. But if you scrape away the material clouding the mirror, all appearance of the images will cease at once.

One must think that it happens exactly this way in melancholic affections. In these, the "mirror surface" is represented by the soot and dense vapor collected in the receptacles of the brain, which is most fit for receiving images. If this vapor is driven into a spiral, it will agitate the man with a strange vertigo. If it is curled into flowing waves by the agitation of the spirits, it will fashion truly ridiculous and **incoherent** <note>original: "ἀσύνετα" (asyneta)</note> phantoms of various images in the man. But if it should be gluey, tenacious, and immobile, it will reflect to the imagination an external object that happened to be impressed upon it, as if in a mirror. As long as the man is agitated by this reflected phantom, he will simultaneously be agitated by the madness of the concept. But once the cloud of the mirror is dispersed, the vain fear of the conceived thing must also vanish.

<margin>Why does someone rave about one specific thing, but is otherwise wise?</margin>
But this also might seem a wonder to someone: why does a melancholic person rave about only one specific object, while remaining wise in all other matters? I respond: this happens because of the continuous reflection of the image onto the imagination from the unmoving vapor, not unlike how in **catoptrics** <note>The study of reflection and mirrors</note> the image of a thing is seen only at a determined angle, while infinite other visible objects placed outside that ray's path escape the sight. From whence this wonderful harmony of things arises, I believe must be explained a little more fully.

<margin>Humors have great power over the soul.</margin>
Until now, there has been no Philosopher who denied that the humors have great power over the soul, just as they do over the body; and experience, the mistress of things, clearly teaches this. For, according to the testimony of **Galen** <note>A famous Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium</note>, the character of the soul follows the temperament of the body. Since they are joined together, it is necessary that they suffer with one another. In those things which exist in relation to something else, when a change is made in one, it is necessary that the other [is changed]...

# The Great Art, Book II, Part I.

<margin>Various effects of the passions.</margin>
As was said in the preceding sections, the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia"</note> and **melancholy** <note>In this period, "melancholy" was seen as a physical imbalance of "black bile" that caused delusions.</note> cause the mind to wander. However, once the melancholic humor is dispersed, the mind is restored to clarity. Likewise, loves, fears, pains (or sadness), and pleasure (or joy) are all **passions of the soul**; for we experience fear and love through the soul as their starting point. Yet, in these states, we see the body suffer and change: those who fear turn pale; the envious waste away and turn a leaden color; lovers sigh. Others are shaken by different passions, which sometimes attack with such great **symptoms** <note>original: "corsymptomatis"; likely referring to bodily manifestations of distress</note> that, unless help is provided in time, they are cast into the clear dangers of death.

<margin>The ridiculous body of the Monkey was granted a ridiculous soul.</margin>
For since matter and form, or body and soul, are (as we have said) correlative in their very existence, it is necessary that when one is changed, the other is changed as well. Therefore, as the body is, so is the soul: the ridiculous body of the **Monkey** was granted a ridiculous soul to match. And this is the primary foundation of the marvelous operations that occur within the soul.

<margin>The quality of food has great power in the soul to stir up imaginative movements.</margin>
The second foundation is the quality of **nourishment**, which can sometimes have such power that it transforms a person into someone else entirely. Thus, gentle people can be changed into angry ones by things that sharpen the **bile** <note>Choler or "yellow bile," the humor associated with anger.</note>. Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar of natural science.</note> testifies that this occurs if one drinks the blood of bears, lions, tigers, and similar ferocious beasts. For there lies hidden in the blood of said animals a certain "kindling" of ferocity and cruelty which, when consumed by a human, imprints those same qualities upon them and stimulates them toward the same impulses and affections. Conversely, Galen teaches in his book *On Food* that the fierce, cruel, and wild can be "degenerated" <note>In the sense of being softened or brought down from a wild state.</note> by things that extinguish the bile and increase the **phlegm** <note>original: "pituitam"; the cold, moist humor associated with a calm or sluggish temperament.</note>. Thus, the eating of "chaste lamb" <note>likely referring to *Agnus Castus*, the chasteberry plant, believed to diminish libido</note> and the frequent use of **water lily** <note>original: "Nenupharis"</note> turns the lustful into the continent. From the continent, however, the frequent eating of **satyrions** <note>A type of orchid believed to be an aphrodisiac.</note>, **skinks** <note>A type of lizard used in early modern medicine as a stimulant.</note>, and other lecherous animals makes them lustful; and so it goes for the rest. Thus, all imaginative operations seem to draw their origin from vapors, the vapors from a disordered disposition of the organs—the spleen, the

<margin>The foundation of Magic from the sequence of transmutations.</margin>

<column-break/>

liver, the heart, and the brain—and these from the quality of the food. This quality then affects the "species" <note>Mental images or representations.</note> impressed upon the vapors of the brain with that same quality by which it represents the objects. Finally, through its own reflection, it alters the imagination, and the imagination further alters the entire soul.

### First Corollary.

<margin>The foundation of oneiromancy.</margin>
From all this, it is clearly evident by what means **dreams** are formed in the sick as well as the healthy, and how one can divine the constitution of bodies from them. Likewise, it shows how a human being, by the mere illusion of the imagination, can be naturally transformed from one thing into another. But whoever desires more on this **Magic**, let him read our treatise *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* regarding the Magic and Sacrifices of the ancient Egyptians, where we bring forward many unheard-of things on this subject from the discipline of hieroglyphics.

### Second Corollary.

It also follows from these things how pregnant women, by means of the imagination, imprint signs of desired things upon their fetuses. But since we have treated this extensively and exactly in our *Magnetic Art*, Book 3, in the chapter on the **Magnetism of the Imagination**, we refer the reader there. Let it suffice here to have demonstrated in a few words that all things are shaped according to the logic of light and shadow. Furthermore, this great force of the imagination shines forth in animals themselves. Indeed, I find that **hens** possess such a strong power of imagination that at the mere sight of a string, they remain motionless, as if struck by a kind of stupor. The truth of this will be taught to you by the following experiment.

# CHAPTER XI.
-> On the radiation of the soul toward the outside. <-

<margin>
On sympathetic rays acting at a distance.
</margin>

THERE HAVE BEEN in these recent times certain individuals who have attempted to revive and defend—in published books—the once-condemned opinion regarding the **rays of the soul** transmitted outside the body. They are of the opinion that the soul vibrates certain rays from itself toward things it intensely desires. By these rays, they claim, friends and relatives of a similar nature can feel a great change, even at a significant distance. In this way (they say), experience teaches that the death of children living in the most remote regions is sensed beforehand by their parents. They tell various stories, or rather fables, about the soul leaving the body of a sleeper; all of which they assert could by no means happen without the radiation of the soul into distant places.

We, however, condemn this opinion as being out of harmony with the **Orthodox Faith**. For we hold, along with all the Orthodox, that such premonitions of parents—when children are placed in great calamities or dangers of life—proceed not from the soul of the parents, but immediately from a **Good Spirit** <note>original: "Genio bono," likely referring to a Guardian Angel</note> or by divine inspiration. Nor do we agree with those who believe that the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasiam"</note> can act upon external objects, change them, or in any way make them subject to its own law. We would demonstrate all these things more fully here, were it not that we have already treated both subjects—partly in our *Magnetic World*, in the chapters on the imagination and the magnetisms of love and enchantment, and partly in our *Hieroglyphic Theology*—openly and at length. Therefore, lest we repeat what has already been dealt with, we refer the curious Reader to those works.

# CHAPTER XII.
-> On actinobolismus, or the radiation of elements and minerals. <-

WE ARE NOT speaking here of the rays of the elementary or manifest qualities <note>Manifest qualities are those perceivable by the senses, like heat or cold.</note>, but of the **sympathetic** or specific rays emanating from the very essence of any thing. It must be noted, therefore, that there is nothing in the world that does not naturally "accord" with something else, and "discord" with another. Similarity of substance gives birth to concord and unity, while dissimilarity produces discord. The former pursues another thing as a "good" for its own conservation; the latter avoids another thing as an "evil" to itself by every means. But since things cannot always achieve their effect through "immediacy of presence" <note>original: "immediatione suppositi," a scholastic term meaning direct physical contact</note>, provident Nature—a kind daughter in all necessary things—instituted this **actinobolia** <note>original: "ἀκτινοβολίαν," meaning ray-emission</note> so that substances which cannot act upon each other at a distance might reach their goal through a secondary transmission of their powers. Hence, to each and every thing contained within the machine of the world, this kind of **actinobolismus** has been granted.

<margin>
The atmosphere is nothing other than an expiration made in the shape of a sphere.
</margin>

What else is this wondrous **atmosphere**, the basis of all sublunary generation, but a certain radiant expiration <note>original: "exspiratio"; an exhalation or vapor</note> diffused into a sphere? If it were possible to see it, it would appear in no other shape than an oval, because the atmosphere (or the "right sphere") is higher from the earth due to the thinness of the expiration, yet closer to the earth at the horizons due to the density of the expiration. What else is the movement of heavy and light objects but a certain perennial radiation, while exhalations diffused into the heights, being ignited from there,

<margin>
The motion of light and heavy things.
</margin>

radiate perpetually toward us? Concerning these, read in our *Magnetic Meteorological Art*. What is the heat of a fire, if not a radiation diffused spherically from the fiery body to those standing near? Who could describe with sufficient eloquence the magnetic radiations <note>original: "actinobolismos"</note> in minerals, and their wondrous powers and properties...

# Great Art, Book II, Part I.

...express you with eloquence? Since we have treated these matters variously and at length in our work *The Magnetic Art* <note>Kircher is referring to his 1641 book *Magnes, sive de Arte Magnetica*, where he discusses all forms of attraction and radiation.</note>, I have deemed it superfluous to make more extensive mention of them here. Among the metals, this is also not the least bit wonderful: that they do not merely establish spheres of radiation through their power, but also, through their material "effluvia" or "efflorescences," they fashion something radiant. Thus, the various crystalline growths of vitriols, salts, and nitre, as well as flakes of snow, are formed into certain little stars; we have decided that all these things ought to be proven by experiments.

### Experiment.

<margin>A wonderful experiment.</margin>
Prepare a lye <note>original: "lixivium," an alkaline solution leached from ashes</note> from a nettle <note>original: "urtica"</note> reduced to ash; expose this lye to the sky at night until it develops an icy crust, and you will see—marvelous to say—the whole and perfect figure of the nettle expressed in the ice itself, with that same layout of fibers and jagged leaf-edges that you would find in real ones. 

<margin>In the ashes of all things lies a seed, and the colors of all things.</margin>
If you then apply a microscope <note>original: "smicroscopium." Kircher was one of the first scientists to use early microscopes to observe biological and mineral samples.</note>, you will see with admiration that the entire figure of the nettle has grown together from minute and almost infinite little stars. I would believe that the same thing happens with any other plant, so that it may appear even from this that a certain seed lies hidden in the ashes of things, which, through its radiation, affects a form similar to its species.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration showing rows of crystalline, six-pointed star or snowflake-like figures. The rows are labeled with letters B, C, D, and E on the left side of the diagram area. Each row contains three slightly different geometric patterns, demonstrating variations in stellar formation.</image-desc>

Thus manna, nitre, vitriol, and alum, when inspected with a microscope, are nothing other than

<column-break/>

starred bodies of the most diverse shapes. But why snow especially should express star-shaped corpuscles, various men have tried to explain in various ways. Some, following Democritus, attribute everything to atoms; some to the "plastic power" <note>The "plastic power" or "virtus plastica" was a contemporary term for the biological force that gives shape to living things.</note> of snow; others, driven by despair, have judged that the cause of so hidden a matter can by no means be defined. We say that this starry formation <note>original: "plasma"</note> of snow comes from nowhere else than from a **warm spirit** concentrated within the snowy flakes; which, while it is surrounded on all sides by cold corpuscles, finally rushing out through whatever door is given, forms the snowy body into a starred or radiant figure by "drilling" through it. This is clearly demonstrated by the multitude and variety of the rays: for some have the shape as in B, others as in C, and some as in D. There are not lacking those that have the shape we have placed in E: which certainly do not come from the plastic virtue of the snow, since that gives a constant and perpetually determined shape to things. Therefore, it is from the warm spirit concentrated within the snowy flakes, which—according to the thinness or density of the matter—divides them into figures now of one kind, now another, yet all of them star-shaped. You will learn all these things by this experience: for if an glowing coal or a red-hot iron ball is placed in the middle of a thin sheet of ice (the kind we usually find frozen over water in the morning at the start of winter), you will soon see that as the heat spreads from the center, the ice is formed into a starry crust. The same, therefore, must be thought to happen in soft snow. However, how crystals and aluminous bodies "degenerate" into starry prisms will be discussed in our *Subterranean World* <note>original: "Mundo nostro subterraneo," referring to his massive 1665 encyclopedia of geology and the underground world.</note>.

# CHAPTER XIII.

## On the Sympathetic and Antipathetic Radiation of Medicinal Things.

<margin>The foundation of a more secret medicine.</margin>
In no thing does the radiation <term>actinobolismus: the "casting of rays" or projection of an internal power</term> of natural things shine forth so clearly as in medicinal matters: for this is twofold, tending either toward life or toward destruction. To understand this, it must be noted: just as all things were created for the sake of man, so too particular powers have been granted to individual things by which they can preserve man. For he who intends the end also intends the means to achieve it, such as the virtues of natural things. Since, therefore, there is no member in the human body that does not suffer its own infirmities, the most kind Creator has provided for each with opportune remedies. Since members were hidden in the deepest

<column-break/>

recesses of the body, inaccessible to herbs and plants, He willed to co-create in those plants certain powers modeled after light spreading its rays in a circle, which, permeating the whole body, would penetrate the corresponding member by radiation <term>actinobolismus</term>. Hence it happens that medicines, with the rays of their power unfolded, strengthen and comfort that member which corresponds to it by a certain proportion of nature. Thus all **Cardiac** <note>medicines for the heart</note> medicines seek out not the liver, nor the brain, nor the spleen, but the heart by their radiation; **Hepatics** <note>medicines for the liver</note> comfort not the heart, nor the kidneys, nor the lungs, but the liver by radiation. Thus **Diuretics** seek not the heart, liver, or brain, but the kidneys, the emulgent veins, and the bladder. In this way, the radiation of **Diaphoretics** <note>medicines that induce sweating</note> forces the bile lying hidden in the whole body into the viscera, and from there secretes it as something harmful.

# The Actinobolism of Natural Things. 115

### Corollary.

<margin>The power of compound medicines.</margin>
From this it is clear by what means compound medicines—endowed with various qualities—act upon the body equally, with no one quality hindering another, just as rays of different light act without becoming confused. Since the specific virtues of each ingredient remain in the compound even when their "primary qualities" <note>In Aristotelian physics, the four primary qualities are hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> perish, it happens that once such medicines are received into the stomach, as if in their natural place, the individual species radiate toward the limbs that correspond to them by a certain natural proportion. They do this without any mixing or confusion of their rays, just as we have shown regarding rays of light. Through this *actinobolism* <note>original: "actinobolismo," from the Greek for "throwing out rays." Kircher uses this to describe how objects project their internal power outward.</note>, they wonderfully comfort those limbs. Consequently, when all the limbs are comforted, the natural heat and the "vein of life" must also be strengthened; the more this prevails, the more the disease-causing force will fail. Thus, we can imagine as many centers of different virtue in a medicine as there are species that enter into it. If there are many cardiac ingredients, they will all radiate toward the strengthening of the single heart; pulmonary species will radiate toward the preservation of the single lung, and hepatic species toward the single liver. In this way, with these virtues gathered together, the whole man is comforted and must necessarily prevail over any deadly quality.

<margin>What Antipathetic Actinobolism is.</margin>
On the other hand, the antipathetic actinobolism of inferior or poisonous things happens in this way: the poison of certain things, as soon as it reaches the stomach, immediately attacks the heart with its radiation as if it were the primary fortress to be captured. Thus do mineral poisons—Arsenic, Ochre, and Orpiment <note>Auripigmentum (yellow arsenic trisulfide).</note>—act. The poison instilled by the bite of a serpent infects the nearby blood beneath the skin through radiation; by its pestilential radiation, it infects more and more of the nearby blood until it creeps toward the vitals, where, unless it is repressed by *antactinobolism* <note>A counter-radiation or defensive power.</note>, it finally contrives the ultimate destruction of the man. Individual limbs also have their own poisons; for some things, when consumed, do not

<column-break/>

seek the heart immediately, but rather the lungs—such as the "sea-lung" <note>original: "pulmo marinus," likely referring to a type of jellyfish or medusa believed to be toxic.</note> when swallowed. From this, the lung becomes ulcerated and corrupted, and the man must necessarily perish from a slow wasting disease. The "Sardonic Celery" <note>original: "Apium Sardonicum," the water dropwort, which was said to cause a facial convulsion resembling a grin—the "sardonic smile."</note>, as well as the Tarantula, invades the workshops of the spirits, the arteries, and the muscles with the radiation of its poison, turning the man toward laughter and jumping. The bite of the Dipsas <note>A legendary serpent whose bite was said to cause unquenchable thirst.</note>, as soon as it begins to radiate, leads the liver into rot. The poison of a rabid dog, by its radiation, transforms the person into canine behaviors; hence they perpetually bark, bite, and fear water. The brain of a cat stirred by heat <note>original: "æstro perciti," meaning in a frenzy or heat.</note> brings about feline behaviors. Schenck <note>Johann Schenck von Grafenberg (1530–1598), a famous physician known for his massive collection of medical observations.</note> tells of a girl who, from eating the brain of a cat, was so transformed that she imitated all the gestures of cats, expressed their voice exactly, and hunted mice with her fingers curved like talons. The poison of the Asp, being an enemy to the nerves, strikes the man with its radiation, inducing a stupor in all the limbs. Likewise, the corrosive actinobolism of sublimated Mercury finally finishes a man by "boring through" all the vitals. 

<margin>The wonderful power of poisons.</margin>
You see, therefore, that different limbs and parts have different poisons, all of which act upon the said limbs not by their own substance, but by the diffusion of a radiant virtue. However, one cannot counter this poisonous radiation except by the radiant quality of a substance contrary to it, by which the poisonous quality is blunted; just as shadows and the radiation of darkness are destroyed by the radiation of light. But concerning these things, see the one who treats them more extensively in *The Magnetic World* <note>Referring to Kircher's own work *Magnes*, or a specific section of it.</note> in the chapter on the magnetism of poisons. And from all these things briefly brought forward, it is clearly evident that there is nothing in the nature of things that is not endowed with a certain radiant virtue for certain ends established by the Author of Nature for man. This radiation is established in all things according to the pattern of light, so much so that the wise reader—just as from the magnetisms of things, so also from the actinobolisms of natural things—may easily reach the highest inner secrets of nature by using these individuals as if they were the two wings of nature. But now, leaving these things behind, let us turn our pen to other matters.

# PART TWO
## ON OPTICAL ACTINOBOLISM.
### OR ON VISUAL RADIATION, WHICH IS THE ROOT AND FOUNDATION OF THE ENTIRE SCIENCE OF OPTICS.

# PREFACE.

<image-desc>Decorative initial 'C' featuring a landscape scene with a central sun-like face and ornate floral scrollwork bordering the letter.</image-desc>

Since in the preceding parts we have spoken enough and more than enough concerning the radiant action of light, shadow, and other things propagating their powers into the distance through actinobolisms <note>original: "actinobolismis," from the Greek for "throwing out rays." Kircher uses this to describe how objects project their internal power or form outward.</note>, nothing remains but to say something about optical actinobolism. Even though I am not unaware that nearly countless authors have handed down whole volumes on this art—which is common knowledge even to the bleary-eyed and barbers <note>original: "Lippis & Tonsoribus," a Latin idiom for something so well-known it is discussed in barbershops.</note>—and thus the more learned might deservedly accuse me of wasting time in teaching an art so well known to all. Nevertheless, they will cease to grumble once they rightly understand our aim in teaching these things and the goal we have proposed. For we do not intend here to hand down the whole science of optics, but only that art which concerns the radiant projection of things; and that not precisely for its own sake, but in relation to our Magic of Light and Shadow <note>Referring to Kircher’s major work, *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae*, which deals with mirrors, lenses, and projections.</note>, in which—using these as certain foundations—we shall produce exotic effects. Leaving aside, therefore, those things commonly taught by opticians, we shall follow those things proper to our purpose, namely optical actinobolism.

---

## DEFINITIONS.

I. **Optical Actinoboly**, or visual radiation, is nothing other than the arrival of images and species <note>original: "specierum," referring to the "likenesses" or formal qualities of objects that travel through the air to the eye in traditional physics.</note> of objects at the organ of visual power in the form of a cone or pyramid.
II. A **Direct-viewing ray** <note>original: "orthopticus," from the Greek *orthos* (straight) and *optikos* (viewing).</note> is a visual ray tending straight toward an object and cutting it perpendicularly; it is also sometimes called the axis of the right radiant cone.
III. An **Upward-viewing ray** <note>original: "anopticus," from the Greek *ano* (upward).</note> is a visual ray turning upward, such as when we behold the height 

<column-break/>

of mountains, towers, etc.
IV. A **Downward-viewing ray** <note>original: "catopticus," from the Greek *kato* (downward).</note> is a ray opposite to the former, by which we look down at objects from a height.
V. An **Oblique-viewing ray** <note>original: "loxopticus," from the Greek *loxos* (slanting).</note> is a visual ray incident upon objects obliquely or laterally.
VI. The **Optical pyramid** or **cone** is the solid figure formed by visual radiation produced from the object into the organ, whose base is the thing seen and whose vertex is the organ of the eye itself.
VII. The **Section of the pyramid** is the name given to the interposition of some intermediate <term>diaphanous: any material, like air, water, or glass, that allows light to pass through.</term> body between the eye and the object, or between the vertex and the base, by which the visual cone or pyramid is cut.
VIII. Moreover, the **Intermediate plane** <note>original: "planum mesophanum."</note> is that transparent plane interposed between the eye and the thing seen in which the section occurs.
IX. A **Straight-cut section** <note>original: "orthotome."</note> occurs when the section is equiangular to the axis, or when the axis of the visual pyramid is cut at right angles in the intermediate plane.
X. An **Oblique-cut section** <note>original: "loxotome."</note> occurs when the section is at an oblique angle to the axis, or when the axis is cut by the intermediate plane at acute or obtuse angles.
XI. A **Straight-plane object** <note>original: "orthoplanon."</note> is the base of the pyramid that is perpendicular to the axis.
XII. An **Oblique-plane object** <note>original: "loxoplanon."</note> is the base of the pyramid that is slanted, or founded on an oblique plane.
XIII. An **Upward-plane object** <note>original: "anoplanon."</note> is the base of the radiant pyramid depicted on a plane in a higher location.
XIV. A **Downward-plane object** <note>original: "catoplanon."</note> is the exact opposite of the preceding, grounding its base on a floor or pavement.

## HYPOTHESES.

**I.** Distinct vision is only achieved under an acute angle; the shape encompassed by the visual rays is a cone or a pyramid, whose peak rests in the eyes and whose base rests upon the outer edge of the thing seen. From this, those things are properly seen whose images <note>original: "species"; in Renaissance optics, this refers to the "form" or "likeness" of an object traveling through the air to the eye.</note> radiate into the eye. *Euclid, Optics, Book 1.*

II. Larger things appear under a larger angle, smaller things under a smaller one, and equal things under an equal angle. *Euclid & General Perspective.* Thus, nearby things are seen under a larger angle, and remote things under a smaller one; the floors of temples appear to slope upward to those entering; and the more remote parts of planes lying below the eye 

<column-break/>

appear to be raised high. Consequently, the horizon is also viewed as being in a higher place than it truly is, with lines on the right inclining toward the left, and those on the left toward the right.

III. Regarding planes that hang above the view: the more remote parts appear to glide down toward the bottom.

IV. Among equal magnitudes that stand upright before the sight, the more remote ones appear raised higher; conversely, those that hang above the sight appear depressed or lower when compared to those nearby.

V. Parallel lines produced to infinity on a plane appear to eventually meet at a point on the horizontal line, which is called the "primary" or "principal point" by opticians.

# CHAPTER I.

->On the Structure and Vision of the Eye.<-

<image-desc>A circular anatomical diagram of the human eye is situated in the lower part of the first column. It shows the various layers and internal structures labeled with letters: A (anterior surface), B and C (outer membranes/sclera), D and E (inner membranes), F (pupil/iris area), G, H, I (posterior interior/retina), K, L, M (internal humors with L as the crystalline lens), N (suspensory ligaments), and Z (the optic nerve exiting at the posterior). Above the first paragraph is a large decorative woodcut initial 'O' featuring a face within a circular medallion.</image-desc>

Anatomical experiments on the eyes of animals and humans, performed by the most skilled surgeons, have taught us that the eye is by no means spherical throughout its entire substance. Instead, observe this shape which you see depicted here, where **ABCB** is a somewhat hard membrane <note>original: "pellis," literally "skin." Here referring to the sclera and cornea.</note> formed into the shape of a vessel containing all the other internal parts. **DEF** is another interior membrane, finer and stretched within the aforementioned first one. **ZH** is the optic nerve, composed of countless filaments stretched out, from where it is propagated into the remaining circuit **GHI**. There, mixed with infinite small veins and arteries, a certain kind of soft and very tender flesh is composed, performing the role of a third membrane <note>The retina.</note>.

**KLM** are three types of transparent humors <note>The fluids of the eye: aqueous, vitreous, and the crystalline lens.</note> filling the entire space contained within the membranes. Depending on their density or rarity, they refract images into the shape seen here; the middle humor is likened to crystal, while the others are likened to water. The first membrane enjoys an unequal curvature, being more prominent in its upper part. The interior surface of the membrane **EF**, where it faces the back of the eye, is entirely black and dark, and it has a round opening **EF**, which 

<column-break/>

by voluntary motion—via muscles and certain tiny tendons and filaments **BN** originating from the second membrane—can now be contracted and now dilated. Furthermore, in this miraculous factory <note>original: "fabrica," referring to the anatomical "construction" or "workmanship" of God/Nature.</note>, it is clearly seen that the crystalline humor is not circular, but lenticular <note>Lens-shaped, like a lentil.</note>, established by nature for the exact representation of things. Therefore, through these humors, the images of external things are transmitted and presented to the sensing soul. Vision occurs by the exact same principle by which we previously saw the images of colored things—passed through a lenticular pupil into a dark place and caught on white paper—exhibited in the back <note>original: "fundo," the fundus or retina.</note> of the eye. Thus, the room in which the images are exhibited represents the interior state of the eye: the opening represents the pupil; the lenticular glass represents the crystalline lens and the other adjacent humors; and the paper <margin>The marvelous construction of the eye.</margin> destined to receive the images represents the back of the eye. Just as all images of external things, along with their colors and proportions, are exhibited on paper in a darkened room through an opening and a lenticular pupil; so too, by the radiation of the objects acting upon the visual power in the back of the eye (acting like the paper), all images of things seen are sketched with their colors and universal symmetry through the opening **FF**, before they are apprehended by the imagination. I would never have believed this, had an experiment first by a certain most sagacious anonymous optician <note>Likely referring to Christopher Scheiner or Johannes Kepler, who pioneered the "eye as camera obscura" theory.</note>, and then the same performed by myself, not made me certain of this fact.

## I. An Optical Experiment.

<image-desc>A diagram and a detailed woodcut illustration related to optics. The upper diagram shows light rays originating from three geometric symbols (a triangle, a star, and a crescent moon) passing through a narrow aperture and diverging as they travel toward a curved plane. Below this is a circular woodcut illustrating a cross-section of a human eye, showing light rays converging at a focal point on the retina through the lens and humors.</image-desc>

Take the eye of a bull, or of some other large animal—or even a human eye, if the opportunity for a dissection <note>original: "anatomiæ inſtituendæ"; performing an anatomy or dissection.</note> should arise. After washing this eye, you will strip away the thicker membrane from the back part, cutting away the denser sections little by little, until the internal fluid <note>original: "humor"; referring to the vitreous humor of the eye.</note> begins to show through. Once this is done, place the eye in a certain hole <note>Such as a hole in a darkened room's shutter.</note> so that the outer, illuminated part faces directly outward. When the room has been darkened, it is wonderful to relate <note>original: "mirùm dictu"</note> how any ray-emitting objects <note>original: "actinobola"; from the Greek for 'throwing rays.'</note>—or rather the images <note>original: "ſpecies"; in 17th-century science, this refers to the 'form' or 'likeness' of an object that travels through the air.</note> of the objects—penetrating the eye through the crystalline humors, will display their likenesses on the back of the eye. They will appear with their own colors and natural characteristics, so perfectly arranged inside that they seem to be painted with a brush, though in an inverted fashion. Thus, the demonstration of images represented in a dark place through a glass pupil <note>A lens.</note> is exactly the same as the images represented on the back of the eye through the intervening fluids.

## II. A new and wonderful experiment, exhibiting any objects in darkness.

Giuseppe Bonacorsi <note>original: "Joſephus Bonacurſius"; a 17th-century Italian nobleman and scholar known for his interest in light.</note>, a man most celebrated for his nobility as well as the integrity of his life and the fame of his learning, was recently discussing with me the nature of light and its more hidden effects. Among other observations, he brought forward this one: namely, that it is possible for some-

<column-break/>

one to see objects in the darkness just as if they were standing in the middle of the light. This matter was at first held to be a paradox; but after he brought forth the reasons for his assertion, it immediately appeared that it was by no means a deception, as it rested upon such a probable foundation. A great desire to test the matter then burned in my mind, especially since I saw how much the consideration of the previous experiment favored the proposed claim. Furthermore, I have not infrequently found in myself that, upon being woken from sleep at night, all the objects in my bedroom were represented as clearly and distinctly as if they were illuminated by a candle.

Encouraged therefore by this fortunate encounter with the most learned Bonacorsi, I set about the experiment and found the truth of the matter to be not only as described, but I also discovered that many things could be concluded from this single experiment. These will provide a great light to the field of Optics and the untying of insoluble questions. Therefore, curious Reader, begin the experiment with this diligence. In a certain place that can be perfectly closed so that no light shines in from any side, leave a paper window <note>A window covered with translucent paper instead of glass.</note> upon which you will paint any images, or rather shadows of things. Let the window face the Sun so that it can be illuminated by it. Once this is done, gaze at the paper window with fixed eyes for some time until the back of the eye has perfectly absorbed its image. Then, with the window closed in the dark place, place a white paper before your eyes. And behold, wonderful to relate, on that paper you will first see something like a rising dawn, appearing first as saffron, then red, then purple. Finally, you will see a circle painted with every kind of color (such as those in a rainbow), and after that, the inverted shape of the window. This will eventually fade into a most beautiful blue color mixed with intense red. The image, which at first appears black in the bright circle, then yellow, is sometimes upright and sometimes inverted. These phantoms <note>original: "ſimulacra"</note> will eventually turn into a very thick shadow, and thus, as the spirits <note>In traditional physiology, "visual spirits" were thought to be the subtle fluids that carried sight from the eye to the brain.</note> are consumed and the images vanish, the image is returned to its origin—that is, to darkness—and escapes the eyes. This is the experiment that I wish all curious investigators of nature to observe. Furthermore, it remains to be asked how the images of things remain in the eye, and how that variety of colors is caused. To the first, I respond that the images of light and colors, as well as the shapes, behave toward the eye in exactly the same way as light behaves toward the phosphorescent stone <note>original: "lapidem phoſphorum"; likely the 'Bologna Stone,' a famous mineral that glowed in the dark after exposure to sunlight.</note>, which we described in Book 1, Chapter 8. For this stone, when exposed to the Sun, perfectly shows the absorbed light in the darkness in the form of glowing coals...

# Optical Ray-Projection

Thus I say it happens in the eye, which, having absorbed the likenesses <note>original: "ſpecies"; in 17th-century science, this refers to the visual form or "image-bearing" rays of an object.</note> of other images illuminated by light, retains them for a little while because the humors <term>humors: the transparent fluids within the eyeball</term> of the eye are natural to it and clear; it happens that in the dark, the light received displays them in the darkness as well. Nor should anyone object to us here that these colors are merely "phantastic" <note>imaginary or illusory after-images</note>: for the inverted form of the likenesses shows this to be false.

<margin>Demonstration of the experiment.</margin>

<image-desc>A schematic optical diagram demonstrating image projection within the eye. An external object AB (a cross) represents the sun. Light rays (AT, BS) pass through a narrowed pupil GH and lens I to form an inverted image ST on the fundus E of the eye CD. A secondary process shows rays (SGM, THN) reflecting from the fundus out through a dilated pupil GH to project an inverted image MN onto a surface labeled "charta" (paper).</image-desc>

But why it is formed inverted, we have decided must be explained by the following demonstration. Let there be, therefore, the eye CD, the back of the eye <note>original: "fundus"</note> E, and an object illuminated by the Sun AB. Specifically, a cross depicted in a bright window: the pupil of the eye GH, and the center of that same pupil I. If anyone, therefore, looks at the object illuminated by the Sun for a little while with steady eyes; the likenesses poured out from the object, and falling through the lines AT and BS onto the back of the eye, will paint the object there according to the preceding experiment; which object, according to proposition 4 of part 2, will necessarily be inverted on the back ST. For when the pupil is contracted into the smallest little circle due to the intense inspection of the bright object, it happens that the lines intersecting at I also display inverted likenesses of the external things. But in the dark, when the pupil gradually dilates—for example, at GH—it follows that the likenesses reflected from the back of the eye through the pupil GH and the lines SGM and THN represent the thing on the paper <note>original: "charta"</note> without any [further] intersection being made, just as it appears on the back of the eye. But we have shown in the preceding experiment that all likenesses in it are inverted; therefore, they are also inverted on the paper MN, as the figure clearly shows. They will therefore appear inverted on the paper. However, it usually happens from time to time that they also appear upright on the paper: this occurs then, when the pupil is strained and narrowed by a voluntary motion: for then, due to the intersection of the lines carrying the likenesses, it will also appear upright on the paper. The diversity of colors, however, occurs according to the degrees declared in the preceding book; for first

<column-break/>

a saffron color <note>original: "croccus color"</note> will occur, which happens because of the abundance of light impressed upon the eye; as this fails by certain degrees, the color also changes from saffron to red, from red to crimson, from this into blue, and finally, verging into darkness, it vanishes along with the light and the likenesses.

And this genuine and most vivid idea of the eye is most perfectly reflected by the ingenious introduction of visible likenesses through a single convex lens into a dark place, and their most pleasant representation on a piece of paper; so much so that the introduction of the aforementioned likenesses through a single convex lens is nothing other than an ingenious imitation of the eye's own visual power in representing the same. And just as many variations occur in the natural perception of things presented to the eye, so too in their artificial transmission. For the eye, remaining fixed and unmoving, perceives everything directly opposite it via a straight ray <note>original: "orthodromo radio"; a ray following the shortest, direct path.</note> more clearly and distinctly than those things which withdraw to the sides: the same happens in a lens, through which the likenesses transmitted onto the paper are more distinct the closer they are [to the center], and more dull the further they are from it. Because both in the lens and in the crystalline humor <term>crystalline humor: the natural lens of the eye</term>, likenesses falling through the central axis and near it suffer hardly any refraction <note>The bending of light as it passes through different materials.</note>, whence they are painted exactly; moreover, as the picture of the likenesses is in the eye, so a clear vision follows a clear picture, and a dull one follows a dull one.

Again, just as the unmoving and unchanging eye perceives objects at unequal distances from itself with unequal visual power—some clearly and distinctly, others obscurely and confusedly—so also a fixed convex lens projects the likenesses of things placed outside onto a fixed paper with a plainly different effect. The reason for both is that nearby objects project a distinct base <note>the focal plane</note> of likenesses, which presents visible things in an orderly fashion further from the lens or crystalline humor, while distant objects project them shorter [closer to the lens]. Therefore, since the paper receives that base in a tube, and the back of the Retina <note>original: "fundus Retinæ"</note> receives it in the eye, it is impossible for either the paper or the retina membrane to receive both the nearer and more distant base at the same time. Again, just as an object at some very remote distance from any eye is not discerned at all, so in the introduction of likenesses through a lens, there is eventually some such distance that the likenesses on the paper vanish entirely; there is also such proximity that it is never discerned. The reason is that the common base, in which the well-ordered likenesses are represented, falls outside the retina in the eye, and outside the paper held up to the tube or lens—falling in front of it <note>original: "cis"</note> for distant objects, and behind it <note>original: "trans"</note> for those too near.

<margin>Conclusion.</margin>

From which it is clear, first, how the introduction of likenesses through a convex lens graphically expresses the natural organ of the eye by imitating it in all things. The reason for which, from the former, is almost unique and...

# Great Art, Book II, Part II.

<margin>A convex lens mimics the organ of the eye.</margin>
The most powerful factor is the refraction of likenesses <note>original: "specierum"; in 17th-century science, "species" refers to the visual forms or "images" emitted by objects</note> through the crystalline humor <term>crystalline humor: the natural lens of the eye</term>, which is similar to and proportionate with a glass lens. For this lens, by refracting the rays—which would otherwise scatter haphazardly—forces them into an orderly arrangement. It disposes them upon a single base so that a most beautiful painted image of the objects results. In this one thing, however, a certain difference is found: the paper held behind a glass lens is flat, whereas the retinal tunic <term>retinal tunic: the retina</term> of the eye is concave. If someone were to construct a massive globe—just as our Scheiner <note>Christoph Scheiner (1573–1650), a Jesuit physicist who proved that images are formed on the retina</note> says the Most Serene Archduke of Austria, Maximilian, experienced—and entering it, were to collect the likenesses of external things inside that concavity through a convex lens, he would certainly find that the likenesses appear much more distinct, more orderly, and across a wider space than those displayed on a flat surface, following the model of the eye. From this it is clear how kindly God provided for the nature of the eye, wishing to arrange the painting of the likenesses not on a flat but on a concave tunic, so that in this way He might better provide for the sight.

Second, it is clear that the crossing <term>decussation: the point where light rays intersect and flip the image</term> of rays occurs within the eye itself before the image of the object is formed on the retina. A figure beautifully shows all of this; you can also try this experiment for yourself: if you shave away the sclera <note>original: "schlerode"; the white, opaque outer layer of the eye</note> at the back of the eye and let the light of a candle enter through the pupil, you will perceive that it necessarily falls upon the retinal tunic with the rays crossed, according to Proposition 8 of the preceding book. From this, the inversion of images at the back of the eye results.

<margin>Who are the Nearsighted?</margin>
Third, it is clear that the Nearsighted <note>original: "Miopes"</note>, or those who have "short sight," always keep an object close to themselves, and a concave lens is necessary for them to see well. For since they possess a crystalline humor formed from segments of a small sphere—the nature of which is to force received rays into a short space by refraction—it happens that they always "paint" a distinct and very accurate image, but one which very often does not reach the formal sensor of sight (namely, the retinal tunic), but is finished within the vitreous humor <term>vitreous humor: the clear gel-like fluid filling the eyeball</term>. Because of this, the eye perceives the object either not at all or very confusedly, because the base or section of the common cone of light—where the likenesses meet in a common "painting"—either does not reach the retinal tunic at all, or reaches it when the rays are already confused among themselves. Now, the eye feels nothing except what is offered by the visible likenesses, and in the manner in which it is offered. If they are clear, it sees clearly; if distinct, distinctly; if they are offered confusedly, it sees confusedly. In the Nearsighted, therefore, since remote objects by their nature collect rays into a common base more quickly than near ones, remote things appear quite foggy; because those things shape their likenesses into a more distant base, and these into a nearer one: and thus the latter reaches the retinal tunic, while the former are—

<column-break/>

<margin>who are the farsighted.</margin>
—smothered in the middle of the vitreous humor. Since, therefore, a concave lens has this property of spreading rays through refraction, and by this means (together with the convex lens of the eye) extends the likenesses toward the retina, it happens that the Nearsighted, having adopted such a glass <note>original: "specillo"; here referring to a lens or spectacles</note>, are indeed excellently helped to see remote things well. Yet, this occurs under a smaller apparent size, because the angles at the crossing point are made smaller. In the Farsighted <note>original: "Presbytæ"</note>, however, or those who look at things from a distance, the process works in the opposite way.

Thus it is clear, fourth, that an eye reinforced with a convex lens is nothing other than a tube—partly natural, partly artificial—adorned with two convex lenses: namely, the crystalline humor and the convex glass. Indeed, when a tube is used with a convex glass, everything will appear both larger and more distinct. This is a clear experience obvious to all, and most usefully invented to help the farsighted; since they have a crystalline humor that is very broad and composed of segments of a larger sphere, it happens that objects (especially near ones) transmit the visible image or "painting" beyond the formal instrument of sight (the retinal tunic), and thus elude the power of seeing. However, the convex lens fulfills their wish upon its arrival, for it recalls that freely wandering image and restrains it within the prescribed limits. See more on these matters in our *Catoptric Magic* <note>original: "Magia nostra Catoptrica"; likely a reference to another section of Kircher's work on mirrors and lenses</note>.

Finally, it is clear that an eye reinforced with a convex lens is nothing other than a tube, partly natural and partly artificial, adorned with two convex lenses: namely, the crystalline humor and a convex glass. Indeed, a tube equipped with two convex lenses is like a purely artificial, inanimate eye.

Therefore, experiments of this kind—in which nature first wonderfully paints the likenesses of external things on the back of the retina, just as on the walls of a dark room—have truly provided me with the occasion for many speculations. They have opened the door to countless hidden mysteries in natural philosophy and the "sanctuaries of nature," so that now, with the help of these experiments, I am confident that I can discern the vision of any animal from the very back of its eye. I can also discern the nature of fascination <note>the belief in the "evil eye" or the ability to influence others through the gaze</note>, the causes of certain marks on infants in the mother's womb, the reasons for the innate light of animals, and many other things; all of which, since they are not the purpose of this current undertaking, we reserve to be treated elsewhere.

Therefore, a double pyramid concurs in the act of vision: the first is extrinsic, resting on the base of the object itself; and the second is intrinsic and inverted, establishing its base at the back of the eye. The first presents the likenesses of the objects to the visual power, the latter more...

-># Optical Radiation<-

<margin>The visual pyramid. He establishes [the image] in the back of the eye, near the optic nerve.</margin>
By making these images more familiar and internal to itself, [the eye] arranged them so that the soul—stimulated by the visual spirits <note>Visual spirits were thought to be subtle fluids or gases that carried sensory information from the eye to the brain.</note> nearby—might use them to create perfect sensation and vision. For as the base of the exterior pyramid is, so is the base of the interior pyramid: whatever the color of the external object, such is the color of the internal one. This compares exactly to the way we previously taught regarding the representation of forms <note>original: "specierum"; the visual "species" or images cast by objects</note> in a dark room <note>A reference to the *camera obscura* effect.</note>. With these things thus established, it seemed appropriate to set forth in this place some propositions concerning optical radiation <term>actinobolismus: from the Greek for "throwing rays"; the study of how light rays travel and intersect</term>. These serve as a summary of the entire nature and behavior of optics, so that among such a vast multitude of things to be discussed, we might grasp countless details through a few, very clear, and well-organized principles. Let it be, therefore:

### Proposition I.

*All straight lines that exist on direct and horizontal planes—including those inclined toward vertical walls—and are parallel within that plane: all, I say, tend toward the primary point of the mesoptic plane <term>mesoptic plane: the theoretical middle-plane or "canvas" where the image is projected</term>, from which every projection takes its origin.*

Just like the lines of the earth, other straight lines that stand at parallel intervals to the primary ray, if extended to infinity, will finally seem to meet with that same principal ray and with each other.

We shall demonstrate all of this part by part.

Let BD and EG be equal; therefore DX and DG will be equal and parallel to BI and BE through Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 31. Because of this, the mesoptic plane BHE can be extended through DG as a parallel. Since this plane and the "sight-table" <note>The surface on which the image is perceived</note> are cut by the radiant surface DAG, the common sections DG and RS will be parallel through Euclid, Book 11, Proposition 16. Therefore, due to the similarity of triangles DAX and RAE, as DA is to AR, so is DX to RE. However, AD is greater than AR; therefore DX (which is BI) will be greater than that same RE. Thus, lines BR and IE, when produced, will eventually meet, namely at point K, which is shown again as follows. Since BI and RE are parallel to DX, and therefore to each other...

...through Euclid, Book 11, Proposition 9, and since all of them go straight away from the viewer, it is necessary that the gaps between them gradually diminish according to the sight. Consequently, those lines that are stretched out straight are gradually drawn together. Since indeed all principal lines will seem to flow together like rays from the circumference to the center of a circle (according to hypotheses 4 and 5), the lower lines will seem to rise and be carried upward; the upper lines will seem to sink down toward the principal ray as if from a higher place; and finally, those on the right will decline to the left, and those on the left to the right. All of them, with an equal inclination, join themselves to the principal ray which occupies the middle place, until they all meet at the same point of sight. The principal ray falls upon a solitary point of the mesoptic plane, which we named the "primary point" above. But since this is the sole foundation of all optics, and everything that follows depends upon it, I have decided to explain it with a more thorough demonstration.

Let the eye be at A, the mesoptic plane be HBE, and the straight lines facing the eye be BD and EG, extended to infinity. Let the mesoptic plane be perpendicular to both BD and EG, and let the primary point in it be K. I say that the projections of the straight lines BD and EG, proceeding from the extreme points B and E, meet each other at the primary point K.

# Sciagraphy
<page-num>125</page-num>
<header>Sciagraphy.</header>
<sig>Q 3</sig>

to be, which better represents the optical <term>actinobolism</term> <note>original: "actinobolismum"; the radiation or emission of light rays in straight lines from a source.</note>. It seemed appropriate, therefore, to briefly declare its nearly infinite use, so that we do not appear to have omitted anything in the art of light and shadow.

<margin>Construction of the mesoptic instrument.</margin>
First, let a parallelogram ABCD be made, joined together by four small wooden rods. The sides AB and CD should be five palms in length, while AC and BD should be four palms long. Over this frame, stretch a very fine and entirely transparent veil <note>original: "velum"; here referring to the screen or "drawing plane" of the device.</note>, of the kind that noblewomen everywhere are accustomed to using to cover their faces.

Second, at point E on side CD, a transverse, mobile rod—the "cursor" of the instrument—should be passed through in such a way that it can be pushed forward or pulled back at the operator's will. At point F of the cursor EF, let another transverse rod GF be attached, inserted into rod EF so that it can be raised or lowered as needed for the objects being drawn. You will then have the finished instrument, as the figure shows.

<margin>The multiple and remarkable uses of this instrument.</margin>

->**The multiple and remarkable uses of this instrument.**<-

**T**he use of this instrument is so broad and vast that there is almost no theorem or problem in the whole of optics that the theory of this instrument does not encompass. First, it demonstrates to the eye, as if by proof, the nature of the optical ray—both luminous and opaque—as well as the logic of shadows and all other types of projections, as will be clear to any expert examining it. Second, given any object—whether it be a shape, a solid body, an image, a statue, or even a house, temple, city, field, forest, or mountain—all these things can be drawn with no effort by the help of this instrument, according to the natural position in which they are placed. Third, with the help of this instrument, you will perform wonderful metamorphoses of objects, and even the drawings for all kinds of <term>prodigious clocks</term> <note>These "prodigious clocks" often referred to complex sundials projected onto irregular surfaces or anamorphic art that only looked correct from a certain angle.</note>. However, so that the reader may proceed as quickly as possible in the following sections, we will provide some very brief examples of each proposed matter.

<margin>The threefold drawing: orthographic, scenographic, and sciagraphic.</margin>
The drawing of things can be established in three ways: either <term>orthographically</term>, <term>scenographically</term>, or <term>sciagraphically</term>. We say an orthographic description is performed by this instrument when the object or thing to be drawn is positioned parallel to the mesoptic parallelogram (the veil); thus we draw the frontages of houses, towers, temples, and whatever is carried to our eyes by direct rays. To this category, we also refer all those figures drawn either as <term>ichnographies</term> <note>floor plans or ground plots.</note> or scenographies, where we are instructed to paint a similar version on the veil. We call it a scenographic drawing when we draw a <term>loxophanous</term> <note>original: "loxophanum"; appearing slanted or oblique.</note> object, or one in an oblique position, such as things placed at an angle to the horizon or on a vertical plane with receding sides. We call it a sciagraphic drawing when we are ordered to draw the projection of a body's shadow; in that case, the body to be drawn sciagraphically must be placed between the rod GF and the veil. In all objects, however, where we desire to paint things with the greatest transformation, the orthography of the thing to be transformed must first be painted on the veil itself. These things having been performed, let us now begin the drawings themselves.

---

### Proposition I.

->To draw any polygonal figure—whether three-sided, square, etc., and whether regular or irregular—on the mesoptic veil, both scenographically and orthographically.<-

**T**he method by which all these things are to be cast geometrically onto a plane will be discussed a little later. For now, let us see how they can be accomplished with our polygraphic veil. First, if someone desires to draw an object orthographically, he shall place the figure parallel to the veil; if scenographically, he shall expose it to the horizon, or to a receding or inclining vertical plane. This being done, you will fix the instrument in its place using rod EF, according to the size or smallness of the image, so that it cannot be moved by any means. Then, placing the eye at the sighting-hole (the extremity G of rod GF) and with the hand resting upon the wooden support (which is held up by two props attached to the sides for this purpose), you will trace the figure placed beyond the veil onto the veil itself with no trouble, following the line of sight directed at the object's shape, using red ochre, chalk, or any other material that colors the cloth but can be easily erased. I demonstrate this figure described optically on the cloth thus: Since the tip of the pen is always in the same line as the point G (where the eye is located) and the points of the object figure, the projected optical figure will necessarily be drawn on the cloth. For such a drawing represents nothing other than a section of a straight or oblique pyramid of the <term>species</term> <note>In 17th-century physics, "species" were the formal qualities or "images" shed by objects that traveled through the air to the eye.</note> radiating from the object into the eye. If the section is a right section in a right pyramid, the painted figure will necessarily be similar to the object; but if the section is a right section of a pyramid whose base is incident obliquely, or an oblique section in a right pyramid, the figure will be represented on the veil according to the logic of the optical section of the pyramid. But let us demonstrate the matter with an example.

### Corollary I.

<margin>How even someone unskilled in painting can draw any proposed images.</margin>
From these foundations, it is clear how every kind of painting can be outlined with the help of this instrument, even by one unskilled in painting; namely, if the eye is applied to the aperture A, and a brush <note>Latin: "penicillo"</note> follows the path of the visual ray that marks the boundary of the original model <term>prototype</term>; for the desired design will be left on the cloth or mesoptic veil.

### Corollary II.

<margin>How the entire view of a city can be optically projected.</margin>
If you place this instrument in a high location so that the layout of a city appears from every side, you will describe it on the scenographic veil <note>A screen used specifically for architectural or theatrical views.</note>—following all the towers, churches, and palaces (with the eye at A, at the end of the rod GF, and the brush following the path of the visual ray falling upon the original)—drawn with most perfect symmetry.

### Corollary III.

<margin>How the layout of a province can be described.</margin>
From this it is clear how the locations of cities, fields, and forests can be most conveniently expressed on the veil according to their natural position. 

But at this point, one might ask: in what way are the aforementioned descriptions made on the veil to be transferred onto paper? It is answered that this can be done in two ways. First, by pricking with a needle: this is done if you place the veil over prepared paper and press points into the paper according to the design. Second, if the drawing was made with a certain red chalk <note>original: "rubrica"</note> called "scum of lead" <term>spuma plumbi</term> <note>Likely referring to a lead-based pigment or graphite.</note>; you will have what you seek faster than said, if you press moistened paper onto the veil; for the paper will draw into itself all the color clinging to the veil, along with the things drawn.

### Corollary.

From these things, it is clear by what method we can know the quantities of the height and width of the individual parts of any structure from a single station without moving from the spot, provided that the smallest part of the height or width—or even the interval between two columns in the building—is known. By this artifice, we discovered the height of the Dome of St. Peter's <note>The famous Basilica in Rome.</note>—knowing only the height of one of the columns of those that surround the <term>cornice</term> <gloss>original: "Coroniden"</gloss>—to be nearly 600 <term>geometric feet</term>, starting from the ground of the Roman College <note>The Jesuit educational center where Kircher worked; he is describing measuring the city's landmarks from his own window.</note>, together with the width, height, and distances of the columns of that same <term>frontispiece</term> <gloss>The principal face or facade of a building.</gloss>.

<margin>The method for measuring inaccessible things from a single station.</margin>
It must be observed, however, that this measurement is not at all accurate except at a very great distance; for at such a distance, you will commit a scarcely perceptible error. But the closer you are to the object being measured, the greater the errors that must necessarily be committed, unless you proceed with great skill. The reason for this is nothing other than <term>optical projection</term>, which, when viewed up close and from nearby, always determines a height to be that much larger the closer it is to the base, and that much smaller the higher up it is; consequently, a known measure taken in one spot can by no means be equated to the remaining interrupted parts. In a more remote distance, however, since the visual angle under which the entire height and length to be measured is seen becomes quite acute, the remaining parts will also have a scarcely perceptible difference of inequality. Nevertheless, how the dimension of things viewed from up close can be found must be explained in a few words. First, it is known from the following propositions that just as any geometric figure can be reduced to an optical one, so conversely an optical one can be reduced to a geometric one; that is, there is no line optically projected whose quantity cannot be found through reduction to a geometric line—which reduction the following propositions teach. And this is the first method. The second method is done through arithmetic, which it seemed fitting to declare with some examples. Let, therefore, the height BC be twelve palms; the height ED, however, be 14 feet, encompassed under the same angle; the distance AD being 60 palms. It is

# The Ray-Projection of Shadow-Drawing #
<note>original: "Actinoboliismus Sciagraphicus." This title refers to the mathematical behavior of light rays in creating perspective drawings.</note>

-> R <-

...the organ <note>original: "organum"</note>, from which various aspects arise, partly true and partly illusory; both of these have been discussed in the preceding sections. The second is the meeting of the projected illusion with a certain flat object; for that place where the cast illusion of the thing falls displays a certain figure, which we call a **Projection**; this occurs as if the thing itself were projected onto the plane by the force and efficacy of the sight. Some also call this a **Section**, because it is the common intersection of the plane and the visual rays falling through the object being viewed; by this manner of speaking, they also name those figures shown by sliced cones or cylinders, about which more material for discussion will be given in the following book. Therefore, a **Projection** is nothing other than the transcription of a superficial or solid figure onto a plane. To achieve this, three things are primarily necessary: the object to be projected; the eye, from which the optical rays flash out to all parts of the proposed object; and the plane, onto which the object itself is transcribed through the extension of the rays. But since not everyone has such an instrument at hand, we will briefly teach by what method the said practices can also be perfected by geometric reasoning.

Note that in every optical task, two planar spaces, four lines, and two points must be considered. The first plane is called **natural** or **physical**, and it is that plane which serves the optical projection. The other is the **optical plane**, which the optical projection occupies; we have marked the former with letters ABCD, and the latter with EDCF.

There are four kinds of lines: the **ground line**, the **horizontal line**, the **radial line**, and the **diametrical line**.

The **ground line** <note>original: "linea terræ"</note> is the line which is the base of the optical plane, such as line CD.

The **horizontal line** is the line equidistant to the ground line CD, terminating the optical plane, such as line AB.

The **radial line** is that which is drawn from a certain point of the optical figure to be delineated to the horizontal line, at the point which is called the **principal point**, such as lines NM and FM.

The **diametrical lines**, or **diagonals**, are those which are drawn from certain points of the optical figure to be delineated onto the horizontal line, at the point which is called the **eye point**, such as lines NR, CR, and DR. There are therefore two most important points to be considered in optical projection: the **principal point**, which is marked with the letter M, and the **eye point**, marked with the letter R, which are always established on the horizontal line.
