# The Great Art, Book II. Part II. #

## Proposition I. ##
### Given a point in the geometric plane, the principal point, and the eye point, to find that point in the optical plane. ###

Let NOPQ be a geometric square, in which the given point is Z, the eye point is R, and the **principal point** <note>In modern terms, the principal point M acts as the central vanishing point on the horizon.</note> is M. It is required to find this point in the physical plane AB CD. From the points N and O on the ground line CD, let lines be drawn to the principal point M—specifically, lines NM and OM. Next, let the arc ZV be drawn from point N, passing through the chosen point Z. For if you draw a line from point V to the eye point R, it will intersect NM at point C, which is the point sought. Consequently, the line NC in the **optical plane** <note>The "optical plane" is the surface of the drawing where the 3D perspective is represented.</note> will represent the line NZ from the geometric plane. By this method, you shall assign all points and lines given in any geometric plane to the optical plane. The demonstration of this matter is clearly evident from Proposition 1 and our **mesoptic instrument** <term>mesopticum: a specialized perspective-calculating device described by Kircher</term>.

<image-desc>A geometric perspective diagram showing a rectangular frame ABCD. Inside, a smaller trapezoidal area DENO represents the perspective projection. Lines converge from points N and O to a central principal point M, and from a side point S to an eye point R. Within the projected square is a woodcut illustration of a double-headed imperial eagle. Various points are labeled with letters A through Z to illustrate the geometric transformation from a ground plane to an optical plane.</image-desc>

## Proposition II. ##
### To project a given square in perspective, and an Eagle within that square. ###

Let the given square be NOPQ. In the preceding figure, the eye point R and the principal point M are given. It shall be projected in perspective thus: From points N and O, using the distances NP and OQ, draw the hidden arcs PS and QN. Once this is done, let **radial lines** be drawn from N and O toward M, and **diagonal lines** <note>These diagonal lines help determine the depth or "foreshortening" of the square.</note> from points S and N toward the eye point R. Where SR and NR intersect the radials NM and OM, mark points E and D. These points, joined by the straight line DE, will yield the desired perspective square DENO. Note that ND corresponds to side NP, and EF or EO corresponds to side OQ, and finally, side DE corresponds to side PQ; the side NO is common to both. 

The method is made very easy by our **mesophanos** <term>mesophanum: from the Greek for "middle-appearance," another name for his perspective machine</term> described above. In that device, the optical space ACBD—a veil or screen erected perpendicularly—represents the geometric square NOPQ together with the inscribed figure on a straight horizontal plane. Let the eye be placed at the **dioptra** <note>a sighting hole or viewfinder</note> G of the rod GF, at the same distance from the plane of the veil as point R is from point M. If the rod also has the height BD, it is clear that the eye looking from G through the veil (or the geometric square NOPQ) will see the square DENO delineated in perspective within the optical space, exactly as you see it done here. See the preceding Proposition I, where you will find everything demonstrated more at length.

#### Corollary. ####

Furthermore, if someone were to depict an Eagle in the geometric square, the boundary points of the Eagle in the perspective square would be found by exactly the same method described in the proposition. But these things appear more clearly in the diagram.

-># The Art of Shadow-Drawing <note>original: "Ars Sciagraphica"; the study of projecting shadows or 3D objects onto a 2D surface.</note><-

If you extend threads above the points marked on the **geometric plane** <note>The flat, "top-down" plan view of an object.</note>, namely above NO, and others above the optical points SN, they will intersect the optical plane at points which, when joined by straight lines, will provide the sought goal of the proposition. The threads themselves are represented by lines SR and MO.

### Proposition III.
#### To delineate a triangle or a square that is distant from the ground line in the geometric plane.

**L**et there be given, for example, a triangle ACD to be projected optically. First, let perpendicular lines be drawn from each point of the triangle ACDB to the **ground line** <term>linea terræ: the horizontal line where the drawing surface meets the ground</term>. Let these be, for example, the hidden lines ES, PA, PK, GV. Second, from points E, P, and G, using the distances ED, PA, PK, and GC, let hidden arcs be described, which terminate on the ground line at points G, H, I, and K. Third, from points G, P, and E, let **radial lines** <note>Lines converging toward a central vanishing point.</note> be drawn to point I. Then, from the points of the arcs K, I, H, and G, let diagonals be drawn to M. Where those radial lines intersect the diagonals, the points of intersection joined by straight lines will give the optically projected triangle, namely MNP, which was sought: the reasoning for all of which, as before, is clear from the **mesoptic instrument** <term>mesopticum: a specialized drafting tool designed by Kircher for calculating perspective</term> in the preceding Proposition I.

Below the line, a triangle (ACD), a square (VSCD), and a rhombus containing an eagle are shown. Construction arcs project these points onto the ground line. Above the line, radial lines from a vanishing point (I) and distance points (M, O) intersect to form the projected perspective versions of the shapes. An eagle emblem is rendered within the projected rhombus on the right side.</image-desc>

### Consectary <note>A logical conclusion or corollary.</note>

<margin>
A triangle
is half of a
parallelogram.
</margin>

**F**rom this it is clear, since every triangle is half of its square parallelogram VSCD, it can be assigned in the optical square simply by drawing line IH parallel to the ground line: for once this is done, MNIH will be the optically projected square that was sought. You will also accomplish the same very easily using threads attached at points L and M.

### Proposition IV.
#### To delineate a rhombus optically, and an Eagle within the Rhombus.

**L**et the given rhombus be ABCD, the **principal point** <note>The central vanishing point on the horizon.</note> E, and the **eye point** <note>Also called the distance point, used to determine depth in perspective.</note> O; you shall delineate it thus. First, draw perpendicular lines to the ground line from each boundary of the rhombus: CG, AB, and DE. From G, with the distance GC, describe arc CA; from A, with the interval AB, describe arc BI; finally from F, with the interval FD, describe arc DI. Then from points F, A, and G, draw radial lines to F <note>The text likely refers to the vanishing point E here; "to F" may be a typesetter's error or refer to a specific point on the instrument.</note>, and through points I, E, and A, extend diagonals to O, the eye point. These will intersect the radial lines at points which, when joined by straight lines, will constitute the sought optical rhombus FGMA. The reasoning relies on Proposition 3 of the mesoptic instrument. You will perform the same most easily with threads fixed at F and O, extended above the geometric and optical points, as we taught in the first proposition.

#### To project a circle optically.

**L**et circle A be the one to be projected optically. First, divide it into as many parts as you like, and through these points, perpendiculars must be erected to the ground line, as was done in the preceding [propositions]...

# Proposition VI.
->To project a regular body optically.<-

**F**irst, project the base of the given body—namely, a cube—optically according to Proposition 3. Second, once this is finished, take the perpendicular of the body's height, which is to be placed above the ground line AD—for instance, at point D:

<image-desc>A geometric construction diagram illustrating the perspective projection of a cube. The top portion shows a plan view with points labeled B, N, P, K, L, H, G, F, E, and I. And again, at any distance away, another equal line at A, so that the line AB, parallel to DH, is erected perpendicularly above the ground line. Third, then, from the outer points AB, let lines be drawn to any point on the horizontal line SC, chosen however you like—for example, point C—and let these be lines AC and CB. Fourth, having done this, from the points of the base of the figure DEFG, once optically projected, let lines be drawn to the ground line, which end at line AC, [namely] parallels EM (or GM) and FO. Fifth, from these points M and O, let perpendiculars be raised to the ground line AD, which end at line BC; let these be lines MN and OP. Sixth, from points N and P, again draw lines parallel to the ground line; finally, if you draw perpendiculars from points D, G, E, and F of the base figure, these will intersect lines NL and PK at points which, when joined by straight lines, will constitute the given body projected optically—such as the present cube.

# Proposition VII.
->To project a tetrahedron optically, so that it appears to stand on the plane at a single point.<-

**F**irst, let one of the sides of the **tetrahedron** <term>tetraedron: a triangular pyramid with four faces</term> be placed as the **geometric plan** <note>A flat, top-down map of the object's proportions.</note> below the ground line, as in the example, below line HA. Let an equilateral triangle ABCD be made, either at a distance from the line or not.

<image-desc>A geometric construction diagram illustrating the perspective projection of a tetrahedron (triangular pyramid). It includes a horizon line with vanishing points S and L, a ground line H, and various rays extending from a plan-view triangle (labeled A, B, C, D) to create the three-dimensional form of the pyramid in perspective.</image-desc>

2. Let this triangle be projected optically according to Proposition 3, and let it be in the **optical plane** <note>The area of the drawing where the 3D effect is created.</note> ABCD.
3. Let the line CD, or AD, or DB (which are equal and are drawn from the center of the equilateral triangle in the geometric plane) be transferred to the ground line from any point—for example, H; I say, let one of these be transferred from H to I.
4. Then, from H, let an infinite perpendicular line HS be drawn; and having intercepted one of the sides of the equilateral triangle in the geometric plane—for example, AB—let it be transferred from point I onto line HS, for instance, to K; and you will have the determined height of the figure above the plane.
5. From points H and K, let two lines HL and KL be drawn to any point of the horizontal line, for instance, L.
6. Let lines AM, CO, or BO be drawn from the points ACB of the triangle in the optical plane to the line HL, parallel [to the ground line].
7. From points M and O, let perpendiculars be drawn to the ground line (or parallels to HK), which intersect line KL at points N and P, from which **hidden** <note>Construction lines that are drawn lightly or dashed because they are not part of the final visible object.</note> parallel lines are again drawn to the ground line. For where the perpendicular lines drawn from angles A, C, and D intersect these, there will be the points which, when joined by straight lines, will designate the body which was to be projected according to the given position.

# Proposition VIII.

> *Given a square, a figure with grid cells and an image placed within them, to describe the proposed figure of an Eagle in another optical quadrangle together with a figure that cannot be recognized unless the eye is positioned at a certain fixed point.*

**L**et there be a geometric square ABCD, in which an **Eagle** is drawn. This is to be projected optically so that it can only be seen from a certain given point; proceed as follows. On any flat wall, or even a horizontal surface, let a line IS be made; at its endpoint I, let another line AB be drawn at right angles <note>Latin: *ad angulos rectos*</note>, equal to one of the sides of the given square, so that the ends of line AB are equidistant from the center line IS. This line AB is then divided into as many parts as the side of the square is divided; then, from the points A, H, I, K, B, and the middle spaces, let lines be drawn to point S. Next, let the "eye-length" <note>The distance from the observer's eye to the plane of the drawing.</note> be line SO. From point O to point B, let a straight line be drawn; and where that line intersects the lines AS, HS, IS, KS, and BS, draw lines from those same points parallel to AB. You will then have a square divided optically on the wall or horizontal plane, into which you will also draw the figure of the Eagle according to the proportion of the squares corresponding to the geometric square. For if you sketch this figure on a vertical plane, such as a wall, and then place your eye at point O of the rod SO (which is fixed perpendicularly to the wall), the Eagle will appear in its natural shape just as it did in the square.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating perspective and anamorphic projection. At the top right is a square grid labeled ABCD containing a drawing of an eagle. Below and to the left is a construction for an anamorphic projection: a baseline is marked with points A, H, I, K, B, and lines radiate from these points to a point S on the right. An observer's eye location is marked as O, with a line SO representing the distance from the plane. The diagram illustrates how the proportions of the original grid are projected onto a distorted triangular grid (craticula) so that the image appears correctly only when viewed from the specific point O.</image-desc>

In the same way, you may represent any other figures optically, which, when viewed from a distance, appear as nothing but confusion, but when the eye is placed at point O, they will represent a natural figure. But these are common matters. Note, however, at this point: if the said figure were to be scattered <note>Anamorphic distortion was often called "scattering" or "dissipation" of the image.</note> upon a floor <note>Latin: *pavimento*</note>, then the Eagle should be drawn in the geometric square ABCD in such a way that the body of the Eagle in square ABCD stands perpendicularly to the horizontal line: and according to this sketch, the Eagle would be drawn in the **grid-like** <term>craticulato: from 'craticula', a small grid or lattice used by artists to scale images</term> triangle SBA. The figure of the Eagle will then appear scattered on the horizontal plane when viewed from O, the point of the rod SO, which is erected perpendicularly to the horizon.

# Proposition IX.

> *To transform an image geometrically by another method.*

## First method.

**L**et the figure of the Eagle be transformed on a certain **middle-view** <term>mesoptico: referring to a plane situated between the eye and the object, often used in calculating distortions</term> plane AB.

1 After describing the quadrangle CD within the middle-view plane AB around the image of the Eagle, and dividing it into smaller rectangles, let each of the outermost side-lines perpendicular to the base (or the root of the middle-view plane) be extended: HD to I, and CX to Y. Then, from the endpoint K, with a perpendicular line sent out to E, let lines KI and KY be drawn, extended to infinity. Then, through the final points of the remaining lines from K, lines extended to infinity will provide the space within which the **anamorphosis** <term>anamorphosis: a distorted projection that requires a specific vantage point or mirror to be viewed correctly</term>, or transformation of the figure, is to be made.

2 Then the entire visual radiation propagated from E through the middle-view plane is projected onto the plane of the horizon by this skill. You shall transfer the height EK from K to L, so that line KL is equal to line KE and stands perpendicular to line KI; but extend line HI from point I to M, along line IM parallel to line KL.

3 Let the side HD of the image's quadrangle, together with its divisions, be transferred from M onto line MN, as indicated by points M, O, P, Q, N. Straight lines drawn from point L through these points will intersect the side KIR at points through which lines drawn parallel to the base YI of the middle-view plane AB will produce the quadrilateral ZGFR. This is the transformation of the straight image CXHD onto the horizontal plane, with each and every rectangle appearing transformed. If you paint the image of the Eagle within this, as if in a grid, according to the proportions of the original gridded prototype, you will have the transformation of the image.

### *The same transformation performed mechanically by light. The second method.*

**I**f you carefully pierce the outlines of the eagle image on the <term>mesothetic plane</term> <note>an intermediate screen or plane placed between the eye and the surface of projection</note> with a needle, and place a light at point E (the position of the eye), the light shining through the holes will describe the transformation of the eagle image onto the projected plane in the space FR GZ, in exactly the same way we described it geometrically in that same space just a moment ago.

### *The same transformation by shadow, using our mesoptic instrument. The third method.*

**I**f the <term>mesothetic plane</term> AB is transparent, like our <term>mesoptic instrument</term> <note>a device used for viewing or projecting optical transformations</note>, you may produce the transformation of the image by shadow in this way. Let any figure, such as this Eagle, be painted on a veil with a thicker color, so that the outlines on the transparent plane are made somewhat opaque by that thicker paint. Once this is done, if you place a light at point E as before, the shadow of the outlines coated in the thicker color will describe the desired transformation of the image on the plane. Alternatively, if the projection were to occur on various planes, something opaque would have to be applied to the principal points of the eagle's outlines painted on the veil, so that the shadow of the opaque body would show the points of the image to be transformed in the distant space.

### *First Corollary.*

**F**rom these things it is clear that all transformations can be achieved by shadow and light. Indeed, you may see the wonderful effects resulting from these in the *Magic of Light and Shadow*.

### *Second Corollary.*

**I**t is also clear that if the mesoptic plane were a mirror, and the eye were placed at a distance—at the same distance and height from the plane as the light EK is—the transformed image would appear in its natural form within the mirror.

### *Proposition X.*

-> How to describe any figure in a convex cone so that it cannot be seen in any way, except <term>catoptrically</term> <note>original: "κατοπτρικῶς," meaning by means of reflection in a mirror</note> from a determined point, namely with the eye placed on the extended axis. <-

**F**irst, we will provide the method taught by Niceron in his *Curious Perspective* <note>referring to Jean-François Niceron's 1638 work, "La Perspective curieuse"</note>, which is as follows. From a single center, describe eight equidistant circles, the circumferences of which you will divide into as many parts by eight rays, as you see in ST, figure 11 of <term>Plate I</term> <note>original: "Iconismi I"</note>.

2. In this diagram, you will draw any figure in its natural position.

3. You will prepare a cone similar and equal to this one. Let the diameter of the diagram ST be drawn, taken twice on the line CD; then from D, with the distance CD or CA, let a semicircle DBA be described, which you will divide into two quadrants by the line CB.

4. You will draw a line from A to B, and divide the arc CX (drawn with the distance AC) into eight equal parts. If you draw hidden lines from A through these parts, they will cut the side CB at points through which eight circles drawn in the quadrant CBD will give the cone's optical projection. In this, following the diagram of the Eagle correctly depicted within ST, you will paint the eagle distorted and scattered; it will, however, appear exactly like the original when viewed from a certain point. See Figure 11.

5. Once this is finished, you will fold the quadrant so that the two sides CD and CB are joined at point B, and you will have your prepared cone. If you wish to see the figure, the eye must be as far from the cone as the apex of the cone is from the plane on which it stands. And thus you will achieve your goal.

Note here: if a similar figure were to be drawn in a concave cone, the opposite ratio of projection must be held. For the narrower spaces will occupy the upper part of the open cone, and the wider ones will be toward the bottom, near the apex. The dictates of reason will teach this to everyone better than I can explain it even with many words.

This also being done, you will wrap this perforated paper around the cone again so that it takes the shape of a natural cone; then, having removed the wooden cone and cut away the part of the cone DE, place a candle or light inside at point E. The light will project the transformed image through the holes of the paper cone onto the flat surface. If again from the ho-

## Proposition XI.
### To represent an image optically in a cylinder.

<margin>See figure V.</margin>
**F**irst, following the rules of "curious perspective," let there be a geometric square ABCD, along with the image of the Imperial Eagle inscribed within it. From a center point F assumed on some plane, let a circle be drawn whose diameter is equal to the thickness of the cylinder. You shall divide its radius FN into four equal parts, and at the third part P, placing the compass, you shall describe 14 circles—exactly as many as there are transverse lines in the square. Let the first circle be at such a distance from the center as a sufficient reflection in the mirror requires; let the subsequent remaining circles increase in the proportion of 20 to 21, or you may simply draw these circles as parallel without worry. Third, let the first circumference LSTVXY be divided into 16 equal parts, through which lines drawn from the center F to the circumference of the final circle will show the little optical squares corresponding to the geometric squares, leaving aside parts SL and LY as superfluous. Fourth, in these optical spaces, following the sequence and proportion of the members of the inscribed Eagle, you shall sketch—as if through a <term>grid</term> <note>original: "craticulam," a common technique where artists use a grid to transfer or scale images</note>—a highly scattered figure of the Eagle. However, the appearance of this figure, when reflected in a cylindrical mirror placed at the center of the circle F, will restore the natural figure <margin>See figure VI.</margin> of the Eagle once again, as shown in the attached Figure VI of Illustration I.

## Corollary.

**I**t is also clear from what has been said how the aforementioned method of drawing can be performed much better and more easily by the help of the cylinder itself: namely, if you first draw a figure on a paper cylinder similar to one depicted straight on a plane, with the eye fixed at a certain assumed point, and then expose the drawing, perforated along its outlines, to a light at a proportional distance. For the light passing through the holes will project a transformed and highly scattered image, which—once the cylinder is shaped into a mirror and the image is reunited and reflected into its original and natural state—will appear true to the eye. You can also perform this transformation geometrically in exactly the same way we prescribed above in Proposition 10; I would show all of this in detail, were it not already evident from the preceding examples. Whoever desires to know these things more extensively should consult the *Apiarium* of the most learned Father Bettini, or the *Curious Perspective* of Niceron; they will easily supply every deficiency in this part. For it is not our purpose to dwell on things already handed down by others, but only to touch upon them superficially as they are directed toward a further goal.

# CHAPTER IV.
## On the Art of Scenography.
### §. I. Rules to be observed in the description of Scenes and other paintings.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'N' featuring a detailed landscape with classical architecture and trees within the letter's frame.</image-desc>

WE say nothing here of the three kinds of stage scenes—Tragic, Comic, and Satiric—as they are commonly very well known; rather, we shall only open up the method by which they can be most easily outlined by an optical ray. Indeed, the representation of scenes claims for itself no small part of our undertaken study; for the name of <term>Scenography</term> <note>the art of perspective representation, especially as applied to architectural and theatrical design</note> is taken from "scenes" as the principal subject matter of this science. Since scenes are usually fashioned from lines, plane surfaces, solid parts, and lights and shadows composed in various ways, and since this knowledge is necessary for all painters, we shall add certain things here summarily as a <term>finishing touch</term> <note>original: "coronidis loco"</note>.

**1** It must be known, therefore, that in every representation of scenes, once the common section of the <term>mesoptic plane</term> <note>the intermediate plane where the perspective projection is formed</note> is given, the primary point must immediately be established according to the given height of the eye; for all lines drawn in any planes whatsoever extend to this point. This may be observed in porticos, when we view them not from the front, but along their length; for here we see the tops of all the columns, the capitals, and the bases, and the directions of the architraves and cornices all strive toward the primary point, which serves as the place of the eye. To this point also...

->Scenographic Ray-Projection.<-

...these common lines belong to those by which pavements, floorings, and whatever else is established at the level of the horizon are joined to upright walls.

2 Next, since much importance is placed on the height of the eye, it will require no small skill to place the principal point <note>In modern terms, the "vanishing point" on the horizon line</note> appropriately—whether high, low, or in a middle position. From this, we read that every mode of seeing is distributed into Optics, Anoptics, and Catoptics <note>Kircher uses these terms uniquely: Optics for level vision, Anoptics for looking up, and Catoptics for looking down</note>, which were known even to the ancients. Therefore, when the history <note>original: "historia," referring to the subject matter or narrative scene of a painting</note> that is required to be represented on a plane is on that surface drawn through the eye and the horizon, the scene must be established with an orthoptic <note>straight-seeing</note> ray. When the history stands above the eye line, it is established with an anoptic ray; and finally, with a catoptic ray when the history is below the eye line. The use of Anoptics is for designing those things that exist either on mountains, in the high air, or on the upper stories of houses; for we view these by looking up from below. Catoptics, however, shows those things that are in valleys, or underground and in other lower places, when we look down at them from higher places. Those things established in the middle belong to Orthoptics, which is again twofold: either the height of the eye equals human stature, or it is surpassed by it. If the former, it is manifest that the heads of all standing men must fall on that straight line which is the projection of the horizon. If the latter, the closer men will necessarily appear taller than those further away. But with these things established, let us now reveal the method of the whole of <term>scenography</term> <note>the art of representing three-dimensional scenes on a flat surface, particularly for stage sets</note> according to the triple method of Optics, Anoptics, and Catoptics.

# THE ART OF PAINTING

## Foundations of Scenography.
# PROBLEM I.
### On the artistic drawing of pavements.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial T featuring scrolling floral vines and a small bird-like creature in the lower right of the box.</image-desc>

**I**f you wish to draw the pavements of temples, walkways, or any things enclosed within walls: First, at the ground line QR, let there be a square ABCD, whose side AD is divided into any number of equal parts; for the sake of brevity, we have divided it here into four parts. Then, from the points of division A, F, L, E, and D, let radial lines be drawn to any point assumed on the horizontal line MGX—say, to G, the "most rightward" <note>original: "δεξιωτατὸν"</note> point, which we previously called the principal point. From any assumed point M on the same horizontal line, let the diagonal MND be drawn; and where it intersects the radial lines, lines drawn through those points parallel to the ground line will give the square ADNS, optically projected along with the small squares, circles, and other ornaments previously inscribed in the geometric square. You will have the same result if you draw diagonals from M to each point A, F, L, E, and D; for the side NA will be cut at points through which parallel lines will give the optical square ADNS as before. If you wish to continue the projection of this optical square toward G, decreasing proportionally, proceed as follows: From the eye point M, draw another diagonal to the last point S of the side of the optical square; and where this diagonal intersects the radial lines AG, FG, LG, and EG, lines drawn through those points parallel to the previous ones will give the proportional degradation <note>The visual compression of objects as they recede into the distance</note> of the optical square. Finally, if you draw another diagonal from M to K, the last point of this square, it will intersect the radial lines at points through which parallel lines will give a third square decreasing proportionally, so that the whole projected space AKOD is equal to the geometric square ABCD continued three times in length. By this art, you can project the degradation of squares decreasing proportionally toward G into infinity; the reasons for all of which depend on Proposition 1, Chapter 1, which you should consult. <margin>Another case of projection.</margin> If, however, the principal point is not in a straight but in an oblique position, as in X, having drawn radial lines as before from X to AD and the remaining points, and having drawn the diagonal from M to C, it will intersect the rays AX, FX, LX, EX, and DX at points through which parallel lines will give the desired projection of the pavement in an oblique position.

# Conclusion.

**F**rom this projection it is clear by what method you may erect columns perpendicularly <note>original: "normaliter"</note> upon the floors of temples, gardens, the walkways of Princes, and the projections of colonnades; you will then have the desired result, about which we will speak more extensively in the following sections.

## PROBLEM II.
### To construct an optical quadrangle.

**F**irst, let line AB be taken as the base, upon which a triangle ABC is described. Let the base be divided into any number of equal parts, and let a "radiating" or "diminishing" floor be made, just as we taught before—namely, by drawing lines from the center C through the points of division. Second, draw any diagonal AD, and let C be the eye point <note>the vanishing point</note>. Then, draw parallel lines through the common points where the diagonal and the rays intersect. This will be the foundation of all Scenography <note>the art of perspective scenery</note>, namely the floor of the theater. Third, extend AC to O, and BC to E, by a space equal to AC and BC. Fourth, above the ends of the parallels, erect perpendiculars between the lines (or rays) CO, CB, CA, and CF; let the outermost points be joined again to form an optical quadrangle. In this, the projection EO IH is **anoptical** <note>viewed from below looking up, like a ceiling</note>; AEDB is **catoptical** <note>viewed from above looking down, like a floor</note>; HO BD and its opposite EAIF are **loxoptical** <note>the side or oblique views</note>; and finally, C will be **orthoptical** <note>the direct, straight-ahead view</note>. If, therefore, you paint magnificent palaces within the loxoptical projection, it will be a **Tragic** scene; if private houses, it will represent a **Comic** scene; if trees, it will represent a **Satyric** scene. In the anoptical <note>ceiling</note> area, you may depict clouds, stars, the Sun, the Moon, or even the projection of cross-beams, which is entirely similar to the projection on the floor.

## Conclusion I.

**I**t is therefore clear that an optical quadrangle of this kind contains the principles of all Scenography. For if columns are placed in the spot of the vertical parallels, you will have a certain colonnade <note>original: "peristylium"</note>, or a most beautiful series of columns presenting themselves to the eye according to the model of nature through proportional and oblique <term>diminution</term> <note>original: "loxodroma degradatione"</note>. If you wish to enclose this with a paneled ceiling, you shall draw oblique beams in the anoptical space in place of the parallels, placed upon each corresponding column; these will, by a similarly proportional diminution, represent the arrangement of beams in a ceiling according to nature’s model. If, however, you desire to sketch windows in perspective anywhere, extend threads from the center C (to which they are tied) to the points HH; for within the threads CH, CH, painted windows will have their own perspective projection in any place. Do the same on the opposite side between the two threads CI, CI. If you sketch doors within the lines CR and CQ, those too will have their own projections. You see, therefore, that by the help of threads alone, drawn from the center C, all the symmetry of optical projections can be found. Finally, if instead of the vertical parallels you sketch trees or garden walkways woven with various arches of trees and shrubs according to the diminishing parallels, you will have the perspective projection of said works shaped according to the model of nature. All of these things will be better understood from the figure than I could explain even with many words. This entire optical quadrangle, then, depends on the first diminution of the floor; the perpendiculars erected upon its parallels will give the projection of walls and any upright objects, while two threads drawn from the center will give the <term>oblique alignment</term> <note>original: "λοξοδρομίαν" (loxodromian); refers to the slanting path or receding lines of perspective</note> of the floorings, doors, and windows situated in order. For within these, the windows, doors, images, or painted statues will yield the desired projections. See Figure II of Illustration II.

## Conclusion II.

**F**rom this it is also clear by what method men and other animals on a floor must always be sketched smaller and smaller according to the optical projection. For if you paint statues or men within the lines CS and AC, as you see has been done, and you paint corresponding men in any place according to this measure between the parallels of the floor (which encompass the height of the image), you will have the desired result. By this arrangement, men, animals, and trees are placed on any perspective plane according to that proportion of lessening that optics requires. See Figure III of Illustration II.

<margin>*Rules to be observed in Painting.*</margin>
From all these modes of Scenographic projections, although none is by its own nature more excellent than the others—for all are perfect if they are established according to the rules of the art—nevertheless, due to the diversity of places in which they are set and from which they are viewed, it happens by accident that they do not equally please the eyes of those approaching. For if an immense light comes from that side where the shadows are painted, the image would offend the eyes, since it is necessary that shadows be opposite the light. Again, if an image is made according to the catoptical <note>floor-view</note> method and is presented to be seen from a lower place, it does not show the same beauty as if it were viewed from a higher place; and in the same way, that which is made according to the anoptical <note>ceiling-view</note> method appears less perfect if it is looked down upon from above. For a painting truly satisfies the eyes of the beholders...

...is sufficient when it occupies that position according to which its designation was established. A similar deception occurs when something is viewed from an angle <note>original: "ex obliquo"</note> that was distorted from a direct view, as clearly appears in the images transformed in the preceding propositions; these, when viewed from the front, represent nothing, but when seen from an oblique view with the light-ray transmitted through a narrow hole—lest it wander outside the region of its original design—they exhibit the object in its proper and natural form.

## §. II.

->*Rules for the wonderful painting that always keeps its eyes turned toward you, wherever you turn.*<-

**A** truly wonderful method has been discovered by which a human face is expressed so vividly that it always gazes at the viewer with a fixed stare, no matter where they stand, just as if the image had moving eyes that it could turn by its own power to every place the spectator moves. Since many wonder at this thing yet cannot assign a reason for it, we have considered it our duty to give painters some instruction regarding the design of such images. It should be known, therefore, that although flat images never appear more perfect than when they are seen from a predetermined distance and height of the eye, nevertheless, the depicted image does not stray from the likeness of truth in the same proportion that the eye of the viewer is moved from its proper place. For unless you approach very closely to the perpendicular of the <term>mesoptic plane</term> <note>the central line or plane of vision in perspective</note>, the same arrangement of the painted object and the correspondence of its parts always presents itself to you, wherever you turn.

<margin>The Practice of Painting.</margin>
Therefore, to produce paintings where the image looks at you from everywhere: do it this way. Let a man stand before you as a <term>prototype</term> in whatever pose you wish, who should look back at your eyes perpetually, constantly, and with eyes fixed immovably. If you paint the face of this man looking at you in this manner to the life, you will have what you sought; for he will always seem to look at you wherever you turn. The reason for this is that the radiation from both eyes of the person looking into the painter's eyes forms <term>visual pyramids</term> <note>in Kircher's optics, vision is imagined as a pyramid or cone of light-rays stretching from the object to the eye</note>, the bases of which are the eyes of the image. Since these were founded from the beginning to the life and persist perpetually in those same points, they will follow you perpetually as they press upon your eyes wherever you turn. They preserve that position and regard acquired from the beginning with a certain wonderful force and property; however, we never see this happen if the eyes are sketched haphazardly, nor does this ever succeed in the eyes of a marble statue. We give the reason for this:

<margin>Why the eyes of statues do not look back.</margin>
Because the eyes of statues are for the most part spherical in shape and prominent beyond the surface of the plane, it happens that the base of the visual pyramid also undergoes a perpetual change, and the eyes in an oblique view do not encompass the whole base of the eye; consequently, there will be no view from the said statue in every direction. Therefore, this kind of all-encompassing view of an image can only occur on flat surfaces in the manner described. For this reason, some paint an image of Death with a bow so skillfully that the arrow placed on the bow seems to want to shoot at you—not without horror—no matter where you turn. Innumerable things of this kind can be painted by artists on various occasions, so shaped after the pattern of nature that nothing seems to be lacking in them except life. For not only eyes depicted in this manner, but also instruments directed toward you by <term>optical ingenuity</term> will simulate a projection in every direction, as Figure VI of <term>Iconism II</term> <note>Refers to the second set of engraved plates/illustrations in the book</note> clearly teaches; but let us leave these things to industrious painters.

## §. III.

->*Rules concerning the anoptical method, by which we are directed to describe writings, pedestals, and windows so that they appear equal to the eyes below despite being at a great height.*<-

**T**he greatest industry of painters also consists in this: that they represent things situated at a great height in a natural position, especially if columns, beams, or windows are to be established. Vitruvius first observed this method in Book 6, Chapter 2, with these words:

<margin>Vitruvius, Book 6, Chapter 1.</margin>
> *One appearance seems to be at hand, another on high; it is not the same in a closed space, and different in the open; in these matters, the work requires great judgment as to what should actually be done: for the eye does not always perceive true effects, but the mind is often deceived by its judgment. Therefore, since things that are true may seem false, and some things are approved by the eyes as being other than they are, I do not think there should be any doubt that subtractions or additions ought to be made according to the nature and necessities of the locations.*

A <term>stylobate</term> <note>the top step of a temple platform or a continuous base supporting a row of columns</note> ought to be so adjusted that it has an addition through the middle by means of unequal <term>scamilli</term> <note>original: "scamillos impares." These are small "offsets" or leveling blocks used in classical architecture to correct for the optical illusion where a perfectly level horizontal line appears to sag in the middle</note>. For if it is directed by a level, it will appear hollowed out to the eye. These things are to be understood as follows: that for the topmost surface of the stylobate, when it is constructed level with the horizon, an addition must be made in the middle by placing another block, as it were, like a <term>plinth</term> <note>a square base</note>, upon which the base plinth stands as if on a small stool or step <note>original: "scamnulo"</note>, lest by the obstruction of the cornice it be withdrawn from view as if received and driven into a hollow. Truly, Vitruvius's unequal "scamilli" should be made higher the more elevated the place of the stylobate is. Although we have few examples of this in the structures of the ancients, there is one principal example...

# The Art of Scenography

<margin>The Roman Pantheon</margin>
It should be seen as remarkable that the Pantheon, the most beautiful and ancient of all temples, is surrounded by three unequal "crowns" or tiers around its circumference, like little pedestals <note>original: "scamillis," a term used by Vitruvius for small blocks or leveling steps used to correct optical illusions</note>, which support the bases of each level so that they can be seen in their entirety from a lower vantage point. The lowest tier—or rather the one placed above the first level to support the second—is the shortest; the next or middle one is taller; and the third is the highest of all. The entire logic of these tiers clearly depends on optical rays and the projections of the cornices. For this reason, in domes or vaults, the curve of the arches should not begin immediately from the surface of the highest cornice, but rather as much higher as the sightlines of those looking up from the lowest part of the chamber are "stolen" from view. The ancients also very frequently used these pedestals for the bases <note>original: "stylobatis"</note> that they placed under solitary columns or statues of famous men, so as to display a more august majesty as if from a raised platform. They did this especially so that—as Vitruvius says otherwise occurs—the lowest parts of the statues do not appear sunken into a "well" when viewed from the ground.

<margin>Trajan's Column in Rome</margin>
The Column of Trajan provides an example of this remarkable craftsmanship above all others; it still stands in Rome today as a singular monument and ornament of the City. On this column, the spirals <note>original: "helices," referring to the continuous narrative relief wrapping around the column</note> are drawn so skillfully that the upper intervals of the spirals, though twice as large as the lower ones, nonetheless appear equal when viewed from the bottom. Therefore, if statues are to be placed on a column, or levels are to be arranged so that the lower appears equal to the upper, and all appear equal to each other, proceed as follows: Let the column be AD, and its levels be AK, KI, IH, HG, GF, FE, and ED. From point B, representing the eye, let a quadrant AC be drawn, divided into as many equal parts as there are levels in the column DA. From the center B, lines drawn through the parts in the quadrant AC will intersect the column AD at points; within these, if windows, paintings, inscriptions, images, and the like are placed, they will all appear equal to those standing below at point B. I demonstrate this as follows: according to the stated hypothesis, whatever is seen under an equal angle appears equal; but AK, KI, IH, HG, GF, FE, and ED are seen under equal angles by the hypothesis; therefore, they appear equal. This matter is entirely easy and has great utility in architecture.

<image-desc>A geometric perspective diagram of a column (labeled AD). To the left is a focal point 'B' from which lines radiate towards the column at various heights (labeled I, H, G, E, D). A quadrant arc AC is drawn near point B to show the equal division of angles used to project equal visual segments onto the varying heights of the physical column.</image-desc>

Phidias, most skilled in these calculations, reported a victory over Alcamenes, as is found in Tzetzes <note>Johannes Tzetzes, a 12th-century Byzantine poet and grammarian who preserved many classical stories</note>. Both were perfectly skilled in sculpture, and Phidias, being an expert in optics, was accustomed to making statues according to the nature of the view and the location; Alcamenes, however, worked only according to the established proportions <note>original: "symmetries"</note> of the walls.

<margin>The Story of Phidias and Alcamenes</margin>
Wherefore, when it was eventually required that the Athenian people place two statues of Minerva <note>Athena</note> upon high columns, the work was commissioned to both. Phidias, not ignorant that things in the heights appear very short, made a statue with gaping lips, a distended nose, and other limbs distorted to suit the condition of the location. When placed on high, this statue displayed a great dignity of art; but Alcamenes’ work was a subject of laughter and mockery for everyone.

### §. VI.
-> Rules regarding the light and shadow of Scenes, <-
-> OR <-
-> Regarding the Art of Painting. <-

Having spoken of drawing <note>original: "graphide," the art of drafting or linework</note>, let us now speak of light and shadow, which properly belong to painters. For once the designs are made, they apply light and shadows, and then the proper colors of each thing. Since all those things used in the description of stage scenes are either straight lines, circles, or twisted curves not governed by a certain law, and since the logic of all these has already been proposed, it is clear that nothing else is needed to explain the proposed scenes by this type of projection. Therefore, so that the lights may be appropriately drawn onto the projected forms, I think this must first be cautioned—a point on which I see many people hallucinating: rays of light are admitted differently when diffused from lamps than from the Sun. Things are not illuminated in one and the same way in the open air as they are when placed before windows in an enclosed space. Finally, light is received by one method from multiple light sources, and by another from a single light.

<margin>What must be observed in light and shadow.</margin>
For those things which [receive] light from lamps, or through windows...

# The Great Art, Book II, Part II

...monsters <note>The text likely refers to "monstra" or "displays" from the previous page</note> are illuminated in a confined light, they ought to be expressed according to scenography <term>scenography|the art of representing objects in perspective, especially for stage scenery</term> in such a way that they are bathed sparingly in light, but more abundantly in shadow wherever appropriate. However, those things which admit direct rays of the sun should be designed orthographically <term>orthographically|a method of projection where lines of sight are parallel, showing objects in their true proportions without perspective distortion</term>, so that the drawn figures participate equally in light and shadow from parallel rays. Finally, things in the open air should be shown surrounded by equal light from all sides, as they exclude shadow from almost every part. This must also be carefully noted regarding the science of optics: if a painting is to be shown within a painting, it should not be designed according to the perspective by which it was originally made, but as it is seen in its present position <note>Kircher means that if you paint a room that contains a painting, the perspective of the "inner" painting must match the perspective of the "outer" room</note>. In this matter, many common painters, though not without talent, yet unskilled in optical matters, fail miserably.

Having now established these things properly, nothing remains except to offer something to judicious painters concerning proportion, light, and shadow. Even if these are not my profession, and I have not put any of them into practice, I will gladly share here what my natural judgment—trained by constant speculation—has dictated to me regarding such things. I am mindful of musicians who, although they compose the most excellent harmonies based on the highest judgment, may themselves seem least suited to perform them with their own voices. I am also mindful of Horace himself:

> ->I shall perform the role of a whetstone, which can sharpen<-
> ->iron, though it is itself incapable of cutting.<-
<note>original: "Fungar vice cotis acutum / Reddere, quæ ferrum valet exors ipsa secandi." — Horace, Ars Poetica 304–5</note>

<margin>What logic of light and shadow must be held in painting.</margin>
## Rule I.

**W**hoever desires to reach some degree of perfection in this most noble art should know that the foundations of this art of light, shadow, and optics—which are the basis and foundation of all graphic arts—must be learned. Without these, he will know that he can accomplish nothing with judgment, nor according to the prescriptions of art and nature. Once properly imbued with these, he should diligently inspect the monuments of famous painters, taking care with every diligence and effort to imitate what is best. He should constantly contemplate the differences between shadows and lights: which projections require a clear light and which require a shadowy one, always respecting the place, the time, and the story. He must consider which shadows are darker, which are intermediate, and which are more like total darkness; when they should terminate the edges and borders of images according to nature, and how they should gradually vanish as light is poured over them—always respecting the place, time, and story. For one story is shown at midday, another at dawn, another at night; the differences in shadows necessarily follow these circumstances of time. From these foundations of scenography, they will also learn the perspective projection of houses, temples, towers, instruments, seats, beds, fields, rivers, and the images themselves, along with their natural position of projection. For those who stumble even slightly in these matters of distance commit a grave sin against art, such as by sketching nearby objects smaller than they should be, or distant objects larger.

<margin>How the eye should be adjusted to the light.</margin>
## Rule II.

**I**t contributes greatly to the shadowing of images if painters place distinguished statues before their eyes, or even well-proportioned men, and learn from the natural archetype the bends, habits, gestures, and positions of individual parts with their shadows and lights. They will accomplish all this with singular and excellent success if they position the eye slightly below the object, with light passing through from a white source—and if possible, from a Northern region, not from the South, because of the too intense and variable light by which images are, as it were, blunted and meet with an unhappy result. Our academic Roman painters commit similar errors when they are accustomed to attempting such things at night by candlelight, unless they know how to correct the crudeness of the shadows with the greatest and most singular industry.

<margin>The gestures and proportion of limbs in different positions must be noted.</margin>
## Rule III.

**T**hey should prioritize the human body above all else, observing the proportions of the parts to one another with singular industry. Without this knowledge, almost every gesture becomes both monstrous and ridiculous. Meanwhile, they must observe the condition and circumstances of nature, sex, and age; for the proportion of the human body is one thing in a boy, another in a man, another in an elder, another in a male, and another in a female. The great painter Albrecht Dürer <note>original: "Albertus Durerus," the famous German Renaissance artist known for his treatises on human proportion</note> describes these most judiciously in his complete work. The artist should also discern what position individual parts and the whole have relative to one another: for the proportion of the limbs of a man lying on the ground is one thing, another when standing, another when sitting, and another when placed in any other position. The arrangement of extended, contracted, or curved limbs is different; the gesture of an old man is different from a youth, and different still from a boy.

<margin>Account must be held for the disposition of the body.</margin>
## Rule IV.

**T**hey should study the physiognomy <term>physiognomy|the practice of assessing a person's character or personality from their outer appearance, especially the face</term> of the human body and learn with the greatest study the qualities of the men they intend to sketch. They should know how to distinguish a strong and vigorous body from a soft, tender, and weak one; a manly one from a youthful one; a giant from a dwarf. They must know how to distinguish liveliness from sadness, anger from gentleness, sadness from mourning, and all other passions...

...opposed figures, just as the circumstances of the histories <note>In this context, "histories" refers to narrative or historical paintings</note> shall teach him, the artist should strive to express them with lines, shadows, and light. A distinction must also be observed between the dead and the living, and between those sleeping and those awake.

### Rule V.

**T**he arrangement and positioning of statues must also be observed, so that those running, ascending, descending, rising, sitting, or walking are arranged with the posture of the body ordered according to the proportion of their height; maintaining the line of direction <term>line of direction|the vertical axis or center of gravity of a figure</term> in all things, and the leaning of the limbs. Thus, a Painter intending to express the posture of an ascending or descending image would create a clumsy picture if he situated it perpendicularly and according to a straight line of direction; therefore, an ascending figure should be somewhat inclined forward, and a descending one reclined backward. The same is to be understood for those carrying loads; for the posture of one reaching out a hand is different while lying down than while standing; the posture of one raising a hand is different from one about to receive something from the ground, or from on high. These things are to be observed not only in humans, but also in animals. Hence, regarding the Horse

<margin>Error in the statue of Castor and Pollux on the Capitoline.</margin>
of Castor and Pollux on the Capitoline Hill <note>Famous Roman statues located at the top of the Cordonata stairs leading to the Piazza del Campidoglio</note>, a most foul error was committed by the sculptor, which is still present today: he depicted the horse with two feet on the same side moving together, rather than positioned diagonally. Since this is against nature and the forward movement of animals, it can hardly be said how much of a torment it inflicts upon the eyes of experts. I speak here of a standing Horse: for in these times there is no lack of **Riding Masters** <note>original: "Hippodidascali", from the Greek for horse-teachers</note> who occasionally force horses to walk on one side; however, they are not able to continue this gait for long.

### Rule VI.

**H**aving weighed these things judiciously, there now follows by right that which is considered most perfect in the pictorial art and the ultimate completion of the entire craft: namely, the tempering <term>tempering|the mixing or balancing of pigments to achieve harmony</term> of colors adapted to express each thing to the life. Without this, you can achieve nothing worthy in this art. For if these colors are too bright, the neighboring parts will affect the eyes with a distracting discomfort; if too dark, they will defile the neighbors by obscuring them; if too varied, they will cause confusion. Let these, therefore, be the rules. No color reflecting onto

<margin>The Tempering of Colors.</margin>
the surface of another body carries the tint of its own color onto that surface purely, but it will appear mixed with the reflected colors of the other bodies. If yellow and blue reflect onto a white surface, a green mixture will result, as we have shown extensively above in Book 1. Likewise, red and blue cause purple. And just as opposites placed near one another shine forth more clearly, so colors appear more illustrious when they are distinct and placed side by side. The remaining designations of the passions follow these differences of colors. Thus, a child composed and expressed with a man, a youth with an old man, a woman with a man, the weak with the strong, and the joyful with the sad, come closer to nature and are therefore more pleasing to the sight.

### Rule VII.

**I**t is also of great importance that the Painter affects the nature of inanimate things with the greatest study, such as trees, plants, rivers, and seas, maintaining the distance in each with proportionate color; so that things present have their natural color, while all remote things end in a transition from green to blue by a gradual, proportional decrease of colors. Water also, which is capable of receiving the tint of every color, he should tint with that color which it can be imbued with from the objects present: thus, black and red clouds imbue it with black and red; the greenery of a tree imbues it with a green color. All these things are to be observed according to the example of nature. Its own color must also be given to the sea, now calm, now angry; and its own to the courses of rivers, sometimes interrupted by foaming rocks, sometimes with the waters variously rippling.

### Rule VIII.

**I**n depicting garments as well, they should diligently observe the curves of the hems and the folds of the clothing with their shadows. For the logic of the folds of garments is one thing in a standing man, another in one sitting, and another in the various gestures they perform. These things can certainly be learned by no other method than from nature herself, or from a living model of a clothed man. Whoever observes these things will undoubtedly fulfill all the roles of an ingenious Painter.

Many things were to be said in this place concerning certain exotic mixtures of colors and paintings; but because we have deferred most of those to Book 10, *The Magic of Light and Shadow* <note>Referring to Kircher's own work, "Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae", published in 1646</note>, I have therefore thought it unnecessary to dwell on them longer in this place.

# BY ATHANASIUS KIRCHER
## PRIEST OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS
# THE GREAT ART
# OF LIGHT AND SHADOW
## Book Three.
## CURIOUS GNOMONICS
### CONTAINING THE
### PREPARATION.
### PREFACE.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'L' featuring floral and architectural motifs inside a square frame.</image-desc>

**W**e consider LIGHT in this work of the *Great Art* under a twofold reasoning. First, as it exists immobile in all bodies of the world; then, as it is mobile, producing various sciences in the minds of men through its varied motion. Therefore, after we have discussed all the hiding places of immobile light in the first two books, nothing remains but to investigate each and every path of mobile light in the following; which will be done in three books. For in these, light shows all the motions and occurrences of the Heavens in such a way that we can see those vast volumes of the Heavens no longer from afar, but the secrets of those same things translated into these earthly hovels of our dwellings, pointed out on a bright field as if by a shadowy finger. For which reason we have not inappropriately given it the name *Curious Gnomonics* <note>original: "Gnomonicæ Curiosæ". Gnomonics is the art of designing and using sundials to tell time and track celestial movements.</note>. For whatever is new, rare, excellent, and curious in the whole of Gnomonics, we disclose in the following three books with a singular method, maximum ease, and—unless we are mistaken—most lucid brevity. And lest the tedious treatment of mathematical proofs (which displeases some in Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612) was a renowned Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who led the calendar reform under Pope Gregory XIII. Kircher implies his own work will be more accessible than Clavius's dense proofs.</note>) should offend curious readers anywhere, it seemed best to put forward the theory of all Gnomonics in this book, which we have therefore labeled the *Apparatus to Gnomonics* <note>In this context, "Apparatus" means the foundational tools or preparation required for the study.</note>; so that the reader, proceeding without delay or obstacle through the following books, may more deeply enjoy the sweetest fruits of the Theory. Here practical men will find what they love; there will also be objects for the Mechanicians to applaud. I pass on many things, and most of great importance discovered by me, which will undoubtedly give birth to a new offspring of countless speculations for the theorists. And since the insatiable appetite for knowing is a lover of variety, not at all content with mathematical narrowness but breaking out from time to time into the widest fields of Physics, I have striven to join Physics entirely with Mathematics. From this physico-mathematical marriage a certain new offspring has emerged, which if I call *Physical and Astronomical Gnomonics*, I shall seem to call it by its proper name. These things having been così established, nothing remains but to apply our pen to *Curious Gnomonics*.

XIII. We call the **Cone-cutting Plane** <note>original: "Planum conotomum"</note> that flat surface which, meeting the shadow cone, cuts it in any manner. The parabolas, hyperbolas, and ellipses themselves represent this section.

XIV. Such is NO in the parabola, the line DD in the hyperbola KMD, and finally PR in the ellipse.

VI. When either the light source or the opaque object is moved, the shadow moves as well.

VII. Light and shadow move in opposite directions around a stationary opaque body; thus they take pleasure in opposing sides—right to left, and left to right. Furthermore, the higher the luminous body is, the shorter the shadow it projects from a vertically standing gnomon, and the lower it is, the longer the shadow.

VIII. The ray of light and the ray of shadow move with equal speed.

IX. The center of the Sun, the center of the Earth, and the tip of the shadow always exist in the same circular plane. Consequently, while the Sun travels through 15 parts <note>referring to 15 degrees, which equals one hour of time</note>, the tip of the shadow travels through the same number in the opposite direction. While the Sun describes a circle in the heavens, the shadow's tip will describe a similar circle on an opposite, parallel plane.

X. Shadows projected by equal vertical rods <note>original: "styli recti"</note> fixed into the same plane at the center of the Earth, or onto planes parallel to each other on the Earth's surface, are perceptibly equal to one another.

XI. To our senses, these planes are not distant from each other, nor are the solar rays traveling to opposite parts perceptibly distant.

XII. The tip of any gnomon coincides, for all practical purposes, with the center of the Earth, as does the slanted axis of sundials.

XIII. Although the centers of astronomical instruments are physically distant from the center of the Earth, their surfaces or rims are <term>concentric</term> <note>original Greek: "ὁμόκεντροι" (homokentroi); having the same center.</note> with the celestial circles. Consequently, the entire diameter of the Earth is treated as a single point; for the whole Earth is but a point in relation to the heavens. Therefore, any point on Earth is likewise the center of the heavens.

### ->HYPOTHESES or POSTULATES.<-

I. The Earth is <term>geocentric</term> <note>original Greek: "γειοκεντρικὸς" (geiokentrikos); at the center of the world.</note> and is perceptibly a single point—not that it is truly tiny, but that its size is imperceptible compared to the heavens—which the tip of the gnomon represents in the art of shadow-marking <note>original: "sciathericis".</note>.

II. The shadow ray is extended in a straight line with the light ray from which it proceeds; or, what is the same thing, the shadow ray and the light ray form one continuous straight line.

III. A finite shadow is defined by the opaque body on one side and by the surrounding light on the other, as if by an external boundary.

IV. An opaque body projects its shadow in the direction opposite to the light.

# PART ONE
## THEOREMS,
### First Introduction.
### On the requirements for the Gnomonic Art, or the Astronomy of Shadows.

Since our goal in this Gnomonic Art is to project the entire teaching of the "prime mover" <note>The "primum mobile," or the outermost sphere of the heavens that carries the stars and planets in their daily rotation.</note> onto any given plane—or to demonstrate perpetually, like a radiant finger, everything that astronomers usually investigate using astrolabes and planispheres—there are six primary things necessary to discuss to achieve this.

<column-break/>

First, an exact knowledge of the celestial circles and the gnomonic hours that are to be described.

Second, an accurate judgment for distinguishing the planes upon which the gnomonic projection must be made.

Third, the quality, site, and position of the gnomon, or the indicator or "style" that shows all things.

Fourth, the nature and effect of the projections and sections caused on the planes.

## CHAPTER I.
### On the definition of celestial circles and their roles in Horography.

<margin>What the common intersections of circles are.</margin> Ptolemy, following the three types of sundials <note>original: "horologiorum"; refers specifically to time-keeping devices like sundials.</note> (namely the horizontal, vertical, and meridian types), considers only three "great circles" in his analemma <note>The analemma is a geometric method for projecting the celestial sphere onto a flat surface.</note> in any given position of the sphere. These circles intersect each other at right angles, such as the horizon, the meridian, and the vertical circle properly so-called. For any one of these three circles, according to the demonstrations by Theodosius in Book 1, Proposition 15 <note>Theodosius of Bithynia was a Greek astronomer known for his work on the geometry of a sphere.</note>, is perpendicular to the other two since it is drawn through their poles. The common intersections of these same circles also form right angles with one another at the center of the world. This is because any two of these circles are perpendicular to the third, as we have said, and therefore their common intersection is also perpendicular to that same circle. The common intersection of the horizontal and meridian circles is called the **meridian line** by Ptolemy. However, the common intersection of the horizon and the vertical is called the **equinoctial line**, because it is also the common intersection of the horizon and the equinoctial circle <note>The "equinoctial circle" is the celestial equator.</note>. Finally, the common intersection of the meridian and the vertical is called the **Gnomon**. These are the circles mentioned by Ptolemy, assigning a specific motion to each. We, however, wandering more widely, have undertaken to explain the differences of the circles surrounding the globular surface of the heavens more broadly; we have established more of them, according to the multitude and diversity of the roles they hold in this business of sundial making <note>original: "gnomonico hoc negotio".</note>. Proceeding methodically <note>original: "ἐμμεθόдως" (emmethodos).</note>, we have divided all celestial circles into a triple class. <margin>A triple class of circles.</margin> In the first class are all those circles of longitude which meet and intersect at the poles of the world; such as the meridians, both colures <note>The colures are two principal meridians that pass through the equinoxes and solstices.</note>, the hour circles, and similar ones. In the second class occur all those that are parallel to the horizon, such as the circles of altitude, which the <margin>Almucantars.</margin> Arabs call **Almucantaras**; to these can be referred the parallels of the Sun in an "extremely oblique sphere" <note>This refers to the polar regions where the Sun's path appears parallel to the horizon.</note>. In the third class, we place all those that are considered intermediate: among which there is again a great difference. For some are perpendicular to the axis of the world, such as all the circles of the Sun parallel to the equator; others are <margin>Azimuth.</margin> perpendicular to the horizon, such as the vertical circles, which the Arabs call **Azimuth**; finally, others are perpendicular neither to the horizon nor to the

<column-break/>

axis of the world, but are conceived in the sky with an oblique intersection made with both. Examples of these are the **Zodiac**, and all the circles that can be conceived as being equidistant to it; likewise the circles of positions, the celestial houses, and others: all of which must be dealt with in order.

### DEFINITIONS.

I. The **Meridian circle** is that which is drawn through the poles of the world and the zenith of the place. it stands above the other larger circles on a material sphere, the axis of which is the meridian line; and upon this is measured the altitude of the pole of any given location.
II. The **Equinoctial circle** on the sphere is called that "great circle" which is described from the poles of the world, and is removed equally from both poles of the world in all its parts.
III. The **Zodiac circle** is that which obliquely cuts the equinoctial into two halves; its poles are as far removed from the poles of the world as the Zodiac is distant from the equator toward the North or the South.
IV. <margin>Horizon.</margin> The **Horizon** is a great circle described from the vertex, or the Zenith point, as its pole; it divides the meridian at spherical right angles. It is called by the Latins the *Finitor* <note>meaning "The Bounder" or "The Finisher".</note>, because it separates the seen hemisphere from the unseen; by the Greeks it is called the *horizōn*, the bounding circle or that which cuts off the visible hemisphere from the invisible. <note>original: "ὁρίζων, κύκλος ὁρίζων ἢ ἡμισφαίριον ἀποτέμνων ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀοράτου".</note>
V. <margin>Parallels of the Sun.</margin> The **Parallels of the Sun**, or the circles of the Signs of the Zodiac, are those which are described equidistant to the equator following the motion of the Sun, Moon, and other stars located within the twelve signs of the Zodiac around the earth, the center of the world; they are smaller the further they are distant from the equator. All these can be considered in different ways according to the diversity of the sphere <note>In this context, "sphere" refers to the observer's latitude.</note>. In a "right sphere" <note>The Equator.</note>, they are all perpendicular to the horizon; half appear and half are hidden. In an "oblique sphere" <note>Any latitude between the equator and the poles.</note>, they graze the horizon with an oblique intersection, showing a larger or smaller portion above or below it, according to the arrangement of the signs. However, in an "extremely oblique sphere" <note>The Poles.</note>, they are established as parallel or equidistant to the horizon, remaining in a state of perpetual appearance or perpetual hiding.
Of all these, which are always partly visible above the horizon and partly hidden below, two are the largest of all, described as if from the two poles of the world with one foot of a compass fixed in one of the poles and the other extended all the way to the horizon; one of which...

<meta>This page continues the technical definitions of celestial geometry, specifically focusing on circles that are used to determine the position of celestial bodies and the layout of sundials.
