Art of the Great [Light and Shadow], Book II, Part II.

<margin>Two circles, one always appearing as the greatest, the other of those not appearing.</margin> One is called by Astronomers the "greatest of those always appearing"; the other is called the "greatest of those always hidden." Although one is always equal and a pair to the other, no one should think that both are always of the same size [at every latitude]; for both become larger and closer to each other the more oblique the horizon becomes. Thus, for those living under either of the poles, these types of circles entirely merge into one and coincide with the equator. For those living under the polar circles, the two tropics perform the duty of these circles, and conversely, for those living under the tropics, the polar circles will perform the duty of those same two parallels. For these parallels are always equal to each other in every region and equally distant from the equator, as is established in Book 2, Proposition 6 of Theodosius <note>Theodosius of Bithynia, a Greek geometer of the 2nd century BCE, whose work *Sphaerica* provided the mathematical basis for spherical astronomy.</note>, where he demonstrates one of the properties of the circles of a sphere: A great circle in a sphere which touches a non-great circle <note>original: "circulum non maximum"; a circle smaller than the full circumference of the sphere, like a line of latitude.</note> also touches another non-great circle equal and parallel to it. Therefore, since a great circle (namely, the horizon) touches the greatest always-appearing parallel from above, it will touch the greatest always-hidden circle opposite to it from below. Note here that a "great circle" simply speaking is one thing, and a "greatest" circle with an qualification is another; for these are called "greatest" only in comparison to other smaller circles.

<margin>What are Azimuth circles?</margin>
VI. Vertical circles, called *Azimuth* <note>original: "Azimuth"; derived from the Arabic *as-sumūt*, meaning "the paths."</note>, are great circles intersecting each other at the point of the vertex [Zenith] and the point beneath the feet [Nadir], and are perpendicular to the horizon.

<margin>What are Almucantarath circles?</margin>
VII. Circles of altitudes, called *Almucantarath* <note>original: "Almucantarath"; an Arabic term for circles on the celestial sphere parallel to the horizon.</note>, are circles equidistant to the horizon. The further they are from the horizon, the more they decrease in size; the greatest of these is the horizon itself. They are called circles of altitudes because they determine the height of any star elevated above the horizon; in a diagram, there are 90 such circles parallel to the horizon.

<margin>Circles of the celestial houses.</margin>
VIII. Circles of the celestial houses, or of positions, are of two kinds: According to Regiomontanus <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a foundational Renaissance astronomer.</note>, they are nothing other than those circles which, passing through the common intersections of the horizon and the meridian, divide the equator into twelve equal parts. According to Campanus <note>Campanus of Novara (1220–1296), an Italian mathematician who developed a competing system of "house" division for astrology and astronomy.</note>, they are circles passing through the common sections of the horizon and the meridian that divide the "primary vertical" <note>The prime vertical; the circle passing through the Zenith and the East/West points.</note> into twelve equal parts.

<margin>Parallels of Cities.</margin>
IX. Parallels of cities, or circles of latitudes, do not differ from the arcs or parallels of the zodiac signs: they are circles equidistant from the equator. They can also be called circles of the Sun's declination. And these are the principal circles which will be discussed in this work on Gnomonics <note>The science of using a gnomon (a sundial's shadow-caster) to measure time.</note>.

<column-break/>

From these definitions, you will be able to clearly recognize all the positions and intersections of the circles relative to the meridian and the horizon. Once these are understood, you will have no difficulty in what follows. Therefore, the Reader should labor diligently to firmly impress these upon himself before proceeding further.

## On the roles of celestial circles in Gnomonic Astronomy.

### §. I. On Vertical Circles.

Vertical circles, which the Arabs call *Azimuth*, are great circles that are drawn through the vertex of any place, or *Zenith*, to individual points on the horizon, intersecting each other at the *Zenith* and the *Nadir* <note>The point directly opposite the zenith, beneath the observer's feet.</note>. All these circles form right spherical angles with the horizon, and their planes are perpendicular to the plane of the horizon according to Proposition 22 of the first book of Theodosius. And since the whole horizon contains 360 degrees, through every two opposite points of which any vertical circle passes, it follows that there are 180 vertical circles in total; however, Astronomers imagine them passing through every single point of the horizon as use requires, by which reasoning they are nearly infinite.

<margin>Vertical Circle.</margin>
Among these vertical circles, the Meridian is also numbered, for it also passes through the vertex of any place. Only one vertical circle intersects this meridian at the vertex at right angles; this one is usually called the "Vertical Circle" by excellence [the Prime Vertical]. It passes through the common intersections of the Equator with the Horizon, which are the points D and E in this figure, called the points of true East and West.

The Meridian circle and the vertical circle properly so-called divide the entire upper hemisphere into four quarters: two of which are called eastern—the one that turns toward the South is called the Southeastern, and the one reaching toward the North is called the Northeastern. Two are called western—one of which is called the Southwestern because it runs toward the south, and the other the Northwestern because it faces the North. Although all vertical circles are great circles, they are not usually described in the lower hemisphere hidden from us, but only in the upper hemisphere visible to us, because they have no use among Astronomers in the lower hemisphere, or certainly a very rare use.

Since we have said that all vertical circles pass through the vertex of any place, it is clearly gathered that they never change their position unless the vertex [the observer's location] is changed. Whence in whatever...

->Of the Celestial Circles.<-

In any given hemisphere, these circles are to be conceived as entirely immobile; however, they vary from one hemisphere to another.

<margin>What the Vertical circle is useful for.</margin>
These vertical circles <note>Vertical circles, also known as azimuth circles, are imaginary lines that run from the point directly overhead (the zenith) down to the horizon.</note> were devised by Astronomers for various celestial observations. The first function of these circles is to track and determine the distance or "amplitude" of the Sun and the other stars from the true East and West—specifically, at the moments when the stars rise above or set below the horizon. For the vertical circle that passes through the center of a star at that moment shows us the size of the arc of the horizon between the star and the point of true East.

<margin>What are rising and setting amplitude?</margin>
We call this arc the **rising amplitude**, which is categorized as either Northern or Southern, depending on whether the star is in the Northern or Southern quadrant of the rising horizon. In the same way, the vertical circle shows us the arc of the horizon between a star and the point of true West as it sets; we call this arc the **setting amplitude**, which is likewise divided into Northern and Southern, just as was explained for the rising amplitude. Thus, through vertical circles, we know the extent of the Sun's or any other star's amplitude, both rising and setting—provided, of course, that it has amplitude. All stars positioned outside the equinoctial circle <note>The celestial equator.</note> possess amplitude; only those stars located exactly on the equinoctial circle lack it entirely. Furthermore, Astronomers also call this amplitude (whether rising or setting) the **latitude of rising or setting**.

Secondly, through the vertical circle "properly so-called" <note>The Prime Vertical, which runs exactly East-West through the Zenith.</note>, we know in which quadrant of the world any star is located at any given time. For this reason, these vertical circles are not inconveniently called by some the **circles of rectitude**. Those who are even moderately well-versed in the *Analemma* of Ptolemy <note>A mathematical method or instrument used to project the celestial sphere onto a plane, essential for designing sundials.</note> are well aware of how important this knowledge is:

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram representing an analemma or celestial sphere. It features a central face, vertical and horizontal axes, and several curved lines intersecting the sphere, labeled with letters A, B, C, D, and R.</image-desc>

namely, in which part of the world the Sun is found at any hour of the day. For Ptolemy himself describes horizontal sundials by using this distance of the Sun from the "proper" vertical circle, which is obtained through the remaining vertical circles. Moreover, in the figure above, the vertical circles have been drawn

In this figure, **A** is the common intersection of the horizon with the Northern meridian; **C** is the intersection of the horizon with the Southern meridian; **B** is the vertex of the head <note>the Zenith</note>; **D** is the intersection of the horizon with the Eastern equator; **E** is the intersection of the horizon with the Western equator. Finally, the circle **ADCE** represents the horizon; **ABC** the meridian; and line **ED** the equator.

### §. II. Concerning the Circles of Altitude.

<margin>How the Almucantars are to be conceived in the heavens.</margin>
The circles of altitude—which the Arabs call *Almucantarath* <note>Almucantars: circles on the celestial sphere parallel to the horizon, used to measure a star's height.</note> and most Latin authors call "circles of progression"—are those described as parallel to the horizon from the vertex (or pole) of any location. They divide the quadrant of any vertical circle from the *Zenith* down to the horizon into 90 degrees (for that is how many *Almucantarath* are drawn by Astronomers). Each of these circles is, in turn, divided into 360 parts by the vertical circles, because the entire circuit of the horizon contains 360 quadrants of vertical circles. Thus, the *Almucantarath* and *Azimuth* circles <note>Azimuth: the vertical circles described earlier.</note> create a kind of hemispherical mesh or "web," as can be seen in the preceding figure.

Among all these circles, the **Horizon** is the greatest. No other *Almucantarath* are drawn below it, as they would belong to the hidden hemisphere inhabited by our antipodes <note>Those living on the opposite side of the Earth.</note>. All the others are smaller and unequal to one another, the smallest being the one closest to the zenith. And because the pole of all these circles is the *Zenith* of any given region, it is clear that they do not change unless the *Zenith* and Horizon change together. Therefore, in any given hemisphere, these circles are to be conceived as entirely immobile.

Astronomers devised these circles of

altitude for the purpose of observing the heights of the stars; for by the function of these circles, they measure the elevations above the horizon of all stars, both fixed and "wandering" <note>Planets.</note>.

<margin>Utility of these circles.</margin>

For the altitude of any star is as many degrees as there are from the circle of altitude which it currently occupies down to the horizon. These degrees are indicated by that vertical quadrant...

<margin>The Twilight Line.</margin>
Besides all these altitude circles, another must be understood 18 degrees below the horizon and parallel to it, such as QR. For when the Sun reaches this line before rising, it is the beginning of dawn, or morning twilight; but when it reaches the same after sunset, it is the end of evening twilight. For when the Sun is 18 degrees below the horizon—which degrees must be calculated on the vertical circle drawn through the center of the Sun—the upper hemisphere begins to be illuminated in the morning; in the evening, however, it ceases to be illuminated, according to the common opinion of Astronomers. This circle can be called the parallel of twilight.

### §. III. On the Hour Circles.

<margin>What the measure of time is.</margin>
The markers of the hours, also called hour circles, are great circles that, passing through the poles of the world, distribute the entire equator into 24 equal parts. For since time is the measure of motion, and vice versa, motion is the measure of time, as is established in the books of Physics; and since the Equator is carried most regularly according to the movement of the whole universe, the motion of the equator conveniently measures the time in which the *primum mobile* <note>original: "primum mobile". In the geocentric model, this is the outermost celestial sphere that carries all other spheres from East to West every 24 hours.</note> is moved from east to west. From this it follows that a twenty-fourth part of the time in which the entire equator is rotated once corresponds to a twenty-fourth part of the equator itself, and vice versa. This twenty-fourth part of the aforementioned time, Astronomers have been accustomed to call an **hour**, so that the entire equator revolves once in the space of 24 hours, and one hour, or the twenty-fourth part of the stated time, measures the twenty-fourth part of the equator; and conversely, a twenty-fourth part of the equator measures the quantity of one hour. This twenty-fourth part of the equator contains 15 degrees, so that 15 degrees of the equator correspond to one hour. Therefore, if through each arc of the equator containing 15 degrees, and through the poles of the world, we describe great circles—which will be twelve in number (since each passes through two opposite points on the equator, so that between any two immediate circles 15 degrees are placed)—the entire equator, and each...

<column-break/>

...single solar parallel will be divided into 24 HOUR parts. These are therefore called hour circles, or hour markers, which are to be conceived as entirely immobile in any sphere, just like the meridian, which is also counted among the hour circles. These hour circles indicate the hours, starting from the meridian circle, and thus from midday, according to the custom of Astronomers; so that when the Sun reaches the meridian circle in the visible hemisphere by the motion of the *primum mobile*, it is the twelfth hour. When it reaches the next hour circle, it is the first hour after midday; when the second, it is the second hour, and so on, until it reaches the meridian in the hidden hemisphere, where it is again the twelfth hour, namely midnight. All these things can be easily understood from this figure, in which the meridian is ABCD, the North Pole is A, the South Pole is C, the Equator is BD, the Oblique Horizon is GE, the Vertical is FH; the hour circles, moreover, are those which are drawn through each pole and divide the equator into twelve equal hours (for this figure represents only half the sphere, namely that which is from meridian to meridian).

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing the celestial sphere. The outer circle represents the meridian ABCD. Points A and C are the North and South Poles respectively. The horizontal line GE represents the oblique horizon, and the line BD represents the equator. A vertical line FH represents the vertical circle. Several arcs radiate from poles A and C to divide the equator BD into sections; these arcs are labeled with the letter I and numbers 1, 2, and 3. A point M is marked on the equator.</image-desc>

Hence if it is taken twice, a complete sphere will be had. For there are two such hemispheres exactly similar to each other (as far as the position of the hour circles is concerned), of which the meridian ABC is the circle of the twelfth hour: A 1 C, of the first hour: A 2 C, of the second hour: A 3 C, of the third hour, and so on, as the numbers placed on the equator easily demonstrate. And these circles, which are called hour circles simply and without addition—since the beginning of the day is taken more conveniently from no place other than the meridian circle, as is taught in the sphere—since they pass through the poles of the world and equal parts of the equator, they will always be the same in number in any climate, although they have a different position in various horizons.

<margin>Unequal hours.</margin>
There is another kind of hour circle distinct from the aforementioned; for these do not pass through the poles of the world, nor do they divide all the parallels of the Sun (except the equator) into 24 equal hours; but rather they divide the daytime arc of any parallel into twelve equal parts. By the same reasoning, they distinguish the nighttime arc into the same number of equal parts; which parts indeed...

<margin>Hours from Sunrise and Sunset. <note>original: "Hora ab Ortu, & occasu"</note></margin>
For although they divide each individual parallel into 24 equal parts (in which they agree with hour circles of the first type), they do not pass through the poles of the world; in this regard, they are distinguished from them and agree with the hour circles of the second type. These circles are described on the sphere in this way: all the solar parallels are divided into twenty-four equal parts, beginning from the western horizon (if we desire hours according to the <term>Italian custom</term> <note>The Italian hour system, or "Bohemian hours," began the 24-hour count at sunset.</note>, starting from sunset) or from the eastern horizon (if we prefer hours starting from sunrise, according to the <term>Babylonian custom</term> <note>The Babylonian system began the 24-hour count at sunrise.</note> or that of the Balearic Islands). <margin>Babylonian Hours. <note>original: "Horæ Babyloniorum"</note></margin> Then a circle is drawn through the points nearest the horizon, and similarly through the subsequent points, and so on, until twenty-four circles are obtained, one of which is the horizon, just as in the preceding second type. For if circles are drawn through these points touching the said parallels, all other intermediate parallels will also be divided by them into twenty-four equal parts, beginning from the horizon, as is established from the 18th proposition of the 2nd book of **Theodosius** <note>Theodosius of Bithynia, a Greek astronomer whose work "Sphaerics" provided the mathematical foundation for the geometry of the sphere.</note>. Therefore, these circles are to be understood as touching the parallels DN and GH at the twenty-four points in which they are divided into twenty-four equal parts by the hour circles of the first type. # Book III of the Great Art. Part I of the Preliminary Theory.

**EFGH** is the innermost <term>parallel</term> <note>A circle of constant declination, like the Tropics</note> of the stars that are always visible; the circle **KImn** is the outermost parallel of those that always remain hidden; the circle **KBSD** represents the <term>oblique horizon</term> <note>The horizon as seen from a specific latitude, tilted relative to the Earth's axis</note>, which touches the said parallels at points **S** and **K**, where it also intersects the <term>meridian</term> **KOM**, in which point **O** is the pole; the straight line **POQ** represents the circle of the 1st astronomical hour (either 1:00 AM or 11:00 PM); the circle **PSRT** is for the 1st hour before sunset or after sunrise, touching the said parallels at points **P** and **R**, where the circle **PORQ** intersects them—namely, the semicircle **PSR** from sunrise and the remaining **RTP** from sunset. Moreover, the arcs **PK** and **SR** are the hourly spaces. You see, therefore, in a single glance, the entire concept of hours from sunrise and sunset alongside astronomical hours; from this, the intersections of each with the others are represented such that, from this figure, tables can be constructed, and Italian, Babylonian, and Astronomical clocks <note>original: "horologia"</note> of every kind can be built, as will be discussed in the course of this work; for the entire doctrine of <term>hour lines</term> and solar sundials depends on this.

<margin>The varying condition of circles.</margin>
Furthermore, these last two types of hour circles, although they are to be understood as completely immobile within one and the same sphere (just like the first type), are nonetheless not the same in every sphere. For these circles will vary if they constitute the second type in different spheres, just as the <term>diurnal</term> <note>daytime</note> and nocturnal arcs vary, as is evident from the method of their description. By the same logic, these same circles will vary if they indicate the third type of hours in different regions, just as the parallels of the always-visible stars change. For the more oblique the sphere is <note>the higher the latitude</note>, the larger the diurnal arcs of the northern signs are, and the smaller the nocturnal arcs; whereas for the southern signs, the diurnal arcs are smaller and the nocturnal arcs are larger; and likewise, the parallels that are always visible and touch the horizon are larger.

### §. 4. On the circles of the celestial Houses. <note>original: "Domiciliorum cœlestium"</note>

The circles of the celestial houses are six <term>great circles</term> that divide the entire Heaven into twelve parts, which they call the "Celestial Houses." Those parts of the sky in which the various stars hold different domains are called celestial houses. When the ancient astronomers noticed the powers and influences of the stars, they saw they were not only varied according to the unique nature of each—for not all have the same influence, since some dry things out, some cool, some heat, and others affect things in various other ways—but they also saw that the powers of the same stars were sometimes increased and sometimes diminished depending on their position in the sky. We perceive this clearly in the "luminaries" <note>The Sun and Moon</note> every day; for we commonly see changes in the weather occurring when the Sun touches the horizon

<column-break/>

at sunrise or sunset; likewise when it is at the meridian <note>high noon</note> or at midnight. Similarly, we notice that due to the movement of the Moon through these same four locations, the ebb and flow of the tide happens infallibly, and the greatest storms are almost always stirred up. Anyone will easily observe all these same things in the other more famous stars running through these same places, if only they pay diligent attention. It was for this reason that Ptolemy explained with great care the approaches of the stars to these four locations, especially in conjunction with the Sun.

<margin>Why the heaven is divided into twelve houses.</margin>
When, I say, those ancient observers of the stars had noticed this, they divided the entire sky into twelve parts, in which—chiefly due to the various sites and positions—the stars produce various effects in these lower regions; these parts they called the twelve "celestial houses." Through long observation, they grasped that there were twelve such notable places to be established in the sky. The circles distinguishing these twelve parts they called the "circles of the celestial houses," which are what we are discussing now. Not all authors agree with one another in establishing these. Some make all twelve houses equal, while others make them unequal. However, they do agree on certain points. First, those four locations of the world—namely, Noon, West, Midnight, and East—are called by everyone the <term>cardines</term> <note>literally "pivots" or "hinges"</note> of the world, and by more recent authors, the "angles" or "cusps." Although each of these cardines has remarkable power, Ptolemy—in the 3rd book of his *Astrological Judgments* <note>Referring to the "Tetrabiblos"</note>—prefers the "culmination of heaven" (that is, the meridian pivot) over all others. In the second place, he puts the eastern pivot; thirdly, the western; fourthly and lastly, the midnight pivot. Again, all agree who divide any space contained between any two pivots into three parts, so that they have twelve celestial houses. Finally, they agree because everyone, both ancient and modern, makes the beginning of the first house the eastern pivot, and they distribute the rest according to the succession of the <term>signs</term> <note>the Zodiac signs</note> because of the motion of the planets from west to east, so that the second house is below the horizon on the eastern side, and so on for the others. Hence, everyone also places the same beginning for the fourth, seventh, and tenth houses, since these houses have their beginning in the four pivots of the world according to that succession of the signs. Although astronomers do not differ among themselves in the distribution of this order, in the particular distinction of the houses, some have followed one method and some another. For certain ancients, taking their beginning from the **Horoscope** <note>The Ascendant, or the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific moment</note>, just as all Astro-

# On the Celestial Circles
### V

Astronomers divide the entire Zodiac into twelve equal parts according to the order and succession of the signs, starting from the horizon in the eastern part. (For the <term>Horoscope</term> <note>In this context, the "Horoscope" refers to the Ascendant—the specific point of the Zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a given moment.</note> is that degree or point of the Zodiac, or <term>ecliptic</term>, which emerges above the horizon at the beginning of any event, such as at the birth of a human or the start of a building project, etc.) By the sections of these parts and through the poles of the Zodiac, they draw six <term>great circles</term> <note>A circle on a sphere whose plane passes through the center of the sphere, like the Equator or the Meridian.</note> with which they bisect the whole sky into twelve equal parts, which are called the **celestial houses**. This division of the sky into twelve houses is therefore similar to how astronomers divide the whole sky into the twelve signs of the Zodiac using great circles described through the poles of the Zodiac and the beginnings of all the signs. However, there is an exception: in the division of the sky into twelve houses, the dividing circles do not always pass through the beginnings of the signs, unless the beginning of a sign happens to be on the horizon; furthermore, these circles must be conceived as immobile, whereas the circles distinguishing the twelve signs revolve along with the heavens. Nevertheless, it is true that these circles of the celestial houses never remain exactly the same due to the motion of the Zodiac's poles.

Indeed, if we wished to follow this logic of describing the circles of the celestial houses, it would happen that many stars existing in the northern hemisphere already raised above the horizon would fall into the **first house**; likewise, many stars located in the southern hemisphere that have not yet risen above the horizon would fall into the **twelfth** or final house. Both results are contrary to the definition of the first and twelfth celestial houses. For according to almost all astrologers, the entire first house remains hidden below the horizon, with its beginning being the horizon itself. Likewise, the entire twelfth house is established above the horizon, with its end being that same horizon.

<margin>How Alcabitius and John of Saxony drew the lines of the houses.</margin>
Certain others, among whom <term>Alcabitius</term> <note>original: "Alcabitius"; the 10th-century Arab astrologer Al-Qabisi.</note> and <term>John of Saxony</term> <note>A 14th-century astronomer known for his work on the Alfonsine Tables.</note> are numbered, distinguish the <term>diurnal arc</term> <note>The path an object takes across the sky from sunrise to sunset.</note> of the Horoscope into six equal parts, and the nocturnal arc into as many. Through these sections and the poles of the world, they describe six great circles dividing the whole sky into twelve celestial dwellings. By this division, not only are the twelve houses made unequal to one another—since sometimes those above the horizon are larger than those hidden below the horizon, and sometimes smaller, as is clear from the diurnal and nocturnal arcs of the Horoscope—but also the houses of one day or night are unequal to the houses of another day or night, since the arc of the Horoscope for one day or night is larger than the arc of the Horoscope for another day or night. Noticing this, some divided the <term>equator</term> <note>original: "aequatorem"; the celestial equator.</note> perpetually into twelve equal parts, and through those sections and the poles of the world, they described the circles of the celestial houses.

<column-break/>

In this way, they established houses that were always equal. However, the same problem necessarily happens to all these methods as happened to the previous ones; and for that reason, these methods of dividing the sky into twelve houses are now rejected by all astrologers. Wherefore, all more recent authors, wishing to avoid the aforementioned inconveniences and desiring that six entire houses always remain above the horizon and just as many below it, have followed a different method. They describe these six circles of the celestial houses not through the poles of the Zodiac, nor the poles of the world, but through the poles of the **vertical circle** <note>Also known as the Prime Vertical, the circle passing through the Zenith, Nadir, East, and West points.</note> properly so-called—that is, through the common intersections of the meridian circle with the horizon. By this logic, since the halves of all the celestial house circles are entirely above the horizon and likewise entirely below it (so that the horizon takes the place of one circle), all the aforementioned inconveniences are very easily avoided.

<margin>Discrepancy of Authors.</margin>
Furthermore, these authors also disagree among themselves, as some establish all the celestial houses as equal, while others make them unequal.

<margin>The system of 12 houses according to Campanus.</margin>
<margin>For Campanus, whom many weighty authors follow, divides the vertical circle properly so-called into three equal parts in each of the quadrants intercepted between the four cardinal points of the world, so that the entire vertical circle is distributed into twelve equal parts. Through these parts and the poles of the vertical circle,</margin>
that is, through the common intersections of the meridian with the horizon, he describes six great circles dividing the whole sky into twelve equal houses; as you will see in the figure, in which the meridian is **ABCD**, the vertical circle properly so-called is **BD**, and its poles are **A** and **C**.

<margin>Regiomontanus.</margin>
<term>John of Regio Monte</term> <note>original: "Joannes de Regio monte"; the 15th-century mathematician and astronomer Regiomontanus.</note>, however, divides not the vertical circle but the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The celestial equator.</note> into three equal parts in each of the quadrants placed between the same cardinal points, so that the entire equator is distributed into twelve equal parts. Through these parts and the common intersections of the meridian with the horizon (that is, through the poles of the vertical circle properly so-called), he describes great circles which distribute the whole sky into twelve unequal houses, since they also divide the vertical circle into unequal parts, as is established from the elements of Theodosius; and they will become more unequal the more <term>oblique</term> <note>A "right sphere" occurs at the equator; an "oblique sphere" occurs at any other latitude where the celestial axis is tilted relative to the horizon.</note> the sphere is, as can be seen in this figure. In a right sphere, however, these houses will be equal,

# The Great Art, Book III. Protheoria Part I.

...are equal, since the equator then coincides with the vertical circle. <term>Johannes Regiomontanus</term> <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), an influential German mathematician and astronomer who developed the "Rational" system of house division based on the celestial equator.</note> calls this method of dividing the heavens into twelve houses "Rational," because it is more reasonable than all others and more consistent with experience.

Moreover, <term>Campanus</term> <note>Campanus of Novara (c. 1220–1296), whose system of house division was the standard before Regiomontanus.</note> and Regiomontanus agree with one another, as do all others, regarding the order of these houses, as is clearly seen in the preceding figures in which the numbers of the celestial houses are assigned.

<margin>Various names of the houses</margin> For according to both, the first house begins from the horizon in the east, extending below the horizon so that its end is beneath the horizon; this house is called the <term>Pivot</term> <note>original: *Cardo*. The four "cardinal" points or "hinges" of the chart.</note>, the cusp, or the eastern angle, the <term>horoscope</term> <note>In traditional astrology, "horoscope" refers to the specific point of the Zodiac rising on the eastern horizon.</note>, and the **ascendant**, because it is raised from the lower hemisphere to the upper. Next follows the second house below the horizon, which is called the house **Succeeding** the horoscope. After that follows the third, which is called **Falling** from the horoscope. To this succeeds the fourth house, having its beginning in the meridian circle below the horizon, which is called the Pivot, cusp, or the angle of midnight, or even the angle of the earth <note>original: *angulus terrae*, also known as the *Imum Coeli*.</note>. Then follows the fifth house, which is called **Succeeding** the bottom of the sky, or the angle of the earth. Then follows the sixth, which is called **Falling** from the bottom of the sky. To this succeeds the seventh, beginning from the horizon in the west, which is called the pi-

<column-break/>

-vot, cusp, or western angle. Next follows the eighth, which is called **Succeeding** the angle or western pivot. Then follows the ninth, which is called **Falling** from the sunset. To this again succeeds the tenth, whose beginning exists in the meridian above the horizon, which is called the pivot, cusp, or southern angle, or even the **midheaven** <note>original: *medium coeli*.</note>. Then follows the eleventh, which is called **Succeeding** the midheaven. Finally, the twelfth, whose end is at the horizon in the east, which is called **Falling** from the midheaven.

From these things it is clear that these twelve houses are distributed into three classes: In the first are contained the first, fourth, seventh, and tenth houses, which are called **Pivots** <note>original: *Cardines*</note>, because they are like the hinges for the others and are stronger in their significance. The second class comprises the second, fifth, eighth, and eleventh, which are named **Succeeding** the Pivots, or Secondary, because they hold the second place in their significance. Finally, the third class encompasses the remaining four—the third, sixth, ninth, and twelfth—which are called **Falling** from the pivots <note>original: *Cadentes*</note>, because in themselves they have almost no power of significance. However, it must not be overlooked that these twelve celestial houses are described by astrologers in a square figure when they adapt them for use, as you see here.

### §. V. On the Circles of Positions.

Circles of positions are great circles passing through the common sections of the meridian with the horizon and the centers of the stars. Whence it is manifest that the circles of the celestial houses are also circles of positions, namely when a star or planet stands at the point of any house.

For this reason, the circles of positions are easily understood from the preceding figures. It is also customary for the circle of position of any star to be call-

Moreover, the circles of position were devised so that through them we might know whether a star, or any point in the heavens, is at the specific point of any celestial house; or if it is not, how far it is distant from that point.

### §. VI. On the Circles of Latitude.

**C**ircles of latitude are great circles <note>In spherical geometry, a "great circle" is a circle on the surface of a sphere that has the same circumference as the sphere itself, dividing it into two equal halves.</note> drawn through the poles of the Zodiac and through each degree of the ecliptic <note>The ecliptic is the sun's apparent path across the sky throughout the year.</note>: therefore, they number 180, since each one passes through two opposite points of the ecliptic. Within the number of these circles are also included those circles which form the signs of the Zodiac in the third sense, as is declared in the study of the sphere. The function of these circles, however, is to measure the latitudes of the stars.

<margin>What is the latitude of a star?</margin>
For the latitude of any star is the arc of the circle of latitude passing through the center of the star, contained between the ecliptic and the star. This is twofold: namely, Northern and Southern, according as the star deviates from the ecliptic toward the North or the South. Furthermore, although these great circles which are drawn through the poles of the Zodiac are commonly called "circles of latitude" by astronomers (because they obviously measure the latitudes of stars), the "minor circles" <note>Small circles on a sphere that do not pass through the center, like lines of latitude on a map of the Earth.</note> could also be called circles of latitude. These are described from the poles of the Zodiac parallel to the ecliptic itself through each degree of those great circles—just as the minor circles which are said to be parallel to the horizon through each degree of the vertical circles from the zenith were previously

<column-break/>

called circles of altitude, even though the vertical circles measure the altitudes of the stars.

### §. VII. On the Circles of Declination.

**F**inally, circles of declination are great circles passing through the poles of the world <note>The North and South celestial poles.</note> and through each degree of the equator. Therefore, they number 180, since each one passes through two opposite degrees of the equator. In the number of these circles are also included the Meridian and all the hour circles indicating the hours from noon. The function of these circles is to measure the declinations of the stars.

<margin>What the declination of a star is.</margin>
For the declination of any star is the arc of the circle of declination passing through the center of the star, contained between the equator and the star. This is likewise twofold: namely, Northern and Southern, according as the star has receded from the equator either to the North or to the South.

<margin>The functions of these circles.</margin>
However, even if commonly only these great circles, which are drawn through the poles of the world, are called "circles of declination" by astronomers (because they measure the declinations of stars), the minor circles could also not ineptly be called circles of declination. These are described from the poles of the world parallel to the equator through each degree of the great circles, just as we said concerning the circles of latitude. For these minor circles of latitude and declination have no small use in the construction of the gnomonic <note>The art of making sundials.</note> Astrolabe, as will be seen later.

# CHAPTER II.
## On the fourfold kind of Clocks, which emanate from the discussed hours.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap letter 'S' featuring a detailed landscape with a town, trees, and a radiant sun in the background.</image-desc>
**I**f it is true, as the Stoic School knew, that time is the "norm and guardian of things" because it is the index and test of truth, and preserves the memory and duration of past deeds for posterity, then surely those men are worthy of no small praise who—binding the laws of time with shadowy chains—have attempted by an ingenious device to arrest the fleeing years, months, days, and hours, rendering them as present as if they were permanent things.

<margin>What is time?</margin>
For since time is nothing else than <term>the measurement of the first mover</term> <note>original Greek: "μέτρησις τοῦ πρώτου κινήτου". In Aristotelian physics, the "first mover" refers to the rotation of the outermost celestial sphere.</note> according to before and after, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> testifies; and since this measurement is the rule of all human actions, adopted to avoid confusion; certainly Censorinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman grammarian and author of "De Die Natali."</note> teaches at length that in ancient ages, while time did not yet consist of the name "hours," it was called and distinguished by daily

<column-break/>

actions. Thus they called the evening <term>ox-loosing time</term> <note>original Greek: "βουλυτὸν", referring to the time when oxen are unyoked from the plow.</note>; specifically, as the Poet says,

> When Phoebus took the yokes from his well-deserved horses.

Likewise, designating the time before noon, they would say <term>when the market is full</term> <note>original Greek: "πληθούσης ἀγορᾶς".</note>, as men at that time would assemble in the meeting place, or as Hesiod says, <term>from the wallowing-place and the unyoking of the plows</term> <note>original Greek: "ἀπ’ ἀλινδήτω καὶ λύοντος ἄροτρα".</note>. Thus Homer designates Noon as <term>when a man prepares his dinner from the plows</term> <note>original Greek: "ὅταν ἀρύτρους ἀνὴρ δόρπον ἐποπλίσσηται".</note>. Indeed, as Athenaeus testifies, the ancients for the most part noted the time of daily acts by the word <term>hours</term> <note>original Greek: "ὥρας".</note>, such as the <term>hour of the evening meal</term> <note>original Greek: "ὥρα δόρπου"</note> or the <term>hour of dinner</term> <note>original Greek: "ὥρα δείπνης"</note>. Among the Latins it is also called <term>tempestas</term> <note>Time, season, or weather.</note>: concerning which see us treating it at length in the *Egyptian Oedipus* <note>Kircher's own encyclopedic work on Egyptology and Coptic language.</note>. One may think the same of the ancient Hebrews, who divided the Day into Morning, Noon, and Evening, which parts they called Hours.

So in Psalm 55. For they observed the whole <term>night-and-day</term> <note>original Greek: "νυχθήμερον", a 24-hour period.</note> divided into four parts (which they called Watches). The first watch was from the evening: The second...

# The Great Art, Book III. Preliminary Theory, Part I.

<margin>Gnomonics existed from the beginning.</margin>
The second [hour] from midnight; the third from dawn; the fourth from noon. From this, some conclude that the ancients lacked specific hourly intervals, but they are mistaken. For I am easily persuaded that the art of **Gnomonics** <note>The science of constructing and using sundials (gnomons).</note> and the distribution of hours existed from the beginning, especially when I consider more deeply the remarkable skill of the ancients in discovering things. Since we judge those things which we cannot do without, and which we use by necessity, to be the most useful, it is certainly not probable that the first mortals discovered the use of Music and the more obscure and less necessary intervals of voices, yet neglected the less difficult and more necessary science of Gnomonics. For if, as the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle, who famously defined time in his *Physics*.</note> testifies, "time is the number of motion," and thus the measure of our actions, it must be that either the ancients lacked time by which to measure their actions, or they were not unskilled in Gnomonics.

<margin>Adam knew Gnomonics.</margin>
Almost everyone attributes the knowledge of Astronomy, and indeed Astrology, to our first parents, Adam and his progeny. But who is unaware that neither of these sciences can stand without Gnomonics? For the partitioning of time is supremely necessary to both. Therefore, the division of the day into certain parts was very ancient. <unclear>??</unclear> These they called **Hours**, the principles of which were designated by the senses themselves; throughout the sacred books, the use of hours is clearly indicated. In Exodus 9, Deuteronomy 28, Ezra book 3 chapter 2, and Job 11, mention is made of a "half **hour**" <note>original Latin: *horæ*</note>, and in chapter 12, they prayed prostrate for three hours. In Ecclesiasticus 12: "One hour he will remain with you," and in chapter 30: "Every work in its own hour." From these, such an argument is constructed: If the ancients had hours, they also had instruments by which they knew them; therefore, they also cultivated Gnomonics.

<margin>Gnomonics is a very ancient art.</margin>
Moreover, such instruments were called **horologia** <note>Literally "time-tellers," referring to clocks or sundials.</note>. But regarding these, I have written more extensively in the *Dial of Ahaz* and in the *Egyptian Oedipus*. Furthermore, that **Sciatheric** <note>Shadow-measuring (from the Greek *skia* for shadow).</note> clocks were in use in ancient times is demonstrated by the phrase "the eleven-foot shadow" <note>original Greek: <term>ἐνδεκάτως σκιᾶς</term></note> for the hour of dinner; or "the eleventh element" <note>original Greek: <term>ἐνδεκάτου στοιχείου</term></note>, because the individual hours were distinguished by the marks of letters, as is also testified by the "inscription" <note>original Greek: <term>ἐπιγεγραμμένον</term></note> regarding the clock in **Athenaeus** <note>A 3rd-century Greek rhetorician and grammarian.</note>:

> Six hours for labor are most sufficient; those that follow,
> Indicated by their tasks, say "LIVE" to mortals.
> <note>The Greek letters for hours 7, 8, 9, and 10 are Z, H, Θ, I, which spell *ZĒTHI*, the Greek word for "Live!"</note>

For before Ζ, Η, Θ, Ι, there were Α, Β, Γ, Δ, Ε, Ϛ. <note>The letters representing hours 1 through 6.</note>

<margin>Diverse measures of time.</margin>
Therefore, as the world was refined by the invention of various things over time, it observed a more exact reckoning of time. Just as the beginning of the "natural day" was established differently among various nations, so too were different systems of hours established among them. For Astronomers set the beginning of the day at the meridian <note>Noon</note>, while the Babylonians set it at the eastern horizon <note>Sunrise</note>; the Italians set it at the western horizon <note>Sunset</note>; the Egyptians and Roman Priests from the nocturnal semicircle of the meridian, which is below the horizon <note>Midnight</note>. This custom has remained in the Church to this day. The common people compute the day

<column-break/>

from the rising of the Sun to its setting, which is the "artificial day." Astronomers, however, preferred to begin the day from the meridian circle rather than from the horizon; for as **Clavius** <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician who helped lead the Gregorian calendar reform.</note> teaches in the third chapter of *The Sphere*, the Sun and stars always relate to the meridian in the same way with all rigor, but not so with respect to the horizon, which varies in a marvelous way according to the greater or lesser elevation of the pole above the horizon <note>This refers to how latitude changes the timing of sunrise and sunset, but not noon.</note>.

<margin>Equal and unequal hours.</margin>
There are, therefore, two types of hours (about which we also spoke in the preceding pages): **equal** and **unequal**. **Equal hours**, into which the natural day is distributed, are nothing other than the twenty-fourth parts of one natural day; each of these contains fifteen degrees of the equator. They are called "equal" because throughout the entire space of the year they are always of the same magnitude, given that fifteen degrees of the equator are attributed to each, all of which emerge above the horizon in an equal space of time. Thus, the natural day consists of twenty-four equal hours, the beginning of which is set differently by different people. And accordingly, it is found that these types of hours are numbered differently by different nations. For the Babylonians (according to Pliny, Book 2, and Macrobius, Book 3 of the *Saturnalia*) called the "day" the motion of the Sun from one sunrise to another (whom the **Balearic Islands** imitate at this time), and for that reason they reckoned the hours from the rising of the sun; these are called **Babylonian hours** by most

<margin>How the Balearic Islands count hours.</margin>
writers, because they were in use among the Babylonians. The Athenians, however, in former times, and now all of Italy together with Bohemia, defined the day from one sunset to the next; from there they numbered the equal hours, which are now called **Italian hours**, after Italy, where their use most flourishes. The Umbrians next, as well as the Astronomers, called the entire time from noon to noon a day; thus they computed equal hours from noon. Because these are used by Astronomers in calculating the motions of the heavens, they are customarily called **Astronomical hours**.

<margin>Astronomical Hours. Egyptians. Romans.</margin>
Finally, the Egyptians (according to Macrobius, Book 1 of the *Saturnalia*) and the Roman people numbered the day from one midnight to the following midnight, and from here they observed the elapsed hours. This is what the Roman Church also observes in the celebration of solemnities and fasts. Those hours which are now in use by the French, Germans, Spaniards, and almost all of Europe do not differ much from the Astronomical and Egyptian hours, since all of these count twelve equal hours from noon to midnight, and as many from there to the next noon. Thus, only by changing the numbers of the hours from noon or midnight, these will differ from the others.

<margin>Canonical Hours.</margin>
Furthermore, an **unequal hour** is the twelfth part...

# On the various kinds of hours

<margin>What an unequal hour is.</margin>
...of both the day and the <term>artificial night</term><note>The "artificial day" is the time from sunrise to sunset, while the "artificial night" is from sunset to sunrise, regardless of their actual length.</note>. Formerly, any artificial day and any night were divided into twelve parts, equal to each other—daytime hours equal to other daytime hours of that same day, and nighttime hours to nighttime hours of that same night. Moreover, **unequal hours** are the twelfth parts of the parallel segments that are visible above the horizon and those that lie hidden below it; or, what amounts to the same thing, they are the twelfth parts of all the diurnal and nocturnal parallel arcs. Indeed, in a <term>right sphere</term><note>The celestial sphere as seen from the equator, where the celestial poles are on the horizon.</note>, these parts contain 15 degrees of the parallels ascending the horizon at any time of year, and thus they do not differ from **equal hours**. However, the matter stands differently in an <term>oblique sphere</term><note>The celestial sphere as seen from any latitude other than the equator or poles, where the lengths of days and nights vary.</note>. These unequal hours were used in the past by the Jews (as is established from Sacred Scripture), as well as by the Romans and almost all of antiquity (as histories and the monuments of ancient mathematicians testify); and from this, the sundial—which is commonly called "ancient"—is established.

<margin>The ancient sundial.</margin>
From these hours, the watches of the night were also established; and even now, the <term>Canonical hours</term><note>The scheduled times for daily prayer in the Christian church (Matins, Lauds, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline).</note> are chanted by the Church. Many passages of Sacred Scripture must be understood through these hours; such as when the Lord says: *Are there not twelve hours in the day, etc.*<note>John 11:9</note>, clearly beginning the counting of hours from the rising of the Sun, so that six fall at noon and twelve end at the setting of the Sun. Regarding these hours, the Jews say this in the *Seder Olam*<note>A 2nd-century CE Hebrew language chronology.</note>:
> By the common consensus of the world, days and unequal nights are divided into twelve equal parts, which are called unequal hours. <note>original Hebrew: וכל אחד ואחד מן הימים והלילות אשר אנס שיים נחלקים לדעת כל העולם על י"ב חלקים וקוראין לכל חלק וחלק שעה עיקלה להפריש בינה ובין הישרה</note>

This means: By the common consensus of the world, the day and nights are divided into twelve equal parts, which are called unequal hours. And that the **Sundial of Ahaz** was composed of such hours is testified by Rabbi Eliezer, Abenezra, and Jonathan, who calls it the <term>Stone of Shaya</term> <note>original: אבן שייא</note>, others call it the <term>Stone of Hours</term> <note>original: אבן שעות</note>—that is, the stone of unequal hours. Rabbi Solomon, in the *Parushoth* <note>Commentaries</note> of this passage, calls it the <term>Instrument of Hours</term> <note>original: הכלי שעות</note>, an instrument of unequal hours. What sort of thing it was, we shall say, God willing, in the Mathematical Section. Persius also seems to have made mention of these hours when he sings:

<margin>The Sundial of Ahaz.</margin>
> *We snore away, enough to work off the raw Falernian wine,*
> *while the shadow touches the fifth line.* <note>Persius, Satires 3. Falernian was a famous Roman wine.</note>

By these words, he signifies a morning hour, the one which we count as the eleventh. Martial also, in book 4 of his *Epigrams*, very elegantly included almost all the hours of the artificial day in this epigram:

> *The first and second hour occupy those who offer greetings,*
> *The third exercises the hoarse lawyers.*
> *Rome extends various labors into the fifth,*
> *The sixth is rest for the weary; the seventh will be the end.*
> *The eighth is sufficient for the sleek wrestling-grounds.*
> *The ninth commands us to break the piled-up couches.*
> *The tenth is the hour for my little books, Euphemus,*
> *When your care arranges the ambrosial feasts.*
> *And the good Caesar is relaxed with heavenly nectar,*
> *And holds the small cups in his mighty hand.*
> *Then admit the jokes; our Muse Thalia fears to go*
> *With a bold step to the morning place.* <note>Martial, Epigrams 4.8. This poem tracks the Roman day from the morning "salutatio" (greetings) to the evening banquet.</note>

<margin>Fables of the Rabbis</margin>
Furthermore, in the book *Sanhedrin* of the Talmud, the Hebrews make mention of twelve unequal hours, in which they fabulously tell that man was created by God in a singular mystery; for thus it is read: In the first hour, indeed, God collected his dust. In the second hour, the mass of the body was made. In the third, his limbs were extended. In the fourth, the spirit was infused into him. In the fifth, he stood upon his feet. In the sixth hour, or at noon, he assigned names. In the seventh, Eve was joined to him. In the eighth, they two ascended to the bed, and four descended <note>Meaning Adam and Eve went to bed, and they, plus two children (Cain and Abel), resulted.</note>. In the ninth, he was prohibited from eating from the tree of knowledge. In the tenth, other precepts were given to him. In the eleventh, he sanctified the table. In the twelfth, at the beginning of the night, Adam transgressed. We have treated these things more extensively so that those things which occur everywhere in sacred texts concerning hours—such as the hour of our Savior’s death, the third hour of the coming of the Holy Spirit, and similar things occurring everywhere—might be more easily understood; since those times can and should by no means be taken according to our hours, but according to Jewish or "unequal" hours, as has been said.

<margin>Planetary hours.</margin>
Another kind of unequal hours includes those which are commonly called **Planetary Hours**. They are so named because they are referred not absolutely to the course of the Sun, as equal hours are, but to the ruling planets. For since there are seven planets (which are listed in this order with their spheres: ☽ Moon, ☿ Mercury, ♀ Venus, ☉ Sun, ♂ Mars, ♃ Jupiter, ♄ Saturn), each is said by astronomers to dominate and preside over individual hours of the day in order. For if Saturn dominates the first hour of the day, Jupiter will dominate the second, Mars the third, the Sun the fourth, Venus the fifth, Mercury the sixth, the Moon the seventh, Saturn the eighth, Jupiter the ninth, Mars the tenth, the Sun the eleventh, Venus the twelfth, Mercury the thirteenth, and so on. Then, on the first hour of the following day, the Sun, and so on thereafter—namely, in the order of the planets, not that in which we listed them a moment ago, but always in retrograde. But take the following diagram for this.

<margin>Use of the table</margin>
Furthermore, the legitimate progression of the planets can be clearly seen from this table. Since a natural day contains 24 hours, it is necessary that if Saturn rules the first hour on the Sabbath <note>Saturday</note> (from which the day of Saturn takes its name), then on the following day the first hour is ruled by the next planet in retrograde order, skipping two; namely the Sun, from which the day of the Sun <note>Sunday</note> is named. Similarly, on the next
<margin>Where the arrangement of the table comes from.</margin>
day the Moon, hence the day of the Moon <note>Monday</note>, and for the rest in the same manner thereafter. But as for why two planets should be skipped in this way to establish the 

<image-desc>A circular diagram featuring a seven-pointed star (heptagram). The lines of the heptagram connect the planets in the sequence that determines the order of the days of the week: Saturn ♄ to Sun ☉, Sun ☉ to Moon ☽, Moon ☽ to Mars ♂, Mars ♂ to Mercury ☿, Mercury ☿ to Jupiter ♃, Jupiter ♃ to Venus ♀, and Venus ♀ back to Saturn ♄.</image-desc>

names of the days, Dio Cassius <note>original: "Dion Nicæus"</note> in Book 36 provides a reason based on harmony, or the resonance called the <term>diatessaron</term><note>A musical interval of a perfect fourth. The ancients believed the cosmos was structured according to musical ratios.</note>, in which it was believed by the ancients that the entire power of music was contained and its stable foundation rested. For having considered the 
<margin>The discordance of the diatessaron in all music.</margin>
reason for this kind of harmony, and comparing it with the adornment of the heavens and the order of the celestial spheres and planets, they noted a certain convenience and similarity in them. After one day was named for one planet, they were accustomed to name the following day for the fourth planet after it, though in retrograde order. Thus, after Saturn, the Sun follows in the fourth place, then the Moon, then Mars, etc., as appears in the table. But if you arrange this progression of planets in the way it appears to have been done in the present <term>heptagon</term><note>original: ἐπταγώνῳ; a seven-pointed star</note>, you will see clearly that this arrangement of planets by the days of the week drew its origin

<column-break/>

from the nature of the number seven, which, having completed a triple revolution within the space of twenty-four hours, necessarily results in the planet of the present day <note>This refers to the math: (24 hours mod 7 planets) = 3. Furthermore, the musical mystery contained here has been discussed more extensively, God willing, in our *Mundane Hieroglyphic Music*.
<margin>The wondrous power of the number seven.</margin>

But if anyone now desires more concerning the property of these kinds of hours, let them—besides what we have handed down in the *Physico-Astrological Sciatherics*—also consult Juan de Rojas, Book 2 of the *Planisphere*, Chapter 26, and Poliziano's *Miscellany*, Chapter 8, where Dio reports that the Egyptians were the authors of this order and the naming of the days, as well as others whom we pass over for the sake of brevity. It was from the <term>unequal hours</term> of this first kind that the days formerly received their names, which indeed they still retain; from the planetary hours, I say, and the hourly planets. But although no solar clock or sundial of this kind has been constructed so far as I know, we shall nevertheless show below the method of inscribing hours of this sort on a sundial, and therefore they had to be discussed more fully in this place.

And from these four kinds of hours, four kinds of clocks <note>original: "horolabiorum," referring to sundials or instruments that "take" the hour</note> have also arisen. The first of these is the 
<margin>Hours from sunrise and sunset.</margin>
counting of hours from noon and midnight, which we call the **Astronomical clock**. The second is the counting of hours from sunset, which is commonly called **Italian**. The third is the counting of hours from sunrise, which is called **Babylonian**. Finally, the fourth is called the **ancient** or **Jewish** clock, used by the ancients, consisting of unequal hours, because it perpetually divides the diurnal arcs into twelve equal parts. From this it follows that the hours of one day or night, when the Sun travels through one of those parallels, are equal to each other; but they are unequal when compared to the hours of another day when the Sun has reached another parallel of the same size, if today's hours are always compared to tomorrow's—excepting those that are equidistant from Aries and Libra <note>The equinoxes, when day and night are equal.</note>. Therefore, a clock is nothing other than a sensible sign indicating the hours according to the motion of the heaven; and it is...

<header>On Flat Sundials.</header>

...either natural, artificial, or a mixture of these.

<margin>Natural clock.</margin>
A natural clock is one which, without human artifice, or rather through daily recurring actions, indicates the division of time. Examples include the ebb and flow of the tides in Ireland, in the Strait of Sicily, and other places; the onset of fevers; the blooming of certain flowers; and whatever indicates the hours through natural sympathy, such as the crowing of the rooster, the urination of the Egyptian baboon <note>Original: "Cynocephali Aegyptiaci mictus." It was a common ancient and Renaissance belief, cited by authors like Horapollo, that baboons urinated twelve times a day at regular intervals.</note> repeated twelve times, and similar phenomena. Regarding these, see our *Oedipus* <note>original: "Oedypum nostrum"; referring to Athanasius Kircher's encyclopedic work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*</note>; these are all reckoned among

<column-break/>

natural clocks. Artificial clocks are likewise varied; for they are either mechanical, such as those which show the time by the revolution of wheels; or Solar, all and each of which we have resolved to treat in the course of this work. The mixed type is composed of both the natural and the artificial. Since we shall speak of each of these specifically in the following sections, we have deemed it unnecessary to dwell on them any longer here. Therefore, let us turn our pen to the Planes, upon which the aforementioned clocks are usually drawn.

# CHAPTER III.
## On the Variety of Planes, or Surfaces, upon which Sundials are Drawn.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' with scrolling floral and acanthus leaf patterns.</image-desc>
IT IS ESTABLISHED from the principles of Logic that the position of any thing cannot exist without a relationship to something else. Therefore, all sundials <note>original: "horolabia"</note> acquire their specific positions: for some stand upright, others lie extended, some decline, some are inclined, and some have a mixed position. The naming of this position comes to the planes in relation to their location; this is designated by the vertical line, which, if it falls outside the equator, constitutes latitude, and if outside the meridian, longitude. It is now our duty to speak of these.

First, by the name "Plane," I understand any flat surface on which Sciatheric <note>original: "Sciatherica"; from the Greek for shadow-tracking, a technical term for sundials</note> or Solar Clocks are customarily described. Just as these surfaces are various and differ significantly in position, so too have they been given various names by craftsmen, which we shall reveal in this chapter. Both the position and the name are derived from the celestial circles to which they are parallel. Although the Equinoctial Circle <note>The celestial equator</note> holds the primary place among these, nevertheless, in the logic of sundials—as far as their position is concerned—we should rightly prefer the horizon to the equinoctial circle. This is because the horizon serves as the foundation and basis for the others, as will soon be clear; and almost everything we discuss must first deal with it.

<margin>Horizontal plane.</margin>
2. A horizontal plane, therefore, is one that is parallel to the horizon—namely, a leveled plane, or one made according to a water-level. In the figure placed here, Plane A is to be established as such, so that the positions of the remaining planes may be more easily found from it. For this purpose, on the same plane A, the straight lines KL and MN have been drawn: the former for the meridian line, the latter for the vertical line. Their function is to show the four quarters of the world: namely, East, South, West, and North, as the labeled names also indicate. For since the said

<column-break/>

lines intersect each other at right angles at point O, it follows that if one of them, such as KL, shows South on one side (for example, K) and consequently North on the other side (L), the remaining line MN will indicate East on side M and West on side N; this has already been frequently proven by many. With these things established, the positions of other planes shall be defined. For all other planes are either perpendicular to the horizon or inclined to it; and both types, again, either directly face one of the four quarters of the world, or certainly decline from them in various ways. Hence, it is necessary that there be many differences among Planes. So that these may be enumerated in a certain order, we must begin with the planes perpendicular to the horizon that are most commonly used—those which are typically called "vertical," because they are parallel to the vertical circles, which are themselves perpendicular to the horizon.

<margin>Primary vertical plane.</margin>
3. First among the vertical planes, then, is the proper vertical plane, which is parallel to the proper vertical circle; that is, it is elevated perpendicularly above the horizon from a line parallel to the vertical line MN. In the present illustration, these are the two walls B and F, in which one may consider a double surface: one, which the perspective itself reveals, looking directly North, such as surface F; and the other, which directly faces South, which we have noted in wall B as being imagined on the opposite face. Hence, a double naming of the Vertical Clock also arises. For that which is described on the southern face of wall B is called a Meridional or Southern Vertical Clock; but that which is drawn on the Northern or Boreal face is called a Boreal or Northern Vertical Clock.

In the second place among the Vertical Planes are numbered...

<margin>A vertical plane parallel to the meridian.</margin>
...are called Meridian [planes], which are parallel to the meridian circle, that is, those which are raised vertically above the horizon from a line parallel to the meridian line. These are represented by the two walls D and H, in which again a double surface appears, providing the basis for a double Meridian Sundial <note>original: "Horologii"</note>. For the Sundial inscribed on the Eastern face of wall D is called the Eastern Meridian Sundial; however, the one opposite it on wall H is called the Western Meridian Sundial.

<margin>A declining vertical plane.</margin>
Thirdly, besides the two planes already mentioned, which are in a way regular, there are many other vertical planes called Declining, because they are parallel to vertical circles that are oblique to the primary vertical <note>the primary vertical is the east-west line</note>. If these are compared to the four quarters of the world <note>the cardinal directions: North, South, East, and West</note>, they are all reduced to four types, which can be seen in the remaining four walls of the figure, C, E, G, and I, whose fa-

<column-break/>

ces do not look precisely toward any single quarter of the world. For the face of wall C, the opposite one which the Perspective drawing could not represent, looks toward both the South <note>original: "Meridiem"</note> and the East <note>original: "Ortum"</note> simultaneously, yet neither part directly. Hence, the Sundial drawn on that same surface will be called Declining from South toward East. Similarly, the opposite face of wall I, and the Sundial described on it, will be named Declining from South toward West, because it tends obliquely toward both of these quarters. But indeed, the Sundial depicted on surface G will be named Declining from North <note>original: "Septentrione"</note> toward West, from both quarters of the world which it faces; and conversely, the Sundial made on wall E will be called Declining from North toward East, because that plane is viewed from those same parts.

4. From these things, the distinction of Planes not at a right angle <note>original: "rectorum"</note> to the Horizon will also be easily understood. # On Plane Sundials.

...North <note>original: "Septentrionem"</note>, and the lower part toward the South <note>original: "Austrum"</note>. Third: If the angle of inclination of wall F—namely, toward the North—is equal to the angle of the altitude of the pole <note>this angle corresponds to the observer's latitude</note>, so that it is parallel to the circle of the 6th astronomical hour, both the lower and upper sundials will be called **Polar**. Fourth: If, however, that same angle is smaller or larger, the lower will be said to face the North, and the upper toward the South.

<margin>Planes declining from the horizon.</margin>
5 Second, if the two walls D and H are understood to be inclined in the said manner, they will represent all planes directly facing East <note>original: "Ortum"</note> or West <note>original: "Occasum"</note>; however, to distinguish them from the former, they are not usually called "inclined," but **declining from the horizon**. First, the sundials on wall D will be called declining from the horizon: the lower one toward the East, and the upper one toward the West. Then, the sundials described on wall H will be called declining from the horizon: on the lower face toward the West, and on the upper face toward the East.

6 Third and finally, if the remaining four walls—C, E, G, and I—are similarly conceived as being inclined inward, they will show us all the remaining plane sundials, which are simultaneously called **Declining & Inclined**. For first, wall C will show a double sundial, upper and lower, of which the upper is called "inclined and simultaneously declining from South toward East"; the lower is called "inclined and simultaneously declining from North toward West."

<margin>Declining and inclined.</margin>
Second, the lower sundial described on wall I will be called "lower inclined and simultaneously declining from South toward West," and consequently the upper is "inclined and simultaneously declining from North toward East." Third, the lower sundial of wall E will be "inclined and simultaneously declining from North toward East"; the upper will be "inclined and simultaneously declining from South toward West." Fourth and finally, on wall G, the lower sundial will be "inclined and simultaneously declining from North toward West," and conversely the upper will be "inclined and simultaneously declining from South toward East."

7 And this is the placement and naming of plane sundials, whether they are perpendicular to the horizon or inclined, always taking into account the East or West, North or South. But if, in the planes inclined toward the horizon mentioned in number four, and in the planes that are simultaneously inclined and declining, we wish to observe certain differences in their

<column-break/>

inclinations, we shall find even more distinctions among the planes, in which the sundials drawn upon them appear to acquire different shapes.

<margin>Characteristics of inclined planes.</margin>
And indeed, regarding the Inclined: those planes which are not equinoctial or polar—those whose inclination, clearly, is not equal to the angle of the complement of the altitude of the pole <note>the "complement" is 90 degrees minus the latitude</note>, or to the angle of the altitude of the pole itself—will have that angle of inclination either smaller or larger than the aforementioned angles. First, therefore, if the angle of inclination of wall B is smaller than the inclination of the Equator, the lower sundial can be called "inclined toward the South" and the upper "toward the North," as held in number four; both are parallel to the great circle that intersects the meridian below the equinoctial <note>the celestial equator</note>, specifically on the southern side. Second, if the angle of inclination is larger than the angle of the complement of the altitude of the pole, the lower sundial can again be called "toward the South" and the upper "toward the North," and both moreover are parallel to the circle that intersects the meridian above the equinoctial. Third, if the angle of inclination of wall F, which we set to lean toward the North, is smaller than the angle of the altitude of the pole: both the lower sundial (which is then Northern) and the upper (which is Southern) will be called parallel to the circle that intersects the meridian below the arctic pole. Fourth and finally, if the same angle is larger, the planes will remain with the same names regarding the quarters of the world, but regarding the circle to which they are parallel, they will be said to be parallel to the circle that intersects the meridian above the aforementioned pole.

8 almost the same distinction can be applied to planes that are simultaneously declining and inclined. For the two walls C and I, which are inclined toward the South, either are parallel to the great circle that intersects the meridian at the same point as the equinoctial, or above that point, or below it; and so if these same walls are named according to both surfaces from the aforementioned circles to which they are parallel, it is clear that each wall, C and I, exists in a threefold variation. In the same way, there will be threefold variations for walls E and G, if they are considered insofar as they are parallel to the great circles that intersect the meridian either through the poles of the world, or below, or above those same poles.

# CHAPTER IV.

## On the construction of the Level, and on its use in identifying and aligning Planes.

In this fourth chapter, we will endeavor to provide three things. First, we will teach the construction of the **Level** <note>original: "Libella"; a tool used to ensure a surface is perfectly horizontal or at a specific angle</note>, namely a certain instrument most fit for balancing planes and accomplishing several other tasks. Second, how that same level is to be used in identifying planes, whether they are balanced, upright, or even oblique <note>slanted</note> to the Horizon: and if they are oblique, how great that obliquity is. Third, and finally, by what method planes are to be balanced, or raised perpendicularly, or certainly inclined at any given determined angle. All of these things contribute greatly both to the design and the construction of Sundials; not to mention that the use of these same matters is very great in other
<column-break/>
Geometric and Astronomical problems as well.

### Construction of the Level.

<margin>The manufacture of the Level.</margin>
1 **Do** not be surprised if we have crafted the Level a little differently than it is usually constructed by artisans: for we have done this with the intent that we might extend its use to more things. Thus, we were manufacturing it as follows.

Let a **Gnomon** <note>In this context, the author uses "gnomon" to mean a carpenter's square or L-shaped tool, rather than the shadow-casting pin of a sundial; original: "Gnomon BAC"</note> be made separately from two rules AB and AC, of the same width and length, so that these same rules contain a right angle most exactly at both the exterior and interior meeting point A. Then, with a rule applied to the extremities B and C, let two small lines be marked on these same rules, which will designate two small parts to be cut away from each rule, as you see in the figure. <note>The figure mentioned is likely on the following page or omitted in this section of the text</note>
