Book III of the Great Art. Part II of the Preliminaries.

# Problem VII.

## *The calculation of the ascensional difference.*
<note>The "ascensional difference" is the difference in time between the actual sunrise or sunset and the 6:00 AM/PM time of the equinox. It allows a navigator or astronomer to calculate the length of a day.</note>

From the figure of the analemma <note>A geometric method of projecting the celestial sphere onto a flat surface, often used to design sundials</note>, it is clear that the northern semi-diurnal arc <note>The path the sun takes from noon to sunset</note> exceeds the quadrant of a circle <note>90 degrees</note> by exactly as much as the same arc in the opposite southern sign falls short of 90 degrees. Therefore, in the analemma, the arc of the parallel for Cancer ♋ 3 is sought; but this is in parts where Aries ♈ V is the whole sine <note>The "whole sine" or *sinus totus* refers to the radius of the calculation circle, used as a baseline in trigonometry</note>, and the arc to be found is called the **ascensional difference**. Indeed, the line Aries ♈ V is to the semi-diameter of the equator as the arc of the Sun's declination is to the tangent of the same declination.

<image-desc>A complex circular astronomical diagram illustrating an analemma projection. The outer circle is divided into segments labeled with zodiac symbols including Leo, Cancer, Gemini, Taurus, Aries, Pisces, Aquarius, Capricorn, Sagittarius, Scorpio, Libra, and Virgo. A series of vertical, horizontal, and diagonal lines (chords and diameters) intersect within the circle, labeled with uppercase letters A through Z. Dotted lines and arcs indicate geometric relationships used for calculating solar angles and ascension.</image-desc>

---

Therefore, let it be done thus: as the **whole sine** is to the **tangent of the pole's elevation** <note>The geographic latitude</note>, so the **tangent of the Sun's declination** <note>The angle of the sun above or below the celestial equator</note> is to the other value. If, therefore, you multiply the tangent of the Sun's declination by the tangent of the pole's elevation, and divide the product by the whole sine, it will indicate the sine of the result, the arcs of which are made known in the Table of Sines. You will find the Table of Differences calculated by others scattered everywhere among astronomical authors, such as Clavius, Magini, Orontius, and countless others. <note>References to Christopher Clavius, Giovanni Paolo Magini, and Oronce Finé, famous 16th-century mathematicians and astronomers.</note>

# Problem VIII.

## *To construct tables of solar altitudes and horizontal circumferences.*

Since we have treated the method of calculating these tables for every kind of hour at great length in our *Magnetic Art* <note>original: "Arte nostra Magnetica," referring to Athanasius Kircher's work *Magnes sive de Arte Magnetica* published in 1641</note>, we have deemed it unnecessary to repeat the same thing here. We therefore refer the reader there; however, in this place, we have decided only to set forth the tables that are required there.

### The use of the Almucantar-Azimuth Table.

At the head of the table are the astronomical hours; on the side are the elevations of the pole <note>latitudes</note>, to each of which the three signs Cancer ♋, Leo ♌, and Virgo ♍ correspond on the same side. If, therefore, you wish to know the **Azimuths** and **Almucantars** for a pole elevation of 42 degrees, given the sign and the hour—for example, at the 3rd hour in Cancer ♋—look for the given elevation of 42 degrees on the side. The area for those signs with the 3rd or 9th hour will give 48 degrees and 29 minutes for the **Almucantar**, and 12 degrees and 4 minutes for the **Azimuth**. And so for the rest.

Note here, Reader, that by **Almucantars** we understand nothing other than the circles of the Sun's altitude above the horizon; just as by **Azimuths**, we understand nothing other than the vertical circles by which the Sun's position in any quarter of the sky is determined at any moment of time.

<meta>This page provides the concluding instructions for using the Almucantar-Azimuth tables found on page 214 and introduces a new mathematical problem regarding the calculation of shadow lengths for sundial construction.</meta>

<page-num>215</page-num>
<header>Sciatheric Tables. <note>From the Greek 'skiatheras,' meaning 'shadow-hunting'; these are tables used for the design and construction of sundials.</note></header>

### Note on the preceding Table.

**T**his Table serves only for describing the tropics <note>The paths the sun follows during the summer and winter solstices.</note> on any sundial and on any plane. It shows the common points of intersection where the <term>Almucantars</term> <note>Circles of altitude parallel to the horizon.</note> and the <term>Azimuths</term> <note>Vertical circles that measure horizontal direction.</note> cross each other at every Italian and Babylonian hour. However, since three signs—Cancer ♋, Libra ♎, and Capricorn ♑—are needed to describe hour lines, so that an hour arc can be drawn through the three points found in those signs, most astronomers choose Aries ♈ and Libra ♎ together with Cancer ♋ and Capricorn ♑, just as we did in the preceding Table IV. In this Table, however, we have deliberately omitted Aries ♈ and Libra ♎, not because they are not useful for describing Italian hours, but because the Almucantars and Azimuths which serve the astronomical hours in the preceding table—when the Sun is positioned in Aries ♈ or Libra ♎—also serve the same purpose here for Italian and Babylonian hours. Thus, the Almucantar and Azimuth which correspond to astronomical hour 12 when the Sun is in Aries ♈ or Libra ♎, match Italian hour 18 and Babylonian hour 6, and so on for the others. Therefore, if you wish to use this Table, extract the Almucantar-Azimuth numbers corresponding to the elevation of the pole <note>The geographic latitude.</note> of your region and the hours listed at the top. For the points of Cancer ♋, enter the Table from the side where the pole elevations are described; for the points of Capricorn ♑, enter the Table from the opposite side. For Aries ♈ and Libra ♎, extract the numbers from the preceding table corresponding to Aries ♈ and Libra ♎ as previously mentioned, and you will achieve your goal.

## Problem IX.
### To calculate a table of shadows.

**T**his Table is very necessary for the inscription of the zodiac signs and other celestial circles. Therefore, you shall calculate it for any altitude of the Sun as follows. Let the known altitude of the Sun be E, the horizontal plane AB, the <term>stylus</term> <note>The rod or upright of the sundial.</note> HI, the <term>straight shadow</term> <note>The horizontal shadow cast on a flat surface.</note> GH, and the

A geometric diagram showing a quadrant (arc labeled C, 45, D) used for astronomical or gnomonic calculations. A vertical gnomon (stylus) HI stands on a horizontal base AB. Point G marks the end of the straight shadow on the base, while point F marks the "turned shadow" on a vertical scale. Line IE represents a solar ray at a given altitude E. Auxiliary lines ES (perpendicular to HI) and VI/EV (horizontal and vertical projections) form triangles used to solve shadow lengths via sines. Point S is on the horizontal line through I; point V is on the vertical line through I. The angle EID is marked at 45 degrees.

<term>turned shadow</term> <note>The shadow cast upon a vertical wall or surface.</note> FG. Let a line be dropped from E onto S perpendicularly. Since, therefore, the illuminated triangle IES is similar to the shaded triangle GIH, the angles will be equal to the angles, and the sides proportional to the sides. 

<margin>*Operation by Sines.*</margin>
Let it be done, therefore: as the sine of the known solar altitude ES is to IS (the sine of the complement <note>Equivalent to the modern cosine.</note> of that same solar altitude), so is the gnomon IH—divided into 10, 12, or any other number of parts—to GH, the straight shadow, which becomes known once the operation is performed. If, however, you desire the turned shadows, let it be: as EV (the sine of the complement of the given solar altitude) is to the right sine VI (or ES) of the same altitude, so is the stylus FI—divided into 10, 12, or any other parts—to FG, the turned shadow, which becomes known once the operation is performed. Thus, given any altitude of the Sun, you will investigate the straight and turned shadow.

# Dialing Table. <note>original: "Tabula Sciatherica"; from the Greek "skia" (shadow), referring to the art of gnomonics or sundial making.</note>

### Note on the preceding Table.

**G**iven the altitude of the Sun, look for its degrees among the larger numbers; and, if it has minutes added, look for those on the side. The intersection of both will give the shadow in parts, based on a style <note>The gnomon or rod that casts the shadow.</note> that is divided into 12 parts. For example: if you wish to know what shadow length is produced by an altitude of the Sun 50 degrees above the horizon, look among the series of larger numbers for 50 degrees. At 0 minutes, the common area will give a horizontal shadow of 10 parts and 4 minutes. <note>In this system, a "part" is 1/12th the height of the gnomon, and a "minute" is 1/60th of a part.</note>
If, however, the Sun is elevated at 50 degrees and 40 minutes, take 40 minutes on the side and 50 degrees at the top; the common area will give a horizontal shadow of 9 parts and 50 minutes. But if you desire to know the quantity of the vertical shadow <note>original: "umbræ verticalis"; also known as a versed shadow, used for dials on walls.</note>, take the complement of the Sun’s altitude <note>The complement is the angle needed to reach 90 degrees (e.g., the complement of 30 is 60).</note> from the vertical shadow section; find the intersection of the degree and the minutes on the right side of the Table. For example: let the given altitude of the Sun be 50 degrees and 40 minutes, and someone desires the versed or vertical shadow. Look for the complement of the given altitude, which is 39 degrees and 20 minutes; let the degrees be found within the same column at the bottom, and let the 20 minutes be sought in the small side-table for vertical shadows. The common area will give 9 parts and 50 minutes, which is the vertical shadow sought. You shall operate no differently in other cases.

### Problem X.

*To calculate a table of the Sun’s parallels to be inscribed on sundials.*

**F**irst, let the altitudes of the Sun be obtained from the preceding tables, calculated for the beginnings of the [Zodiac] signs for each hour from noon and midnight. Then, let the calculation be made: As the right sine of the given altitudes is to the sine of their complement, so is the style (divided into 12 parts) to the unknown value. This will produce the sought-after lengths of the shadows for the given hours—specifically, "right" shadows on a horizontal plane, and "versed" shadows on vertical planes—which you may then arrange into tables, as follows.

<header>Book III of the Great Art. Part II of the Apparatus.</header>

### Problem XI.
**To construct a table for inscribing Azimuths, or vertical lines, on a vertical plane.**

If you reduce the tangents of each individual degree of a quadrant into tables—using such parts as the <term>style|The gnomon or pin of the sundial that casts the shadow.</term> is 10 or 100—you will have what is sought.

### Problem XII.
**The calculation of Tables for the horoscopes of the Ascending Signs.**

The tables declaring the <term>horoscopes|In historical astronomy, the 'horoscope' refers specifically to the 'Ascendant'—the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a given moment—rather than a modern astrological chart.</term> of the signs are nothing other than tables showing at what hour any sign of the Zodiac is raised above the horizon, or depressed below it, or situated in the Midheaven <note>original: "medio Cæli"</note> or at the bottom of the sky. For this kind of knowledge for use in <term>Gnomonics|The art and science of constructing sundials.</term>, you shall calculate the tables by this art.

## Rule I.

With the Sun existing in the four cardinal points—Aries ♈, Cancer ♋, Libra ♎, and Capricorn ♑—inquire at what hour before or after noon the beginnings of the 12 signs rise, by this industrious method.

It is asked, for example, with the Sun being in Aries ♈ when the <term>semidiurnal arc|The length of time the sun is above the horizon from sunrise to noon (or noon to sunset).</term> is 6 hours, at what hour the beginning of Cancer ♋ emerges above the horizon in Rome. Seek the <term>oblique ascension|The arc of the celestial equator that rises together with a point on the ecliptic in a specific latitude.</term> of the Sun positioned in Cancer ♋, that is, the arc between the beginning of Aries ♈ and the first degree of Cancer ♋, which you will find from the tables to be 66 degrees and 57 minutes. Resolve these degrees into hours, and you find 4 hours and 28 minutes. When these are subtracted from 6 hours (that is, the semidiurnal arc of Aries), they leave 1 hour and 32 minutes before noon. Therefore, at this hour the beginning of Cancer ♋ ascends above the horizon while the Sun is in Aries ♈, which corresponds to the hour 10 and 28 minutes after midnight.

<margin>Calculation examples</margin>
Again, with the Sun positioned at the beginning of Cancer ♋, the hour is sought at which the beginning of Capricorn ♑ emerges above the horizon. Calculate the oblique ascension of the arc intercepted between the beginning of Cancer ♋ and Capricorn ♑, which is 190 degrees and 12 minutes. These, converted into hours, give 12 hours and 41 minutes. If you subtract the semidiurnal arc of 7 hours and 32 minutes from these, there will remain the hour 5 and 9 minutes after noon—namely, the hour at which the beginning of Capricorn ♑ then emerges above the horizon. And this rule must be observed by you for all the remaining signs. For if the oblique ascension (when it is less than the semidiurnal arc) is reduced into hours and taken away from the semidiurnal arc, the hours that remain until noon will be left, at which time that sign whose oblique ascension was taken rises. But if the semidiurnal arc is taken away from the said hours (if the oblique ascension exceeds the semidiurnal arc), the remaining hours will be those elapsed after noon when the beginning of that sign whose oblique ascension was assumed rises, as is clear in the examples provided. We have not placed the particular tables here, since anyone can very easily calculate them by his own effort <note>original: "proprio marte"; literally 'by his own Mars,' meaning by one's own strength or skill.</note> according to the given rule.

## Rule II.

**On calculating the tables of the mediations of the signs, and their declinations.**

This rule commands nothing else but to find the points of the Ecliptic existing on the meridian circle—that is, the "mediations" of the heavens—when the beginnings of the 12 signs rise, and the <term>declinations|The angular distance of a point north or south of the celestial equator.</term> of those same points. To have the said points, proceed thus: From the oblique ascension of the beginning of any sign, let a quadrant of a circle [90 degrees] be taken away—having first added a whole circle [360 degrees] to the oblique ascension if the subtraction cannot be made. For the remaining number will be the <term>right ascension|The position of a point along the celestial equator, measured eastward from the vernal equinox.</term> of the point of the ecliptic which is then found on the meridian, and which astrologers call the "culminating" or "mediating" point. From the table of right ascensions, that point of the ecliptic will become known, whose opposite point will exist in the same meridian below the horizon, which astronomers call the <term>Imum Coeli|The 'Bottom of the Sky'; the point where the meridian intersects the ecliptic below the horizon.</term>, or the angle, or the cusp of midnight. But let us declare the rule by a paradigm.

### Paradigm.

If therefore you wish to know what point in the ecliptic "mediates" <note>Culminates or crosses the meridian.</note> while Cancer ♋ is rising: take the oblique ascension of the beginning of Cancer ♋, namely 41 degrees and 33 minutes. If a quadrant [90 degrees] is taken from this <note>Presumably adding 360 first: 401°33' - 90° = 311°33'. The following result suggests Kircher is using a specific coordinate shift or there is a misprint in the degree value.</note>, there will remain 51 degrees and 33 minutes for the right ascension, to which in the table of right ascensions corresponds 23 degrees and 57 minutes of Gemini ♊—the sought mediating point of the ecliptic. Its opposite point below the horizon is 23 degrees and 57 minutes of Sagittarius ♐.

Again, the oblique ascension of Libra ♎ is 66 degrees and 57 minutes. If a whole circle of 360 is added to this, they are 426 degrees and 57 minutes. From which 90 being removed leaves 336 degrees and 57 minutes of right ascension, to which in the table of right ascensions corresponds 5 degrees and 6 minutes of Aries ♈—the sought mediating point of the ecliptic when the beginning of Libra ♎ emerges above the horizon. By this industry you will calculate the table of mediations suitable for your elevation [latitude], an example of which see in Problem XX of Book V.

It provides step-by-step rules and examples for calculating these astronomical positions using oblique and right ascensions.</summary>

<header>Tables of Sundial Construction</header>

### Rule III.
#### To find the point of the Ecliptic on the circle of the sixth hour, and to record it in a table.

**S**ince the <term>oblique ascension|The arc of the celestial equator that rises with a point on the ecliptic in a specific latitude.</term> of the beginning of any sign is the <term>right ascension|The distance of a point measured eastward along the celestial equator from the vernal equinox.</term> of that point of the Ecliptic which is situated on the circle of the sixth hour at that same time before noon: thus, from a table of right ascensions, you will find the tables of the said points on the line of the sixth hour. For example, with the Sun positioned at the beginning of <term>Cancer ♋︎</term> <note>original: "♋︎"</note>, since its oblique ascension is 66 degrees and 57 minutes, the right ascension of the point of the Ecliptic then situated on the circle of the sixth hour will be exactly the same number of degrees; to which ascension in the table of right ascensions corresponds 8 degrees and 41 minutes of <term>Gemini ♊︎</term> <note>original: "♊︎"</note> (always taking into account the proportional part if the precise number is not found in the tables). Its opposite point will be 8 degrees and 41 minutes of <term>Sagittarius ♐︎</term> <note>original: "♐︎"</note>. One must proceed in the same way for the others.

## PRELIMINARY EXERCISE II.

### To find the centers of reflection.

**I**n a parabola, the midpoint DK of the section DE will be the center of reflection.

In a hyperbola, let the side AC be prolonged along with the section DX determining the transverse side (or exterior diameter) at point *y* of the section YD. This is divided in half at W, and from here WZ is drawn parallel to CY. When this is transferred into the section of the hyperbola DX, from W to O, it will give the desired point of the center of reflection in that same place.

### Practical Procedure IV
*To describe a parabola by another method.*

**First**, let there be a right cone ABC, in which a parabolic section DP falls in any way, extended to S.

**Second**, let the axis of the parabola DP be divided into any number of equal parts, as also its side DA, and through the points of division let parallels to the base AB be drawn, such as DQ, MR, and so on. In the same way, let hidden <term>perpendiculars|Lines meeting the axis at a 90-degree angle</term> of indeterminate length be drawn through the points of division marked on the axis DP, such as WV, YX, and so forth.

**Third**, with the distance IM or IR, a circle being drawn from center I (the midpoint of line MR), let a perpendicular HK be drawn to it through E—the common point of intersection of DP and MR; this will be equal to the <term>ordinate|A coordinate measured from the axis to a point on the curve</term> WV.

-> <image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the construction of a parabola within a cone. The cone is labeled ABC, with a section DP. Construction lines include DQ, MR (horizontal) and WV, YX (vertical). The resulting curve is labeled "Parabola." and various construction points are labeled with letters G, H, I, K, L, M, N, Q, R, S, T, V, W, X, Y, Z.</image-desc> <-

**Fourth**, then, with the compass placed at each point, such as FG, etc., of the axis DP, let arcs be drawn from C (the vertex of the cone) to the extended axis of the parabola DP, which you will mark with similar letters.

**Fifth**, after intercepting the spaces between C and the points of division F, G, etc., of the side DA, let arcs be drawn from the subsequent points of the extended line PDS; these will cut the ordinates at the points through which the parabola is to be drawn. See the demonstration of this in Propositions 1 and 2, and Apollonius, Book 1, Proposition 11.

### Practical Procedure V
*To describe a parabola in another way, given the center of reflection and any semiordinate.*

**First**, let the semiordinate CD and the <term>center of reflection|The "focus" of the parabola. Kircher calls it the center of reflection because any light ray originating from this point and hitting the parabola will reflect outward in a straight, parallel line.</term> B be given; by their help, both the vertex of the parabola and the points of the parabola will be found as follows. Let the points CB be joined by a straight line. According to Proposition 10,

-> <image-desc>A geometric diagram for constructing a parabola using circular arcs and ordinates. A central triangle/sector is labeled with points A, B, C. Construction arcs are drawn from point B to intersect vertical lines (ordinates) at points such as F, I, T, H. Labels include A, B, C, D, H, K, F, I, T, V, L, N, O, P, Q, R, S.</image-desc> <-

all lines drawn from the center B to the edge of the parabola, and from there drawn perpendicularly to the semiordinate, are equal to line BC. Therefore, having drawn the arc DR, let BR be made equal to BD; and RC, being divided in two at E, will give ER or CE, which, when transferred from center B, gives A, the vertex of the parabola. You will find the remaining points thus: let line EB be divided into as many parts as you wish, which shall be L, M, N, O, P, Q.

**Second**, then, with one foot of the compass placed in B, let hidden arcs be described at the spaces intercepted between C and L, CM, CN, CO, CP. Again, with the compass having intercepted the space BL, and one foot placed on the arc F, let it be moved this far until the other foot touches the semiordinate CD; for from this point H, another arc will be drawn, which, where it cuts the former, there will be the point through which the edge of the parabola runs. Furthermore, with the space BM intercepted, let the compass be moved forward on arc BI until the other leg touches the base CD, and you will have the second point of the parabola on arc BI. You will find the third point T thus: with the space BN intercepted, let the compass move back and forth on arc BT until it touches CD with the other leg, and the leg resting on arc BT will give the third desired point. You shall work in the same way to investigate the other points, as is clear in the example. We have given the demonstration in Proposition 10.

### Practical Procedure VI
*To describe a parabola by the easiest method of all, given the vertex and center of reflection.*

**First.** Let A be the vertex and C the center <note>Kircher uses "center" here to refer to the focal point.</note> of the parabola; which having been assigned from the previous practice, you shall describe a parabola of any size by this industry. Let AC be divided into any number of equal parts—for example, six—and if you desire a larger one, extend beyond C into other and further parts of 12 equal parts—for example, complete the division so that AC is as large as CB; and through the points of division let hidden lines be drawn parallel to AB and perpendicular, which shall refer to the ordinates.

lines at points through which the curve, when drawn, will give the <term>hyperbola</term>.

### Practical Procedure XII.
**To describe a hyperbola by means of a string.**

**L**et A be the <term>center of reflection</term>, B the opposite <term>center</term>, and C the <term>vertex</term>: given these, the <term>hyperbola</term> shall be drawn with the string by this industrious method. In both centers A and B, let thin needles be fixed, to each of which a string is tied: then have another <term>stylus|a writing or drawing tool</term> which has a hole at the bottom like a needle, as appears at D: let both strings be passed through this hole.

Next, let the stylus D be moved on both sides, so that the two strings are always slackened by the motion, and by this movement, the desired <term>hyperbola</term> will be described. All these things depend on Porism 1 of Proposition 10.

# On the description of Conic Sections.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram at the top left showing a horizontal line with points A, C, and B. A line segment rises vertically from C to D. At D, a further vertical segment is labeled E, and several lines radiate from D towards arc-like markings.</image-desc>

To assign the centers of an ellipse given the <term>major semi-diameter|half the length of the longest axis of an ellipse</term> AB: if you transfer the major semi-diameter AE or EB from the common point of intersection of the perimeter and the <term>minor diameter|the shorter axis of an ellipse</term> to both sides of the major diameter—namely to points F and G—the centers will be established. By a similar logic, since two lines drawn from these centers to any point on the perimeter are equal to the major diameter, we may easily describe the ellipse. Let the centers F and G be given on the diameter AB; these, as we said, are obtained if you transfer the semi-diameter AE or EB from point C onto the major diameter. Then, from F toward E, any number of points H, I, K, L, M shall be marked. Next, with the distance AH, let two hidden arcs be drawn on both sides from centers F and G. Then, with the distance BH, let two other arcs be described from the same centers F and G on both sides; where these intersect the previous arcs—namely at N—is where the ellipse must be drawn. Next, taking the distance AI, let arcs be made on both sides from centers F and G; then, taking the distance BI, let other arcs be made on both sides from centers G and F; where these intersect the former—namely at O—those will be points of the ellipse. Then, taking the distance AK, let arcs be drawn on both sides from centers F and G; then, taking the distance BK, let other arcs be made from centers F and G, which will be points on the perimeter of the ellipse; for as it was demonstrated in <note>A "porism" is a type of mathematical proposition; Kircher is citing his own earlier proofs or those of classical geometers like Apollonius.</note> Porism 3 of Proposition 6,

<image-desc>A large diagram of an ellipse oriented horizontally on its major axis AB. The focuses (centers) are labeled F and G. Intermediate points I, K, L, M, E are marked between the focuses. Points on the upper and lower perimeter (P, R, Q, N) are determined by the intersection of circular arcs centered at F and G.</image-desc>

where the previous arcs intersect—namely at P—there will be the points of the ellipse. You shall proceed in no different a manner in investigating the other points of the ellipse. Note here that the more points are assigned on AE, the more perfect the resulting ellipse will be; all of which is demonstrated in Porism 3 of Proposition 6.

*Corollary:*

**H**ence it is clear by what method an ellipse may be described using two strings. Again, let the major diameter AB and the minor diameter CX of the ellipse be given; the foci (or points from the comparison made) will be F and G according to the preceding instructions. If, therefore, you tie two strings to the foci F and G so that they are joined at C, a <term>graphium|a stylus or drawing tool</term> moved while keeping the strings taut will describe the desired ellipse ACBX; but more on these matters will be discussed at greater length in what follows.

# EXERCISE III.

## On the projection of circular surfaces of bodies onto a plane, so that
## they may serve the practical uses of sundial drafting.

### CHAPTER I.

## On the true and certain Geometric method by which we teach
## how to assign a straight line equal to any given arc of a circle.

### P R E F A C E.

<margin>The <term>Quadratrix|the squaring line</term>: Pappus attributes the "Admirable" line to Menelaus, but the <term>Quadratrix</term> to Dinostratus, Nicomedes, and Hippias.</margin>
**A**MONG those lines celebrated in the writings of the ancient mathematicians, two hold the first place: the "Admirable" and the <term>τετραγωνίζουσα|Quadratrix</term>. Pappus attributes the Admirable line to Menelaus, but the Quadratrix (or "squaring line") to Dinostratus, Nicomedes, and Hippias. Both were devised for the purpose of squaring the circle. Leaving the former aside, we shall treat here only of the quadratrix. This quadratrix is described by two imaginary motions: namely, that of a radius and that of a line <margin>of spirals and spiral-shaped lines</margin> moving parallel to the base of a quadrant. While these proceed with a <term>ὁμαλῷ|uniform</term> and <term>ἰσοχρονίῳ|isochronous</term> motion <note>moving at a constant speed and reaching their destination at the same time</note>—the radius traversing the quadrant and the parallel line traversing the vertical radius—wherever their common intersection occurs, a line is drawn. This line is called the <term>τετραγωνίζουσα|Quadratrix</term> from its function <margin>the squaring line</margin> of squaring. However, Pappus criticized this invention because it "begs the principle" <note>original: "principium petit," a logical fallacy where the premise assumes the conclusion</note>. For since it is primarily intended to define the point <margin>squaring</margin> of the quadratrix, and that point vanishes before it is even found—and cannot be obtained by any reasoning from the principles of Dinostratus—Pappus rightly rejects it as useless and impossible to describe. The learned Clavius explained this last proposition of the 6th book of Euclid most skillfully; however, because he could not extricate himself from its difficulties, we share here with students of more subtle Geometry what we have attempted regarding this matter.

### Proposition I.

<margin>Presentation.</margin>
*If the arc of a quadrant is continually cut in half, and the side of the quadrant is cut in the same proportion, and a straight line is drawn from the last point of the side's division through the last point of the arc's division to the corresponding tangent line; this line will cut from the tangent a segment equal to the arc of the quadrant produced by that last division.*

<margin>Presentation.</margin>
**L**et the arc of the quadrant be BD, cut in half <margin><term>ἀποτομίας|at the section point</term></margin> at C, and let its side AB also be cut at E. Let the straight line ECF be drawn from E through the point of <term>ἀποτομίας|sectioning</term> at C. I say that this line, in the tangent line DG, cuts a segment DF equal to the arc DC.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a quarter circle arc BCD within a square framework ABDG. Point C is at the midpoint of the arc. A line ECF originates from point E on the vertical side AB and passes through C to intersect the vertical tangent DG at F. Another line HIK originates from point H on AB (the midpoint of AE), passes through point I (the midpoint of arc CD), and intersects DG at K. Horizontal and vertical lines mark sines and complements for calculation.</image-desc>

Let EA be cut in half at H, and from H through I (the midpoint of arc CD), let the straight line HIK be drawn to the tangent DG. It will be that just as arc DC is to DI (the middle to its own half), so DF is to DK. (For we assume here, from the *Cyclometria* of Lansbergius <note>Philippus Lansbergius (1561–1632), a Dutch astronomer and mathematician</note>, that the periphery, the right sine, and the tangent are equal to one another if the sine or tangent of the periphery is to the sine or tangent of half the periphery as the periphery is to half the periphery. For if they were unequal, as demonstrated by Ptolemy in Book I, chapter 9 of the <term>περὶ τῆς μεγάλης συντάξ.|Great Treatise (Almagest)</term> etc., they would be <term>ἀλόγις|irrational</term>; but they are <term>ἀνάλογοι|proportional</term>, therefore they are equal). For in this case, equality always follows proportion, just as inequality follows disproportion. Therefore, by this hypothesis, the segment DF cut on the tangent will be equal to the arc DC, and its half DK will be equal to the half-arc DI. I have chosen to demonstrate this first with numbers.

<margin>Proof.</margin>
Let the radius, or AB, be 10,000,000,000 parts. Let AE be half of these, 1,953,125 <note>Note: The numbers here reflect the high-precision tables used by 17th-century astronomers</note>. Let arc CD be half of arc BCD, that is 45 degrees, where DB is 90. From the tables of sines, the right sine CL of a 45-degree arc is given as 3,067,956, and the sine of the complement EN is 9,999,952,93. If you subtract LN from LC, NC remains: 1,114,831. Therefore, as EN is to NC, so EM (the radius AD) is to MF: 1,114,836. If you add DM (1,953,125) to this, DF will be 3,067,961. Now let AE (1,953,125) and arc DC (45 degrees) be cut in half: AH will be 976,562.5 and DI will be 22.5 degrees. Its right sine or inscribed line is 15,339,80 and its complement HQ is 9,999,988,23. Again, subtracting AH from the sine leaves QI: 557,417.5. Therefore, as HQ is to QI, so HP is to PK: 557,418. If you add DP (976,562.5) to this, DK will be 1,533,980.5. It is therefore clear that the line HIK cuts <margin><term>συνένωσις|the junction</term></margin> DF in half at K. For just as DF is to DK, so is arc DC to arc DI, and DK is equal to DI. Which was to be demonstrated.

Perimeter: 3.14159265358979323846264338328... / $10^{30}$. <note>This is an extremely precise value for Pi, calculated to thirty decimal places.</note>

Following Archimedes with similar diligence, the distinguished calculators Ludolph van Ceulen <note>original: "Rudolphus à Keulen," the Dutch mathematician famous for calculating Pi to 35 places</note> and Christopher Grienberger <note>a fellow Jesuit mathematician and contemporary of the author</note>, a most eminent mathematician of our Society, found the ratio of the diameter to the circumference. However, the method proposed here is much closer than that of Archimedes. Nor is the Archimedean method as simple as ours, because in his work the limits of 3 $10/70$ and 3 $10/71$ <note>These fractions represent Archimedes' famous bounds for Pi: 22/7 and 223/71</note> diverge too widely. From the first limit, the ratio of the diameter to the periphery is gathered as 10,000 to 31,428; from the other, as 10,000 to 31,418, as Lansberg <note>Philippe van Lansberge, a Dutch astronomer</note> also noted. The mean between these, namely 10,000 to 31,418, is not sufficiently accurate. This was noted by Apollonius of Perga, and seen by Eutocius of Ascalon, Philo of Gadara, and other supreme geometers. But so that we may finally see the origin of the <term>squaring curve</term> <note>original Greek: "tetragonizousa," referring to the Quadratrix, a curve used for squaring the circle</note> more clearly, let it be:

### Proposition II.

<margin>Dinostratus</margin>
> *If, in a quadrant of a given circle, a line is drawn from the final point of the section made on the side of the quadrant to a tangent equal to the final arc (whose endpoint is cut by another straight line drawn from the center), then a perpendicular line drawn from the point of section to the base of the quadrant will mark off the base of the quadratrix.*

<margin>On planes</margin>
Let the quadrant ABD be inscribed in the square BAOD. Let the arc of the quadrant BD be continuously divided into two, first at C, then at E. Let the side AB admit this same <term>inequality</term> <note>original Greek: "anomalian," referring here to the proportional division of the line</note> by being bisected first at F, then at G. Then, following the previous steps, let DI be described as equal to the arc ED; and from G, let a line parallel to AD be drawn, which cuts the added line DN at H; and from the center...

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a quadrant of a circle ABD enclosed in a square BAOD. Points C and E divide the arc BD. Points F and G divide the side AB. Horizontal lines are drawn from F and G. Radial lines are drawn from point A to various points on the arc and the curve of the quadratrix. A vertical line segment DI is shown outside the square, corresponding to arc segments. Points are labeled with capital letters A through N.</image-desc>

...by Proposition 4 of Book 6 of Euclid, as AL is to LM, so AD is to DN. However, DN is equal to the arc BCD. For as KL (one-fourth of the radius) is to ID (a straight line equal to one-fourth of the quadrant), so LM (that is, the radius AB) is to DN (a straight line equal to the quadrant BCD). Therefore, as AL is to LM, so AD is to DN—that is, to BCD, the arc of the quadrant—and thus the lines AL, LM, and the quadrant ACD are in continuous proportion. But Dinostratus also demonstrated (as found in Clavius <note>Christoph Clavius, the leading Jesuit mathematician of the 16th century</note>) that the base, the radius, and the periphery of the quadrant are in continuous proportion. Therefore, AL, cut off from LK, will be the base of the quadratrix; which was to be demonstrated.

### Corollary.

Since the base of the quadratrix is to the radius as the radius is to the circumference of the quadrant, and from our demonstration the base of the quadratrix is to the radius as the radius is to the third proportional, it is clear that the perimeter of the quadrant and the third proportional have the same ratio to the radius. Thus, by Proposition 9 of Book 5 of Euclid, the perimeter of the quadrant and the third proportional are equal to each other.

### Problem I.

To describe the <term>squaring curve</term> <note>original Greek: "tetragonizousan," or quadratrix</note>.
Let a rectangle be described from the given third proportional and the radius of the smaller quadrant AD, and let the sides AB and CD be divided into four equal parts, where the arc of the quadrant BE is also divided.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a grid within a rectangle ABCD. A quadrant arc is drawn from A. A series of radial lines and horizontal lines intersect to define points P, Q, R, and S. A smooth curve (the quadratrix) is drawn through these intersection points from B to D. The points on the arc are labeled M, N, O.</image-desc>

Then, through the points on the sides, let the parallel lines FG, HI, and KL be drawn. From the center A, let arcs be drawn through the points of the quadrant which has been divided into four parts. Where the radius AB cuts the parallel BC, and the radius AM cuts the parallel FG, and AN cuts HI, and finally AO cuts the line KL: a curved line drawn through these points will give the quadratrix BPQRD. ...of the helix; with this distinction established between them, however, that the ordered helix is described by equal radial decreases, and the <term>quadratrix</term> <note>A non-algebraic curve discovered in antiquity to solve the problem of "squaring the circle" (finding a square with the same area as a circle) and trisecting angles.</note> is described by unequal ones.

### Corollary I.

Hence it is clear that if a line is drawn from the center of the quadrant **A**, to any point of the quadratrix, for example at **P**, and from here a perpendicular **PS** is drawn to the base **AD**: this normal line **PS** will be equal to the arc **DV**, which **AP** cuts in the quadrant **TD**. For just as **AF** (that is, **PS**) is to **AB**, so **EM** is to **EB**: but **AB** (that is, **DC**), according to the premises, is equal to the arc **DT**: therefore **PS** is also equal to arc **DV**.

### Corollary II.

From this it follows by what reasoning we can assign a straight line equal to a given arc of any circle, inscribed in the **DC** of the quadrant: for arc **TD** is equal to **DC**, by the preceding, and **VD** will be equal to the straight line **DG**, or **PS**, and arc **YD** to line **DL**. Again, if an arc is given composed of the quadrant **DT** and arc **VD**, a line composed of **DC** and **PS** will be equal to it likewise. But if you desire a straight line equal to the arc of quadrant **DT** taken twice, or a semicircle; **AB** taken twice will give what is sought. Thus the arc of quadrant **DT** taken twice together with arc **DX** will be equal to line **AB** taken twice together with line **ID**, and so on for the others.

### Corollary III.

If a quadratrix has been inscribed in a given circle, how it may be allowed to cut it into a given proportion. First, let **AB**, the third proportional, be cut into the given proportion, namely fourfold; let parallel lines **FG**, **HI**, **KL** be drawn through the points of section to the base **AD**; and carefully note the common points of intersection of these parallels with the quadratrix, namely **PQR**. For if you draw straight lines through these from the center **A**, they will give the arc of the quadrant **DT** cut into the given proportion, such that **TV**, **VX**, **XY**, **YD**, the four parts of arc **DT**, are equal to **BF**, **FH**, **HK**, **KA**, the fourths of **AB**. For just as **AB** is to **DT**: so is **BF** to **TV**; and the remaining parts. But **AB**, by the premises, is equal to **TD**. Therefore, **BF** is also equal to the arc **TV**. You will expedite any other given proportion in the same way. And the use of this in Geometry is distinguished. For with its help, any figures are inscribed in a given circle; and the circle and any given periphery of it is divided into a given proportion. Secondly, any angle into a given proportion, and an <term>isosceles triangle</term> <note>A triangle with two equal sides and two equal angles.</note>, each of whose equal angles has a given proportion to the remainder. From here also depends that most intricate problem: *To inscribe any figure in a circle.*

### Problem II.

*Given two unequal circles, to cut off from the one an arc equal to a given arc in the other.*

Let there be in the attached figure the arc of the smaller circle **BC**, and **IK** of the larger: it is asked that **PK** be cut off from the larger arc **IK**, equal to the arc of the smaller **EC**. Since therefore by the premises **FG** is equal to arc **EC**; and **HM** has been assumed equal to **FG**; and this however is equal to **OK**: then **OK** will also be equal to **EC**, according to that common axiom: *Those things which are equal to the same thing, are equal to each other.* <note>original: "Quæ sunt eidem, &c." referencing Euclid’s First Common Notion.</note> Therefore, the arc **OK**, cut off in the larger circle, is given as equal to **EC** of the smaller circle. Which was to be done.

If you therefore quadruple this arc **IS**, the quadrupled arc will be equal to the given circumference of the smaller little arc **BACD**, which was sought. This would be a significant **paralogism** <note>A piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning.</note>, since not all **isoperimetric** <note>Figures that have the same perimeter or boundary length.</note> shapes contain equal areas. A certain mathematician of no small reputation recently fell into this very error. Therefore, the area of Rhombus CXDE is much smaller than the area of the circle with the same perimeter. Nor would the area of the Rhombus become equal to the circle if its individual sides were arranged into a square. We wished to warn the curious reader of these matters first, lest anyone accuse us of a similar error in reasoning.

...the difference of the circle BDCE: for as diameter is to diameter, and radius to radius, so is circumference to circumference. And because circles are usually divided into 360 parts, if this arc, which is equal to the circumference BDCE, is desired in degrees of circle HLI, let it be as AC is to CF, so 360 of circle HLI is to the fourth number. For in this way, the fourth number will count the degrees of that arc which is equal to the circumference of circle BDCE. In the proposed example, we made the angle BAC the angle of an equilateral triangle <note>An angle of 60 degrees.</note>; from which it follows that FC is the sine of angle FAC, and thus half of the <term>total sine</term> <note>original: "sinus totius"; in early modern trigonometry, this refers to the radius of the circle used as a base for calculations, often set at a value like 10,000 or 100,000.</note> AC, so that the ratio of AC to CF is the same as 2 to 1. Therefore, having performed the operation according to the rule of proportions, the circumference HLI will also be double those degrees which are owed to the circumference DBCE; that is, the arc of circle HLI, which is equal to the circumference BDCE, will be a semicircle, which is 180 degrees. I say, therefore, that the semicircle HLI is equal to the proposed conical surface. For if GI is understood to be placed upon AC itself, and the remaining surface of the semicircle placed upon the conical surface, the curvature of this semicircle will necessarily match the curvature of circle BDCE; that is, all points of the circumference of the semicircle HLI will fall upon the circumference of circle CDBE, because the radii drawn from G also match the lines drawn from A to the points of the circumference CDBE.

From this, it follows that the halves LH and LI are equal to the semicircles BDC and BEC, and each of the lines drawn from G to the aforementioned parts of the circumference HLI corresponds to those lines drawn in the cone from the vertex to each degree of the base. This is also to be understood for any other parts, even if they are not whole degrees, provided their ratio to the whole base is given; for corresponding parts will be found for such parts if they are as the whole circumference of the base is to the proposed parts: that is, as the preceding number is to the following, so the degrees of the whole arc HLI are to the fourth; for this will give the point of the same arc HLI corresponding to the part of the base.

### Another very easy method for casting a <term>cone</term> <note>original: "turbinem"; literally a whirl or top, here referring to a conical shape.</note> onto a plane.

**F**irst, let there be a cone ABC, the surface of which must be cast onto a plane. First intercept CA, or CB, the side of the cone, and from center A, let an arc of a circle of any size be described, which shall be BCDEF.

<image-desc>A geometric construction diagram showing the development of a cone into a plane. At the top left, a triangle labeled A B C represents the cone's elevation. <margin>Second, divide the diameter of the cone AB into 14 equal parts, according to the <term>Archimedean ratio</term> <note>The ratio of 22/7 for pi, here expressed as 44/14.</note> of the diameter to the circumference, which is 14 to 44 as given above.</margin>

...or divide only the half into 7. Then, from the intercepted space of the diameter, transfer 11 of such parts (of which the diameter is 14) sequentially onto the arc described separately, beginning from B: for this space divided into 11 parts will be a quadrant on the <term>horizon of the cone</term> <note>The circular base of the cone.</note> AS or SB. If this is quadrupled in the arc, the whole arc BF will be divided into 4 quadrants, as you see, each of which is a quadrant of 11 parts. If, therefore, you close this arc at AB and AF, ABF will be the surface of the <term>whirl</term> <note>The cone.</note> or the given cone. You will achieve the same thing if you designate an arc equal to the circle or base of the cone in the arc of circle BCDEF; which is done by the problem demonstrated on folio 241. By this art, you will transfer any cone onto a plane with almost no labor. Wherefore, let it suffice here to have indicated only the demonstrative reasons.

### On the Projection of Gnomonic Surfaces.

Then transfer the space *a d*, of the quadrant *b a c*, captured with a compass, thirty times according to the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, etc. Having captured 10 of those parts with the compass, with one foot of the compass on point 1 and the other on point 11, let an arc be described; then, with the same opening, let the remaining arcs be described in order through the following points up to 12, as you see. When this is finished, with one leg of the compass placed on 29, 28, 27, and the other in order, let 12 arcs be described which, by intersecting with the previous ones, will form twelve shapes like rays, not unlike the rays <note>or "warps"</note> used by weavers. You will then have the <term>dodecatomoria</term> <note>original: "dodecamoriam"; the division of a sphere into twelve equal segments or gores.</note> of the sphere projected onto a plane. 

<image-desc>Geometric diagrams illustrating the construction of globe gores. The top diagram shows a single almond-shaped segment (dodecatomoria) with points A, B, C, D, E, F, G. Therefore, let a string or a plaster sphere be made of such a size as *b a*, the radius of the quadrant, onto which you should glue the 12 cut-out rays described just before in their proper order, and you will have the prepared sphere. If, however, you divide one of the semicircles *M c* or *O Z* into another 90 parts, and draw arcs from the poles or tips, you will have the latitudes and declinations of the stars, together with the altitudes of the Sun, according to how you have established the poles of the sphere. For six of the said rays will fill the concave or convex surface of an entire hemisphere whose semi-diameter is *b a*, while three will fill one quadrant of the half-circle *b c a*.

### Corollary.
->To project the central equator with twelve hours onto a plane.<-

By the preceding methods, let a straight line be made equal to the semicircle whose semi-diameter is *B a*, which you shall also divide into twelve equal parts. Then, at each of the twelve parts, let lines be drawn on both sides perpendicular to *V X*, of the same kind as *M c*, all of which should be equal to the arc of the quadrant semicircle *B c a*; for the arcs drawn through every three points—such as *M N O* and *O P Z*—will provide the rays, as will be explained more fully in the following books.

### Problem VIII.
->Another way to apply dodecatomoria sheets to globes.<-

**A**rtisans understand the straight line **AB** to consist of twenty parts: **CB** and **CE** each being one part. They take **EF** equal to this **AB**, and with centers **A** and **F**, and intervals **AB** and **FE**, they describe two arcs **DBG** and **DEG**. These constitute one of the twelve <term>dodecatomoria</term> <note>individual segments or "gores" that make up the surface of a globe.</note> to be applied to a globe. For these to be fitted to a spherical surface by application, it is necessary for these flat segments to be stretched in both length and width, such that **DG** becomes equal to one of the arcs **DBG** or **DEG**, and **EB** becomes six times the arc. For the points **D** and **B** <note>the tips of the gore</note> meet at the poles, and six times **EB** must reach the semi-periphery; or, what is the same thing, each individual arc **EB** must correspond to 30 degrees of a <term>great circle</term> <note>A circle on the surface of a sphere that shares the same center as the sphere, like the equator.</note>.

The semi-diameter of that globe is therefore sought in the given parts of **AB** itself; in 100,000 parts, in which the half-circumference is very nearly 314,159—less by only one unit. But first, the arc **BD** must be investigated in those same given parts of the known **AB**, which is done as follows: For whatever **AB** is 20, the arc **BC** is 1 of those same parts. Therefore, where the same **AB** is 100,000, **BC** is 5,000; and consequently, the remainder **AC** will be 95,000, which is the <term>sine of the complement</term> <note>original: "sinus complementi"; known today as the cosine.</note> of the arc **BD**. To this, in the [trigonometric] table, corresponds 18 degrees, 11 minutes, and 40 seconds, which make 65,500 seconds. However, the half-circumference contains 648,000 seconds. Therefore, the proportion of the half-circumference to arc **BD** will be as 648,000 is to 65,500; that is, as 1,296 is to 131. Consequently, if it is made so that as 1,296 is to 131, so 314,159 (the half-circumference in 100,000 parts) is to the fourth...

# OF ATHANASIUS KIRCHER
## PRIEST OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS
# THE GREAT ART
## OF LIGHT AND SHADOW
### *Book Four.*
# VARIOUS METHODS OF TIME-TELLING
## IN WHICH
## ALL KINDS OF HOURS
## ARE DEMONSTRATED BY A SHADOW-CASTING GNOMON
## UPON A BRIGHT FIELD.
## PREFACE.

<image-desc>A decorative historiated initial letter 'P' featuring a landscape with a sun bearing a human face in the sky above clouds and rolling hills.</image-desc>

**P**reviously, I have set forth all those things which seemed required in any way for the perfect practice of the universal science of sundials <term>Gnomonics</term> <note>The art or science of constructing sundials and calculating the time by the position of the sun’s shadow.</note>. Now, order demands that, having left Theory aside for a little while, we turn our attention to practice. While we do this, there will not be lacking mathematicians "of a keen nose" <note>original: "emunctioris naris"; a Latin idiom for those who are sharp-witted or overly critical.</note> who will chime in that we are dealing with a worn-out subject. But I hope I shall very easily evade their criticism when I bring forth things that perhaps were not so well known to them before. Therefore I proceed with confidence; I know for whom I write, and I know what the world now desires in Mathematics; I am not ignorant of what is pleasing to Princes at this time, at whose urging I publish these works, such as they are. 

The insatiable greed of humans for knowing seeks some practical use in human affairs. When they do not find it in speculative Mathematics—whether because of the thorny traditions of the elements or because of the intricate method of proof—it is no wonder that so few are found who devote themselves to such abstract studies. Indeed, what is deplorable is that the late-night labors and monuments of the greatest men are often held in such low esteem that they seem to have prepared the fruit of such great labor not as material fit for subtle minds, but as wrapping paper for fishmongers and perfume-sellers to make into cones <note>original: "cucullos"; refers to the common practice of using discarded manuscript or book pages to wrap fish, spices, or medicines.</note>. Such were the works of *Adriaan van Roomen*; such were those of the most learned *Viète* <note>François Viète (1540–1603), a French mathematician whose work on algebra was foundational but notoriously difficult for his contemporaries.</note>, before they were brought into the light; such are most works that mathematicians deliver regarding Algebra and other more abstract arguments. 

Deterred by these things, I did not wish "to beat the air," as the saying goes; I did not want to expose myself to the insults of the perfume-sellers for the sake of only three or four mathematicians skilled in more hidden science. Instead, I have judged that the speculations of more abstract and subtle Mathematics should be directed toward some utility for human life. Whereas others hide the very use behind I know not what affected obscurity, I labor all the more to make the same a matter of public right, so tempering the materials that a knowledge of subtle theories never excludes use and practice; and I accommodate the style and matter to every kind of person, of whatever profession they may be. 

Therefore, practitioners will find here what they love; there will be objects for mechanics to applaud. I add many things, most of them of greater importance, both new things thought out by me and inventions that will produce for theorists a new offspring of innumerable speculations. Since human curiosity is a lover of variety, I am not content with mathematical "hovels" <note>original: "gurgustiis"; a metaphor for narrow or cramped intellectual spaces.</note>, but often break out into the widest fields of Physics. I have studied to join Nature to Mathematics in such a way that from this kind of marriage, that offspring of inventions might be born which both this present work and others to be published here and there have demonstrated and will demonstrate. You see therefore, unless I am mistaken, O candid Reader, the reason for my undertaking from these things. This being so, nothing remains except that we now set sail upon our purpose with full sails.

### PART ONE.

## CHAPTER I.
->*On the prerequisites for the Sum of Gnomonics.*<-

<margin>The fourfold method of horography.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'Q' featuring a celestial or scholarly scene within an ornate square frame.</image-desc>
**T**he Sum of all Gnomonics <term>Gnomonics: the art or science of constructing sundials</term> is achieved through a fourfold method: Geometrical; Arithmetical (or by tables); Mechanical (or by instruments); and Teretical <note>original: "Teretica"; from the Greek *teretikos*, meaning observational or contemplative</note>, which is performed through observations. And although many have already written entire volumes on these subjects, we have nonetheless wished to set forth here only those things born of our own speculation, or at least those things explained more obscurely by others, through a new and very easy method, with as much brevity and clarity as possible. While we do this, we accommodate ourselves to the capacity of beginners <term>Tyro: a beginner or novice</term> in such a way that anyone will notice that we care for nothing else except that the beginner may achieve his goal in the exercise he has undertaken. Hence, so that all obstacles of difficulty might be removed, we are accustomed to hint at the demonstrations of the proposed problems in few words, or even for the most part to omit them entirely; since we have pursued their principles and reasons separately in the *Apparatus* <note>Referring to a foundational or introductory section of the book</note> using a demonstrative method, to which we refer the more learned Reader. For I know that mixed demonstrations of this kind hinder the thread of the practical procedure <term>pragmatia: a practical task or exercise</term> not a little. Whoever, therefore, wishes to know the reasons for the proposed Problems more deeply, let them turn to the *Apparatus*, where they will find everything demonstrated at length, according to the references placed next to each Problem. Also, so that the beginner might proceed with an unobstructed practice, we have deliberately omitted those intricate repetitions of many characters <note>Referring to complex mathematical symbols or labels in diagrams</note>; I wanted to warn the Reader about all these things beforehand, lest my intention in the manner of proceeding in this work be hidden from him.

<margin>Various uses of the wonderful quadrant.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative historiated initial 'Q' depicting a seated figure, likely a geometer or astronomer, engaged in study.</image-desc>
**W**e call the quadrant "wonderful" because of the admirable uses it has in the construction of shadow-measuring devices <term>Sciatherics: the science of sundials, from the Greek for "shadow-hunting"</term>. It is also called "horographic" <term>Horographus: hour-drawing</term> because with its help, hours of every kind may be inscribed on any surface. Thus, let it be constructed:

Let there be made on any solid and polished material a square AIKL, from whose corner A, as a center, let a quadrant of a circle IK be described. Through the points of its rim <note>limbus</note> divided into 90 degrees, let straight lines be drawn from the center A to the sides KL and IL. You will then have a prepared square, which is of great use in all Gnomonics.

First, if you draw a line BS parallel to the side AI of the quadrant, which intersects all the rays, it will first serve you for composing tables of tangents and secants. Since all the straight lines from the center A are secants, the parts cut off on line BS, corresponding to the arc CB, are tangents; provided the whole radius <term>sinus totus: the "total sine" or radius of the circle</term> AB is considered divided into 100 parts.

Second, it will serve for tables of shadows, both "versed" and "right," <note>Referring to shadows cast on horizontal versus vertical planes</note> if AB is divided into 12 or 10 equal parts to serve as a style <term>style: the rod or pin that casts the shadow on a sundial</term>.

Third, the same line BS, divided by the "six-part" rays <term>hectamorios: from the Greek for "sixth part," used here for specific angular divisions</term>, will serve for delineating clocks of all kinds more quickly than can be said.

Fourth, for the altitudes of the Sun, and consequently for inscribing hours on any perpendicular surface.

Fifth, for the construction of all kinds of portable clocks, as will become clear in the course of the work.

Sixth, the lines IB, RB, FB, EB, OB, CB represent middle cones, whose axes AI,

# Practical Exercise II.

## To construct a gnomonic triangle for any latitude.

<margin>The gnomonic triangle is the foundation of all horography.</margin>
The **principle** and foundation of all Gnomonics is the determined position of the stylus, so that it has its proper distance from the center of the sundial (or the pole) and the equinoctial. And indeed, in all horizontal, vertical, declining, and inclined sundials (if the equinoctial and meridian planes...

### The First Method.

**Number** the latitude of your region in the limb <note>The graduated edge or scale of an instrument</note> of quadrant AKI, carefully noting point F, where the radius AF for the Roman elevation of the pole—42 degrees—cuts the arc IK. By drawing a <term>normal: a line perpendicular to another</term> from F to P, you will have the proposed triangle. For here, the radius AF, cutting the arc of 42 degrees, will be the base of the gnomonic triangle—namely, the total latitude from the center of the sundial all the way to the <term>equinoctial: the celestial equator</term>. FP, however, is the right sine or tangent of the same degree; finally, AP is the sine of the complement of the elevation of the pole at Rome, or the total sine with respect to the tangent of the same. In this base of the gnomonic triangle, let the place and height of the stylus be found thus: Let a normal be drawn from point P (or the right angle) to the base AF; and this will give, in the line PS, both the location of the stylus at S and its determined height. By this method, you will find the gnomonic triangle for any given altitude. For all lines drawn from center A to the arc IK are the bases of gnomonic triangles for each given elevation of the pole. But, so that you may perceive the entire system of gnomonic triangles at a single glance, I will add here a figure constructed for every ten degrees of polar elevation, in

### Second Method.

### Construction of the gnomonic triangle by tangents for horizontal and vertical planes.

**L**et the length of the gnomon AO be 1,000 parts in place of the radius, or the <term>total sine: the maximum value in a trigonometric table, representing the radius of the circle</term>. Take the tangent of the complement of the <term>elevation of the pole: the latitude of the observer</term> in parts of the stylus, and transfer it from A (the location of the stylus) to point B; you will then have the center of the sundial. Again, take the tangent of the elevation or altitude of the pole in parts of the stylus, and transfer it from A (the location of the stylus) to V; you will then have the common intersection of the meridian and the equator. Moreover, the tangent of the 42-degree elevation of the pole is 900. The elevation

This method is the easiest of all, especially if one has prepared the tangents of the altitude of the pole and the equator proper to one's own elevation. To proceed even more easily, take the length of the stylus AO and transfer it several times onto line AN, so that the space AO, corresponding to the stylus, is considered divided into 1,000 or 10 parts; ON into as many, and NM into as many. ### Practical Task III.

### Construction of the triangle for any declining plane.

**W**e shall investigate gnomonic triangles of this kind in two ways. First, Geometrically, or by means of an <term>analemma: a projection of the celestial sphere onto a plane</term>. Second, by sines.

### The first method is as follows:

**L**et there be some plane <note>original: "planum quodpiam"</note> declining 30 degrees from the meridian, or what is the same thing, 60 degrees from the primary vertical. Then, at any point for the size of the hour-lines—namely, at V—the tangent of the complement of the elevation of the pole should be determined, as well as at NA, where the tangent of the elevation of the pole of 42 degrees is determined. You will then have the triangle ANV, in which A is the center of the declining sundial; the triangle ANV, moreover, will be the gnomonic triangle...

**Second**, from point I, let a perpendicular IM be drawn to CI.

## Practical Procedure IV.
### To find the gnomonic triangle upon a declining plane through numbers, or tangents.

Let there be a plane declining by 30 degrees, in which the location of the stylus is C, and the height of the <term>gnomon: the part of the sundial that casts the shadow</term> CO is 1000 parts. Let a line DE be drawn through C parallel to the base of the plane, which will be the horizontal line, in which the tangent of the plane's declination from the south is CB. Therefore, a perpendicular drawn through B to DE will give the 12th hour on the plane; however, a normal line drawn through C, the location of the stylus, will give

the center of the sundial at A. Therefore, on this line AC, given the center of the sundial, you will consequently find the proposed triangle by this industry: and first indeed the inclination of the gnomon, or the distance of the stylus line from line AB, through sines by this ratio. Since the tangent of the complement of the pole's elevation <note>90 degrees minus the latitude</note> relates to the tangent of the stylus's declination as the <term>whole sine: the radius of the circle used in trigonometric tables, often 10,000 or 100,000</term> relates to the sine of the wall's declination; multiply the tangent of the complement of the pole's elevation by the sine of the wall's declination; and the sum divided by the whole sine will give the desired inclination of the stylus line.

->Example of the Practical Procedure.<-

Here in Rome, a certain plane declines 30 degrees toward the East; its right sine will be 5000. The tangent of the complement of the pole's elevation (for 48 degrees) <note>Rome is roughly 42 degrees North; the complement is 48 degrees</note> will be 1111, which being multiplied by 5000 will give a sum, which divided by 10,000 (the whole sine), will give the tangent of the stylus's declination as 555; and its arc is known from the tables of sines as 29 degrees and 58 minutes.

Having obtained the angle of declination, multiply its complement's tangent by the tangent of the wall's declination, and divide the product by the whole sum, and you will have the distance AB of center A from point B of the horizontal line DE. For if you draw a straight line OC from A through C (the location of the stylus), the points A and O, together with the line OC, will give the triangle AOC upon the proposed plane. Nevertheless, this same thing is found through sines thus: multiply the sine of the stylus's declination by the tangent of the complement of the plane's declination (60 degrees), and divide the product by the whole sine, and the result will give the tangent of the stylus's elevation CO. For just as the whole sine is to the sine of the stylus's declination found a moment ago, so is the tangent of the complement of the plane's declination to the tangent of the stylus's elevation, whose degrees the tables of tangents will provide.

->Otherwise.<-

As the whole sine is to the sine of the complement of the pole's elevation, so is the sine of the complement of the plane's declination to the sine of the stylus's elevation, whose arc in the tables of sines will give what is sought.

## Practical Procedure V.
### To determine the gnomonic triangle of the pole's elevation in sundials inclined to the horizon and declining from the horizon.

<margin>Declining and inclining sundials are always horizontal or vertical somewhere else.</margin>

Since sundials inclined to the horizon are nothing other than horizontal sundials corresponding to different latitudes, the triangle corresponding to a certain latitude will be the triangle sought. Thus, in a sundial inclined 5 degrees to the horizon, the gnomonic triangle will be equal to the gnomonic triangle constructed in a horizontal sundial at a pole elevation of 37 degrees. See <term>Theorem: <gloss>original: θεωρ.</gloss></term> 1 of the 1st part, and below, where we treat the inclining sundial. Furthermore, since sundials inclining from the horizon are nothing other than those declining from the vertical, it follows that the triangle of the pole's elevation upon some plane declining from the vertical always corresponds to some sundial declining from the horizon; thus, the gnomonic triangle on a plane declining 30 degrees toward the West from the horizon is the same as the gnomonic triangle on a plane declining 30 degrees from South toward West at a latitude of 48 degrees. You see, therefore, that all gnomonic triangles on any planes [are related] either to the triangles of horizontal planes

### Practical Procedure VI.
#### *To construct a tilting instrument, or a universal declinatory.*

**A**lthough the declination and inclination of planes were treated at length in Problem 2, if those explanations please someone less, we wished to describe here another instrument for them. In this device, as if in a summary <note>original: "anacephalaeosi", from the Greek for recapitulation</note>, they will find everything said there included. Its use can be universal and nearly infinite in the whole of <term>Gnomonics: the art and science of constructing sundials</term>. It is arranged thus:

Let there be drawn on a very solid plate KMNO, a circle QPNR, divided into four quadrants as you see. Upon the center S of this circle, a small beam is inserted, above whose ends LO (which should have a <term>fiducial line: a fixed line used as a reference for measurement</term> in the middle suited for showing the degrees of declination) two other small beams LF and OE are based. Furthermore, the beam LF should have a semicircle divided into its degrees attached at point F. Let there also be a certain flat plate, which has an axis at FE, to be inserted into the center of the semicircle at F and E, so that in these—acting as poles—it can be lowered and raised at the whim of the maker. Let it also have a small screw at X so it can be fixed upon a given degree. At point Y, a sliding <term>cursor: a movable part of an instrument used for alignment</term> α BY is also inserted, so that it can be pushed in or pulled out at the user's discretion. Let the cursor also have an upright quadrant at points B, above whose edge Bγ a movable fiducial line αγ is led out from the center α. To this cursor YB α, at point α, another certain plate X can be attached; the use of which will be explained in the following sections.

### Practical Procedure VII.

### The construction of the sciatheric or horographic rule, and its marvelous use in all of Gnomonics.

**C**lavius, in his new description of the sundial, and Voellus in his *Horologiographia* <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612) and Jean Voellus (1543–1610) were prominent mathematicians who wrote foundational texts on sundials.</note>, mentioned a certain rule; but because they demonstrate its use in a very limited way, I will first teach how to construct a universal one in this place. By doing so, there is almost nothing in the entire art of <term>Gnomonics: the science of sundial making</term> that cannot be accomplished with the help of this rule. Let us come, then, to the matter.

## Analemmatic-Geometric Horography.
### Problem I.

## *Another method using Tangents, much easier and more universal than the previous one.*

**T**ake the parts of the equatorial radius DB, divided into 10 equal parts (specifically, the parts of the total sine), and take the tangents of the hourly distances from noon. Transfer these from the meridian points G and O on both sides onto the touching lines HI and KL. These hourly distances correspond to angles of 15, 30, 45, 60, and 75 degrees. The lines drawn from the centers A of the vertical sundial and B of the horizontal sundial through these marked points will give the hours on the vertical and horizontal planes. Furthermore, the points on lines HI and KL that are equally distant from the meridian, when joined by straight lines, will give the hours on the polar plane and on both meridian planes.

<margin>Equinoctial sundial.</margin>
If, therefore, you first transfer a circle divided into 24 equal parts onto a surface parallel to the equator—which here in Rome is elevated at 48 degrees <note>While the pole is at 42°, the equator is at the complementary angle of 48° above the horizon</note>—you will have an equinoctial sundial arranged to show the hours, provided you have first erected a <term>stylus<note>the rod or pin of a sundial that casts the shadow</note></term> of indeterminate length <term>at right angles</term> <note>original Greek: ὀρθογωνίως (orthogonios)</note> in its center. The proof of this is so evident from the construction itself that it does not need to be stated. Note, however, that this dial is double: an upper and a lower part. On the lower part, it shows the hours when the Sun is in the southern signs; on the upper part, when the Sun is in the northern signs. The numbering of the hours on the lower part will be inverted and positioned opposite to the hours on the upper part.

<margin>Polar sundial.</margin>
Secondly, if you apply the parallelogram HKIL along with the parallel hour lines onto a plane parallel to the sixth-hour circle—or, what is the same thing, above the axis of the world—so that it faces directly south, and a stylus of the same height as DB is erected normally <note>perpendicularly</note> at point E on the 12th hour line, it will show the desired hours from noon and midnight on the polar plane. We gave the proof of this in the third proposition of the Preliminary Exercises.

<margin>Eastern Meridian.</margin>
Thirdly, if you transfer the parallelogram RSIL (a portion of the parallelogram HKIL) onto a meridian surface parallel to the eastern plane, so that the line of the sixth hour exactly corresponds to line CA in the gnomonic triangle (according to whose position it must be erected), and a stylus of the length BD of the triangle is erected normally from E, it will show the hours from midnight on the meridian plane. The logic, being very easy, is self-evident.

<margin>Western Meridian.</margin>
Fourthly, if you transfer the quadrangle PQHK (a portion of the parallelogram HKIL) onto the western surface of the meridian plane above the triangle CDA, so that the line of the sixth hour aligns with the axis of the world (which the line ABC of the triangle represents), and a stylus is erected normally from E with the length BD as before, it will show the hours from noon on that plane.

<margin>Horizontal.</margin>
Fifthly, if you bring the sundial VOX with its hours onto the horizontal plane with the lines extended as far as you wish, a <term>gnomon<note>the part of the sundial that casts the shadow; used here interchangeably with stylus</note></term> erected normally on it will show the desired hours from noon and midnight. The location of the stylus and its height will be found as follows: transfer the space between C and S in the gnomonic triangle CBD from the center of the sundial B onto the meridian line at point S; that will be the location of the stylus, and its height will be SB.

<margin>Vertical.</margin>
Sixthly, if you finally bring the sundial SGT onto a vertical plane, the gnomon will show the hours from noon and midnight. The location and height of the gnomon are found this way: in the gnomonic triangle ABD, transfer the space AT from A (the center of the sundial) onto the meridian line; the end of this line will show the location of the gnomon, and line BT will indicate its length. Since the reasons for each of these are very clear and have been demonstrated by all writers on sundials, we deliberately omit them so as not to waste time on a matter of no difficulty.
