## Procedure II.

->How you may describe the hours from noon and midnight on a polar sundial with one and the same opening of the compass.<-

<margin>Polar sundial.</margin>
**F**irst, from any point on the equinoctial line GH—for example, from B—describe a circle AGHI using an interval equal to the length of the stylus. Divide its lower semi-circumference GAH into six parts using the same opening from points H and G, just as was done in the previous operation.

Second: if you then draw <term>hidden straight lines<note>construction lines</note></term> through the points of the sections GFHI from I and A as centers, you will have points on the equinoctial line XY. Parallel lines drawn through these to the meridian line will give the desired hours. Thus, we have described the hours on a polar plane with a single compass opening, which was the task. Since a meridian sundial differs from a polar one only in the order of the hours, a polar sundial will become an East meridian sundial if you assign the sixth hour to the twelfth, the seventh to the eleventh hour, the eighth to the tenth, and so on for the rest, as is clear from the previous inscription. It will become a West meridian sundial if you assign six to the twelfth, five to the first, four to the second, and so on.

## Alternatively.

**F**irst, the size of the stylus transferred from point B in both directions onto line GH will give two hours: 3 and 9.

Second, the space GH, transferred from either point I or A onto the line XYI, will give 4 and 8 on both sides.

Third, this same space GH, transferred from points 4 and 8 on both sides toward X and Y, will give 5 and 7.

Fourth, this same space GH, transferred from point 4 toward B, will give 11, and transferred from the point of the eighth hour toward B, it will give the first hour. A third part of the line B 4 and B 8 will give the second and tenth hours. The proof of these things will be clear in what follows. Furthermore, if you draw parallels to the meridian line IA through the hour points found on line XY, you will have the hours described from noon and midnight. See the proof of this in the final operation.

->The description of a vertical sundial with a single opening of the compass.<-

Having done this, you will find the hours with one and the same opening of the circle as follows. First, let a circle be drawn at interval DB, which will cut the equinoctial line EF at points 9 and 3. You shall transfer the diameter of this circle from V on both sides onto the line EF, and you will have hours 8 and 4. Moreover, from points 8 and 4, the same diameter transferred further along the same line will give 7 and 5. This same diameter transferred from points 8 and 4 toward the meridian will give 11 and 1. The points 10 and 2 remain, which you will find...

### Practical Procedure IV.

#### Construction of a horizontal sundial using only a single opening of the compass.

**L**et the <term>gnomonic triangle<note>A right-angled triangle used in dialing to represent the relationship between the gnomon's height and the latitude of the location.</note> be appropriately applied to the meridian line, which should intersect NV <term>perpendicularly<note>original Latin: "orthogonos"</note> at point A.

First, from A, with the distance AB, let a circle be described: I say that this circle marks off the 3rd and 9th hours on the equinoctial line VN. For since AG is equal to the straight lines A9 and A3, the angles AS9 and AS3 will be equal; for they are equal to one right angle, therefore each will be a half-right angle, that is, of 45 degrees, and accordingly it encompasses 3 hours from noon. Rightly, therefore, the said circle will mark off the 9th and 3rd hours on VN.

Second, the diameter of the said circle, transferred from S onto NV on both sides, will give the 8th and 4th hours, which I show as follows. For since the diameter is double AB, that is AM, then by the hypothesis it will be M8 and M4. Or what is the same, S8 and S4 are also double the line AB, or AM. And since 4 and 8 are distant from noon by 60 degrees, that is four hours, and the angles AM8 and AM4 encompass the same number of degrees, it is clear that the lines M8 and M4 correctly cut the 4th and 8th hours on VN.

<margin>Vertical dial.</margin>
<margin>Horizontal dial.</margin>

Third, if you then transfer the diameter MS, or its equal M8, further along the line NV from the points of the 8th and 4th hours, it will mark off the 5th and 7th hours for you. For since M5 <term>bisects<note>divides into two equal parts</note></term> the angle EM4, the angle AM5 will consequently be 75 degrees, which encompasses 5 hours before noon. The same must be said for 5 o’clock in the afternoon. We have therefore correctly assigned 5 and 7. If you again transfer the diameter MG from 4 and 8 toward the south, points 1 and 11 will present themselves. There remain, therefore, the 10th and 2nd hours to be sought, which you will have if you draw <term>hidden lines<note>faint construction lines</note></term> from G or M through S in the quadrant M9, or through P in the arc M3: for these will cut the line NV at points 10 and 2; for the 2nd and 10th hour is the third part of the line A8 or A4. If you then draw lines from D through the points found on NV, you will have a horizontal sundial. But if you transfer the intervals between S and the points of the odd hours from those same odd hour points to either side, you will have the points for the half-hours.

<margin>Provided that the quadrants of the hours are available.</margin>

You will also have the quarter-hours if you transfer the interval between the point of any half-hour and point S on either side: all of which practice itself will teach more clearly. Or more briefly: for the half-hours, let either semi-circumference be divided into 12 equal parts; through which, if you draw hidden lines from points M and S, they will cut the equinoctial line NV at points through which lines drawn from D will assign the half-hours. If, however, you divide the semi-periphery into 24 parts and draw lines through them from points M and S, those will give the quarter-parts of the hours on line NV.

To describe the hours from noon and midnight on five regular planes using Tangents.

## Practical Procedure I.

## Practical Procedure II.
Delineation of a polar sundial by Tangents.

**T**he polar dial <note>A sundial where the dial plate is parallel to the Earth's axis; the hour lines are parallel to each other.</note> is of two types: upper and lower. The upper face looks toward the Zenith (or the South), while the lower face looks toward the Nadir (and the North). Both are one and the same; the only difference consists in the reversed order of the numbers, as shown in the figure.

<margin>Description of a polar sundial by tangents.</margin>
Given, therefore, a <term>style<note>The part of the sundial that casts the shadow, also known as a gnomon.</note></term> AB, divided into ten parts (each of which is considered to be further subdivided into another ten or one hundred parts, so that the style consists of 100 or 1000 total parts), you will find the points for these hours with the help of the table placed here. Take the measurement of the style and transfer it several times onto the line AH. Then, take the tangents corresponding to the hours from the table and transfer them from point B onto line XY; for if you draw lines parallel to IA through these points, you will have described a polar sundial. The reason for this is that, since the equinoctial plane is perpendicular to the polar plane, the <term>sixth-part rays<note>original Latin: "hectemorii radii"; these are the 15-degree increments of the sun's hourly movement.</note></term> of the equinoctial projected onto the plane will necessarily be the hour points. Since these rays, when compared to the meridian, create the angles of the Sun's distance from the meridian for each hour, their tangents will necessarily provide the hour points projected onto the equator.

### Scholium concerning the tables of Tangents.

<margin>Note on the table of tangents.</margin>
**S**ince we arrange all the tables of tangents for a style divided into 1000 parts, we have decided that only the leading numbers—that is, those that remain when the units are set aside—should be used, so that we are not forced to divide every line corresponding to the style into 1000 small parts. For example, the tangent for the 11th and 1st hours is 267 <note>Note: In the table and geometrically for a polar dial, the tangent for 11:00 (75° from the 6:00 substyle) is actually 3732. The author here likely uses 267 (the tangent for 15°) as a general example for 1 hour's distance from the reference line.</note>; if you set aside the last two digits, 67, it leaves 2. If you then take 2 parts on the style and an additional <gloss>67/100</gloss> (that is, 67 parts of one unit that has been divided into 100 parts), it will give you the exact same point as if you had divided the style into 1000 equal parts and taken 267 of them for the tangent of the 1st and 11th hours. I would like you to note all of this carefully, as we will use this method in all the following tables.

Since polar and meridian dials are universal—being the same throughout the whole world if the types of hours and their differences are the same—there will be...

### Construction of vertical and horizontal sundials by Tangents.

**L**et there be a <term>gnomonic triangle<note>A right-angled triangle used in dial-making where one side represents the height of the gnomon (the shadow-caster) and the other represents the distance of the hour lines.</note></term> ADB applied to the plane of the vertical dial, whose equinoctial diameter DB is divided into 10, 100, or 1,000 parts: that is, let it be the <term>total sine<note>In early trigonometry, the "total sine" refers to the radius of the circle being used for calculations, often set to a base of 10 for easier division.</note></term>. If, therefore, you transfer the tangents of the hours (along with their half-hours) in parts of DB from the table of tangents, starting from point D onto the equinoctial line, and draw straight lines from the center A through the end points of these tangents, you will have the desired vertical sundial.

### Another method of describing horizontal and vertical dials.

**H**aving drawn a circle ABCD, where AB is the <term>meridian<note>The line indicating true north and south, corresponding to noon on a sundial.</note></term> and CD is the primary vertical, you would describe both types of sundials from the following table as follows. For the 2nd and 10th hour, count 21 degrees and 7 minutes from the same point B, and a straight line drawn from the center through them will give the 2nd and 10th hour; and one must proceed in this way for the rest. For vertical dials, you will take the numbers corresponding to the given elevations of the pole on the opposite side, as the title teaches.

# CHAPTER III.

## Concerning sundials that decline from the South, or from the primary vertical line.

### Proposition I.

<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'O' depicting a figure (possibly a cherub) within an ornate square frame featuring scrolls and foliage.</image-desc>

I. Every vertical sundial is, in some location, a horizontal one, and vice versa. <note>This fundamental principle of gnomonics states that because the Earth is a sphere, a vertical wall at one latitude corresponds to the flat ground (the horizon) at another latitude.</note>

II. Every dial declining from the vertical is, in some location, both a horizontal and a vertical dial.

III. Every inclined dial is, in some location, horizontal and vertical.

IV. Every dial declining from the horizon is some dial declining from the vertical, and consequently horizontal somewhere, so that all dials are contained within all other dials. The gnomonic triangle <term>Gnomonic triangle: A geometric tool used to calculate how the sun's shadows project onto a tilted surface.</term> beautifully teaches which dials are horizontal, or at what elevation of the pole they must be established, upon a declining or inclining plane. I shall clarify this with an example. A dial that is horizontal under a "right sphere" <note>original: "sphæra recta." This refers to the celestial orientation at the Earth's equator.</note> is a vertical, straight, and declining dial under the pole; on a polar plane, it is everywhere inclined to the horizon; on a meridian plane, it declines 90 degrees from the horizon; on a polar plane, it is at a 45-degree angle, both inclining and declining. It is a mixture, composed of both the inclining and the inclined. The same must be said for every other horizontal dial.

Therefore, if someone knows how to construct a standard horizontal or vertical dial, they will be able to describe all remaining declining and inclining dials with almost no effort. We shall resolve this entire business with four problems.

### Problem IV.

*How to mark the hours from noon and midnight on a sundial that declines from the vertical.*

Four pieces of knowledge are required for this task. First, the declination of the wall <note>The "declination" is the angle by which a wall turns away from facing true South.</note>; Second, the line of the index <note>original: "linea indicis." Also called the substyle line, the line on the dial's face directly beneath the shadow-casting pointer.</note>, or the meridian of the declining dial; Third, the position of the equinoctial line; Fourth, the gnomonic triangle above the declining plane, by whose help the hours may later be marked just as in other horizontal dials. We shall first teach how to find each element geometrically, and then arithmetically.

### Practical Method I.

**L**et two lines be drawn on any declining plane at point E, intersecting each other at right angles, ABCD. Let the declining plane be Southern, declining 30 degrees from the South toward the East; its complement is 60 degrees, which is its declination from the primary vertical. First, from point E, let an arc of a circle be drawn at any distance, in which you will count the declination of the plane. Let arc HF be the declination of the wall if it declines toward the East; let HG be the arc of its declination if it declines toward the West. However, on a Northern plane, the declination from the South toward the East will be IL, and toward the West will be LK, in the opposite position to the previous one.

I. With these premises established, let the tangent of the elevation of the pole at Rome (42 degrees) be transferred from E to N; N will be the center of the sundial. Then transfer from E to M the tangent of the complement of the same. The tangent of 42 degrees is 9.00, and the tangent of the complement, 48 degrees, is 11.11. <note>The author is using a unit scale where the radius is 1000; in modern decimals, these tangents are approximately 0.900 and 1.111.</note>

II. You will transfer the tangent EM from E onto the line of the wall's declination EF, specifically at point O; from here, a line drawn perpendicular to CD at point P will give the point through which a straight line drawn from the center of the dial N will give the line of the style <note>original: "linea styli." This is the substyle line where the gnomon is attached.</note>, or the meridian of the declining plane, upon which the gnomonic triangle must be founded.

<image-desc>A complex geometrical diagram illustrating the construction of a declining vertical sundial. A large circle is centered at point E, with a vertical diameter line AB and a horizontal diameter line CD. Points N and M are marked on the vertical line above and below the center. Arcs labeled IL, LK at the top and HF, HG at the bottom indicate angles of declination. Radiating lines from points N and M intersect with horizontal lines (marked with S, T, V, X) and the circle's perimeter, forming the projected hour lines of the sundial. III. A line drawn perpendicular to the style line NPV at point P will mark the equator QR on the declining plane.

IV. On line QR, starting from P towards Q, let the line PG be defined as equal to PO; this will give point G, which, when joined to point N, represents the world axis <note>The imaginary line around which the Earth and stars appear to rotate.</note> above the plane. The line SP, perpendicular to NG, is the diameter of the equator, and ST, perpendicular to that, is the gnomon <term>Gnomon: The part of the sundial that casts the shadow, usually a rod or a triangular plate.</term>, with T being its location. Thus, the gnomonic triangle for the plane is prepared.

V. Therefore, if you transfer PS onto the style line and describe a circle of any size from the end point V, and divide this circle into 24 equal parts, it will intersect the equinoctial line QR at various points. Straight lines drawn from center N through these points will provide the desired hours from noon and midnight on the given declining plane. (Begin the numbering from point X, where line EB and the equinoctial line intersect—this should be carefully noted.)

<margin>
The description of dials declining from the vertical is easiest of all by means of Tangents.
</margin>

I. **L**et there be a straight line AB, drawn in any way to represent the horizontal. On this line, let point C be chosen as the location for the style, and let the perpendicular CD be equal to the length of the style. Then, taking any number of segments on a separate straight line equal to CD (with the first segment divided into 10 equal parts), take the tangent <note>A trigonometric value used here to calculate the length of the shadow's path.</note> for a wall declining 30 degrees from South toward the East. (The tangent of 30 degrees is 5.77 parts of the style's length). Transfer this distance from C: to the right of the style's location if it declines toward the East, or to the left if it declines toward the West, onto the horizontal line AB. Having marked the end point B, take the tangent of the complement of the wall’s declination—namely 60 degrees—which, relative to a style divided into 1000 parts, is 17.74 parts. Transfer this from C to point A in the direction opposite to B. Point B will be a point on the meridian line, and A will be the common intersection of the horizontal line, the equinoctial line, and the 6 o'clock hour line.

# Practical Operation II.

II. Having completed this, on the meridian line EBF, determine from B toward N the tangent of the pole’s altitude, 42 degrees (which is 900 parts, as previously stated). The tangent of the complement of the pole's elevation <note>If the pole is at 42 degrees, the complement is 48 degrees.</note> is 11.11 in terms of the style's units. In the same direction toward F, take the tangent of the equator’s elevation, 48 degrees. Point E will be the center of the sundial, and F will be the point on the meridian through which a line drawn from A gives the equinoctial line AF. From center E, draw a perpendicular EK to AF; this will provide the style line (the dial's own meridian) on the declining plane. If no error has been made, this line must necessarily pass through the location of the style, because its meridian is perpendicular to the dial and passes through the upright style and center E. Furthermore, if a perpendicular CZ is raised from location C equal to the style, lines drawn from E and K through Z will form the gnomonic triangle EZK above the given declining plane, and the 6 o'clock line will be the straight line EA, drawn through center E and A.

III. With these preparations made, the hour lines can be inscribed in two ways: first, on the horizontal line by using tangents <note>In trigonometry, a tangent helps determine the distance along a flat line that corresponds to a specific angle.</note>; second, by the tangents of the hourly distances from the meridian <note>The noon line.</note> on the equinoctial line <note>The projection of the Earth's equator onto the dial's surface.</note>.

<margin>Method for calculating the tables.</margin>
The first method works as follows: from the position of the style C <note>The style is the physical edge that casts the shadow.</note>, transfer the tangents for hours 10, 11, 12, 1, 2, 3, and 4 onto the horizontal line toward the right; however, transfer the tangents for the lines for 9, 8, 7, 6, and 5 toward the left. For if you draw straight lines from E <note>The center or vertex of the dial.</note> through these points marked on the horizontal line, you will have the desired declining sundial. If the wall declines toward the west, the exact same distances should be used; however, the hour numbers must be changed to their complements relative to 12; those whose distances from the style were toward the right will now have their complements toward the right, and vice versa.

I. Take from the table of horizontal arcs proposed above in Problem 3, the degrees of the arcs corresponding to each hour, or their complements for the given latitude of the place.

II. If the sundial faces east, you will add the degrees of the afternoon hour arcs to the degrees of the wall's declination <note>The angle by which the wall turns away from being perfectly South-facing.</note>: but if it faces west, you will subtract the degrees of the wall's declination from the morning hour arcs—or subtract the arcs from the declination itself, if the arcs are smaller. You will record the tangents of these additions or subtractions in tables, as you see we have done in the following table: and by this skill, you will be able to construct tables for any latitude.

The second method, using the tangents of the hourly distances from the style line on the equinoctial, is carried out with the help of the following small table.

### Problem V.
### To mark the hours from noon and midnight on a surface tilted relative to the horizon.

**A tilted** <note>original: "planum"</note> surface is of two types: upper and lower, as we showed in the second introductory theory. You shall complete a surface tilted to the horizon in this manner. Look in the following table to see which latitude's horizontal sundial corresponds to the degrees of the surface's tilt; for a horizontal dial designed for that specific latitude will provide the markings for the upper tilted surface; the lower surface, however, will contain the remaining hours after both six o'clock marks.

If, therefore, some surface is tilted 15 degrees to the horizon, look in the table established for the elevation of the Roman pole <note>The "elevation of the pole" is a historical term for latitude; Rome is approximately 42 degrees North.</note>. In the column for 15 degrees of tilt, you will find the corresponding number 27. This is the latitude of the region for which a horizontal sundial, once constructed, will satisfy the requirements for the desired tilted surface. The table is made by this logic: the tilt of the surface is either equal to the elevation of the pole, less than it, or greater than it. If it is equal, it will be a polar sundial <note>A sundial whose face is parallel to the Earth's axis.</note>; if it is less, subtract the tilt from the elevation of the pole, and the remainder will give the latitude under which a horizontal dial should be built to become the desired tilted dial. If, however, the tilt is greater than the elevation of the pole, the elevation of the pole subtracted from the tilt will give the latitude of the required horizontal sundial. Therefore, if you wish to know what latitude of horizontal sundial is required, subtract the tilt from 42 (the elevation of the Roman pole), and the remainder will give the desired latitude, namely 11. <margin>Construction of the table.</margin>

<margin>How a dial that is both declining and tilted may be made most easily.</margin> From these things it is clear that a polar sundial is one of the tilted varieties. If, however, this polar dial turns away <note>The term "declining" refers to a dial surface that does not face a cardinal direction like North or South.</note> from the circle of the sixth-hour line toward the right axis, it will be simultaneously declining and tilted. If, for instance, it turns 15 degrees from the sixth-hour circle toward the East <note>original: "Ortum"</note>, in this case the intervals of the lines will remain the same. The style <note>The shadow-casting edge.</note> also always keeps the same position relative to the lines; only the hour changes. If, therefore, as we have assumed, this surface turns 15 degrees toward the East, you will assign to the line passing through the center of the style not 12, as in a polar dial, but 11—anticipating by one hour. If it turns fifteen degrees toward the West <note>original: "Occasum"</note>, the number for one o'clock should be placed on the center line of the style, and so on. If it turns thirty degrees toward the East or West, the center line of the style should be labeled as the tenth hour for the former, and the second hour for the latter. If it turns 45 degrees, the center line looking East will be 9, and the West will be 3; and so on until six, according to the following table.

| If a polar dial turns from the circle of the sixth hour always toward the right axis by these degrees: | | Then the center line of the polar dial will be, if it turns East: | | | If it turns West: |

| **Degrees (G)** | | **Hours (H)** | | | **Hours (H)** |
| 0 | | 12 | | | 12 |

| 30 | | 10 | | | 2 |
| 45 | | 9 | | | 3 |
| 60 | | 8 | | | 4 |
| 75 | | 7 | | | 5 |

And from this table, once the degrees are applied to a polar surface turning from the sixth-hour circle upon the axis of the world, a dial that is both declining and tilted can be constructed faster than a word can be spoken. For if, for example, it turns 30 degrees toward the East, you will assign the 10th hour to the center line, 11 to the next, then 12, 1, 2, 3, 4. If it faces West, assign 1 to the center line, 2 to the next, then 12, 1, 2, and so on for the others. Since these things are easy, they require no further explanation.

### Problem VI.

*To plot the hours from noon and midnight on a surface that is tilted from the horizon.*

Since constructing sundials that tilt from the horizon <note>These are known as inclined-declining dials.</note> is essentially the same as constructing a dial that turns away from a vertical wall—provided you use the **complement of the latitude** <note>The complement is 90 degrees minus the latitude of the location.</note> of the place where the dial is being built—we present all the necessary details for you in the following summary table.

| Under the latitude, or elevation of the pole, | Deg. | Sundials tilting from the horizontal, | Deg. | Are equivalent to vertical declining dials, | Deg. | Under the latitude, or elevation of the pole, | Deg. |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| | 10 | | 10 | | 10 | | 80 |
| | 20 | | 20 | | 20 | | 70 |
| | 30 | | 30 | | 30 | | 60 |
| | 40 | | 40 | | 40 | | 50 |
| | 50 | | 50 | | 50 | | 40 |
| | 60 | | 60 | | 60 | | 30 |
| | 70 | | 70 | | 70 | | 20 |
| | 80 | | 80 | | 80 | | 10 |
| | 90 | | 90 | | 90 | | 0 |

Suppose, for example, it is proposed to construct a dial tilted 10 degrees from the horizon at a latitude of 10 degrees (where the complement is 80 degrees). Under this pole elevation of 80 degrees, a dial declining from the vertical by 10 degrees must be constructed to achieve a dial tilted from the horizon by 10 degrees. Similarly, a dial tilted 70 degrees from the horizon at the **latitude of Rome** <note>Specified here as 42 degrees.</note> is equivalent to a vertical sundial declining by those same 70 degrees, but calculated for a latitude of 48 degrees <note>90 - 42 = 48.</note>. Again, a dial tilted 70 degrees from the horizon at latitude 50 is equivalent to a dial declining from the vertical by 70 degrees at latitude 40, just as the table shows you. We have included everything in the fourth column: for the fourth column shows the latitude numbers under which a vertical declining dial should be built so that it is equal to the desired horizontal tilted dial. Thus, the latitudes in the fourth column are simply the complements of the latitudes in the first column. Therefore, anyone who knows how to describe a vertical declining dial from **Problem IV** will also know how to describe one that tilts from the horizon. However, since some differences occur in the triangle of the pole's elevation and its position, I will briefly explain the whole business so that no doubt remains in the curious reader's mind.

I. Let the figure from Problem IV be repeated. Suppose a dial tilting toward the West <note>original: "in Occasum"</note> by 30 degrees is to be constructed at the latitude of Rome. In the figure, instead of the vertical declination, the 30-degree tilt from the horizon must be used. The angle of the wall's declination (FEH) is taken here as the angle of the plane's tilt from the horizon, below the line CD toward point C if the surface faces upward and toward the West; however, if the lower surface faces West, the angle of declination is above the line CD toward D. If the same dial faces East <note>original: "Ortum"</note>, the same angle must be formed above CD toward C; this must be carefully noted.

<image-desc>A complex circular geometrical diagram for sundial construction. It features a large circle with several intersecting chords, radii, and arcs. A central triangle NEM is identified. Various dashed lines indicate specific projections and angular measurements relative to the horizontal and vertical axes.</image-desc>

II. At point M, you must set the angle not for the elevation of the pole above the horizon (as in a vertical dial), but for its complement—an angle of 48 degrees, for instance. Or, what amounts to the same thing, the triangle NEM must be inverted. Once these things are set, there will be no difference in the rest of the operation from the method used to describe the vertical declining dial proposed here, except that the vertical dial described here must be applied to a primary vertical wall according to its inclination to the horizon in order to show the hours correctly. The reason for what has been said is that the horizon...

In this matter, the zone should be conceived as its own <term>vertical circle</term> <note>A circle that passes through the Zenith and Nadir, perpendicular to the horizon.</note>, and the other circles of positions drawn from the poles of that vertical circle as declining from the horizon, much like those that decline from a standard vertical wall. Just as vertical circles (which share the axis of the horizon as their common intersection) relate to the horizon, so do the <term>great circles</term> <note>The largest circles that can be drawn on a sphere, sharing the sphere's center.</note> of position drawn from the poles of the primary vertical relate to that primary vertical itself. However, all these things will be explained more fully in the following sections.

### Problem VII.
#### *Concerning dials that are both tilted and declining, of which there is an infinite variety.*

Since these sundials—which exist in infinite variety—are somewhat complicated because of the sheer number of lines involved, we will conveniently teach the method of constructing them in the following sections using a different method: namely, through direct observation.

---

# CHAPTER IV.
## *Concerning the Gnomonic Sphere, or the method of constructing every kind of sundial by means of a globe or a sphere divided into celestial circles.*

### Problem VIII.
#### *To construct a gnomonic sphere.*

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'I' depicting a person, likely a scholar or astronomer, seated amidst books and scientific instruments.</image-desc>
**O**n a solid, perfectly round sphere, choosing a point **A** to represent the North Pole, let a <term>great circle</term> **B, C, D** <note>In this context, the equator of the globe.</note> be described. After dividing this circle into 360 parts, draw 12 great circles through every

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing a celestial or gnomonic sphere. It illustrates various great circles and lines including the Horizon, Meridian, Equator, and Vertical circles. Points are labeled with letters A through S. The axis of the world (AE) is shown tilted relative to the horizon. Labels like "Horizon", "Meridian Line", "Vertical", and "Equator" are visible within the sphere.</image-desc>

15 parts and the pole **A**. These will divide the entire sphere into 24 equal parts; these will be the <term>hour circles</term> <note>Also known as meridians.</note> meeting at **A** and **E**, the poles of the world. If the size of the globe allows, circles for the half-hours and quarter-hours should also be inscribed, but in a different color so they can be easily distinguished from the hour circles. Add the hour numbers to each circle, and the globe will be ready for use.

Flat surfaces (for we are dealing only with these here, omitting spherical, cylindrical, and conical surfaces on which sundials are often described) are divided into three types.

The first and simplest surface is the **Horizontal**, and a sundial inscribed on it is called a Horizontal or "lying" dial.

The second is the **Perpendicular** surface, which stands at a right angle to the horizon <note>Essentially a vertical wall.</note>. This is of three kinds: it is either built along the East-West line (which cuts the meridian at right angles); or it is built along the North-South meridian line (which cuts the East-West line at right angles); or finally, it is built along some intermediate line between the meridian and the East-West line.

On the first type of surface, a **Southern** dial is described on one side and a **Northern** dial on the other.

On the second type, an **Eastern** dial is described on one side and a **Western** dial on the other.

On the third type—which is also twofold, as it is built either between South and East, or between South and West—we describe **Declining** dials, which turn away from either the South or the North.

The third type of surface is one that is not built at right angles to the Horizon but forms a certain angle of **Inclination** with it <note>This refers to a tilted or slanting surface.</note>. This type is also threefold.

The inclination either occurs along the meridian line, with the bottom edge of the plane joined to the East-West line;

Or the inclination occurs along the East-West line, with the lower edge of the plane joined to the meridian;

Or finally, the inclination occurs along some intermediate line between the Meridian and the East-West lines.

A sundial can be very easily inscribed on any of these surfaces using the globe we put together above. For since any flat surface is part of a great circle passing through the center of the Universe (for the size of the Earth...

## §. I.

### *A Horizontal Astronomical Sundial for 50 degrees latitude.*

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing a horizontal sundial. The circle is labeled with points A, C, E (center), D, and B. Lines radiate from E to the circumference. <margin>Note that all following circles ought to be equal to the circle of the globe; for here they have turned out somewhat smaller due to a fault in the drawing. However, it corrects the space if you describe a circumference from the same center of circles equal to the circumference on the globe, about which we thought you should first be advised.</margin>

To describe a horizontal sundial, therefore, a circle must be described on a plane parallel to the horizon, which should be made of the same size as the <term>great circle</term> of your globe. This will be done if the distance of sixty degrees is taken with a compass on the globe's equator; with that opening of the compass, which gives you the semi-diameter of the sought circle, let circle **ACBD** be described from center **E**. This circle having been divided into four equal parts by two diameters at right angles, **A** and **B** will be the <term>meridian line</term>, and **CD** will truly be the line of the sixth hour. Then, transfer the distance **GI** from the globe into the circle described on the plane from **B** to **F**, and from **B** to **G**: the lines drawn from the center **E** through **F** and **G** will be the one-o'clock hour in the afternoon. Similarly, transfer from the globe the distance **G, K** into the same circle from **B** into **H**, and from **B** into **I**: the lines drawn from the center **E** through **H** and **I** will be, one the hour line of ten in the morning, the other the hour line of two in the afternoon. The same must be done with the remaining lines.

For the erection of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of the sundial that casts the shadow.</note>, let there be transferred

from the globe the arc **H, A**, which is the <term>elevation of the pole</term> <note>The latitude of the observer’s location.</note> of your place, into the flat circle from **B** to **K**; the line drawn from **E**, the center of the sundial, to **K** will show you the angle at which the <term>axis of the world</term> <note>The line around which the heavens appear to rotate, which the gnomon must parallel.</note> ought to be raised above the meridian line.

## §. II.

### *A Vertical Astronomical Sundial for 50 degrees latitude.*

For surfaces of the second kind—those which are indeed perpendicular to the Horizon—and especially for those raised on the <term>Oriental</term> <note>East-West</note> line, let there be described from **G** or **H** (the common intersection of the Meridian and Horizon) through point **F** of the vertex, a

great circle **F, C, P**; this will represent the said surface to us. Let its intersections with the hour circles be **F, Q, R, S, T, V, C**, which will give the vertical distances of the common hours from the meridian line. To delineate a vertical sundial, therefore, let a circle again be described on a plane, equal to the great circle of the globe in the manner we have said: let it be **A, C, B, D**. Having divided it into four parts by two diameters at right angles, the line **AB** will again be the meridian, and **CD** the line of the 6th hour. Therefore, transfer the distance **FO** from the globe into the circle described on the plane from **B** into **F** and into **G**; the line drawn from the center **E** through **F** will be the one-o'clock hour in the afternoon; through **G**, however, the eleven-o'clock hour in the morning. One must act no differently with the remaining hours.

For erecting the gnomon, let the arc **FA** (which is the complement of the pole's elevation) be transferred from the globe from **B** to **K**; the line drawn from **E** through **K** will show the angle at which the axis of the world ought to be raised above the meridian line.

### §. III.

### *An astronomical declining sundial for 50 degrees latitude.*

**T**o describe the third species of these surfaces—those perpendicular to the horizon which rise from a line intermediate between the Meridian and the East—it is first necessary to know how much they <term>decline</term> <note>original: "declinant"; "declination" in sundialling refers to how many degrees a vertical wall faces away from true South or North.</note> from the Meridian toward the West or East. Once this is known, let the <term>complement of the given declination</term> <note>The angle remaining when the declination is subtracted from 90 degrees.</note> be numbered on the circle of the Horizon of our globe, starting from its common intersection with the meridian **G**: to the right if toward the East, or to the left if toward the West, as far as **L**, for example. Then, from **L** as a pole, let a <term>great circle</term> <note>A circle that shares the same center as the sphere, dividing it into two equal halves.</note> be described through **F** and the vertex **P**. By this method, in all planes—whether they are only declining, or both inclined and declining at the same time—the distance of the <term>substyle line</term> <note>original: "substylaris"; the line on the sundial's face directly beneath the gnomon or "style."</note> from the meridian, and the height of the <term>Axis</term> <note>The gnomon or rod that casts the shadow.</note> above the substyle must be investigated. I wished to advise this here so that it need not be repeated hereafter.

It should be noted, moreover, that the meridian line, on all surfaces perpendicular to the horizon, is itself also perpendicular to the horizon or to its level.

### §. IV.

### *A sundial inclined to the Horizon for 50 degrees latitude.*

**S**urfaces of the third kind, which are <term>inclined</term> <note>original: "inclinatæ"; a dial plate that is not perfectly horizontal or vertical, but tilted like a roof.</note> to the horizon, are marked out in this manner.

<image-desc>Two circular geometric diagrams for sundial projection. The left diagram (labeled with A, B, C, D) shows a declining dial with a "Stylus" and numbers 1-12 along the bottom arc. The right diagram shows an inclined dial with radiating lines originating from a center point labeled A¹² and numbers 1-12 around the perimeter.</image-desc>

<margin>See the figure of the gnomonic globe</margin>
**FOP** will be the circle on the globe representing the given surface. Let its intersections and distances with the hour circles be **F, Y, Z, a, b, c, d**. In the circle **A, C, B, D**, the declining sundial shown in the figure will be described by exactly the same method we taught for the horizontal and vertical dials.

To erect the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of the sundial that casts the shadow.</note>, one must first seek the substyle line, upon which the gnomon must be raised. In horizontal dials and all others directly facing the South or North, that line is one and the same as the meridian line. In declining dials, however, it is investigated thus: From the pole to the circle representing the given plane, let an arc of a great circle be drawn perpendicular to that circle, **A, e**. The arc **F, e** will be the distance of the substyle from the meridian; and **A, e** will be the quantity of the angle by which the Axis is to be raised above the substyle.

Thus, in the attached figure of the declining sundial, the arc **F, e** is transferred from **B** into **H**, and the arc **A, e** from **B** into **K**. The line drawn from the center **E** through **H** will be the substyle line; the line drawn from **E** through **K**, however, will give the angle **HEK**, at which the axis must be raised above the substyle.

If the inclination occurs on the meridian line, let it be numbered from the vertex **F**; toward the equator if the surface faces South, but toward the pole if it faces North (we are numbering the given inclination of the surface toward the equator; by "inclination" I mean the angle which the surface itself makes with the horizon) as far as **f**. From that point, as if from a pole, the great circle of the sphere **B C, h** is described, which represents the given surface. Its intersections with the hour lines are transferred to the plane by the same method we taught above. The Gnomon is raised on the meridian line so that it forms an arc with it equal to **A, h**.

### §. V.

### *A sundial inclined to the primary vertical for 50 degrees latitude.*

**I**f, however, the inclination occurs on the Eastern line <note>The line representing due East on the horizon.</note>, that too must be numbered from the vertex **F**, not on the meridian, but on the Eastern circle (which they usually call simply the <term>vertical</term> <note>The Prime Vertical, an imaginary circle passing through the Zenith and the East and West points of the horizon.</note>), as far as **i**. From **i**, the end of the number, as if from a pole, the circle **G, l, H** is described, which will give you the hour distances.

# §. VI.

### A declining and inclined sundial for 50 degrees latitude.

**I**f, finally, an <term>inclination</term> <note>original: "inclinatio"; the tilt of the sundial's face away from the vertical plane.</note> occurs on some line intermediate between the Meridian and the East; then first that line of <term>declination</term> <note>original: "declinatio"; the angle at which a vertical wall faces away from true South.</note> must be designated, which is done through the known declination of the surface in the manner described above. Let circle F, O, P represent this, and in it, starting from the vertex F, count the inclination of the given surface as far as M. From M, without a number, let a <term>great circle</term> <note>A circle sharing the same center as the sphere, dividing it into two halves.</note> n, m, p be described as from a pole; this will give the required distances of the hour lines from each other and from the meridian.

To construct the sundial from this, a circle should again be described on the proposed plane, equal to the great circle of the globe. Because the position of the meridian line is uncertain on these surfaces, a line parallel to the horizon must first be marked through the center of the described circle. Taking the arc IL from the globe (which is the arc of the circle representing the sundial's plane, intercepted between the meridian and the horizon), let it be transferred from the common point of intersection of the circle and the horizon. The line drawn from the center of the sundial through the end of this arc will be the meridian of the proposed plane. Then, by transferring the distances of the hour lines from the meridian onto the circle on both sides in the manner already frequently taught, the declining and inclined sundial will be drawn, which was the task. The location of the substyle line and the height of the axis must be investigated as before. We have omitted the figure here because it was poorly engraved by the Sculptor; however, the Reader will easily understand it if he correctly compares this with the preceding sections. From this, it is easy to see that it is not strictly necessary to take the distances of the hour lines from the meridian circle when making sundials; they can also be measured from the horizon or any other great circle described on the globe, provided that circle is first properly drawn as a straight line on the given surface. Note also, Reader, that we have established these sundials for 50 degrees of altitude—the central meridian of Germany—but the measurement of the arcs of the globe projected optically does not perfectly correspond to the intervals of the circles except on a material and solid globe. I wanted to warn you of this first, lest you might accuse us of committing some error.

## On constructing sundials of all kinds very easily through observation.

### Preparation I.

### The projective instrument, or Observational instrument.
<note>original: "Instrumentum καταπτητικὸν" (kataptētikon); from the Greek for looking down or falling upon, referring to an instrument used for geometric projection.</note>

**L**et a board be prepared, which we shall call the "horographic instrument," made of polished wood or any other hard, solid, and polished material, marked here with the letters ABCD. On any side, a part of the board E should stand out, fashioned into a round or square shape. Furthermore, the board ABCD must be fixed at the back at center H upon a versatile globe N, so that the board can be conveniently turned in every direction and, if necessary, fixed in any position with a pulley S. Thus you will have the prepared instrument, by whose help you will delineate the given lines of the celestial circles on a given plane or surface faster than words can say, in the following manner.

### Problem IX.

### To delineate astronomical hours on the surfaces of the five regular solids in a single operation.

**W**e shall demonstrate the practice using only astronomical hours; by following this method, anyone can later inscribe any other lines on the aforementioned planes in a similar fashion.

### Practice I.

### To describe a tetrahedral sundial.

**L**et a sundial first be delineated on each of the sides of a <term>tetrahedron</term> <note>A pyramid with four triangular faces.</note>; first, you will fix the tetrahedron upon the surface of the table so that it cannot be moved from its place. Ensure that one side faces directly toward the south, and another cuts the meridian line EV on the <term>isogonal</term> <note>original: "isogonos"; having equal angles</note> plane. On each side of the tetrahedron, fix <term>styles</term> <note>The pins or rods of the sundials.</note>—whether straight, slanted, long, or short, it matters not—as the convenience of the side for receiving the sun's rays allows. This being done, expose this system to the shining sun at any time of day, and rotate it until the gnomon of the <term>archetype</term> <note>The master or model sundial used as a reference.</note> sundial precisely touches the meridian line, or the twelfth hour of Cancer ♋. Without delay, mark the shadow tips of the gnomons on each illuminated side, labeling each with the hour 12 according to the archetype; for when the sun is positioned in Cancer at the 12th hour, the shadow of the styles will fall on the marked points.

Then, by rotating the entire system, move the shadow of the archetype gnomon over the remaining hour points in Cancer ♋. In addition, mark the shadow tip of the gnomon on each side of the tetrahedron, labeling each with the hours corresponding to the archetype; this is the first observation.

Again, let the entire <term>sciatheric</term> <note>original: "sciathericum"; relating to the use of shadows to tell time.</note> system be rotated (this is what we call the entire assembly of the table with the archetype and the solids upon which we propose to describe the shadow-work, fixed to the table) until the shadow tip of the gnomon falls on each point of the Tropic of Capricorn ♑ on the archetype. At the same time, mark the shadow tip of the gnomons fixed to the sides of the tetrahedron, labeling each point with the hours corresponding to the hours of the archetype. By drawing straight lines through the points of one and the same hour noted in the first and second observations, you will produce the required hours on the sides of the tetrahedron. In this manner, you will be able to inscribe hours on pyramids of all kinds—four-sided, five-sided, or six-sided—with almost no effort.

<margin>What is a sciatheric system?</margin>
<margin>What a tetrahedron is, and how it is composed.</margin>
<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing the net of a tetrahedron, composed of four equilateral triangles joined together.</image-desc>

A tetrahedron is a solid body bounded by four equal <term>isopleural</term> <note>equilateral</note> triangles. Therefore, if four equal equilateral triangles are fashioned from some material and arranged as you see in this figure, the desired body will be created from them if they are properly folded together.

### Practice II.

### To describe a cubic sundial.

<margin>What a cube is and how it is composed.</margin>
**A** cube is a solid figure contained within six equal squares. Thus, if six squares are projected onto a plane, as you see in this figure, and each is cut out and properly joined together, a cube will be formed. On its sides, you shall complete the descriptions of the celestial circles as follows.

I. Since the side of the cube BF represents a vertical plane facing South, and its opposite faces North; while BG represents the meridian plane of the West, and its opposite the meridian plane of the East; and finally GE represents the horizontal plane: 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing the net of a cube, composed of six squares arranged in a cross shape. The squares are labeled with letters: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H.</image-desc>

First, sundials will be described on each side if you inscribe the proper sundial on each plane according to the operations used in the preceding sections.

II. Indeed, by observation, you may complete the dial-writing on each side of the cube in exactly the same way we used for the inscription of the Sciatheric tetrahedron. Since this matter is very clear, it does not require an example.

## Practice III.
### Describing an octahedral sundial.

<margin>What an octahedron is, and how it is constructed.</margin>
An **o**ctahedron is a solid figure contained within eight equal equilateral triangles. It is constructed thus: let eight equal <term>isopleur</term> <note>original: "isopleurae"; meaning equilateral triangles.</note> triangles be made from some solid material, and let them be arranged as the figure indicates. When the sides of this figure are properly folded together, it will constitute the desired <term>octahedron</term> <note>A three-dimensional shape with eight faces.</note>.

<image-desc>A woodcut diagram showing the geometric net of an octahedron, consisting of eight equilateral triangles arranged in a staggered row (four pointing up, four pointing down) forming a parallelogram-like shape.</image-desc>

<margin>The nature of the planes of this body.</margin>
In this body, one of the eight sides will always be a horizontal plane, while the rest will be either inclined toward the horizon or declining from it. If on the horizontal plane one side of the triangle represents the meridian line, the two sides—the Eastern and Western—will be parallel and declining 60 degrees from the horizon; the remaining sides will be simultaneously declining and inclined toward the horizon. Therefore, once this body is fixed upon the <term>horographic table</term> <note>The workspace used for calculating and drawing sundials.</note>, you shall position it so that one of the sides of the horizontal plane coincides with the meridian line EV on the table. You will easily achieve this if you apply a plumb line to the extreme points of said side and move it back and forth until the plumb line touches the meridian line EV on both sides.

Once this is finished, you will describe the hours on each of the sides of the octahedron (which should first be fitted with their own <term>styles</term> <note>The pins or rods of the sundials that cast the shadow.</note> proportional to the size and capacity of the surfaces) in exactly the same manner using the master sundial as we showed in the preceding sections.

## Practice IV.
### Describing a dodecahedral sundial.

<margin>What a dodecahedron is, and how it is constructed.</margin>
A **d**odecahedron is a solid figure contained within twelve equal equilateral pentagons with equal angles. You shall construct it thus: let twelve equilateral pentagons be constructed from some material, as you see here; if you fold these correctly together, the desired <term>dodecahedron</term> <note>A twelve-faced solid.</note> will emerge.

<image-desc>A woodcut diagram showing the net of a dodecahedron, consisting of twelve regular pentagons. One central pentagon is surrounded by five others, and a second identical cluster is attached at one edge.</image-desc>

This body admits no other regular plane besides the horizontal one; rather, all will be either inclined toward the horizon, declining from it, or both declining and inclined simultaneously. If any side of the horizontal pentagon is made into the meridian line, the pentagon facing the West will decline 35 degrees above the horizon, and its lower opposite will always be parallel to the upper one. The remaining pentagons facing the <term>Zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly above the observer.</note> will be mixed—simultaneously inclined and declining from the horizon from the South and North toward the East or West—by as many degrees as the angle of the pentagon comprises, namely 72. The pentagons facing the <term>Nadir</term> <note>The point in the sky directly below the observer.</note> are the lower ones, simultaneously inclined and declining from the horizon, turning from South to North and toward the East or West.

<margin>The nature of the sides.</margin>
If, however, one side of the horizontal pentagon is positioned on the six o'clock hour line—that is, if it cuts the meridian at equal angles—the pentagon facing South will be inclined 72 degrees above, and its opposite and parallel lower one facing North will be the same. All the others will be mixed, always inclining by 72 degrees either from the South and North toward the East and West, or from the horizon.

Therefore, you shall position the dodecahedron fixed upon the sundial table and equipped with styles so that one side of the horizontal pentagon corresponds to the meridian line EV on the table, or to the six o'clock hour line on the same table. Once this is done, you will inscribe the hours on each of the pentagonal surfaces with the help of the master sundial, in exactly the same way as we taught in the first practice. Meanwhile, this should be noted: the smaller the <term>gnomons</term> <note>Another term for the styles or pins that cast the shadow.</note> used, the more hours can be inscribed on the said planes.

## Practice V.
### Describing an icosahedral sundial.

<margin>What an icosahedron is, and how it is constructed.</margin>
An **i**cosahedron is a solid figure contained within 20 equal equilateral triangles. You shall construct it thus: let 20 triangles be described on some solid material in the order and position that appears in the figure; these, when lightly scored and folded, will constitute the proposed <term>icosahedron</term> <note>A twenty-faced solid.</note>.

<image-desc>A woodcut diagram of the net of an icosahedron, composed of twenty equilateral triangles arranged in a central double row of ten triangles with two flaps of five triangles each on the top and bottom.</image-desc>

All of these are [inclined] from their primary circles—the vertical, meridian, or horizon—by 30 [degrees].

### Problem X.

**To inscribe hours on irregular bodies.**

*How to inscribe hours on the concave or convex surface of a cylinder or column, as well as on a parallelepiped, and a concave or convex pyramid.*

**P**lace a hollowed-out cylinder ABCD—with its axis ending in the center to serve as a gnomon, and also equipped with a style on the exterior surface—

<image-desc>A woodcut diagram on the right side of the upper text block showing a section of a cylinder (labeled a, b, c, d, s) with numbered radial hour lines (1 through 12) and a shadow cast from a central point.</image-desc>

Then, rotate the system back and forth on the table until the shadow of the archetype's gnomon touches all the hour points of the Tropic of Cancer <note>original: "♋"</note>. At the same time, carefully note where the ends of the shadows fall on both surfaces of the cylinder, just as was done in the previous steps. Then, rotate the system again so that the shadow points on the archetype reach the Tropic of Capricorn <note>original: "♑"</note>; or, if those cannot be reached on that dial, the points should be noted on the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The celestial equator.</note> or any other Northern parallel. Mark the points on both surfaces of the cylinder accordingly. If you join these individual points—each

corresponding to one and the same hour—with a straight line, you will have the hours inscribed on the surfaces of the given body. You shall proceed by this exact same method in delineating a parallelepiped sundial (or prism) and a pyramid of any number of sides. See the diagrams of the prisms and pyramid placed here.

### Demonstration of the operation performed.

**F**rom this it is clear that no body can be so irregular that hours cannot be inscribed upon it by the stated method. Because we shall speak at length about this in the following sections, we only wished to briefly introduce the technique here. The demonstration of this business is very easy. Since all these bodies are fixed upon the same horizontal plane, imagine to yourself that the Sun stands still, and in place of the Sun, this entire complex of shapes moves. Since the motion of the system is made according to the intervals of the hours described on the archetype, this motion produces the same effect on the shadows across the different planes of the bodies as the rays of the Sun would do by projecting the shadows of gnomons on different stationary planes. For what the Sun's motion produces on the stationary surfaces of bodies, the system—

<margin>Demonstration of this description.</margin>

—being rotated toward a seemingly stationary Sun produces, with the shadows of the gnomons projected on the various surfaces in equal measure to the movement of the archetype's shadow. Secondly, if the system is inclined so that the archetype shadow runs through the Tropic of Cancer, the Sun will have the same elevation above the table at that time as it does when it truly and realistically describes that Tropic above the horizon of the place where the sundial is being made. The same must be said for any other parallel. Therefore, since the shadows of the remaining surfaces move uniformly with the motion of the archetype shadow, the same lines will necessarily be delineated on all of them: namely, the Tropic of Cancer if the archetype shadow follows Cancer, or the parallels of Leo and Gemini if the archetype shadows run through them; and let the same judgment apply to all others. I said "toward a seemingly stationary Sun" because this entire operation must be performed in that momentary space of time during which it is unlikely the Sun has moved perceptibly. For if you were to delay during the operation, the sundial would not be free from error. Let these remarks suffice regarding sundials made through observation.

# CHAPTER VI.
## Concerning the Sciatheric Ruler,
### By whose benefit all kinds of sundials may be constructed.

<note>The term "Sciatheric" comes from the Greek words for "shadow" and "hunting"; it refers to the science of shadow-tracking, or gnomonics.</note>

#### Problem XI.

->**Given the Sciatheric Ruler, to inscribe astronomical hours upon any given plane.**<-

##### Practical Exercise I.

->***To draw a horizontal astronomical sundial.***<-

###### Rule I.

**H**aving drawn two straight lines at center N, intersecting at right angles, let CD represent the equinoctial line <note>The east-west line on a sundial.</note> and AB represent the meridian <note>The north-south line.</note>; on the <term>latitude scale</term> <note>A specialized graduated scale used to adjust for the user's distance from the equator.</note> inscribed on the Ruler, take the elevation of the pole <note>The local latitude.</note> corresponding to your region, intercepted between points S and Y, and transfer it from point N of the sundial toward B; this B will be the designated center of the horizontal sundial.

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram illustrating the construction of sundials. It features a central rectangle containing several horizontal scales. Above the rectangle is a triangle with its vertex at point A and base on a line containing points C, N, and D. Numerous lines radiate from A and N to markings on the horizontal scales. To the left of the rectangle are the labels "VERTICAL:" and "HORIZONTAL:". To the right are the labels "ZONAL:" and the letters "M" and "Y". Inside the scales are markings for "east," "west," and "Latitude Scale." There are numerical markings for latitudes 42 and 48 degrees.</image-desc>

###### Rule II.

**A**pply the <term>horographic ruler</term> <note>A specialized instrument for drawing sundials, also called a Sciatheric Ruler.</note> by its side KBM upon the equinoctial CD on the dial, so that point B of the ruler corresponds exactly to point N of the sundial. Then, with the ruler remaining in this position, mark the points on the line CD according to the hour points inscribed on the ruler. 

To each of these points, add the corresponding hour number; for lines drawn from the center of the sundial (B) through these points will provide the desired horizontal sundial.

###### Rule III.

**T**he method for erecting the <term>style</term> <note>The gnomon or blade that casts the shadow.</note> is as follows. At the base of the gnomonic triangle—or what is the same thing, by dividing the line NB in half at point I—place the compass at I and describe a circle that touches the lines CD and KM at points N and B. Then, from point N onto the circumference of this circle, transfer the distance intercepted between N and the third (or ninth) hour points on both sides, as you see done at PQ. If you draw a straight line through these two points, it will intersect the line NB at a point that will be the location of the <term>gnomon</term>; its height, however, will be terminated at P or Q. Thus, what was proposed has been achieved.

##### Practical Exercise II.

->***Drawing a vertical sundial by means of the ruler.***<-

<margin>Finding the style.</margin>

**I. H**aving drawn, as in the previous exercise, two lines—the meridian and the equinoctial—either anew or using the same lines AB and CD for both sides of the dial: on the latitude scale of the ruler, take the elevation of the pole for your region (for example, 42 degrees) intercepted between S and X, and transfer it from N toward A.

**II.** With the ruler applied as before, mark the hour points on CD; for straight lines drawn through these from point A will provide the vertical sundial. You will find the location and height of the style in this way: draw a circle between N and A, just as we did before for the horizontal sundial, and on its circumference transfer the distance intercepted between N and the third (or ninth) hour point on both sides, namely at V and Z. A straight line drawn through these will intersect AN at O, the desired location of the style, the length of which will be OZ or VO.

### Practical Exercise IV.
### To draw a polar sundial.

I. Two lines having been drawn, as was done for the horizontal sundial, apply the ruler above the line ENB so that point B of the ruler corresponds exactly to N. If you were to erect a square plate at the 12th hour in place of a <term>style</term> <note>The metal pin or blade of the sundial.</note>, with a height equal to the width of the ruler, it would show the desired hours on the situated ruler.

### Practical Exercise V.
### To draw an equinoctial sundial.

I. Let a circle be made on any plane, described with an interval of the width of the ruler, divided into four quadrants by its diameters GO and MN; GEO will be the line of the twelfth hour, and CD will be the line of the sixth hour. Any circle divided into 24 equal parts will give the desired sundial, if you apply it to the given plane so that 12 corresponds to the meridian; indeed, by means of the <term>gnomonic ruler</term>, you will accomplish this with almost no effort. Apply the ruler at its point S to the center of the given plane. See the figure for Chapter 2, Problem 1.

II. By applying the ruler at points G and O, the points of the hours should be marked on the tangent lines HI and KL; for from these, lines drawn from the center of the circle E and ending at the circuit of the semicircle NCBD will give the desired equinoctial sundial, as the figure shows. The style erected from center E is of infinite magnitude <note>meaning it represents a line of indefinite length rather than a fixed point</note>, for it represents the axis of the world, and it will show the hours upon a plane applied to the equator, so that the line of the twelfth hour corresponds exactly to the meridian line.

A line drawn through this point parallel to line CD will give the horizontal line of the sundial. Thus we have described the declining dial, which was the objective.

# Practical Exercise VII.
## To construct an inclined astronomical sundial.

Note first: this plane can have a double aspect. For the angle of its inclination either leans toward the North or toward the South. If the angle of the plane with the horizon leaning toward the North is equal to the angle of the pole's elevation <note>The local latitude</note>, the inclined plane sundial will be the same as a polar sundial. If, however, the angle leaning toward the South is equal to the complement of the pole's altitude (that is, the altitude of the equator), the inclined sundial will be the same as an equinoctial sundial.

Note second: If the upper part of the plane, facing South and the <term>Zenith</term> <note>The point directly overhead</note>, has an inclination less than the altitude of the pole: subtract the degrees of inclination, and the remainder will be the altitude of the pole above the plane, according to which a horizontal dial must be drawn to produce the inclined dial. For example, suppose a plane is inclined by 30 degrees, upon which a sundial must be described; subtracting 30 from 42 (the elevation of the pole at Rome), 12 remains. Therefore, if you describe a sundial for the latitude of 12 degrees, you will have the dial inscribed on the given inclined plane. If, however, the inclination exceeds the altitude of the pole—say, for example, it is 50 degrees—you should subtract 42 from 50, and the remaining 8 will give the latitude of the region...

### Practical Procedure II.

->To inscribe hours from sunrise and sunset on a vertical plane.<-

->The drawing of the hours from sunrise.<-

<margin>How the Babylonian hours are to be inscribed.</margin>
**I**f you wish to inscribe the hours from Sunrise <note>Known as Babylonian hours, which begin at dawn.</note> on the same dial, let all the points of the hours marked on line AE be transferred from A toward F on the other part of the sixth-hour line, along with the double series of hours. For if you connect the points 7 and 7 on the equinoctial and the straight line of the sixth hour, that will give you the 1st hour from Sunrise; if you connect 8 and 8, you will have the 2nd from Sunrise; if 9 and 9, you will have the 3rd, and you will proceed with the rest just as in the previous description of the hours from Sunset. The 12th hour will be common to both dials. If, however, you wish to provide the 11th hour from Sunset, you shall join point 7 on line AF with the point for the fifth hour on the equinoctial, for that will give the sought-after hour; for the 10th from Sunset, point 8 on line AF joined with 4 on the equinoctial will give the result; and so on for the others. You shall follow the opposite logic if the 13th, 14th, 15th, and following hours from Sunrise are to be inscribed. The demonstration is clear from the construction itself; you shall investigate the center of the sundial, the gnomon, and its placement in exactly the same way as was done for the astronomical sundial.

<margin>The Babylonian Sundial.</margin>
You will inscribe the hours from Sunrise on the same dial if you maintain the arrangement of lines from the opposite part of the horizontal line AE with the hours on the equinoctial. For a <term>Babylonian sundial</term> <note>A system where the day begins at sunrise, used in ancient Mesopotamia.</note> is nothing other than an inverted <term>Italian sundial</term> <note>A system where the day begins at sunset, common in early modern Europe.</note>; if you paint the hours from Sunrise onto it, you will have a Babylonian one. Thus, if you transfer the points of the hours from Sunset from the center of the gnomon to the horizontal line for both, these, when joined with the corresponding points on the equinoctial, will give the hours from Sunrise. The matter presents no difficulty at all. For the method of constructing tables of this kind, as well as the following ones, see Theorem IX, page 251.

### Practical Procedure V.
## How to describe the hours from Sunrise in the same meridian plane.

<margin>A Babylonian sundial in the meridian plane.</margin>
**IF** you describe a Western <term>Italian sundial</term> <note>A system where the day begins at sunset; hour 24 is the moment of dusk.</note> on a <term>meridian plane</term> <note>A vertical surface facing exactly East or West.</note>, you will have an Eastern <term>Babylonian sundial</term> <note>A system where the day begins at sunrise.</note>; and if you describe an Eastern Italian sundial on the meridian plane, you will have a Western Babylonian one. The only difference will be in the numbering of the hours. In the Eastern Babylonian dial, the first hour begins after the 24th, and so on for the rest; in the Western dial, however, the last hour here in Rome will be 15, but everything else remains the same. Thus, we have inscribed the hours from Sunrise and Sunset, which was our goal.

### Practical Procedure VI.
## How to describe a polar sundial on a polar plane, or the circle of the sixth hour.

**DE**scribe an astronomical polar sundial with half-hours, according to the rules handed down in the preceding sections, by drawing two lines AB and SN, intersecting at right angles at point G.

II. For the foundation of the sundial, you will describe two lines—namely, the line for the 12th hour and the 24th hour—by this industrious method: let the line for the 9th hour be extended straight to point T, and from the point of the 9th hour, describe a <term>quadrant</term> <note>A quarter-circle used for measuring angles.</note> S Γ. If, therefore, you draw a straight line through I (the boundary of the <term>polar elevation</term> <note>The angle of the Earth's pole relative to the horizon at a specific latitude.</note> as measured from T) and through the center of the quadrant, that line will cut the line AB at point X. A line CD drawn through X perpendicular to AB will give the 12th hour. If you desire the 24th hour (the horizontal line), transfer the space GX from point G toward A to point V; a line drawn through V parallel to SN will give what you seek. Alternatively, let a perpendicular line be erected from point 9 to the line IX; for where this cuts the line AB at point V, a line RQ drawn through that point parallel to SN will give the 24th hour, or the horizontal line.

## Practical Procedure VII.
### *How to describe the hours from sunrise and sunset on a plane parallel to the equator.*

**T**his method of describing the hours is by far the easiest, and we shall explain it quite briefly.
I. Let an astronomical <term>equinoctial sundial</term> <note>A sundial where the dial plate is parallel to the Earth's equator and the pointer is perpendicular to it.</note> be drawn according to Practical Procedure V; the 12th hour line will be CD, and the 6th hour line will be BA.
II. Let the remaining hours follow at equal distances from one another. Once this is done, if tangents are drawn to the circle through each hour at the point where they intersect the perimeter, you will have both the <term>Italian</term> <note>A system where the 24-hour day begins at sunset.</note> and <term>Babylonian</term> <note>A system where the day begins at sunrise.</note> sundials completed. The tangent line MZ represents the horizon, and the hours shall be inscribed in the manner you see done here. The length of the <term>stylus</term> <note>The physical rod or blade that casts the shadow.</note> will be found as follows: from point C, where the <term>meridian</term> <note>The North-South line.</note> and horizontal lines intersect, let an arc EXN be drawn. Starting from N, count the complement of the altitude of the pole, which is 48 degrees <note>For a location like Rome at roughly 42° latitude, the complement (90 minus 42) is 48 degrees.</note>. If you draw a straight line EXC through the end of this degree, it will cut the 6th hour line at point X, marking the limit of the stylus's height. Therefore, the size of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of the sundial that casts the shadow; used here interchangeably with "stylus."</note> standing perpendicularly at center N will be NX. You should seek the stylus by this industrious method. Because of an error by the engraver, the arc EXN was omitted in the figure; we wanted to place our intention regarding the size of the stylus before your eyes more clearly through this explanation.

<image-desc>A complex circular horological diagram demonstrating the construction of different hour systems. It features a central point C with radiating lines labeled with Roman numerals (I-XII) for astronomical hours and Arabic numerals (1-24) for Italian and Babylonian hours. ->At angle C, at the common point of intersection of the meridian and the horizontal, let the angle of the complement of the pole's elevation be established—for example, 48 degrees for Rome. The line CB, forming said angle at C with line CN, will cut the line NB at B. It will designate NB as the sought-after size or height of the stylus. The gnomonic triangle NBC will then stand above the given plane. Therefore, the size of the stylus will be line NB, its location will be at N (where it stands perpendicular), and NB (or NA) will be the semi-diameter of the circle of the "greatest of those always visible" <note>This refers to the circumpolar circle, containing stars that never set below the horizon from the viewer's latitude.</note>.<-

## Practical Procedure VIII.
### *How to delineate an Italian sundial on a given plane declining from the primary vertical.*

**F**irst, let an astronomical sundial be made on the said plane according to Practical Procedure VI, together with the half-hours. If, by the help of the table proposed in Practical Procedure II of this problem, you draw straight lines through any two points where the hours from sunset pass through the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The line the shadow follows on the spring or autumn equinox.</note> and the horizon, you will have the desired Italian sundial. Since these intersections are common to all astronomical hours delineated on any planes whatsoever, you will be able to describe all kinds of declining, inclining, and tilted dials, and those mixed from these, with almost no effort by the help of the said table.
