# CHAPTER II.

## The inscription of Planetary, or unequal, hours on a given plane.

### Problem XIII.

### To delineate unequal, or ancient, or <term>Planetary hours</term> <note>Also called "Temporal hours," these divide the time from sunrise to sunset into 12 equal parts. Their length changes depending on the season.</note> on a given plane.

### Practical Procedure I.

->Let the given plane be horizontal.<-

<margin>I:</margin>
**I.** Once you have described the <term>parallel of 18 hours</term> <note>A specific reference line used in gnomonics to calibrate the scale of the dial based on the sun's path.</note> (marked XY) on a horizontal astronomical sundial according to Practical Procedure III of *Gnomonic Geography*, you will find the unequal hours using the following table, which we have calculated for half-hour increments, in this manner:

| Astronomical Hours | III | 3 ¼ | 4 ½ | 5 ¼ | VI | 6 ¾ | 7 ½ | 8 ¼ | IX | 9 ¾ | 10 ½ | 11 ¼ | XII |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Unequal Hours | XII | ½ | I | 1 ½ | II | 2 ½ | III | 3 ½ | IV | 4 ½ | V | 5 ½ | VI |

Begin the operation from the 6th unequal hour, which always coincides with the 12th astronomical hour <note>Unequal hour 6 is noon; Astronomical hour 12 is also noon.</note>. Therefore, when you are about to describe the fifth hour, see where the astronomical hour 10 ½ intersects the parallel XY of 18 hours. For if you draw a straight line through this point and the 5th unequal hour (or the 11th astronomical hour) on the <term>equinoctial line</term> <note>The line on the sundial representing the sun's path during the equinoxes.</note>, you will have the hour you seek. Likewise, if you draw a line through the 9th astronomical hour at the place where it intersects the 18-hour parallel, and through the 4th unequal hour on the equinoctial (for, as appears in the figure, the unequal and astronomical hours are exactly the same on the equinoctial), or even through the 10th astronomical hour, you will have the fourth unequal hour. Proceed in the same way with the others until you have completed first the whole hours, and then also the half hours; the <term>gnomonic triangle</term> <note>The right-angled triangle formed by the style, its height, and its shadow-casting edge.</note> is the same in all these as in the previous examples.

<margin>Time, devourer of things, and you, envious old age <note>original: "Tempus edax rerum tuque invidiosa vetustas." A famous quote from Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book 15, reflecting on the destructive nature of time.</note></margin>

Suppose, therefore, that the 5th <term>unequal hour</term> <note>original: "hora 5. inæqualis"; these are hours that change length with the seasons.</note> is to be described for the <term>Tropic of Capricorn</term> <note>The sun's path on the winter solstice, the shortest day of the year in the northern hemisphere.</note> (♑︎). A thread extended from the center of the sundial (V) through this point will cut the Tropic of Capricorn (♑︎) at a point; a straight line drawn through this point and the 4th unequal hour (or the 10th astronomical hour) on the equinoctial line will provide the 4th unequal hour. You shall work in this same manner for the remaining hours until you have completed half the arc. Move the ruler to the 1st hour of the diurnal arc ANB, and note where the ruler cuts the equinoctial line. A straight line drawn through this point and through the center of the sundial (V), extending beyond the center, will cut the Tropic of Cancer (♋︎) at a point. When this point is joined to the 7th astronomical hour (which is the 1st unequal hour) on the equator, it will give the 1st hour sought. In a like manner, you will inscribe the rest of the hours in order. For the mathematical proof of this, see <term>Preliminary Theory III</term> <note>original: "Protheoria III"; likely a reference to an earlier theoretical chapter in the same volume.</note>.

# Practical Procedure II.
### To describe the proposed hours on a vertical plane.

First, let a <term>vertical astronomical sundial</term> <note>A sundial designed to be placed on a wall facing a cardinal direction, usually South.</note> be fashioned using only faint lines, together with the <term>parallel of 6 hours</term> (which is the same as the parallel of 18 hours) and the tropics. Once you have these tropics described (using the practice to be explained shortly hereafter), you will describe the <term>ancient hours</term> <note>Another name for unequal or planetary hours.</note> on this plane in exactly the same way as in the preceding sections. This is done first with the help of the table proposed in this Practical Procedure.

### Practical Exercise IV.
#### To describe the same on a polar plane.

SINCE the <term>polar sundial</term> <note>A sundial whose face is set parallel to the Earth's axis of rotation.</note> is the same as the meridian one, differing only in its orientation and the hours shown, the method for drawing it is also no different. Therefore, anyone who has properly understood the method for the meridian sundial cannot be in doubt here. Let the figure alone suffice in place of instruction.

### Practical Exercise V.
#### To describe unequal hours on an equinoctial plane.

NOTHING is easier than to engrave the proposed hours on an <term>equinoctial plane</term> <note>A sundial face that lies parallel to the Earth's equator.</note>. Therefore, work as follows: Divide the <term>nocturnal arc</term> <note>original: "arcum nocturnum"; the path the sun takes below the horizon during the night.</note> of Cancer (♋) AHB into 12 equal parts; likewise, divide the arc CFD of Taurus (♉) and Virgo (♍) into the same number of equal parts. For straight lines drawn through the points marked in both arcs will give the lines of the ancient hours—

# C A P U T IX.

## On another description of Italian-Babylonian Sundials.

### Problem XIV.

->To engrave the hours from Sunrise and Sunset upon any given plane with the greatest ease.<-

->Practical Exercise I.<-

*To construct an instrument by benefit of which the hours from sunrise and sunset may be inscribed more quickly than said.* <note>The Latin phrase "dicto citius" translates to "faster than it can be said," implying extreme speed or ease.</note>

**F**IRST, let a circle MANB be described, divided in half by a line or diameter MN. Secondly, from M, count on both sides the semi-diurnal arc <note>The arc of the sun's path from noon to sunset.</note> from the proper Table proposed in the first Preliminary Exercise—for example, here in Rome, 113 degrees and 3 minutes—and through points D and E, which terminate the daytime arc of Cancer (♋), let line DE be drawn; the arc will be divided into two segments, daytime and nighttime, with the Sun positioned in Cancer. Again, let the daytime arc of Aries (♈), that is, arc NE or ND, be transferred from M on both sides, and let line AB be drawn. Thirdly, starting from B, let the whole circle BMAN be divided into 24 equal parts, and starting from E, let the same circle be divided into as many parts, as the figure shows. Through these points, you shall draw straight lines from the center O, or in place of lines, you shall attach a ruler. Let the circle be made of thin paper or some other transparent material; or if the ruler is attached, let it be entirely cut out, leaving only the <term>armillis</term> <note>Small rings or supports.</note> to support the ruler; and you will have the instrument prepared.

## Practice II.

### *Given the gnomonic triangle, the tropics, and the equator, to describe Italian hours on a horizontal plane by means of the constructed Instrument.*

**F**irst, let the <term>gnomonic triangle</term> <note>A right triangle used in sundial construction where the vertical side represents the gnomon's height and the hypotenuse points to the celestial pole.</note> be drawn on a horizontal plane, and let the two tropics be marked along with the equator, having previously noted the points for the hours starting from noon and midnight. Then, apply that transparent hour-circle prepared a little earlier, with its line MN aligned to the <term>meridian line</term> <note>The north-south line.</note> AB, such that the center of the instrument is distant from the equinoctial point by the amount of the equinoctial semi-diameter in the gnomonic triangle. Also, in the instrument, let the line BA (or DE), which cuts the circle into two segments of the daytime and nighttime arcs of the longest day, be parallel to the equator, and consequently let the line NM be aligned with the meridian. 

Once this is done, see where the hour lines in the transparent circle (or a ruler placed above the hour points) drawn from the center of the circle intersect the CD equinoctial line of the sundial. For if you draw a thread from the center of the sundial through these points, it will intersect the tropic at points which, when joined with the corresponding hour points from noon and midnight, will give the <term>hours from Sunset</term> <note>These are "Italian hours," which begin counting at 1 immediately after sunset.</note>, the inverse of which is the <term>Babylonian sundial</term> <note>Hours counted from sunrise.</note>. In that place, you will put 1 for 23, 2 for 22, and so on for the rest.

<image-desc>A rectangular diagram labeled "Horizontal A" showing a gnomonic projection with lines fanning out from points A and B toward vertical lines C, D, and E. It includes a small inset detail labeled 42.</image-desc>

<margin>
How the numbering of hours is to be established on the instrument.
</margin>

Note, however, in this place: if you desire to have the points of the hours in the <term>Tropic of Cancer</term> (♋), the numbering of the hours must be established from point B through M, A, D, N, and E. But if you desire the points in the <term>Tropic of Capricorn</term> (♑), the same numbering must be established from E through B, M, A, D, and N, as the divided circle itself shows. Thus you see the ruler placed above point 18 intersects CD at a line in a point through which a thread drawn from center A will intersect the Tropic of Cancer (♋) at Aries (♈) <note>Signifying the equinox point</note>: for through this point, and through the 12th astronomical hour, a straight line drawn will give the sought-after line of the 18th hour.

Moreover, so that you may know with which points of the hours from noon and midnight on the equinoctial line these points of the hours from Sunset found on the tropics ought to be joined: consult this small table, which we have also transferred onto the <term>sciatheric rule</term> <note>A specialized calculating ruler for sundial makers.</note>.

### Problem XV.

->**To describe the ancient, or unequal, hours on a given plane using a tool.**<-

->**Construction of the Tool.**<-

**L**et the same circle described a little earlier remain, divided by the line AB into two segments: the <term>diurnal arc</term> <note>The path of the sun above the horizon.</note> and the nocturnal arc of the longest day. You will work well and without confusion if you describe the lines drawn through the points of the arc of Cancer ♋ in a distinct color from those drawn through the points of the arc of Capricorn ♑. You will then have a perfect instrument, by the help of which you will most easily mark the remaining hours, as follows.

# Appendix,
## Or
## The Wonderful Artifice of defining the endpoints of the hours.

I shall reveal here, as a <gloss>finishing touch</gloss> <note>original: "colophonis loco"</note>, a certain wonderful artifice for defining the endpoints of the hours through any given parallel of the Sun. I believe nothing more beautiful, easy, or exact has been devised in this field; for of all the methods found up to now, as far as I know, it is both the most universal and the most elegant. It can be varied in infinite ways, and I do not doubt that it will provide the occasion for clever minds to discover countless similar things. This invention was suggested to us by Proposition 5, Book 2 of the *Astrolabe* of <term>Clavius</term> <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who was the main architect of the Gregorian calendar.</note>, number 36, and Proposition 6, number 37, where the shrewd reader will find the foundations of our device. I find the author of this demonstration to be <term>Father Grienberger</term> <note>Christoph Grienberger (1561–1636), a Jesuit successor to Clavius, known for inventing the equatorial mount for telescopes.</note>, from whom Clavius drew many other ingeniously demonstrated things in his works. Leaving aside the demonstration, which the reader can see in the cited place, we shall set forth only our findings here. But, lest we proceed <note>original Greek: "αμεθόδως" (without a system)</note> in such a singular invention, we shall begin the matter "from the egg," as the saying goes.

# Proposition I.
### *Given a point of any solar parallel noted at any hour, to find the termination of the remaining given hours through that point in infinite ways.*

First, let the points of the solar parallels be given on the 12 o'clock line of the sundial; these you will easily obtain from the <term>analemma</term> <note>A geometric construction used to project the paths of the sun and stars onto a flat surface.</note> described on pages 273 and 274. By this industry, let two lines be drawn on a certain flat surface intersecting each other at right angles, AB and CD, of which AB designates the <term>meridian</term> and CD the <term>equinoctial</term>. From the analemma, let a horizontal <term>gnomonic triangle</term> <note>A triangle used to calculate the height and angle of the shadow-casting style.</note> be established upon AB, where A is the center of the dial, B the meridian point of the equinoctial, D the location of the <term>style</term> <note>The pin or blade that casts the shadow.</note> and its length DV. Having extended the radius of the equator VB, let the lines of the rays emerging from V be described on both sides around it—that is, the <term>declinations</term> <note>The angle of the sun above or below the celestial equator.</note> of the signs of the Zodiac from the cited analemma. For where this radiant Zodiac intersects the meridian line, there will be the points of the solar parallels assigned on the meridian, or 12 o'clock line. With the help of these points, we shall terminate the remaining hours in infinite ways, as we said: for in this artifice of ours, after the description of the hour lines, nothing else is required except one single point where some hour is terminated, and additionally the points of the equinoctial through which either the whole hours or at least some parts of the hours pass.

<margin>Points which terminate at the completion of the whole hours.</margin>
For the termination of all the whole hours, the equinoctial points of both the whole hours and the half-hours (or at least one of the half-hours) are required; for the termination of the half-hours, the points of the quarters are needed; and finally, for the termination of the quarters, the points of the eighths—or at least one of them—is necessary, as will be clear from the following.

If, therefore, the meridian point of Cancer F is found from the foundation (for example), we will find the remaining points from it in the other hour lines as well, both for Cancer and for Capricorn. Let a ruler be applied to point F and to the individual points of the hours and half-hours found on the equinoctial; for in those applications, all the hour lines will be terminated where the ruler intersects them, both for Cancer and for Capricorn (except for the 12th hour of Capricorn, since that itself is terminated from the foundation), namely in this order:

<margin>Example of the operation.</margin>
The first hour of the afternoon is terminated from the point of the equinoctial looking toward the half-hour beyond six, either before or after noon. Then, from the nearest point of the 7th hour, either before or after noon, the 2nd hour is terminated, and so on until one reaches the hour to be terminated which is not contained in the <term>diurnal arc</term> <note>The path the sun takes across the sky from sunrise to sunset.</note> of Cancer. For then that same hour will be terminated in Capricorn, such as the 8th hour and the rest up to the 4th hour; after that, however, starting again from the 5th hour, the remaining hours will be terminated in Cancer. The same is true if one chose to establish the termination from the point of Capricorn E.

Furthermore, once all the points have been found in this way, it will be permitted to examine any one of them,

between the fifth hour and the third, which is clearly the fourth hour. If, therefore, you count six hours <term>exclusively</term> <note>Meaning you begin counting from the next hour, not including the starting hour itself.</note> from the fourth hour—for instance, up to the 10th hour—the point of the 10th <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The equinoctial line is the path the shadow follows when day and night are of equal length.</note> hour will be that which exists in the same straight line with the points of the fifth and third hours. If, however, the point of the third hour (by which you wish to prove the point of the fifth hour) were in <term>Capricorn</term> <note>The Tropic of Capricorn represents the Sun's path during the winter solstice.</note>, then the point of the 4th equinoctial hour itself—which is clearly the middle between the fifth and third hours—would be the one lying in the same straight line with the points of the fifth and third hours; and so it goes for the rest. Indeed, by the same logic, you may examine the same point of the fifth hour from other points, and through the point of the fifth hour, all others. But so that you may more easily remember these two rules, I have chosen to set them down separately below, and also to add a third, from which it is gathered: if some point of any hour is taken on the equinoctial, and the ruler is applied to it and to the termination point of any [other] hour, which other hour is terminated by that application—a matter which pertains to the very method of marking boundaries handed down at the beginning.

### Rule I.

*By which the point on the equinoctial is found which exists in the same straight line with two points of two hours of Cancer or Capricorn, of which one is sought and the other is given, or of which both are given.*

**F**irst, let it be asked which hour is the middle between the two assigned hours of Cancer or Capricorn. Then, let it be asked which hour, counting exclusively from that middle hour, holds the sixth place. For the point of that hour on the equinoctial will be the one that lies in the same straight line with the points of the two hours of Cancer or Capricorn. 
   Hence, if any two of those points are given, the third will always be found by the application of the ruler.

### Rule II.

*By which, again, a point of the equinoctial is found which lies in the same straight line with two points, one of which exists in Cancer and the other in Capricorn.*

**L**et the hour be sought which is the middle between the hours of the <term>tropics</term> <note>The "tropics" here refer to the solstitial points of Cancer and Capricorn.</note>. Its point on the equinoctial will be the one being sought.
   Hence, again, from any two given points, their third will be found.

### Rule III.

*By which it is found which point of the tropics lies in the same straight line with two points, one of which is also in either tropic, and the remaining one in the equinoctial.*

**F**rom the equinoctial hour, let six hours be counted exclusively: for the point of the tropic hour—which stands at an equal distance from that hour found in the sixth place as the other assigned hour in the tropic does—will be that which exists in the same straight line with the remaining two. If, therefore, that later-found tropic hour is contained within the <term>daytime arc</term> <note>The portion of the sun's path that is above the horizon.</note> of the assigned tropic hour, both hours will be in the same tropic. If, however, that later-found hour is not contained in the daytime arc of the other tropic hour, they will be in different tropics.
   And so, if any two out of the three points are given, the remaining one will be given by the application of the rule.
   For example, I desire to know the point of the 7th equinoctial hour, and the point of the 12th hour of Cancer, and with which point of the tropic they lie in a straight line. By counting 6 hours exclusively from the 7th hour, I find the 1st hour: then, by counting again one hour beyond the 1st hour (because the 12th hour is one hour away on the other side of that same 1st hour), I find the 2nd hour; since this is an afternoon hour and is contained within the daytime arc of Cancer, the points of the 2nd hour, the 12th hour of Cancer, and the 7th equinoctial hour will be in the same straight line.
   Again, I desire to know the point of the 10th equinoctial hour, and the point of the 8th hour from midday at night in Cancer, and with which other tropic point it exists in the same straight line. By first counting six hours from the 10th hour exclusively, I find, for example, the 4th hour in the afternoon: then by counting nine hours from the 4th hour (which is how many hours the 8th hour of Cancer is distant from the 4th hour), I find the 12th hour of midnight. Since, therefore, that hour is not contained in the Tropic of Cancer, the points of the 12th hour of Capricorn, the 8th of Cancer, and the 10th equinoctial hour will be in one straight line: and so for the rest. These operations we show to you more concisely in the following table. Thus, in the first example, look for the 7th hour in the equinoctial at the side, and the number in the transverse series under 12 at the top of the table will give 2, the sought number; for this hour, with 7 and 12, in the same straight line

For from this, we teach how to determine the point of any hour in countless ways; not only through the <term>tropics</term> <note>The paths of the Sun during the summer and winter solstices.</note>, but through any given <term>parallel</term> of the Sun, with an ease and readiness that is almost incredible, and with an infinite richness and variety of combinations. ->The Great Art, Book IV. Part I of Curious Gnomonics<- <note>original: "Artis magnæ Liber IV. Gnom. Curiosæ Pars I." Gnomonics is the traditional science of using a gnomon, or sundial's shadow-caster, to measure time.</note>

### Explanation of the Wondrous Table.

To help the curious reader grasp the wonderful concept of the diagram in <gloss>Table 8</gloss>, we have organized a table here. In it, every combination of hour-markings is presented with such ingenious skill that it provides endless use for countless practical applications in the work of sundial-making; for this reason, we have called it "wondrous." Its use is as follows: If you have this Table at hand, you can use it to determine the endpoints of the hours without needing the complex reasoning or calculations mentioned earlier, in this manner:

Search for the hour whose fixed point is already known (from which the points of other hours are to be found) on the top or bottom edge of the Table. Then, look within the main area of the Table under that hour for the hour you wish to mark. By looking directly to the right or left sides of that row, you will find the hour on the <term>equinoctial line</term> <note>The straight line on a sundial where the shadow falls during the equinoxes.</note> from which the alignment must be made. That is to say: if a ruler is applied to the given fixed point and to the hour found on the equinoctial line, it will cross the hour line you are trying to mark at the exact point you seek.

<margin>Use of the Table.</margin>
In a horizontal sundial, this will relate to the northern arc (the <term>boreal parallel</term> <note>The path of the sun's shadow during the summer solstice.</note>) if the intersection happens above the equinoctial line toward the center of the dial. It relates to the southern arc (<term>austral parallel</term> <note>The path of the sun's shadow during the winter solstice.</note>) if the intersection occurs below the equinoctial line. 

If the ruler is applied to both points found on the equinoctial, and the proposed hour is contained in both the northern and southern parallels, then one application of those points will find one, and the second application will find the other. However, if the hour you wish to mark is only found in the northern parallel, it will be marked from both of those equinoctial points for the northern parallel alone; one point will be the mark for the hour starting from midnight, and the other for the same hour starting from noon. Examples will make this clearer.

From point **F**, for example—the 12th hour in <term>Cancer</term> <note>The sign representing the summer solstice.</note>—suppose all the remaining hours are to be marked for both Cancer and <term>Capricorn</term> <note>The sign representing the winter solstice.</note>. Take, for instance, the 1st hour, which appears in both. On the top edge, I look for hour 12 (the "terminating hour" through which the 1st hour is to be marked). Inside the table under 12, I find the 1st hour. From there, I move across to both sides until I reach the right and left edges, where I find "half an hour before 1" on the left and "half an hour before 7" on the right. 

I conclude, therefore, that the marking of the 1st hour through point **12 F** must be established from two points on the equinoctial line: those belonging to the half-hours before the 1st and 7th hours. You will find this to be true if you apply the ruler to these points: from the half-hour of the 7th, you will find the 1st hour marked for Cancer; and from the half-hour of the 1st, the same hour is marked for Capricorn. If we had used point **E** (Capricorn) instead of point **F** (12th hour of Cancer), the point for the 1st hour of Cancer would have been found from the half-hour of the 1st, and for Capricorn from the equinoctial point of the half-hour of the 7th—that is, in reverse order.

Again, using the same point 12 (**F** or **E**), let us say the 7th hour is to be marked. In Rome, this hour does not exist in Capricorn, but both (morning and evening) exist in Cancer. Since the 7th hour sits under the "terminating" 12th hour in the Table, it corresponds to the half-hours before 10 and 4 on the right and left sides. If the ruler is applied to these two equinoctial points and to point **F**, the half-hour before 4 will mark the 7th hour from midnight, while the half-hour before 10 will mark the 7th hour from noon—and both will be in Cancer. The logic is exactly the same for other hours to be marked or used as markers, as the equinoctial points for such markings are always found in this way.

One could also use the same Table to mark hour lines by first picking a point on the equinoctial and applying a ruler to it and a point of an already marked hour. The Table will immediately show which other hour line is being marked by that ruler's placement. It works like this: find that equinoctial hour on the left or right side of the Table in the section where the "terminating hour" is listed at the top or bottom. Move across from that equinoctial hour until you reach the cell directly under the terminating hour. The hour in that cell is the one being marked by the ruler. (Unless the hour in that cell is the same as the terminating hour, in which case the ruler will show no other point except the one on the terminating hour line itself.)

As you can see, the use of this table is vast, as it allows for nearly infinite...

...various points can be used to define the hour lines, or at least to verify whether the termination points have been correctly found. This applies not only to the <term>tropics</term> <note>The lines representing the sun's path at the summer and winter solstices.</note>, but to any other opposing <term>parallels</term> <note>Lines on a sundial corresponding to the sun's path on a specific day of the year.</note>, provided that some point of those parallels is found fundamentally on the meridian line or the line of the sixth hour.

<margin>The Utility of this Table.</margin>
The excellence of this table is further enhanced by the fact that it allows one to see, almost at a single glance, all those hours that define and limit one another through various hour points found on the <term>equinoctial line</term> <note>The straight line on a sundial where the shadow falls during the equinoxes, when day and night are equal.</note>. If, for example, you wish to define other lines through the 12 o'clock point on the Tropic of Cancer, and you select that same 12th hour on the top edge of the table, you will find under it all the hours—both the full hours and their halves and quarters. Simultaneously, on the right and left sides in the same row as those hours, you will find the hours of the equinoctial line from which those same hours are defined through the 12 o'clock point. If, however, you select an hour of the equinoctial on the right or left side and proceed across, you will again find all the hours to be defined from that equinoctial hour; the defining hours will be those written directly above each hour to be defined on the top edge.

If you study this same table more diligently, you will see that from the full hours of the equinoctial line, an even hour (such as 12, 2, 4, 6, etc.) only defines other even hours. Through an odd hour, only odd hours are defined. Thus, if any two hours have been marked—one even and the other odd—all the remaining hours, both even and odd, can be defined by means of them. This is done by applying a ruler to the individual points of the equinoctial that pertain to the full hours, and to the points of those two defined hours: first to the even hour, and then to the odd hour. From this, you will also easily deduce something that must be carefully observed: when only full hour lines are drawn on the sundial, it is still necessary to find the half-hour points on the equinoctial. It is sufficient if one point is found on the equinoctial that corresponds to a single half-hour. For instance, from that point, through the point of (for example) 12 o'clock in Cancer, one of the odd hours may be defined, which you will immediately recognize from the table. If, for example, a point for the half-hour before 9 o'clock is found on the equinoctial, you will find from the table that from that point, through the 12 o'clock hour, the 5th hour is defined. Since 5 is an odd hour, all the other odd hours will be defined through it if the ruler is applied to its termination point and to the individual full hours of the equinoctial, as has been said.

<margin>How half-hours are defined.</margin>
If, however, half-hours are also drawn on the sundial, it is required that at least one quarter-point be found on the equinoctial, so that from it, through the 12 or 6 o'clock point, one of the half-hours may be defined, as indicated by the table. For through the termination point of that half-hour, all other half-hours will be defined—partly from the half-hours and partly from the full hours of the equinoctial.

Finally, to define the lines for the quarter-hours, it will be necessary to find a point on the equinoctial for a "semi-quarter," which is to say, for the eighth part of an hour. From there, through 12 or 6, one of the quarters will be defined, from which the others can be derived.

<margin>The Table is extended to the eighth-parts of an hour.</margin>
This explains why we have progressed as far as the eighth-parts of the hours of the equinoctial line on the sides of the tables. Namely, so that the same table might also serve for the definition of quarters; since these are the smallest parts commonly drawn on sundials, it was sufficient to extend the table that far.

However, anyone wishing to describe even smaller parts on a sundial can easily extend the table. In the descending sides, between the hours and parts placed here, one should interpose the fourth-parts of the quarters—that is, the sixteenth-parts of the full hours. On the top and bottom edges, one would insert the eighth-parts between the hours and their defining parts, as well as between the hours and parts of hours contained within the main area of the table.

Indeed, since it is very rare for quarters to be drawn—usually only half-hours or even just full hours—anyone can extract a smaller, specialized table from this universal one for their own use, so there is no need to carry around such a large table. But let us now explain the use of this table separately through specific <term>canons</term> <note>Standardized rules or instructions for calculation.</note>, so that what must be done to define the lines may be found more easily.

## Following are the Rules for the Table provided above.

### Rule I.

> *Given the hour of some parallel arc, to find from which point of the equinoctial it must be defined, using a known hour of the same or an opposite parallel arc.*

**S**earch for the known (defining) hour on the top edge of the Table, for example, and find the hour you wish to define within the main area under that same hour. Directly across from this hour, on the left or right side, you will find the equinoctial hour...

### Rule II.

*To investigate, from a assigned hour on the equinoctial, by which hour of a parallel arc a proposed hour may be bounded.*

**S**eek the equinoctial hour on the left or right side of the table, and from there proceed across through its area until you fall upon the cell of the hour to be bounded. If you then go up or down from that same cell, you will find on the top or bottom side the hour sought, namely, that by which the proposed hour can be bounded.

### Rule III.

*To discern, from an assigned hour on the equinoctial, which hour is bounded by a given and bounded hour of any parallel arc.*

**S**eek again the equinoctial hour on the left or right side, and the bounding hour—or the one already bounded—on the top or bottom edge: for within the area, directly below or above the bounding hour, will be the hour to be bounded which is sought.

## Cycle I, A, B: A Recapitulatory Summary <note>original: "Anacephalæoticus"; a concluding summary that brings points together.</note> of the Great Table.

<margin>Summary of the Table.</margin>
**S**ince, however, not everyone can carry these massive tables around with them, and striving for the convenience of the curious reader, we have arranged this great <term>Pinax</term> <note>A register or mathematical table.</note> into a cyclic system. We have done this with such industry that everything found in the large table is presented here as if in an epitome <note>A brief summary or condensed version of a larger work.</note>.

The propositions of the preceding three rules will also be easily adapted to the following Cycle, into which we have compressed the superior table. We have done this with the intention that, whenever necessary, everything that the table contains at greater length can be described in a smaller space.

### Solution to the proposition of Rule I by the Cycle AB.

**P**lace the hour to be bounded (found among the hours of the middle Cycle, which is the outermost ring of the moving wheel) under the bounded or bounding hour (found in the outermost Cycle, namely the fixed one). For with the Cycles placed in that position, the 12 o'clock hours of the outermost Cycle will correspond to the bounding hours in the innermost Cycle—which is for the hours of the <term>equinoctial line</term> <note>The line on a sundial representing the equinox, used as a baseline for calculations.</note>—or those parts of them that would have been found on the right and left sides in the table if the proposition were to be solved by it.

---

### Solution to the proposition of Rules II and III.

**P**lace the equinoctial hour (found in the innermost Cycle) under the 12 o'clock hour of the outermost Cycle of bounding hours: for in that arrangement of the Cycles, the bounding hour in the outermost Cycle will correspond to the hour to be bounded, which is to be taken in the middle Cycle; or conversely, the hour to be bounded in the middle Cycle will correspond to the bounding hour found in the first Cycle; depending on whether the proposition of the second or third rule is to be solved.

With these things observed: if, for example, the 6th hour to be bounded is placed under the 10th bounding hour, you will see under the 12th bounding hour the hours 2 and 8 of the equinoctial, from which, according to the first rule, that bounding must be made.

Again, if for example the 2nd or 8th equinoctial hour is placed under 12 of the Cycle of bounding hours, then according to the second rule, the 10th bounding hour in the outermost Cycle will correspond to, for example, the 6th hour to be bounded of the middle Cycle. Or according to Rule III, the 6th hour to be bounded in the middle Cycle will correspond to the 10th bounding hour of the outermost Cycle: and so for the rest, using the lines that distinguish the cells in place of the nearest smaller parts than are contained in the cells, when one must descend to quarters or eighth-parts.

## Hourly Cycle II, CD: Serving for the description of Parallel Arcs in any Astronomical sundial, to be completed with almost no effort.

#### Explanation of the Cycle.

**T**his Cycle comprises two parts: one fixed wheel and another moving wheel.

The fixed wheel consists of two Cycles: the outermost, which is assigned to the equinoctial, and contains 12 full hours with half-hours, quarters, and half-quarters or eighth-parts of an hour; and an interior Cycle, whose hours, half-hours, and quarters are those for which the points in the description of the arcs are either sought or found. Accordingly, this same interior Cycle can quite appropriately be called the "Cycle of hours to be bounded." The moving wheel has a single Cycle of hours, half-hours, and quarters, which, since they pertain to the hours and parts of hours of the parallels, we have chosen to name the "Cycle of Parallel hours," or even of "bounding hours," because it is in this cycle that those hours are properly taken by which it is desired to determine other hours. Therefore...

## Use of the Attached Cycle.

<margin>though the said hours are determined by the 12th parallel.</margin>
We shall explain the use of the proposed Cycle through the three Problems that follow.

## Problem I.

*To recognize, from an assigned hour on the Equinoctial, which hour is determined on the arc of any parallel, by a given and determined hour of the same.*

**I**n this Problem, two things are given and assigned: namely, the point of some hour on the equinoctial line, and a point on some hour line which relates to the arc of a certain parallel. A third thing is sought: namely, the hour line in which the point of the same parallel arc may be found if a straightedge is applied to the two assigned points. This is found with no trouble from the attached Cycle in this way: Place hour 12 of the Moving Wheel (also called the Cycle of determining hours, which the index of the painted hand points to) under the assigned hour on the equinoctial found in its own Cycle. Then, if you look again in the Cycle of determining hours for the hour of the parallel, the hour of the parallel being sought will correspond to it in the neighboring Cycle of hours to be determined—specifically, that which is determined from the given points. 

For example, if the given hour on the equinoctial is the fifth or the eleventh, before or after noon, and the hour of the parallel through which you wish to determine another is, for instance, six in the morning: if we set hour 12 of the Cycle of determining hours under hour 5 or 11 of the Equinoctial Cycle, we will find across from hour six of the Cycle of determining hours, specifically in the Cycle of hours to be determined, hour 4. This hour will be completely determined through the given and assigned hours, provided that same hour is contained within the layout of the proposed sundial. The same logic applies to other hours and their parts placed in the proposed Cycles. 

If the determining hour were assigned as 12, it would not be necessary to move the Moving Wheel at all, since in the Static Wheel, under the equinoctial hour, the sought hour to be determined is already placed. You should understand this applies not only to whole hours, but also to half-hours, quarters, and even the eighth-parts described in the Equinoctial Cycle. Thus you see that from hour 1 or 7 of the equinoctial, the second hour is determined; likewise from hour 1 and 1/2, the 3/4 hour after the second is determined, then the third, and finally from 1/8 past the first, the third quarter after the second, if you see—

## Problem II.

*To investigate, from an assigned hour on the equinoctial, by which hour of a parallel a proposed hour is determined.*

**H**ere also two things are given: the equinoctial hour and the hour to be determined. A third is sought: namely, which hour of the parallel it is, so that a line drawn from the given equinoctial point exhibits the point of the parallel arc on the assigned hour line. Again, place hour 12 of the Cycle of determining hours under the hour of the Equinoctial Cycle. The hour in that same Cycle of determining hours which corresponds to the assigned hour (found in the Cycle of hours to be determined) will be the one through which the determination must be made. 

For example, if you place hour 12 of the Cycle of determining hours under the 9th hour of the equinoctial, you will see across from hour 5 of the Cycle of hours to be determined (which is proposed as the example to be determined) the hour 1 placed in the Cycle of determining hours. It is through this hour that the proposed fifth hour can be determined, provided a point in the first hour is not desired.

## Problem III.

*Given an hour of a Parallel, to inquire from which point on the equinoctial it must be determined through a given parallel hour.*

**T**he thing sought in this Problem is a point on the equinoctial line, and both given values are hours of the parallel: one is the determining hour, and the other is the hour to be determined. Look for each of these in its own Cycle—the one to be determined in the Cycle of hours to be determined, and the determining one in the Cycle of determining hours. By rotating the moving wheel, set the latter under the former. In this position of the Cycles, the hour in the Equinoctial Cycle that corresponds to the twelfth hour of the Cycle of determining hours (the one the hand index points to) will be the one from which the proposed hour can be determined, if a point of that same hour exists on the equinoctial line. 

In this way, if hour four of the cycle of determining hours is set under hour three of the cycle of hours to be determined—since the half-hour past three (or nine) in the Equinoctial Cycle corresponds to the twelve of the cycle of determining hours—it will be concluded that Hour three is determined through hour four from the point...

### Note concerning the first and second Problems.

**W**hen the determining hour and the hour to be determined occur as the same value, the Problem is rendered useless, since an hour cannot be determined by itself. However, one useful thing can be gathered from it: from that hour, one may easily judge which two hours are determined simultaneously from the same point on the <term>equinoctial</term><note>The celestial equator, used as the primary reference line for timekeeping.</note>. For there will always be two hours determined from that assigned point on the equinoctial which are either equally distant on both sides of the determining hour (when it coincides with the hour to be determined), or are equally distant on both sides of the hour assigned on the equinoctial.

Furthermore, anyone who desires to know the use of all these stated things more exactly should consult our following <term>Sciatheric Ouranographia</term><note>original: "Ouranographiam fciathericam." A title meaning "Shadow-measuring Description of the Heavens."</note>, where he will find everything treated more extensively through examples and various <term>paradigms</term><note>In this context, models or worked examples.</note>.

# BY ATHANASIUS KIRCHER
## PRIEST OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS
# THE GREAT ART OF LIGHT AND SHADOW
### Book Five.
## GNOMONIC OURANOGRAPHY, OR ON THE DOCTRINE OF THE ENTIRE PRIMUM MOBILE
### TO BE REPRESENTED SCIATHERICALLY UPON ANY PLANES.
## P R E F A C E.

<image-desc>A large, ornate woodcut initial letter 'P' featuring a landscape background with trees, foliage, and a small building or tower. The letter is decorated with classical architectural scrollwork and leafy flourishes.</image-desc>

*Having <term>PREVIOUSLY PRESENTED</term> the better-known <term>Horography</term> <note>The art of constructing sundials to tell the hours.</note>, the requirements of order now seem to demand that we follow the doctrine of the celestial circles with the same method. And although I am well aware that our <term>Clavius</term> <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a renowned Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who wrote extensively on gnomonics.</note> dealt with this matter most learnedly; yet, because his work on <term>gnomonics</term> <note>The art of using a gnomon (the part of a sundial that casts a shadow) to measure time or celestial positions.</note> seems so difficult to most that there are few who can either grasp the author’s mind, or, if they do grasp it, endure the tedium of the most intricate figures in his stubborn demonstrations: I have applied myself with singular care to this end, so that by a new and hitherto unseen method, I might advance such a distinguished and curious doctrine as much as possible, and free talented minds from so many entanglements.*

*However, since I have learned by experience that most people long for practical application, and noticing that demonstrations attached to the <term>Problems</term> bring more hindrance than help to <term>Tyros</term> <note>Beginners or students in a particular field.</note>; it seemed best to weigh the entire apparatus of gnomonic proofs separately. This we have provided in the first part of this Work, so that the pragmatic exercise might run its course with a steady foot, and that I might simultaneously benefit both the theoretical and practical students through this modest study of mine. I have also deliberately remained silent regarding the demonstrations and reasons for many problems recently invented by me, or have indicated them only obscurely; this was done so that I might open a wider field of discovery to curious minds by searching and investigating, while they are held by the desire to know the reasons proposed in the problems.*

*You shall learn, therefore, Reader, in this work how to delineate all types of <term>Planispheres</term> <note>Maps of the celestial or terrestrial sphere onto a flat plane.</note>, or <term>sciatheric astrolabes</term> <note>Shadow-measuring instruments used to determine the positions of stars and the time of day.</note> upon any given surface, with a method and ease that has been provided by no one else, as far as I know. And these are the things about which I thought the Reader should first be warned: so that if perhaps he should see <term>unproven</term> <note>original: "ἀναποδείκτους" - Greek for 'without proof' or 'unproven'</note> propositions, he might know it happened for the reason we have stated. Just as various positions of the stars occur according to different optical projections, so we will teach here various astrolabes according to the diversity of the planes. Thus you will see universal astrolabes on polar, meridian, and equinoctial planes; and particular ones on the rest. But leaving aside the twists and turns of words, let us get to the matter itself.*

### *To Delineate the Triangle of the Radiant Zodiac.*

<margin>First method of constructing the radiant Zodiac.</margin>

**T**HE RADIANT Zodiac is nothing other than a triangular figure of the declination of the signs, caused by the rays of the Sun. We imagine these rays to be spread out—intersecting each other at the beginning of the signs, either at the center of the earth or at the tip of a <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note>—onto a plane perpendicular to the equator, or a polar plane. These rays are nothing else than the sides of the <term>sciatheric cones</term> <note>From the Greek 'skia' (shadow); these are the three-dimensional cones of light and shadow formed as the sun moves in its circular path throughout the day.</note> which the Sun describes around the apex of the gnomon on the said plane. You shall delineate the said Zodiac in this way:

First, from the Table of the Sun’s declination proposed on folio 276, look up the declination of each individual sign from the equator toward the South or the North, which we have placed here separately.

II. With the arc CD drawn around line AB, let the declinations of the signs be numbered from B on both sides according to the little table placed here at the side. First, for Aries (♈) and Libra (♎), you will have drawn the chosen lines; they will intersect from the arc CED at points through which straight lines drawn from A will display the sought-after radiant Zodiac.

## Corollary I.
From this it is clear how the radii of the middle of the signs, or of any number of parts, can be inscribed in the Triangle: namely, if you determine them by lines drawn from A, using the declinations numbered on both sides from B in the first figure, or from C in the second, corresponding to the middle, third, or sixth parts of the signs. #### To construct an Analemma for describing conic sections.

**L**et the circle ABCI be divided by two diameters, AI and CB, intersecting each other at right angles at the center D; BC will be the horizontal line, and AI the vertical line. Starting from B, divide this on both sides into 4 quadrants, and each one into 90 degrees, as you see.

2. Once the altitude of the pole has been numbered from C as far as E, let the line EDS be drawn through the center D, which will be the <term>axis of the world</term> <note>The imaginary line around which the heavens appear to rotate.</note>, which the <term>equinoctial line</term> <note>The celestial equator.</note> XY intersects at right angles at the center D.

<image-desc>A detailed geometric diagram known as an Analemma. It consists of a circle with a grid of horizontal lines and radiating lines from the center D. An axis line EDS and an equinoctial line XY are prominent. The upper arc is graduated with degrees (labeled 70, 80, 90, 80, 70). Two parallel vertical lines QR and a horizontal line MN are drawn relative to the gnomon's height. Various points are labeled with letters A, B, C, G, K, L, M, Q, R, S.</image-desc>

III. Let the individual degrees equally distant from the points of the horizontal line BC be joined by straight lines—or, to avoid confusion, every 10th or 5th degree, as we have done here—and through these same degrees let other lines be drawn from the center; thus the desired <term>conic triangles</term> <note>Triangles representing the cones of light and shadow cast by the sun at different times of the year.</note> of the stars' declination will be established.

IV. Let QR be drawn parallel to the vertical line AI, at a distance from it equal to the height of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The vertical rod or blade of a sundial.</note>; from the segments of the world axis PD, the equator DL, and the plane line PL, the gnomonic triangle PLD for a vertical plane will be formed. If, however, you desire the same gnomonic triangle for a horizontal plane, you will draw MN parallel to the horizontal line BC, at a distance from it equal to the length of the gnomon; it will be formed from the segments of the world axis SD, the equator DL, and the plane DSL, serving the horizontal plane. The lines QR and MN will intersect the cones at those points through which <term>hyperbolas</term> <note>The curved lines traced by the tip of a gnomon's shadow on most days of the year.</note> must be drawn when transferred to the meridian line, as will be seen later in practice. This <term>analemma</term> <note>A geometric projection of the celestial sphere onto a flat surface.</note> will serve for the conic sections of all the parallels of the stars' declination in the whole world. Hence the instrument will become more universal if the equinoctial and the axis of the world are 
<margin>How the instrument may be made universal.</margin>
joined and can be set at the center D to turn above the given altitude of the pole and the equator. This will also serve for inscribing the conic sections of the diurnal arcs on any plane, as will become clear in the following pages.

## Preliminary Exercise IV.

*To describe the Net, or the Almucantar-Azimuth Instrument; that is, to describe the Almucantars <note>Lines of altitude parallel to the horizon.</note> and Azimuths <note>Vertical circles or bearings relative to the horizon.</note>, or the horizontal and vertical circles on a horizontal plane, by means of a shadow-measuring ruler.*

**T**herefore, you will describe the Almucantar-Azimuth Net for a horizontal plane as follows. First, let there be made separately a circle of any size HRTV, divided into four quadrants intersecting each other at right angles at the center D by two diameters, HT and VR. Let a gnomonic triangle be applied to the meridian line HT; the radius BC will be the <term>axis of the world</term> <note>The imaginary line around which the heavens appear to rotate.</note>, AC the equator, and DC the gnomon <note>The vertical rod or pillar that casts the shadow.</note>, from which you will cut off an equal portion AB in the hour-writing quadrant, shown separately in Figure 2. If, therefore, you draw BY parallel to AI, the side of the quadrant, this parallelogram ABIY will provide the cut-out "expanded ruler," which shall be applied by its center B to the center D (the location of the stylus) assumed separately on the horizontal plane; this is done so that one side of the ruler, BY, perfectly matches line DV or DR, and the other side of the ruler, AB, perfectly matches line HT. If, therefore, you mark points according to the degrees of the applied ruler on line DV or DN, the circles drawn through them from the center D will give the desired Almucantars, or horizontal circles. But if

The circle contains a series of horizontal parallel lines (almucantars) in the upper half and radial lines (azimuths) originating from the center point D in the lower half. the center A of the lines described on the ruler is applied to center D in such a way that the side AI perfectly matches line DT or DH, the end points of the degrees of line BY will give points on line AI. If you draw straight lines from center D (the location of the stylus) through these points to the periphery of the circle, these will be the vertical lines, or the desired Azimuths in one quadrant, which may then be transferred to the other quadrants.

<margin>
*The Almucantar-Azimuth Instrument.*
</margin>

This instrument has such a remarkable use that there is hardly any kind of line that cannot be projected onto a plane by its help, as will be demonstrated more extensively in what follows. For this reason, we have decided to title the instrument the "Almucantar-Azimuth" instrument. For if anyone, with the diligence mentioned, describes the Almucantars and Azimuths for every single degree on a large scale, he will possess a mechanical instrument that performs the same function as the Almucantar-Azimuth tables, as will be seen in the following sections.

## Preliminary Exercise V.

*To describe Almucantars and Azimuths on a vertical plane.*

**L**et the vertical gnomonic triangle ABC be applied to AC, the meridian line of the plane, with three points marked: A for the pole, C for the equator, and O for the stylus. If you draw line VR through O perpendicular to AC, and another line parallel to VR through C, VR will be the horizontal line and MN the <term>equinoctial line</term> <note>The path the shadow follows when the sun is on the celestial equator.</note>. This having been done, apply the ruler (constructed a little earlier and having a width equal to the height of the stylus) to the horizontal line VR in such a way that BY perfectly matches said line. If you then mark the points of the degrees in this position on the horizontal line VR, and draw lines through them parallel to the meridian line, you will have the vertical circles, or Azimuths, described on the given plane.

<margin>
*Another method for describing Azimuths.*
</margin>

You will obtain the same results if, from point O, you draw a circle onto line AC (the length of the stylus OB being transferred) from the end of the stylus assumed above or below the horizontal. For if you divide this circle into 360 parts and draw straight lines through the points of division onto the horizontal VR, the lines drawn through these points parallel to the meridian AC will give the desired Azimuths.

### How to work for the Almucantars <note>original: "Almucantaris"; these are circles of altitude on the celestial sphere, parallel to the horizon.</note>.

**I**n the hour-drawing quadrant <note>A tool used to calculate the positions of hour lines.</note>, transfer the segments AB or DB from the gnomonic triangle (keeping the previous size of the stylus <note>The vertical rod or gnomon that casts the shadow.</note>). Each radius ending on side BY of the expanded ruler—specifically those intersecting AB at 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, etc., from A toward B in the hour-drawing quadrant—should be transferred as previously mentioned. Or, if the points are too close together, first transfer every 5 degrees, or every 10 as we have done here, or even every 15 degrees onto line AK of the hour-drawing quadrant. Then, draw lines through these transferred points parallel to the side of the quadrant AB; with the help of these, you will track down the points for the **conic sections** <note>The mathematical curves (like hyperbolas) formed when a cone is intersected by a plane; in gnomonics, the path of a shadow is a conic section.</note> on the vertical lines, or **Azimuths** <note>Lines representing the compass bearing or horizontal direction.</note> of the Net, through which the hyperbolas of the Almucantars must be drawn as follows (here, due to limited space, we have only drawn lines 80, 70, 60, and 50, marked with the letters N, D, B, and Y).

First, in the quadrant, apply the Azimuth marked 80 degrees with the letter N over the line parallel to the vertical line of the net marked with that same number (80), with such care that they align perfectly. Once this is done, you will mark every 15 degrees in order by piercing the paper with a needle; or, these same points can be transferred from the quadrant to the net's azimuth using a compass, labeling the points 15, 30, 45, 60, and 75. 

After this is done, apply line D (70) designated in the quadrant to the 70-degree azimuth on the plane of the net; as before, carefully mark each of the 15-degree points on this 70-degree Azimuth, labeling them with numbers as you did just before. Then, by applying the quadrant line B (60) to the vertical or 60-degree azimuth of the net, you will mark the said degrees on it, as has been described. And so, by applying the remaining parallels (50, 40, 30, 20, 10) in order to the vertical Azimuths of the Net for 50, 40, 30, 20, and 10 degrees,

you will mark every 15 degrees as was done before. # Problem I.
## *To draw the arcs of the Zodiac signs on a given plane.*

### Practical Application I.
### *To draw the parallels of the Zodiac signs on an equinoctial plane.*

**S**ince on an equinoctial plane <note>A sundial face set parallel to the Earth's equator.</note> the arcs of the signs are nothing other than circles, you may draw them on that same plane with almost no labor. Draw two lines intersecting at right angles at the center E: AB as the meridian or 12 o’clock line, and CD as the 6 o'clock line. If, therefore, in the "radiant Zodiac" <note>A reference to a specific diagram used as a calculation tool.</note> on line VZ representing the axis, you determine the size of the stylus <note>The gnomon or rod that casts the shadow.</note> from O toward either side LO or NO, and draw a straight line through L or N parallel to the radius of the equator AB; it will cut the rays of the signs at points through which circles drawn from E will give the desired result.

<margin>The double equinoctial, lower and upper.</margin>
Let the size of the stylus in VZ be determined as OL, as is clear in the following radiant Zodiac, and let LM, parallel to AB, cut the rays of the signs at points P, Q, and R. If, therefore, circles are drawn from the center E of the equinoctial plane at intervals LP, LQ, and LR, they will provide the desired arcs of the signs. The equinoctial line itself is not found on this dial, but rather vanishes entirely (just as the horizon vanishes on a horizontal dial, as shown above) because the equator is parallel to the plane. Therefore, at the time of the equinox, the gnomon casts an infinite shadow on an equinoctial plane, which is always larger the closer the Sun is to it. From this, a "double equinoctial plane" arises: the upper and the lower. On the upper plane, the shadow dwells for the six northern signs; on the lower, for the six southern signs.

<margin>Finding the horizontal line.</margin>
The horizontal line separates the upper part from the lower, and you find it thus: From E toward I, set the length of the stylus EI, and from I let a line be drawn containing the angle SIE of the

<image-desc>A circular gnomonic diagram. A vertical meridian line is marked AB, and a horizontal 6 o'clock line is marked CD, intersecting at center E. The left side is labeled "Horiz:" and the right "zontal", together forming "Horizontal". The top of the vertical axis features the symbol for Cancer (♋) and the bottom features Capricorn (♑). A diagonal line is labeled with the number 42, likely representing the latitude of Rome. Various concentric circles represent the paths of the sun through the different signs of the Zodiac.</image-desc>

elevation of the pole <note>The latitude of the observer.</note>. Where the drawn line intersects the meridian AB, draw a line through 그 point parallel to the 6 o'clock line CD; this will give the horizontal line, which divides the lower plane from the upper. But these things are too simple to deserve further explanation.

<margin>Another method.</margin>
You may also draw these arcs with the help of an Almucantar-Azimuth instrument. For if you apply it to the equinoctial plane so that its center D exactly matches the center E of the plane and the meridian line, all the circles from 1, 2, 3, up to 23 1/2 will represent the circles of the signs' declination. The shadow of the gnomon will show the degree of declination from the equator every day, and consequently the declinations of the signs when the Sun is at their beginning. See another method in Problem IX, Section III, Application I.

### Corollary.
**F**rom this it follows that the arcs of the signs on this plane are of the same projection as that which the Sun makes under a very oblique sphere at the horizon, and under a right sphere on the primary vertical plane.

## *The universal conic projection of the arcs of the Zodiac signs on a polar plane.*

For this reason, I have joined them here...

The First Method.

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram for constructing a sundial. Two primary intersecting lines meet at a central point N. Having drawn two lines intersecting each other at right angles at center N, of which AB represents the meridian line and EB the equinoctial line, let NA or NB represent the length of the style <note>The gnomon or "pointer" that casts the shadow.</note> (which must always be equal to the space intercepted between the 12th and 9th hour, as mentioned above and shown in the description of the polar sundial). Transfer the hour lines from O onto the line OB (which is the equator of the radiant Zodiac provided here) in this order: take the length of BN or AN with a compass (representing the style's height) and transfer it from point O, the center of the radiant Zodiac, onto the equinoctial line OB. Next, take the hour lines in order from between point B and the common points of intersection of the equator and the hours—for example, B 1, B 2, B 3, B 4, B 5—and transfer them from the same point O of the radiant Zodiac onto the radius of the equator, marking each point with its respective number, as seen here. Lines drawn through these points parallel to the axis YZ will provide the hour lines inscribed within the radiant Zodiac. You will then apply these parallel lines, together with the Zodiac, to the dial so that the equinoctial line OB of the Radiant tool matches perfectly with the equinoctial line EB of the polar dial, and the 12th hour line of the Radiant matches the 12th hour line of the dial.

<margin>
How the hour lines are first inscribed on the radiant Zodiac.

<image-desc>A triangular projection diagram labeled with apex A and base line M. Radiating lines from A meet a curved bottom edge marked with zodiacal symbols. Once this is done, carefully mark the points where the rays and the 12th hour line intersect on both sides of that same meridian line; for through these, the Sun's parallels—both Northern and Southern—will pass. Then, moving the parallel for the 1st hour on the Zodiac over the 1st hour line on the dial, mark the points for the rays as before on the 1st hour line. Next, mark the same on the 2nd hour line by applying the 2nd hour parallel of the Radiant onto the 2nd hour of the dial. Proceed in this way with the others until you have completed the seasonal hour inscription <note>original: "hectemoriam"; referring to the division of the day or the zodiacal arcs into parts.</note>. For curves drawn through the points belonging to the same parallel of a sign will give the arcs of the signs on the polar dial. If you transfer half of these arcs to the other side of the dial, you will have the complete arcs of the signs as required. The style shall be erected perpendicularly at point N, with its height equal to the space NB, or the distance to the 3rd or 9th hour.

<margin>The Second Method.</margin>
The second method for inscribing the arcs is both the easiest and most enjoyable. Operate in this way: let the full and half hours be marked on a polar or meridian sundial. Once this is done, apply the Radiant Zodiac with its vertex O over point 9 on the equinoctial line of the sundial, so that the equinoctial lines perfectly correspond (the Radiant Zodiac should be drawn on transparent paper soaked in oil <note>This was a common early modern technique for creating tracing paper.</note>). Once this is done, mark the points of the rays on the 12th hour line, as before. Then, move the vertex O over the half-hour after 9, and the line of the 1st hour will be intersected at points through which the arcs of the signs will pass. Then, move the vertex O again over 10, and the 2nd hour will be intersected at the points through which the arcs of the signs will pass; proceed in the same way with the rest, always applying the vertex O over the half-hours. By marking the common points of intersection between the rays and the hours on the full hours, the curved lines drawn through these will give the arcs of the signs <note>These arcs show the sun's path during different months, such as the summer or winter solstices.</note>.

<margin>The Third Method.</margin>
The third method is done with the help of the "latitude of shadows" from a universal table serving all polar and meridian dials throughout the whole world, which we have drawn from Table VI on page 292. Let the hours be inscribed on the polar plane, as shown. Place the table of shadows before you, and for the points of the arcs of the signs on the 12th hour, take the shadow parts corresponding to the 12th hour from the table. Transfer those points—based on the parts into which the style <note>the gnomon or shadow-casting rod</note> is divided into 12—from point N (the location of the style) to both sides of the 12th hour line. Secondly, for the points of the signs on lines 1 and 11, take the parts from the table corresponding to hours 1 and 11; for these, transferred from the location of the style to both sides of the 1st and 11th hour lines, will mark the points through which the arcs will pass. In the same way, you will find the points of the arcs of the signs on the remaining hour lines with the help of the table. This method is entirely easy and universal.

<margin>The Fourth Method.</margin>
The fourth method is by conic sections, which are described by the movement of a single string; it is wonderfully ingenious and pleasant, and is completed without the hours being drawn beforehand.

First, proceed thus: let there be two lines CD and AB, as before, intersecting each other at right angles at A.

Thus, we have delineated the arcs of the signs on a polar sundial in various ways, which was the task at hand.

## Problem III.
### To describe the arcs of the signs on a meridian sundial.

Since a meridian sundial differs from a polar one only in its position and the order of the hours, the description of the arcs of the signs in it will be exactly the same. This only must be noted: instead of the 12th hour line in the polar dial, use the 6th hour line here; and establish point E as the location of the style and the beginning of the conotomic projection. In a word: if you transfer the Zodiac from the polar dial into the hour lines of the meridian sundial, you will have what you seek. The rest differs in no way from the polar dial. But since this has been spoken of at length in the preceding sections, we refer the reader there.

## Problem IV.
### To inscribe the arcs of the signs on a horizontal plane.

See various methods for inscribing the arcs of the signs in the works of diverse authors; we share only our own inventions along with a most easy and universal method for the curious reader.

### Section I.

<margin>Universal Corollary</margin>
Given the parallel of any star, to find—from the cone which it would describe by its motion around the center of the gnomon <note>original: "gnomonis"</note>, if it projected a shadow on an equidistant parallel plane—the parabola, hyperbola, or ellipse which it would delineate in any other given cone-section <note>original: "conotomo"</note> plane. For you will have **G** as the focus of the hyperbola for Cancer ♋. You will have the opposite **H** if you cut off from **OB** the segment **OH** equal to **NG**. Then, with **NO** halved at **K**, let any number of points **Q, R, S, T, X** be assumed in **VN**, through which hidden circles are drawn from **K**. Then, having placed the compass at point **G**, let other hidden circles, or merely arcs of circles, be drawn through **V, Q, R, S, T, X, N**: for where these have cut the previous circles on the other side of the sundial, the other part of the hyperbola for Cancer ♋ must be drawn through those points. If again you draw circles on both sides from **H** (as the center or focus) at the intervals **HM, HN, HO, HP, HQ**, they will cut the previous circles at points through which the opposite hyperbola must be drawn. If you desire to describe the hyperbolas of the remaining parallels, you will proceed in exactly the same way as in the description of the tropics, retaining points **GH**, whether assumed arbitrarily or made from comparison—that is, the centers and foci of the reflections. ### Practical Exercise III. ###
#### To describe the hyperbolas of the arcs of the zodiac signs on a horizontal plane solely by the drawing of a string. ####

<margin>Third method by the help of a string.</margin>
**F**irst, take from the analemma <note>A geometric construction used to project the celestial sphere onto a flat surface.</note> of the base of the cone (the section or hyperbola of which you desire) the diameter GK, along with the diameter of that same section IA. The base KG will be halved at I; and from this perpendicular axis ID, take IB as double the length of IG, and IC as three parts where the line GI is four. Thus, the line GC is necessarily 5 parts, and equal to the line CD—for 3 taken from 8 leaves 5. In this way, you will determine the points C and D on the axis IB by comparison. You will find the vertices A and B as follows: make DE equal to DG, and EF equal to GC (or DC), and divide CF in half at A, which is the vertex of the hyperbola to be drawn. The vertex B of the opposite section is found if BD is made equal to AC, or AB equal to FD. Furthermore, let a movable ruler of length DG be fixed around the center D. A string of length CG (or EF) has one end fixed at C and the other at the tip of the ruler. Thus, a drawing tool, by loosening or tightening the taut strings along the ruler's reference line, will describe the hyperbola GEK. Or otherwise: let two needles be fixed at the foci <note>The points that define the shape of the curve.</note> C and C, and let two strings be wound around them, which, when twisted together, are led through the eye of a needle to the vertex A. Then, by gradually loosening the strings, move the needle from A in either direction; by its motion, the hyperbola will be described in exactly the same manner as we showed in the preceding problem. And this is the method of Father Grienberger <note>original: "Patris Grinbergerii"; Christopher Grienberger (1561–1636) was a Jesuit mathematician who succeeded Clavius in Rome.</note> of blessed memory; truly remarkable and ingenious.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing the construction of a hyperbola. It features a triangle with base GK and a vertical axis containing points A, I, B, and D. A dashed curve representing the hyperbola passes through point E and terminates at G and K.</image-desc>

### Practical Exercise IV. ###
#### To describe the conic sections of the arcs of the signs on a horizontal plane through tangents. ####

<margin>Fourth method by the help of tangents.</margin>
**U**se the following table, having first applied the gnomonic triangle of the meridian AB to the horizontal plane. The line drawn normally <note>at a right angle</note> to the center of the clock A will be the sixth-hour line; the line drawn normally to B will be the equinoctial line; and finally, the gnomon <term>gnomon: the part of a sundial that casts the shadow</term> QC is drawn normally to Q. Let the horizontal astronomical sundial be described according to the methods and rules prescribed previously. Then, with the stylus <note>the vertical rod of the sundial</note> CQ divided first into 10 equal parts (corresponding to 1,000 parts of the whole sine <term>whole sine: the radius of the reference circle used in trigonometry</term>), transfer the tangents of the signs in parts of the stylus from the center of the clock A onto the corresponding hour lines, beginning from Cancer ♋, according to the order noted in the table. To find point 12 for Cancer ♋, take the tangent 14.45 in parts of the stylus, and transfer it from the center A to the meridian point Q; for that will be the desired point 12 in Cancer ♋. If, however, you desire point 12 in Capricorn ♑, take the tangent 33.05 and transfer it in parts of the stylus from center A to point R on the meridian line; for that will be the point sought. You will find the points of other parallels in the same way for any given hour. But since these things are very easy, let it suffice to have declared them with one or two examples.

<margin>The fifth method.</margin>
**T**he same technique can be achieved from a table of shadow lengths, if you derive the quantity of the shadow through the altitudes <note>original: "altitudines"</note> corresponding to each hour, and determine that quantity from the location of the <term>style</term> <note>The physical rod or blade of the sundial that casts the shadow.</note> within the hour lines. <margin>The sixth method.</margin>
**Y**ou will also mark the arcs of the [zodiac] signs with the help of an <term>Almucantar-Azimuth instrument</term> <note>An instrument used to measure both altitude (almucantar) and horizontal direction (azimuth) of celestial bodies.</note>, and by the assistance of an Almucantar-Azimuth table, in this way: Look where the Azimuth and the Almucantar circles intersect when the Sun is positioned at the beginning of Cancer (which the Almucantar-Azimuth table will suggest to you). For if you calculate the Azimuth and Almucantar numbers in the shared area of Cancer and at the 12th hour—those from the meridian on both sides, and these in the found Azimuth—where those lines intersect, there will be the point for the 12th hour in Cancer. You will proceed in this same way for investigating the remaining points on the hour lines. ### Problem V. ###
### To describe the arcs of the signs on a vertical plane. ###

**T**he arcs of the [zodiac] signs are described on a vertical plane in exactly the same way as on a horizontal one: the only difference is in the application of the <term>gnomonic triangle</term> <note>The geometric triangle formed by the gnomon's height, the shadow, and the line connecting the tip to the shadow's end.</note>. Thus, the angle of the complement of the pole's elevation <note>Latitude</note>, which on a horizontal plane was established at the equator, is established on the vertical plane at the common intersection point of the axis and the meridian. But let us run through the individual steps briefly.
