...the sixth, CS of the equinoctial. Then, the astronomical hours should be marked on the intended plane, upon which you will scribe the intersecting arcs using this technique. First, let the radius of the equator CB in the radiating Zodiac <note>A specialized geometric tool or diagram used to project the paths of the sun across different signs.</note> be divided into ten, or a hundred, or a thousand equal parts in the place of the <term>total sine</term> <note>The radius of the reference circle used in trigonometric calculations, often set to a large power of 10 to avoid fractions.</note>. Then, using the table from § 1 of the preceding problem, you will transfer the secants of the hour distances from the meridian, measured in parts of the line CB, from B onto CZ, the radius of the equator. For through such points, the hour radii drawn obliquely from A will intersect the radii of the signs at specific points. When each of these is intercepted from A and transferred again from the center A of the sundial onto the corresponding hour lines, they will provide the required points for the arcs of the signs. Thus, the spaces between A and the points of the radii 12, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, cut off from the radius of <term>Cancer</term> <note>♋</note> and transferred from the center of the vertical sundial onto the 12, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 hour lines, will give the points through which the <term>hyperbola</term> <note>The geometric shape formed by the shadow's path on most sundials throughout the day.</note> of <term>Cancer</term> <note>♋</note> will pass. The same must be done for the others.

## The Second Method: Very Easy via Two Threads.

**F**irst, let two lines be made at right angles at E, intersecting each other; but let a normal line TAS be drawn to the line AB at A. Second, apply the gnomonic triangle for a vertical dial to this line AS, so that AS matches the line AB of the world axis. CB will be the <term>style</term> <note>The physical rod or blade that casts the shadow.</note>, BD the radius of the equator, and AD the meridian line, or 12 o'clock, as the first figure here shows. If, however, you desire the hours of the signs for a horizontal plane, you will apply the horizontal gnomonic triangle (that is, the inverted triangle for a vertical dial) to line AT. Third, with the interval ED, let a semicircle ADB be described, divided exactly into 12 parts. Connect each point of the divisions equidistant from D with hidden straight lines, carefully noting where they intersect the line ED; let these points of intersection be E, F, G, H, I, K. Fourth, let the radiating Zodiac be applied again with its center at point B of the gnomonic triangle in the second figure, so that BD corresponds to the radius of the equator. Everything in the semicircle of the first figure should be cut away except the edges AE, AB, and ED; in the radiating Zodiac, everything should also be cut away except the edge of the signs' declination and the edge of the equator BV. You will then have an instrument prepared for scribing the arcs of the signs very easily.

## Practice of the Preceding Instrument.

**W**ith the help of this instrument, given any hour, we can find the point on it through which a given parallel of the Sun passes faster than said, and consequently find the arcs of all parallels with almost no effort. Suppose the point for <term>Cancer</term> <note>♋</note> is to be found at the 3rd or 9th astronomical hour. Extend a thread from B, as if fixed to the center, over the point of the parallel of <term>Cancer</term> <note>♋</note>, and another thread from A, as if from the center, over the given 3rd hour on line ED. For if you transfer the space intercepted between A and the point where the threads intersect from the center of the sundial to the line of the third hour, that will be the sought point of <term>Cancer</term> <note>♋</note> at the given hour. Suppose again the point for <term>Capricorn</term> <note>♑</note> is to be marked on the 12 o'clock line. Let two threads be extended from A and B: the former through the 12 o'clock point on line ED, and the latter from B through point M of the parallel of <term>Capricorn</term> <note>♑</note> on the edge of the signs. If you then transfer the space between A and the intersection point of the threads from the center of the sundial to the 12 o'clock line, you will have what was sought. You shall determine the same for finding points of other parallels.

---

# Gnomonic Sky-Drawing <note>original: "Ouranographia Gnomonica"</note>

...having been marked, if you inscribe the arcs of the signs according to the practices handed down in the preceding sections, the result will be a vertical sundial equal to a horizontal and declining one. However, I have thought it necessary to declare a bit more fully with how much caution one must proceed in this practical procedure <term>Pragmatia</term> <note>A term used by the author to refer to the technical or "business" of the geometric construction.</note>.

Let there be, therefore, a plane declining toward the East by 30 degrees at the latitude <note>original: "elevationem poli," literally the elevation of the pole.</note> of Rome, according to the previous instructions. First, you will investigate the declination of the substyle line <term>linea styli</term> <note>The line on the dial face directly beneath the gnomon's rod.</note> from the meridian, which we taught how to find above on pages 349 and 357. Second, find the height of the style above the plane; you will also find this practice handed down in the cited place. Let there be, therefore, a gnomonic triangle of the pole's elevation above the given plane $EZK$, based on the substyle line $CE$ in the declining dial; $ZK$ will be the radius of the equator, $CZ$ the style <note>The physical rod that casts the shadow.</note>, and $EZ$ the axis. Thus, the tangent of the wall’s declination transferred onto the horizontal line will give point $R$, through which a straight line drawn from $E$ will give the meridian, or the 12 o'clock line. Furthermore, the tangent of the complement of the declination transferred to the opposite part of the horizontal line will give point $A$, the common intersection of the primary vertical, the six o'clock line, and the equinoctial line. If you connect $K$ with point $A$ in a straight line, you will have the equinoctial line <note>The line the shadow follows during the Spring and Autumn Equinoxes.</note> depicted on the sundial.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the construction of a sundial (gnomonic projection). It features a vertical axis with points E, Z, C, and K. A triangle EZK represents the gnomonic triangle relative to the plane. Several rays emanate from point Z, crossing horizontal and angled lines to mark points on the zodiacal arcs at the bottom. If, therefore, you adapt the gnomonic triangle above the declining plane (equal to a horizontal dial found elsewhere) to the radiating Zodiac in such a way that $EZ$ is the axis, $ZK$ the radius of the equator, $ECK$ the substyle line (or the meridian of the declining plane), and $ZC$ the style. Again, if by the benefit of Table 2 on page 358 (proposed in the problem of the declining sundial) you transfer the secants of the tangents from the substyle line on the equinoctial from the center $Z$ of the radiating Zodiac onto the radius of the equator, and draw straight lines through the points from $E$; these will cut the radii of the signs at points whose intervals from $E$, when transferred from the center of the dial onto the corresponding hour lines, will give the sought-after arcs of the signs on the declining dial.

<margin>Another method.</margin>
Furthermore, if you inscribe the arcs of the signs in a horizontal sundial that is equal to the declining vertical one (as has been said) through exactly the same practices handed down for the horizontal dial—making the necessary adjustments <note>original: "servatis servandis," a common Latin phrase in technical writing meaning "with the things that ought to be observed having been observed."</note>—you will have the sought-after arcs of the signs on the given plane. If, however, anyone is affected by weariness from this sort of thing, he will be able to use the mechanical operations which we will produce in the following sections, by which he will obtain the desired effect with almost no trouble.

### Problem VII.

->To inscribe the arcs of the signs in sundials inclining to the horizon.<-

Since inclining sundials <note>Dials on surfaces that are tilted or sloped rather than being perfectly horizontal or vertical.</note> are nothing other than horizontal dials under a certain specific latitude (which the table on page 359, proposed in the problem of inclining dials, teaches): if, therefore, you inscribe the arcs found through the cited table according to the procedures handed down in Problem IV regarding the inscription of the arcs of the signs in some horizontal dial corresponding to the inclining one, and you elevate the plane from the horizon according to the degrees of inclination so that the meridian line corresponds to the meridian, the gnomon will show the sought-after parallels of the Sun. Since this problem is very easy, it does not seem to require further explanation.

### Problem VIII.

->To describe the arcs of the signs in dials declining from the horizon.<-

Since those declining from the horizon are nothing other than declining vertical dials elsewhere: if, through the second table on page 360 in Problem VI, you find a constructed vertical declining sundial corresponding to some dial declining from the horizon, and in it you inscribe the arcs of the signs according to Problem VI, you will have what you sought. Or, if you inscribe the arcs in the horizontal dial equal to this vertical declining one according to the practices handed down in Problem IV, the same arcs will be produced for the sought-after dial declining from the horizon.

# Problem IX.

### A Recapitulation <note>original: "Anacephaleoticon," a summary or condensed explanation</note> and Universal Method, by which the arcs of the signs are taught to be inscribed through the termination of hours on any given plane: and this is taken from the Wonderful Abacus <note>A mathematical table or chart used for calculation</note> placed above on page 400.

Whoever knows the common intersections of the hour circles and the parallels of the Sun, he will possess an excellent and very useful <note>original Greek: "polychreston"</note> method for inscribing solar hyperbolas <note>The curved paths that the tip of a shadow traces on a flat surface throughout the day</note> on any plane; which method we set down briefly here; excerpted from the "Wonderful Abacus of the Termination of Hours" proposed above on page 400.

## Explanation of the Table.

First, the hours marked in the top row AB denote the hours through which the others are to be terminated: the hours in column AC are the hours on the equinoctial <note>The line on the sundial where the shadow falls during the equinox</note> of the sundial after midday; the hours in column BD are the hours on the equinoctial before midday: the intermediate terminated hours will give the desired points of the solar parallels.

In any sundial, therefore—for example, a horizontal one, or any other of any plane—let the astronomical hours <note>Standard 60-minute hours counted from noon or midnight</note> be described with their half-hours. Once this is done, you will terminate the hours, or rather describe on it the solar parallels that terminate the hours, by the following artifice.

### Practical Canons <term>Canones Pragmatici</term> <note>Rule-based procedures for the technical construction of the dial</note>.

If you wish for the description of the parallels through the 12th hour, or through the first column: first, with the help of the **Radiant Zodiac** <note>A tool previously described by Kircher for projecting celestial coordinates onto a plane</note>, you will seek the points of the parallels on the meridian line of the sundial. But if through the 1st and 11th hour, or the second column: the points of the parallels must first be investigated in the said hour lines. If through the 2nd and 10th column, you will seek the points of the said arcs of the signs in the same hour line. Therefore, once the points of the signs are given in any hour lines, you will find the points in the remaining hours through which the arcs of the signs must be drawn with the aid of the preceding table. If, therefore, the termination is to be established through the first column, that is 12, which we have chosen as an example; one must proceed as follows.

## Canon I.

### To find the tropical points in hour 1 and 11.

1. **If** you wish to terminate the first hour, apply the ruler above hour 12 at the point of Cancer <note>symbolized as $\sigma$ or ♋</note>, and above the 1/2 hour before 1 on the equinoctial, that is, 1/2 [of the hour] terminating the 1st hour. If again you place the ruler above hour 12 at the point of Cancer, and above the middle hour, that is 1/2 before 7 as column BD notes; where hour 1 is cut, there is the tropical point of Cancer. You see, therefore, that the hours which must be terminated always occupy the middle column.

### Rule II.
*To find the points of the parallels at the 2nd hour.*

**A**pply a ruler over the point for Capricorn <note>Symbolized by ♑, the winter solstice</note> on the meridian line (the 12 o’clock line) and over the 1st hour on the equinoctial line <note>The straight line the shadow follows during the spring and autumn equinoxes</note>, as column AC shows, which corresponds to the 2nd hour in that region of the column; see where the ruler intersects the 2nd hour line, for the Tropic of Capricorn will pass through that point. Again, apply the ruler over the 12th hour of Capricorn and over the 7th hour on the equinoctial, as column BD demonstrates, and see where the 2nd hour is intersected; the Tropic of Cancer <note>Symbolized by ♋, the summer solstice</note> will pass through that point. You will find the points for the remaining parallels in a similar way.

### Rule III.
*For the points of the parallels at the 3rd hour.*

**A**pply the ruler first over point F (the 12th hour of the Tropic of Capricorn) and over the halfway mark between 1 and 2, as the first column teaches, and see where the 3rd hour is intersected: the Tropic of Cancer will pass through that point. Again, apply the same ruler over E, and over the halfway mark between 7 and 8 in column BD, and see where the 3rd hour is intersected; Capricorn will pass through there. If, however, you apply the ruler over point X of the parallel for Sagittarius <note>♐</note> and Scorpio <note>♏</note>, and over the halfway mark between 1 and 2, the intersection on the 3rd hour line will give you the point through which the opposite parallel of Gemini <note>♊</note> and Aquarius <note>♒</note> passes. By applying the ruler over point Y of the parallel for Aquarius and Pisces <note>♓</note>, and over the halfway mark, it will give the intersection point for the opposite parallel of Gemini and Leo <note>♌</note>. Furthermore, the ruler applied over E and the halfway mark between 7 and 8 in column BD will mark the point on the 3rd hour line through which Capricorn will pass. And so, you shall proceed according to the order of the hours contained in the columns until you have found the points of the parallels for every single hour.

### Rule IV.
*If, however, the points of the parallels at the 11th hour are known, you will find the points through which the parallels must pass on all remaining hour lines by the aid of column 2, marked with the number 11 or MN, using this method.*

**I**f you desire to find the point for Cancer, for example, at the 2nd hour: see which hours on the equinoctial (that is, in columns AC and BD) correspond to it, and you will find 12 1/2 and 6 1/2. If, therefore, you apply the ruler over the point for Cancer at the 11th hour and over the halfway mark between 12 and 1 on the equinoctial, it will intersect the 2nd hour at the point through which Cancer will pass. If you apply the ruler over the point for Capricorn at the 11th hour and over the halfway mark between 6 and 7, the ruler will give the desired point for Capricorn at the 2nd hour. And if you apply the ruler over the point for Capricorn on the 1st hour line and over the halfway mark between 12 and 11, it will give the point of intersection on the 10th hour line through which Cancer shall pass. You will also have the point for the Tropic of Capricorn at the 2nd hour if you apply the ruler over the point for Capricorn at the 1st hour and over the halfway mark between 9 and 8. Whatever we say here regarding the Tropics should also be understood for the remaining parallels, as we showed in Rule I.

### Note.

**I**f the points of the parallels are known on the 10th hour line, the third column marked with that same number will serve you; if they are known at the 9th hour, the fourth column will serve you for determining the points of the remaining hours, and so on for the others. Therefore, let these brief remarks suffice. He who desires more may consult Book 4, where we have explained this "Wonderful Abacus" <note>A calculation table or chart</note> at length. Indeed, this craftsmanship is so immense and proceeds by such a vast series of combinations that it seems it can scarcely be exhausted; we have drawn it out from a certain hidden property of the hyperbolic section <note>The mathematical curve (hyperbola) formed by the shadow on a flat surface</note>, which we pointed out in Book 3, part 2, theorem 12. I do not doubt that the curious and sagacious reader, if he penetrates these matters, will find innumerable other things pertaining to this subject that have been discovered by no one else. But having briefly indicated these things, let us now move on to others.

## Problem X.
### Mechanical inscription of the arcs.
### Practical Application I.
*To inscribe the arcs of the signs using an observational instrument.*

**V**arious instruments have been devised by craftsmen for inscribing the arcs of the signs <note>The curved lines on a sundial representing the zodiac signs</note>. But since their construction is for the most part laborious, we shall set those aside and introduce those that are both easy to use and easy to obtain. Thus, you will describe the arcs of the signs with almost no effort on any surface by means of the observational instrument proposed here. Therefore, on the table ABCD of this instrument, let there be placed at the elevated part E a prototype of any sundial together with the inscription of the Zodiac—that is, the arcs of the signs exactly inscribed upon it. Then, let the plane of any declination—be it vertical-inclined or declining—be placed upon the surface of the table; so that if the plane declines 30 degrees from the meridian EV toward the East, you will arrange the vertical plane in such a way that the base of the plane contains the angle of said declination with the line EV of the table.

### Practical Exercise II.
### *To accomplish the same on any plane by the guiding of a thread.*

<image-desc>A complex gnomonic diagram and apparatus. It shows two inclined planes. **O**nce the 12 o'clock line **AB** has been drawn on any plane, and the axis **AC** has been erected and fixed upon it according to the <term>gnomonic triangle|A right-angled triangle used to calculate the height and angle of the gnomon based on local latitude</term> of the given plane, you will attach to it a "radiant Zodiac" <note>A circular scale showing the degrees or signs of the Zodiac</note> inscribed on a wooden plate, so that the radius of the equator **OB** is perpendicular to the axis **OA**. Let it be fixed at point **O** in such a way that it can rotate around the axis, but cannot change its position. When this is finished, let a thread be extended from **O** so that it freely brushes the surface of the radiant Zodiac plate. If you extend this thread over the radius of Cancer <note>♋, the summer solstice</note> so that it always runs straight over said radius all the way to the wall, it will indicate the point on the wall through which the <term>Tropic of Cancer|The line marking the sun's highest point in the sky during the summer solstice.</term> must be drawn. If the Zodiac triangle is rotated around the axis while the thread remains straight over that same radius, the thread extended to the wall will describe the desired curve for Cancer. If you extend the thread over the remaining radii, you will describe the corresponding arcs on the wall. The logic is perfectly clear to anyone who correctly considers the path of the thread on the radiant Zodiac as representing a ray of the Sun. Having described the arcs in this manner—

# Gnomonic Sky-Mapping <note>original Latin: "Ouranographia Gnomonica," from the Greek "ouranos" (sky) and "graphia" (writing/mapping).</note>

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram at the top left illustrates an inclined plane with points A, B, C, I, and D. ### Another method by means of a hollow hemisphere.

**I**f one has already inscribed hours of every kind, as well as celestial lines, into a hollow hemisphere: then cut out the two tropics <note>The lines representing the sun's path at the summer and winter solstices.</note> and the equator. With the center of this hemisphere applied to the tip of the <term>stylus|The rod or needle of a sundial that casts the shadow.</term>, and a thread drawn from that same center through the 12 o'clock point onto the wall—so that the thread corresponds to the 12 o'clock mark in both the hemisphere and on the wall—it will be perfectly positioned. If, therefore, you extend the thread straight through the shapes of the Tropic of Cancer (♋) and Capricorn (♑) onto each individual hour point on the wall, the end of the thread will mark those specific hour points. When these are joined by straight lines on the wall, they will form the sundial together with the curved arcs of the zodiac signs.

## Problem XI.
### How to inscribe Almucantars and Azimuths on given planes.
### Practical Exercise I.
### On horizontal and vertical planes.

**T**ake the expanded ruler <note>original: "regula expansa"</note> ABIY, which was also described in Preliminary Exercise IV. Apply it over the line so that point A coincides with D (the center or the location of the <term>gnomon|The part of a sundial that casts the shadow, here serving as a reference point for the calculation.</term>), and the side BY coincides with line **Ia**. Having done this, mark the points of the degrees indicated on side BY onto line **Ia**. Through these points, if you draw straight lines using A as your center, they will give you the vertical lines, or the desired <term>Azimuths|An astronomical measurement of the direction of a celestial object along the horizon.</term>. You will then add the numbers to these in the same order as they are marked on the ruler.

Again, if you apply the side of the ruler BY to the line **VR**, so that B takes the position of the center or gnomon-site D, and you mark the points of the degrees upon it; the circles drawn from the gnomon-site D through these degree points will provide the desired <term>Almucantars|Circles of altitude parallel to the horizon, used to measure how high the sun is in the sky.</term>.

### Practical Application II.

## To inscribe Almucantars and Azimuths on an equinoctial plane.

**L**et two lines, AB and CD, be drawn intersecting at right angles at A; CD will be the horizontal line, and AB will be the equinoctial diameter. Or, to line AB, let a <term>gnomonic triangle|A right-angled triangle used in sundial construction where the angles correspond to the local latitude.</term> be fitted with such care that the angle *Abd* contains the degrees of the elevation of the pole <note>The local latitude.</note> for the given region. The angle *A*, or *dbc*, will then contain the angle of the complement of the pole’s elevation—namely, the angle of the equator—and point C will be the vertex point <note>The Zenith, the point directly overhead.</note>. If, therefore, you have drawn a horizontal sundial and placed it upon this plane so that its center corresponds to center C and its meridian line corresponds to line AC, the <term>stylus|The rod or needle that casts the shadow.</term> *db* will show the vertical circles <note>Azimuths.</note> every fifteen degrees. Indeed, the description of vertical circles on an equinoctial plane is exactly the same as the description of hour lines on a horizontal plane.

->[A circular astronomical diagram representing a celestial sphere or projection. A vertical axis is marked A at the center and B at the bottom, with a secondary axis extending upward to point P. A horizontal axis is labeled C and D, with the words "HORI" and "VERTICALIS" (Horizontal and Vertical) inscribed along it. Numerous intersecting arcs and radiating lines are marked with degree measurements (30, 45, 60, 75, 90). A conical projection is sketched over the center, with its apex at P and base points labeled K, L, M, N, I, O along a horizontal plane.]<-

Therefore, just as all the hour circles from noon and midnight, and the axis of the world, relate to the horizon and its parallel plane, so do the <term>Azimuths|Vertical circles used to measure the horizontal direction of a celestial body.</term> and their common intersection of the axis relate to the horizon and the equator and its equidistant plane. There is only this difference: what is called the "equinoctial" in a horizontal sundial is called the "horizontal" in this place; and what is the "six o'clock line" there becomes the "primary vertical line" here. If, therefore, you transfer line *Ab* in the gnomonic triangle to S, and from that same point describe a circle divided into 360 parts, straight lines drawn from S through those divisions will give points on the horizontal line CD. Other straight lines drawn from C (the center) through those points will be the desired vertical lines. The demonstration of this fact is clear from what has been said.

<margin>
Astronomical hours on a horizontal plane are the same as vertical lines on an equinoctial plane.
</margin>

Furthermore, you may inscribe <term>Almucantars|Circles of altitude parallel to the horizon.</term> from the <term>analemma|A geometric projection of the celestial sphere onto a flat surface.</term> proposed in Preliminary Exercise III of this chapter in this way: Place the equator with the world axis so it can rotate around the center of the analemma, in such a way that the equinoctial occupies the position of the horizon, and the world axis occupies the position of the horizontal axis. Once this is done in the analemma proposed on page 404, let a length DP equal to the world axis SE be taken; at its point P, let a perpendicular line KL be drawn, which will intersect the horizontal line BC at T. If, therefore, starting from T, you transfer the spaces MNIO, etc., from point A of the horizontal line on the equinoctial sundial plane onto the meridian toward C, you will have the points (or vertices) of the hyperbolas. If you then describe <term>conic projections|The curves formed by intersecting a cone with a plane: hyperbolas, parabolas, and ellipses.</term> through these points according to the rules and practices delivered in Preliminary Exercise III and the preceding sections, they will give you the desired Almucantars. Note carefully which side of the cone the equinoctial line is parallel to; for through that point, not a hyperbola, but a **parabola** must be drawn—such as the 48th Almucantar in this equinoctial sundial. If, however, it neither touches the cone nor cuts the base, that Almucantar will be an **ellipsis**, such as the 60th here, which should be well noted. Note further that the Almucantars described from T toward L belong to the lower plane.

This is the easiest method of all and much faster than the previous one; therefore, I would advise the Reader to use it.

### Problem XII.
### To inscribe Almucantars and Azimuths on a polar plane.

**A**zimuths <note>original: "Azymutha." Lines showing compass direction.</note>, or the vertical lines inscribed on a <term>polar plane|A sundial face that lies parallel to the Earth's axis, pointing toward the celestial poles.</term>, are the same as the hour lines on a vertical sundial if they are taken every fifteen degrees. Therefore, if you apply a vertical sundial to a polar plane so that the meridian line corresponds to the polar meridian, and in place of the hours you put individual fifteen-degree increments up to 90, you will have the vertical lines inscribed on the polar sundial. 

For just as the hour circles relate to the axis of the world on a plane equidistant to the vertical, so do the vertical circles relate to the axis of the horizon on a polar plane (or the circle of the 6th hour). The only difference is that where the equinoctial line is on the vertical dial, the horizontal line is on this one; and where the 6th hour line is on the vertical dial, the vertical line <note>The line representing the Zenith/Nadir direction.</note> is on this one. Therefore, if you apply the gnomonic triangle to this sundial as you would on a vertical one, and at the interval EB above the horizontal line you draw a circle from point A on the meridian line—divided into 360 parts, or into five, ten, or fifteen-degree increments according to the capacity of the plane—and draw hidden straight lines from the center to the horizontal; these other straight lines will give...

### Corollary I

<margin>The Gnomonic Secret.</margin>
**H**ence is revealed a certain wonderful method by which, with the help of this <term>Net|A grid-like projection or coordinate system used in instrument making.</term>, you can delineate any plane declining from the vertical faster than it can be said. If, from the <term>Almucantar-azimuthal table|A table providing the coordinates for altitude and direction circles.</term>, you mark with a small needle on the subject plane the common intersections of the verticals and Almucantars, corresponding in order to the astronomical hours in the table; for straight lines drawn through these from the center of the sundial will give the hours of the declining plane.

### Corollary II

**H**ence it follows further, that there is no kind of celestial lines or circles which cannot be given in any plane, faster than it can be said, by the help of this Net through the tables of the said celestial circles. Truly a great and distinguished secret in the art of sundials. But since we shall declare all these things more extensively in the following books, we refer the reader there.

### Problem XIV

*Regarding the circles of position, or the delineation of the twelve celestial houses in any given plane.*

**W**hat the circles of position are, and what the lines of the <term>celestial houses|Twelve divisions of the sky used in both astronomy and astrology to track the positions of stars and planets.</term> are, was said in the First Preliminary Apparatus, where we brought forward a twofold method: one by Campanus, who <margin>The Method of Regiomontanus.</margin> draws the circles of position through the common intersections of the horizon and the meridian, and through each degree of the primary vertical; the other is the rational method of Regiomontanus, who describes the circles through the same intersections of the horizon and meridian, and through each part of the equator. <margin>The Method of Campanus.</margin> We shall teach how to inscribe both methods on any given plane. We presuppose, therefore, in this place, that the tropics, the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator.</note>, and the horizontal line have been previously delineated on the given plane according to the preceding instructions. Once this is done, operate as follows.

### Practice I

*To describe the circles of the celestial houses on a horizontal plane.*

<margin>The line of positions according to the method of Regiomontanus on a horizontal plane.</margin>
**T**herefore, once the often-proposed gnomonic triangle has been applied above the meridian line CA, as was done in the horizontal sundial, ST will be the equinoctial line, and DB will be both the <term>style|The part of the sundial that casts the shadow.</term> and the vertical line. If, therefore, you apply an expanded scale on a ruler (the width of which should be as great as the equinoctial radius AB) to the edge of the degrees above the equinoctial ST, and mark the points every five degrees, or every ten degrees, along it: the lines drawn parallel to the meridian through each point will give the sought lines of position according to the mind of Regiomontanus. And the lines drawn parallel through each 30-degree point will be the lines of the celestial houses, and each 15-degree parallel will be the middle of a house.

->Another method<-

### Corollary

<margin>A notable summary of the description of the celestial houses.</margin>
**I**t is clear that a polar dial, or a meridian dial, on a horizontal plane, is nothing other than a diagram of the <term>celestial houses|The twelve divisions of the sky used in astrology and astronomy to track the positions of celestial bodies.</term>, according to <term>Campanus|Johannes Campanus (c. 1220–1296), a mathematician who developed a specific system for dividing the sky into houses based on equal divisions of the prime vertical.</term>. If, therefore, you fix it to a given plane, it will represent to you the complete houses with their midpoints, for which you may replace the hour numbers with the house numbers, as you see done here. 

However, since the Sun is always at the end of some house before it is at the beginning—because the position of the celestial houses is opposite to the position of the hours—it follows that a shadow falling on one of those lines, for example on 11, shows that the Sun is at the end of the 11th house and is moving toward the beginning of the 10th. The same must be said of the degrees of position, which terminate at the meridian, which is the 90th circle of position. For the meaning, use, and quality of these houses and circles of position, see our *Physico-Astrological Gnomonics*.

### Practice II.
#### To describe these same houses on a vertical plane.

**F**irst, let the gnomonic triangle constructed for the vertical be applied to the meridian: then prepare an expanded ruler of the same width as the radius of the equator in the gnomonic triangle: apply this to the equinoctial line, and mark points upon it at every five, ten, and fifteen degrees: if you draw straight lines through these points from the location of the gnomon, you will have the circles of position, of which the 90th is the meridian. If, however, you draw lines from the location of the style through each 30-degree point of the divisions, you will have the celestial houses according to <term>Regiomontanus|Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), whose system of house division was based on the equator rather than the prime vertical.</term>, as is clear in the first figure. Again, having placed the center of the ruler at the location of the style, so that the side of the ruler resting on the horizon is parallel to the equator, the rays drawn from the center of the style will represent the lines of position according to Campanus. If, therefore, you mark points in the underlying plane next to the degrees on the side of the ruler, straight lines drawn through them from the location of the style will give the circles of position, and the celestial houses according to Campanus through each 30-degree point, as is clear in the second figure. The logic is so clear from the position and the drawing of the circles themselves that it requires no explanation. You will also achieve the same result if you describe a circle from the location of the style divided into 12 equal parts; for straight lines drawn from the center of the circle through the points of division will give the lines of the celestial houses on a vertical plane, according to Campanus.

### Corollary.

**I**t is clear, therefore, that an equinoctial dial placed on a vertical plane reflects, by its hour lines, the lines of the celestial houses with their midpoints according to Campanus.

### Practice III.
#### To inscribe these same houses on a meridian plane.

**T**ake the <term>dodecatemoria|A ruler or scale divided into 12 equal parts, traditionally used for zodiacal or house divisions.</term> ruler, or the <term>hectemoria|A ruler divided into 6 parts.</term> ruler, which you will apply above the equinoctial MN, drawn on the meridian plane, so that the meridian line, or the width of the ruler, corresponds to the 6 o'clock line CD: then mark the hectemoria or <term>trimoria|Divisions of three.</term> points along it on the equinoctial MN; for lines drawn through them parallel to the horizontal line on the meridian plane will give the midpoints and the full celestial houses, in both the oriental and occidental planes, according to Regiomontanus.

# Book V of the Great Art: Curious Gnomonics <note>Gnomonics is the art and science of using a gnomon—the part of a sundial that casts a shadow—to measure time and the positions of celestial bodies.</note>

### Problem XV.

*How to describe the celestial houses on any given irregular plane of a house using an observational instrument.*

**F**irst, let the <term>celestial houses</term> <note>These are twelve divisions of the sky used in astrology to determine the positions of planets relative to the horizon at a specific time and place.</note> be drawn on a horizontal dial, or any other irregular plane. Place this "echo-drawing" <note>original: "æcographia", likely referring to a preliminary sketch or template</note> on part E of the table. Once the table is placed against any given planes, rotate the entire system until the shadow falls upon the lines of the celestial houses that end at the <term>tropics</term> <note>The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, representing the sun's northernmost and southernmost limits.</note>; at that same moment, you will mark the shadows on the flat gnomons already prepared. For if you draw straight lines through the resulting points, you will have the celestial houses delineated on the given planes.

---

### Problem XVI.

*Horoscopography of the Signs. To determine by a shadow on any plane which sign of the Zodiac is rising or setting at any given moment.*

**W**e shall treat in this problem the site and position of the stars, and the placement of the <term>signs of the Zodiac</term> in the heavens; so that the position and placement each one holds in the sky may become known through a shadow.
Although <term>Clavius</term> <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a Jesuit mathematician and astronomer who was a primary architect of the Gregorian calendar.</note> touched upon these matters at great length, many of my students and other distinguished men have complained to me more than once about his excessive obscurity regarding this subject. Therefore, to promote their laudable efforts in the business of gnomonics, I have applied myself seriously to making this task easier. The result is that, with the help of the trigonometric art, I have finally—though not without great effort—uncovered a method soon to be revealed, which I believe is easier and more efficient than any handed down until now. And since this kind of line can be described on no plane better or with less confusion than on the <term>equinoctial plane</term> <note>A flat surface aligned with the Earth's equator.</note>, we shall begin our description from there.

### Practice I.

*Given the parallels of the Sun and the horizontal line on an equinoctial plane, to describe the lines of the ascending signs on the same.*

<margin>He who knows how to describe the hours from sunrise and sunset also knows how to describe the lines of the ascending signs.</margin>

Since the lines of the <term>ascending signs</term> <note>The signs of the Zodiac appearing on the eastern horizon.</note>—or the common sections of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The sun's apparent path across the sky during the year.</note> and any plane—relate to the hour lines in exactly the same way as the lines for hours from sunrise and sunset relate to the hour lines from noon and midnight on any plane; and just as the lines for hours from sunrise and sunset always touch the circle of those stars that are always visible or always hidden

...if you have drawn straight lines from center E in the morning quadrant AC, and have drawn tangents at the points where they intersect the <term>tropic of Cancer</term> <note>The line marking the Sun's northernmost point in the sky, reached at the summer solstice.</note> [♋]; they will give you the sought-after lines for Cancer [♋], Leo [♌], Virgo [♍], Libra [♎], Scorpio [♏], and Sagittarius [♐]. # Practical Operation IV.
## To describe the lines of the ascending and descending signs on a horizontal plane.

**F**irst, let a ruler be made with an expanded scale, which should have a width as great as the <term>equinoctial semi-diameter</term> <note>The radius of the circle representing the celestial equator on the sundial's surface.</note> *b C* in the gnomonic triangle for the horizontal plane. On its part *c e d*, you will determine the points of the degrees corresponding to each sign according to the table placed here, as was done in Practical Operation II of this Problem; you will then have the points of the ascending signs for the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The line on the dial where the shadow falls during the spring and autumn equinoxes.</note>. Then, on the other part of the ruler at *b*, you will determine the points of the degrees of the equinoctial in the second table for the <term>tropics</term> <note>The summer solstice (Cancer ♋) and winter solstice (Capricorn ♑).</note> of ♋ and ♑, carefully marking the points. Therefore, given a horizontal plane in which the two tropics ♋ and ♑, along with the equinoctial line *ST* and the <term>meridian</term> <note>The north-south noon line.</note> *ace*, have first been drawn, you shall scribe the lines of the ascending signs in this way: Take the side of the ruler *ced*, distributed into degrees (which is done if you draw straight lines from center *d* of the quadrant *d e 90*), and apply it above *ST*, so that point *e* of the ruler matches the middle point *c* of the equator, and *cd* aligns with the whole of *ST*. Once this is done, mark the points on the equinoctial *ST* according to the numbers in the first table of ascending signs on both sides of the meridian; these will be the points upon which the shadow of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The pin or blade of the sundial that casts the shadow.</note> will fall when the Sun is positioned in Aries ♈ and Libra ♎. Now, to have the points on the equinoctial when the Sun is positioned in the tropics, take the side of the ruler at *b* for the tropics, divided into its degrees (which is done if you draw straight lines from center *e* of the quadrant *e d 90*), and apply it above the equinoctial as was done just before, marking the points on it according to the numbers described in the second table of ascending signs. If, therefore, you draw hidden straight lines from the center of the dial *A* intersecting the tropic of Capricorn ♑, the straight lines of the ascending signs will pass through any two points of a single sign. For example, to scribe the line of Taurus ♉, having already found point *O* on the equinoctial, *N* will be the other point on the equinoctial after noon, through which a straight line drawn from center *A* will cut the tropic of Capricorn ♑ at *S*. Therefore, a straight line drawn through *S* and through *O* will give the line of the ascending Taurus ♉. The same is to be established for the rest.

<margin>Operation by tangents.</margin>
This whole business can be expedited without a ruler by means of tangents alone in the parts of the ruler's width, or the semi-diameter of the equator *cb*. Take the tangents of the ascending signs corresponding to their degrees, and transfer them from location *C* of the equinoctial to both sides; you will then have the points for the equinoctial when the Sun is in the equinoxes, namely positioned in Aries ♈ and Libra ♎. If, however, you transfer the tangents contained in the second table for the degrees of the ascending signs to both sides on the said equinoctial, you will have the points on the equinoctial for when the Sun is positioned in Cancer ♋ or Capricorn ♑; through these, the hour lines drawn from the center of the dial will intersect the tropic at points which, when joined with the previous points of one and the same sign, will give the lines of the ascending signs. Take care to note diligently so that you do not confuse the points of both tables marked on the same equinoctial. You will have the lines for Aries ♈ and Libra ♎ if you draw straight lines parallel to the equinoctial through the vertices of the opposite <term>hyperbolas</term> <note>In gnomonics, the shadow of the gnomon tip traces a hyperbola across the dial on most days of the year.</note> of Cancer ♋ and Capricorn ♑, as the figure demonstrates. For the method of calculating the table for any elevation of the pole, see page 302. Dotted lines show the lines by which the descending Sun indicates the rising of the signs; the lines that are not dotted show the ascending signs while the Sun is ascending.

### Corollary I.
**S**ince the lines of the ascending signs are related to the hours in which they rise (drawn from the center of the dial to the tropics) in the same way that the hours from sunrise and sunset are related to the hours at noon and midnight, cutting the two largest circles of those always visible and always hidden into 24 equal parts...

# Great Art, Book V. Curious Gnomonics.

...points. And since the hours from sunrise and sunset always touch the aforementioned great circles of the stars that are always appearing and those that are always hidden at those points where they are cut by the hours from noon and midnight; it follows that the points of contact, when joined with the points on the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The line on a sundial representing the celestial equator; on this line, day and night are of equal length.</note>, give the lines for the hours measured from sunrise and sunset. <margin>A notable summary of this observation.</margin> In the same way, I say, the lines of the ascending signs touch the <term>tropics</term> <note>The lines representing the solstices: the Tropic of Cancer (summer) and the Tropic of Capricorn (winter).</note>. If, therefore, the hour lines are drawn from the center of the sundial through the points of the degrees that correspond to the hours of the signs' ascension—for example, when the Sun is positioned in Capricorn (♑)—these lines will intersect the Tropic of Capricorn at the points through which (along with the points on the equinoctial found through the first table) the tangents drawn will provide the desired lines of the ascending signs. See other methods in the works of other authors; we have placed only these here, which combine novelty with ease of use, and from whose highly universal principles countless other methods can be derived.

### Corollary II.

From this it is clear that at a latitude of 23 ½ degrees <note>This latitude corresponds to the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.</note>, a sundial drawn for sunrise and sunset coincides with the lines of the ascending signs.

### Another method.

If in this present <term>Practical Instruction</term> <note>original: "Pragmatia"; a technical exercise or demonstration.</note> it perhaps displeases someone that tangents to <term>hyperbolas</term> <note>On most sundials, the path of a shadow throughout the day forms a hyperbolic curve.</note> cannot be drawn so easily, we will add another practice here. By this method, the lines sought are produced by lines drawn through the points of the <term>culminations</term> <note>original: "mediationum coeli"; refers to the points where the zodiac signs cross the meridian or "middle of the sky."</note> on the meridian, and through the points of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere.</note> found on the circle of the sixth hour.

<margin>1. Operation by the analemma.</margin>

<image-desc>A technical gnomonic diagram labeled "1. operatio per analemma." The image shows a triangular framework with vertex O at the top. Lines radiate from O across a field containing several hyperbolic curves. At the base, there is a complex scale with letters A, L, N, O, B, M, and smaller letters like P, R, S, T, V, X, Y. The bottom-most arc contains astrological symbols for zodiac signs, including Leo (♌), Cancer (♋), Gemini (♊), Taurus (♉), Aries (♈), and Pisces (♓). It appears to be a tool for projectively determining planetary or zodiacal houses/lines on a sundial.</image-desc>

You will find the points of the culminations through the following tables in this way. First, by the <term>analemma</term> <note>A geometric construction used to project the celestial sphere onto a flat surface.</note> placed above in the figure for Practical Instruction IV, let the horizon be *a b*, the axis of the world *c d*, the equator *e f*, and the vertical line *g h*; let *IK* be the horizontal plane of the sundial. If you then count from point *E* of the equinoctial toward *g* (if the declinations of the culminations are northern) or toward *a* (if they are southern), and straight lines are drawn through the ends of these counts and the center; these will intersect the line *IK* at points which, when transferred from point *m* of the analemma (from the position of the <term>style</term> <note>The shadow-casting blade or pin of the sundial.</note> on the sundial) onto the meridian line, will give the desired points of culmination. 

But these will be found even better through the "Radiant Zodiac," as follows. Apply the gnomonic triangle *AB, CD* so that, as in the figure of Practical Instruction IV, the semi-diameter of the equator *bc* matches the radius of the equator *OB* in the present figure. Then *ac* will be the meridian line, *db* the style, *ab* the axis, *au* the line of the sixth hour, and *ST* the equator. If you then calculate the declination of the culminations from the first table in both directions from point *B* of the "Radiant Zodiac" (toward *C* if the signs of the culminations are northern, and toward *D* if they are southern), the lines drawn from *O* through the ends of these calculations will intersect the meridian line *ac* (or the 12 o'clock line) at points. These points, when transferred from the position of the style *a* or the center of the sundial *d* onto the meridian, will give the points of culmination through which the ascending sign must be drawn. For example, by calculating 22 degrees and 32 minutes from *B* toward *C*, the line drawn from *O* through that point will intersect the meridian line *ac* at a point which, when transferred from the center of the sundial *a*, will give the point on the sundial's meridian through which the line for Leo (♌) must be drawn.

To obtain the points of the ecliptic at the sixth hour, count the declinations of the points of the ecliptic from point *B* toward *C* according to the second table. Once this is done, if you draw straight lines from the "Radiant Zodiac" *O* through the ends of these counts, they will intersect the line *LM* of the sixth hour at points. When these points are transferred from the center of the sundial *a* onto the line of the sixth hour—either before or after noon (according to whether the table is for the sixth hour before or after noon)—they will provide the points which, when joined by straight lines with the culmination points belonging to the same sign, will give the desired lines of the ascending signs.

<margin>Note concerning the use of these shadow-measuring tools.</margin>
Furthermore, once the points of the <term>mid-heaven crossings</term> <note>original: "mediationum"; the points where zodiac signs cross the meridian.</note> have been found through the preceding rules, you will be able to describe the lines of the ascending signs with almost no effort: provided, of course, that you draw tangents to the <term>tropics</term>; for those will be the lines you seek. We have already taught how these tables are calculated for individual polar altitudes <note>i.e., local latitudes</note> above on page 303. However, since not all the lines touched by the shadow of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The vertical rod or blade of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note> show that those specific signs are rising at that time, it must be understood that only those six signs which rise during the day—which are always those numbered according to the succession of signs from the position of the Sun—are shown by the shadow. For example, if on the 22nd of February, with the Sun being at the beginning of Pisces (♓), the shadow of the stylus falls upon the line for Scorpio (♏), do not think that Scorpio is rising at that time, since it is not above the horizon at that hour. Thus, if the shadow falls on the line for Taurus (♉), you will know for certain that it is rising then, since it is above the horizon and is one of the six signs counted from the Sun's position. Therefore, all signs from Pisces (♓) through to Virgo (♍) inclusive will be indicated by the Sun’s shadow on February 22nd when they are above the horizon, but the others will not. To avoid confusion, this sundial can be divided into two parts, one of which

will show the lines of the signs that are rising at that time from Cancer (♋) to Capricorn (♑) in descending order, and the other from Capricorn (♑) to Cancer (♋) in ascending order without exception; I have thought it best to include these here. ## Problem XVII.

### To describe the particular risings of fixed stars on a horizontal plane.

<margin>Shadow-measurement of the fixed stars.</margin>
It is truly a new invention, and one handed down by no one else that I know of: to describe the hourly markers of the fixed stars. That is to say, by which the rising of any fixed star may be demonstrated by the shadow of the Sun at any moment, even if the star itself cannot be seen. Let us, therefore, first reveal the secret. First, investigate the determined distances in hours from the Sun for some fixed stars located between the tropics while it is rising; and calculate these on a quadrant of a circle from *e* toward *n*, if the hour is before noon, and from *e* toward *m* in the afternoon; for at the end of the counting, a straight line drawn through the center will intersect the <term>equinoctial line</term> at the point where the shadow of the Sun, positioned in Aries (♈) or Libra (♎), falls at the same time that some star is above the horizon—

## Problem XVIII.

**How to describe the entire system of fixed stars on a plane in such a way that the rising of the fixed stars is perpetually shown by the shadow.**

<margin>Illustration IV.</margin>
Although the projection of these kinds of stars can be done on any plane, nevertheless, since no plane is more convenient or more naturally suited for this kind of projection of the star-bearing hemispheres than the equinoctial <note>The plane of the Earth's equator projected into the sky</note>, it seemed best to exhibit them on that plane above others. Therefore, let the hemispheres of the fixed stars be delineated on both equinoctial planes with all the figures of the stars, as you see done here. The drawing shall be organized as follows: Let an Azimuth-Almucantar Net <note>A coordinate grid used in astrolabes to measure horizontal and vertical positions</note>, which we taught how to construct above in Preliminary Exercise IV, be fitted to the equinoctial plane so that the center of the Net represents the pole of the world, while the 90th Azimuth represents the meridian line (or the diameter of the equinoctial), and the remaining lines drawn from the center to the circumference represent the meridian or hour circles. The concentric circles parallel to the equator shall represent the circles of the stars' declinations; and thus you will have the Net prepared.

<margin>The Equinoctial Net.</margin>
In this Net, therefore, according to the tables of latitude and longitude—or of the declinations of stars—published by Clavius, Grienberger <note>Jesuit astronomers famous for their work on the Gregorian calendar reform and star catalogs</note>, and others, let the two hemispheres of fixed stars be drawn: on the upper for the northern hemisphere, and on the lower for the southern. Or, if instead of a gnomonic drawing of the fixed stars, any two star-bearing hemispheres are used, they will serve the same purpose. They shall be fitted to the equinoctial plane in this way: First, on a somewhat thick board, let a circle be described with the radius of one of the hemispheres, and let a larger concentric circle be drawn on the plane, as you see; let this latter circle be divided into 24 equal parts. Lines drawn from the center through the points of division will give the hour lines from noon and midnight, as is apparent, and this circle shall always remain immovable. You will hollow out this board according to the smaller concentric circle on both sides, so that the spheres of the hemispheres can be conveniently inserted into it and rotated within the cavity at the user's discretion—just as the "nets" or "spiders" <note><term>araneæ</term>: the rotating openwork plate of an astrolabe</note> are usually inserted into astrolabes. These spheres can then be moved at will on opposite faces around a style <note>The gnomon or rod that casts the shadow</note> (which should be erected perpendicularly at the center of the circle and of indeterminate size), as if around an axis in the plane of the equator. You will then have a timepiece for showing the stars, as follows.

### The Use of This Timepiece.

Once the plane is situated according to the required altitude of the equator and the meridian line of the equinoctial dial: If you wish to know the position of the whole sky, observe the shadow of the style showing the hours on the rim. Suppose, for example, the shadow of the style falls on the third hour of the afternoon: to know the position of the whole sky, move the degree of the Sun (which the Sun occupies on that day) under the shadow of the style, and you will have the hemisphere positioned to know the placement of the entire northern hemisphere. For those stars contained under the hour lines occupy the same place in the sky as the hour circles in the heavens; thus you will immediately see which stars are in the middle of the sky, which are on the line of the sixth hour, and which are situated in other regions of the sky. If, however, you desire to know the position of the stars in the southern hemisphere at the same time (which the Sun has not yet entered), you will apply the southern hemisphere over the same hour line upon which the shadow falls in the upper one: and you will have what you sought.

<margin>Explanation of the figures in the Illustration.</margin>
But so that you may better distinguish all these things, we have placed three figures here: the first shows the astrographic drawing; the second, the rising of the stars throughout the whole world; the third shows the application of the sphere upon the axis of the world. The use of the second figure is this: apply the Roman meridian over the sign currently rising, and you will have the rising signs corresponding to the remaining locations.

<margin>How to describe right ascensional lines on a vertical plane.</margin>...from noon and midnight. Therefore, if you apply our shadow-measuring ruler <note>original: "regulam sciathericam"</note> with its scale expanded over the equator of a horizontal sundial (the width of which should be equal to the radius of the equator of the gnomonic triangle), and you mark the points on it according to the rule of degrees on both sides; the lines drawn through those points will give the sought-after lines, or ascensional circles. For a vertical dial, you will obtain these circles if you draw straight lines from the center of the vertical sundial through the points of the degrees marked on the equinoctial line; these are the <term>ascensional lines</term> <note>These lines represent Right Ascension, the celestial equivalent of longitude.</note>. However, the ruler must be of a width equal to the radius of the equinoctial circle in a gnomonic sundial constructed for a vertical plane. You will have the same results on a <margin>On a polar plane.</margin> polar plane if, on the applied ruler (which should have a width equal to the height of the style <note>The "style" is the physical blade or pin of the sundial that casts the shadow.</note> above the equinoctial of the polar plane), you mark the points of the degrees according to the expanded scale; for these points, drawn parallel to the meridian, will provide the sought-after lines. The same method shall be observed for inscribing these on a meridian plane. Finally, for an <margin>For an Equinoctial plane.</margin> equinoctial plane, a circle divided into 360 parts (with a style of an undetermined quantity assumed and erected perpendicularly in the center) will satisfy the requirement.

## Problem XX.

### *To describe Mecography <note>From the Greek 'mēkos' (length/longitude) and 'graphia' (writing); the mapping of longitudes to show world time.</note>, or the longitudes of places, on a horizontal sundial; so that at any given hour, you may know what time it is in the whole world.*

**T**he description of the longitudes of cities does not differ from the preceding instructions, except only in the position of the first meridian of the Canary Islands <note>Before the Greenwich Meridian was adopted, the Canary Islands (the "Fortunate Isles") were often used as the zero-point for longitude.</note>, which you will find in this way. Let the ascensional or meridian lines be described as before with the help of the ruler. Then, count from the meridian toward the western part of the sundial the distance of the first meridian from Rome, which according to Ptolemy <note>The famous 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian geographer.</note> is 36 degrees, but according to the accurate observation of more recent authors is 30 degrees.

<image-desc>A circular diagram of a gnomonic projection designed for a horizontal sundial. The center point radiates multiple lines (meridians) marked with degrees (15, 30, 45, 60, 75, 90). Along these radiating lines, various historical and geographic location names are placed: TOLU, NEW SPAIN <note>Mexico</note>, PERU, BRAZIL, CANARY ISLANDS, GADES <note>Cadiz</note>, ROME, CONSTANTINOPLE, BABYLON, MOGOR <note>The Mughal Empire in India</note>, INDIA, SUMATRA, CHINA, and JAPAN. At the top of the central circle, there is a small protractor-like scale labeled with numbers 1 through 6. Dotted lines and arcs intersect the main meridian rays, forming a complex geometric grid typical of early scientific instruments for timekeeping and navigation.</image-desc>

According to Ptolemy's observation, therefore, count on the ruler from the first meridian (marked O) toward the meridian line, every fifteen degrees, at each of which you will place the names of places distant by that longitude denoted by degrees, and the Mecography will be finished. Truly, the figure will explain the matter better than I could explain even with many words.

### Usage.

**F**rom this Mecography, you will understand more quickly than a word can be spoken which peoples are experiencing noon at any given moment, and what hour it is in any city assigned to a particular meridian. For if the shadow of the gnomon falls on the 70th meridian, to which the city of Babel is assigned, you will know for certain that it is noon in that very place; and so for the rest.

On a vertical plane, the same Mecography <margin>How the mecography of regions is to be completed on a vertical plane.</margin> will be completed if you first inscribe the meridians or ascensional circles, and place the same names of locations with the same degrees; observing this, that the first meridian should always be toward the western part of the plane—specifically, the part into which the Sun casts its shadow after noon; the rest should then be calculated toward the meridian.

## Practical Exercise I.
### To describe the <term>Mecography</term> <note>From the Greek *mēkos* (length) and *graphein* (to write), this refers to the mapping of geographic longitudes on a flat surface.</note> of places on an equinoctial plane, by which the hour in any part of the world can be known.

<margin>Illustration V.</margin>
Just as astronomical hours are inscribed on no plane more easily than the equinoctial one, so too can no plane be found more suitable or convenient for the longitudes of places. We shall therefore inscribe the hours and the meridians of longitude in two ways: first, geographically; second, by the placement of names alone. The first method is as follows: Let two hemispheres be drawn with all their meridians, parallels, and the geography of places, as you see here. You shall attach these—the northern above and the southern below—to a <term>style</term> <note>The style is the physical rod or blade of the sundial that casts the shadow.</note> erected perpendicularly, so that they can move freely as if around an axis, just as we did a little earlier with the hemispheres of the fixed stars. Thus, if you first expose the sundial to the Sun in its proper position, and place the meridian of the principal location (to which the longitudes of the other places are calculated, as Rome is here) under the shadow of the style; then the hour lines, or meridians in the geographical drawing on the hour-rim, will show the sought-after hours in the cities contained under those same meridians. In this present illustration, we show the geographical drawing in the first figure for only one hemisphere, namely the northern one, together with the hour circle inscribed on the margin, which also represents the equinoctial. The second figure shows the method of applying the said hemispheres upon the axis by means of a quadrant, so that they may be fit for showing the hours; the upper hemisphere will show the time when the Sun is in the North, and the other when it is in the South. The third figure shows another method, which we explain in the following Practical Exercise.

## Practical Exercise II.
### To achieve the same goal by another practice.

<margin>Geographical Rose.</margin>
One who is content with the simple placement of names should take this "Geographical Rose" of ours, such as the second figure here displays. Having duplicated it for the lower and upper planes, and inserted it into the cut-out hour circle, let him attach it to the perpendicularly erected style so that it can revolve freely around it like an axis. Then, when the Sun is shining and the sundial is positioned, align the Roman meridian under the shadow of the style; the hour-rim will then show what hour it is in all the places to which those hours correspond.

## Problem XXI.
### To delineate the space of the <term>Sun-runner</term> <note>original Greek: "ἡλιοδρόμου" (heliodromou); this refers to the path the sun takes through the sky throughout the year.</note>, or the Torrid Zone, on any given plane by a gnomonic projection.

The purpose of this projection is to see at which place within the Torrid Zone the Sun is directly overhead, and also for which place it is currently noon. You shall first set up the work on a horizontal plane in this way: First, according to chapters 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 of various "horographies" <note>Descriptions or drawings of hours.</note>, let an astrological sundial be drawn according to the practices taught there; or draw the individual lines of the ascensional circles according to the preceding Problem, together with the individual arcs of the Sun's declination according to the Problem following this one. These will be 47 in total; let the hour lines serve as meridian circles, and the arcs of declination as circles of latitude. If, therefore, you geographically insert the places between the tropics by means of an accurate map (using the longitudes and latitudes of the cities contained in said map) into the space of the <term>Sun-runner</term> or the gnomonic space of the Solar limit, you will have what was sought.

## Problem XXII.
### To delineate the parallels of the diurnal arcs on any given plane.
### Practical Application I.

1 **D**raw on a separate sheet of paper two radiant cones of the diurnal arcs, according to the rules handed down in the second Preliminary Exercise of this work, and let them be joined at the common vertex B, forming the figure BSHT.

2 Within each cone, apply the <term>gnomonic triangle</term> <note>A right-angled triangle representing the height of the sundial's pointer (gnomon) and its relationship to the dial's surface.</note> ABC for the horizontal and vertical planes, as the figure shows.

<margin>
How the instrument is to be adapted to polar and meridian planes.
</margin>

2 From point S, let a semicircle GFI be described with the interval SC, divided into 12 equal parts; you will join each pair of points equally distant from F with straight lines, which will cut the line SF at specific points. These points, transferred from S toward C, will mark the hour points from noon and midnight on the line SC, as the figure clearly shows with the hour numbers added; and you will have an instrument prepared for inscribing the <term>diurnal arcs</term> <note>The curved paths that the sun's shadow follows across a sundial over the course of a day.</note> on horizontal and vertical sundials. For polar and meridian dials, however, proceed as follows: In a polar sundial, where the length of the <term>style</term> <note>The physical rod or edge of the gnomon that casts the shadow.</note> is DB, assume a point on the sixth hour line only as far distant from the equinoctial line as the length of the drawn gnomon DB is. 

[Image: A complex gnomonic diagram featuring two circular arcs labeled with hour numbers (1 to 15) and degrees. The arcs are centered at points G and H, with a common vertex at point B. A horizontal line is labeled "HORIZ:" and a vertical line is labeled "VERT:". Lines radiate from vertex B across various degree markers (15, 30, 45, 60, 75). Geometric points are labeled with letters: A, B, C, D, F, G, H, I, S, T, and R. Dotted lines and projections indicate the intersection of solar rays with different planes, forming hyperbolic and circular paths.]

From this point, let the <term>secants</term> <note>In 17th-century geometry, these are specific lengths derived from trigonometric ratios used to project points from a sphere onto a flat map or dial.</note> of the hour distances from noon be transferred; that is, the secants of 15, 30, 45, 60, and 75 degrees from vertex B of the radiant cone onto line BH. For if you draw lines normal to BH through these transferred points—or what is the same thing, parallel to line ABA—they will all intersect the rays of the diurnal arcs. These, then transferred from the equinoctial line of the polar or meridian sundial to the corresponding hours, will give the points through which the <term>hyperbolas</term> <note>The mathematical curve (a conic section) that the sun's shadow usually traces on a flat sundial.</note> of the diurnal arcs must be drawn, as will be clear in what follows.

## Use of the Instrument <note>original: "Usus Organi"</note>

**W**ith the help of this instrument, therefore, you will describe the parallels of all the arcs on a horizontal plane more quickly than can be said, and without any confusion of lines on the plane of the horizontal sundial.

Let two threads be drawn from points A and B: the one drawn from B onto the limb SHT will represent the lines of the diurnal arcs, and the other from A onto the line SC will represent the rays of the hour lines. Suppose, then, first, that a diurnal arc of 13 hours is to be described on the chosen plane (for the arc of 12 hours is the <term>equinoctial line</term> <note>The straight line the shadow follows during the Equinox, when day and night are of equal length.</note> itself on the sundial).

To describe diurnal arcs with the help of two threads.
</margin>

Apply thread B over point 13 on the limb SH, and fix it there. Then you will draw the thread from A through point C at 12 on the line SC. For where the two threads intersect each other, there will be the point of the 13-hour diurnal arc; which, being transferred from A onto the meridian line from the center of the sundial, will give the point through which the 13-hour diurnal arc will pass. Then, having placed thread A at the point of hour 1 and 11 on line SC, you will note the intersection of the two threads: the distance...
