...for the distance between this point of intersection and A, transferred from the center of the sundial onto the lines for the 1st and 11th hours, will provide the points sought for the <term>diurnal arc</term> <note>The path the sun's shadow follows on the dial plate during a specific day of the year.</note> at those hours.

Likewise, apply thread A over the hour points 2 and 10 on the line SC; the space between A and the common point of intersection of the threads, transferred from the center of the sundial to the 2nd and 10th hours, will give the sought points. In no different a manner, you will investigate the points of a diurnal arc of 13 hours in the subsequent hours through the intersection of two threads (one of which always remains stationary over the edge SH, while the other is moved through the hour points on SC).

<margin>How a diurnal arc of 18 hours is to be described.</margin>
Again, if a diurnal arc of 14 hours is to be described, you will fix the moved thread from B over the number 14 on the edge SH; then, the other thread A, moved through the individual hour points on the line SC, will give spaces with the other thread B. These spaces, transferred from the center of the sundial onto the corresponding hour lines, will prepare the points through which the diurnal arc of 14 hours will pass—the use of which is greatest in describing hours from sunrise and sunset. If, however, you place thread B over the 18th degree, fixed on the edge HS, the other thread A, moved through the hour points on SC, will give the spaces between A and the point of intersection of the threads. These, transferred from the center of the sundial onto the corresponding hour lines, will give the points through which the diurnal arc of 18 hours will pass. Although this arc does not fall within the <term>tropics</term> <note>The boundaries of the sun's path at the solstices; an 18-hour arc refers to high latitudes or specific seasonal calculations.</note> but outside them, it is nonetheless of great use in describing <term>unequal hours</term> <note>Also called "temporal hours," where the day and night are each divided into 12 hours regardless of season, meaning the hours change length throughout the year.</note>, as has been said partly in the description of such hours and will be said partly in the following sections.

Where you should note that whenever two threads intersect each other, then the arcs described by the points of intersection will be **hyperbolas**; and where two threads are parallel anywhere, a **parabola** will be described by them. This happens in a sundial when thread B is placed over point T on the edge SHT, and the other thread A over 12 on the line SC. For since in this position the threads are parallel, a parabola will be described according to the practices and methods handed down in the *Preliminary Exercises* <note>original: "Progymnasmatis"</note>; see the reasons for all of these in the *Theoretical Foundations* <note>original: "Protheoriis"</note>. However, when the threads do not intersect, know that **ellipses** are to be described.

You see, therefore, Reader, a method no less pleasant than it is ingenious, by the rule of which you will inscribe the arcs of the signs, months, and days with no less ease than the aforementioned diurnal arcs: namely, if you place thread B over the given degree of the sign's declination on the edge SHT, and move the remaining thread A over the hour points on SC. For the spaces between the point of intersection and A, transferred into the sundial from the center onto the corresponding hour lines, will give the arc of the sought sign, month, and day.

## Practical Application II.
### For the Vertical Plane.

**If**, therefore, you desire to delineate diurnal arcs on a vertical sundial, with two threads attached at A and B of the <term>gnomonic triangle</term> <note>A right-angled triangle representing the height of the gnomon relative to the dial plane.</note> assumed for a vertical sundial: so that B is always moved on the edge SHT over the degree of the given arc, and the other over the hour spaces, they will give the spaces between the points of intersection of the threads and A, which, when transferred from the center of the sundial onto the hour lines, produce the desired diurnal arcs. The practice differs in no way from the previous one, except only in the application of the gnomonic triangle, as you see.

## Practical Application III.
### To describe the parallels of diurnal arcs on a polar and meridian plane with a single movement of the thread.

**H**aving transferred onto the radius BH the <term>secants</term> <note>A trigonometric function used here to determine distances on the dial plate.</note> of the hour distances in parts of the style divided into 10 parts, and having described parallels normal to each other at the points, as we taught a little while ago in Practical Application I, begin the operation thus. If you direct the thread fixed at B over the arc—for example, a diurnal arc of 13 hours—it will cut the parallels (namely the hour lines) into spaces. These intercepted spaces, transferred from the equator of the sundial into the corresponding hour lines, will give the points through which the diurnal arc of 13 hours will pass. By this art, you will transfer the space B 12 in the <term>radiant cone</term> from the place of the gnomon in the polar sundial on both sides of 13 onto the meridian. Likewise, the space intercepted between the 3rd hour line and B on the radius B 13, when transferred from the point where the 3rd hour line cuts the equinoctial of the sundial into the 3rd hour line, will give the point in it through which the sought arc will pass. You will proceed no differently for inscribing other arcs.

Since meridian planes have the same projection of signs and hours, you will also inscribe diurnal arcs in them by the same method. Therefore, nothing more remains to be said about them.

## Practical Application IV.
### To describe the parallels of diurnal arcs on an equinoctial sundial.

**S**ince the parallels of the equator on an equinoctial plane are all circles, you will thus delineate the diurnal arcs on it with almost no trouble. Let a line BO be determined in the radiant cone equal to BD, the <term>style</term> <note>The physical rod or edge that casts the shadow.</note> of the sundial, and let OR be drawn normal to O, parallel to BH. If, therefore, the thread fixed at B is placed over the number of the diurnal arc of 13 hours, it will cut off a space on the line OR, at which interval from the center...

on the equinoctial plane, a circle drawn from the center of the sundial will provide an arc of 13 hours. If, however, you move the threads over the arc for 14 hours, a space will be cut on line OR; a circle drawn from the said center to that space will give the <term>diurnal arc</term> <note>The path traced by the shadow of the gnomon on the dial face during the course of a day.</note> of 14 hours. ## Problem XXIII.
### To describe the Climates of the whole world gnomonically.

A **Climate** <note>In historical geography, a "climate" (clima) was not a weather pattern, but a latitudinal zone or band of the Earth defined by the length of its longest day.</note> is nothing other than a zone parallel to the equator, bounded by two circles parallel to the equator, encircling the whole earth. Its width is such that from its southern boundary to its northern boundary, the longest day increases by half an hour. Since it has been said that one parallel differs from the next following one by a quarter of an hour <note>15 minutes of daylight difference.</note>, it follows that a "climate" consists of three parallels: two forming the boundaries, and one passing through the middle of the climate. This is not because it divides it exactly in half (for the climates are always narrower toward the North and South) but because of the equality of the time difference. However, to embrace many things in a few words, see the following Table of Climates; from which, as if from a synopsis, the things mentioned will become known.

Thus, when you are about to represent the climates gnomonically on a sundial, you will describe the parallels of the climates by this universal new artifice, which has been handed down by no one else, as far as I know, until now. 

->[Large circular geometric diagram with a vertical diameter A-E and various labeled radial arcs. The lower quadrant is divided into segments labeled with geographical names: Chile, Magellanic Land, Paraguay, Madagascar, Mozambique, Canary Islands, Meroë, Syene, Alexandria, Rhodes, Rome, Venice, Podolia, Rostock, Wolfsberg, and Vardø. Labels include A, B, C, D, E, I, T, O, R, b, and d.]<-

Let an arc BDC be described separately on paper from point A, which you will divide on both sides into 66 1/2 degrees; CD will represent the latitude of 12 climates to the South, and DB the latitude of 12 climates to the North. AD will act as the radius of the equator. Next, you will transfer the same hour points onto the line CI, just as was done in the <term>Practical Application</term> <note>referring to the previous geometric demonstration (Pragmatia).</note> cited shortly before. This being done, with thread A placed over the latitude of the first climate through Meroë <note>An ancient city in modern-day Sudan, often used as a reference point for the first climate zone.</note> on the edge BD, and the other thread from *b* over the hour points: the spaces between the intersection points of the threads and *b*, transferred onto the corresponding hour lines from the center of a horizontal sundial, will give the points through which a drawn arc will provide the first parallel. Again, having moved thread A over the latitude of the second climate through Syene <note>Modern Aswan, Egypt; traditionally the location of the second climate.</note>—namely, over its latitude on circle BD—and with the thread from *b* extended over the hour points on CI: the intervals between *b* and the intersection points of the threads, transferred from the center A of the sundial onto the corresponding hour lines, will give the points through which the arcs of the second climate will pass. And so on, according to the given latitudes of the climates...

# The Great Art, Book V. The Curious Gnomon.

...you will proceed according to the latitudes proposed in the table, using threads, until you have inscribed all the arcs of the climates. Indeed, the greater part of these will fall outside the <term>tropics</term> <note>The regions between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.</note>, and in the process, you should mark the <term>hyperbolas</term> and <term>ellipses</term> <note>These are geometric curves (conic sections) formed by the shadow of the gnomon's tip on the dial face.</note>. For if the threads are parallel, a <term>parabola</term> must be described instead of a hyperbola; and at 66 ½ degrees <note>This latitude corresponds to the Arctic and Antarctic Circles.</note>, it will be an ellipse, and so on for the others. The reason we have placed the climates outside the tropics is so that, with the help of those arcs, many things regarding the construction of various hours can be expedited, as has partly been said and will partly be said in the following sections.

<margin>Description of Climates on a vertical polar, meridian, and equinoctial plane.</margin>
On a vertical plane, you will inscribe the said climates simply by changing the <term>gnomonic triangle</term> <note>The right-angled triangle formed by the gnomon, its shadow, and the distance from the base of the gnomon to the shadow's tip.</note>, as was done in the preceding section. On a polar plane, you will describe the climates if you transfer the hour-spaces of the preceding <term>Pragmatic figure</term> <note>A practical working diagram used for calculations.</note> onto the radius of the equator, drawing lines through the points terminating the parallels to the line IC. For a thread applied from point A above the degrees of the climates on the border BD will cut the spaces in the parallels; these, when transferred onto the hour lines of the sundial, will give the points for the arcs of the climates. The same method of description shall be observed for a meridian sundial. On an equinoctial plane, the <term>Rete</term> <note>Latin for "net" or "grid," referring here to a specific calculating instrument or grid described earlier in the work.</note> constructed in Pre-exercise IV will provide the desired result.

Note at this point that there is such a great diversity of opinions regarding the position of the climates that there is scarcely a geographer who agrees with another. We have organized this <term>sciatheric</term> <note>Related to the art of dialing or the use of shadows (from the Greek "skia" for shadow).</note> climatography in this place according to the Table taken from **Junctinus** <note>original: "Junctino"; referring to Francesco Giuntini (1523–1590), a Florentine theologian and astronomer.</note>. However, if anyone prefers to use the **Ptolemaic** description, they may do as they please. We subjoin his table here.

Book 5 of the Great Art: Gnomonics. Curious Matters.

## Problem XXIV.
### For the Polar Plane.

### To describe the individual parallels of solar declination on a horizontal sundial.

**O**nce the line AD is drawn, describe the arc BC, which you will divide on both sides, starting from D, into 23 and a half degrees; <note>original: "23. gradus 1/2"; this corresponds to the obliquity of the ecliptic, the tilt of the Earth's axis which determines the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.</note> the points on BC will be the solar terminal points. If, therefore, you desire to describe the individual parallels of solar declination of this triangle on a horizontal plane, take the gnomonic triangle for a horizontal dial and apply it so that the <term>equatorial radius</term> <note>The distance from the center of the sundial to the celestial equator line.</note> AE perfectly matches the equatorial radius AD. If the hour points are then transferred onto CE, as we instructed in the preceding sections, the <term>organ</term> <note>original: "organum"; here meaning a geometric tool or calculation device.</note> of solar declinations, or for describing the parallels, will be prepared.

**W**ith the sundial layout drawn on a polar plane, transfer the radius of the equator from the preceding tool into line AD starting from A—the <term>secants</term> <note>A trigonometric value used here to project the curved path of the sun onto a flat dial plate.</note> of the hourly distances from the meridian in parts of the total sine—and let the parallels be drawn through these points. Then, a thread A applied to the individual degrees of declination on the scale BDC will give segments on the parallel hour lines; when these are transferred to the corresponding lines of the sundial, they will show the points where each parallel of solar declination passes. The same should be said for meridian planes. On a vertical plane, you shall engrave the said parallels simply by inverting the gnomonic triangle, as was also handed down in the preceding parts.

A sophisticated gnomonic diagram. At the top is a geometric construction with points A, B, C, D, E. Point A is at the apex, with lines radiating down to a base line. Below this is a large, fan-shaped instrument or scale. It features numerous concentric arcs and radiating lines. A plumb line or indicator hangs from a central point D. The bottom edge of the fan is divided into boxes labeled with the names of the months, paired according to solar declination: MAY/JULY, APRIL/AUGUST, MARCH/SEPTEMBER, FEBRUARY/OCTOBER, JANUARY/NOVEMBER, and a single box for DECEMBER. Within the fan, there are also numerical scales and zodiacal symbols.

Once the astronomical sundial has been drawn on any horizontal plane, you will describe the solar declinations on it using this art. With threads fixed at points B and A of the instrument, you will fasten one of them over the first degree of solar declination (if the sundial is large); the other is applied over each individual hour point of line CE, carefully noting where thread B intersects thread A. For if you transfer the spaces mediated between the intersection points and A onto the corresponding hour lines from the center of the sundial, the first parallel of solar declination will pass through those points. Likewise, by applying thread A over the second degree of the scale BD, and the other over the individual hour points, let the spaces cut between B and thread A be transferred to the corresponding lines of the sundial, and you will have the points of the second solar parallel. You shall proceed no differently in the description of the following parallels, and you will have what was sought.

### Corollary I.
#### To determine the lines of the time of sunrise and sunset on the sundial.

<margin>Sunrise and sunset.</margin>
**F**or each of the parallels of solar declination, you will add its time of sunrise and sunset in a separate space on the edge of the sundial (which the <term>semidiurnal arcs</term> <note>The time or angle the sun travels from noon to sunset.</note> will provide). The shadow of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The vertical or angled rod that casts the shadow.</note> falling upon those parallels will show the sought-after time of sunrise and sunset.

### Corollary II.
#### To determine the time of twilight within the lines of the sundial.

<margin>Twilights.</margin>
**L**ook in the table of twilights to see how long the twilight is for any parallel of declination, and write down the numbers for the duration of twilights throughout the year in a separate space, and the shadow will show what is sought.

### Corollary III.
#### To determine the rising and setting amplitude.

<margin>Rising and setting amplitude.</margin>
**S**ee from the table of <term>amplitudes</term> <note>The angular distance from the true East or West point where the sun rises or sets.</note> how much any parallel of declination deviates from the rising point of the equinoctial; the number assigned to this declination will give the rising amplitude of that day on which the gnomon's shadow is observed to fall.

### Corollary IV.
#### To determine right and oblique ascensions, etc., with ascensional differences on the sundial.

<margin>Right and oblique ascensions.</margin>
**I**f you assign the corresponding right and oblique ascensions, etc., from the tables placed above to the individual parallels of declination in the table, you will have what was sought. But all these things are clearer in the diagrams than they deserve to be described in words. See the figure for all these things in the *Physico-Astrological Gnomonics*.

...expanded, as Figure 1 of the Illustration <note>referring to the plates on the previous page</note> shows, marked with its numbers ABKH as you see. This rule should have an attached space KHCD along its length, whose side KC is equal to the width of the rule KH or AB; furthermore, let it have an attached space EAFC along its width. You will then have a mobile stylus or <term>axis</term> <note>In sundial making, the "axis" or gnomon is the part that casts the shadow.</note> suitable for showing the hours under any latitude. Indeed, you shall scribe the hours on any given plane by this industrious method, as shown in Figure 2 of this Illustration.

First, let a solid round disc ABCD be made of such a size that it exceeds the aforementioned rule; in this disc, let two lines AB and CD be drawn, intersecting each other at right angles in the center V. AB will be the <term>meridian line</term> <note>The North-South line.</note> and CD will be the <term>equinoctial line</term> <note>The East-West line representing the celestial equator.</note>. This being done, apply the rule at its point K above point V, and let the side HB match the line VD of the plane. Then, at every fifteen degrees, points should be marked on the equinoctial line CD; these points, when transferred to the other part VC, will give the hour points on the equinoctial, to which you will scribe their respective numbers, as you see. Thus, the sundial will be prepared for <term>universal</term> <note>original: "catholicum". In this context, "catholic" means general or applicable everywhere, rather than referring to the Church.</note> use. You shall insert the expanded rule, or mobile axis, into the sundial thus prepared. In the meridian line AB, let a thin groove or slit be made, into which the expanded rule—representing the mobile axis—is inserted at its point K, so that it can be rotated at will around a pin or any other small pointer inserted at V, as if around an axis. However, the pin must be transfixed through point K of the rule (as the center) in such a way that the said rule does not sit loosely in the slit, but tightly and strictly—that is, so it can be moved with some resistance. Otherwise, it could not be held firmly at a given degree of the <term>pole's elevation</term> <note>The latitude of the observer's location.</note>. You will then have a prepared universal sundial. See Figure 3.

### Use of the Universal Sundial.

*The Universal Horizontal Sundial.*

First, its use on a horizontal plane will be as follows. Arrange the disc of the sundial according to the four cardinal directions of the world, and press the rule down into the slit VX until the plane of the disc cuts the given degree of the pole's elevation on the edge of the rule DH6. The portion projecting above the plane represents the <term>axis of the world</term>, and its end, along with the meridian line, will represent the angle of the pole's elevation above the horizon. Therefore, when the sun shines, the shadow of the world axis (or the edge of the rule) will necessarily point to the desired hours among the points on the equinoctial line VS. The reason is clearly evident: since the rule, by its elevation and depression, represents the elevation of the pole above the horizon of any given region; for by the elevation and depression of the axis, as is clear in Figure 3, a triangle is always formed that is appropriate to some latitude. For example, here the triangle VH6, or CD6, is always the same as that which fits the elevation of the pole at Rome. H6 is the portion of the world axis, V6 the meridian, HI the vertical <term>gnomon</term>, and finally the whole triangle VH6 provides the hours. Since the axis, when depressed or elevated, forms the <term>gnomonic triangles</term> <note>The geometric triangles used to calculate shadow lengths and angles.</note> for individual latitudes, and the equinoctial semi-diameter VH always remains the same and perpendicular to the equinoctial line drawn on the plane, it must necessarily show the hours when directed to the given latitude. Thus, we have constructed a universal horizontal sundial, which was the task at hand.

*The Universal Vertical Sundial.*

If, however, you wish the hours to be shown to you vertically <note>On a wall.</note>, nothing else needs to be done except to depress the mobile axis in such a way that, with the slit of the horizontal plane, it no longer represents the altitude of the pole above the horizon, but rather its <term>complement</term> <note>The angle remaining to reach 90 degrees (e.g., if latitude is 42°, the complement is 48°).</note>. This completed, you shall elevate the instrument or disc so that it corresponds exactly to the vertical line XP. When situated thus (as will be discussed shortly), because of the gnomonic triangle formed by the axis, it will necessarily show the projection of the hours on the equinoctial vertically.

*The Universal Equinoctial and Meridian Sundial.*

If you wish the hours to be shown to you according to the position of an equinoctial plane, once the disc is positioned according to the practice to be revealed shortly, the shadow of the axis CD—standing out above the plane only as much as the width of the scale—will show the desired hours. Similarly, if placed in this same way according to the position of a polar and meridian plane, it will show the same hours. Experience itself will teach all these things better than we can explain them with many words. I add this: whoever has well penetrated the reasoning of this sundial will find open to themselves a new method of constructing any <term>declining</term> <note>A sundial on a wall that does not face a cardinal direction (North, South, East, West) exactly.</note> dials with the greatest ease.

# The Great Art, Book VI. Part I of the Sundial Proteus.

...once the axis point is chosen, let the radial Zodiac described above in the Preparatory Exercises be applied at its end point C, so that the equinoctial radius <note>The line representing the sun's path during the equinox.</note> matches the semidiameter CD, and the remaining radii touch the axis. Carefully mark the intersection points of the Sun's parallels—or the radii of the 12 signs—with the axis, adding the symbols of the zodiac signs to each intersection; for this reason, the axis must have some thickness. Next, let a solid disc be made, as shown in Figure 5, whose semidiameter CB is equal to the interval CV of the equinoctial radius in the radial Zodiac; this disc is inserted onto the axis MN in such a way that the same <term>equinoctial line</term> <gloss>original Greek: ἰσημέριος (isēmerios)</gloss> always stands at point B, which represents the equinoctial point. Onto this axis, you will transfer the intervals of the radial Zodiac around VB, and IV from B into the axis BM, and BH on both sides. Once small circles are drawn around the points transferred onto the round axis MN, the instrument will be prepared to be situated as a <term>sundial</term> <gloss>original: horolabium</gloss> anywhere in the world, without any prior knowledge of the meridian <note>The North-South line</note>, as follows. You will therefore insert this circle with its portion of the axis into the mobile axis of the rule at point D, as Figure 3 shows. Once this is done, if you wish to know the hour on a horizontal sundial, you shall set the axis CHB according to the given latitude of the region. Then, you will move the entire globe together with the axis and the disc fixed to it back and forth until the shadow of the disc’s edge touches the parallel that the Sun is currently describing, as marked on the axis; you will then have a sundial situated for showing the hours much more accurately than by the benefit of a magnet <note>Kircher argues that geometric alignment using the sun's current declination is more precise than using a magnetic compass, which suffers from magnetic declination.</note>.

<margin>Demonstration of the proposed matter.</margin>
A vertical, meridian, polar, or equinoctial dial is situated by exactly the same reasoning. The logic is clearly evident: Since the disc represents the equinoctial circle, and the shadow in the equinoctial plane perpetually describes circles which are parallels of the Sun (as demonstrated in the preceding sections), it follows that throughout the day, while the Sun stays in a particular sign, the shadow remains equal, since it is nothing other than the semidiameter of that parallel which the Sun is currently describing. Therefore, just as a portion of the axis perpetually projects circles onto the equinoctial plane, so by a converse reasoning, a circle or disc placed perpendicularly on the axis will perpetually project a shadow onto the same point throughout the course of the day. Furthermore, just as the Sun describes a right cone each day around a stylus perpendicular to the equinoctial plane—the base of which is a circle, and all lines from the vertex of the cone to the circumference of the base are equal—so the shadow of the Sun will similarly describe a right cone around a disc placed perpendicularly on the axis, but in an inverse manner. Indeed, the base of the cone itself which the Sun describes is the circumference of the disc; the vertex, however, is the point of the parallel marked on the axis, upon which the shadow perpetually falls on that day, as the lines from the base to the vertex of the cone are perpetually equal. Since the axis has some thickness, the circles of the parallels on the axis will represent a section of the cone parallel to the base, and consequently all lines intercepted between the base and the section will be equal. You will easily grasp all of this if you imagine the portion of the radial Zodiac FCG in Figure 4 rotating around the axis AB: by this revolution, point C will describe the equinoctial; the remaining radii for **Cancer** ♋ and **Capricorn** ♑ will perpetually touch the same points F and G on the axis. It is impossible, however, for the shadow of the disc to touch this point of the axis unless the disc and axis are in their proper positions. Whenever, therefore, the sundial is so situated that its shadow touches the point of the given parallel, then the axis will necessarily correspond to the axis of the world, and the disc to the equator. Consequently, the perfectly situated sundial will indicate the desired hours. Which was to be demonstrated.

### Problem II.

## The Universal Concave Cylindrical Sundial.

This type of sundial also has remarkable uses, and it can even extend to the very minutes of the hours, provided it is constructed skillfully and with industry. Let us therefore first teach its construction, and then also its use. It is of two types: the first is made with a fixed stylus; the second with a mobile one. Both follow exactly the same logic. Therefore, to have explained one is to have explained both. Let the given body be a concave cylinder ABCD, as Figure 7 shows, whose cavity FEG is semicircular. You shall delineate the sundial in it as follows. According to the Preparatory Exercise on page 328 regarding the projection of surfaces onto a plane, let that entire cylindrical surface be projected onto a plane, which becomes AB CD, as Figure 6 has it. You will divide this into two equal parts by the lines EF and GH; EF will be the equinoctial line, and GH the line of the sixth hour.

<margin>Construction of the instrument.</margin>
Next, having placed a circle <note>i.e., the point of a compass</note> at points E and F with the interval EA or BF, let semicircles be drawn, each of which will be divided into two quadrants by the line EF. Each of these quadrants—FIB, FID, and EAO, EOC—you will first divide into three parts if you want the full signs <note>The 12 signs of the zodiac, each spanning 30 degrees.</note>; and again into three other parts if you desire a division of tens of degrees, or even a division of fives. You will then connect with straight lines the individual points of division that are equally distant from the equinoctial points O and I. You will then have the parallels of the Sun described, to each of which you will add the symbols of the signs, as you see done here. You shall describe the lines of the astronomical hours in this way.

<margin>Inscription of the hours.</margin>
Let the equinoctial, or one of the lines parallel to it, be divided first into two equal parts by the line GH, then—

# On Portable Sundials

...GH, then SF, and ES; the line is again divided into six equal parts (following the method provided in Preparatory Exercise III) which will represent whole hours; you will divide each of these again into half and quarter hours, as you see, and the hours will be inscribed: however, AC and BD represent the 12th hour. You will insert this paper, drawn in this way, into a piece of wood hollowed out into a semi-cylinder so that, once glued, it perfectly fills the entire interior space; or, if you have described the <term>horary</term> <gloss>original: horarium; relating to the hours</gloss> scale on a brass plate, you will then bend it into a semi-cylinder.

<margin>The stylus and its length.</margin>
Let this concave space be bounded by a rectangular frame <note>original: "limbo parallelogrammo"</note> divided in two, in the point **X** of which (as Figure 7 shows) a semicircle is to be described. You will divide the quadrants of this semicircle into 90 equal parts, as you see, and the degrees of the lines drawn from the center **X** are to be marked on the square frame. However, from point **Y**, a transverse <term>stylus</term> <gloss>The gnomon or pin that casts the shadow</gloss> is to be inserted of such a length as is the width, or the distance, of the equinoctial from the tropics <note>This ensures the shadow reaches the correct points on the scale during the change of seasons.</note>: let the tip of the stylus be in the plane of the frame itself, and the tip in the equinoctial plane: and you will have the instrument prepared.

## Use of the universal concave cylindrical sundial.

Take the time-telling instrument <note>original: "horofcopium"</note> in your hand, and let the <term>plumb line</term> <gloss>original: perpendiculum</gloss>, which must be attached to point **X** at the center of the semicircle above the degree of your latitude, fall freely. Specifically, if it is before noon, use the morning quadrant; if after noon, the afternoon quadrant. Then, with the plumb line always remaining steady over the degree of the given latitude, turn the instrument back and forth until the shadow of the stylus tip falls precisely onto the <term>parallel</term> <gloss>The line representing the Sun's path for a specific day of the year</gloss> which the Sun completes on that same day; for that shadow will show the current hour with its minutes. If, however, the hour and its parts are already known, the hour will show the Sun's parallel together with its <term>declination</term> <gloss>The Sun's angle north or south of the equator</gloss>, the sunrise and sunset, the twilight, the length of the day and night, etc. The demonstration of the instrument is clear from its very design.

## Another much shorter method of describing the same sundial by means of a movable stylus.

Let a circle, or disc **ACB**, be divided as Figure 9 shows, into 12 hours with their minutes, just as was done in the previous sundial by parallel lines; done in such a way, however, that with all the width of the circle removed, only the zone of the equator remains, as you see. This being finished, let there be a movable stylus reduced into the form of a plate **DE**, the end **D** of which terminates in a tip fit for showing the hours. On this plate, you will describe the Sun’s parallels in exactly the same way as was done in the preceding one; so that if the brass semi-disc **ACB** was equal to the previous semi-cylinder, you will transfer its entire width with all the distances of the parallels from one another onto the plate of the movable stylus, adding to each their numbers and symbols, as you see: the plate, however, must be inserted into the back of the frame **ABFE** so that it can be moved forward like a sliding <term>cursor</term>.

<margin>The condition of the stylus in this sundial.</margin>
If, therefore, you desire the hour and its minutes, move the plate forward until the side **AB** of the frame intersects the Sun’s parallel. Then, with the instrument and the plumb line directed to the degree of the elevation of the pole <note>The local latitude</note>, rotate it this way or 그 way until the shadow falls on the middle line of the semicircle **ACB**; for there the shadow will show you the sought-after parts of the hour. The logic of this instrument is also very clearly evident, since it is nothing other than the inverse of the previous one: for just as in the first one the fixed stylus related to the <term>Zodiac</term> inscribed in the concave according to the expanded parallels; so in this one, the movable stylus marked with the width of the Zodiac relates to the always-immobile circle. But let these things suffice for the industrious.

## Problem III.

### Construction of another universal time-teller.

Let a <term>planisphere</term> <gloss>A flat map of the celestial sphere</gloss> be made, of the kind we described in the *Magnetic Art*, Chapter 1, concerning "Magnetic Astronomy." Once it is constructed, let a movable rule **AB** be attached at the center with a quadrant **AV** inserted at its end **A** in such a way that the quadrant constantly follows the motion of the rule. Moreover, let there be a certain slider **N** in the quadrant equipped with its own stylus, and let the rule **AB** be of such a width as is an arc of 18 degrees; and you will have the instrument prepared. To know the hour in any part of the world, first take the altitude of the Sun, in exactly the same way as is usually taken with an <term>astrolabe</term> <note>A classic astronomical instrument used for navigation and timekeeping</note>: move the slider on the quadrant **AV** to the found altitude of the Sun.

<margin>Various uses of this instrument.</margin>
Then, with the rule **AB** placed above the degree of your latitude on the quadrant ***D***, turn the shadow of the slider’s stylus until it falls onto the Sun’s parallel for the current day, and let the shadow simultaneously be parallel to the horizon (which is important to note); then the shadow of the stylus on **AB** will reveal to you the sought-after hour within the hour lines with its parts. Where the horizontal rule **AB** intersects the Sun’s parallels, it will mark the sunrise and sunset, and the length of day and night; the width of the rule will assign the twilights <note>original: "crepuscula"</note> upwards and downwards. We have therefore constructed the time-teller <note>original: "horofcopium"</note> that was to be made.

### To describe universal spherical sundials.

Since the sphere is the true figure of the heavens, the hours will be demonstrated by its benefit with almost no effort, as follows.

<margin>How an armillary sphere may indicate the hours.</margin>
Let an <term>armillary sphere</term><gloss>A model of objects in the sky, consisting of a spherical framework of rings</gloss> be constructed with a horizon, tropics, equator, and Zodiac; let the equator, however, be divided into 24 equal parts by circles drawn from each pole, and the sphere will be prepared. For if this is positioned according to the given latitude of the region and the four cardinal directions of the world, the shadow of the axis on the equator (and on its parallels divided into 24 equal parts) will show the desired hours. The reasoning is evident from the positioning itself.

->*Another way by an astronomical globe.*<-

<margin>How a solid sphere may be made into a sundial.</margin>
**S**et the degree of the Sun for the current day under the meridian, and the index of the hour circle above the 12th hour. Then, in that degree of the Sun for the current day, place a certain elliptical needle standing <term>equiangular</term><gloss>original Greek: ἰσογώνιος (isogonios)</gloss>. Then, with the sphere positioned as before, turn it back and forth until the needle is <term>shadowless</term><gloss>original Greek: ἀσκία (askia)</gloss>—that is, without a shadow—and the index on the hour cycle will show the desired hour. The reasoning is clearly evident from the position.

->*Another way by any other globe.*<-

**D**elineate on any perfectly round globe a <term>region of equal course</term><gloss>original Greek: ἰσοδρόμου (isodromou)</gloss>, which is the space of the torrid zone, as was said above. You will insert this globe into a semicircle divided into its own degrees, so that its poles can be moved at will above a given degree of latitude. Once this is done, a stylus of any length placed at the <term>vertex</term><gloss>The highest point or zenith</gloss> will show the desired hours on the globe positioned toward the south. A concave hemicycle can be made by exactly the same reasoning. There are, moreover, certain other universal sundials which, because we have reserved them for the following treatises, we have decided to omit here on purpose. Indeed, those which are found in the works of <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612) was a Jesuit astronomer and mathematician who was the main architect of the Gregorian calendar.</note> Clavius (Book 8) and other <term>gnomonists</term><gloss>Experts in the art of sundial making</gloss>, we also omit on purpose, lest we seem to have enriched our art with the belongings of others, and thus with commonplace equipment.

### Problem V.

> *To project a gnomonic astrolabe onto a given hemicycle or hemisphere for a given latitude with almost no effort.*

In describing this, you will proceed by a twofold path: either with a compass or by projection onto a plane. We will teach both methods with as much brevity and clarity as we can. The practical application <note>original: "Pragmatia"</note> of the former is as follows: 

First, take a compass with its legs spread wide; with one of its legs placed at **N** on the edge of the circumference and the other through the point <term>nadir</term><gloss>The lowest point, directly opposite the zenith</gloss> (or the lowest point of the hemicycle, **A**), let a semicircle be described within the prepared vessel. The horizon, or the edge NHGD of the circular vessel, will be divided into two equal parts. Again, with one leg of the compass placed at **G** and the other through **N**, let another semicircle be described, which intersects the former at **A** at right angles; the whole horizon will be divided into four quadrants, each of which you will divide into its own degrees. By placing one foot of the compass at this degree, and drawing the other through the 48th degree of the HA quadrant, you will describe a semicircle, which will be the equator. Next, calculate the maximum declination of the Sun on both sides <note>The maximum distance of the Sun from the equator, roughly 23.5 degrees.</note>; by drawing arcs parallel to the equator, you will have the tropics. You shall also draw the parallels of the remaining zodiac signs using the method of the declination table, as has been described in various places previously. With the symbols of the signs written on the outside along the horizon, the <term>style</term><gloss>the gnomon or upright rod that casts the shadow</gloss> will be like this one, AO, terminating upright in the center of the horizon. From this, two threads intersecting in the same place can serve as the index, as the lines ND and HG show here.

### Inscription of the hours from noon and midnight.

Divide the equinoctial line NKD into 12 equal parts. Then, having measured the space of the DA quadrant with the compass, let arcs be described within the tropics from the subsequent hour points of the equator through hour points a full quadrant apart; thus you will have the <term>astronomical hours</term><gloss>standard hours of equal length used by astronomers</gloss>.

### Inscription of the hours from sunrise and sunset.

Divide the arc of the tropic of Cancer (♋) into the hours corresponding to its longest daylight period, as you see in the figure, and similarly divide Capricorn (♑) into the hours corresponding to its daylight period. Then, starting from the 24th hour (which the horizon represents), draw a circular arc through the first three points found on the tropics and the equator; you will have the 23rd hour. Again, through the points of the next hour found on the tropics and equator, draw a circular arc, <margin>Italian and Babylonian hours.</margin> and you will have the 22nd hour. Proceed in this manner for the other hour lines until all are finished, and the <term>horoscope</term><gloss>literally "hour-viewer"; here meaning the sundial face</gloss> from sunset will be complete. With the same diligence, you may write the hours from sunrise, or Babylonian hours, in the same hemicycle; for as has been often said, this is nothing other than the reverse of the previous system.

### Inscription of the ancient or unequal hours.

Divide each tropic into 12 equal parts, starting from the sunrise side of the horizon. An arc drawn through the first three points found on the tropics and equator will give the 1st hour. Through any three following points, another arc drawn between the tropics will give the 2nd <term>unequal hour</term><gloss>historical hours where the day and night are each divided into 12 parts, meaning the length of an "hour" changes with the seasons</gloss>, and so you shall proceed. The sixth hour will correspond to the 12th astronomical hour [noon], and the 12th unequal hour will be the same as the 24th hour from sunrise and sunset. Nothing, therefore, is easier than the description of unequal hours in a hemispherical sundial.

### Inscription of Almucantars and Azimuths.

All circles drawn through each of the 360 degrees of the horizon circle, intersecting at the pole of the horizon A, will give the <term>Azimuths</term><gloss>lines of horizontal direction or bearing</gloss>. The <term>Almucantars</term><gloss>circles of altitude or height above the horizon</gloss> will be given by circles described from center A through individual degrees, or groups of five or ten degrees, on the quadrants AV, AG, AN, or AD.

### Another practical method, or the method by projection of the globe onto a plane.

Let the surface of the hemicycle be projected onto a plane, according to the practical methods handed down on page 332, using <term>dodecamoria</term><gloss>twelfth-parts, often referring to the 30-degree divisions of the zodiac</gloss> or by drawing the description of the <term>sun-path</term><gloss>original Greek: ἡλιοδρόμους (heliodromous)</gloss> space on a plane with two straight lines intersecting at right angles, equal to the curves VAG or MAD of the hemicycle, and using the <term>Cyclotetragonic instrument</term><gloss>a specialized tool for "squaring the circle" or mapping circular coordinates to a grid</gloss>, as shown here. Next, divide VAG, which represents the meridian, into 180 parts (or two quadrants of 90 equal parts each); divide the semicircle MAN in the same way. Then, placing one foot of the compass at the 42nd degree <note>The latitude of Rome, where the author likely designed this.</note> of quadrant AG, and the other through the 48th of quadrant AV, draw a circle through each and every point found at that same degree.

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram illustrating the projection of a spherical coordinate system. A central vertical line (the meridian) is marked A at the top. The network of lines creates a grid used for calculating time and solar position.</image-desc>

In the dodecamoria parts, these joined arcs will represent the equator. From this arc, on both sides of the same 42nd degree, draw arcs 23 and a half degrees distant from the equator; these will be the tropics of Cancer (♋) and Capricorn (♑). The dodecamoria parts themselves will give the hours from noon and midnight, as you see. For the remaining hours, proceed with the same diligence as before. If you then transfer all these points or dodecamoria parts into the cavity of a hemisphere so they all meet at the pole (that is, at the 42nd degree), the joined points will recreate the same description as seen here, once all parts extending beyond the horizon are trimmed away. # CHAPTER II.

### *Concerning a new method of projecting every kind of hour and celestial circle onto the concave and exterior surfaces of any bodies whatsoever.*

**I**N the preceding sections, we discussed the projection of gnomonic <term>astrolabes</term><gloss>instruments used to determine the positions of celestial bodies</gloss> onto given straight or circular surfaces; now, however, we must discuss how they can be drawn on polygonal bodies that can be moved from place to place. While we do this, I truly know not whether those aforementioned astrolabes on the various and irregular exterior surfaces of bodies—with their various placements and positions of <term>gnomons</term><gloss>the part of a sundial that casts a shadow</gloss> and styles—command more admiration, or if it is instead the projection of that same apparatus of celestial circles onto the internal and concave surfaces of those same bodies using a single fixed style? Certainly, having weighed both, the latter will seem more in conformity with the operations of nature and, as they say, preferable to the other by many <term>parasangs</term><gloss>an ancient Persian unit of distance; here meaning "by a great distance"</gloss>. It is added that a shadow gathered in a concave space demonstrates everything better and more clearly than on external surfaces. For on the latter, the shadow is wandering and loose; while it takes on various forms on various planes, it mostly deviates from its natural path. Thus, it does not present itself as agreeably to observers as it does in concavities where, as if held back by a bridle and barriers, that confused multitude of projected lines reveals itself most conveniently to the sight. The practical inscription of these lines was the only thing that made the task difficult; while we were intent on overcoming this difficulty, a certain method finally occurred to us that is both very easy and most certain. Since it is new and most reliable, I have chosen to share it here with the Reader, as no plane can be encountered so irregular that one cannot inscribe any species of lines upon it with the greatest ease, and that by the aid of the <term>Almucantar</term><gloss>a circle of altitude on the celestial sphere parallel to the horizon</gloss>-Azimuth table alone. Therefore, let there be

## Problem VI.
### *To construct a scaphium.*

**W**e call <term>scaphia</term><gloss>bowl-shaped or hollowed-out sundials, from the Greek "skaphe" meaning a boat or tub</gloss> all those clocks which are described in the concave segments of some sphere, which the halves of the sections represent in the "wondrous quadrant" CI or NO on page 336. To describe astrolabes in a scaphium by the easiest method: First, the horizon of the scaphium having been divided into 360 parts, let hidden arcs be drawn through them and through the center of the scaphium, and you will have the <term>Azimuths</term><gloss>arcs spanning from the zenith to the horizon used to measure horizontal direction</gloss>. You shall inscribe the Almucantars on them thus: In the wondrous quadrant, let the radius of the scaphium AN be taken from center A, and let AO be its axis, or style. If concentric circles are drawn from the center of the scaphium through the individual points where the lines of the degrees intersect the segment or circular line ON, you will have the Almucantars.

<image-desc>A technical diagram for the geometric construction of a concave sundial. The top section features a curved scale labeled with degrees and hours, with radiating lines converging at a point marked 'C'. A central vertical axis 'A' serves as the gnomon or style. Below, a secondary curved scale measures degrees from 10 to 90. Various intersection points are labeled with letters to guide the mathematical placement of hour and altitude lines within the "bowl" of the dial.</image-desc>

You shall inscribe the hours on the said circles by this industrious method. Take the Almucantar-Azimuth table and see at which Azimuth and Almucantar the Sun is at the 12th hour in <note>original: "♋"</note> Cancer, and you will find the Almucantar at 71 degrees 28 minutes. The table shows the Azimuth of 90 corresponds to the 12th hour. Therefore, having found the common point of intersection of the Azimuth and Almucantar, count down 71 degrees and 28 minutes at the 90th Azimuth in the scaphium, and the end of the counting will give the sought-after point for the 12th hour in Cancer. Likewise, the Azimuth and Almucantar for the Sun in Cancer at 51 [degrees] and 19 minutes at 40 minutes <note>referring to coordinate adjustments</note> will give the point for the 1st and 11th hours on both sides. In the same way, you will investigate the points of the other hours, and you will simultaneously have the points through which the drawn arc will give the <term>tropic of Cancer</term><gloss>the northernmost circle of latitude where the sun can be directly overhead</gloss>. Similarly, you will investigate the points of the hours in the equator and in the <term>tropic of Capricorn</term><gloss>the southernmost circle of latitude where the sun can be directly overhead</gloss>; for through each of the three similar points of the hours, the drawn arcs will give the astronomical hour lines. If, however, you desire the description of the hours from sunrise and sunset, you will take the table assigned to these and operate in exactly the same way as in the preceding section. For the inscription of the Sun's parallels, the same table used for the hours will serve. Likewise, use the appropriate table for describing the <term>celestial houses</term><gloss>twelve divisions of the celestial sphere in astrology</gloss>. For the ascending and descending signs of the Zodiac, you shall operate through the proper table. Which tables [are found] everywhere...

### Problem VII.

### To project astrolabes <gloss>astronomical instruments, here meaning sundial faces</gloss> onto the interior and exterior surfaces of a cube by another method, using a <term>horographic rule</term><gloss>a specialized scale or ruler used in the 17th century to calculate and draw hour-lines for sundials</gloss>.

Let there be a cube ABCDHIK, whose interior side looking south <note>original: "meridiem respiciens"</note> is BEC, the side looking

<image-desc>A perspective drawing of a cube (ABCDHIK) with dotted lines indicating interior planes and points. Labels include A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K, L, M, and S. A central vertical gnomon line is shown from point G.</image-desc>

east is BMA, and the west is CLD, and the north is AFD. And let MG be the length of the <term>gnomon</term><gloss>the part of a sundial that casts a shadow</gloss> on the plane looking east, at M, the intersection where the horizontal sixth-hour line and the equinoctial point meet at a right angle. Furthermore, let EG be the vertical gnomon of the interior south-facing plane, erected perpendicularly on the horizontal line E. Let GL be the gnomon of the west-facing plane. Finally, let GF be the gnomon of the north-facing plane. If, therefore, you describe on any piece of paper equal to the interior plane, separately for the given gnomon EG, whatever hours you wish according to Problem 6, Book 4, and any circles according to the precepts delivered in the preceding sections, you will have a gnomonic <term>horolabium</term><gloss>a sundial</gloss> drawn on a vertical plane for those hours which the plane is capable of receiving.

<margin>The eastern, western, and similar parts of the cube.</margin>
Likewise, if you describe those same hours and lines on the eastern, western, and northern planes for the given gnomons MG, GL, and FG according to the rules delivered previously, you will have a sundial in which all the lines correspond to one another with a certain wondrous harmony, drawn on the interior planes; in this, a single apex of any assumed gnomon terminating at point G will show on the four divided surfaces that which four different gnomons would do on the four exterior planes.

<margin>How the bottom of the cube is to be drawn.</margin>
One difficulty still remains to be solved in this place regarding the horizontal plane, which the bottom of the cube represents: since some hours must necessarily be placed there, it is asked how those hours, or the part of the <term>tropics</term><gloss>the lines representing the summer and winter solstices</gloss>, are to be drawn? I respond: by this industrious method. Let the gnomon of the said horizontal plane be equal in length to one of the sides of the cube, and let its location be at S, the center of the bottom, for example; let a horizontal sundial be drawn separately along with any other lines for the given length of the style GV, or for any side. Then, from that drawing so described, let all those parts be cut away which exceed the floor of the base HSKI. For this, having been glued to the bottom, it will necessarily correspond to the hour lines of the remaining vertical planes (unless an error has been made somewhere).

Indeed, on the exterior surfaces, the sundials drawn appropriate to each plane will show the same hours outside that the single apex G shows inside. Thus, we have drawn a cube showing the hours both inside and out, which was the task to be done.

Let a line AA be drawn on any separate plane, and on this...

### Another very easy method to accomplish the same.

Cut out from stiff paper a trapezoid equal to CABD. From its midpoint, inscribe a circle divided into 360 parts, and having drawn straight lines from the center to the edge, add the respective numbers to each. Apply this trapezoid to the rim of the vessel CABD so that side matches side perfectly. Wherever the lines drawn from the center of the trapezoid intersect the edges of the rim CABD, make marks with the degrees; for the lines drawn perpendicular to the rim through these points will give the <term>azimuths</term><gloss>arcs of the horizon used to measure horizontal direction</gloss> on the said planes. Alternatively, apply the sides of the projected polyhedron's trapezoid to each side of the actual trapezoid and proceed as before. You will inscribe the <term>almucantars</term><gloss>circles on the celestial sphere parallel to the horizon, representing altitude</gloss> on these using exactly the same method and industry, along with the hours, as we did above using the <term>remarkable quadrant</term><gloss>a specialized calculating instrument described earlier in the text</gloss>, and as we shall teach in the following sections. See the preceding figure.

### Corollary.

By this industrious method, you will describe <term>horolabiums</term><gloss>sundials or hour-tracking instruments</gloss> on the surfaces of all bodies, whether regular or irregular; for he who perceives the logic of one will not be able to remain ignorant of the logic of others.

### Problem IX.

### To delineate the hours together with the celestial circles on a concave cylinder using gnomonics.

Since it is difficult to perform the drawing of the things soon to be discussed directly on the concave surfaces of bodies, it seemed more advisable to first complete it on flat paper, so that it may then be inserted and glued into the concavity for use. As for how a drawing can be established on flat paper that exactly corresponds in every way to the position and site of spherical or any other interior surfaces, accept this brief explanation. Let the cylinder be ABEO in the first figure of Illustration 7, in whose concavity the hours and celestial circles must be described. On a separate piece of paper, as Figure 2 shows, let a quadrangle ABCD be made, whose opposite sides AD and CB represent the length of the cylinder, while sides AB and CD represent its circumference—that is, equal to the circumference of the cylinder at both the bottom and the top. The surface is found by this method:

<margin>Projection of a cylindrical surface onto a plane.</margin>
Since, according to the demonstrations of Archimedes, the diameter is to the circumference in the proportion of three and one-seventh <note>The ratio 22/7, a common historical approximation of Pi.</note>, and relates as 14 to 44, you will have a line equal to the circumference. First, divide the diameter into 14 parts, and both sides AB and DC into 44 parts equal to the parts of the diameter. If you then divide this entire line (equal to the circumference) into four equal parts, 11 parts of the whole will be equal to the arc of a quadrant of the cylinder. Furthermore, for a better practice, you may assign a straight line equal to any circumference by using the line they call <term>pragmatic</term><gloss>from the Greek 'pragmatike'</gloss> or the <term>quadratrix</term><gloss>a mathematical curve used to determine the length of an arc or square a circle</gloss>. But since this was treated extensively from page 317 to 327, we refer the reader there. With these things thus performed, side AB of the quadrangle will be equal to the circumference of the cylinder; the space of the quadrangle AEDF will be equal to one of the quadrants of the interior surface of the cylinder; and the entire surface of the quadrangle ABCD will be equal to the surface of the concave cylinder.

### The Inscription of Azimuths.

Having provided this art, for a quadrangle equal to the interior surface of the cylinder, you will divide either side AB or DC into 360 parts if the vessel is large, or by every five, ten, or fifteen degrees if it is narrow. By drawing parallel lines downward from each degree, you will have the azimuthal lines of the cylinder inscribed on the plane, as appears in Figure 2 of the Illustration.

### The Inscription of Almucantars.

<margin>Operation 1: By the remarkable quadrant.</margin>
You shall inscribe the almucantars as follows. First, take the horographic quadrant described above on page 336. On its side AK, determine from A toward K the quantity of the semi-diameter of the cylinder's base, which is AN; on the side of the quadrant AI, determine the height of the cylinder's axis, which is AI itself. Second, carefully note where the lines drawn from the center A through the individual degrees of the quadrant intersect line N 80. From this line, if you transfer the intervals of the individual degrees to the sides AD and BC of the cylindrical quadrangle and connect them with straight lines, they will represent the circles of the almucantars to you, as is evident in the example.

To mark the rectangle, consult the <term>Almucantar-azimuth</term><gloss>A coordinate system combining altitude (almucantar) and horizontal direction (azimuth)</gloss> tables for the principal pole elevations <note>In this context, "pole elevations" refers to geographic latitudes.</note> calculated by us earlier in the Apparatus on page 293. With their help, you will be able to mark both the hours and any other <margin>Marking the hours.</margin> celestial circles with almost no effort, whether on this present cylinder or on any other internal surfaces of solid bodies. Spread out before you the dialing-plate <note>original: "pinacem horologum"</note> suited to the latitude of your region, taken from the universal table, just as the following plate, calculated for the latitude of Rome, demonstrates. This table <note>original: "abacus"</note> is composed partly of <term>azimuths</term><gloss>arcs of the horizon used to measure horizontal positions</gloss>, or horizontal circumferences, and partly of <term>Almucantars</term>, or the altitudes of the Sun above the horizon, as the titles show. If, therefore, you intend to mark the astronomical hours on our cylindrical rectangle, look for the <term>Azimuth</term> and <term>Almucantar</term> corresponding to the 12th hour when the Sun is positioned in <term>Cancer</term><gloss>the astrological sign marking the Summer Solstice</gloss> in the table. You will find that the <term>Azimuth</term> is indeed 90, while the <term>Almucantar</term> is 71 degrees and 28 minutes. Look for that value on the upper or lower line AB of the cylindrical rectangle, starting from the noon points X and F; then, on that same <term>Azimuth</term> line, you will count 71 degrees and 28 minutes downward. For where the 71st <term>Almucantar</term> with 28 minutes intersects the meridian <term>Azimuth</term>, there is the point for the 12th hour—the exact spot which the Sun's ray strikes at the 12th hour while it stays at the beginning of <term>Cancer</term>.

The points for the 1st and 11th hours in <term>Cancer</term> are found on the cylindrical plane in this way: Look for the <term>Azimuth</term> corresponding to these hours in the <term>Cancer</term> column—namely, 51 degrees and 19 minutes—along with the <term>Almucantar</term> of 67 degrees and 40 minutes. Look for the former from the meridian point X or F on the line EF or EC at the base of the cylinder; look for the latter among the <term>Almucantars</term> marked on the plane. For where the <term>Almucantar</term> of 67 degrees and 40 minutes intersects that <term>Azimuth</term> of 51 degrees and 19 minutes before and after noon, there will be the points for the 1st and 11th hours, through which the <margin>Finding the points on the equinox.</margin> tropic of <term>Cancer</term> must also be drawn. You will proceed no differently in marking the remaining hour points. Once their description is finished, you will seek the points of the hours in exactly the same way for the Sun positioned in <term>Aries</term> and <term>Libra</term> <note>These signs represent the Spring and Autumn Equinoxes.</note>; for where the <term>Almucantars</term> in the column of the table marked for <term>Aries</term> and <term>Libra</term> intersect the corresponding <term>Azimuths</term>, there will be the points for the equinoctial hours.

The hour points for the Sun positioned at the beginning of <term>Capricorn</term><gloss>the sign of the Winter Solstice</gloss> will also be found by the exact same method we have described: namely, by noting the intersection of a given hour and sign's <term>Azimuth</term> and <term>Almucantar</term>. The same must be done for drawing the points of the other hours into a single line, and you will have a finished sundial. ### Inscription of hours from sunrise and sunset on a given cylinder.

# The Great Art of Light and Shadow, Book VI. Part I of Proteus <note>Kircher uses the name of the shape-shifting sea god "Proteus" to title this section on the various transformations and projections of sundial geometry.</note>.

<margin>
Shadow is the fleeting trace of light, the indicator of light in flight; 
What it snatches away is certain, what it teaches is ambiguous.
<note>original Latin: "Luminis umbra fugax, fugitivi luminis index, Quod rapit est certum, quod docet ambiguum." This is a poetic reflection on how a sundial marks the certain loss of time even as its readings can be difficult to interpret.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
A segment of a concave cylinder displaying the lines of hours from sunset, noon, and midnight.
</margin>

<margin>
The shadow and the light race toward the desired goal; it was just running, and has not yet ceased, for all things in life are in flux.
<note>original Greek: Η σκιὰ φῶς δὲ τρέχει τὸ ποθούμενον· ἔτρεχεν ἄρτι Οὔπω ἀνήρθησεν πάντα τρέχειν βίω. This epigram parallels the Latin verse above, emphasizing the constant motion of time.</note>
</margin>

### Inscription of the celestial houses along with the hours from sunrise on a cylinder.

Work according to the rules previously given by extracting the degrees and minutes of the <term>Azimuths</term><gloss>circles of horizontal direction</gloss> and <term>Almucantars</term><gloss>circles of altitude above the horizon</gloss> according to the three signs of Cancer ♋, Aries ♈, and Capricorn ♑. Carefully note the common intersections of these circles; for those will be the points through which the lines, once drawn, will designate the <term>celestial houses</term><gloss>the twelve divisions of the sky used in astrology to determine the positions of planets and stars</gloss>. The matter is entirely easy; therefore, we have judged it unnecessary to dwell on it any longer. See the example of the celestial houses inscribed in the following figure.

### How to inscribe unequal, or planetary, hours into the same quadrant.

**E**xtract, for example for the 9th hour, the degrees and minutes of the Azimuths and Almucantars for when the Sun enters the specific hours of ♋︎ <note>Cancer</note> and ♑︎ <note>Capricorn</note>. If you then join a straight line through the three points of intersection of the Azimuths with the Almucantars found in the quadrant, you will have what you seek. You shall operate no differently for the other hours. <note><term>Unequal or Planetary Hours</term><gloss>An ancient system where the periods of daylight and darkness are each divided into 12 hours, meaning summer hours are longer than winter hours.</gloss></note>

Therefore, once the quadrilateral has been marked with its hours and circles, as has been said, you will insert it, adapted into the form of a cylinder, into the cavity of the cylinder in such a way that the sides BC and AD completely converge into a single line. From this point Y, draw a line to R, which will represent the sloping line of the cone's side. We have placed a practical diagram (<term>Pragmatia</term>) here separately under Figure 5, where LM represents the semidiameter of the conical base; LN, the axis; and finally, NM, the side of the cone. You will divide this arc into 44 parts, such that each part is equal to one of the 14 parts into which diameter AO of Figure 3 is divided. Thirdly, let each quadrant be divided into 90 equal parts, starting from point N on both sides. Then, through each degree (if the vessel is large), or through every five, ten, or fifteen degrees (if it is narrower), you will draw straight lines to the center V, which will represent the <term>azymuthales circulos</term> (azimuth circles – great circles passing through the zenith and nadir, perpendicular to the horizon). The apex of the stylus, corresponding to the center of the horizon or the rim of the cone, will show the hours and the circles that the Sun traverses at that hour.

->*Problem XI.*<-

->*To inscribe a sciatheric planisphere into a concave cube.*<-

EFGH will represent the plane of the primary vertical, BFDH the western, AECG the eastern, and ABCD the northern. When finished, you will insert this plane into the cubic vessel so that each side corresponds to its own side. # Problem XII.
## *To inscribe the same set of lines upon a pyramid, or a concave tetrahedron.*

**L**ook first at Figure 6 of the preceding Diagram 6, in which there is a pyramid ABCD, upon whose interior sides it is necessary to inscribe the hours. First, as was said in the preceding sections, the concave part of the pyramid must first be transferred onto a pyramidal plane in the following manner. Let the base of the <term>tetrahedron</term><gloss>a four-sided solid</gloss>, or inscribed pyramid ABC, be transferred to paper from center V, as appears in Figure 9. From the center V of its circumscribed circle, let lines be drawn that divide the circumference into 360 parts, or even into 36 parts (which are the decades of the circle); for these lines will represent the vertical circles projected onto the horizontal plane of the pyramid. Then you shall inscribe the three surfaces onto the pyramidal plane thus: Take the side of the given pyramid BD or CD, and with this distance let an arc of a circle HGFE be described, into which you will transfer the sides of the base of the pyramid. With the lines EL, FL, GL, and HL drawn to the center, you will have the prepared plane, onto which you will first inscribe the Azimuths in this way: take one of the sides of the base of the pyramid drawn separately and divided into its Azimuths—I mean side AB (as Figure 9 shows)—and transfer it along with its divisions onto the lines of the pyramidal plane EF, FG, GH. For if you draw straight lines from the center L through these types of points, you will have the azimuthal lines inscribed on the pyramidal plane. To these you shall inscribe the Almucantars by this art: From center V of the separately drawn base of the pyramid, transfer onto side AB of the quadrant ABD in Figure 8 each of the lines intercepted between V and line XB or XA. From the transferred points K, L, M, N, O, P, straight lines shall be drawn to side AC at point R, or the apex of the pyramid (therefore, the space AR must be as large as the axis of the pyramid). Once this is done, the Almucantars will be inscribed on the Azimuths as follows: See where the radii of the degrees of the quadrant intersect the line KR in the quadrant, and transfer these spaces of the intersections to Azimuth 90 of side GFL, which side will be facing South, and consequently line KL will be the meridian line. Next, see where the radii of the quadrant intersect line MR—for example, the 60th Azimuth—and transfer these intersections onto line ML, the 60th Azimuth on line GF of the pyramidal plane. Then transfer the intersections drawn on line IR, the 30th Azimuth, onto lines HL, GL, FL, and EL. For if you join the points of the same degrees into curved lines, you will have the desired Almucantars. Thus, having inscribed the Azimuths and Almucantars on the pyramidal plane, you shall inscribe the rest of the set of hour lines in the exact same manner and order with the help of the preceding tables as was done in the previous cases. But practice and experience itself will teach you everything better and more easily than I could explain even with many words.

### Problem XIII.

> *Given any prism of any number of sides, to inscribe upon it the system of circles described previously.*

From the preceding instructions, it is clear how the previous system of things can be inscribed within the hollow of any given prism—as appears in Figure 5 of this **Plate** <note>original: "Iconismi"</note> showing a hexagonal prism.

**First**, the base of the given polygon should be separately circumscribed by a circle divided into 360 parts, as Figure 6 demonstrates.

**Second**, the sides of this base are to be transferred onto a line, AB, so that a rectangular plane is created, distributed into its own surfaces according to the height of the body, just as was done with the surfaces of the <term>parallelepiped</term><gloss>a six-faced solid with parallel sides</gloss> previously, and as Figure 5 sufficiently declares.

**Third**, the points of the sections on the sides of the base—made by lines drawn from the center to the circumference—should each be transferred to their corresponding surfaces of the plane of the polygonal body. From these points, parallel lines should be drawn downward (except in pyramidal bodies, where the lines will meet at the apex of the pyramid); for these lines will be the desired <term>Azimuths</term><gloss>lines of horizontal bearing or direction</gloss> of the body.

**Fourth**, the spaces between the center O of the base of the polygonal body in Figure 6 and the points LM of the division of the sides are to be transferred onto the **beneficent quadrant** <note>This likely refers to a specialized drafting tool or scale used for calculating altitudes</note> BVS, and parallels should be drawn downward, as was done in the description of the cube. With the help of these, the <term>Almucantars</term><gloss>lines of altitude above the horizon</gloss> will be inscribed upon the Azimuths in exactly the same manner as was stated in the preceding sections.

**Fifth**, once the Azimuths and Almucantars have been inscribed in the polygonal body by the said method, you will easily inscribe the remaining system of hours and celestial lines with the assistance of the previously provided tables. Therefore, I advise you to make the <term>Practical Procedures</term><gloss>original: "Pragmatias"</gloss> used in the preceding pages familiar to yourself through frequent exercise; for with their help, nothing will occur in later sections so difficult that you cannot easily perceive its reasoning. See Figure 5, in which we have inscribed the signs, the astronomical hours, and the <term>celestial houses</term><gloss>divisions of the sky used in astrology</gloss>. This plane, when folded into a six-sided prism, shows the desired teaching on the inside.

### Corollary.

There is nothing in the entire breadth of <term>Gnomonics</term><gloss>the art of sundial making</gloss> that cannot be achieved with the greatest and most admirable shortcut and brevity through these Almucantar-Azimuth tables alone, which we have proposed to you in the preceding sections, and the method for calculating which we have taught elsewhere. This is a secret known to few, and we shall clearly demonstrate it in our *Combinatorial Art* <note>A reference to Kircher's *Ars Magna Sciendi*, where he explores universal logic and combinations</note>.

### Problem XIV.

> *To describe sundials of every kind with almost no effort on an observatory instrument in the concave surfaces of all bodies, both regular and irregular.*

Let any given <term>polyhedron</term><gloss>a solid with many flat faces</gloss> equipped with its own <term>style</term><gloss>the shadow-casting pin or gnomon</gloss> be placed upon the table of the instrument proposed above on page 367, and secured there so that it cannot be moved from its place. Then, let the "prototype" <note>a master template or reference dial</note> dial also be placed in its previously established position. Turn the whole system together—the prototype and the polyhedron intended to be marked with hours—back and forth until the style of the prototype dial passes over each of the hour points on the <term>Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn</term><gloss>the lines representing the summer and winter solstices</gloss>. If at the same time you carefully mark each point where the tip of the shadow touches the polyhedron, these points, when connected into a curved line, will give you the desired Tropics. And if you join the points of similar hours with straight lines, those will give you the desired hours. But since these things have already been said above, the reader will find a fuller instruction from the preceding sections.

### Problem XV.

> *To inscribe sundials of every kind in a tetracyclic column—that is, in four parts hollowed out in the manner of a cylinder.*

Let there be a **tetracyclic** <note>literally "four-wheeled" or "four-chambered," referring here to a column with four concave vertical channels</note> column, which Figure 1 of the present Plate VIII exhibits to you, with the <term>ground plan</term><gloss>original: "ichnographia"</gloss> of the cylindrical hollow XYZN, as the base of Figure 1 of the Plate shows. Its hemicycle <margin>ABC</margin> faces South, <margin>FED</margin> the East, <margin>KLM</margin> the West, and <margin>IHG</margin> the North. In each of these, you will delineate gnomonic astrolabes. First, let the Azimuths and Almucantars be drawn with the same diligence we used above in the description of the concave cylinder. This will also be easily done with a semicircle made of stiff paper or other material, equal to one of the four semicircular segments and divided into 180 parts. For this, when inserted into each semicircle—ABC, FED, IHG, MLK—will immediately assign the points through which perpendiculars drawn to the base of the tetracycle will give the Azimuths. You shall inscribe the Almucantars in these in the very same way we inscribed them in the aforementioned cylinder. Moreover, you will inscribe the Zodiac, the fourfold kind of hours, and the rest of the system of celestial circles in these in the very same way, by the benefit of the Almucantar-Azimuth table appropriate to each, as all these things were partly in the preceding—
