...we have inscribed on the preceding <insert>surfaces</insert>, and partly we shall inscribe on those following. In the Quirinal garden of the Pope <note>The Quirinal Palace in Rome, then a papal residence</note>, the most learned Theodosius Rossi of Priverno, a Roman legal scholar and Papal mathematician, recently designed a device of this kind. In this work, in place of traditional **styles** <gloss>the shadow-casting pin of a sundial</gloss>, the Urban Bees <note>original: "Apes Urbanae." A reference to the three bees on the coat of arms of Pope Urban VIII (Maffeo Barberini)</note> indicate the hours and other data with their stings, accompanied by this verse from Virgil:

> *To some, by lot, fell the guard-duty at the gates.* <note>original: "Sunt quibus ad portas cecidit custodia sorti." From Virgil's Georgics, Book IV, describing the labors of bees.</note>

In a similar way, you will mark these things on the five-circled prism shown in Figure 3; but let us briefly explain the process. Within this, with the help of the Almucantar-Azimuth table, you will mark the hour lines as before.

### Corollary I.

<margin>Drawing on another tetrahedral pyramid, figure 4.</margin>
It is clear from this how a **tetrahedral pyramid** <note>a four-faced solid, each face being a triangle</note> sundial can be skillfully drawn first on a flat surface, both according to its interior and exterior surfaces, as Figure 4 shows. Once folded, these can show the hours and other data on each of the four inclined faces looking toward the four quarters of the world, on both the inside and outside, as Figure 5 demonstrates. By this same industry, you can describe a synopsis of celestial teaching on any other body, such as a **starred cone**, as Figure 6 shows. All of these things will become clearer in the following sections.

### Corollary II.

By this art, you will be able to inscribe all kinds of sundials on six-circled, seven-circled columns, and so on, with truly admirable skill, where all the styles show either the same hours or different types of lines. All of this can also be successfully accomplished with an observation instrument. At the top of the column, a **naval ensign** <gloss>original: "aplustre"; used here as a decorative pointer or vane</gloss> can be erected in the center, showing the winds within a circle divided into 32 parts. Furthermore, a machine could be made that demonstrates as many different aspects of the sphere in 32 concave surfaces divided according to the 32 winds. We will speak more extensively about this machine in our *Horographic Magic*. The same things can be described on a cone with as many concave surfaces. All of this can be gathered more clearly from the present figure than I could explain even in many words.

## Problem II.
### To describe a four-circle horological cross.

<margin>How the hours are to be inscribed on the Cross</margin>
Let a Cross be made of any material, the ends of which are hollowed into semicircles, as is evident in Figure 2. This being done, you will inscribe the hours in the semicircles and on the styles in exactly the same way as was done in the previous Problem. On the sides of the cross, however—having attached a **sixth-part quadrant** <term>sixth-part quadrant: a tool divided into six 15-degree sections, each representing one hour of the sun's 90-degree path from noon to the horizon</term> <note>original: "quadrante hectemorio"</note> to the end points of the arms MN, QP, and LI—the hour lines should be drawn straight. Where these lines touch the sides, hour lines should be drawn parallel to each other and to the sides **at the same height** <note>original Greek: "ἰσοϋψῶς" (isoipsos)</note>. Thus, you will have the horological cross described; the hours, moreover, shall be written in the order you see here. It must be observed, however, that the perpendicular side of the quadrant always represents the 12th hour line, while the transverse side represents the line for the 6th hour of the morning or evening. The cross itself, placed upon the equinoctial plane in any location in the world, will demonstrate the hours. But these matters are too easy to deserve a description in more words. See the figure.

### Corollary.

**From this it is clear that, by the exact same method by which we described the four-circle version, one can describe** a five-circle, six-circle, seven-circle, eight-circle, nine-circle, ten-circle, and finally any bodies with semicircular cavities.

## Problem III.
### To describe the Name of JESUS as a sundial.

<margin>Illustration VIII.</margin>
**L**et the shape of the name **JESUS** be carved into some solid wood, such as boxwood or ebony, about a finger's width thick, together with 12 or 24 rays, as appears in the attached figure. Then, with the rays extended and shaped in the solid wood, you will mark two of them separately; let them be the two rays ABC and DCI. At the first tip, A, let a sixth-part quadrant AEC be attached, or let a quadrant AEC divided into six equal parts be drawn. The straight lines drawn through the points of these divisions will intersect the side DC of the solid ray DCI at certain points; note these carefully. Through these points, hidden circles drawn from Y (the center of the entire figure) on both sides of the figure will intersect each individual ray at points. When these points are joined by straight lines on the **shadow-tracking** <term>sciatheric: relating to the use of shadows to tell time</term> faces of the rays, they will give the hour lines. In these, you will inscribe the hours in the order you see done here, the sequence of which is as follows.

<margin>How and in what order the hours are to be inscribed.</margin>
All lines descending perpendicularly at the tips of the rays are the lines for the 12th hour. Again, all transverse lines drawn from the tips of the rays perpendicular to the 12th hour line are the lines for the 6th hour, wherever they may fall. From these, you will inscribe the numbers of the hours in their natural order for the remaining intermediate lines up to 12. If you observe these things well, you will never be able to err in inscribing the hours.

<margin>The Name of Jesus as a sundial.</margin>
Indeed, you shall make the Name of **JESUS** into a sundial by this industrious method. Let the characters of the name **JESUS** be made of solid material of the same thickness as the rays, marked with the letters AB, CD, EF, GH, and IKL. To each of their tips, let a sixth-part quadrant be attached, and let the outermost points of the lines drawn from the center be marked where they strike the surface of the quadrant. Through these points, parallel lines drawn on the shadow-tracking faces will give the hours inscribed on the sides. Truly, all these things are shown better by figures than by many rambling words. Therefore, consult the figure...

## Problem IV.
### *To describe an eagle sundial.*

<margin>Illustration IX</margin>
In wood, or some other material, let the Imperial Eagle be shaped, which then—as was done in the preceding figure—having been cut out, provides faces or sides for inscribing the hours. The order or inscription of hours is the same in all of them; the position also, as in the preceding examples, is the same in the plane of the equinoctial; for the shadows of the tips falling on the opposite faces will show the hours. In the heart of the Eagle, we have depicted a universal sundial of the hours from sunrise and sunset; its <term>style</term> <note>original: "stylus"; the gnomon or pointer of a sundial</note> at the center, or point X, will show the hours perpendicularly.

## Problem VI.
### *To construct a universal ring sundial.*

Let there be a ring of any material of the width of a half-finger, AEFG, and let it have a <term>crena</term> <note>a notch or aperture</note> at point A; from which a <term>dodecamorius</term> <note>original: "quadrans BDC dodecamorius"; a quadrant divided into twelve parts</note> quadrant BDC shall first be described on the plane, as you see: and lines being drawn from the center A through the points of division, they will cut the circumference of the ring at points through which parallels drawn according to the width of the ring will form the sought-after sundial; the ring shall be raised according to the plane of the equator, and the notch shall correspond to the meridian: for the Sun, penetrating the notch, will show the sought-after hours in the shaded part of the circle.

# CHAPTER II.
## On Portable Universal Sundials.

### Problem VII.
### To prepare a gnomonic globe, in which a movable stylus may demonstrate the theory of the entire first mover. <note>The "first mover" (primum mobile) in Renaissance astronomy refers to the outermost sphere of the heavens which carries all other spheres in its daily rotation from east to west.</note>

### Practical Exercise I.
#### The first drafting of the globe.

---

<margin>Illustration X.</margin>
**F**irst, let a globe be made as round as possible, from whatever material you choose. Let its primary vertical circle be DBE C, its meridian BAC, and its horizon DAE; divide this horizon into 360 parts. If, therefore, you draw circles through each point or degree marked on the horizon by the aforementioned method—which will be done if you press points onto the surface using a rule that is movable at the pole and applied to the arc AE—and if all these circles intersect at the poles B and C, they will provide you with the <term>Azimuths</term> <note>original: "Azymutha"; vertical circles passing through the zenith and nadir, used to measure horizontal direction.</note> inscribed on the globe. You shall inscribe the <term>Almucantars</term> <note>original: "Almucantaras"; circles of the celestial sphere parallel to the horizon, used to measure the altitude of a celestial body.</note> as follows:

<margin>The first method using the wonderful quadrant, page 336.</margin>
Secondly, take the length of the stylus BV, or BS; determine this on the AC side of the "wonderful quadrant." <note>The "wonderful quadrant" (*quadrans mirificus*) was a specialized calculating tool invented by Kircher for solving spherical trigonometry problems geometrically.</note> Then, having drawn a line perpendicular to CA from point A, determine the length of the globe's semi-diameter upon it. Afterward, draw a circle through point A touching the line at A, which represents the surface of the globe; lines drawn from C will represent rays falling from the tip of the stylus V onto the surface of the globe. See, therefore, at which points on the wonderful quadrant the lines drawn from C intersect the arc BA; for these points, transferred from pole B of the globe onto either quadrant BE or BD, will give the points through which the circles drawn from the same pole B will provide the Almucantars.

<margin>The second method using the quadrant V-BE of the 1st figure of this Illustration.</margin>
However, if anyone should weary of this labor, he may describe the said Almucantars more briefly by this clever device: draw a line from E, as shown in the 1st figure of Illustration 9, perpendicular to the tip of the stylus V. From this, if you arrange lines from the center V through the degrees of a quadrant divided into 90 parts, the touching points of the circles drawn will give the desired Almucantars. Once these have been correctly established, first inscribe the astronomical hours on it by this art: take the Almucantar-Azimuth table provided in the preceding sections for the hours from noon and midnight. See in which Azimuth and Almucantar the Sun is located at the 12th hour when the Sun occupies <note>original: "Sole ♋ occupante"; meaning the Sun is in the zodiac sign of Cancer, the Summer Solstice.</note> Cancer; you will find here at Rome it is 90 degrees and 71 degrees 30 minutes. The known meridian BC will represent the former; while the Almucantar of 71 degrees 30 minutes described on it will give the point for 12 o'clock when the Sun is in Cancer. Likewise, look in the table for the common intersection of the Azimuth and Almucantar for the 1st and 11th hours, which you will find by calculating 51 degrees 20 minutes from point A of the meridian on both sides, and 69 degrees 30 minutes from B on the same; you will then have the desired points for the said hours. Proceed in no different a manner for investigating the points of the remaining hours. You shall inscribe the <term>Babylonian hours</term>, <term>Italian hours</term>, and <term>ancient hours</term> <note>Kircher refers to different systems of timekeeping: Babylonian hours started at sunrise, Italian hours at sunset, and ancient "unequal" hours divided daylight into 12 parts regardless of season.</note> by exactly the same artifice, using the specialized tables placed in the preceding pages. For through the individual points of the hours when the Sun is in the Tropics, curves drawn with a flexible piece of parchment or some other device will give the Tropics; the points of the hours in the Tropics of the same type, joined by straight lines, will give the desired hour lines. But if you apply a flexible rule to pole B, which represents a movable quadrant on the globe, and transfer onto it the points of the sections of the arc BA of the wonderful quadrant (or of quadrant BVE), you will be able to perform all the said operations with almost no effort, without any other division of Azimuths and Almucantars being made on the globe, using only the horizon B divided into 360 parts. This is done by placing this movable quadrant over a given Azimuth and counting the Almucantars on that same Azimuth, starting from the pole of the horizon B. For the limits of the counting will give the points of the desired hours without difficulty.

### Use of the Gnomonic Spherical Astrolabe.

**T**he stylus SB should have a foot attached at right angles at B, which foot you shall insert into the pole of the globe so that it can be moved within it like an axis in whatever direction you please; however, the line of the stylus must always touch the globe at point B. The stylus can also be made <term>two-armed</term> <note>original: "διβραχίων"; a Greek term meaning having two arms or branches.</note> on the other side, consisting of a double arm such as VS, so that you may then use <margin>Position of the stylus.</margin> either one. Therefore, having placed the stylus in the movable pole and positioned the globe so that the circle BAC matches the meridian of your region: once this is done, while the Sun is shining, rotate the stylus here and there until its shadow makes no intersection with any vertical circle—that is, it is straight relative to the globe. In this position, its tip will show at a single glance on the surface of the globe the time in any hour system, and on any circle in which the Sun is actually positioned.

# The Great Art, Book VI. Part II of Proteus.

...if you have fixed a movable <term>stylus</term> <note>The rod or pin of a sundial that casts the shadow; also called a gnomon.</note>, all the things demonstrated on the globe will be shown on the surfaces of the said bodies. But let us declare each one with brief examples.

### Practical Exercise II.

**To inscribe the said things on a conical surface.**

**F**irst, let a cone ABC be given, as is evident in Figure 2, on whose winding surface you wish to describe the hours and other markings. Therefore, given the length of the stylus AS or AN, which should be movable at point A on the axis of the cone, as was said in the preceding section; then, with the help of the preceding table, let the hours be inscribed by this art: let the base of the cone be divided into 360 parts, through which, if you draw straight lines from the point of the apex A, those will give you the <term>Azimuths</term> <note>Vertical circles or lines representing horizontal direction/bearing.</note>. Next, let a quadrant be described from S through point A of the vertex of the cone, through whose rim (divided into 90 degrees) straight lines are drawn to touch the surface of the cone at points; circles drawn through these from A will give the sought-after <term>Almucantars</term> <note>Lines or circles on a dial representing the altitude of the sun above the horizon.</note>. Having described the Almucantars from the previously mentioned tables, you will inscribe the hours and other things on the cone, as was said. This cone, situated toward the four quarters of the world so that Azimuth 90 corresponds to the meridian, and with the movable stylus turned toward the Sun so that the stylus is in the same vertical plane in which the Sun <margin>The method of the gnomon in this shadow-marking art.</margin> actually remains, its tip will show what is sought. However, for the stylus, one can take the figure of any animal at the movable apex—the tip of whose tail or beak (as you see), or even the end of a scepter in a human figure—terminating at the final point of the stylus, as Figure 2 shows.

### Corollary.

<margin>Cylinder XY in Figure 3.</margin> **B**y the exact same reasoning, a cylinder will be described: nor is there any difference, except that in a cone the Azimuths meet at a point; in a cylinder they are equidistant, as appears in Figure 3 marked with the letters XY. All other things are the same; therefore, I have deemed it unnecessary to delineate it with more words.

### Practical Exercise III.

**To inscribe the said things on a pyramid.**

**L**et there be a four-sided pyramid ABCE, as Figure 4 shows, on whose sides it is required to describe an astrolabe. First, let a circle divided into 360 parts be inscribed in its square base, and lines produced from the center to the sides of the square will give the points through which straight lines drawn from the vertex A of the pyramid will assign the Azimuths (moreover, let the first, or 90th Azimuth, represent the meridian line AC). And you shall perform this operation on as many other sides of the pyramid as you like. Therefore, having drawn the Azimuths, let a quadrant divided into 90 degrees be described from S, the apex of the movable stylus; let a thread be drawn from its center S, and with the quadrant placed above Azimuth 90, look in the table of Almucantars for the degrees of the Sun's altitude while it is positioned in the 12 signs; for a thread extended from the center of the quadrant <margin>The practice of the delineation.</margin> through these onto Azimuth 90 will give the points for the 12th hour for all signs. Likewise, let the quadrant attached to the movable stylus be moved over Azimuth 51, and through the appropriate degrees of altitude for the said hour (the Sun being positioned in the individual signs), a thread extended from the center over the found Azimuth will give the points for lines 1 and 11 in the individual signs of the Zodiac. You shall proceed no differently regarding the finding of points for the hours in other Azimuths; once these are found, if you join the points of all the hours pertaining to the parallels of the Sun with curves, those will give you the arcs of the signs: but if you join the points of the parallels belonging to one hour with lines, those will give you the sought-after hour lines. Thus, with the pyramid situated so that the 90th Azimuth is in the meridian plane, the movable stylus—furnished with the form of some animal—turned toward the Sun's Azimuth, will show the sought-after <term>horography</term> <note>The art of constructing sundials or "hour-writing."</note> on the surfaces of the pyramid.

### Practical Exercise IV.

**To inscribe sundials on a prism.**

**L**et there be a prism whose base is SNM, in which an inscribed circle is divided into 360 parts, as you see in Figure 5, and straight lines produced from the center through the points of division will give points on the sides of the base, from which perpendicular and mutually parallel lines drawn will give the Azimuths, the first of which can be assumed either at any angle SNM or in the middle of the sides, such as at Y or V—it is all the same. Here, let the first be assumed at V in the middle of the sides. This being done, let a quadrant OY be described from the apex K of the movable stylus YK, or let one described separately be attached to the stylus YK so that the center of the quadrant matches the apex K of the stylus; and let the quadrant be movable together with the stylus. This being done, by the benefit of the preceding tables, you will inscribe the hours and other things on the sides of the prism, as was said, always moving the quadrant together with the movable stylus over the Azimuth which the table indicates as corresponding to the hours: in the found Azimuth, let the points of the Almucantars be sought with the help of a thread drawn from the center of the quadrant, as we taught how to do before, and you will have a sundial furnished with a single movable stylus. For if you first situate it as in the preceding sections and turn the stylus toward the Sun's Azimuth, it will show the desired things on the planes of the prism.

# Of Portable Sundials.

### Corollary I.

From these things it is clear: given any <term>prism</term> <note>A solid geometric figure whose two ends are similar, equal, and parallel rectilinear figures, and whose sides are parallelograms.</note>, to describe the <term>sundial markings</term> <note>Original Latin: "horolabia."</note> upon it by the stated method, the prism will be more irregular the more sides it has. In tetrahedrons, pentahedrons, hexahedrons, heptahedrons, decahedrons, etc., a circle inscribed in the bases of the prisms and divided into 360 parts will give the points through which lines are drawn perpendicularly and parallel to each other. These will be the <term>Azimuths</term> <note>Vertical circles or lines representing horizontal direction/bearing.</note>, upon which you will inscribe the <term>Almucantars</term> <note>Lines or circles on a dial representing the altitude of the sun above the horizon.</note>, by attaching a quadrant with a movable <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note>, as was done in the preceding sections. By drawing a thread from the center onto the Azimuths according to the table, and marking the solar altitude points corresponding to the hours, the exact same operation is to be applied to the remaining parts until you achieve your goal.

### Corollary II.

It is also clear that the same art of describing the hours can be applied to any given concave bodies.

### Problem VIII.

->To construct a marvelous globe, in which no <term>stylus</term> <note>The rod or pin of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note> is present, yet all the aforesaid things are demonstrated through light in a shaded dial-field.<-

We call this globe "marvelous" because few have been able to comprehend the methods of its construction, even among those who wish to be seen as mathematicians; to many, the matter has seemed a paradox. Indeed, its layout is exactly the same as the globe in the preceding Problem, from which we have derived it; only the stylus differs. You shall make the stylus in this way: Let a solid disc be made of some harder material, three fingers thick, or even thicker depending on the size of the globe (for the thicker it is, the more suited it will be for our task). Its diameter should be the same size as the movable stylus SBV in Figure 1 of the preceding Problem.

<margin>A stylus toothed in the manner of a comb.</margin>
First, you will divide the rim of this disc into 360 degrees. Once the division is finished, use a very fine saw—the kind that craftsmen use for making smaller and more delicate things, constructed from an iron wire—with this saw, I say, you will cut into each degree of the disc's rim (or every two degrees if the degrees are too small). Use such skill that the rim resembles a circular comb with its saw-cuts, and let all the saw-cuts on the outermost circular surface be equidistant. You will then have a stylus suitable for demonstrating the hours and the things inscribed on the globe, as Figure 6 demonstrates. You shall insert this <term>slotted disc</term> <note>Original Latin: "ferratilem orbem," literally a "sawn" or "iron-cut" disc.</note> into the globe so that the axis of the globe also passes through the center of the disc (that is, the center of the disc L coincides with the pole of the globe). The entire disc should touch the pole of the globe—that is, it should be perpendicular to the axis of the globe—and the saw-cut LB or LA should correspond to the meridian, equal to the stylus BV or BS of the globe in Figure 1. The layout of the globe remains the same. Therefore, if you expose this globe, together with its disc fixed immovably at the globe’s pole, to the shining Sun after first orienting it, you will always see three bright lines in the shaded field. The middle one, at its light's extremity, will demonstrate everything that the shadow of the tip of the movable stylus previously showed in the illuminated field. To ensure the whole globe is in shadow, you can surround it with another disc of any size; thus the thing will excite greater wonder.

### Corollary I.

<margin>See figures 7, 8, 9, 10.</margin>
From these things it is clear that if you place this slotted disc upon the cone QRS in Figure 7, the pyramid TVX in Figure 8, the cylinder GHIK in Figure 9, the cube ABYZ in Figure 10, or a prism of any number of sides—in which the sundial markings have been inscribed by the previously mentioned method—the immovable slotted disc will demonstrate, by a triple light and not without wonder, all those things which the movable stylus showed by its shadow in the preceding sections. We have not wished to extend the practical instruction further here, as we believe the wise Reader will easily perceive all instruction from the provided figures themselves.

### Corollary II.

If, however, you wish for the slotted disc to be movable, a single notch assigned for showing the hours will suffice. For if you turn this notch directly toward the Sun's Azimuth, the extremity of the light will show the desired things. From this also result wonderful things which we pass over in silence, lest we be overwhelmed by a multitude of inventions.

### Corollary III.

<margin>A slotted board can be of any shape.</margin>
If, instead of slotted discs, you attach a square board, or a triangle, or one of any number of sides cut like a comb, and align our quadrant with each of the slits or notches in such a way that the side of the quadrant corresponds to the notch and its center to the end of the notch; and then work according to the Almucantar-Azimuth table, you will see certain wonderful spectacles created in the hour lines and the solar parallels. Thus, by this artifice, it is possible to twist the said lines into any shape, and there will be as many different styli as there are Azimuths. But it seemed best only to hint at the mystery, so that we might leave the curious reader matter upon which to exercise his ingenuity. Nevertheless, we add some examples of hour lines transformed into the figures of animals, lest the matter...

## Problem IX.

*A paradoxical gnomonic problem, proposed to all Mathematical Horologists.*

To construct a <term>Horoscopium</term> <note>In this context, a device for telling the hour, not a modern astrological chart.</note> without a stylus, without a fixed plane, and without the appearance of lines, within a confused heap of infinite surfaces and various bodies placed at random. This is done with such ingenuity that it can still demonstrate the hours certainly and exactly according to the teaching of the <term>Astrolabe</term> <note>A portable medieval instrument used for astronomical measurements and telling time.</note>. The eye itself will perform the function of the stylus, yet will be stable in no single place. This is a certain matter, and has been reduced to practice by me more than once, to the wonder of those watching.

## Problem X.

*Given any image, to describe all types of hours upon it using an observation instrument.*

Let any mass of irregular bodies, or images of any things, be placed upon our <term>Tireticum</term> <note>Original: "Tireticum." A specific mechanical drawing instrument described by Kircher earlier in the work for transferring coordinates from one surface to another.</note> instrument (the use of which was handed down above on page 367). For example, let it be the following stellar system; let the tips of the stars AB serve in place of styli, showing the hours on the underlying plane of the circle VX. Let the teeth be within the gear-work; these, projecting into the octagon placed beneath the circle, and then the tips of the starry body GO, DE, FH, IK, LM, shall demonstrate the hours on the planes opposite

<margin>Practice of the drawing.</margin>
to them. You shall inscribe them on the said surfaces in this manner: Having placed the given body upon the horographic table <note>A specialized table for drawing sundial lines.</note> of the observation instrument and the prototype sundial, let it be fitted in its own place, as has often been said in the preceding sections. Then, let the system be rotated together with the prototype sundial with such industry that while the stylus touches the individual points of the hours in the <term>tropics</term> <note>The lines on a sundial representing the sun's path at the summer and winter solstices.</note>, at the same time the ends of the shadows—which the tips of the starry body AB, G, O, I, D, F, H, I, K, L, M make on the subject planes—are marked, with the hour numbers added. For if you draw straight lines through the points of the same hours, you will have the hours sought; furthermore, the curved points of the individual hours found in the tropics, when joined, will give the tropics on the said planes. One must reason no differently concerning other planes. This same body can also be described geometrically through the practices handed down in the preceding <term>Pragmatias</term> <note>Kircher uses this term to mean "practical exercises" or "instructional procedures."</note>.

### Corollary I.

From this it follows that statues and images fashioned from any material whatever can be inscribed in a similar way, by taking the extremities of the ears, horns, tails, or other parts of the image as the tip of the indicator.

### Corollary II.

There is no body or figure so irregular that the hours cannot be inscribed upon it by this method faster than it can be said. However, leaving all these things to the industry of the curious reader, let us turn our pen to other matters.

# CHAPTER III.

->*On portable sundials of various forms, to be constructed from solar altitude tables by the use of shadows, both straight and turned.*<-

<image-desc>An ornate initial woodcut letter 'V' depicting a landscape with classical architecture and a reclining figure.</image-desc>

I COME to another way of drawing <term>horoscopia</term> <note>devices for telling time</note> no less varied than the preceding one: by the aid of which a desired <term>horolabium</term> <note>Literally "hour-taker," another term for a sundial or time-measuring device.</note> shall be fashioned from the altitude of the Sun and from shadows both straight and turned. There is a nearly infinite variety and multitude of these: some by the help of a plumb line equipped with a bead; some by the shadow of a fixed stylus performing the function of a plumb line; others indeed by a stylus, but a movable one that mimics the setting and receding of the Sun. Some even mark the hours by light itself in a shaded field. All of these, however, find their reasons for construction from the altitudes of the Sun. Therefore, he who has perfectly penetrated the logic of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The shadow-casting part of a sundial.</note> and the shadow in different planes will certainly not be able to be ignorant of the logic of all the things to be proposed here. Let us come to the matter.

# Practice II.
## Second method without a gem, using only a plumb line.

Let ABC be an isosceles right-angled triangle in the form you see in the 2nd figure of the Illustration. Let the space EC of the whole side be divided into 12 parts as before, and the parallels drawn to the base BC (which should be divided into 90 degrees, which will happen if from the center you determine the degrees on the base through each degree of the quadrant BC with the plumb line extended) will represent the parallels of the signs, while the dotted lines will represent the parallels of the midpoints of the signs. In this, therefore, if you write the hours with the help of the Sun's altitudes, as you did in the previous section, you will have the desired hour-indicator <note>original: "horodicticum".</note>, whose hours are shown here by straight lines. Its use is this: through the sights attached to side AB, once light is admitted, the thread at the common point of intersection of the hour line and the parallel will show the desired hour without a gem.

# Practice III.
## To inscribe Italian hours on a quadrant.

Let quadrant ABC be made, equipped as before with tropics and the equator; then take the table of solar altitudes for Italian hours <note>Italian hours were a system where the day began at sunset (24:00).</note>, which you will extract for yourself from the <term>Almucantar</term>-Azimuth <note>A coordinate system used to find the height and compass direction of a celestial body.</note> table proposed on page 289: or if you grow weary of this labor, the table proposed in Problem X can be of use to you. From this, therefore, you will mark the hour points on the tropics and the equinoctial of the quadrant as before, beginning from the 24th hour in reverse order. For if you draw an arc through each of the three points, you will have the Italian hours inscribed on the quadrant. We are brief because we are revisiting things that are almost common knowledge.

### Use of the Instrument.

<margin>How an unknown polar altitude may be found.</margin>
**T**o determine the hour of the day, turn the **pastoral staff** <term>pastoral staff (pedum): a curved, pivoting arm used to set the instrument for a specific latitude or date</term> attached to pole B, so that its extremity E touches the degree and sign of the Sun in the radiant Zodiac LN. Once this is done, move the cursor T by its prominent tooth above the degree of latitude on the staff, and the **gem** <note>original: "gemma"; a sliding bead or marker on the plumb line</note> of the thread above the degree of the Sun in the Zodiac RP; then, with the instrument tilted, turn the **sighting holes** <term>sighting holes (dioptra): small apertures through which sunlight or stars are viewed</term> X and Y toward the Sun, until the ray corresponds to both holes X and Y—which in our instrument represent the head and tail of the **Dove**—and the gem will show the sought hour. With this same instrument, you will have the sunrise and sunset if you let the thread hang freely so that it is parallel to the hour lines; for the hour which it marks on the rim will give the hour of rising and setting. You will find the unknown altitude of the pole for any place if you first have a known hour: for if you move the cursor back and forth on the staff until the gem demonstrates the current known hour, the degree which the cursor points to will give the altitude of the pole, or the latitude of the region sought. Note, however, that the cursor—especially if it is moved to a sign near the tropics—should be moved one or two degrees higher; and thus you will achieve the desired time without any notable error. The reason for this is that the tilted staff recedes somewhat from the parallels of the scale of latitudes; however, this recession almost never exceeds 2 degrees. **Oronce Fine** <note>original: "Orontius Finæus" (1494–1555), a famous French mathematician and cartographer</note> once fell into this **mathematical error** <term>paralogism (paralogismus): a piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning, here referring to a geometric miscalculation</term>; concerning this, see his small works on sundials.

## Practical Exercise V.
### To inscribe ancient hours on a quadrant.

<margin>Use of the quadrant of ancient hours.</margin>
**L**et a quadrant ABC be made, as appears in Figure 5, in which **ancient hours** <note>original: "antiquæ horæ"; also called "unequal hours," these divided the period from sunrise to sunset into 12 equal parts, meaning the length of an hour changed with the seasons</note> are to be inscribed: proceed as follows. Let the rim BMC of the quadrant be made somewhat wide, so that the Zodiac can be inscribed in the same manner as will be described shortly; once this is done, extending the side AC or AB of the quadrant indefinitely, let the arc of the quadrant BC be divided into 6 equal parts, which should be determined by hidden lines from the center A. Then you will divide each hidden line in two and draw perpendiculars to the points of division, which, where they cut line AC or AB, will leave centers from which arcs drawn through the center A of the quadrant will give the sought unequal hours. You will construct the Zodiac thus: let all the noon altitudes of the Sun be numbered from B toward C on the rim of the quadrant, through which, if you draw straight lines from the center, they will distinguish the Zodiac, as you see. The said Zodiac could also be made within the width of a movable rim; for by this industrious method it could easily be accommodated to any altitudes of the pole. The use of the sundial is this: Let the thread, equipped with its gem, be brought down from center A above the degree of the Sun in the Zodiac; let the gem then be moved precisely to the 6th unequal hour line (which is precisely 12 o'clock astronomically, or noon); this done, let the ray of the Sun enter through the sighting vanes, and the gem will show the sought unequal hour.

## Practical Exercise VI.
### To describe sundials on a vertical plane.

**L**et a square ABCD be made, whose side AB is divided into 12 equal parts, whose dotted lines demonstrate the middle parallels of the signs. Then, starting from the parallel of **Cancer** ♋ and ♋ AC, and the outer lines of the square BD, let all the points of the hours be designated in them, according to the order placed in the table of Solar altitudes with the help of quadrant STV. Then all the points of the hours in the parallel of **Gemini** ♊, or **Sagittarius** ♐ on both sides, and so on for the rest: with the points determined in this way, you will join the individual points of those same hours with curved lines, and you will have a perfect sundial. However, so that you may determine the points more conveniently; attach a quadrant STV divided into 90 parts to side TD, whose side TS denotes the size of the **style** <term>style (stylus): the shadow-casting pin or blade of a sundial</term>, while the lines drawn from S to side BD denote the solar rays. If, therefore, you transfer the spaces of the shadows of style AC intercepted from point T on line TD into the parallels of the Sun according to the table, you will finally reach your goal, placing a movable style perpendicularly above line AB at the point or degree of the Sun's parallel. For if you turn the small square together with the style until the shadow falls on the parallel of the Sun, its extremity will give you the sought hour: and these will be "turned" shadows of the style. If, however, you wish the hours to be shown to you by the same plate in a horizontal position, you will complete the aforementioned drawing with the help of the altitude of **straight shadows** <term>straight shadows (umbræ rectæ): a term from medieval trigonometry referring to shadows cast on a horizontal plane</term>, taking the outer sides AC and BD for the lines of **Cancer** ♋, but the middle line NM for the line of **Aries** ♈, and then proceed as before, and you will have a **shadow-measuring device** <term>sciathericum: a general term for an instrument that tells time by shadows, such as a sundial</term> demonstrating the hours on a horizontal plane. But since these things are very easy, I shall by no means linger on them.

Thus, when the Sun is passing through Taurus ♉, Gemini ♊, Cancer ♋, or Leo ♌, the gnomon will be fixed in the center point of side CD; when the Sun is in Capricorn ♑ and Aquarius ♒, the gnomon is placed in the center point of side DT, and so on for the others, as the figure shows.

### Use.

Let the knife be fixed upon a table, or even held in the hand by its blade, with such skill that the handle is perpendicular to the horizon. The shadow of the gnomon, fixed in the location corresponding to the Sun's position and parallel to the lines CH, DI, EK, FL, and GM, will show the desired hours on the handle when it is held facing the Sun.

## Practice VIII.
### To describe the same lines in a concave quadrant.

Let a solid, hollowed-out quadrant be made in the form you see in Figure 1, the width of which is CD. On its quadrantal surface CD, EF, first draw 12 equidistant lines representing the parallels of the Sun and the midpoints of the signs. This is done as follows: with diameter CD, describe a circle divided into 12 parts. If you join any two points equally distant from points C and D with straight lines, they will cut the line CD at points through which lines drawn parallel to the sides CE and DF will give the sought parallels. Then, other transverse parallels drawn from each degree will intersect the parallels at right angles. If, therefore, you join the points corresponding to the same hour on this quadrantal surface using a table of solar altitudes, you will have a **horoscope** <note>original: "horoscopium"; here referring to a map of the hours, not a modern astrological chart</note> inscribed in a concave quadrant, as Figure 1 shows. However, since it is difficult to complete the drawing on a concave surface, you may first project the said quadrantal surface onto a flat plane (as we taught on page 324) and, once drawn, bend it back into the quadrant. This will give you the desired sundial, in which AB will act as the gnomon. If you expose the quadrant to the Sun so that the transverse shadow of the gnomon AB is parallel to the lines of the altitude degrees in the concave part, the intersection of the shadow line and the Sun's parallel will give you the sought hour. Indeed, the entire shadow on the concave rim will also always infallibly demonstrate the altitude of the Sun.

## Problem XII.
### To describe the same things with a fixed gnomon on horizontal and vertical planes, with the hour lines contracted into various figures of images.

## Practice I.
### To describe a Tortoise-shaped Sundial.

Let a circle of any size be made and divided into 12 equal parts, as Figure 3 shows, and the lines drawn from the center will represent the 12 lines of the signs. This having been done, you will determine all the hour points from the center N on the line of Aries ♈ using a table of **reversed shadows** <note>original: "umbras versas"; a trigonometric term relating to the horizontal component of a shadow</note> of the solar altitudes. Then, determine the same points from N on the parallel of Taurus ♉, then the same on the parallel of Gemini ♊, and so on for the rest. If you draw curves through each of these points on the same lines, those lines will be contracted into the shape of a tortoise—which is what was required. To determine the points on the lines of the signs more easily, first assume a certain length for the gnomon, such as CA for example. From its tip C, describe a quadrant divided into 90 parts; for straight lines drawn from its center C to the line AB will provide a scale which, when applied to the parallels or transferred with a compass, will determine the hour points on said parallels.

<margin>The clock-tortoise.</margin>
The use of this instrument is as follows: to find the hour, turn the hanging disk toward the Sun from the opposite degree of the Sun, and the end of the gnomon on the line of the sign in which the Sun actually exists will show the hour sought. For example, if the Sun is in the 1st degree of Cancer ♋, you turn the disk (suspended from the 1st degree of Cancer ♋) toward the Sun so that the gnomon falls directly onto its parallel, and you will have what you seek. Thus, the tortoise, an earthly animal, earns celestial honors, being brought into the Zodiac with the other animals. If, however, you wish to restore it to its former condition—that is, to the horizon, which it is accustomed to graze with its slow-moving step—inscribe it on a horizontal plane using **upright shadows** <note>original: "umbras rectas"; the vertical component of a shadow</note> of solar altitudes, and you will achieve your desire. For when turned toward the Sun so that the gnomon falls on the Sun's parallel (which it actually describes that day), the end of the shadow will exhibit the result. By this same industry, you may draw hour lines in the shape of bees, spiders, and similar animals.

## Corollary I.

From this it is clear: if the parallels have an equal division, the hour lines will also obtain a similar form. If they are unequal, they will take diverse forms, with differences as great as the inequality of the parallels. Secondly, it is clear that the order of the signs of the Zodiac

<margin>Various transformations of images.</margin>
does not necessarily have to be preserved, but can be transposed for the purpose of figuring different animals, according to whether the animal to be formed requires a shorter or longer shadow. But all these things I leave to the industry of the curious reader; for the infinite multitude and variety of inventions that occur in this place could be further brought forth...

### Corollary II.

**Hence** it is clear how one and the same <term>stylus</term><note>The rod or pin that casts the shadow.</note> on a cylindrical vessel can determine the hours through both the direct and inverse shadow.

### Corollary III.

<margin>An excellent method for describing hours on flat tablets.</margin>
**It follows** finally how the hours usually depicted on vertical cylinders could be described on flat tablets with the stylus remaining fixed in the middle or at the side: provided, of course, that for the <term>parallel</term><note>A line on the dial representing the Sun's path on a specific day of the year.</note> of that sign in which the stylus is fixed, you take a proportional line from which the points of the hours are transferred. Then, for the next parallel, take another proportional line which is as far from the center of the quadrant as the tip of the stylus is from that same next parallel. This will be AF, or the length of the stylus in Figure 7, above line F, and EA above line E, and so on—and this is done with a great economy of construction. For it will cause the distances of the hours on the parallel to be wider, and consequently, the hours will be denoted more exactly.

## Practical Exercise II.

->Another way to scribe the hours on the rim of a portable orb.<-

3. From M, with the distance MF or MH, let a semicircle be made, which you shall distribute into 6 equal parts; for if you describe semicircles through each of these divisions which terminate in GI on the opposite side of the diameter, you will have the Zodiac described.

You shall delineate the hour lines by this industry: from the table applied here for the three signs Cancer ♋, Aries ♈, and Capricorn ♑, compute the numbers corresponding to the hours in the three lines of the signs GSI; for a curve drawn through each of the three points will give the sought hour-line.

## Practical Exercise III.

->To describe another kind of quadrant demonstrating all types of hours.<-

**Here** we have added another kind of quadrant arranged in a square, which is general and accommodated to all types of hours. The radiant Zodiac is EGH; the scale of the latitude of regions is AC, IK. Let its delineation be thus: from point E, let a semicircle be described divided into two quadrants, and from E through the degrees of each quadrant, let hidden lines be drawn to lines AC and IK; the said lines will be cut into a scale of the latitude of regions, as the figure shows. Moreover, the lines EG, GH, and EH, drawn through 23 degrees and 30 minutes, will determine the radiant Zodiac; other manifest lines, at whose extremities perpendiculars are drawn to the base of the figure CD, will give the hours from noon and midnight, to which the hours from sunrise and sunset correspond a little lower down. You will have the lines of the signs in the radiant Zodiac if you divide the semicircle drawn from E with the interval XE into 12 equal parts; for through the points equally distant from X, straight lines drawn as far as lines EG and EH will give the sought spaces of the signs. ### Problem XIII.

*To describe an ingenious cylinder that demonstrates what hour it is in any location.*

<margin>Illustration XIII.</margin>
**L**et there be two cylinders, A and B, of which the former is hollow and the latter solid; however, in such a way that this one [B], inserted into cylinder A, may be rotated at the maker's discretion. On cylinder A, the hours should be described on the cylindrical surface (previously projected onto a flat plane) in the manner commonly used everywhere by <term>gnomonists</term><note>Specialists in the design and construction of sundials.</note>. First, count 60 degrees from D on both sides in a circle, and let perpendicular lines be drawn from the endpoints to the base. Again, let 8 degrees be counted from D on both sides, and with straight lines drawn downwards, let the entire space enclosed by these two lines be cut out. This having been done, divide one of these four perpendiculars into 24 equal parts: through which you shall draw arcs, within whose spaces you shall write the names of locations, in the order evident in Figure 1. Furthermore, you will divide the remaining part of the circle of the cylinder MV into six equal parts: and with perpendiculars drawn to the base, you will have the lines of the zodiac signs, as Figure 3 teaches. In these, according to the given size of the <term>stylus</term><note>The shadow-casting rod or pin.</note> MN, you will determine the points of the hours of the Sun's altitudes with the help of the table already often cited: for through the determined points of those same hours, the drawn curves will give the hours; and the side MO will be the scale of the Sun’s altitudes. Therefore, having described the hour lines in the outermost cylinder VMO in the said manner, you will divide the upper circle of cylinder B into 24 equal parts, with perpendiculars drawn through them to the base. Again, with any of these perpendiculars divided into 24 parts, you will draw circles through them, and little compartments <note>original: "loculamenta"</note> will be made, within which you shall write the numbers of the hours, in the order which follows here; so that the morning hours are written in red, and the afternoon hours in black or another color. Let the spaces of the circles be equal to the spaces inscribed for the position of locations on the surface of cylinder ZAHK. This also having been completed, you will insert cylinder B into the hollow cylinder A, and you will have the finished cylinder. Its use is this:

<margin>Use of the cylinder.</margin>
With the stylus MN moved forward over the line of the Sun's parallel, turn it toward the Sun so that the shadow falls over the lines of the Sun's parallel, and the end of the shadow will give the sought hour. Once this is found—if, for example, it was a morning hour—move the hour written on the upper circle of the inner cylinder until it is above the compartment marked (*ROME*), and immediately the hours shining through the slit AR, corresponding to the other regions, will give the sought hours for the whole world. The matter is so easy that it does not even need further explanation.

*Another way, much easier and more concise.*

**L**et ABCD be the cylinder of the previous base; let a ring EF be made in it, divided into 24 equal parts and marked with the same number of hours. Let the cylindrical surface ABCD be similarly divided into 24 spaces, as you see, in which, as in the preceding, the names of the regions are inscribed. If, therefore, you set the solar hour found on the outermost surface of the cylinder on the moved hour-ring above the space assigned to Rome, the hours on the ring will correspond and consequently align with the spaces of the regions which they touch; you will have, as if in a summary, the corresponding hours for every single region in the whole world. But all these things can be seen even more easily from the following table, which will also serve for drawing the preceding cylinder. See the use of the table on the following page.

# UNIVERSAL TIME-CHART
<note>original: "Horarium Catholicum"</note>

<margin>Length of the day in the Northern Signs; of the night in the Southern [Signs].</margin>

<image-desc>A large, detailed rectangular grid titled 'HORARIVM CATHOLICVM' (Universal Horarium). The table is structured with a central grid of numbers, flanked by city names on the left and their corresponding regions on the right. Roman numerals are used for morning hours and Arabic numerals for afternoon hours.</image-desc>

-> Morning hours <note>original: "Ante meridiem"</note> <- -> Afternoon/Evening hours <note>original: "Post meridiem"</note> <-

<margin>Usage.</margin>
**S**eek the current hour—whether morning or afternoon—at the top of the table; then find the region or city at the side, and the intersecting cell will show the hour in that region. For example <note>original: "Verbi gratia"</note>, if it is 1 o'clock in the afternoon here in Rome, and you wish to know what hour it is in Goa in India; follow the column for 1 p.m. at the top straight down until you reach the row corresponding to Goa at the side; there you will find the desired hour: 6. Likewise, in Bengal it will be 7; in Xi'an 8; in Manila 9; in Kyoto, Japan 10; and so on for the rest. Note that the Roman numerals I, II, III, IV, etc., indicate hours before noon [AM]; while the Arabic numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, etc., signify hours after noon [PM].

# Book VI of the Great Art. Part III of the Proteus.

## Explanation and Use of the Universal Timepiece.

We have placed on the Cylinder a universal figure of the hours, through which everything pertaining to the measurement of time is found faster than a word can be spoken. Its use is as follows.

First, when the Sun is in the Northern signs <note>The zodiac signs of the spring and summer (Aries through Virgo), when the sun is north of the celestial equator.</note>—that is, from the 21st of March until the 24th of September—take the degree of the <term>altitude of the pole</term> <note>This refers to the latitude of the observer's location.</note> on the left-hand side. If the specific degree is not marked, it must be taken between the two nearest degrees; for any space between two adjacent degrees should be understood as divided into three degrees. A straight line drawn from that degree to the signs of ♈ <note>Aries</note> and ♎ <note>Libra</note> will serve you at that latitude for the Northern signs. However, the line corresponding to this on the right-hand side is to be used for the Southern signs—that is, from the 24th of September until the 21st of March. Furthermore, the beginning of the line on the left near the degree of the pole's altitude is assigned to the sign of ♋ <note>Cancer</note>; the next point to the beginning of ♊ <note>Gemini</note> and ♌ <note>Leo</note>; the following point to the beginning of ♉ <note>Taurus</note> and ♍ <note>Virgo</note>; and finally, the point where all lines drawn from the pole's altitudes meet belongs to the beginning of ♈ <note>Aries</note> and ♎ <note>Libra</note>. Conversely, the beginning of the line on the right near the pole's altitude is the beginning of ♑ <note>Capricorn</note>; the following point is the beginning of ♒ <note>Aquarius</note> and ♐ <note>Sagittarius</note>; and the next point is the beginning of ♓ <note>Pisces</note> and ♏ <note>Scorpio</note>. Any space on the line between two points should be understood as divided into 30 degrees.

Next, if you draw a line from the Sun's position noted on the proposed latitude line, parallel to the straight lines extending from left to right—which a thin thread stretched from the Sun's position to the opposite position of the Sun will show you—this parallel line will indicate the length of the day and night, and the hour of sunrise and sunset in <term>Italian</term> and <term>Babylonian hours</term>, <margin>Finding the sunrise, sunset, and the length of days and nights.</margin> as indicated by the numbers assigned to the lines for the length of day and night and sunrise and sunset. But if you descend straight down from the hour of sunrise and sunset in the Italian and Babylonian hours (provided you do not take the same hour on the outermost lines near the pole's altitudes), you will find on the bottom-most line of hours from noon and midnight the hours of sunrise and sunset in <term>Astronomical hours</term>, <note>Astronomical hours are the 24-hour cycle starting at midnight or noon, much like modern timekeeping, as opposed to systems that start at sunset (Italian) or sunrise (Babylonian).</note> which are used in Germany, France, and Spain. For example: At a latitude of 42 degrees, which is roughly that of Rome, if you draw a parallel from 42 degrees toward the right, you will find that when the Sun is at the beginning of ♋ <note>the Summer Solstice</note>, the length of the day is 15 hours and a little more; the night is a little less than 9 hours. Sunrise in Italian hours is a little before the 9th hour; in Babylonian hours, however, sunset is a little after the 15th hour. And if you descend straight down from the hour of sunrise and sunset, you will find the Sun rises a little before 4:30 AM (from midnight) and sets a little after 7:30 PM (from noon). You will find these values not just in one place, but in several, as indicated by the numbers for sunrise and sunset marked in various places. When the Sun is at the beginning of ♊ or ♌, you will find the day contains almost 14 3/5 hours—that is, 14 hours and 36 minutes. The night is almost 9 2/5 hours—that is, 9 hours and 24 minutes, and so on. You proceed in the same way for the Southern signs and for any other latitude.

<margin>Determining the hour of noon in any kind of hour system.</margin> Third, if you ascend straight up from the 12th hour of noon, which bisects the bottom side, as far as that parallel line which we said was to be drawn through the pole's altitude, and from there ascend to the left along the line parallel to the straight lines forming the <term>Rhombuses</term>, you will land at the top of the table on the hour of noon and midnight in Italian hours when the Sun is staying in the Southern signs. But on the contrary, if you ascend to the left, you will land on the hour of noon and midnight in Babylonian hours when the Sun occupies the Southern signs; but to the right on the hour of noon and midnight in the same Babylonian hours when the Sun runs through the Northern signs; provided that you assign the daytime hours from sunrise and sunset to noon, and the nocturnal hours to midnight. For example: At the same altitude of 42 degrees, with the Sun at the beginning of ♋, if you ascend straight up from the 12th hour on the bottom side, you must stop a little below the transverse line drawn for the 15th and 9th hour. For a little below this line, the parallel line drawn through 42 degrees is extended. To the left, therefore, you will find at the top almost the 16 1/2 hour of noon, and almost the 4 1/2 hour of midnight in Italian hours; to the right, however, you will find a little more than the 7 1/2 hour of noon, and a little more than the 19 1/2 hour of midnight in Babylonian hours. But with the Sun being at the beginning of ♑ <note>the Winter Solstice</note>, you will find to the left that 4 1/2 hours makes noon, and almost 16 1/2 hours makes midnight in Babylonian hours; to the right, however, you will find a little more than the 19 1/2 hour for noon, and a little more than the 7 1/2 hour for midnight in Italian hours.

Fourth, you will find in the same way which Italian, Babylonian, or unequal hour <note>Unequal or "Temporal" hours divided the daylight and darkness into 12 hours each, meaning an hour's length changed depending on the season.</note> corresponds to any Astronomical hour, by taking the hours from midnight in the first half of the bottom line, and the hours from noon in the second half. That is, if you ascend straight up from the given astronomical hour, then go left or right, as we said regarding the hour of noon and midnight. But when, in Astronomical hours after noon, after the straight ascent as far as the parallel drawn through the Sun's degree on the latitude line, it is not possible to proceed to the left or right, the given Astronomical hour must be taken in the first half of the bottom line,

...lines, and it must be carefully observed which hours from sunrise or sunset are nocturnal at the top of the table. Furthermore, the end of the <term>right ascension</term> <note>The position of a celestial body measured along the celestial equator.</note> will indicate the corresponding <term>unequal hour</term> <note>Also known as "seasonal hours," these divide the period of daylight and the period of darkness into 12 hours each, meaning the length of an "hour" changes depending on the season.</note> between the spaces marked with thicker lines, ending at the top and bottom lines of the table, or between spaces distinguished by dotted lines, ending between the top line of the table and the midpoint of the bottom line. The former are the diurnal unequal hours of the Northern signs and the nocturnal of the Southern; the latter are the diurnal of the Southern signs and the nocturnal of the Northern. But if the right ascension from a given <term>Astronomical hour</term> <note>Standard hours of equal length, counted from noon or midnight.</note> after noon falls outside the unequal hours as far as the aforementioned parallel, a similar hour must also be taken in the first half of the bottom line. 

**For example:** At a pole altitude of 42 degrees <note>Roughly the latitude of Rome or Chicago.</note>, with the Sun at the beginning of Cancer, you will find that 10:30 from midnight corresponds to nearly the 15th Italian hour, and slightly more than the 6th Babylonian hour; and finally, nearly the 4 1/2 unequal hour. Conversely, from a known Italian, Babylonian, or unequal hour, you will find the corresponding Astronomical hour if you proceed in the opposite manner—namely, either to the right or to the left from the Italian or Babylonian hour—until the said parallel line, and then descend straight down. He who desires more on these matters should consult the Table of <term>Theodosius Rubeus</term> <note>Theodosio Rossi, an Italian mathematician and astronomer.</note>.

### Problem XIV.

*By what new method Astrolabes can be described on a horizontal plane, with a gnomon erected perpendicularly from the center.*

**I**n *The Magnetic Art* <note>original: "Arte Magnetica"</note>, book 2, part 3, we handed down a method by which every kind of celestial circle is projected onto a plane in such a way that the hours and other things pertaining to hours are perfectly shown by a magnetic needle. This is done by the motion of the meridian under the plane of the Solar <term>Azimuth</term> <note>The horizontal direction of the sun.</note>. In this case, however, the hours will be shown while the meridian remains fixed, and with a <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note> erected perpendicularly from the center of the horizon. Since I know this has been handed down by no one as of yet, I thought the reasoning for its construction should be briefly laid down here, lest we seem to have omitted anything desirable in this great art. 

Let there be made, therefore, an Astronomical Shadow-measuring Timepiece <note>original: "horolabium Sciathericum Astronomicum"</note> ABCD, according to the rules in *The Magnetic Art*, book 2, part 3, problem 4, in which the meridian line is AE, and the horizon is LVSXRM. In this timepiece, a magnetic needle will show the hour if you turn it exposed to the Sun above a horizontal plane until the meridian AE passes precisely under the plane of the Solar Azimuth. This will be achieved by the shadow of a very fine thread extended over a glass cover and under the same plane of the meridian; for while the shadow of the said thread touches the meridian, the magnetic needle will show the desired hour at the intersection point of the Solar parallel. But if you desire the hour without moving the meridian in the same timepiece, you shall operate thus: let a gnomon of any size be erected from the center of the figure; for its shadow on the timepiece—having been previously situated magnetically toward the four parts of the world—will show the requested hour at that point where it cuts the parallel of the Sun. It shall be so situated that the AE part of the meridian faces South, and FB faces North; which is to be noted above all. By this art, you will describe all the doctrine of the <term>prime mover</term> <note>The outermost sphere of the heavens in classical astronomy.</note> handed down in *The Magnetic Art* with almost no effort in the said timepiece, using only a perpendicularly erected gnomon.

### Corollary.

**F**rom these things it is clear that if one were to delineate each kind of hour in particular concentric systems—that is, described from the same center—he would have one timepiece that is indeed multiple, distinct, and unconfused, in which one and the same gnomon would demonstrate different doctrines in different concentric spaces. This matter is both profound and brings wonderful pleasure to those who behold it. Hence, I thought this reasoning should be included in Part 1, Chapter 5 of *The Magic of Light and Shadow* <note>original: "Magiæ lucis & umbræ"</note> concerning Magnetic timepieces, where the curious Reader will find the method of construction perfectly handed down along with a figure.

It remains now for us to summarize everything that has been said so far, which will be done when we have explained the Universal Timepiece <note>original: "horarium Catholicum"</note>, which is shown in Figure 4 of Illustration 9.

# THE THIRD PART OF THE DIALING PROTEUS.
## THE MARRIAGE OF GNOMONICS AND PHYSICS, OR
# GNOMONICS
### Physico-astrological.
## PREFACE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' with swirling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
**I**t might rightly seem a **paradox** <note>original: "παράδοξον"</note> to someone that a shadow could be produced which points out the motions of the heavens and the hidden effects of the stars as if with a finger, had not common usage already made it almost commonplace. Therefore, relying on these foundations and attempting something further, we will strive to demonstrate in this work that there is nothing in the nature of things—at least nothing that has some relation to time—which cannot be constantly shown by the movement of Light and Shadow. For this reason, we have thought it not unfitting to call this book "Physico-astrological Gnomonics," since in it the cycles of physical things are so joined with the periods of the stars that the movements of shadow or light, just as they serve as the common measure of time, demonstrate both the movement of the heaven and the generations, deaths, changes, fertility, sterility, qualities, and virtues of natural things depending on this movement with a certain wonderful dexterity.

<margin>What Physico-astrological Gnomonics is.</margin>
Hence, this Physico-astrological Gnomonics is nothing other than the science by which, with the help of a <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow, usually a pin or a blade.</note>, all those physical things that have a connection with the movement of the sky are taught to be demonstrated. To propose this distinctly and clearly, let us begin with:

## CHAPTER I.
### Concerning the Gnomonic Year and its parts.

<margin>Illustration XIV.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring architectural columns and a central figure holding a celestial globe or compass within the letter's frame.</image-desc>
**W**e say that the Gnomonic Year is nothing other than the space which the shadow of some gnomon completes from the meridian point of the tropic back to that same point. We also call this same space the **solar path** <note>original: "ἡλιόδρομον"</note>, or the goal of the solar course. For within this space of the tropics, the Sun, in its perpetual motion, moves, promotes, and brings to ultimate perfection the generations of all <term>sublunary</term> <note>Literally "below the moon"; refers to the earthly realm where things are subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens.</note> things. Within this space, it arranges the four seasons of the year, distributing to each its own duties fit for the preservation of the sublunary world. Within this space, it communicates itself so equally to the entire terrestrial world that there is no nation so remote, no region so hidden from the light, that it does not participate in an equal portion of light.

<margin>The Sun's wonderful power in the world.</margin>
Within this space, it disposes the degrees of heat suitable for each region. Within this, with its attendant the Moon and the other Planets, the secretaries of nature, it decides on the increase and decrease, life and death of every single thing. Within this space, it opens the various armories of Nature in the **twelve-fold division** <note>original: "δωδεκατημόριον"</note> of the signs which they call the Zodiac, as if in twelve palaces, upon which depends the preservation of all things in the universe. But since the said Zodiac is the foundation of the entire solar course, we shall here undertake an exact anatomy of its individual signs, so that the nature, property, and effect of each sign may be better understood.

<margin>The quality and condition of the Zodiac.</margin>
The Zodiac, therefore, is the foundation of all Astronomy, which for this reason the ancients placed in the sphere. For when they observed the Sun moving under it with a perpetual and constant motion, and the planets also wandering under it, never receding more than six degrees from its middle at most; they expressed it like a band twelve degrees wide <note>Referring to the 12 degrees of celestial latitude that define the zodiacal belt.</note> to indicate the boundary of the planets, and placed it in an oblique position between the tropics. Thus it happens that it intersects any horizon at an oblique angle, producing oblique angles and generating the perpetual inconstancy of the rising and setting of the signs, as well as the change and diversity of days and nights. In this also, the Sun, in a wonderful order...

<meta>catchword: order</meta>

<summary>This page introduces "Physico-Astrological Gnomonics," a science that uses the movement of shadows on a sundial to understand not just time, but the Sun's physical and astrological influence on the earthly world. It begins a detailed look at the Gnomonic Year and the role of the Zodiac in regulating nature.</summary>

# Book VI of the Great Art. Part III of Protheus.

The seasons behave differently for them than for us. For when the Sun passes through Aries (♈︎) and Libra (♎︎), according to some, summer is established for them, whereas for us spring and autumn begin. When the Sun holds the tropic of Cancer (♋︎), it is winter for them, while it is summer for us. Thus, they do not strictly have a spring or autumn, but rather, as the Sun recedes furthest from the equator, it is considered winter for them just as it is for us. Unless one prefers to say that while the Sun is in Aries and Libra, all the way to Taurus (♉︎) and Scorpio (♏︎), it is summer for them; from Taurus and Scorpio to Gemini (♊︎) and Sagittarius (♐︎) it is spring and autumn; and finally, from Gemini and Sagittarius to Capricorn (♑︎) and Cancer (♋︎) it is winter—and likewise for the other parallel signs. They can assert this without any error: for in Cusco and Quito, provinces of Peru, they begin the harvest around the equinoxes, which they call the time of summer; the rest of the time, which is somewhat cooler, they call winter. Yet this can by no means be perfectly called winter; for their heat at that time is nearly as great as the summer heat for inhabitants at 46 or 47 degrees of polar elevation <note>The latitude of central Europe, including parts of France and Switzerland</note>, when the Sun is elevated 66 degrees above the horizon at the summer solstice. Nevertheless, I do not doubt that the heat will be somewhat weaker for the peoples at the equator when the Sun is in Libra, due to the nights always being equal to the days; whereas for those in oblique latitudes, it is more intense because of the longer days. Therefore, our "physico-astrological" sundial-making cannot apply to these inhabitants, nor to our <term>Antoeci</term> <note>original: "Antæcis"; people living at the same longitude but opposite latitude</note>, or those peoples occupying the Northern Hemisphere: for when the Sun permeates the southern signs, a completely different and diametrically opposite arrangement of seasons is produced for us. Let these teachings, therefore, be for the inhabitants of the Temperate Zone and those living under an oblique horizon. These things having been established, let us now turn our pen to explaining the powers of the signs.

### The gnomonic Zodiac is, therefore, nothing other than the <term>sun-path</term> <note>original Greek: "ἡλιόδρομον"</note> space enclosed by the tropics, of which much has been said previously. This space measures the motion of the Sun over a year by the shadow of the gnomon, according to those lines of Manilius:

> *But the starry belt shines in its vast circle,*
> *And makes the world remarkable with its veiled light:*
> *Here, ever-burning Phoebus <note>The Sun</note> guides the reins,*
> *And wandering Delia <note>The Moon</note> follows the Sun in her chariot,*
> *And the five stars <note>The planets</note> struggling against the turning world*
> *Perform various dances by the law of nature.*

<margin>The seven-zone belt of the gnomonic year.</margin>
We divide this into the "dwellings" of the twelve signs by seven curved lines, such that the right side always contains the small chambers of the ascending signs, and the left contains those of the descending signs. Within these spaces, we also arrange the nature, quality, and effects belonging to each sign, so that the shadow of the pointer indicates the state and condition of the time almost every day under this Roman horizon. To ensure all this is done with greater system, we have first arranged within this Zodiac or <term>sun-path</term> space an ecclesiastical calendar. In this, by the perpetual change of the Sun’s motion, the shadow—now approaching the zenith, now declining from it—demonstrates the feasts and solemnities of the entire year according to the order of the twelve months.

### Problem 1.

->*To arrange an Ecclesiastical Calendar on*<-
->*an astronomical shadow-caster so that the shadow*<-
->*of the gnomon, besides the teaching of the*<-
->*primum mobile, also demonstrates the*<-
->*feasts of the Saints occurring through*<-
->*the course of the whole year, month*<-
->*by month, upon the Roman*<-
->*horizon.*<-

First, let a horizontal shadow-caster <note>sundial</note> be constructed for all degrees of the Sun's declination, as shown above in Gnomonic Geography. Then, see to which degrees of the Sun the beginnings of the twelve months respond, and what declination those degrees have. For if you inscribe the corresponding feasts on the parallels of solar declination, you will have a calendar ordered according to the twelve months. Let us briefly clarify the matter with an example. Since the feast of St. John the Baptist falls on the 24th day of June—specifically at the first degree of Cancer, where the maximum declination of the Sun is 23 degrees and 30 minutes—the said feast shall be inscribed on the line of the summer tropic. Likewise, the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary falls on the 15th day of August, when the Sun enters the 22nd degree of Leo. Look up the declination of this degree in the table provided in the third book, which you will find to be 18 degrees. You will therefore place the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary on this parallel in the space for feasts. Furthermore, if you describe the parallels of the declination of the signs with slightly thicker lines to distinguish them from the others, <margin>The teaching of the primum mobile <note>The "first moved" outer sphere of the heavens</note> is to be drawn from here.</margin> they will give you the hyperbolas of the 12 signs. If you also arrange within the spaces of this Zodiac—destined for this use according to the solar declinations—the twilight of night and day, the quantity of the day, the rising and setting of the Sun, right and oblique ascensions, and the rising and setting amplitudes, along with the qualities and properties of the signs; you will have the desired Astronomical Calendar Shadow-caster, of the kind we place here before your eyes.
