->On Portable Sundials.<-

## Explanation of the Hemerological-Astronomical Sundial.

The <term>sciatheric device</term> <note>From the Greek *skia* (shadow) and *thera* (measuring); a device that "hunts" or measures time using shadows, such as a sundial.</note>, which we present to you here in the form of an Imperial Eagle, consists of ten spaces in which we have encompassed the entire doctrine of the <term>prime mover</term> <note>In traditional astronomy, the *primum mobile* is the outermost sphere of the heavens that carries all others.</note>. The first border contains the 12 months with the degrees of the Sun's declination. The second circular space contains the feasts of the Saints corresponding to each month. The third contains the degrees of the Sun corresponding to the days of the 12 months. The fourth contains the signs of the Zodiac with the qualities appropriate to each. The fifth contains the twilights. The sixth contains the length of the days and nights. The seventh contains the sunrise and sunset. The eighth contains the rising and setting amplitudes <note>The angular distance of a celestial body from the east or west point of the horizon.</note>. The ninth contains the right and oblique ascensions. The tenth contains the houses of the Planets. 

This system is expressed in the symbol of the Imperial Eagle, whose scepters, inserted into its double head, are the <term>styles</term> <note>The gnomon or pin of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note>. The one on the right shows the astronomical morning hours, and the one on the left shows the afternoon hours, with this inscription: *From midday and midnight.* In the talons of the feet, we have arranged two other scepters, one of which shows the Babylonian hours <note>Hours counted starting from sunrise.</note>, and the other the Italian hours <note>Hours counted starting from sunset.</note>, with this inscription: *From sunrise and sunset.* Therefore, when this shadow-measuring device is placed on a horizontal plane and situated according to the four cardinal directions, the shadow of the style will perfectly demonstrate all the aforementioned things. We have summarized the use of the entire device in these verses:

> *Whoever loves the various labors of the Sun and Moon,*
> *Let him see what the shadow marks within its circles.*
> *It teaches the signs, days, months, the setting and rising of the Sun,*
> *How long the night is, how long the day, and how long the twilights.*
> *How far the Sun declines from the central orbit, and at what time*
> *Any stars may be raised, or at what time they may fall.*
> *Here is given the measure of midnight and of midday,*
> *The hour which takes its name from the astronomers.*
> *The shadow indicates in its circles those hours which King Ahaz* <note>A reference to the biblical "Dial of Ahaz" mentioned in Isaiah 38:8.</note>
> *Once showed, along with the ancient Masters.*
> *The hours which Babylonia counts from the rising of the Sun,*
> *And those which the Latin land teaches from its setting.*
> *The mystical scepters of the Eagle of the House of Austria,*
> *Ruling over the vast world, mark all these things in the field of light and shadow.* <note>original: *Luc-umbri*</note>

Having thus surveyed the <term>summary</term> <note>original: *Perioche*</note> of our calendar-based shadow-measuring device, nothing remains but for us to investigate the causes of the effects associated with the individual signs and the <term>twelve divisions of the zodiac</term> <note>original: *dodecamoriisque*</note>.

# Physical Inquiry I.
## On the Influence of the Signs.

Within the space assigned to the twelve signs, the curious reader will find certain letters with which we point out the qualities belonging to each sign, which we also set before your eyes in the following single summary table.

### *Table of the Qualities of the Signs.*

| | | Nature of the Signs. | Bodily Humors. | Elements. |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ♈ | Hot and dry. | <term>Cholera</term> <note>Yellow bile; associated with a fiery and ambitious temperament.</note> | Fire. |
| 2 | ♉ | Cold and dry. | <term>Melancholy</term> <note>Black bile; associated with a thoughtful or somber temperament.</note> | Earth. |
| 3 | ♊ | Hot and moist. | Blood. | Air. |
| 4 | ♋ | Cold and moist. | <term>Phlegm</term> <note>Associated with a calm or stolid temperament.</note> | Water. |
| 5 | ♌ | Hot and dry. | Cholera. | Fire. |
| 6 | ♍ | Cold and dry. | Melancholy. | Earth. |
| 7 | ♎ | Hot and moist. | Blood. | Air. |
| 8 | ♏ | Cold and moist. | Phlegm. | Water. |
| 9 | ♐ | Hot and dry. | Cholera. | Fire. |
| 10 | ♑ | Cold and dry. | Melancholy. | Earth. |
| 11 | ♒ | Hot and moist. | Blood. | Air. |
| 12 | ♓ | Cold and moist. | Phlegm. | Water. |

<margin>The source of the power of the <term>dodecamoria</term> <note>The twelve-fold divisions of the Zodiac.</note>.</margin>
It is first asked, therefore, whether the signs truly and actually possess these qualities; whether a power of this kind is bestowed within the twelve-fold spaces themselves, or whether it belongs to the <term>asterism</term> <note>The actual group of stars forming the constellation.</note> or stars of which the signs consist? Certainly, it is the opinion of all astrologers that the said properties reside in the asterisms of the signs themselves, and this is so firmly fixed among astrologers that if you were to deny it, you would seem to overturn all of Astrology. For upon these properties, as if upon a foundation, rests the entire science of the <term>triplicity of the trigons</term> <note>The grouping of signs into threes based on their element (Fire, Earth, Air, Water).</note>, the <term>oekodespotia</term> <note>From the Greek *oikos* (house) and *despotes* (master); refers to the planet that "rules" or acts as the lord of a particular sign.</note> of the planets, and the effects of ascendants and horoscopes. From this, they constantly assert that the revolutions and conjunctions of planets moving from a watery trigon into a fiery one—such as moving from Cancer ♋, Scorpio ♏, or Pisces ♓ into Aries ♈, Leo ♌, or Sagittarius ♐—bring about the greatest changes in the world, such as shifts in religions, empires, and Republics, and other similar transformations of things, which they insist upon to the point of boredom <note>Original Latin: *ad nauseam*.</note>. Hence arises that great "affinity" of the Planets with the signs of the Zodiac in which they are found; for in these signs they obtain certain powers by which their strengths become hotter and more potent. Therefore, astrologers, diligently observing their various states, have reduced them to seven distinct types, which are: house, <term>exaltation</term> <note>Latin: *altitudo*, literally "height." A sign where a planet's influence is particularly harmonious.</note>, trigon, term, <term>chariot</term> <note>Latin: *carpentum*; a specific dignity or protective state of a planet in a sign.</note>, person, and joy, about each of which something must be said.

### *The Houses of the Planets.*

First: That place where the power of a planet, finding qualities friendly, beneficial, and...

<meta>This page continues the technical and astrological explanation of the Zodiac signs and their relationships to the planets, which began on the previous page with a table of elemental qualities. ...and when a sign is most congruent for reducing its own effects, and is more valid, stronger, and more virtuous, it is called the **house** of that planet. For this reason, because the sign of Leo is masculine, hot, and dry—matching the nature of the Sun—it is called the house of the Sun.

♋ <note>Cancer</note>, being a nocturnal and feminine sign, is assigned as the house of the Moon.

♊ <note>Gemini</note> and ♍ <note>Virgo</note>, the signs closest to the houses of the Moon and Sun, are assigned to Mercury; he is nearest by reason of the Moon’s position, and by reason of his conjunction, he never departs more than 27 degrees from the Sun.

♉ <note>Taurus</note> and ♎ <note>Libra</note>, both being fertile signs and the third signs from the houses of the Sun and Moon, are accommodated to Venus. By reason of her maximum conjunction with the Sun, she does not distant herself more than 48 degrees; she holds the third place in a certain way and is the third planet from the Moon, being supremely fertile.

♈ <note>Aries</note> and ♏ <note>Scorpio</note>, since they abound in much bile and have a certain hidden power of harming, constitute the house of Mars.

♐ <note>Sagittarius</note> and ♓ <note>Pisces</note>, being more fertile than all others, are attributed to Jupiter, the greatest friend of the luminaries <note>The Sun and Moon</note> and most fertile; for these signs gaze upon the houses of the luminaries—the mothers of fertility—with a <term>trine</term> <note>An aspect of 120 degrees, considered harmonious and beneficial</note> radiation.

♑ <note>Capricorn</note> and ♒ <note>Aquarius</note>, soft and very cold, being opposite the houses of the luminaries, belong to Saturn, the most remote and coldest of all. The houses truly opposite to these are called the **exiles** or **detriments** of the planets: therefore, they say the detriment of the Sun is Aquarius; of the Moon, Capricorn; of Saturn, Leo and Cancer; and so on for the others, as the little table shows.

## On the Exaltation of Planets.

**SECONDLY**: The **Exaltation** of a planet is what Astrologers call that place in the Zodiac where the planet has greater virtue after its own house. They recognize this in three ways: First, from the progress of the planet toward signs of its own nature and those most congruent to its effects; Second, from the place in which it shows its powers more after conjunction with the Sun; Third, from the sign in which it can more aptly and easily produce its effects. Therefore, the exaltation of the Sun is the sign of ♈ <note>Aries</note>, and its <term>depression</term> <note>Also called the "Fall," the point where a planet's influence is weakest.</note> is Libra, because from Aries it proceeds to the northern semicircle which is more congruent for the generation of things; from Libra, it moves to the southern, which is hostile to generation in our hemisphere. The Moon is exalted in ♉ <note>Taurus</note> and depressed in Scorpio; because once the conjunction with the Sun is made in Aries, it immediately proceeds to Taurus, where it exerts its powers most greatly; but when the conjunction is made in Scorpio, it proceeds toward Sagittarius, and when made in Libra toward Scorpio—

<margin>Detriments and falls of the planets.</margin>
—in which it cannot produce its own effects so perfectly. Jupiter is exalted in ♋ <note>Cancer</note> and humbled in ♑ <note>Capricorn</note>, because in the former it more easily stirs up the Northern winds, of which it is the parent.

♂ Mars, in the opposite way, has its exaltation in ♑ <note>Capricorn</note> and its depression in ♋ <note>Cancer</note>: for that sign, being most remote, tempers his excessive heat; the remoteness is measured from the vertical.

♀ Venus, being moist, is exalted in the sign of Pisces, where many waters are found; she is depressed in ♍ <note>Virgo</note>.

♄ Finally, <note>Saturn</note> is exalted in ♎ <note>Libra</note> and depressed in ♈ <note>Aries</note> because of the repugnant qualities of this <term>dodecamorion</term> <note>A 30-degree division of the Zodiac.</note> with him.

## On the Trigons.

**THIRDLY**: The **Trigons** are considered. A <term>trigon</term> <note>Also known as a triplicity; a group of three signs belonging to the same element.</note> is the dominion of a Planet arising from the dignity of its house and exaltation. For although the signs forming a trigon may be of different natures, they are nonetheless bound in friendship to one another by sex and radiation, especially when they are governed by the planets themselves. There are four triangles of signs, just as was shown in the preceding pages. The **Fiery** is constituted of three signs: ♈ ♌ ♐; the **Earthy** of three signs: ♉ ♍ ♑; the **Aerial** from ♊ ♎ ♒; and finally the **Watery** from ♋ ♏ ♓. The Sun ☉ and Jupiter ♃ rule the Fiery, because they are masculine and diurnal, as are the signs themselves. The Moon ☽ and Mars ♂ rule the Earthy and cause winds mixed from the south and east; Saturn ♄ and Mercury ☿ are assigned to the Aerial because of the North-East winds they cause. Mars is placed over the Watery, to whom Venus is joined by day and the Moon by night. All of these are the opposite for our Antipodes.

<margin>The terms of the Egyptians.</margin>
**Fourthly.** Furthermore, there are certain degrees in every sign in which a Planet, while existing there, is more robust and effective; these degrees were called **terms** by the Egyptians. Thus, the space from the first degree of ♈ <note>Aries</note> up to the end of the sixth is called the term of Jupiter; from the 6th to the 12th, of ♀ Venus; from the 12th to the 20th, of ☿ Mercury; from the 20th to the 25th, of ♂ Mars; from the 25th to the 30th, of ♄ Saturn; and so proceeding through the degrees of the twelve signs.

<margin>The chariot of the planets.</margin>
**Fifthly.** The **Chariot** is that place of any Planet in the Zodiac in which, while it exists there, it has several dignities joined together; and it is called a chariot because, like a King with a great company of friendly stars, it triumphs as if in a carriage of honor and riches.

<margin>The persona of the planet.</margin>
**Sixthly.** The **Persona** of a Planet, called the <term>Almugia</term> <note>A term from Medieval Arabic astrology referring to a specific relationship between a planet's position and the Sun or Moon.</note> by the Arabs, is when it looks back in the same way...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of planetary "dignities" (the strength of planets in certain zodiac signs) but shifts into a major scientific critique. Kircher argues that traditional European astrology is flawed because it fails to account for the Southern Hemisphere, where the seasons and astrological effects are reversed.</meta>

<header>The Great Art, Book VI. Part III of Proteus.</header>
<page-num>388</page-num>

...regards the Sun, or the Moon, just as its house regards the house of the Sun, or the Moon; so that it is western in relation to the Sun, and eastern in relation to the Moon.

<margin>The Joy of a Planet.</margin>
Seventh, it is called the **Joy of the Planets** when a planet rests in a house belonging to another, joined by friendship, fortune, and the goodness of the other planets existing there; for then it rejoices in their good, participating in the goodness found there.

You see, therefore, that while these things were wisely established by the ancients, no universal science can be built upon them. It appears clearly that the ancients had absolutely no account of the <term>Antipodes</term> <note>People living on the opposite side of the Earth</note>, nor of the different configurations of horizons. They judged that the twelve divisions of the signs provided the same effect everywhere. In this they were greatly mistaken; indeed, I show that Astrology is absolutely nothing unless it is established for a specific horizon. For if the twelve divisions of the signs were imbued with such-and-forth qualities by their own nature, they would produce the same effect everywhere; but experience today teaches that the Antipodes and our <term>Antaeci</term> <note>People living at the same longitude but opposite latitude</note>, as well as those <term>Amphiscii</term> <note>People in the Torrid Zone whose shadows fall both north and south</note> who live under the Torrid Zone, experience entirely different things. For a sign which experience has taught us is hot and dry, they find to be imbued with entirely contrary qualities, namely cold and moist. Thus, a hot and dry sign bringing us vehement summer heat will cause them vehement cold, and consequently the House of the Sun can in no way be appropriately established for them. Hence, the houses in which the stars are exalted for us, and in which they rejoice and triumph, are ruinous and detrimental for our Antaeci and Antipodes, since these astrological "dignities" are supposed to follow nature exactly.

<margin>The uncertainty of Astrology.</margin>
But if anyone should object that no certain account can be had of the conditions of places among the Antipodes and Antaeci, he will be more than convinced by daily voyages as well as the observations of Europeans staying in those places. In the Province of Chile—which is a province of South America bordering the Southern Sea, extending from the 30th to nearly the 50th degree of latitude, and is nearly our Antaeci—this is testified by Father **Alonso de Ovalle** <note>original: "Alphonsus Dualle"</note> of our Society. He was born and raised there, and while I am writing this, he has been sent to Rome as a procurator; he is not ignorant of Astronomy.

<margin>Quality of the signs in the opposite hemisphere.</margin>
He says that all the effects of the Sun are contrary to the effects occurring in our hemisphere. Therefore, in his homeland, that sign which brings us intolerable heat is the cause of exotic and intolerable cold for them. He notes that he could never perceive any warmth from **Leo** or the **Dog Star** <note>Sirius, associated with the "dog days" of summer</note> that could temper such enormous cold. On the contrary, **Aquarius**, which we experience as raging with enormous cold, is the cause of intolerable heat for them. Thus **Aries**, the "gate of generation" for things in our hemisphere, is not undeservedly established as the "gate of destruction" for them. Since the Sun, approaching our zenith, accelerates the generation and life of things, but by receding from the zenith gradually brings about the destruction and death of things, reason itself teaches that the sign of Aries brings destruction to them, while **Libra** brings generation and life.

But under the **Torrid Zone** <note>The tropics</note>—as I have heard by word of mouth from the Procurators of our Society from Peru, Brazil, and the Philippine Islands—the qualities of the signs are so confused that you can hardly discern what is moist or dry, cold or hot. Thus, under the Equator, they experience the vertical signs of Aries ♈ and Libra ♎ as being of a mostly moist and hot temperament; but the tropical signs <note>Cancer and Capricorn</note> incline more toward dryness and cold; the remaining intermediate signs are allotted various other temperaments. From such great variety, exotic effects are caused that are entirely distinct from the effects of the Temperate Zone.

<margin>Variety of effects in the Torrid Zone.</margin>
From this, there is an entirely different constitution of plants, animals, humans, and other things originating there, such that they have almost nothing that corresponds to our things. But you may see more on this in our treatise *The Art of Anacamptics* <note>A work on optics and sundials</note>, Book 7, Part 1.

<margin>Horoscopes in the Torrid Zone.</margin>
If anyone, therefore, were to construct a <term>genethliacon</term> <note>A birth chart or horoscope</note> under the Torrid Zone or in the Southern Hemisphere according to the standard astrological rules, it is certain that it would signify absolutely nothing of what the Astrologers promise. In those places, neither the nature of the signs is the same, nor can the coordination of the houses and other "dignities" assigned to the planets be maintained. Thus, the signs and the powers the planets obtain within them would have to be entirely reordered.

Having established these points, it is clearer than the midday sun that Astrology is by no means universal. Nor can <term>natal themes</term> <note>original: "themata genethliaca"; these are birth charts or horoscopes</note> constructed for the Torrid Zone or its neighboring places remain valid. These facts are so true, based on what has preceded, that only an astrologer of a disturbed mind could contradict them. Indeed, since the arrangement of oblique horizons is so varied, I say that these qualities will vary in every single location. Thus, no chart can be constructed that is entirely certain and safe unless it is for a specific horizon or climate. The entire astrological business depends not only on the light of the stars and their various positions and arrangements, but also on almost infinite circumstances. These circumstances are varied in nearly every horizon by the natural makeup of the place, the position of mountains, the nature of the waters and the soil, and even the natural inclination and disposition of the parents—as we have shown at length in Book 1, Chapter 19. Unless all these things are properly weighed, it is impossible for an exact and perfectly complete celestial chart to be made. 

Hence, one would be a laughingstock who, living in the polar region or Frigid Zone, promised himself anything regarding the fortune of a person born there, or regarding rains and the changes of seasons. For that region neither receives the required division of the <term>houses</term> <note>The twelve sections of an astrological chart</note>, nor do the <term>dodecamoria</term> <note>The twelve-fold divisions of the zodiac signs</note> of the signs maintain the same properties there as they do under the 5th, 6th, 7th, or 8th climates <note>A "climate" in ancient geography was a strip of latitude; these numbers refer to the Mediterranean and Northern European regions</note>.

Furthermore, since the Planets appear continuously above the horizon of the Frigid Zone for a space of 3, 4, 5, or 6 months, or are hidden below it for that same interval of time, it would be the mark of a rash—not to say foolish—man to attribute to them the same effects during this manifestation or concealment that we, living in the Temperate Zone, ascribe to them. For who does not know that many other effects are caused in those parts by this perpetual appearance or occultation of starlight than are caused in our regions? If even in European, Asian, and neighboring regions we frequently find such a great difference in natural makeup—due to the different site of the soil and earth receiving the diffusion of solar and lunar light in different ways—surely those peoples will undergo a much greater diversity from the perpetual appearance or concealment of light, just as the position of the sphere they inhabit and the natural makeup of the earth is more different from ours.

From these things, rightly considered, we infer that for a <term>gnomonic</term> <note>Related to the use of a gnomon, the shadow-casting part of a sundial</note> celestial chart to be exact and serve for divinations, it must be tailored to only one climate, whose nature and long-term quality [is experienced...]

## C A P U T II.

->*Concerning the various effects which the Sun, the Moon, and the twelfth-parts of the twelve signs produce while passing through,*<-
->*and concerning the selection of times for beginning matters opportunely.*<-

---

<margin>What an astrological election is.</margin>
**T**he Sun and the Moon, as was declared at length in the first book, are the moderators and leaders of sublunary <note>Meaning things "below the moon," or the earthly realm subject to change.</note> things, without which neither generation nor any life of living things could be preserved by any means. Therefore, so that it may be clear at what times and in which <term>twelfth-parts</term><note>Latin: *dodecamoria*; these are subdivisions of the zodiac signs used to refine predictions.</note> they provide effects suitable for the preservation of things, we have thought it necessary to arrange in this place a <term>Sciatheric</term><note>From the Greek *skiatheros*, meaning shadow-catching; a device like a sundial that uses shadows to indicate time or astrological data.</note> instrument, in which the shadow of the <term>gnomon</term><note>The pin or blade of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note>, like a finger, may demonstrate the time for making <term>elections</term><note>The practice of choosing the most astrologically auspicious moment to begin an undertaking.</note> at the opportune moment. For an "election" is nothing other than a certain opportunity of time which the Sun and Moon hold according to their position and disposition in the Zodiac; so that if someone initiates actions serving Medicine or Agriculture at that same time, they may achieve an infallible effect, as irrefutable experience teaches. For man is ruled by two principles, namely nature and will; nature is subject to the stars, but the will is free. Therefore, effects and operations that are purely natural clearly obey the stars as secondary causes established for these and other things by God—such as health, or infirmity, and the long or short life of men. Other matters are purely and merely voluntary, which exceed the astronomical limits of power, such as doing this or that good or evil, or something conducive to either. Still others are mixed, such as making a journey, which depends on the man's will to do or not to do. However, whether the journey will be favorable depends on the stars and the constitution of the air. If, therefore, someone perfectly knew the influence of the stars as agreeable or disagreeable to our body, he could beyond doubt judge with certainty concerning the fortunate or unfortunate state of a journey.

<margin>How judgment should be formed regarding the election of things.</margin>
Again, if someone certainly knew the influence of the stars as agreeable or disagreeable to the humors of a sick person, he could beyond doubt form a perfect <term>crisis</term><note>A medical turning point where a patient either begins to recover or declines toward death.</note> regarding the health or despair of the patient. Finally, if someone about to treat business with a certain Prince knew the alteration which the present state of the stars might effect in that Prince, he could similarly form a probable judgment about the success of the business. But since these things can be done only with difficulty, the astrological knowledge of elections is for the most part deceptive, unless it is bolstered by experiences. Because, however, elections achieve more certain effects in the business of agriculture, medicine, and navigation than in undertaking general business matters; for this reason, we have thought it necessary to arrange this Sciatheric instrument according to experiments suitable only to the Roman sky.

### Problema II.

->A Medical-Agricultural-Economic Sciatheric Instrument<-
->for the opportune selection of times.<-

<margin>Illustration XV.</margin>
**L**et a horizontal gnomonic Zodiac be drawn according to the precepts delivered in the fourth book, together with the declinations of the signs; which you shall divide into its spaces by its hyperbolas in exactly that manner which the present figure teaches.

### Explanation and use of the figure.

**T**he gnomonic Zodiac is divided into eight spaces in total. The first space contains the signs; the second contains <term>phlebotomic</term><note>Related to bloodletting, a common medical practice of the time.</note> elections, that is, the opportune time for cutting a vein and letting blood; the third space shows the time fit for taking medicines; the fourth is deputed for baths; the fifth contains elections for building, or the construction of edifices; the sixth, the time for hunting; the seventh assigns the opportune time for cutting timber for use in construction; finally, the eighth is destined for sowing, planting, grafting, and other works pertaining to agriculture.

<margin>Explanation of Illustration 11.</margin>
In each of these spaces, we have indicated the elections to be made by a triple kind of letter: the first of which, **B**, signifies Good <note>Latin: *Bonum*</note>, that is, the time is most opportune. The second letter, **I**, signifies a certain mediocrity or Indifference <note>Latin: *Indifferens*</note> of time in choosing elections. The third letter, **M**, denotes a Bad <note>Latin: *Malum*</note> and inopportune time for making elections. If, therefore, the lunar shadow of the gnomon falls into any space of the <term>sixth-parts</term><note>Latin: *hectemoria*; divisions of the dial face.</note> of the gnomonic Zodiac, the letters within that same space will show the opportunity or inopportunity of the elections to be made. Thus, with the lunar shadow falling into the sixth-part space of Aries, the letters of that same space—I, B, M, I, I, B, B—show an indifferent time for phlebotomy, a good time for taking medicines, indifferent for baths, as well as for buildings; for hunting...

The Mystic Dove—which is our <term>Sciathericon</term> <note>A shadow-catching instrument or sundial.</note>—expresses the state of the Church Militant <note>The Church on Earth, currently "at war" against sin and trials.</note> <term>symbolically</term> <note>original Greek: ἐν τύπῳ (en typō)</note> through the perpetual inconstancy of the Moon and the alternating shifts of light and shadow. In this Dove, the Holy Spirit is seen directing His Church. The Miters—in which we have delineated the shadow-climes of the world alongside the Keys—denote the Successor of Peter and Vicar of Christ, according to the inscribed mottos. We further denote the various institutions of the Orthodox Church by certain allegorical titles: <margin>The Mystic Zodiac.</margin> thus, through the "baths" and "anointings," we understand the Sacraments of Baptism, Confirmation, and Extreme Unction; through "bloodletting," we understand the Sacrament of Penance, by which the soul is restored to health after the superfluous humors of sins that suffocate the spirit are drawn away; through the "taking of medicine," the most holy Sacrament of the Eucharist is understood, leading to the perfect health of body and soul. The Sacrament of Holy Orders is denoted by "hunting" and "fishing," according to the verse: *I will make you fishers of men* (Matthew 4), signifying the Apostles or Priests. Finally, through "planting" and "sowing," Matrimony is understood. The twelve signs of the Zodiac denote the various conditions of men. Furthermore, the Pamphili Dove <note>A reference to the family of Pope Innocent X, whose coat of arms featured a dove with an olive branch.</note> rules over this mystic sky, carrying an olive branch, the symbol of peace and tranquility. We must uniquely petition Him in whose hands are the hearts of Kings, with the greatest confidence and most ardent outpouring of prayers, so that we may at last experience this peace as quickly as possible after the floods of overflowing evils and the nearly desperate state of the Christian Commonwealth.

### Investigation II. Physical.

<margin>Whence comes such a great variety of things within the circle of the year.</margin>
**H**aving seen the nature and properties of the Signs, let us now see in what manner the constitution of their qualities arrives. For it is certain that the <term>twelve divisions</term> <note>original: dodecamoria; the 30-degree sections of the Zodiac.</note> are, in and of themselves and by their own nature, indifferent; they possess no hidden power implanted in them by which they provide the aforementioned qualities. Therefore, the cause of all things must be attributed to the Sun and the Moon, his co-helper. But let us give the reasons for each.

The Sun, therefore, entering **Aries**, while his strength grows through the increasing flow of his healing ray, causes the body of the earth—which had been overwhelmed by winter’s squalor—to finally be opened by the Phœbean arrows <note>Sunbeams; Phœbus is a name for the sun god Apollo.</note>. Along with the internal heat, the earth admits the moisture of the melted snows from without. By this benefit of heat and moisture, plants and animals are affected: some are disposed toward grass, herbs, and leaves; others toward the "seed" of animals. Yet, because the solar heat is not yet sufficient to consume the excessive moisture, the vapors raised from the earth and condensed are mostly resolved into rains at this time, which is the reason why we experience such an inconstant weather constitution in April.

When the Sun enters **Taurus**, as he acquires greater and greater strength, the greater part of the earth’s moisture is consumed, and the fluid gradually breaks out from the roots where it resided into the leaves, branches, flowers, and seeds. From this comes all that luxury of all things which we experience in the month of May; from this, all kinds of birds and animals, touched by the ray of such beneficial light, are stimulated into fertile motions.

Furthermore, when the Sun enters **Gemini**, the entire terrestrial moisture having been consumed by the Sun's powerful ray, the earth now begins to decline toward dryness; the rains cease, as the vapors are turned into air by the heat of the Sun. The maturing crops are prepared for harvest; the moisture implanted in plants is gathered by the help of plastic power <note>The "form-giving" force in nature.</note> from the stalks, branches, and flowers into early fruits.

When the Sun enters **Cancer**, as he strikes the earth with the greatest force of heat being near the zenith, not only is the moisture implanted in the earth entirely consumed, but the earth itself, disposed toward perfect dryness, is soaked through with external heat. Thus it happens that, once the moisture of the plants is "cooked out" into the fruits, the leaves turn yellow, and the earth gaps open with cracks, showing signs of immoderate heat. Since the days are also at their longest and decrease very slowly, the earth, as if baked by the heat, exhales the excessive temperatures such as we experience in the <term>dog days</term> <note>The hot "canicular" days of mid-summer.</note>. From this come various and dangerous illnesses, which many ascribe to the Dog Star, but we more truly attribute to the Sun affecting the earth in the manner mentioned.

Furthermore, with the Sun positioned at the end of **Leo** and the beginning of **Virgo**, as the nights grow by a large increase, the sweltering earth is somewhat tempered by the nocturnal cold. The attracted and condensed vapors are gradually prepared for new rains, by which the earth, suffering from the vehement heat, is refreshed for a little while and soaked with new moisture to ripen the fruits that usually come forth in Autumn.

When the Sun runs through **Libra**, as rains multiply due to the shortness of days and the length of nights, the earth, filled with new moisture, acquires a certain imbalance; whence, <margin>The decay of things from a lack of heat.</margin> from a lack of heat, trees are deprived of leaves and fruit. Finally, all things seem to verge toward old age. These effects take on greater increases as the Sun enters **Scorpio** and **Sagittarius**, up until the Solstice, when the earth—with all external heat banished—lies squalid and mournful. Yet it is by no means idle; for, compressed by rains and ice, it conceives new seeds of things to be generated, as it were. These are gradually brought forward in **Capricorn**, **Aquarius**, and **Pisces** by the "inwardly nourishing spirit," until finally, as the Sun returns to **Aries**, they sprout again into new offspring.

## The Contest of the Sun and Moon, of Day and Night, of Heat and Cold.

You see therefore from what has been said, that the same course of the Sun—its approach and its withdrawal—is the reason why the seasons of the year are sometimes sweltering, sometimes freezing, and sometimes temperate. For since the delay of the Sun above the horizon breathes in heat, while the night indeed brings cooling, it happens that in the winter time, the night brings in much moisture and consequently cools the entire tract of the sky, and the air itself thickens because of the cold; for it is the function of cold to condense fluid things. This occurs to such an extent that the Sun, in that tiny space of time in which it shows itself to us, is soon snatched away immediately to the lower parts of the sky below the horizon; it has no ability nor power to break through the thickness of the air, nor to gradually instill its heat through the benefit of the short time in which it shines. And thus, all things are benumbed by stiffness and ice.

<margin>The length of days and nights induces the change of things.</margin>
But as the day gradually grows, we feel the Sun itself becoming stronger, and now these clouds, now those are driven away, until, given an equal share of the field, it makes the contest equal and struggles with equal force against the night; this happens when the vernal equinox <note>The time in spring when day and night are of equal length.</note> is reached. Emerging from there as the victor, it continues to press and pursue the night and all cold all the more sharply, the more unfairly it had been treated by her. Having become in a way the Lord of the sky, with the known boundaries of night reduced into a narrow space, the Sun extends its heat through this entire region even to a heavy dominion. And since there is a change in all things, as soon as the Sun, frolicking widely, has badly punished <term>Cancer</term> <note>The zodiac sign marking the Summer Solstice.</note> to the envy of the Moon (who rules the night), it is ordered by the inviolable law of the fates to change its ground. Retreating to <term>Leo</term>—who shares the closest friendship with him—and being conscious that it must lose its possession, the Sun pours out all its strength with as much effort as possible and hurls those <term>canicular</term> <note>The "dog days" of summer, named after the star Sirius (the Dog Star).</note> heats through the whole air.

Within this, circular segments are divided and labeled by the four seasons: 'SPRING', 'WINTER', 'AUTUMN', and 'SUMMER'. The diagram includes concentric circles, diagonal intersecting lines, and shaded circular phases representing celestial bodies or their shadows at different times of the year. Received at last by the Virgin, the Sun is commended to <term>Astraea</term> <note>The goddess of Justice, often identified with the constellation Virgo, who holds the scales of the next sign, Libra.</note>, who tries to settle peace between the Sun and Night and give equal power to each, but she accomplishes nothing. Indeed, the night, armed with Scorpions and Archers <note>The zodiac signs Scorpio and Sagittarius.</note>, attacks the Sun and, after a long-driven contest, finally puts him to flight. The sovereignty of things is entrusted for a time to the cold itself, until, with forces resumed, the Sun attacks his adversary anew. But as to why all years are not equal—since we experience some as sterile, others fertile, some humid, some hot or cold or dry—I would ascribe that either to the natural constitution of the Sun, or to the arrangement of the <term>wandering</term> <note>The planets (from the Greek 'planētēs', meaning wanderer).</note> and fixed stars, or even to eclipses. For stars of a humid temperament, concurring with humid "wanderers," will cause a humid climate; dry and hot ones, operating immoderately beyond the usual heat, will also fill the lower world with malignant influences, from which various types of monsters <note>In this period, "monsters" referred to any unnatural or extraordinary phenomenon in nature.</note> arise; and so on for the rest. We have seen, therefore, the Sun's twelve...

# Great Art, Book VI. Part III of Proteus.

...having run through the works and effects of the twelve signs of the Zodiac; now let us investigate what the course of the Moon, repeated twelve times in that same Zodiac, provides.

## On the effects of the Moon in the Zodiac.

We stated in the first book that the Moon, traversing the Zodiac in its monthly space, performs the same function for sublunary things <note>Things on Earth, beneath the sphere of the Moon.</note>, according to a certain analogy, as the Sun performs in its annual space. Hence, the first lunar quarter corresponds in every way to the solar spring quarter, the second to the summer, the third to the autumn, and the fourth to the winter solar quarter. Since, therefore, the light of the Moon is modified in various ways by its varying aspect <note>The angular relationship between two celestial bodies.</note> to the Sun, there should be no doubt that it also produces very different effects along with it. Hence, the influence of the <term>Syzygy</term> <note>The alignment of the Sun, Moon, and Earth, occurring at the New and Full Moon.</note> is different from the influence of the opposition of the luminaries; this, in turn, is different from the square and trine influences, both of which differ from the sextile. All of these differ from the <term>platic</term> and <term>partile</term> <note>Technical terms for the precision of an aspect: 'partile' is exact to the degree, while 'platic' is within a wider range of influence.</note> aspects. From this, almost innumerable modifications of Lunar light with Solar light result, as is clear from the art of combinations, which relate to one another in exactly the same way as mixtures of colors, which are infinitely variable.

If, therefore, the Sun and Moon meet in fiery signs <note>Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius.</note> corresponding to a particular horizon, they will bring with them not only a violent intensification of quality, but even a malignant and harmful quality. In the watery <term>dodecatemories</term> <note>The twelve divisions or signs of the Zodiac.</note>, the Moon will suffocate everything with destructive cold and moisture; in the fiery signs, it causes rot through a harmful mixture of light; but in the airy signs, because of the tempered mixture of light, it brings fertility and abundance to things. All of these can be varied in infinite ways according to the aspects of the remaining planets. But so that these things may be better understood, let us encompass the individual points in brief rules or canons.

<margin>The science of elections is most useful.</margin>
All the arts declare that the science of <term>elections</term> <note>The practice of choosing the most auspicious time to begin an action based on the stars.</note> is necessary for the proper and successful completion of human operations—especially those arts which do not work alone, but in cooperation with nature. For unless the Physician takes account of the Moon and the "critical days," he kills while he heals, or does not properly complete what he has prepared. The sailor, too, if he commits himself to the sea in winter during a harmful lunation, is not safe from capsizing. The farmer, if he sows grain in the month of August, will not harvest fruit in our regions; he therefore chooses the autumnal quarter, to which, if he adds a fertile lunation, he will do better. Nor should he prune vines in December, but in February; nor plant them in September, but in March. Travelers, if they do not first consider the winds and rains and their causes, are afflicted by many inconveniences. All things, therefore, in the judgment of a wise man, have their time. Since this is so, nothing remains except that we prescribe here some canons for properly performing agriculture, recognizing the change of weather, and taking medicine at the opportune time.

## Agricultural-Economic Canons concerning Farming.

1. When the MOON is waxing, all humors <note>The vital fluids in plants and animals.</note> increase; when it is waning, they decrease in all seasons.
2. When the Moon is positioned in watery signs <note>Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces.</note>, all planting should be omitted because of a certain suffocating force of the humors.
3. But in earthy signs <note>Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn.</note>, because of the beneficial power of the humor, planting should be opportunely undertaken.
<margin>Astrological rules to be observed in Agriculture.</margin>
4. In fiery signs, the aspect must be taken into account: if it is a square, the election should be omitted; otherwise, if it is a trine or opposition, it will then temper the harmful dryness of the sign with heat. Finally, in airy signs <note>Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius.</note>, planting should always be opportunely undertaken.
5. When the Sun enters Leo [♌] and the Moon is positioned below the earth, because of the absence of an excessively moistening virtue, you may cut timber for use in buildings that will not be subject to any rot.
6. When about to plant trees or vines, choose the Moon positioned in Taurus [♉] together with Venus [♀]; for since Venus is hot and moist, her light will temper the cold lunar light and make it most suitable for sowing and planting in the most appropriate sign. If, however, the Moon is not found in Taurus, it will provide the same if positioned in Cancer [♋]; if not in Aquarius, it will provide the same if positioned in the sign of Pisces [♓] or Libra [♎].

However, in the casting of seeds, care must be taken that the election is made while the light is increasing, not decreasing; otherwise, besides the seed becoming flabby from moisture, it will also be susceptible to worms.

## Medical Canons, or on the elections of medicinal matters. On the quarters of the Moon conducive to phlebotomy, or bloodletting.

The first quadrature <note>The first quarter moon.</note> of the Moon is an opportune time for bloodletting to be applied to youths, specifically during the "Lunar Spring." The second quadrature, namely the "Lunar Summer," is suitable for the youthful and mature state. The third quadrature, the "Lunar Autumn," will benefit mature men and the elderly. The fourth quadrature, the "Lunar Winter," will be of use to the decrepit.

Fiery signs, Aries [♈] and Leo [♌], are beneficial for phlegmatic people: for all veins can be opened at this time, except for the cephalic <note>The vein in the arm associated with the head.</note> and the veins of the head. In Sagittarius [♐] as well, all may be opened except for the hips; the reason is that the specific nature of this—

# Physico-astrological Gnomonics.
<note>Physico-astrological Gnomonics: The art of using sundials and shadows to determine the proper times for physical and medical actions based on the stars.</note>

The nature of the [zodiacal] signs is to dry out the watery moisture of the blood in phlegmatic people, and to restore its natural heat.

<margin>The reason why veins should be opened under certain signs.</margin>
As for the fact that in Aries [♈] all veins can be opened, except for those of the head, the reason for this is that since the brain is of a moist and cold <term>complexion</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, 'complexion' refers to the balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—and their qualities (hot, cold, wet, dry).</note>, and the sign of Aries is most contrary to this complexion; experience, the mistress of things, has taught that a [vein] section made in this sign destroys the temperament of the head rather than helping it, due to the efficacy of the contrary qualities. And by this same logic, the remaining signs are to be applied in a parallel manner; for our blood is wonderfully subject to alterations. For besides food, it is especially subject to the alteration of the air, and it is altered by it: in summer air it seethes, in autumn it slows, in winter it thickens, and in spring it warms; just as it warms in the morning, seethes at midday, slows in the evening, and thickens at midnight; so that it undergoes rarefaction and condensation in a kind of perpetual cycle. Since the blood provides the spirits <note>In early medicine, 'spirits' were subtle fluids that carried vital force and sensory information through the body.</note>, and the spirit is the unique instrument of animal motion, it is no wonder that a person is altered so variously at different times.

# Physical-Astrological Gnomonics

...gnomonical science, and the mechanical arts; against the evils of the State, political science and law are the medicine; against accidental occurrences, providence, armed by the exercise of the sciences, fights. With this providence, the most wise Creator ordained individual things so that, since each was created for the use of the <term>microcosm</term> <note>The "microcosm" refers to the human being, viewed as a miniature version of the entire universe.</note>, each should also have its own character by which it might demonstrate through an external <term>phytoptic</term> <note>Literally "plant-viewing"; the study of the external appearance of plants to determine their internal properties.</note> seal what it signifies internally, according to that famous and distinguished golden saying of <note>Polemon of Laodicea, an ancient Greek philosopher known for his work on physiognomy.</note> Polemon: <note>original: "Σιγώντων μὲν ἐστιν ὑπόθεσις, λαλεῖ τοῖς σημείοις ἡ φύσις τὰ τρόπους ἑκάστου ἀνακαλύπτουσα."</note> *Nature speaks through signs, revealing the character of each, even while it remains silent.* Nature provides a kind of silent response regarding each thing while it speaks through signs, by which it manifests the virtues of each; these virtues are indeed nothing other than certain stars, or the forms of plants corresponding to the celestial stars. I have no doubt that whoever knows their occult connection will perform miracles in the more secret arts of medicine. For every celestial star is a herb in spiritual form, corresponding in power to the inferior stars born from the earth.

<margin>How the superior stars exist in inferior things.</margin>
With this foundation known, the constellations and compositions of celestial and earthly herbs will not remain hidden; thus, he who knows the star of Rosemary or <term>Wormwood</term> <note>original: "Absynthii".</note> will also know the hidden virtues of those herbs. He will also observe that in earthly herbs, there are as many virtues as there are colors of flowers. Therefore, nothing was created in the family of plants rashly or in vain, but in the right way, with ordained causes, and in accurate number, at the opportune time and place; just as we recognize the internal character of a man through his external composition, so too the genuine powers of herbs are known through the external signs carved into them by the most wise Architect. And, what is most worthy of admiration, all the celestial stars, which were created clearly visible in the heavens in their own bodies, also lie hidden and enclosed in the earth in their own spirits: and just as the celestial Sun generates all things in a terrestrial way by its invisible heat; so the terrestrial Sun creates and regenerates all things invisibly by its own invisible heat. Through the celestial Sun, the Spirit of the Lord works all things in nature naturally: but through the terrestrial Sun, the same Spirit works all things, but by an invisible reasoning. And just as the superior Sun is intrinsically present in all things by its invisible power, being the natural heat of all things; so too the terrestrial Sun, by its invisible power, is the native heat in all things, the balsam, the lamp, and the oil of all things. That is called the Spirit of Life hidden in all things; this is called the **Sulfur of Nature** existing in all things by its own proper and genuine name; for the superior things are in the inferior, and the inferior in the superior, yet not as they are in themselves, but according to...

<margin>The analogy of worlds.</margin>
...the nature and mode of the superior things. Therefore, the lowest things show the highest; the physical show the intellectual: through the natures and properties of the inferior and earthly, we ascend into the natures and properties of the superior and celestial. Since indeed these inferior, external, and visible things are the notes of the superior, and the symbols of the internal invisible things, by which we may be led by the hand to the knowledge of the internal superior things.

<margin>The creature is the shadow of God.</margin>
Every created thing is nothing else but the shadow of God, and the figure of the internal paradise—that is, that insight by which the Creator's "back parts" <note>A biblical reference to seeing the effects or "after-effects" of God in creation rather than His direct essence.</note> and effects (the invisible things) are seen through those things which have been made. But our "hieroglyphical Oedipus" <note>Kircher is referring to his own work, "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," where he attempts to solve the "riddles" of ancient symbols.</note> treats these things in a broad survey in his volume on the hieroglyphical Theology of the ancients. Since, therefore—to return to the plan—there is a certain wonderful connection of superior things with the inferior, and according to the celebrated pronouncement of the <term>Mecubalim</term> <note>The "Mecubalim" are practitioners of the Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition.</note>: <note>original: "nulla herba inferiùs sit, quæ non habeat suam plantam in supernis, quæ dicat ei, cresce;"</note> *there is no herb below that does not have its own plant in the heavens saying to it, "Grow!"*; and since, furthermore, certain members of the human body are like stars of the microcosm, and the plants of the microcosm have a certain relation both to the superior and inferior stars, we have decided to arrange here the analogy of the planets with both the microcosmic and <term>megacosmic</term> <note>The "megacosm" or macrocosm refers to the vast universe as a whole.</note> Zodiac, just as in the preceding parts we showed the interplay of the human body parts with the twelve signs of the Zodiac, so that students of the more secret medicine may have something to contemplate from this work of Light and Shadow.

## Physical Inquiry III.

### On the Sympathy of Celestial Stars with Terrestrial Stars.

<margin>The dignity of man.</margin>
**I**t is certain that the Heavenly Farmer implanted certain seeds into man at his birth <insert>into this small world</insert>, so that whichever seeds each person cultivates, those will grow. If he cultivates the vegetable seeds, he will become a plant; if the sensual seeds, he will become like a beast; if the rational seeds, he will emerge as a heavenly animal; if the intellectual seeds, he will be an Angel, transformed into the likeness of the Son of God through his actions. And if, perhaps content with no created thing, he retreats into the center of his own unity, he becomes one spirit with God in the "solitary darkness" of the Father, who is set above all things and stands before all. Thus, there is nothing in this universe that is not found in man, the son of the world, for whose sake all things were created. Since all things are directed toward man as their end goal, it was certainly necessary for all things to conspire for his preservation. Since both man and the other creatures made for him are subject to the heavenly motions, the celestial bodies will surely act upon the lower bodies that correspond to them through a certain similarity. Again, since the members of man are like internal stars preserving the life of the <term>microcosm</term>, and the life of the members cannot be preserved without nourishment taken from the outside, and since nourishment often infects the members and leads to their destruction due to the conflict of contrary dispositions: hence, provident Nature, the minister of God, ordained for each member its own <term>prophylactics</term> <note>Preventative or protective treatments.</note>, or preservatives of the members. And so that these might be known, she impressed upon each thing certain "characterisms" or external signs which, according to a wonderful analogy, would point out that member or humor that corresponded to them by a certain hidden sympathy.

<margin>Why plants, by their similarity, cure the limb they regard.</margin>
The question is asked, therefore: from where does this power to strengthen the limbs come? I respond first: from the different degrees of celestial heat with which each thing is imbued according to the requirement of its nature. Thus, for example, the celestial heat in the Liver <note>original: *Hepar*</note> is the same as that in the plants that regard it. For the constitution of the liver is one way in winter, another in summer, and another at other times; and by the same reasoning, the constitution of the Liverwort <note>original: *Hepatica*</note> plant is different at different times. Whoever, therefore, knows the laws of this natural marriage in both, will find that Liverwort applied to the liver at the opportune time performs a miraculous effect in strengthening it, defending it against both excessive inflammation and coldness. He will apply it skillfully and wisely who has an excellent knowledge of the secret properties corresponding to the four parts of the year, the months, and even the day—Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter—which this present **sundial** places before your eyes, as has been said. Secondly, I say that this power comes from a certain hidden sympathy that plants have toward the limbs, by which they seek each other out and rejoice in a friendly encounter. Hence, the aforementioned Liverwort, once taken internally, immediately runs to that member which is related to it by a certain natural similarity—namely, the liver. The member, dilated with joy as if by a friendly guest and closely united to it by a friendly attraction, is awakened from its lethargy and receives a maximum increase of vigor. Thus, Lungwort <note>original: *Pulmonaria*</note> flows to the lungs, the member assigned to its protection, as soon as it has been taken in; Motherwort <note>original: *Cardiaca*</note> rushes toward the heart, the fountain of life, through whatever gate is opened; for individual plants have innate seeds of the temperament of that member which they regard. From this, Nature expressed the outlines of said members in the fibers of those plants. As...

# Physico-Astrological Dialing

...subject. When I first observed this, I can hardly express how astonished I remained at such an unusual industriousness of nature. <margin>The wonderful power of nature.</margin> From this, experience has also taught that the liver of animals, when used as food for the liver, possesses great efficacy in strengthening the members they correspond to. I will not speak here of <term>Phytomancy</term> <note>The practice of divining the medicinal properties or omens of plants based on their physical appearance.</note>, by which we can sagaciously investigate the diseases to which each limb is subject by comparing the fibers and markings of plants to the lines of the hands; for the lines of a plant that resemble the lines in the hands indicating a certain disease are helpful in driving that disease away. Thus, nature has arranged a certain line in the leaves of the Malabathrum <note>original: *Melabathri*; likely the Indian bay leaf or cinnamon leaf.</note>, mirroring the line in the hand of someone suffering from colic, for the purpose of driving away that colic. Likewise, those subject to apoplexy have a line shaped like an anchor impressed upon their hands; since the Sweet Flag <note>original: *Acorum*</note> also expresses this shape in its leaves, it is a most proven remedy against apoplexy. See what we have handed down regarding these types of natural "signatures" in our *Egyptian Oedipus* <note>Kircher’s massive 1652 work on Egyptian lore and "universal knowledge."</note>, in the treatise on hieroglyphic medicine, which I have unearthed according to the dogmas of the ancient Egyptians—a subject, as far as I know, touched by no one until now.

Furthermore, it was clear from the first book that plants have the greatest affinity with the heavens. Hence, there is almost no month or zodiac sign that does not produce its own peculiar herbs, which acquire different qualities according to the various constitutions of climates and horizons, and according to the various degrees of heat. Thus, every native land contains within itself the "wombs" of its own element and provides for itself what is necessary. <margin>Every region brings forth its own remedies for the diseases found there.</margin> Nature produces and tempers herbs for every land and region, for its own people, its own climate, its own sky, and its own age. And just as the nature of places—due to certain hidden exhalations of the earth—produces certain diseases peculiar to individual regions, so it also produces specific herbs in that native soil as a remedy for the disease. Therefore, I wonder greatly why things are sought so anxiously from India which we have right here, meeting us within our own domestic walls. For it is certain that Indian plants, just as they are not accustomed to the soil of our regions, are neither fit for driving away the diseases peculiar to a specific homeland, nor are they in any way "friendly" to us, because of the diversity of climate and celestial influence. An example for us can be found in the *Arum* <note>Cuckoopint or Jack-in-the-pulpit.</note>, which provides the Egyptians with a most pleasant food; yet for us, on account of its notable sharpness and a certain caustic power, it is both harmful and unfit for eating. Likewise, the *Persea* tree <note>A fruit-bearing tree of ancient Egypt, often identified with *Mimusops schimperi*.</note> bears fruits which are counted among poisons by the Parthians and Egyptians, yet are counted among the better fruits for us. Therefore, individual plants in individual regions have certain corresponding places in the heavens, by whose benign influence they grow and are perfected for the benefit of man. Hence, the ancient physicians, by prudent counsel, assigned specific herbs to individual signs as well as to the planets. To avoid being overly long in describing them, I place here a catalog of them from Apuleius <note>Likely referring to Pseudo-Apuleius, the author of a famous 4th-century herbal.</note>.

# CHAPTER IV.

# On the physical clock of planetary governance, by which the shadow of the Sun shows which member of the human body each planet looks upon when positioned in the 12 signs.

<margin>What an unequal hour is.</margin>
We call this the **physical clock of planetary governance** because it demonstrates with shadowy fingers <note>A poetic reference to the gnomon or pointer of a sundial.</note> the dominion of each planet over the seven days of the week—governing powers which we read the ancients assigned to the individual hours of the natural day. Truly, so that these things may be better understood, it is useful to begin a little further back. Therefore, a **planetary** or **unequal hour** <note>In pre-modern timekeeping, the "artificial day" from sunrise to sunset was always divided into 12 hours. Consequently, an hour in summer was much longer than an hour in winter.</note> refers to the twelfth part of the artificial day, lying between the rising and setting of the Sun, or between its setting and rising. Regarding these, the ancients assigned individual planets to each hour by this logic: the first hour of the day, starting at sunrise, was always attributed to that planet from which the name of the day itself was taken. For it will be established from what follows that each day received its name from an individual planet.

Thus, on the **Day of the Moon** (Monday), the first hour was said to be the Moon's, the second Mars's, the third Mercury's, the fourth Jupiter's, the fifth Venus's, the sixth the Sun's, and so on through all the remaining hours, counting the planets in a circular order until reaching the first hour of the following day. If these are numbered correctly, they will always fall upon the planetary designation from which the day takes its name, as was said: regarding this, see the following table, in which we have noted the planet reigning during the first hour of both the artificial day and night.

But if you wish to know the governance of the remaining and succeeding hours of the day and night, take from the table itself the planet reigning in the first hour of that day or night. Finding this in the horizontal and bottom row of the table, you will give the second hour to the next one to the right, the third to the one after that, and so on, maintaining the order of hours and planets and repeating from the beginning on the left until you have finished the count of hours. For example, let the sixth hour of the Day of the Moon be proposed. Since the Moon (☽) dominates the first hour, having found the character for the Moon at the foot of the table, it gives the second hour to Saturn (♄), the third to Jupiter (♃), the fourth to Mars (♂), the fifth to the Sun (☉), and the sixth to Venus (♀). You conclude, therefore, that Venus governs the given hour; do the same for the others.

For the ancients believed that not only was one of the seven planets—the moderators of the world—set over each week, but also over each hour, and that by their providence everything in the world is governed. They learned the <margin>The harmonic governance of the planets.</margin> dominions of each from the "harmony of things" which they established with the things subject to them. For if someone refers the harmony—which the Greeks call *diapason* <note>original: *διαπασῶν*; the musical interval of an octave, literally "through all [notes]."</note>, by which the universal power of all music is believed to be contained—to these stars by which all the adornment of heaven is distinguished, following the same path as they move, and beginning from that supreme sphere attributed to Saturn (♄), skipping the following days and naming the lord of the fourth; then skipping two others and adding the seventh; and finally proceeding in this manner to review the presiding spirits in order and thus count the days: he will find that they all agree through a certain musical logic with that celestial distinction and arrangement. All of this is beautifully shown by the heptagon <note>A seven-sided figure.</note> placed here, which Dio Nicæus <note>Dio Cassius (ca. 155–235 AD), a Roman historian who explained the planetary week in his "Roman History."</note> confirms in almost the same words in his *Life of Caesar*:

> "For if one applies the harmony called the *diatessaron* <note>original: *διὰ τεσσάρων*; the musical interval of a fourth.</note>, which is also believed to hold the glory of music together, to all the stars by which the whole order of heaven is arranged... naming the lord of the fourth... and proceeding in this way to review the successions of the weeks... one finds the order of the days follows a musical principle." <note>This quote from Dio Cassius explains why the sequence of days (Sun, Moon, Mars, etc.) differs from the physical order of the planets (Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, etc.).</note>

The diagram above represents the planetary heptagon. At the top of the outer circle is the symbol for the Moon (☽). Moving clockwise, the symbols are Saturn (♄), Jupiter (♃), Mars (♂), Sun (☉), Venus (♀), and Mercury (☿). A seven-pointed star is inscribed within the circle, with lines connecting the planets in the sequence of the days of the week: Sun to Moon, Moon to Mars, Mars to Mercury, Mercury to Jupiter, Jupiter to Venus, Venus to Saturn, and Saturn back to Sun.

-># Physical-astrological Gnomonics<- <note>The study of sundials as they relate to natural and astrological influences.</note>

Some also count the hours of day and night in this way: they begin counting immediately from the first hour, so that you assign it to Saturn, then the following to Jupiter, the third to Mars, the fourth to the Sun, the fifth to Venus, the sixth to Mercury, and the seventh to the Moon. This follows the sequence of the celestial spheres handed down by the Egyptians. You repeat this cycle until, passing through 24 hours, you find the first hour of the following day attached to the Sun. Then, if you do the same thing for those 24 hours in the same way as before, you will assign the first hour of the third day to the Moon. If you observe this same pattern for the rest, any given day will take on a presiding spirit <note>original: "genium"</note> corresponding to itself according to the decrees of the ancients; concerning these things, see our *Hieroglyphic Astrology* where it is treated more extensively.

At this point, the Hebrews ask how the moral days of the Christians agree with natural ones, since Moses is adapted from the whole of physiology <note>In this context, "physiology" refers to the study of the physical laws of nature.</note>, and therefore seems preferable to all others because God is proved to be the same author of both nature and the Law? I respond that the Author of nature is the founder of both the Hebrew Law and the Christian Law—that is, the law of scripture and the law of grace. In the former, He expressed the planets and the signs of heaven; in the latter, however, it will be clear from what follows that He has declared all these things more beautifully. Indeed, the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note> is observed first by the Church, both so that we do not coincide with the Saturnine Sabbath <note>Saturday</note> of the Hebrews, and because the world and light began on that day; and after the week of ages and times, there will be rest in it through a return to the first principle. In the Sabbath, however, there is no return. The Sun is the Lord of the stars, not Saturn. Likewise, the movable feasts instituted with the greatest judgment by the orthodox Church harmonize strongly with nature.

<margin>The liturgical year of the Orthodox Church is established according to the model of nature.</margin>
We celebrate Easter at the first lunation, when Christ rises, and the trees and seeds rise again. We celebrate the Ascension when things, with heat prevailing, send forth spirits and breath upward. The coming of the Holy Spirit, when much heat of the Sun descends to us. The coming of Christ <note>Advent/Christmas</note>, when the Sun begins to return to us; and the feast of Saint John <note>the Baptist</note> when it begins to recede, according to the saying of John: *He must increase, but I must decrease* <note>original: "Oportet me minui, illum autem crescere" — John 3:30. This refers to the summer solstice (St. John's Day) when days begin to shorten, and the winter solstice (Christmas) when they begin to lengthen.</note>. We celebrate Lent when the Sun is in Pisces, and when humors <note>The bodily fluids thought to control health and temperament.</note> are exuberant, we fast usefully. In the morning of the year—namely, in the springtime—Christ rises; at midday, He ascends to heaven and sends the Spirit (summer is the midday); in Autumn, Matthew writes the Gospel of the departing one, as if in the old age of the year. In midwinter, which is the decrepit age, Christ is born; and at midnight, when the day begins to increase. The twelve Apostles are marked by the twelve months; Matthias is intercalated in the leap year <note>original: "bissexto"</note> in place of Judas. You see, therefore, how aptly the institutions of the Church correspond to the seasons of nature.

But leaving these things behind, let us hasten to the construction of the Shadow-clock <term>Sciathericum: a device, like a sundial, that uses shadows to tell time or show celestial data.</term>.

### Problem IV.

*To construct a Shadow-clock of planetary governance, by which the shadow of the Sun shows which planet reigns through the individual days and hours of the week, and which member of the human body each planet looks upon when positioned in the 12 signs.*

<margin>Illustration XVII</margin>

**F**irst, in a wave of a sphere, or in a certain oval figure, let the planetary clocks be arranged according to the seven days of the week. We have amply taught how these should be constructed above in Book 4. You shall place the characters of the planets on each of their hour lines in exactly the way you see done here.

Second, let the Zodiac be described within the oval figure, which you will divide on both sides into seven spaces, each of which will be assigned to individual planets. Within these spaces, letters corresponding to the twelve signs will be placed in the order you see done in the figure.

### Use of the Shadow-clock.

**F**irst, if you wish to know at any moment which planet governs in heaven according to the mind of the ancients: with the instrument exposed to the Sun and properly situated, first observe the day within the elliptical ring for which you desire to know the dominion of a certain planet. For instance, if on the Day of the Sun <note>Sunday</note>, look at the Shadow-clock assigned to the Day of the Sun or the Lord's Day; for in that dial, the shadow of the gnomon will show both the hour and, within the hour lines, the character of the governing planet. Thus, at the second hour, it will show the dominion of Mercury ☿, at the third hour the Moon ☽, and so on for the others. Likewise, the Shadow-clock of the Moon shows the dominions of the planets for the Day of the Moon <note>Monday</note>. The Shadow-clock of Mars will teach the dominions of the individual planets on the Day of Mars <note>Tuesday</note>. The Shadow-clock of Mercury the same governance on the Day of Mercury <note>Wednesday</note>, and so on for the rest, as the figure clearly shows. For there are individual Shadow-clocks corresponding to the individual days of the week.

Furthermore, once the planetary hour and the character of the dominant planet are obtained, enter with it into the space attributed to it within the Zodiac; then see which twelfth-part <note>original: "dodecamorium," a 30-degree segment or sign of the zodiac.</note> of the Zodiac the shadow of the gnomon strikes. The common area, or the common intersection of the space of the found planet and a certain sign, will give a letter signifying which member of the body the Zodiacal sign looks upon with the discovered planet. But let us declare the matter with an example. If you wish to know, for instance, which member the Sun positioned in Aries ♈ looks upon together with Saturn ♄, see where the sign of Aries ♈ (which the shadow of the gnomon strikes at that time) intersects with the space of Saturn ♄: in the common intersection of both, the letter I will occur, which in any of the four corners...

# CHAPTER V.
## Concerning the Sundials of the secondary movers, or concerning the representation of the motions of the Planets by shadow.

<margin>Difficulty of the undertaking.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative historiated initial 'C' showing a landscape scene with figures and classical architecture, possibly a garden of knowledge.</image-desc>
**S**INCE in the preceding sections we have handed down various modes and methods of showing the teaching of the "first mover" <note>The "Primum Mobile," or the daily rotation of the heavens.</note> on various planes <term>by means of shadows</term> <note>original: "σκιαθενικῶς" (skiathenikōs)</note>; nothing remained except that we should also find a way by which, with the same diligence, the "secondary movers"—that is, the motions of the planets—can be shown by shadow. This undertaking seemed nearly <term>impossible</term> <note>original: "ἀδύνατον" (adynaton)</note> because of the almost infinite diversity of the said motions, the as-yet unexplored knowledge of their periods, and the various conditions of the planets' direction, station, and retrograde motion. Considering all these things, we were very nearly ready to cast aside almost all hope and spirit regarding the proposed subject. Nevertheless, lest our Art of Light and Shadow be deprived of such a wonderful industry and a technique unseen until now, we have moved every stone to reach our desires. At last, a certain method occurred to us, which although it is by no means universal, can nevertheless be made universal in that manner which we shall reveal shortly.

### Physical Inquiry IV.
#### On the nature and qualities of the planets.

AND since it is our purpose to present a theory not only of astronomical but also of physical science, it seemed appropriate to treat also the nature of the individual Planets, so that we may assign to each its suitable qualities and effects. Let us begin, therefore, with <term>Saturn</term> <note>The symbol ♄ is used in the text.</note>.

### §. I. On the nature of Saturn.

<margin>What kind of body Saturn is.</margin>
The planet Saturn is said, by the opinion of all Astrologers, to be malefic, <term>unbalanced</term> <note>original: "ἄμετρος" (ametros)</note> or intemperate, cold, and dry, and endowed with the greatest power for harm: the reason for which is sought. We say, therefore, that this planet is a celestial body endowed with such virtue that as soon as the Sun's...
