When the rays of the Sun strike [the planet Saturn], its power—mixed with said solar rays—is carried to the earth in various configurations relative to the Sun and other planets. For the most part, it produces harmful effects; it promotes the melancholic humor in human bodies by a certain hidden force, and hence aggravates those bodies, even wearing them out with premature old age and decay. If left to its own devices, it fosters and excites a dry and cold quality in these lower realms, and even in human bodies, as Ptolemy testifies in these words: *The star belonging to Saturn has a greater power in cooling and, in a moderate way, drying.* <note>original Greek: "ὁ τῷ Κρόνῳ ἀστὴρ πλέον ἔχει τὸ ποιητικὸν ἐν τῷ ψύχειν, καὶ ἡμέρᾳ ξυρανεῖν"</note> There is no one who does not know how much these two qualities—cold and dry—harm the heat and moisture of human life. Therefore, the nature of this planet is prone to corruption. Yet, since nothing exists in nature that does not consist of its own goodness—for just as great benefits often come from poisons tempered by art without causing harm—so too from the mixture, radiation, and harmonious temperament of this star (however ill-omened) with other planets and stars, extraordinary benefits flow:

<margin>The most excellent men were melancholics.</margin>
For while it fixes the minds of men, it renders them most fit for labor, industry, and speculation, as Aristotle testifies. Hence, it is certain that whoever flourished in genius, or was outstanding in Philosophy, the administration of the Republic, poetry, or the cultivation of other arts, was melancholic. From this class we produce Socrates, Demosthenes, Archimedes, Plato, Galen, Caesar, Virgil, and others. Both historians and their own great works, immense labors, unconquerable endurance, deep thought, and tireless study of inventions—by which they achieved immortality—bear witness that they were such men.

Nor does Saturn (♄) exert its power only on the intellect, but also in stirring the humors of the body, though not in the same way for everyone. Just as wine, due to the <term>idiosyncrasies</term> <note>From the Greek "ἰδιοσυγκρασίας," meaning the unique physical temperament or "mixture" of an individual's constitution.</note> and varieties of natures, does not affect everyone it inebriates in one and the same manner, nor acts in the same way; for it drives some to talkativeness and thence to brawls, others to vomiting, some to silence, sleep, or laughter, and most to tumults and arms; so the melancholic humor, serving under Saturn, moves some to laughter, like Democritus, and others to tears, like Heraclitus. Some it moves to talkativeness, like Thersites; some to eloquence, like Nestor; to silence and patience, like Socrates; to fear, like Pisander; to cheerfulness, like Lucullus; to sadness, like Crassus; to deep thought and the hidden knowledge of things, like Archimedes. It affects others differently according to the condition, quality, and quantity of the rising soot and vapor which it excites in the "Saturnine" blood. For if the fumes, while seeking the citadel of the mind directly, disturb the animal spirit mixed within it, it follows that they create, foster, and feign various imaginations, thoughts, reasonings, and phantasms. You can recognize the imagining of such things in the melancholic juice and in fermented blood in any way possible. For its slimy humor, caught untimely in thick matter, becomes like a poison, which indeed lies dormant in certain living bodies like sulfur removed from a flame; but in others it blazes up, and like ignited sulfur, it not only burns but fills everything with noxious vapor. Unless this were restrained by the "darts" <note>An astrological metaphor for the aspect rays of other planets.</note> of the other planets, if left to its own devices, it would turn everything upside down. Hence its immoderate influence renders men misanthropic, solitary, always driven as if into despair, suspicious, aspiring to nothing high, and infested with the most turbulent and terrifying dreams. In the humors, it excites hypochondriacal and colic pains, quartan fevers, epilepsy, elephantiasis, and other such things; one and the same power stirs all these according to the different constitution of the Saturnine humor in different men. Indeed, in the earth and the air, it produces similar effects corresponding to itself according to a certain analogy, which were discussed in the preceding sections.

<margin>What the body of Saturn is like:</margin>
If anyone, therefore, were to fashion a spherical mass composed of Larch resin and the crushed roots of Nightshade, Aconite, Mandrake, and Henbane, and were to set the finished mass on fire; that mass, evaporating Saturnine fumes on all sides, would produce the same effects in the human body as the breathing out of the body of Saturn in the system of the world when struck by Solar fire. Yet, just as these species, when mixed with others as in a <term>Theriac</term> <note>A famous ancient "universal" medical concoction used as an antidote to poison.</note>, provide a life-giving medicine, so too is Saturn when mixed with the beneficial light of the remaining planets.

With these things briefly premised concerning the nature of Saturn, let us now proceed to construct the *Sciathericon* <note>A Greek-derived term for a shadow-measuring instrument or sundial.</note> itself, in which not only its motion under the Zodiac at any moment is shown by the shadow of the Sun, but also its aforementioned properties are designated with singular industry.

On the heads of these dials, the characters of the zodiac signs are placed, while in the subsequent spaces, the numbers for the degrees are inscribed. This is done so that after a thirty-year period, the previous numbers can be erased and the revolving dials can be reinscribed with new numbers and the degrees of the planet's motion for a new series of years. In this way, the motion will be continued perpetually every thirty years, with the lines and boundaries remaining the same; only the change in numbers and the adjustment of the dials is required. <margin>Use of the same.</margin>
Once the Sciathericum is exposed to the Sun and properly situated, look for the common intersection of the <term>hyperbola</term> <note>The curved path the sun's shadow traces on a flat surface during a single day</note> which the Sun describes on that same day with the curve or bend marked with the number of the current year. At that point, the degree which Saturn holds at that time will present itself. For example, if the Sun is entering the point of **Aries (♈)** and you wish to know which degree of the Zodiac Saturn occupies: see which line the Sun describes over the surface on that same day; where this line intersects the curve for the year 1644, there you will find the sought-after degree of Saturn. But these things can be better understood from the <term>illustration</term> <note>original: "Iconismo"; likely referring to the engraving on page 405</note> than declared with many words.

### Problem VI.
### To construct a Sciathericum for Jupiter (♃).

Jupiter—called <term>Zeus</term> in Greek—is named the "Preserver," the "Savior," the "Hospitable," the "Beneficent," the "Healing Deity," and the "Benign," not only by the Greeks but also by Latin poets and orators. He is also called the "Father of both gods and men," and not without great reason. For since his nature is remarkably temperate, he possesses qualities that are perfectly suited for preserving the world.

<margin>The nature of Jupiter.</margin>
From this it happens that, whatever he is mixed with, he always strikes sublunary things <note>Things on Earth, beneath the moon's sphere</note> with an incorrupt flow of rays. With his beneficial rays, he breaks the harmful power of both Saturn and Mars. Like a certain moderator and arbiter of the strifes between Mars and Saturn, he keeps both in check. For as Ptolemy rightly says: <note>original Greek: "ὁ τοῦ Διὸς ἀστὴρ εὐκράτου ἔχει τὸ ποιητικὸν τῆς δυνάμεως μεταξὺ γινομένος τῆς κινήσεως αὐτοῦ τῆς τε κατὰ τὸν Χρόνον ψυκτικῆς, καὶ τῆς κατὰ τὸν Ἄρεα καυστικῆς θερμαντικῆς, καὶ ὑγραίνει."</note> "The star of Jupiter has a temperate productive power, being situated between the cooling movement of Saturn and the burning, heating movement of Mars, and it also provides moisture." Therefore, the cause of such healthy powers should certainly be attributed to nothing else than the Jovian disk or globe itself, which is like a celestial and aromatic <term>spice-box</term> <note>original: "pixis"; a small box or vessel, often used for medicine or incense</note> imbued with most excellent powers.

<margin>Jupiter has dominion over the spirit.</margin>
When these powers are breathed out by the striking of the Sun's ray, they bestow life and spirit upon the entire world below the moon. For this reason, Jupiter is judged to preside over the blood, the heart, the spirits, the lungs, and the other vital members in the "lesser world" <note>The human body, often called the "microcosm" in Renaissance philosophy</note>; and consequently over all other things having a certain analogy to them, as the table in the preceding chapter teaches. If he flows kindly into these, he constitutes a noble human temperament fit for performing great deeds. And to settle the matter briefly, he shares almost all faculties in common with the Sun. Since we have treated this more extensively elsewhere, I did not wish to be longer here.

Having properly examined these things: you shall delineate the Sciathericum of Jupiter and its motion under the Zodiac in exactly the same way as you did for Saturn (♄). I shall explain the matter in a few words. The tropical or periodic year of Jupiter is nothing other than a complete revolution from a certain point of the Zodiac back to the same point. Since this occurs in a space of about twelve years, you will first describe the gnomonic Zodiac, as was done in the preceding sections.

<margin>Construction of the Sciathericum for Jupiter.</margin>
Then you will divide the same across its entire width into twelve rotations by a wavy line. Or, so that we are not forced to change the curves every twelve years, you may divide it into thirty spaces, as was done in the Sciathericum of Saturn. To each of these boundaries, you will add the number of the years, as is clear in the figure. Within the individual year-curves, you will arrange the locations of the said planet in the Zodiac according to the degrees and signs imprinted on the revolving dials, as described from the Ephemerides. You shall also ascribe the Jovian effects on different classes of things within the spaces of the signs, and you will have the sought-after Sciathericum, as the figure shows. The use differs in no way from the use declared in the preceding section; except that just as the numbers of the Saturnine Sciathericum must be changed after a thirty-year period, so must the numbers of this one after the same period of years. Thus we have constructed the Sciathericum of Jupiter, which was to be done.

### Problem VII.
### To construct a Sciathericum for Mars (♂).

That the star of Mars is of a fiery and clearly glowing nature is sufficiently shown by the epithet <term>Pyroeis</term> <note>Greek for "The Fiery One"</note> by which the Greeks entitle him. For he has a burning heat and a power to do harm—that is, he is favored by an affinity for fiery moisture. He is an inauspicious star and, along with Saturn, a "malefic" <note>A planet believed to have a harmful influence in astrology</note>, as one for whom it is more fitting to burn and destroy than to preserve. This is recognized in what yellow bile produces in human bodies. Hence he induces many vices and evils of both body and mind. For from his vehement heat and the vehement commotion of bile, he excites the worst disturbances, which are followed by violent and inconsiderate passions even in the actions of a composed mind, as if in the battle line of which fight brawls, contentions, homicides, wars, and similar things. Just as...

# Physico-Astrological Dialing

Just as Nature has established the globe of Jupiter within the universe to promote vital activities through its benign influence, so too has she joined to it the star of Mars, a body filled with pestiferous exhalations with which it strikes the lower world.

<margin>The quality of the body of Mars (♂).</margin>
If one were to construct an ignited sphere made of pitch, resin, arsenic, antimony, sulfur, mercury, orpiment, and similar substances, it would produce the same effects in humans that we see Mars causing in the lower world: manias, frenzy, violent inflammations, burning fevers, skin infections, the plague, and the like. For this reason, the Greeks quite rightly attributed <term>the gall bladder</term> <note>Greek: "kystin cholēdokon"</note> to it from among the internal organs, which the Latins called the "little bag of bile," the small storehouse of the choleric humor. As Ptolemy rightly says: <quote>It has a nature that is mostly burning, and it produces a color like fire, since it is placed very close to the sun's sphere.</quote> <note>original Greek: "Μάλιστα δὲ καυστικὸν ἔχει φύσιν ᾧ πύρει χρώματα ποιεῖσθαι πρὸς τὸν ἥλιον ἐγγύτατα ὑποκειμένους αὐτοῦ τῆς ἡλιακῆς σφαίρας."</note> Furthermore, just as almost all violent and acute diseases originate from bile, so too do all the pestilences of the sublunary world originate from the harmful evaporation of the globe of Mars. Unless this were mitigated by the mediation of Jupiter and the benign aspects of other planets, as has been said, it would destroy the world itself with its savagery. Hence, Nature willed to place it in the greatest eccentricity of all <note>The 17th-century view that Mars has a notably non-circular orbit, which keeps it further from Earth at times to lessen its "heat"</note>, so that its pernicious force might be tempered by the most remote distance.

<margin>Why Mars has the greatest eccentricity.</margin>
And although Mars is of such a nature as we have described, lest Nature be said to have acted like a cruel stepmother in the arrangement of natural things, she endowed it with such gifts that, along with its disadvantages, it also provides the greatest benefits. Indeed, the world could not be preserved without it, and therefore it is most necessary to the world. It seems to provide for the "greater world" <note>The macrocosm or universe</note>—when it is weighed down by a multiple heap of humors—what <term>Spanish flies</term> <note>Latin: "cantharides"; these blister beetles were used in medicine to create "counter-irritation" and draw out toxins</note> provide to the "microcosm" <note>the human body</note> when it is placed in the final crisis of life due to deadly symptoms. Endowed with a certain caustic and most poisonous quality, these beetles dissipate the gathering of disease-causing matter by attracting it from the center to the surface, thus freeing the person in danger. So it is that there is no evil in the nature of things that does not eventually yield to the good of the whole and the preservation of the universe. But see our more extensive discussion on these matters regarding the <term>Egyptian Typhon Mars</term> in our <term>Hieroglyphic Astrology</term> <note>Likely referring to Kircher's "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," where he correlates Egyptian mythology with celestial bodies</note>.

<margin>Construction of the Sciathericon of Mars (♂).</margin>
With these things established, you shall construct a <term>Sciathericon</term> <note>A specialized planetary sundial</note> for Mars in exactly the same manner as the previous ones. However, since the period of Mars is approximately two years, these periods must be multiplied on a winding line of this kind, so that we are not forced to change the numbers of the Sciathericon every two years. If, therefore, you distribute the width of the gnomonic Zodiac into thirty segments, you will have a thirty-year <term>Ephemeris</term> <note>A table of planetary positions</note> inscribed by the Zodiac; once these have revolved, the <term>revolving dials</term> <note>original: "verticilli"</note> must be changed along with the numbers according to the said method. The effects that Mars provides in each sign will always remain the same; however, it will undergo accidental changes insofar as the Martian force will be increased by the aspect of other planets. Thus, in fire signs, along with the aspect of fiery planets, the Martian force will be increased; in water signs, it will be tempered; and so on for the rest, as has been said.

### Problem VIII.

-> To construct the Sciathericon for Venus (♀) and Mercury (☿). <-

The planet Venus is a beneficial planet of the same nature as Jupiter: moderate, moist, and warm. She is called Venus because of the temperate nature of her moisture and the innate beneficial power she possesses and pours forth. Experience has taught that her nature is such that she supplies a sweet and slightly moist juice to lower bodies and substances for as long as they are being generated. However, she does so in such a way that she dews them rather than drenching or flooding them, following the nature of dew rather than rain; perhaps for this reason she is called "Alma" <note>Nourishing or Kind</note> from the word for "nourishing." As for her other quality, namely coldness: just as we have established one kind of heat that fosters and nourishes—such as that of the Sun, then Jupiter, and that which imitates innate heat—and another that burns and destroys—such as that of Mars and the yellow bile—so in the nature of cold, we establish one that is <term>well-tempered</term> <note>Greek: "eukraton"</note>, such as is found in the ray of Venus and in sweet phlegm, over which the "Cyprian" <note>A common poetic name for Venus, born from the sea near Cyprus</note> presides. The other is <term>unbalanced</term> <note>Greek: "akraton"</note>, corrupting, and intemperate, such as is found in Saturn and the melancholic humor.

<margin>Composition of the globe of Venus (♀).</margin>
If one were to make a globe from mastic, amber, musk, rose water, or Malmsey wine, and heat it with a fire placed beneath, he would create a small globe similar in quality and effects to the globe of Venus, arising from its exhalation. The fire heating the Venusian globe is the nearby Sun; being struck by the Solar rays, it breathes out all kinds of qualities that are health-giving to both worlds. Hence it fills the air with temperate, moist, and most fertile winds, granting a pleasant clearing of the weather, the timely sending of rains, and successful voyages for ships. It grants an abundance, growth, and goodness of useful animals and crops; hence comes the luxury of good things. Luxury has the pleasures of Venus attached to it; for this reason, in man, she is said to preside over the liver, the source of pleasure and physical titillation. But let these few words out of many suffice.

<margin>Composition of the globe of Mercury (☿).</margin>
The planet Mercury is so named because of its versatile nature, by which, like Proteus, it transforms itself into all things. And although we denied above in Book I that Mercury has great power over these lower regions, both because of its tiny body and because of the solar rays, by which...

...by which its power is somehow absorbed and suffocated. However, if the various experiments observed by astrologers regarding its nature are true, I would say this happens primarily because it is so close to the Sun, and almost always lies hidden beneath its rays, never departing from it by more than twenty-eight degrees. It is also a neighbor to the Moon, which is closest to the Earth; hence, a nearly equal power emerges in drying and absorbing moisture. Because of its speed as it moves around the Sun, it is the cause of sudden changes in either direction; therefore, it has great power in identifying and altering the qualities and humors of bodies. Thus, at one time its breath is found to be cold, at another humid, sometimes hot and parched, and occasionally windy, because it very quickly takes on the nature of the Sun when nearby, or that of the Moon or Venus when it mixes with them. But since the nature of this planet <note>Mercury</note> is not yet perfectly understood, we shall refrain from saying more about it.

With these matters properly completed, let us now see by what method the <term>Sciatheric</term> <note>from the Greek "skia" (shadow) and "thera" (hunting/capturing); the art of sundial construction</note> instruments of the said planets can be constructed.

<margin>
Construction of Sciatheric instruments for Venus (♀), the Moon (☽), Mercury (☿), and the North (☊) and South (☋) Nodes.
</margin>
First, let a gnomonic Zodiac be made for both, which you will divide into thirty divisions according to latitude. In each of these, you will describe the locations and degrees extracted from the <term>Ephemerides</term> <note>astronomical tables providing the positions of celestial bodies at regular intervals</note> according to the order of years assigned to each, using the same diligence you see here. By also adding the effects and properties in the spaces designated for this purpose, you will have finished Sciatheric instruments. These numbers will last for thirty years; once these have passed, the years must be changed and other numbers inscribed on the boundaries, as was stated in the preceding sections.

### Problem IX.
### To construct a Sciatheric instrument for the North Node (☊) and South Node (☋), or the Eclipses of the Sun and Moon.

It remains for us to also explain the Sciatheric demonstration of the "labors" of the Sun and Moon—that is, of eclipses. You must remember first of all that the Zodiac itself is intersected through its middle by a continuous line called the <term>Ecliptic</term> <note>the apparent path of the Sun across the sky; eclipses only occur when the Moon crosses this line</note>, and the Sun never departs from it, always following that same path. But the Moon, wandering by several degrees, ranges through almost the entire Zodiac and does not always meet the Sun directly under the ecliptic; most of the time she passes freely, having only "greeted" him from a distance. For instance, while the Sun is in some degree of Aries (♈), the Moon often passes beyond the tropic, sometimes up to five degrees away from the ecliptic, sometimes less; or, having slipped toward the lower signs, she is carried in the same way beyond or on this side of the tropic of Cancer (♋), and does not touch the ecliptic at all. Yet it is necessary, if an eclipse is to occur, that both the Sun and the Moon (as they approach a Northern or Southern sign) fall directly under the ecliptic so as to shadow the Earth between them, just as if a line dropped from there, dividing the machine of the world, were being drawn through. Therefore, whether the Earth itself is to be placed opposite the Moon so that its shadow (stretching that far) obscures it, or the Moon is placed in front of the Sun to withdraw its light from the Earth: it is necessary for both planets to be found under the ecliptic. You must conceive in your mind that in two places on the ecliptic, at an equal interval of degrees, that line—or circle—through which the Moon travels crosses transversely. Where it bounces away from the ecliptic, it leaves an open gap; but where it joins the ecliptic, astronomers call one part the **Head of the Dragon** and the other the **Tail**, or better, as Ptolemy calls them: <term>the ascending and descending nodes</term> <note>original Greek: "syndesmon anabibazonta kai katabibazonta"</note>.

<margin>
Explanation of the Head and Tail of the Dragon.
</margin>
These points seem to us to move through the heavens no differently than the Sun and the rest of the planets travel in an uninterrupted course; hence it happens that they are always found somewhere in opposite places of the Zodiac. It is called the **Ascending Node** when it seeks our zenith, and the **Descending Node** when it recedes from it. The motion of both nodes is different from the motions of the other planets: for in 21 days it completes one degree, just as the same number of years are counted in the cycle of Lunar conjunctions; and this is the number they call the **Golden Number**, or the nineteen-year cycle, about which we speak more fully in the Ninth Book. These two nodes are therefore those most famous points observed with the greatest diligence by astronomers, and they have great power and efficacy in the changes of the lower world. This is not because some power resides in the points themselves (which are merely imaginary), but because the eclipses of the Sun and Moon cause various effects according to the nature and quality of the signs in which they are found. For an eclipse of the Sun and Moon occurring in the Northern node produces one effect, while one happening in the Southern node produces another. Likewise, an eclipse in either node produces one effect when positioned in Aries, Taurus, or Gemini (♈ ♉ ♊), and another in Cancer, Leo, or Virgo (♋ ♌ ♍), and so on for the rest. For in Aries, or the springtime, when heat is needed, the air receives a more notable harm in promoting the generation of things from the privation of light than in Leo, where the vehement heat is somewhat tempered by an occurring eclipse; and so on for the others. However, so that you may know the effects of individual eclipses, I have thought it best to subjoin here those collected from various authors.

<margin>
From where the Golden Number takes its origin.
</margin>

->Physico-astrological Gnomonics.<-

## Rules, under whose direction Astrologers are accustomed to divine from eclipses, drawn from Ptolemy, Cardano, and others.

**E**clipses of both luminaries <note>the Sun and the Moon</note> possess great power over the changes of the year: therefore, before a judgment is offered regarding the quality of the year, eclipses must be considered. One should inquire into the nature not only of the eclipses of that same year, but even those of past years, because the effect of eclipses is often deferred to another time. Therefore, so that the effects of eclipses may be well understood, the following rules shall be observed.

I. Eclipses of the Sun cool the earth greatly: therefore, they ought not to be universal for the globe, since they are of a destructive quality, which nature flees.

II. Eclipses of the Moon are always drying in themselves, and they cool only a little.

III. When great eclipses are multiplied, sterility necessarily follows in the subsequent years, because the earth is cooled and dried out.

IV. If with this there should follow copious rains or floods, which are certainly accustomed to happen when the cold has increased; then a dire famine follows, and the greatest penury of things.

V. Eclipses have three powers: a potent one by reason of conjunction or opposition; a general one, because they cool slowly and thus are extended over many days; and a proper <note>specific</note> one, which is held by the name of the place where they occur.

VI. The Lord of the eclipse <note>the planet ruling the sign or house where the eclipse occurs</note> has great power in the eclipse, therefore its nature must be attended to: So says Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the 2nd-century astronomer and author of the *Tetrabiblos*</note>.

VII. Fixed stars accompanying the place of the eclipse, which at that time are either rising or holding the Midheaven <note>the highest point in the sky</note>, have the most influence: for which reason their locations must be considered with the utmost care.

<margin>Lords of the eclipses.</margin>
VIII. Saturn, when he is the lord of the eclipse, causes corruption from cold: he brings about long illnesses, wasting diseases, consumptions arising from <term>catarrhs</term> <note>excessive buildup of mucus</note>, fluxes, and <term>quartan fevers</term> <note>a fever that recurs every four days, often associated with malaria</note>; he brings exiles, terrors, and a scarcity of animals, diseases of beasts, horrendous cold, ice, fog, thick clouds, copious darkness, snows, shipwrecks, the death of fish, floods of rivers, the tainting of waters, the rotting of fruits, caterpillars, locusts, and other things of that kind.

IX. Jupiter, when he predominates in an eclipse, gives an abundance of useful things, the destruction of harmful ones, a healthy air—windy and humid—moderate increases in rivers, the death of fierce animals, and an abundance of gentle ones; by this healthfulness, he subdues the ruinous nature of the lunar quality.

X. Mars effects bilious diseases <note>illnesses related to "yellow bile," one of the four humors</note>, eruptions of blood, acute infirmities, <term>tertian fevers</term> <note>fevers recurring every three days</note>, hot, pestilential, and wasting winds, lightning, hurricanes, drought, the surging of the sea, sterility of crops, and conflagration.

XI. Venus brings fecundity, temperate winds, humidity, timely rains, useful overflows of waters, and a wealth of living things.

XII. Mercury brings dry diseases, daily fevers, consumptions, coughs, shortness of breath, strong, disordered, and unstable winds, and fiery thunders; however, if he strikes while <term>occidental</term> <note>setting in the west after the sun</note>, he diminishes lightning and the destruction of animals or plants.

XIII. The "images" of the stars <note>constellations</note> and the signs of the Zodiac, according to the diverse qualities with which they are endowed at the time of the eclipse, exert their influence.

XIV. Astrologers believe that the lords of the eclipses vary in their actions according to the variety of the <term>houses</term> <note>astrological divisions of the sky</note> in which either the eclipses occur or the lords themselves reside.

<margin>What the color of the eclipse signifies.</margin>
XV. A black and leaden color of the luminaries at the time of an eclipse signifies Saturnine effects; white signifies Jovial <note>from Jupiter</note> effects; reddish signifies Martian effects; yellow signifies Venerean effects; and a variegated color signifies Mercurial effects. When these colors are diffused through the entire bodies of the luminaries, they extend themselves to many provinces. So says Ptolemy.

XVI. "Hairy stars" <note>comets</note> appearing at the time of eclipses partake of the nature of Mars and Mercury and kindle the bile; whence they also provoke wars. So says Albumazar <note>original: "Albumazar," the Latinized name of the Persian astrologer Abu Ma'shar</note>.

XVII. An eclipse of the Sun or Moon falling upon a flowering tree renders it sterile for the year. So says Cardanus <note>original: "Cardanus," referring to Gerolamo Cardano, a 16th-century Italian polymath</note>.

XVIII. An eclipse of the Sun falling upon a flowering harvest brings sterility. The same author.

XIX. Eclipses are accustomed to bring rains, especially if they are aided by Saturn and Venus; but drought, if by Jupiter and Mars.

XX. Eclipses in earthly signs dry things out and bring sterility; in watery signs they moisten and cause plagues along with sterilities; in airy signs they bring winds and seditions along with pestilence; in fiery signs they bring fires and heat, wars, and much death.

XXI. All these things happen chiefly to those regions which are either under the sign of the eclipse or are joined to it in any way; and to those men whose personal nature agrees with those same signs.

XXII. Cardano pronounces that for as many <term>equinoctial hours</term> <note>standardized 60-minute hours</note> as elapse during the time of eclipses, the effects will last for that many years in a solar eclipse, and for that many months in a lunar eclipse.

XXIII. An eclipse falling on the eastern <term>finitor</term> <note>the horizon</note> signifies that the future effect, as far as its beginning <note>original: "exordium"</note>, will occur in the next four months; but as for its completion <note>original: "perfectionem"</note>, the effects will be more vehement in the first...

[...the first] third of the total duration. So says <note>Abu l-Hasan 'Ali ibn Abi l-Rijal, known as</note> Avenragel.
XXIV. If it occurs in the mid-heaven <note>the highest point of the sun's path</note>, the intensity of the effects will be in the middle third of the total duration.
XXV. If it occurs on the western horizon <note>the descendant</note>, it will be in the last third; and it is the same if the Lord of the eclipse <note>the ruling planet of the sign where the eclipse occurs</note> is in those same places. So says <note>Girolamo</note> Cardano.
And these are the effects which Astrologers are accustomed to consider in eclipses; many of these are true and founded in nature, though some also savor of I know not what astrological vanity. I would not always ascribe the stated effects to the influences of the planets; but rather, at times, to the disposition of the Solar body itself as it influences the lower world, about which more was said at length in chapters 1, 2, and 3. However, if anyone wishes to follow those astrological rules, they have my permission. But let these remarks on the effects of eclipses suffice: now let us return at last to the Problem at hand.

<margin>Construction of the Shadow-chart for the Lunar Nodes ☊ ☋.</margin>Let the preceding gnomonic Zodiac be repeated, which a line in a winding flow divides into the form of a serpent: and let there be as many lines, or curves, as there are years in the periodic motion of the <term>Lunar Nodes</term> <note>the points where the moon's path crosses the ecliptic; originally "Draconis nodus" or Nodes of the Dragon</note>, namely, almost 19 years, with the numbers of the individual years added at the ends, as the figure shows: or, so that the <term>Sciathericon</term> <note>a shadow-chart or astronomical sundial</note> is consistent with the others, you may divide it into thirty curves; here we extend the Dragon's node for a space of only 8 years. In these coils, you should describe the positions of the nodes from the <term>Ephemerides</term> <note>astronomical tables showing the positions of celestial bodies</note>

as they descend, according to the degrees in that order which you see done here, through spaces of thirty years, with the time of both Lunar and Solar eclipses written in. To the signs of the Zodiac, you shall assign the natural effects which the Sun and Moon produce when they are eclipsed in them, and you will have the Shadow-chart prepared, the use of which is as follows.

<margin>Use of the Shadow-chart.</margin>### Use of the Shadow-chart.

IN the Shadow-chart exposed to the Sun, observe the shadow of the <term>style</term> <note>the needle or blade of a sundial</note>: having found this, see where the parallel of the Sun, crossing the shadow, cuts the curve of the current year: for in that spot it will immediately appear whether, and when, an eclipse will occur in that year. Thus, for example, in the year 1645, the coil marked A B C will show that on the 21st day of August a solar eclipse will occur in the form which the figure represents, to which the effect of that same eclipse corresponds in the same sign. But since the figure shows all these things most clearly, I have thought it superfluous to say more words about them. You see, therefore, by what method Shadow-chart Ephemerides can be displayed, in which the motions of the planets can be gathered for individual days without difficulty: The likes of which may be seen in my <note>Kircher's</note> Museum, in which all the positions of the planets, their declinations, latitudes, regressions, directions, and other conditions are demonstrated by a shadow in a certain wonderful manner, not without the admiration of those looking on. After 18 years have passed, you will change the transposed coils into other places according to the Ephemerides, and with the series of years written in, you will have a Shadow-chart of eclipses for another 18 years without any change of the lines.

# CHAPTER VI.

## Concerning the Horoscope of the Ascending Signs and the Stars.

<margin>Division of the fixed stars.</margin>
<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial letter 'A' containing a seated figure, possibly a scholar or deity, within a classical frame decorated with foliage.</image-desc>
THE ANCIENTS distributed all the stars into forty-eight constellations <note>original: *Asterismos*</note>, and gave them names based on their shape, their power of influence, or some memorable deed, metamorphosis, or fable, as will be shown more fully in our *Hieroglyphic Astronomy*. These they further divided into three classes: Northern, Southern, and Zodiacal. Setting aside the Southern and Northern stars, we shall place upon our shadow-dial <note>original: *Sicatherico*, referring to a *Sciathericum*, an instrument for telling time by shadows</note> only those contained within the space of the "runners" <note>original: *διαδρόμων* (diadromōn), referring to the paths of the planets</note>. All of these are distinguished by their size as well as their powers; the greater or lesser force of their action can be considered in relation to the planets, and is determined either in terms of the multiplication and balance of influences, or in terms of the intensity of their effects. If we speak in the first way, the fixed stars are sometimes nobler in action than the planets: both because in such a variety of stars favoring one another, a great variety of effects occurs; and because the influences of the planets are tempered by the fixed stars themselves and are preserved for a long time. For while the planets, in their constant motion, wander through various regions of the heavens, they sow the seeds; the fixed stars, however, nourish the cast seed and bring it to maturity.

<margin>Why the Planets possess such great power.</margin>
If, however, they are considered in the second way, the planets will undoubtedly be stronger; both because they are closer to the Sun and the Earth, and because, as they perpetually run beneath the Zodiac (the nobler part), they are strengthened by the Sun. But since enough has been said about their nature and properties in the preceding pages, let us proceed to the constellations of the Zodiac. Astrologers, therefore, instructed by long experience, noted that when the Sun was in this or that zodiacal constellation, it produced different effects—not only throughout the course of the whole year, but also in its daily motion when positioned at the four "cardinal points," namely the points of rising, setting, noon, and midnight. Noting also that six signs are always above and six below the ethereal horizon, dividing the space of the heavens into twelve equal parts, they followed the lead of nature and distributed the sky into twelve parts, like twelve regions, which they call "houses" <note>original: *domus*</note>, but by very different methods.

<margin>Various divisions of the houses.</margin>
Some, following the Arabs, divided the heaven into twelve parts by six great circles meeting at a common point on the horizon and meridian, and dividing the primary vertical circle into twelve parts. Some, leaving the common points of the horizon and meridian, divided the equator into twelve parts by the said circles; others held to other methods. He will hold the true method, consistent with natural discipline, who assigns to each house a space of twelve <term>unequal hours</term> <note>also called "seasonal" or "planetary" hours, these divide the period from sunrise to sunset into 12 parts regardless of the season, making summer hours longer than winter hours</note>. For the ancients, with the greatest genius, devised a common measure of time for the convenience of all the nations of the whole world, namely through the motion of the equator and the Zodiac. They chose the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>the celestial equator</note> because its parts are found to be twenty-four equal ones, to which the motions of the unequal parts of the Zodiac are reduced in a certain proportion. But because the motion of that same circle is not connected to astrological influence primarily and by itself, but only by accident, nor does its measure of time distinguish day from night; therefore, it was worthwhile to find another way of measuring the motion of the Zodiac, from which (as from a naturally principal efficient cause) all influence flows into lower living things—the sense of life, and motion:

<margin>The Zodiac is the life of all things.</margin>
from this the Zodiac is named <note>The author derives "Zodiac" from the Greek *zoon*, meaning "living being"</note>, because in it there is nothing inanimate or artificial, but rather the images of animals, objects, men, beasts, women, creatures of land and water, perfect beings, and monsters are contained; by this very fact, it is designated as the fountain of all life. Therefore, when the ancients noted that the Zodiac unfolded with an unequal motion above the horizon and created unequal sections with the horizon, it followed that they assigned six hours to the individual spaces from the rising [the ascendant] to the noon line, six more from the noon line to the setting, then six more to the bottom of the sky <note>the *Imum Coeli* or the midnight point</note>, and finally six others back to the horizon. Thus, both shorter and longer days, and nights, were always divided into twelve parts. And from this emerged the first division of the houses of heaven, by which twelve unequal hours are necessarily assigned to each house; so that just as the motion of each sign is measured by two unequal hours, so the size of any domicile should be of two unequal hours;

<margin>How unequal hours are taken.</margin>
so that in this way the action or influence of one and the same sign may become known through the signified time, and likewise the measure itself and the thing measured may be applied with the meanings of the houses to discern the generic and specific powers and qualities within the houses.

<summary>This page explains the astrological division of the sky into twelve houses and the relationship between fixed stars and planets, arguing that the Zodiac is the source of all life. It advocates for a system of house division based on unequal (seasonal) hours to better reflect natural influences on the world.</summary>

## Use of the Shadow-casting Horoscope.

In this figure, we have arranged a two-part <term>Sciathericon</term> <note>From the Greek "skia" (shadow) and "thēraō" (to hunt or track); a device that tracks the Sun's shadow, essentially a sundial.</note>: this was done by us with the intention that you might be able to distinguish the moments of the rising signs without confusion. For the first, or upper part, serves for the half-year period when the Sun is ascending from Capricorn ♑ to Cancer ♋; the lower part, however, serves the other half of the year when the Sun is descending from Cancer ♋ to Capricorn ♑. Since only six signs rise during any given "artificial day" <note>An "artificial day" refers to the time from sunrise to sunset, as opposed to a 24-hour "natural day."</note>, it follows that only the lines of the six ascending signs show the rising signs on any proposed day. These are specifically the lines of those six signs which rise during the day, which are indeed calculated from the location of the Sun according to the succession of the signs; for the Sun only falls upon those positions of the ecliptic on that day which the lines represent, since the remaining signs do not rise during the daylight at that time.

For example, when the Sun is in the beginning of Aries ♈, only these six signs rise during the day: ♈ ♉ ♊ ♋ ♌ ♍. When the Sun sets, the beginning of Libra ♎ appears. Consequently, none of the following six signs—namely ♎ ♏ ♐ ♑ ♒ ♓—should be thought to rise, even if the shadow marks them in the lower diagram. Similarly, when the Sun is positioned at the beginning of Libra ♎, the six signs rising that day are ♎ ♏ ♐ ♑ ♒ ♓; and as the Sun sets, Aries ♈ rises. Therefore, on any given day, to understand which signs are rising, the location in the Zodiac must be known. If it is in the ascending signs, the shadow of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The pin or blade of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note> shows the rising signs <note>original: *horoscopos*, here referring specifically to the "Ascendant" or rising point of the zodiac.</note> on the upper shadow-dial; if it is in the descending signs of the lower shadow-dial, the shadow must be observed there.

Let us clarify the business with an example. Someone wishes to know at the beginning of October, with the Sun positioned at the beginning of Libra, which signs are rising: since Libra is one of the descending signs and at the equinox, let him observe the shadow on the lower shadow-dial. As this shadow proceeds either on the equinoctial line or a nearby parallel, it will first show point G; since the line for Scorpio ♏ passes through this, it shows that at that moment Scorpio is rising. When the shadow falls on line F, it shows Sagittarius ♐ is rising; at E, Capricorn ♑; at O, Aquarius ♒; and finally at C, it will signify that Pisces ♓ is rising. The same must be determined for the rest of the signs in order. If, however, the Sun is in the ascending and equinoctial sign of Aries ♈, the lower shadow-dial will be idle for half a year, and the shadow will signify the rising points of the ascending signs on the upper dial. Thus, the shadow at point F will show Taurus ♉ rising, at E Gemini ♊, and the same judgment is made for the rest of the signs in order. Furthermore, if you place the fixed stars on these shadow-dials—those which emerge above the horizon at the same time as a certain sign—the shadow will also show the rising and setting of the fixed stars.

<margin>Use of the tables in the Illustration.</margin>
Furthermore, so that you may know which signs are at the four "cusps" or angles of heaven at any moment—that is, which is the <term>Horoscopos</term> <note>The Ascendant.</note>, which culminates in the <term>Medium Coeli</term> <note>The Midheaven, or 10th house cusp.</note>, which is at the Western angle <note>The Descendant, or 7th house cusp.</note>, and finally which is in the <term>Imum Coeli</term> <note>The bottom of the sky, or 4th house cusp.</note>—you will find a table attached to each shadow-dial. From this, you will know the constitution of the remaining signs, and indeed of the entire heaven, faster than a word can be spoken. If, for example, the shadow somewhere shows Taurus ♉ rising, the table of the upper shadow-dial shows in the transverse series of signs that at the same moment Scorpio ♏ is descending; the 16th degree of Aquarius ♒ is in the Midheaven; the 16th degree of Leo ♌ is in the "Angle of the Earth" <note>Another term for the Imum Coeli.</note>, and so on for the rest.

<margin>Use of the shadow-dial for the celestial houses.</margin>
Additionally, so that you may know in which "house" both the Sun and the remaining signs are when any sign rises, we have inscribed the 12 celestial houses on both shadow-dials according to the rational method of <term>Regiomontanus</term> <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), an influential mathematician whose system of house division was standard in the Renaissance.</note>. In the upper dial, we have described the <term>above-earth</term> <note>original: ὑπεργείους (*hypergeious*), houses above the horizon.</note> houses; in the lower, we have described those positioned <term>below-earth</term> <note>original: ὑπογείους (*hypogeious*), houses below the horizon.</note>, which correspond exactly to the tables. Thus, a shadow found on the upper shadow-dial within the space FG shows the Sun to be in the 12th house; found within space EF, it signifies the Sun in the 11th; within DE, in the 10th; within CD, in the 9th; within BC, in the 8th; and finally within BA, it will signify the Sun is positioned in the 7th house.

If, however, the shadow is found anywhere on the rising line of Taurus ♉, it does not follow from this that it is in the "house of Taurus" where the shadow is found; rather, you will consider the Sun to be in the 1st house then, with the remaining stars consequently occupying that cusp or place in the sky which the table demonstrates. Furthermore, in the lower shadow-dial we have placed the same lines of the 12 celestial houses, but as indicators of the nocturnal or subterranean ones. Thus, when the Sun is positioned in the 10th house in the upper dial, the lower shows the opposite house—namely the 4th, or the "bottom of heaven" (Imum Coeli). Which sign occupies it at that moment, the table will demonstrate. For example, if the Sun is occupying the 10th house and the shadow simultaneously marks the ascending line of Taurus ♉, the table will show that at the same time, the 16th degree of Leo ♌ is in the 4th house. In this way, the gnomon in the lower dial always demonstrates the houses opposite to those described in the upper. It should also be noted in this place that the shadow demonstrates the celestial houses by one logic, and the hours and signs by another; for when the shadow falls on one of the rising lines, or hours, that sign to which the line belongs...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the construction and use of shadow-casting horoscopes (Sciatherica), specifically how to read the lines of the celestial houses on a sundial, before transitioning into a major new section on the geographical problem of determining longitude.</meta>

<page-num>414</page-num>
<header>The Sixth Book of the Great Art. Part III of Proteus.</header>

...is owed to have ascended, and another, which follows, to begin to ascend; or, it will signify that the hour which the line marks has ended and another is beginning. The lines of the <term>celestial houses</term> <note>In astrology, the sky is divided into twelve "houses" that govern different aspects of life; Kircher is explaining how to mark these divisions on a sundial.</note> behave in the opposite way; for these indicate not the ends, but the beginnings of the houses, so that the shadow of the <term>stylus</term> <note>The gnomon or pin of the sundial that casts the shadow.</note> falling upon any of the said lines shows the Sun to exist in that circle of position which is the start of that celestial house indicated by the ascribed number. Since the celestial houses are numbered from west to east, while the Sun is carried by its daily motion from east to west, it necessarily follows that the Sun exists at the end of any house before it exists at its beginning. Therefore, just as a shadow falling on the hour lines indicates an hour already passed from its beginning to its end; so the shadow of the stylus falling on one of the lines of the celestial houses indicates that the Sun has already been carried through that entire house from its end to its beginning. Furthermore, if anyone describes the planetary or "ancient" hours in this shadow-tracking device and places two <term>unequal hours</term> <note>Also called "temporal hours," these divide the daylight into 12 equal parts, meaning the "hour" is longer in summer than in winter.</note> for each house, he will have a description of the celestial houses according to the true and legitimate method of which we spoke previously. Finally, in these houses, the <term>house-rulers</term> <note>original: "œcodespotæ," the planets that "own" or rule specific signs or houses.</note> can be added to the lines of the signs for anyone, together with their nature and quality, as well as those things pertaining to physical causes. But all these things we leave to the execution of the curious Reader.

# CHAPTER VII.
## *On the longitude of places.*

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut drop cap for the letter 'Q'. Inside the 'Q', there is a landscape scene featuring a ship on the water and a castle or city on a distant shore under a cloudy sky.</image-desc>

<margin>What the longitude of places is.</margin>
**J**UST as we come to a knowledge of the stars themselves through their motion from the beginning <note>original: "$\gamma$," likely referring to the first point of Aries, the start of the zodiac.</note> considered according to the longitude of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The Sun's path across the sky.</note> and the order of the signs, together with the latitude of those same stars—that is, their deviation from the ecliptic—by no dissimilar reasoning we are accustomed to obtain the positions and distances of individual places by means of longitude and latitude. We therefore call the longitude of any given place the arc of the equator included between two <term>meridians</term> <note>Imaginary lines running from pole to pole.</note>, one of which we imagine to be described through the western extremity of our habitable Earth, and the other through the offered place. More briefly: the longitude of a place is nothing other than the distance of the place itself from the fixed West. By the "fixed West," we understand the intersection of the equator itself with the extended meridian established through the ultimate boundary of the West, which some describe through the Azores Islands, some through the Hesperides <note>Often identified with the Cape Verde Islands.</note>, and many, following Ptolemy, through the Canary Islands, which they call the Fortunate Isles, as do we. Moreover, the arc of any of the <term>parallels</term> <note>Lines of latitude.</note> intercepted from their common intersection with that same fixed meridian even to the meridian of the given place is mostly taken for the longitude of that place: for it has the same ratio to the whole parallel as the aforementioned arc of the equator has to the whole equator. Furthermore, that arc of the equator which is intercepted by two meridians passing through any two places is called the *difference of longitude* of those same places—that is, the arc of the same equator, or of its own parallel, by which one of the given places is more easterly than the other. 

But just as nothing is easier than to understand the concept of longitude, so nothing is more difficult than to determine it; so much so that it may not undeservedly be called the <term>Gordian knot</term> <note>An ancient metaphor for an intractable problem, famously "solved" by Alexander the Great cutting it with a sword.</note>, in the untying of which all mathematicians have thus far sweated; yet no one has so far provided anything singular. Orontius <note>Oronce Finé (1494–1555), a French mathematician.</note> <margin>Difficulty in finding longitudes.</margin> investigates it through observations of the meridian Moon and a fixed star; but by a method so laborious, so perplexed, and so difficult that no one unless he were Euclid or Ptolemy could be sufficient for it. By a similar method, Morin <note>Jean-Baptiste Morin (1583–1656), a French mathematician and astrologer.</note> boasts that he has found it. Some have thought they could reach it through <term>Magnetic Variation</term> <note>The difference between true north and magnetic north; Kircher wrote a whole book on this, as he mentions next.</note>; regarding these, see our *Magnetic Geography*. Some through the eclipses of the <term>Medicean stars</term> <note>The four largest moons of Jupiter, discovered by Galileo and named for the Medici family.</note>. Another, not so long ago, asserts that he has discovered the true science of longitude through the spots or shadows of the lunar mountains. But I fear lest, just as all other methods attempted thus far, they are from the number of those they call "Metaphysical speculations." For it is not enough in this place to devise various reasons by which it might be done; but a method is sought by the common prayers of geographers that is easy and obtainable in any place; whoever finds it ought surely to be judged to have contributed no less effort than if he had <term>squared the circle</term> <note>A famous impossible mathematical problem: creating a square with the exact same area as a circle using only a compass and straightedge.</note>. Therefore, no other method in establishing the longitude of places has been employed by mathematicians thus far, except by the observation of the beginning, middle, or end of some lunar eclipse. By which...

...how this ought to be established throughout the whole world, we teach extensively in our *Geographical Council*; to which we refer the reader in due time.

Since it is our intention to describe a **Universal Clock** in this place, which shows the hours not only everywhere in general, but especially in the Colleges of our Society of Jesus spread throughout the entire world; and since this cannot be achieved without a knowledge of longitudes; I have applied myself with the greatest study to determine the Earth’s globe according to various observations of <term>eclipses</term> <note>By timing when an eclipse began in different cities, Jesuit scientists could calculate the longitudinal distance between those locations.</note> carried out in Europe, the East Indies, China, Peru, Brazil, Canada, and Mexico by the mathematicians of our Order, as well as according to the distance of their meridians. Indeed, having obtained the time difference that emerged in the observation of a certain eclipse—for example, in Nanjing (China), Goa (India), Mozambique (Africa), Pernambuco (Brazil), and other cited places—it was certainly not difficult to determine the longitude of said places, both in relation to each other and to other intermediate locations. According to these findings, we have constructed this present **Horological Tree** of the entire Society. However, the method for investigating longitudes and the reasoning behind the observations performed at different times by the Fathers of our Society scattered across the world, we treat extensively and as a specialist in our *Geographical Council*; where we also show the way in which the whole Earthly Globe can be corrected in a brief summary. Leaving these things aside, let us turn to our own matters.

## CHAPTER VIII.

->*Star-Gazing, or Lunar and Nocturnal Shadow-Science, by which the hour of the night is shown partly through the shadow of the radiating Moon, and partly through the rays of the fixed stars.*<-

**T**he observation of the night and its hours is a matter entirely necessary for astronomers, both for the exact observation of <term>phenomena</term> <note>original: "φαινομένων"; referring to observable celestial events like eclipses or planetary conjunctions</note> and for handling other business, since the restoration of the whole of Astronomy rests solely upon this as its hinge. Therefore, we must treat these matters in this section, lest we seem to have omitted anything that can in any way be related to our **Art of Light and Shadow**. The first place is thus held by Lunar Clocks. Even if these do not show the hours with total exactness due to the variety and inconstancy of the Moon's motion—indeed, it is impossible for them to reach the perfection of a Solar clock—we shall nevertheless strive with such industry to construct them so that they indicate the usual nocturnal hour as close to the truth as possible.

Let this clock-face be placed upon another disk, EFGH, divided into 30 proportional parts

...also with a triangular <term>style</term> <note>The "style" or "gnomon" is the part of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note>, because at night the lunar shadow cast by the edge of a triangle distinguishes the hours better and more clearly than the tip of a <term>gnomon</term> <note>A pin or pointer.</note>; for the tip is false and deceptive in a lunar shadow, as has been demonstrated elsewhere.

I have said that the outermost circle ought to be divided into 30 parts by proportional division, or similar to the division of hours. This is achieved if you divide a circle into 30 equal parts: for if this is placed above the plane of the equator in the gnomonic triangle, it will mark points on the equator through which straight lines drawn from the center of the clock will divide the outer circumference into the desired 30 parts. Alternatively, by this art, the equinoctial semi-diameter in the gnomonic triangle may be transferred to the meridian from point M; and with this as the center, let a circle be drawn divided into 30 equal parts. Marked with as many lines, it will intersect the equinoctial line of the clock at points which, when led back from the center of the clock, will yield a circle proportionally divided by a thirty-fold division.

### Practical Instruction II.
### *To describe a vertical lunar dial.*

<margin>Vertical lunar dial.</margin>
Let a vertical astronomical dial (constructed according to the rules handed down in Book 4, as was done in the preceding <term>shadow-science</term> <note>original: "Sciatherico"; referring to the study of sundials/shadow-clocks</note> section) be enclosed within a ring divided into 30 parts, similar to the division of the clock, so that it can be turned this way and that: you will then have a perfect lunar clock. If, therefore, you count the age of the Moon on the outer rim and align the 12th hour of the clock to that number, the shadow of the Moon will show the sought-after hour on the same rim of the vertical circle.

### Practical Instruction III.
### *To construct a lunar clock on an equinoctial plane.*

<margin>Equinoctial lunar dial.</margin>
No plane is more fit or better suited for describing clocks of this kind than the equinoctial plane: therefore, I would recommend it above all others for the use of a nocturnal clock. Arrange its construction as follows. Let both the innermost and outermost rings be divided—the latter into 30 days, the former into 24 hours equally. The axis normal to the plane shall be the style of the clock. This clock, once placed on its plane and situated according to the meridian line, will show the hours thus: count the age of the Moon from the beginning of the circle, and move the versatile <note>In the sense of "rotatable" or "adjustable."</note> ring to this position; then the style's shadow, cast by the Moon onto the same rotatable hour-ring, will show the nocturnal hour as before. However, this clock has one inconvenience: it requires a double hour-scale; one upper, which shows the hour when the Moon is passing through the northern signs; the other lower, for when the Moon is passing through the southern signs.

### Practical Instruction IV.
### *To delineate lunar hour-scales by another method.*

To incite the reader to such a laudable study of Astronomy through the greatest variety of things and inventions, we have devised here another shadow-clock for lunar time.

In a horizontal clock, let 24 circles be inscribed, to each of which you will assign a number for the age of the Moon. To the hour lines, however, assign numbers in the order shown in the following table; with the style erected as in the preceding sections, it will be a perfect lunar clock. Once situated, let it first be exposed to the rays of the Moon: then look for the age of the Moon on the rim of the clock. For if you proceed within its circle as far as the shadow of the style, that shadow will show you the desired hour within the circle corresponding to the Moon's age. But so that this business may be done with less confusion, we have placed two clocks here: one, A, which shows the hours when the Moon is waxing; the other, B, when it is waning. These two clocks shall be situated according to the magnetic needle attached to each. The style of each, as in the previous ones, will be oblique and of indeterminate size; the shadow of these, in whichever clock is first situated as I said above, will show the hours within the circles corresponding to the phase or age of the Moon. The arrangement of the numbers was extracted with singular industry from the horizontal clock proposed in Practical Instruction I.

### Use of the Table for the duration of Lunar light above the horizon.

If you wish to know how many hours the Moon shines above the horizon at night, first look for the age of the Moon in column AB, and in the last column CD, within the same horizontal row of numbers, you will find the hours of the Moon's light above the horizon at night. Thus, you see that at the 10th age of the Moon, the Moon shines at night for 8 hours; at the 23rd age of the Moon, for 5 3/5 hours; and so for the rest.

In this, therefore, a solid gnomonic triangle—erected according to the instructions given elsewhere—will show, by the shadow of its peak cast by the Moon, the sign which the Moon is actually entering, together with the <term>declination</term><note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> it has from the equator.

### Practical Exercise VII.

*To describe on a horizontal plane a <term>Household Celestial Lunar Dial</term><note>original: "Sciathericum ☽ Oecuranomicum"; a shadow-measuring device that tracks the Moon's position within the "houses" of the zodiac.</note>, which indicates the house and the degree the Moon occupies at any moment of the night within the tropics.*

<margin>Celestial houses on a Lunar Shadow-Dial.</margin>
**D**escribe the celestial houses according to the problems on folio 444, together with the <term>pentads</term><note>groups of five degrees</note> and <term>decads</term><note>groups of ten degrees</note> of the degrees, just as you see done in that location. Add to each house the qualities that the Moon communicates to the lower world when it is present in them, as we have stated above; and you will have a perfect Shadow-Dial. In this, the shadow of the <term>gnomon</term><note>the part of a sundial that casts the shadow</note> shows the house which the Moon occupies at any given moment.

### Practical Exercise VIII.

*To describe Almucantars and Azimuths on a Shadow-Dial, that is, to determine the altitude of the Moon and its distance from the meridian by its shadow.*

<note>Almucantars are circles of altitude parallel to the horizon; Azimuths are vertical circles used to measure horizontal direction.</note>

**L**unar Azimuths and Almucantars are described in a manner not at all different from Solar Azimuths and Almucantars. Therefore, he who has learned the method from the precepts taught in Book 5, folio 439, will describe the same here with almost no effort. Or, if he has already described the Shadow-Dials for solar Almucantars and Azimuths, they will also show the lunar altitudes and lengths during the night.

### Corollary.

**I**t follows from these things that what was said in Book 5 concerning the doctrine of the <term>first mover</term><note>the outermost sphere of the heavens in Aristotelian cosmology</note> can be adapted to a lunar clock. However, since these have little use at night, I thought they should be omitted on purpose. There are other lunar instruments which you will find here and there in the works of <term>Münster</term><note>Sebastian Münster (1488–1552), a German cartographer and cosmographer.</note>, <term>Apianus</term><note>Peter Apianus (1495–1552), a German humanist known for his astronomical works.</note>, and others; namely those by which we come to a knowledge of the nighttime hour by inspecting the Pole Star through the center of a perforated disk and two stars of the Little Bear at the place where they intersect a transverse rule, using a toothed wheel divided into twelve parts fixed to the center of the first disk. But since these things are almost trivial, we have chosen to omit them and bring forth only our own inventions here.

### Problem XIV.

*To find the hour of the night through the inspection of fixed stars.*

**W**hoever is skilled in the methods of <term>Astrolabes</term><note>an ancient astronomical instrument used for solving problems relating to time and the position of the stars.</note> will come to a knowledge of the hour of the night at any time with almost no effort. I would gladly present their uses and applications in this place, were it not that the subject is too common and well-worn, and in some way outside our purpose, which keeps us from our intent; since our goal here is nothing else than to demonstrate the gnomonic or shadow-measuring art according to its full extent. However, so that we may also exhibit some specimen in this place regarding the finding of the hours of the night by the benefit of fixed stars, we wished to teach a simple, exact, and concise method here, lest we seem to have omitted anything in this *Art of Light and Shadow*.

### Practical Exercise I.

*To investigate the hours of the night with this night-scope.*

<margin>To find the night hour with an Astrolabe.</margin>
**T**ake the altitude of any fixed star known to you and inscribed on the <term>rete</term><note>the rotating star-map on an astrolabe</note> using the astrolabe that we proposed in our *Magnetic Horologiography*; and apply the pointer of this star over the <term>Almucantar</term><note>altitude circle</note> of the star found just before. Once this is done, the rule drawn through the position of the Sun in the Zodiac will show the sought-after hour on the rim.

### Practical Exercise II.

*To investigate the same hours through tables without an instrument, by calculation.*

<margin>Alternatively by Arithmetic.</margin>
**F**irst, observe any star at its <term>culmination</term><note>the point at which a celestial body reaches its highest altitude on the meridian.</note>; then seek the <term>right ascension</term><note>the distance of a point east of the First Point of Aries, used to locate stars.</note> of the star and of the Sun at the time you begin the observation. Then, if the hours of the star's ascension are fewer than the hours of the Sun's ascension, you shall add 24 hours to them, and from the sum subtract the day of observation, and the remainder will give the sought-after hour of the Sun from noon. But if the hours of the Sun's ascension are fewer than the star's ascension, you shall subtract them from 24, and the remainder will give the sought-after hour.

### Practical Exercise III.

*The construction of a new astronomical instrument.*

**W**e now bring forth a new instrument, both for identifying stars at night and for finding the hours, which has been handed down by no one else yet, as far as I know. You shall begin its construction thus: First, let an axis be fixed upon the base BC, adapted to the elevation of your region, which shall be AC. Then, insert onto this a disk XII, VI, XII, VI, divided into 24 equal parts, which represents the equator. Thirdly, insert onto this another semi-circle FR, which has a rule attached at E, the center of the equinoctial, which also rotates together with the semi-circle RF above the center E and is equipped with pulleys to secure it; for it is around the axis like a movable and versatile meridian divided into twice 90 degrees; from whose center K, a rule KG is drawn out, which, raised or lowered according to the <term>declination</term><note>the angular distance of a star north or south of the celestial equator.</note> of the stars, grazes the rim of the semi-circle, and is also fixed by pulleys if necessary. To this again, as if to an axis, let a system of some constellation...

### The Use of the New Instrument

To find the hour of the night, first adapt the equinoctial circle (which is divided into 24 equal parts) placed at right angles to the axis CA at point E, and directed to the altitude of your <term>equator</term><note>The observer's latitude relative to the celestial equator.</note>. Then, take one of the constellation charts drawn on paper (in which each star is to be perforated—that is, holes are made at the positions of the stars, with the names of the individual stars added) and insert it perpendicularly into the rule KG. This must be done with such care that the midpoint AB of the constellation is as far from the center K of the semicircle KFR as the radius assigned to each constellation. Furthermore, the meridian BC in the constellation illustration must always lie in the plane of the axis CEA. Once this is properly completed,

After this is done, place your eye at the center K and rotate the semicircle KFR together with the first constellation chart until one of the brighter stars shines through its hole. As soon as you catch it, look: the index E will, at that very moment, show the sought hour on the equinoctial <term>limb</term><note>The graduated outer edge or scale of the instrument.</note>, provided you have first converted the difference in degrees between that star and the position of the Sun into hours. Furthermore, with this instrument, the individual fixed stars can be identified more quickly than can be said—even by someone unskilled in Astronomy—simply by keeping the eye fixed at K; for each star will appear perfectly through its own hole. This instrument has countless other uses in Astronomy, which the lack of time and the growing size of this book do not permit us to detail here; therefore, we leave them for the wise reader to consider further.

### Construction of a Table for the New Celestial Perspective.

<margin>Illustration XXII.</margin>
This is how the tables are constructed. Suppose, for example, the constellation of the Dragon <note>original: Draco</note> and the Little Bear <note>original: Ursa Minor</note> is to be drawn: first, let two lines be drawn at right angles intersecting each other at point A, namely BC and DE. Point A will be the vertex of the constellation, BC the <term>meridian</term><note>The north-south line of the map.</note>, B the upper part, C the lower part; and along this line, <term>tangents</term><note>Geometric values used here to calculate the flat placement of objects on a curved sky.</note> are taken downward and upward on the table, as will be explained later. DE, however, shall be the primary vertical line, with D as the left side and E the right. F is the pole of the <term>Zodiac</term><note>The path the sun follows through the stars.</note>, and G is the pole of the world <note>The North Celestial Pole.</note>, as is clear in Figure 1. With these established, if you wish to inscribe individual stars in the order they occur in the table:

1. Take the <term>radius</term><note>original: semidiametrum</note> for the size of the constellation, which might be, for example, HI in Figure 1, which you will divide into a thousand equal parts. Once this is done,

2. Take the table and see which tangent corresponds to the first star of the Little Bear according to the straight distance, and you will find 168 C. Again, see which tangent corresponds to the same star according to the transverse distance, and you will find 255. In the first example, the letter C signifies that the tangent is to be taken below line DE; in the second, the letter E indicates the tangent is to be taken toward the right side, E.

3. Therefore, take 168 parts of the first tangent within the radius HI divided into 1000 parts, and transfer them from point A of the vertex toward C—for example, to point S. Then, draw a perpendicular transverse line 255 units long at S, where from S

you will determine the tangent in parts of the radius HI, for example at V; for there will be the genuine position of the chosen star. However, the instrument is made easier if RSV, like a sort of cursor <note>A sliding guide on a mathematical instrument.</note>, is moved above line CB. For it will mark the tangents of the vertical distances on line BC, and the tangents of the transverse distances on RSV. The first inventor of this technique was Father Christopher <note>original: P. Chri-jus.</note>

Grienberger <note>Christopher Grienberger (1561–1636) was a Jesuit mathematician and colleague of Galileo.</note>, who also established unique tables which he calls a "new perspective of celestial images." We have chosen to place some of these here for the construction of the attached constellations.

### Explanation of the Constellations.

**T**hese constellations, constructed by the help of tangents, are arranged in such an order that they perfectly show the <term>longitude</term><note>The position of a star measured along the ecliptic.</note> of individual stars on the rim, when a string is stretched from the pole of the Zodiac F through the center of the star; for this will immediately show the star's longitude on the rim. Where the pole of the Zodiac is not available, a string placed over two similar degrees marked at the top and bottom, or on the sides, will show the star's longitude. In all the constellations, the lines are the same: A is the vertex of the constellation; BC is the meridian of the illustration, or the line of vertical distances; DC is the line of transverse distances. Beneath each of these is placed a line labeled "radius" <note>original: semidiameter</note>, which is the measure of the distance of the plane—or the star-bearing paper—from the eye. Furthermore, anyone who desires the tables of all the other constellations should consult the catalog of the longitudes and latitudes of the fixed stars constructed by Father Grienberger, where he will find them all reduced into tables with great diligence.
