# ATHANASIUS KIRCHER, PRIEST OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS
# THE GREAT ART OF LIGHT AND SHADOW
### Book Seven.
# PROMETHEUS, OR THE ANACAMPTIC ART, OR REFLECTED ASTRONOMY.

->Where the secrets of the heavens are enclosed within earthly dwellings by Promethean genius,<-
->that is, by celestial fire drawn down with mirrors.<-

## P R E F A C E.

*The human mind, like a small portion of divine fire, is incapable of rest while it strives for great heights; it leaves nothing unattempted until it finally reaches its intended goal. In this present book, as we strive for such heights—that is, as we attempt to bring the heavens down to earth, and try to enclose the immense volumes of the heavens within the small shacks of earthly habitation—we undertake a most difficult, if not to say daring, task. Nevertheless, having begun, and having broken through every difficulty, obstacle, and impediment with the invincible constancy of the mind, God willing, we have succeeded. We have enclosed the heavens within the hidden recesses of our houses. One thing seemed to be missing: namely, a soul, which might govern this celestial machine with vital light. Light and fire, I say, were lacking, without which the whole machine would rightly remain fruitless and lifeless. Yet, drawing that light down from heaven demanded a power greater than human. Therefore, driven by the impulse of an internal fire, while we left nothing untried, Prometheus <note>In Greek mythology, Prometheus stole fire from the gods to give to humanity. Kircher uses him as a symbol for the scientist "stealing" sunlight with mirrors.</note> was finally consulted, and he revealed many and various ways of drawing fire down from heaven. This was not done by striking one flint against another, nor by the incantatory rhythms of witches, but by a small piece of the purest mirror. When this was properly exposed to the Sun, it clothed itself in the stolen splendor of the Sun, and entering our "heaven" <note>Referring to the room where the projection is made.</note>, it animated it so wonderfully in an instant that it may rightly be said to have seized all the laws of the heavens. Thus, because of this "stolen" light, the name* Prometheus *has been quite fittingly given to this book.*

*Furthermore, although about ten years ago my "Catoptric Gnomonics" <note>original: "Gnomonica Catoptrica." This refers to the science of telling time via reflected light.</note> saw the light of day in Avignon; yet, because I am now better instructed by daily experience, and have found more and more concerning those hidden effects of reflected light; and since I have noted besides that in various places these first fruits of my inventions are being put into practice by various craftsmen—not without applause and the admiration of onlookers—it seemed right for the perfection of the work to publish all those mysteries of the <term>Anacamptic art</term> <note>From the Greek "anakamptikos," referring to the science of reflected light (catoptrics).</note> which I have discovered anew, for the common good. I did this especially as I realized they constitute a significant portion of our "labors of light." You will see, therefore, in this book—besides those things we have published elsewhere—many new things handed down by no one else. Among these are experiments in linear reflection, by which we display celestial motions not just by a bright spot of light vibrating on the walls, but by entire lines projected by reflected light. If I seem to have achieved anything in this, I pray that you ascribe it to that one God, the Best and Greatest, the true Prometheus of all things. But leaving aside the winding paths of words, let us begin our undertaking from the very egg <note>A Latin idiom, "ab ovo," meaning from the very beginning.</note>.*

---

## SUMMARY OF THE BOOK.

Since the entire business of optics, and thus our entire Great Art of Light and Shadow, is perfected by a triple ray—namely, the direct, the reflected, and the refracted—it seems that after the study of the direct ray of the Sun (which we have therefore called <term>sciatheric</term> <note>From the Greek for "shadow-tracking," referring to traditional sundials.</note>), the <term>reflected</term> <note>original: ἀνακαμπτικὸς (anakamptikos)</note> ray should hold the second place by a certain right. Since we have treated this in a complete work titled "Catoptric Gnomonics," printed long ago in Avignon, nothing remains but to add new inventions to it and to demonstrate the secrets of the same <term>immaterial reflection</term> <note>original: δι' ἀνδύλου (di' andylou). This is likely Kircher's Greek for "immaterially" or "without matter," referring to the nature of a reflected image.</note> more clearly across all kinds of mirrors. So that this may be <term>methodical</term> <note>original: εὐμέθοδος (eumethodos)</note>, let us draw the thread from the principles of the art.

# DEFINITIONS.

<margin>I.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'C' with intricate floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>
**A** luminous body is said to be anything that diffuses light. Transparent <note>original: "Diaphanum"</note> is that which is passable by light. Non-transparent, opaque, or <note>original Greek: *ἀδιαφανῆ*</note> "impenetrable to light" is defined by Aristotle as that which light cannot pass through.

<margin>II.</margin>
Lux, Lumen, and Splendor <note>Kircher distinguishes between the internal essence of light, its transmission, and its reflection.</note> are distinct. **Lux** is said to be that which is innate to a glowing body. **Lumen**, however, is nothing other than the visible quality produced from *Lux*, diffused far and wide through a transparent medium. Finally, **Splendor** is *Lumen* reflected back from a smooth and polished body. Therefore, it is clear from what has been said that just as *Lumen* is generated from *Lux*, so *Splendor* is generated from *Lumen*.

<margin>III.</margin>
The polishing of bodies is nothing other than the continuity of the parts of the surface of a polished body, without any perceptible pores, inequality, roughness, or division; hence, a mirror can be nothing other than any body polished by the aid of art or nature.

<margin>IV.</margin>
A luminous ray is not properly the straight line through which light is transmitted, whether that line be real or imaginary; rather, it is the light itself vibrating out, or the straight-flowing stream of light.

<margin>V.</margin>
The line of incidence is that line according to whose direction the luminous ray of a shining body falls upon the surface of a polished body.

<margin>VI.</margin>
The line of reflection is that line according to whose direction an image, or the form of light received upon the surface of a mirror, is turned back and reflected to the sight or any other object, being unable to penetrate further due to the opacity of the polished body and the <note>original Greek: *ἄβατον*</note> "impenetrable" medium.

<margin>VII.</margin>
The point of incidence is that point where the line of incidence falls upon the surface of the mirror; it is the same as the point of reflection, since the reflection of forms to the sight, or another object, always occurs from the point of incidence.

<margin>VIII.</margin>
The perpendicular or normal line is that which, drawn from the point of incidence, is at right angles to the flat surface of the mirror. In polished bodies that are convex or concave, the normality of this line must be calculated from a line touching the convex or concave surface of the polished body, upon which it is erected <note>original Greek: *κατὰ τὰς ὀρθὰς*</note> "at right angles."

<margin>IX.</margin>
The surface of reflection is the surface containing the line of incidence, the line of reflection, and the perpendicular line produced from the point of contact upon the surface of the mirror itself.

<margin>X.</margin>
The cathetus <note>A technical term in geometry for a line falling perpendicularly on another.</note> of incidence is the line which is normal to the flat surface of the mirror from the point of the seen form of the luminous body, or from any other point on the line of incidence; likewise, the cathetus of reflection is that line which is drawn perpendicular to the flat surface of the mirror from any point on the reflected line. The "surface of incidence" is that which is bounded by the cathetus of incidence and the line or ray of the luminous body.

<margin>XI.</margin>
The angle of incidence is that angle which the cathetus of incidence subtends, or which the line of incidence causes together with the line that is the common intersection of the surface of reflection and the mirror itself. The angle of reflection is that which the cathetus of reflection subtends, or which the reflected line constitutes with the line common to the surface of the mirror and the reflection.

<margin>XII.</margin>
The triangle of incidence is that which the incident ray of the luminous body establishes with its cathetus; the triangle of reflection is that which the repercussion of the received form or the radiant light causes upon the same surface with its cathetus; moreover, the hypotenuses or chords of these triangles meet together with their bases at the single point of incidence and reflection.

<margin>XIII.</margin>
The line of the surface of reflection is the line upon which the double triangle of incidence and reflection is founded.

# Postulates, or Petitions.

<margin>I.</margin>
**N**ature does nothing in vain, nor does she fail in necessary things.

<margin>II.</margin>
A radial line is formed according to straight lines; or, what is the same thing, the rays of any lights and the multiplications of forms are extended according to straight lines.

<margin>III.</margin>
A straight line may be drawn through any three points designated on a surface of reflection.

# THE FIRST PART OF THE ANACAMPTIC ART. <note>Anacamptics is the study of reflected light, what we now call catoptrics.</note>
## ON THE NATURE OF REFLECTED LIGHT
### and its effects in the nature of things.

## CHAPTER I.
### *On the craftsmanship of the world, and its marvelous constitution.*

<margin>The marvelous arrangement of the zones.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative initial letter 'S' showing a classical building and mountains.</image-desc>
**I**f that worldly Sun of the entire universe were fixed and did not vary its path, the effects on lower things would not vary, but the result would be exactly the same always and everywhere. For certain parts of the terrestrial globe would be numbed by perpetual cold, just as they are by perpetual darkness; other parts would be uninhabitable for animals due to the heat of the Sun constantly looming over them; and some would be situated in a middle state. Again, if the moving Sun were whirled in its rotation forever under the same circle of the equator from East to West, it would indeed provide some light to all inhabitants of the terrestrial globe, but it would not vary the effects; some would enjoy a perpetual winter, others autumn, some spring, and others a perpetual summer. Because of this, the world would necessarily perish. Furthermore, if the earth were of another shape besides spherical—namely, square or triangular—all the aforementioned inconveniences would befall the world. 

Hence, by a certain admirable design of nature, it was brought about that the earth, gathered into a sphere, might aptly receive the rays of the Sun. The Sun, however, is neither fixed in one place nor revolving under the same perpetual parallel, but moves back and forth between the North and South at such an interval as is sufficient to illuminate the entire earth. It maintains this order of motion with such marvelous and invincible constancy, and such unalterable justice, that no nation in the world can complain that the Sun or nature has failed them in supplying the necessary heat. Thus, for the people living under the frigid zone <note>The Arctic and Antarctic regions.</note>, it repays an absence of one, two, three, four, five, or six months with a presence of just as many months. For those living under the temperate zone, as much as it shortens the days in winter time, it lengthens them by the same amount in the summer. Under the torrid zone <note>The tropics.</note>, however, it administers all things with an equal lot of alternating days and nights. In this, if it were to overstep the laws of justice by even the slightest amount, it would undoubtedly lead the economy of the lower world into the greatest confusion. 

Hence, He <note>Referring to the Creator.</note> established this orb of the earth so exactly in proportion to the distance of the Sun from the center of the world, that it can be neither larger nor smaller. <margin>The Earth can be neither larger nor smaller.</margin> For if it were larger, the Sun would be insufficient to illuminate the terrestrial hemisphere, and all sub-polar regions would be squalid and condemned to perpetual cold, as will be demonstrated in the ninth book. If, however, it were smaller, the Sun would illuminate the earth more than is proper, and would induce a great intemperance of heat and a <term>dyscrasia</term> <note>original: "dyscrasiã"; a medical term referring to an unhealthy imbalance of bodily fluids or "humors".</note>. Thus, all things are established so exactly that the Sun, in illuminating the earth, neither lacks sufficient heat nor causes harm with excessive heat.

## CHAPTER II.
### *On the necessity of the reflected ray, and its effects in the lower world.*

<margin>A Paradox.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative initial letter 'S' showing a landscape with a river.</image-desc>
**I**f the Author of nature were to reduce this mass of the earthly habitation either to the size of a fist or to nothing at all, a person situated in the center of the earth, or anywhere outside of it, would feel nothing except that light which the reflected light of the Sun would cause in their own body. The same would happen if the rays of the Sun passed through the terrestrial body without being reflected. Therefore, the reflected ray is the cause both of heat and of the degrees of heat suitable to each region. 

To show this, it must first be supposed that nature achieves its effects in all things following the shortest lines, as is demonstrated at length in the first theorem of this work. It has been shown elsewhere that the shortest lines of this kind are the solar rays reflected from the point of incidence, and they are more effective the closer they approach the perpendicular. Secondly, the denser and more compact a body is, the more fit it is for reflecting solar rays effectively—not unlike a ball, which bounces back higher the harder the body it strikes. Such a body also retains the heat caused by reflected rays longer the denser it is; just as fire thrives more in coals than...

<margin>The earth is full of "all-seeds."</margin>
...than in flame, or in iron than in coal. Thirdly, the terrestrial body is full of spirits and a fetus-like mixture of every kind of <term>seminal reasons<note>original: *seminalium rationum*. A philosophical concept suggesting that the seeds or blueprints of all physical things were implanted in the world at creation by the Creator.</note></term>, and it overflows with moisture everywhere; all of these things were ordained by the Author of Nature both for the beauty of the universe and to manifest the variety of things in the world. These mixtures of the celestial bodies—the Sun, Moon, and stars—poured out with their own specific seeds using light as a vehicle, finally produce that variety which we contemplate, struck with the greatest admiration, in this massive machine of the Universe.

These things having been duly established, let us now see how all these things are arranged for the use of the sublunary economy by the reflected ray. Therefore, when light strikes the harder body of the earth and is denied passage, it is beaten back either upon itself or toward the opposite side; from this percussion, since the ray—which was at first single—is now doubled, and since there are infinite rays resting upon the earth, these are multiplied immensely in a short time by being driven back by the reverberation. 
<margin>How heat is produced.</margin>
From this multiplication or condensation of the rays, the air is violently split; once split and stripped of its moisture, it passes into a state of the greatest rarity, which is followed by intense heat. The air, violently struck and ignited by this multiplication of rays, makes the earth it surrounds a participant in its heat; once heated, the earth evaporates the moisture it contains, and that which is flatulent is dissipated into a breath, exhaling as it is lifted by the force of the heat. From this eruption of vapors and terrestrial exhalations, the material for the greatest meteorological impressions is supplied: hence rain, hail, winds, and the like. Furthermore, the hidden seeds of things follow along with the vapors and exhalations, all of which are the cause of innumerable prodigious effects in the sublunary world. Having therefore seen that perpetual *constitution* <note>original: *κατάστασιν*</note>, or the universal *reflection* <note>original: *ἀνάκλασιν*</note> of sublunary things caused by the reflected ray, let us now turn our pen to examine the particulars.

# CHAPTER III.
## *On the reflected ray under the torrid zone, and its effects.*

<image-desc>A large historiated woodcut initial 'T' depicting a pastoral landscape with trees and figures.</image-desc>

<margin>The torrid zone is most temperate.</margin>
**IT IS SO** arranged by human nature that unless it is supported by the service of the senses and adopts the experience of things as its ally, it is easily liable to the greatest errors and most absurd opinions. This seems to have happened exactly this way for many, even among the first class of philosophers: Aristotle, Democritus, Anaxagoras, and others after them who were Christians, such as Lactantius, Origen, and others. For the knowledge of the circuit of the earth is an argument of such great wisdom that even the wisest of mortals dared to boast of this science communicated to him by God, when he says in Wisdom 7:17:
> *For he himself gave me true knowledge of the things that are, to know the disposition of the whole world, and the virtues of the elements, and the beginning, and the ending, and midst of the times: the alterations of the turning of the sun, and the change of seasons: the circuits of years, and the positions of stars;* 

The aforementioned philosophers, being destitute of this knowledge, when they wished to philosophize about the nature of the world’s circuit, it is no wonder they fell into foul errors. Among these errors, this was not the least: they thought the torrid zone <note>The "Torrid Zone" refers to the tropics, the area of the Earth between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.</note> was inaccessible due to the heat of the Sun, parched with dryness, and devoid of humans, animals, and plants. Against them, modern men, taught by experience, have found that the torrid zone is not only not inaccessible due to heat, but is most highly cultivated for human habitation, and of all the zones it is the most pleasant and delightful, filled with an innumerable variety of animals and vegetables. By a hidden counsel of nature, it is so constituted that by a completely contrary reasoning, the vertical Sun—which usually brings summer to us—brings winter to them. 
<margin>The vertical Sun brings winter, while at its most distant it brings summer.</margin>
That is, it produces the most fertile and copious rains; from the frequent and almost daily fall of these, the zone acquires a constitution that is not "torrid," but exceedingly humid. Yet when the Sun gradually declines from the zenith <note>the point directly overhead</note>, the Sun—which ought to bring winter, as it does for us—brings the most serene and temperate weather. Thus in Lima, Peru, at 12 degrees south latitude, in the months of May, June, and August, the Sun is nearer to Europe and more remote from them; yet at that time, a sky so clear and serene is seen by the Peruvians that those watching cannot marvel at it enough. For at that time, neither rains fall, nor is snow scattered; the rivers are diminished, and some of them fail, being entirely dried up. But a little later in the year, as the Sun travels toward Jupiter <note>This likely refers to the Sun moving toward a specific astronomical alignment or toward the northern tropic; Kircher uses planetary symbols to denote celestial positions.</note> and grazes the zenith, then the force of both snow and rain floods down, and the rivers are increased. In the opposite zone, among the inhabitants of Panama, New Spain, and the adjacent islands, they experience the total opposite.

For from the beginning of November until April, they always have a most peaceful and clear sky, as the Sun is declining furthest from the northern <term>zenith<note>original: *vertice*. Literally the "vertex" or highest point in the sky directly above an observer.</note></term>. The time of rains, however, takes its beginning from June until September; so much so that this can be a perpetual rule: under the <term>torrid zone<note>The tropical regions of the Earth located between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn.</note></term>, a great dryness and aridity occurs when the Sun recedes from the zenith; and when it returns to the same, the greatest and most abundant humidity is caused. Because of this humidity, the heat is also not as intolerable as some have thought, who believed:

->*that the zone with the flashing Sun*
*is always reddening, and always parched by fire;*<-
<note>original: *quòd zona corusco, Semper Sole rubet, & torrida semper ab igne*. These lines are from Virgil's *Georgics* (Book I, 234-235), describing the ancient belief that the tropics were an uninhabitable wasteland of fire.</note>

but rather it is extremely temperate. We must therefore explain why the Sun's approach to the zenith under the torrid zone causes humidity, and its recession causes dryness, whereas under the temperate zone, its approach causes a dry constitution and its recession a most humid one. We must also explain why it produces such a great variety of things—animals, plants, and minerals—so entirely different from those in Europe. This will be explained by first presupposing this demonstration.

Therefore, when the Sun under the torrid zone always strikes the earth and ocean with a <term>normal<note>In geometry and physics, "normal" refers to an angle that is perpendicular (90 degrees) to a surface.</note></term> influx at midday, and the ray, <term>retorted<note>original: *retortus*. This refers to the ray being "bent back" or reflected upon itself, which Kircher believes multiplies its heating power.</note></term> upon itself, fills the air on all sides with immense heat by its great multiplication, it must consequently produce the most powerful and effective of all actions. From this powerful action, that immense change into monstrous things, which those positioned under the torrid zone contemplate, necessarily follows by this reasoning: the earth, struck by the glowing heat of the surrounding air, draws out from its innermost bowels an immense abundance of vapors and exhalations on both land and sea. The truth of this matter is taught to us by an experiment taken from the <term>distilling art<note>original: *arte stillaticia*. Early chemistry or alchemy focused on distillation.</note></term>, in which the more powerful the fire is, the more abundant the vapor emitted by the herbs inserted into the <term>alembic<note>A chemical apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distilling chemicals.</note></term>. Therefore, once this abundance of vapors and exhalations has been drawn out by this most powerful ray, even in a short space of time, it cannot be consumed so quickly as they are carried into the colder region of the air (being now situated outside the <term>anacamptic<note>Reflected.</note></term> sphere of the reflected ray, I say, where the heat gradually fails); they must gradually thicken and be resolved, pouring down into most copious rains. Since this action lasts daily for nearly a whole month, it happens that all the fields are filled with excessive moisture, rivers overflow, paths are blocked, and animals retreat from the deserted plains to the mountains. The bodies of both living creatures and plants acquire a most humid constitution; the leaves of trees, dilated by excessive moisture, degenerate from their natural form; in a word, all things are changed. Furthermore, since a mixture of <term>seminal reasons<note>original: *seminalium rationum*. See the note on the previous page; these are the hidden biological "blueprints" or seeds of all life believed to be dormant in the environment.</note></term> is stirred up by these exhalations and vapors, it 

<margin>Why there is such a great variety of things under the torrid zone.</margin>

impregnates the air with a fetus of various mingled seeds. When these are released by that warm and moist environment, it produces an innumerable variety of both insects and plants that differ entirely from ours. Hence, from the latent mixture of various mingled seeds, dispersed far and wide together with the resolved vapors, there is born that multitude of monstrous things—worms, serpents, insects, and plants—which all foreigners look upon with admiration under the said zone. Hence, trees struck by the most vehement heat of the Sun are resolved into oils, balsams, and various kinds of resins. Animals themselves brought from Europe to these regions degenerate so much that they seem scarcely recognizable anymore. Because the air is also tainted by various and different <term>impressions<note>In this context, atmospheric conditions or qualities.</note></term>, bodies are infested with unusual and exotic diseases and infirmities. All these things, as I have said, obtain their origin from that varied heap of seeds attracted and diffused in the air. Furthermore, when the Sun declines from the zenith and the rains are diminished, they begin a dry constitution. But let us declare these things a little more fully.

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing the Earth (corpus ICKL). A horizontal line marks the diameter through the center C, with points A, C, and B. A vertical axis runs from S at the top to L at the bottom. An arc representing the sun's path or ecliptic is marked with points D, E, and F. Point K is on the right circumference. <margin>The geometric cause of the powerful heat under the torrid zone.</margin>

Let the body of the earth be ICKL, the torrid zone ACB, and the oblique motion of the Sun from the tropic D to the tropic F through the equinoctial E. Therefore, when the Sun is positioned in either of the tropics D or F, it will excite the most powerful heat in the underlying normal planes at A and B due to the perpendicular influx: from this also come vehement rains. But the tropic ray DC will then strike the region of the equator obliquely, where it will cause less heat according to the smaller angle of reflection DCE, and consequently a diminution of rains. But under the opposite tropic B, it will cause much less heat still, according to the more obtuse angle of reflection DBS; whence, consequently, they will participate somewhat in the nature of the neighboring temperate region—namely, a more intense cold. And thus, the heat will always be as much more intense or relaxed as the Sun is more distant from the inhabitants. From these things, truly, the wonderful sagacity of nature shines forth, which...

# Theory of the Anacamptic Art <note>original: *Artis Anacampsticæ*. "Anacamptics" is the branch of optics dealing with the reflection of light or sound.</note>

[Nature] has for the most part enclosed this <term>torrid zone<note>The tropical regions near the equator.</note></term> between vast oceans, or even enriched its inland regions with the world's greatest lakes and rivers. Such are the Amazon, the Marañón, the Santa Marta, and the River Plate in America; and in Africa, the Nile, the Niger, the Zaire, and the Cuama. These were provided lest the earth, deprived of moisture or the material for rain, be destroyed by the force of the burning Sun. Against the Sun's "darts" <note>original: *spicula*. A poetic way of describing harsh solar rays.</note> she also opposed the very rapid movement of the Sun toward the west, and the nearly constant twelve-hour cycle of day and night. By these, the air scorched during the day is tempered by the nightly cold and the pouring out of abundant dew. From this equality of temperature, it is a wonder how temperate and delightful the zone is rendered. I would not deny, however, that the torrid zone is of a very different nature in many places; for in some spots it is extremely humid, in others stiff with cold, and in others burning with vehement heat. The cause of this is nothing other than the diverse nature of the underlying soil, the arrangement of mountains, and the dominion of the winds. I have written of these things at length in my work *The Subterranean World* <note>original: *Mundo nostro subterraneo*. This refers to Kircher’s famous 1665 treatise on geology and geography.</note>, where you will find the causes explained. Thus it happens that the Sun under the torrid zone is at times most burning and far more penetrating than the heat of the "Dog Days" <note>The hottest days of summer in the northern hemisphere, associated with the rising of the star Sirius (the Dog Star).</note> in Europe; yet this heat is easily kept away by the lightest shade or covering. Consequently, one lives much more safely and securely under a dwelling of straw or reeds there than here in Rome, in rooms that are hidden away and darkened with every possible care.

<margin>
Wonderful properties of certain particular places.
</margin>
Why are the summer nights under the torrid zone not hot? Why, on the very ridges of mountains amidst piles of snow, are men often burned by intolerable heat? Why, in the province of <term>Collao<note>A high-altitude region in the Andes, primarily in modern-day Peru and Bolivia.</note></term>, is there cold even under a weak shadow, yet such great heat from the Sun immediately nearby? Why is the coast of the Peruvian Province bordering the sea so legendary and gravelly, yet wonderfully healthy? Why are the cities of Plata and Potosí located under the same climate, yet the former is joyful, temperate, and fertile, while the latter is entirely harsh, wrinkled, and fruitless?

## CHAPTER IV.

### On the reflected ray under the temperate zone, and its effects.

<insert>

</insert>
The <term>temperate zone<note>The regions between the tropics and the polar circles.</note></term> is that entire space contained within the tropics and the Arctic and Antarctic circles. Since it has a different position—namely, outside the goals and limits of the Sun as we said in the preceding—it causes different effects. Let the <term>sphere of the world<note>The Earth.</note></term> be represented by the oblique circle DGEF, with HI as the equator, BL and KM as the tropics, and GE as the axis. Let BC be the temperate zone and N be the rays of the Sun. These rays, traveling obliquely into the space of the earth at BC, will be reverberated <note>reflected</note> toward O. Since the rays are not reflected back onto themselves, but toward the opposite side, the heat will not be as intense, nor will it have as much power to stir up humors as

under the torrid zone. Heat, however, is produced in this way: since the Sun sends infinite rays into the space BC—specifically, as many as there are points it touches on the surface BC—it happens that from each point, the reflected rays must necessarily intersect each individual incident ray. From this, infinite triangles emerge, which we call here <unclear>reverberating</unclear> triangles of heat; for under these, the multiplication of heat occurs. Thus, the heat becomes more intense the more acute the triangle is at vertex A (with its sides closer to the normal line), and more moderate the more obtuse the triangle is at angle A (with its sides

...at sunrise and sunset, heat will be stirred up. These are geometric models Kircher uses to calculate how much heat is "trapped" by the reflection of light rays between the atmosphere and the ground.</note></term> caused by the incident and reflected rays increase and multiply the heat in a rated proportion above the horizon. 

Thus, with the Sun positioned in **Cancer**, the midday caumatic triangle is **ABC**; in **Leo** and **Gemini**, it is **BDC**; in **Virgo** and **Taurus**, **BEC**; in **Libra** and **Aries**, **BFC**;

in **Scorpio** and **Aquarius**, **BGC**; in **Sagittarius** and **Capricorn**, **BHC**; and finally in **Capricorn**, it is **BIC**. Concerning the hours of the day, it will be compared such that the caumatic triangle at midday in **Cancer** is **BAC**; at the 1st and 11th hour <note>Kircher is using a 12-hour system from sunrise; these represent the hours closest to noon.</note>, the triangle becomes **BDC**; at the 2nd and 10th hour, **BEC**; at the 3rd and 9th hour, **BFC**; at the 4th and 8th hour, **BGC**; at the 5th and 7th hour, **BHC**; and finally at the 6th hour <note>Sunset/Sunrise</note>, **BHC**. 

Furthermore, the same can also be considered according to the various <term>climates<note>In historical geography, "climates" were zones of latitude determined by the length of the longest day.</note></term>. Thus, under the sixth climate, for example, with the Sun positioned in **Cancer**, the <term>gnomonic triangle<note>A triangle based on the shadow cast by a sun-dial's pin (gnomon).</note></term> **BAC** is formed; under the seventh **BDC**, under the eighth **BEC**, under the ninth **BFC**, under the tenth **BGC**, under the eleventh **BHC**, and finally under the twelfth it becomes **BIC**. 

Whoever examines these things deeply will undoubtedly see a new gate opened for himself to investigate the degrees of heat through the doctrine of triangles. Therefore, according to the diversity of the caumatic triangles, different degrees of heat are caused in the constitution of oblique horizons. From this arises the great variety of climates in the production of things, which we shall examine shortly.

# CHAPTER V.
## Concerning the reflected ray of the Sun under the Frigid Zone, or under the most oblique sphere.

<image-desc>Woodcut initial letter 'Z' containing floral patterns and architectural elements.</image-desc>

<margin>The stay of the Sun above the horizon compensates for the weakness of heat under the frigid zone.</margin>

The **FRIGID ZONE** is the name given by geographers to that space contained within the polar circles, in which the Sun always makes the longest day greater than twenty-four hours, all the way to the pole itself, under which it establishes a six-month day. For as the Sun enters **Aries** <note>The Spring Equinox.</note>, the horizon begins to be illuminated, and the presence of the luminary lasts until it enters **Libra** <note>The Autumn Equinox.</note>. 

However, it is called the "frigid zone" because of the weakness of the solar rays. For the caumatic triangles of reflection are very obtuse; a notable lack of heat follows this obtuseness. Indeed, unless the long stay of the Sun above the horizon for many months compensated for the weakness of the solar rays, nature would seem to have placed this zone in vain, as it would be intolerable in its rigor. By a wonderful counsel of nature, it was brought about that the perpetual stay of the Sun above the horizon for many months would restrain and subdue that most stubborn cold, which an obtuse ray could not pierce. 

Therefore, the Sun—born again and emerging from the kingdom of the underworld above the horizon, under which it was buried for a six-month space—beholds the mountainous heaps of piled-up snow, the seas raised into icy Alps, the rivers, the mountains, and in a word, the whole earth subjected to the tyranny of <term>Hyperborean<note>A term referring to the extreme North.</note></term> rigor. Not unmindful of its duty, the Sun soon emerges into a most fierce battle with the cold, its enemy. 

<margin>The struggle of Nature.</margin>

It attacks the offspring of the stubborn cold with its sharpest "darts" <note>The Sun's rays.</note>, and a massive conflict arises. The cold, more obstinate in the claim of its own right, is finally forced to surrender, conquered by the constant solicitation of the Sun dwelling perpetually upon it. This cold, thoroughly dissipated within one month of the Sun's rising by the joined forces of **Taurus**, is ordered to leave the soil along with the offspring of snow and ice, and the earth is restored to its pristine liberty. 

Furthermore, having now become more powerful with **Gemini** called in as allies, the Sun imbues the earth (now freed from superfluous moisture) with a great luxury of grasses and herbs. Finally, having attained perfect dominion over the earth in the remaining two months <note>Cancer and Leo.</note>, it brings forth an offspring of various fruits, until approaching **Virgo**, and now as if weighed down by old age with failing strength, it is once again committed to its six-month burial. 

Thus, under the <term>parallel sphere<note>The perspective from the poles, where the celestial equator is parallel to the horizon.</note></term>, the Sun labors from **Aries** until **Taurus** in dissolving the snow and ice. From **Taurus** until **Gemini**, it is occupied in drying the earth, pushing the same forth into grasses and herbs. From **Gemini** to **Cancer** and **Leo**, it spends two months in ripening the fruits. But in the remaining space of **Virgo**, as if weary of such a long stay above the horizon, it seeks the underworld again, and all things return to their former squalor. 

You see, therefore, the marvelous industry of nature, distributing light everywhere with such an equal balance that what the ray could not conquer (since here it never rises more than twenty-three and a half degrees above the horizon), the persistent duration of its stay does conquer. For since the caumatic triangle of reflection there is most obtuse, it could not suffice to dissipate such squalor and horror unless that long stay gradually, bit by bit, strengthened and multiplied the heat caused by such a small reflection. 

Let the parallel sphere be **ABC**, the equator and horizon together **BC**, the poles of the world **AC**, and the Sun in the tropic of **Cancer** **DE**, where in circling the horizon it forms a radiant cone.

# CHAPTER VI.
## On the effectiveness of reflection regarding the change of the air, plants, and animals, specifically under the five said zones.

<margin>The Torrid Zone of various natures.</margin>

**U**NDER the <term>right sphere<note>The celestial sphere as seen from the Equator, where the poles lie on the horizon.</note></term>, or the **Torrid Zone** <note>The Tropics</note>, the most powerful perpendicular action of light is followed by an equally powerful attraction of vapors, stirred up with sudden motion. Since these vapors cannot be processed by the Sun with equal speed as it glides toward the west, they are resolved into rains which temper the sweltering air. Because this effect lasts for almost an entire month, the constitution of the air is rendered humid; vegetables flourish most luxuriously, weighted down with moisture. Bodies are burdened by the tedious heat until the Sun, moving closer to **Cancer** or **Capricorn** <note>The solstices.</note>, now forms caumatic triangles that gradually move from the "natural nature" of light into a triangular form, thus bringing about serenity and dryness. Directly opposite to this most powerful normal <note>Perpendicular</note> action is the radiation under the pole, which is tangent or parallel to the horizon and is the weakest of all. In the **Temperate Zone**, however, as the caumatic triangles grow more acute, they become sharper the closer the Sun is to the zenith. From this proximity, various degrees of heat emerge, followed by the temperaments of natural things growing under the same zone.

Hence, animals proper to the Temperate Zone degenerate in both color and form under the Torrid Zone: sheep grow humps, dogs go bald, birds change colors, and countless similar things which the experience of modern times has taught. Under the **Frigid Zone**, animals—swelling to a massive size due to excessive moisture and the expanding cold—change from a black color to white. Herbs and plants proper to the Temperate Zone, when planted under the Torrid Zone, acquire such a different constitution that they are scarcely recognizable; many degenerate into a fringed growth of leaves and acquire something of an aromatic quality. Some conceive such horror from the unaccustomed region that, impatient of the soil, they prefer to die rather than become accustomed to it.

<margin>Properties under the Frigid Zone.</margin>

Under the Frigid Zone, all leaf growth, luxuriating in undigested moisture, becomes watery; thus apple, cherry, plum, and similar trees planted there acquire the temperament of **Moneywort** (which they also call **Venus's Navel**), **Bean-caper**, or **Water-lily**. Under the Torrid Zone, men are rendered so varied in inclination by the perpetual change and the violence of the heat that they are constituted as entirely different from Europeans. Indeed, you will find most to be /cunning, deceitful, fickle, fierce, and lustful/, recommended by no praise of talent, prudence, or fortitude, even when the greatest cultivation is applied; the particular constitutions and nature of these places greatly promote this variety. Under the Frigid Zone, men obtain a temperament diametrically opposite to those mentioned: for due to the intemperance of moisture and cold, they are for the most part /dull, senseless, slow, timid, cold, of the most obtuse talent/, and unskilled in managing affairs, having been allotted (as the saying goes) <term>a soul instead of salt<note>original: "animam... pro sale sortiti." A Latin idiom implying the soul serves only to keep the body from rotting, like salt preserves meat, suggesting a lack of higher intelligence or wit.</note></term>. Those of the **Middle Zones**, however, although varied, obtain a better and more temperate complexion, as we have demonstrated more extensively in our *Chromocritica*; even if according to certain degrees; so that a better, more perfect...

...and the temperament of heat and cold, if it falls between the thirty-fifth degree of latitude and the fifty-fifth, and is always more perfect the closer it approaches the forty-fifth degree; they contract a greater imbalance in all things the more they approach the torrid and frigid zones on either side. ### Corollaries, in which experiments regarding the transplantation of trees, plants, and other things are presented.

<margin>New experiments on the transplantation of herbs.</margin>
From all this, it is clear that the degrees of heat can so alter a plant that they make it of an entirely different species. Thus, experience has found that **Cinnamon** brought from India and planted in suitable soil in Europe degenerated into **Laurel** <note>Sweet Bay</note> due to a lack of heat; and indeed, that Laurel contains some traces of Cinnamon within itself is more than sufficiently declared by its very scent, its <term>Solar power<note>In Kircher's time, aromatic and "hot" plants were believed to be governed by the Sun's astrological influence.</note></term>, and the aromatic quality with which it is imbued. I have it on the report of eyewitnesses that **Pepper** sown in Portugal and tended with diligent cultivation eventually degenerated into our local **Ivy**; this will seem not at all far-fetched to anyone who rightly compares the caustic power of Ivy and its sharp flavor, the shape of its berries, and its leaves with the properties of Pepper. We know that the **Persea** <note>Possibly the *Mimusops laurifolia* or a related species mentioned by ancient authors as toxic in Persia but edible in Egypt.</note> in Arabia and Persia possesses a deadly quality, yet here it provides a most sweet-tasting food. **Arum** <note>Cuckoopint or Lords-and-Ladies</note>, on the other hand, is useless in Europe because of its gnawing, acrid power, yet in Egypt, it is a most sweet type of vegetable. It has been found by Portuguese physicians that the **Nutmeg**, which grows under the torrid zone, turns into a plant similar to a **Chestnut** when transplanted to Europe. The **Cypress**, when placed in more Northern regions, either refuses to grow at all or is known to degenerate into something like **Savin** <note>A low-growing, scrubby juniper.</note> even with diligent care.

<margin>The marvelous power of the veins of the earth.</margin>
I said "in suitable soil"; for such species are not thought to grow everywhere they are planted, but only in soil appropriate to them. Thus, in Italy, the Laurel is the same as the Cinnamon on the island of Ceylon; and Ivy is the same as the Pepper of Cochin in India. In Livonia <note>Modern-day Latvia and Estonia.</note>, Savin or garden Cypress is the same as the Cypress tree. For there are certain "veins" diffused throughout the entire earth, which if anyone understood, he could undoubtedly produce plants grafted into them of the same species as the aromatic herbs that India supplies us, even if, lacking sufficient color, they might fail in the perfection of their natural gifts. Certainly, whoever rightly compares our local **Turpentine** and **Larch** trees with the plants from which balsams flow in the West Indies will see that they are, as it were, of the same species; but in India, as if in their native soil, they "degenerate" <note>Here used in the sense of "diverge" or "transform."</note> into a nobler nature. The same must be said of the **Acacia**, or **Tragacanth**, which under the temperate zone gives us **Arabic Gum**, but in New Spain <note>Mexico</note> produces **White Balsam**, or that health-giving gum they call **Tacmac** <note>Tacamahaca, a medicinal resin.</note>. Nor is this metamorphosis hidden even in different climates: for the herbs that grow in Italy and Germany are very different. **Hyssop** and **Southernwood**, which have a most pleasing scent in Germany, are found here <note>in Italy</note> to have a very dull scent.

<margin>The difference between plants in Germany and Italy.</margin>
In contrast, **Basil** is found here in Italy to be most sweet and of a very sharp scent, while in Germany it is of a duller scent. We know that the stalks of **Fennel** in Italy are of a most sweet flavor and are used at the table at any time of the month, as are gourds and beans; in Germany, they are left as fodder for pigs, donkeys, and goats. I could bring forward innumerable examples of this sort here, were I not to believe they are known to everyone. All these things find their origin in <term>anacamptic actinobolism<note>Kircher's term for the way light rays are emitted and then reflected back from the earth, creating localized microclimates.</note></term>, or reflected radiation; for these provide the suitable and necessary conditions according to the requirement of each zone, region, and climate. These things are so true and evident that we see nature itself has played at representing the three zones on the highest mountains of Europe.

<margin>The property of the zones on the highest mountains.</margin>
Let **Mount Etna** stand as a representative of all, in which herbs proper to all three spheres are found: the plain around the base of the mountain is sweltering and humid, producing plants proper to the torrid zone such as **Amomum**, **Cashew**, **Malabathrum** <note>Cinnamon leaf</note>, **Plantain**, and **Sweet Flag**. Around the middle of the mountain, it produces all kinds of herbs belonging to the temperate zone. Finally, around the sandy summit—filled with snow, desolate, cold, and windy—it produces those herbs which the cold regions are accustomed to bring forth, thus constituting a frigid zone. This occurs because the reflected ray relates to the regions of the mountain in exactly the same way as it relates to the three aforementioned zones of the world.

<margin>The qualities of plants according to the various regions of mountains.</margin>
The nature of plants follows these mountain zones: torrid, temperate, and frigid. In the plains, or fervent soil, plants grow with an ample and cheerful appearance, with a swelling, smooth, leafy stalk and fleshy fruit. Around the middle of the mountains, they have a bright, smooth stalk...

# CHAPTER VII.
->On the causes of the change of things in various climates of the earth.<-

WE are not speaking here of the specific qualities of each plant, but of the primary or secondary ones which they acquire through transplantation: for only he knows that these arise from more or less heat and moisture, and the other qualities of the soil in which they grow, who has understood how much the change of locations can achieve in the mutation of humors. I shall clarify the matter with experiments.

### *Experiments in transplantation.*

Take any herb you like—for example, **Basil** <note>original: "Ocymum"</note>—and plant it in various places; for instance, in arid and dry places, without care and neglected; then plant another in a domestic garden, cultivated with singular care and continuous irrigation. You will find a manifest difference between them in odor and taste. Indeed, to one who tastes it, the one in the arid places will be found sharper and hotter than the one that grew up with cultivation and watering; so much so that the former seems to have reached the third degree of heat, while the latter has scarcely reached the first. For in the one cultivated with frequent irrigation, the force of heat is, as it were, blunted; whereas the one planted in arid places grows up content with its natural moisture, all superfluous and external moisture having evaporated. The same thing happens in other plants that are planted in different locations—humid, wet, arid, or sweltering. Hence, for these stated reasons, wild herbs are much more effective in medicines than garden varieties, for through cultivation they decline somewhat from their native character.

This is not only true in plants and vegetables, but also in animals. Hence there is such a great difference between domestic and wild animals, even of the same species. <margin>The miraculous metamorphosis of a certain animal.</margin> Herrera <note>Antonio de Herrera y Tordesillas (1549–1626), a Spanish historian famous for his accounts of the Americas.</note> reports that there is an animal in America that first becomes accustomed to the air like a bird; then it assumes the nature of a quadruped, with its wings degenerating into front feet; finally, when old age comes on, it commits itself to the sea; and at last, it is thoroughly transformed into a beast, or sea monster. Certainly, in the case of divers <note>original: "urinatoribus", referring to professional breath-hold divers.</note> who from youth become accustomed to being under water, the organs of respiration are so transformed by the perpetual moisture that they differ little from fish. Read what natural histories relate about **The Fish-Cola** <note>original: "Pisce Cola," referring to the Sicilian legend of Colapesce, a man said to have lived in the sea.</note> and others, and about the inhabitants of Lake Colai in the works of the aforementioned Herrera. However, since we have dealt with such matters extensively in our *Chromocritica* <note>Kircher’s work on the nature of color and light.</note>, I did not wish to be longer here.

# CHAPTER VIII.
->On the Line of luminous action, its terminus, and the quantity of heat.<-

In this place, we call the **Line of luminous action** that which terminates the action of radiant diffusion. We say this is equal to the line composed of the incident and reflected ray, and it can occur according to three cases; for either the reflected line is equal to the incident line, and then the obstacle—or **reflective object** <term>anacampticum: from the Greek "anakamptikos," meaning reflecting or bending back.</term>—will necessarily occupy the midpoint of the line of action. For example, if the line of action is AC, the reflective object will be at B, and the ray from A to B, and the ray reflected from B to A, will be as large as half the line of action AB. Which I confirm by this experience. Let a candle be placed at A, whose...

...light spread through opening B, fails at the smallest **natural minimum**. This occurs if you move back so far that the light is completely obscured by darkness. Then, let a very polished fragment of a mirror be inserted into opening B, and you will note that the light reflected at point A is obscured at the same distance as the straight ray at C. If, however, in the second case the reflected line is shorter in—

<image-desc>A horizontal line segment with four vertical marks. The letters A, I, S, and C are placed below the marks from left to right, creating three equal intervals.</image-desc>

—it will be established beyond the midpoint of the line of action, as at S; and the line of reflection SI will be equal to SC: which you will experience if you observe the light introduced through opening S into C, and the same light, with a mirror placed at S, reflected at I; for you will see that, as far as the senses can tell, it suffers a decrease and vanishes into nothing. Thirdly, if indeed the reflected line is—

<image-desc>A horizontal line segment with four vertical marks. The letters I, A, V, and C are placed below the marks from left to right, creating three equal intervals.</image-desc>

—longer than the incident line, then the <term>anacamptic</term> <note>original: "anacampticum"; from the Greek for "reflecting" or "bending back." This refers to a reflecting object like a mirror.</note> object will necessarily be placed on this side of the midpoint of the line of action, as at V, and the reflected line VI will exceed the incident line AV by the quantity VC. You will find the truth of this matter if you correctly observe the light transmitted through opening V into C, and the same light reflected to the opposite side from a mirror placed at V; for you will find both the magnitude and the brightness. And this experiment is always true, that is, whether the ray falls upon the mirror at right angles or oblique angles, the incident and reflected lines taken together will always equal the total line of action.

<margin>The reason why the line of action is equal to the incident and reflected lines combined.</margin>
Having seen the experiment, let us look at the reason. There have been those who said that light, blocked by the obstruction of an opaque body, becomes more illustrious, or, being hindered from extension, gathers itself for intensification, as if compensating in its own subject for what it could not pour into another; they refer the cause of this to <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>original: "antiperistasim"; a Scholastic philosophical concept where a quality is intensified by being surrounded by its opposite (e.g., heat being concentrated by surrounding cold). Kircher rejects this as a cause for light reflection.</note>. But since nothing is opposed to light, as it is immaterial, nor is there anything that can plot its destruction, light is not intensified by its encounter with a circumstance of its opposite (which they call **antiperistasis**); rather, because the rays are struck back by the opaque body, the neighboring medium glows with a more excellent degree of light. For that which it ought to have imparted to the medium immediately following, it spends upon itself by reciprocating back when the opaque body resists; and thus, by accident and not of its own accord, the light hindered from further progress is intensified. From what has been said, therefore, it is clear that the line composed of the reflected and incident rays is always equal to the total line of action. But since all these things depend on the terms of the beginning and ending of things, I have decided to describe them a little more precisely.

**Great** is the controversy among Philosophers regarding the limits of natural powers, and concerning their boundaries—where they begin and where they end; their opinions take their origin from a diverse misuse of names rather than from the thing itself. To me, certainly, that view has always been pleasing: that all things are started and finished by intrinsic boundaries, whether they consist of stable things or flow by motion:

<margin>How things begin and end.</margin>
for that which is first and last of any thing is either the whole thing itself, or a part, or some indivisible point. None of these can rightly be called "extrinsic," since they all exist within the thing itself; therefore, all things arise and cease by intrinsic beginnings and ends. However, we are not dealing with this at present, since it is established that light in its entire sphere rises and sets all at once. Again, it is established that the activity of light is limited by no boundary of smallness, if we speak of the indivisibles of intensity; but we are not treating that either. We say, however, that light cannot exist by its own power in isolation under just any degree of intensity, but that there is some limit of smallness beyond which it is not permitted to proceed by dividing without its destruction; which we consequently call, not incongruously, the <term>minimum naturale</term> <note>original: "minimum naturale"; a philosophical term referring to the smallest amount of a natural substance or quality that can still retain its identity and exist in nature.</note>. If, moreover, another smaller light is added to a larger one, however tiny it may be, nothing prevents this smaller light from being sustained by the help of the larger, provided that together on both sides they at least reach the **natural minimum**. Furthermore, this weakness of subsisting is common not only to these qualities which admit a diversity of "lesser" and "greater," but also to all bodies that vary in magnitude; for just as these bodies cannot save themselves from destruction without some mass, so those qualities cannot save themselves without some degree of excellence. For once they are thinned beyond their strength, they perish, collapsing into nothing with no contrary intervening, but only by a defect of measure, which is required by the irrefrangible law of nature as a necessary condition for each thing's own protection. And indeed, if it were not so, every outpouring of light would be extended infinitely, which is repugnant, as will be seen in what follows. Therefore, this ray propagated from a luminous body as far as the **natural minimum**, we call the **line of action**, namely, the boundary of radiant diffusion: for along this line the diffused light gradually faints and fails with a uniform deformity, not according to an arithmetic proportion, but a geometric one—that is, in equal spaces, with unequal or proportional decreases.

<margin>Light is spread uniformly.</margin>
Which I show thus: since it is established from that whole axiom that every effect must be proportioned to its cause, it is certain that the effect can never be of a power entirely equal to the cause; but it is always so much smaller as the cause is rendered weaker, both by itself and by the length of the space in which it produces the action. Wherefore, if the action is divided by equal spaces, the decrease of the effect will take its origin solely from the weakness of the agent;

It also introduces the "natural minimum," the threshold of intensity required for light to exist before it fades into nothingness.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of light intensity from page 534, moving from the way light fades over distance to how it multiplies when multiple sources are combined, particularly in the context of reflection.</meta>

<page-num>535</page-num>

-> Theory of the <term>Anacamptic</term> <note>From the Greek *anakamptikos*, meaning "reflecting" or "bending back." This refers to the science of reflected light, or Catoptrics.</note> Art. <-

<margin>Light increases in geometric proportion</margin>
will result; therefore, just as the source is weaker, the effect is further diminished; not in an equal amount, but in proportion to the power of the source. For example, if a light whose power is 12 spreads half of itself (6) through a given space, I say that a light of 6 will spread 3 (likewise half of itself) through an equal space. For as a source of 6 is to a source of 12, so the effect of 3 is to the effect of 6. If a light of 6 produced a greater light than 3 through that space, then another light equal to it would also produce more than 3; therefore, joined together, they would propagate an effect greater than the half of both combined. These two lights would then be more powerful with their forces joined than a light of 12 acting by itself, which is false. Furthermore, that two lights of 6 acting together produce an effect composed of the action of both is clear from this: just as the power of a part relates to the power of the whole, so does the power of the whole relate to the light of the whole. Since the power of equal lights is equal, and equal power produces an equal effect, then two lights are equal in both force and effect to a single light of 12. For where a light of 12 produces a light of 6 at a certain interval, a light of 6 produces 3; when doubled, these produce a light of 6. From this it is clearly evident that light is diminished by proportional decreases over equal spaces, which was to be demonstrated.

Since this triangle is composed of a double radiation, it must necessarily intensify both light and heat, just as was evident from the preceding experiment. The light and heat will always be more intense the more acute the triangle is at point **L**. Furthermore, it will always be sharper as it approaches the normal (perpendicular) radiation at **B** in the first figure, where the caumatic triangle of reflection will "degenerate" into a parallelogram; and thus, it intensifies heat much more than in triangle **NLO**, as we said occurs under the <term>torrid zone</term> <note>The area of the Earth between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, known for its intense heat.</note>. However, the further the light is from **B**, the more this caumatic triangle **NLO** will produce an obtuse angle around **L**. The more obtuse it is, the more relaxed or diminished the heat it will cause, until in the <term>subpolar region</term> <note>The areas just below the Arctic or above the Antarctic circles.</note> the solar radiation once again "degenerates" into a parallelogram, as is clear in this figure;

<margin>The condition of the caumatic triangle.</margin>

<image-desc>A small circular diagram showing two rays (labeled 'R') intersecting a curved surface within a larger circle, forming a triangle labeled 'R' at the point of convergence, illustrating the reflection of light rays and the formation of a "caumatic triangle."</image-desc>

but this happens without effect or intensity of heat, since the radiation strikes the earth at such an extreme slant that it does so only by contact <note>Original: *per contactum*; meaning the rays merely graze the surface rather than hitting it directly.</note>. From this it is also inferred that the more acute the <term>anacamptic</term> <note>Reflective; referring to the angle at which light bounces back.</note> triangle is, the more intense the heat will be: for the more acute it is, the larger the portion of air it always illuminates; but it is always smaller the more obtuse it is, and consequently it obtains a more "obtuse" (dulled) heat, as is clearly evident from what has been said.

From this arises a certain easy method of detecting the degree of heat in any anacamptic triangle, namely by this ingenious device. Let the caumatic triangles be **BOC**, **DOE**, **IOM**, **NOG**, etc. Since solar heat always decreases more the further it recedes from the equator, the said triangles will represent the intensity and remission of heat in each degree of the Climate, so that the

same proportion of the remission and intensity of heat exists as the proportion of the chord subtending the caumatic angle to the chord of the other triangle; or better, the same proportion as the <term>versed sine</term> <note>A trigonometric function (1 - cosine). In Kircher’s era, these were essential for calculating angles in astronomy and optics.</note> to the sine of its complement <note>The "sine of the complement" is what we now call the cosine.</note>. Thus, under the equator, the final degree of heat relates to the final degree of intensity as the versed sine **A** of 0 degrees relates to the sine of its complement—that is, to the total sine, or the radius **AO**. For the Sun, while it is reflected back upon itself (the Sun declining from **A** to **B**), not only makes the ray a simple line reflected back on itself, or—if we look at the width of the radiation—a sort of cylinder whose middle line or axis represents the total sine in the present figure. Again, as the Sun declines from **A** to **B**, the reflected ray from **O** to **C** forms a triangle, whose base **BC** (the chord cutting the total radius at **α**) creates the versed sine **αA** and its complement **αO**. I say that the decrease of heat relates as the versed sine **αA** does to its complement **αO**, such that the parts of the triangle **Aα** designate cold, and **αO** designate heat. In this way, you will see a certain proportional decrease of heat according to the Sun's descent or elevation, down to 0 degrees, at which point the entire force of heat perishes, compressed into point **O**, and the force of cold is signified by the radius, or total sine **AO**. This occurs in the subpolar region, where the Sun, entering the equator, grazes the horizon, and strikes the earth with no triangle or radiant cone, but its ray is terminated by a tangent line.

<margin>The increase and decrease of heat and cold.</margin>

Furthermore, if we establish point **A** under the equinoctial for the chord of 0 degrees, we will see that there is no degree of cold there, just as there is no chord subtending a caumatic triangle. From this point, however, the chord gradually decreases until **XY**, where it will signify that there is no heat, but that cold absorbs all heat. Thus, to explore the degrees of heat under any given altitude of the Sun compared to the heats of the torrid zone:

### Explanation of the Table.

The first column shows the versed sines, according to which cold is intensified. The second column shows the altitudes of the Sun, both the maximums for the entire year and the specific ones for each day. The third column shows the complements of the versed sine—namely, the quantity of the axis of the burning triangles, according to which the increase of heat occurs. The fourth shows the elevations of the pole <note>Latitude.</note> corresponding to the maximum altitudes of the Sun.

You see, therefore, by what proportion the heat is now intensified and now diminished according to the Sun's declination from the <term>zenith</term> <note>Original: "vertice," referring to the point directly overhead.</note>.

### Corollary I.

<margin>Light and heat are equal in all places.</margin>
And from this wonderful proportion, a great secret in the nature of things is revealed: namely, that all places of the whole world, and even the locations directly under the pole, possess equal degrees of heat. You will experience this if you multiply the quantity of the daylight arc under each altitude of the pole placed here by the complement of the versed sine (or the axis of the burning triangle) corresponding to the Sun's maximum altitude. For the sum will always give as much as emerges from the individual parts. Since heat is proportionally intensified from the pole to the <term>equator</term> <note>Original: "æquinoctialem."</note> according to the increases in the altitude of the meridian Sun, it happens that as much as is lost in one place is gained in another. Every deficit of heat resulting from the weakness of the ray resting on the horizon is compensated by the length of the day, or the duration of time spent above the horizon at given latitudes. The same is to be understood regarding the increases and decreases of cold, and regarding the altitudes of the Sun at individual hours. 

But perhaps someone will say it cannot be true that the heat under the pole is equal to the heat pressing upon the <term>torrid zone</term>. But I respond that this is true if the earth is considered simply and without respect to the specific nature of locations; and I say the Sun can achieve as much in 180 days (or a six-month space) by being perpetually above the horizon—even if at an unequal altitude—as it can under the equator during a 12-hour span above the horizon at an unequal altitude. When weighed in the equal balance of the intellect, the heat of both is equal. Likewise, the Sun can do as much in a space of 24 hours at 23 degrees above the horizon...

### *Corollary II.*

**F**rom this it also follows why, under different climates, herbs and fruits come forth at various and different times; under the tropic of <gloss>Cancer ♋︎</gloss>, fruits which are born around the equinox, and are accustomed to come forth here in April, come forth almost one month later in Germany, and almost one month later in Sweden and Norway, all the way to the pole. The same must be said of other things: for which there is indeed no other reason than the resistance of the earth, which, having been chilled more than is proper by the length of the nights, resists the heat; which chill cannot be overcome except by the length, or increase, and the delay of the Sun above the horizon.

### *Corollary III.*

**F**rom this proportional increase and decrease of heat caused by the reflected ray, and from the sharpness or bluntness of the <term>caumatic triangles</term> <note>From the Greek 'kauma' (burning heat). These are geometric models used by Kircher to calculate the intensity of solar heat based on the angle of incidence and reflection.</note> mentioned above, it follows finally that the <term>anacamptic sphere</term> <note>From the Greek 'anakampto' (to bend back). This refers to the layer of the atmosphere where light is reflected and heat is contained.</note>, or sphere of reflection established around the earth, is of an oval shape. Let the earth be A, and the anacamptic sphere BDCE, in which you see that under the equinoctial line BC—where the reverberation of the external mass of rays is more powerful—the rays establish a higher sphere of reflection than under the poles DE, where, due to the very oblique incidence of the rays and the lack of heat, the vapors are not raised so high. In the intermediate regions, indeed, according to a greater or lesser proximity to the Sun, the rays are also extended with a proportional decrease or increase. 

From all these things, when thoroughly considered, the infinite goodness of God the Best and Greatest—who constructed the world with such order, such proportion, and finally such harmony—shines forth; so that while He makes His sun rise upon the good and the bad, He provides this with such equity and justice that no nation in the whole world can ever complain that divine providence or nature, its servant, has failed them in any place. So that even from this very fact, we are bound in countless ways to serve solely such a munificent Giver of things. Therefore, having discussed the nature and efficiency of reflected light, nothing remains except that we show its nature by mathematical reasoning in the following part. This might not poorly be called an <term>Isagoge</term> <note>An introductory manual or treatise.</note> to the Anacamptic Art, or the science of reflections.

# PART TWO OF THE ANACAMPTIC ART
## THEORETICAL PRINCIPLES

### Theorem I.
->*Nature acts in all things according to the shorter lines.*<-

<image-desc>A technical diagram illustrating the principles of physical motion and light. At the top, points D, E, S, and F represent different positions of the Sun. Below this, a semicircular arc is labeled A, C, and B, with point C at the zenith. A horizontal chord connects points I and K. At the bottom center, point L is marked. <margin>All natural things act through the shortest lines.</margin>
**A**bundant evidence from all the works of nature testifies that Nature acts in all things according to shorter lines, and acts more strongly and powerfully if those lines are <term>normal<note>In geometry, "normal" means perpendicular or at a right angle (90 degrees) to a surface.</note></term>. For all natural motions occur in this way: heavy objects descend perpendicularly upon the surface of the horizon, and they know no other motion. For it is impossible for a heavy body to fall to the underlying surface of the earth through lines DC or FC, for example, as they are longer and more oblique. The Sun also, the shorter and more perpendicular—or rather, the straighter—the ray with which it strikes the earth, the more powerful an effect of heat it will produce. For instance, the Sun positioned at E will heat the earth’s surface ACB more effectively than when positioned at D or S; for no other reason than that in the former case it acts by a shorter and straighter or, so to speak, more perpendicular line; whereas in the latter case it acts by a longer and more oblique line. And the longer or more oblique the line according to which any action is completed, the always weaker the effect it will achieve.

From this it is clear why all things boil under the force of the most intense heat in the torrid zone; conversely, under the poles of the world, all things grow stiff from the harshness of the cold, as was shown a little while ago. From this it is also clear that the greater the approach made toward the <term>equinoctial<note>The celestial equator.</note></term> line, the more vehement the future heat will always be. The reason is that the Solar rays will approach closer to the shorter and more perpendicular line. Again, arrows shot violently from bows are carried by a shorter line, according to the angle of their release, as appears in the figure above. For let the arc be ACB, and the chord IK. I say that the arrow must only be shot according to the shorter line CE, and that it is impossible for it to happen through other longer lines, since the force of the push is not carried except into the shorter line.

<margin>Demonstration.</margin>
From this it also follows that all shots from machines and military engines of war, unless they are directed perpendicularly, obtain no power in shattering walls. Hence, also, motion is faster from the same starting point to the same end point through a shorter line: for since, according to the first <term>petition<note>In logic or geometry, a "petition" (postulate) is a fundamental assumption accepted without proof.</note></term>, nature does nothing in vain, nor fails in necessary things; it is clear that she necessarily acts according to shorter lines.

<insert>A |——| B |——| C</insert>

Which is demonstrated as follows: Let nature work through motion or action according to the line AC. I ask whether she can complete the whole intended operation through motion or action along the line AB, or not. If the former is true, and yet she acts through the line ABC, then every action she performs through the line BC is in vain <note>original: "frustranea"</note>, since she attained her goal at point B. Since nature, as stated, does nothing in vain; and she would act in vain if, having attained her goal at B, she were to act further along the line BC: Therefore, she acts not at all in BC. Therefore, she will only perform what was proposed according to the shorter line AB. 

And this is clear by running through many examples of natural things; for animals, whose mover is the soul, are moved toward a goal according to the shorter line, as is clear in the straightness of the threads which spiders weave; for even if they are sometimes found to be circular, they are nevertheless woven from straight threads, both the warp and the woof, for the sake of the shortness of the line. The same is also clear in dogs, who, ignoring two sides of a triangle, run through the third <note>The hypotenuse of a right triangle.</note>, just as if they knew by natural instinct that two sides of a triangle are greater than the third. Therefore, nature in all lines acts by the shortest. Which was to be demonstrated.
