Book VII of the Great Art. Prometheus Part II.
<note>The "Great Art" refers to Kircher’s *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae* (The Great Art of Light and Shadow). "Prometheus" is the title of this specific section, named after the mythological figure who brought fire/light to humanity.</note>

## Theorem II.

*In every reflection made by any mirror whatsoever, the angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection.*

Since any <term>form<note>In this context, "form" refers to the visual image or the ray of light itself.</note></term>—whether through a plane, convex, or concave mirror—is contained within the shortest lines (as we shall demonstrate shortly), it follows that the lines produced from the same points (namely, from the point of the incoming forms and the reflected forms) to the surface of the mirror are the shortest. These shortest lines contain equal angles both with the lines touching the surfaces of the mirrors and with the <term>perpendiculars<note>Lines at a 90-degree angle to the surface.</note></term> drawn from their point of meeting upon the surfaces of the mirrors. Furthermore, the angles which the rays of the incoming and reflected forms create on the surface of the mirror are nothing other than the <term>angle of incidence<note>original: "angulus incidentiæ"; the angle at which light hits the surface.</note></term> and the <term>angle of reflection<note>original: "angulus reflexionis"; the angle at which light bounces off.</note></term>, which are always equal and contained within the shortest lines. Thus, the proposition is clear.

## Theorem III.

*Every object seen, or any other form reflected from any mirror, is contained within the shortest lines.*

Let there be a mirror, on whose surface is a straight or curved line **HDE**; let the point of the form or object seen be at **C**, and the eye (or the location of the reflected form) be at **F**: I say that the lines **DC** and **DF** are shorter than all other lines drawn from points **C** and **F** to any other points of the mirror. Or, to propose it better: I say that the lines of incidence and reflection, which contain equal angles with the perpendicular drawn from the point of their meeting upon the surface of the mirror, are shorter than all lines produced from the same endpoints over the same surface of the mirror that contain unequal angles with the perpendiculars drawn from their points of meeting.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the law of reflection. A horizontal line H-D-E represents the mirror. Above it, a dashed horizontal line contains points C, G, and F. A vertical line K-G-D is the normal (perpendicular) to the mirror at point D. Solid lines CD and DF show the path of a reflected ray where the angles are equal. Another potential path is shown via point E (lines CE and EF). Below the mirror, construction lines extend to points L and M to facilitate the geometric proof that the path C-D-F is the shortest possible distance.</image-desc>

Let us now take, for the sake of example, a plane mirror **HDE**, whose line is the straight line **HDE**. Let the lines of incidence and reflection be **CD** and **DF**. Now, either the center of vision (the location of the reflected form) will be on the line **CGF** (which is parallel to the line **HDE**) or it will not. If it is, let the center of the eye be **F**; and if the perpendicular line drawn from **D** intersects the line **CF** at **G**, it will divide the <term>triangle<note>original: "trigonum"</note></term> **CFE** (the surface of reflection) into two equal triangles. I show this as follows: If the angles **CDH** and **FDE** (which are the angles of incidence and reflection and are equal by hypothesis) are subtracted from the two right angles **GDH** and **GDE**, those that remain will be equal, according to the <term>common notion of the mind<note>A reference to Euclid’s Common Notions/Axioms: "If equals be subtracted from equals, the remainders are equal."</note></term>. Since triangles **CGD** and **FGD** remain, they are equal; therefore the angles are equal to the angles, and the sides facing the equal angles are proportional, according to **Euclid, Book 6, Proposition 4**.

With these things established, let lines **CE** and **FE** be drawn from **E** (or any other point of the mirror) to the points **C** and **F** (the endpoints of the incoming and reflected form), which have a common base with the triangle **CDF** parallel to the line **HDE**. Thus, while the triangle **CFE** has unequal sides and angles, the triangle **CFD** is equal <note>meaning its two halves are symmetrical</note>. I say that the sides of the triangle **CD** and **DF** taken together are smaller than the sides **CE** and **EF** of triangle **CFE** taken together.

I demonstrate it thus: Let line **CD** be extended beyond point **D** in a continuous straight line to point **L**, so that line **DL** is equal to line **DF**. Furthermore, let line **CE** (which is the longer side of triangle **CFE**) be extended beyond point **E** to point **M**, until line **EM** becomes equal to line **EF**, and let line **LM** and line **EL** be joined. Because angle **FDE** is equal to angle **DFC** (by **Book 1, Proposition 29**), and angle **DEC** is equal to angle **CDF** (as is clear from the premises), and angle **EDL** is equal to angle **FCD**, then angle **FDE** will be equal to angle **EDL**. But line **DL** is equal to line **DF**, and line **DE** is common to both triangles **DFE** and **ELM**. Therefore, by **Book 1, Proposition 4**, line **EF** is equal to line **LF**, and thus also to line **EM**, and therefore the angles **ELM** and **EML** are equal. Thus, the total angle **CLM** is greater than angle **CML**. Therefore, by **Euclid, Book 1, Proposition 19**, line **CM** is longer than line **CL**. Consequently, the two sides **CE** and **EF** accepted together are greater than the two sides **CD** and **DF** taken together. Which was to be demonstrated.

Furthermore, if the center of vision (the location of the reflected form) is not placed on the line **CGF** parallel to **DE**, but at **B**, let a line be drawn from **B** to **A** parallel to **CF**, and extend line **DC** to **A**, the perpendicular **DG** to **K**, and **DF** to **B**, as well as **AE** and **EB**, as you see. ### Theorem IV.

#### *The angles of incidence and reflection are equal.*

**L**Et the plane surface of the mirror be $CBA$, the ray of the luminous body be $MB$, and the ray of the reflected form be $BN$: I say that the <term>angle of incidence<note>original: "angulus incidentiæ"</note></term> $MBA$ must always be equal to the <term>angle of reflection<note>original: "angulus reflexionis"</note></term> $NBC$. For since, as demonstrated in the preceding sections, the form of a luminous body is perceived through any mirror along the shortest lines, and the lines $MB$ and $BN$ (as the rays of incidence and reflection) are the shortest lines, beyond which nature would act in vain; it is clear that reflection cannot occur outside of these. Let it be granted that the light of body $M$ reflects from $S$ into $N$: therefore, the angle of reflection $NSC$ will be greater than the angle of incidence $MBA$: thus the angle is unequal to the angle. Therefore, according to the previous demonstration, the lines $MS$ and $SN$ taken together are greater and longer than lines $MB$ and $BN$, as is clear from what was demonstrated just before. Therefore, nature would be acting through them in vain, which, as it is against the common axiom of the Philosophers, neither can nor should be said. Therefore, since nature acts in all things through shorter lines, and in reflection the shortest lines are the incident and the reflected, and they would not be the shortest unless they established equal angles on the surface of the mirror: therefore, the angle of incidence and reflection are necessarily equal, which was to be demonstrated. 

<margin>Why the angle of incidence and reflection are equal.</margin>

But since perhaps not everyone will perceive our meaning in the preceding geometric demonstrations, especially those who are little accustomed to geometric considerations, it seemed fit to set the aforementioned things before their eyes a little more clearly by a physical method. Why, then, the angle of incidence is always made equal to the angle of reflection, and the line of the reflected ray always obtains the same position as the line of the incident ray: we establish this cause. Because when light, falling upon the mirror with a very swift motion, is unable to penetrate it because of its opacity, nor can it be fixed in its flat surface (since the force and nature of the prior impetus and motion still persist in it), the fixation being denied, it is rebounded back toward the part from which it proceeded (provided that the incidence occurs perpendicularly) and according to lines having the same position as the prior ones.

That the motion of reflection happens to light because of the resistance of the polished body is clear from the fact that a stronger reflection follows a stronger impulse and resistance of light. And the natural motion of heavy bodies teaches us that this is so.

# Great Art, Book VII. Prometheus Part II.

Regarding reflection: if anyone should ask me why it occurs, I respond that it arises from the force of the incident light, the repulsion of the mirror, and the perpendicular resistance—much like what happens in the natural motion of heavy bodies. For when a heavy body descends along a <term>perpendicular<note>A line at a right angle (90 degrees) to the surface.</note></term> line, we see things directly opposite, both by the repulsion of the polished body and the motion of the descending heavy body. We find no other motion there except a normal one, <margin>of the straight line</margin> <note>original Greek: τᾶς ὀρϑᾶς</note> and that which is <unclear>of the straight line</unclear>. From this, it follows that the body must return perpendicularly to the place from which it departed, or else no reflection occurs. However, when something heavy descends obliquely onto a surface, or along a sloping line, it will be reflected according to the same angle at which it struck. Light, indeed, possesses the same nature of reflecting as the motion of weights, or a ball thrown against a floor, or any other projected object. For since it is not natural for it to simply ascend or descend, it moves in reflection according to its initial line until it meets an obstacle that causes its motion to stop. Then, springing back, it will depart toward the opposite side at the same angle it would have followed in a straight path if it had encountered no obstacle at the point of reflection.

### Theorem V.

*The higher the luminous body is, the larger the angles of incidence and reflection it will cause, and consequently, the stronger the reflection.*

Let ABC be the plane of the mirror, the luminous body be at M, and the place of reflection at N. It is clearly evident that as the Sun rises above the horizon ABC, the higher it ascends, the larger the angles it will produce. For the angle created when the Sun is at D—namely, DBA—is larger than the angle MBA, which it makes when positioned at M. Now, if angle MBA were equal to angle DBA, then since the <term>arc<note>A segment of the curved path of the sun's travel.</note></term> AM is 30 degrees and AD is 60 degrees, 30 would be equal to 60, which is impossible. Indeed, 60 is twice as large as 30; therefore, when the Sun is at D, angle DBA will be twice as large as angle MBA made by the Sun at M. Thus, the higher a luminous body ascends, the larger the angles it will cause; this was the point to be noted. Having established this, I say consequently that the Sun's ray falling from D to B is refracted from B to F more powerfully and effectively than the ray MB reflected from B to N. For as was shown in the preceding sections, a luminous ray produces a more powerful reflection the more it approaches the perpendicular. It approaches the perpendicular more closely the further the luminous body is from the horizon and the higher it is elevated. It is clear, then, that the force of reflection always increases until the ray of incidence and the ray of reflection are united in one and the same perpendicular line, and thus they produce the most powerful action in the aforementioned throw of the ray. For where the incidence is higher and more perpendicular (as is seen in the motion of heavy weights), there the impetus and force of motion are greater; therefore, the repulsion of the plane is greater.

From this, it is gathered that the force of heat is greater under the <term>equinoctial<note>The Equator, where the sun passes directly overhead.</note></term> than in any other region of the world, whether it declines toward the North or the South. This is because the solar rays falling perpendicularly onto the terrestrial globe multiply the force of heat, as the reflection is made back upon itself. Moreover, the more or less cities or regions approach it, the more or less heat they will feel.

### Theorem VI.

*Sound, or the voice, follows the nature of the light ray in reflection.*

It should also be well noted that whatever has been said so far regarding the incidence of light and the reflection of opposing <term>forms<note>In this context, "forms" (species) refers to the visual images or rays carrying the appearance of an object.</note></term> can all be very aptly applied to sound.

A human figure, labeled S, stands at the right, observing or participating in the acoustic reflection from a vertical wall labeled R-h. Dotted lines show various paths of incidence and reflection, including perpendicular and oblique angles.</image-desc>

Sound is in all things the rival of light, particularly in its spherical diffusion, which is made uniformly-difformly (except that the motion of light is instantaneous, while that of sound is successive). For just as the reflected form of light is nothing other than the image and daughter of the primary light, so the reflected voice is nothing other than the image and daughter of the primary voice. Just as we have shown the reflection of light to occur by the extension of straight lines, by the same reasoning, the reverberated appearance of the voice must be judged to occur by the aid of straight lines. And first, indeed, the incidence of any voice against a solid and smooth wall at a perpendicular returns by retracing the same path according to which it fell, and the wandering appearance of the voice first emitted... ## Theorem VIII.

*In every reflection, it is necessary that the center of sight (or the location of the reflected form), the point of the seen form (or the point of the radiating body), the terminus of reflection, the perpendicular, and both Catheti, consist in the same surface of reflection.*
<note>A "Cathetus" in historical optics is a line drawn from a point (like the eye or the object) perpendicular to the reflecting surface.</note>

For if that perpendicular were terminated at another point outside the surface of reflection, it would be perpendicular in another surface, which is contrary to the 11th definition of this work, and it would have a right angle smaller than a right angle, which is impossible. Therefore, it is clear that the point of the form, the reflection, the eye, and the perpendicular are necessarily in the same surface. Suppose, however, that the perpendiculars were not in the same plane of reflection, but ended in another plane—for example, at points G and V. In that case, GN and OV would be parallel and not parallel to DC. Therefore, the angles ANG and BOV would be equal to the right angles ANE and DCO. Thus, a line could be drawn from another plane to this specific plane which would actually intersect all other lines—all of which are impossible. <margin>Everything seen in a mirror is seen on the perpendicular of incidence.</margin>

And from this follows what is most especially to be noted: namely, that in any mirror, every single point viewed is seen on the perpendicular of its own incidence. For since the uniform position of the point of the thing seen (which is E) with respect to the surface of any mirror from which its form is reflected occurs only according to the perpendicular of its incidence; and since the "form" <note>In 17th-century science, the "form" or "species" was the visual information traveling from an object to the eye.</note> seen in the mirror is nothing other than the orientation of the thing seen toward the mirror (otherwise that form would not be seen as an image); it will therefore necessarily be seen on the perpendicular of incidence. This was the proposition.

...the line of incidence AC is formed, and from point A let the perpendicular <term>cathetus</term> <note>A line dropped at a 90-degree angle to a surface.</note> ABE be drawn upon the line of the mirror BC D, and let it be extended as far as point E, until the line BE is made equal to AB itself. Then, let the line EC be continued and extended beyond C to point F. I declare that if the eye is positioned at any point on the line CF, reflection will always occur toward it, and the form of point A will be seen. For let the line AC be joined; then the angle ABC will be equal to the angle CBE because, as is evident from the previous statements, both those angles are right angles. Since, therefore, by our hypothesis the line BE is equal to AB, and the side BC is common to both, the triangles ABC and CBE are <term>isogonal</term> <note>having equal angles</note>; thus the angle ACB is equal to the angle BCE. But the angle FCD, according to the first theorem of the second book, is equal to the angle BCE. Therefore, the angle FCD is equal to the angle ACB. Consequently, since line AC is the line of incidence, CF will be the line of reflection: under that line, therefore, the reflection will be made to the eye. We have thus found the place where, once the eye is positioned, reflection occurs toward it, which is what was proposed.

<margin>Reflection occurs from a single point.</margin>
## Corollary I.

It follows from this aforementioned Theorem that the form of a point of a seen object is not reflected from a mirror to the same eye except from one point only. For if the reflection were to occur from another point, a perpendicular could also be raised at that point, which, once raised, would divide the triangle of reflection into two equal parts; but this is impossible, since a perpendicular dividing the triangle of the surface of reflection into two equal parts cannot be raised except at the single point where incidence and reflection are identified. Therefore, the proposition is clear.

---

<margin>Why, at the banks of rivers, houses and trees appear to extend as far below the water as they stand above it.</margin>
## Corollary II.

It also follows that the distance of the location of the image from the surface of a plane mirror below the mirror is the same as the distance of the seen point from that same surface existing above the plane mirror. As seen in the preceding figure, lines AB and BE are equidistant both from the mirror surface BCD and from the point of reflection by the equal lines CE and CA, one of which extends above and the other below the mirror. And from this, the reason is clear why, when we stand at the banks of rivers, pools, springs, and other waters, the tops of things appearing on the opposite bank seem to project as far below the water as they tower above it, and appear to be extended descending in a straight line.

---

<margin>The line from the center of vision to the location of the image equals the lines of incidence and reflection combined.</margin>
## Corollary III.

Finally, it is gathered from these things as well that the line drawn straight from the center of vision to the found location of the image—for example, the line FCE—is equal to the line of incidence and reflection added together, namely AC and CF. This is not difficult to prove. For since the line AB, or the cathetus of incidence, is set as equal to the line BE, the extended cathetus of incidence, and since the point of reflection C is common to both, it follows that AC is equal to EC, and the entire triangle ABC is similarly equal to the entire triangle BEC. Since, therefore, AC (as was said) is equal to the line CE, and the line CF is the line of reflection, it follows by the common mental notion—"Things which are equal to the same third thing are equal to each other"—that AC, CF, and CE are equal among themselves. Therefore, FC and CA taken together (namely the lines of incidence and reflection) will be equal to the whole line extended all the way to the location of the image, namely FCE. Which was to be demonstrated.

# THE REFLECTIVE ART <note>original: "Anacampticæ Artis." From the Greek word for "turning back" or "reflecting."</note>
# PART THREE.
# THEORETICAL.

## Theorem XI.

### *Concerning the properties of cylindrical and conical mirrors, insofar as they relate to the business of reflection.*

<margin>Various classifications of mirrors.</margin>
**SINCE** we have spoken at length in the preceding sections about the properties of plane mirrors in the rebounding of light, the order of our reasoning now seems to require that we say something also about mirrors of a different nature. Seven types of regular mirrors are enumerated by those skilled in <term>Catoptrics</term> <note>The branch of optics dealing with reflection.</note>. The first, and simplest, is the plane mirror, which we have dealt with until now. In addition, there are three convex types: namely, the spherical, the cylindrical, and the conical. There are also three concave types: namely, the columnar (or cylindrical), and the conical (or pyramidal). These are called "regular mirrors" because of the smooth surfaces of which they consist. For since a regular (or uniform) reflection cannot occur except from regular bodies—and regular bodies can generally only be bodies with plane surfaces, or of a single concave or convex surface—and every regular convex or concave surface is either part of the surface of a sphere, a column, or a cone: it follows that as many regular mirrors are established by the Teachers of Catoptrics as there can be regular surfaces. Furthermore, all mirrors of this kind are of such a nature that they unfailingly reflect a ray of incident light at an angle equal to that which the incident ray makes with the surface of the mirror, as shown by extensive experience. See Alazen <note>original: "Alazen." Referring to Alhazen (Ibn al-Haytham, c. 965–1040), the medieval Persian polymath known as the "father of modern optics."</note> Book 3, number 8, part 5; and Vitello <note>original: "Vitell." Referring to Witelo (c. 1230–1280/1314), a Polish friar and philosopher whose work "Perspectiva" was a standard text on optics.</note> Book 5, theorem 10. Leaving aside concave mirrors, as they are less suited to the kind of reflection required for our purpose, we shall treat here only convex mirrors—namely spherical, cylindrical, and conical—briefly and as clearly as possible, so that we do not appear to have omitted anything that seems to pertain to our <term>Catoptric Gnomonics</term> <note>The study of sundials that use reflected light to show the time.</note>.

## Theorem XII.

### *If a ray of light falls upon a convex, conical, or cylindrical mirror, the angles of incidence and reflection will necessarily be equal.*

**LET** us say, for example, the convex mirror is FGD, and a light ray falling from B onto point D is reflected toward A: I say that the angles BDG and ADF are equal. For since CDA and CDB are equal (according to Theorem 4) because of the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>The "normal" line, drawn at a right angle to the surface at the point of contact.</note> CD, from which AD and BD must be equally distant; therefore, the angle CDA, combined with ADS, constitutes a complete right angle, which the perpendicular lines SD and CD establish. Therefore, the angle CDB added to BDO will also constitute an angle equal to the former. Thus, the right angle CDS will also be equal to the entire angle CDO.

## Experiment.

**L**et a disc be made of thick wood, and in this disc (which should be perforated through its thickness from the circumference all the way to the center) let a hole be made, starting at the 45th degree in both the eastern and western quadrants of the disc. Once these are made, let the center of this disc be hollowed out with enough space so that the bodies of the mirrors can be conveniently inserted. Having done this, if you insert one of the mirrors into the center of the wooden disc and align one hole toward the Sun, you will see the entering ray of the Sun, upon falling on the mirror's surface, be reflected back through the other hole. This would be impossible to happen if the angle of incidence were not equal to the angle of reflection.

## Theorem XIII.

> *In every surface of reflection from columnar <note>cylindrical</note> or convex conical mirrors, it is necessary that the center of sight (or light), the point of reflection, and the point on the axis where the perpendicular—drawn from the point of reflection to the surface of the mirror—falls, all consist within that same surface.*

**T**hat the center of sight, the point of reflection, and the reflected point are in the "surface of reflection" <note>the plane containing the path of the light</note> is evident from Theorem VIII of this book; the same must be said for any other mirrors. In every surface of reflection, there are necessarily lines of incidence and reflection containing the three aforementioned points. And if the surface of reflection cuts the mirror along the line of its length, it is clear from what was said previously that the entire axis, and the point where the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection falls, are in this surface. But if the common section of the surface of reflection and the mirror is an <term>acute-angled section</term> <note>original: "sectio oxygonia." A classical term for an ellipse formed by cutting a cone or cylinder at an angle.</note>, it is clear that this section is sloped upon the axis of the column, intersecting the axis at the point where the perpendicular falls, which is produced from the point of reflection upon the surface that touches the column at the point of the section. Therefore, what was proposed is evident.

## Theorem XIV.

> *When the common section of the surface of reflection and a convex cylindrical mirror is a circle, reflection from any point on that circle always occurs within the same surface.*

**L**et the specular cylinder be FDBTGC, and let the common surface of reflection and the mirror be BPI. Now, let any point you please be marked on the circle BPT. It is manifest that the semi-diameter <note>radius</note> of that circle BPT is perpendicular to the surface of the mirror touching it at that given point of reflection. Therefore, any such perpendicular extended outside the surface touching the cylinder in that same surface will consist entirely within the surface of reflection, which the line BPT represents, and it will stand perpendicularly upon it. Since, therefore, any such perpendicular is in the surface of that circle, and the reflected form of light (which is A) is similarly in the surface: then in this surface alone will the reflection of any point of the thing seen (or the reflected form) occur, made from any of the points of that whole circle or its visible (illuminated) portion. This is what was proposed.

### Corollary I.

**O**f all the reflection surfaces formed from the same convex cylindrical mirror to the same eye, there is only one whose common intersection with the mirror's surface is the line of length of the mirror itself. Likewise, if the line of length happens to be the common intersection of the reflection surface and the convex cylindrical mirror, the reflection to the eye from any of the points on that line will always occur in the same surface. Consequently, other points [on the mirror] will require other locations for the eye.

### Corollary II.

**I**f the eye and a straight line parallel to the axis of the convex cylindrical mirror are in the same plane, reflection can occur to the eye from the entire side of the cylinder, and the image will be seen as a straight line equal to the parallel line. Furthermore, if the eye is outside the plane of the straight line parallel to the axis of the convex cylindrical mirror, reflection will necessarily occur from the side of the cylinder.

### Corollary III.

<margin>How the image is seen in a cylindrical mirror.</margin>
**I**f our vision is parallel to the surface of reflection in the cylinder, the common intersection of both the reflection surface and the mirror will be either a circle or a straight line. If, however, it is from the side, and the section of the axis is oblique <note>original: "λοξός" (loxos), a Greek term for slanted or oblique.</note>, the common intersection of both surfaces (reflection and mirror) will be an ellipse. All other reflection surfaces, however, cut the axis of the column and the column itself, because the perpendicular drawn from the point of reflection cuts the axis; and the lines common to these surfaces and the surfaces of the column are the "sections" <note>This refers to conic sections—the shapes made by slicing through a solid cylinder or cone.</note> which Geometers assign to columns and cones.

## Theorem XVII.

> *Similarly, when the surface of reflection and a convex cylindrical mirror share a common intersection that is a circle parallel to the bases of the mirror, the reflection of the form of a single point (whether seen or luminous) to the eye occurs from only one single point of the entire surface of the mirror.*

<margin>Reflection in conical or cylindrical mirrors cannot [occur except at a single point]</margin>
Let the arrangement be as before, and it is clear that under this hypothesis, the surface of reflection ABG will be parallel to the bases of the column; likewise the circle, which is the common intersection of surface ABG and the column: its axis is CD, parallel to the cylinder's bases, let it be GH, and its center E. I say that from the circle GH—the common intersection of surface ABG and the mirror surface—the reflection of form B to A cannot occur except from one point G. For since in convex spherical mirrors reflection from the circle upon which it occurs cannot happen except from one single point: therefore, it cannot happen in these columnar mirrors either, except at the unique point G. But if it were granted that reflection could occur from another point of the mirror (such as point L) just as it does from point G, let a line LK be drawn from the given point L perpendicular to the surface of the cylinder. Therefore, the extended perpendicular <gloss>toward the axis above</gloss> can occur <note>This gloss clarifies the direction of the perpendicular line toward the central axis.</note> on the axis CD at point I, and the line LK will intersect line BA at point K; from this other <insert>point</insert> let a line be drawn to E, the center of circle GH, and KE will be orthogonal to axis CD, for it is in the surface of reflection intersecting the axis CD at right angles. Therefore, the two lines KE and KI, with line EI being part of the axis CD, will form a triangle containing two right angles: but this is impossible <note>In Euclidean geometry, no triangle can contain two right angles as the sum of all angles must be 180 degrees.</note>. Therefore, it is also impossible for the form of point B to be reflected to location A from any point of the whole mirror surface other than point G. Which was to be demonstrated.

### Corollary I.

To whatever point marked on the visible surface of a columnar or convex conical mirror a straight line is drawn from the center of vision, that extended line will necessarily intersect the mirror. Likewise, conclude that every plane surface appearing to the eye in some line of length on the surface of a convex conical or cylindrical mirror, and touching the mirror, intersects the surfaces produced from the eye which touch the extremities of the visible portion; and all those surfaces are extended between the eye and the surface of the mirror.

## Theorem XVIII.

> *If the species <note>original: "species." In medieval optics, "species" refers to the visual form or "likeness" of an object traveling through space.</note> of opposite forms fall upon the surface of the mirror from a straight line parallel to the axis of a convex cylindrical mirror, it is possible for them to be reflected from the entire line of length of the mirror to the eye, and their images will appear straight and equal to the things seen.*

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram of a vertical cylinder for an optical proof. Points T, N, E, G, B, F, A, D, H, K, and Z are shown. Point E is positioned as the observer's eye above the cylinder. Lines trace the reflection of points from a straight line TH onto the cylindrical surface.</image-desc>

Let there be a columnar Mirror, to whose axis ZK a straight line TH is parallel; therefore, the line TH will be parallel to the line of length of the cylindrical mirror, which, existing in the same surface THZK with line TH and with axis ZK; it is possible for all points of line TH to be reflected to the eye E. Since it is possible that the points of reflection of all points of line TH are in the line of length of the column, which is GA: because that line is common to the surface of reflection (in which the eye E is), the axis ZK, the line TH, and the surface of the column. Therefore, the image of the form of line TH will appear straight, because any perpendicular drawn from a point of line TH will be in the same surface as the eye and the axis, and the locations of the images of points TH will be proven to be arranged according to a straight line, as in plane mirrors. The proposition is therefore clear. Truly, see this proposition demonstrated more fully in Vitello <note>Witelo (c. 1230 – after 1280) was a friar and theologian whose treatise "Perspectiva" was a standard text on optics for centuries.</note>, proposition 30, folio 282.

### Theorem XIX.

*When radiant light falls upon the surface of a cylindrical mirror standing perpendicular to the horizon, all points of the circles (or circular segments) that are parallel to the cylinder's bases and visible to the eye, as well as all points of the lines of length <note>Vertical lines running straight down the side of the cylinder.</note> parallel to the cylindrical axis, will be reflected onto a plane. Through their conic incidence and reflection, they will describe a circular grid; the luminous rays of this grid are formed by the lines of length of the cylindrical mirror, while the luminous circles are formed by the circles on the cylinder that are parallel to its base.*

LET the light of the Sun be **A**, the cylindrical mirror **FGBC**, the circles parallel to the cylinder's bases **FG** and **ED**, and the lines of length of the cylinder **FB** and **GC**. I say that when the ray of the Sun **A** falls upon the surface of the cylindrical mirror standing perpendicular to the horizon, all points of the circles **FG**, **HI**, **ED**, and **RX** (which are parallel to the base **BG**) illuminated by the Sun, as well as the lines of the cylinder's length reflected onto the plane, will describe a circular grid **OMPN**. Specifically, the circles **FG**, **HI**, **ED**, and **RX** will, by reflected light, form the circles **OMP**, **N**, **OX**, **GS**, and **VQ** on the plane. Furthermore, the lines of length parallel to the cylinder's axis will, by the reflected light of the Sun, describe the rays of the circular grid, or the very radii of the circle. For as was said in the preceding sections,

<margin>Light reflected from a cylinder or a mirror cone projects a bright circular grid.</margin>

the entire visible surface of the circle is illuminated by the Sun, and consequently, all points of this surface are illuminated. Again, according to the aforementioned theorems, there is a reflection to the eye (or to the location of the reflected form) from only one point. Since infinite points are understood to exist on the illuminated surface of the mirror, and it is impossible for them all to be reflected to the same point (for if this happened, it would create unequal angles of incidence and reflection, which is against Theorem 3 and Postulate 3 of this work, as well as the common opinion of Opticians), therefore, lest nature fail in necessary things <note>A common philosophical principle of the time: "Natura in necessariis non deficit," meaning nature always provides the necessary means to achieve an end.</note>, different points will necessarily be reflected to different places. They are reflected in such a proportion that the distance between one point and another [on the mirror] corresponds to the distance between one reflected form and another. Let there be a straight line perpendicular to the axis of the mirror, always in the same "surface of reflection" <note>The plane containing the incoming ray, the reflected ray, and the normal to the surface.</note> with the lines of incidence and reflection that constitute equal angles. Finally, one must understand that there are as many surfaces of reflection in a cylindrical mirror as there are possible circles parallel to the base, and as many as there are lines of length parallel to the axis. Since two or more surfaces of reflection cannot exist simultaneously (as is clear from what was demonstrated above), it follows that each one claims its own proper place in the reflection produced on the horizontal plane. 

Just as the Sun's ray **A**, falling on the cylindrical mirror, will illuminate the entire surface of the mirror visible to the eye; so let it first illuminate circle **FG**, which is parallel to base **BC**. I say that all points of that semicircle will send the appearance of their radiant form onto the plane into the circle **MOZDP**. For as was said previously, a diametrical reflection can occur on the convex surface of a cylinder: so that a ray falling from **A**, for example onto point **G**, is reflected from there to **B**, with the lines of reflection and incidence forming a single straight line. Thus, point **G** reflects the form of light onto the opposite part of the circle **ZOMP**; and the other limit of the light ray does the same. This being done, it is necessary that the remaining intermediate points project the species <note>A technical term in old optics meaning the "image" or "form" of the light.</note> of light onto the intermediate points between **B** and **Y** on the plane corresponding to the illuminated surface of the mirror, in the proportion we have described. Therefore, the light **A** from all points of the circle **FB** will be reflected onto the horizontal surface in the circle **ZOMDP**, which they describe perfectly. Truly, the circle of the cylinder **HI** will reverberate the ray received from the Sun circularly into the circumference **OX** of the plane. Similarly, the other circles **ED** and **RX**, reflecting the received light onto the plane, will delineate circles **CS** and **VQ**; indeed, however many intermediate circles parallel to the bases are possible, they will describe just as many circles on the plane. All the radiant projections of these circles will be nothing other than cut cones <note>He is describing the geometry of the light rays as they travel from the cylinder to the floor.</note>, whose bases are the circles described on the plane, and whose convex surfaces terminate at the circumference of each circle of the cylindrical mirror parallel to the base.

<margin>Circular projection of light.</margin>

Furthermore, since according to the preceding Theorem there is no line of length on the mirror from which the entire species cannot be reverberated, it follows that the Sun's ray...

...not only circles, but also the diameters of those circles (which will be as many as there are lines of length parallel to the mirror's axis) to be inscribed into the circles according to the model of the art; for all points on the lines of length that reflect the form of the light will follow straight lines on the plane inscribed within the circles, all meeting at the center, or the lowest point of the cylinder’s axis. ## Corollary I.

<margin>The bases of luminous projections from a cylinder's surface are circles, ellipses, hyperbolas, parabolas, or straight lines.</margin>
These most wonderful projections of reflected light, struck back from the surface of a cylindrical or conical mirror, are followed by experiments so <term>extraordinary<note>original Greek: παράδοξα (paradoxa)</note></term> as to seem like miracles. These have not infrequently left me astonished at the majesty of nature hidden in all things, and they compel me to repeat that saying of Briantes: <term>How nothing, O man, is not of the gods<note>original Greek: Ὡς οὐδὲν ὦ ἄνθρωπε τῶν μὴ οὐχὶ θεῶν (Hōs ouden ō anthrōpe tōn mē ouchi theōn). This sentiment reflects the idea that the laws of physics and geometry are divine in origin.</note></term>. I could never have brought myself to believe this, had I not been made certain by frequent and long-lasting experience, and found these things to be infallible and free from any experimental error. 

It is a marvel, I say, and altogether <term>divine<note>original Greek: θεῖον (theion)</note></term>, how a single radiant projection from a conical mirror onto any surface—no matter how irregular or broken—can most exactly describe and represent all those parallels the Sun passes through, and any conic sections on any planes proper to each horizon. Indeed, a cone inclined to the latitude of a given place will, by its reflected light, describe the same figure that is usually drawn on a plane by the tip of a <term>gnomon<note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note></term>, created by the intersection of the dial's plane and the cones originating from the center of the world as the Sun moves through its parallels. 

Thus, beneath the poles it will form circles; beneath the "frigid zone" it will form ellipses; beneath the "temperate zone" it will form parabolas and hyperbolas; and finally, at the equator, following nature’s model, it will follow straight lines. These figures, once drawn upon a plane, will not move from their place like a ray reflected from a flat mirror (which jumps from one hour to the next). Instead, for the entire day, that conic section it describes will remain immobile in the same place. On the following day, however, as the Sun moves one degree in the <term>Zodiac<note>The belt of the heavens divided into twelve signs, representing the Sun's annual path.</note></term>, the projection will move and describe another parallel. Thus, when the Sun is in the <term>tropics<note>The solstices, the highest and lowest points of the sun's path.</note></term>, the cylinder will describe the tropics all day long. This is truly a matter full of wonder, and I know not if it has been observed by any mathematician until now. But let us proceed to the experiments themselves.

## Corollary II.

### Luminous projections reflected onto a plane from a cylindrical or conical mirror perpendicular to the horizon beneath the poles will describe cut cones, whose bases are circles.

<image-desc>A woodcut diagram illustrating the catoptric projection of light from a sun (top right) onto a vertical cylinder (AB) which stands upon a horizontal plane. The reflected rays form concentric circular patterns on the base. A horizon line is marked 'H'. Letters A, B, G, H, M, N identify specific points and planes in the geometric proof.</image-desc>
<margin>A cylinder standing perpendicular to the horizon projects circles; just as the Sun under the pole [projects] the shadow of a gnomon.</margin>
If a cylindrical mirror is placed beneath the pole in a "most oblique sphere" <note>An astronomical term for a location where the celestial pole is directly overhead, such as the North or South Pole.</note>, where the pole is seen elevated 90 degrees above the boundary line: I say that if the Sun, positioned at **O**, illuminates it, the reflected ray will describe a perfect circle. Since in such a constitution of the world the Sun always moves parallel to the horizon (as is clear from the description of the sphere), its ray reflected from the cylindrical mirror onto the plane will describe—according to the preceding Theorem I—a cut cone, the base of which is the luminous circle **GH**. 

The circle parallel to this one, from which the cone is said to be "cut," is **MN**; this is the line where the points of incidence and reflection are conceived. Since this line is circular and parallel to the Sun's own parallel, it will tend to describe a circular line, or what is the same thing, a circle. For it will describe such a figure as the Sun's ray describes in the section of the cylinder. Since in such a position of the world that section is a circle, it will also project a circle. For, as we said above, just as in flat mirrors reflection can occur at only one point, in convex cylindrical and conical mirrors it can occur—and indeed always does—not in just one point, but along an entire line, whether that line be circular, straight, or along the length of the cylinder or cone. Therefore, the Sun, by its reflected rays, will project a circle on the plane, which will be smaller the higher the Sun is, and larger and wider the lower the Sun is. Thus the proposition is clear.

Under the Frigid Zone, the reflected <term>radiation<note>original: actinobolismus</note></term> is elliptical; that is, the reflection made by a cylinder inclined at 80 degrees describes an ellipse.

### Corollary III.

*The sun's ray falling upon the surface of a cylindrical mirror under the frigid zone will describe an ellipse on a plane via its reflected ray.*

For if a cylindrical mirror is elevated over the meridian line to the height of the pole at, for example, 80 degrees, or another elevation appropriate to the frigid zone: I say that the sun's ray, by falling upon it, will describe an ellipse on a plane with its reflected ray. This is because when the sun falls upon the mirror in this position obliquely, and the cylinder cuts the incident rays <term>according to the bending<note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν ἔγκλασιν (kata tēn enklasin). This refers to the specific angle of inflection or refraction formed by the intersection.</note></term>: and since, according to Proposition 16 of <term>Pappus<note>Pappus of Alexandria (c. 290 – c. 350 AD), one of the last great Greek mathematicians of antiquity.</note></term>, an oblique section of a cylinder produces an ellipse: it follows that the sun's ray, in its incidence, will form an elliptical line on the convex surface of the cylinder, which will be the common section of the cylinder and the surface of reflection. Accordingly, since the reflected ray—following what has been said thus far—strives in all things to mirror the nature of the incident ray, that which is reflected will similarly describe a figure on the plane similar to the one from which it was reflected, namely, an ellipse. Which was to be demonstrated.

<margin>
Under the Temperate Zone, however, it will describe hyperbolas and parabolas.
</margin>

### Corollary IV.

*The sun's ray falling upon the surface of a cylindrical mirror under the temperate zone will describe, via the reflected ray, sometimes parabolas (as under 66 degrees) and sometimes hyperbolas; however, if placed under the equator on the meridian line so that the mirror's axis is parallel to the horizon, it will mimic a straight line on the plane.*

<margin>
The reflection of a ray from conical or cylindrical mirrors depicts the same conic sections that the tip of a <term>gnomon<note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note></term> does across the whole world.
</margin>

For since a cylindrical mirror elevated in an oblique sphere obliquely cuts the horizon at a certain height of the pole; and since the incident sun's ray cuts the cylinder or cone in the same way as it does the horizon parallel to it; and since that section—depending on the greater or lesser elevation of the pole—produces sometimes parabolas and sometimes hyperbolas (the latter in the cone, the former in the cylinder): it will follow that the reflected ray, as has been said, will similarly delineate that figure of a conic or cylindrical section on the <term>conotome<note>A plane that cuts a cone.</note></term> plane which the sun's rays form on the surface of the cylinder or cone. However, under a right sphere, or under the equator, it will describe a straight line following the section of the cylinder.

### Experiment.

If a cylindrical mirror is braced at right angles to the horizon in any climate of the world, its reflected ray will make a projection on the plane similar to that which it would make if it were placed under the poles, or under a very oblique sphere; namely, it will produce a circular one. The reason for this is that since the circles of altitude in which the sun is positioned at every moment are everywhere parallel to the circles of the mirror, and the axis of the cylinder passes through the <term>Zenith<note>The point directly overhead.</note></term> and <term>Nadir<note>The point directly below.</note></term> (the points of the crown and the feet) and exists on the same common line with them: it follows that in all places, the reflected ray will make the same section on the plane. Thus, the sun will describe a circle of the same magnitude at, for example, 23 degrees of altitude, in whatever horizon it may be, as it would when positioned under the pole at 23 degrees of altitude, or in the <term>Tropic of Cancer ♋<note>The northernmost latitude where the sun can be directly overhead.</note></term>; since under the poles, the sun's circles of altitude do not differ from the sun's parallels. Nor will there be any difference between the said projections, except that the circle projected under the pole grows and shrinks over the space of half a year from <term>Aries ♈<note>The spring equinox.</note></term> to <term>Libra ♎<note>The autumn equinox.</note></term>; whereas in an oblique sphere, it grows from sunrise to noon and shrinks from noon to sunset over the space of an artificial day, as will be clear to anyone attempting the experiment. 

But if the cylindrical mirror is elevated to a certain height of the pole, the reflected ray will describe for you that conic or cylindrical section which the tip of some stylus would describe on a plane specific to the location of said pole height. For example, let a cone be elevated over the meridian line to an elevation of 66 degrees: there will be described for you in any horizon that parabola which the tip of a stylus would describe in the horizon of the said elevation. And so for all others. The reason for this is the same as the preceding: for since the circles of altitude no longer cut the axis of the cylinder at right angles, but rather <term>according to the bending<note>original Greek: κατὰ τὴν ἔγκλασιν (kata tēn enklasin)</note></term> in this position, it is necessary that an oblique section is also produced similar to that which would occur at its own proper elevation; if that section be an ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola, it is necessary that an ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola be produced here as well. Finally, if the cylinder is placed in the position of a right sphere, by turning it toward the sun so that the sun's ray strikes it perpendicularly, the reflected ray will describe—at any place and hour—on the opposite plane that straight line which it would describe if, with the sun positioned at the equator, it were placed in a right sphere, as was shown above. Therefore, by a single ray reflected from the surface of a cylinder or cone, the conic sections of all the horizons of the entire world can be represented at any place, time, and hour. Which was to be demonstrated. Note, however, that we do not take these lines of conic sections as mathematical abstractions, but as physical ones, endowed with some width; this is especially to be observed.

### Regarding the Cylinder and Cone.

<meta>This page continues the technical geometric proofs regarding how light reflects off cylindrical surfaces. It transitions from the specific case of the frigid zone to a general theory of "anacamptics" (the science of reflected light), comparing how cylinders and cones project light differently than flat mirrors.</meta>

<header>Theory of the Art of Reflection.</header>

...carried out, whether it be the side of a cylinder or a circle: the locations of the reflections and the images will behave in the same way as they do in plane and convex spherical mirrors.

II. If the eye is positioned outside the surface of a convex cylindrical mirror on a plane that is oblique to the axis, the shared intersection of the surfaces of reflection and the mirror will be an ellipse; and multiple reflections can occur on that same visible surface from which the light reaches the same eye.

III. If a ray of light falls perpendicularly upon a cylinder standing upright on the horizon, the <term>radiant projection<note>original: radiosa projectura</note></term> will be a cut cone whose base is a circle of light, and the section of the cone will be another circle parallel to the base. Since the circles of the Sun's altitude are parallel to the circles of the cylinder and are at right angles to its axis, and since the Sun is positioned at every moment in one of these circles parallel to the horizon, it follows that the rays falling on the cylinder cause a circular section common to the surfaces of reflection and the mirror. Since this shared section is a circle, it is necessary that the projection of the reflected ray also creates a circle on the plane. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that this projection were an ellipse. Then a section perpendicular to the axis would be causing an ellipse. This would mean the angles of incidence and reflection would be unequal. Thus, it would project both a circle and an ellipse at the same time; all of these things are absurd and are proven to be impossible. Therefore, it will project only a circle. This is also evident from the following: since in this position all points of incidence and reflection conceived in the circular section are equally distant from the point on the axis, the reflected rays from the points of incidence all make equal angles at the outermost surface of the cylinder. Necessarily, the surface of reflection in which those rays are conceived will be conical with a circular base. If one were to argue a circle is not projected, then one must say that the projection occurring beyond the circle is on a different surface of reflection; we have already proven this to be impossible. Therefore, in this position of the cylinder, a circle remains projected. This is what was to be shown. I wanted to demonstrate this at greater length so that the error of those who deny a circle can be projected by a cylinder in this position might be more easily recognized.

<margin>The reflected <term>radiation<note>original: Actinobolismus</note></term> on a plane cut from a cone aims for circles, ellipses, and other sections depending on the inclination of the cylinder or cone to the plane.</margin>

IV. You may gather from this that the projection of reflected rays will describe the same kind of <term>conic section<note>In geometry, a conic section is a curve obtained as the intersection of the surface of a cone with a plane. The four types are the circle, ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.</note></term> or cylindrical section on a plane as the incidence of the rays makes on the surface of the cylinder itself. Thus, if the circles of the cylinder are parallel to the circles of altitude—which happens if the cylinder is placed upright to the horizon—it will infallibly describe a circle of light on the plane for the reasons stated. If you incline the cylinder slightly, so that an intersection occurs between the circles of altitude and the cylindrical circles (according to the 11th theorem of Book I of <term>Apollonius of Perga's Conics<note>Apollonius was a Greek geometer known for his work on conic sections.</note></term>), it will no longer describe a circle but an elliptical figure. This figure will always become more drawn out and blunt the more you incline the cylinder, until the axis of the cylinder is placed parallel to the horizon. In this position, a ray falling on it at right angles will cause a straight line on the opposite plane, since that section is linear; in the same way that a circle directly opposite our sight appears as nothing but a straight line.

V. It also follows from this that a straight luminous line is always infallibly described on a plane whenever the cylindrical circle exists in the same <term>Azimuth<note>The Azimuth or vertical circle is an imaginary circle passing through the zenith and nadir, used to define the position of celestial bodies.</note></term> or vertical plane that the Sun holds at that time. For in this way, the Sun's Azimuth, the section of the cylinder, and the reflected line of light will all be in the same surface, as is clear from what was demonstrated above.

VI. But if the cylinder is inclined so that its axis coincides with the <term>axis of the world<note>The imaginary line around which the heavens appear to rotate, passing through the celestial poles.</note></term>, and the circles of the cylinder are parallel to the Sun's paths, the reflected ray of the Sun will describe that figure or section of the cylinder which the Sun's parallel makes with the cylinder—namely, an ellipse. However, if a cone is inclined in the said manner, it will make either an ellipse, a parabola, a hyperbola, or a similar conic section, which the Sun is accustomed to describe by its motion through the shadow of the <term>apex<note>The tip of the cone.</note></term> on a plane, which is the common section of the clock-face plane and a cone having the Sun's path as its base.

VII. From this, it is gathered that different positions of the cylinder correspond to different circles in the heavens, and the luminous projection of the reflected rays occurs according to the intersection of these celestial circles with the cylinder. Either the cylinder is placed upright to the horizon, and thus the axis of the cylinder corresponds to the vertical line and its circles correspond to the <term>Almucantarath<note>original: Almucantarath. These are circles of altitude parallel to the horizon.</note></term> (circles of altitude or horizontal circles); or it is considered parallel to the horizon, and thus the axis will correspond to the diameter of the horizon and the circles to the <term>Azimuth<note>Vertical circles.</note></term>; or finally, it is viewed as inclined, and thus the cylindrical axis regards the world axis, and the circles regard the circles of the <term>Zodiac<note>original: signorum (of the signs).</note></term> or the Sun's parallels.

<margin>Reflection from plane mirrors mimics the Sun's daily motion.</margin>
<margin>Reflection from conical or cylindrical mirrors mimics the Sun's proper motion.</margin>

VIII. From all this, a certain wonderful property of the Plane, Cylindrical, and Conical Mirror is gathered. For the reflection of a plane mirror moves according to the daily motion of the Sun, completing 15 degrees of the equator every single hour. But the cylindrical or conical reflection observes the Sun's <term>proper motion<note>Unlike the daily motion (rising and setting), the "proper motion" is the Sun's slower journey through the signs of the Zodiac over the course of a year.</note></term>, which follows the succession of the signs of the Zodiac. It does this in such a way that its projection, as long as the Sun remains in a certain parallel (that is, for an entire day), remains unmoved in one and the same place; but on the following day, according to the Sun's movement in the Zodiac, the projection also moves...

It highlights a unique property where cylindrical mirrors can "freeze" the Sun's daily motion, only shifting as the Sun moves through the Zodiac from day to day.</summary>

# The Great Art, Book VII. The Fourth Part of Prometheus.

...it may be moved: Thus indeed, with the cylinder raised to a certain polar altitude, it can without difficulty describe any parallels of the Sun throughout the entire year on any surface, no matter how irregular; as we have shown more fully in Book 3. This matter is altogether wonderful, and I do not know if it has been known until now.

IX. It is also gathered by what means, with the help of this cylinder, the remaining circles which it reflects can be shown on any <term>clock<note>In this context, Kircher is referring to sundials or "horologia," which track time using the Sun's position.</note></term>; whether they form straight lines, circular lines, or finally <term>conic sections<note>The shapes created by slicing a cone: the circle, ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.</note></term>. And here it should be briefly noted that although—besides the ellipse and the circle—the remaining sections, such as the hyperbola and parabola, cannot strictly match a cylindrical section; nevertheless, the luminous projection created by reflected rays so closely resembles conic sections (the parabola, I mean, and the hyperbola) that in mechanical operation, a difference can hardly be found between them. For I do not know what hyperbolic quality even the cylindrical section affects. All these things will be more clearly revealed to those who consult experience, the teacher of all things, than I could demonstrate even with a flood of words. These are the things we thought should be set forth regarding the doctrine of the theory of our <term>Anacamptic Gnomonics<note>original: Catoptricæ noſtræ Gnomonicæ; the art of using reflected light to tell time.</note></term>; if these are well understood, I have no doubt they will open a field of infinite inventions to the clever reader. See also the more extensive treatment of these matters in our work, *The Anacamptic Art*.

# THE ANACAMPTIC ART
## PART FOUR
### PRACTICAL PROBLEMS.

->Wherein all things considered in the aforementioned <term>theory<note>original: ἐν τῷ θεωρίᾳ</note></term> are brought into use and practice.<-

## CHAPTER I.

*On clocks that are constructed by reflection from flat mirrors projected onto regular surfaces.*

<margin>
**Hypotheses and Postulates.**
I. Every angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection.
II. Every point of incidence and reflection must be considered the same as the center of the world <note>Kircher treats the small mirror as the center of the celestial sphere because the Sun is so far away.</note>.
III. The plane of any reflected sundial is as far from the center of the world as the point of reflection is from the plane onto which the rays are reflected.
IV. The reflected ray performs the same function in the drawing of celestial circles as the Sun does via the tip of a <term>gnomon<note>The part of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note></term> using a direct ray on a plane. The only difference is that the latter does it in a direct order, while the former does it in a reversed order.
V. The reflected ray moves uniformly with the movement of the Sun.
VI. The reflection of the Sun from a cylinder or cone describes a complete parallel of the Sun.
VII. The reflected ray of the Sun from flat mirrors imitates the daily motion; from cylindrical and conical ones, it imitates its own proper motion.
VIII. The angle of reflection is always as great as the angle of the Sun's elevation above the horizon in horizontal sundials: In others, however, it is as great as the angle between the plane of the mirror and the...
</margin>

<image-desc>A large decorative letter 'N' at the start of the chapter, containing a woodcut illustration of a scenic landscape with classical buildings and trees.</image-desc>

NOTE first, that the reflected ray can be considered in various ways according to the different condition of the polished and mirror-like bodies it strikes, as was discussed at length in the preceding sections. For it either strikes flat or spherical surfaces, or cylindrical or conical ones. What sort of effects, and how wonderful they may be in both cases, will become clear in what follows. Note secondly, that the planes upon which the reflection ends can also be taken in two ways; for the reflection is either projected onto regular planes—such as the horizontal, vertical, meridian, polar, or equinoctial planes—and in this case, <term>Anacamptic<note>Reflected light</note></term> clocks do not differ from <term>Sciatheric<note>Shadow-casting</note></term> ones except by their site and position alone, being nothing other than certain ordinary sundials turned upside down. Or, the light is projected onto irregular planes, which consist of a varied mixture of planes and a collection of different surfaces. It is now time that we teach how both are to be constructed, beginning with reflections from flat mirrors onto regular surfaces. But first, let the hypotheses and postulates be set forth in the usual manner.

...the central ray of the Sun.

IX. Reflection always occurs on the opposite side from the source, with respect to the perpendicular line.

X. A reflected ray from a <term>mirror<note>original: "Speculo"</note></term> parallel to the horizon will describe a clock on a vertical plane—whether it be a vertical, declining, or an oriental or occidental meridian clock.

XI. A reflected ray from a vertical parallel mirror will describe a horizontal clock on a horizontal plane.

XII. A reflected solar ray from a mirror inclined toward the <term>axis of the world<note>The imaginary line around which the Earth or the celestial sphere rotates.</note></term> will describe a clock according to the arrangement of the plane onto which it is reflected.

XIII. In no vertical <term>catoptric<note>Relating to the reflection of light by mirrors.</note></term> clock can more than 12 hours be shown.

## Theorems.

**IF** a solar ray in a <term>right sphere<note>A celestial sphere viewed from the Earth's equator, where the celestial poles lie on the horizon.</note></term> falls upon a mirror parallel to the horizon, the reflected light on the opposite wall will describe a straight line when the Sun is positioned on the equator, but it will describe <term>conic sections<note>The curves produced by the intersection of a plane and a cone: the circle, ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola.</note></term> when the Sun is in the <term>tropics<note>The two latitudes (Cancer and Capricorn) marking the farthest north and south the Sun reaches at the solstices.</note></term>. See the demonstration of this in Book 3, preliminary theorem 2.

In every reflection, things on the right are on the left, upper things are lower, and straight things are inverted; and conversely, things on the left are on the right, lower things are upper, and inverted things are straight.

If the Sun moves along a circle parallel to the equator, and the plane onto which the reflected ray falls is parallel to the <term>great circle<note>A circle on the surface of a sphere whose center is the center of the sphere, such as the equator.</note></term> touching both bases of the conic surfaces, the light projected from the center onto the plane will be a conic section called a **parabola**. This is demonstrated in Book 3, preliminary theorem 2, Theorem 4.

If the Sun moves along a circle parallel to the equator, and the plane onto which the shadow of the <term>gnomon<note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note></term> or the reflected ray falls is parallel to the great circle cutting both cones, the projected shadow of the center, as well as the reflected light, will be a **hyperbola**. This is demonstrated in the cited place, Theorem 5.

If the Sun moves along a circle parallel to the equator, and the plane onto which either the direct ray through the tip of the gnomon or the reflected ray from the same center falls—a plane, I say, equidistant from the great circle, and neither parallel to the bases of the cones, nor touching them, nor cutting them—the projected shadow of the center, as well as the reflected light, will be an **ellipse**. This is in the cited place, Theorem 6.

Light and shadow moved in opposite directions around a stationary opaque body describe a cone of shadow, just as reflected light describes a luminous cone.

With the Sun positioned at any point outside the equator, the solar ray, and thus the shadow of the tip of the <term>style<note>The pointer or blade of a sundial.</note></term>, is projected into a curved line, as is the reflected ray, which is the common section of the clock plane and the conic surface whose base is the parallel opposite the Sun's parallel. Cited place, Theorem 1.

🕈 See the demonstration of these theorems in our *Catoptric Gnomonics* pages 52, 55, 57, 61, 65, 69, and 72.

# Proposition I. Problem I.
## To delineate an Astronomical Anacamptic Clock on a regular plane parallel to the horizon.

Therefore, once the meridian line has been established on any given plane according to the rules handed down in <term>Gnomonics<note>original: "Horographia"; the art of drawing sundials.</note></term>, let a horizontal astronomical clock DEFG be constructed. This should be done using the benefit of our <term>Gnomonic<note>original: "Sciathericæ"</note></term> or shadow-measuring rule, or by any other practice taught there; however, it must be done so that the hour lines, originating from the center, incline toward the South, in a position entirely opposite to shadow-casting clocks, as you see here. Once this is completed, if you erect a support at point A to the height of a shadow-casting style, and at its summit R you attach a small piece of a mirror in such a way that the plane of the mirror R is parallel to the plane of the primary vertical; you will have the <term>Anacamptic<note>From the Greek 'anakamptikos', meaning reflective.</note></term> or reflected clock that you were seeking. The demonstration of this matter is evident from the construction of the shadow-casting clock proposed in the cited place: for it is nothing other than an inverted horizontal clock; and what the direct rays LMNO would do—passing through the mirror R in a shadow-casting plane behind the wall DAE—the reflected ray now does in the plane EDGF opposite to it.

# Corollary I.
From this it is clear that clocks of every kind—<term>Italian<note>Hours counted from sunset.</note></term>, <term>Babylonian<note>Hours counted from sunrise.</note></term>, unequal hours, and others representing the motion of the <term>prime mover<note>The outermost sphere of the heavens which carries the stars and planets in their daily rotation.</note></term>—when inscribed upon this horizontal clock according to the laws to be observed in shadow-casting, perform the same function in this reflected anacamptic clock.

<margin>
*A clock showing the hour by both direct and reflected rays.*
</margin>

# Corollary II.
If you delineate a shadow-casting clock on the other side: I say that the style, or support, will show the hours toward the North with its shadow on the shadow-casting plane; but the attached mirror toward the South will demonstrate the same hours on the anacamptic plane. It is also clear by what method the same tip of the style may demonstrate the hours simultaneously in opposite planes, both by shadow and by reflection: namely, if you place a small mirror-ball in the place of the tip, for this will provide both by its shadow and by its reflection in the opposite planes.

<margin>
*An hour-marker without a style, and a shadow in the middle of the Sun, by which it can show the hour.*
</margin>

# Corollary III.
Since reflected light on a horizontal plane illuminated by the Sun is somewhat weaker and can be difficult to see without a style, it may be made manifest in two ways: first, by the natural site of the location being so adapted that it casts a shadow over the anacamptic plane; or even—which will seem more marvelous—if you shade the plane with your hand or any screen, for in this way the ray of light, which previously did not appear, will soon be made visible by the shadow and manifest the point of time that was sought.

# Proposition II. Problem II.
## To describe an Astronomical Anacamptic Clock on a regular plane that is parallel to the primary vertical.

Therefore, on any plane equidistant to the primary vertical, let a vertical astronomical, Italian, Babylonian, or any other kind of clock be made according to the various rules handed down in dial-making; however, let it be done so that the hour lines proceeding from the center face the <term>zenith<note>original: "verticem"</note></term> in a position entirely opposite to vertical shadow-casting clocks, as you see in the example.

### Proposition III. Problem III.
### To delineate an astronomical Eastern and Western meridian sundial, or one of any other kind, on a meridian plane at an equal distance.

<margin>Placement of the mirror in Eastern and Western sundials.</margin>
Let an Eastern and Western sundial be made, as in the preceding sections, with the aid of our <term>shadow-measuring rule<note>original: "regulæ nostræ Sciathericæ"</note></term>, or by any other practice described in the first book. These should be placed on opposite planes looking precisely toward the East and the West, yet in a position entirely contrary to shadow-casting ones. Once this is completed, if you fix a small piece of a mirror above the <term>axis of the world<note>The imaginary line around which the Earth/heavens rotate; in sundial making, this is the angle of the gnomon pointing toward the celestial pole.</note></term> (which should be as far from the reflective plane as the tip of the style of a shadow-casting sundial is from its own plane) in such a way that it is parallel to the polar plane, you will have the sundial you seek. Note, however, in this place, that such sundials are made with a double mirror: one indeed above the axis of the world from the eastern region, and the other in the same position from the western region; the former will indicate the morning hours, the latter the afternoon hours. For more on the construction of this sundial and the placement of the mirror, see the following sections.

### Proposition IV. Problem IV.
### To delineate a reflective polar sundial on eastern and western planes equidistant from the meridian surface.

The reflective <term>polar sundial<note>A sundial whose plane is parallel to the Earth's axis.</note></term> here coincides entirely with the meridian one; the placement of the mirror will also not differ from the previous one. The reason why a sundial of this kind can be described on a polar plane is that the sun's ray, if blocked by such a plane, cannot reach the mirror. Additionally, the reflected light on this plane does not present itself so conveniently to the eyes; all of which the skilled reader will understand better than I could describe at great length.

### Proposition V. Problem V.
### To delineate an equinoctial reflective sundial on a plane parallel to the equator.

<margin>Placement of the mirror in an equinoctial sundial.</margin>
Since the equinoctial plane is double—upper and lower—a double mirror is also required to describe this kind of sundial. Therefore, let an inverted equinoctial shadow-casting sundial be made on any plane parallel to the equator (namely, the lower and the upper); and let a small piece of a mirror be fixed parallel to the equinoctial plane so that it is as far from the reflective plane as the tip of the style in an <term>equinoctial sundial<note>A sundial where the dial plate is parallel to the Earth's equator.</note></term> is from the shadow-casting plane; and you will have completed what you sought. Note, however, that this type of reflective sundial has some inconvenience because, as in the preceding polar sundial, the mirror does not easily catch the sun's ray, nor does the light present itself conveniently to the eyes.

->*Corollary.*<-

<margin>Placement of the mirror on declining planes.</margin>
Hence it is clear how, given any plane—whether <term>declining<note>A "declining" plane is one that does not face exactly North, South, East, or West, but is turned at an angle.</note></term> or not—a reflective sundial can be delineated upon it. For if you describe an inverted sundial suited to the given plane, and fix a small piece of a mirror at the tip of the given style, you will by no means be frustrated in the desired effect. And let these remarks on regular reflective sundials suffice.

# CHAPTER II.
## On delineating any reflective sundials on any given irregular surfaces.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'D' depicting a landscape with a river, a small bridge, and rolling clouds.</image-desc>

WE HAVE SPOKEN thus far about the method of describing sundials on regular planes. However, these can rarely be of use because of many inconveniences that can occur in their delineation. Therefore, leaving these behind, let us turn our pen to describing a more universal method. Before we do this, it must first be noted that only the position of the mirror is to be considered in this chapter, without regard for the nature of any interior plane. There will be a threefold position of the mirror: horizontal, vertical, and polar. The horizontal position of the mirror is when the mirror occupies a site equidistant to the horizon. The vertical position is when it is placed on a vertical plane; and finally the polar position—
