...finally, when it is parallel to the polar plane. If, therefore, the plane of any interior wall or vault is situated so that a large part of it faces South, or if the walls face East or West, the **Mirror** will most conveniently be placed in a horizontal position. If, however, the interior walls of a house face North, and the sides face East and West, the **Mirror** will most conveniently obtain a vertical position. Finally, if the interior walls or partitions of a house face East and West, no matter how irregular their planes may be, the Mirror will have a polar position; that is, it will be fixed above the axis of the world <term>at right angles<note>original: "πρὸς τὰς ὀρθάς"</note></term>. Judgment is therefore needed to discern the planes toward which the ray of reflected light is directed. For just as a plane facing North conveniently receives rays reflected from a Mirror in a vertical position, that same plane is entirely unsuited for receiving rays reflected from a Mirror in a horizontal position. You shall judge the others in the same way.

<margin>Necessary instruments.</margin> Secondly, it must be noted that since the interior constitution of walls is diverse and uneven, and contains a various mixture of planes, it is impossible to delineate sundials on them according to the practice handed down in <term>Sciatherics<note>The traditional art of shadow-casting sundials.</note></term>. Other instruments will be needed, by whose help we may obtain the desired effect. Such are those whose construction we have taught in our *Reflected Astronomy*, or *Catoptric Gnomonics*—namely, the **Anacamptic**, the **Azimuthal**, and the **Optical** instruments. The **Anacamptic** will serve for inscribing the hour lines and the parallels of the signs on the sundial. By the benefit of the **Azimuthal** instrument, we inscribe horizontal and vertical circles onto the same. Finally, the office of the **Optical** instrument is to manifest to us the points of the hours and signs on an inaccessible or very remote reflective plane, as will be shown in the following pages.

## Problem I.

### To construct the anacamptic instrument.

Just as in all external works that are to be performed legitimately and properly, certain organs—commonly called <term>auxiliary aids<note>original: "συμβοηθήματα"</note></term>—are assumed to make the work easier; so too, for the easier description of reflected sundials, we have decided that we would perform a service not ungrateful to the studious reader if we eased the difficulty of the work by providing certain instruments. This is in memory of Heron, who asserted that no external work could be done without machines. You shall set up the matter thus: Let a square, such as CADB in the present figure, be described in copper, brass, wood, or any other solid material. This square is to be divided into two parallelograms by the line QS. Once these things are properly prepared, a solid limb of a brass semicircle, exactly divided into 180 degrees, should be erected at right angles from point O, above the meridian line OR, as the limb of the solid semicircle OSR appears in the figure. This must be fixed and soldered at point O of the square ABCD, as well as at point R, so that it cannot be moved from its place. Once this is finished, a solid semicircle divided into 180 degrees should be cut from a similar material. You will accurately distribute this into 12 parts or hours, along with their hour quadrants, with hour lines drawn from the center M through the points of intersection. In the present figure, QAS refers to this semicircle. Furthermore, this solid semicircle must be fitted to the plane QS above the line SQ of the square ABCD with <term>hinges<note>original: "vertebris"</note></term> GH, and so joined to it that, like a door turning on its hinges, it can be raised or lowered at the user’s will within the semicircular limb OSR. A screw should be made at S to fix the semicircle QAS above the semicircle OSR. When these are also properly prepared, <margin>Description of the Radiant Zodiac.</margin> the **radiant Zodiac**, or movable hour-scale, should be described in the following manner: To the size of the semi-diameter of the semicircle OSR, or even the semicircle QAS, you will separately describe a semicircle ABC, divided into two quadrants by the line CO. Afterward, taking 23 degrees and 30 minutes with a compass from the limb of quadrant OSR or the semicircle QAS, transfer them to the arc CED described separately...

Its square ABCD, placed parallel to the horizon and directed toward the four cardinal points, represents the horizontal plane. If it is placed parallel to other planes, it represents that plane to which the Mirror is equidistant. The rim of the solid semicircle OSR will always represent the immobile meridian passing through the poles of the world and the <term>zenith<note>original: "verticis punctum" — the point directly above the observer.</note></term>. The solid semicircle QAS, moved and fixed above the meridian (I mean the rim of semicircle OSR), will show the depression or elevation of the reflected or inverted equinoctial. Finally, the radiant Zodiac, moved above the equinoctial circle, will represent the movable hour line along with the projection of the Solar rays for each hour, with the Sun positioned at the start of the signs. The center of the semicircle, placed above the line representing the reflected axis of the world, will represent the center of the world, or—according to the 13th Theory of the previous part—the tip of a style or the point of reflection. Therefore, we have constructed the <term>anacamptic instrument<note>A specialized tool for designing reflective sundials.</note></term>, which was the task to be performed.

## Problem II.

# On the position of the mirror in a horizontal plane.

## Problem IV.

### By fixing a fragment of a mirror to any plane parallel to the horizon, to delineate a vertical reflected astronomical clock on any opposite parallel vertical wall.

Let the plane of the mirror be **ABS**, parallel to the horizon: let the mirror be placed at **S**, the center of the plane, so that it projects a reflected ray into the opposite shadowed interior wall of some house, marked **XVNT**. I maintain that a vertical reflected clock <note>a sundial that works by reflecting sunlight from a mirror onto a wall</note> can be drawn on said wall. By taking the reflection instrument that we described in the first problem and placing it upon the plane **ADBC** in such a way that the center of the semicircle **QAS** corresponds exactly with the center of the mirror **S**; if you then align the square **ADBC** with the meridian line by means of a magnet <note>a compass</note>; it is manifest that in this position, the instrument—with the semicircle **QAS** raised to the complement of the elevation of the pole <note>the co-latitude; for example, if the latitude is 42°, the instrument is set to 48°</note>—attains the position of the reflected sphere under which you desire to describe the clock, as we shall show later.

Once the instrument is aligned and the semicircle **QAS** is raised, as was said, above 48 degrees, for example—the height of the equator at Rome—the semicircle **OSR** will provide you with these degrees. This semicircle performs the dual role of supporting the semicircle **QAS** and acting as the pointer for the degrees to which it must be raised. Once it is stabilized with the whole instrument, and especially by the little screw <note>original: "cochleola"</note> at the semicircle **OSR**, and the semicircle **QAS** is secured, you shall scribe the hours on the opposite wall in this manner.

The "Radiant Zodiac" **TV**, which serves the function of a mobile hour-circle, should be moved to the 12th or 11th hour, or any other hour delineated on the semicircle **QAS**. A thin thread should be extended from the center through any line on the Radiant Zodiac **TV** to the wall in such a way that it is neither too depressed nor too elevated, but only lightly grazes the surface of the Radiant Zodiac. Once this is done, you will observe with the greatest diligence the points on the wall where the thread ends. When this is finished and the points are duly marked on the wall, you have completed the first operation. 

Next, while the Radiant Zodiac remains in the same position as before—namely upon the line of the 12th, 1st, or 11th hour marked on the semicircle **QAS**—and while it rests immovably, you shall extend the thread to any other line figured on the said Zodiac from the center of the semicircle **QAS**, only grazing the surface of the Zodiac. (This must be observed exactly in all other operations performed with the help of the thread, so that we are not forced to repeat one thing so many times.) Extend it all the way to the wall, and having marked the point of intersection as found in the second operation, you will join them with a straight line; you will then have the first, eleventh, and ninth hour. For example: with the Zodiac placed above the eleventh hour and the delineation made as described, the reflected ray of incident light—when the Sun is positioned in the circle of the eleventh hour—falls upon the mirror parallel to the horizon, placed at point **M** at the center of the semicircle; it [projects] the eleventh hour onto the shaded wall, in...

### Demonstration.

Once the instrument is established in the proposed site and directed according to the quarters of the world <note>the cardinal directions</note>, the equator of the instrument, which is the **semicircle QAS**, will lie in the plane of the reflected or inverted celestial equator (we have said, moreover, that all those circles are "reflected" which, due to the repercussion of light, take an inverted position from their direct ones; we have thought it necessary to warn the reader of this here, lest those terms, rendering him uncertain while reading, should delay the operation). Now, I demonstrate that the **semicircle QAS**, or the reflected equator, is correctly placed in this position as follows. Since, according to the Theorem of the previous part, every reflection occurs in the opposite direction from the perpendicular of the surface of reflection, but the reflected equator, according to the Theorem of this first part, recedes from the perpendicular of the surface of reflection only as much as the direct equator is removed from the same—both being as much as the **Roman elevation of the equator** <note>the altitude of the celestial equator above the horizon, which is the complement of the latitude. For Rome, with a latitude of roughly 42°, this elevation is 48°</note>, namely 48 degrees receding from the perpendicular—therefore, both will obtain their genuine position, the latter suited to direct lines, the former to reflected lines. Therefore, the reflected equator will obtain a position turned toward the direct equator, namely through the **semicircle QAS**, moved to the said degree of elevation. 

Suppose it were denied that it obtains its genuine position when elevated to the forty-eighth degree; then let it be placed elevated to 36 degrees. Therefore, with the Sun in Rome positioned, for example, in the equator elevated by 48 degrees: then the reflected ray would establish angles equal both to the elevation of the equator and to its complement. Thus, the triangle of the surface of reflection would be divided by the perpendicular line into two equal parts and not into two equal parts: therefore the angles of incidence and reflection would be equal and not equal. But all these things involve a contradiction and are against Theorems 2, 6, 7, and 8. Therefore, it remains that the reflected equator, raised above the 48 degrees of the Roman equatorial elevation, obtains the proper position for describing the clock. 

Furthermore, since according to the first hypothesis of this section and Theorem 13, the point of reflection of the mirror ought to be considered the same as the center of the world, or of the equator; therefore, with the Sun positioned in the equator, it is necessary that the reflected ray describes the same thing on the **wall XVNT** as it would describe if, having penetrated the mirror, it were projected in a straight ray onto the lower wall, as we have demonstrated in 2, 12, 13, and 14, with the only discrepancy being the inversion of the sundial. Therefore, the center of the mirror is also well-assigned. 

Furthermore, the **solstitial Colure** <note>one of the two principal meridians of the celestial sphere</note> and the mobile hour-circle, or the **radiant Zodiac TV**, moved to the individual hours, will obtain the position of the individual hour-circles passing through the poles of the world; and finally, the rays of the signs of the Zodiac will correspond exactly to the diameters of the **Ecliptic** <note>the sun's apparent path</note>, insofar as they are the common sections of it and the meridian, with the beginnings of the signs placed under the meridian. Wherefore, if the plane of the quadrant of the <margin>Demonstration of the operations performed by the instrument.</margin> **Meridian** is then conceived to be extended all the way to the wall, it will produce on the wall the hour-line of that hour—that is, the common section of that hour-circle with the wall—above which the movement happens to occur. 

And this is why we commanded that the hours be inscribed above by a double operation. For when the **mobile hour-circle TV**, or the **radiant Zodiac**, has been placed upon any hour-line marked in the **semicircle QAS**, the said Zodiac or mobile hour-circle will necessarily obtain that position which the aforesaid hour-circle obtains in the heavens, to which it is indeed parallel: wherefore if the said hour-circle were to run out all the way to the wall, it would express the same line on it as the celestial hour-circle running out to the wall would express. But since the mobile hour-circle cannot touch the wall, being removed from it, and therefore a line cannot be marked on it directly, we wished to represent it by means of a certain string extended from the center all the way to the wall, acting as a substitute for the mobile hour-circle. For when the string is drawn in such a way that it rests freely upon the surface of the said mobile hour-circle, if you draw a straight line through two points marked on the wall by the help of the string, the line drawn will represent for you the desired hour-circle. I said two points are to be marked, not because more cannot be marked, since by one continuous alignment of the string a whole hour-line can be drawn on the wall; indeed, infinite points can be drawn on the wall for the same surface of the mobile hour-circle while the string rests freely,

### Problem V.

#### To inscribe the arcs of the signs on the aforementioned catoptric sundial by means of our anacamptic or reflective instrument.

Two things are especially to be observed in the aforementioned method of constructing a vertical sundial.

<margin>
The necessary securing of the instrument.
</margin>

First, the instrument must be stabilized as firmly as possible in its place or center. For since the reflected ray consists in an indivisible point <note>meaning the ray is perfectly focused and any tiny deviation is amplified</note>, the instrument, if moved even slightly and imperceptibly, will also divert the ray elsewhere, along with compounding errors.

The arcs of the signs, or the parallels of the Sun, are nothing other than the daily and nightly circles of the Sun traced by its revolution at the beginnings of the signs, all parallel to the equator. Let us see by what method these may be delineated on the given plane **XVNT** with the help of our instrument.

<image-desc>
A technical geometrical diagram illustrating the projection of celestial arcs onto a plane. The diagram features a grid labeled "ARCVS DIVRNI" (Daily Arcs) with a vertical axis showing zodiac symbols (Scorpio, Libra, Virgo, Leo, Cancer) and a horizontal axis with Roman numerals (IX to III). Various lines and dashed arcs represent light rays or projections connecting a central focal point (near letters R, S, T, V) to points on the grid. Points are labeled with letters including A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, K, L, M, and N. At the bottom, there is a graduated semi-circular scale marked with numbers 1 through 6. The diagram demonstrates the "anacamptic" or catoptric (reflective) method for constructing a sundial.
</image-desc>

Note therefore first, since the surfaces of the **radiant Zodiac** <note>original: "Zodiaci radiosi"; a component of the instrument representing the ecliptic path</note> or the movable hour-scale cannot be extended all the way to the wall for the stated reason, it is necessary that their common sections with the wall, and the points through which the arcs of the signs of the Zodiac are to be drawn, be investigated with the help of a thread, or the optical instrument mentioned in Problem III, or by other means. Being content with the first two, we will expedite it in the following manner.

Let the radiant Zodiac, or the movable hour-scale, be moved to the 12th hour in its semicircle and be well-fixed in that position. From point **S**, let a very thin thread be sent out to the wall, as we said above, with such care that the thread, freely grazing the plane of the movable hour-scale **T, V**, rests upon it perpetually. For if that thread is applied to the individual rays of the signs,

Then, having moved the **movable hour-scale** <note>original: "horario mobili"; the adjustable part of the instrument used to set the time</note> to the first or eleventh hour marked on its semicircle, we will find—with the same thread freely grazing the plane of the hour-scale and resting on the individual rays—the points for those same signs on the wall, through which the lines for the 1st or 2nd hour are to be drawn. Again, by moving the movable hour-scale to the 2nd or 10th hour, and drawing the thread through each ray of the signs to the wall, you will have the points for the beginnings of the signs for the 2nd or 10th hour. The same reasoning applies to all other hours that can fall upon the wall—that is, those whose points can be marked on the wall while the thread grazes the plane of the hour-scale. If you then aptly join the points of the rays that correspond to each sign marked at different hours with slightly curved lines, you will have also described the arcs of the signs <note>the paths the sun follows across the sky at different times of the year, such as the solstices</note>, which the reflected ray will traverse when the Sun is at the beginnings of those signs.

However, all points for **Aries** <note>♈</note> and **Libra** <note>♎</note> must fall on a straight line, provided no error was made in the operation; namely, on the common intersection of the equator with the plane of the sundial, as we demonstrated in Theorem 15 of the previous section, and as **Theodosius** <note>Theodosius of Bithynia, an ancient Greek astronomer whose work "Sphaerica" was a standard textbook on the geometry of the sphere</note> demonstrates in Book 1, Proposition 15. Furthermore, we shall delineate the points of these same arcs of the signs—and indeed the arcs themselves—by another method, without taking any account of the hours. For if we move the movable hour-scale to various positions on the semicircle **QAS**, spaced slightly apart, and in each position mark points on the wall for the individual signs using a thread, all the points for the signs will be found, even if no account of the hour was taken. Indeed, the more frequent the intervals on the semicircle (or the **movable equator QAS**) in which the movable hour-scale is placed, the more frequent the points will be, and the less distance between them for each sign; consequently, the arcs of the signs themselves will be drawn more precisely.

### Another method of delineating the said arcs by means of our optical instrument.

<margin>The optical instrument is useful for a great variety of surfaces.</margin> **But** if, furthermore, a wall should be irregular, discontinuous, or too far removed from the center of the mirror (as is often the case in the interiors of houses, chambers, vestibules, and other places where walls extend quite far), the layout of the sundial can only be completed with difficulty using the aid of a thread. This is because a thread extended a bit too long in this case easily curves; and once curved, failing to represent the direct projection of the reflected ray, it could introduce incorrigible errors into the rest of the sundial. Therefore, to remedy this problem, we consulted the most clear-sighted **Science of Optics** <note>original: "Optica"</note>, which penetrates every difficulty of mathematics, and it supplied a certain instrument; how excellent and infallible its use is will appear clearly from what follows.

Suppose, therefore, that some great irregularity of the walls is encountered; by the aid of the said instrument, we shall describe the hours and arcs of the signs on any irregular surface no less easily than on one that is perfectly straight and flat, in the following manner. Let us say, for example, that the third hour falling upon the said irregular surface of the wall is to be delineated using the direct reflective instrument. Move the movable hour-scale, or the **rayed Zodiac**, to the 3rd hour marked on the movable semicircle **QAS**. Once it is fixed, let the optical instrument be placed between the wall and the reflective instrument, as appears in the figure. A thread is then drawn alongside the rays of the signs from the center **S** of the movable Zodiac, resting freely upon it, extending to the **transverse rod CD**. By raising, lowering, and twisting this rod in various ways, you will turn it toward the movable Zodiac **TV** so that the rod **CD** maintains the same position relative to the movable hour-scale (or rayed Zodiac **TV**) according to the line of sight, and both are in the same plane. Once this is established, you will fix the optical rod **DC** using the small screws attached to the side for this purpose. Then, you will align the **small arms** <note>original: "brachiola"</note> according to the position and projection of the rays described on the rayed Zodiac with the visual ray, so that the thread drawn from the center through the rays—also passing directly through the **sights** <note>original: "dioptras" or "pinnacidia visoria"; small plates with holes used for precise aiming</note> of the arms—appears to constitute a straight line. Once this is done, it is manifest that the small arms maintain the true position of the reflected hour-scale or rayed Zodiac. If, finally, your eye is placed between the movable hour-scale and the said optical instrument, and you mark the points on the wall where they fall as seen through the sights of the arms, it is manifest that these are the points upon which the reflected ray will strike at the given 3rd hour when the Sun is positioned at the beginnings of the signs. If you join these points with a straight line, you will have simultaneously delineated the desired 3rd hour. Furthermore, if you perform the same operation for the subsequent hours and join the Zodiac points marked on the wall with straight lines, you will have delineated—even on any surface of a wall, however irregular—a sundial together with the parallels of the signs. When the reflected ray of the Sun from the mirror falls upon this, it will show everything that the shadow of a **gnomon** <note>the part of a traditional sundial that casts the shadow; here, the mirror takes its place</note> usually shows on any plane. But if perhaps someone suffers from a defect of the eyes such that they cannot discern the points to be marked on the wall by sight, this can be done perfectly at night with the aid of a light or a candle. For if between the rayed Zodiac and the optical instrument and its small arms, a candle...

...you will have placed the candle with such care, raising, lowering, and turning it in every direction, until the sights <note>original: "dioptrae"; sighting holes or markers used for alignment</note> of each arm merge into a single shadow; know then that this spot, where the union of the shadows projected from the two arms of the sight occurs, is the genuine place where the reflected ray of the Sun falls when the Sun is at the beginning of that sign which the direct ray drawn through the sight indicates. Note, however, that the arrangement of the arcs of the signs drawn here is inverted from that which is found in a direct vertical sundial. For the Northern signs from Aries <note>♈</note> to Cancer <note>♋</note>, and from there to Libra <note>♎</note>, will occupy the upper part of the dial; whereas the Southern signs from Libra <note>♎</note> to Capricorn <note>♑</note>, and from there back to Aries <note>♈</note>, will occupy the lower part in a vertical catoptric <term>catoptric: relating to mirrors or reflected light</term> sundial. We have provided the demonstration of this fact in Theorems 12, 14, and 15 of the previous book of our *Catoptric Gnomonics* <note>The study of sundials that use mirrors</note>. But all these things can be better understood from the preceding figure. If you truly desire to have the daily arcs, you will prepare a radiant Zodiac, such as we taught in Book 5: you will fix this to the movable equator on the reflective instrument; and then proceed just as we did in describing the lines of the signs, and you will have what you sought.

### Corollary.

<margin>Ecclesiastical Almanac.</margin>
**FROM** these things which have been said so far regarding the inscribing of the arcs of the signs, it is clear by what method a complete Almanac <note>original: "Ephemeris"</note> of the fixed feasts occurring throughout the whole year, and of other solemnities, can be arranged within the Zodiac of the aforementioned sundial. Likewise, it shows which degree the Sun is declining from the equator, along with the duration of twilight at any time of the year, and many other things pertaining to nature and Medicine. These include the qualities of the years and parts of the Zodiac, the vigor of herbs and plants to be noted at certain times of the year, together with other more common astrological selections: in a word, everything we have handed down in our *Physico-Astrological Gnomonics* can be applied here.

### Problem VI.

#### To inscribe the vertical circles, or Azimuth lines, on the said sundial with the aid of the Azimuth instrument.

<margin>Application of the Azimuth Instrument.</margin>
**Y**OU shall describe these circles, or lines, on the sundial with the aid of the Azimuthal instrument <note>An instrument used to measure the horizontal angle or compass direction of a celestial body</note> in this manner. The Azimuth instrument having been placed at the center S in such a way that the line AB corresponds exactly to the meridian line. Thus, having placed the semicircle of the instrument MSN over the 90th degree—that is, the meridian line—

You shall act in no other way for the remaining subsequent vertical lines to be inscribed by the help of the thread. Furthermore, I shall demonstrate that the Azimuthal circles are correctly inscribed on the sundial as follows.

it also represents various vertical circles <note>Vertical circles, or azimuths, are imaginary lines that run straight up and down from the horizon to the point directly overhead</note>. Since the common sections of the horizon and the vertical circles passing through the poles of the horizon divide the horizon—and thus also the circle ABCD—into equal parts (as the horizon and the said circle share the same center in this position); and consequently, the straight lines drawn from the center through the points of division are the common intersections of the verticals and the horizon: it is clear that the movable semicircle MSN, when moved to these lines, represents a vertical circle at as many degrees as the line on which the semicircle rests is distant from the line of the sixth hour (or the primary vertical). Therefore, a string drawn all the way to the wall represents the reflected ray of the Sun at that same time in that specific vertical circle. Thus, the string in this setup of the instrument will perform the same function as the ray of the Sun; it will show those points on the wall where the Sun, positioned in that vertical, must necessarily fall. Therefore, we have correctly inscribed the vertical circles, which was the task to be performed. Furthermore, since the common sections of the vertical circles and the plane of the sundial are parallel (because the plane of the primary vertical is equidistant to the plane of the dial), it is evident that those straight lines which are parallel to the meridian are the common sections of the verticals and the plane of the dial; however, the primary vertical itself cannot be projected onto the dial, as it is parallel to it. Thus, we have described the vertical circles. Which was the task to be performed.

### Problem VII.
### To describe the Almucantarath circles, or circles of the Sun’s altitudes, on the same sundial.

**L**eaving the instrument in the same position in which we previously placed it, move the semicircle MSN over each of the fifteen degrees of Azimuth <term>Azimuth: the horizontal direction or compass bearing of a celestial body</term> marked on the outer edge—

indeed, having moved the semicircle MSN (which represents the movable vertical) above the 12th hour, or 90 degrees of Azimuth, and with a string drawn from the center R through every fifteen degrees of altitude marked on the quadrant MS of the movable semicircle MSN all the way to the wall; there will immediately appear to you the points for the 15, 30, 45, 60, and 75-degree altitude circles, in which the Sun will be found at the 12th hour throughout the course of the entire year. Once this is done, move the semicircle—I mean the movable vertical MSN—above the Azimuth or 75th degree, and stretching the string through each of the aforesaid fifteen degrees of altitude marked on the quadrant MS, the aforementioned degrees of altitude will appear more quickly than can be said. Finally, having moved the semicircle MSN over the remaining 60, 45, 30, and 15 degrees of Azimuth, you will investigate the points of altitude in the same manner as described, namely by drawing the string through every fifteen degrees of altitude. 

<margin>The practice of describing the circles of altitude and the longitude of the Sun.</margin> Furthermore, once the points of the circles marked on each vertical are found, if you connect any similar points belonging to the <term>Almucantarath: circles on the celestial sphere parallel to the horizon, representing equal altitude</term> (15, 30, 45, etc.) with slightly curved or hyperbolic lines, you will have the Almucantarath circles described. These will be nothing other than the common sections of the horizontal circles and the plane of the sundial, or <term>conic sections: the curves resulting from a plane intersecting a cone</term> called hyperbolas, which the Sun describes on the said plane with its radiant cone being intersected by the plane. For whenever the reflected ray falls upon any of these, it will show the Sun elevated above the horizon by exactly as many degrees as were assigned to that line. The demonstration of this will not be difficult if you have well understood the position of the parallels of the horizon in relation to the verticals, which the instrument (as has been often said) perfectly represents. If an irregular surface should occur in this description, the operation would need to be completed with the help of an <term>optical instrument: likely a lens or a projection device to ensure accuracy on uneven walls</term>; you shall observe this also in all other irregularities of walls. Thus, we have also inscribed the parallels of the horizon. Which was the task to be performed.

# Reflective Dialing <note>Latin: *Horographia Anacamptica*</note>

Once this is done, raise the semicircle **QAS** above the 90-degree mark described on the semicircle **OSR**. By extending a string through the 48th degree—taking the elevation of the equator at Rome as an example—all the way to the wall, mark a point on the meridian line. For through this point, if you draw a line perpendicular to the horizon, you will have the line of the house which they call the **Midheaven**, or the **Heart of the Heaven** <note>Latin: *Medium cœli* or *Cor cœli*; in astrology, this is the cusp of the 10th house, the highest point in the sky</note>. Having completed this, move the semicircle **QAS** to the 60th degree described on the semicircle **OSR**. Once it is fixed, draw a string through the aforementioned equatorial elevation of 48 degrees all the way to the wall. If you draw a straight line from the point on the horizon through the point marked on the wall, you will have the line for the **11th** or **9th house**. Finally, if you move the semicircle above the 30th degree described on the semicircle **OSR**, and draw the string through the 48th degree of equatorial elevation and mark the point on the wall, you will have the line for the **12th** or **8th house**—provided that you first draw the line from the common intersection of the horizon and the meridian through the point already found. You can also complete this same layout while the semicircle **QAS** of the equator remains in its natural state. For once the aforementioned instrument is adjusted and the equator is raised above the given equatorial elevation, if you mark points by extending a string from the center through the 30th, 60th, and 90th degrees of the equator all the way to the wall, the lines drawn through these found points from the spot where the meridian intersects the horizontal line will provide the lines of the **celestial houses**. Furthermore, the demonstration of this will be clearly visible to anyone who carefully compares the path of these circles with the position of the instrument.

<margin>Houses according to Campanus.</margin>
Furthermore, according to the method of **Campanus** <note>Giovanni Campano (c. 1220–1296), an astronomer known for a specific method of dividing the celestial houses</note>—who draws these houses through the same common sections of the horizon and meridian, dividing the **prime vertical** <note>Latin: *verticalem proprie dictum*; the vertical circle passing through the east and west points</note> into 12 equal parts—you shall draw them with the aforementioned instrument as follows. Let the semicircle **OSR** be placed parallel to the plane of the vertical circle, so that it occupies the same position. In this position, the semicircle **QAS** will represent the movable semicircle of the celestial houses, passing through equal portions of the prime vertical. Once this is done, you will move the semicircle to the 60th degree of the semicircle **OSR**. By drawing a string from **E** to the wall through any chosen degree on the quadrant **SA** of the semicircle **QAS**, you may draw it as you please, so long as the string rests freely on the quadrant. Once this is done, if you draw a line through that point from the center of the horizon **C**, you will have the start of the line for the **11th** or **9th house**. Again, by moving the semicircle to the 30th degree and drawing the string to the wall as before, if you draw a line from **C** through the point found, you will have the start of the line for the **12th** or **8th house**. If you desire the midpoints of the houses, the string extended on the wall at every fifteen-degree interval will designate the points through which the lines of the **middle of the houses** are to be drawn from the center.

### Corollary

<margin>The difference between the circles of the celestial houses and the hours.</margin>
The circles of the **celestial houses** are transcribed onto a plane by the same law as those **hour lines** which distinguish the astronomical hours. Just as the latter meet at the poles of the world, the former meet at the common intersection of the horizon and the meridian. And just as the hour lines pass through equal parts of the equator, so the dividers of the celestial houses pass through equal parts of the equator (or, as Campanus prefers, through equal parts of the **primary vertical**). Therefore, the lines of the celestial houses are the same as the hour lines in terms of the method of drawing them, even though they are "as different as the whole sky" <note>original: *toto cœlo diversæ*, an idiom meaning they are completely different in nature</note> in terms of what they indicate. For the hour lines indicate and perfectly show the beginnings and ends of the hours; the lines of the celestial houses, however, demonstrate only the beginnings, not the ends or boundaries. This is so much the case that a reflected ray falling on one of them shows that the Sun exists in that circle of position which is the start of the celestial house signified by the assigned number. We assign this reason for it: the Sun exists at the end of any house before it exists at the beginning. <note>In the sky's daily rotation, the Sun moves through the houses in reverse numerical order, reaching the "end" of a house's space before it hits the cusp or "beginning" of the next.</note>

For the celestial houses are numbered from the West toward the East. Thus, just as a reflected ray in a dial falling upon an hour line shows that the hour has already passed; so, if it falls into one of the celestial houses, it shows that the Sun has already been carried through that entire house from its end to its beginning. For example, if the reflected ray falls on one of these lines, for instance on line 10, it will show that the Sun is now at the beginning of the 10th house and at the end of the 9th; and the same judgment applies to the others.

## Problem IX.

### To construct a reflective Italian and Babylonian sundial,
### or the hours from Sunrise and Sunset.

In the analemma <note>A geometric method for projecting the 3D celestial sphere onto a 2D plane, used by ancient and Renaissance astronomers to design sundials.</note>, let the meridian be **RSH**, its center **K**, the diameter of the horizon **HI**, the vertical diameter **RS**, the axis of the world **FG**, the diameter of the equator **MB**, the diameter of the parallel of Cancer <note>Symbol: ♋</note> **DC**, and the diameter of Capricorn <note>Symbol: ♑</note> **AN**. Let semicircles be described around these diameters, and from the points **I**, **Z**, and **K**, which are the common intersections of the horizon and the parallels, let perpendicular lines **KF**, **ZX**, and **LO** be raised to the said diameters of the parallels.

<image-desc>A circular geometric diagram of an analemma. It consists of a main outer circle with a horizontal diameter HI and a vertical diameter RS. Multiple intersecting arcs and lines are labeled with letters including A, D, R, O, P, C, B, N, T, Y, L, Z, K, X, F, M, G, and H. The diagram shows the projection of celestial circles onto a plane, with specific focus on the tropics (represented by Cancer ♋ and Capricorn ♑ symbols in the surrounding text) and the horizon.</image-desc>

Once this is done, **DO** will be the portion of the parallel of Cancer <note>The Summer Solstice line</note> above the earth, as will the portions of the other semicircles **AX** and **AF**; while the portions **OC**, **XN**, and **FB** will be below. Or to put it another way, let **OC** be the portion of the parallel of Capricorn <note>The Winter Solstice line</note> above the earth, while **DO** of the same is situated below the earth. And from this, it is clear why we have omitted the opposite or southern signs: because since the individual parallels of the signs are equally distant from the equator, what we say regarding the northern parallels of the signs, we also mean for the southern ones. It follows that day and night in opposite signs are entirely equal, such that the Sun, when in a northern parallel, describes a day arc of as many hours as the night arc it describes when situated in the southern parallel—which is opposite the northern and equally distant from the equator—and vice versa. For the night arc of Cancer <note>original: ♋</note> is as great as the day arc of Capricorn <note>original: ♑</note>, and vice versa. But these things are better known even to those slightly steeped in spherical science than they need to be said: therefore let us proceed with our project.

You shall divide the semicircles as follows: Divide the semicircle **DOC** into 12 equal parts starting from point **C**, beginning from the midnight hour, because astronomical hours take their start from the 12th hour of the night. For **Italian** and **Babylonian** hours, however—that is, hours from Sunrise and Sunset—divide the whole circle, for example Cancer **DCPQ**, separately into 24 equal portions, counting the hours from Sunrise toward **D**, and the hours from Sunset toward **C**, beginning from point **O**; for here **PDY** represents the day arc of Cancer (or the night arc of Capricorn), and **PCY** represents the day arc of Capricorn (and the night arc of Cancer), as you see.

For **unequal hours** <note>Also called "planetary" or "ancient" hours, these divide the period between sunrise and sunset into exactly 12 hours, regardless of the season, meaning an "hour" is longer in summer than in winter.</note>, or the ancient or planetary hours, the individual portions of the parallels placed between their common intersections with the horizon and the meridian circle must be divided into 6 equal parts, and the entire day arc of Cancer **PDY**, as well as **PCY**, the day arc of Capricorn, must each be divided into 12 equal parts. For that point where any parallel cuts the meridian will be the 6th unequal hour; the first point of division from there toward the common intersection of the parallel and the horizon will give the 5th and 7th hours; the following point the 4th and 8th hours; and so on for the remaining hours, of which take the following examples. We have divided here only the parallel of Cancer and Capricorn, for the division of these together with the equator will suffice to easily delineate any of the said sundials.

To mark the hours from Sunrise or Sunset in our reflective sundial, you will proceed as follows. Once the instrument is set in its natural position: take the circle **DPCY** (divided into day and night hours from Sunrise and Sunset) and cut it along the line **QQ**. Apply the cut-out semicircle **QDO** over the semicircle **QAS** of the reflective <note>original: *anacamptici*</note> instrument so that its center exactly matches the center of the semicircle **QAS**, and the meridian line exactly matches the line **DC**. Once this is done, let the movable hour-indicator be placed over all the points of the hours from Sunrise or Sunset; by extending a string through the ray of Cancer <note>original: ♋</note> all the way to the wall, mark the points of incidence along with the assigned hours. You have now finished the first operation: for the points found will be the hour points from Sunrise and Sunset upon which the Sun, when positioned in Cancer, will project a reflected ray. If you then lead the string through the ray of Capricorn <note>original: ♑</note>, you will have, by one and the same operation, the points of the hours from Sunrise and Sunset upon which the ray of the Sun, when positioned in Capricorn, will fall.

Again, let the movable hour-indicator, or the radiant Zodiac, be moved—not over the points of the hours already described, but over the lines...

Finally, the horizontal line will give the line of the 24th hour. Thus, you have the Italian and Babylonian hours, etc., which was the objective.

When all these things have been performed exactly, move the movable hour-arm, or the radiant Zodiac-arm, to the hours described in the semicircle RNX applied to semicircle

## Corollary.

<margin>How the hours mentioned in the Gospel are to be understood.</margin>
And from these hours, we will be able to know the time and the hours used throughout Holy Scripture. For instance, if one wishes to know which hour was that "ninth hour" according to St. Matthew chapter 27 <note>original: "S. Math. 2. cap." - Likely a scribal error for chapter 27, where the crucifixion is recorded.</note>, at which our Lord Christ is said to have expired: the answer is that it was the third hour of the afternoon. Since the ancient hours coincide with equal astronomical hours at the equinox, and our Lord Christ died shortly after the equinox, it is clear that He expired around three in the afternoon. Likewise, it is asked which hour was that "third hour" at which the Holy Spirit is remembered by Luke in Acts chapter 2 to have descended upon the Apostles on the day of Pentecost. The answer is that this occurred nearly one quarter-hour after eight in the morning. For since the arrival of the Holy Spirit occurred around the summer solstice, when the unequal hours are at their longest, it will be clear by the said method (dividing the parallel of Gemini) that it occurred a little after eight in the morning, as Peter said: <note>original: "Non enim, ut vos putatis, hebrii sunt, cum hora sit diei tertia"</note> *For these men are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day.* This could by no means be said of our third hour of the morning <note>i.e., 3:00 AM</note>, as that time is unsuitable for drinking and eating. But concerning these and similar hours, see where I have treated this work more extensively elsewhere.

## Problem XI.

### *To describe the ascending signs of the Zodiac above the horizon on the said sundial.*

<margin>The utility of this inscription</margin>
**V**arious methods and ways of inscribing the lines of the signs of the Zodiac ascending above the horizon on sundials are handed down by different authors, such as Clavius, Schöner, Maurolico, and others; but they are so obscure and difficult that they easily deter even the most experienced practitioners from the practice of inscribing them. Lest we seem to have omitted anything regarding those matters belonging to the doctrine of the *primum mobile* <term>primum mobile: the outermost celestial sphere in the geocentric model, believed to carry all other spheres in its daily rotation</term> to be inscribed on our catoptric <term>catoptric: a branch of optics dealing with reflected light, particularly from mirrors</term> sundials, and considering the labor and difficulty faced by beginners, we have found an easy and brief method: by which we can almost without any trouble delineate this ingenious inscription of lines by the help of our instrument, just like all the other things. But before we proceed further: it seemed best first to explain what those lines properly signify, and what use or utility they have in sundials; for thus it will happen that, once these things are understood, we may approach the execution of the aforesaid practice more ready and capable. Therefore, the ascending signs of the Zodiac in this context are nothing other than straight lines which are the common sections of the plane of the sundial and the ecliptic <term>ecliptic: the circular path on the celestial sphere that the Sun appears to follow over the course of a year</term>; or lines that represent the various intersections of the ecliptic with the plane of the sundial, according to the various sites and positions it holds relative to the horizon while the beginnings of the signs emerge above the horizon. These indeed have a greater and more illustrious use than almost all the lines mentioned previously: for from these, at almost any moment, we can know the position of the entire heaven. For when a reflected ray falls upon any line of the ascending signs, we know which sign is emerging above the horizon at that time, and consequently which one is setting—since it is necessary that the opposite sign sets. Consequently, we infallibly know which sign at that same time occupies the middle of heaven <term>medium coeli: the "Midheaven," the highest point of the ecliptic at a given moment</term>, and likewise the opposite sign which occupies the angle of the earth <term>imum coeli: the "Bottom of the Sky," the lowest point of the heavens, directly opposite the midheaven</term>. For if a reflected ray of light falls, for example, on the line for Gemini (**II**) at point A, I would understand without any delay that Gemini is rising, or emerging above the horizon, and at that same moment of time the first point of Sagittarius (**♐**) is descending; Aquarius (**♒**) exists in the middle of heaven, and Leo (**♌**) is positioned in the angle of the earth; and so on for the rest: as you will easily discover through these opposite tables.

Therefore, once the four cardinal points of the heavens <note>The four cardinal points are the Rising (Ascendant), Setting (Descendant), Midheaven (Zenith), and Lower Midheaven (Nadir).</note> are known in this way, it will not be difficult to know the positions of the remaining signs of the Zodiac in the intermediate parts of the sky. Thus, if the locations of the stars in the Zodiac were known, along with their declination or latitude, you will be able to know which fixed stars exist in this or that part, even if they are not currently visible. But having explained these things in passing, let us now see by what method they should be inscribed by our reflective instrument <term>anacamptic instrument: a device designed to calculate or project time and celestial positions using reflected light</term> as an "anacamptic" problem.

<image-desc>A complex scientific diagram depicting an astronomical or horological quadrant labeled with letters A, T, V, S, B, H, R, M, C, D, and Q. Therefore, with the instrument directed in the manner used thus far, turn the semicircle QAS (which is raised to an elevation of 42 degrees <note>42 degrees is the latitude of Rome, where the author, Athanasius Kircher, lived and worked.</note> and fixed toward the sundial or wall on which you wish to describe the said lines) and you will find the first points of the ascending or emerging signs above the horizon—namely Taurus ♉, Gemini ♊, Cancer ♋, Leo ♌, and Virgo ♍—by the help of the tables placed here in the following manner.

First, look in the first table to see at what hour, with the Sun positioned at the beginning of Aries ♈, the sign of Taurus ♉ rises above the Roman horizon: you will find in the first table that this happens at the 4th hour and 51st minute. Count these hours and minutes on the Eastern quadrant of the reflective semicircle QAS, starting from the 12th hour; and at the end of the count, if you extend a thread over the plane of the equator of the semicircle QAS all the way to the wall, the point where the thread reaches will be the point that the reflected ray will strike when the said sign emerges above the horizon while the Sun is in Aries ♈.

However, so that you can draw a straight line through two points, look similarly in the second table for the hour at which the said sign Taurus ♉ rises above the horizon with the Sun positioned in Capricorn ♑: and you will find, for example, that this happens at 4 hours and 28 minutes before noon. Seek this hour, therefore, in the Eastern quadrant of the semicircle; and having applied the "mobile hour line" (or the radiant Zodiac) upon it, and having extended the thread through the Capricorn ♑ line (where the Sun is then said to "dwell") to the wall, you will have the second point. If you join this to the first point by a straight line, you will have the line of the ascending sign Taurus ♉ for the whole year.

Again, if you wish to inscribe the line of the ascending sign Gemini ♊, work as follows. First, look in the first table for the hour when Gemini ♊ emerges above the horizon with the Sun positioned at the beginning of Aries ♈; you will find it happens at 3 hours and 26 minutes before noon. Look for the hours found in the semicircle QAS in the Eastern quadrant, and by the end of the count, with a thread extended from the center to the wall as was done above, mark the point on the equator; for this will be the point where the reflected ray of the Sun (positioned at the beginning of Aries ♈) falls when the sign Gemini ♊ is ascending above the horizon. Again, look in the second table for the hour when Gemini ♊ emerges above the horizon, with the Sun holding the beginning of Capricorn ♑; and you will find, for example, 2 hours and 34 minutes after noon; which you will seek in the Western quadrant of the circle, and [advance...] <note>The text ends mid-sentence as it moves to the next page.</note>

However, for the lines of Aries (♈) and Libra (♎), which you can only obtain from the tables with difficulty, you shall inscribe them thus: Since it is noon when the sign of Aries is ascending and the Sun is at the beginning of Capricorn, as appears from the second table, it is clear that the common section of the flat sundial and the ecliptic then passes through that point where the meridian line cuts the Tropic of Capricorn (♑). A line drawn perpendicularly through this will give the sign of ascending Aries (♈). In the same way, a straight line drawn through the point where the meridian line cuts the Tropic of Cancer (♋), parallel to the equinoctial line, will give the sign of ascending Libra (♎), as is evident in the figure on page 452.

## Problem XII.
### Recapitulatory <note>Original Greek: ανακεφαλαιωτικόν (anakephalaiotikon), meaning a summary or summing up.</note>.

**By which "mesoptic" instrument all things mentioned thus far are inscribed with wonderful ease and diligence upon any wall of any surface.**

<margin>This mesoptic instrument is the epitome of the entire reflective art.</margin>
**L**et the Mesoptic <term>mesopticum: an "intermediate-vision" device used to project or sight coordinates</term> instrument be ABCD, covered with a transparent veil, upon which a vertical sundial is drawn in reverse (if you desire a reflected sundial), just as the dotted lines represent here. Let the small beam GE be positioned so that the angle GFE maintains the complement of the pole's elevation, which is 48 degrees <note>If the latitude is 42 degrees, the complement—the angle required for the dial's tilt—is 48 degrees.</note>. If you then wish to sketch a reflective sundial on any wall: first, the instrument must be positioned magnetically <note>i.e., using a compass</note> so that the surface ABCD exactly matches the primary vertical plane. Then, let a rule fixed at center F be applied to the instrument, unmoved, over the line for the 7th hour. Next, placing your eye at G, see which parts of the intended wall the rule intersects; a straight line drawn through these will give the reflective 7th hour. Then, moving the rule over the dotted line of the 8th hour, look again through the sighting-hole <term>dioptra: a sighting tube or aperture for taking measurements</term> at G to see which parts of the opposite wall it matches; a straight line drawn through these will give the desired 8th hour. By this skill, you shall inscribe all subsequent hours. When this is finished, if you glue a fragment of a mirror at point G parallel to the horizon, the reflected ray of the Sun will show the desired hours on the wall.

If, however, you wish to inscribe Italian or Babylonian hours in a direct position on the said veil, you will determine the desired hours on the wall by applying the rule over each individual hour line while looking through the opening at G. With this same diligence, you may inscribe the arcs of the signs, the celestial houses, the ascending signs, and the planetary hours; in a word, everything we have taught in the preceding sections, provided you have first described the said lines on a vertically placed veil. If, however, determining the lines on the wall through the sight G should prove too difficult, by placing a light at G, the rule will determine each point more easily and surely by the shadow it casts on the opposite wall.

# CHAPTER III.
## On drawing portable reflective sundials in the hollows of various vessels.

### Problem XIII.
### To draw a portable reflective sundial, along with the inscription of celestial circles, in a concave hemisphere.

<image-desc>A circular diagram representing a concave sundial or hemicyclium. The bowl-shaped device is set on a base. The interior is marked with concentric and intersecting lines representing celestial circles. The outer rim is graduated in degrees (10, 20, 30 up to 90). Points are labeled N, G, D, V, K, and A. Roman numerals and Hindu-Arabic numerals for hours and degrees are visible.</image-desc>

I. Let a hemispherical vessel be made from any solid material, as follows: its horizon <note>The rim of the bowl representing the observer's horizon.</note> NGDV should be divided into four quadrants NG, GD, DV, and VN, beginning the numbering of the degrees from points N or D toward points G and V.

II. Let the meridian GAV be divided into two quadrants, or into 180 degrees (alternatively, twice 90). By beginning the numbering from points G or V, point VA will be 90 degrees at the Nadir <note>The point directly opposite the zenith, or the very bottom of the bowl.</note>, which is the pole of the horizon.

III. From point G toward A (the pole of the horizon), count the altitude of the pole <note>This refers to the geographic latitude of the observer.</note> on the quadrant GA—such as here in Rome, 42 degrees. This endpoint will be the world pole, from which the axis is to be drawn. In this diagram, because of the optical projection, the point does not appear.

IV. Use a pair of dividers with spreading legs in this way: with one foot placed on the world pole <note>The celestial pole, the point around which the stars appear to rotate.</note> already found, and the other passing through the points N, K, and D, draw the semicircle NKD; this will be the equinoctial <note>The celestial equator.</note> within the hemisphere.

V. From this point where the equinoctial line intersects the meridian line AV, count the declinations <note>The celestial equivalent of latitude, measuring distance north or south of the equator.</note> of the zodiac signs on both sides toward V and A. Through these points of declination, using the world pole as your center, draw arcs of circles extending down to the horizon. You will then have the Zodiac described according to its parallels, onto each of which you will paint its respective signs. Proceed with the remaining lines of the *primum mobile* <note>The "first moved" sphere in Aristotelian astronomy; essentially the primary celestial coordinate system.</note> as was done in the fifth book.

### *Marking the astronomical hours.*

**F**irst, let the equinoctial NKD be divided into 12 equal parts. Once this is done, keeping the dividers set to the interval NK, draw an arc from the nearest point on the equator between the tropics; this will represent the seventh hour before noon. Then, placing one foot of the dividers on the following point and the other between the tropics, describe the arc for the eighth hour. Once the hour arcs for the eastern side have been drawn, place one foot of the unmoved dividers on the equinoctial points of the eastern quadrant and the other between the tropics to draw the arcs for the afternoon hours. You will then have the astronomical hour-dial you desired. Or 
<margin>Alternative | method.</margin>
else, do it this way: Attach a flexible ruler made of parchment to the pole and apply it to each of the 15-degree marks noted on the equator. If you draw the arcs between the tropics according to this placement, the result will be the same as in the previous operation.

### *Marking the hours from Sunrise and Sunset.*

**L**et each tropic be divided into degrees or hours corresponding to the shortest and longest days respectively. For example, here in Rome, the tropic of Capricorn ♑ should be divided into 8 hours and 56 minutes. The tropic of Cancer ♋, however, should be divided into 15 hours and 4 minutes. Begin the numbering of the Italian hours <note>Hours counted from sunset (24:00).</note> from the western horizon, counting backwards through the daylight arc starting from hour 24. For the Babylonian hours <note>Hours counted from sunrise.</note>, begin from the eastern horizon in forward order through the daylight arc.

### *Marking the planetary, or ancient, hours.*

**F**irst, let each tropic be divided into 12 equal parts, starting the hour count from the western points; thus, the first hour after sunrise is the first planetary hour <note>Also called "unequal hours," where the day and night are each divided into 12 hours regardless of the season.</note>, the meridian hour is the sixth, and sunset is the twelfth. Second, if you draw arcs through each of the three points for the hours on the equinoctial and the two tropics that are equidistant from the horizon, you will have what you seek.

### *Marking the Azimuths and Almucantars.*

**P**lacing one foot of the dividers on point A, the Nadir <note>The point directly below the observer, opposite the Zenith.</note> (which represents the point beneath the feet), and the other through every five, ten, or fifteen degrees designated on the quadrant VA, let circles be drawn; for these will represent the horizontal circles or <term>Almucantars</term> <note>Circles of altitude parallel to the horizon.</note>. You shall describe the <term>Azimuths</term> <note>Vertical circles intersecting at the zenith and nadir, used to measure horizontal direction.</note> by this craft: Apply a flexible parchment ruler attached to the horizon pole at A, and draw arcs above every single degree of the horizon (if the instrument is quite large) or above every five, ten, or fifteen degrees (if it is smaller); these will be the desired Azimuths. The demonstration is clear from what we said above in Book 5 regarding the marking of Almucantars.

### *Marking the celestial houses.*

<margin>Two methods | for the | celestial | houses.</margin>
**I**f you wish to mark the celestial houses <note>The twelve divisions of the sky used in astrology.</note> into the concave surface according to the method and opinion of Regiomontanus <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a famous Renaissance mathematician and astronomer.</note>, apply the flexible parchment ruler to the common intersection point of the meridian and the horizon, and draw lines over every two-hour space on the equinoctial and between the tropics, and you will have what you seek. If you follow the method of Campanus <note>Campanus of Novara (c. 1220–1296), who devised a different system of house division based on the prime vertical.</note>, applying the ruler from the same point to every 30 degrees of the prime vertical will yield the same result.

In this hemispherical vessel thus prepared, you shall fix a style <note>A gnomon or pointer.</note> at the center A, at the height of the radius of the great circle. At its summit, you shall attach a very small piece of mirror <unclear>regarding the perspective</unclear> <note>Original Greek: "ὡς τὰς ὄψεις" (hōs tas opseis), referring to the visual alignment or optics.</note> in such a way that it is positioned parallel to the vertical. This done, rotate the instrument on a horizontal plane until the reflected ray touches the sun's position among the parallels; it will then be situated to demonstrate the hours and the other celestial circles marked upon it. For since both the ray reflected from the mirror and the shadow of the tip of the style describe a perfect cone with equal motion of light and shadow over the space of 24 hours around the style, it necessarily follows that the same reflected ray on a North-facing surface will show exactly what the shadow shows on a South-facing hemispherical surface. All these things are clear at greater length from the Theory of this Apparatus. In the hours, therefore, no difference occurs, except that those which in a direct sundial face South, in a reflected one face North, the evening hours and so on, as the hours described here in the figure show. <margin>Another method.</margin>
...by means of horizontal circumferences and the table of <term>Almucantars</term> <note>Almucantars are circles on the celestial sphere parallel to the horizon, used to measure the altitude of stars or the Sun.</note>. Since Almucantars are nothing other than 90 circles drawn from the pole of the horizon—the <term>zenith</term> <note>The point directly above an observer.</note>—through each individual degree of the quadrant, and <term>Azimuths</term> <note>Vertical circles that intersect at the zenith and divide the horizon into degrees of direction.</note> are 180 great circles meeting at the said zenith point and dividing the horizon into 360 equal parts: if you calculate the Azimuth for given hours on the horizon from the Almucantar-Azimuth tables, and then calculate the altitude of the Sun within that same Azimuth toward the pole of the horizon (or the center of the vessel), I say that the result of this calculation will provide the point of the desired hour. For a more extensive treatment of all these matters, consult Problem 11 in the *Proteus Sciathericus* <note>original: "Proteo sciatherico"; a reference to Athanasius Kircher's 1623 work on sundial construction.</note>.

On this surface, by the benefit of the Almucantar-Azimuth tables, you will mark the hours and other lines in exactly the same manner as was performed there. The only difference to be observed is that in a reflective cylinder, the plane of the sundial which faced South in that instance should here face North. When this is

### Problem XIX.

> *Given any concave body, however irregular, to delineate a reflective astrolabe in it using an observatory instrument.*

Let the given concave body be placed on the instrument's table so firmly that it cannot move from its spot. Then let the <term>prototype</term> <note>The original model or template used for projection.</note> be fitted into its own place, as has already been said often. Once this is done, let a mirror be placed in the vertical plane of the vessel at any chosen spot—for example, on the tip of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts the shadow or, in this case, holds the reflective element.</note>—and with the system exposed to the shining Sun, let the operation be carried out according to the prototype exactly in the way described on page 367, and you will achieve your wish. We assume, however, that to delineate a reflective <term>astrolabe</term> <note>A complex astronomical instrument used to solve problems relating to time and the position of the Sun and stars.</note>, the prototype is a gnomonic astrolabe; for in this, following the path of the shadow across a certain type of lines, the reflected ray will describe that same type of lines in the concave vessel, as has been demonstrated elsewhere at length. If, therefore, the shadow moves along the lines of astronomical hours, the reflected ray will also describe those same hours. If it moves through <term>Babylonian</term> <note>Hours counted from sunrise.</note> or <term>Italian hours</term> <note>Hours counted from sunset.</note>, the reflection of light in the vessel will describe the same; if through the <term>hyperbolas of the signs</term> <note>The curved paths the Sun's shadow follows on different days of the year.</note>, the reflected ray will describe those as well. And so for the rest.

### Corollary.

**F**rom this it is clear that no object can be so irregular that the aforementioned lines cannot be inscribed upon it using the described method. However, because it is difficult to draw lines on these types of concave surfaces, the sides of the vessel should be joined together so precisely that they can be disassembled once the points have been located through observation; then the lines should be drawn on the separate pieces. Once delineated, they can be glued back together if the object is wooden, or soldered if it is metal. I felt it necessary to advise you, the reader, of this first, so you would not think I had failed to anticipate the difficulty of the task.

# THE FIFTH PART OF THE ANACAMPTIC ART.
## ON LINEAR REFLECTION.
# OR
->CONCERNING<-
## ANACAMPTIC SUNDIALS,

> *In which, by the reflected light itself, the entire lines of the primary motion and any circles of any given plane are projected by a new and hitherto unseen method.*

---

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'V' featuring a landscape with a tower and buildings in the background, framed by elaborate floral motifs and scrolls.</image-desc>Having now considered the nature and properties of reflection emanating from flat mirrors, and now ascending a little higher, we have deemed it necessary to investigate with the greatest study what wonderful things and useful applications reflection possesses on the surfaces of cylindrical and conical mirrors. We do this so that the curious reader may learn how great, incredible, and altogether paradoxical effects emanate from simple principles, and having learned them, may be able to turn them to uses shortly to be revealed. But lest we seem to treat the matter with mere bombast of words, let us prepare ourselves to teach the practice itself; this will happen once we have first presupposed some things necessary to be known.

First, therefore, it is to be presupposed that cylindrical mirrors, as well as conical ones, have this property: they reflect light linearly—either into circles, hyperbolas, parabolas, ellipses, or into straight lines—as was explained at length in the second part of this book. Whenever, therefore, a right cylinder stands upright on the horizon, it will cast the reflected light in such a line as the shadow of a straight <term>gnomon</term> <note>The vertical rod or pin of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note> in a plane parallel to the equator—namely, a circle. But if the cylinder is placed on a horizontal plane such that the length of the cylinder is <term>normal</term> <note>Perpendicular, or at a 90-degree angle.</note> to the plane of that <term>azimuth</term> <note>The horizontal direction or arc of the horizon where the Sun is currently located.</note> in which the Sun is actually positioned, the reflected light will necessarily describe a straight line on the plane.

It is to be presupposed secondly, that any section of the cylinder parallel to the base can perform the same reflection as the whole cylinder. Thus, if a cylinder is cut into rings, each one has the same faculty as the whole. From this very source, as if from a fountain, the reasons for all the <term>spherographic</term> <note>Techniques related to representing the celestial sphere on a flat surface.</note> miracles emanate, as will now be stated. Let it be, therefore:

### Proposition I.

> *Whenever the light of the Sun falls upon a ring of a cylindrical section, erected <term>at right angles</term> <note>original Greek: "πρὸς ὀρθὰς" (pros orthas), meaning perpendicular to the plane.</note> to the horizon, and coinciding with the azimuth in which the Sun is actually positioned—or what is the same thing, existing under the same plane of the azimuth—the reflected light will always describe a straight line.*

Let the ring of the cylindrical section be **A**, and let the Sun be in the Azimuth **LVH**, whose rays fall into the <term>catoptric</term> <note>Reflective; from the study of mirrors.</note> ring directly opposite to it—for example, at points *nopq*. I say that all the reflected rays are to be reverberated into one line **XTKSY**. Since it has been demonstrated previously that the angles of incidence are equal to the angles of reflection, and the <term>normal</term> <note>original: "cathetus," the line perpendicular to the surface at the point of reflection.</note> is in the same reflective surface: if we imagine the rays **Vn**, **Vo**, **Vq**, **Vp** to be reverberated by some impossibility into any line other than **XY**, then, this being posited, the line of incidence and reflection would be in the same surface as the normal, and yet not in the same surface. But this implies a contradiction; therefore, they will be reflected into the same line **xy**. For the angles of the lines so incident on the mirror are equal to the angles of the reflected lines, and the normal of reflection together with said lines will always be in the same surface. For example, the angle of incidence **VnH** is equal to the reflected angle **HnY**, and the normal **nH** is in the same surface with them; while the remaining angles of incidence **VoI**, **VpL**, **VqM** are also equal to the angles of reflection **IoS**, **LqR**, **MpT**, and their normals **ILM** exist in the same reflective plane; therefore they will necessarily reflect into points **TRSY** of the line **XY**. Since there are infinite points in the line *nopq* of the reflective ring in which reflection may occur, it happens that all also reflect into the same line as the points *nopq*, as we showed a little before,

### Proposition II.

> *Whenever sunlight is reflected onto a <term>catoptric ring</term> <note>A mirror shaped like a ring or a section of a cylinder.</note> that is parallel to the horizon and intersects the Sun’s <term>azimuth</term> <note>The horizontal direction of a celestial object, measured as an angle from the north or south.</note> at right angles <note>original Greek: εἰς τὰς ὀρθὰς, "at right angles"</note>, the reflected ray will describe a radiant cone in the plane, the base of which is a circle.*

**L**et the catoptric ring be AB, parallel to the horizon; let the Sun be C, whose rays fall upon the mirror AB. I say that the light falling with its radiant cone will describe the circle DGEF as the base of the cone. Since, according to the preceding principles, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, and in this position of the mirror (as is clear from the figure) the incidence of the lines occurs upon a section of the cylinder parallel to the horizon: it follows necessarily that lines falling upon a circular surface parallel to the horizon will be reflected onto a circular surface. This is because there are as many surfaces of reflection

<margin>Reflected light projects circles onto a plane parallel to the ring.</margin>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the proof. Light rays from the sun (C) strike a horizontal ring (AB). A vertical line G descends from the center of the ring to the center of the illuminated circle.</image-desc>

as there are points of reflection established in this position of the mirror, as was shown in part 3 of this book. The <term>catheti</term> <note>In optics, these are the lines perpendicular to the reflecting surface at the point where the light hits.</note> of reflection are also nothing other than the planes of the azimuths, or rays extended perpendicularly <note>original Greek: ὀρθῶς, "uprightly" or "at right angles"</note> from the centers of the ring's reflections to the horizon. Examples of these in the first figure are HILM; and here, the cathetus AB is in the middle of the reflection surface CBE, between the incident line CB and the reflected line BE. It will therefore occur in no other circle or line than DGFE; otherwise, the angles of incidence and reflection would be both equal and unequal, which is absurd. Since they are therefore equal, they will produce a luminous circle. They will do the same as the Sun does in a circular rainbow <note>The author refers here to a "round iris," likely meaning an atmospheric halo or circular rainbow effect.</note> with respect to our eye.
