# Proposition III. I.

*Whenever sunlight reflected onto a <term>catoptric ring</term> <note>A mirror shaped like a ring or a section of a cylinder.</note> of a conic section—existing in the same plane as the equator—falls upon a surface; it will produce a radiant cone that forms a circle on a parallel <term>anacamptic</term> <note>Reflective</note> plane; however, on a horizontal plane, it will form hyperbolas, parabolas, or ellipses, depending on how high or low the Sun is in the sky.*

**L**et there be a ring **C**, existing in the same plane as the equator, or—what is the same thing—fixed perpendicularly to the axis of the world **EF**. Furthermore, let some plane **AB** be parallel to the ring, and let the solar rays fall upon the catoptric ring: I say that the light from the radiant cone will describe a circle on the parallel plane **AB**, but on the plane **HI** it will describe hyperbolas, parabolas, or ellipses, according to the position of the Sun. That it describes circles in the first plane, I show as follows: Since the ring has the same position relative to the plane parallel to itself as it had in the figure of the preceding proposition, the reflected ray will describe here the same thing as it did there;

<margin>Reflected light projects circles onto a parallel plane.</margin>

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating catoptric projections. A point of light F casts rays through a ring (annulus C) onto two surfaces. The first surface AB is parallel to the ring and shows a circular projection (D-E). The second surface HI is a horizontal base plane showing a curved projection of a conic section (parabola or hyperbola). Lines and points A, B, C, D, E, F, H, and I mark the optical paths and intersection points.</image-desc>

but there it was demonstrated that a circle was going to be projected; therefore here also it will project a circle in the same plane. If indeed the radiant cone is intersected by the horizontal plane, which the line **HI** represents, the reflected lines will necessarily describe in that same plane the line which the section **HI** produces in the cone. But according to our principles of <term>Conics</term> <note>The mathematical study of shapes like circles, ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas formed by cutting a cone.</note>, since the side of the cone **FE** is parallel to the plane **HI** in this present example, nothing is produced but a parabola; therefore in the horizontal plane it will project a parabola. Whenever therefore, etc. Which was to be demonstrated.

### Corollary I.

From this it follows that if the catoptric ring were placed in the same position as the axis of the world—or, what is the same, the position of an <term>hour circle</term> <note>A great circle through the celestial poles, used to measure time.</note>—it will project the equinoctial hour onto the horizontal plane by the linear reflection of the circle. The reasoning depends on the first proposition; for here it has the same position relative to the plane as it has there; therefore it will provide the same effect. If, however, the radiant cone is cut by the plane **HI** in such a way that the plane passes through the cone without cutting the base, a luminous ellipsis will necessarily be born. And if the plane **HI** cuts the base of the light cone in any way (provided the side of the cone is not parallel to **HI**), by conic principles a luminous hyperbola will necessarily be born in the said plane. Since these have been demonstrated in the preceding sections, I have thought it superfluous to repeat them so often here.

### Corollary II.

From this it is clear that by these three propositions the path is paved to the most hidden mysteries of the anacamptic art, unseen until now; which, however, we deliberately keep silent, so that we may leave some occasion of discovery to the curious Reader. But now, these preliminaries having been established, let us begin the practice itself.

# Problem I.

## *To indicate the hours and celestial circles in the interior parts of a house by means of linear reflection.*

**F**irst, in a location **ABCD** facing precisely East or West, a <term>catoptric ring</term> <note>A mirror in the shape of a ring, used to reflect light into geometric shapes.</note> **O** should be fixed in an opening in the wall or a window (which can later be closed) at the position of the <term>world axis</term> <note>The imaginary line around which the heavens appear to rotate; in sundial making, the stylus or mirror is aligned with this to match the Earth’s rotation.</note>, so that the ring exists in the same plane as the equator.

Second, according to the previous instructions, the <term>parallels of the Sun</term> <note>The paths the Sun appears to follow across the sky at different times of the year, such as the Solstices or Equinoxes.</note> along with the hour lines should be projected from the point of reflection **O** of the ring onto the interior walls, whether they are regular or irregular.

<image-desc>A technical diagram of catoptric gnomonics. It shows a room labeled ABCD with an opening EFGH. A sun symbol 'L' shines through a small aperture or point 'O' (where a mirror or ring is placed) onto the wall 'D'. Rays reflect from point 'O' to the interior walls, tracing hour lines (numbered 1 through 9) and other geometric points labeled B, E, F, G, H, M.</image-desc>

<margin>A wonderful sundial.</margin> You will achieve this easily with the help of an <term>anacamptic</term> <note>Reflective; from the Greek "anakamptos" meaning "bent back."</note> and optical instrument. However, let the parallels of the Sun be "blind"—that is, they should not be visible; instead, let only the signs be painted on the edge of the walls, each corresponding to its own parallel. The hour lines, however, should be drawn clearly. Once this is done, you will see—not without wonder—that the mirror, by its reflected light, will describe a complete luminous line. This is the same line that the Sun would describe with a shadow on the opposite plane **EGH** if the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note> were as large as the distance from the mirror to the wall. Which sign's parallel it refers to is shown by the reflected line at the degrees of the signs where it intersects the margins **D** and **B**. If, however, you wish the hours to be represented for you, a very small part of a flat mirror should be inserted at the top of the ring, or the steel ring itself may be polished into a small flat surface in that same spot. This flat surface will reflect light in a central luminous line, which will always move from East to West with the Sun, showing the hours between the lines, just as the luminous line shows the sign, degree, and <term>declination</term> <note>The Sun's angle North or South of the celestial equator.</note> of the Sun, remaining fixed throughout that entire day. This might rightly seem like a <term>paradox</term> <note>In 17th-century science, a "paradox" was a statement that seemed to contradict common sense but was nonetheless true.</note>, had not frequent experimentation with the matter made me certain of it. See more regarding this device in the *Magic of Light and Shadow*, Problems 6 and 7.

# Problem II.

## *To demonstrate the hours and parallels of the Sun by linear reflection on a plane parallel to the equinoctial.*

<margin>The various positions of the mirror cause various projections.</margin> **F**irst, let a ring be fixed to the world axis, so that it is in the same plane as the <term>equinoctial</term> <note>The celestial equator.</note>. Second, on any plane parallel to the ring, according to the distance of the ring from that plane, let an equinoctial sundial be drawn, together with the parallels of the Sun, which will be represented as circles on this plane. I say that the ring will project onto that plane, by a radiant cone, the same circles which the shadow of a gnomon (equal to the axis between the point of reflection and the plane) would describe. If, however, you arrange the ring so that it lies in the plane of some <term>meridian</term> <note>A great circle passing through the celestial poles and the zenith of a specific location.</note>, or if the ring represents one of the hour circles, the reflected light of the mirror placed opposite the Sun will project a straight luminous line onto that plane—namely, the same hour line that a gnomon would project with its shadow.

## Problem III.

### *To project the hours and celestial circles at the same time onto a plane in an equinoctial sundial using a Reflective Armilla.*

In the two preceding problems, we showed the manner in which different projections are represented according to the different positioning of the mirror; now, however, we shall demonstrate the manner in which those cylindrical mirrors ought to be fitted so that they project both the hour lines and the celestial circles simultaneously.

<margin>The construction of the reflective armilla.</margin>
Therefore, let two reflective rings of the same cylindrical section be made, which are intertwined with one another so that, when inserted, they represent the two <term>colures</term> <note>Great circles on the celestial sphere that intersect at the poles; one passes through the equinoxes and the other through the solstices.</note>, or even so that one represents the horizon and the other the primary vertical or the meridian, such as are **AB** and **CD**. Furthermore, let the connection of these circles be as accurate as possible, so that nothing protrudes at the common points of intersection, but rather they appear to be cut from a single reflective sphere. You shall mount this Reflective System upon a support with such skill and method that you can turn it in every direction at will, as appears in the figure; we shall henceforth call this device the **Reflective Armilla** <note>original: "Armillam Catoptricam"; from the Latin "armilla" meaning bracelet or ring.</note>. Indeed, by its aid, the hours and the circles are traced in a single projection. Let this Armilla, without its support, be fixed to the <term>world axis</term> <note>The imaginary line around which the heavens appear to rotate, aligned with the North and South poles.</note> in such a way that circle **AB** is parallel to the equator and the other, **CD**, is parallel to the meridian. The ring **AB** will project the circles; the other, **CD**, having been rotated so that it corresponds to the <term>Azimuth</term> <note>The horizontal direction of the sun, measured as an angle from the North or South.</note> of the Sun, will project a line. Where the intersection of the circles and the straight lines occurs, that is the determined point of the hour. If, therefore, you have inscribed the numbers of the hours on <term>blind lines</term> <note>Lines drawn on the surface that are meant to be "filled in" or highlighted by the reflected light.</note> traced upon the plane, you will have a sundial which, without any material stylus, will demonstrate the hours by the projection of light alone.

It consists of two interlocking circular rings, labeled with points A, B, C, and D, representing celestial colures or circles. A central axis or gnomon is labeled N. The device is mounted on a decorative turned wooden or metal stand (labeled V) with a circular base (labeled T). ## Problem IV.

### *To trace Azimuths and Almucantars onto a horizontal plane by linear reflection.*

Let the Armilla, together with its support, be placed on some horizontal plane at a stylus length of **NV**, upon which <term>Azimuths</term> and <term>Almucantars</term> <note>Circles of altitude parallel to the horizon, used to measure how high an object is in the sky.</note> have been traced with blind lines in the order we taught in the *Sciatherics* <note>original: "Sciathericis"; the study of sundials and shadows.</note>, Part 5, page 404. Once this is done: let the Armilla be fixed with its support on any horizontal plane; upon which, at the given stylus length of the support **NV**, the Azimuths and Almucantars should be traced in the order and method we taught in the aforementioned <margin>To create an astronomical grid with light.</margin> page of the *Sciatherics*. Let them be drawn with blind lines, however, so that nothing is seen except the numbers of the Azimuths (starting from the meridian and described on the outer circumference of the circle), and let the numbers of the Almucantars be written on the meridian line. If, therefore, you desire to see in which Almucantar or Azimuth the Sun lingers at that time: let the machine be exposed to the Sun, and let the Armilla be positioned so that circle **AB** is parallel to the horizon; let the reflective circle **CD**, however, exist in the same Azimuth as the Sun. Then the circular reflection on the meridian will strike the number of the Almucantar which the Sun holds at that time; the luminous line on the circumference will show the Azimuth of the Sun where it lingers at that time; and the points of intersection of the luminous lines will show the point of the hour and the <term>sign</term> <note>The zodiac sign or seasonal marker.</note>. Thus you see by what wonderful artifice, without any drawing of lines, these circles can be shown by the linear reflection alone.

### *The inscription of astronomical hours on this reflective grid.*

<margin>Astronomical hours projected by light.</margin>
If you further desire to inscribe the hours, or any circles whatsoever, upon this <term>anacamptic</term> <note>Reflective.</note> grid, proceed thus: On the horizontal plane, with the help of Azimuth-Almucantar tables, you will describe the hours or circles in precisely the same manner we taught in the preceding sections. Once this is completed, if you wish to explore the current hour, you shall fix the Armilla so that circle **CD** perfectly represents the meridian and **AB** the horizon. Point **T**, the common intersection of the meridian and horizon, looking perfectly toward the south, ought to be flattened slightly, or a small piece of a plane mirror should be attached parallel to the vertical plane; thus a luminous ray will be produced, which, always proceeding from East to West within the luminous circle, will show the hour lines and whatever other circles are described on the same grid.

In the first place, let there be a concave cylinder—the greater its capacity, the more perfectly it will render the projections of the luminous lines. Let its interior surface first be projected onto a plane according to the precepts delivered in the preceding sections: and the Azimuths along with the Almu-

<term>Almucantars</term> <note>Circles of altitude on the celestial sphere, parallel to the horizon.</note> are likewise to be inscribed by the same method on the cylindrical plane, yet in such a way that the lines themselves remain hidden and only the numbers appear: those of the <term>Azimuths</term> <note>Vertical circles intersecting at the zenith, used to measure horizontal direction.</note> on the rim of the horizon, and those of the Almucantars on the meridian line. Therefore, etc., which was the thing proposed.

### Corollary I.

From this, a certain hidden method is also clear to the wise Reader for inscribing these same things upon any other planes whatsoever. Given, therefore, any concave body, you shall display the aforementioned apparatus of celestial circles within it through linear reflection.

### Corollary II.

<margin>The hidden power in the reflection of mirrors.</margin>
Whoever has well understood what has been said thus far should know that the way is open for him to discover countless other things. I could say much here concerning conoid bodies and others, such as <term>paraboloid</term>, <term>hyperboloid</term>, and <term>ellipsoid</term> surfaces, and their wonderful properties in the business of reflection. But I have thought it best to suppress these things here in silence, both because of the countless occupations that keep me busy in other matters, and so that I might provide an opportunity for others, who perhaps enjoy greater leisure, to investigate such admirable and unseen things. Whoever desires more of this kind should consult our *Magic of Light and Shadow*, where he will find the core of the speculations proposed here.

### Notes concerning what has been said.

First, it must be observed: In cylindrical fragments, hyperbolas tend to slightly resemble ellipses; you will remedy this if you cut the ring from a <term>catoptric cone</term> <note>A cone used for reflective projections.</note>. However, in practice, a difference of any significance is hardly detected. Second, the <term>reflective emission of rays</term> <note>original: "actinobolismus anacampticus"; referring to the path light takes when bouncing off the curved mirror.</note> must be carefully observed; for they are not described from the center of the ring, but from as many centers as there are points of reflection on the circumference of the ring. Hence, in describing the hour lines, one must proceed with the greatest care; they relate not to the center of the ring, but to individual points on the ring's circumference as the tip of the <term>style</term> <note>The pointer or gnomon of a sundial.</note>. Third, a clock of this kind is completed more successfully and safely by using observation and mechanical means rather than purely geometrical ones. Since rings can hardly be made so exactly that their surfaces are perfectly round and equal in every part, you will remove this imperfection if, as I said, you begin the business through observation or by our <term>Tiretic instrument</term> <note>A specialized drawing or measuring tool invented or promoted by Kircher.</note>. Otherwise, if the work is organized correctly, it can hardly be said how much admiration a machine of this kind excites in the minds of those who see it. Fourth, the place for displaying this work must also be appropriate: dark and closed; for in this way the radiant lines will both illuminate the place and better display the machine to the eyes of the spectators.

And let these things suffice regarding the <term>Anacamptic art</term> <note>The science of reflected light or catoptrics.</note>. I do not doubt that wise minds, leaning upon these foundations of ours, will in their own time give birth to a countless offspring of new inventions. A reflective astrolabe of this kind was commissioned to be drawn not long ago in his most magnificent Palace by the Most Eminent <term>Cardinal Spada</term> <note>Bernardino Spada (1594–1661), a patron of the arts and sciences in Rome.</note>; as this work is truly clever in the highest degree, so it seizes everyone with the greatest admiration, so that one might not undeservedly say of it what was once said of my own device drawn at Avignon:

->*And thinks the author of the art is Jove.*<-
->*Jupiter the Author is present; for who but another Jupiter*<-
->*Could thus compress the immense stars into a light house?*<-

But, since the aforementioned Cardinal—a most wise Prince and one cultivated in every kind of literature—played upon that device with remarkable subtlety; here are his witty...

# ATHANASIUS KIRCHER
->PRIEST OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS<-

## THE GREAT ART
### OF LIGHT AND SHADOW
### BOOK EIGHT.

## THE ANACLASTIC ART,
->OR<-
## REFRACTED ASTRONOMY.

->In which the secrets of Gnomonic Astronomy <note>The art of making sundials and measuring time via shadows.</note> are curiously taught by means of lines and shadowy circles, through anaclastic description—that is, the new science of refractions—projected onto any interior surfaces of vessels.<-

### PREFACE.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial letter 'N' featuring intricate foliage and floral patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>

The Anaclastic art follows the <term>Anacamptic art</term> <note>original: "Nacampticam artem"; the study of reflected light, which Kircher discussed in previous chapters.</note>, both being daughters of the same mother, Optics, and not at all unlike one another. The former has performed its duty brilliantly up to this point, attempting to capture the immense volumes of the heavens within the shaded retreats of houses using "stolen" light—that is, by a ray reflected from a mirror—by a truly <term>Promethean</term> <note>In Greek mythology, Prometheus stole fire from the gods to give to humanity; Kircher uses this as a metaphor for "stealing" the sun's light to use in a darkened room.</note> skill. This art, however, as if begrudging such secrets to the public light, exhibits those same wonders not out in the open, but craftily hidden under water, established by a skill that is almost like an enchantment. The former shows the miracles of the heavens in a dark place by means of light; the latter shows them in a luminous field of water by means of shadow. Therefore, we have decided that the nature of this art in representing the heavens must be demonstrated hereafter with the greatest industry we can manage; especially since there is hardly anyone who has handed down anything on this subject or noticed our particular method. I know that some have handed down certain rules for making an <term>anaclastic clock</term> <note>A sundial that works by bending light through water or glass.</note>; but I have seen no one who has reached that universal method for the teaching of the entire <term>primum mobile</term> <note>The "first moved" sphere in ancient astronomy, which carries all the stars and planets around the Earth.</note> by the Anaclastic art. For this reason, we think it not undeserved to call this part "Refracted Astronomy." Furthermore, since we shall occasionally turn from Geometry in this treatise toward physical contemplation, our speech will also be a little more free—not everywhere restricted to letters, figures, or bound by the chains of mathematical demonstrations—but more relaxed with conjectures, following a certain philosophical liberty. We shall do this, however, so that while preserving our method as much as possible, we may proceed <term>in an orderly manner</term> <note>original Greek: εὐτάκτως (eutaktōs).</note>.

---

### PART ONE.

## PHYSIOLOGICAL PRELUDE,
->Explaining the nature, effects, necessity, utility, diversity of media, and other<-
->matters pertaining to the Anaclastic business, or the study of refractions.<-

### CHAPTER I.
->On the Etymology and nature of refraction.<-

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial letter 'A' with elaborate foliage and scrollwork decoration.</image-desc>

The <term>Anaclastic Art</term> is defined here as nothing other than a certain and demonstrative faculty by which, through the help of refractions, we teach how to represent the doctrine of the entire "first moved" heaven within water upon any surfaces of bodies, along with other wonders and paradoxes unknown to the ignorant. Moreover, it is called <term>anaclastic</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνακλαστικὴ (anaklastikē).</note> from the verb <term>to refract or break back</term> <note>original Greek: ἀνακλάζειν (anaklazein).</note>; it is also called <term>diaclastic</term> <note>original Greek: διακλαστικὴ (diaklastikē); "breaking through."</note> because of the diversity of the media through which the light passes...

<summary>Athanasius Kircher introduces Book Eight, focusing on "Anaclastics" or the science of refraction, which he proposes to use for creating astronomical instruments and sundials under water. He distinguishes this from the science of reflection (Anacamptics) and claims to be the first to develop a universal method for mapping the heavens through refracted light.</summary>

--- Page 523 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Kircher begins to distinguish between the science of reflection (Anacamptics) and his new focus, the science of refraction (Anaclastics). He explores the physical reasons why light bends when it moves from air into a denser substance like water.</meta>

<page-num>587</page-num>
<header>A Physical Discussion on Light.</header>

<margin>The difference between reflection and refraction.</margin>
We define <term>refraction</term> <note>original: "κατάκλασιν" (kataklasin)</note> as being distinct from those things which pertain to <term>reflection</term> <note>original: "ἀνάκλασιν" (anaklasin)</note>, or the bouncing back of light from mirrors. Although both involve a kind of "breaking"—for in both cases the rays are truly broken, one by the surface of a mirror and the other by the surface of a denser medium, and these broken parts form a straight-lined angle—they are nonetheless different. In a broad sense, any ray that should be a single line but instead splits into two contiguous straight lines (as rays do) is said to "deflect." However, because rays are affected differently by mirrors than they are by water, they must be given different names. From a mirror, rays bounce back toward the direction from which they came; but from the surface of water, they incline into the depths, moving in a direction opposite to their origin. Furthermore, a ray in <term>catoptrics</term> <note>The study of reflection and mirrors.</note> is not so much "broken" as it is primarily "reflected." Its "breakage" is not as obvious to the eyes as it is when a ray falls into a denser medium. In the latter case, something that is naturally straight appears broken to our sight, as is clearly seen with a stick dipped in water. Therefore, we correctly call this science <term>Anaclastics</term> (the science of refraction) and the other <term>Anacamptics</term> (the science of reflection).

<margin>The object of Anaclastics.</margin>
Anaclastics, therefore, considers as its formal object a ray refracted toward the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>An imaginary line standing at a 90-degree angle to the surface.</note> in a denser medium. Since this matter has wonderfully tormented the minds of almost all philosophers until now, it seemed right to us to philosophize a little on such a remarkable and prodigious effect.

It should be noted that, by its own nature, one ray is no different from another; they all share the same nature and properties. However, whether they fall upon an object straight or at an angle determines if one ray surpasses another in strength, power, and virtue. From this, the action of luminous bodies varies in infinite ways, and multiple types of refraction arise. The strongest and most robust of all is the ray that hits an object <term>perpendicularly</term> <note>original: "πρὸς τὰς ὀρθὰς" (pros tas orthas)</note> or at right angles. The ray that falls at <term>oblique</term> <note>original: "εἰς τὰς λοξὰς" (eis tas loxas)</note> or unequal angles is less strong. We rightly and genuinely name the former the "most upright" <note>original: "ὀρθότατον" (orthotaton)</note> and the latter the "most slanted" <note>original: "λοξότατον" (loxotaton)</note>. From this, it follows that after the perpendicular ray, the strongest is the one closest to the perpendicular.

<margin>The causes of refractions.</margin>
Various thinkers have established various causes for this brilliant effect. Some point to the principles of the lever and the balance; some to the "crowding" of rays; others have devised different causes, which you may see in the works of <term>Kepler</term>, <term>Scheiner</term>, and others. We say that the cause of this refraction is the **resistance** of the ray. For the force of a perpendicular ray is strengthened and increased because its angles (which it makes equal on all sides with the surface of the object) are gathered and forced together. In an oblique ray, however, that same force is broken and weakened because the angles are unequal and dispersed. Thus, a perpendicular ray penetrates straight through all media, no matter how much they differ in transparency, without any hindrance to itself. Even if it is more compressed in a denser medium—as if confined in a narrow space—and wanders more freely, dilating and spreading out in a thinner medium, it remains certain that a denser medium resists the spreading and transition of visible "species" <note>In 17th-century physics, "species" were the images or forms of objects traveling through the air to the eye.</note> slightly more than a thin or less dense medium, even if this cannot be perceived by any sense.

<margin>The motion of natural things.</margin>
This is also why all natural motions that occur <term>most perpendicularly</term> <note>original: "ὀρθοτάτως" (orthotatos)</note> are stronger than those occurring <term>most obliquely</term> <note>original: "λοξοτάτως" (loxotatos)</note>, as can be seen everywhere in pushes, throws, and strikes. For nature affects either the unity of parts or their separation; both are achieved most efficiently through straight motion. The shorter the distance between things, the more they are understood to be united, and straight lines are the shortest paths between points. Therefore, motion that unites things—such as the movement of weights toward the earth or steel toward a magnet—must happen in a straight line. Otherwise, not all parts of the motion would tend toward the same end; instead, somewhere in the middle of the journey, that which was meant to be united to another would deflect from this desire for union. Since the union of parts consists mostly in action along the perpendicular, all things certainly aim for this out of an innate appetite for perfection. Thus, when sunbeams fall obliquely, since they cannot penetrate the density of an object in that position, they tend toward a middle path—that is, they decline from the line they were traveling toward the perpendicular—so that they might act with more unity. By some necessity of nature, what was lost in power due to the density of the medium is recovered by leaning toward the perpendicular, as nature always strives for the shortest path. See below for other arguments drawn from the theoretical section.

## CHAPTER II.

### Concerning the variety of media capable of refraction.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'M' depicting a landscape with trees and a building within the frame of the letter.</image-desc>

**A** refractive medium is any transparent body denser than air: thus vapors, water, wine, oil, distilled waters, and also glass of every kind can have the capacity to refract images. Regarding water, wine, and oil, these will be treated extensively below.

<margin>The quality of glass in refractions.</margin>
Glass, just as it is provided with diverse shapes, also refracts in diverse ways. All flat glasses have this property: they change the shape of an object more as they become thicker, and less as they become thinner. Thus, sheets of <term>Selenite</term> <note>Transparent gypsum or foliated mica, used in the ancient and early modern world for windows before clear glass was common.</note> do not change the shape of an object at all. Yet flat glasses have this remarkable trait: while the same surface applied to the eye contracts the thing seen, if the opposite side of the same surface is moved further away, we see the same thing spread out wider than it was previously contracted; we shall provide the reason for this matter elsewhere. Convex glasses, shaped like segments of a sphere, contract the thing seen when held obliquely to the eye, just as they contract a ray of the Sun passing through. However, hollowed-out glasses, where the concave surface is parallel to the convex—or "homocentric" <term>concavo-convex</term> <note>Lenses that are curved on both sides like a bowl, maintaining a consistent thickness.</note> lenses—perform much more effectively than simple spherical glass segments, because the refraction in this type is doubled. Hence, rays in convex lenses converge by that much more, while in concave ones they diverge by that much more.

<margin>The nature of refraction in glass.</margin>
Therefore, convex lenses held obliquely to the optical axis lead the object along the inclined diameter of the glass before the image is inverted; but afterwards, the opposite occurs. Concave lenses do the opposite, because in these, no intersection ever occurs, as the rays are always moving further and further apart from each other. Plano-convex and plano-concave lenses, when looked at straight on, leave the shape alone but vary the size; for plano-convex lenses make an object appear smaller when brought near the eye than when moved away; plano-concave make it larger when brought near than when moved away, until inversion happens in them, for then the opposite occurs—as our colleague <term>Scheiner</term> <note>Christopher Scheiner (1573–1650), a Jesuit astronomer and physicist famous for his studies on the eye and sunspots.</note> rightly notes in his work on the eye. Yet these same plano-convex lenses, when viewed with an oblique ray, spread the thing seen along the diameter before inversion, and once thus spread, they sometimes raise it and sometimes lower it (depending on the various surfaces of the glass and the position of the eye), and after inversion, they contract the thing seen. Plano-concave lenses viewed obliquely demonstrate contraction or refraction in a great variety of ways. This refraction is indeed the mother of all portents, and it reveals the unique causes of wonders. For by the illusions of such refractions made in different media, small masses are led into immense magnitude; curves appear as straight lines and straight lines as curves; squares as rounds; flat things as solids and solids as flat; swollen things appear depressed, convex things hollow, and direct things appear reflected. Things that are whole and continuous seem to be broken and torn apart. Nature not only disguises the things that are, but even invents things that are not. Greater things lie hidden under these than anyone could imagine for themselves. Few, in fact, know the wonders which <term>conical</term> <note>original: "κονιοειδῶν"</note>, <term>plug-shaped</term> <note>original: "ἐμβολοειδῶν"</note>, and <term>parabolic</term> <note>original: "παραβολοειδῶν"</note> glasses—glass bodies polished into the form of a parabola, hyperbola, and ellipse—can achieve in representation through their refractions. Whoever penetrates into this hidden science will surely know that he has exhausted the greatest part of Natural Magic. But all these things are discussed more fully in our *Catoptric Magic*. Furthermore, things seen are shifted from their true places in a marvelous manner: upward, downward, to the right, and to the left. Hence, through such glass, the Sun when viewed will be shaped into an ellipse; and a single Sun will be seen multiplied, as in <term>parhelia</term> <note>Atmospheric "sun dogs" or mock suns caused by ice crystals.</note>. From this, you will hunt down the truest reasons for <term>parhelia</term> and <term>paraselenae</term> <note>Mock moons.</note> as if from a certain prototype; we treat these in more detail in what follows.

<margin>The heavens are not solid.</margin>
Therefore, since glasses undergo the most irregular refraction according to their various shapes, it is necessary that they also show various appearances of refracted things. But bodies of water and air, since they are born of thin and moist vapor and consist of contiguous and transparent parts, and assume a regular surface more easily, reflect light more orderly than they refract it. Consequently, those prodigious appearances of the stars do not appear, which *would* be seen if the heavens consisted of crystalline spheres. Hence, against <term>Empedocles</term>, <term>Aristotle</term>, and <term>Anaxagoras</term>, it is concluded demonstratively that all that space which the wandering stars occupy is pure ether, distinguished from our air only by its thinness. For if that body were different from air and had as many spheres as there are distinct planets—that is, if they were solid bodies like glass or crystal—what monsters would those infinite encounters of refractions produce? What illusions would they exhib-

...will display; the fixed stars and other celestial bodies, scattered widely through so many media and distinguished by so many surfaces, will never be seen in their true place if they are viewed anywhere other than at the pole of the horizon <note>The zenith, or the point directly overhead.</note>; indeed, those which are most remote will appear close and nearly touching. Certain stars, though separated by one or two degrees, will be seen joined together by the deceptive nature of refractions; and conversely, when they reach the pole of the horizon, those which appeared joined elsewhere will seem to be pulled apart and distant enough from one another. Therefore, with these experiments, the solidity of the celestial spheres <note>The traditional Aristotelian view that the heavens were made of solid, crystalline shells.</note> cannot be maintained by any reasoning, nor does the "sphere of fire" <note>A region of fire once thought to exist between the Earth's atmosphere and the Moon.</note> hold up against the experience of refractions. For it was shown in the preceding pages that visual rays, passing from a dense medium into a thinner one, cause massive changes in the things seen. But since none of these changes have been noted in the observation of the stars until now, the proposal is clear.

<margin>What a comet is.</margin>
It can also be demonstrated that comets are nothing other than air, or an ethereal body, illuminated by the rays of the Sun. This occurs by the refraction of the solar rays themselves as they fall into a crystalline sphere, projecting a cone that acts as a kind of tail. When Aristotle had surveyed the world of the sciences with incredible sagacity and saw that the wonders of miraculous effects could not be sought from physics alone, he turned to optical speculations. From these, he demonstrated that halos—the stars of the air—are formed by refraction; "mock suns" <term>parelia</term> <note>Also known as sun dogs; bright spots that appear on either side of the sun.</note> are formed by reflection; and the rainbow is formed partly from refraction and partly from the reflection of visible rays. Not content with these, he also added reasons to show that a halo is only created around the largest stars, and that mock suns are never produced above or below the Sun, but only at its side. However, this was proven false by the mock suns seen at Rome in the year 1632. He also claimed that rainbows do not only appear in a full circular form, but are never seen from the Northern region looking toward the South.

Have not many things been observed in our own times by the help of refraction which at first seemed paradoxical? The journey of the Dutch to the North <note>Refers to the 1596–1597 expedition of Willem Barentsz, who sought a Northeast Passage and became trapped on the island of Novaya Zemlya.</note> is well-known, in which they report this among other most memorable things: Having been trapped in the ice and overwhelmed by night, they had seen the Sun for the last time on November 3, 1596. From the altitude of the pole, which they calculated to be 76 degrees, they were certain by astronomical principles that the Sun would not return before February 11, 1597. Yet it happened that on January 24, seventeen days before the legitimate time, they saw the Sun again—its top edge appearing at the very point of noon. At that time, after a few hours, they noted a conjunction of Jupiter and Moon in the second degree of Taurus, so that no one might think the correct count of days and nights had been neglected by them due to the continuous darkness. To remove all doubt, on January 27 they saw the whole Sun emerge. Therefore, on January 25, the center of the Sun had risen.

Captured by wonder at this matter, many have given various causes for such a rare phenomenon. We say that the cause must not be attributed to an error of the sailors wrongly observing the latitude of the place, as some thought. For if you take this away from sailors—that they cannot have any certainty about the altitude of the pole within five degrees—you would overturn almost the entire nautical science of this century; which those followers of the lucky Neptune <note>A poetic reference to sailors and navigators.</note> will not bear with an even mind. Therefore, a single, prodigious refraction of the Sun of several entire degrees in that watery medium must be established as the cause of this so rare phenomenon.

<margin>Remote islands that are invisible occasionally appear.</margin>
If anyone should wonder why such an enormous refraction of this kind has not happened in other places, however humid and vaporous, let him know that the Northern air is denser and more watery the closer it is to the pole. It is no wonder if refractions larger than usual are caused in our parts. Hence islands in the farthest sea, which would be invisible when the sea is free of vapors, present themselves to the eyes of onlookers raised up on high with wonder, as we shall discuss elsewhere <note>This describes the "Fata Morgana" or superior mirage, where distant objects appear elevated or distorted.</note>.

And from these things, the final cause <note>The "Final Cause" in Aristotelian philosophy refers to the purpose or "end goal" of a thing's existence.</note> of refractions finally appears clearly. For since the world is so arranged that the movement of the Sun between the tropics produces a perpetual change of days and nights for different climates, provident Nature—by equalizing light with darkness so she could not be said to have acted as a stepmother to the world—strove to grant to each individual more light, other things being equal, than darkness. I say she gave more of that light than of the evil which is the opposite of good, namely darkness. To preserve the world with this equity, she assumed refraction as the unique instrument by which she might help the individual regions of the world in their necessities. For these images of the Sun and Moon, before they are born and while they are being born, gladden with their beneficial sight the parts covered by the horror of darkness and fertilize them with the sprinkling of dew. By this it happens that for the peoples living under the pole, the six months of darkness to which they were otherwise condemned without refraction are changed into a perpetual twilight, leaving a night of only four months, so that the nature struggling in those regions might be prudently aided.

For since refraction can often exceed an entire degree—indeed, as seen from the preceding, it sometimes reaches two degrees—it happens that in such...

In the parallel sphere, however, since its own motion (with the help of refraction) places the Sun above the horizon sooner than it would be without refraction, it follows that the slower the daily motion is, the longer the image of the refracted Sun remains above the horizon. This is by a wonderful plan of nature to aid a suffering world <note>Kircher suggests that refraction is a divine gift to those living in cold, dark polar regions, giving them more daylight than geometry alone would allow.</note>. Finally, let us recognize with most grateful hearts the generous bounty of the Creator in these matters. For that which those vapors take away from the efficacy of the solar splendor through their dullness, the shape bestowed upon them by the Creator compensates; for while they seem to restrain the Sun so it does not shine too long for all peoples, they actually hold it back, shortening the hated shadows of light <note>Meaning the darkness.</note>, prolonging the light, and cutting short the night while enlarging the day. For as has been said, light is present longer for all nations and darkness for a shorter time: so that we may draw great encouragement and help for carrying out and continuing the works of light by the Sun, the very source of light. But having pursued these matters perhaps more at length than was proper, let us now explore the nature of refraction itself according to the standards of demonstration.

# D E F I N I T I O N E S .

->*The figure found on this page should have been placed on the following page.*<-

I. **Anaclastic <gloss>refracted</gloss> vision** is vision composed through a different medium.
II. **An <gloss>anaclastic</gloss> or refractive medium** is that into which an incident ray does not travel straight to the target but is reflected elsewhere by being broken; it is refracted more as the medium is denser, and less as the medium is rarer.
III. **The point of refraction** is the point on the surface of a transparent body, such as B.
IV. **The <gloss>anaclastic</gloss> perpendicular line** is what is called the absolute perpendicular; it is that which, standing normally to the horizon, represents the axis of the horizon, such as line BO.
V. **The line of refraction** is that which extends from the point of refraction to the center of vision, such as BG.
VI. **The cathetus <note>A line falling perpendicularly to a surface.</note> of incidence** is the line produced normally from the point of the thing seen above the surface of the body in which the thing is seen, and from which the refraction occurs, such as FX.
VII. **The angle of incidence** is the smaller angle comprised of the ray of incidence and the perpendicular, such as angle GBO; it is also called the line of the extension of the form.
VIII. **The <gloss>anaclastic</gloss> or refracted angle** is the smaller angle comprised of the ray of refraction and the perpendicular EBO, such as angle FBE.
IX. **The angle of refraction** is said to be that which the line of refraction contains with the line of incidence produced continuously through the transparent body from whose surface the refraction occurs; or, the angle of refraction is from the continued ray of incidence and the ray of refraction, such as FBM or GBH.
X. **The surface of refraction** is that surface in which the lines of incidence and refraction are contained.

# P R O N U N T I A T A .
<note>Axioms or self-evident principles.</note>

I. All refraction occurs according to straight lines.
II. Nature does nothing in vain <note>original: "Natura nihil agit frustra." A central tenet of Aristotelian philosophy.</note>.
III. Nature acts through the shortest lines.
IV. The operations of nature are stronger at the perpendicular.

# PRELIMINARY CONSIDERATIONS
## ON THE NATURE OF REFRACTION,
### AND THE REFRACTED RAY.

## Theorem I.

> *Whenever a ray strikes a medium obliquely <note>at an angle</note> that is of a different density or rarity than the previous medium, the ray will not continue in a straight line at the point of entry, but will be refracted toward the perpendicular line. If, however, it strikes the surface directly <note>at a 90-degree angle</note>, no refraction will occur.*

**L**ET there be a vessel full of water, CBDE, and let the Sun be at position G, whose ray is GB. Let this ray strike the liquid CD in the vessel CED at point B, where there is a <term>gnomon<note>A vertical rod or pointer used here to mark the "normal" or perpendicular line to the surface.</note></term> EB, which is perpendicular to the horizon. I maintain that the ray GB, passing through the tip B of the gnomon, will not propagate in a straight line (as would happen if the vessel lacked water), but rather the ray, broken at point B, will move back toward the perpendicular line, or the gnomon EB. Consequently, the shadow will undergo a decrease. I shall demonstrate this by experience.

## Experiment.

**L**et the vessel CDE be emptied and positioned in exactly the same way as before. You will see that the shadow, which previously fell at E due to refraction, will now fall in a straight line at M in the empty vessel. Therefore, the ray GB, entering the <term>heterogeneous<note>original: "heterogeneum"; a medium with a different physical makeup or density, such as moving from air into water.</note></term> medium CBD, is not directed straight to M, but is refracted toward the <term>normal<note>original: "normalem"; the line perpendicular to the surface.</note></term> EB at point F. However, if the Sun’s ray strikes the liquid CBD perpendicularly—such as from O to B—no refraction will occur, but the shadow will merge into itself, and the object will be seen in its natural state as it truly is. We shall assign the physical reasons for this later.

<image-desc>A circular scientific diagram illustrating the principles of refraction. A hemispherical vessel (marked with arc C-E-D) contains a liquid medium (humor) with its surface at the horizontal line CD. A vertical line EB represents a gnomon or normal. A light source G (Sol) casts a ray GB that strikes the surface at point B. Without the medium, the ray would continue straight to point M on the bottom arc. Due to refraction, the ray bends toward the normal EB, following the path BF. ## Theorem II.

> *A refracted shadow, or the image of a seen object, reaches the eye in straight lines.*

**L**et the preceding figure be repeated. Let ray GB strike the liquid CBD and depart refracted at F. I maintain that the end of the shadow F, or an object seen in that same place, will not reach the eye G through curved lines—as many have wrongly believed—but through straight lines, specifically through lines FB and BG. I will teach this through experience.

## Experiment.

<margin>A notable observation.</margin>

**L**et a thin, straight <term>tube<note>original: "syphon"; here referring to a hollow sighting tube rather than a device for moving liquid.</note></term> be made, which is adapted with such skill above the rim of the vessel and to the <term>Azimuthal quadrant<note>An instrument used to measure the horizontal angle (azimuth) of a celestial body.</note></term> CGO (which we will teach how to construct in the following sections) that it can be moved around point B like a <term>fiducial edge<note>original: "regulae fiduciae"; a straightedge used for precise alignment or measurement.</note></term>. Then, let this small tube, together with the quadrant, be directed toward the Sun so that it diffuses the ray received straight through the entire length of the tube in a straight path. You will see, not without wonder, that the light which ought to have been projected in a straight line toward M according to the length of the tube, is seen refracted from it at F. For since the light cannot deviate, being enclosed, it must necessarily proceed by a straight path, and consequently through a straight line. For if it arrived at point F through other detours, let us suppose it then came through GB to M. But this contradicts the stated experience: therefore, it arrives at F in a straight line. Having often contemplated this most lucid experiment with no small pleasure, I immediately began to consider that remarkable opinion of certain philosophers...

...to mock the foolishness of the "wise" <note>likely referring to traditional scholastic philosophers</note>, who think that refracted forms reach the sight through I-know-not-what tunnels and hidden circles. ### Theorem III.
*The angles formed at the point of refraction by lines that are partly direct and partly refracted, when extended into a continuous line, are always equal to one another.*

**I**N the present figure, let the refracted line BF be continued from B to point H, and let the incident line GB be continued from B to M: I say that angle GBH is equal to angle FBM, and angle HBO is equal to the refracted angle EBF. For by the law of sectioning, these are vertical angles <note>opposite angles formed by two intersecting lines</note>, and are therefore equal to each other. For a ray of the Sun, if it strikes a liquid medium obliquely, it is broken toward the perpendicular upon impact: and if the path from which it bounced back is extended, it will be reflected back to where it emerged, receding from the perpendicular into the same position. The same thing happens in things seen outside the water when the eye is placed under the water; thus, if the eye is placed under the liquid at F, the ray carried through B will not tend toward H, but toward G, being refracted at B, and there it will perceive the thing seen. Thus, a ray of the Sun GB, forming an angle of 45 degrees with the horizon, will not strike point M on the 45-degree arc inside the water, but will incur at point F on the 35-degree arc; and if the Sun were placed here at F, it would not project a ray to H, but to point G at 45 degrees, as before.

### Experiment.
<margin>A refracted image is not seen in its actual place.</margin>
**H**ence it is clear that the refracted image of an object meeting the sight is not seen in its actual place. I demonstrate this by a common experience. Let a coin be placed at the bottom of the previously mentioned vessel; then, move back from it by such a distance until the image of the coin is completely hidden from your sight: once this is done, have the vessel filled with water, and you will soon find the previously hidden coin becomes visible by the help of refraction. See what wonders we exhibit by the help of this experiment in the following pages.

### Corollary.
<margin>The refracted image of a thing is seen at the meeting of the perpendicular and the extended line of refraction.</margin>
**T**he refracted image of an object is seen at the intersection of the <term>cathetus<note>A technical term in optics for the perpendicular line drawn from the object to the refracting surface.</note></term> and the extended line of refraction. Let the thing seen be at F, which, carried through FB and refracted at B, meets the sight at G: hence, from the line GB, extended straight to M, it will show the thing seen at M, at the meeting of the intersection of the cathetus FX and the extended line of refraction. See the demonstration in Experiment 7.

### Theorem IV.
*A thing seen underwater by refraction <note>original: "anaclasticè"</note> appears higher the farther it is from the eye.*

**L**et the sight, therefore, be at A, and the points seen under the water be the equidistant points B, C, D, E; let the surface of the water be FK, and the perpendicular from the sight be AB. I say that the further the thing seen is from the sight, the higher its elevation will appear. Or, what is the same thing, the refraction will be greater the farther it is from the line AB: that is, the refraction of point E will be greater than D, and D...

Furthermore, the larger they are, the higher the refracted images appear on the vertical normal of refraction, as is evident in points S, R, and H. ->*Corollary I.*<-

**F**rom this it is clear why the Stars, the Sun, the Moon, and the rest of the celestial bodies are occasionally seen above the horizon before they have actually risen: for the horizon is always submerged in the depth of dense air, rising vapors, and mists, from which the image of the hidden Sun is elevated by the refracted ray.

**H**ence it is also clear why a sphere hidden under water looks both larger and concave when viewed perpendicularly; because the part that is further from the eye appears higher <note>meaning closer to the surface</note>, while the center stays in its place; the oblique radii will be seen, and because of this, they appear larger.

### *Theorem V.*

->*Because of refraction under water, all things appear larger.*<-

**T**heon <note>Theon of Alexandria (c. 335–405 AD), a Greek scholar and mathematician who commented on Ptolemy's Almagest.</note> in his *Commentaries on the Almagest* <note>The Almagest is the definitive ancient Greek manual on astronomy by Ptolemy.</note> attributes the cause of this phenomenon to this principle: Things seen under larger angles appear larger; those seen under smaller angles appear smaller. This is incorrect <note>original: "Perperam"</note>: for this cannot be called the immediate cause by any reasoning. Therefore, we demonstrate the truer cause in the following proof <note>original: "apodixi" (from Greek for demonstration)</note>.

->*Experiment.*<-

**L**et there be a sphere cast onto the flat bottom of a vessel of water, marked IL, whose extremity L—of the diameter—reaches the surface of the water. Therefore, since the refraction is described uniformly around it, it will also describe a larger circumference over MN than over LI; for while the diameter LI lies straight between the two parallels NL and MI, MN lies obliquely due to refraction. Let the diameter IL be parallel to NO, and from M let MO be drawn; the angle MON will be a right angle, because it is an angle in a semicircle. Therefore, the power <note>original: "potentia" - in geometry, this refers to the square of the line's length</note> of ON and OM is equal to that of MN itself, and ON is equal to LI. Therefore, the power of MN exceeds the power of ON by the power of MO. Thus, MN is larger than LI; and therefore, the circle is larger than the circle. Which was to be demonstrated.

### Corollary I.

<margin>Why the stars seem to move more slowly near the horizon than at the meridian.</margin>
**F**rom this it is clear that the bottom of any body of water, when viewed obliquely, is much further from the surface of the water than it truly appears to the eyes. Vitellio <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1285) was a Polish friar and physicist whose work on optics, *Perspectiva*, was a standard text for centuries.</note> reports that this illusion has been the cause of death for many <note>Likely referring to drowning accidents caused by misjudging the depth of water.</note>. It is also clear that things seem to move more slowly due to refraction in water than in the open air. Since the perpendicular BT, along which the image proceeds, appears shorter than it really is—becoming, for example, the seen image AT—it is clear that the refracted ray spends as much time traveling through it as it would if it traveled through the whole of BT in a vessel empty of water. For this reason, the stars near the horizon seem to move more slowly than at the meridian. For between two equal movers traveling through unequal spaces, the one moving through the shorter space will appear to move more slowly, while the one moving through the longer space will appear to move faster.

Since the end of the rod E appears to the eye at V when refracted, according to the laws of refraction, the line EV represents the part of the rod under water, and the line BE represents the part above the water. Thus the whole rod will appear as BEV; since these do not continue in a straight line, it must necessarily appear broken at the point of refraction, E. From this principle it also depends why ships seen from a transparent medium through a vaporous medium appear deeper; why the same things seem to move when the medium is disturbed by refraction; and why the stars and sunbeams seem to tremble near the boundary of Light and Shadow.

<margin>The surface of refraction necessarily passes through the center of the world.</margin>

Therefore, if the plane of refraction falls on that point, it also falls on the vertex of the solar cone.

III. It follows that the plane of refraction necessarily falls on the ray of incident refraction, and the perpendicular, or vertical line. I prove the first part thus: the plane of refraction falls on the center of the eye (or light) and the point of refraction: but these are the extremities of the line of incidence: therefore it falls on the whole line, since the whole line lies in that plane in which its endpoints lie. I prove the second part thus, because it falls on the point of refraction and the eye, which bound the line of refraction. The third, because it falls on the center of the earth, as was said, and on the point of vision: these, however, lie on the vertical, because a straight line extended from the center of the earth through the eye into the sky is vertical; therefore, the plane of refraction is also vertical.

IV. It follows that every plane of refraction—and only a plane of refraction—is a vertical plane. From this, the following new theorems are derived:

# Great Art of Light and Shadow, Book VIII. The Science of Refraction, Part I. #

The points of refraction are labeled D, E, and F, where perpendicular lines are drawn toward which or from which the refraction occurs. I maintain that to an eye positioned within the atmosphere at point H, the Sun (ABC) is seen not directly, but through refraction; it appears larger than usual and elevated. 

<image-desc>A circular diagram illustrating atmospheric refraction. A smaller central circle with center G is surrounded by a larger circle. An arc labeled D, E, F represents the boundary of an atmosphere. Light rays from a solar body labeled A, B, C strike the atmosphere's boundary and bend (refract) as they travel to an observer at point H located within the atmosphere.</image-desc>

This occurs because the light of the Sun (ABC), falling from a thinner medium <note>In 17th-century physics, the "thinner medium" refers to the vacuum of space or the ether, while the "vaporous medium" is the Earth's atmosphere.</note> onto the surface of the vaporous medium (DEF), refracts toward the perpendiculars GD, GE, and GF, according to the principles previously established, and meets the eye at point H on the vaporous horizon. By this refraction, it happens that the Sun begins to appear to an eye at H even before it has actually risen; however, this does not happen through direct rays, but through refracted ones. This proposition is the converse of the first one: for just as when the eye is placed in the thinner medium, the visual ray falling into the denser medium is refracted *toward* the perpendicular (from B to F), so too if the eye were placed under water at F and the object was outside the water, the visual ray from point B would be refracted *away* from the perpendicular toward point G. The same logic applies to the Sun: while our eye is situated in the misty atmosphere, the visual rays carried through the medium and refracted at the surface DEF do not travel in a straight line, but recede from the perpendiculars to points A, B, and C. Therefore, whether the eye is inside the water and the visible form outside, or the form is inside and the eye outside, the angles of refraction for those same media will always remain the same.

From this it is clear that for an eye within the atmosphere and away from its center, the Sun—wherever it may be visible—is seen refracted toward the perpendicular. This I prove as follows: no solar ray passing from any point of the atmosphere to the eye will pass through the center of the atmosphere if its path is extended in a straight line, except for the single vertical ray at the <term>zenith: the point in the sky directly above an observer</term>. Therefore, apart from this one, no other ray is perpendicular to the atmosphere; consequently, all others are oblique and, therefore, refracted.

### Theorem X.

->The Sun and the stars are variously refracted in all their parts, both in length and width, according to the observations of Scheiner.<- <note>Christopher Scheiner (1573–1650) was a Jesuit astronomer and rival of Galileo, famous for his detailed studies of sunspots and atmospheric optics.</note>

The **contraction** of the Sun arises from the unequal elevation of its highest, middle, and lowest parts above the horizon. This stems from the fact that they are refracted unequally relative to their perpendiculars. This is caused by the unequal inclination of the rays proceeding from those parts as they strike the surface of the atmosphere. Since the lower parts of the Sun strike this surface more obliquely and the upper parts more directly, it is necessary that the lower parts of the Sun are refracted more than the higher parts, appearing stretched higher and more intensely squeezed together.

Almost everything said so far is illustrated in the provided diagram. In this diagram, the smaller circle ABC, described from center A, represents the Atmosphere; the larger circle ADE represents the "heaven" or path of the Sun. In the vertical line AF, an eye G is positioned within the atmosphere. Whether the eye looks at the Sun at the zenith (DE at point F), or at the horizon (HI at point I), or at the <term>nadir: the point directly below the observer, opposite the zenith</term> (KL at point M)—for we assume here that the Earth does not block the view—the eye G will always see the Sun refracted, but not always contracted.

For the Sun (DE) seen at the Zenith (F) will be contracted equally through the refracted lines GN and GO. Since the incident rays DB and EC strike the perpendiculars AP and AQ, the refracted rays GN and GO must approach them; thus, the Sun seen through them must be refracted and appear smaller or "contracted," with the diameter NO being smaller than the true diameter DE. However, this vertical refraction and contraction escapes our senses because the incidence of rays DB and EC is nearly straight; it is understood through reason alone, as the effect is too slight to perceive.

But the Sun (HI), when positioned on the true horizon <margin>AI, re-</margin> <note>The text cuts off here, continuing the discussion of the Sun at the horizon on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how the Earth's atmosphere acts like a lens, distorting the perceived shape and position of the Sun. # Theory of Refractions #

The Sun, labeled AI, appears refracted and unevenly contracted at HR through the refracted radiations GR, GS, and GH, which are produced by the incident rays HT, VX, and IY. Because the angle HYI is greater than SXV, and SXV is greater than RTH, the ray GY is refracted more than GX, and GX more than GT. Therefore, if the straight line GX is extended outside the vapors to S, it becomes higher in its proportion than the extended line GR; and GH becomes higher than either GS or GR. This is because, within the Atmosphere, due to the more oblique incident ray IY, it approaches its perpendicular AY more closely than GS approaches its own AX, and so on.

Therefore, the entire refracted Sun HR appears smaller than the unrefracted Sun IH; and the lower refracted semi-diameter HZ appears smaller than the upper refracted semi-diameter ZR.

However, if the eye at G views the Sun KL at the <term>Nadir</term> <note>The point directly below an observer, opposite the Zenith.</note> labeled $\beta \gamma$, it appears through the refractions G $\alpha \beta$ at $\epsilon$, and G $\gamma \delta$ at $\delta$, outside its true locations K and L, under a diameter $\epsilon \delta$ that has been enlarged by refraction. Since the incident rays K $\alpha$ and L $\gamma$ create equal inclinations on all sides, it is necessary for the spreading of the Sun to be uniform; therefore, the Sun appears larger, but still spherical. From this, it seems agreeable to reason and conformable to the laws of Refraction that the same Sun, when placed outside the Nadir in the lower hemisphere and approaching the boundary, is unevenly enlarged. As it moves away from the Nadir, it appears taller than it is wide because of the more oblique incident rays. Experience itself seems to support this doctrine. These findings are drawn largely from the observations of <note>Christoph Scheiner (1573–1650), a Jesuit priest and rival of Galileo, famous for his detailed studies of sunspots and atmospheric optics.</note> Scheiner.

### Corollaries ###

I. **FROM** these points, it is established first that the Sun, viewed by an eye remains stationary outside the center of the earth, displays nearly every variety of shape and size as it moves around.

II. At the <term>Zenith</term> <note>The point in the sky directly above the observer.</note> it appears round, but smaller than it truly is; at the Nadir, it appears round, but larger than it truly is.

III. Between the Zenith and the Horizon, it appears smaller in height than in length; yet both dimensions appear diminished.

IV. At the sensible horizon, the sight is diminished in height alone, while in length it appears natural.

<margin>Variations of the Sun caused by refraction.</margin>
V. Between the Horizon and the Nadir, it appears more extended in height than in length, though both dimensions exceed the truth. The reason for this is that only the vertical planes are the planes of refraction, and in this position, the planes of length cannot be such.

VI. The same things will happen if the eye, moved around the periphery of a circle located within the vapors, observes a stationary Sun. However, if the eye moves along a diameter that does not pass through the Sun, an observer placed outside the center of the Atmosphere will see it as unequal; if placed at the center, the observer will see it as equal and of its natural size.

## Rules of <term>Anaclastics</term> <note>The branch of optics dealing with the refraction of light, specifically through lenses or the atmosphere.</note> derived from the preceding, useful for dioptric astronomy. ##

I. **A**ll points of the open sky, except for the vertex, are subject to refraction, and consequently, all appear higher than they are. From this, it follows again that the portion of the sky that appears is more than it seems: more due to elevation, yet less due to contraction. The other celestial circles follow this same condition.

II. No stars positioned away from the Zenith are seen in their true places once they reach 40 degrees of altitude. Likewise, no stars demonstrate their true altitude above the horizon while they are far from the Zenith; and stars located on the sensible horizon are actually partially below it. Almost all phenomena of the <term>prime mover</term> <note>In the Ptolemaic system, the "primum mobile" or first moved sphere, which carries all the stars in their daily rotation around the Earth.</note> depend on this.

III. Whoever calculates the altitudes of the pole from stars near the horizon exposes themselves to the manifest danger of error; the same danger faces those who observe the vertical distances of stars.

<margin>Civil time affected by refraction.</margin>
IV. Civil days—from sunrise to sunrise, or sunset to sunset—are shorter or longer according to the amount of refraction (setting aside the Sun's own proper motion). However, the days measured from midnight to midnight, or Astronomical days, are always equal, since refraction does not interfere here. In the former case, at the beginning and end of the Sun's motion near the horizon, refraction can bring about some increase to the day. Hence it is also clear that even at the time of the equinox, the day is longer than the night everywhere in the world; Nature prolongs this by the help of refraction, not without divine providence.

V. Stars placed away from the point of the vertex are never seen in their true places, though this is not very obvious to the senses when they are at roughly 40 degrees of altitude. Consequently, they never show their true altitude above the horizon when away from the vertex, even if the sense fails to notice it, especially when they are further removed from said vertex.

VI. All stars located on the sensible horizon are, in reality, below it; and those that appear to be on the physical horizon are actually above it.

<margin>The rising and setting of stars vary due to refraction.</margin>
VII. The distance between stars positioned simultaneously on the same vertical line, although it is visible, is not the true distance. Rather, the perceived distance is always less than the true distance, though this is not subject to error. The reason is clear from Theorem 10. For it is proven by the same that the Sun at the point of the vertex is round, and just...

# The Great Art, Book VIII. The Art of Refraction, Part I. #

...but smaller than is accurate; in the middle it appears round, and larger than is accurate.

VIII. The Sun, at the equinoxes, appears to decline slightly toward the North or the South. <note>Refraction makes the Sun appear higher in the sky than its true astronomical position, which can make it seem to have shifted its seasonal path slightly.</note>

IX. From this, it follows that two stars—where one is rising while the other is setting, and both touch the horizon—should by no means be considered diametrically opposite in reality.

X. Civil days <note>A "civil day" refers to the full 24-hour cycle from sunrise to sunrise or sunset to sunset.</note>, from sunrise to sunrise or from sunset to sunset, vary in length according to whether refraction is great or small; therefore, this method is least reliable for the business of astronomical observation.

XI. Days measured from midnight to midnight are always equal: for since refraction only occurs vertically (relative to altitude) and not longitudinally, refraction cannot hinder them at all. The same must be said for astronomical days measured from noon to noon.

XII. Artificial days <note>The "artificial day" refers specifically to the period of daylight, from sunrise to sunset.</note>, or the diurnal arcs, are always longer throughout the entire world, and the nights are shorter. Since the refraction of the Sun occurs toward the perpendicular, the Sun rises earlier in the morning than it ought to, and sets later in the evening than is right.

XIII. All Solar clocks <note>Sundials.</note> that are constructed based on altitudes are erroneous; those who set clocks according to the rising and setting of the Sun are also in error. Thus, by a truly wonderful providence of the Divine Power, men always and everywhere have more light than darkness; indeed, this greater or lesser refraction, depending on the higher or lower elevation of the Sun, presents unequal and yet proportional durations of time.

### *Rules concerning the Shadows of Gnomons.* ###

<term>Gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note>

XIV. Shadows can be considered in three ways: first, as they appear on mobile or immobile dials; second, as they are considered under a <term>right sphere</term>; and third, as they are considered under an <term>oblique sphere</term>. <note>In historical geography, a "right sphere" refers to the view from the Equator, while an "oblique sphere" refers to the view from mid-latitudes.</note>

-><margin>Cautions regarding sundials due to the fallacy of refractions.</margin><-
XV. On mobile sundials, such as cylinders, rings, and similar instruments constructed based on the Sun's altitude, the shadow demonstrates the same hour and position of the Sun that the Sun would show if it were not refracted. However, the matter is different for fixed sundials equipped with a <term>Zodiac</term>, because of the oblique rising and setting of the Sun. Thirdly, fixed <term>Sciatheric</term> <note>original: "Sciatherica"; the art of dialing or shadow-measurement.</note> instruments under a right sphere suffer no change; however, under an oblique sphere, they will wander somewhat from the line that an unrefracted Sun would show. For as is clear from the preceding, the Sun has one <term>amplitude</term> <note>The angular distance from due East or West at rising or setting.</note> when refracted below the horizon and another when unrefracted. Indeed, the greatest variation in refractions demonstrates that shadows undergo the greatest changes under a <term>parallel sphere</term>. <note>The "parallel sphere" refers to the view from the Earth's poles, where the celestial equator is parallel to the horizon.</note>

XVI. Hence the rising and setting of the stars, as well as the rising and setting amplitudes, are wider toward the North in Northern climates.

XVII. Hence stars that have not yet set for us have already risen for the <term>Antipodes</term>. <note>People living on the exact opposite side of the globe.</note>

-><margin>The nature of wondrous refraction in the right and parallel sphere.</margin><-
XVIII. Just as under a right sphere and those oblique spheres near it, refraction affects only the hourly times; so, marvelous to say, under a parallel sphere and those near it, it anticipates or postpones entire days. This happens because of the extreme obliquity of that sphere. For in that location, the Sun remains at the horizon for a very long time due to the inclination of the <term>ecliptic</term> <note>The Sun's apparent path across the sky over the year.</note>. Therefore, if its refraction equals even a single degree—which no doubt happens often—several days pass while the Sun traverses such an arc in the ecliptic that corresponds to one degree taken vertically. For one degree in the vertical circle of this sphere corresponds to 20 degrees, 30 minutes, 29 seconds, and 21 thirds in the ecliptic. Since refraction can quite often exceed a whole degree, and indeed most probably reaches two degrees at times, it happens in such a case that the Sun will emerge above the horizon in the parallel sphere five days earlier; this is because 50 degrees, 11 minutes, 44 seconds, and 4 thirds in the ecliptic correspond to two degrees taken vertically. The opposite happens in a right sphere, where the ecliptic has a small inclination to the horizon, and the "first motion" <note>The daily rotation of the sky.</note> soon carries the Sun away from the horizon; this does not happen in a parallel sphere, where only the "second motion" <note>The Sun's own annual movement along the ecliptic.</note>, which is proper to it, lifts the Sun above the horizon.
