## CHAPTER II.
### On the calculation of Anaclastic Tables.

Having seen the causes resulting from refractions in various media through the previous experiments, the order of our study now demands that we see by what method rays of this refracted <term>anaclastic</term><note>From the Greek 'anaklasis', meaning breaking back or reflection; here it refers specifically to the mathematics of refracted light.</note> type can be investigated and organized into tables. Since I see that this has been done by no one, we—believing ourselves to be the first to "break the ice" in this most difficult matter—have, with truly great labor, established complete refraction tables for every degree and minute, and for various media through very laborious experiments, so that the needs of students <note>original: "Tyronum," referring to beginners or young scholars</note> might be served. There are indeed some tables in the tenth book of Vitellio <note>A 13th-century scientist whose work on optics was a standard reference for centuries.</note>, which Kepler also followed; but I have found no one who has calculated them degree by degree down even to the seconds. I am speaking, however, of tables of refractions from air into water, wine, glass, and similar denser media; for many have described refractions in the media of vaporous air <note>atmospheric refraction</note>, and fairly accurate tables were established by Tycho Brahe, Kepler, Scheiner, and others. But to come to the matter, some Lemmas <note>A lemma is a "stepping stone" proposition used to prove a larger theorem.</note> must first be set forth here, which contribute greatly by smoothing the way for the task of investigation.

### Lemma I.
#### *The more obliquely light falls into a denser medium, the greater the angle at which it is refracted.*

I show this matter first by experience, and then by reason itself. Let the figure from Proposition I, Theorem I be repeated. Where **GB** is the ray of incidence and **CD** is the surface of the denser transparent body. I say that the more obliquely the light falls on point **B**, the more it is refracted by a larger angle. First, let the alidade <note>A sighting device or pointer used to measure angles.</note> **GB** be raised to **G**, and the light falling through it from point **B** will be refracted at **F**, and the refracted angle will be **EBF**. Then, let the same be lowered to **S**, and it will refract the light sent through point **B** at **M**: therefore, the refracted angle **EBM** will be larger than angle **EBF**. 

But this refracted angle is always so much wider as the Sun is closer to the horizon; conversely, it is so much smaller as it is closer to the zenith. And this experience is certain and infallible; for unless the refracted angle increased continuously with the obliquity of incidence, there would be no universal cause of refraction. Since oblique incidence is the cause of spreading <note>original: "dispersionis"; in this context, the deviation of light from a straight path.</note>, as that obliquity increases, the spreading increases, as Kepler well notes. 

-> ![A geometrical diagram illustrating refraction at a plane surface. A horizontal line CD represents the surface of a denser medium. A vertical line AB is the normal. Incident rays GB (less oblique) and SB (more oblique) enter the medium at point B. The ray GB refracts towards F, and the more oblique ray SB refracts towards M. The diagram includes several auxiliary points and lines (E, N, Q, P) used to measure the angles of incidence and refraction, demonstrating that a more oblique incident ray results in a larger angle of refraction.](image_placeholder) <-

For if the angle of refraction in oblique incidence—say at 80 degrees—stopped increasing, and it remained the same at 80 as it was at 82, 83, or 84 degrees of incidence (for example, at 30 degrees). Therefore, the medium would have resisted the spreading of light up to an 80-degree inclination, but at 82 degrees and others for 2, 3, or 4 degrees, it would no longer resist. But a medium always resists the spreading of light because it is a denser medium; therefore, it prevents the light from being scattered. But it is always impeded as long as it scatters, until it falls perpendicularly upon it; for then the ray is refracted into itself <note>Meaning the light enters straight and does not bend at all.</note>. It is therefore clear that it must be proven...

## Lemma II.

*The more obliquely light falls, the greater the resistance it always encounters from the same medium than if it entered more directly, with respect to the medium itself.*

Let the light be **A**, and the denser medium be **BM**; let **AB** and **KM** be parallel rays of the Sun, with their distance being **ML**. Since angle **BLM** is a right angle, and **LBM** is assumed to be an oblique acute angle, then **LBM** will be smaller than **BLM**. Thus, the side **LM**, which subtends the smaller angle **B**, will be smaller than the side **BM**, which subtends the right angle **BLM**. But **LM** measures the width of the medium encountered by the light falling directly <note>falling at a right angle or perpendicularly</note>, because **BLM** is a right angle; whereas **BM** measures the width of the light encountering it from an oblique angle. Therefore, there is more density <note>meaning more material to pass through</note> in **BM** than in **LM**. Consequently, there is greater resistance. For since refraction is an "affected motion" <note>an early term for motion altered by a medium</note> occurring when light strikes the surface of a denser medium, and since the surface terminates at infinite points—or rather, the motion of the infinite points of light is more affected here—this must be considered in terms of density no less than physical bulk. Thus, the light is more affected if it encounters a "denser" path; and it encounters a denser path when entering obliquely, as has just been shown.

From this it is evident that refractions near the horizon increase by steep proportions of growth. Since **BLM** and **BCA** are right angles, and **LBM** is common to both triangles, the triangles **BAC** and **BLM** will be similar. Therefore, as **CA** is to **AB**, so **LM** is to **MB**; but **AB** are the secants of the inclinations **ABC**, which increase suddenly at the end of the quadrant <note>approaching 90 degrees</note>. Therefore, **BM** also increases; and we have said that in **BM**, relative to **ML**, the refractions increase, as it were, beyond the fact that they increase proportionally to the inclinations themselves. Thus, the refractions also increase suddenly, which was to be proven.

## Problem I.

*To calculate tables of refractions.*

Having obtained the composite refraction for any inclination, we shall calculate the elements of refraction and the composite (or whole) refractions for the other inclinations using the following method, following the system of Kepler. First, let the medium be water; let the radius of incidence be inclined at 80 degrees; the angle of deviation <note>original: "reflexionis," but the context clearly indicates the angle of deviation or the "breaking" of the ray</note> be 30 degrees; and the refracted ray be at 50 degrees, the <term>secant</term><note>A trigonometric function representing the ratio of the hypotenuse to the adjacent side.</note> of which is 155,572. Calculate as follows:

As the secant of the 50-degree angle is to the secant of the 0-degree angle (or to the <term>total sine</term><note>The "total sine" or "sinus totus" refers to the radius of the mathematical circle used in calculations, typically set at 100,000 in early modern tables to avoid decimals.</note> of 50 degrees), so is the refraction angle of 30 degrees to the proportional refraction of the 80-degree inclination. Once the operation is performed, it will yield 19 degrees and 17 minutes; to which is added 10 degrees and 43 minutes (because the medium appears denser to the refracted ray under water than to a direct ray, in the proportion of 155,572 to 100,000), resulting in 30 degrees and 0 minutes. Thus, once this is obtained, since simple refraction is proportional to the inclinations, the distribution into the remaining inclinations can be made. Then, each should be multiplied by the secant of the refracted angle, which is not yet fully known: the search for the secant must be repeated as many times as necessary until there is no remaining discrepancy.

## Practical Example.

When the refracted angle was set at 50 degrees by distribution, the result for simple refraction was 12 degrees and 4 minutes. These, subtracted from 50, leave 37 degrees and 56 minutes, the secant of which is 126,787; its excess above the total sine (the secant of a 0-degree angle) is 26,787. This value, multiplied by 12 degrees and 4 minutes and divided by the total sine, shows 3 degrees and 14 minutes for that part of the refraction derived from the secants, which previously had to be subtracted from 50. Let this now be subtracted from the already diminished 37 degrees and 56 minutes, leaving 34 degrees and 42 minutes. The excess of this secant above the total sine is 21,633, which, when multiplied by 12 degrees and 4 minutes, shows 2 degrees and 37 minutes. The previous result of 3 degrees and 14 minutes was therefore too much. Thus, subtracting this 2 degrees and 37 minutes from 37 degrees and 56 minutes leaves 35 degrees and 19 minutes; the excess of this secant shows 2 degrees and 43 minutes. But even that does not quite match. Therefore, once again, this being subtracted from 37 degrees and 56 minutes leaves 35 degrees and 13 minutes, the excess of which (22,402), multiplied by 12 degrees and 4 minutes, shows 2 degrees and 42 minutes. Since this differs from the previous result by an imperceptible amount, the calculation may rest. Therefore, the refraction due to secants at an inclination of 50 degrees will be 2 degrees and 42 minutes. By this method—which is truly most laborious—we have constructed the following table, in which the composite refractions from air into water are shown for every single degree of incidence relative to the perpendicular ray, based on the dual elements 1 and 2.

## Rules for the Calculation of Refractions in Water and Air.

### Rule I.

As the secant of the refracted angle of 50 is to the total sine, so the angle of refraction **B** (30) is to the simple refraction of 19 degrees and 17 minutes.

Therefore, by inversion of the ratio: As the secant <note>The secant is a trigonometric function representing the ratio of the hypotenuse to the adjacent side</note> BI is to the tangent HI, so CH is to HL; and by division, as the total sine <note>original: "sinus totus"; in historical trigonometry, this refers to the radius of the circle used for calculation, here treated as a base value of 100,000 or 10,000,000</note> is to the tangent HI, so CL is to LH. Furthermore, as the refracted CE is to the simple CL, so CE is to CL.

If, therefore, it is assumed that arc CE is 80 degrees and arc CH is 30, and consequently arc HE is 50, then BS will be 155,572, HI will be 55,572, BH will be 100,000, and CL will be found through A.

### Canon II.

The **U**nrefracted inclination <note>The angle at which light hits the surface before bending</note> G of 80 degrees has a total refraction of 30 degrees; and this, subtracted from 80, leaves a refracted angle of 50 degrees, the secant of which is 15,557,239. As this secant is to the total sine, so the total refraction of 30 is to its simple part. Therefore, this simple part will be 300,000,000 / 15,557,239, which is 19 degrees and 17 minutes <note>A minute is 1/60th of a degree</note> of one degree—that is, the denominator signifies the parts of one degree. Therefore, multiplied by 30, it will give the total refraction in those same parts as 466,717,170; and from this, the numerator of the simple part (300,000,000) being subtracted, it leaves the congruent part <note>The "congruent part" likely refers to the secondary corrective value in the author's refraction model</note> as 166,717,170 / 15,557,239, which is 10 degrees and 43 minutes.

### Canon III.

**A**S the unrefracted inclination of 80 is to its simple refraction B (100,000,000 / 15,557,239 degrees), so the unrefracted inclination C of 50 is to its own simple part. Therefore, multiply B by C and let the product be divided by A; the fraction of one degree will be found to be 1,500,000,000 / 124,457,912, or 12 degrees and 3 minutes. From this, 50 degrees—that is, the unrefracted inclination—will be of the same parts: 6,222,895,600 / 124,457,912. Subtracting the fraction of the simple angle from this will leave, for the refracted angle, 4,722,895,600 / 124,457,912, or 37 degrees and 57 minutes, the secant of which is 12,681,543. Now I say that:

> Just as the total sine 10,000,000 is to the secant sine 12,681,543, so 12 degrees and 13 minutes is to the other value.

### Canon IV.

**I**N an inclination of 80 degrees, it is established that the total refraction is 30; therefore the refracted angle will be 50. And because, as the secant of the refracted angle is to the total sine, so is the total refraction to its simple part; Let it be that as 155,572 (the secant of 50 degrees) is to the total sine 100,000, so 30 is to the fourth proportional, that is, to 3,000,000 / 155,572. This fourth number will be the simple part of the total refraction; and because the denominator denotes parts of one degree, multiplied therefore by 30, it will give 30 degrees in those same parts: 4,667,160 / 155,572. And from here, the simple part being removed, it will leave for the congruent part: 1,667,160 / 155,572.

### Simple part for an inclination of 50°

**A**S the inclination of 80 degrees is to the inclination of 80 degrees, so is its simple part—that is 1,000,000 / 155,572, or in the smallest numbers 750,000 / 38,893—to the simple part of the inclination of 50 degrees, which is 37,500,000 / 3,111,44 of a degree, or 468,750 / 38,893, which is a simple part of 12 degrees and 3 minutes.

### First approximation to the congruent part.

**F**irst, the simple part 468,750 / 38,893 (which is 12 degrees and 3 minutes) should be subtracted from the inclination of 50 degrees, and there will remain 37 degrees and 57 minutes, the secant of which is 126,815. Subtracting the total sine of 100,000, the difference of 26,815 remains. Then, let it be that as the total sine 100,000 is to 26,815, so the simple part 468,750 / 38,893 is to the fourth proportional; and the first congruent part will be found. That is, the numerator of the fraction of the simple part should be multiplied by the difference, producing the numerator of the quotient, and the denominator should be multiplied by the total sine, producing the denominator of the quotient. And thus this fraction, 12,569,531,250 / 3,889,300,000, reduced to degrees and minutes, makes the first congruent part 3 degrees and 14 minutes. And from this single example <note>original: "paradigmate"</note>, it is clear by what method you ought to elicit the congruent parts of the remaining refractions by calculation. But so that you may have a direction for your calculation, it seemed best to place before your eyes here a Table of Refractions calculated with incredible labor, together with the operations performed; so that if anyone has not fully grasped the methods of calculation, they may draw some light from the proposed table.

### Use of the Table.

**L**ook in the column (titled Degrees in Air) for the degrees of the incident rays; and the following column will give the refracted angles in degrees and minutes. For example, if you wish to know which refracted degree corresponds to degree 80, see this degree in the column titled Degrees in Air, and the column titled <insert>Refracted Degrees in Water</insert> <note>While the table headers simply say D and M for brevity, the text here clarifies that these columns represent the final angle of light once it has entered the water.</note> will give 50 degrees, 0 minutes, which is the refracted degree under water: you shall proceed in the same way for the others. The column titled "Complement" serves this purpose: so that if I wish to perform the operation from the opposite side, it may be permitted; let him reach the goal through the complements of the degrees.

## Problem II.
### To construct an anaclastic mesoptic instrument.

**F**irst, let a cup be made as a perfect semi-sphere <term>hemicyclus</term><gloss>a half-circle or bowl-like structure</gloss> CBDE, the interior concave surface of which you will divide into four quadrants by two semi-circles representing the meridian and the vertical [lines]; and it will give point E as the Nadir <term>Nadir</term><gloss>The point on the celestial sphere directly below an observer, opposite the Zenith.</gloss>, the point opposite the vertex: and let the meridian be CED, the primary vertical be BE: B the center of the world <note>The "center of the world" refers to the central point of the instrument's spherical representation, mimicking the cosmos.</note>: the horizon BCVD divided into 360 parts, or four quadrants: CED is the meridian, the quadrant ED of which you will divide exactly into 90 equal parts, starting from E.

Secondly, to this vessel so prepared, you will adapt an Azimuthal quadrant <note>An instrument used to measure the azimuth, or horizontal angle, of a celestial body.</note>, with such diligence that it can be moved freely around the axis in center B; so that this may be done more conveniently, it is necessary that the side of the quadrant BO be equipped with two small handles, so that in them, as if on certain hinges...

->[image: A complex geometric diagram illustrating an astronomical or optical instrument for measuring refraction. Thirdly, you will attach a ruler—or <term>alidade</term> <note>A pointer or sighting device used to measure angles.</note>—to the center B of the quadrant, crafted as finely as possible and equipped with its own sights, or even a narrow tube like the one labeled GB. You will then have the quadrant ready for use.

### *Method for observing refractions with the aid of this instrument.*

<margin>Practical method for observing refractions.</margin>
**T**he degrees of refraction can be observed by two paths using this instrument: by the visual line, or by the rays of the Sun. Let us explain both. When you are about to determine the points of refraction in the anaclastic <note>Refractive.</note> semi-circular vessel: First, fill the vessel with water until the center point B is exposed immediately beneath the water's surface. Next, direct the alidade over every ten degrees of the quadrant, beginning at 10. Carefully note which degree the line of sight hits under the water on the quadrant ED; record this precisely, for this will be the refracted angle, which you should note separately alongside the 10-degree angle of incidence. Again, move the alidade to the 20-degree mark, and by looking carefully, note which degree the sight reaches on the quadrant ED. Record this along with its minutes in the same way, and so on for the rest, until you have completed all the decades of refraction. Then, you may turn to observing the individual degrees. To better determine the points, you should mark the points under the water that correspond to the sight with a fine needle in your other hand. This method, if performed exactly and if the quadrant is correctly adjusted, is quite certain and reliable.

However, to construct a table with the help of solar rays, proceed as follows: First, create an exact description of the azimuths and <term>almucantars</term> <note>Circles of altitude parallel to the horizon.</note> on some horizontal plane, as we taught in the fifth book. Then, at a selected time at noon when the Sun enters the first degree <note>Likely referring to the beginning of a zodiacal sign or a specific solar position.</note>, observe which degree the rays passing through the alidade indicate on the quadrant ED. This will be the refracted degree corresponding to the maximum almucantar for that day; note this separately. You will then repeat this operation as the Sun reaches each almucantar. Note, however, that in each observation, the vessel along with the quadrant ED must be directed toward the Sun’s azimuth. <margin>Another practical method for investigating refraction.</margin> In this way, you will be able to record both the azimuths and the almucantars in a single operation. But since this is more laborious, we will add another practical method here, as follows:

Let two entirely equal semi-circles be made, equipped with equal <term>gnomons</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note> and identical quadrant divisions. Let these be exposed to the Sun together: one filled with liquid, the other empty. The gnomon of the empty one will show the direct path of the rays, while the other will show the degree of the rays refracted beneath the liquid. By this industrious method, we have discovered the refractions of any liquids whatsoever, as will be discussed shortly.

From this operation, it is clear how not only refractions from air into water, but also into oil, wine, and other liquids of different thicknesses—and even into glass and crystal bodies—can be observed and reduced into tables. Indeed, so that you may see a specimen of the refractions in water, wine, <margin>Refraction into oil, wine, and glass.</margin> oil, and glass, observed by us with the greatest labor, we subjoin the tables of refractions here. We do this so that we do not seem to have withheld anything from the curious maker; from these tables, you will see, not without pleasure, the differences in refraction from one medium to another. From air to wine and oil, we found scarcely any difference except in the minutes; therefore, we will present them here only in decades of degrees as we observed them. From these, the wise reader (or anyone else with the leisure) can easily investigate the refractions of the remaining degrees by following the rule for finding a proportional mean.

### On the Refractions of the Atmosphere.

<margin>Diversity of refractions.</margin>
**N**o task in Astronomy is entangled with so many difficulties as that concerning the refractions of the stars arising from the air. For since there is hardly any horizon that does not differ from another in the density of its air, it follows as a consequence that in different places, stars observed near the horizon—even with the most exact instruments—nonetheless produce as many errors as there are observers of the stars. Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the famous Danish astronomer known for his accurate celestial observations.</note> also noted this inconsistency of refractions, as did Ke- <note>Johannes Kepler (1571–1630), who developed the laws of planetary motion.</note>

Book 8 of the Great Art. The <term>Anaclastic Art</term> <note>From the Greek "anaklasis," meaning refraction; this branch of optics deals with how light bends as it passes through different materials like air, water, or glass.</note> Part I.

...and Kepler. He adds that the atmosphere is exceedingly uneven and of uncertain height; if we held this height as a certainty, the exact investigation of refractions would not be difficult. For as the practitioners of optics demonstrate that the height of the "twilight matter" <note>The layer of the atmosphere capable of reflecting sunlight after the sun has set.</note> is equal to 12 miles, it does not follow that this same matter which causes twilight is also the cause of refractions. Since the refractive matter of the stars is liquid, moist, and vaporous—indeed, the very evaporation of water—it follows that this same smoky and fiery material (as such exhalations are) will struggle upward above this refractive air just as air struggles out of water. Therefore, the "smokes" will occupy the higher places; and since they possess a certain opacity, they will indeed reflect the light of the Sun to us before its rising, yet they are not suited to refract that same light. 

Since, therefore, there is such a great variety of refractions, it is difficult to establish anything certain regarding this business. Certainly, the refractions of the stars observed by Tycho Brahe at <term>Uraniborg</term> <note>Tycho Brahe’s famous observatory on the island of Hven.</note> differ notably from those which <term>Schiner</term> <note>Christoph Scheiner (1573–1650), a Jesuit priest and astronomer who, like Kircher, studied sunspots and optics.</note> and others observed here in Rome. Indeed, this refraction is not only noted to be different under different horizons, but the same refraction is found to vary not just from day to day, but from hour to hour. For refraction is one thing in summer and another in winter; one way at sunrise and another at sunset; one way in inland regions and another in coastal areas; one way in the mountains and another on the plains. And although these differences do not always extend to many minutes, when they are multiplied in the business of astronomy, they cause errors that are utterly intolerable. We include here tables of stellar refractions so that we do not appear to have omitted anything from our Art.

**Usage.** Look up the degrees of the Sun (☉), the Moon (☽), or a Star (*) in the appropriate tables, and the figures in the corresponding rows will give the desired refraction; for example, 10 degrees of the Sun's altitude corresponds to 10 minutes and 0 seconds, and so it is for the rest.

### Problem III.
### To construct an anaclastic quadrant for use in sundial making.

Let two opposite quadrants be made, ABC and CDE, of which the former is called the <term>mesotonos</term> <note>original: "μεσότωνος"; a term referring to the scale of incidence, literally the "middle-tone" or "intermediary" scale.</note>, or the quadrant of the incidence of rays; the latter is the anaclastic, or refractive quadrant. Each of these should be divided into 90 equal parts, but with this difference: quadrant ABC is to be marked with distinct degrees and rays drawn to the center, while quadrant CDE is marked with hidden <note>faint or dashed</note> degrees and signs. Once this is done, place before your eyes one of the three anaclastic tables of your choosing from those proposed just above. Although these tables differ slightly in their minutes, in the business of <term>sciatherics</term> <note>The art of designing and constructing sundials.</note> no noticeable difference is to be feared. Therefore, you may use either one safely. First, see which refracted degree corresponds to the first degree of incidence; look for the degree of incidence in quadrant ABC, beginning from point B; then look for the refracted degree in quadrant CED, beginning from point E (or vice versa), and draw a line from the center through this degree or the minutes of the degree. This will be the refracted line. Then, arrange each refracted degree in order according to the incident rays occurring in the table onto the edge ED of quadrant CED, just as was done for the first degree. You will then have an anaclastic quadrant CEG prepared for every degree, the use of which in every refractive business is almost infinite, as will be seen shortly.

<image-desc>A complex geometric diagram of an "Anaclastic Quadrant." It consists of two circular sectors sharing a common center point C. The left sector, ABC, is marked with a scale from 0 to 90 degrees and contains several solid and radial lines. The right sector, CDE, also has degree markings (labeled 10, 20, 30, 40 on the outer arc) and various lines of refraction labeled with letters G, S, N, and E. Dashed lines connect the corresponding points of incidence and refraction between the two sectors. Letters A, B, C, D, E, and G define the primary structure, while smaller letters S and N mark specific internal points.</image-desc>

<margin>The method for finding the angles of refraction.</margin> We have omitted the specific "angles of refraction" in these tables because anyone can find them simply by subtracting the refracted angle from the angle of incidence. For example, if I wish to know what angle of refraction from air into water corresponds to 80 degrees of incidence: I subtract the refracted angle corresponding to 80 from 80 itself, and the result is 30, which is the angle of refraction. By the same logic: if I wish to know how great the angle of refraction is from air into glass; I subtract the refracted 7 from the 10 degrees of incidence, and 3 will remain as the angle of refraction. Let the same judgment apply to all others.

From this it is clear that in the same denser <term>diaphanous medium</term> <note>A transparent substance, such as air or glass.</note>, the angle of refraction from a larger angle of incidence will be greater than the angle of refraction from a smaller angle of incidence; and also that the excess of the larger angle of refraction over the [smaller] refraction angle will be less than the excess of the larger angle of incidence...

## Prelude.

### On the construction of the horizontal refractive net.

**I**n the preceding refractive quadrant, on line CE, determine the size of the style <note>The "style" or gnomon is the rod that casts the shadow.</note> as desired—let it be, for example, C, S—and from point S to line CD, let a parallel line SQ or GN be drawn, which will represent the horizontal line, or the horizontal refractive plane.

Once this is completed, transfer the line SQ along with its divisions from the refractive quadrant onto a separate straight line CD of any size. Placing one foot of the compass at point R (the midpoint of line CD) as the center, let eccentric circles be drawn through the transferred points of the circle. These will provide the desired refractive <term>almucantars</term> <note>Almucantars are circles of altitude parallel to the horizon; here, they are adjusted for the way water bends light.</note>, as is evident in the following figure.

Furthermore, if you divide the outermost circle into 360 parts, or into 4 quadrants, and draw straight lines from the center point R through the points of division, these will provide the <term>azimuths</term> <note>Azimuths are vertical arcs used to measure the horizontal direction of a celestial body.</note>, and thus complete the refractive net in all its parts. The demonstration of this depends on the preceding experiments. See the figure for the following Problem.

# Refractive Astronomy

Find the hour points in Aries <note>The zodiac sign of Aries represents the Spring Equinox.</note>, beginning from the 12th hour. For the common intersections of the **Azimuths** <note>Vertical circles used to measure horizontal direction.</note> with the **Almucantars** <note>Circles of altitude parallel to the horizon.</note> must provide the hour points, which, when joined by a straight line, will give the Equator. In the same way, you will seek the hour points in the tropic of Capricorn using a table, which always shows you the common intersections of the Azimuths with the Almucantars for a given hour. You shall mark the hours from sunrise and sunset in a similar manner using their own table, always beginning from the 23rd hour, joining the common points of intersection with straight lines; thus you will have the desired hours. You will delineate the <term>planetary hours</term> <note>Also known as "unequal hours," these divide the day and night into 12 equal parts regardless of the season, meaning an "hour" is longer in summer than in winter.</note> by exactly the same method using their specific table.

### Use.

<margin>Placement of the vessel.</margin>
**P**lace the refractive <term>sciatheric</term> <note>From the Greek 'skia' (shadow) and 'therao' (to hunt/measure); a device for measuring time by shadows.</note> vessel on the meridian line and fill it with water until the tip of the gnomon <note>The pointer or rod of the sundial.</note> is submerged just beneath the water; it will show the desired hours within the lines by means of refraction. On these same lines, if the vessel were emptied of water, the shadow would wander far astray. Thus, we have described the horizontal refractive sundial, which was the task at hand.

## Problem V.
### To describe a vertical refractive sundial.

When you are about to describe a vertical refractive sundial, you must choose a vessel shape suitable for this specific type of clock. Just as we chose a vessel with low sides for the horizontal sundial—so that the Sun’s ray would not be blocked by the shadow of the rims—here, a vessel with high margins must be selected so that the shadow can move more freely upon the vertical refractive plane. Let the prepared vessel be **ABCD**, whose vertical plane intended for the sundial is **ABQD**. In this vessel, we shall describe the refractive hour lines, once we have first taught the method for constructing the vertical refractive net.

### Use of the sundial.

If, therefore, you desire to know the hour of the day, or other matters pertaining to the <term>prime mover</term> <note>In Aristotelian astronomy, the outermost sphere that moves all others; here referring to general celestial motion and time</note>, you shall fill the positioned sundial with the clearest water until the tip of the <term>style</term> <note>The gnomon or pin that casts the shadow</note> is hidden immediately beneath the water, and you will achieve your purpose: for the images, which previously appeared by no means in the vessel when it was bare of water, you will now behold appearing clearly and beautifully from the depths to the heights, not without wonder and pleasure.

### Corollary.

**First**, from what has been handed down, it is clear by what method—given any vertical plane inclining in any direction—an <term>anaclastic sciatheric</term> <note>A shadow-measuring device that works through refraction</note> can be described upon it.

**Second**, by what method—given a concave body of any sides—you can skillfully inscribe the hours with their circles by the help of the anaclastic art on each of the sides, however much they may decline, using only one style. But since all these things are clear from the preceding, I did not wish to dwell on them any longer, as we hasten to other more beautiful things, and also to leave material for the curious reader to investigate new things.

### Problem I.

> To inscribe the hours and the apparatus of the other celestial circles anaclastically in a concave hemisphere, so that a gnomon erected perpendicularly from its center shows everything, yet shows none of them unless the vessel has been filled with water. This we also entitle the Sundial of Ahaz.

<margin>The Sundial of Ahaz.</margin>
<insert>A large historiated decorative woodcut initial 'T' featuring a figure, possibly a prophet, seated in a landscape with buildings in the background.</insert>
I SHALL set forth in this place a Sundial in the likeness of that which the Sacred Scriptures record that Ahaz once constructed in 2 Chronicles, chapter 32, and Isaiah 38; of which Josephus also makes mention in Book 10, chapter 3. Therefore, Isaiah the Prophet called upon the Lord, and he brought the shadow back ten degrees by the lines by which it had already descended on the sundial of Ahaz. The Hebrew reading has <gloss>Steps of Ahaz</gloss> <note>original: "Maghnaloth Achaz"</note>, meaning the ascents or degrees of Ahaz; the Chaldean <term>Targum</term> <note>An ancient Aramaic translation or paraphrase of the Hebrew Bible</note> has <gloss>the form of the stone of hours</gloss> <note>original: "tsurath eben schagnoth"</note>. Regarding this Sundial, it will be treated most extensively in our *Sacred Encyclopedia* in the chapter on Sacred Gnomonics; where we shall also, God willing, produce the true reasons for its construction, as far as it has been possible to draw from the monuments of the ancient Orientals. However, we call this present anaclastic sundial the "Sundial of Ahaz," not because it was built according to the laws of refraction, but because, just as the shadow on that sacred sundial of Ahaz retreated by a manifest miracle, so in this present anaclastic sundial the shadow naturally retreats; namely, by this ingenious device. Note on which hour line the shadow falls in the bowl when it is empty of water; you will find that the same shadow, once the vessel is filled with water, has retreated many degrees below the water; for this is the nature of refraction, that as much as the direct shadow-ray moves forward, so much does the anaclastic shadow-ray move back. # The Eighth Book of the Great Art. The Anaclastic Art, Part I.

<page-num>616</page-num>

...of our <term>anaclastic</term><note>The study of refracted light, particularly how it behaves when passing through water or glass.</note> science: the center of the Sun, the point of refraction, and the refracted ray, together with the lines that bound them, must stand within the same plane of refraction. Therefore, in whatever vertical plane the Sun may be, its shadow even under water will hold the opposite part, exactly as it does in a vessel lacking water. For if it were possible for the shadow of the <term>style</term><note>The upright rod of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note> to be refracted from M into P, the points M and P would simultaneously be in the same plane of refraction and not be; indeed, the refraction would occur toward the perpendicular and not toward the perpendicular—all of which are absurd and contrary to experience. It is therefore clear that the <term>Azimuths</term><note>Vertical circles or directions used to measure horizontal angles.</note> of refractions admit no lateral width in themselves. Which was to be demonstrated.

<margin>The marking of Azimuths and Almucantars.</margin>
The Azimuths having thus been described, you shall mark the anaclastic <term>Almucantars</term><note>Circles of altitude on the celestial sphere parallel to the horizon; in this context, they are marked inside the bowl to show the Sun's height.</note> by this practical procedure. Let the anaclastic quadrant CEG be transferred into one of the sides of this <term>concha</term><note>A shell-shaped or hemispherical vessel.</note>, using the same industrious method we taught shortly before; the anaclastic horizon will then be MLT. If, therefore, from the center N of the vessel, you draw concentric circles through the remaining points of the anaclastic quadrant transferred into the meridian, you will have the Almucantars marked anaclastically among the Azimuths. The first of these is the anaclastic horizon, in which all refractions terminate; the remaining circles will represent the other Almucantars in which refraction occurs, until they vanish at point C, the center of the horizon (which the Arabs call the <term>Nadir</term><note>The point directly opposite the zenith; the "bottom" of the celestial sphere.</note>), ending with the refraction at the point of ninety degrees.

Thirdly, once the Azimuths and Almucantars have been described in the hemispherical vessel according to the given rules, you shall mark any kind of circles within them with the help of the following tables. First, let the astronomical hours be marked in the first place.

### §. I.
### The anaclastic description of astronomical hours in a given vessel.

To mark the 1st and 11th hour, proceed as follows. See where the Azimuths of this hour are intersected by the Almucantars in Capricorn ♑, Aries ♈, Libra ♎, and Cancer ♋. For the arcs described through these common intersections will give the desired 1st and 11th hours. You shall seek the Azimuths on the edge of the horizon starting from the 12th hour (or the meridian point H) on both sides. You will find the Almucantars among the anaclastic circles parallel to the horizon: where these intersect the Azimuths, mark the points of the given hours. 

For example, the first hour (with the Sun positioned in Capricorn ♑) corresponds to 75 degrees and 3 minutes, which is its Azimuth. Having calculated this on the edge of the quadrant from C toward T, see where the Almucantar of 25 degrees and 23 minutes (which corresponds to that same hour) intersects the aforementioned Azimuth: for there will be the point of the first hour in the <term>tropic of Capricorn</term>. In like manner, you shall join the remaining points found for Aries ♈, Libra ♎, and Cancer ♋ that belong to the given hour with an arc, and you will have the desired hour line. Thus you shall draw the arcs of the remaining hours. If, however, you wish to mark the signs of the <term>Zodiac</term>, you will find the points of the remaining parallels in exactly the same way as the tropics. For curved lines joined through the points of the hours belonging to the parallels will give the parallels of the signs. The matter is entirely easy and suffers no difficulty.

## Section III.
### The anaclastic inscription of unequal hours.

**T**ake the anaclastic table of <term>unequal hours</term> <note>Also known as "temporal hours," these divide the period from sunrise to sunset into 12 equal parts, meaning their length changes depending on the season.</note>, the use of which is exactly the same as the preceding ones. Observe where the Azimuths and Almucantars of the first hour from the rising of the Sun in the three signs—Cancer ♋, Aries ♈, and Capricorn ♑—intersect each other in the vessel <note>Refers to the bowl or container of the water-refracting sundial.</note>. For a curve drawn through common intersection points of this kind will give the first unequal hour you seek. You shall proceed in the same manner to find the remaining hour curves.

### *Corollary.*

**B**y exactly the same reasoning, you will inscribe the ascending and descending signs of the Zodiac, and other matters pertaining to the doctrine of the "first mover." <note>The *Primum Mobile*, or the outermost sphere of the heavens in Aristotelian cosmology.</note> All of these things are described at length in our *Sciatheric Proteus*. <note>Refers to Kircher's earlier work *Pantometrum Kircherianum* or *Ars Magna Lucis et Umbrae*, specifically the section on his "Protean" multi-functional sundial.</note>

### §. V.
### *The design of the indicator.*

**T**he indicator <term>index<explanation>the gnomon or pointer of the sundial</explanation></term> must be of such a size that its tip touches the center of the horizon. In its place, you may use anything else; for example, the tip of the beak of a little drinking bird, or a statue pointing with a stylus, provided the tip reaches the center of the horizon. It should also be noted that the tip must lie immediately hidden under the water poured into the bowl; otherwise, it would not point correctly. <note>The refraction occurs at the water's surface, so the pointer must be positioned precisely at the interface to account for the "bending" of the light ray.</note>

Therefore, let a very thin plate be made of copper or brass, onto which you will transfer the surface of the interior plane of the cylinder according to the rules handed down for the reflective <note>original: *anacamptico*</note> cylinder.

# Problem VIII

->To complete the same anaclastic sphaerography <note>The art of drawing the circles of the celestial sphere on a surface.</note> in a cup or conical bowl.<-

I. Let the cup be ABE, as Figure 3 shows, the interior surface of which you shall project onto a plane according to the rules provided for the conical cup on page 146. Let Figure 4, SZX, represent the projected plane, the perimeter of which you will divide into four equal parts, with lines drawn from each division into the center Z; thus the whole cone will be exactly divided into its quadrants.

II. Divide each of these into 90 equal parts or degrees, as appears in the figure. When this is done, if you draw straight lines through every 5 or 10 degrees to the center Z (or the vertex of the cone), you will have the vertical lines or **<term>Azimuths</term>** <note>Vertical circles stretching from the zenith to the horizon, used to measure horizontal direction.</note> inscribed on the cone.

III. Having described these, you shall inscribe the Almucantars by this industrious method. Take the anaclastic quadrant, and on its side AD you will determine the radius of the cone AP, or apply the same to the radius PB, so that one side corresponds to the axis of the cone PE, as you see done in Figure 5, MNO; the line MO will represent the sloping inner side of the cone itself or the cup, and MN the axis of the cone or gnomon. Furthermore, on the line MO, you will find the points of the Almucantars to be inscribed on the Azimuths as follows.

VI. Observe carefully where the anaclastic lines, drawn from center N through the edge IO of the anaclastic quadrant, intersect the line MO. For the points transferred through each of these intersections onto one of the lines SZ, TZ, XZ (as Figure 4 shows), drawn in circles from the center or apex Z, will assign the sought-after Almucantars.

V. To this grid of Almucantars and Azimuths, you shall inscribe the science of the **<term>primary motion</term>** <note>The apparent daily rotation of the heavens from east to west.</note> by means of tables proper to each type of hour and circle, in the exact same way we handed down in the preceding sections, and as Figure 4 clearly teaches here. For the only difficulty consists in the positioning of the plane of whatever body is given; otherwise, the laws for the indicator of the conical cup will be the same as the preceding ones. We have therefore inscribed the cup accordingly; which was to be done.

# Problem IX

->To inscribe the aforementioned things in a tetrahedral or pyramidal vessel.<-

Although the method for inscribing the aforementioned things on the surfaces of such polygonal bodies is more laborious than that which we taught for bodies consisting of homogeneous and circular surfaces, we shall not dwell on it too extensively for that reason. Instead, we shall refer the reader to Part 2 of *Proteus* <note>Likely referring to another volume or section of Kircher's work dealing with changing forms.</note>, where he will find everything described more fully. Therefore, let the sphaerographic delineation be performed anaclastically in the first place in a concave **<term>tetrahedron</term>** <note>A solid with four triangular faces; a triangular pyramid.</note> or inverted equilateral pyramid, which we have marked with the letters ABCD in Figure 6.

First, let the whole pyramid be translated onto a plane in the exact same way as was done in Problem 5 of the preceding part, and as appears here in Figure 7.

Second, the vertical lines shall be inscribed on the said plane also in the same way as was done there. And here in Figure 9, by drawing vertical lines from the center of the base of the pyramid R into the circumscribed circle divided into 360 parts: for where those [lines] intersect the line LO, there will be the points of the verticals to be transferred onto the sides of the pyramid.

Third, you shall also transfer the verticals of one side into the anaclastic quadrant by the same industrious method you used there, which we have thought to set down here again. And up to this point, the whole method of delineating is the same as the delineation made for the tetrahedron in the place cited. The description of the Almucantars to be made on the Azimuths is handled a little differently here.

Fourth, having transferred in Figure 9 the spaces of the Azimuths RB, RC, Rd, Re, Rf, Rg, Rh (the halves of one side of the plane of the tetrahedron) from R, the midpoint of the base of the pyramid, onto the side AB of the anaclastic quadrant; then at the same time, let the axis of the tetrahedron be determined on side AC of the same quadrant, and the lines drawn from C into the transferred points will represent the verticals of the sides of the equilateral tetrahedron. Thus, you shall inscribe the Almucantars on these: or perhaps it will be more advisable...

### Problem X.

*The refractive inscription of celestial circles onto a triangular column or prism, a parallelepiped, or indeed any column with any number of sides.*

**L**et the bodies be given in the illustration <term>Iconiſmo; a diagram or visual representation</term>: namely, A is a prism, B is a parallelepiped, C is a five-sided column, and D is a six-sided column. In the hollows of these, one must accurately perform the refractive mapping of the sphere. Proceed as follows:

**First**, you must first project the interior surfaces of each body onto a flat plane, in the exact same way as was done on page 491 and in various other places.

**Second**, let the vertical lines be inscribed using circles circumscribed around the bases of each body. If you divide these into 360 parts and draw parallel lines every 5 or 10 degrees at the points where the sides intersect the perpendiculars, you will have the azimuths described. You will see the practice of this better in the cited passages.

<margin>Inscribing the altitude circles.</margin>
**Third**, you shall inscribe the altitude circles <gloss>Almucantars</gloss> upon them using the refractive quadrant. Apply it above each azimuth and observe where the refractive rays drawn from the center of the quadrant intersect each vertical line. The points of intersection transferred onto the vertical lines of the proposed bodies' sides will provide the points through which the curved lines will mark the desired refracted altitude circles. With the help of the tables, you shall then inscribe everything that we inscribed on the previous bodies.

# CHAPTER III.

->*On inscribing refractive sundials on any concave surfaces of bodies by a very easy method through observation.*<-

### Problem XI.

*Given one refractive sundial, to delineate many others on any irregular planes whatsoever, faster than it can be told.*

**A**lthough there is almost no object so irregular or strangely shaped that the lines of the hours and celestial circles cannot be inscribed within its concave surfaces using the method we gave previously—namely, the geometric-arithmetic method—the work grows alongside the variety of surfaces encountered within the bodies, and the task becomes full of tediousness. Therefore, we have devised another way by which you may easily achieve your desire through observation or mechanical operation.

Let the instrument described on page 367 (and repeated here) be brought back. On its flat board, first take one of the refractive vessels already drawn—whether spherical, cylindrical, or conical, as you prefer—with its gnomon <term>gnomon; the part of a sundial that casts a shadow</term> and lines properly adjusted according to the first three problems described in this book. This we shall hereafter call the **Prototype** <note>original: "Prototypum"</note>. Fix it to the surface of the board so it cannot move. Let the sides of the square board face the four corners of the world <note>The cardinal directions: North, South, East, and West.</note>, and let the vessel be placed on the meridian line of the board near the side facing North. Once this is done, place any body on whose concave surface you wish to complete your spherical mapping upon the same meridian line. It should be fixed to the board in the same way, so that both bodies, along with the board, are fixed to a movable globe <note>likely a ball-and-socket joint or gimbal</note> and can be easily moved in every direction. You will then have all the requirements to begin the inscription.

<margin>Practical method of inscription.</margin>
**Thirdly**, once the instrument is exposed to the Sun together with the vessels fixed to the board, rotate the board along with the vessel until the shadow of the gnomon <term>gnomon; the part of a sundial that casts the shadow</term> hits the point of the twelfth hour on the Tropic of Cancer ♋ <note>The Summer Solstice</note> in the cup already anaclastically drawn. At that same moment, observe where the tip of the gnomon’s shadow hits in the new cup being drawn (or any other concave vessel used, however irregular); mark that spot and label it with the number 12. Then, as the shadow of the gnomon on the first cup moves over the subsequent hours, always mark the points where the shadow falls in the second cup until you have completed all the hours using this method. For if you connect the individual points marked in the concave vessel with a curved line, you will have the Tropic of Cancer ♋ marked along with the hour points.

**Fourthly**, rotate the board together with the vessel again until the shadow of the first cup falls on the 12th hour point of Aries ♈ or Libra ♎ <note>The Equinoxes</note>; in the second vessel, mark the tip of the falling shadow in the same way. Then, by turning the board so the shadow of the first cup moves over each of the hour points in Aries, mark the shadow in the other vessel at each movement. The marked points, when drawn into a curved line, will provide the equinoctial line <term>Equinoctial; the celestial equator, where day and night are equal</term> along with the hour points. In the same way, you shall draw the Tropic of Capricorn ♑ <note>The Winter Solstice</note> along with its hour points in the proposed cup, provided you turn the shadow over each of the points of the Tropic of Capricorn ♑ on the template.

### Corollary I.

By a similar practice, you may inscribe the remaining hours, celestial circles, and various lines into the proposed cup. For if the hours from sunrise and sunset are to be inscribed, you will turn the shadow falling on the prototype cup over each point of the hours from sunrise and sunset on the Tropic of Cancer ♋, and mark these in the other cup according to where the shadow falls; thus you will have the desired points. If you find the same points through the said method for Aries ♈ and Capricorn ♑, and connect the three points belonging to a single hour with straight lines, you will have the desired hours from sunrise and sunset. In the same way, you can draw unequal or planetary hours <note>Ancient hours that varied in length depending on the season</note>, the celestial houses, the ascending signs of the Zodiac, or any other type of hours or lines inscribed on the prototype cup, solely by following the incident shadow of the prototype onto the proposed cup.

### Corollary II.

**H**ence it is clear that many vessels of any shape can be fixed to this board at the same time, and the described marking can be completed in all of them with one and the same labor.

### Problem XII.

But now we must also discuss how anaclastic dials can be described so that, even with the gnomon of the style placed outside the water, its shadow nevertheless demonstrates the hours anaclastically beneath the water, since the path of the incident rays is then different...

# The Great Art, Book VIII. The Art of Refraction <note>Latin: *Ars Anaclastica*</note>, Part II.

...the arrangement of refracted lines; for experience itself teaches that the more the tip <note>Latin: *apex*</note> of the pointer <note>Latin: *stylus*</note> is raised above the water, the more the refracted lines recede from the perpendicular; and the more it is depressed below the surface of the water, the more they approach the perpendicular. Therefore, whether the refracting point is at F, or at E, or at I, or at any other place on the line IEF, the refracted ray will always be FD. Thus, whether the tip of the pointer is at A inside the water, or at O, or at E, according to the stated ratios, the refracted

Therefore, with the help of tables and the <term>anaclastic quadrant</term> <note>A specialized instrument used to calculate the angles of refracted light for sundial construction.</note>, sundials can be described inside the water with the tip of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of a sundial that casts the shadow.</note> placed however far outside or inside the water; for nothing else is required here except that you mark the point of the shadow projected on the surface of the water by the tip as the Sun rises or sets. For this will be the point of refraction, in which the shadow of the tip E is refracted toward D, just as if its refraction had occurred at the tip of a gnomon placed at F. You will reason no differently concerning other points of refraction projected from the tip. If, therefore, you apply the <term>anaclastic</term> quadrant, the refracted lines drawn from the center of the quadrant to the side BD will give the points of the <term>Almucantars</term> <note>Lines on a celestial map or instrument representing circles of altitude parallel to the horizon.</note>. Once the almucantars and azimuths <note>Lines representing the horizontal direction or bearing of a celestial body.</note> have been described in the vessel ABCD, as was done on page 688, you will have a grid in which you may "fish" for the hours refractively <note>Latin: *anaclasticè*</note> under the water. 

However, since this method might seem rather laborious, I maintain that such sundials should be completed by a easier mechanical method, namely through observation. By this method—having placed the tip of the pointer either inside or outside the water—you can describe any sundial inside the said vessel with the help of another <term>anaclastic sciatheric</term> <note>Relating to the art of shadowing or sundial making through refraction.</note> instrument already made, using this industry: Having exposed both vessels upon the table described a little earlier, fixed in the solar rays, tilt the table until the shadow successively touches all the hour points in Cancer <note>The summer solstice symbol: ♋</note>, and you shall mark each of these at the same time in the vessel prepared for describing the sundial. Then you will rotate to the hour points in the tropic of Capricorn <note>The winter solstice symbol: ♑</note>, and impress the same in the other vessel according to the shadow of its own gnomon; and you shall proceed likewise in designating the hour points for Aries <note>The equinox symbol: ♈</note>. For if you connect these three individual points of one hour with a straight line, you will have a sundial drawn to the said tip of the pointer, whether it projects outside the water or lies hidden within. For the vessel, when filled with water, will perfectly show the hours by the shadow of the tip both outside and inside the water.

From this it is clear that no place at all can be given to the tip of the pointer, whether outside or inside the water, where a sundial cannot be designated upon the interior surfaces of any vessel—no matter how irregular—through the practical observation method delivered here.

# CHAPTER IV.
## On Anaclastic-Anacamptic Sundials, or Reflected-Refracted Dials.

### Problem XIII.
*To construct a reflected-refracted time-piece.*

ALHTOUGH nothing new arises in these sundials, I will nevertheless briefly indicate the method of constructing them here, leaving further investigation to the curious Reader.

Therefore, when you are about to project an <term>anaclastic</term> <note>From the Greek *anaklasis*, referring to the refraction or "breaking" of light as it passes from one medium (like air) into another (like water).</note> astrolabe into a vessel <note>Latin: *concha*, literally a shell, but here referring to a bowl-shaped basin.</note> ABCD, you shall first make a simple anaclastic dial in the semicircular part ADC, according to the rules delivered above. Let the pointer <note>Latin: *stylus*</note>, however, be led out from D and end at C, the center of the horizon; then pour in water until the tip of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The part of the sundial that casts the shadow.</note> is hidden immediately beneath it; and you will have a vessel fit for showing astronomical matters. If, however, you wish the said hours to be shown to you by a reflected ray, you shall adapt a small piece of mirror to the tip of the gnomon in such a way that its plane is in the plane of the primary vertical; for when water is poured in until the mirror is hidden immediately beneath the water, the ray of the Sun falling upon the mirror will, by a reflected ray refracted beneath the water, show the hours; not indeed in the quadrant ACD, but in CBD. This will happen if you swap the vessel’s quadrant ACD with the quadrant CBD; and quadrant ACD, which at first faced South, will now face North. See the following figure.

<image-desc>A scientific diagram of a reflected-refracted sundial. A chalice-shaped vessel (concha) is labeled with points A, B, C, D, G, R. A vertical stylus or gnomon CD stands in the center. The sun is shown at the top right, with a ray ("radius Solis") entering the vessel, refracting at the water's surface, hitting a small mirror (speculum) labeled S at the top of the gnomon, and reflecting downward toward the base. Labels include S for the mirror, C for the center of the water surface, and D for the base of the gnomon. The vessel is partially filled with liquid.</image-desc>

### Problem XIV.
*Another construction of a paradoxical refracted-reflected sundial.*

IF anyone should desire to describe both the refracted and the reflected sundial separately in the same vessel, he shall work in this manner. Let there be a pointer CD, whose tip, hidden immediately beneath the water, will serve for indicating the anaclastic hours in the semicircle ADC; the other part of the semicircle, CBD, will remain for delineating the <term>anacamptic-anaclastic</term> <note>A dial combining both reflection (*anacamptic*) and refraction (*anaclastic*).</note> sundial, which you will complete by this industry. Let a small piece of mirror be attached to the gnomon at S, a point immediately below the tip in the plane of the primary vertical; then, at the height of this gnomon, you shall construct an anaclastic dial according to the practical methods (either by gnomonics or mechanically, through observation) delivered in the preceding sections; and you will have the sundial prepared. However, it will not show the hour unless the vessel is full of water; with the mirror being a little bit below the water, the ray of the Sun, falling upon the mirror not directly but by refraction, will then show the hours beneath the water. From this, the sundial will appear all the more wonderful, since only one or the other will demonstrate the hours: for if the vessel is full of water, the anaclastic dial will faithfully show the hours, and the reflected-refracted one will be in error. If, however, you empty the vessel down to the center of the mirror, the reflected-refracted one will begin to show correctly, and the other will be in error. This matter will seem like a paradox to those ignorant of the nature of things.

If, however, someone desires both to show correctly at one and the same time, he shall delineate the same sundial in both parts of the semicircle, with a tip common to both; for the tip of the pointer will be the very edge of the mirror, which, projecting a shadow into the quadrant ACD (facing south), will show the anaclastic hours there; the center of the mirror, however, will reverberate the reflected ray of the Sun into the part of the vessel facing North. These two sundials will describe every day a <term>shadow-light</term> <note>original Greek: *σκιαφωτεινὸν* (skiaphoteinon), a term used to describe a phenomenon involving both light and shadow.</note> cone—that is, a dark-bright or light-dark cone; one half of which is in the shadowed part ACD, and the other in the bright part, revealing a great secret in the more hidden Philosophy, concerning which I shall speak elsewhere.

IN ORDER that you may have a direct sundial and a refracted one at the same time, nothing else is required except that you add a direct one to the reflected-refracted sundial described in the preceding problem, by this industry. Upon a sheet of selenite, which they commonly call Talc, let the hour...

# ATHANASIUS KIRCHER
## PRIEST OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS
# THE GREAT ART
# OF LIGHT AND SHADOW
## BOOK NINE,
# GNOMONIC COSMOMETRY,
->THAT IS,<-
### *Concerning the investigation of the position, magnitude, quantity, and height*
### *of the parts of the world through the reasoning of light and shadow.*
## PREFACE.

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial letter 'C' featuring a central figure in a medallion, possibly a scholar or divine personage, surrounded by elaborate acanthus-style floral scrolls.</image-desc>By Gnomonic Cosmometry <note>The science of measuring the world and the universe using the principles of sundials and shadows</note> in this place, we mean that science by which—through the help of certain observations and phenomena—we arrive at a knowledge of the dimensions of worldly bodies by the reasoning of light and shadow. We shall present this in two parts in this ninth book: the first part demonstrates the dimensions of any nearby and accessible things by the aid of shadow and light. The other teaches how to explore, through the reasoning of light and shadow, the distance of inaccessible celestial bodies both from the earth and from each other, as well as their mass. We will treat both with as much brevity and clarity as possible, so that the curious reader may know how great a harvest of wonderful things is produced for us by the shadow—that work of nature’s play.

<header>PART ONE. SCIATHERIC GEOMETRY, OR GNOMONICS,</header>

# PART ONE.
## SCIATHERIC GEOMETRY,
### OR GNOMONICS,

->*By which new method the distances, lengths, widths, depths, and the direct, reflected, and refracted shadows of given things are investigated.*<-

### Introductory Theorem I.
#### On the utility of the shadow in Gnomonic Cosmometry.

<image-desc>Large decorative drop-cap 'P' depicting a landscape with a building and a celestial body (possibly the sun) in the background.</image-desc>

AFTER we have discussed at length in the preceding pages the various effects that the movement of light obtains in different planes during its astronomical motions, it now follows that we should establish a treatise here on the logic of shadows and the demonstrations of their magnitudes, according to the varying elevation of the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars above the horizon. From these things, seekers of truth will not only understand the logic behind the change in the size of shadows and their proportion to vertical gnomons <note>A gnomon is the part of a sundial that casts the shadow</note> (or any bodies standing perpendicular to the horizon), but also what their use is in that part of learned Astronomy which they call <term>meteoroscopy</term> <note>original: "μετεωροσκοπίαν"; the observation of celestial phenomena or things high in the air</note>. This will be more clearly gathered from the following introductions. The shadow is a great and almost incredible thing; by its help, we measure not only the motions of celestial bodies (as seen previously), but also the infallible magnitude, breadth, circumference, and distance of those same bodies from one another, along with the other quantities of individual parts, all by the aid of this "shadowy ray." Therefore, we may quite fittingly apply the words of Claudian <note>Claudius Claudianus, a late Roman poet</note> to the shadow:

> When Jupiter beheld these shadowy labors on the globe,
> He laughed, and gave these words to the Gods above:
> "Has the power of mortal care progressed this far?
> Now my own labor is mimicked by the art of shadow.
> The laws of the pole, the decrees of fate, and the rules of the heavens
> This work of light and shadowy art has translated.
> Now bold industry, turning its own world,
> Rejoices, and rules the stars with a shadowy mind."

### Introductory Theorem II.
#### On the straight and turned shadow.

<margin>The shadow is twofold: straight and turned.</margin>
Among shadows, some are called "straight" and others "turned" <note>original: "rectas" and "versas"</note>. A **straight shadow** is that which a body standing at right angles to the horizon (or a plane parallel to it) projects onto its flat surface. They call it a **turned shadow** when it is projected from some body parallel to the horizon's flat surface onto the plane of another surface standing at right angles to the horizon. Here it may be known that the ratio of the right sine of the Sun’s altitude at any time to the sine of its complement <note>The "sine of the complement" is known today as the cosine</note> is the same as the ratio of a perpendicular body (or a gnomon erected <term>orthogonally</term> <note>original: "ἰσογώνως"; at equal or right angles</note>) to its shadow. Likewise, the ratio of the sine of the complement to the sine of the Sun's altitude is the same as the ratio of a style fixed normally into a vertical plane to its "turned" shadow.

<margin>Investigation of the quantity of shadows through sines.</margin>
Therefore, you will find the quantities of these shadows with almost no trouble. Multiply the sine of the complement of the Sun’s elevation by the height of the gnomon (divided into specific parts), and divide the product by the right sine of the Sun’s elevation; you will then have the known quantity of the straight shadow. Likewise, multiply the magnitude of the gnomon by the right sine of the Sun’s altitude, and divide the sum by the sine of the complement, and the quantity of the turned shadow will result. See what we have treated more extensively on these matters in the third book. From this, it is gathered that the shadow sometimes equals the gnomon in size, which happens when the Sun is elevated at 45 degrees; or it is less than the same when the Sun occupies more than 45 degrees above the horizon; but it exceeds the height of the gnomon when the Sun is positioned below 45 degrees. At sunrise, an infinite shadow is projected, but at the zenith <note>directly overhead</note>, no shadow is projected at all.

<margin>Various differences of shadows.</margin>
Furthermore, it is established that when the Sun travels through the parts nearer to the tropics, the midday shadows obtain the smallest differences; but when the Sun is near the points of the equinoxes, the greatest differences between them are established for several days at noon. It is also established that for those living under a "right sphere" <note>the Equator</note>, as well as those between the equator and either tropic, the midday straight shadows are sometimes turned toward the South and sometimes toward the North. For this reason, they are called <term>Amphiscians</term> <note>original: "ἀμφίσκιοι"; those whose shadows fall both ways</note>, such as the Arabs of whom Juvenal <note>A Roman satiric poet</note> makes mention, who, having come to Rome, wondered that the shadows always turned in only one direction.

> You Arabs have come into a world unknown to you,
> Marvelling that the shadows of the groves do not go to the left.

# The Great Art, Book 11. The Art of Refraction, Part 1.

<margin>The nature of shadows as they appear in different zones of the earth.</margin>
When the Sun reaches the zenith, the shadow of those living in the Torrid Zone <note>the region between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn</note> is, as it were, consumed within itself; for this reason they are called <term>Askioi</term> <note>original: ἄσκιοι; Greek for "shadowless"</note>. Just so, those living outside the Torrid Zone in the Temperate Zone are called <term>Heteroskioi</term> <note>original: ἑτερόσκιοι; Greek for "those with shadows on one side"</note>, that is, "Side-shadowed." Under the parallel or frigid sphere, they are called <term>Periskioi</term> <note>original: περίσκιοι; Greek for "those with shadows all around"</note> because of their circular shadows, as if called "Circum-shadowed." But having dismissed these matters as being well-known to the common public, let us turn to other things.

### Preliminary Discussion 3.

### *The Paradox of the Shadows of the Sun and Moon.*

It is commonly believed that two luminaries at the same altitude above the horizon project the same shadow. However, it has been proven that the <term>Sun</term> <note>symbol: ☉</note> and the <term>Moon</term> <note>symbol: ☽</note>, even when positioned at the same altitude, nevertheless project shadows of different sizes: the Sun's is smaller, while the Moon's is larger. I shall demonstrate this briefly. Let there be two circles, CBN and SGE, described from the same center A; the horizon is CAN, and the <term>gnomon</term> <note>a vertical rod used to cast a shadow for measurement</note> is AD, set perpendicular. Let us first place the Sun at B and the Moon at G: while the Sun is at B, the shadow is AE; the Moon being at the same altitude of the circle at G, its shadow—

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing two concentric circular arcs representing celestial spheres. A vertical gnomon AD is positioned on a horizontal line CAN. Rays are drawn from a sun symbol at point B and a moon symbol at point G through the top of the gnomon at point D, intersecting the horizontal axis at points E and F. Various points are labeled with letters B, S, C, D, A, F, E, N.</image-desc>

—its shadow would be AE. But the Sun’s shadow is actually AF, which is smaller than the Moon’s shadow AE, even when both luminaries are at the same altitude and under the same angle CAB. The proposition is therefore clear. From this, it follows that if there were a great distance between the center of the world and the <term>apogee</term> <note>the point in an orbit furthest from the Earth</note> of the Sun, the sizes of the shadows would appear to differ at different times even when the Sun is at the same altitude. 

Thus, it is also clear that the shadow of the Sun when at its apogee is smaller than when it is at its <term>perigee</term> <note>the point in an orbit closest to the Earth</note>. Let me explain. Suppose there are <term>Antoeci</term> <note>people living on the same meridian but in opposite hemispheres at equal distances from the equator</note>, who live under the same meridian and at the same latitude, but in different hemispheres—the Southern and Northern—such as those at 45 degrees of latitude in opposite hemispheres. If, I say, two Antoecan observers—one who exactly observed the midday shadow of the Sun at 6 degrees of <term>Cancer</term> <note>symbol: ♋</note>, where the Sun is at its apogee; and the other in the Southern Hemisphere who observed the same midday shadow when the Sun was at 6 degrees of <term>Capricorn</term> <note>symbol: ♑</note> (where it is at its perigee)—then these observers would find some difference in the shadows caused by the Sun's eccentricity. 

Consequently, a great benefit would be conferred upon astronomy, and many things concerning the eccentricity of the Sun, hitherto unknown, could be gathered. This realization moved me to believe that a serious recommendation should be sent via letter to our Fathers living in the Kingdom of Chile and in Canada (as Antoeci) to observe such a thing. For by this means, the quantity of solar <term>eccentricity</term> <note>original: ἐκκεντρότητος; the amount by which an orbit deviates from a perfect circle</note> might perhaps be obtained more accurately and easily than through the usual theoretical rules.

### Preliminary Discussion 4.

### *How great a difference in shadows the semi-diameter of the Sun creates.*

It should also be noted that in calculating the altitude of the Sun from the center of the Earth based on the measurement of shadows, both straight and <term>reverse</term> <note>umbra versa; a shadow measured on a vertical scale</note>, the calculation always misses the mark by as much as the Sun's semi-diameter appears to occupy in the heavens. 

<image-desc>A geometric diagram featuring a circle. At the top, a sun symbol emits multiple diverging rays. These rays strike the top of a vertical gnomon labeled 'h'. The rays continue to a horizontal baseline, where they intersect at points labeled with Greek letters α (alpha), β (beta), and γ (gamma). A smaller interior circle represents the globe or the horizon projection.</image-desc>

For shadows projected onto the flat surface of the horizon reveal the elevation not of the center of the Sun, but of the highest part, from which the ray descends through the top of the gnomon to the plane. But altitudes taken from reverse shadows are almost always found to be smaller by a quarter of one degree (where the whole circle has 360). This difference happens not from uncertainty in measurement or calculation, but from the rays of the Sun, which pour out from everywhere—not only from the center but also from its whole circumference or surface, as we experience during an eclipse. Thus it happens that the straight shadows of all bodies...
