# The Geometry of Shadow-measurement

...[the shadows] <note>This text continues from the previous page, discussing the geometry of shadows cast by the sun's disk.</note> of the right and versed types are always smaller than those which rays proceeding from the center of the Sun would establish. Since, therefore, according to Peurbach <note>Georg von Peurbach (1423–1461), a celebrated Austrian astronomer who measured the apparent size of the sun</note>, the diameter of the Sun appears at an angle of 31 arc minutes at its apogee <note>the point in orbit furthest from Earth</note> and at 34 arc minutes in the opposite position, it happens that rays are carried to the earth not only from the middle of the Sun's surface, but also from the highest and lowest points. If the circle of the Sun's altitude is V d, the horizon is Kf, upon which the gnomon Ae stands at right angles, and another perpendicular h R rests upon this; the center of the Sun is C, and its diameter is b d. I say that the central rays Ce and CK determine the true shadows Af and AR; the other rays flowing from the ends of the solar diameter, dg and Ab, cause only the apparent shadows Ag and AR. For from the angles e g h and b AK (or AVR), only the apparent altitudes of the Sun are found. Hence, if you divide the difference of each altitude into two equal parts, subtracting one from the higher elevation or adding it to the lower, the true altitude of the Sun's center will be revealed. I have thought it necessary to set all this down here so that in that most subtle measurement of celestial bodies, which we attempt through shadows, some account might be taken of this excess or deficiency.

### Preliminary Discussion V.
->*Rays produced from one or various parts of the Sun to different parts of the earth are parallel.*<-

Let AE and AL be rays drawn from the same point of the Sun through V and C, the tips of equal gnomons. I say that V E and CL appear parallel; for since V E is the smallest part of the ray AE, so that its ratio to the whole disappears; and the lines VC and EL are parallel,

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating solar rays. A point A (the Sun) is at the top, from which two long rays AE and AL extend downwards to a horizontal ground line. Two vertical gnomons of equal height, marked V E and C L, stand on the ground. A horizontal line segment VC connects the tops of the gnomons. The diagram demonstrates that because the distance to A is so vast compared to the distance between the gnomons, the rays AE and AL are effectively parallel.</image-desc>

it will be as EV is to AV, so EL is to CV. But the difference between EV and AV is imperceptible; therefore, the difference between CV and EL cannot be judged by the senses either; and thus V C and EL are equal, but also parallel. Therefore the rays AE and AL, although they flow from the same point, will appear parallel because of their infinite distance.

# CHAPTER I.
->*On investigating the height of accessible things by the reasoning of light and shadow.*<-

### Problem I.
*To construct a geometric sciathericon <note>an instrument used for measuring heights or time via shadows</note> which demonstrates the heights of all things by the shadow of a stylus divided into 12 parts.*

### Practical Exercise I.
*To construct a sciathericon for exploring altitudes in practice.*

**L**et two lines be made on any plane positioned most exactly, intersecting each other at right angles, AB and CD; of these, let AB designate the meridian line and CD the equator. Then, having described the two tropics: let the place of the gnomon be N; and starting from this point, let the meridian line be divided into any number of equal parts (we have divided it here into 100 equal parts). Through each part, let circles be drawn from the center N within the tropics. This having been completed, take a gnomon of such a size as is the radius of the circle described through the 12th division point, which you shall erect <term>at right angles</term> <note>original: ἰσόγωνον (isogonon); meaning perpendicular to the base</note> at the center N, and the Sciathericon will be finished. Moreover, let the numbers of the parts of the shadows be inscribed on the individual circles, together with the proportions of the shadows, both right and versed <note>referring to vertical and horizontal shadow measurements</note>.

### The Use of the Sciathericon
**T**he use of this Sciathericon is immense and encompasses the principles of all Geometry; therefore, we shall explain it in parts. Thus, when the Sun is shining and the Sciathericon is positioned, if you desire to know the heights of any things—for instance, houses, columns, pyramids, trees, or other objects—measure the size of the shadows yourself (or through someone else) in a known measure of feet, cubits, or poles. Once you have this, the Sciathericon will show you the heights of the objects faster than it can be said. For if you find the measured shadow of a pyramid, tree, house, roof, or any other thing to be, for example, 20 feet, and on the Sciathericon the gnomon touches the 3rd circle, you may assume with certainty that the shadow of the objects is four times less than the height, as the inscribed...

# Practical Procedure II.

## To construct a Light-Shadow Measuring Instrument.

Let there be any oblong board AE, in the middle of which another parallelogram BDSN is erected perpendicularly; its middle FC is to be perforated with a thin slit—

->[A geometric diagram of the surveying instrument. It features a horizontal base AE and a vertical rectangular plate BDSN. The left side of the base is a "Scale of direct shadows" marked 5 to 60. The right side shows a "Scale of altitudes" with an arc XC graduated from 10 to 80. A central vertical slit FC allows light to pass through, projecting onto the scales.]<-

—and then let the middle line AE be drawn, of which the section AC demonstrates the ratios of shadows, and the section CE demonstrates the altitudes of the Sun. In AC, you will describe the shadow ratios in this way: let the whole line AC be divided into 100 equal parts, or even fewer (for instance 72, which is a number sufficient for our operations), while FC, which represents the <term>style|The vertical rod or edge that casts a shadow; also called a gnomon</term> or gnomon, should have 12 of those parts into which AE was divided (whether 100 or 72). For if you draw straight lines through the points of division parallel to SN, you will have a ready-made shadow scale. In CE, however, you will describe the altitudes by this method: let straight lines be drawn from the center F through the edge of the <term>quadrant|A quarter-circle used for measuring angles</term> XC (which is attached to line FC) onto the line CE; you will then have the points for the Sun's altitude, through which parallel lines drawn to SN will provide the scale for the Sun's altitude, and thus the entire instrument will be prepared.

The use of the instrument is as follows: Let the instrument be set up, having first been positioned with a <term>level|A tool used to ensure the base is perfectly horizontal</term>, and let it be observed toward the Sun so that the light gliding through the notch FC hits the middle line CA; immediately, the ratios of the shadows marked by the transverse lines will present themselves by way of the incident shadow BD. If, therefore, the shadow falls on the 6th point of line AC, a doubling of the shadow of objects will give the height. If it falls on 12, the shadow will be equal to the heights, and so on for other proportions. If, however, you wish to know the Sun's altitude corresponding to the shadow, turn the other part of the instrument toward the Sun, as before, so that the light through the slit FC holds the middle line CE, and the end of the light-line will assign the sought-after altitude of the Sun.

# Practical Procedure III.

## Use of the instrument when placed in a vertical plane.

Take the preceding instrument and erect it so that CA represents a vertical 

line: let it be observed in this position toward the Sun, so that [the light] through the slit FC falls upon the line CA, and immediately the ratios of <term>turned shadows|Also called *umbra versa*, these are shadows cast on a vertical surface, like a wall, rather than the horizontal ground</term>—which are the opposite of the previous ones—will be indicated, as you see. If, however, you turn the other part of the instrument CE vertically toward the Sun, so that the light through the slit FC falls on CE, the shadow and the light on the same line will show you the point of the sought-after Sun’s altitude. Therefore, in the first position, if you desire the height of objects, see which line in the shadow scale the shadow BD intersects. Thus, if it falls on the 24th point of the turned shadow, a doubling of the horizontal shadow of the objects will give the heights of the objects. If it falls on the 12th point, the found shadow will be equal to the height of the objects. If it falls on the 48th point, the horizontal shadow will be quadruple <note>four times</note> the height of the objects. Furthermore, if the shadow is less than 12 parts and falls on the 6th point, half the shadow will give the height. And so on for the rest.

# Corollary I.

<margin>Direct and turned shadows are equal.</margin>
From these things it follows, first, that a turned shadow on a vertical plane relates to a direct shadow on a horizontal plane as the sines of the complements of the Sun’s elevation relate to the <term>right sines|A standard trigonometric sine</term> of the same: and vice-versa, as was shown in the preceding theory of shadows. Therefore, the shadow of the Sun when elevated at 70 degrees on the horizontal is the same as the shadow which the Sun elevated at 20 degrees produces on the vertical: these two shadows are always equal. Likewise, the shadow of the Sun at 60 degrees and the shadow at 30 degrees are equal; the former on a vertical plane, the latter on a horizontal plane: and you shall argue similarly for the others.

# Corollary II.

<margin>Use in describing Sundials.</margin>
It also follows from this that this shadow-measuring instrument, regarding its scale of Solar altitudes, has a use in describing all <term>clocks|Specifically sundials or solar timekeeping devices</term> and celestial circles.

# The Ninth Book of the Great Art: Cosmography and <term>Gnomonics</term>. Part I.
<note>Gnomonics is the art or science of constructing and using sundials or gnomons.</note>

<note>Azimuth refers to the horizontal angle of the sun, measured along the horizon.</note>

### Corollary III.

I will briefly indicate how the lengths of shadows on any plane can be obtained, assuming a <term>stylus</term> of 12 parts.
<note>A stylus, or gnomon, is the rod on a sundial that casts the shadow. Traditionally, it was divided into 12 parts for mathematical calculations.</note> 
If the plate **SNFB** is so arranged that it is equipped with certain hinges so it can be rotated around **SN** like a pivot, and inclined according to the ratio of the plane, and can be moved to any proposed degree—which would happen if a quadrant divided into 90 degrees were placed opposite side **DN**, within which the moved plate could be fixed at the proposed degrees by a small pulley—for in this position, through the edge of the quadrant **XC**, lines produced from center **F** would intersect the middle line **CE** at the sought points of solar altitudes. You will complete the measurements thus: On any plane parallel to the horizon of the Sun, note the shadow of a string in parts of that same string; this happens if you apply the string directly over the shadow itself. Having done this, if the shadow occupies three parts of its own length, you will say the shadow of any object is four times its altitude; if it occupies 4, it is triple; if 12, it is equal; if 24, it is double; if 48, it is quadruple. If you apply this string normally to a vertical plane, it will also show you the ratios of the <term>versed shadows</term>.
<note>Versed shadows (umbra versa) are shadows cast onto a vertical surface, as opposed to "straight shadows" (umbra recta) cast on a horizontal surface.</note>

# Practical Application IV.

## The shadow of a string performs all the same tasks.

Let a string equipped with its lead weight be divided into 12 equal parts, in each of which knots are made to better distinguish the parts; it will be a perfect instrument. By the benefit of this string, the measurement of things...

### Corollary I.

From this it follows how we can also "hunt" for altitudes with the help of a string: namely, if we see which solar altitude the shadow parts correspond to. This can also be done by this industrious method without a table. Let **CB** be the string and **AB** the shadow, to which you apply the string at point **B** on the horizontal plane so that it makes a right angle **CBA** with the shadow. Then, if you join the extreme points **A** and **C** with a straight line, the angle **BAC** will give the sought altitude of the Sun.

### Corollary II.

<margin>To know the hour of the day by the shadow of a string.</margin>
It also follows how, with the help of this string at any time, you can know the hour of the day. For if in the table of "straight shadows" for making clocks shown above, you find the shadow parts given in **BA**; by ascending in the column of the found shadow, the sought hour will be offered.

### Corollary III.

If a circle is divided into 360 degrees, or into four quadrants (each divided into 90 equal degrees), and situated according to the four cardinal directions of the world, a string hanging over the center of the circle will—faster than it can be said—show the Sun's Azimuth on the circumference of the circle, or the horizontal circumference.

# CHAPTER II.

## *<term>Catoptric Geometry</term>, or concerning reflected shadow and light, and <term>Mesoptic Geometry</term>, or refracted light.*
<note>Catoptrics is the study of light reflection, while "Mesoptics" (more commonly called Dioptrics today) refers to the study of light as it is refracted or "bent" through different mediums.</note>

**T**he principles which we previously proposed regarding the equality of the angles of reflection and incidence are the same principles used in reflected <term>Gnomonic Geometry</term>. Therefore, we have deemed it unnecessary to repeat them again here. Let us proceed, then, to the matter at hand.
<note>Gnomonics is the art of measuring time or distance using the shadows cast by a sun-pointer, or gnomon.</note>

### Problem II.

*To measure the heights, distances, and depths of things with a mirror through the reflected shadow of objects in mirrors.*

### Practical Method I.

*To construct a Universal Catoptric-Measuring instrument.*

**L**et there be two rectangular rules, **EC** and **AB**. Let rule **EC** be divided into 100 equal parts, and **AB** into the same number of parts equal to the first. Let rule **AB** be inserted into rule **EC** at point **E** in such a way that it can be moved perpendicularly up and down within it, like the slider on an <term>astronomical staff</term>.
<note>The "astronomical staff" or "Jacob's staff" was a common navigational and surveying tool used to measure angles.</note>
Furthermore, rule **EC** must be attached to a rod **F** so that it can be directed according to the position of the objects to be measured, and can be extended or pulled back at the operator's pleasure. It would be better, therefore, if the rod were equipped with a versatile globe **X** (a ball-and-socket joint) into which the rules are inserted, styled after the instrument proposed in the study of Magnetics. At the point where rule **EC** and the globe meet, place a mirror in the same plane as the rule, and you will have an instrument prepared for measuring any objects.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the measurement of an object's height using a catoptric instrument. A person's hand at the bottom holds a supporting rod (D) connected to a horizontal rule (EC). A mirror (Speculum) is placed at point E. A vertical rule (AB) with a graduated scale from 0 to 50 is attached to the horizontal rule. Dotted lines represent light rays reflecting from the top of a distant tower (point A) onto the mirror at E and then to the observer's eye at the top of the vertical rule (A). The tower stands on base C, and its height is marked V. Geometric points labeled include A, B, C, D, E, F, V, and X.</image-desc>

### Practical Method II.

*To measure accessible heights with a reflected ray.*

**T**ake the distance from the mirror to the height to be measured in a known unit of measure; let it be, for example, 50 feet. Once this is done, extend the rule **EC** so far that between the mirror **F** and the rule **AB**, as many parts are intercepted as the number of feet you just found between the height to be measured and the mirror—namely, 50. This being finished, lower or raise the rod **AB** within its notch **E** until, looking through the tip **A**, you see the summit of the height being measured in the mirror **F**. The parts on the rod **AB** intercepted between **A** and **E** will give the sought height of the object being measured—namely, 25 feet.
**The proof:** Since angles **C** and **E** are right angles by definition, and angles **AFE** and **VFC** are equal (as the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection), angles **A** and **V** will also be equal. Therefore, the triangles have equal angles and proportional sides. Thus, as **FE** is to **EA**, so is **FC** to **CV**. But the base **FE** is 50 parts, just as the base of the larger triangle **FC** is also 50, and **EA** has 25; therefore **CV** will have the same number. Thus, **AE** in the parts of **EF** will give **CV**, the sought height.

### Practical Method III.

*To measure an inaccessible distance with a reflected ray.*

**L**et distance **CV** be the width of a river to be measured, and let the mirror be erected vertically. Take a space on the bank **CF** of 50 feet in a known measure. Once this is done, let **EC** be extended until 50 parts are intercepted between **E** and the mirror **F**, specifically the same number of feet the known measure **CF** contains. Then let the rule **EA** be lowered or raised until, through the tip **A**, the mark **V** (chosen as the endpoint of the measurement) appears in the vertically upright mirror **F**. The parts intercepted between **A** and **E** will give the sought distance **CV**. For since triangles **FCV** and **FEA** are proportional—owing to the two right angles **C** and **E**, and the two angles of incidence and reflection—it will be as **FE** is to **EA**, so is **FC** to **CV**; or as **EF** is to **FC**, so is **EA** to **CV**. But in **FE**, as many parts were taken as the feet we found in **FC**; therefore, since the sides of the triangles are proportional, there will also be in **EA**...

### Practical Application IV.
*To measure an inaccessible height through two stations by means of a catoptric ray <note>original: "catoptrico radio"; referring to the use of reflected light from a mirror</note>.*

**Let** the inaccessible height AB be investigated, where the distance CB is also inaccessible. With a mirror placed in two stations, F and C, and having observed from each station the apex <note>the highest point</note> A of the elevated object in the mirror, two catoptric triangles DCE and HGF will be formed, which are proportional to the triangles CBA and FAB. Therefore, let it be that as the difference of the stations IF is to HG, so the known distance FC is to another value; the sought height AB will then be produced. Again, let it be that as the difference IF is to HI, so the known interval between stations FC is to another; the inaccessible distance CB, which was desired, will be produced.

### Practical Application V.
*To measure an inaccessible height from the same location using a mirror.*

**Let** the inaccessible height OP be measured from location D, from which it is permitted neither to move backward nor forward. You shall erect in that same location D a ladder or a pole DA, upon which you will establish two stations for the mirror at D and A. Having observed from each height the point O (the apex of the elevated object) in the mirror, catoptric triangles EFD and ABC will be formed, proportional to triangles DOP and AOL. Therefore, let it be that as the difference of the stations FG (which you will obtain if you establish triangle GDE as equal to triangle CBA) is to FE, so the known measure AD (the interval between the first and second mirror stations) is to another value; the sought height OP will be produced. To truly find the inaccessible distance DP, let it be that as FE is to ED, so OP is to the sought distance PD.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram in the upper right showing a mountain with a tower. The height is measured from a fixed station D using a vertical scale DA. Furthermore, if you wish to know the height of the mountain and the tower separately, operate in this way: Let it be that as PE (or CA) is to EG (or CB), so the measure DP identified just before is to another; the axis PN of the mountain's height will be produced. Again, as ED is to GF, so DP is to another; the sought height NO of the tower positioned on the mountain will be produced. Alternatively, let the height NO be subtracted from the total line PO found just before, and the mountain height PN will remain; or subtract NP from the total, and the sought tower height NO will remain.

### Practical Application VI.
*To measure the depths of things through one or two stations.*

**Let** the known height be DA and the distance be DV. With a mirror erected perpendicularly at A, extend a rule <note>term: regula; a straight measuring rod or scale</note> until you see the mark V on the level ground through its extremity B. Then, let it be that as the parts of the rule AC are to the parts of the rule CB, so AD is to another; the sought distance DE will be produced.

Let there be two stations for the mirror on the mountain's level ground, A and D. Whoever, therefore, examines these examples of <term>catoptric geometry</term> <note>geometry performed using mirrors and reflections</note> more deeply will certainly find that no case can occur in all of practical geometry that cannot be solved by this catoptric trigonometry. Since the proofs are exactly the same as the demonstrations proposed by <term>Father Clavius</term> <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), a leading Jesuit mathematician and astronomer</note> in Book 1 of his *Practical Geometry*, we have thought it best to omit them here, lest the book be stuffed with things already delivered by others. ...ment above the center of the circle divided into four quadrants (each consisting of ninety degrees), if it is positioned and rotated, the middle line will show the point of the Sun's altitude on the rim of the azimuthal circle. <note>The "rim of the azimuthal circle" refers to the horizontal scale of a sundial or surveying instrument used to measure the angle of the sun from the north.</note>

### Problem IV.

*To measure things through a refractive ray, involving both shadow and reflected light; that is, to measure the heights of objects under water.*

If you wish to know how much greater a refractive <term>anaclastic<note>original: "anaclasticì"; from the Greek *anaklasis*, meaning refraction or the bending of light as it passes from one medium (like air) to another (like water).</note></term> shadow is compared to a reflective <term>anacamtic<note>original: "anacamticum"; from the Greek *anakampsis*, meaning reflection.</note></term> one—that is, the ratio of the shadow refracted under water on a horizontal plane to the shadow on a plane outside the water—proceed as follows. Construct a geometric refractive instrument with this design: make a vessel of any kind in the shape of a <term>parallelepiped<note>A six-sided solid figure where all faces are parallelograms; essentially a rectangular tank.</note></term> that is hollow inside, with the side ABCS open.

<image-desc>A perspective technical diagram of a rectangular basin or tank. The vertices and key points are labeled with letters (A, B, C, G, E, O, F, H). Inside the basin, lines originate from point G on the upper left rim and extend downwards, showing the paths of refracted light rays hitting the bottom surface (marked with line FH). The bottom surface features a numerical scale from 10 to 80. Additional dashed and solid lines show light paths outside the tank (line EO) and reflections.</image-desc>

In this vessel, first divide the median line FH on the bottom into points representing the refractive or refracted altitudes of the Sun. This is achieved if you draw straight lines to the line FH from center G of the quadrant GIF through degrees divided according to the refractive method (which we taught above in Book 8, Part 2, Problem 3). These lines will intersect the aforementioned line at points where parallel lines, once drawn, provide a scale of refractive shadows.

But if, by the same method, you project the scale of the Sun’s altitude onto the extension of the floor side EO, and with the help of the quadrant GIF, use a direct ray according to Problem I, Practice II: then the shadow AGB outside the water on the floor side EO will show the direct altitude of the Sun. Conversely, the refractive or "anaclastic" altitude of the Sun will be shown in the water on the median line FH. Therefore, to investigate the difference between the direct and refracted shadows, first mark the shadow outside the water on the instrument facing directly toward the Sun at line ED. Then, with the vessel filled to the brim with water so that the edge AGB of the vessel's rim is at the same level as the water's surface, you will immediately see by how many parts one exceeds the other: specifically, the refracted shadow within the water on line FG, compared to the direct shadow outside the water on line EO. 

If, therefore, following these comparisons, you construct a scale of refracted shadows based on the refracted altitudes of the Sun, and you attach the ratios and proportions of the shadows to each point, you will be able to find the heights of all things using this scale of refracted shadows in exactly the same way we found them in previous sections with the help of the <term>Sciatheric<note>original: "Sciatherici"; relating to the use of shadows for measurement or timekeeping, specifically sundial science.</note></term> instrument. If, however, you attach a small piece of a mirror vertically at point F, the reflected light under the water will show the refracted shadow on the same line EH; while outside the water, the reflected ray will demonstrate the direct shadow on line EO.

### Corollary

From what has been stated, it follows how any length, whether below the water or on the bottom of the water, can be determined with the help of this instrument. All the quantities of things below the water, when compared with those outside the water, can lead us to knowledge of these unknown objects. Whoever thoroughly understands these foundations of ours should know for certain that a door is opened to a certain new Geometry, by which lines and surfaces projected refractively can be investigated no less quickly than quantities measured directly in any medium. However, I deliberately make an end here, lest having entered this new ocean of infinite inventions, I may not be allowed to retreat. But let it suffice to have provided the ingenious and sagacious Reader with a handle to continue the weaving of the inventions I have begun.

### *On the difficulty of our undertaking.*

<margin>Difficulty in measuring celestial bodies.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'C' at the beginning of the text, embellished with intricate foliage, floral scrollwork, and classical ornamental patterns.</image-desc>
**A**s we set out to investigate the size of celestial bodies, we approach a matter so difficult and so entangled by the disagreements of authors that we can scarcely find whose opinion we should follow first. On one hand, the different theories of the world's systems <note>The "systems" refer to the competing models of the universe prevalent in the 17th century.</note> led us into great perplexities; on the other hand, the unreliability of observations made until now, and the deceptions of the mediums through which observations are carried out, are so great that it seems to be a work for an angelic mind rather than a human one, nearly driving us to despair. For who does not know how much the Ptolemaic system <note>The ancient geocentric model where Earth is the center of the universe.</note> differs from the Copernican <note>The heliocentric model where the Sun is the center.</note> or the Tychonic <note>The system of Tycho Brahe, where the Sun orbits the Earth, but the other planets orbit the Sun.</note>; how different and unequal the distance of the planets from the Earth is; and finally how varied the theory and method of <term>Cosmometry<note>The science of measuring the universe and the celestial bodies within it.</note></term> is among different authors. Terrified by these things, I was nearly on the verge of omitting such a laudable exercise entirely, as if it were slippery and deceptive. When, however, I saw on the contrary that I could provide the same in this gnomonic Cosmometry as the experts Ptolemy, Copernicus, and Tycho achieved in their astronomical calculations based on their various hypotheses; who, however much they differed, still agree so perfectly with the calculation that the celestial bodies computed according to these three hypotheses were found to err by scarcely one degree of difference. Intent, therefore, on this parallel comparison of things, while I applied myself more sagaciously to this task, at last a certain method occurred to me by which, abstracting from every hypothesis, one could arrive at true knowledge of the size of the world's bodies with the same certainty that one can arrive at a knowledge of calculation through light and shadow. Concerning these matters, it is the plan in this second Part to treat them in my usual way—briefly, easily, and clearly. But so that we may proceed in order, we will first treat the principal bodies of the world: the Earth, the Moon, and the Sun; and then the other planets in order. To do this better:

<margin>God's wisdom in the construction of the world.</margin>
It must first be assumed that a certain <term>parallax<note>original: "parallaxim"; the apparent shift in the position of an object when viewed from two different points. Astronomers use this to calculate distances to stars and planets.</note></term> is given, based on the sensitivity of the measuring Earth in relation to celestial bodies. For it was the will of God the Creator, Greatest and Best, that man, as His image, should lift his eyes from these earthly things to those heavenly ones, and diligently contemplate the monuments of His great wisdom. The entire distribution of the world's machine tends toward this: that it might make known to us this will of the Creator, as if attested by right; and therefore the proportion of the terrestrial globe to the celestial sphere was made sensible <note>Meaning 'perceivable or measurable by the senses'.</note>; so that what was hidden from the eyes of individual men might be supplemented by the diligence of all those living across the whole surface of the earth, aided by its size, and in this way learn the positions of the wandering stars <note>Planets</note> in the diameter of the world through those earlier distances with respect to the surface, or the angle, as will be seen shortly after. But even so, the most wise Architect of the world did not cease to instruct the human race. For just as when the distance between a man's eyes was not sufficient to know the true distance [of the Moon] from the earth, the vastness of the orb of the earth had to come to the aid of the weakness of sight: so also when here the departure of the Earth's surface from its center...

...it would vanish compared to the incredible height of the upper planets from the Earth; and here too, not in vain or unexpectedly would the mind wander through the circuit of the heavens, but even the human mind could reach these; God has engineered another and much larger type of <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent shift in position of an object when viewed from two different locations.</note>; if perhaps there were someone among men who would desire to follow this reasoning without offending piety, and without misrepresenting His works, which <margin>What the annual parallax of the orbit contributes.</margin> Erasmus Reinhold, following the mind of Copernicus, calls the "annual parallax of the orbit." And even if Tycho Brahe transferred that reasoning from the immobility of the Earth to the mobility of the Sun, the optical observer has no reason to choose one system over the other. But by the help of both types of parallax, we investigate heights inaccessible to sight in the following Problem 4 and in Rule 7, Problem 10, to which we refer the curious reader.

I suppose secondly, that the Sun illuminates the Earth, since day is nothing other than that portion of the terrestrial globe which the Sun illustrates for a certain number of hours. Since the body of the Earth is also opaque, dense, and <gloss>non-transparent</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀδιαφανὲς</note>, the light of the Sun, having encountered it as an obstacle, necessarily illuminates the surrounding reflected air; this clarity and splendor we not inappropriately call "day."

I suppose thirdly, that the terrestrial globe casts a shadow: for what else is night but the shadow of the Earth, which is moved around the Earth alternately with illumination, or day? See what we have explained at length in the Introduction concerning light and shadow, which lunar eclipses make manifest; since we speak of this more fully elsewhere, we deliberately pass over it here.

I suppose fourthly, that this terrestrial shadow is conical, from which it follows again that the Earth is round and the Sun is larger than the Earth.

I suppose fifthly, that the rays of the Sun falling upon the surface of the Earth are parallel, without any sensible error. These things being thus supposed, let us now approach the matter itself, taking the beginning of our demonstration from the Earth as the base and foundation of all things. Let it be, therefore:

## Problem I.
### To find the size of the terrestrial globe by shadow or light alone.

**P**tolemy, in his *Geography*, relates the ways in which the ancient astronomers investigated the size of the Earth. There are also other ways which practitioners are most often accustomed to use; leaving all those aside, we shall demonstrate in this place only how the same size of the Earth can be concluded by the shadow alone, lest by adopting others we seem to have overstepped the limits of our art. But to demonstrate the matter <gloss>experimentally</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἐμπείρως</note>, we will first set forth certain things about determining the shadow, so that the matter may be so much clearer and more evident. Let two cities be selected in some very flat region, situated under the same meridian, whose distance you must have known by the most exact measurement. These being obtained, at the time of the summer solstice at the noon hour, with a <term>gnomon</term> <note>A vertical rod used to cast a shadow for astronomical measurement.</note> erected on some most exactly leveled plane (which will achieve a more exact effect the taller it is), let the angle be observed in both places at the same moment of time, which the ray of light falling upon the gnomon makes with the same at the top: for this will manifest the distance of both cities in degrees or minutes. These degrees will hold the first place in the rule of proportions; the known distance between the cities in a certain measure, as was said, will hold the second; and finally, the 360 degrees of the entire terrestrial circle will hold the third place. Thus, when the second is multiplied by the third and the sum is divided by the first, the fourth number will emerge, demonstrating the sought-after size of the entire terrestrial globe.

With these known, nothing else was required except that he also have the same distance known in degrees; which...

# Shadow Geometry

...which he discovered with the following cleverness. Since at the time of the solstice the city of Syene, located directly under the tropic, becomes <gloss>shadowless</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἄσκιος</note> at the noon hour, and the shadow is consumed into itself without any angle being made with the <term>gnomon</term> <note>The vertical rod or pillar of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note>; taking this as known, he erected a gnomon at Alexandria at the same moment of time and on the same day, diligently observing the angle which the gnomon made with the shadow at its tip. For this was, as we shall demonstrate shortly, equal to the meridian arc between the two chosen cities. But let us demonstrate the matter with a diagram. 

->Let the circle, or the globe of the Earth, be represented with its center at A, the meridian as DBE, the city of Syene at point E, and Alexandria at point B; let the arc BE be the distance of the given cities, recorded as $6183 \frac{1}{3}$ <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient unit of distance, roughly 185 meters, though its exact length varied.</note>.<-

Note: the arc will be obtained in eight known degrees by this industry: at point B, Alexandria, at the eleventh hour of the solstice, having erected the gnomon BC, let the angle C of the shadow's tangent be observed; for this will give the sought-after distance in degrees. I demonstrate it thus: since, by the supposition that the Sun's rays are parallel due to the immense distance of the Earth from the Sun (without sensible error), let the line BC (the <term>style</term> <note>The shadow-casting edge or pin.</note>), being extended into the center A, fall between the two rays DC and EG. When this happens, by Proposition 29 of the First Book of Euclid’s *Elements*, the alternate angles DCB and BAE will be equal; therefore, arc DB will also be equal to arc BE. Thus, the former was found to be $8 \frac{1}{4}$ degrees; therefore, arc BE will also be known in those same degrees. Let it be done, therefore, that as the degree of arc BE ($8 \frac{1}{4}$) is to the known distance BD of the given cities ($6183 \frac{1}{3}$ stadia), so are the 360 degrees of the great meridian circle of the sphere to the other value. The sought-after quantity of the Earth in its great circle will come out to be 252,000 stadia, with 700 stadia corresponding to one degree. Furthermore, with the circumference of the Earth known, its diameter and then its solidity will easily become known through the rule of the proportion of circles to their diameters. If, however, the same observation were made during the Equinoxes, the difference of the angles produced by each shadow in the given cities would provide the sought-after space between them in degrees.

### *Another, and much more exact method, to find the size of the Earth through shadows collected within bowl-sundials.*

I find that the ancients, with truly great genius, detected the magnitude of the Earth through shadows collected within <term>scaphia</term> <note>Hemispherical, bowl-shaped sundials.</note>, about which the Arab astronomer Arazael <note>Likely referring to Al-Zarqali, known in Latin as Arzachel.</note> writes at length in the book he titles *The Measure of the World*. Ptolemy testifies that Eratosthenes also used these. The *scaphium* was, as Macrobius explains in his *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, a certain stone vessel hollowed out in the shape of a hemisphere with a curved perimeter, designated below by lines with the number of the 12 hours of the day, which the shadow of a protruding style distinguishes as it passes by with the transit of the Sun. For this is the function of such a vessel: that the shadow of the style runs from its first extremity to the other in the same amount of time as the Sun strives to cross the middle of the sky from its rising to its setting—namely, the rotation of one hemisphere. For the complete rotation of the whole sky concludes a day and a night. And therefore, it is established that as much as the Sun moves in its own circle, so much the shadow moves in this vessel. I read that mention of these was also made by Martianus Capella: *The bowl-sundials,* he says, *are bronze vessels which distinguish the paths of the hours by the height of a style in the middle of their base, which style is called a gnomon.* See Pliny, book 2, chapter 2, and Vitruvius, book 9, chapter 9. See such bowl-sundials figured above in our *Horologiographia*, and in *Anacamptic Astronomy*, part 2, problem 1. With the help of these bowl-sundials, Eratosthenes found the quantity through the shadow in this way. Supposing first, according to Cleomedes, that the rays of the Sun produced from one or various parts of the Sun to various parts of the Earth are parallel. I cite the words of Cleomedes:

> The rays sent from different parts of the sun to different parts of the earth are parallel. <note>original Greek: Τὰς δὲ ἀποπεμπομένας ἀκτῖνας ἀπὸ διαφόρων μερῶν τοῦ ἡλίου ἐπὶ διάφορα μέρη τῆς γῆς παραλλήλους εἶναι.</note>

Which we also demonstrated above in Prolusion 5. Let the center of the Sun be A, and the place on Earth where the Sun strikes perpendicularly be Y. Let AY be continued into the center of the Earth E. Then, let the place where the Sun strikes obliquely be I, where the ray AO falls through O, the tip of the gnomon, into V in the bowl-sundial TID; the magnitude of the shadow becomes VI. Now, since rays AV and AE are parallel according to the prolusion, angle VOI will be equal to the alternate angle IEY, and therefore the periphery VI in the bowl and YI on the surface of the Earth will be made similar. Therefore, however many degrees the shadow IV is in the bowl itself, the interval of the places YI will be just as many degrees. Let it be, then, to retain the example of Eratosthenes, that Syene is at Y, upon which the Sun is <gloss>shadowless</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἄσκιος</note> on the day of the solstice; while Alexandria...

# Book IX of the Great Art. Cosmography. The Gnomon. Part II.

...but when it is at I, where at that same moment at midday it is marked, the limit of the shadow falls at point V. Let the curved shadow in the *scaphium* <term>scaphium</term> <note>A bowl-shaped sundial used in antiquity</note> be measured at $7 \frac{1}{5}$ degrees, as Cleomedes asserts. 

<gloss>The angle in the bowl is found to be the fiftieth part of its own circle. <note>original: "Ἡ δὲ γωνία τῇ σκάφῃ πεντηκοστὸν μέρος εὑρίσκεται τοῦ οἰκείου κύκλου"</note></gloss>

The periphery IV—that is, the distance between Syene <note>modern Aswan, Egypt</note> and Alexandria—will also be the same number of degrees. Therefore, given the travel distance of 5,000 *stadia* <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters</note>, the circumference of the whole earth is concluded to be 250,000 *stadia*, as stated above.

Note here, however, that some error crept in among the ancients, which later and modern "Lyncean" <note>Referring to the Academy of the Lynxes, an early scientific society famed for sharp observation</note> astronomers have detected: namely, that those ancients considered only the central solar ray, neglecting the rays from the edges, as if they introduced little or no error. Yet, as we showed above in Preliminary Exercise 3, because the apparent semi-diameter of the Sun is 15 minutes and 38 seconds (for we found it to be that much with the greatest diligence), it often exceeds [the calculation]. I rightly think this was the sole cause of such diversity in determining the latitudes of even the most famous cities, such as Rome, Alexandria, etc. Astronomers alone know how much it matters when 15 minutes and 38 seconds are omitted—which must either be subtracted from or added to the central solar ray.

With similar industry after Eratosthenes, Posidonius that philosopher (to whom Pompey the Great lowered the symbols of imperial power when he went to hear him speak) took the cities of Rhodes and Alexandria, which lie under the same meridian, and their distance. Then, using the star Canopus at its highest elevation—comparing this difference with the distance—we read that he finally found the size of the terrestrial meridian. King Alammon <note>The Abbasid Caliph Al-Ma'mun, r. 813–833 AD</note> of the Arabs followed a similar method, as I read in the work of Abulfeda the Arabian geographer. Having sent out geometers along the straight path of the Red Sea heading north into the plains of Sinjar, he discovered that while proceeding under the same meridian, one degree of the heavens corresponds to $56 \frac{2}{3}$ miles, and the circumference of the earth is 20,400 miles. Maurolyco found another remarkably subtle method, but since it is found everywhere and is cited by Clavius and other astronomers, we refer the reader there. Let us return to our shadows.

### Problem II.

*To investigate the magnitude of the Atmosphere—that is, the greatest height of air that can be illuminated by the Sun—from its distance from the earth by means of reflected light.*

I presuppose first, from the common observation of astronomers, that twilight begins (or what is the same thing, the atmosphere is first illuminated) when the Sun is positioned 18 degrees below the horizon. Second, that the Sun, being larger than the earth, illuminates more than half of it—namely, 28 minutes beyond the 180th degree, as will be shown later. With these things supposed, you will discover the height of the atmosphere through the shadow of the earth, or the bright solar ray grazing the earth. Let the earth and its center be H, and the circle of the atmosphere be MXN. Let a tangent line QR be drawn at point F, which will be the physical horizon, just as OP is the astronomical horizon. Since the atmosphere first begins to be illuminated when the Sun is depressed 18 degrees below the horizon:

-># The Geometry of Shadow-making<-

->Yyy 3<-

...becomes PD, an arc of approximately 18 degrees, assumed for the purpose of better forming the demonstration, and let D be the center of the Sun. From this center, a straight line is drawn to the center of the Earth, H, just as a line is drawn from the shadow-point C to V. Where this line intersects the physical horizon QR, there lies the beginning of the atmosphere. Thus, having drawn a straight line from center H to K, a triangle FHK is formed, in which FH is known from the preceding as the semi-diameter <term>semi-diameter</term> <note>The radius of the Earth</note> of the Earth. It remains for us to investigate the side FK; this will be done if we first investigate the arc FHK. That arc is investigated as follows: First, arc FG is a quadrant of 90 degrees; arc GT is, by supposition, 18 degrees; therefore, the total arc FIT is 108 degrees. From this, if you subtract arc TI (which we said was 90 degrees and 14 minutes, because it is half of the sphere illuminated by the Sun), there remains arc FI, of 17 degrees and 46 minutes. Half of this arc is 8 degrees and 53 minutes, which is the angle FHI. Therefore, the angle that was sought is known. According to this arc, a triangle should be formed whose side FH is the semi-diameter of the Earth in miles; then HK, the distance of the atmosphere from the center of the Earth in the same units, will be known. If you then subtract a length equal to the Earth's semi-diameter from HK, there will remain LK, the distance of the atmosphere from the surface of the Earth—namely, the sought distance of approximately 43 miles. We have therefore found the height of the air or atmosphere, which was the task at hand.

### *Otherwise by sines.*

Let it be that as the total sine <term>total sine</term> <note>In historical trigonometry, the 'total sine' refers to the radius of the circle used for calculations, often set to 100,000 or 1,000,000</note> HF is to the tangent of the arc of 8 degrees 53 minutes (FK), so the known semi-diameter of the Earth HF is to another value. The line FK will result, which is the distance from the point of the eye to the point of intersection of the Earth's shadow and the solar light, or the atmosphere. Again, let it be that as the sine of the complement <term>sine of the complement</term> <note>Equivalent to the modern cosine</note> of the arc of 8 degrees 53 minutes is to the total sine, so the known semi-diameter of the Earth is to another value. The line HK will result, from which if the semi-diameter of the Earth HF is subtracted, it leaves LK, the height of the atmosphere.

However, to handle this business more exactly, we should no longer establish the illuminating center of the Sun as the reference, but rather the edge of the solar diameter; in this, we diverge from Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), a foundational figure in optics</note> and his other commentators. For when a straight line drawn from the center of the Sun grazes the Earth and, continued, reaches the physical horizon, the first beginning of dawn cannot yet occur. Instead, it must have already passed, since a part of the atmosphere is already whitening and illuminated, insofar as light is diffused from the upper part of the Sun, as was said in the third preliminary exercise of this book.

---

Therefore, if at the beginning of dawn the center of the Sun is depressed 19 degrees below the horizon, it is fair to establish the calculation from the highest edge (which is 16 minutes higher) due to the Sun's diameter; this edge is depressed below the horizon by only 18 degrees and 44 minutes. Furthermore, it is not necessary to account for the fact that more than a hemisphere is illuminated by the Sun, since it does not matter where the point belongs, as long as it pertains to the point of the atmosphere first illuminated. We have seen fit to include all these things here as a caution.

<margin>The beginnings of dawn are different in different parts of the world.</margin>

Note, however, in this place, that the atmosphere receives a different height according to the varying nature and disposition of regions. Under the equator, as the vapors are excessively rarefied, even if it spreads into a larger sphere, the higher they ascend, the closer the vapors must necessarily approach the nature of pure air; consequently, they are less capable of illumination and refraction. But under the cold Zone, condensed vapors are much more capable of such illumination and refraction. From this, it follows that the beginning of twilight, or dawn, will occur at a different distance of the Sun below the horizon. Hence, observers situated at different latitudes—namely, in the torrid, temperate, and cold zones—should be urged to determine the beginning of dawn in each of the mentioned regions, so that something certain can be established concerning the limit and beginning of dawn. For as for the beginning of dawn being established when the Sun is depressed 18 degrees below the horizon (the opinion of almost all astronomers), I would easily believe that this happens in places under the temperate Zone. But as for what is said about the beginning of dawn under a right or parallel sphere, the reasons indicated just above seem clearly to conflict, namely because of the very great difference of refractions in the said regions; but as I said, all these things would have to be observed most exactly so that the truth might become known from them.

### *Corollary.*

<margin>A machine measuring dawn.</margin>

From this it is clear by what method a machine can be constructed from the proportions of the dimensions of the Sun and Earth, together with the distance of both, which would indicate the beginning of dawn everywhere. Namely, if ABC, a globe of the Sun, were fixed to its parallelogram DCHI at center H such that it could revolve freely around the Earth; and a tangent line VC, similarly mobile on the physical horizon and attached to the parallelogram, would infallibly demonstrate the beginning of dawn. But about these things, more elsewhere. Therefore, let it suffice to have merely indicated them.

### Problem III.

*By what method clouds, or sky-beams <note>original: "trabis"; likely referring to a "chasma" or a beam-like meteor or aurora.</note>, and other appearances of meteors <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including clouds, rain, and wind, not just falling stars.</note> in the air, can be investigated through the logic of light and shadow.*

Depending on the different positions of clouds, different methods of measuring them can be established. For either a cloud sits exactly at the zenith <note>Directly overhead.</note>, or it inclines away from the zenith. The more vertical a cloud is, the better the result the meteorometric <term>meteorometric: the science of measuring atmospheric phenomena</term> task will achieve; however, the further it is from the zenith, the more its inconsistent ratio will waver more and more, as is well known in Optics.

Suppose first a cloud **AIBK**, observed during calm weather, of a size not so great, but of a moderate size separated from others, of the kind that most often occur in mid-summer; and let its shadow be projected onto a flat plain as **LGNF**. By this skill, you will investigate its distance from the earth. Let there be two assistants for this task, who, standing at the extreme boundaries of the shadow **LN**, receive you in the middle at **F**. You, indeed, with the same polymetric staff <note>A surveying instrument used to measure multiple angles simultaneously.</note> from point **F** in the middle of the shadow, will carefully observe the width of the cloud **AB**, noting the degrees, or the angle, which the visual lines make with the extreme parts of the cloud **AB**, which let us say is 10 degrees; and let the width of the shadow **ED** be measured by some known measure, which let be 100 feet. Let normal lines <note>Perpendicular lines.</note> **AD** and **BE** be drawn from the boundaries **AB** of the cloud to the extended diameter **LM** of the shadow, at points **D** and **E**; and from the same points **AB**, the ends of the little cloud, let other lines **AL** and **BN** be drawn to the boundaries of the shadow **L** and **N**. These lines, with the perpendiculars **AD** and **BE**, intercept the angle of the Sun's elevation. Let the line **EF** also be drawn. Various triangles will be formed, and since they are proportional, as **DAF** is to **DAL**, so the base **DF** is to **DL**. But the angles of triangle **ALF** are known—**L** being a right angle, and **F** frequently so—and the side **LN** is known to be 50 feet; the angle of triangle **ADL** is also known. Therefore, the sides of each triangle will also be known. If, therefore, it is made so that the sine <note>original: "sinus rectus"</note> of 4 degrees is to the sine of 33 minutes, as **LF** (50 feet) is to the other [segment] **DL**, then **DL** will come out to be 16 feet, which, when added to line **DL**, makes 66. Again, say: as the sine of 4 degrees 33 minutes is to the cosine <note>original: "sinum complementi"; the sine of the complement (90 minus the angle).</note> of 85 degrees 27 minutes, so **DF** (66 feet) is to the other; then **DA**, the sought altitude of the cloud from the earth, will come out. If, however, you desire the width of the cloud **AB**, you will add 16 twice to the line **LN**, and you will have what was sought.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the measurement of a cloud's altitude. A cloud labeled A, I, B, K is in the sky. Lines project down to ground points L, D, G, F, E, N. A human figure is depicted standing at point F on a small mound. Vertical lines AD and BE represent the cloud's height relative to the ground points.</image-desc>

### Case II.

If, however, the cloud is further from the zenith, you will operate thus: Let the vertical line be **VC**, the cloud **AB**, the Sun at **E**, the shadow of the cloud **C**, and the ray of light-shadow **EBC**. Thus you will investigate the altitude of the cloud. Let there be two observers, one at **C** and the other at **G**, at any interval. Let both observe the extreme boundary of the shadow **B** at one and the same time, and let the parts or degrees cut on any geometric instrument be carefully noted at each station. You shall also exactly measure the space between **G** and **C**. Let angle **G** be 30, **B** be 60, and the space **GC** be 100 feet. Let line **CL** be drawn parallel to **GB**, and **IK** parallel to **AC**. Then, let it be made so that **IN**, the difference of the tangents of the observations made, is to **NK**, as the known measure **GC** is to **CD**. And **CD** will come out—namely, the distance of **C** from the perpendicular **BD** dropped from the cloud to the earth. Once this is obtained, let it be made again so that the total sine <note>The radius of the unit circle in trigonometric tables of the time.</note> is to **IK**, the tangent of 60 degrees, as the distance **CD** (found just before in a known measure) is to **DB**. Thus **DB**, the sought altitude of the cloud, will come out. By this art, you will measure almost all types of clouds.

Sun rays EBC cast a shadow. Geometric points V, L, I, N, K, D are used to construct triangles for trigonometric calculation. Line BD represents the altitude of the cloud.</image-desc>

## Problem V.

### *Investigating the heights of mountains through the observation of light.*

**S**ince the heights of mountains are sometimes so great that they far exceed the middle region of the air <note>In traditional Aristotelian physics, the "middle region" of the atmosphere was where clouds, rain, and snow formed.</note>, their peaks relate to that middle region just like rocks rising out of the sea relate to its surface. The rays of the Sun appear on their sharp peaks long before sunrise; let us now see by what method we can arrive at the height of such a mountain from the knowledge of the light which usually appears on the summits long before the Sun rises above the flat horizon. To achieve this, it must be noted that a mountain is taller in proportion to how much earlier the light shines upon its peak before the common sunrise. Indeed, once we have the arc between the point where the Sun first begins to illuminate a mountain and the point on the horizon between them, we can arrive at the knowledge not only of the mountain's height but also the diameter of the physical horizon. This is because the base of the triangle, which the light line forms with the peak of the mountain, is nothing other than the semi-diameter of the physical horizon. Once the height of the mountain is obtained through this first illumination (according to Problem II), the base of that triangle will also be known in parts of the world axis, or the calculated vertical line <term>catheti: a mathematical term for a line falling perpendicularly, like the side of a right triangle</term>. However, so that this matter may be treated a bit more exactly, we shall attempt to explore the height of the more famous mountains according to the accounts of historians. But first, a quite famous passage occurs in Aristotle’s *Meteorology*, Book 1, concerning the height of Mount Caucasus. There is hardly anyone among the authors who has understood this passage well; we provide its genuine interpretation from the corrected manuscripts of the Vatican Library as follows: <note>original: "Ὁ δέ Καύκασος μέγιστον ὄρος τῶν θερινῶν ὀρῶν & πάλιν ἕ ὕψῃ. σημείον δέ τῷ εἶῷ ὕψους, ὅτι θεῷ καὶ ἀπὸ τῶν κορυφάων βαδίων, & εἰς τὴν λίμνην εἰς πλεόντων. ἔτι δέ ἡλίου τῆς νυκτὸς ἀυτῷ ἀχρὶ μεχρὶ τῶ τρίτῶ μέρους, ἀπό τὲ τῆς ἔω, & πάλιν ἀπὸ τῆς ἑσπέρας:"</note> *“Caucasus is a mountain toward the summer sunrise <note>The "summer mountains" were those located toward the northeast, where the sun rises during the summer solstice.</note>, greatest in both extent and height. Proof of its height can be gathered from this: it is visible both from the place they call the 'Depths of the Black Sea' and from those entering the mouth of the Maeotian Lake <note>The Sea of Azov.</note>. Furthermore, its highest parts are illuminated by the solar rays at night for a third part of the time, both at dawn—that is, in the morning—and again in the evening.”* If we follow Aristotle's report here, using the rule for investigating the atmosphere or the quantity of twilight proposed in Problem II (where we determined it to be 52 miles), we find by the doctrine of sines that the height of the mountain is 270 miles. This is altogether ridiculous and can in no way be possible, since hardly any mountain has been found in the whole world whose vertical height extends to 4 or 5 miles. From this it is clearly evident that either Aristotle was deceived by the report of others, or he spoke carelessly. For however you interpret this passage, we will always see the height of Mount Caucasus exceeding 52 miles. Therefore, it would be worthwhile to test this matter in the city of Caffa <note>Modern-day Feodosia in Crimea.</note>, situated on the isthmus of the Tauric Chersonese, from which Aristotle claims Caucasus can be seen. I truly wonder why, in a place so frequented by Europeans, an experiment on this matter has not yet been conducted by philosophers. If it were done, something certain could finally be established regarding the genuine interpretation of this passage. Passing over this place as corrupted by a false report, let us turn to another that corresponds better to calculation.

<margin>Height of Mount Athos.</margin>
Mount Athos is in Macedonia, most famous for the excavation by Xerxes <note>Refers to the Canal of Xerxes, dug across the peninsula in 480 BCE.</note>. It is located 87 miles from the island of Lemnos in the Aegean Sea. According to Pliny, at the solstice, this mountain is said to cast its shadow into the forum of the city on Lemnos called Myrrhina; hence the inhabitants are said to have placed a bronze heifer as a marker for the end of the said shadow. Plutarch mentions this in his book *On the Face in the Moon*. "Neither of us," he says, "has been to Lemnos, yet we have often heard that iambic verse tossed about in every conversation: <margin><note>original: "Αθως καλύψει πλεύρα Λημνίας βοός."</note></margin> *Athos shall cover the flanks of the Lemnian heifer.* For the mountain's shadow terminates near a certain bronze heifer, stretched out over the sea no less than 700 stades <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance; 700 stades is roughly 80 miles.</note> away." These are the words of Plutarch. And indeed, the height of this mountain could easily be found if the altitude of the Sun were determined at the moment Athos strikes the heifer with its shadow. It is certainly true that at noon on the solstice, whether summer or winter, this shadow could by no means be projected that far. Since the position of Mount Athos relative to Lemnos is North-West <note>original: "Eurozephyrus"; a wind/directional term</note>, and given the shortness of the shadow that the Sun makes at noon on the solstice when it is elevated nearly 72 degrees (at latitude 41, where we place Lemnos and Athos), this clearly contradicts the claim. The height of the mountain would have to be excessive and utterly incredible—indeed, exceeding all the mountains in the world. Therefore, it must necessarily occur in the evening time, when...

# Book 9 of the Great Art. Gnomonic Cosmometry. Part I.

...where the Sun stands 2, 3, or 4 degrees above the horizon, it will cast this "Lemnian shadow." <note>This refers to the ancient proverb that the shadow of Mount Athos reached as far as the island of Lemnos.</note> Let **Myrrhina** <note>the ancient capital of the island of Lemnos</note> be represented by **C**, and Mount Athos by **AB**; furthermore, so that the mountain's shadow may reach the forum at **C**, let us place the Sun near its setting, for then, as the Sun sinks lower, longer shadows fall from the mountains. Let the distance **BC** be 700 <term>stadia</term> <note>An ancient Greek unit of distance; 700 stadia is roughly 80 miles</note>, or 437,500 feet.

[The diagram illustrates the Sun (D) shining over the peak of Mount Athos (A), casting a long ray across a body of water (700 Stadia) to the city of Myrrhina on the island of Lemnos. Point C marks the "Forum" where the shadow falls.]

According to geographical accounts, these 700 stadia, when resolved into degrees, give 1 degree and 16 minutes on the circumference of a great circle. Let us therefore suppose the Sun is elevated by 3 degrees. It follows that as the <term>total sine</term> <note>In period trigonometry, this refers to the radius of the calculation circle, used as a base for ratios</note> is to the distance **BC** (700 stadia or 437,500 feet), so is the tangent of 3 degrees to the other value; this gives the height of the mountain as 44 stadia. If, however, you set the Sun at 2 degrees above the horizon, following the same rule, you will find the mountain to be 32 stadia high. Since the length of the shadow—that is, the distance of the city of Myrrhina from Athos—is established by historical accounts, nothing else is needed to investigate the height of the mountain except the angle of the shadow at **C**, which the Sun's altitude reveals. If someone standing on Lemnos were to observe the angle of the falling shadow, the mountain's height could be obtained without any difficulty. Just as the total sine relates to the 700 stadia distance from Athos to Lemnos, so the tangent of the shadow's incident angle relates to the height; the fourth term will necessarily provide the sought-after height of the mountain.

<margin>The height of Mount Olympus.</margin>
By this industrious method, the heights of all mountains can be investigated. Using this method, **Xenagoras** <note>A Greek mathematician mentioned by Plutarch</note> famously boasted that he accurately measured the height of **Mount Olympus** by the shadow of its summit, finding it to be 10 stadia and 96 Greek feet. By this same art, **Mount Pico** in the Canary Islands, seen from a distance of 4 degrees, was found to have a height of 43 stadia; this height is indeed immense, and thus it seems to exceed all other mountains in altitude. But let these remarks on the height of mountains suffice; whoever desires more of this kind should consult our work *Mundus Subterraneus* (The Subterranean World), where we professedly investigate the heights of mountains and the depths of the seas.

## Corollary.

From these points, it is clear that once an exact height of the mountains is obtained, one can also obtain both the exact distance of those sailing at sea from a particular mountain, and the difference in <term>refraction</term> <note>The bending of light through the atmosphere, which affects where a star or peak appears to be</note> caused by the mountain peak when viewed from one place near sunrise or sunset. I believe the knowledge of these things brings great advantages, which will be hidden from no one who has deeply penetrated the secrets of <term>anaclastics</term> <note>The study of refracted light</note> discussed in the preceding book.

### Problem VI.
## To investigate how much of the terrestrial globe the Sun illuminates.

**B**efore we pass on to describing the magnitude of the celestial bodies and their shadows, let us first treat the quantity of the surface illuminated by a larger luminous body. This knowledge is presupposed for the art of finding the shadows which illuminated bodies cast from themselves. Since the Sun is larger than the Earth, according to the rules of shadows, it must necessarily illuminate more than half of the sphere of the smaller Earth. How great this excess is remains to be found by the following clever method.

[The diagram shows a large Sun (A) and a smaller Earth (I). Rays (BC, DC) converge at a point (C) behind the Earth. The line MN represents the midpoint of the Earth, while EF shows the actual further extent of the Sun's light.]

Let the globe of the Sun be **A**, and the Earth **I**. Let **EFC** be the terrestrial shadow, **BC** and **DC** the rays of the Sun, and the quantity of the Earth illuminated beyond the midpoint **NM** be at points **E** and **F**. The question is: how large is that arc **NE** or **MF**, beyond which the Sun illuminates the Earth, which is smaller than itself? I say, therefore, that this arc consists of as many degrees or minutes as there are in the arc of angle **C**, which the shadow constitutes. That is, the arc of excess by which the Sun illuminates the Earth beyond the halfway point is equal to angle **C**, which the two lines terminating the shadow create. This is true not only in the illumination of the Earth, but in any other two bodies, where one...

# Shadow-Measuring Geometry

...illuminates [the Earth], I shall now demonstrate. Let the rectangle **MNEF** be formed, as appears in the present figure from the points of contact and the midpoint of the sphere; and let lines **IE** and **IF** be drawn from the center **I** to the points of contact. Since these are right angles—for the angles at **F** and **E**, according to Proposition 18 of Book 3 <note>original: "18. juxta 3" – Euclid's Elements, Book 3, Prop 18 states that a tangent to a circle is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact.</note> and Proposition 32 of Book 1 of Euclid’s *Elements* <note>Euclid's Elements, Book 1, Prop 32 concerns the sum of angles in a triangle.</note>, are equal to four right angles—the angle **EIF**, together with angle **C**, will be equal to two right angles. Or, the angle **FIC**, together with the half-angle of the shadow **ECI**, is equal to one right angle. Therefore, the angle **EIC**, together with **ECI** (the half-angle of the shadow), will equal one right angle; that is, if you subtract angle **ECI** from 90 degrees, there will necessarily remain the angle **NIF**, which is equal to angle **ECI**. Its arc **NF** is the excess of the illuminated globe beyond the midpoint.

However, this arc is equal to the arc of angle **ECI**, which would be described as equal to the interval **IN**. Therefore, the arc **NF**, by which the Sun illuminates the Earth beyond the midpoint, is equal to the angle **ECI** of the Earth's shadow. This has been found by practitioners on Earth to be nearly 14 degrees beyond the midpoint of the sphere—that is, **RE** is 104 degrees <note>90 degrees for the hemisphere plus the 14-degree excess.</note>. If you double this number, you will have the arc **ERF**, 204 degrees, which we say is the arc of illumination defined by light on the body of the Earth. If the number 180 is subtracted from this, it leaves the total excess by which the Sun illuminates the Earth beyond the midpoint. By this skillful method, given any two bodies, you will find how much one illuminating the other shines beyond or below the midpoint.

### Corollary I.

From this it follows first: whenever a spherical body illuminating another is larger than the body being illuminated, the angle of the shadow necessarily gives the angle of the excess of illumination beyond the midpoint of the smaller sphere, as is evident from the previous demonstration.

### Corollary II.

<margin>cylinder-like <note>original: "κυλινδροειδῆ"</note></margin>
Whenever the spherical body being illuminated is equal to the body illuminating it, the illumination will necessarily be hemispheric; that is, the rays terminating the shadow will touch the ends of the diameter. Consequently, the tangent lines, together with the shadow, will constitute a parallel, shaded cylinder running out into infinity, which they call <term>cylinder-like</term> <note>original: "κυλινδροειδῆ" (cylindroeidē). This refers to a shadow that does not taper to a point but remains a constant width.</note>.

### Corollary III.

If, however, the illuminating body is smaller than the body being illuminated, the larger body will necessarily be illuminated less than halfway, by as much excess as the angle of the smaller body's shadow would be if it were illuminated by the larger one. I will explain the matter: Let **A** be the larger opaque body that is illuminated, and **I** be the smaller illuminating body. Let tangent lines be drawn from points **E** and **F** to the globe **A** at points **B** and **D**. Since these lines are not parallel, they will necessarily meet at point **C**. I say, therefore, that the globe **A** is illuminated by the smaller globe **I** only below the midpoint of the sphere, by an amount equal to angle **C**, which is equal to angles **BAV** and **DAY**.

The reason is very clearly evident from the preceding, for it is the inverse ratio of all things. If, therefore, the Sun were the Earth and the Earth were the Sun, the Earth would illuminate the Sun below the midpoint **YV** by a deficiency as great as angle **C**, to which angles **VAB** and **YAD** are equal. This arc, since it is 28 minutes, will make the arc of illumination **DXB** equal to 28 minutes [less than the hemisphere]. The shaded arc **DSB**, however, will be greater than the arc **YD**, that is, by 28 minutes. If you then add 28 minutes to 180 degrees, the shaded arc will be 204 degrees <note>The text here seems to conflate minutes and degrees for the sake of the example, or refers to a specific calculation where 28 units of arc are added to the 180-degree base.</note>; if you subtract this from the whole circle, there remains an arc of 156 degrees, which is the sought-after arc of illumination. You see, therefore, how beautifully light and shadow agree.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the optics of illumination between a smaller sphere (I) and a larger sphere (A). Two tangent lines originate from points E and F on the circumference of sphere I, pass through points D and B on sphere A, and converge at point C. Sphere A's illuminated area is delineated by points Y and V, while the shaded region behind it represents the umbra (shadow), labeled with point S. Other geometric labels include M, N, R, T, Z, and X. The diagram demonstrates that a smaller light source illuminates less than half of a larger opaque body.</image-desc>

### Corollary IV.

From this it is also clear that if a smaller body illuminates a larger one, the shaded arc of the larger sphere will be as great as the luminous arc would be in the smaller body if it were illuminated by the larger one. Conversely, the arc of illustration in the larger body will be as great as the shaded arc would be in the smaller body if it were illuminated by the larger one. Whoever examines this relationship more deeply will find the distances and sizes of any spherical bodies with almost no trouble.

# Problem VII.
## *To calculate the thickness of the heavens and their distance from the earth, according to the doctrine of Ptolemy.*

I set forth, therefore, what Ptolemy proves concerning the Constitution of the heavens: the thickness of each Heaven is divided into three orbs; the first and the last are eccentric in one respect, and homocentric <term>homocentric: spheres that share the same center, usually the Earth</term> in another; the middle one is simply eccentric <term>eccentric: a circle whose center is offset from the center of the Earth</term>, around which the <term>epicycle: a small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one</term> revolves (this is a certain solid globe in which the planet is conceived to be immersed). If this heaven, thus constituted, be divided in two by a great circle equidistant from its poles, it will offer to those looking at it from the section where it was divided the appearance presented by that figure **ABC**, in which three orbs appear: the middle one is entirely eccentric, which includes the epicycle within itself, namely **AMOP**; the others are eccentric in a certain respect, such as **ABCL** and **FDEP**.

Let this, then, be the Heaven of the Moon: our purpose is to investigate that diameter **AC**, from which we will then easily recognize the entire lunar circuit **ABC**. To understand this matter, it is worthwhile to see what admirable skill Ptolemy used: for he first investigated the proportion of the semi-diameter <note>original: "semidiametri", often referred to as the radius today</note> of the epicycle to the distance from the center of the earth to the center of the epicycle; that is, in the circle **ABC**, which we want to represent the epicycle to us, the proportion of the straight line **IA** (the semi-diameter of the epicycle) to the straight line **XI** (the distance from the center of the earth **X** to the center of the epicycle **I**) by this method.

He observed three lunar eclipses at Alexandria, which, having taken into account the motions of the Moon and the epicycle, were so arranged that the first was at **X** in the following figure, in which the Moon was totally eclipsed, being at, for example, 13 degrees [of a sign]. The second was at **B**, from the Northern part, in which half of the Moon and more than a third of its diameter failed <note>i.e., was eclipsed</note>, while it occupied 25 degrees of Aries in the Zodiac. The third was at **C**, also from the Northern part, in which the Moon was eclipsed by half while it was at 14 degrees of Virgo. These things ought to be explained more fully by us; but partly to avoid the boredom that would arise from the subtle relation of motions and numbers, and partly because we are hurrying to other matters, we have touched on them briefly; especially since those same things can be readily found by anyone in Ptolemy, or in Regiomontanus <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a celebrated Renaissance mathematician and astronomer</note>, who pursue them more copiously.

Therefore, to approach Ptolemy's most subtle discovery: let straight lines **DX**, **DB**, **DC** be drawn from the center of the earth **D** (in the following figure) to the individual locations of the failing Moon, and the straight line **DX** through the center of the epicycle **LX**; then let the straight lines **FG**, **CB**, **BF** be drawn. From these we shall then proceed to track the proportion of the line **DL** to the line **LX**, which we seek.

From the doctrine of triangles, it is held that in rectilinear triangles in which the proportion of the angles is known, the proportion of the sides is also known; this is taught at length by Father Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612), the Jesuit mathematician who led the Gregorian calendar reform</note> in his book on rectilinear triangles in his *Theodosius* <note>Clavius's commentary on the *Sphaerica* of Theodosius of Bithynia</note>.
