Therefore, by proposition 10 of Clavius’s *Rectilinear Triangles*, all angles of the triangle **DFB** being known, the proportion of its sides to one another will be known; wherefore the proportion of side **DF** to side **FB** is known. In the same way, in the rectilinear triangle **FDC**, angle **D** is known through the observation of the eclipses, and the external angle **AFC**, standing upon the arc **ABC** known through calculation, is also known, therefore (as we were saying a little while ago regarding the other triangle) the internal angles **DFC** and **DCF** will also be known. Therefore, the proportion of side **DF** to side **FC** will be known; and from the known proportion of side **DF** to side **FC** and **FB**, the proportion of sides **FB** and **FC** to each other will then be recognized. ### Problem VIII. ###

-> *Another way to investigate the distance of the Moon from the Earth by its shadow and its parallax.* <-

From the arcs MN and MNO, we will thus know the proportion of the straight line DL to the straight line DH; that is, how many times the minimum distance of the Moon from the earth contains the radius of the earth. Let this triangle HLD be considered; in it, angle HDL is known because of the known arc MN upon which it stands. Furthermore, angle MHO is also known because of the given arc MO; therefore, the interior angle HLD in triangle DHL will also be known. For two internal angles HDL and HLD are equal to their external and opposite angle by the 32nd proposition of the first book <note>This refers to Euclid’s *Elements*, Book 1, Prop. 32, which states that an exterior angle of a triangle is equal to the sum of the two opposite interior angles.</note>. Therefore, the radius of the concave lunar sphere encompasses 33 and more than **7/10** of one radius of the earth.

Let circle DYZX be the Moon, the sensible Earth <note>The "sensible" earth or horizon refers to the perspective of an observer on the surface, as opposed to the "astronomical" or "rational" perspective from the center of the earth.</note> at the Moon be AP, and let RO be the physical or sensible horizon, and XY the astronomical or insensible horizon. This, subtracted from 180 degrees, leaves angle EAC. Now, since two angles A and C are known in triangle EAC, the third angle AEC cannot remain hidden. Since the angles and one side of any triangle are known, the remaining sides of the same will also be known.

<margin>Calculation by sines.</margin>
Therefore, let it be done: as the sine of angle E is to the known line AC (the radius of the earth), so is the sine of angle CAE to the other side. This will produce line CE, the distance of the Moon from the center of the earth.

From here, with a easier outcome and less labor, Ptolemy progressed both to measuring the thickness and circumference of the lunar Heaven, and to measuring the spheres of the remaining planets, according to the rules which mathematicians—especially Archimedes, the light of mathematicians—hand down concerning the proportion of the diameter to the circumference and the dimension of the sphere. This seems altogether to escape the senses: for how can it be that the pole star, which is distant from the pole by only a few degrees, describes a circle so vast that within its circuit can be confined a body of which the Sun is the smallest part?

## Problem IX.

### To find the width, or thickness, of the earth's shadow.

**IN ORDER** that we may gradually, and by parts, come to the knowledge of the size of the celestial bodies, let us first examine the earth's shadow as a foundation, so that from it the curious reader may be able to see how many and how wonderful things may emerge. We call the "earth's shadow" that entire dark or shadowy cone which the opacity of the earth, illuminated by the Sun, causes. There are, however, two primary things to be observed in it: first, the thickness of the shadow, or the diametrical width at that place where the circle of the Head and Tail of the Dragon <note>These are the lunar nodes, the points where the Moon's path crosses the Ecliptic (the Sun's path).</note> and the Moon situated within it cuts it at the time of an eclipse. Second, the length of the shadow, or what is the same thing, the length of the axis of the shadowy cone. As for the thickness, it should be noted that the diametrical width of the shadow always decreases starting from the radius of the earth, and is always greater or smaller depending on the Moon’s position in its eccentric and its epicycle <note>Technical terms for the circular paths used in pre-modern astronomy to explain planetary motion.</note>: it is smallest at the apogee <term>apogee: the point in an orbit farthest from the Earth</term> and greatest at the perigee <term>perigee: the point in an orbit closest to the Earth</term>. From these points, the eclipse also becomes larger or smaller. Therefore, so that you may know how great the width of the diameter of the earth's shadow is in any eclipse, you shall work as follows.

Suppose, therefore, that at the time of a lunar eclipse, half of the Moon is obscured; you will observe its obscuration with the greatest diligence. This is done if you carefully consider the figure of the Moon admitted through a hole onto a tablet, and at the same time, you have the Moon's latitude obtained from the *Ephemerides* <note>Daily astronomical tables</note> or by calculation; for this latitude doubled will give the sought diameter of the shadow. But let us declare the matter by an example. Let the circle of the shadow, which the section of the nodes produces, be BDFC; the ecliptic DAC; and the Moon about to pass through the shadow B. Suppose it has already passed through with its greatest obscuration <margin>halved <note>original: *dichotomos*</note></margin>, and let its latitude from either of the Moon's nodes be given at that same moment of time—for example, 44 minutes. I say that this is the semi-diameter of the earth's shadow. For since the latitude of the Moon is nothing other than the declination from the nodes, or from the ecliptic DAC, which AB represents—which

<image-desc>A circular diagram showing the Earth's shadow as a large circle labeled B at the top, D on the left, C on the right, and F at the bottom. A horizontal line, labeled DAC, passes through the center A, representing the ecliptic. A smaller circle, representing the Moon, is centered at point B and is tangent to the horizontal ecliptic line at the center point A. A vertical line connects B, A, and F.</image-desc>

declination, since it is 44 minutes by supposition, therefore the semi-diameter AB of the earth's shadow ABCD will be the same number of minutes, which when doubled will give the full thickness of the shadow as 88 minutes, which is what you were seeking. <margin>The quantity of the semi-diameter of the earth's shadow.</margin> By this industrious method, those most excellent craftsmen Tycho and Copernicus found the semi-diameter of the earth's shadow, with the Moon positioned at its apogee, to be 45 minutes; and with the same Moon positioned at its perigee, to be 47 minutes. However, so that you may receive full instruction in this matter, we must deal here somewhat with the lunar eclipse, since one can by no means be understood without the other.

Note, therefore, that just as there is a very great variety of lunar eclipses, so too there are various causes constituting them. The first is the unequal latitude of the Moon: for if this is either zero or at least very small, it makes the eclipse much greater, both in magnitude and duration, since the Moon must run through the middle of the shadow; but the further it is from the ecliptic, the more quickly it extricates itself, so much so that sometimes it barely grazes the shadow. The second cause is the unequal and unstable thickness or density of the earth's shadow, and also the anomaly arising from the unequal distance of the Sun from the earth. For when the Sun is further away at the apogee of its eccentric, it causes the shadow to be extended longer; but when the Sun is nearer, the shadow is shortened (as is clear from the laws of shadows). Hence Copernicus found the semi-diameter of the shadow at the place of the transition of the Moon at its highest point (or at the apogee of its epicycle), with the Sun positioned at the apogee of its eccentric, to be 39 minutes and 48 seconds. But with the Sun at the perigee of its eccentric and the Moon remaining at the apogee of its epicycle, the semi-diameter of the shadow was found to be 38 minutes and 53 seconds.

Again, with the Moon at the perigee of its epicycle, namely in...

# The Great Art, Book IX. The Gnomon of Cosmometry. Part II.

...positioned at the lowest point, and with the Sun at its apogee <note>The point in an orbit farthest from the Earth.</note> at the highest point of its eccentric path, the radius of the Earth's shadow was found to be 49 minutes and 46 seconds. However, with the Sun at its perigee <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note> and the Moon remaining at its own perigee, the observed radius of the shadow was 48 minutes and 51 seconds; and this occurs at the maximum eccentricity of the Sun. The third cause is the unequal divergence of the Moon from the Sun. For a fast-moving Moon shortens the duration of an eclipse, while a slow one draws it out longer. From this, it follows that the duration of time at both the apogee and perigee of the epicycle is nearly equal, provided the latitude is the same in both cases. For as much as the shadow is thicker at the perigee, the Moon's motion is that much faster; thus, a Moon with no latitude <note>Meaning it is exactly on the ecliptic line.</note> passes through the Earth's shadow in nearly equal time whether it is at its apogee or perigee, even though the shadow itself differs. From these facts, various total or partial eclipses result.

<margin>
What is an eclipse with delay, and without delay?
</margin>

Total eclipses occur when the entire Moon is darkened. These are of two types: with delay and without delay. A **total eclipse with delay** is when the Moon remains immersed in the shadow for some time. A **total eclipse without delay** is when the entire Moon is indeed darkened, but it emerges from the shadow again immediately. In this case, the sum of the Moon's radius and its latitude is equal to the radius of the shadow, as appears in the following Example I, where AB is the radius of the Moon and AG is its latitude; these two joined together equal the shadow's radius. A **partial eclipse** is when only one part of the Moon fails; this is three-fold: either half the Moon's diameter fails, or more, or less than that. More than the radius fails when, at true opposition, the Moon's latitude is less than the shadow's radius, yet greater than the difference between the radii of the shadow and the Moon. Half of the radius fails when the Moon's latitude during the eclipse equals the radius of the shadow, and the Moon appears <term>halved</term> <note>original: διχότομος (dichotomos); a term describing the Moon when it appears exactly bisected.</note>. Less than the radius fails when the Moon's latitude is greater than the shadow's radius, or less than the combined radii of the shadow and the Moon. From these clarified points, the following rules emerge to help investigate the Earth's shadow.

<margin>
Rules for investigating the magnitude of a lunar eclipse.
</margin>

### Rule I.

If, in a total eclipse without delay, you halve the apparent diameter of the Moon and add that half to the Moon's latitude at that same moment, you will infallibly obtain the required latitude—or thickness—of the Earth's shadow.

### Rule II.

If the eclipse of the Moon is partial, and the maximum darkening is equal to the Moon's radius, then according to the previous demonstration, the Moon's latitude will be equal to the shadow's radius.

### Rule III.

If, however, only a quarter part of the lunar diameter is darkened, and the Moon is at the same distance from the Sun and Earth as it was during the darkening of the <gloss>previously mentioned</gloss> eclipsed Moon—namely 44 minutes—you will find the thickness of the shadow if you subtract a quarter of the apparent lunar diameter from the Moon's latitude at that time; for the remainder will give the required thickness of the shadow.

### Rule IV.

If, however, two-thirds of the radius are darkened, you will find the thickness of the shadow if you add one-third of the Moon's apparent diameter to the Moon's latitude. By following these four rules, you will be able to find the latitude of the Earth's shadow in any occurring eclipse with almost no effort, as will be shown shortly in the practical application.

## Problem X.

### *To find the apparent diameter of the Moon and the Sun, and from these, finally, the size of their bodies and the shadow of both.*

<margin>
The difficulty in astronomical observations.
</margin>

The sharpness of human vision is so weak when it comes to grasping the size of celestial bodies separated by almost infinite distances, that it is scarcely possible for the eye to reach them unless aided by various instruments. Added to this is the varying state of the medium <note>The atmosphere or air through which light passes.</note>, by which the eyes are marvelously deceived, thinking that which is large to be small, and that which is small to be large, or that which is angular to be round. Thus we see the flame of a torch appearing pyramidal to those watching up close, but appearing spherical when far away, as was shown at length in the second book. Hence, even in reality, we perceive a circular shape when it is actually radiating semicircular light. Therefore, the apparent diameter of the stars is subject to the greatest errors, and it seems hardly possible that anything exact can be determined in this matter; nor do I think the tube <note>The telescope.</note> is to be greatly trusted, owing to the variety of refractions.

Another method must therefore be held to, so that the truth may be obtained in such a subtle business, which we shall produce in the following sections. However, the curiosity of human ingenuity has found certain other instruments—some of which we shall explain here—which astronomers are accustomed to use, in the absence of better ones, to track down the apparent diameters of celestial bodies as much as possible. The first is the Diop- <note>The text cuts off here, likely referring to the "Dioptra," an ancient surveying and astronomical instrument.</note>

## Geometrical Shadow-Casting

->**Ptolemy’s Sighting Rule** <note>original: *Dioptra Ptolemæi*</note>, the construction of which is as follows.<-

Let AB be a long board of 4 cubits <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length, approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note>, upon which, near point A, another rule is erected at a right angle. In the center line of this vertical rule, at point D, let there be a small hole. To this, you will attach another board, F, to the line AB, in such a way that it can be moved back and forth at a right angle within a sort of small groove. This mobile board should have two small holes, L and F, which are equally distant from the center line D on both sides; thus you will have the instrument prepared. You shall then investigate the apparent diameter of the Sun and Moon in this way: With the instrument set out while the Moon or Sun is shining and positioned on the meridian <note>The imaginary line passing through the celestial poles and the zenith of a person's location; observing at the meridian avoids certain atmospheric distortions.</note> to avoid refractions, look through hole D at the Moon. In the same action, move the sighting rule FL back and forth in its groove until you can see the two extremities of the body of the Sun ☉ or Moon ☽—that is, the highest and lowest points of the diameter—within your sight. The angle IDE, or angle YDX, will be the angle under which the Moon or Sun is seen, and which the diameter of the Sun or Moon subtends. This diameter can be taken in various other ways, for which see **Tycho Brahe** in his *Progymnasmata* <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601) was a famous Danish astronomer; his *Progymnasmata* (Introduction to the New Astronomy) was a foundational text for early modern astronomy.</note>.

Note, therefore, that with the apparent diameter of the Moon ☽ and its distance from the Earth known, we can describe the Earth’s shadow according to true proportions by this reasoning. Let the radius <note>original: *semidiameter*</note> of the Earth be known as AE, through the ends of which two lines are drawn which, meeting at point B, constitute an angle of the same number of minutes under which we recently detected the apparent diameter of the Moon ☽. This is done so that either line EB or AB contains 52 Earth radii—that is, the distance of the Moon ☽ from the Earth. ### Another easier method to measure the length of the earthly shadow.

**D**elineate two spheres, AI (the Sun) and O (the Earth), and the Moon, upon a straight line, for example A and I, so that their semidiameters relate to one another as 5 ½ to 1. Let the distance between the drawn spheres also be the distance of the Sun from the Earth. If you then enclose these two bodies within two lines, BMC and DNC, they will form a cone DBC, proportional to the cone of the Earth's shadow NMC. This can also be established geometrically. Since triangles ABC and AO (which is produced from the parallel OI, drawn to the side BM) are similar by the 13th proposition of the 5th book of <note>original: "Euclid."</note> Euclid’s Elements, it will be: as AC is to IC, so is AB to OB, or to its equal IM. By dividing, as AI is to IC, so is OA to OB, or IM. By the initial assumption, AB consists of 5 ½ equal parts, of which IM is one. Therefore, OA will be 4 ½. The ratio is thus the same: 4 ½ is to 1 as the line AI (which contains 1142 semidiameters of the Earth) is to the other number, which explains the quantity of the earthly shadow IC.

<margin>The quantity of the earthly shadow.</margin>

Which is found by the "golden rule" <note>The Rule of Three, a mathematical method to find a fourth value from three known ones.</note> to be approximately 254 semidiameters of the Earth. Such then is the size of the Earth’s shadow. From this, you may gather a universal rule for investigating the shadow of any celestial body.

### A universal rule for investigating the shadow of any celestial body.

**L**et it be: as the excess of the Sun’s diameter over the diameter of the celestial body is to the body’s diameter, so the distance of the Sun from the body is to another value, found by the golden rule; for that value will be the length of the shadow.

# Problem XII
->To find the radius of the Sun in terms of the Earth's radius.<-

**L**et the Sun be A, its apparent radius <note>original: "semidiameter"</note> BC, which we taught how to find in the preceding sections; let D be the center of the earth. In triangle BCD, we have three known terms: namely, half of the angle BDC, under which we found the apparent radius of the Sun (which we assume to be 15 minutes when the Sun is at its apogee <note>The point in the orbit farthest from Earth.</note>); CD, which according to the preceding proposition is 1147 terrestrial radii; and the right angle CBD. Therefore, just as BC is to CD, so the diameter of the earth is to the diameter of the Sun; thus the diameter of the Sun will be to the diameter of the earth as 5 is to 1, and a little more. You will learn all these things perfectly through our **Uranometric instrument** <note>A specialized tool for measuring the heavens.</note>, as will be described.

# Problem XIII.
->Another much easier method of investigating the diameter of the Sun and Moon through the observation of their images projected into a dark place.<-

**A**t the time of observation, with all the windows of some room closed, let the light of the Sun or Moon be received through some round hole (X) onto a flat board, the outline of which should be traced with ink or red chalk. Let DEL be the body of the Sun or Moon, and X the hole: HRIq is the figure of the sun or Moon represented in the dark place on the board.

Because the rays of the Sun intersect each other in the hole X, they will necessarily leave a shaded angle equal to the luminous angle at the vertex. Thus, it will happen that as qR (the diameter of the projected light inside the room) is to the known distances RX or qX, so the known apparent diameter of the Sun DL is to the other; from this will come LX or DX, the distance of the Sun from the earth. If, however, the distance of the Sun from the earth was already known, and you desire to know the diameter of the Sun: let it be as the known RX or qX is to the diameter qR; so is XL or XD to the other, and the sought-after diameter will be produced.

->To find the magnitude of a solar eclipse, proceed as follows.<-

**B**efore the start of the eclipse, let the rays of the failing Sun or Moon be transmitted by the skill described into the interior wall of a house, or a board prepared for this, in which you will describe a circle divided into 12 digits <note>A traditional unit for measuring eclipses, where the diameter of the celestial body is divided into 12 parts.</note>; and move this back and forth until the depicted and divided circle corresponds on all sides to the projected circle of light. The segment of light will immediately reveal the Sun in diameter, providing the sought-after ecliptic parts or digits.

## The true art of measuring lunar and solar eclipses with the greatest ease.

<margin>Total and partial eclipse.</margin>
**U**niversal Rule: When the Moon is positioned opposite the Sun and has a <term>latitude</term><note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the ecliptic (the Sun's path).</note> that is either greater than or equal to the sum of the radii of the shadow and the Moon, its light will suffer no harm. But when it has a smaller latitude, it will suffer some loss, or the loss of its entire light; how this may be hunted for <note>original: "venari"; a common metaphor in early science for calculating or discovering a value</note>, you will now learn. Furthermore, as has been said before, an eclipse is twofold: partial or total. A partial eclipse is when the Moon touches the Earth's shadow with only a part of itself. A total eclipse is threefold: either without delay, with delay, or central. We shall provide examples for each of these in their proper place, so that the curious reader may better perceive this admirable work of nature, and may look up to and admire the near-divine skill of the human mind in uncovering it. But let us come to the matter at hand.

### Paradigm I.

### Given the latitude of the Moon from the ecliptic, and the diameter of the Moon and the shadow, to measure the magnitude of the eclipse.

**L**et there be in this diagram a circle designating the shadow at the place of the Moon’s passage, BCDE; B to the North, C to the East, D to the South, and E to the West. The center of this circle is A, the radius of the shadow is AC, and the radius of the Moon is GD.

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram illustrating a lunar eclipse. A large circle representing the Earth's shadow (umbra) is centered at point A and marked with cardinal points B (North), C (East), D (South), and E (West). A horizontal line CAE represents the ecliptic. A chord FGH traces the Moon's path through the shadow. Three moon discs are drawn along this path: at the start of the eclipse (F), at the point of maximum obscuration (G), and at the end (H). Lines connect the center A to the points F, G, and H, forming triangles for calculation. Various celestial symbols, including the Moon phase and zodiacal signs like Gemini, are present around the perimeter.</image-desc>

Furthermore, let the line CAE represent the ecliptic. Let the lunar path be FGH, such that F is the beginning of the defect, the Moon already touching the shadowy circle of the Earth's shadow—the dimmer and depriver of light—before the true opposition. Let the middle of the eclipse, or true opposition, occur at G. The end of the eclipse and the complete emergence of the Moon occurs at H. Let lines AF and AH be drawn, each containing the sum of the radii of the shadow and the Moon. Likewise, let a perpendicular line AG be drawn from the center of the shadow onto the line HF, which it will cut exactly in half at point G (according to the 3rd proposition of the 3rd book <note>Referring to Euclid's Elements</note>). Therefore, AG is the latitude of the Moon at the middle of the eclipse. I desire now to explore by how many <term>digits</term><note>A "digit" is a traditional unit for measuring eclipses, representing one-twelfth of the diameter of the celestial body.</note> the Moon is eclipsed; operate thus: Subtract the latitude of the Moon from the sum of the radii of the shadow and the Moon. The remainder will give 4 minutes and 54 seconds, which you should place into the rule of proportion thus: 36 minutes and 2 seconds <note>the total diameter of the Moon in this example</note> make 12 digits; how many digits do 4 minutes and 54 seconds produce? In this way, you will find 1 digit and 38 <term>scruples</term><note>A "scruple" (scrupula) here refers to a sixtieth of a digit.</note> (sixtieths of a digit). It is established, therefore, that the whole Moon does not disappear, but only 1 <math>\frac{38}{60}</math>—nearly two-thirds—of the lunar disk is obscured.

<margin>To investigate by how many digits the Moon may be eclipsed.</margin>
<margin>What the points of incidence are in an eclipse.</margin>
Furthermore, if you desire the minutes of the fall, or the <term>points of incidence</term><note>The distance the Moon travels from the moment it first touches the shadow until the maximum point of the eclipse.</note>—which are nothing other than the minutes of the Zodiac which the Moon traverses while overtaking the Sun from the beginning of the eclipse until its middle (if it be partial or total without delay), or from the beginning until the start of total obscuration (if it be universal with delay)—if, I say, you desire these points, operate thus: Let FG be the minutes of the fall, or the sixtieths of incidence, to which the sixtieths of completion (namely GH) are equal. These are explored by the penultimate proposition of the first book of the Elements <note>Euclid's Elements, Book 1, Prop 47—the Pythagorean Theorem.</note> in this manner: First, resolve the minutes into seconds by multiplication. Let AF be 3860 seconds and AG be 3566 seconds. The square of AF will be 14,899,600 seconds, and the square of AG will be 12,716,356 seconds. Subtract the square of AG from the square of AF; the remainder will be the square of GF (or GH), which is 2,183,244. Its square root is 1478 seconds, which makes 24 minutes and 8 seconds. These are the sixtieths of incidence or completion—that is, the loss of light and its recovery. To learn how much time corresponds to these sixtieths, do this: The hourly motion of the Sun is 149 seconds, and that of the Moon is 2160 seconds. The Moon's excess speed is 2011 seconds. Using this as a divisor, distribute the 1478 seconds of incidence (having first resolved them as is customary in the third rule); you will calculate the time of incidence as 44 scruples <note>minutes of time</note>, which is approximately three-quarters of an hour. And this method is to be observed in all partial eclipses.

**L**et the radius of the Moon (GB) in some eclipse be 17 minutes and 44 seconds, and the radius of the shadow be...

Therefore, the apparent Northern latitude of the Moon is 2 minutes 10 seconds.
According to the tables for the <term>seventh Climate</term> <note>A "climate" was an ancient geographical zone defined by the length of the longest day of the year; the 7th climate was roughly in the northern regions of the known world.</note>; if these tables do not fail us, around the eighth Climate 

<image-desc>A circular astronomical diagram showing a total solar eclipse. The central solar disk is completely covered by the lunar disk (A). Labels include B at the top, H and E on the left, G in the center, F and C on the right, and D at the bottom. The path of the moon passes directly through the center of the solar disk.</image-desc>

no latitude of the Moon would appear, but there would be a central meeting of the luminaries. However, in the seventh Climate, the ecliptic digits would be 11 with a third, because the semi-diameter of the Sun is 16 scruples with a <term>dodrans</term> <note>original: "dodrante"; a Roman fraction meaning three-quarters (9/12).</note>, and the Moon's is 17 scruples with an <term>uncia</term> <note>original: "uncia"; a Roman fraction meaning one-twelfth.</note>.
And the minutes of incidence (GF) are 33 minutes 47 seconds.
The hourly motion of the Sun is 151 seconds; that of the Moon is 2509.
The excess of the Moon is 1908 seconds. Therefore, the time of the fall is one hour and 4 minutes.

### Note I.
->On the proportion of motion to the Visual Diameter.<-

**T**he visual diameter of the Sun in the <term>eccentric</term> <note>A circle whose center is off-set from the Earth.</note> subtends 31 minutes, but at the opposite point it is 34; yet always, the proportion of the Sun's motion in an hour to its visual diameter is 5 to 66. Indeed, the visual diameter of the Moon at the <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in orbit farthest from Earth.</note> of the eccentric and the <term>epicycle</term> subtends 29 minutes; but at the apogee of the eccentric and the opposite of the epicycle's apogee, it is 36; yet always, the proportion of the Moon's motion in an hour to its visual diameter is 48 to 49. Let all these things be understood.

# Astronomy of Light-Dials.

In the past, there were two primary methods in use for observing the diameters of the luminaries <note>The Sun and the Moon.</note>. They either hunted for the quantities of the luminaries through <term>hydrology</term> <note>The use of water-clocks (clepsydrae) to measure time by the flow of water.</note> and the measurement of water, as <margin>Ptolemy <note>Claudius Ptolemy, the influential 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer.</note> observed the diameters of the luminaries.</margin> Cleomedes <note>A Greek astronomer known for his work *On the Circular Motions of the Celestial Bodies*.</note> testifies and teaches in Book 2, near the beginning; or they did so by the timing of the equinoctial risings, or by marking shadows, which they observed with great diligence at sunrise on the day of the Equinox using a <term>Scapha</term> <note>A bowl-shaped sundial.</note> or a hollowed-out hemisphere, just as Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial who wrote a famous commentary on Cicero’s *Dream of Scipio*.</note> describes clearly and at length in Book 1 of *The Dream of Scipio*, almost at the end. Through water-clocks, the diameter of both the Sun and the Moon was found to be the seven-hundred-and-fiftieth part of its own circle <note>That is, 1/750 of its 360-degree orbit.</note>, which is 28 <term>scruples</term> <note>original: "scrupula"; here referring to minutes of arc.</note> or minutes, and additionally 48 seconds. Through shadows, however, it was found to be the ninth part of an equinoctial hour, which contains one part and two-thirds <note>original: "partem cum besse"; a "bes" represents two-thirds of a unit.</note>, of which 360 make up a complete circle. But because such observations are deceptive and so slippery that it is easy to be greatly mistaken, Ptolemy rejects both methods in Book 5, Chapter 14. He shows that he discovered with a <term>dioptra</term> <note>An ancient sighting instrument for measuring angles or altitudes.</note> that the Sun is always contained within nearly the same angle; he estimated its quantity later from lunar eclipses while the Moon was near the peak of its <term>epicycle</term> <note>A small circle whose center moves around the circumference of a larger one, used to explain planetary orbits.</note>. At that time, it appeared to subtend the same angle as the body of the Sun. Having done this, he found the Sun's diameter to be 31 minutes and one third <note>31' 20''.</note>; because when the Moon was at its greatest distance from the Earth, such a diameter was shown by its eclipse. By a similar reasoning, he hunted for the diameter of that same Moon when it was lowest and nearest to us, finding it to be 35 minutes and one third, as he himself explains in Book 6, Chapter 5.

Furthermore, as usually happens in difficult and obscure matters, more recent authors disagree somewhat with Ptolemy, though they do not entirely agree among themselves. Albategnius <note>Al-Battani, a major 9th-century Arab astronomer.</note> sets it the same, yet Ptolemy asserts the diameter of the nearest Moon compared to its diameter when furthest at the new and full moon to be only about 29 and a half minutes. But the Sun’s incidence near its <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in the orbit of a celestial body where it is nearest to the Earth.</note> is 33 minutes and two-thirds, in which matter he followed partly his own observations and partly the distances of the Moon noticed elsewhere; see his chapters 30 and 43. Purbachius <note>Georg von Peuerbach, a 15th-century astronomer.</note> follows Albategnius for the most part, as is apparent from this place and from Proposition 215 of the *Epitome* <note>The *Epitome of the Almagest*, a summary of Ptolemy's work.</note>, which Regiomontanus <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg, a student of Peuerbach who completed the *Epitome* after his master's death.</note> finished after his teacher's death, delivering it as if by hand. He also handed down rules on how one may calculate the diameters of the luminaries from their hourly motions using his own tables, of which it may suffice to declare one example: in the solar eclipse of the Year [15]44, its hourly motion was 2 minutes and 21 seconds. Just as 5 is to 66, so 2 minutes and 21 seconds is to 33 minutes and 13 seconds. Above, however, from Purbachius's eclipse tables, we placed the Sun's diameter at 33 minutes and 30 seconds. Moreover, that there can be an analogy and similarity between the motions and diameters is clear enough from the above; from which it is established that when either luminary is furthest from the Earth, and therefore appears smallest to the eyes, it proceeds with a slower motion, etc. Wherefore it follows that although it is possible for a universal eclipse of the Sun to occur at some time, it can never appear naturally so due to the reason of <term>parallax</term> <note>The apparent change in position of an object when viewed from different locations.</note>, such that the whole Sun is eclipsed for the whole Earth universally.

### A Clear Proof.

> *As the Sun moves from apogee to perigee, the shadow of the Earth continuously decreases, and vice versa.*

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the relationship between the Sun's distance and the Earth's shadow. A large personified Sun with a face is shown at the top. Below it, a smaller circle labeled 'A' represents the Earth. Lines of light pass the Earth to form a conical shadow (the umbra) pointing downwards to a vertex labeled 'C'. Points E (a further position) and B (a nearer position) on the vertical axis represent different positions of the Sun. Points G, H, F, and D are used as geometric markers to show how the length of the shadow cone (the axis AC or AF) changes depending on whether the Sun is at point E or B. As the Sun moves closer (to B), the shadow cone becomes shorter (ending at F).</image-desc>

That the Earth's shadow decreases as the Sun approaches its center is manifest from this diagram, in which the Earth itself is A, the more distant body of the Sun is E, and the nearer is B. Therefore, when the center of the Sun is at B, the shadow extends as far as C; however, when the Sun is positioned at E, the shadow is consumed at F, which is closer to the Earth. Hear a brief proof. Let us suppose ED, BG, and AH, the semi-diameters of the Sun and the Earth, to be parallel. Since ED and BG are equal semi-diameters, they hold the same proportion to AH, by the 7th proposition of the fifth book of the *Elements* <note>Referring to Euclid's *Elements of Geometry*.</note>. By the 4th proposition of the sixth book, EC is to AC as ED is to AH; and EF is to AF as BG is to AH. Therefore, by the 11th proposition of the fifth book, EC is to AC as EF is to AF; and by the 17th of the same, EA is to AC as BA is to AF. But the first, EA, is greater than the third, BA, by hypothesis; therefore the second, AC, is greater than the fourth, AF, by the 14th proposition of the fifth book. Now, AC is the length, or axis, of the shadow when the Sun holds position E, just as AF is when the Sun is at B, closer to the Earth. And by the 14th proposition of the second book of the *Elements*, the cone ACH is to the cone AFH as AC is to AF. It is manifest, therefore, that the shadow of the Earth [decreases] together with what was said, and conversely increases in all directions, etc. Similarly, it is now clear that the Moon cannot fail [to be eclipsed] at a distance...

# The Ninth Book of the Great Art: Cosmom. Gnomon. Part II.

...standing at a true latitude from the ecliptic of 65 minutes. For the maximum semi-diameter of the Moon is 18 
<margin>The maximum limit of a lunar eclipse.</margin>
minutes and 4 seconds, and that of the shadow (if the Sun is at its highest point) is 46 minutes and 57 seconds; which, when joined together, make 65 minutes and 1 second. Therefore, if the full Moon has such a latitude, whether North or South, it will not fall into the shadow, but, merely grazing its edge, will shine with its whole disk, etc.

<margin>Why the Moon does not eclipse every single month.</margin>
It is also now sufficiently clear why the Sun and Moon do not eclipse every single month with a loss of their light, owing to the latitudes of the Moon—either the true latitudes, as in the case of the Moon, or the apparent ones, as in an eclipse of the Sun. For unless these three bodies—the Sun, the Moon, and the Earth, or our point of view—come upon the same straight line, or with no latitude or a very slim one, a failure of either light cannot occur. From this it is manifest that those same eclipses become the greatest and most terrible of all if the centers of these three bodies occupy the same straight line. Otherwise, they are smaller in proportion to the degree of latitude, etc. A total eclipse occurs when the whole body is obscured while the centers of the three bodies are positioned in what the Greeks call <term>obstruction <note>original: ἐπίπροσθεσιν (epiprosthesis), referring to one body being placed directly in front of another</note></term>, or as others say, <term>perpendicular alignment <note>original: κάθετος (kathetos)</note></term>.

A partial eclipse occurs when the same bodies do not occupy the same straight line. Let students read Cleomedes <note>A Greek astronomer from roughly the 2nd century AD</note>, who philosophizes on the first elements of Astronomy. Furthermore, the limits of eclipses for both luminaries have been discussed above. Aristotle, at the end of the second book of *On the Heavens*, among other reasons by which he demonstrates the roundness of the earth, draws an argument also from the eclipses of the Moon, which it suffers when it runs into the shadow of the earth while its disk is full. For it is established that shortly before and after the full moon, it never appears horn-shaped <note>crescent</note>, but always <term>gibbous <note>bulging or convex on both sides</note></term> and swollen; on the contrary, however, when it is failing while entering the shadow, or emerging from it again, it is always seen as horn-shaped. From this it is clear that the edge of the shadow, which distinguishes the shining part of the Moon from the darkened part, is neither a straight line nor a hollow one, but curved, and therefore the surface of the shadow itself is round and circular.

Otherwise, these kinds of <term>sections <note>original: ἀποτομαὶ (apotomai), meaning cuttings or segments</note></term> of the Moon's light would by no means occur in all lunar eclipses. From this it follows that the earth itself is spherical; for a shadow imitates, as much as it possibly can, the shape of the body by which it is cast.

Moreover, I know that students of these disciplines wonder by what skill it was discovered that the Sun, which appears scarcely a foot wide, far exceeds this great mass of the earth; and conversely, that the Moon, which to the judgment of the eyes equals the Sun, is nevertheless smaller than the same earth. Likewise, that the shadow of the earth is conical.

Finally, they wonder that the failure of the luminaries can be predicted for many years ahead, marking not only the place in the heavens, but even the hour of the day. Nor indeed do such things hold our admiration without merit. For the sharpness of human genius could never have penetrated into the knowledge of such great things unless some God led the way, as Plato most gravely says in the *Epinomis*. Therefore, these gifts of God must be preserved and propagated with all zeal. However, although the method is complete, in order to invite students I wish to recount a bare history, as it were, of the method without demonstrations, as briefly as possible.

### The method of the doctrine of eclipses preserved by Ptolemy.

<margin>Observation of parallax.</margin>
I. Ptolemy explored the parallax of the Moon with wonderful sagacity, and distinguished the true latitude of the Moon from the apparent, as he teaches in chapter 32 of book 5 <note>of the Almagest</note>. For in eclipses of the Moon it is necessary to have knowledge of the true latitude; likewise, the darkening of the Sun cannot be foreknown without the apparent latitude, and thus the doctrine of parallaxes, as is evident.

<margin>Distances of the Moon from the earth.</margin>
From this, among other things he judged, he announced by a geometric way that the maximum distance of the new or full Moon from the earth is 64 and one-sixth earth radii. Furthermore, from other observations he held the known proportions of the semi-diameters of the eccentric and the epicycle, and the eccentricity of the Moon, as was reported above.

<margin>Observation of semi-diameters.</margin>
II. Then he hunted for the quantities of the apparent diameters of the Sun, the Moon, and the shadow at conjunction and the full moon from observations in this way. First, by the use of a <term>dioptra <note>a classical surveying/astronomical instrument for measuring angles</note></term>, he noticed that the luminaries were contained by the same angle while the Moon was at its furthest distance. Next, he employed two eclipses of the Moon; in one of which, when the latitude of the Moon was 48 and a half minutes <note>original: scrupulorum (scruples), used here as minutes of a degree</note>, the shadow darkened a quarter of the Moon's diameter; in the other, however, it darkened half the diameter, while the Moon had a latitude of 40 minutes and two-thirds. In both eclipses, the Moon was moving near the top of its epicycle. From this it was clearly established that a quarter of the diameter of the furthest Moon occupies 7 and a half plus a third minutes in the Heavens according to our sight. These taken four times show that the diameter of the Moon was then 31 minutes and a third, to which the observed diameter of the Sun was equal. Finally, the semi-diameter of the shadow was revealed in the later eclipse as 40 minutes and two-thirds; for the center of the body of the Moon then touched the outermost edge of the shadow. From this it was similarly opened up that the diameter of the shadow is to the diameter of the Moon as 13 is...

# Photo-sciatheric Astrometry
<note>The title refers to "Astrometria Photo-sciatherica," or the measurement of stars using the science of light and shadows.</note>

to point 5. And he discovered this constant ratio in all other eclipses of the Moon. Although it is clear from these observations that the diameter of the shadow exceeds the diameter of the Moon, it does not immediately follow from this that the Moon is smaller than the Earth.

III. Therefore, by this geometric path—that is, according to the doctrine of plane triangles—he compares the apparent semi-diameters of the Moon and the shadow with the distance of that same Moon, measured in <term>semi-diameters of the Earth <note>The radius of the Earth used as a standard unit of measurement.</note></term>. Here he finds the semi-diameter of the Moon to be only 17 <term>minutes <note>original: scrupulorum</note></term> and 33 seconds, and that of the shadow to be 45 minutes and 38 seconds, where the semi-diameter of the Earth is taken as 60 minutes.

It is clear, therefore, that both shadows are conical—that is, shaped like a <term>turning post <note>original: metæ; a cone-shaped boundary marker used in Roman circuses</note></term>—eventually tapering to a sharp point, and because of this, the Sun is larger than the Earth, even if it only appears to be a foot wide, etc.

A certain judgment regarding the quantities of these three bodies could not have been made unless the <term>parallaxes <note>The apparent change in position of a celestial object when viewed from different points on Earth.</note></term> of the Moon had first revealed its distance measured in Earth radii. For if we assume the distance between the Moon and the Earth to be 84 Earth radii (keeping other hypotheses unchanged), it will be found, according to the same geometric doctrine, that the semi-diameter of the shadow is exactly equal to the Earth’s semi-diameter. In that case, the Earth's shadow would be <term>cylindrical <note>original: cylindracea</note></term>, or cast in the shape of a column, and would have no end, to use Pliny's words. Again, if we assume an even greater distance for the Moon, such as 170 Earth radii, the semi-diameter of the shadow (specifically at the place where the Moon passes through) would be shown as 2 Earth radii.

<margin>Distance of the Sun from the Earth.</margin>
Therefore, at this lunar distance, if the other hypotheses are not changed, the shadow will necessarily exist as a <term>paraboloid <note>original: παραβολοειδὴς (paraboloeidēs)</note></term>—that is, in the shape of a basket or a spinning top—so that the width increases infinitely along with the length, etc.

IV. Furthermore, from these points, Ptolemy argues by the same method that the distance of the Sun from the center of the universe contains 1,210 Earth radii; likewise, the Sun's semi-diameter contains five and a half of those same radii. Thus, the diameter of the Sun relates to that of the Earth as 11 to 2. Finally, he found the axis of the shadow to be 268 of those same radii. Therefore, according to Ptolemy’s opinion, the eccentricity of the Sun contains approximately 1,148 and a quarter Earth radii; however, this is shown by <term>Albategnius <note>The Latinized name of the Arab astronomer al-Battani (c. 858–929 AD).</note></term> to be 1,146 radii. See his chapter on this, etc.

<margin>Proportions of celestial bodies from knowledge of diameters.</margin>
V. Now it is easy to find the proportions of the three bodies from the knowledge of their diameters. For, according to the final proposition of the 12th book of <term>Euclid’s Elements <note>A foundational mathematical work from ancient Greece; Book 12 deals with the volumes of spheres.</note></term>, spheres are in a triple ratio of their diameters to one another. A triple ratio is produced by the cubic multiplication of the terms of a given ratio. Since the Sun's diameter is to the Earth's diameter as 11 is to 2, the body of the Earth will be to the Sun as 8 is to 1,331. For these cubes are produced from each term. Therefore, the Sun is more than 166 times larger than the Earth. In a similar way, you will find that the Moon is scarcely a fortieth part of the entire terrestrial globe, and only a 1/6644 part of the solar body, because its diameter relates to the Sun’s as 10 to 187, etc.

<margin>A heaven-measuring instrument.</margin>
You see, therefore, how many other things follow from the certain discovery of the Moon's parallax; for besides the fact that this has its use in predicting solar eclipses, Ptolemy first reasons from it how many Earth radii the lunar interval comprises. Then, from this very interval, he hunts for the ratio of the diameters of the Earth, the Moon, and the shadow; from which it is simultaneously revealed that the Earth's shadow is conical. From these points, he further gathers both the distance and the size of the Sun. Finally, by reversing the path, he establishes and proclaims the parallax of the Sun from its distance, which is otherwise hardly observable with instruments, etc. I have chosen to mention these things as briefly as possible for the sake of students. But if anyone desires to know what the Arabs have handed down concerning the sizes of other stars, let him read Albategnius, chapter 50, <term>Alfraganus <note>Latinized name of al-Farghani, a 9th-century astronomer.</note></term>, discourse 22, and others; although their opinions vary greatly, as is the case in an uncertain matter full of conjectures. For this reason, Ptolemy bypassed this entire topic. But now that we have explained these things as clearly as possible, let us proceed further.

# Great Art, Book IX. Cosmometry. Gnomonics. Part II.

...the larger [arm] can be moved through all the degrees of the semicircle. This being finished, and two lines IK and IM having been drawn in the middle of the arms meeting at I, a semicircle CGE should be described from I as the center, divided very exactly into 180 parts. This being done, with the compass opened from I, let the arc MN be described according to the length of the ruler IM; along this arc from I, at the interval of only one degree, let a line be drawn to arc MN, which will mark off one degree of that circle which would be described by the distance IM. Divide this degree M again into 60 parts, or minutes; this degree, divided into its minutes, serves for measuring the apparent diameters of the celestial bodies, as will be seen later. The larger this arc is, the more exact the measurements it will provide.

When this is done, let another semicircle or quadrant FHC be drawn, which should serve as a slider <note>original: 'cursoris', referring to a moving part of the instrument</note> mobile on center K on the line KD. Let the line IK or IB be divided into any number of parts you wish, say 1000 or 10000, or even more at the craftsman’s discretion; for the finer the division, the better and more safely you will work. Each of these parts should be considered divided again into 100 parts. Divide the line IM on the larger arm into the same number of parts. Then, on each line IB or IM, beginning from the center I, count 3436 parts—which is the number of miles we have found the Earth's radius <note>original: 'semidiametrum terræ'</note> to have—and transfer this space of the Earth's radius onto line IB and IM as many times as you can. When this is also performed, take two silk threads, strengthened beforehand with wax, which you will divide into spaces equal to the spaces of the Earth's radius; attach small pins <note>original: 'obolis', literally small coins, used here as anchors or pivot weights</note> to the centers of semicircles CGE and FHK to which the threads may be tied. You will then have the instrument prepared, as you see.

### Canon I.

-> To find the distance of the Sun and the Earth. <-

<image-desc>A vertical astronomical and geometric diagram occupying the right side of the page. At the top is a personified Sun (Sol) with a radiant face. Count 56 parts from point I of the Ouranometric instrument (mentioned on the preceding page) toward D, representing the distance of the Moon from the Earth (which we found above to be 56 Earth radii at its average distance). Extend the thread there so that it forms a right angle with line AD (which is easily done if, having moved the quadrant FHK to the said 56th point, you then draw the thread through 90 degrees). Then, from center I of the other semicircle CGE, let the second thread be extended through the 87th degree. Where these two threads meet, carefully note the parts of the threads (which ought to be always equal to the parts of line IEFK, not in number, but in the physical space by which one is compared to the other). These sides will give the distance of the Sun from the Earth, and from the Moon. Or, if the threads are not divided into parts, take the distance with a compass...

# Astronomy of Light and Shadows

This small triangle is similar to the large triangle formed by the distance of the Sun and the Moon from the Earth, together with the third side, which is the distance between the Sun and the Moon. Therefore, once one side is known, the remaining sides will reveal themselves. In this figure, the distance of the Moon from the Earth is assumed to be known; therefore, the remaining sides will also be made known. Thus, side AB—representing the mean distance <note>original: 'distantia mediocri'</note> of the Earth from the Sun as 1142 Earth radii <note>An Earth radius, or semidiameter, was the standard unit for celestial distances in this period.</note>—will give the sought-after interval between the Sun and the Earth.

Alternatively, this can be done by sines <note>referring to trigonometric calculations</note>. Let the Earth be B in the present figure. For the Moon when it is <term>dichotomous</term> <note>original Greek: 'διχοτόμω'; meaning half-illuminated, as during a quarter-moon phase</note>, let the part ION be the circle separating the shadowed portion from the bright portion. Let line IN be placed beneath it, directed toward our eye at B. Because the bright part ION always looks directly at the Sun, it follows that if line CO is extended perpendicular to line IN, it will reach the center of the Sun. Furthermore, let angle B be 87 degrees—the distance by which the half-illuminated Moon recedes from the Sun. Thus, the triangle ABO will have known angles: at B, 87 degrees by supposition; at the center of the Moon, a right angle; and the remaining angle A will be known as 3 degrees. Consequently, the sides will be revealed. Just as the sine of angle A is to the distance BZ (the Moon's distance from Earth, namely 56 Earth radii), so the sine of the right angle is to the other side; this will yield AB, the sought distance of the Sun from the Earth.

## Rule II.

### *Given the apparent diameter of the Sun (or the angle of vision) and the distance of the Sun from the Earth, to find the diameter of the Sun in Earth radii.*

Suppose the angle of vision, or the apparent diameter of the Sun, is 31 minutes at its mean distance from the Earth, which is 1142 Earth radii. You will find how many Earth radii the Sun's diameter contains with the help of the strings, using this method: Let two extended strings be joined at center I of the semicircle CGH. One string should be drawn through 90 degrees, and the other through 31 minutes on the MN scale of the larger arm of the square <note>original: 'normæ'</note>; that is, so the angle it makes at I is 31 minutes (the apparent diameter the Sun occupies in the sky). On the string or line IM, 1142 numbered parts will create an <term>isosceles triangle</term> <note>a triangle with two equal sides</note> exactly similar to the one formed by the lines of sight from the eye at the center of the world to the visual diameter of the Sun. Since the two strings IN and IM form the angle of vision at I, and their length is 1142 parts (the mean distance of the Sun), it follows that as IN (or IM) is to NM, so is the Sun's distance to its diameter. Since the side IN is known to be 1142 Earth radii, NM (the Sun's diameter) will also be known in those same units. Once this is obtained—since volumes are in a <term>triplicate ratio</term> <note>meaning the volume of a sphere increases by the cube of its diameter</note>—you will easily arrive at the knowledge of the magnitude or solidity of the solar body.

## Corollary.

**G**iven the distance of the Moon from the Earth and its apparent diameter, the magnitude of the lunar diameter relative to the Earth will be revealed by this exact same method. Once the proportion is found, the magnitude or solidity of the Moon will soon be known through the rule of the triplicate proportion of diameters, which we have described extensively not only in the preceding pages but in the third book of our *Magnetic Art* <note>original: 'Artis nostræ magneticæ'</note>.

## Rule III.

### *To investigate the distance of the Moon from the Earth using our instrument.*

**L**et the figure proposed on page 648 be repeated, where through the observation recorded there, we found triangle AEC. In this triangle, angle ACE is 45 degrees, and the angle of the shadow CAV (or DAE) is 46 degrees and a little more; when these are subtracted from 180 degrees, they leave angle CAE. The angle of <term>parallax</term> <note>the apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different points</note> will be AEC. Once these are found, you will find the distance of the Moon from the Earth with almost no effort using our Ouranometric instrument described on page 659. Place the semicircle FHK with its center above line KI at 3436 parts, which represents AC, the Earth's radius in known miles. Then, let one string attached to center I be drawn through the 45th degree of the quadrant CG; let the other string attached to the center of the semicircle K be drawn through the 46th degree of quadrant HF. At the point where these two strings intersect, look at the number of parts marked on the strings. Or, if they are not marked, apply the string over line IM (which is divided into parts equal to those of line IK); the parts cut off on line IM will give the sought altitude or distance of the Moon from the Earth.

# Problem XIV.
### To describe the proportions of the diameters of all the Planets to the Sun, and from these, finally, the lengths of the shadows.

## Rule I.
### The quantity of the diameter of the Sun, the Earth, and its shadow.

First, by the methods handed down above on folio 651, take the apparent diameter of the Sun and the Moon. The diameter of the Earth to the diameter of the Sun is as 5 is to 26, or as 1 is to 5 and a little more.

If you then transfer its length to the line **IM**, it will give you the sought length in units of the Earth's radius.

### Canon II.

#### To investigate the distance from the center of the earth, its size, and its shadow.

<margin>Discovery of the diameter and shadow of the body of Mercury.</margin>

**Y**ou will obtain the distance from the center of the earth in this way. Observe when Mercury <note>The symbol ☿ represents the planet Mercury.</note> recedes furthest from the Sun, and when it is at its greatest wandering in its <term>epicycle</term> <note>In the older geocentric model, an epicycle was a small circle centered on the circumference of a larger circle; it was used to explain the complex movements of planets.</note>. For it has been noted by astronomers that Mercury has a distance from the earth equal to that of the Sun when the Sun is at its average distance from the earth, namely 1142 earth radii <note>original: "semidiam. terræ"</note>. The Ephemerides <note>Astronomical tables or almanacs giving the positions of celestial bodies.</note> and tables will give you these positions. Given the time, take the apparent diameter of Mercury using the Uranometric instrument described on page 750, which Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the famous Danish astronomer known for his incredibly accurate naked-eye observations.</note> says he found to be 2 minutes. Then, on the line IM, or on the lines themselves, determine the distance of Mercury from the earth as 1142 of its radii, and draw the lines from center I through 2 minutes (or 10 seconds of the arc MN). For if you join the endpoints of the 1142 earth radii with a straight line, it will give you the diameter of Mercury's body in parts of the earth's radius; you can also obtain this mathematically with a compass. However, you will get it more accurately using sines as follows: as the <term>total sine</term> <note>In historical trigonometry, the 'total sine' is the radius of the circle used for calculation, often 100,000.</note> is to the right sine of half the angle of the vision (or the apparent diameter), so is 1142 to the other value; the diameter of Mercury's body will result. With that known, you will find its shadow thus: the furthest distance of Mercury from the Sun has been found by experts to be 571 earth radii; and the diameter of the Sun, as is clear from the table of proportions to be placed in the following sections, is to the diameter of Mercury as 26 is to 1 and ¾. Therefore, if with the help of lines you construct a triangle according to these proportions, so that the lines of the solar diameter attached to the extreme points touch the orb of Mercury at its given distance from the Sun, the meeting of the lines will give the length of Mercury's shadow (illuminated by the Sun) in parts of the earth’s diameter—namely 43—and the tip of the shadow will be 614 earth radii away from the Sun.

### Corollary.

**F**rom these things, it will be easily recognized whether the star Mercury can eclipse Venus <note>The symbol ♀ represents the planet Venus.</note> with its shadow. Since the tip of Mercury's shadow is 614 earth radii from the Sun, and Venus is 855 radii from the Sun (as will be seen in the following pages), the shadow cannot reach it.

### Canon III.

#### To find the distance of Venus from the earth and the Sun, its shadow, size, and other proportions, through shadow and light.

**B**efore we proceed further, the epicycle of Venus must first be outlined here, so that from its proportion we may arrive at the magnitude of the whole orb. It should be noted, therefore, that Venus at its maximum elongation is 48 degrees from the Sun. This being established, let the center of the earth be O; using this as the center, draw the arc ABC above the line OB, on which you count 48 degrees on both sides. Having drawn lines OC and OC, if you describe a circle from B within these, this will be the sought-after epicycle of Venus. Its <term>apogee</term> <note>The point in an orbit furthest from the Earth.</note> is N and its <term>perigee</term> <note>The point in an orbit closest to the Earth.</note> is X; within this circle Venus travels in various ways. While it traverses the semicircle NCX in the evening—that is, after the setting of the Sun—it is called <gloss>evening star</gloss> <note>original: "ἑσπέρος"</note> or Vesper; if indeed it traverses the semicircle XCN, it appears in the morning before the Sun and is called <gloss>light-bringer</gloss> <note>original: "φωσφόρος"</note> or Lucifer. It has been observed in these most recent times by the truly sharp-eyed <note>original: "Lynceis Astronomis," referring to the Academy of the Lynxes, the scientific society of which Galileo was a member.</note> astronomers that Venus undergoes almost the same phases, increases, and decreases of light in a year's time that the Moon <note>The symbol ☽ represents the Moon.</note> undergoes in a month's time. Thus, emerging from the light of the Sun from N into Q, it appears like a <gloss>full moon</gloss> <note>original: "πανσέληνος"</note>; in R it appears <gloss>gibbous</gloss> <note>original: "ἀμφίκυρτος"</note>; in A <gloss>dichotomous</gloss> <note>original: "διχότομος," meaning half-illuminated like a quarter moon.</note>; and finally in PT it appears <gloss>horned</gloss> <note>original: "κερατοειδής"</note>, or like a crescent. This truly <gloss>paradoxical</gloss> <note>original: "παράδοξον"</note> <gloss>phenomenon</gloss> <note>original: "φαινόμενον"</note> concerning the nature of the celestial world has provided modern scientists with distinguished material for philosophizing. From this wonderful phenomenon, the difficulty is solved that twisted the minds of almost all ancient astronomers in a marvelous way, as they were unable to grasp why Venus appears smaller near its perigee and larger near its apogee. The cause of this is very easily clear from knowledge of modern phenomena.

# Photo-Shadow Astrometry

...the apparent diameter of Venus <note>original symbol: ♀</note>, or the right sine of half the visual angle under which the said diameter is seen, is to the total sine, so is the apparent diameter of Venus to the perigean distance of Venus from the Earth, and the fourth proportional will give the result sought.

### *Corollary*

<margin>The Moon does not reach the shadow of Venus.</margin>
**H**ence it follows that the maximum shadow of Venus is 132 <term>Earth radii<note>A "semidiameter" of the Earth; the standard unit of measurement used by Kircher for cosmic distances.</note></term>, and its tapering point from the Sun is 957 Earth radii. From this it is inferred that the Moon does not reach the shadow of Venus, since the Moon is at a distance of 1034 Earth radii from the Sun.

## Rule IV.
### *To investigate the shadow of Mars <note>original symbol: ♂</note>.*

**F**rom the distance of Mars from the Sun, and the proportion of the diameter of one to the other, the shadow of Mars is investigated in exactly the same way as was done in the preceding sections. Since, therefore, its distance from the Earth, according to the aforesaid rules, is 1628 Earth radii; with the help of threads on our instrument, you will make a triangle into which you will insert the circles of the Sun <note>original symbol: ☉</note> and Mars <note>original symbol: ♂</note> according to the proportions of their diameters; and the shadow of Mars will immediately be revealed as 147 Earth radii.

### *Corollary*

<margin>The shadow of Mars reaches the shadow of no other planet.</margin>
**I**t is clear from this that Mars can eclipse none of the other planets with its shadow; since Venus <note>original symbol: ♀</note> and Mercury <note>original symbol: ☿</note> are too close to the Sun; while Jupiter <note>original symbol: ♃</note> and Saturn <note>original symbol: ♄</note>, being further from the Sun, are more distant than the shadow of Mars can reach.

### *To investigate the magnitude of Mars.*

**T**he magnitude of Mars is obtained, as in the preceding sections, by its apparent diameter and by its distance from the Sun. Its apparent diameter was found by craftsmen to be approximately 2 minutes <note>of arc</note>: and its distance from the Sun 1628 Earth radii. If, therefore, with these things known beforehand, you set up a triangle with the help of threads whose sides are 2 minutes apart (or form an angle of 2 minutes), while also maintaining its distance from the Sun: it will immediately be clear how many Earth radii are contained in the diameter of Mars. From this, consequently, the proportion of the spheres will emerge, and it will be as 1 is to 13, so is Mars to the Earth. Furthermore, you will see that the Moon <note>original symbol: ☽</note> is contained 40 times in the Earth, Venus 6 times, and Mars 13 times; but the Earth is contained 140 times in the Sun. Thus Mars will be slightly more than triple the size of the Moon, and more than double the size of Venus, and slightly less than half the size of Venus <note>Kircher's comparison here seems to suggest a specific ratio of volumes or diameters; he likely means Mars is smaller than the Earth but larger than the other "inner" bodies mentioned.</note>; and finally, compared to the Sun, as 1 is to 1820.

## Rule V.
### *To investigate the shadow and magnitude of Jupiter <note>original symbol: ♃</note> through the shadow of Jupiter itself.*

<margin>The magnitude of Jupiter.</margin>
**T**he distance of Jupiter from the Earth is found through <term>parallax<note>The apparent displacement of an object when viewed from two different lines of sight.</note></term>; its magnitude, however, is found through its diameter and its apparent distance from the Sun. They investigate its distance from the Earth through the shadow of Jupiter in this way: Since in these recent times that marvelous phenomenon of the "companions" <note>The moons of Jupiter, first discovered by Galileo in 1610.</note> of Jupiter and Saturn has been revealed; many things indeed unknown to previous times have become known through their motion. Indeed, the daily motion of the companions around Jupiter was observed to be 42 hours; in which time it was also discovered that they are hidden twice. With these things preserved, we will investigate its distance from the Earth following <term>Scheiner<note>Christopher Scheiner (1573–1650), a Jesuit priest and astronomer who was a contemporary and rival of Galileo.</note></term>. Let Jupiter be R, the orbits of the companions be LKIH, the Earth F, and the Sun G near the horizon: let the hiding places <note>occultations</note> of the companions be *a, o, PQ*; and the shadow of Jupiter be *RX*. Form, therefore, the triangle *RFG*, whose sides *RF, RG, GF* represent the distances of Jupiter from the Earth, from the Sun, and of the Sun from the Earth (which triangle you will easily form with the help of threads from the previously known distances). Since, therefore, due to the interposition of Jupiter, the companions are hidden first on the side *TK*, and then in its shadow *OPO*, nothing is required to know the sides of the triangle except that we know the arc *TO*, which they traverse from their first occultation until they reach the shadow of Jupiter. We know this very easily by this industrious method: as the 42-hour daily motion of the companions is to a full circle (an orbit of 360 degrees), so are two hours (the time, namely, which they consume in the arc of occultation) to another value: the sought arc *TO* will come out to be 17 degrees. To this angle at the vertex *FRG*, it will be equal by 15 degrees and 1 minute. The distance of the Sun from the Earth on line *FG* will also be known; therefore the remaining sides *RF* and *RG* will be known. Extend, therefore, in our <term>Ouranometric instrument<note>Referenced on page 750 of the original work; a device used for measuring or calculating celestial positions.</note></term> a thread through *I*, and another through the 17th degree of the quadrant *GH*. Then take a certain ruler, on which you mark off 1142 Earth radii in the parts of line *IM*. You will adapt this space marked on the ruler between the threads so that one thread is normal <note>perpendicular</note> to the ruler, and the other thread terminates the intercepted space; and you will have all the sides of the triangle known in the parts of the intercepted space, or line *IM*. Or even more easily on line *IK*, intercept 1142 Earth radii; then with one thread extended from *K* through 90 degrees, and the other through 17 degrees, mark the intersection of the threads, for this will give the triangle whose sides are known in the parts of *IM* or *IK*. But by the use of sines, the operation...

# The Great Art, Book IX. Cosmometry. Gnomon. Part II.

...Let it be that as the tangent of 17 degrees is to the secant of 17 degrees, so 1142 is to another value; there will result the line RG, the distance of the Sun from the Earth; to another; there will result the line RF, the distance of the Earth from Jupiter. Again, let it be that as the tangent of 17 degrees is to the whole sine <note>The "whole sine" (sinus totus) was a standard trigonometric term in the 17th century referring to the radius of the calculation circle, usually assigned a value of 100,000.</note>, so 1142 Earth semidiameters <note>A "semidiameter" is the radius of a celestial body; in this case, the radius of the Earth is used as a standard unit of measure.</note> are to another; there will result the line RG, the distance of the Sun from Mars.

### The Shadow and Magnitude of Jupiter

**Y**ou will determine the shadow of Jupiter <term>♃</term> in this way. Subtract the minimum distance of the Sun (1101) from the maximum distance of Jupiter (4753); the remainder is the maximum distance of Jupiter from the Sun <term>☉</term>, which is 3652 Earth semidiameters. Having obtained this, you will find through the preceding rules that the diameter of the Sun to the diameter of Jupiter has a ratio of four and one-fifth, namely as 21 is to 5. Therefore, let it be that as 21 is to 5, so 3652 is to another value; the sought-after shadow of Jupiter, 869 Earth semidiameters, will result.

<margin>Jupiter's shadow does not eclipse Saturn.</margin>

### Corollary

**F**rom this it is evident that Jupiter's shadow does not eclipse Saturn, because Saturn is removed by 8365 Earth semidiameters: whereas the shadow of Jupiter, when added together with its distance from the Sun, extends only 4521 semidiameters. Furthermore, having the distance—namely the average distance of 3990 Earth semidiameters—and its apparent semidiameter of 2 3/4 minutes <note>A "minute" is an angular measurement equal to 1/60th of a degree, used here to describe how large the planet appears in the sky from Earth.</note>, the proportion of the diameters, and consequently the proportion of the spheres, will be obtained, as was stated in the preceding sections.
