## Rule VI.
### To investigate the shadow, distance, and magnitude of Saturn <term>♄</term>.

<margin>The visual diameter of Saturn is 19 minutes.</margin>
**F**rom the parallax of Saturn <term>♄</term>, Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the preeminent naked-eye astronomer whose data Kircher relies upon.</note> found—following the instructions given above—that its average distance from the Earth is 10,550 Earth semidiameters. Therefore, if you determine this interval by means of measuring-threads along with its apparent diameter of 19 minutes, the proportion between the diameters of Saturn and Earth will be produced. From this, once mechanically arranged, the magnitude of Saturn is found, as well as its shadow, which we have found to extend to nearly 12,527 Earth semidiameters. However, anyone who is aware of the irregularity of Saturn’s body <note>original: "Saturnini corporis inæqualitatem." Kircher is likely referring to the "ears" of Saturn—the rings—which appeared as strange bulges in early telescopes and made measuring a clean diameter difficult.</note> will see that its diameter can only be acquired with great difficulty.

### Corollary.

**I**t follows from this: if the fixed stars are no further from us than 13,000 Earth semidiameters, as some authors maintain, they could be eclipsed by Saturn's shadow. Anyone, therefore, who applies himself to this observation will undoubtedly find himself discovering many new and paradoxical things for the world.

## Rule VII.
### To investigate the distances of the fixed stars from the Earth by means of a shadow.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the measurement of stellar distance relative to Earth's shadow. A star (A) is positioned at the top. The Earth is represented by a circle (ABC) with center (B). Below the Earth, a vertical rod or "stylus" (EF) is erected. A shadow (DF) is cast on a plane (DFV). Lines connect the star (A), the Earth (B), and the triangulation points (E, F, D) to demonstrate the geometry of shadow-based measurement.</image-desc>

**S**ince the distance of the fixed stars from the center of the Earth is so great that it can hardly be explored with a certain dimension through instruments, and since no parallax is granted by which we might arrive at their further distance from the Earth: nevertheless, despite these impediments, I say that if a star were so bright that it cast a shadow—such as Sirius <note>referred to here as "Canicula," the Dog Star</note>, Lyra, etc.—we could arrive at the desired knowledge by its help. We demonstrate the matter thus. Let the terrestrial globe be **ABC**, its center **B**, the fixed star **A**, the stylus <note>A gnomon or upright rod used to cast a shadow.</note> **EF**, and the shadow of the stylus **DF**, erected normally on the plane **DFV**; let **DA** be the ray of the star **A**. I say that the altitude of the star can be made manifest by this industry. For since **FE** is perpendicular to **DV**, the triangle **EFD** is <gloss>right-angled</gloss>, whose base **DF** is known from the magnitude of the apparent shadow, and **EF** is known from the combined height of the erected stylus, as has been said. Therefore, the angle **DEF** is known; when this is subtracted from two right angles, the exterior angle **AEB** will remain.

Furthermore, angle **AEB** is the complement of the angle of the star's elevation above the horizon, which, once explored, makes that known. Therefore, in the triangle **EAB**, with angles **AEB** and **EBA** known, together with the side **EB** (which consists of the Earth’s semidiameter), the side **AB** will become known. Thus, the distance of the star from the center of the Earth is established, if we admit the established hypothesis—namely, that the shadow **DF** is notable, and that some ratio of the Earth's semidiameter **FB** to **AB** is understood that falls under the senses, which was to be demonstrated. But if indeed no shadow were sensible, the business would have to be dispatched by a certain tube, or a canal applied to an index through which the star was to be viewed; for the support of the tube would be in the place of the stylus, the line of sight in place of the ray; and finally, a line drawn normally from the opening of the tube to the support would exhibit the "shadow."

## Another very subtle method for investigating the distance of the fixed stars from the Earth.

**B**y another investigation, truly most subtle, you will investigate the distance of the fixed stars from the Earth through the parallax of the annual orbit <note>The "annual orbit" refers to the Earth's path around the sun, a concept central to the Copernican system, though Kircher often frames this within a Tychonic or geo-heliocentric context.</note> with altogether admirable skill in this manner. Let **A** be the insensible Earth, **BC** the orbit, the sphere of the fixed stars **Solis HG**, let the star be at **G**, and let the proportion of lines **BA**, **AG**, and **BG** be sensible. First, let the Earth **A**, the Sun **C**, and the star **G** be in the same straight line; there will be no parallax, because the lines **CG** and **AG** drawn from the Sun and the Earth to the star will coincide. Now let the Sun be not at **C**, but at **B**, and let the line **AB** be drawn to **D**, or **H**, the place of the Sun among the fixed stars. And because the Sun at **B** is that point to which Tycho refers the eccentricities, apogees, and simple motions of the orbits of the Planets: therefore, from the rules usually handed down in astronomy, the quantity of the angle **DBG** (between the line from the Sun through the Earth and the line from the Sun through the star) will become known; and at that same moment, the place **F** of the star **G** among the fixed stars, as it appears from Earth **A**, will become known through an instrument. Therefore, the arc between **D** (the place of the Sun) and **F** (the observed place of the star) will be obtained, which is the measure of the angle **DAF**. And because the proportion of **BA** to **AG** is sensible, but **B** is outside the line **AG**; therefore the lines **BG**, **CG**, and **AG** will be inclined, and the angle **DBG** will be equal to angles **BAG** and **AGB** joined together, as an external angle is to the internal op-

# The Great Art, Book IX. Gnomonic Cosmometry. Part II.

...equal to the opposite angles of the triangle BGA, and the parallax will be BGA; when these are established, the side BG will become known: namely, the distance BG of the Sun from the star;

<margin>A most ingenious method for investigating the distances of the fixed stars from the earth.</margin>

AG indeed is the distance of the star from the earth; BA is also the distance of the Sun from the earth. The only difference here is that EF is not the parallax, because it measures neither the angle BGA nor EGF; rather, DE measures the angle DAE, or BAG. If, however, the two angles A and G in the parallactic triangle BAG are equal to the external angle HBG (which is equal to the internal opposites joined together): the whole arc DEF will be given as known. From this, the arc DE is subtracted, leaving EGF, the angle of the <term>parallax of the shadow</term> <note>original: "parallaxsis umbræ"; a technical term relating to the displacement of a shadow or body relative to the observer's position</note>, by whose help the quantity of the diameters of the worldly bodies then becomes known by a truly divine stroke of genius.

### Rule VIII.

->To investigate the heights of Comets from the earth.<-

Let two locations differing in altitude be taken under one and the same meridian; and let the distance of a Planet be observed at one and the same hour from some fixed star existing on the same meridian, and let the parallax be carefully noted, if there be any; the sought-after height of the comet will then become known from the angles and sides of the triangle. I shall clarify the matter with an example.

<margin>Observation of a Comet made by Tycho.</margin>

By this industry, Tycho <note>Tycho Brahe (1546–1601), the famous Danish astronomer known for his accurate celestial observations.</note> and Hagecius <note>Thaddaeus Hagecius (1525–1600), a Czech astronomer and physician.</note>—the former in Uraniborg, the latter in Prague, which locations are under almost the same meridian—each observed at a prearranged hour and day, taking a star existing in the same vertical line, which they call the Vulture <note>original: "Vulturem"; the star Altair in the constellation Aquila was historically referred to as the "Falling Vulture."</note>. Let the meridian of the earth's globe be AB. Uraniborg is A, Prague is B. Let the star of the Vulture be F, C be the Comet in the same vertical line FCE; the distance of each, FC, was seen to be 17 degrees and 52 minutes. Wherefore, each observer beheld it in the same place in the Heavens: an evident sign that the Comet was higher than the Moon and other Planets that possess a sensible parallax. For if it had been at D, the observer at Uraniborg would necessarily have seen it at E. Therefore, it would have had a lower altitude, and consequently a greater distance from the star F, as the line AE clearly shows. From this it is clear that those Comets which are found to have a smaller parallax than the Moon were also above the Moon, as the very nature of parallax proves. Furthermore, you shall attain the distances in this way: Multiply the semi-diameter of the earth by the <term>total sine</term> <note>original: "sinum totum"; in historical trigonometry, this refers to the radius of the sine table used in calculations, often a large integer like 100,000.</note>, and then divide the product by the right sine of the maximum parallax; the result will give the sought-after distance of the Comet from the earth. If you subtract the square of the earth's semi-diameter from the square of that distance, the square root of the remainder will give the distance of the Comet from the earth's surface. For just as AI, the right sine of the parallax ACI, relates to the total sine IC, so the semi-diameter of the earth relates to the other, and the sought distance IC will be produced.

### Another Way.

<margin>parallax</margin>

Once you have the maximum <gloss>parallaxes</gloss> <note>The original text breaks the word "parallaxibus" across the line and margin.</note> of any two planets or phenomena in the sky, and the distance of one of them from the earth, you shall multiply the given distance by the sine of that phenomenon's maximum parallax, and divide the product by the sine of the remaining parallax; the fourth number resulting from the division will give the sought distance of the phenomenon.

### Device I

->Given the proportion of the diameter of the Sun and the remaining planets along with their distances, to mechanically determine the lengths of the shadows.<-

# The Great Art, Book 10. Part 1 of Magic.

...the radius of the glass sphere to the Solar radius is as 5 to 26. These two globes should be placed next to the first column at a distance of 1142 parts, where the radius of the earth is 1 part. Then you will illuminate the glass sphere with a light placed inside, and you will see—not otherwise than if you were present in person in the heavens—how far the globe is illuminated beyond the halfway point of the earth; and how great the shadow of the earth is, and consequently, if you take the distance of the Moon <note>original: ☾</note> from the earth, you will clearly see the passage of the Moon through the terrestrial shadow; and you will look upon all these things that have been said thus far as if you were another judge of nature. But if you make another globe which, according to the second column of the table, relates to the earth as 5 to 17, and you place this globe in its proper place according to the distance that the Moon is from the earth—namely, at the average distance of 56 terrestrial radii—if, I say, you place this globe between the Sun and the earth, you will discover all the mysteries of a Solar eclipse, and which peoples are able to see the Solar eclipse and which are not. Indeed, if you appropriately apply the motion to both bodies, you will also see the duration of the eclipse itself, and other things which astronomers pass down in such intricate ways; and you will look upon how much of the earth's surface its shadow covers, clearly and with incredible pleasure of the mind, having been made higher than the heavens themselves.

<margin>How apogee and perigee can be shown in the Cosmometric sphere.</margin>
If, however, you move the bodies proportionally according to the apogees and perigees <note>The points where a celestial body is furthest (apogee) or closest (perigee) to the Earth.</note> of the Sun <note>original: ☉</note> and Moon <note>original: ☾</note> and the other eccentric points, from this you will also find the diversity of the shadows and their thickness, just as if you were moderating the very reins of light. I said a glass globe because, since this sphere represents the Sun, it ought to be illuminated so that from the light diffused into all the bodies, the nature of eclipses can be better discerned. It can, moreover, be illuminated in two ways: first, by placing a candle inside; but since a candle placed inside does not illuminate the sphere on every side—which is of great importance in this business—it could be covered with the thinnest paper: for in this way it can communicate light more equally to the whole sphere. The second method, as it spreads a greater light, so it can achieve a better effect: a sphere or crystal ball, to which a light is applied from behind at such a distance from the sphere until it illuminates the whole sphere like a globe of fire, and you will have a Sun that rivals the celestial Sun in all things, as has been said. A concave mirror, which receives the light appropriately, will also perform the same task.

### Machine II.
### *To adapt the bodies of the planets to the body of the Sun and the earth according to the proportions shown in the table.*

If, indeed, according to the second and fifth tables, you make the remaining bodies of the planets having the stated proportion to the body of the Sun, and you arrange them according to their distance from the Sun as before, with the earth meanwhile holding its place in the middle; there will offer itself to you a spectacle not only wonderful, but pleasant beyond what can be said. For first, how great the length and width of the shadow produced by the Sun illuminating the body of each planet will be seen: whether the same shadow touches the earth or other bodies? And how much one shadow is greater than another? How much of the earth they obscure with their shadow? And similar things of this sort will be clearly open to view <margin>A wonderful spectacle.</margin> with demonstrative proof <note>original Greek: τεκμηριώτως</note>. From this it will be clearly revealed whether the stars have their own light, or whether it is communicated from the Sun. It will also be seen whether the Moon can acquire any reflected light from the earth illuminated by the Sun during a new moon; and innumerable other things, which I leave to the curious reader to consider.

### Machine III.
### *To construct a Cosmometric Sphere.*

This sphere could be better constructed according to the system of Copernicus. Therefore, let there be made in some very large hall a sphere according to the system of Copernicus; for I have found this most suitable for our machine, because the glass sphere placed in the center in the position of the Sun will be better able to achieve its operation in this layout. According to the given proportions of the bodies, and the distance of each body or sphere from the Sun and the earth, let orbs be made, each of which has a motion corresponding to its planet. This device will be explained at length in our *Thaumaturgic Mechanics* <note>A reference to Kircher's other mechanical works</note>; for you will have a perfect Sciatheric sphere <note>A sphere used for measuring shadows or telling time by the sun.</note>, in which it is permitted to gaze upon all the miracles of the heavens extraordinarily <note>original Greek: περιτῶς</note>. If, however, the bodies of the planets were at an equal distance from the Sun, they would cast shadows according to that quantity which the figure shows: thus the earth would cast shadow A; Saturn <note>original: ♄</note> shadow B; Jupiter <note>original: ♃</note> C; Mars <note>original: ♂</note> shadow D; Venus <note>original: ♀</note> E; Mercury <note>original: ☿</note> F; all different, according to the difference of the sizes of each. Many mysteries pertaining to Astronomy could have been brought forward in this place. But since those can be gathered from other places in this work, lest we overstep the limits of our purpose, we have deliberately kept silent. Now indeed, weary of the abundant light of the world, [we rest] under its shadow...

# The Great Art, Book IX. Cosmometry. Gnomon. Part II, etc.

looking down upon the orb of the lands from above—narrow, and for the greatest part covered by the sea, and even in that part where it stands out, widely desolate, and either scorched <note>referring to the tropical "torrid zone" believed to be uninhabitable</note> or frozen—he would say to himself: "This is the point which, among so many nations, is divided by iron and fire. Oh, how ridiculous are the boundaries of Mortals! It is truly a point in which we wage war, in which we sail, in which we arrange kingdoms." These are the words of Seneca <note>Seneca the Younger (c. 4 BC – 65 AD), a Stoic philosopher who often wrote on the insignificance of earthly strife compared to the vastness of the cosmos</note>: which we conclude with these following verses.

->To see how small a portion of the universe it is,<-
->Which we carve into proud kingdoms with magnificent words,<-
->Dividing it by the sword, purchasing it with shed blood,<-
->Leading triumphs from a part of a meager clod of earth;<-
->For that mass, when viewed by itself separately,<-
->Is indeed great: but if you compare it with the ceiling<-
->Of the starry sky, it will be like a point, or like a seed.<-
->This is the seat of men, this the home of wild beasts<-
->And of birds: from this narrow prison, how much<-
->The flowing moisture of the Ocean steals from the Earth!<-
->Add here the sea, add the lakes and the wide marshes,<-
->And the rivers which undermine mountains from their steep<-
->Summits, or stand motionless in sluggish pools.<-
->While these things snatch by force, and those drown the world in a whirlpool,<-
->The greatest part of the tiny earth is hidden under the waters.<-
->What remains floats like a small island in the great deep:<-
->Even of this, how much is either desolate with sands,<-
->Or swells into vast mountains without fruit or tree?<-
->Or burns with excessive flames? Or is numb with cold?<-
->Or lies untamed, refusing to be softened by human cultivation?<-
->Or is deadly to living things with its poisonous juices?<-
->Oh, the shame! Oh, the headlong madness of a foolish prayer!<-
->How small a portion of reality it is, in which glory raises itself,<-
->Anger roars, fear terrifies, grief burns, and poverty<-
->Compels one to seek wealth by the sword, by snares, by flame and poison!<-
->Truly, even human affairs seethe with trembling tumult.<-

But what need is there to traverse the Heavens, when Astronomers have so declared these things that it is permitted for us, even placed on this narrow orb of lands, to contemplate the amplitude of the Heavens? Therefore, if ever the smallness of the earth appears visible to us, if ever we gape to fill our minds with fleeting things; let the untiring journeys of the Heavens come to our mind; let us contemplate the pleasant turnings of the wandering stars <note>the planets</note>; let us measure in our mind the most ample and most pleasant field of the <term>Aplanis</term> <note>From the Greek 'aplanes,' referring to the sphere of the "fixed stars" which do not move relative to one another</note>, and the innumerable flocks of fixed stars that graze within it. For thus, satisfied by the delight and beauty of Celestial things, and conceiving the Idea of the Astronomers—not only in that part which approaches more to the dignity of the image, but also in that which supplies to us a greater harvest of pleasures—we shall at last be rolled, perpetually happy, toward that supramundane sphere <note>A reference to God or the infinite divine realm</note>, whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere.

# OF ATHANASIUS KIRCHER
## PRIEST OF THE SOCIETY OF JESUS
# THE GREAT ART
## OF LIGHT AND SHADOW
### Book Ten.
# THE MAGIC OF LIGHT,
## AND OF SHADOW.

->In which the more hidden effects of Light and Shadow, applied to various uses, are discussed.<-

## PREFACE.

### On Magic, and the purpose of this book.

<image-desc>A large woodcut drop cap 'I' featuring decorative scrolls, leaves, and vine motifs.</image-desc>

**I**t seems the same thing has happened to us in this work as to those who, while preparing a sumptuous banquet filled with every kind of delicacy for their friends, set aside the rarer courses for the final meal. Since we have so far discussed at length in nine whole books the miracles and wonderful works of Light and Shadow, and the admirable things that can be done by their means, we believed we would win favor with the curious Reader if, in this last book—as if in a certain recapitulation <note>original: "anacephalæosi", a Greek-derived term for a summary or summing up</note>—whatever was rare, curious, paradoxical, and prodigious, hidden under the gloom of Shadow and the darkness of Light, we were to bring out into the open and apply to rare and prodigious human uses, and to what I might call <term>recurring wonders</term> <note>original Greek: παίγνια ἀνακύκλωτα (paignia anakyklota), meaning cyclical toys or amusements that repeat their effects</note>. Our goal is that the Reader, contemplating the inexhaustible treasures of hidden riches even within the lowliest things, might recognize that great and admirable Divinity by whose nod all things stand, and whose craftsman’s hand has worked such greatness in all things; and having recognized Him, might praise and love Him, and finally possess Him forever. 

For this reason we have titled this section "Magic"—not that kind which we detest as a deceptive, superstitious, impure, and impious habit handed down by the Devil as Master, at whose very name Christian ears should shudder; but rather that **natural magic**, which we establish as twofold: one contemplative, the other practical. **Contemplative Magic** is a certain more secret and abstruse wisdom regarding things deeply hidden within the mysterious majesty of nature; parts of which Aristotle and Theophrastus (in the book *On Marvelous Things Heard*), and many others, have touched upon while contemplating the hidden miracles of nature. The other is **practical magic**, the producer of unusual works, such as we propose in this book (and which has more commonly taken the name of Magic for itself), which pours forth into the light, through undiscovered methods, whatever is admirable in the individual disciplines and arts. Strong in this art, Archytas <note>Archytas of Tarentum (428–347 BC), a Greek philosopher and mathematician credited with inventing the first self-propelled flying machine</note> is said to have suspended a wooden dove with certain counterweights so that it flew through the air by the propulsion <margin>Archytas's dove.</margin> of an enclosed breath of air. A work of this kind...

<meta>This page serves as an introduction to Book 10, where the author defines "Natural Magic" and its various branches, specifically focusing on the "Magic of Light and Shadow" which he divides into three specialized fields of study.</meta>

# The Great Art, Book 10. Magic, Part 1.

<margin>Archimedes’s burning mirror.</margin>
Archimedes displayed his work in a marvelous sphere and in a burning mirror <note>A legendary device said to have been used to set fire to Roman ships by concentrating sunlight.</note>. Severinus Boethius used to exhibit bronze serpents that hissed and statues that blew trumpets, and he performed many other things, on account of which he complained that he was accused and condemned as if he were steeped in the evil arts <note>Boethius (c. 480–524 AD) was a philosopher whose mechanical inventions, like water clocks and sun-dials, were so advanced they were sometimes mistaken for sorcery.</note>. Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a scholar and friar rumored in folklore to have created an "android" or magical automata.</note> is said to have brought forth a dry tree trunk adorned with leaves and flowers within the space of about two hours, along with countless other things; so much so that there are as many types of *Natural Magic* as there are branches of the practical sciences. 

<margin>Albert’s Chemical Tree.</margin>
Thus *Chemical Magic* produces portentous transmutations and mixtures of metals. Medical magic draws out truly extraordinary effects in curing illnesses. *Music*, and the other mathematical sciences—*Geometry*, *Arithmetic*, *Statics*, *Optics*, and *Astronomy*—produce such unusual effects that no one could easily explain the reasons for them, unless they were thoroughly skilled in the mysteries. And to these, one can rightly add the *Magic of Light and Shadow*, which, since it consists of certain subtle principles not obvious to everyone, should undoubtedly excite great wonder in the minds of the spectators. 

<margin>Horographic Magic.</margin>
We have divided this into three parts. The first part we have called *Horographic Magic*, or concerning marvelous *Clocks*; in this, we elevate the movement of *Light* and *Shadow*, and the actions of rays, to produce clock-like effects that are utterly paradoxical and—*if I may say so without boasting*—I will not say have never been written about by anyone, but have never even been seen. 

<margin>Parastatic Magic.</margin>
The second part contains *Parastatic Magic* <note>Relating to the representation or projection of images; often a precursor to the magic lantern.</note>, through which the <term>wonders</term> <note>original Greek: θαύματα</note> and marvelous operations of both reflected and refracted rays are brought to light through fires, various lights, and colors. 

<margin>Catoptric Magic.</margin>
The third part is called *Catoptric Magic* <note>The branch of optics dealing with mirrors and reflection.</note>, by which a <term>metamorphosis</term> <note>original Greek: μεταμόρφωσis</note> or transmutation of various things into other things is performed with the help of all kinds of mirrors. To these, finally, certain supplementary works are attached at the end. In all of these, we have aimed to personally test each experiment before it was made public, so that we would not sell uncertainties as certainties and defraud the curious reader of both time and money. For I know how many rare, marvelous, and unheard-of things many people promise, and how much empty nonsense they babble; yet reason and experience—if you carefully bring these claims back to the anvil—cry out against them, and they truly achieve nothing except to drive the student to a dead end and utter despair. I criticize their haste in handing down these matters all the more freely because I am confident that these works will be more pleasing to noble lovers of truth. Having briefly introduced these points, let us now approach the work itself.

PART ONE.

# HOROGRAPHICAL MAGIC
## OR
## CONCERNING EXTRAORDINARY CLOCKS.

->In which everything relating to the more hidden<-
->description of the hours is clearly, faithfully,<-
->and genuinely revealed.<-

### Definition of Horographical Magic.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'V' featuring ornate floral and leaf patterns.</image-desc>

**W**e call this section <term>Horographical Magic</term> <note>From the Greek "hora" (hour) and "graphia" (writing/drawing)—the art of constructing sundials and clocks.</note>, because where the previous books end, this begins. It teaches methods far removed from common human use, to be observed not only in the drawing of the hours, but also in the delineation of other celestial circles. By these methods, effects are produced whose causes are not easily grasped, even by the most skilled. For this reason, we have quite rightly named it horographical magic.
<margin>The wonderful power of Light and Shadow.</margin>
Indeed, there is a wonderful power in Light and Shadow. As they intermingle with all things and constitute everything in the sensible world, they seem to perform the same function as the <term>World Soul</term> <note>The "Anima Mundi," an ancient philosophical concept of an intrinsic spirit that connects all living things on Earth.</note> does in Plato's *Timaeus* <note>One of Plato's dialogues that speculates on the nature of the physical world and the creator.</note>—namely, acting as the cause and origin of all sensible effects and exotic operations. Yet, only he who has established a wise combination of all things can truly know this power. But let us now begin the matter itself.

---

### CHAPTER I.

*Concerning hidden horography, to be established by a ray that is partly direct and partly reflected or refracted.*

**A**s the subjects of direct, reflected, and refracted clocks were treated at length in Books 4, 7, and 8, it remains for us to apply the rules delivered there to the presentation of more hidden effects. Let it be so.

---

*Problem I. Preparatory* <note>Original: "Parafcevasticum," a term derived from Greek meaning a preliminary or introductory exercise.</note>

<insert>
*To describe a <term>horodictic egg</term> <note>Literally a "time-showing egg."</note>, in which a certain bright spot in a dark place demonstrates the hours in place of a pointer.*
</insert>

<margin>Proposition I.</margin>
**W**henever light, falling upon a shape that is in some way opaque, casts a shadow; to those situated in a dark place, the shadow will present itself on any opposite translucent plane in a shape similar to the proposed opaque object. 
<margin>Proposition II.</margin>
Again, whenever light falls into any shaped opening, or upon the opaque edges that terminate it, the light will again express a shape similar to the shape of the opening on an opposite translucent plane to those situated in a dark place. You will find all these things demonstrated at length in Book 2. Relying on these principles, let us see by what method <term>clocks</term> <note>Original: "Horologa vasa," literally "clock-vessels."</note> are to be arranged in dark places without any <term>stylus</term> <note>A gnomon or pointer that casts a shadow.</note>, using only light or shadow.

**T**ake the egg of a hen, a goose, an ostrich <note>Original: "struthio-cameli."</note>, or any other bird—the larger it is, the better (as is evident in the first figure of Illustration 24, marked with the letters ABCD). Remove the white and the yolk through two holes, C and D, made at the poles of the shell. Parts of an axis should be passed through these holes and secured so that the time-teller, holding the egg by both protruding ends of the axis, can turn the egg toward the Sun as desired and fix it in place where he wishes. 
<margin>Construction of the horodictic egg.</margin>
In the middle of the egg's length at point A, let another very tiny hole be made, through which the Sun's ray, penetrating, may show the hour with a round light on the opposite side. However, the hours in

Through these points of division, hidden straight lines drawn from A will intersect the semi-circle of the egg ACBD at specific points; through these points, parallel lines drawn on the egg will produce a <term>polar sundial</term> <note>A sundial whose plane is parallel to the Earth's axis</note>. You shall then inscribe the <term>sun-path</term> <note>original: heliodromus; a scale showing the sun's path through different signs of the zodiac or seasons</note> by the exact same method we prescribed in Book 5. *But if these things should perhaps seem difficult to anyone, he may, with the help of the observational instrument we described on page 269, inscribe both the hours and the sun-path without any difficulty at all, provided the egg is placed on the hour-mapping board in such a position that the meridian equinoctial ray entering through the hole makes an angle with the plane equal to the <gloss>complement of the pole's altitude</gloss> <note>The angle remaining when the local latitude is subtracted from 90 degrees</note>. For by this method, using an original model of any kind of sundial, those various types of dials—along with the sun-path and the entire science of the <term>prime mover</term> <note>In older astronomy, the outermost celestial sphere that carries all others; here refers to the motion of the heavens</note>—will be described upon the egg.*

<margin>The use of the time-telling egg.</margin>
The use of this egg is marvelous. First, if you fit the egg tightly into the shutter of a window in a dark room, with the ends of its axis protruding so that it blocks every ray of light, and the equinoctial or line CD on the egg is positioned exactly in the plane of the equator: it will happen that when the shutters are closed and the room is darkened, a ray of the Sun sent through the hole will form a very bright little star on the opposite side of the illuminated egg—like a small torch in a glowing shadow. This "star" will run between the circles all day long, showing the time and the hours to the great astonishment of the beholders, who cannot see where this little light originates or how it so constantly indicates the hours and the other secrets of the heavens.

## Corollary.

From this it is clear how this same artifice can be exhibited in all bodies that transmit light, provided they are not entirely transparent. Such materials include certain types of marble, paper, parchment, an empty eggshell, and similar things, whatever their shape may be.

## Problem II.

->How to represent the shadow of the figure of Death in a dark place, so that although the shadow is perpetually unstable—now growing, now shrinking—it nevertheless always shows the hours with its extended shadowy hand to those standing inside.<-

<margin>See fig. 2. Illustration 24.</margin>
First, make a paper cylinder ACBE, of the same shape as the <term>Nuns' Wheels</term> <note>original: Rotæ Monialium; revolving hatches used in convents to pass items through walls without the nuns being seen</note> used for conversations, which is permeable to light. In this, you will expose a figure of Death with a scythe, cut out from thick paper at position D, to the Sun. You shall then describe the hours on the inner surface of the cylinder. Take the tip of the finger as the end of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>original: styli; the part of a sundial that casts the shadow</note> I, and following this rule, inscribe the hours on the cylinder according to the rules proposed in Book 4. Once the cylinder is positioned magnetically so that the part BEF turns inward and ACL turns outward, the time-telling image of Death will be constructed. As soon as the sun shines, the shadow of Death appearing to those inside will demonstrate the depicted hours with its left hand. The same can be done with a paper cube, as follows.

<margin>Another method using a cube.</margin>
Let a paper cube BDCEQNO be made of thin paper, with the corners that terminate and support the paper made of fine, thin wood. Inside its sides, a sundial should be described in the exact manner handed down in the "Shadow-measuring Proteus" <note>Problem 7, page 349</note>. Let the given size of its gnomon be the side of the cube, and its tip be at A, the final point of the shadow of the figure of Death. You will describe the figure of Death on the side of the cube ECNO, which you will cut out so skillfully that the remaining parts perfectly express the figure of Death.

<margin>Telling time through light.</margin>
Once this is done, with the windows closed in some location, let this cube (having been previously positioned magnetically) be inserted into the shutters so that the paper sides and bottom can be seen from every angle. When the Sun shines, a certain bright and phantasmagoric shadow of Death will be projected onto the opposite side of the cube, the fingertip of which shows the hours drawn there. We have often displayed this experiment, not without fear from the beholders, who could not grasp by what artifice this shadow was represented, nor how, since it is always changing, it nonetheless demonstrated the hours so constantly on the opposite side with its extended finger. If you wish to show a black shadow, you shall fashion the figure of Death (or some other thing) from a metal plate, thick paper, or wood; it is sufficient, however, that only the extremity of the skeleton be formed.

<margin>Telling time through shadow.</margin>
You will erect this in that position on the open side of the cube CENO, so that the tip of the finger falls on point A. The Sun, casting the shadow of the skeleton outside the cube, will display a black shadow of Death to those inside in the dark place, which demonstrates the hours just as before.

From these things it is clear that any figure, whether bright or shadowy, can be displayed by the said method, such as we have shown here in the "Shadowy Eagle" (figure 4). In its breast N is a small crack through which the Sun's ray...

# Book 10 of the Great Art: Part 1 of Magic

### Problem III.

*To exhibit the figures of the seven planets in light or shadow, so that each one, on the individual days of the week, demonstrates the hours of its rule with the same attributes.*

**F**irst, let a cube, a rectangular prism, or a paper cylinder be made—a receptacle, to be sure, most fit for this business. Second, let a wheel be made of thicker paper divided into seven segments: BA, CA, DA, EA, FA, GA, and HA. In each of these, let the figures of the seven planets (or any other things) be depicted, as the figure for this Problem teaches. Each figure should hold either a scepter, a spear, or something similar in its hand, the tips of which should all fall upon the center of the wheel, A, where we also establish the apex of the hour-telling shadow or light. Third, you shall cut out these figures along their outer edges, as was done in the previous examples. Then, fix this wheel in the window of the room so that it can be rotated around as desired, with the center of the wheel falling upon the upper side of the cube. Fourth, with the wheel thus established and rotatable, you shall make an opening in the side of the cube or cylinder equal to one of the segments. Then, on the opposite side of the paper system, you shall describe the planetary hours <note>an ancient system where the day and night are each divided into twelve hours, each ruled by a planet in sequence</note> according to the method handed down in Book 4, with as many circles responding to the seven days of the week, in which you shall write the characters of the ruling planets in order. Thus, you will have the sought-after planetary horoscope <note>here meaning a device to see the planetary hour</note>.

<margin>Use of the planetary clock.</margin>
The use of the clock is this: When you wish to observe the planetary hour—for example, on a Thursday—you will turn the wheel in such a way that the segment with the image of Jupiter aligns precisely with the opening made in the side of the receptacle. The solar rays entering and grazing the edges of the figure of Jupiter will project a "light-shadow" <note>original: "lucumbri," a term for light shaped by a cutout to act like a shadow</note> figure of Jupiter upon the sides of the paper receptacle. I say the tip of the scepter in the image’s hand will show the sought planetary hour to those positioned outside the cube in the room. Once the hour is obtained, if you wish to know which planet is ruling, proceed within the circle assigned to Thursday up to the hour indicated by the light terminating the scepter; in that same place, the character of the ruling planet will appear.

### Corollary.

**F**rom this single light-shadow <note>original: "lucumbri"</note> paradigm, it is clear by what means entire historical scenes constructed by this kind of hour-telling artifice, as well as family coats of arms and other <unclear>unknown</unclear> <gloss>great wonders</gloss> might be exhibited to the point of a miracle. But since we must hasten to other matters, we wish to leave those for the curious Reader to investigate further.

### Problem IV.

*In a discontinuous place, with unequal walls and various surfaces and all kinds of planes—such as might be found in the rugged, jagged hollow of some overhanging mountain, or even within the ruins of Palaces and Churches—to delineate clocks by this art so that no one can conceive the mechanism, and no one can discern either the lines or the shadow showing the hours except from a certain fixed point.*

**L**et the place in which the clock is to be delineated be the interior porch (A B) of some building, discontinuous with a multiple variety of planes, as Figure V shows. First, take our following "Mesoptic" instrument <note>a sighting or projection device for complex surfaces</note> and fix it at some location that seems more convenient to the prudent engineer for delineating the clock (namely at point O), so that it cannot be moved from that spot. Before this is done, however, you shall prepare the instrument with this art: On the "veil" <note>a transparent screen or grid</note> of the instrument, you shall delineate from point G (as the center) a vertical clock, set to the elevation of the pole <note>latitude</note> of your region, just as was described at length in Book 4. Or, if you do not wish to mark the veil, the points of the hours marked on the wooden frame will suffice. This being completed, you should have a long rod equipped with red chalk or charcoal; or, if the place is higher than even a long rod can reach, the task must be carried out by a luminous ray in the dark, or by the reflected light of the Sun during the day using a mirror. This industry should be performed first at night, or even during the day if the business is to be carried out within a chamber. With the place darkened and the veil first positioned magnetically <note>aligned with a compass</note>, you shall place a light at point G by the dioptra <note>a sighting tube or hole</note>, and the "fiducial rule" <note>original: "regula fiduciæ," a straightedge used for sighting</note> shall be led from C, the center of the clock, through the points of the hours. ## Horographic Magic

The most uneven irregularity of surfaces will project a shadow line; if you paint a colored line along this shadow on the said surfaces, that same line will show the desired hour. You shall do the same for painting the remaining hour lines. However, to do this by means of **reflected light**, proceed as follows. Place a **mirror** in the middle of the drawing board of our <term>Tiretic instrument</term><note>A specialized drafting device or "observatory" used by Kircher for perspective and surveying, previously described on page 270.</note>, in which a horizontal sundial has been depicted. Then, rotate the entire machine so that the tip of the gnomon's shadow always grazes the hour points on the <term>tropics</term><note>The lines representing the Summer and Winter solstices.</note>. At the same time, mark the points reflected from the mirror onto the wall. These reflection points, joined into a curved line, will give you the tropics on the wall, along with the endpoints of the hour lines.

Therefore, once everything has been properly prepared, as we said at the beginning, you shall fix the instrument in a certain place so firmly that the surface of the <term>veil</term><note>A transparent grid or piece of fabric used as a reference plane for projection.</note> is precisely in the primary vertical plane, and the small beam *EF* corresponds to the meridian line. Once this is done, let a thread be stretched over the point for, let us say, six o'clock in the morning. Then, placing your eye at the **aperture G**, observe which parts of the discontinuous surfaces of the objects the stretched thread touches. If you draw a line through these points (marked one by one with red ink), you will have the line for the sixth hour on the said surfaces. If, however, a rod cannot reach every location, one should proceed in the said manner by placing a light source opposite the **diopter G** <note>a sighting hole or tube</note>. Using a <term>fiducial rule</term><note>A straightedge used for measuring or sighting.</note> extended from *CE*, you shall sketch the hour lines according to the shadow of the rule (which is the easiest method of all). Once this is finished, place the thread over the point for the seventh hour and, through aperture *G*, observe which points on the wall it falls upon; the line drawn according to these will give the seventh hour line. Proceed in the same way for describing the other hour lines. The tip of the gnomon can be any point on the axis. You will find the point thus: with your eye at aperture *G*, look through the center of the sundial *H* marked on the cloth; for this visual ray represents the **axis of the world**. Therefore, the tip of any object falling upon this visual ray can serve as the tip of the style that demonstrates the hours. Whether you erect a column in place of a style, or hang something falling from above into the ray, or extend something protruding from the sides that touches the visual ray, the hour will always be shown. Thus, you will have prepared a sundial which will only appear correctly to an eye placed at point *G*; outside of that spot, you will see nothing except a confused scattering of fragmented lines. For this reason, all who see it will be struck with wonder, and will be unable to perceive the logic of this by any means. That this sundial is correctly constructed, I demonstrate as follows.

Since a vertical sundial has been depicted on the cloth, and the "veil" represents the plane of the primary vertical, and the axis is established according to the appropriate angle, the eye applied to the aperture and directed at the hour lines will perform the same function as the light of the Sun illuminating the axis at point *G*. For example, when the Sun is positioned in the circle of the sixth hour, casting a shadow from point *G*, it must also necessarily fall upon the line of the sixth hour described on the veil; consequently, passing through the transparent veil according to the <term>actinobolic</term><note>original: actinobolæ; referring to the "throwing" or radiation of light rays in a pyramid shape.</note> diffusion, it will fall upon that line on the wall which the ray of the eye had determined according to the line on the veil. Or even in this way: if a physical axis is conceived to be extended from point *G* through the center *H* along the visual line to the opposite wall, the end of the axis on the wall will necessarily be the center of the sundial, and the axis, by hypothesis, will be in the position of the axis of the world. Since we also suppose the sundial on the veil to be correctly drawn, when the Sun shines, the shadow of the axis will necessarily fall upon one and the same hour line on the veil and on the various objective planes. Since the sundial depicted on the veil is nothing other than a section of the actinobolic (or radiant) pyramid from point *G* onto the objective walls...

### Corollary

From this, it is clear how other types of hours, as well as the projections of circles, can be described on similar planes. For if you inscribe the hours from sunrise and sunset, or the parallels of the zodiac signs, onto the polygraphic <term>veil</term><note>A "veil" or *velum* was a grid-like drawing aid used by artists and mathematicians to map 3D space onto 2D surfaces.</note>; and then proceed by the aforementioned method, you will have the hours from sunrise and sunset, and the parallels of the signs, inscribed upon the said planes in a truly marvelous fashion.

To this category belong all those clocks which we taught how to construct in our "Sciatheric Proteus" <note>original: *Proteo nostro Sciatherico*. This refers to Kircher’s own invention, a multi-purpose sundial named after the shape-shifting god Proteus.</note>; I would not wish these to be confused from here on.

### Problem V

*To construct a Reflective Astrolabe <note>original: *Astrolabium Anacampticum*. "Anacamptic" is an archaic term for catoptrics, the study of reflected light.</note>, so that a ring in the hand of a statue demonstrates both the hours and the full parallels of the Sun with lines of light: that is, to arrange a mirrored ring so that a beam of light projects onto a wall the entire parallel of the sun which the Sun describes on any given day on any plane, showing the movement of the entire "prime mover" <note>The *primum mobile*, or "first moved," in Aristotelian astronomy was the outermost sphere of the heavens that carries all others.</note>. This light beam will observe not only the movement of the Sun from east to west (the daily motion), but also its own progression through the signs of the zodiac so constantly that throughout the day, a radiant or bright hyperbola, for example, will appear projected immovably on a wall, but on the following day, it will be seen to have ascended or descended by one degree with the Sun. Furthermore, within this line of light, we can skillfully arrange another brightness so that, as the sun moves from east to west, an added light moves along that stationary line to perfectly demonstrate the hours; I believe nothing more wonderful in this genre has ever been observed.*

We read in a Hebrew work titled *Shiltei ha-Gibborim* <note>original: *Schiltegibborim*, meaning "Shields of the Mighty," a 17th-century work by Abraham Portaleone.</note> that Solomon placed a statue in the Forest of Lebanon from whose eyes flashing rays showed the course of the entire heavens. Most people consider this story a fable, and many claim it was a magical statue; we, however, assert that the matter is purely natural and arises from this, our "Magic of Light and Shadow." In fact, we shall attempt to present something even more ingenious in this place.

First, let the reflective <note>original: *anacampticum*</note> clock (Eastern or Western) be delineated on the veil of our mesoptic <term>instrument</term><note>A "mesoptic instrument" was Kircher's term for an optical device used for observing and projecting images.</note> according to the rules passed down in the catoptric art. Let the site be enclosed on all sides; let window T face the rising and setting Sun. Once the instrument is arranged in windows S and T such that the veil is in the meridian plane, then, applying your eye, see where the hour lines described on the transparent veil intersect the wall. Lines drawn through those points will give the desired clock. Furthermore, if you describe the rest of the celestial circles and the apparatus of hours on the same veil, and then transfer them to the wall using this method, nothing remains but to arrange the mirrors that show the time by reflected light in both windows in this manner:

In both windows S and T, at point G of the bar GF, let two ring-shaped segments of a cylindrical or conical mirror be placed, so that their plane is in the equinoctial plane. To each of these, you should glue a small piece of flat mirror <gloss>to the eye</gloss><note>original: ὡς τῆς ὄψεως - Greek for "for the purpose of sight/view."</gloss>; and the clock will be prepared. When the Sun rises, the ray entering through the window will reflect the light hitting mirror T onto the opposite wall A. Since the segment is cylindrical, it will project—according to the precepts of our Catoptric Art—the entire parallel of the Sun in which the Sun is then positioned, remaining stationary all day. From the flat mirror, however, it will project a circular light that travels through the bright parallel throughout the entire morning, showing the hours and other celestial circles. As the Sun enters the meridian, the mirror of window S will gradually begin to be illuminated and will show the same things on the opposite wall. 

It can hardly be expressed how much admiration this excites in viewers, as they do not grasp how the bright solar parallel remains stationary all day, yet on the next day is seen to have moved up or down a degree with the Sun; while the light from the flat mirror proceeds through that bright parallel from east to west with a steady and constant motion, as if it were alive or being carried by someone. If you place these cylindrical mirror segments (or the ring) on the finger of a statue standing near the window, positioned on the axis of the world, you will then have that miracle of Solomonic wisdom which the Hebrews so greatly admire; a statue, I say, whose ring shows the science of the entire "prime mover" in a dark place.

When these things are performed correctly, it will produce the greatest admiration in viewers to see the hours and other details shown on a plane with no <term>gnomon</term><note>The part of a sundial that casts a shadow.</note> and no shadow, but by a single bright point caused by the intersection of the circular and straight lines of light—and only when the sphere is directed in a certain way. ### Problem VII

->*How to describe a fantastic clock on a wall such that it shows the hours by a reflected ray of the Sun only in the dark and with closed windows; but when the windows are opened, the entire fantastic mechanism with all its lines and colors vanishes in an instant, leaving the wall without any lines.*<-

Let ABCD be a closed place, F a window, and G a hole or small crack through which the "species" <note>In 17th-century optics, "species" refers to the visible images or forms cast by objects through light.</note> of things may enter the room. The delineation of the sundial will be managed thus: at point H, let a hole be made of the size the business requires. Then, taking our <term>mesoptic instrument</term><note>A perspective-calculating tool invented by Kircher.</note>, let an inverted horizontal sundial be painted on its transparent cloth, as you see. Then, with the small rod EF pulled out so that the end G corresponds exactly to point G of the window, and with the eye applied to point G, let the appropriate sundial be drawn on the exterior area according to the sundial described on the cloth, in exactly the same way as was done a little earlier; and you will have the sundial completed. 

Furthermore, to make this sundial truly magical—that is, inconceivable—act as follows. First, with the chamber closed on all sides, outside it in an open place or space KK, you will arrange long poles, or <term>sarissas</term><note>Long pikes used by ancient Macedonian phalanxes; here used as large physical markers.</note>, reeds, or stretched ropes into rays, so that their "species," radiating through the window hole G (or the tip of the rod EF), correspond everywhere to the lines of the sundial depicted on the veil. All of this you will easily manage with the help of this mesoptic instrument of ours applied from the outside. 

Once this is also finished, if you desire to see the fantastic clock: remove the mesoptic instrument and close the window. Behold, suddenly the "species" of the reeds, pikes, and poles (which were arranged in a confused manner outside) radiating through the hole G, will exhibit the depicted sundial inside. In this, a bright spot will both illuminate the dark wall of the chamber along with the dim light entering at the same time, and on that illuminated area, it will show the hours—delineated not with real color, but with a truly fantastic one—to the great perplexity of the onlookers. When the window is opened, however, this entire fantastic machine, vanishing in a moment, will leave nothing except empty walls destitute of all color. 

A clock of this kind, once exhibited by me at <term>Avignon</term><note>Kircher taught at the Jesuit college in Avignon, France, in the 1630s.</note>, seized everyone with such admiration that many afterwards confessed that this exotic spectacle seemed to them to be nothing but the work of an evil spirit...

### For describing the hours in a crystalline globe.

Nothing can seem more portentous than this, especially if the glass is sealed at a glass-blowing lamp in such a way that the selenite sheet, with the clock and pictures, can never be removed again. By this art, certain solid spheres are prepared in Venice, inside which they represent little demons painted on selenite through hidden grooves in such a way that they seem to have either grown into them naturally or to have been placed there by magical art.

### Problem IX.
->*To establish another clock, in whose plane many bright circles of different colors are cast, yet only one of those circles is capable of showing the hours with a bright azimuth.*<-

First, let a horizontal clock be made from an Almucantar-azimuth <term>Almucantar-azimuth<table>An astronomical table used to map the sun's altitude (almucantar) and its compass direction (azimuth) onto a flat surface.</table></term> table; once this is done, you will fashion a reflective <note>original: "anacampticum"</note> cylinder by this industry. Let a mirrored cylinder A be made, adorned either from glass, steel, or from rounded crystalline selenite, in which the cylinder is covered with paper or some other 

<margin>See figure 1, problem 9, illustration 25.</margin>
material, so that only the cylindrical mirror sections EFGH stand out. Or, if you prefer to accomplish the matter with more secret craftsmanship, you may insert as many rings into the cylinder, each of which is made of a different color of glass and darkened with mercury; or if you cannot obtain colored glass, let the darkening material of the mirrors be of a different color, of which more will be said below. These things having been done, let the mirrored segments CBD be placed upon this cylinder in the manner of colures <note>original: "colurorum"; astronomical circles that intersect at the poles</note>, and you will have the machine prepared. Thus, when this cylinder is placed on the meridian line of the clock, so that the center of the cylinder's base is distant from the position of the clock's stylus by the space of the radius of the cylinder's base; then with the greatest admiration you will see as many circles projected onto the plane as there were mirrored segments in the cylinder. All will be of different colors: the first bright, the second red, the third green, the fourth purple. Yet out of all these, only one determines the hours—namely, that one which is as distant from the plane as the height of the stylus for which the clock was constructed, specifically ring E. Moreover, it will show the time by this industry: rotate the reflective colures CBM until the reflected light is projected in a straight line, and where this cuts the outermost bright circle E, there it will show the desired hour. The remaining circles, although they serve for nothing but ornament in this case, can nevertheless serve if you construct particular clocks for them. Thus, if there were as many clocks as there were reflective mirrored circles, that circle would show the hours which was as distant from the horizontal plane as the height of the stylus of the clock whose hours it demonstrates.

### Corollary.
This prodigious machine could be most conveniently displayed within some round building, such as the Pantheon here in Rome; a cylinder of such thickness as would be a third part of the said opening <note>the "oculus" or circular hole in the roof</note> would be placed in its orifice. For the Sun, radiating its rays into the different colored rings and projecting circles into the entire interior of the building, would imbue it with a wonderful variety of colors, with no one even suspecting the cause of the miraculous radiation.

# Horographic Magic.
<note>original: "Magia Horographica"; the art of drawing or writing the hours, specifically through technical or "magical" means</note>

Now, however, standing upon these same foundations, we shall hand down certain things removed from common human understanding; so that the curious reader may know how many wonders can be derived from foundations of this kind. Therefore let there be:

### Problem X.

> *To delineate a miraculous sundial <term>horoscope</term> <note>original: "horoscopium"; here referring to a device for showing the hour rather than an astrological chart</note> in a glass sphere so that, first, a little globe hanging in the center of the water shows the hours by its shadow on the opposite part of the glass—just as the shadow of the earth falls on the opposite region of the Heavens, if the eye could reach there. Second, that it shows the hours described upon itself by its own shadow in the space of 24 hours. Third, that it exhibits eclipses of the Moon according to the model of nature.*

<margin>See figure 2, Plate <term>Iconism</term> 25.</margin>
Four things must be provided in this horological mechanism. First, the little globe must be fixed in the center of the water; how this is done we have taught in Book II of *The Magnetic Art*, Part I, regarding Magnetic Statics. Second, the inscription of the hours on the globe and its revolution upon itself; the method for which is handed down in Chapter 24 of our *Magnetic Magic*. Third, the description of the hours on the surface of the sphere, which shall be done according to the method handed down in Book 6, Part 1, Problem 5. Let there be, therefore, a glass sphere **ABCD** and a little globe **G**; **E** is the shadow acting as the hour index in the shadow of globe **G**, which revolves upon itself; **DB** are the hours described around the circuit of the sphere; **BD** is the horizontal circle dividing the upper from the lower hemisphere. In the hemisphere **CBDG**, therefore, the <term>horolabium</term> <note>a clock face or dial</note> will be delineated with all the celestial circles, precisely by the reasoning and method which we handed down at length in Book 6, Part 1, Problem 5: and you shall have the magical clock you sought. Its use will be this: the sphere being situated according to the 12 o'clock line described on the rim of the sphere, and exposed to the bright Sun, it will happen that the rays falling upon the middle globe will cause the shadow of the globe to show the hours and the rest of the celestial lines on the opposite part of the sphere, refracted equally on all sides. In this, a thing will seem wonderful and almost miraculous: while the shadow of the globe is seen to show the hour on the rim of the vessel, diffused through the medium of the liquid just like the terrestrial shadow through the medium of the ether, the middle axis of the shadow—in its own revolution made upon its own center—will also show the hour, which will always correspond to the hour shown by the shadow on the rim of the glass sphere.

<margin>A shadow-measuring <term>schiatheric</term> demonstration of eclipses.</margin>
By what means eclipses of the Moon can be demonstrated, I now reveal. Let the shadow-measuring <term>schiatheric</term> <note>relating to the use of shadows to tell time or measure</note> markers of the "head and tail of the dragon" <note>original: "capitis & caudae draconis"; these are the Lunar Nodes, the two points where the Moon's orbit intersects the ecliptic, where eclipses occur</note> be inscribed in the Zodiac of the glass sphere, precisely in the manner we taught it should be done in Part 3 of the *Physico-Astrological Proteus*, page 408. Let a golden figure of the Full Moon also be depicted in the serpentine coils <note>referring to the path of the ecliptic</note> at that place in the Zodiac where you know beforehand that eclipses will occur; and the shadow **GE**, necessarily passing through that point of the Zodiac, will exhibit a segment of a failing Moon on the figure of the Moon. All these things happen so naturally that one might think himself snatched up into heaven to see everything firsthand. This mechanism, moreover, is very easy and is constructed with almost no trouble.

It should be noted, however, that all these things will be exhibited more perfectly if the sphere is placed in a dark room, in a window or a hole exactly the size of the sphere: for since the shadow of the little globe can scarcely be seen due to the abundance of light (because of its thinness), the circular segment of the conical shadow ought to be observed on the hour lines themselves.

### Problem XII.

> *A Siren with a mirror, as soon as it is exposed to a glass sea, swimming in the center, will show the hours in a reflected-refracted manner.*

<margin>See figure 3, Plate 25.</margin>
Let there be a vessel of any form **AB**, in the opposite sides of which you describe a clock at the height of the mirror from the bottom, according to the precepts handed down in the *Anaclastic Art* <note>the study of refracted light</note>. This will be achieved if you pierce the mirror in the hand of the Siren in the center; for the ray of the Sun, passing through that hole, shows the refracted hours on the opposite part of the vessel beneath the water; but this [shows them] from the mirror in a refracted-reflected way; in a word, it will show the hours equally by a refracted ray and a refracted-reflected ray. By what means it is brought about—through the magnet **D** placed at the bottom of the vessel **CD**—that the statue, moved through the water, stabilizes itself so that its mirror maintains its position in the vertical plane, we have said in the preceding problem, and figure 3 declares it sufficiently. When these things have been performed with the greatest diligence, if you desire to exhibit a pleasant spectacle to friends, you shall release the Siren with her mirror, hidden somewhere and tied; she, feeling herself released, will immediately betake herself to the center, where she will situate herself as if commanded, soon to show the hours—now refracted, now refracted-reflected—beneath the water by her pierced mirror.

### Problem 13.

*To describe a sundial with such ingenuity that, within an infinite multitude of confused lines and pins placed in various positions, this chaotic mess of things will nevertheless display an orderly clock, exactly demonstrating the hours, when viewed from a certain point.*

**F**irst, let a machine **CEFD** be made, whose tube **AB** contains a <term>polyhedral glass</term> <note>a multi-faceted lens that can multiply or recombine images</note>; once this is done, you shall delineate the sundial as follows. Separately on paper, let a vertical sundial be drawn, as Figure 4 shows, which you will then cut into various parts, writing the hour number it designates on each line to avoid confusion. This done, first take the pieces for the 12th hour. With your eye applied to the tube **A**, use your other hand to arrange them on the board **CEDF** so that, to those looking through the glass, they appear as a straight line for the 12th hour. Then, in the same manner, take the pieces for the first hour and apply them to the board **CEFD** so that the line drawn from the center has the proper distance from the 12th hour; it will achieve this if the rectangular edge of the sundial is properly established and the parts are correctly adapted to one another.

You shall proceed no differently for the rest of the hour lines to be inscribed on the plane **CEDF**, until you have constructed the entire sundial. The sign that you have worked correctly will be this: if, to those looking through the tube **A**, the sundial displays the same figure it had before the parts were cut—namely, a rectangular one. Once the sundial is drawn, you will adapt the <term>gnomon</term> <note>original: "stylus"; the rod that casts the shadow</note> in this way. With the machine exposed to the sun and situated with such care that the plane **CDEF** is in the primary vertical plane, apply your eye to the tube **A**. With your other hand, twist the gnomon here and there somewhere on the plane until the shadow of its tip falls exactly on the common point of intersection for the hour and the sun's <term>parallel</term> <note>lines on a sundial indicating the sun's path at different times of the year</note>; for the gnomon fixed there will always perform its duty exactly. By this industry, you will fashion a "magic sundial" which, seen from outside the point **A**, reflects nothing certain and lies entirely scattered. You can paint whatever you like among the lines, form any figures, and delineate any number of pins and gnomons; it is all the same, for none of these things obstruct the sundial refracted through the glass. For if you have a mind to contemplate a specific hour, you will apply your eye to point **A** of tube **AB**: and behold, suddenly that whole multitude of lines vanishes, and nothing offers itself to the sight except the clock, in which the tip of the gnomon perfectly shows the hour by its shadow. It can hardly be said how much admiration this excites in viewers if handled secretly, as they cannot grasp where such a multitude of pins and lines has gone from their sight; it is truly a great trick of the eyes.

### Corollary.

**T**his artifice can excite even greater admiration if you view the sundial through the tube from some dark room onto an opposite wall illuminated by the sun, upon which anything else besides a clock might be painted. The sagacious reader will easily discover innumerable other things from this single <term>mechanical trick</term> <note>original: "technafmate"</note>. Furthermore, the method by which an entire sundial, together with its hour-telling shadow, can be suddenly represented on any wall, will be discussed in "Catoptric Steganography" <note>the art of hidden writing or imaging using mirrors</note>.

Therefore, once all these things are prepared, the gnomon must be adapted with this skill. Position the <term>metamorphic figure</term> <note>the distorted "anamorphic" image</note> according to the quarters of the world, together with the cylinder; and from some other <term>sciatheric</term> <note>shadow-measuring</note> clock, according to an hour known to you, you will adapt any other gnomon to the metamorphic plane by this art: so that the shadow of the gnomon falls precisely on the common point of intersection for the hour and the sun's parallel corresponding to the hour of the other clock; and fix it in this position. Moreover, anything else can be used in place of a gnomon, provided that its extremity falls on the axis of the world. And you will have a wonderful sundial which, when exposed to the sun so that the part of the mirror showing the sundial is turned away from the sun; the plane—

### Problem XV.

->Another method, much more secret and impenetrable to all.<-

> *By which a clock appears in a mirror, reflected not just from a horizontal plane, but from various disconnected surfaces, such that no one can grasp the manner in which it is done.*

I. First, on a piece of fairly sturdy paper wrapped around a cylinder, let a vertical <term>horoscopic</term><note>A device for observing the hours, here referring to a sundial layout.</note> dial be drawn from a designated point; the description of this will be aided by our <term>mesoptic instrument</term><note>An optical tool Kircher previously described for calculating perspectives and reflections.</note> described on page 124. Once the dial is drawn, remove the paper and pierce it with a needle along the path of the hour lines; or, as you might more wisely do, cut out the individual hour lines, leaving only enough space around the center so they may hold together.

II. This being done, stand the paper—folded back into a cylinder—in its original place, positioned normally and exposed to the Sun. Behold: the rays of the Sun passing through the hour-slits will depict the dial upon whatever objects and planes are present. Because of the roughness and inequality of these surfaces, the dial will appear greatly deformed and distorted. You should then paint the dial onto those objects exactly following the luminous projection. And since nothing but the dial is represented in the mirror, you may paint anything you like on the <term>metamorphotic plane</term><note>A surface containing a distorted image that only looks "correct" from a specific angle or through a specific mirror; often called anamorphosis.</note> between the said hour lines to further hide the artifice.

III. Have a cylindrical mirror prepared of exactly the same size as the wooden or paper cylinder was. Place this in the position of the paper one. Behold: the forms of the dial, transformed across various planes, are recollected in the mirror through a certain <term>optical epharmosis</term><note>original: "epharmosin"; a Greek term meaning "fitting together" or "adaptation." Here, it refers to the mirror's ability to "correct" a distorted image.</note> and will show the hours exactly. See what we have handed down from page 124 to 130; for those pages will bring great light to the things presented here. A <term>stylus</term><note>The gnomon or pointer of the dial.</note> or hour index will also be fitted as in the preceding section.

### Corollary.

From this method, it is clear by what means the same thing can be shown in any plane mirror. However, since we shall treat this more fully in the following pages, we intentionally remain silent on it here.

### Problem XVI.

->To construct a catoptric sundial in such a way that the hours do not appear unless the eye is applied to a specific, determined point in the intermediate space.<-

<margin>See Figure 5, Illustration 25.</margin>
I. First, let a cylindrical mirror **DC**, two palms in length, be made of any material and placed in the center of a square table **XT**. Second, over this you shall fit another paper cylinder **AE**, **BC**, double the size of the first, which tightly encloses the inner one. This should have a wide, hollow wooden base **BC**, which—fitting into a <term>clepsydra</term><note>A water clock.</note> or hydraulic vessel **HI** of nearly the same width as the paper cylinder's base—will float upon the water. Furthermore, in the middle of the hydraulic vessel, let there be a <term>diaphragm</term><note>A partition or floor.</note> **LR**, through which water, dripping steadily from vessel **H**, discharges itself into the lower part of the vessel **I**. For this reason, it must be equipped with a <term>stopcock</term><note>original: "epistomio"; a valve or tap.</note> at **R**, or more wisely, a curved <term>siphon</term> **LIM**.

III. When this is opened, the water in vessel **H**—exiting either through the stopcock or the siphon according to a measure of 12 hours (for the middle paper cylinder must be divided into that many hours or parts)—will slowly descend. Thus, through a hole or slit in the paper cylinder (which must be made in the middle, and through which the inner mirror shines), it will show the desired hour reflected from the table.

IV. You shall inscribe the hours on the plane of the underlying table by this art: first, having taken any space separately, let a <term>dioptra</term><note>A sighting device or eyepiece used to ensure the viewer looks from the correct spot.</note> **G** be fixed, to which the eye is applied to see the hour.

V. Having filled the hydraulic vessel **H** with water, you will draw as many circles from the center of the table as the surface of the inner cylinder **DC** is divided into—namely 12. You will describe the twelfth hour in the first circuit of the table according to the method we taught on page 130 for painting transformed figures; or even mechanically, by applying the eye to the sighting-vane, paint the number of the 12th hour in the first circuit of the plane. If this number is recognized exactly in the mirror, you have correctly completed the metamorphosis of the number in the first circuit. This being drawn, open the stopcock; the water will descend along with the cylinder until the mirror is in the position where it can receive the reflection of the second circle and the hours inscribed upon it. Then, with the stopcock closed, you will inscribe hour 1 or 2 in that same circle using the same method as in the previous operation. Third, with the stopcock opened again, let the floating cylinder descend until the mirror is in the place where it can receive the reflection of hour 3 from the circular space...

<margin>Use of the catoptric clock.</margin>
The use of this <term>catoptric</term><note>Related to the science of mirrors and reflection.</note> clock is as follows. Fill the <term>clepsydra</term><note>A water clock that uses the flow of liquid to measure time.</note> until the mirror inside the opening of the paper cylinder shows "Hour 1" to those looking through the <term>dioptra</term><note>A sighting tube or aperture used for precise observation.</note>.
