This is done with such ingenuity that no one will ever be able to grasp the secret mechanism in their mind; only the current Hour 1 (and no other) will appear in the mirror to those looking through the tube, and nothing else. Note here that the internal circular cylinder must be a pendulum fixed somewhere at point E; otherwise, if it were not, the paper cylinder would have no free path for its ascent and descent. I remember once performing a rough experiment of this clock here in Rome. It so dazzled the eyes of the onlookers that many men, by no means unskilled in natural philosophy, thought it could only happen through some kind of enchantment. We have given the explanation for this matter in various places already cited. To make the clock appear even more wonderful, an index PQ can be placed on the side of the paper cylinder upon a fixed board the length of cylinder DE; as the paper cylinder descends, this index will show the hours on the upper part of the cylinder, while the mirror shows that same hour. On ordinary hydraulic <term>sciatheric</term><note>Devices that tell time using shadows, from the Greek 'skia' (shadow) and 'therao' (to seek).</note> vessels, additional details can be inscribed according to the rules in Book 4 to increase the sophistication of the artifice.

## Problem XVII.

->*How to inscribe the astronomical shadow-science upon an eight-cycle column, so that Aeolus, sitting atop the column, simultaneously shows the blowing wind in the circuit and, within the cylindrical hemicycles, the hours and other celestial apparatus. See Figure VI, Problem 17.*<-

Let there be a cylinder CDEF, with Aeolus <note>The Greek god of the winds.</note> placed upon it at A, sitting upon a dolphin B. This figure should be able to turn upon the axis of the cylinder with a trident rod, which will serve as the index for both the winds and the hours. The circumference of the cylinder is divided into eight parts, and in each part, the figures of the winds with their names shall be placed. Within the cylindrical <term>hemicycles</term><note>Half-cylinders or curved recessed channels carved into the column.</note>, let various hour lines be described: within G, the astronomical hours; within H, the Italian and Babylonian hours; within I, the half-cycle of the planetary hours; and within K, the line of the <term>celestial houses</term><note>A term from astrology referring to the twelve divisions of the sky.</note>. These should be drawn according to the rules provided on page 355; and thus you will have a finished clock.

You shall construct the statue of Aeolus as follows. Of whatever material the statue is made (following the current figure), it must be equipped with a staff or rod to point out the winds and hours. This statue should have a <term>matrix</term><note>A hollow socket or female joint.</note> inside the head, into which the tip of the cylinder’s axis is inserted to allow the statue to move easily. For if it is balanced in this way, it will be driven by any agitation of the air and will come to rest in the direction toward which it is pushed. The cylinder itself should also be movable around its axis. This cylinder, situated according to the four cardinal points of the world and placed in an open location, will force Aeolus—agitated by the blowing wind with his index toward the part from which the wind blows—to show the wind there. If you wish the astronomical hours to be shown to you, turn the cylinder until the shadow of Aeolus’s rod is precisely parallel to the <term>azimuth</term><note>An arc of the horizon used to determine the direction of a celestial body.</note> of whichever hemicycle you choose; the tip of the shadow in G will then show the astronomical hour. If you move it with similar industry to H, it will show the hours from sunrise and sunset; if to I, the planetary hours; and finally, K will show the celestial houses on the columnar hemicycle. Only the eight principal winds are placed here; if you wish to inscribe the remaining 32 collateral winds, the column must be hollowed out with as many hemicycles, in each of which something specific pertaining to astronomical doctrine may be delineated. This machine, placed in the garden of some Prince, will excite great pleasure in spectators, in addition to their admiration. By what means a machine of this kind can be made within domestic walls to show the winds <term>sympathetically</term><note>In this context, 'sympathetically' refers to 'action at a distance' or magnetic connection, a favorite topic of Kircher's.</note> will be explained in the *Mechanical Thaumaturge* <note>original: "Thaumaturgo mechanico". ### Problem XVIII.

> *To construct a heliocaustic <note>original: "heliocausticum," meaning solar-burning</note> clock, or "Solar-burner," with such ingenuity that it not only demonstrates the hours using light as an indicator, but also announces the hours at each interval by igniting a fire and creating a noise, functioning just like common clocks that strike with the help of wheels.*

<margin>Illustration XXVI.</margin>
**Three** things are primarily necessary for this clock. First, a crystal ball, or if that cannot be obtained, a spherical vial full of liquid. Second, a spherical shell <note>original: "concha," likely a bowl-shaped metal or wooden enclosure</note>. Third, the layout of the clock inside the shell, together with the items necessary for the ignition and the sounding of the hours. In place of a crystal ball, a spherical vial can easily be obtained by this industrious method: have a glass ball blown for you at a glass furnace, as exactly round as possible. This will have exactly the same properties as a crystal ball; for when exposed to the Sun, it burns so powerfully that in its burning it can be compared to a parabolic mirror. Once this is obtained, have a shell or hemicycle made of such a size that the glass ball, placed in the center of the shell, allows the tip of the burning cone—or the focus—to precisely touch its concave surface. Then, you will delineate a clock of any kind within this shell. Let it be, for example, an astronomical clock within the heliodromic space <term>heliodromic: the path the sun travels between the tropics</term>, as appears in Figure 2, Illustration 26. Let the spherical shell be LMNO, on whose concave surface is drawn the sun-path space with astronomical hours, according to the method we taught in Book 6, Proposition 1. Let A be the glass ball full of water placed in the center of the sphere, so that it represents the Earth in relation to the heavens. Let R be the Sun, whose rays, penetrating the ball, are united at point B, so that the caustic point of ignition, B, ends precisely on the concave surface of the shell. I say that this bright burning point will demonstrate the hours, no differently than rays of the Sun sent through a hole onto the said spherical surface, or the tip of a shadow-cone on the clock. For since the rays constitute a burning cone BAR, and the axis is always straight and unrefracted (being normal or perpendicular to the surface) according to what we demonstrated in Book 2, Part 3, Proposition 12 and in our *Anaclastics* <note>Anaclastics is the study of the refraction of light</note>, whenever the cone is formed by the Sun, it necessarily does the same thing as an unrefracted ray of the Sun or a shadow falling on the spherical surface from the tip of a style. But these things demonstrate the hour perfectly on a clock. Therefore, so does the focus of the burning cone, which was to be proven.

Furthermore, since the convex surface of the glass ball is concentric with the concave surface of the shell, it follows that all lines from the center of the glass ball to the concave surface of the shell are equal to each other, by the 15th definition of Euclid. Moreover, all lines drawn from the center of the ball to its own circumference are equal to each other. Therefore, by subtracting the radii of the ball from the radii of the shell, all the lines from the concave surface of the shell to the convex surface of the ball will remain equal to each other. But these are nothing other than the axes of the burning cones projected by the different movements of the Sun from the surface of the ball onto the concave surface of the shell. Therefore, the focus—namely the end of the caustic cones—will necessarily, always and everywhere, touch the concave surface; therefore, it will cause burning everywhere on said surface. Thus, while showing the hours, it will simultaneously cause ignition, which was to be demonstrated. Now, we must explain how the burning is to be arranged.

## Use of the machine.

The machine should be positioned with the spheres in such a way that the 12th astronomical hour and the 6th planetary hour <note>In ancient timekeeping, the "planetary hours" divided the daylight into 12 equal parts regardless of the season; thus, the 6th planetary hour always corresponds to noon.</note> always occupy the middle of the sphere. Then, once the "first mover" <term>XY</term> <note>referring to the main drive mechanism labeled in Fig. I</note> has been directed to a specific astronomical hour and set in motion, all the statues enclosed in the spheres will move together, sitting upon their small globes and pointing out the hours on the circumference of the spheres with their staffs. However, only that statue enclosed in the sphere marked with the name of the current day denotes the true planetary rule. 

Suppose, for example, that today is September 24th, a Wednesday: I desire to know which planet governs at the 12th astronomical hour; the statue sitting on the globe marked with the name of Mercury <note>original: ☿</note> will point with its small rod to the 6th hour, and next to it, the symbol for Mercury <note>original: ☿</note>. I shall therefore say that Mercury governs at this hour. 

Again, on the same Wednesday, the summer solstice day of June 21st, let us inquire after the rule of the third astronomical hour after noon: look, therefore, where the circle of the third hour—which the statue points to in the fourth sphere, or that of Venus <note>original: ♀</note>—intersects the <term>Tropic of Cancer</term> <note>original: ♋; the northernmost point of the sun's path</note>; there you will also find the planetary hour with the symbol of the reigning planet written next to it. 

Finally, on the same day of the solstice, December 21st <note>original: ♑, the Tropic of Capricorn</note>, at the third hour of the afternoon, let the ruling planet be sought: see where the third hour circle—which the statue in the fourth sphere (Venus) demonstrates on the equator—intersects the Tropic of Capricorn; for there you will find the planetary hour corresponding to the astronomical hour, together with the symbol of the reigning planet. Thus, as the Sun runs through any given parallel, you will find the planetary hours together with the governing planet assigned to it. If, however, you wish to know the rule of the planets on a Sunday, you shall proceed in exactly the same way as in the preceding example, and thus in the sphere assigned to any current day, you will find the rules of the planets for every individual hour.

If anyone desires more on this subject, let him consult our *Magnetic Magic*, where he will find a treatise written expressly on these matters.

## Problem XXII.

*To construct a magnetic clock in which a little Lizard, or any other small animal fashioned from light paper, demonstrates the hours by ascending and descending over the space of 24 hours. See figure 2 of Illustration 27.*

Among other machines which are accustomed to excite wonder in spectators, I display one of this kind in my Museum; it is adorned with such artifice that a little Lizard, by ascending and descending on a certain column, demonstrates the individual hours so vividly that there is almost no one who perceives the logic of the Lizard’s movement. For it proceeds upward and downward with a natural motion, yet it does not cling to anything; it is not carried by wheels, nor is it supported by any external prop; if you pull it away, as soon as it is replaced on the column, it will seek out its proper hour again. 

You shall therefore decorate this machine with this ingenuity: Let a hollow receptacle <term>ABCD</term> be made in the form of a square column, as Figure 2 teaches: in the middle of which a thin and slender ruler made of ebony or a brass plate is inserted, marked with the letters <term>EF</term>. Within the hollows of this column, you will fit a very strong magnet, suspended by a cord with such ingenuity that the face of the magnet is parallel to the magnetic axis, and the same face lightly grazes the interior surface of the brass ruler <term>EF</term>; and you will have the first requirement for moving and animating the lizard.

<margin>The time-telling lizard.</margin>
Again, so that the little Lizard may ascend and descend by itself every 24 hours and show the hours, you shall act thus: In the top of the column <term>AB</term>, you shall make a hydraulic wheel marked with the letter <term>V</term>, which completes one revolution in the space of 24 hours. This wheel should have 24 conical small vessels firmly inserted around its circumference, as the figure shows: the vessels, moreover, should be pierced at the bottom with a very fine hole. This wheel, thus prepared and turned upon an axle and poles, must be placed within the vessel <term>AB</term>; a cord must be wrapped around the axle, at the end of which the magnet (of which we made mention a little while ago) must be tied. This magnet will have a double duty: by its weight, it drives the wheel <term>V</term> inserted within the vessel <term>AB</term> over the space of 24 hours; and by descending simultaneously within the square column, it will drag with it a steel needle secretly passed through the middle of the lizard’s body: and the lizard will be seen... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with the catchword "lacer-" (lizard) on the next page.</note>

...the little lizard <note>Latin: *lacertula*</note>, by its own accord, by ascending and descending in the order of the hours, demonstrates the time to the great admiration of those watching. ### Problem XXIII.

->*To construct a clock in which a Dove, flying through the air, shows the hours on the same square column. See Figure 3, Plate 27.*<-

**In** this machine, let the same square concave column remain; only the axis V should project out by three inches. A cord is wound around this axis from the back part, at the end of which the same magnet is tied, as before. To the front part of the axis, however, another small cord—or rather a thread—should be wound, as subtle and thin as possible, namely the finest silk thread, so that from a distance it is barely perceptible to the senses. Let there also be a hidden tube in the base of the column, within which the thread unwound from the axis, together with any attached weight, may descend. However, the unwinding of both cords—both the internal one from which the magnet hangs, and the external one from which the dove hangs—must occur in one and the same direction. These things having been properly performed, let a Dove N be made from very fine paper, through the body of which a very fine steel needle is secretly passed. To the tail of the dove, on one side, a very fine and barely sensible thread is attached; on the other side, it hangs vertically, directly across from the magnet hidden inside the column. It will happen that as both cords are unwound from the axis in the same direction and at equal rates, the Dove N, attracted by its beak <note>Latin: *rostello*</note> to the internal magnet, will now ascend and now descend with a steady motion, hanging entirely free in the air. For, attracted by the force of the stone <note>The "stone" refers to the loadstone or magnet.</note>, since it cannot join itself to the same because of the restraint of the vertically attached thread, it will hang in the middle of the air and demonstrate the hours on the column, now by ascending and now by descending, to the greatest admiration of the spectators. The display will be enhanced if the panel EF is made of mirrored material; for in this way two doves will be seen to struggle in the middle of the air, attacking each other with their beaks. See the figure, which will explain everything exactly.

### Problem XXIV.

->*Concerning Sympathetic Time-telling, as used by Botanists and Zoologists, or animated clocks.*<-

**There** is a great controversy among authors as to whether a "sympathetic" clock can exist—that is, one which demonstrates the hours by hidden force alone, without any artificial mechanism? <margin>*The sun-turning clock.*</margin> Some affirm the matter with doubt; some reject it entirely. There are those who so abhor the idea that they seem to close their ears at the very first proposition. We, taking a middle path, say that it is entirely possible for something to exist in this sublunary <note>The region below the moon, meaning the Earthly realm.</note> world which has such a "sympathy" and consensus with the Sun that, when the Sun moves, it follows the Sun incessantly, balanced by its own magnetic industry. Therefore, if this thing were placed inside a small globe divided into 24 equal parts, and balanced in the center of water, with a stationary pointer placed across from it; there should be no doubt that this clock would demonstrate the hours perfectly and perpetually. I have shown all these things more extensively in Book 3 of our *Magnetic Art* <note>Kircher is referring to his own work, *Magnes; sive de arte magnetica* (1641).</note>, in the chapter on Botanical Clocks, to which place we refer the curious reader, where he will find the specific material, the method of operation, and even the series of the entire history described. In what manner a Botanical clock can be constructed is also spoken of at length in the cited passage of the *Magnetic Art*. There remains only the doubt concerning an "animated" clock—namely, whether any animal can exist that naturally demonstrates the hours? Certainly, the Egyptians taught that a certain kind of ape, the dog-headed baboon <note>Latin: *cynocephalus*</note>, performs this, as it indicates the equinoctial time <margin>*The time-telling baboon.*</margin> through twelve urinations repeated every hour, as we shall show at length in our *Hieroglyphic Astronomy*. Some also assign this to certain animals of America which demonstrate the time of day by emitting certain cries; such as the animal they call "Sloth" <note>Latin: *Pigritia*</note>. In the subpolar regions, Olaus <note>Olaus Magnus (1490–1557), a Swedish writer and cartographer.</note> reports that a certain kind of Gull <note>Latin: *Lari*</note> demonstrates the hour for lying down and rising to men in those months where they enjoy perpetual sun for the space of one, two, three, or four months. They add that the rooster has a certain knowledge of time and solar motion implanted in its nature, which it demonstrates by its morning song. There are innumerable stories of this kind told by authors, all of which we shall pursue at length in other works. And regarding solar statues...

...regarding those things which perpetually turn themselves toward the Sun, see our *Hieroglyphic Mechanics*, where we shall bring forth certain unheard-of things from the more recondite philosophy of the Egyptians concerning the statues of Memnon, Serapis, Isis, and Anubis. <note>Kircher refers to his own works on Egyptian "magic," where he believed the ancients used complex mechanics to make statues appear to speak or move. The "Statue of Memnon" was a famous Colossus in Egypt said to sing at dawn.</note> Furthermore, one secret published in this century has shaken the minds of the curious with the greatest perplexity. It is a certain kind of clock displayed in a cup, the practice of which is as follows.

<margin>The magical clock.</margin>
Someone wishing to know the hour lets down a ring held by a fine thread into a cup. They say that as soon as it has rested a little, it announces the hour by striking the sides of that cup with sounding blows. If these things that are told are true, I ask here: who determines the ring to strike this hour rather than another? Why would it designate the astronomical hour <note>The standard 24-hour day starting at midnight.</note> rather than the Italian, Babylonian, or planetary hours? <note>Historical timekeeping systems: Italian hours started at sunset; Babylonian at sunrise; planetary hours varied in length based on day and night.</note> For every distribution of hours is made by human institution and depends on the free choice of human will. I hear it said that the movement of the blood and the pulse of the **systole** and **diastole** <term>systole and diastole</term><note>The contraction and relaxation of the heart.</note>—agitated in accordance with the motion of the heavens—causes this effect. But I ask here: what philosopher has ever demonstrated that the movement of the blood matches the celestial motion? Who has ever learned by experiment that the pulse of the blood in the nerves is a clock? And even granted (though not conceded) that the blood completes its cycle in the **microcosm** <note>The human body, viewed as a miniature version of the universe or "macrocosm."</note> in the space of 24 hours according to the motion of the heavens: who will cause the sound? Who determines the sound of exactly so many strikes, and no more or fewer? Why, when the Sun is positioned at the meridian point, does it make only 12 strikes, and not 6, or 18, or 17? Since I see everyone fall silent at these questions, and I find no one who can assign any reason for such a prodigious sound, I rightly view it as suspect. Indeed, those people do not seem tolerable who, while no natural reason is available to them, are not ashamed to descend into the "motion of the earth" <note>Kircher remained skeptical of Copernican heliocentrism, here grouping it with "foolish opinions."</note> and other foolish opinions, provided they can somehow persuade certain incredulous people and the unskilful crowd of this paradox. I remember that I myself have very often taken up the experiment of this thing, but always with a failed result. But why does it provide the accustomed effect for them, and not for me? Here they accuse me of a lack of diligence. But I marvel here not so much at a judgment so weak in discerning natural things, as at that primarily stupid superstition of idle men, who have such easy faith in these kinds of rambling delusions that they think no one besides themselves possesses sufficient industry to perform such things. Truly, an intolerable vanity. To explain myself briefly, then: I say that this clock is in no way natural, but that this effect is from the number of those which are performed only with either an implicit or explicit **pact with a demon**. <note>Kircher frequently attributed phenomena that lacked a "natural" or "magnetic" explanation to demonic interference or fraud.</note> All things of this kind are those which have no connection with natural causes, and for which no reason founded in nature can be assigned. However, since we have sufficiently refuted this kind of clock in our *Magnetic Art*, I have judged it superfluous to waste time and paper in refuting it again here.

### Problem XXV.
### On rotating clocks.

Lest anything be missing from this curious doctrine of **horodixis** <term>horodixis</term><note>The art of showing or telling the time.</note>, the composition of those instruments which demonstrate the hours by various adaptations of wheels entwined in proportion to each other seemed to claim this place for itself, as if by right. But since we saw this material was situated far outside the boundaries of light and shadow, we deemed it more advisable to defer it to another work titled *The Nature of Things Animated by Machines, or The Mechanical Wonder-worker*, lest we seem to have jumped across the limits of our purpose. In that work, we will treat most abundantly the method of perfectly constructing said clocks, and the proportion of the wheels to the movements of the celestial bodies—how, for instance, besides those movements of celestial bodies ever noted by craftsmen, we can also exhibit the movements of all natural things, shaped by wheels, sinews, and ropes according to the model of nature. In that book, if God grants me life, the curious reader will contemplate the whole nature of things animated by machines with incredible pleasure of the mind.

The longer tube <term>NCD</term> should be joined at <term>N</term> to the vessel <term>AB</term>, and below at <term>M</term>, it should be joined to the vessel <term>MXYD</term> along with the rest of the base. ### The Practice of the Clock.

**B**efore all else, you will measure the intervals of the hours with the help of an exact <term>Clepsydra [water clock]</term>, or even a <term>sciatheric [sundial-based]</term> clock, by the flow of water. While the water from vessel <term>AB</term> works its way into tube <term>NC</term> and from there through tubes <term>CG</term> and <term>CH</term> with valve <term>L</term> open, the water should rise precisely by as much as the space of one hour between the twelfth and the following hour within tubes <term>KG</term> and <term>IH</term>. If you achieve this, then the water, by its ascent or descent in showing the hours, will attain the desired effect, with the small globe <term>X</term> floating on the water always showing the current hour in both glass tubes. To have the globe show the hours through the descent of the water, proceed thus: with valve <term>L</term> closed, open valve <term>M</term>, and the water will show the hours as it falls. For vessel <term>AB</term> will first be filled with water which, through the middle tube joined to vessel <term>AB</term> at <term>N</term>, will flow drop by drop through the valve or stopcock at <term>L</term> into both tubes <term>GK</term> and <term>HI</term> while ascending. However, after it has risen to twelve, to show the hours by descent, you will open the valve <term>M</term> and close valve <term>L</term>. Thus it will show the hours by descent in the same order as before. The water will be discharged through valve <term>M</term> into vessel <term>MVXDOE</term>, which will be emptied through another valve <term>O</term> and poured back into the upper vessel, <term>AB</term>.

### Precautions.

I. You must ensure that the water poured into the machine's vessels is very pure and separated from all dregs; otherwise, it would easily block the valves with its sediment. Water passed through an <term>alembic [distilling apparatus]</term> would serve this purpose best, or even <term>burnt wine [distilled alcohol]</term> <note>original: "vinum Crematum," referring to brandy or spirits, which were used in clocks to prevent the growth of algae or the water from freezing.</note>.

II. The valves or stopcocks should have a very fine opening, like a bristle, so that the water flows through only drop by drop, and they must be equal in both tubes. For you will determine the hour intervals according to their flow, as was said above. The decorations that can be added are left to the industry of the artist. We present such a clock for inspection to all foreigners who come to see my <term>museum</term> <note>referring to the Museum Kircherianum in Rome, Kircher’s famous collection of curiosities and scientific instruments.</note>.

III. In place of the floating globes, little fish, sirens, angels, or similar small figures made of wax or another light material can be placed on the water.

# <term>Technical Wonder</term> III.
<note>original: "Technasma." A Greek-derived term Kircher uses for a clever mechanical device or artistic artifice.</note>

## To construct a wonderful Sympathetic-magnetic Clock from the Kircherian Museum.

1. **L**et a machine be made according to the layout you see here, constructed with hour-columns P.Q. and R.S., which are secured by the transverse timber P.R. Let the columns be hollow and divided in the middle by a diaphragm. At point X in both columns, let a rotating clockwork be placed, driven by a weight. In this arrangement, a strong magnet is attached to one end of a cord, and to the other end of the cord, another weight is attached, though lighter than the first. It will then happen that the magnet, fastened to the cord within the first partition of the diaphragm, will be moved either up or down by the benefit of the rotating clockwork. On the exterior surface, in the hour-space, it will show the hours in order by means of a little lizard or a crab, made of very light paper with a steel needle fixed inside it. For the magnet hidden inside, moved by the rotating clockwork, will draw the steel needle (fixed to the paper lizard or crab) after itself according to the series of hours. In this way, the lizard will be seen to walk forward, to the wonder of all, since even if it is pulled away and then placed back in its spot, it clings there. It is held by no other thing. In one column it will show <term>astronomical hours</term>, and in the other, <term>Italian hours</term>, or another kind of hours.
<note>Astronomical hours begin at noon; Italian hours were counted as 24 hours starting from sunset. Kircher often designed clocks that showed multiple systems simultaneously.</note>
The reader may consult our *Magnetic Art* <note>original: "Artem nostram Magneticam," referring to Kircher's 1641 book *Magnes*.</note> and the section of the present work on prodigious clocks, and he will clearly perceive the method of constructing a clock of this kind.

2. In the middle of this structure, let three glass globes be placed above the columns. In the middle of these, place a similar small globe of glass or wax, into which a strong piece of magnet is inserted, and an angel on the hour-rim of the globe to show the hours. To ensure the globe completes its circuit in the space of 24 hours, let it be done thus: Above Column N.O., let a rotating clockwork be placed, marked with the letter N, moved by a steel plate. Above this clockwork, let a strong magnet be placed which, rotated in the space of 24 hours, will move globe I (divided into 24 parts) along with itself because of the piece of magnet enclosed within it. On this, an immobile figure of an Angel or a <term>Siren</term> sitting upon the globe will show the current hour.
<note>Kircher often used mythological figures like Sirens or Tritons in his fountain and clock designs.</note>
Furthermore, let the glass globes C.R., likewise divided into 24 parts or hours, hold small globes in their centers that are able to turn and are equipped with their own magnetic pieces; on these, other sitting figures may show the hours on the rim of the globes, whether astronomical, Italian, or <term>Babylonian</term>.
<note>Babylonian hours are counted as 24 equal hours starting from sunrise.</note>
For the magnet M, placed on the middle Column above the rotating clockwork, will not only turn the upper globe in a 24-hour period, but by its lateral motion will also move the small globes contained within the side glass spheres. We display an assembly of this kind of clock today in our <term>Museum</term> for the great admiration of all; we have also placed a little bird on the upper transverse rim, which, by moving forward along with the motion of the clock, points out the hours. I have thought it best to communicate all these things to the curious reader in a few words. Farewell, and look with favor.

### PART TWO,

# PARASTATIC MAGIC,
## OR
### CONCERNING THE PRODIGIOUS REPRESENTATIONS OF THINGS THROUGH LIGHT AND SHADOW.

### PREFACE.

<margin>Wonderful examples of parastatic operations.</margin>
**P**arastatic Magic <note>The term "parastatic" comes from the Greek word *parastasis*, meaning to "bring before" or "represent." Here, it refers to the art of creating lifelike illusions.</note>, or Representative Magic, is nothing other than that more recondite science of Light and Shadow. By various mixtures of Light and Shadow, and through the use of reflections from mirrors <note>original: Catoptricas</note> and the bending of light <note>refraction</note>, wondrous spectacles are exhibited to an audience. It is said that by this means, *Roger Bacon* once presented himself to distant pupils by means of his own shadow. With this aid, the Arab *Arzachel* <note>original: Arazel</note> would suddenly produce whatever the audience desired, as if in a theater. By this support, *Dinostratus* used to decorate rooms with images of grapes and the heads of every kind of animal. Finally, by this power, it is said that all the Emperors from Julius Caesar to Charles V were represented to the *Emperor Rudolph II*, as if upon a stage. For this reason, many people have not been ashamed to accuse them of "Magic" <note>Meaning dark or forbidden sorcery.</note>, while many others have attributed such hidden effects to the secrets of nature. Let us see how we might produce similar things from the hidden science of Light and Shadow. In the preceding Part, we treated—as far as the strength of our intellect permitted—the prodigious movement of Light and Shadow ordered for the demonstration of hours and time. Now, order requires that we also explain the wonders of immobile Light and Shadow through these said prodigious representations <note>original: parastases</note> of things. So that this may be done with better method, we shall first discuss representations in the air and water, and then those involving fire.

---

### CHAPTER I.
### Concerning Aerial Representations.

**N**ATURE is a painter. While she paints and fashions various likenesses of things within all objects in a wonderful way, she instructs us in the method we must observe in the secret representation of things. However, because "it is not permitted for everyone to go to Corinth" <note>A Latin proverb meaning that not everyone has the means or skill to achieve something difficult or expensive.</note>, I thought it necessary to indicate briefly in this place the ways in which Nature acts as a painter, and how we might be able to imitate her. Nature, therefore, paints unusual spectacles of things in four ways. First, in the sky; some of these are set forth by God beyond the intention of nature as omens of evils or 

<margin>Wonderful things that nature paints in the Sky.</margin>
blessings about to come upon the world. For example, in the Books of the Maccabees, armies are formed in the air, and the clash of charging troops is heard. Likewise, at the time of the Nativity, He painted a star in the air as a herald of the arrival of the Eternal Light into the world. The records of almost all historians tell of infinite spectacles of the sky of this sort. You may read of them collected in the works of Lycosthenes, Aldrovandus, Gesner, Cornelius Gemma, and others. These the Greeks call apparitions <note>original: φάσματα (phasmata)</note> and wonders <note>original: τέρατα (terata)</note>, while the Latins call them prodigies, omens, or portents...

# The Great Art, Book X. Part II of Magic.

...of civil [turmoil], schisms, wars, and other calamities. Second, various meteorological impressions, multiform <note>original Greek: παντόμορφος (pantomorphos)</note> comets, beams, crosses, and other multifaceted shapes, halos, parhelia <note>Also known as "sun dogs," these are bright spots in the sky caused by ice crystals.</note>, leaping goats <note>A historical term for a type of flickering meteor or atmospheric light.</note>, falling stars, and the like; which are treated in books on meteorology. Thirdly, nature now and then, with an admirable balance of light, just like a mixture and balance of various colors, paints such diverse images of things in aerial mirrors with such industry that no human art or industry seems able to reach it. And regarding the Rainbow, that wonderful craftsmanship of nature’s painting, enough and more has been said in the first book. It remains for us to look at two modes: first, how Nature is accustomed to perfectly and completely depict images of every kind in the air at certain places and times; second, how she is accustomed to shape the same on steep precipices of mountains, in the bends of forests, and finally in animals, plants, and stones. Let it be so.

Indeed, when I was passing through Messina in the year 1636, I learned many things about a prodigious manifestation of this kind, truly worthy of admiration. To discover the truth of the matter more closely, I went to Rhegium <note>Modern-day Reggio Calabria.</note>; where, having consulted many of the more skilled inhabitants of the town about this miracle of nature, all affirmed that the matter was exactly as I had heard reported. In order to philosophize more solidly about such an admirable prodigy of nature, I thought the site’s location, the nature of the land, and the vapor of the sea should be observed with the greatest diligence; through which I easily arrived at the cause of such hidden effects, as will be explained later. But, so that the prodigy may be affirmed with greater certainty, I will add here the letters of a certain one of our Fathers, who describes such spectacles of nature at length in a certain letter given to Leo Sanctius of our Society, a man indeed most learned in every respect, and at that time Prefect of Higher Studies in the Roman College.

## The First Manifestation of Nature.
### Or concerning the Morgana of the people of Reggio in the Mamertine Strait, or the Strait of Sicily.

->Most Reverend Father in Christ.<-
->The Peace of Christ.<-

<margin>Wondrous spectacles of things in the Strait of Sicily.</margin>
**E**specially at the time when the burning Sun cooks the Mamertine Sea with heat and fervor, nature—opening the inexhaustible riches of her pictorial storehouse—exposes to view, primarily in that tract of sea, what is to be seen near Reggio, a town of Calabria no less ancient than it is famous among the Lyceums and Academies of the ancient philosophers. For it happens that at the mentioned time, a certain theater suddenly opens in the vaporous air, adorned with such a variety of things, and with such an apparatus of scenes, that there is almost nothing there that does not show itself to be seen: the architecture of castles arranged most orderly; a certain marvelous magnificence of palaces and buildings projected according to all the rules of Perspective in an infinite order of columns; with a catoptric <term>catoptric: relating to reflections or mirrors</term> scene succeeding in the place of those gradually vanishing. You may see here shady tracts of forests, rows of Cypresses and other trees arranged in a quincunx <term>quincunx: an arrangement of five objects like the dots on a die's five-face, four at the corners and one in the center</term> in a wonderful series, immense fields filled with troops of men, herds of oxen, and flocks of sheep; all with such a variety of colors, such an artful mixture of Light and Shadow, and such lifelike gestures; that no human industry seems able to produce anything similar. The people of Reggio call this spectacle the Morgana. And since this matter is known to few, I undertake to treat it in this place.

<margin>Letter to Father Leo Sanctius concerning the Morgana of the people of Reggio.</margin>
*On the morning of the Assumption of the Most Blessed Virgin, while I was standing alone at the window, I saw things so many and so new that I am never satiated or tired of thinking of them again. It seems to me that the Most Holy Madonna caused a vestige of Paradise to appear in this Lighthouse <note>original: "Faro," referring to the Faro di Messina or the Strait of Messina</note> on the day that she entered there. For if the eye up there still has, like the intellect, the voluntary mirror where it sees what pleases it: what I have seen I can call the mirror of that mirror. The Sea that bathes Sicily swelled, and became for about ten miles in length like a black mountain spine; and the sea of Calabria leveled out, and in a moment there appeared a most clear and transparent crystal that seemed like a mirror, which with its top rested on that mountain of water, and with its foot on the Shore of Calabria. In this Mirror there suddenly appeared, in a light-dark color, a row of more than 10,000 pilasters of equal width and height, all equidistant, and the recesses between pilaster and pilaster were of the same shimmer. In a moment then the pilasters were halved in height, and arched into the shape of those aqueducts of Rome, or the structures of Solomon; and the rest of the water remained a simple mirror, as far as the piled-up water of Sicily: but only for a little while, for soon above the arcade a large cornice was formed; and shortly after, above the cornice, royal castles were formed in quantity, arranged in that vast plaza of glass, and all...*

# Parastatic Magic <note>From the Greek word for "standing beside," referring to illusions where images appear to stand before the viewer.</note>

*...and all of one shape and workmanship: shortly after, of the castles there remained a quantity of towers, all equal: shortly after, the towers changed into a theater of colonnades: shortly after, the theater stretched out and created a double row: shortly after, the row of colonnades became a very long facade of windows in ten rows: from the facade it became a variety of forests of equal pines and cypresses, and of other varieties of trees. And here the whole thing disappeared, and the sea, with a little wind, returned to being the sea.*

*This is that Fata Morgana, which for twenty-six years I have estimated as improbable, and now I have seen it as true, and more beautiful than what was described to me. Of this, I now believe it is true that it is accustomed to appear in various flying colors more vivid and beautiful than those found in art or permanent nature: because I never saw light and shadow similar to these. I desire that Your Reverence teach me who the architect and who the smith might be, and with what art and material he stamps in a single point such various and many splendors. You live among the true Roman splendors and contemplate the most true divine ones: while I remain praying to God to be always propitious to you, and recommending myself to your Holy Sacrifices.*

->*From Reggio, 22nd of August 1643.*<-
->*Servant in Christ, Ignatio Angelucci.*<-

<term>Damascius</term> also remembers this prodigy in the *Life of Isidore the Philosopher* found in <term>Photius</term>. In our own time, men of good faith have reported that near Sicily, in a field named <term>Tetrapyrgio</term>, and in many other places, images of fighting horsemen are seen, especially in the summertime when the noon heat is most intense.

Similar things were seen in Neritum <note>Modern-day Nardò.</note>, a city in the interior of Apulia, where today the most illustrious <term>Fabius Chisius</term> <note>Fabio Chigi, later Pope Alexander VII, a close patron of Kircher.</note> acts as Bishop—a man supreme in all things and born for great tasks, incomparable in talent and prudence, and as I write this, the Apostolic Nuncio in Germany. In the capital of this diocese, I say, similar phantasms of nature are seen, as <term>Scipio Mazzellus</term> relates in his description of the Kingdom of Naples on page 117, in these words:

> *Then nearby one sees Salice and Nardò, a very ancient city called Neritum by Ptolemy, which is very civilized, rich, and populous; where often, when the southern winds are blowing, one sees in the air, as if in a mirror, some images of those things that are around: the common folk, who do not know the cause, attribute it to diabolical illusion, whereas it happens on the contrary because of the layout of the place and the nature of the air, which thickens because of excessive humidity.*

It can hardly be expressed how much this parastatic phantasm and in what a marvelous way it has twisted the minds of many, while they cannot comprehend how things appear in a cloud that do not appear in any neighboring fields. Therefore, as was said above, so that I might philosophize more solidly about the hidden causes of so worthy a wonder, I traveled to Reggio, comparing all the circumstances of the phenomenon with the layout of the site, the nature of the land and sea vapor, and its properties, and finally I uncovered the causes. For first, I observed a mountain in the region of Sicily named Tinna of the Sea, opposite Reggio, ending in a black tract at Pelorus; the shores indeed, as well as the seabed, roll down much gravel or sand composed of <term>selenite</term> <note>A translucent variety of gypsum.</note>, antimony, glass, and other translucent material from the nearby mountains filled with these minerals. Under the most intense heat of the Sun, this material is raised on high together with vapor, creating diverse and various surfaces. These surfaces, in the thicker vapors in the middle and opposite the mountain—as if darkened by the shadowy tract—finally coalesce into a polyhedral <note>Multi-faceted.</note> mirror, most perfect in every respect. In this mirror, therefore, having various positions relative to the eye, various images of the objects are reflected.

<margin>Causes of the aerial mirror, which they call Morgana.</margin>
An artificial series of columns happens either from a single column standing on the shore, which by multiple reflection goes off into an infinite multitude of columns; in exactly the same way as we see even a single image between two mirrors directly opposite each other reflect an infinite multitude of completely similar images within said mirrors, as will be shown more extensively in <term>Catoptric Magic</term> <note>The study of reflection and mirrors.</note>. Thus one man, reflected various times and often within the specular <note>Mirror-like.</note> surfaces of the clouds, looks like an army. The same is to be said of trees, herds, and animals.

When indeed other objects succeed the columns, such as trees, castles, or animals, the cause is this: since our eye stands in different ways to the diverse surfaces of the perpetually moving specular vapor, it happens that according to the rules of the angles of incidence and reflection, different things are also seen under a set angle, according as the surface of the specular vapor reflects them into the eyes. But some wonder here how that sandy, mirror-like matter is raised up. But these people will cease to wonder when they have more deeply considered the violent force of attraction by which the Sun, while it draws up vapors, is accustomed to lift up various materials of things on high together with itself. Who does not know that hairs, straws, small sands, stalks, and similar debris are found everywhere in spherical hail? These are certainly clear signs that the said things, raised into the air together with the vapor, were mixed there with the released vapor, and then, congealed by the force of cold, descended to earth again. If it is true what meteorologists report, that sometimes stones, wood, iron—

# Great Art of Light and Shadow, Book X. Magic, Part I.

...indeed, it has been reported that it rained frogs and similar small animals; certainly, these could not have grown in the upper region of the air unless the material had been drawn up there first. For the same reason, that extremely fine and almost imperceptible glassy matter is elevated along with the vapor of the sea and is shaped into a mirror-like surface. You now have the cause of the observed phenomena. Now it remains for us to explain certain histories here, which most people hiss at as empty human fictions.

<margin>Various apparitions are not always the illusions of the devil.</margin>
Pomponius Mela <note>A Roman geographer of the 1st century AD.</note> reports that in Mauritania, behind Mount Atlas, there are regions in which various apparitions are accustomed to appear among the mountains around noon, which mimic the gestures of men in every way: you might see dances there, or hear the sounds of trumpets and drums. Pliny also reports that within the region of Imaus <note>A name used in antiquity for the Himalayan or Ural mountain ranges.</note> in Scythia, there is a place where every year, in a vast plain, various spectacles of things appear in the shapes of men and animals, and like an army; by these, travelers are not infrequently led into pathless ways and devious precipices, and finally into manifest destruction. Regarding the river Ob <note>A major river in western Siberia.</note>, Haithon the Armenian <note>Also known as Hethum of Korykos, a medieval historian.</note> reports that there is a region which no one has yet penetrated because of the multitude of formidable apparitions that appear from that part of the river. He testifies that there the neighing of horses, the bleating of sheep, and the shouts of men are heard very frequently; so much so that, thinking this the region of Devils, no one has yet attempted it out of horror. 

Indeed, all these cited histories can be very well explained through those natural apparitions arising in that vaporous "glass" as if in a mirror. For it is possible that the site and nature of the places are such as we described in the Strait of Sicily <note>The Fretum Siculum, famous for the 'Fata Morgana' mirage.</note>, in which at certain times of the year, elevated glassy vapors show those horrific apparitions which they fear so much, just like mirrors. Furthermore, that they hear various voices of animals should be no cause for doubt, as this can happen through the voices of nearby animals reflected in a concave cliff or mountain; for the vapors do not necessarily require the sea to be spread beneath them; the nature of a place swelling with glassy vapor is sufficient.

<margin>A wonderful story regarding the appearance of a certain American Idol.</margin>
All these things are confirmed by what Herrera <note>Antonio de Herrera y Tordesillas, a major historian of the Spanish Americas.</note> reports about a certain place in the Kingdom of Guatemala in America; for he says that the worship of a certain Idol named Anazothleo <note>Likely a Latinized or corrupted spelling of a local Mayan or Pipil deity.</note>, which flourished in that place, took its origin from the fact that at fixed times of the year, this idol appeared in a cloud like some God, surrounded by a troupe of minor deities. However, that by which he says the Indians were mocked was that very Idol—which we mentioned before was accustomed to be worshipped with the highest veneration at a nearby lake—represented with all the exact circumstances and ceremonies of adoration which they themselves used, by a certain vapor emitted from the lake at the same time, acting as a mirror. The Indians, however, being ignorant of nature, thought the mystery—which had been excited by the images reflected from the overhanging cloud—was an apparition of the Gods, and thus the Devil miserably imposed upon their dull minds through a work of nature. But soon, when the fraud was detected by the Dominican Fathers, the Idol was cut down and burned, and the impostor ceased to appear in the said place. I do not doubt that natural apparitions of this kind have given occasion for idolatry in many places, since nothing is easier than to wonder at and look up to those things whose causes and reasons we do not grasp; and we are mocked by them all the more firmly the more they are thought by us to be worthy of great admiration. Indeed, it is likely that Mauritanian shepherds dressed in wild skins and dancing to flutes, seen in such vapors, spread that rumor which Geographers then accepted as true, handing down to posterity that Satyrs and Silvani were accustomed to appear at fixed times in the said region of Mauritania, performing dances with trumpets and flutes.

It is clear, therefore, that an aerial mirror is made by nature, in which the multiplied images of things exhibit themselves to men as if they were portents, without any work or mockery of demons. We must now declare by what art we might be able to do this, by applying active forces to passive materials.

### Parastasis II.
<note>A Greek-derived term meaning 'presentation' or 'exhibition'.</note>

->That is, the artificial exhibition of aerial apparitions.<-

In the preceding section, we have seen the work of nature regarding representable things: now we must declare by what reasoning we can provide the same through the art of Light and Shadow, by applying active forces to passive materials.

Let there be made, therefore, an oblong iron box curved in the manner of a channel: then you will place within it selenitic coals <note>original: 'carbones seleniticos'; likely referring to minerals like gypsum or transparent stones that Kircher believed could create reflective vapors when heated.</note>, sods swollen with antimony, and other clods dissolvable into glassy matter (the Chemists here understand me), and with a fire placed beneath the channel, let the coals be burned for so long until they glow with the greatest fervor and heat conceived. Once this is done, let a curtain of black color be stretched out from the region of the channel: then you should have prepared water composed of various kinds of vitriols <note>Sulfate minerals.</note> and salts, which as soon as you have poured it onto the glowing coals, behold—wonderful to say!—just as in a most lucid mirror, infinite images filled with a certain variety of colors are reflected from the established place, and in the mirror-like vapor...

<header>Parastatic Magic <note>The magic of representation or simulated appearances.</note></header>

...reflected by vapor to the eye, or even to the envy of Nature herself working in the *Morgana Mamertina* <note>The Fata Morgana mirage observed in the Strait of Messina.</note>; you will gaze, stunned with the greatest pleasure, as a curtain of glassy vapor obscures the transparency. From this, the reflection of objects into a determined place will burst forth with such a variety of colors from a seedbed of salts, that I judge nothing more beautiful can be seen in human affairs. However, for the matter to be perfectly established, it requires chemical mastery and a dexterous mind.

From this single experiment, we have demonstrated to the eyes of our friends the reasons and the cause of that so unusual phantom appearing at stated times in the Mamertine Strait <note>The Strait of Messina, between Sicily and Italy.</note>, so that there was no one who dared to doubt any longer the cause of such an unseen effect. I shall proceed no further here; let it suffice to have suggested the matter only to sharp minds.

<margin>An admirable mirror.</margin>
Certainly, he who has searched into these things deeply will be able to conceive of them; he should know that a mirror—one that no mind could grasp as it far exceeds the ways of common nature—will show everything. Yet, let no one persuade himself that every vapor is suitable for exhibiting things of this kind: for it is clear that this is false from the fact that this business does not achieve the desired success in every place where vapors are raised. It happens only in those places which both the layout of the site and the particular property of the vapor have made fit for exhibiting these things. By the same reasoning, not every vapor produced by art, but only that established according to the model of nature—such as we have already indicated—will be fit for this <term>parastasis</term> <note>From the Greek 'parastasis,' meaning a representation, appearance, or standing-forth.</note>. The task, therefore, requires not just any hand, but a Chemical hand, as I said, to achieve its effect.

### Corollary.

From this mechanism, you may gather that by breath alone, and the movement of vapor, innumerable things can be exhibited that are entirely paradoxical to the human mind; these we leave to be further weighed by the curious reader and the sagacious engineer. It is our part, in such a multitude and variety of things to be said, to suggest many things only in few words.

# CHAPTER II.

## Concerning the industry of Nature the Painter, by which she forms everything in human fetuses, animals, plants, and stones.

How great the power of the imagination of women can be in forming images in conceived fetuses was treated at length in *The Magnetic Art* <note>Kircher's own work, *Ars Magnetica* (1641).</note>. For it is certain that the imaginative power can not only imagine, but also paint with suitable color the likenesses of things in young fetuses, while it possesses a certain power of hindering the maternal matter so that it cannot be likened to the parents. Examining this knot diligently, Ludovicus Mercatus <note>Luis Mercado (1525–1611), a prominent Spanish physician.</note> says there remains another impediment by which the seed cannot operate freely, nor can it make the child like the parents—namely, a vehement and varied imagination. This is conceived not only during conception but even throughout the whole time of formation, since this formation dominates the maternal matter in the same way that higher powers dominate lower ones, and lower ones obey higher ones. For this reason, that image grasped through a vehement imagination is imprinted on the fetus rather than the likeness of the father.

<margin>The imaginative power.</margin>
Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> agrees with these views in Question 4, Article 8, asserting that the imagination is a certain power in a bodily organ, from which the bodily spirit is changed toward the imagined species; in this, a formative power is shaped which works in the seed. Therefore, a change sometimes occurs in the offspring because of the imagination of the parent during union. From this, it is clear that the spirit from the imaginative power exercises its strength and outlines the image of the formation more effectively in the aforementioned way than the formative power itself, which proceeds from the nature of the parent's limbs.

So great, then, is the force of the <term>plastic spirit</term> <note>The 'spiritus plasticus,' a theoretical biological force believed to mold and shape living matter.</note> that wonderful forms are produced from a vehement imagination: hence so many marks, moles, and "signatures" of fruits, red wine, meat, and animals result from being impressed at the time of birth. Some occur if a cherry, a strawberry, or wine is thrown or poured onto the face or bosom of a woman carrying a womb, and the pregnant woman takes it badly; then a mark of the thing will be seen impressed and painted on the fetus. The same happens if a cat, or a mouse, or a weasel unexpectedly leaps upon a pregnant woman;

<margin>From where do the marks on fetuses come?</margin>
for immediately a mark will be imprinted on the fetus, with the species of the thing radiating through the fantasy, and conveyed by the help of the spirits to the place on the fetus corresponding to the touch; unless perhaps the woman immediately wipes the limb touched by the animal with her hand, and moves that same hand to another part of the body. You may see innumerable examples of this matter in Cornelius Gemma, Weinrich, Lycosthenes, Gesner, Lemnius, and many others.

Therefore, when we read of "monster-bearing" women who gave birth to a fetus deformed with a canine or feline shape, or they confessed to have mixed with dogs;

<margin>An example of a monster-bearing woman.</margin>
as happened in Tuscany in the time of Pope Pius III to a certain woman, who gave birth to a dog...

->The Great Art, Book 10. Magic, Part 1.<-

...having relied on a shameful union with a dog, she was brought before the Pope for the sake of penance; or as happened to another woman in Avignon, who, giving birth to a dog, declared she had endured a dog; for this reason, by order of Francis <note>Francis I (reigned 1515–1547)</note>, King of the French, she was burned together with the dog. It must be said against the Atheists of this time (who impiously assert that a true human can be conceived from a beast, and thus that the human soul is mortal no differently than that of a beast) that these monsters could not possibly have come from the seed of a dog. Just as no other animal can be generated from a human, since these kinds of females differ in quality, nor do they agree in the time of gestation in the womb, and they differ in properties by a distance as wide as the heavens, as was discussed at length in Book 2. Therefore, it must be asserted that such animals, or monsters, are made not from the seed of a brute, but of a human, since such a form is communicated to the fetus by the frequent thought and imagination of the woman.

<margin>History of women giving birth to monsters.</margin>
For even if a dog should enter a woman, nonetheless nothing is generated from that seed, but it vanishes as something unsuitable for the female womb, or turning into rot, is finally cast out with other waste. However, when human seed is conceived, a monster is produced by the force of imagination and thought, because that woman, disturbed by that unspeakable encounter and anxious with fear, constantly thinks she will give birth to a dog. For this reason, St. Jerome relates that he freed a woman suffering under the suspicion of adultery when she produced an offspring not at all similar to the father, because a painting hanging in the woman’s house was not unlike the infant. Therefore, the only painter of such marks is the imagination: the brush is the bodily spirits; the colors are the images radiating from the imagination; the canvas is the tender body of the infant; and the prototype of the infant’s body is the maternal body, whose parts have a singular correspondence with the parts of the infant.

So great is the power of the imagination of pregnant women that whatever they have conceived in the mind, they easily depict in the conceived fetus. Cornelius Gemma <note>A 16th-century physician and astronomer interested in wonders and prodigies</note> reports that when the Emperor Charles V arrived from Spain in Belgium, protected by a well-equipped fleet and surrounded by a most grand display of nobles, as he walked through those coasts, the Belgian women (then carrying in the womb and anxious with excessive curiosity) gave birth to infants with black and curly eyebrows due to the sight of the Spaniards and the working of a most vivid imagination. He also repeats this regarding animals, which occasionally outline monstrous births in the womb from the sole vehement sight of some thing. In the shells of eggs,

<margin>The imagination is the painter of all things.</margin>
above-mentioned authors report that birds have also painted now serpents, now human figures, or something similar.

### The miracles of Nature the painter in stones and plants.

In the roots of plants, it is more well-known than it needs to be said that nature paints and fashions likenesses of all things. I report only those things which I myself have observed. There are four species of stones in which icons of plants and trees and images of fruits are seen wonderfully depicted by nature.

<margin>Various kinds of rocks.</margin>
The first rock is *Borsycites*, which is said by Pliny to be branched in black with white or blood-red foliage. The second is that which Imperato <note>Ferrante Imperato, a Neapolitan apothecary and natural historian</note> calls "Wooded," others call the "Stone of Sinai," and others call *dendrites* <term>dendrite: a stone with tree-like branching mineral marks</term>, composed of many layers like an onion, the inner surfaces of which represent most beautiful images of plants and trees, and indeed even forests. The third is that which, placed by Imperato among the porous kind, has images of fern fronds, whence the stone is called "fern-leaf." The fourth is called "grain-stone," which reflects the likenesses of wheat and other fruits. In Agate and marble, or Jasper, there is almost nothing that nature does not paint: you will see in it now cities, now forests, now rivers, and animals of every kind. I remember that I saw a perfect Crucifix in an Agate.

<margin>Crucifix in Agate.</margin>
Authors of the Jerusalem itinerary testify that an image of St. Jerome, depicted in stone, is also seen near the cave of Bethlehem.

<margin>A natural alphabet found in stones.</margin>
In the ferns <note>likely fossilized plants or dendritic patterns</note> extracted from the Tolfa mine <note>Famous for alum and mineral specimens</note>, I have sometimes extracted an entire alphabet, formed with letters of various wandering lines, in exactly that shape which Figure 1 of the Icon shows. Who does not know that Mandrake and certain bulbs of *Satyrium* <note>A genus of orchids</note> display the rudiments of a human figure? There is also found a <term>anthropomorphos: human-shaped</term> flower that perfectly mimics a human; another species of *Satyrium* mimics bees and flies. Ambrosinus <note>Bartholomeo Ambrosini, director of the Bologna botanical garden</note> testifies that a human image was found in the root of white Bryony and is still preserved in the public Museum of Bologna. Nor does nature figure likenesses of man only in roots and plants, but also of other things from time to time. Who does not know that when the root of the "unhappy" <note>likely the *Pteris aquilina* or Eagle Fern</note> is cut according to a certain law, nature has depicted the Imperial Eagle? In a certain root, called <term>ophioides: snake-like</term> from its effect, it has sketched a serpent, and so in other roots of herbs. Sliced onions show the volumes of the heavens. The root of the *Astragalus* has images of stars. Experience will teach you that in the trunks of various trees, cut according to different sections, you will find various figures. In the roots of plants you will also behold wonderful images of things depicted. In the trunk of Guaiacum wood, a dog's head with the figure of a bird...

## C H A P T E R  I I I.

->Concerning the accidental and casual representation of things, and how it can be induced in objects by art?<-

**W**e spoke in the preceding chapter of the likenesses of things depicted on various bodies by the brush of nature; now it remains for us to treat in this place of the accidental representation of things. We call it "accidental" because the likenesses are imprinted on things by no certain intention of nature, nor even by skillful sculpture or painting, but purely by chance—because the different parts of some complex whole, meeting the eye at a certain and determined point, constitute such and such a figure.

<margin>A medal shaped in a mountain.</margin>
Thus at Palermo <note>Latin: *Panormi*</note>, on the concave side of a high mountain situated in the region of the city, the rocks with the projections of shrubs—even if by chance—present themselves to the eyes with such a projection that they perfectly express a medal with the head of an Emperor in the center.

<margin>A human head expressed on Mount Scylla.</margin>
Those walking toward the theater of the port of Messina also see the Scyllaean promontory, opposite Pelorus, which displays a head with eyes, nose, and beard with such skill that it seems sketched by a brush. The smooth rocks provide the bright parts, while the shrubs, thickets, broom-plants, fern-beds, or even mossy cliffs provide the shadows of the mountain. I remember seeing certain mountains mimicking the figure of a trireme <note>A type of ancient galley ship with three banks of oars.</note>, others a man sitting on a horse,

<margin>A mountain rising in the shape of a galley.</margin>
and some a man—or Bacchus—sitting on a barrel. Only he who has traveled through various regions of the world will discover innumerable sights of this kind; for it can hardly happen that such a variety of cliffs, occurring everywhere, such a difference in planes, and such a multitude of shadows, would not occasionally sketch something—though these things represent nothing unless viewed from a certain point.

<margin>The Altar of Jupiter on Olympus.</margin>
Pausanias relates in his *Boeotia* <note>Kircher refers to the *Description of Greece* by the ancient geographer Pausanias.</note> that there is a mountain in the vicinity of Olympus which was called the Altar of Jupiter for no other reason than that it perfectly expressed an Altar with incense. Pierre Belon <note>Latin: *Bellonius*</note> also relates that for those traveling through the desert of Sin, various fissured rocks at dawn resemble an army of men, even causing fear to those who are unaware of the phantom. Those rocks of Russia, too, which Ortelius <note>Abraham Ortelius, a famous 16th-century cartographer.</note> mentions, I judge to be forms of men, camels, cattle, and other things—the work of "Formative Nature" <note>original: *naturæ formatricis*</note> rather than a miraculous metamorphosis.

<margin>Wonderful specters in the Hermitage of Saint Maurinus.</margin>
I remember having once observed similar works of nature with no small wonder in the Hermitage of Saint Maurinus near the city of Narbonne <note>Latin: *Rhegium Narbonensis*</note> in the Province of France, with as great a variety of figures as the imagination can fashion for itself. Olaus Magnus reports that in the middle of the Northern Sea, nature has placed a cliff most perfectly expressing a monk with his hood. Also on the island of Malta, as I myself observed on the eastern part of the island, a rock hanging from a prominent precipice perfectly emulates the figure of a man in a toga suspended from the cliff, from which the place gets its name from the phantom: "The Hanged Friar" <note>original: *Frate impiccato*</note>.

<margin>A wonderful painting of an image in Chile.</margin>
Everything seems to be surpassed in wonder by that which Father Alonso de Ovalle <note>original: *P. Alphonsus Dovalle*</note>, the Procurator of the Province of Chile, relates while staying here on business, concerning a certain wonderful image of this kind visible among his people. The place is by the Southern Sea, commonly called *del Zur* <note>The Pacific Ocean.</note>, named Arauco, where a mountain is so filled with emeralds, turquoises, and similar precious stones that from a distance it offers a spectacle to be viewed—not without pleasure for the beholders—depicted by the native splendor of such varied stones. In a hollow of this mountain, however, from a certain and established point, the image of the Most Blessed Virgin with her son in her arms is seen depicted with such a variety of colors that almost no one could persuade themselves it is a work of "nature at play" <note>original: *ludentis naturæ*; a common Early Modern concept where nature seems to mimic art or humor.</note>, but all hold fast to the idea of a divine apparition. Indeed, it seemed a wonderful sight to the natives, since it offered itself to be seen only from a specific place; from which, if you withdraw even slightly, the figure now vanishing, nothing more than rocks and precipices [is seen]...

Kircher distinguishes these accidental visual alignments from intentional "plastic magic" and provides global examples ranging from Sicily to Chile.</summary>

# Parastatic Magic

...so that you might think you see more than is there; consequently, the place has been accustomed to be frequented in a wonderful manner over time. The fame of this spectacle spread even to our Fathers <note>Kircher is referring to his fellow Jesuit priests.</note>; who, intending to examine the matter more deeply, traveled to Arauca <note>original: *Araucum*; likely referring to the sanctuary of Our Lady of Arantzazu in Spain, famous for a Marian apparition associated with a thorn bush and rocks.</note>. They inspected the work, and found it to be—not as the simpler folk believed, a divine apparition or a miraculous representation—but a mere optical projection <term>optical projection; Latin: *proiectio optica* — the way light and shadow fall to create a recognizable shape</term> into the eyes, expressed by the chance proportion of light, shadow, stones, and colors, meeting the gaze in the form of a woman clutching her son in her arms.

Lest, however, the devotion of the people toward the Mother of God <term>Mother of God; Latin: *Deipara*</term> be hindered by this so miraculous spectacle, they instituted a solemn procession to that place every year, as if it were a place reserved by divine providence for devotion to the Mother of God. Event showed that this devotion was by no means unpleasing to her; for gradually it began to shine with such great wonders that now, in all that world, hardly a more celebrated place is held. Thus, God the Best and Greatest <note>Latin: *Deus Optimus Maximus*, a standard Roman epithet adopted by Christians</note>, on the occasion of this image falling under the eyes in an unusual way, seems to have chosen this place for himself to propagate the glory of his name and the cult of his Mother. From this it appears that nothing in the nature of things 

<margin>Nothing is casual or accidental.</margin>

can appear so casual and accidental that it does not lie hidden under the secret disposition of divine providence, the moderator of all things; even if to us, because of hidden ends and the inaccessible reasons of divine counsel, it seems for the most part to have no cause. I also heard not long ago that in one of the islands of the Archipelago <note>The Aegean Sea islands</note>, nature played with a similar artifice in forming an image of the Mother of God. And these are the things I thought should be said concerning the accidental representation of images.

Nothing therefore remains except that, following the example of nature, I should also teach in this place the method by which Princes can introduce similar images into the discontinuous surfaces of mountains, fields, valleys, and gardens with similar art; which, however, do not represent anything certain except from a fixed point. This can be done in a twofold manner, either by a scenographic <term>scenographic; Latin: *scenographica* — related to perspective and stage-like projection</term> or orthographic <term>orthographic; Latin: *orthographica* — related to top-down or straight-line projection</term> method, as we will now explain.

### Representation I. Optics.

*How to adapt rocks in the mountains, and to arrange trees and plants in vineyards and gardens with a certain skillful cultivation, so that from a certain and fixed place they represent whatever you wish; but outside of it, absolutely nothing, not even a trace of the thing, appears.*

**I**ntending, therefore, to delineate something worthy of royal magnificence, which may seize the minds of the beholders into admiration: take our instrument, or "mesoptic window" <note>original: *fenestram mesopticam*; a specialized perspective frame used for drawing</note>, which we described in the *Art of Scenography*, Book 2, page 124. On its cloth or veil, first delineate that image which you desire to represent in the said subjects—such as an Eagle here.

-> [An engraving of an optical projection apparatus used for creating anamorphic art. It features a large vertical frame (B) holding a transparent screen or grid. A diagonal surface (A) is positioned in front of it, displaying a distorted image of an eagle. A vertical rod with a sighting hole or eyepiece (G) is located to the right. A dashed line (D) represents the visual ray extending from the viewpoint at G, through the screen, to the projected surface. The entire mechanism is mounted on a wooden frame with supports labeled C, E, and F.] <-

Having done this, fix the instrument in a determined place from which the representation <term>representation; Latin: *parastasis* — a projection or appearance</term> of the image will be given to be viewed. Applying the eye to the sight <term>sight; Latin: *dioptrum* — an observation hole or vane</term> of the small bar G, carefully observe which parts of the representational objects the outlines of the image painted on the cloth cut according to the optical ray. For according to these parts, either the painted or sculpted object will give an image similar to that which is painted on the cloth, which will meet the eyes nowhere else except from the location of the instrument. 

Moreover, only the primary points of the sketch can be marked on the representational objects or the level ground of the gardens. First, either by the eye determining the sections on the objects which the outlines of the image project; or by a light placed in the location of the sight G, and the image formed and cut out of a board or paper in an opaque plane and in the place of the veil; for this, by its light, will determine the sketch of the first picture in the space assigned for the drawing. Or by a shadow, with the figure attached to any transparent veil; for with a light placed at G, this will determine the sketch in the proposed space by its shadow, in exactly the same way we taught for making sundials in the first part of this work, problems 2 and 3. For by these three modes, the matter is accomplished with almost no trouble.

<summary>Kircher explains that "miraculous" natural images, like a Marian rock formation at Arauca, are actually optical illusions governed by divine providence. He then provides technical instructions on using a "mesoptic window" to create anamorphic landscape art that only appears as a coherent image from a single viewpoint.</summary>
