# Great Art, Book 10. Magic Part II.

<margin>Anthropomorphic <note>original: "ανθρωπόμορφος"</note> field, figure 22.</margin>
is brought into effect. And so that you may perceive my mind more clearly, I have seen fit to place here in figure 2 of Illustration 28 <term>Iconismus: a technical term used by Kircher for an engraved plate or diagram</term> the image of a man which, when inspected up close and along the longitudinal base LM, will represent mountains, cities, valleys, precipices, rocks, rivers, lakes, trees, and similar images of a rough field. If, however, you look at it from a distance above the straight base MD, immediately an image of a human figure—composed of the various shadows of the trees, rocks, and rivers—will present itself to the eyes of the beholder, not without pleasure, as the figure shows more extensively. In like manner, any field could be so arranged that, when viewed from a certain place, it would exhibit a similar apparition. For if you were to scribe this figure onto the veil of the <term>mesoptic instrument: a device Kircher designed for calculating perspective and anamorphic distortions</term> and work according to the handed-down practices, you would easily reach the proposed goal.

### Corollary I.

From these things it is clear by what method any figure or image can be described on the walls of some gallery with a long stretch of walls, so that it can be seen from only a single determined point of sight; outside of that point, however, the whole picture would reflect forests, men, animals, lakes, gardens, fishponds, mountains, and similar things.

Once our mesoptic window is placed, you will first paint the image to be projected onto the slanted wall upon its veil, and then you will work with the eye applied to point G, as has been said; for the optical rays determining the outlines of the image on the cloth will also determine the scattered projection of the image on the wall in such a way that it can be seen from no other place except from point G.

### Corollary II.

<margin>Church pavements.</margin>
It is also clear by what method the same things can be described on the floor of some church or gallery; so that a determined figure appears only at the entrance to the church or gallery, but as one moves forward, the appearances of the images utterly vanish.

### Corollary III.

From these things it follows that there is no place so irregular, nor any scattered with such discontinuous surfaces, that any image cannot be painted on them with the help of this instrument; it will demonstrate the image only under a certain point, and under no other, as is clear in figure 2 of Illustration 28 of this work.

### Corollary IV.

<margin>Other wonders of gardens.</margin>
It is also clear by what method you can exhibit wonders in gardens through the skillful grafting of plants and trees—such as coats of arms, and the likenesses of Princes, and various figures of animals—so skillfully arranged from a given point that they seem to be drawn with a brush. This can also be done on the disordered rocks of mountains, on the steps of stairs, between columns, and in other places which might seem like miracles to men; and even if no deception underlies them—indeed, they are most certain and demonstrative, and easily put into practice—this art could even be used to construct a city which, from a high place, would represent something specific. Just as histories relate that the architect Dinocrates <note>An ancient Greek architect who proposed carving Mount Athos into a colossal statue of Alexander the Great holding a city.</note> wished to shape Mount Athos for Alexander the Great. Fields and gardens can also be varied to emulate a figure proposed by the artist when viewed from a distance, as is beautifully clear in figure 2 of this Illustration. All of these things we leave for the curious reader to investigate further.

## Scenographic Representation <note>original: "Parastasis"</note> II.

-> *How to describe one and the same image, or different images, on a panel with such art that none may be seen except from a determined point.* <-

<margin>How one image may be rendered fivefold by a change of sight alone.</margin>
On a certain panel, let any image be drawn—for example, of Christ our Savior. After this is done, with very thin threads stretched perpendicularly across the plane of the image, you shall set the panel with the threads in such a slanted position that the threads meet the eye as one continuous white surface. Once this is done, and the panel fixed in this position, an image—for example, of the Blessed Virgin—should be drawn on that same white surface of the threads, according to the position of the eye at a slant. Then, from the opposite side of the image on the same surface of threads, another image—for example, of Saint John the Baptist—shall likewise be fashioned from a slanted position. Thus, it will have three different images, the middle of which will exhibit Christ to a straight ray <term>orthopticus: viewing something directly or at a 90-degree angle</term>, the second will exhibit the Virgin to a slanted ray <term>loxopticus: viewing from an oblique or diagonal angle</term>, and the third will likewise exhibit the Precursor <note>John the Baptist</note> to a slanted ray. If, however, you wish to exhibit other images on the same panel to an upward ray <term>anopticus</term> and a downward ray <term>catopticus</term>, the threads must be drawn crosswise, so that they exhibit a sort of grid with the vertical ones on the plane of the image. With these placed, let one image be drawn from the upper part on one surface of the threads, and another from the lower part according to the upward ray on the opposite surface of the threads; and one and the same panel will exhibit five different images, none of which can be seen except in a certain and determined place. This is a very beautiful thing, easy to do, and pleasing to spectators. In what manner a representation of these images can be exhibited with mirrors will be told in the following treatise.

# Parastatic Magic <note>The term "Parastatic" refers to the art of making images appear or be presented, often through optical illusions.</note>

To this subject belong those common exhibitions where various images are painted on both sides of paper folded in the manner of prisms. Likewise, there are those triangular "staircase" sticks, arranged step-by-step, upon which an image is scattered; a mirror placed at an oblique angle then demonstrates the image anew by uniting its forms. Since Barbarus <note>Daniele Barbaro (1514–1570), an author on architecture and perspective.</note>, Dantes <note>Ignazio Danti (1536–1586), a mathematician and cosmographer.</note>, and the *Curious Perspective* <note>Refers to the work *La Perspective curieuse* by Jean-François Niceron (1613–1646).</note> treat these matters at length, we have decided to omit them here, contenting ourselves only with those things which are of our own invention.

# CHAPTER IV.
## *On Representation through the transmission of images into a dark place.*

->*Representation III. Of Light and Shadows.*<-
->*In which various likenesses of things are represented in the dark.*<-

**A**LTHOUGH we dealt with the radiation of images into a dark place in various ways in the second book of this work, we only handed down the commonly known facts there. Here, it seemed appropriate to hand down certain more hidden modes of representation. Note, therefore, that there is a twofold mode of representing things in a dark place. The first is by the radiation of images into a dark place; the other is by light or fire. Let us follow each in order.

Representation of the first kind is done both with a glass lens and without one, as explained in the cited place. However, things are exhibited best of all in a dark place with a glass—that is, a lenticular crystal—so that appearing in their natural size, they may occasionally strike the viewer with awe <note>original: "horrorem," here meaning a sense of wonder or being overwhelmed by the realism.</note>. But so that neither the hole nor the lenticular glasses betray the method of the representation, you shall hide the artifice with this industrious trick: 

Opposite the hole in the dark place, let a certain receptacle be made in the shape of a cube or a parallelepiped (as Figure 3 of Illustration 28 shows), which encloses the entire area of the hole. It should be covered with thin and very fine paper, the side of which opposite the hole should have the true proportion of distance required to represent the images genuinely. Once this is done, the likenesses of things from outside, radiating through their own images onto the white paper, will present themselves to those watching from the opposite side as if in a theater. Thus, whatever is outside will appear thoroughly lifelike through this industry, represented with the greatest convenience and with a greater concealment of the experiment. For neither the hole nor the lenticular pupil is seen, but only the images are represented on the bright, translucent paper, filled with an innumerable variety of colors. This is done by the same reasoning we taught above in the first part of this work, propositions 2 and 3, for making "prodigious clocks" <note>likely referring to sundials or devices that project time using light.</note>.

<margin>*The "Wonder-Machine" for representing images.*</margin>
I remember a distinguished craftsman in Germany used a machine of this kind to exhibit fields, cities, forests, stage scenes, and spectacles of every kind so skillfully that no one could persuade himself that these things were being shown by a natural art. The machine was built in the shape of a cube, ABCD, whose outer sides were opaque and had a hole equipped with a lenticular glass on each side. Within the hollow of the cube, however, another cube, EF, was erected, formed and covered with the finest translucent paper. Its sides were distant from the sides of the first cube by exactly the proportion required for the best possible representation of the images of things. This machine had a hole in the center of its bottom, F, large enough to precisely accommodate a man; for while the machine stood on its support, a person would insert himself through the lower hole. Then, he would soon block the gaps where the light entered with a head-wrap or some other thing, so that no light could get in. 

Once this was done, he fixed the machine wherever he wished; for it was constructed of such light material that it could easily be carried by two people without labor. When these things were prepared, if he desired to show pleasant spectacles to everyone, he would have the men's heads inserted through the bottom hole and open the little windows serving the passage of the images. And behold! within the hollow, various likenesses of things soon appeared on the paper sides of the inner cube, each distinct in its variety of colors. 

Here you would have seen mountains, fields, forests, men, beasts, hunts, and other theatrical spectacles exhibited so skillfully that no art of painting would suffice to delineate them with such great variety. Added to these were the gestures of each person, the faces of the men standing around outside, their gestures, looks, speech, the movement of their teeth, and the flight of birds, which were represented so lifelike that I do not remember seeing anything more pleasant in my whole life. For the hollow of the inner cube was illuminated by external light so that one could conveniently read there. 

This machine also provided the greatest utility: if the projections of forests, hills, mountains, and fields with rivers, waters, and ruins, as well as the likenesses of men and animals, were to be drawn to the life, he would turn the machine toward them. And behold, with no trouble at all and the greatest pleasure, the likenesses of said things, exhibited within the sides of the middle hollow cube, offered themselves to be traced upon the paper so lifelike that anyone, no matter how...

I understood that not long ago in Paris, a similar machine was constructed in the form of a **sedan chair** <note>original: "Sedilii gestatorii," a portable covered chair carried by porters</note>, which was sold at a high price; but as people have written to me and as is widely admitted, the entire reasoning for its invention was taken from this machine described by us.

->Another way to represent the same at night.<-

**I**f you place the aforementioned machine in a room at night, and there exhibit various likenesses of things under sufficient illumination, they will project their images through the outermost hole onto the sides of the internal concave cube, just as those shown in the Sun are displayed by light. I said "proportionate illumination" because at night a tiny light accomplishes nothing, but an intense light is required to display the said <term>exhibition</term> <note>original: "parastasin," a term Kircher uses to mean a demonstration or visual display</note>.

### Exhibition IV. Theatrical.

->On the equipment of Stages, and lights created by art.<-

<margin>*The excellence of theatrical equipment.*</margin>
**W**e must now discuss the method by which Scenes, Comedies, Tragedies, and similar spectacles can be exhibited to the life in the dark. Of all the works constructed and elaborated by human hands, which are accustomed to provide both the greatest delight to the sight and incredible wonder to the mind, in my judgment, the form and graceful appearance of some scenic apparatus should not be held in the lowest place. For there, within a small circuit and by the teaching of the <term>optical faculty</term> <note>the science of perspective and light</note>, magnificent palaces, huge temples, and many buildings—both near and distant—are arranged with marvelous distribution, along with wide-ranging squares furnished with different kinds of buildings, and furthermore some roads produced in a very straight line, which are divided in the middle by the meeting of other transverse roads. Indeed, triumphal arches, sublime columns, pyramids, obelisks, and many other things are placed there, shining with a multitude of greater, smaller, and medium lights—special regard being given to symmetry; these lights are composed among themselves with such artistry that they seem to rival and imitate diamonds, <term>fire-stones</term> <note>original: "pyropos," likely referring to rubies or garnets</note>, sapphires, emeralds, and other shining and most precious stones. Here you will see the Sun and the shining Moon gradually 

<margin>*Wonderful theatrical spectacles.*</margin>
emerging from the darkness and ascending by degrees to the heights, and finally hiding themselves beneath the waters, with the stars arranged with such admirable industry that they play upon the very eyes of the spectators; truly, the industry of the artist cannot be praised enough according to his merits. Nor will their minds be rendered less astonished when they behold, one after another, an Angel gliding through the air, or a planet swimming through the sky, or the appearance of some other new and unusual thing. Furthermore, what is more beautiful and pleasant than the choruses of dancers and singers equipped with royal pomp and magnificent preparation, seen with the novelty and elegance of many garments? What is rarer than the exotic exhibitions which I remember seeing in various places—but especially here in Rome—paradoxical even to the point of being a miracle? We would gladly describe their equipment here along with the prodigious machines, were we not reserving them for the *Mechanical Wonder-worker* <note>Kircher's reference to his other planned or existing writings on mechanics and stagecraft</note.

<margin>*Summary of what has been said.*</margin>
Therefore, if you arrange the said scenes around the machine described, a fantastic theater filled with every variety of things will appear to you in the concave space of the interior cube. Here, all the actions of the world—the fall of lightning from heaven, the flashes of the sky, the running of animals, the flight of birds, the various manners of men, and the customs of nations—all of it within a tiny space; I consider that nothing more marvelous than this can be done.

### Exhibition V. Chromatic.

->Or, on various artifices of colors and their prodigious mixture.<-

**O**mitting the common mixtures of colors in this place, we shall deal here only with those that savor of something hidden. But among other color artifices, that invention of the Turks certainly holds a high place, by which paper is usually painted with a certain infinite variety of colors; the painting sometimes turning into the overflowing waves of the sea, soon into variegated marble, and then into the multicolored feathers of birds; an altogether admirable invention, teeming with secrets.

->The method of painting paper in the Turkish manner.<-

**G**um <term>tragacanth</term> <note>a natural gum obtained from the dried sap of Middle Eastern legumes, used as a binder and thickener</note> is immersed in the purest water for three days until it is dissolved into a white liquor: then it is strained and poured into a small box <note>or tray</note> of the same width as the sheets of paper, but with a depth of two or three fingers. It must be observed, however, that the water of this kind should not be too thick, nor too thin: otherwise, the colors thrown in would either not unfold themselves properly because of the thickness of the water, or because...

# Representational Magic

...due to excessive thinness and liquidity, they would retain the given shapes less faithfully.

<margin>The condition of the colors.</margin>
The lighter the colors are, the more suitable they will be. <term>Lacca</term> <note>A red pigment derived from insects or resin, often called "lake" color</note> for red; Indigo, as they call it, for a blue color seems most fit, especially if some white color is mixed with the Indigo to dilute its excessive saturation. We are forced to use <term>Orpiment</term> <note>A bright yellow mineral (arsenic trisulfide) used as a pigment</note> for yellow and <term>ceruse</term> <note>White lead, a common but toxic white pigment</note> for white; although they are heavy by nature, we must use them when lighter options are lacking. Each is ground separately upon a marble slab with water, dissolved egg white, <term>ox gall</term> <note>Bile from cattle, used in marbling to help colors spread and stick to the paper</note>, and a small quantity of what they call petroleum oil; they are then strained into their own small dishes, neither too thick nor too liquid, but tempered in a middle way. It must be observed, when they are sprinkled with a brush into the previously prepared water, that each falling drop spreads itself in an equal and uniform tenor over the surface of the water in a sufficiently wide circle. If this does not happen, some gall is poured in anew and mixed until the desired result is achieved.

The colors are to be sprinkled one by one, in no certain order, but in that which experience teaches to be most convenient; when the surface of the water is entirely hidden, covered by the colors, the sprinkling should stop. Another sign of this is when the colors appear sufficiently gathered together and distinguished by their native brilliance, rather than appearing diluted and dull—unless perhaps a fault of this kind arises either from the color itself, which might be naturally less bright, or from an excess of infused gall, which happens not infrequently. For if the water is burdened with more colors than is proper, besides the fact that they sink to the bottom and stain the water, they also obey less effectively the <term>reed</term> <note>original: "calamo," a stylus or pointed stick used to drag patterns</note> or comb that marks them, and they display less clean and well-defined lines of color—in which, however, the entire splendor and beauty of this kind of painting is seen to reside.

<margin>How the colors of Jasper are made.</margin>
Once the colors have been infused and the surface of the water is covered with various drops of color in the manner of <term>Jasper</term> <note>A variety of chalcedony; here referring to the mottled or "marbled" look of the stone</note>: if you wish to paint the paper so that it resembles this kind of Jasper, you then lower the sheet of paper gradually into the water, beginning from its farthest edge until you reach the opposite side. Then, the entire outer edge of the paper adhering to the sides of the box is pressed with a lightly running finger, so that all the color that usually remains in such an edge is taken up by the paper itself, leaving nothing behind. Finally, the edge of the paper is grasped and slowly removed, then laid out in a flat place to be dried.

<margin>How feathers are depicted on paper.</margin>
Or, if you wish to express not Jasper but other figures, such as vortices, feathers, and the like: then indeed, by drawing a reed back and forth from one side of the box to the opposite, you will cut through all the drops and draw them out lengthwise. After these things are done, you will draw a comb—consisting of needles arranged in a long row—from the top side of the box to the bottom. In this way, the transverse paths of the colors will be cut perpendicularly and will express leaves or feathers; finally, you may twist these individual feathers as you wish with the help of the same reed. However, this entire work requires a swift craftsman; for although the colors float, they nevertheless gradually sink and stain the water if they rest upon it for too long. For how long the same water can be used can hardly be asserted with certainty, since it depends on experience; when it is observed to be stained with colors and more turbid, it must then be poured out, the box diligently cleaned, and another batch of water used anew.

Whoever observes the aforementioned method well will undoubtedly find a gateway opened for himself to infinite other inventions, which I leave to the curious reader to investigate.

### Another method, more secret than the first.

<margin>A new invention for tinting images.</margin>
In this century, a certain wonderful artifice for tinting images has come forth from France. One sees images depicted in every kind of color, but not always or everywhere, except most especially when they are exposed to the light. (For it is not painted images that are tinted by this method, but only those engraved in copper.) These, when tinted by this artifice, show not even a trace of color in the evening by candlelight or during the day in the shade; but when exposed to the Sun and various lights, they show images depicted in a kind of fantastic and all-encompassing color, rivaling the colors of the heavenly rainbow and those found in the tails of peacocks and the feathers of other birds—with a golden, crimson, saffron, purple, and red variety. Some of these colors are most clear in the light while others lie hidden, but when those are brought out from their hiding place, the remaining ones vanish. This thing is more deceptive to the sight than can be described, since this color is by no means earthly, nor applied with a brush, but produced by the industry of hidden nature through <term>evaporation</term> <note>Kircher is likely describing an early form of structural color or a chemical reaction involving thin films of vaporized substances on the surface of the paper or engraving</note> onto the paper, as we shall say shortly. When I first saw this invention, I was somewhat stuck, I confess, at the sight of such an unusual thing; but quickly sensing the hiding places of nature, by the grace of God, from the principles of nature...

<header>The Great Art, Book 10. Part 2: Magic.</header>

...from the principles, I extracted the whole process without very intense study, and I freely share it with the curious reader without any expected compensation. Proceed as follows: Take common salt, and twice as much <term>sal ammoniac<note>Ammonium chloride; used historically in alchemy and dyeing.</note></term>, Roman vitriol, Cyprian vitriol—specifically the green and the blue varieties—and Tolfan alum, commonly called *de la Rocca*; take an equal amount of each. Let them all be mixed together and placed in a steam bath well known to chemists. As soon as you feel the liquefied mixture of salts beginning to evaporate, expose your copper-engraved images to the vapor. The colors naturally inherent in the salts and vitriols, mixed with the vapor, will soon tint the images through this "genesis of colors."

<margin>The true cause of the <term>chromatism<note>Color-changing properties.</note></term> in Nephritic wood, by which it tints water.</margin>
<margin>All types of colors exist within Sal Ammoniac.</margin>
Furthermore, this genesis of colors gave us the opportunity for further philosophizing regarding those "phantom colors" produced by water tinted by <term>Nephritic wood<note>original: "ligno Nephritico." A wood from Mexico (Eysenhardtia polystachya) famous in the 17th century for its medicinal properties and its blue fluorescence in water.</note></term>, which was brought not long ago from New Spain (about which we treated extensively in Book 1, Part 2, Proposition 1). The reason, cause, and origin of these colors, which eluded us in the cited passage, has finally manifested itself clearly to the intellect through the study of this mystery. For I think that the said water, appearing in different ways according to the different motion of shadows, has the same origin as these saline colors we are now discussing, which are induced upon images through evaporation. Since the said wood swells with sal ammoniac, and in sal ammoniac all the seeds of colors lie hidden (as was said in the place cited above), it happens that those colors are released, communicated to the liquid, and exhibit the colored water in different ways according to the different incidence of light. And this I believe to be the genuine cause of the colors appearing in said water. If, however, anyone brings forward a better cause for this chromatic wonder, I promise we will not be unwilling to subscribe to their view.

# CHAPTER V.
## On Anaclastic Representation.
### Or, on the exhibition of things through refracted rays in water and glass bodies.

## Representation VI.
### In which wonderful spectacles of things are exhibited under water, through glass spheres and polygonal glasses.

## Experiment I.
### To construct an image with such industry that, seen from the same point, it gradually disappears into nothing by decreasing, and grows from nothing back into a perfect image. See figure 1, Illustration 29.

<margin>Illustration XXXI.</margin>
**REFRACTION** is a wondrous thing: for by its aid, things otherwise hidden and unseen emerge into the light, presenting themselves to the sight; by its aid, stars not yet risen are seen as if already risen; by its aid, mountains and islands unseen in the sea offer themselves to be viewed at certain times. Let us see, therefore, by what method we might also exhibit various spectacles by this means. Let two vessels, B and C, be made, separated inside by the joining of a partition. Let B be like a basin or a lip; let the lower one be of any size, each equipped with its own <term>stopcock<note>original: "epistomio." A valve or tap to control the flow of water.</note></term>. Furthermore, let the vessel have two columns upon which another vessel, A, is placed, with a stopcock V. Fill both vessels A and B with very clear water. In the bottom of the basin B, place any image you like, so that from a certain point O (which you shall never change thereafter), it can be seen from a distance under the water. This being done, once stopcock S is opened, let the water of vessel B flow down into vessel C: and behold, the image placed at the bottom will gradually decrease so much that not even a trace of it remains (always observing from that certain fixed point). One can hardly say how much this holds the spectators in astonishment. If you wish to restore it to its original form, open stopcock V; the water flowing down from A will fill the basin B anew. As the water increases, the figure of the image will grow until it reaches its perfect form; and that which previously did not strike the eyes at all will now rise up piece by piece into a perfect image, presenting itself to be seen.

## Corollary I.

**From this** it is clear that if a golden figure of the Sun is placed at the bottom of the vessel in this instrument, the motion of the Sun from sunrise to sunset can be perfectly exhibited, along with the differences in hours, which you shall scribe on the inner surface of the vessel <note>original: "κατὰ τὴν τήρησιν" — according to observation</note>.

## Corollary II.

**It is also clear** that this work will be much more wonderful if the figure at the bottom is scattered; for in that case, no matter how the point of the eye is changed, nothing of the figure will appear <note>This refers to an anamorphic image that only resolves when viewed through the specific refractive medium of the water.</note>.

Under the glass bottom, let there be a certain wheel containing various figures around its circumference; this wheel, when turned, will hide some figures and reveal others, especially if the cover of the vessel has an opening as large as the ima-

# Corollary.

**FROM** these things it is clear by what method a likeness of the **Planets** can be exhibited every hour: namely, if a wheel, rotated every six hours, brings the ruling Planet to a stop. Who does not see that this spectacle has a certain appearance of <term>hydromancy<note>Divination by means of water; here used metaphorically to describe the "magical" appearance of images in liquid.</note></term>? # Experiment III.
## *To exhibit the appearances of things through glass spheres or vials.*

<margin>Various appearances through the transmission of light.</margin>
**ANY** figures may be painted upon glass vials shaped into a sphere. It should be noted, however, that figures painted on the glass in light and airy colors have this property: that when exposed to the Sun or another light, at a certain distance, they exhibit an image projected onto a white cloth with all its colors. Therefore, with these figures painted on the glass spheres, if you place a light behind a vial full of water, it will demonstrate each species of the images painted on the circumference of the glass upon the paper placed in front, just as if they were cast off from the objects themselves. If you apply this projection to the machine indicated in display 3, you will exhibit here all those things which we exhibited there. All these things will be exhibited more perfectly if you project the species onto white paper through an intermediate lens, just as we teach in our new <term>Steganography<note>original: "Steganographia." This refers to Kircher’s work on secret communication, which included using mirrors and lenses to project hidden text.</note></term>. There is also another method, which they are most often accustomed to exhibit at the <term>Nativity scene<note>original: "praesepe." A traditional Christmas display of the birth of Christ.</note></term> on the feast of the Birth of the Lord. They place a vial full of water within an opening of some wall at a distance; then, on the edge of some wooden disk, they attach images emulating the history of the feast, separated from the vial by as small a space as possible. Then, candles placed below move the disk around by their heat: and behold, from the other side, through the vial, the images will offer themselves to the viewers as if floating on the water in a quite delightful spectacle.

# Experiment IV.
## *To exhibit wonderful spectacles through glass prisms, or triangular glasses.*

<gloss>Displaying a rainbow.</gloss>
**IN** the first book, enough was said concerning the material of the glass prism, or triangular glass; now opportunity demands that we apply their theory to produce unusual effects. The triangular glass is known for pouring forth innumerable colors from itself; however, for the display apparatus to be successful, they ought to be made a little larger than usual. Therefore, you will first exhibit a rainbow if you permit the rays of the Sun to pass through the glass in a dark place: for in the concavity, it will perfectly express a rainbow with all its distinctions of colors.

# Corollary I. For Displays.
## *So that a room may seem dressed in the most excellent tapestries. See figure 2 of Plate 29.*

**LET** 3, 4, 5, or as many triangular glasses as you wish be joined into one, so that they touch each other at their solid angles, as you see done here in **CD**. You shall expose this "poly-triangular" device to the Sun within a hole, and immediately the ray of the Sun penetrating the glasses will paint the whole room with a certain heavenly and luminous ornament, such that it might not incongruously resemble paradise. If these rays are received by a concave mirror, you will soon see new spectacles of color, much different from the former ones; if, however, you look through the glass, all things shown to you from outside will seem to exhibit something heavenly with an infinite variety of colors.

# Representation Magic

<margin>A heaven in a room that can be displayed.</margin>A system exposed to solar rays, placed around the axis of a window opening and rotated like a wheel, will offer itself as a most pleasant spectacle. For all the brightest figures, driven in a circle, will represent the starry sky within a dark room, to the great wonder of the viewers. All these things will occur with even greater admiration if they are viewed represented on the sides of the interior of a hollow paper cube, which we mentioned above in **Representation III**.

### Experiment V.

->*How you may see a whole room, or chamber, and all the people in it, appear green or infused with a given color.*<-

Mizaldus <note>Antoine Mizauld (1510–1578), a French physician and occult writer.</note> and Porta <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), an Italian scholar and polymath known for his work on optics and natural magic.</note> exhibit this spectacle by means of a lamp whose oil is tinted with a verdigris color <note>original: *aerugineo colore*</note> along with the wick. I find the matter has better success through a glass sphere, or vial, either made of green glass or filled with water tinted with a verdigris color.

<margin>Painting the faces of men with a given color.</margin>For if you place such vials in the window openings with lights positioned behind them, they will soon infect the entire room and all the furnishings, as well as the faces of the men, with a verdigris color. The same will happen if you imbue the water of the vials with yellow, red, blue, or black color; for everything will be imbued with the said colors. If, however, you place vials tinted with yellow and red water, a golden color will be born, according to those things we said in **Book 1, Problem 3**, concerning the mixture of colors. Thus, by the mixture of colors, vials imbued with different colors will also imbue the chamber with different colors. This is especially true if the light is placed in the center of the vial, the method for which we taught in the *Magnetic Art*, **Book 3**.

### The Author’s Critique.

->*Whether, according to Anaxilaus, Albertus, and Porta, a house can be represented full of serpents and other animals; and whether men can be transformed into any animal by the help of light when a lamp is lit.*<-

Porta, citing Anaxilaus <note>Anaxilaus of Larissa, a 1st-century BC Pythagorean magician mentioned by Pliny the Elder.</note> and Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, the 13th-century philosopher often associated with alchemical and magical texts.</note>, reports many things by which he thinks a lamp alone, when lit, can represent anything in chambers, and thus can show men conspicuous with the heads of donkeys or horses. It seemed fitting to examine the truth of this matter in this place; partly so that the curious, enticed by the novelty of the thing, do not fall into very grave errors; and partly so that the truth alone, all pretenses and impostures having been expelled, may find its place. But lest we do an injustice to a man otherwise highly deserving of the Republic of Letters <note>A common term for the international community of scholars.</note>, we have thought it necessary to cite his words first. Thus he says in the last book of his *Natural Magic*: *“I have thought long and hard,”* says Porta, *“whether the ancients, being ignorant of such secrets, were telling the truth in what is said of them and promised by impostors. I was not a little rejoiced when I found many among the ancients who took care of these things, especially Anaxilaus, giving credit to the assertion of Pliny; and we have sweated not a little in discovering these things to complete our history.”*

<margin>Ridiculous spectacles.</margin>*“To make the heads of bystanders appear like those of horses or donkeys, proceed thus: Cut off the head of a horse or a donkey—not a dead one, lest its power be weak—and fashion a clay pot of the same capacity filled with oil, so that it sits above its own fat. Close the mouth with a lid and stubborn mummy-clay <note>original: "mumies luto," likely a reference to bitumen or a strong sealing paste.</note>, apply a slow fire so that the oil is kept boiling for three days, and the boiled flesh runs into the oil so that the bones are seen bare. Pound them with a pestle, and let the powder be mixed with the oil, with which the heads of the bystanders are to be anointed. Similarly, let hemp wicks be placed in the middle of lamps, neither near nor far as the matter requires, and you will be seen with a monstrous appearance. Oil extracted from a recently decapitated human head induces a human face on animals; thus with the heads of various animals you will render bodies monstrous, if the houses are illuminated by these lit wicks.”* Close your heart to this trust! For as secrets were hidden by the ancients, they are not easily dug out from their words. However, Anaxilaus teaches otherwise, *“and not in vain”*: *“Let the virus <note>Here referring to the secretions or semen.</note> of horses be taken from mating, and when lit in new lamps and wicks, the heads of men will be represented monstrously to the sight as equine; the same is handed down concerning donkey heads.”*

These are the things Porta promises. Let us therefore examine each one according to the principles of nature, so that we may be able to discern what is to be believed in such a slippery business. First, he commands that the heads of animals be cut off and preserved in a new pot full of oil along with their fat; the bones are also to be pounded in a pestle, and an ointment made from the powder mixed with the oil, with which the heads of those to be transformed must first be anointed. See, I pray, this ridiculous method, and laugh at the great imposture detected! For he thinks the shape of a horse’s or donkey’s head is so impressed upon the oil by this art that, when the wick is lit, it exhibits the species of the impression made outside itself. But what connection does an oily liquid have with the shape of a donkey’s head? What proportion does a lit wick have for representing a shape? I do not see it.

# The Great Art, Book 10. Magic, Part II.

<margin>Refutation of the so-called "donkey-illusion."</margin>
...to be able to produce a <term>parastatic<note>From the Greek 'parastasis,' meaning a representation or an appearance; here referring to an illusory image.</note></term> effect. For either this donkey’s head leaves a sensible figure of its shape impressed upon the oil, or it does not leave it, but acts only by some sympathetic power. Both ideas are proven to be ridiculous and fabricated. I shall show the first to be no less ridiculous than it is false by this argument: All water, as well as other liquids, by the very inconsistency of their flowing nature, have this property: they are entirely incapable of receiving the impression of any fixed figure. We are not speaking here of the images of things reflected from water—for those are not impressed images, but are struck back from the mirror-like surface to the eye—but rather of those which are displayed in the very midst of the liquid. Since this is the case, who does not now see that the impression of a sensible figure of a horse's head <note>Kircher uses 'equini' (horse) and 'asinini' (donkey) somewhat interchangeably here to refer to the beast-head illusion.</note> in oil is impossible? Furthermore, for oil to represent things, it ought to be especially clear and transparent. But who does not see that from this boiling of a donkey’s head in oil, the oil—I will not say remains in its natural state—but degenerates into a thick and dense broth, with all the transparency of the oil destroyed? Therefore, the impression of the image of a horse’s head is impossible. But let us examine the other side, by which they think this monstrous display occurs through some insensible operation arising from a certain <term>occult sympathy</term>. This reasoning is no less stupid than it is unskilled, being founded on no principles of nature whatever.

<margin>A second refutation.</margin>
Which I prove thus: Every actual representation of images, which is what we are properly discussing here, necessarily depends in its being and its becoming upon a real, actually existing <term>prototype<note>The 'prototypon' is the original object that emits the light or 'species' that the eye perceives.</note></term> object. For just as no one can see an object unless it truly and really (or at least apparently) exists; and just as light cannot exist without a glowing body; so images projected into a dark place can in no way represent a thing unless there truly and really exists a radiating object, for which the images serve as a kind of substitute to produce vision. But for a man to be seen as conspicuous with a horse's head, some sensible prototype is necessarily required to express it; but this can in no way be conceived as "insensible" within the oil. Therefore, this principle is also false and irreconcilable with the principles of nature. I said "true and real" to exclude the deceptions by which mages, with the help of a Demon, can impress a figure upon the eyes, displaying things to the sight that do not truly exist outside the eye—just as we see happening to those suffering from <term>scotomia<note>A medical term for dizziness or dark spots in the visual field.</note></term> and <term>melancholy</term>, who see many things that have no existence outside their own vision. But we are speaking of oil which, having had a horse’s head placed in it and macerated for a long time, is said to obtain the power of representing things under the form of a horse’s head; which we say is a most foul lie and mere imposture, an art repugnant to all principles of nature. Of this same grain are all those <term>parastatic phantoms</term> falsely ascribed to **Albertus Magnus**; such as when he thinks that if they take the blood of a young donkey and anoint the heads of men, they will see the men under a donkey-like form. And so that you might see a man as conspicuous with three heads, the **Pseudo-Albertus** prescribes this operation:

<margin>Albert's magical metamorphosis.</margin>
-> *Take the hairs of a dead donkey, and make a small cord and dry it. Take the marrow of the bone of the principal right shoulder, and mix it with a virgin rod, and smear the cord, and place it over the threshold of the house; and those entering the house will appear to have three heads; likewise, those who are in the house will seem like donkeys to those entering.* <-

Since there are as many superstitions in this experiment as there are words, I have judged it unworthy to waste time in refuting it. To these ravings are also recalled all those things which **Wecker** reports from **Albert** and **Porta**, in which nothing is more foolish than that the **Pseudo-Albertus** wants to display a man under the form of an Angel by similar trifles. And let these remarks suffice concerning the transformation of men into animals. However, by what means this metamorphosis can be performed by a natural action with the help of mirrors will be discussed in the following treatise on *Catoptric Magic*. Another trifle is that many people think that by this method they can also delineate the images of said things on a wall in a certain room. And first indeed, **Porta** thinks he can display a house full of grapes by this method:

<margin>The house appears as if full of grapes.</margin>
-> *When the grape already begins to lose its flower, let a vessel full of pure oil be placed below, into which you shall submerge the cluster with its leaves; let it be secured so the wind does not pull it here or there; let the sun strike it, with a lid made of gypsum and skin, leaving however a hole through which the stem may be let in; thus let it remain. When the grape has reached perfect maturity, it is pressed with a cloth, and the pressed liquid is kept in oil for a few days under the sun; finally, when it is lit in lamps, you will see everything full of grapes, and you will seem to be surrounded by leaves and trees.* <-

Fine words indeed, and wonderfully composed for persuasion; but it is the habit of charlatans to sell their vermin-infested goods to the simple and credulous crowd with beautiful words. For who does not see that a grape placed in oil not only fails to reach maturity, but, being macerated by the penetration of the oil, will degenerate entirely into another compound? Even granted—though not conceded—that it should reach maturity; yet who, from our prior reasoning...

...our eye <note>original: "videt," referring back to the observer in the previous page's argument</note> does not see that the juice of pressed grapes mixed with oil possesses no power for representing anything? This experiment is therefore false, just like all the others, such as those that claim to display a "silver house" if one puts juice from the tails of black lizards mixed with oil into a lamp; or those that claim to show a whole house full of snakes, if there were a wick made from the fat and the sloughed-off skin of a black snake and a funeral cloth, and this were burned in elderberry oil. Forgive me, Reader, if you see me lingering longer over these kinds of madness; for I have done this with the intention that curious and unskilled youth should take every care to guard themselves against such fabrications, through which they not infrequently enter into pacts and illusions of demons. They should not assent to these things for any reason unless they have first examined them with the exact scale of reason according to the principles of nature, persuading themselves in all things not so much of what *has been done*, but what *ought to be* possible. Time reveals many things cited everywhere by authors of no small reputation, which, creeping even into the schools against everyone's opinion, experience—the mistress of things—has nevertheless taught and proven to be false, lying, and full of deceits and impostures. In the imitation of nature, one must not choose just anything, but that which is most consistent with the operation of nature. Now, we must discuss the manner in which these things should be displayed according to the operation of nature.

### Experiment VI.

->*To exhibit a room full of figures of grapes, fruits, and crawling animals.*<-

<margin>The Pantoptic Machine.</margin>
These apparitions can be shown in two ways: either by the help of our "Parastatic" <note>An instrument for projecting images, a precursor to the magic lantern.</note> instrument proposed in Experiment 3, through the injection of images into a dark place, or by the help of glass. The first is set up as follows: Let any number of very tiny holes be made in the sides of our "pantoptic" <note>Meaning "all-seeing."</note> machine; then, outside the machine, directly across from the holes, let an image of a grape or another fruit be exposed to the Sun. The radiant images of the grape, projected through the holes onto the outermost sides of the interior cube, will display everything inside full of the figures of grapes, according to the number of holes. The same will happen if, instead of a grape, you place apples, pears, melons, and other fruits, or even the figures of any animals; if indeed you stand different things on all sides, each will reflect different figures on their corresponding sides.

### *Another way.*

<margin>How the representation of things is to be managed through polyhedral glasses.</margin>
Let a glass or crystal <term>polyhedron<note>A many-sided solid shape; here, a faceted glass that acts like a prism or a multi-lens.</note></term> be made with any number of sides, on each of which the same image is painted. When this is exposed to the rays of the sun, it will project the image onto the opposite wall of a darkened room according to the number of sides, so that the whole room will appear full of images. For example, if you paint grapes on the sides of the polyhedron, the room will be filled with grapes; if snakes, it will be filled with the likenesses of snakes, and so on for the rest. This matter will have greater success if the figures are projected through an intermediate lens. However, the thing will by no means achieve the desired success unless the polyhedron is somewhat large; nor is it necessary that it be fashioned from a single piece of crystal into various faces; rather, pieces of the purest glass joined together so that they form one polyhedron are sufficient. See more pertaining to this matter in *Catoptric Magic* <note>Kircher's term for magic involving mirrors and reflection.</note>.

# CHAPTER VII.

## *Concerning Pyroparastasis, or the exhibition of Fiery Spectacles.*

In the preceding pages, we have spoken at length about aerial spectacles; it remains for us to say something about <term>Pyroparastasis<note>From the Greek 'pyro' (fire) and 'parastasis' (representation/display).</note></term>, or fiery representations. In this, however, we shall proceed in such a way that we treat only what pertains to Light and Shadow, deliberately putting off the other miraculous works of fire for the *Subterranean World* <note>Kircher’s famous work *Mundus Subterraneus*, published in 1665.</note>, in which the wonderful power of fires in the production of things will be treated as a main subject.

### Experiment I.

->*Concerning the friction of fire.*<-

Fire is the treasure of all nature; just as nothing exists without it, so without it all things rush toward destruction. Therefore, by a singular providence of nature, it is implanted in each and every thing, and as it is the most necessary of all, so it is lacking nowhere. It can be drawn out not only from flints, but from any thing. Thus, certain <margin>The peoples of America.</margin> peoples of America are accustomed to draw fire instead of using flint by the rotation of one of two sticks placed into each other within a notch in the other. Which woods easily catch fire by friction was stated above in Book I: Laurel, Buckthorn, Holm Oak, and Linden. From all of these they make a drill, so that it may resist more sharply by friction and complete the work more stubbornly; but the "receptacle" <note>The base board or hearth used in friction fire-starting.</note> is made from ivy, wild vine, and similar dried woods, entirely void of all moisture. I have used laurel on laurel, or a fennel stalk on a fennel stalk, taking <gloss>or sunē <note>A possible variant or printer's correction for the action of taking/using the wood.</note></gloss> it over the other quickly and vehemently—

### Whether a stone can be made that ignites by spit alone, and burns under water.

**Among** authors of secret things, I find a certain arcanum <note>A secret or mystery, often used in alchemy to describe a hidden formula.</note> for creating a stone that excites a flame when moistened by any liquid, even spit. Many marvel at this experiment; but since I have never heard of any craftsman who has actually attempted such a thing, I shall manifest what I have discovered by putting the experiment to the test, after I have first provided the composition of the stone. The mixture for the stone is this: Cast a <term>magnet stone</term> <note>In this context, Kircher is likely referring to a specific mineral believed to have "attractive" or occult properties, not just a modern lodestone.</note> into a pot or similar vessel immersed in <term>quicklime</term> <note>Calcium oxide, which generates significant heat when contact with water occurs.</note>, adding a certain amount of <term>colophony</term> <note>A form of resin obtained from pines.</note>. When you have filled the vessel, smear it with potter's clay, leaving a vent hole, and place it in the furnace until it is thoroughly cooked. Then, having removed it, let it be cast into the pot again, smeared once more with clay, and placed back in the furnace. You shall repeat this process until it glows intensely. For this mixture, as soon as it touches moisture, turns into flame. So the Authors hold.

But I, who have tested the matter by experiment, have found none of these things to be true; wherefore I would not wish the Reader to blindly believe everything found scattered among Authors, unless it has first been made clear by manifest experiment. For there are many things which, according to theoretical reasons, seem most certain and infallible, yet when brought into practice, they never obtain any success. Taught by these failures, I have refused to assert anything in this entire book unless a previous experiment of the same had made me more certain. For if the things narrated by Authors concerning this stone were true, there would be no Prince who would not carry such a thing with him; and there would be no further use for tinderboxes in the future, since we could so easily obtain a supply of flame from elsewhere.

But I shall also show by reasoning that it cannot be done. The ingredients of this stone are Magnet, Colophony, pitch, and quicklime: none of these will provide the desired effect. The Magnet is cold and dry by nature and can contribute nothing of itself to any inflammation; pitch, likewise, will do nothing except by contact with fire or "periphlogian" vapor—that is, in the presence of another flame. If you add water, you will do the same as if water were poured on other combustibles, since water is <term>incompatible</term> <note>original Greek: ἀσύμβατον (asymbaton), meaning two things that cannot exist together or are fundamentally inconsistent.</note> with fire. <margin>Whence comes the heat from cold water poured on lime.</margin> However, water poured on quicklime does excite a certain heat-producing smoke, but I have seen no one who observed it bursting into flame. Indeed, nothing can be inflammable unless it is imbued with some fatty moisture; but after the long torments of the furnace fire, lime turns into a very dry substance, destitute of all moisture and fatness, not unlike ashes, whence it is incapable of all inflammation. That it excites such great heat, however, happens because of the great struggle between the air existing in the highly porous lime and the water poured over it, from which a violent agitation of the air arises, and from that violent agitation, a great heat must necessarily be born. 

<margin>Nothing can burn under water.</margin>
It is easy, however, to make a mixture from magnetic lime, saltpeter, quicklime, camphor, sulfur, turpentine resin, and "burning water" <note>Usually refers to distilled alcohol or "aqua vitae."</note> which, when placed near another flame, is very easily ignited, and when cast into water greatly increases its inflammation—yet never *within* the water; since a flame cannot possibly last without air, which would happen if it burned under water. From this, the lying imposture is evident, which some think they can create—a mixture that burns beneath the waters themselves. This is the nonsense of nonsenses. For who is ignorant of the fact that it is against all principles of nature for a fire, and especially a flame, to be overwhelmed on all sides by waters and yet either burn or be ignited?

### Whether an inextinguishable fire can be given?

**I am not** ignorant that many, because of subterranean lamps found in various places, preserved and burning there from time immemorial, have falsely persuaded themselves that a lamp can be made which burns perpetually. Concerning this quite difficult business, I think it should by no means be discussed now, since I have not yet taken the experiment of them all; but we reserve this matter as proper to the *Subterranean World* <note>A reference to Kircher's other famous work, *Mundus Subterraneus*.</note>, where, opening our mind more fully on this, we shall show various ways in which a perpetually burning lamp can be made after the model of nature. Therefore, I do not speak in this place of an inextinguishable fire, but of a powerful flame of fire, not extinguishable by any whirlwind of winds or violence of rains, which I share as proven by my own experience. Take 10 lbs of varnish, 4 lbs of live sulfur, 2 lbs of resin oil, 1 lb of saltpeter, 2 lbs of frankincense, <margin>A flame difficult to extinguish.</margin> 6 oz of camphor, 1 lb of petroleum, and 14 oz of the best "aqua viva" <note>Likely high-proof distilled spirits.</note>. Let them be mixed together and exposed to a slow fire, and a mixture will be made. When tow <note>Coarse flax or hemp fibers.</note> is imbued with this, placed in pots, and ignited, it yields an inextinguishable fire.

<margin>The power of sulfur with wax.</margin>
<margin>The power of feather alum.</margin>
**Purest sulfur** dissolved equally with wax provides what is sought, if you form a candle from that mixture. They also say a wick made of <term>feather alum</term> <note>Often a historical term for asbestos, which was known for being fireproof and could be used for "perpetual" wicks.</note> with oil...

# Pyroparastatic Experiments I.
## Carrying a light beneath the water, useful for divers.

**W**e said in the first book that the bottom of the sea, especially in deeper places, is so dark that <term>divers</term> <note>original: "urinatores"; from the Latin 'urinari' meaning to dive or plunge into water. In this era, these were usually breath-hold divers looking for pearls or coral.</note> can do nothing without a light. Therefore, some describe how a light can be carried to the interior of the sea with an uncorrupted flame in this manner. Let a lantern of any size be made, first properly equipped with its glass windows, yet so joined together that no water can flow into it. In this, you will place a light made with a wick of the preceding mixture's composition. However, since a flame cannot be preserved without air, let the lantern have a long "trunk" or tube made of leather, whose outer orifice should be made of cork-wood, which holds the tube and serves as a vent. They say this lantern is not extinguished under water because all these things are necessary for preserving combustion. I myself certainly know that this experiment was put into practice by certain divers in Malta, but with unsuccessful results. It is an excellent speculation, as are all the reasons produced by the ingenious <term>Mersenne</term> <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French polymath who corresponded with Kircher and wrote about the physics of "submarine navigation."</note> in his *Submarine Navigation*; but these are difficult to put into work. For who can guarantee that the leather channel will be immune from the entry of turbulent water through the external orifice? Who then would relight the extinguished lantern, and who can vouch for the durability of the tube? For if even thick ropes barely suffice in storms, how much less a leather material? But you will say that this should be attempted in a calm sea. I do not agree with this either. For air will indeed creep in, but around the lantern in the deeper parts of the sea, it will so degenerate into a watery nature that the flame must necessarily be extinguished, smothered by the excessive humidity of the air. Nevertheless, I do not deny that a similar lantern could be made for depths that are not so great, using a sufficiently wide leather tube; indeed, I remember that I once exhibited fire and terrifying spectacles under the water itself in rivers by such a device, provided you construct the lantern in that manner...

# Experiments of the Flame. II.
## Linen thread as well as incombustible paper.

<margin>Why linen thread does not burn in fire.</margin>
**I**f someone wraps a linen thread around a tin cup previously filled with cold water, he will find that an applied flame can in no way burn it, though a glowing coal would burn it. The cause of this thing is none other than the natural cold of both the water and the metal, which, while they act upon the flame, render it unstable and wandering; by this instability, the thread is preserved from all harm. The same will happen if someone moves a leaf of paper directly to the cone of some candle flame and blows violently upon it from the upper part: for the paper, cooled by the breath, will receive no damage from the flame placed beneath it.

# Experiment III.
## Concerning Camphor.

<margin>Camphor burns in water.</margin>
**C**amphor is an exceedingly flammable material and easily persists even with those things that are contrary to fire. Hence, when cast into water and lit, even in the middle of the contrary element, it will be as easily ignited as if it had been joined to the driest tinder. I have seen some who lit a snowy globe mixed with camphor, not without the admiration of those standing by. I also know of some who, by inserting a piece of camphor into a piece of ice worked into a sphere and lighting it, provided a great increase of light. I knew a <term>charlatan</term> <note>original: "Circumforaneum"; literally one who haunts markets, used here for a traveling performer or street magician.</note> who, when he wished, vomited fire to the great wonder of men.

# Experiment IV.
## To exhibit a flying Dragon in the air, and other portentous images of things.

**I** know that by this invention some of our Fathers in India were rescued from the greatest dangers of the Barbarians. They were being held in prisons, and while they knew no way of liberating themselves from servitude, someone more clever than the rest invented some such machine...

# The Great Art, Book X. Magic Part II.

...having first threatened the Barbarians <note>The author uses "Barbarians" to refer to non-European or non-Christian peoples encountered by missionaries</note> that unless they returned his companions, they would soon see portents and experience the manifest wrath of the Gods. When the Barbarians received this threat with laughter, he fashioned a dragon out of the thinnest paper. In its center, he skillfully arranged a mixture of sulfur, pitch, and wax so that, when ignited, it would illuminate the machine and simultaneously present these words to be read in their own language: **THE WRATH OF GOD** <note>original: "IRA DEI"</note>. Once this was done, he attached a very long tail and committed the machine to the air.

<margin>Fraud for the sake of freedom.</margin>
As soon as it caught the wind, it ascended into the air with the terrifying appearance of a fiery dragon. When the Barbarians saw the unusual movement of the phantom, they were struck with the greatest astonishment; remembering the words of the Fathers <note>Refers to the Jesuit missionaries</note>, they feared they were about to pay the predicted penalties of an angry Deity. Therefore, they suddenly opened the prison and freely allowed those they were detaining to depart. Meanwhile, the machine, having been seized and inflamed by the fire, ceased its spontaneous movement with a noise like applause. Thus, the Fathers obtained by a display of nature—and by instilling mere terror—what they could not achieve with much gold. And although these things are known even to children in Europe, nevertheless, because I have often been asked by various people to describe the construction of the machine, I shall do so here opportunely and with as much brevity as I can. I add this: if someone had a falcon trained with such skill that it obeyed the voice of the falconer, he could perform truly miraculous works. For with a string tied to the falcon’s foot, the bird could lead the aforementioned machine through the air wherever it wished at the falconer’s command, and thus perform utterly prodigious feats by this artifice.

### Construction of the Flying Machine.

Let a rectangle **ABCD** be made from very thin reed rods, the length of which should be in a **sesquialtera ratio** <term>a 3:2 proportion</term> to its width. Within the middle of this, let two reeds be inserted crosswise and fastened so firmly that a string tied at the point of intersection can withstand the force of the machine as it flies away. To this, as if to the trunk of a body, both the head and the tail of the image—formed from the same reed rods—should be attached, exactly in the manner shown to you in the present figure.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a dragon-shaped kite or flying machine. The body is a diamond-shaped frame (points A and B marked) covered in a light material. The head (A) is that of a dragon with an open mouth and eyes. The tail (B) is long and tapering. The words 'WRATH OF GOD' (IRA DEI) are printed across the center of the body. A cord or string is attached to the underside at point E.</image-desc>

Once the skeleton of the dragon is thus formed, cover it with the thinnest paper and paint it with appropriate colors; then attach the string (the longer it is, the higher you will drive the machine) in the proper place. Therefore, at a time when the air enjoys neither too much wind nor too much stillness, you shall commit the prepared machine to the air from a high place. As soon as it catches the wind and is released into the aerial regions, it will exhibit to those watching from a distance the true appearance of a dragon, not without fear or the suspicion of a miracle. Furthermore, the more strongly you pull the string, the more the machine—filled by the wind—will be driven with greater force when slackened, so that it might even pull the one holding it upward into the heights. By this art, on the day of the Ascension of Christ the Lord, flying Angels can be displayed in the air with almost no trouble. The wonder of these spectacles will be greatly increased by the arrangement of certain pipes around the circuit of the machine, which, animated by the motion of the air, will cause a certain sweet harmony, along with small bells attached to the same.

### Nighttime Spectacles.

If you wish to display various nighttime spectacles, the entire machine must be made hollow inside and of a solid, least-transparent, yet very light material. However, in the bottom and the sides, let the figures of the things you desire to represent be cut out, and cover them again with very thin paper previously soaked in oil <note>Oiling the paper made it more translucent, allowing the light to shine through better</note>. This will result in the figure of the animal being seen through the light of the candles placed inside. If, however, you desire to show a portentous spectacle, you shall cut out letters which, illuminated by the interior candles, will offer themselves in the darkness to be seen and read in the sky.

<margin>Various aerial exhibitions by night.</margin>
It can hardly be said how much horror and admiration a spectacle of this kind provides, since people cannot conceive who could have placed letters in such a remote tract of air, nor how they remain fixed in the sky. By this artifice alone, as if by certain miracles, I believe an entire army could be turned to flight, especially one of Barbarians, such as the Turks, who are accustomed to take everything for which they do not grasp the reason as omens and portents. If someone truly wishes for the machine to vomit fire after various demonstrations, he will achieve this if he equips the machine with small channels filled with gunpowder <term>pulvis pyrius</term> and inserts a sulfurous thread into a glowing candle. This thread, consumed when it reaches the point of the said sulfurous fuse, will ignite the sulfurous fuel; this, connected to the channels, will animate the whole machine into fiery furies...

### Corollary.

## Concerning the Eagle of Regiomontanus, and the Dove of Archytas.

**T**hat famous eagle, which Regiomontanus <note>Johannes Müller von Königsberg (1436–1476), a celebrated German mathematician and astronomer known as Regiomontanus.</note> is said to have displayed through the air for the Emperor Charles V at Nuremberg—as well as the Dove of Archytas <note>Archytas of Tarentum (c. 400 BC), a Greek philosopher and mathematician credited with inventing the first self-propelled flying machine, a wooden pigeon.</note>—was produced by no other means than this very same artifice. This will be clear to anyone who looks deeply into the principles we have hinted at here. For those who wish these things to have been performed by a certain precise balance, or a hidden proportion of weights, without any secret dependency on a mover, are greatly deluded; such things are repugnant to all principles of Statics <term>Statics: the branch of mechanics concerned with bodies at rest and forces in equilibrium</term>, as will be discussed at length in our *Mechanical Thaumaturge* <note>Referring to one of Kircher's other works on mechanical wonders.</note>. Indeed, it can hardly be said what great miracles acute and wise minds can elicit even from the lowliest principles, if they know how to combine things skillfully, arrange them aptly, and produce them with hidden dexterity.

### To display wonders by light shining in the darkness.

**W**e spoke in the first book of the wonderful power of those things that shine by night; now let us teach how to apply this prodigious light. If you first form statues out of any material, and insert bioluminescent material <note>original: "noctilucam materiam"</note> into their eyes, mouth, and ears, and place them in a suitable location at night, they will provide a source of horror to those who look upon them, and can subsequently be the cause of the greatest events, as the following example will teach you.

<margin>A wondrous history concerning bioluminescent materials.</margin>
We read in the *History of the Scots*: When the Picts had killed Alpin, the father of Kenneth II, King of the Scots; and Kenneth could not draw his subjects, who were struck with fear, to take revenge by any persuasion—and indeed the greatest part of the nobles and soldiers of his father's kingdom had already fallen in battle—he devised a clever scheme. He kindly received the gathered princes of the regions. He then honored them with hospitality and a banquet; the following night, while all was silent, he sent individual men into each of their chambers. In his right hand, each man held a staff made of rotting, bioluminescent wood <note>original: "putri ligno noctiluco"; refers to foxfire, a bioluminescent fungus on decaying wood</note>, and wore a garment made of unscaled fish skin <note>likely the skin of bioluminescent sea creatures or simply reflective scales</note>, which itself shines in a wondrous manner at night. Then, using a bull's horn instead of a trumpet, they each bellowed in a terrifying voice that the King must be obeyed: that the Picts would soon pay the penalty for their crimes, and that they were messengers sent from God. It was easy to deceive the sleepy men, as they could see them neither coming nor going. For

<margin>Victory against the Picts was granted to the King of the Scots; it is said by the help of bioluminescent matter.</margin>
they had wrapped the glowing garment in a cloak as they departed, and hidden the staff under the same. When it grew light, they came to the council, and each narrated what he had seen and heard. The King, fearing lest the story might become public knowledge and the ruse be uncovered, first informed the others that he too had seen a portent of this kind. Then he commanded them to be cautious, lest by publishing the divine warnings they might turn the heavenly will—which was undoubtedly favorable—into an enemy. And so, with no one recognizing the trickery, they consented to war. That the machine instituted by such astute and clever counsel was by no means in vain, the outcome proved. For the Picts were defeated once, twice, and a third time, and finally so destroyed by the Scots to the point of internal slaughter that not even a remnant survived. You see, therefore, how great and how unusual the spectacles are that can be displayed by bioluminescent material of this kind.

## Experiment V.

### To display a fiery rain, or what is the same thing, a fiery fountain.

<margin>The Fiery Fountain</margin>
**T**here is in piddocks, or sea-dates <note>original: "phaladibus, seu dactylis marinis"; Pholas dactylus, a species of boring mollusk known for its bioluminescence</note>, which were discussed at length in Book 1, a certain humor, the liquid of which, when resolved into drops, presents exactly the appearance of fiery sparks. You shall display a fiery fountain with this liquid in the following way. Let two vessels, A and B, be made; the first lead from the top of vessel A into the bottom of vessel B; the second from the top side of vessel B into the top of vessel A; the third from the bottom of vessel A to the outside. In a word, let a Hero’s Fountain <term>Hero’s Fountain: a hydraulic machine invented by Heron of Alexandria that uses air pressure to spout water</term> be made. This being done, let vessel A be filled with the aforementioned bioluminescent humor, and the machine closed so that no air can enter. If you wish to display a pleasant spectacle in the dark, pour water into the lip of the upper vessel A, which is concave like a basin; this water will expel the air latent in vessel B through the tube DC. The air, pressing against the humor in vessel A (since they cannot occupy the same space), will expel the humor through the tube AG, and it will display a fiery rain, or a fountain, or, by spreading as it falls, a fiery lily. Innumerable other things of this kind can be displayed, all of which we leave to the curious reader to deduce, lest we seem to have descended too much into particulars. See what we have treated in our *Magnetic Art* <note>Kircher's *Magnes; sive de Arte Magnetica* (1641)</note> concerning the wondrous spectacles that can be achieved by the help of Phosphorus or Phengitis <note>A translucent or luminous stone</note>. For now, let it suffice for us to have indicated these few things for the deduction of innumerable others. Regarding fiery artifices, or the various mixtures of flammable things, see our *Subterranean World* <note>Kircher's *Mundus Subterraneus* (1665)</note>.
