## CHAPTER VIII.

### On Dioptrics, or on all-seeing glasses, Telescopes, their various forms, and effects.

<note>Dioptrics is the branch of optics dealing with the refraction of light, especially by lenses.</note>

There are three things we consider in all glasses used for a telescope, which we require as necessary to produce the intended effects: the material, the form, and the proper adaptation of the glasses.

§. I.
#### On the glass material.

<margin>Signs of perfection in glass.</margin>
We require the material to be transparent, homogeneous, and continuous. Perfect transparency in glass removes all color; imperfect transparency leaves something in it that remains as color. To perfect transparency, the material must also be homogeneous: thus, little stones, grains of sand, bubbles, and parts of different density or transparency are excluded, as well as other earthy impurities which greatly hinder the purpose. Because of these, the surface is rendered extremely unequal and discontinuous. To obtain their due perfection, the glasses must be equally continuous, solid throughout, and not at all porous or "veined." For there lie hidden in glass—however seemingly equal—certain veins, spirals, waves, coils, vortices, clouds, and "smokes." These are introduced into the glass by the carelessness of the craftsmen while they pull, drive, whirl, twist, turn, pluck, and spoil the ignited and soft material taken from the melting pots in various ways. This one thing brings ruin and "pestilence" to the orderly and pure arrangement of visible images. All of these defects are as clearly visible as a slight disturbance in clear water.

§. II.
#### On the form of the glass.

The form given to this material is artificial—specifically, the surface is either flat or spherical, and the latter is either hollow <note>concave</note> or bulging <note>convex</note>. A lens may have these shapes on both sides, or it may have one face convex and the other flat. Thus, all skillfully crafted glasses are either flat or curved. Curved lenses originate from the circle <note>spherical</note> or from the section of a cone <note>conic sections like parabolas</note>. If the former, they are concave, convex, or a mixture of these; hence some are <term>plano-concave</term> (flat on one side, hollow on the other), some <term>plano-convex</term> (flat on one side, bulging on the other), and some <term>concavo-convex</term>. If the latter, they admit the same combinations of concavity and convexity. In this way, elliptical, parabolic, and hyperbolic glasses are produced, whether concave, convex, or mixed. By these means, whatever is prodigious and hidden in the whole of <term>parastatic Magic</term> <note>original: "Magia parastatica"; Kircher's term for the science of optical projections and illusions</note> is achieved. But let us say something briefly about each, following both our own experiments and those of Scheiner. <note>Christoph Scheiner (1573–1650) was a Jesuit astronomer and a pioneer in the study of sunspots and optics.</note>

<margin>Various forms of glasses.</margin>
I. Flat glasses held straight to the optical axis show the natural shape of the object.

<margin>Effects of Flat, plano-concave, and plano-convex glasses.</margin>
II. Plano-convex and plano-concave glasses held straight to the optical axis leave the shape as it is but vary the size. When moved toward the eye, plano-convex glasses make the object appear smaller than when they are moved away. Conversely, plano-concave glasses make it appear smaller as they are moved away, until inversion occurs; then the opposite happens. Plano-concave glasses never invert the object because the rays refracted by them never meet <note>they diverge</note>.

<margin>Effects of plano-concave or plano-convex glasses.</margin>
If, however, plano-convex glasses are held at an angle to the optical axis, they shift the seen object along that oblique diameter toward an inversion; thus distorted, they sometimes raise the image and sometimes lower it, depending on the glass surface and its position to the eye. After inversion, they contract the object seen. Plano-concave glasses inspected obliquely diminish the object across its diameter and show it much more contracted; this varies greatly depending on whether the convexity or concavity was derived from a large or small sphere.

<margin>Effects of homocentricly concave or convex glasses.</margin>
III. All spherical glasses that are <term>homocentricly</term> <note>having the same center</note> concave and convex, when moved obliquely to the eye, contract the transparent object being viewed. Segments of the same sphere that are equally thick and held at the same angle contract the object equally. However, segments from different spheres—specifically those from a smaller sphere—contract the image sooner (at a shorter distance from the eye), while those from a larger sphere do so later (at a longer distance). It should also be noted that thicker segments of the same sphere contract the image sooner, and thinner ones later. Finally, all glasses of this type increase the size of the object as the eye approaches the glass and diminish it as the eye recedes.

<margin>Effects of double-sided or concavo-convex glasses.</margin>
IV. Glasses that are convex or concave on both sides perform the same as the "mixed" ones <note>plano-convex/concave</note>, but more intensely. When both sides are either convex or concave, they act much more effectively than the plano-convex or plano-concave versions. The reason for this is that the refraction in these is doubled; thus, rays in double-convex lenses converge twice as much, and in double-concave lenses, they diverge just as much. It does not matter whether both surfaces have the same degree of curvature or different ones; one side always increases the power of the other according to its own strength.

...the power of any lens is derived from the spherical surface, of which it shares a portion. Therefore, convex lenses placed obliquely to the optical axis elongate the object according to the inclination of the glass's diameter before the image is inverted; but afterwards, the opposite occurs. Concave lenses, relative to the optical axis and the diameter in position, and the distance of the glass from the eye or the object from the glass, do not cause the rays to cross each other at any point, as they recede further from one another. These glasses also shift seen objects from their true locations in a marvelous way—upward, downward, to the right, to the left, etc. You may also experience this with the Sun, using a similar glass tinted with colors, or with the full Moon using a lenticular glass. For you will see either celestial body transformed into an ellipse, and shifted in location according to the position and state of the glass; and if you place two or more such glasses in different positions between your sight and the stars, you will multiply those same stars. ## §. III.
## On Lenses.

<margin>What a Lens or lenticular glass is.</margin>
In a Lens, all optical miracles truly lie hidden; for this reason, I have decided to treat them at somewhat greater length. A lens is a glass body fashioned from two segments of a glass sphere, whether those segments are equal or unequal. Thus, a glass ball or sphere fashioned from two hemispherical segments provides the greatest effect of all lenses. A complete lens, therefore, is always fashioned from two such segments whose common base is a circle; if these segments are equal, the section will be from equal spheres; if unequal, from unequal spheres. Concave lenses are spherical segments removed from a solid transparent body, terminated either by two spherical surfaces opposite at the vertex, or by one spherical and one flat surface. The cavities of smaller spheres make sharper lenses than those of larger ones; however, the hollow segments of larger spheres produce more obtuse lenses. Doubled or complete concave lenses are more powerful than simple ones; this should also be understood regarding convex lenses applied in a certain way for certain effects. Lenses that take their origin from conic sections are either parabolic, hyperbolic, or elliptic. Among these, elliptic and hyperbolic lenses excel above all others.

<margin>The wonders of parabolic lenses.</margin>
And if craftsmen were so industrious that they could reach the perfection of this art, I say that by their legitimate adaptation, true miracles in optics could be performed. For I assert that with the help of these, the most remote things, even in the heavens, could be seen as distinctly as those we commonly see on earth. But the business is so subtle that certain rules can hardly be assigned to bring it into practice. However, if some accidental industry should lead someone into such a "blessed error" that they deviate from a spherical shape into an elliptical or hyperbolic one, I assert that he will have achieved something he can perpetually boast of. I know that not long ago an eminent Mathematician handed down certain rules for manufacturing them; but since up to now no craftsman has been found who has succeeded, nothing is left to us of such a noble invention besides the desire for it. For the work of polishing of this kind is so subtle that no sharpness of the eyes suffices to discern the figures of the lenses; indeed, it frequently happens that while someone thinks he is working on a spherical section, he finds he has wandered off—by a truly blessed error—into a hyperbolic one. On the contrary, while we think we are working a hyperbola, we most often end up with a spherical shape; and it is a wonder that we cannot even judge the truth of the matter except by the effects. If someone knew how to exactly manufacture **cyclo-hyperbolic** lenses, he would produce the most excellent of all lenses. For these, besides the fact that they collect a great deal of light, produce truly wondrous effects in the "parastasis" <note>representation or display</note> of things, as will be discussed at length in what follows. I do not doubt that the most excellent craftsmen, Torricelli and Fontana, will attempt something regarding this matter—the former all the better as he possesses a greater knowledge of theoretical subtlety than the latter. <note>Evangelista Torricelli and Francesco Fontana were leading 17th-century figures in the development of telescopes and lens-grinding techniques.</note>

<margin>The cyclo-hyperbolic lens is the most excellent of all.</margin>

## §. IV.
## On the arrangement of Lenses.

Just as a house is made from brick, lime, and sand, yet a man who possesses sand, lime, and bricks does not have a house—for there is a need for skillful construction—so too if you have lenses, you must arrange them in the proper proportion. Therefore, a fit and necessary disposition and arrangement of lenses among themselves is required. Furthermore, one type of arrangement is immediate, and another is mediate. The former consists in the lenses being properly placed in tubes; the latter is seen in how the tube itself, together with the lenses, is aptly accommodated both to the eye and to the thing to be viewed. For there is a certain marvelous play of art with nature, which, since we demonstrated it in Book 2, Proposition 1, we refer the reader there, lest we seem to repeat the same things so many times. From these, the shape of the lens fit for the tube is sufficiently known; for it is either spherical...

<margin>The quality of lenses is discerned only through use.</margin>

However, whether a good or bad shape adheres to the lens is evident only through practice and common experience. That these things have been performed correctly is made known through the diligence of the craftsman in his labor, the quality of the instruments, and good fortune; use, the teacher of all things, teaches this better, as I have said, than any subtlety of industry, skill, or learned genius. ### §. V.
## On the effects of Lenses.

<margin>The lens resembles the eye.</margin>
I. **A** single convex <term>lens<note>Kircher uses the word "lens" (lentil) because of the glass's bean-like shape.</note></term> placed in a tube presents objects with the utmost perfection, so much so that the transmission of <term>visible species<note>In 17th-century optics, "species" refers to the "forms" or "images" cast by light from an object.</note></term> through one convex lens is nothing other than an artificial imitation of the eye’s own visual power in presenting those same things. Truly, this lens will be more excellent the closer it is to perfection—so much so that if the lens is not only a portion of a great sphere (for example, one whose radius encompasses twenty or more Roman <term>palms<note>A Roman "palmus" was about 8.8 inches or 22.3 cm.</note></term>), but is also wide enough itself (perhaps one or two palms), you could display any great spectacle with it, provided a blameless form is induced upon good material. For with such a lens, you will display the images of external things in a wonderful manner, along with their living colors. 
<margin>The projection of images through a lens.</margin>
With this, you may create <term>chorographic<note>Regional maps.</note></term>, <term>topographic<note>Local or site-specific maps.</note></term>, and <term>prosopographical<note>Portraits or depictions of faces.</note></term> tables. With the same lens, you will view tiny things and things from a small sphere as if they were very large. With the same large lens and a large sphere, you will present small letters to the sight as if they were very large. Regarding all of these, we shall speak more expansively in what follows.

<margin>The difference between a convex and concave lens.</margin>
II. A hollow lens—whether it be <term>plano-concave<note>Flat on one side, curved inward on the other.</note></term> or concave on both sides, and whether it be a segment of a small or large sphere—receives any visible object and projects it confusedly at any distance upon a paper, so that the passing rays are never united, but instead, entangled by mutual radiations, they cause a perpetual chaos and confusion. From this, the difference between a convex and concave lens is clear: for the former always distinguishes and perfectly organizes a confused image that has been received and transmitted; the latter, on the contrary, perpetually confuses the same. Thus, the duty of a convex lens is to distinguish and organize those images received confusedly, at a proper distance according to its power.

III. A concave lens, placed after a convex one and not far before the seat of the organized image, shows that same image on the paper larger, more distinct, and at a greater distance than the convex lens alone would have done. That same lens, if placed very close to the station of the common base, will display very small but very pure images on the paper, and will make the distance of the paper from the lens the shortest possible. Truly, the more it approaches the convex lens, the larger the image it will display, but it will not equal the former in clarity and purity; it will also require a longer distance for the paper.

<margin>A hollow lens between two convex ones.</margin>
IV. A hollow lens placed between two convex ones serves various uses. When both are situated within the common organized meeting point of the convex lens (or the one facing the object), then an image will always be painted on the properly positioned paper in an inverted position, while it will be seen by the eye in an upright position, and that image will be enlarged. If the convex lens approaches the hollow one while the paper is moved back, it will be diminished; if it moves away while the paper approaches, it will increase. This is because, in this case, the lens receives confused images from the hollow one, and then organizes them onto the paper; and because they had not yet <term>crossed over<note>original: "decussatæ". This refers to the point where light rays intersect, causing the image to flip.</note></term>, it projects them onto the paper as crossed, and thus an inverted position occurs. If, however, both the hollow and the convex lens are placed outside the common meeting point of the [first] lens, then the image on the paper is always upright thanks to the first convex lens, but it is always inverted in the eye. This image is enlarged by moving the convex lens or the eye closer to the hollow one and moving the paper back, and diminished by moving it closer; because in this case the hollow lens always confuses the images on the paper which the convex lens organizes, and because they had already crossed once, it crosses them a second time, and on this account, it sets them upright on the paper, and so the eye sees them inverted.

<margin>A wonderful helioscope.</margin>
V. Finally, if you adapt two similar lenses in the same way into a tube, it will compel any earthly objects, and even any stars, into the service of your sight with incredible size, clarity, and amplitude, albeit in an inverted position. For since those [celestial] bodies are all round, the inversion of the entire view does not disturb the sight regarding their visual configuration; which is otherwise in earthly objects. But if you place two colored lenses in a tube, you will have a wonderful <term>helioscope<note>An instrument for looking at the sun without blinding the observer.</note></term>, which will manifest all the hidden miracles of the Sun. And from this was born that <term>microscope<note>Kircher was an early pioneer in using the microscope to study disease and nature.</note></term>, by which a fly is amplified into an elephant, and a flea into a camel, 
and those...

->**Parastatic Magic**<note>original: "Magia Parastatica." This refers to the art of making "species" or images appear or be displayed, specifically through optical instruments.</note><-

...and those things, which otherwise escape the sharp sight of the eye due to their smallness, appear large. It is also clear that two convex lenses placed in a tube exhibit a far more excellent, clearer, and larger spectacle of external things. You also have, through two convex lenses, the position of the <term>species<note>In early modern optics, "species" are the visible forms or images cast by an object through light.</note></term> displayed upright on a paper; and through three convex lenses properly arranged, you have the position projected upright into the looking eye.

The image would be raised into a <term>hyperbolimorphous<note>A shape based on a hyperbola; here referring to a specific distortion or correction of an image's shape.</note></term> form if there were someone who could construct one exactly. But on these matters, see the most learned *Apiaria* of Bettini <note>Mario Bettini (1582–1657) was a Jesuit philosopher and mathematician whose work "Apiaria Universae Philosophiae Mathematicae" discussed mathematical and optical curiosities.</note>.

<margin>Another method for the uprighting of images.</margin>
There is also another certain method and reasoning for setting images upright. Let a certain machine be made, such as we described in the preceding Illustration 29, Figure 2. In this, above the board ABD, we place a board A, perpendicular to AD itself, imbued with a very white surface. At B, however, we place a mirror equal in size to A, parallel to the horizon. In a certain diaphragm C, let a tube DE be inserted, equipped with a single, and indeed the best, convex lens, which may run back and forth through the hole C for the exhibition of the images; and you will have the instrument ready. Its use is this: in some closed room, part D of the tube is extended outside the shutters through a hole made for this purpose; and the images of external things, having entered through the tube, will appear on the white board A, though indeed overturned; yet these will soon present themselves upright to those looking into the subject mirror B. And let these things suffice concerning the uprighting of images.

## Practical Application I.

### In what way should the images of things transmitted into a dark place be forced into an upright position?

**T**his is a matter desired by many, and it has a notable use in the <term>parastasis<note>The formal presentation or display of an image.</note></term> of things to be exhibited in their natural position: wherefore I thought the secret should be briefly opened in this place before we proceed further. It is done in this way. Take two convex lenses: if you arrange them so that after one has achieved the <term>ordered convergence<note>The focal point where light rays meet to form an image.</note></term>, or the location of the image,

<image-desc>An optical diagram illustrating the path of light rays through two convex lenses to create an upright projected image. Point A at the top of an object sends rays through lens DE, which cross at a focal point C. These rays then pass through a second lens GH and are projected onto surface IL. In the final projection, point I corresponds to the original point A, showing the image has been re-inverted to its natural upright position. The diagram is labeled with letters A through L to mark lenses, focal points, and image coordinates.</image-desc>

which the convex lens draws from the object, another convex lens follows it; this second lens, without a new ordered convergence, will project the image in an upright position onto the opposite paper. The right sides of the image will correspond to the right sides of the object, the left to the left, the top to the top, and the bottom to the bottom; in exactly the same way as usually happens in plane mirrors. However, when you transfer these images onto paper by their outlines or colors, they will become right-to-left and left-to-right again to your gaze: which you will avoid in our practice if, by perforating the paper, you turn the picture toward the reverse surface. Let the object be AB; let there be two lenses DE and GH, arranged thus; let the ordered convergence, or location of the image, be C, and the paper be IL: it is manifest that the image of point A, having been overturned at E through lens GH, and from here projected again at I, will appear in its natural position. The same must be said for the rest of the radiation.

You see, therefore, how the images of things in the dark can be set upright. For the images first—as was shown at length in Book 2—having been transmitted through a hole and passed through a lens, fall onto the paper inverted because of the <term>decussation<note>The crossing of light rays in the shape of an 'X' as they pass through a small aperture or lens.</note></term> of the rays made in opposite directions at the narrowness of the hole. But if, after the proper distance of the rays converging in the first lens GH, you also place the lens DE, the images refracted in it before the convergence of the rays in the second lens will show the images upright on the board IL. These images can also be viewed ingeniously through the pupil...

## Practical Application II.

### On the wonderful constitution of natural things to be investigated through the Microscope.

**S**o great is the fallacy of our senses that <gloss><unclear>it is almost scarcely</unclear></gloss> possible to arrive at a perfect knowledge of natural things unless they are supported by something by which the hidden recesses of things might be brought to light. For since, according to that exclamation of the Philosopher <note>Referring to Aristotle.</note>, "nothing is in the intellect that was not first in the sense," how shall we philosophize rightly and solidly concerning the fabric of natural things if we are ignorant of the most hidden compositions of their parts? This, however, is that divine science of Optics, which leads that which is hidden from the deepest shadows into an admirable light. Certainly, it was believed until now that many bodies were destitute of all life and soul, which nevertheless the study of <term>dioptrics<note>The branch of optics dealing with the refraction of light, particularly through lenses.</term> has discovered to be alive. Who could believe that vinegar and milk teem with an innumerable multitude of worms, unless the art of the <term>microscope<note>original: "smicroscopa ars". The word "smicroscopium" was an early term for the microscope used by Kircher and his contemporaries.</note></term> had taught it in these recent times to the greatest admiration of all? Who could ever have brought it into their mind that the green color in the leaves of citrons is composed of every kind of color, unless the art of the microscope had detected it? All these things experience, the irreproachable mistress of things, has taught us. By this means, I recently detected the leaves of the liburnum and the mastic tree to be entirely full of vermin, and all kinds of herbs to be composed of diverse and marvelous textures of filaments. <margin>Wonders of the Castor oil plant. Wonders of the Cherry tree.</margin> The leaves of the Castor oil plant <note>original: "Ricinus".</note> inspected through these instruments are woven with an innumerable heap of stellar figures, to the greatest delight...

# The Great Art, Book 10. Magic, Part II.

<margin>Nature’s wondrous diligence in the construction of the smallest animals.</margin>
...you will observe with wonder. You will discover the bark of a Cherry tree depicted throughout with an immense abundance of tiny little trees. In a word, you will find that individual roots, leaves, fruits, and seeds consist of diverse figures just as they are distinct in species. If all these things were brought to light by the aid of this <term>Dioptric Magic</term> <note>The branch of optics dealing with the refraction of light through lenses.</note>, no one should doubt that the "Republic of Letters" <note>The international community of scholars and intellectuals.</note> would shortly possess a vast treasure. I shall not speak here of the wondrous constitution and structure of the bodies of the smallest animals, such as <term>mites</term> <note>original: *Acari*</note>, lice, gnats, and other little worms of both the flying and crawling insect varieties. You will find that nature, even in the smallest things, has exhibited Lions, Bulls, Horses, Dogs, Cats, Donkeys, Eagles, Geese, and aquatic creatures of every kind. What else is a flea to us but a wingless locust? What is a mite but a hairy bear? And so it is with the rest. You will also see with amazement that hairs or bristles are actually hollowed out into channels and tubes.

<margin>The verminous blood of those with fever.</margin>
I omit here how much can be learned about the marvelous formation and sprouting of limbs in the "seed" of birds—that is, in eggs—while they are actually being incubated; about the differences in colors implanted in individual natural things; about the <note>original: *sanguine febrientium verminoso*</note> <gloss>verminous blood of those suffering from fever</gloss> <note>Kircher is often credited here with an early observation of microorganisms, though he likely saw blood cells or clumps, believing them to be tiny "worms."</note>, and countless other things hitherto unknown to all physicians and penetrated by none of them. You will see that not only animals, but also individual herbs produce their own natural living creatures, sprouting from their putrefied moisture as if from seed; there is no kind of fly or caterpillar that does not recognize some "mother" from among the aforementioned things. Truly, through such <term>microscopic</term> <note>original: *smicroscopia*</note> instruments, while such a great multitude, distinction, and variety of motions, colors, and nearly invisible parts appear in tiny animals produced suddenly or by chance from decaying matter, it can hardly be put into words how much the mind of the observer is seized with admiration for the infinite power, wisdom, and goodness of God. He is, as it were, "playing in the world," revealing His greatest self even in the smallest things.

<margin>All things are truly different than they appear.</margin>
From these things it is clearly evident that all things seen by us are, in reality, far different than they appear. Long experience has taught that this is true not only of the things we encounter everywhere here on earth, but also of the discs of the celestial bodies. Who would have believed that the <note>original Greek: *ἀμαξίαν* (amaxian)</note> <gloss>wagon-load / dense cluster</gloss> of stars was an accumulation of nearly innumerable stars? Who would have believed the Sun was spotted? Who would have believed the waxing and waning of Venus? Who would have ever believed the remaining miracles of the Heavens, which were discussed at length in the first book, unless the <term>Dioptric tube</term> <note>A telescope.</note> had opened them to us?

<margin>The construction of microscopes.</margin>
But, to return to where we digressed: microscopes are made in various ways; any section of a glass sphere suffices for this business. Some use two convex lenses, which were discussed in the fifth section. Some use huge glass spheres filled with water. On the other hand, others use a nearly new and most clever invention: they enclose tiny glass beads—the diameter of which does not exceed the diameter of the smallest pearls (of this size: O)—inside a small tube. If you place the foot of a flea between your eye and a lamp against the surface of this bead, you will see (wondrous to say) the leg of the thigh bristling like a horse's leg; a hair placed over it will resemble a huge beam. It is truly most wonderful how such massive things can be represented in such a tiny sphere. Let the tube be **A**; **C** the glass orb inserted in the bottom of the tube; the lamp **D**, and the eye **E**. The Most Serene Cardinal Giovanni Carlo de' Medici, out of his distinguished affection for these studies, gave me such tubes as a gift not long ago; and I found those things to be true by experiment which the most wise Prince frequently told me about them.

<margin>Various ratios for microscopes.</margin>
If anyone constructs a lens from two spherical segments so that the sharper segment leans toward a <term>hyperbola</term> <note>A specific type of geometric curve; Kircher suggests this shape improves magnification or clarity.</note>, and then moves very tiny objects to that point: he will find by experiment that what I have said about the miracles lurking in the composition and structure of natural things is true. Moreover, he will perfect this lens if he describes a hyperbola on one side and a spherical section on the other, which he will find on page 426. Let these few words be enough for clever minds; the figure of the lens placed here will explain the concept more clearly. Similar to this is what René Descartes describes in his *Dioptrics*. However, both the use and the shape differ: he makes the interior surface entirely flat and the exterior hyperbolic, the focus of which is in that place where one wishes to locate the object—

### Practical Matter III.
## *On Telescopes and their effects.*

Telescopes and <term>Helioscopes</term> <note>literally "Sun-viewers"; instruments designed specifically for observing the Sun without damaging the eyes.</note> differ in this: the former reach an accessible distance, the latter an inaccessible one.

<image-desc>An optical diagram illustrating the path of light through a telescope. Light rays labeled 'A' enter from the left through a large plano-convex lens marked 'PO'. These rays converge toward a focal point 'V' but are intercepted by a smaller biconcave lens marked 'MN'. After passing through the concave lens, the rays are refracted and continue on to a final focal point or eye position, also labeled 'V', at the far right. The lenses and optical components are aligned on a central horizontal axis marked with the letters 'U' and 'p'.</image-desc>

<margin>The principle of Telescopes.</margin>
The former are for terrestrial objects, while the latter are for celestial objects—namely the Sun (from which they take their name) and the stars. Telescopes, like helioscopes, are for the most part equipped with glasses tinted with color. However, the shape of the glasses does not differ at all. The most common use in Telescopes employs two glasses: one concave and the other convex. This convex glass collects, expands, and, as it were, brings the objects near; the concave glass thins out and distinguishes them. Let the object be **A**; the rays will be forced into one path by refraction through the <term>plano-convex</term> <note>Flat on one side and curved outward on the other.</note> transparent lens **PO**. The rays which, for example, propagate in a straight path and meet at **V**, are so refracted because of the interposed concave lens **MN** that at their exit they move away from the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>The line at a right angle to the lens surface.</note>; part of them are scattered and their density is, as it were, thinned, while part of them meet in an angle further away at **V**. From this diagram, unless I am mistaken, the reader will easily perceive the principles of the Telescope. But anyone who desires the reasons for this arrangement of lenses in relation to the structure of the eye should read what we have handed down more extensively in Book 2, Propositions 1 and 2.

Again, if you fit two similar convex lenses into a tube and apply the eye correctly, you will see any terrestrial objects with incredible magnitude, clarity, and breadth, though in an inverted position. From this it is clearly evident that what some say—without much consideration—is false: that to construct an optical tube, two glasses are necessarily required, one concave and the other convex. For experience has long since taught that two convex lenses demonstrate an object much more excellently, clearly, and grandly than a convex with a concave, even if the orientation is upside down. If it could demonstrate them in an upright position, it would seem that nothing could be added to the excellence of such a tube. <term>Descartes</term> <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the famous philosopher and mathematician who wrote extensively on optics.</note>, for the manufacture of an optical tube of a better sort, prescribes two <term>hyperbolic</term> <note>Non-spherical lens shapes that theoretically eliminate certain types of blurriness, though they were nearly impossible to grind accurately in the 17th century.</note> glasses in his *Dioptrics*: one convex and the other concave. The concave is placed near the eye, and the convex near the objects. In this, however, three notable difficulties occur, which, if they were overcome, would surely snatch the palm of victory from all others. The first is the difficulty in preparing such glasses. The second is the orderly arrangement of the focal points, without which you will accomplish nothing of value—and how difficult this may be, let the judgment of the expert decide. There is also the constant and unchanging application of the eye, by which the <term>visual spirits</term> <note>According to early modern science, these were subtle fluids or "vapors" that traveled through the nerves to enable sight.</note> are wonderfully fatigued, and the eyesight is hindered more than can be said, especially if one must dwell upon something for a long time. If you can find a remedy for these things, I otherwise strongly approve of the invention, even though I have heard of no craftsman to this day who has brought such a thing into a finished work; for mostly, such hyperbolic mechanisms degenerate into spherical ones, as we have said elsewhere. But with these things already tasted beforehand, let us discuss the [use] of Telescopes...

<margin>Two lenses inserted into a tube perform wonders.</margin>

The Great Art, Book 10. Magic, Part 2.

...let us pursue its use in exotic representations.

### Presentation I.

**To represent mountains, rivers, seas, immense plains, vast chasms, lakes, forests, and all kinds of animals within them, using a new art with an optical tube <note>original: "tubo optico"; a telescope</note> in such a way that absolutely nothing of these things appears outside of it.**

<margin>*A new invention for representing things through a tube.*</margin>
While I was completely absorbed in conducting experiments in Dioptrics <term>Dioptrics: The branch of physics dealing with the refraction of light, especially by lenses.</term>, quite unexpectedly and by chance, I came across exactly what I had been searching for with such great effort. This taught me more than enough that all the most excellent things discovered by various people to date were detected not so much by study as by practical use. For while I was standing at a window surveying the Roman countryside with a Telescope <note>original: "Telescopio"</note>, behold! In place of the fields, I observed seas, lakes, rivers, mountains covered in snow, shrubs, pools, shipwrecks, and—amazing to say—whales in the middle of the fields; yet none of these things appeared at all outside the tube. Astonished by the novelty of the thing, while I investigated the cause of such an unusual effect, I finally saw after diligent investigation that the cause of this was a certain board of a lattice-work, parallel to the horizon, which had been decayed by rain and was spread out with various irregularities, providing such wonderful spectacles. Taking this opportunity to attempt something more subtle, I constructed a machine that would show through a tube anything one might desire, even if none of the things to be represented appear outside the tube.

### A new universal-presentation experiment.

<margin>*The exhibition of wonders.*</margin>
On some board parallel to the horizon and exposed to a window, let sand, ashes, straw, and any pile of things be cast, provided they are so small that they cannot be seen through the tube from the place where they are viewed. Then, pour water over the outer edge of the board so that the smallest bits of straw stand out above the water. Once this is done, with the telescope open, move back until you catch the surface of the board in the proper proportion. And behold! A vast plain will suddenly appear to you looking through the tube, and you will perceive an immense sea filled with a great multitude of ships so vividly that you could swear you were standing in vast fields looking at the deepest oceans. Here you will see immense rocks, chains of mountains stretching into the sea in an immense tract, chasms, and similar things, according to the heap of things thrown randomly on the board. For the splendor of the water perfectly represents the sea; the standing straws and stalks represent ships; the flints represent mountains; and the roughness of the board itself represents the cracks and furrows of a country plain. All these things will be represented more vividly the more proportionately they are arranged. When I demonstrated this presentation <note>original: "paraſtaſim"</note> to friends, it can hardly be said how much pleasure and wonder they received from such a variety of spectacles, especially since none of these things shown by the tube appeared outside of it. Father Fulgentius, a religious of the Order of Saint Francis, also exhibits all these things with wonderful skill.

### Construction of the universal-presentation machine.

<margin>*How the whole world can be represented with a tube.*</margin>
In the preceding experiment, we took a sample of things thrown together randomly; in this one, we shall provide an artistic arrangement of things to be displayed. Let a square drum <note>original: "tympanum"; a rotating cylinder</note> be made of wood, equipped with its own axis, of such a length that it can be conveniently rotated within a window, and of any width you like. The individual sides of this drum will present different scenes to you, in almost the same way we taught above concerning Catoptric <term>Catoptrics: The branch of optics dealing with reflections and mirrors.</term> mirrors. Thus, the first side, for example, will represent seas with ships; the second, gardens, cities, and most pleasant fields; the third, a rural plain crowded with a multitude of people and animals; the fourth, rivers, mountains, hills, waterfalls, and vast wildernesses. And if you desire more things of this kind, you can make a drum with five sides, six sides, or as many sides as you wish. Once these things are duly completed: if you then desire to see the spectacles of the first side, rotate the drum until that side stands parallel to the horizon. You shall arrange the things to be represented as follows. Let very small mountains be formed from wax; then, cover the part of the board that will represent the sea with silver leaf and polish it with a tooth so that it acquires a shine. You will form rivers from similar material, yet so small that they do not appear distinctly outside the tube from the place where you are looking. Within the silver border, make tiny stalks stand out in the shape of ships; if you can give them motion by means of small strings, you will exhibit the matter even more vividly. But if you wish to show mountains—blue ones, on this side or that side of the sea, separated as if by an immense distance—you will achieve your goal if you place a fragment of a convex or spherical mirror. For this vividly represents an island seen from a great distance within the sea. <margin>*Vivid exhibition of distant mountains.*</margin> [Set up] the remaining sides of the drum with similar industry...

<header>Parastatic Magic</header>

<meta>catchword: PART</meta>

...you will adorn with diligent industry. Experience will teach all these things better than I can declare with many words.

<margin>Adaptation of the tube.</margin>
Once the sides of the drum have been arranged in the manner described, take the tube <note>a telescope</note> of the size I mentioned and of the best quality. Move it back and forth until you achieve the proper distance. You will know you have this when you see the proposed objects most clearly and perfectly. You will then behold spectacles worthy of admiration, looking at everything I have described as if they were real and life-sized: immense seas, islands scattered across infinite space, curved shorelines, fishing boats, and similar sights we have prescribed. If you wish to change the scene, turn the drum, and another side will exhibit most pleasant gardens, garden walks planted according to all the rules of perspective, and bubbling fountains, to the great delight of the mind.

<margin>How Mount Etna may be shown.</margin>
In this way, you will produce different scenes of things according to the variety of the drum’s sides, which can be seen only through the tube and by no other means outside of it. In this manner, you may represent smoking Mount Etna: if you pour a few drops of water onto small pieces of quicklime <term>Quicklime: Calcium oxide, which reacts violently with water to produce heat and steam—here used to simulate volcanic smoke.</term> placed in a hollow on the board, it will begin to smoke and churn with heat, perfectly representing a fire-vomiting mountain to the viewers. From this, it is clearly evident that there is nothing in the nature of things that cannot be exhibited to the life by similar industry. If all these things are achieved with a certain secret industry, it can scarcely be said how much admiration they excite, since none of the things represented can be seen outside the tube. You shall set up the secret arrangement as follows:

<margin>Requirements for a perfect representation.</margin>
First, let the parastatic drum be made inaccessible to the spectators by a barrier. Second, let the tube be fixed in its proper place so that, directed at the drum, it remains perpetually immobile, and any object may be represented simply by applying the eye. Third, the matter will be more worthy of admiration if viewed from a dark place, into the side of which the tube has been inserted. Fourth, let the place be so arranged that you can either look toward the horizon or, at least, so that a wall positioned opposite the drum is illuminated by the Sun. If the wall is white, it will represent all things most perfectly; for the light reflected from the board will provide splendor to the seas and light and colors to the rest. However, if illumination from an opposite wall is lacking, the illuminated parastatic side of the drum itself will represent things in exactly the same way. The distance of the eye from the board is determined according to the proportion of the tube: small tubes require a smaller distance, larger ones a greater one. I exhibit spectacles of this kind at a distance of about 30 feet. In larger tubes, a space of 100 feet can be used; but these have the disadvantage that while they represent large things, they are not as clear as the smaller tubes. This matter must be left to the judgment of a prudent craftsman.

<margin>How the same things may be shown in a dark place.</margin>
If you project the images of the things arranged on the parastatic board onto the wall of a dark room or onto an exposed linen cloth, the same things will be represented in the dark much more miraculously, since nothing can be seen outside the window that might project such images.

# Representation II.

## *By what means can things in the air, as well as rainbows, clouds, the Sun, Moon, and Stars, be represented?*

<margin>How the Sky, Sun, Clouds, and Rainbow are shown.</margin>
**W**e have represented earthly things; now it remains for us to report on the sublime. Proceed as follows: First, place two convex lenses <note>original: "vitra convexa"</note> of the best quality into the optical tube; for with these, you will represent everything as if in the air, though inverted. Then, on the board itself, let things representing the sublime be depicted. First, let the entire parastatic surface be drenched in liquid or covered with silver leaf; for when inspected through the tube, this will represent a bright and serene sky. Within this, if you arrange a piece of mirror <note>original: "frustrum speculare"</note> so that the reflected ray of the Sun is caught by the tube, you will see a shining Sun in the clearest sky. If, furthermore, you adapt white chalk into the shape of clouds, it will represent clouds wandering through the sky. Carded tufts of cotton <term>Cotton: The Latin "gossypium" refers to cotton wool, used here for its fluffy, cloud-like texture.</term> will perform the same task. You shall form a rainbow <note>original: "iridem"</note> thus: On glass or clean paper, place a rainbow painted and cut out with all the required colors in an inverted position; and you will see in the air a rainbow so natural that nothing more seems possible to express the truth of the thing. An industrious craftsman can exhibit countless other similar things, such as a certain Religious of the Order of Saint Francis <note>The Franciscans or possibly the Minims, an order Kircher often collaborated with in Rome.</note> here in Rome, who not long ago exhibited these things to the great admiration of those watching. The matter is entirely easy and has small principles, like all other secrets: as long as they are unknown, they are held in admiration; when they are known, they become cheapened. I do not doubt, however, that with these foundations laid, many inventions of other things will emerge in their own time. And let these be the things I thought should be briefly communicated to the curious Reader.

# PART THREE,
## CATOPTRIC MAGIC,
### OR CONCERNING THE MARVELOUS EXHIBITION OF THINGS THROUGH MIRRORS,
### P R E F A C E.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'E' depicting a scholar seated at a desk in a study filled with books and scientific instruments.</image-desc>
**H**aving dispatched all those matters which seemed in any way to contribute to <term>Parastatic Magic</term> <note>From the Greek 'parastatikos,' meaning 'presenting' or 'representing.' In this context, it refers to the art of creating apparitions or showing objects through lenses and light, discussed in the previous section.</note>, let us now examine the inner sanctuaries of <term>Catoptric Magic</term> <note>The study of reflection and mirrors, derived from the Greek 'katoptron' (mirror).</note>, lest we seem to have hidden any of the mechanisms of secret devices from the curious Reader. For Catoptric Magic is nothing other than a certain recondite faculty of exhibiting things with the help of mirrors that seem to exceed all grasp of the human intellect.

<margin>The wondrous power of burning mirrors.</margin>
By the aid of this Catoptric Magic, we read that of old, Archimedes at Syracuse and Proclus at Byzantium—who were both well-equipped with such devices—burned ships in the harbor and conquered the most savage enemies using only the armaments of nature (the sun). Vitello relates the same concerning the flat mirrors of Anthemius, as does Pliny in Book 33, Chapter 9, regarding the silver and gold mirrors of Praxiteles. Relying on this Catoptric Magic, we have heard of some in our own age who, during times of siege, detected the enemy's hidden machinery through the communication of secrets by the <term>Catoptrologic Art</term> <note>The practical application of mirror-science for signaling or observation.</note>. By slaughtering the enemy to utter destruction, they liberated both their cities and their fatherland. There were even those who, through the support of this art, performed such feats that—since they could be understood by no one—they were suspected of the infamous crime of <term>necromancy</term> <note>The practice of communicating with the dead; here, it implies the author's contemporaries often mistook advanced physics for dark magic.</note> and suffered punishments worthy of their sordid refusal to share their optical secrets. Whether you look to public use or the private recreation of Princes, you will find here countless things taught by no one else (as far as I know) until now. The impostures of many will also be brought into the open and exposed, against which I would wish the Readers to beware. But leaving behind boastful words, let us now approach the matter itself.

---

### H Y P O T H E S E S.

**I.** The image of any object appearing through a mirror is seen in the manner required by the meeting of the line of reflection with the <term>cathetus of incidence</term> <note>In traditional optics, the 'cathetus' is the perpendicular line drawn from the object to the surface of the mirror.</note>.

**II.** Every reflection weakens light and colors; and the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, for nature operates through the shortest possible lines.

**III.** Every form [image] is produced according to a perpendicular line upon the surface of each mirror. Reflection truly happens along the same line as the ray of incidence; moreover, between the points of the form falling on the surface of any mirror and the surface of the opposite mirror, it is necessary for infinite pyramids to be shaped, having cones and bases mutually on both sides.

**IV.** In every reflection made on the surface of any mirror, a straight line dividing the angle contained by the lines of incidence and reflection into two equal parts is necessarily perpendicular.

**V.** In any mirrors, the center of sight, the point of the form seen, the point of reflection, and the boundary of the perpendicular... <note>The text on this page ends mid-sentence.</note>

# CHAPTER I.
## On the construction of mirrors.
### Practical Operation I.
### First method.

<margin>The method of backing mirrors with a tin plate.</margin>
I am not unaware that many authors treating of Catoptrics have handed down in their books various methods for the construction of mirrors. We, having been instructed by Venetian craftsmen, are accustomed to construct them in this way. First, the backing <note>Original: 'terminatio,' referring to the reflective coating that 'ends' the transparency of the glass.</note> of the mirrors, which is prepared for glass and crystal, is made by means of lead or tin placed under the glass sheet; this is the most efficient and best method of finishing mirrors. Take a tin foil <note>Original: 'stannea bractea'.</note> made of the best English tin <note>English tin was highly prized in the 17th century for its purity and brightness.</note>, which you shall stretch upon a table that is as flat as possible. This foil, thus extended, you shall apply to the glass with such skill that no wrinkle or spot remains in the foil. Then, you shall surround the glass, along with the foil, with a wooden or metal frame. This being done, you shall allow <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury.</note> poured over it to flow here and there until the whole of it is absorbed by the tin foil; and you will have a finished mirror. Nature taught us this craftsmanship in the construction of the eye: for she placed a certain blackness behind the transparent parts, not unlike the glass which finishes the sight with a polished foil. And by this same industry, we finish not only glass, but also sheets of <term>Selenite</term> <note>A transparent variety of gypsum; the text notes it is commonly called talc.</note>, which they commonly call talc. These, having been reduced to a mirror by the said method, and then curved around a cylinder, produce a cylindrical mirror; around a cone, a conical one; around a pyramid, a pyramidal one; and finally, applied to any sides whatsoever, they create the desired mirror. In performing experiments, I have known nothing better than this practice. Truly, since exotic bodies of this kind require the greatest craftsmen and can only be obtained at great expense, nothing better or more efficient can be found than this method for taking various experiments concerning the properties of different surfaces.

### Second method.
## On steel mirrors.

Although steel <note>Original: 'chalybea'.</note> mirrors are excellent and exhibit the likenesses of things most perfectly, because they are nevertheless very greatly subject to rust, craftsmen have devised a certain mixture from which a very smooth and absolutely perfect mirror may be cast. For some construct them thus: from three parts of copper <note>Original: 'aeris'.</note>, one part of tin and silver, and an eighteenth part of antimony. Some leave out the silver for the sake of economy. Certain others make plates from a pound of tin and a third of a pound of copper already melted together, adding an ounce of <term>tartar</term> <note>Potassium bitartrate, used as a flux in metallurgy.</note> and a half-ounce of white <term>orpiment</term> <note>An arsenic sulfide mineral used here to whiten the alloy.</note>, and boiling them over coals until they emit smoke. Finally, the molten metal is poured into molds formed to straightness and heated, smoothed with the resin of the larch <note>Original: 'lacryma laricis'.</note> and the ash of a vine, and brought into the shape of a mirror. Then, they polish it with water and sand attached with glue to a board, then with <term>emery</term> <note>A dark granular rock used as an abrasive.</note> or smooth pumice, afterwards with <term>Tripoli earth</term> <note>A fine-grained siliceous silt used as a polishing abrasive.</note>, and finally with the lime of burnt tin to the ultimate polish.

Silver mirrors, however, are constructed with less trouble, since silver by itself provides what we require from mirrors. Indeed, they are both more brilliant and at less risk of breaking.

### Third method.
## On convex mirrors.

When you are about to construct convex or spherical mirrors, take 1 ounce of <term>Marcasite</term> <note>An iron sulfide mineral used here as part of a reflective coating.</note>, 1 of tin (such as they use for soldering), and 2 parts of quicksilver: let them be melted and poured into cold water. Then the whole should be put into a clean linen cloth to be strained, and the "juice" squeezed out. This, poured into a glass sphere that has not yet been put to any use and shaken about, will soon finish it into a mirror. But as we intend to treat all these things formally in our work *The Subterranean World* <note>Kircher's famous 1665 encyclopedia of the earth sciences.</note>, we deliberately refrain from saying more about them here.

### Practical Operation II.
## On the construction of a concave spherical mirror.

The measure of a concave spherical mirror is a circle, of which even the smallest segments—since they have the same center—will observe the same laws of reflecting the incidence of rays as in the largest segments. For this reason, mirrors that are in some way equal are said by many to be so not in quantity, but in power; and they are as much greater than mirrors cut from a larger periphery as the diameter of the larger circle [exceeds] the diameter of the smaller...

I would like you to note all of this carefully. I said a little earlier that mirrors made from any segments of the same circle, however unequal they may be, are still equal in power in a certain way, though not precisely. Indeed, it has become known to the more secret masters of <term>catoptrics</term> <note>The branch of optics dealing with the reflection of light, especially by mirrors.</note> that some segments cause a greater union in reflecting rays than others, and thus acquire a more effective power for both illuminating and burning. I,

as far as I have been able to gather from tireless scrutiny, judge that a mirror segment spanning a cavity of 18 degrees is the most suitable of all, both for illuminating most powerfully and for burning most effectively. For it gathers and constricts the rays reflected toward the axis around the fourth part of the diameter from the <term>vertex</term> <note>The central point or "peak" of the mirror's curve.</note> of the mirror, so that it seems to resemble something parabolic; for it collects almost all the solar rays within a linear space of 1/12 of a <term>digit</term> <note>A "digit" was a traditional unit of measurement, roughly the width of a finger (about 1.9 cm).</note>. If the other common requirements for a mirror are present—namely, skill in the work, suitable material, evenness of the surface, smoothness, and a polish exceeding all others—then it will ultimately achieve its value. Such a mirror with a diameter of 9 digits will perform as well as a huge mirror weighing 80 pounds and measuring 3 feet in diameter. For this

is so perfect that nothing in it is redundant; it reflects <term>idols</term> <note>In 17th-century optics, "idols" or "images" referred to the visual representation of an object produced by light rays.</note> more perfectly and from a greater distance, and by tightening the rays, it burns better. Thus, whatever is added to a mirror beyond this degree can rightly be seen as added for free and without any utility. I know that a certain French nobleman constructed similar things to the great admiration of all; the secret is known to few.

### Practical Project III.
### On the construction of cylindrical and conical mirrors.

<margin>Selenite mirrors, or those covered in talc.</margin>

The best convex cylindrical mirrors are made from any metal, or even from the <term>mixture</term> <note>A specific alloy of metals, often including tin, copper, and arsenic, used to create highly reflective "speculum metal."</note> which I indicated above, cast into a properly prepared mold, which then, once polished, will provide the intended effects. The wider they are, or the more capacious the base, the more clearly they will return the <term>phasmata</term> <note>Greek-derived term for "apparitions" or "reflected images."</note>. For cylinders and cones, both concave and convex, I use a very fine process without such great labor and expense by covering them with <term>selenite leaves</term> <note>Thin sheets of transparent gypsum or mica, used here to create a reflective surface.</note> reduced into a mirror.

Once the form of a <term>parabola</term> <note>A specific geometric curve that has the unique property of reflecting all parallel incoming light rays to a single focal point.</note>, described according to the rules indicated in the third book, has been cut into some solid material like iron or brass,

### Corollary

From these things it is most clearly evident that from this so-hidden mastery, a focal form can be given which, by its burning, may express any figure whatsoever; I believe nothing more wonderful than this has been produced by anyone. Through this, any thing can be represented by any other thing. Since these matters have been unheard of until now, they should rightly excite curious searchers of nature to investigate such exotic effects with the highest study.

## Proposition I

> *In plane mirrors, the figure of the seen object and the position of its parts are not changed according to the quantity of length and width.*

LET there be a plane mirror AB, the form of the seen object FL, and the <term>catheti</term> <note>Lines drawn perpendicular to the surface of the mirror.</note> FZ and LH. There will be two points, Z and H, on the common surface of reflection. The lines FZ and LH shall be extended continuously to points D and G, at the same distance from Z and H as E and L are from them. Let the center of vision be E, and the cathetus EB having been drawn above the mirror AB, it is clear that the form of points L and F is reflected from some points of the mirror into E. The location of the images' forms will be points D and G, which are as far below the surface of the mirror as points L and F are above the

<image-desc>A geometric diagram illustrating the optics of a plane mirror. A horizontal line AB represents the mirror's surface. A vertical line segment FL above the mirror represents an object. Lines of reflection extend from points F and L to meet at an observation point E (the eye) to the right. Points Z and H are marked on the mirror surface AB where the perpendicular lines from F and L meet it. Below the mirror, a mirrored image DG is shown as a symmetrical projection of FL. Geometric lines connect the object, the mirror's surface, the observation point, and the virtual image.</image-desc>

mirror. Therefore, if line FL is straight, line GD will also be straight. If FL is an arc of a circle, line GD will also represent an arc of a circle, always of the same curvature and arrangement. Therefore, the line FL will always appear to be of the same size and figure as it is outside the mirror. The proposition is therefore evident.

### Corollary

From this proposition, it is first clear that heights, depths, and oblique lengths are seen reversed by plane mirrors when they stand perpendicularly upon the surfaces of the mirrors. See Euclid, Theorem 7 of the *Catoptrics*. And see our own *Anacamptic Art* <note>original: "artem nostram Anacampticam"; "Anacamptics" is an older term for the study of reflected light or catoptrics.</note>, where you will find this proposition demonstrated more extensively: also that right things appear left, and left things right, as is clear from the proposition.

# The Great Art, Book 10. Magic, Part III.

### Proposition II.

*To position a mirror in such a way that the viewer sees not their own image, but in its place another image previously unseen.*

Let there be a horizontal line FB, upon which AB rests <term>perpendicularly</term> <note>original: *normaliter*</note>. Let a certain flat mirror be raised to two-thirds of a unit above the plane of line EB. Below this horizontal line EB, let another plane IT be established parallel to plane DB, in which 

-> [image description: A geometric diagram showing a horizontal base line F-G-K-E-B. A vertical line AB rises from the right. A diagonal line runs from F to B. Above this, a line segment DB represents a mirror or plane. Below the horizontal line, there is a construction with points I, H, T, and L, showing reflections from point I to the viewer at G via the elevated plane DB.] <-

the form to be represented in the mirror is placed—for example, at I—while the eye is positioned at G; and let the horizontal plane QB be open. I say that the appearance of the image positioned at I will be projected to the mirror at point D, and from there reflected to G, the center of the eye; and consequently, the eye will perceive in the mirror the form of the object positioned at I. For since the angle of the radiating image IDB <note>The angle of incidence.</note> is equal to the angle of the resulting image GDF from D to G (that is, to the center of the eye), and since every form is perceived under the same angle at which it falls upon the mirror, the form of the object positioned at I will necessarily be seen in no other place than at point G. For suppose it were seen, for example, at point E. But since the angle of reflection at D would then be unequal to the angle of incidence IDB, the object would therefore be seen at point E and yet not be seen <note>A logical contradiction in optical geometry.</note>, which is absurd. Therefore, it will be seen at point G alone, which was to be demonstrated.

### Proposition III.

*To look upon one's own image flying under a certain arrangement of the mirror.*

Let a right-angled triangle ABC be made, on the plane of whose side AC a mirror LH is placed. On the plane of side AB, let another mirror DE be placed, and let the <term>perpendicular lines</term> <note>original: *catheti*</note> DG and EM be drawn from DE. Let side A be positioned on a flat surface upon which the figure of the viewer is raised, 

-> [image description: A geometric diagram illustrating the optics of a reflection experiment. It features a right-angled triangle ABC with hypotenuse AC. A mirror segment LH is placed on the hypotenuse, and another segment DE on the base AB. Lines of sight from an eye at point K reflect off LH to points on a vertical line representing the viewer (G and M), creating an illusion of a flying image at points N and O.] <-

the feet of whom at point G are slightly elevated above the line AB. Let M be the crown of the viewer's head, and let the eye or sight be at K. Let the angles of the incident lines GD and EM be equal to the angles of the reflection lines DH and EL; and with side BA extended to N, it is clearly evident that the entire image GM is reflected from the surface of mirror ED into mirror LH, and from mirror LH reflected to the sight K. And since the location of the image of each point's form is at the intersection of its <term>perpendicular of incidence</term> <note>original: *cathetus suæ incidentiæ*</note> with the line of its reflection: let the line BDEA be extended, for this is the perpendicular of the forms of points G and M reflected from points D and E to the mirror LH. And from K, through points L and H, lines will mark out—making with line AC angles equal to angles ELA and DHA—the space ON on the extension, the image of the form of the entire line GM. 

<margin>So that one may seem to fly in a mirror.</margin> 

And the point which is the image of the form of point G (namely, the feet of the viewer themselves) will be higher in the air than point O, which is the image of the form of point M (the crown of the viewer's head). Therefore, from point K, the person looking into the mirror LH will see their own image flying in the air, because they will see their feet placed higher in the air than their head. Thus, under a certain arrangement of the mirror, the image of the viewer will be seen flying, which was to be shown.

### Proposition IV.

*To set up two flat, rectangular, and equal mirrors so that a viewer sees their image approaching in one mirror and receding in the other.*

## Proposition V.

*By means of two flat mirrors, the same object can be represented several times, even to infinity. And this Proposition is the foundation of all Catoptrics.*

Let there be two flat and parallel mirrors EB and CD, an object O between both, and the eye at A, from where you can see mirror EB: from object O, let a perpendicular CE fall upon this mirror EB, which will also be perpendicular to mirror CD, and in the same extension the <term>spectra</term> <note>images or visual appearances</note> of object O will appear, according to the common sense of perspective.

Next, let a plane be understood as drawn through the same perpendicular and through the eye A, which makes with the mirrors common sections—straight and parallel lines, for example, EB and CD.

Finally, let EF be equal to EO, and in the second figure, let CG be equal to CO; and in both, let FM, OL, M<unclear>a</unclear>, LS, <unclear>a</unclear>s, sh, be equal and double the distance of CE. I say that one and the same object O, with the eye existing in the same place A and looking into Mirror EB, appears at points F, L, M, S, a, h, s, and so on.

And first, that the object O appears at F is proved in this way. Let the line AF cut the straight line EB at H, and let OH be joined. Since, therefore, the angles at E are right angles, and the sides FO, EF, are equal to sides EF, EH; the angles EHO and EHF will be equal, and because AHB is equal to EHF, the angle of incidence OHE will be equal to the angle of reflection AHB, and consequently point F, in which the ray AH cuts the perpendicular OE, will be the location of the <term>spectrum</term> <note>reflected image</note> of object O.

I say secondly, the same object O appears a second time at point L; for first, CO twice, and OE twice—that is, GO once and OE twice—are double the distance of CE, and thus equal to OL. Therefore, taking away the common OE, there will remain GO and OE, which is EG, equal to EL. Next, let the ray AL cut the straight line EB at I, and the straight line IG cut CD at K, and let KO be joined. Since, therefore, around the right angles at C, the sides CG, CK are again equal to sides CO, CK, and around the right angles at E, the sides GE, EI are equal to sides LE, EI, then as before the angle of incidence OKC will be equal to the angle of reflection IKD; and again the angle of incidence KIE will be equal to the angle of reflection BIA. Consequently, the object O, falling first into mirror CD, will be reflected from K into mirror EB at I, and from I it will be reflected again to the eye A. Thus the eye A, through the ray AI, will see by the benefit of both mirrors the same object O, through two reflections, at point L, where the visual ray AI cuts the perpendicular OE.

I say thirdly, the same object O is seen a third time at point M: for first, let ER be taken as equal to EM, which is greater than double CE, and point R will be beyond C. Finally, let AM be drawn, cutting EB at N, and NR cutting CD at P, and PF cutting EB at Q, and let OH be joined. Since, therefore, both EM, ER, and EO, EF are equal, and EN, EQ are common, the angle of incidence OHE will be (as before) equal to the angle of reflection BQP, and the angle of the second incidence QPC equal to the angle of reflection DPM, and the angle of the third incidence PNE equal to the third reflection BNA: and in this manner the object O will reach the eye A, and through ray AN, the same object will now be seen for the third time at point M.

I say fourthly, the same object appears again at S. For let EV be taken as equal to ES, and CV will also be equal to CL, for GV and LS are equal, because when equals EG and EL are taken away from equals EV and ES, the remainders are equal; moreover, OL is equal to LS: therefore GV and OL are also equal, and by adding the equals CG and CO, CV and CL will also be equal. Therefore, with AS joined and cutting EB at T, and TV cutting CD at X, and XL cutting EB at y, and yG cutting CD at Z; it will be shown, as before, that the incident ray OZ is reflected to y, and the reflected ray Zy is reflected again to X, and yX is reflected to T, and XT is reflected from T to the eye...

### Proposition VI.
#### To demonstrate the same principle universally.

**L**et there be an eye A and an object O, and let the <term>spectrum</term> <note>original: "spectrum"; here meaning the visual image or phantom appearance of the object</note> of object O be represented at B. Let the straight line CD bisect BO into two equal parts at right angles at point C, and the ray AB at D. At point D, let a piece of a plane mirror EF be fitted along the line CD, and let OD be joined. The angles CDB and CDO will be equal, because around the right angles at C, the sides CO and CD are equal to the sides CB and CD. Furthermore, the angle FDA is equal to the same CDB, being opposite at the vertex D. Therefore, the angle of <term>incidence</term> ODC is equal to the angle of <term>reflection</term> FDA, and the ray AD sees the object O at point B, where the ray AD intersects the perpendicular line OC.

### Corollary.

**I**n this way, the same object could be represented to the same eye at assigned locations by multiplying the mirrors—provided no other impediment occurs—and by employing other parallel mirrors, a multiplication of the same object may be achieved across infinite other locations.

#### Another demonstration of this matter, shorter and clearer.

**L**et the plane and parallel mirrors be EB and CD, the object O, and the line COE, which is perpendicular to both mirrors, extended in both directions to infinity. I say that to an eye located anywhere at A, from which the mirror EB can be seen, the object O will be seen multiplied without end.

In the first figure, let EF be taken equal to OE; then from F, let any number of segments EM, Ma, as, etc., be marked off toward the same side at will, each equal to double the distance CE, etc., and let the rays AHI, ANM, Aba, ABs, etc., be joined. I say that from points H, N, G, B, the appearances of the image O are reflected to the eye A, and thus in the perpendicular line OES, they are seen at locations I, M, a, s. For on the other side of the object O—that is, toward C—let OR, RC, and Ct be marked off, equal to double CE, and equal in number to FM, Ma, and as.

Therefore, if first OH is joined, since EO and EF are equal and EH is perpendicular, the angles EHO and EHF must be equal. And because AHE is equal to the same EHF, the image of O, falling upon the mirror at H, will be reflected to the eye through the ray HA, and through the same ray, it will be seen in the perpendicular OE at F.

Secondly, let RN be joined, intersecting the mirror CD at B and P; let another line PF be drawn, intersecting the mirror EB at Q, and let OQ be joined. As before, the angles EQO and BQC will be equal, and the image incident at Q will be reflected to P. That the angle of reflection DPN is also equal to the angle QPC is proved in this way: Let CE be equal to CO. Since OR is double CE, it will be equal to two COs—that is, to O and two OEs—which is to say, to OF. Thus RO and F will be equal, and the common segment O being subtracted, R and OF are equal. By adding the equal segments Cr and CG, CR and CF will also be equal, and CP is perpendicular; therefore, the angles CPR and CPI are equal. But the angle OPR is equal to the vertex angle NPD. Therefore, the angle of incidence QPC is equal to the angle of reflection DPN, and the image of object O is reflected from H to P, from P to N, and finally from N to A. This is because the angles RNE and BNA are also equal, given that ER and EM are equal (since RO is equal to FM and EO to EF) and EN is perpendicular.

Thirdly, for the same reason, Ec and Ea are equal: and thus the angles BbA and Ebc (or Ebd) are equal, so that if a line is drawn from M, the segment bdD is equal to MdC or odC, because CM and Cc are equal—as is evident if the equals CF and CR are applied to the equals FM and RO. Likewise, the angle deB is equal to eE, because ER and EM are equal, and BfD is equal to gfc, due to the equality of CF and CR; and finally fgB is equal to ogE, due to the equality of EF and EO. From this, it is established that the image of object O, falling at g, is reflected from g to f, from f to E, from E to d, from d to b, and finally to the eye A; and therefore the same object is represented to the eye at point A. For the demonstration is always the same.

In the second figure, at point C, let CG be marked off equal to CO, and afterwards GV, VK, etc., equal to double CE, and similarly on the other side from the object O...
