# CHAPTER III.
### *On convex spherical mirrors.*

**F**IRST, in convex spherical mirrors, we consider the surface of reflection as a sphere dividing the mirror into equal parts.

Second, if tangent lines are drawn from the center of sight <note>The position of the observer's eye.</note> to the sphere of the circle, they determine that portion of the mirror from whose points the reflection of forms to the sight will occur; this portion decreases as the sight approaches the mirror, but increases as it recedes.

Third, a line drawn from the center of the mirror to the point of reflection and extended bisects the angle contained by the lines of incidence and reflection; every line of reflection meets with the <term>cathetus of incidence</term> <note>The perpendicular line dropped from the object to the reflecting surface or its center.</note>, and there fixes the location of the seen image.

Fourth, a single sight <note>One eye at a fixed point.</note> cannot see the phantom <note>original: "idolum"; the reflected image.</note> of the same form reflected from different points of the same mirror.

Fifth, the forms of all points equidistant from the center of a convex spherical mirror are reflected to the sight according to equal angles under the catheti of incidence and the visual diameters contracted at the center of the mirror.

Sixth, if from any point of a convex mirror the line of reflection is extended and cuts the circle (which is the common section of the reflection surface of the mirror) in such a way that the part of the extended line within the circle, or which constitutes the chord, is equal to the radius of the circle, the location of the seen image will always be within the convex part of the mirror, and consequently, in this case, the location of the seen image will always be inside the mirror. See the most elegant demonstration of this in <term>Alhazen</term> <note>Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), the medieval Persian polymath whose "Book of Optics" defined the field.</note> Book 2, number 5. And with the help of this theorem, we have uncovered many wonderful and almost prodigious things in representations, which we shall discuss in the following pages.

<margin>Euclid, Theorem 20 of the Catoptrics.</margin>
Seventh, in convex spherical mirrors, the distance of the image from the surface of the mirror is less than the distance of the object itself outside. <term>Euclid</term>, Theorem 20 of the *Catoptrics*.

<margin>Vitellio, Book 6, number 4.</margin>
Eighth, in the same convex spherical mirror, while the center of sight remains unmoved and the form of the thing seen remains unmoved, the image of the thing is always seen in the same size; but if the image of the thing approaches closer to the mirror, it will appear larger, and the further it is removed from it, the smaller it will appear; however, the reverse is not true. <term>Vitellio</term> <note>Witelo (c. 1230–1285), a Polish friar and physicist whose work on optics was a standard text in the Renaissance.</note> provides a detailed demonstration of this in Book 6, number 4.

<margin>Alhazen, Book 15, number 6.</margin>
Ninth, the image of an arc concentric to the mirror in a convex sphere appears curved and parallel to the arc of which it is the image; however, the image of a straight line not equidistant to the mirror (which, if extended, would not touch or cut the surface of the mirror) appears curved when the sight is not in the surface of incidence. <term>Alhazen</term>, Book 15, number 6.

Tenth, from the surface of a convex spherical mirror composed of different spherical surfaces, the reflected forms appear as monstrous images. For since the centers of the various spherical surfaces are different, and the location of the image of any point in spherical mirrors occurs on its cathetus of incidence drawn from the point of sight to the center of the mirror—and these centers are diversified in such irregular mirrors—it is clear that the forms of different points are drawn out in different directions. Since the reflection happens from the whole surface,

## CHAPTER IV.
### On concave spherical mirrors and their prodigious operations.

<margin>The mirror shows the intensification of heat and cold.</margin>
**N**othing has so tormented the minds of optical scientists as the prodigious operations of the concave spherical mirror. For this mirror, with the first light of the Sun, so intensifies heat in the air that it burns white and black objects, marks bricks, and causes lead drawn into thin sheets to melt; it also reflects cold <note>Early modern scientists believed cold could be reflected just as heat was; we now understand this as the mirror reflecting the object's own thermal radiation away or reflecting the "cold" of a void.</note> in such a way that the difference between winter and summer is best discerned through reflection; and it presents letters to be read on a distant wall. With the secondary light, however, it renders various images—upright, inverted, large, and small—and sometimes demonstrates many things from one object, such as the whole object or just parts of it (like a single eye of the viewer), or two images of one thing in different locations. It also determines various locations for the images: beyond the mirror, between the mirror and the object, at the location of the object itself, or beyond the object (that is, behind it, and then the object appears smaller than its image in the mirror); and finally, on the surface of the mirror. Likewise, it shows transposed positions, as appears in reflected letters: forward, backward, upward, downward, to the right, and to the left.

<margin>Effects of the concave mirror.</margin>
Furthermore, it shows that <term>species</term> <note>original: "species"; here meaning the visual forms or "images" projected by an object.</note> are perceptible on their own, as appears from the projected edge of a sword or the light of a candle; likewise from snow or ice, which cools through its image even from quite a distance. It also returns speeches and voices like an Echo, so that those who are very far away hear as if they were close by. Finally, in the dark when illuminated by the Sun, it paints things that are outside onto paper or a wall with a miraculous picture: it pours the forms of things into the middle of the air, displays letters to be read from a distance, and similar wonders, which shall be treated in order in the following sections. But, so that all these marvels may be better understood, we have thought it necessary first to demonstrate certain things here concerning the concave mirror. Let this, therefore, be the first Proposition.

### Proposition I.

*The location of the image in concave spherical mirrors is at the point of intersection of the line of reflection produced behind the mirror and the <term>cathetus</term> <note>A perpendicular line drawn from the object to the reflecting surface or the center of the sphere.</note> of its incidence, which is drawn perpendicularly through the center of the mirror and the object seen.*

Let the mirror be DBA, the line of incidence SED, the line of reflection FD, and the cathetus GEBH, which passes through the center of the mirror and the object itself, and is called the diameter of incidence.

<image-desc>A geometrical diagram of a concave spherical mirror labeled DBA. A central vertical axis line is labeled with points H (top), G, B (at the mirror vertex), and E (the object, represented by a small eye figure). A ray of light ED strikes the mirror at point D and reflects along line DF. A dashed line GD represents the perpendicular to the mirror at the point of incidence. The reflected ray FD is extended backwards to point H on the central axis.</image-desc>

The line GD is the perpendicular of the location or point of incidence, according to which you see that the angle EDG and the line of reflection are equal, both with respect to the mirror itself or the line touching the mirror at D. Let the line of reflection FD be produced continuously from D. I say that where it cuts the cathetus of incidence GH, at that point is the location of the image. For since Nature in her actions strives for brevity—that is, she achieves her effects through the shortest possible lines—and since no lines are shorter than the lines of reflection with the cathetus of incidence, she therefore achieves her end through these two and no others. Therefore, the object E, which is seen by the eye F, is perceived at H, because the line of reflection meets the axis at H.

For if E were to fall beyond the mirror in a straight line—as that is the most direct and shortest path of all—it would fall at H. From this, the eye is deceived, as experience proves, when it thinks the object E is located at H. The reason is that, since the eye is a material and corporeal power, it cannot recognize a reflection, just as it cannot reflect itself upon itself. Therefore, it judges the line, or ray FD, to be continuous, originating from point D and then proceeding directly to the eye. Indeed, if the ray flowed from the eye through lines DH and AC, and neither the solidity of the mirror nor a denser medium prevented it from going further, it would pass straight to point H. ### Proposition II.

->*The focus, or the gathering of forms in a concave spherical mirror, does not occur at the very center of the spherical mirror segment, nor beyond it, but on this side of the center.*<-

<margin>All rays flowing from the Sun's disk are parallel.</margin>

**S**ince all the axes of the pyramids of light emerge from the same point—namely, from the center of the Sun—and the distance of that point from the surface of the mirror is, for us, almost infinite, and the surface of the mirror is of a small or rather imperceptible size compared to the size of the solar body and its immense distance; therefore, the lines falling upon the mirror, whether from the center of the Sun or from any point of the solar body, are all considered to be parallel <note>original: "æquidistantes"</note>, not unlike the lines of direction on the surface of the earth, all of which are assumed by Opticians and Astronomers. This being assumed, I say that the place where the forms or principal rays gather from the surface of a concave spherical mirror is not distant from the surface itself by half the semi-diameter of the sphere of which the mirror is a part; or, what is the same thing, it does not occur at the center itself, nor beyond it, but on this side of the center. I demonstrate this as follows: Let the Sun be A, the center of the concave spherical mirror be B, and let the ray AB pass through both

A central ray (the axis) travels vertically down through center point 'B', focal point 'F', and hits the mirror surface at 'C'. <margin>Demonstration.</margin>

The angle of incidence FEC is equal to the angle of reflection DEG; however, angle BEC is equal to angle BEG, for BE is the semi-diameter dividing the circumference in two: therefore, angles BEF and BED are equal by common notion (if equals are taken from equals, etc.). Since BC and DE are parallel, then by the 29th proposition of Book 1 <note>A reference to Euclid's Elements</note>, angle BED will be equal to angle BEF, and therefore the angles at the base BE are equal. Thus, by the 6th proposition of Book 1, sides BF and FE are equal; but FE is longer than FC, by the 5th proposition of Book 3; therefore, BF is longer than FC. This was to be demonstrated. Therefore, since rays near the center of the mirror are not bent to the midpoint of the semi-diameter, much less are those further away, by 29. 1.

### Corollary I.

<margin>The heat-producing focus is located in spherical mirrors, but in that portion of the axis which is between the center B and the mirror surface C; the focus will be closer to the surface of the mirror the further the points of incidence and reflection are from the point where the principal rays hit, or from the axis of the mirror; conversely, it will be closer to center B the closer the points of incidence and reflection, or the parallel rays incident to the axis BC, are.</margin>

**F**rom this proposition, it is clearly established that the focus is by no means located at the center of a spherical mirror; but in that portion of the axis which is between the center B and the surface of the mirror C. The focus will be closer to the surface of the mirror the further the points of incidence and reflection are from the point where the principal rays hit, or from the axis of the mirror; conversely, it will be closer to center B the closer the points of incidence and reflection, or the parallel rays incident to the axis BC, are.

### Corollary II.

<margin>Burning in spherical mirrors occurs at different points on the axis.</margin>

**H**ence it is also clear that in concave spherical mirrors, <term>ustion</term> <note>original: "ustio"; the act of burning or concentrating heat to ignite something</note> does not occur in only one point, but in several, according to the diversity of the incident lines. However, regarding which part of the diameter the focus occurs in, there are different opinions from different people: <term>appropriate</term> <note>original: "καταλληλη" (katallēlē); meaning corresponding or suitable</note> experience will settle the dispute. For if you adapt the reflecting lines to the rays incident on the entire circuit of the circle, they will show those locations on the axis CK, which for the most part will be established in the fifth part, or between the fifth and fourth part. Those who say, like Maginus <note>Giovanni Antonio Magini (1555–1617), an Italian astronomer and mathematician</note>, that all the rays of the Sun falling on a mirror made from a sixth part of a circle meet at the fourth part of the diameter, are mistaken; since they do not even gather at that point from a seventh part. Rather, they are pulled back toward the mirror surface away from that fourth part the further the incident rays are from the middle of the mirror and the axis, as has been said.

## CHAPTER V.

### *On cylindrical mirrors and their properties.*

<margin>The image in a cylindrical mirror takes on various shapes.</margin>
**I**n convex cylindrical mirrors, these properties are found. If the sight and the straight line are parallel to the axis of the mirror and in the same plane, the image can be reflected from the whole side of the cylinder; and the image is seen as a straight line equal to the parallel line. But if the sight is outside the plane of the straight line which is parallel to the axis of the mirror, reflection occurs from the side of the cylinder, and the image appears slightly curved and smaller than the parallel line itself. If, however, the sight is in the common section—the plane of the straight line and the axis of the convex cylindrical mirror being normal to each other—reflection will occur from the periphery of the mirror, which is the common section of the plane of the line and the surface of the mirror; and the image will appear curved. Finally, if the sight, being equally distant from the ends of the straight line, is outside its perpendicular plane to the plane of the mirror's axis, the image will appear most curved. Furthermore, in mirrors of this kind, the same deceptions will occur as in convex spherical ones: but see the demonstrations of these things in our *Reflective Art* <note>original: "Arte nostra Anacamptica"; Kircher's own work on the science of reflections.</note>.

See the demonstration of this in Witelo <note>original: "Vitellionem"; Witelo was a 13th-century friar and a seminal authority on optics.</note>, theorem 46.

The reflection of the lines of return <note>original: "anacampticæ." This refers to the paths of reflected light.</note> cannot be joined, which only happens when they become parallel. Therefore, if you progress toward infinity along the continuation of this reflected line, you would always see a flame of such a size as the surface of the mirror appears. Thus, if there were a mirror whose diameter was fifty feet, you would see a flame—even if caused by a very small light—so huge that it might appear to be a mountain of fire.

## Corollary II

<margin>How a flea may be changed into an elephant.</margin>
It is clear from this wonder in the mirror that an object, however small, may so fill the entire capacity and surface of a concave mirror, however large, that if you place even the smallest thing—say a poppy seed or any tiny animal—at the point of inversion, it will turn out to be as large as the surface of the mirror. Thus, if the mirror is twenty spans wide, a flea, a spider, or something similar placed there will equal the surface of the mirror in its size.

## CHAPTER VI
### On conic mirrors and their properties.

<margin>Various forms of the convex and concave conic mirror.</margin>
The properties of convex conic mirrors are these: if a straight line falls obliquely on the vertex of a convex conic mirror, it will be reflected from the conical side to the eye located between said line and the surface of the mirror, and its image will appear slightly curved. If the straight line is parallel to the width of the mirror, and the eye is outside the plane parallel to the base of said line, it will be reflected from an ellipse, and the image will appear greatly curved. But if the straight line neither falls obliquely on the vertex of the conic mirror nor is parallel to its width, the image will present itself with varying obliquity according to its varied position. Indeed, oblique lines existing between these two modes, which approach by their motion the lines extended along the length of the cone, have convex shapes again. Those that approach the lines equidistant to the width have clearly convex shapes, and the entire image takes on a conical figure; the closer it is to the mirror, the larger it will appear, and the farther away, the smaller.

A concave conic mirror has exactly the same properties as a hollow cylindrical one; for in this, lines appear equally less curved and hollow. I would gladly demonstrate all these things in this place, had I not already provided it in part in my *Anacamptics* <note>Referring to the author's previous work on the science of reflections.</note> and if <term>Vitello<gloss>Witelo (c. 1230 – 1280/1314), a Polish friar and natural philosopher who wrote a massive, influential treatise on optics titled Perspectiva.</gloss></term> and others had not already demonstrated all these things at length.

## CHAPTER VII
### Distinction II
### On parabolic, hyperbolic, and elliptical mirrors, and their properties.

**T**he sublimity of conic speculations is so great that it seems not to have been acquired by one’s own study, but to have been infused into man by the divine. These lines obtain such infinite use throughout Geometry and similarly in <term>Catoptrics<gloss>The branch of optics dealing with the reflection of light, especially by mirrors.</gloss></term> that a person who is well-versed in these matters should not undeservedly be judged a great Geometer. Devices like lenses or mirrors designed to concentrate sunlight to start fires.</gloss></term> by many leagues. In spherical concaves, just as the lines of incidence are reflected back into the axis of the mirror, so in these mirrors all the lines flow together, reflected into a single point of the axis, in which they perform such powerful operations that they may deservedly seem <gloss>and marvelous</gloss> <note>original Greek: "και παραδοξα"</note>; unless irrefutable experience had long ago established their truth. We are therefore going to speak of their construction, structure, and admirable operations, so that the reader may have something with which to exercise his intellect.

# The Great Art, Book 10. Part 3 of Magic.
<note>The title "Magia" here refers to "Natural Magic," which in the 17th century meant the study of the hidden forces of nature through mathematics and mechanics.</note>

**B**, with the vertex located at **A**, and the line **FBG** being perpendicular to the axis, let both **BF** and **BG** be double the length of **AB**; then the whole line **FG** is four times the length of **AB**. This represents the <term>latus rectum</term><note>Latin: latus rectum, meaning "upright side." In geometry, it is the chord through the focus of a conic section perpendicular to its major axis, defining the curve's width.</note> of the parabola, as shown by Marino Ghetaldi in Proposition 6 on the Parabola. Moreover, the points **FG** will be on the parabola according to Proposition 11 of the first book of the <term>Conics</term><note>A reference to Apollonius of Perga's foundational work, "Conics," which defined the mathematical properties of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas.</note>, because the square of **EB** (or **BG**) is equal to the rectangle formed by the segment of the axis **AB** and the latus rectum **FG**. Since **FG** is four times **AB**, the rectangle of **FG** and **AB** will also be four times the square of **AB**. Additionally, the square of **FB** is also four times the square of **AB**. Therefore, the square of **FB** (or **BG**) is equal to the rectangle formed by **FG** and **AB**; thus, points **FG** lie on the parabola.

Other points are found in this manner. On either side of the vertex **A**, let two equal parts **AC** and **AD** be cut off; and on the other side of point **C**, let the line **CE** be equal to **CB**. Taking the distance **BD**, let four arcs be drawn with that same distance from centers **B** and **E**, intersecting each other on both sides at points **H** and **I**. I say that points **H** and **I** are on the parabola. For since **BH** and **EH** are equal distances, and **CB** and **CE** are equal, it is necessary that the line **HC**, once drawn, is perpendicular to **EB**; the same logic applies to the line **IC**. I say the square of **CH** (or **CI**) is equal to the rectangle of **FG** and **AC**. Since the radii **BH** and **BD** are equal, and the square of **BH** is equal to the squares of **BC** and **CH**, and the square of **BD** is equal to that same square of **BC** plus four times the rectangle contained under **B**, **A**, and **C** (by Proposition 8 of the second book of Euclid), once the common square **BC** is removed, there remains the square **CH** equal to four times the rectangle **BAC**. Moreover, four times the rectangle under **BA** and **AC** is the same as the rectangle under **AC** and **FG** (which is four times **AB**). Therefore, the square of **CH** is equal to the rectangle contained by the axis segment **AC** and the latus rectum **FG**. By Proposition 11 of the first book of the *Conics*, point **H** is on the parabola; and indeed, point **I** is on the same parabola for the same reason.

But let us give another example. Let any other two equal portions **AK** and **AL** be taken on the axis on either side of the vertex; and on the other side of point **K**, let line **KM** be equal to **KB**. Using centers **B** and **M** (for the focus **B** is always one of the two centers), let four other arcs be drawn with the distance **BL**, intersecting each other at points **N** and **O**, which will also be on the parabola for the reason already stated.

Ghetaldus draws perpendiculars **CH** and **KN**, and cuts them at points **H** and **N** by describing circular arcs from center **B** with distances **BD** and **BL**. But because we have no need for such perpendiculars in the description of the hyperbola and the ellipse, we preferred to do without them in the parabola as well, and in their place assume two other secondary centers **E** and **M**.

### How to describe a Hyperbola.

Let the <term>transverse diameter</term><note>The segment of the axis between the two vertices of the hyperbola.</note> be **AB**, the vertices of the hyperbola be **A** and **B**, and the center be **C**. Let the foci (or points established by comparison) be **D** and **E**, such that the rectangle **BDA** (or **ABE**) is equal to a fourth part of the "figure"—that is, the rectangle contained by the transverse side **AB** and the latus rectum. This latus rectum is found as follows: from **AD**, let perpendiculars **AL** and **HDI** be erected to **AB**. Let **AF** be taken equal to **AD**, and let the line **BF**, once extended, cut off from **DI** the line **DG**. Let **AM** be equal to **DG**, **AK** be double **AM**, and **AL** be quadruple **AM**. I say that **AL** is the latus rectum; and points **H** and **I** are on the hyperbola if **DH** and **DI** are double that same **DG** (that is, equal to **AK**), and the whole line **HI** is equal to the latus rectum **AL**.

For since as **BD** is to **DG** (or to **AM**), so **BA** is to **AF** (or to **AD**), the rectangle **BDA** will be equal to the rectangle **BAM**. Since **BDA** is equal to a fourth part of the figure, then **BAM** is also equal to a fourth part of the figure. And because that same rectangle **BAM** is a fourth part of the rectangle **BAL** (since **AL** is four times **AM**), then **BAL** itself is the figure, and **AL** is the latus rectum of the hyperbola.

Now, if point **H** is understood to be on the hyperbola, then by Proposition 21 of the first book of the *Conics*, as **BA** is to **AL** (that is, as the half-diameter **CB** is to the half-side **AK**), so is the rectangle **BDA** (which is the rectangle **BM**) to the square of **HD**. However, as **CA** is to **AK**, so is the rectangle **CK** (or rectangle **BM**, for each is a fourth part of the rectangle **BM**) to the square of **AK**. Therefore, the rectangle **BM** to the squares **AK** and **DH** has the same proportion; they are consequently equal to each other, and the lines **AK** and **DH** are equal. Therefore, by taking **DH** equal to **AK** (or double **DG**), point **H** is established on the hyperbola, whose transverse side is **AB** and whose latus rectum is **AL**. In this, the hyperbola agrees with the parabola: in both, the <term>ordinate</term><note>A line segment from a point on the curve to the axis, perpendicular to that axis.</note> applied through the foci is equal to the latus rectum, which seems worthy of observation. For although in the hyperbola the axis segment **AD** is not 1/4 of the latus rectum, it is nonetheless a mean proportional between the transverse side and **FG**, which is the difference between **AM** (the fourth part of the latus rectum) and **AD** (or **AF**). # Catoptric Magic
<note>Latin: "Magia Catoptrica." Catoptrics is the branch of optics dealing with reflections from mirrors. In this era, understanding the geometry of curves like parabolas and hyperbolas was essential for designing burning mirrors and telescopes.</note>

...is of the fourth part of the figure, and with the common segment **AO** removed, **OM** remains, which is equal to the square of **AN**, and therefore to **AD** or **AF**; it is the mean proportional between **OF** and **FM**; that is, between **AB** and **FM**.

Any other hyperbolic points one might wish for are easily found through the intersections of arcs, just as with the parabola. If a point **P** is taken anywhere outside either focus—for example, above **E**—two intervals **AP** and **BP** are determined between that point **P** and each vertex **A** and **B**. Circles described from the <term>foci</term><note>Latin: "focis." Early mathematicians often called these "points of comparison" or "burning points."</note> **E** and **D** using these two intervals will intersect each other at the hyperbolic points **Q** and **R** for both hyperbolas of the opposite sections, should one wish to describe both.

The foundation of this practice is Proposition 25 of the third book of the *Conics* <note>Referring to the "Conics" of Apollonius of Perga.</note>, where it is shown that the lines **EQ** and **DQ**, which connect the points **D** and **E** (the foci) with a hyperbolic point (for example, **Q**), differ from each other by the <term>transverse side</term><note>Latin: "latere transverso," the distance between the two vertices of the hyperbola.</note> **AB**. These are the same intervals **AP** and **BP** by which we found the point **Q** through the intersection of arcs; for the line **BP** exceeds the line **AP** by the length of the transverse side **AB**.

The reasoning for this other method is the same: if one wishes to find another point **Q** near vertex **A**, let them take two equal segments **AS** and **AT** above and below **A**. Then, with center **E** and interval **ES**, and with center **D** and interval **DT**, describe arcs that intersect each other. The intersection of these arcs will give the point **Q** or **R** for the hyperbola to be drawn. Indeed, the interval **ED** is greater than the interval **DT** by the amount of the transverse side **AB**. For if **AB** is subtracted from **ES**, **EB** remains (which is **AD** and **AS**). But **AS** is equal to **AD**; therefore, after the subtraction, the interval **DT** remains, and so on for the others.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing the construction of a hyperbola. A horizontal axis contains points E, B, A, D. Arcs centered at the foci E and D intersect to define the curve. A rectangle and auxiliary lines demonstrate the proportional relationships between segments.</image-desc>

## Problem III.
->To describe an Ellipse.<-

<image-desc>A circular diagram containing an inscribed ellipse. The construction shows how the ellipse (an elongated circle) is derived from the proportions of a larger circle. Lines (ordinates) are drawn perpendicular to the major axis to define the curve's boundary.</image-desc>

> Let **AB** be the <term>major axis</term><note>The longest diameter of an ellipse.</note>, which is also the transverse diameter, and let **C** be the center of the Ellipse. Let the <term>foci</term><note>Latin: "foci, seu puncta ex comparatione facta," literally "the foci, or the points made from comparison."</note> **D** and **E** be such that the rectangles **BDA** and **AEB** are equal to a fourth part of the figure. Let **HDI** and **AL** be perpendicular to the axis, and let **AF** be equal to **AD**. Let the joined line **BF** intersect **DH** at **G**. Let **AM** be equal to **GD**, and let **AK** be double **DG** (or **AM**), and **AL** be four times **DG**. I say that **AL** is the <term>latus rectum</term><note>The "upright side," a constant segment used to define the width of the curve relative to its axis.</note>, and the points **H** and **I** lie on the ellipse if **DH** and **DI** are taken to be double the same **GD**. For since as **BA** is to **AF** (or **AD**), so **BD** is to **DG** (or **AM**), the rectangle **BAM** will be equal to the rectangle **BDA**. But **BAM** is the fourth part of the rectangle **BAL**. Therefore, **BDA** is also a fourth part of the same. Since the side **BA** is the transverse side, **AL** will be the latus rectum.

If point **H** is placed to touch the ellipse, it will be (by Proposition 21 of the first book of the *Conics*) as **BA** is to **AL**—that is, as **CA** is to **AK**—so the rectangle **BDA** (or **BAM**) is to the square of **DH**. But as **CA** is to **AK**, so is the rectangle **BAM** (or **CAK**, because each is a fourth part of the rectangle **BAL**) to the square of **AK**, if **AK** is taken as common. Therefore, one and the same rectangle **CAK** has the same proportion to two squares, **DH** and **AK**. Thus the squares **DH** and **AK** are equal, and the lines **AK** and **DH** are equal. However, **AK** is double **DG**. Therefore, **DH** is also double **DG**. Since **DH** was defined this way from the beginning, the point **H** on that line lies on the ellipse. The same reasoning applies to points **I**, **N**, and **O**, if **DI**, **EN**, and **EO** are double the line **DG**. And from this, it is also clear that in an Ellipse, the <term>ordinates</term><note>Latin: "ordinatas," lines drawn from a point on the curve perpendicular to the axis.</note> **HDI** and **NEO** are equal to the latus rectum **AL**.

# The Great Art, Book 10. Magic, Part 3.

...as follows; between the foci <note>original: "foci"; the two points that define the shape of an ellipse</note> D and E, let any point P be taken, and with centers D and E, at intervals BP and AP, let arcs be described intersecting each other at Q, R, S, and T; for these points Q, R, S, and T will be on the ellipse. For since the points D and E are established by the comparison made; if point Q, for example, were understood to be on the ellipse, the straight lines DQ and QB together would be equal to the axis AB; but the intervals AP and BP, by which we found the intersection point Q, are also of this nature. Therefore, point Q found in this way is on the ellipse; for otherwise, lines equal to AP and BP could be inclined from points D and E to different points, which is contrary to the 7th proposition of the first book of the <note>Refers to Euclid's *Elements of Geometry*, a foundational mathematical text.</note> Elements.

From this it is clear that the points V and X, where the minor axis terminates, are obtained if lines equal to the semi-axis AC are inclined from points D and E to the perpendicular VCX; for in this way the straight lines DX and EX together are also equal to the axis AB, and the square of CX or CV is always equal to the <term>fourth part of the figure<note>In early modern geometry, the "figure" of a conic section refers to a specific rectangle related to its parameters, often the latus rectum.</note></term>; and thus it is the mean proportional between CA and AK. For the rectangle BDA, together with the square of DC, is equal (by the 5th proposition of the second book of the Elements) to the square of CA—that is, the square of DX—and thus to the squares of CX and DC. Therefore, when the common segment CD is removed, the square of CX remains equal to the rectangle BDA, or the rectangle LAK, all of which are equal to the fourth part of the figure BAL.

### Problem IV.

#### *To construct, by means of a parabola, a burning mirror that will burn an object at a distance of twelve feet.*

**F**irst, let a compass be made of solid, dry wood in the manner of a pole, as appears in the figure, 15, 16, or however many feet long you wish, consisting of two spikes: one at point A, fixed immovably at the center of the compass, and the other attached to a mobile slider D. Let this compass, starting from center A, be diligently divided into any number of feet and inches, each of which is again divided into 12 or 10 parts, according to one's judgment. Let the vertex of the section be B, which we propose should be eight feet distant from the center A; the <term>semi-ordinate<note>A line segment drawn perpendicular to the axis of a parabola.</note></term> CD—drawn from C at a distance of four feet from both A and B—will mark the space DF to be cut out in the parabola FB. Therefore, on a certain very large separate plane, let a line AC of four feet be drawn according to the scale of feet marked on the compass. In like manner, let the line CD be drawn as a semi-ordinate to AC, standing normally <note>at a right angle</note> at C. Having done this, you will find the distance AD on the compass in this way: since it was shown in the third book of this work that the distance AD is equal to the distance AB together with CB—or what is the same thing, the distance of the center or focus from the vertex together with the distance of the semi-ordinate from the vertex—and since AB is established as eight feet by hypothesis, and BC is established as four feet by hypothesis, the distance AD will necessarily be 12 feet, which was what was sought. Therefore, move the slider with the spike to this twelfth foot marked on the compass; and let each foot be divided into 10 or 12 parts, or any other number of parts, such as DN.

-> [The image depicts a large beam compass being used by a hand to plot points on a grid. The tool is labeled with a scale from 1 to 13. The geometry shows how moving the slider along the angled arm creates the specific curve of the parabola.] <-

Next, let a plate of iron or brass be fixed at D upon a flat table, so that the table is subject to no wrinkles but has a smoothness like those prepared for <term>engravers<note>original: "chalcographis"; literally "copper-writers," referring to printmakers who needed perfectly flat plates.</note></term>. On this plate, let a line be drawn from D exactly parallel to the line AC and equal to DN, which you shall divide into as many parts as we divided DN; then from the points of division, parallels shall also be drawn to the semi-ordinate CD. When these things are finished, move the mobile spike of the slider over the points of division in DN, and see where it intersects the parallel line G as it is moved; for there will be a point of the parabola. Again, move the point of the spike over the following point in DN, and having fixed it there, see where line H is intersected while it is moved; for there will be H, the third point in the parabola. Thus you shall proceed with the rest until point F. For if you connect these points exactly into a curved line, you will have the segment FD of the parabola, which, when cut out from the plate, will provide a <term>template<note>original: "modulum"</note></term> to make a mold in some chalky material, in which a parabolic mirror may be cast that will burn a given object at a distance of 12 feet.

However, because a compass longer than 16, 18, or 20 feet can only be made with difficulty, we shall here teach a most exact method by which we can solve the given problem with the help of numbers...

## Problem V.
### To present a segment of a parabola whose center, or focus, is at a distance of twenty feet.

**W**e propose this method as being easier and more certain than the one preceding it. By this method, given any distance proportioned to the intended effect—for instance, 20 feet—we can set the proposed object on fire. Let **W** be the center of reflection, or focus; let **X** be the vertex of some parabola whose distance is 20 feet. From roughly the middle of this parabola, a piece of the parabola is to be cut away, 5 feet in length along the division of the axis, such as **CD** for example. Since the diameter of the mirror is to be five feet, you will draw the <term>semi-ordinate<note>In geometry, a semi-ordinate is a line segment perpendicular to the axis of a conic section, like a parabola, extending from the axis to the curve itself.</note></term> from point **Z** on the axis. Now, by our hypothesis, **ZX** is 5 feet, which is one-fourth of the 20-foot line **XW**. Consequently, according to what we demonstrated in Book 3 on <note>original: "de conicis sectionibus"; refers to the study of shapes like circles, ellipses, and parabolas.</note> Conic Sections, the semi-ordinate **WY** is 40 feet. The ratio will be as **XW** is to the square of **WY**, so **XZ** is to the square of **ZD**. Therefore, just as **WY** is double **XW**, so **ZD** will be double **XZ**; consequently, **XW** is equal to the axis of the parabola. If you add the five feet of **ZX** to this, **WD** will be 25 feet. 

If, therefore, you cut a certain <term>template<note>original: "modulum"; a physical guide or pattern used by craftsmen to ensure a shape is cut or cast accurately.</note></term> from a sheet of material according to the line **DC**, you will produce a template for a burning mirror that burns at 25 feet. The larger the segment of the mirror, the further away it will burn: for example, if **ED** were five feet, the line of reflection **CW** would be 30 feet, while the width of the mirror would be **CD**. 

But now to the calculation. Let us suppose a foot is divided into 100 equal parts, or 1000; this will yield 100 or 1000 semi-ordinates for one foot. **ZX** will be 500 parts of one foot, **ZD** 2000, and **WY** 4000. The square of **ZD** will then be 4,000,000; the square of **WY** 16,000,000. Thus, as line **XW** is to the square of **WY**, so **XZ** is to the square of **DZ** (4,000,000), the square root of which is 2000. Again, just as **XZ** (500 parts) is to the square of **ZD** (4,000,000 parts), so 501 parts—which are equivalent to five feet and 1/100th part (namely, the distance to the first semi-ordinate)—is to the square of the semi-ordinate drawn from it. This will yield 4,008,000, the root of which is 2001 and 222/1000. Since 222/1000 parts is almost less than one whole unit, you can take this semi-ordinate as 2002 without hesitation or any sensible error; this semi-ordinate will be two parts longer than the first semi-ordinate, which was 2000. Again, to find the third semi-ordinate, let it be as **XZ** (500) is to the square of **ZD** (4,000,000), so 502 is to the square of the semi-ordinate sought. This yields 4,016,000, the root of which is approximately 2004; and thus the first semi-ordinate is 4 parts longer than the 2000-part line. You will proceed in this manner to find the remaining semi-ordinates. 

When you have investigated these quantities of the semi-ordinates by the said method, nothing remains but to arrange them in a table and then mark them on a sheet, as the figure shows you. For a curved line drawn with the greatest care through the terminating points on the sheet will give **XW** as 20 feet. Or, if this were too much, a sheet of width **ZX** (five feet) and length 30 feet and more, taking the parabolic segment cut out with the greatest diligence, will give the template with which we may designate the <term>matrix, or mold<note>original: "matricem, seu formam"; the hollow form into which molten metal—likely bronze or speculum metal—is poured to cast the mirror.</note></term>, in which the cast mirror may burn at 20 and 30 feet.

To obtain perfect semi-ordinates, work as follows. Let **AB** be 1/100th part of a Roman foot, which is again divided into 10, as the figure shows. Then let line **EF** be drawn, which you will similarly divide into 10 parts. Let its width be **GH** or **EI**. From **I** to **IG**, or from **Q** downwards to **IG**, it will be 1/10th of **EI** or **GH**. From 2 to **IG**, it will be 1/100th, and so on for the rest. To give the line **BD** as 19 and 9/10, you will take 19 parts from **EF** and transfer them from **B** to **R**. Again, from **IH**, you will take 9 units up to **Q**, and these are the 9/10ths. From this, it is clear that **AD** is almost equal to a straight line, such that the difference can scarcely be detected with a compass. By this skill, one will be able to seek further semi-ordinates. Thus, if **AB** is continued for a full foot, the semi-ordinate drawn from such a point (namely, 600) will be 2190 and 9/1000. If the semi-ordinate **CA** (2000) is subtracted from that, there remains a difference of nearly 90 and 9/10 for the 100th semi-ordinate. From this, it is clear that a parabola is curved along an axis of one foot by exactly 90 and 9/10 parts, of which 100 parts make one foot.

### Problem VI.

*Given the distance of the <term>burning point<note>original: "puncti ustorii". In modern geometry, this is called the focus.</note></term>, to describe a parabolic section on material however small, which nevertheless burns at the greatest distance.*

Let the distance of the burning point be given as a certain number of feet. For the <term>latus rectum<note>The "straight side" or parameter that defines the shape of the parabola.</note></term>, take a straight line four times the given distance, namely AE. Let the base of the given parabola be CD, bisected at E; then, let a circle be described through the three points C, B, and D, with EA extended to B. I say that BE is the distance of the focus from the vertex of the parabola: for just as the latus rectum AE relates to the <term>semi-ordinate<note>Half of a line segment crossing the parabola's interior, perpendicular to its axis.</note></term> EC, so EC relates to EB—all of which has been demonstrated at length by us in Book 5, Part 3, on conic sections. Moreover, so that the parabola can be drawn to the furthest part CD, you will describe the semi-ordinates in the manner done in the cited book, as will be indicated in the following pages. However, if the burning base were too small, but the distance was very great, you can manage the task through numbers. Suppose, for example, a parabola is to be constructed that burns at 60 <term>palms<note>A unit of measurement based on the width of the hand.</note></term>, but its base is four palms: first, let the distance be quadrupled so that you have the latus rectum, which will be 240; and the half of the base will be 2. The third proportional number will be found if you calculate as 240 is to 2, so 2 is to four <note>Kircher is describing a proportional calculation to find the focus-to-vertex distance</note>, the desired distance of the focus from the vertex. Again, let 2 and 2 be multiplied by themselves, and the quotient produced will give the result sought.

### Problem VII.

*Given the focus, to find the vertex of the parabola.*

Let the part of the axis of the parabola be AB, and the line applied to it in order (the ordinate) be BC: the vertex E is sought, with the focus of the parabola being A.

Let a segment AD equal to AC be cut off, and let BD be divided in half at E; for point E will be the vertex of the parabola.

In numbers, if AB and BC are 100, and their squares are 10,000, the square of AC will be 20,000; and AC, or AD, will be 141 15/33. The line BD will be 41 15/33, and BE will be 20 23/31. Finally, AE will be 120 23/31.

If BE and BC are given, the focus A will be found if ED is taken equal to BE, and the chord DC is cut in half at F; for the perpendicular FA gives the focus A. In this way, a circle described from A through D cuts the ordinate BC.

But if BA is understood to be cut into 25 parts, each will contain 4 out of the 100 that make up the whole of BA. To find the parabolic points on each of these perpendiculars (two of which are B and C), it shall be performed, for example, on the perpendicular GD in this way: First, the line AG contains 14 parts out of 25, and thus 56 hundredths of the whole BA. This means DI is almost 6 1/2, and so for the rest. However, if the square of BA is divided by the square of AC, and the quotient is added to AC itself, the diameter of the circle (or the semicircle) that passes through BC and has its center on the axis itself will be produced. Thus, the said semi-diameter will be 505: for the square 10,000 divided by 20 makes 1,000; and 1,000 with 10 makes 1,010, and half of this is 505. ## Comparison of concave, spherical, parabolic, and elliptical mirrors, and their use in making mirrors.

### Problem VIII.

### To determine the segment of a spherical mirror.

Let B be the vertex of a spherical mirror, A the focus at an interval AB of $\frac{1}{2}$ palm, and the angle which the reflected ray makes with the axis—that is, angle BAC—be 30 degrees. Let BG be perpendicular to AB, and angle GBC be 7 degrees 30 minutes. Let BC meet AC at C, and let AE be taken as equal to AC. I say that EC will be equal to EB. Since AC and AE are equal, the angles at the base of the isosceles triangle ACE will be equal, and each will be 15 degrees, because together they are equal to the angle BAC of 30 degrees. Next, if the angle GBC of 7 degrees 30 minutes is subtracted from a right angle <note>90 degrees.</note>, there remains the angle ABC of 82 degrees 30 minutes. The two angles ABC and BAC together will be 112 degrees 30 minutes, and the remaining angle ACB will be 67 degrees 30 minutes. Therefore, adding angle ACE of 15 degrees, the total angle ECB will be 82 degrees 30 minutes, equal to angle EBC; and consequently EB and EC are equal.

And the arc BC, described from center E with the interval EB, will be the curvature and concavity of a spherical mirror, in which the ray EC at point C, parallel to the axis AB, will necessarily be reflected to A through the reflected ray CA. For the angle of reflection FCA will be equal to angle CAB (30 degrees); and because ACE is 15, the remaining ECF will also be 15. This means the two angles of incidence and reflection made with the radius (or <term>normal<note>original: "catheto". A line perpendicular to the surface at the point of impact.</note></term>) of the curvature BC will be equal.

But if from C toward AB, a perpendicular is dropped...

### For the Parabolic Mirror.
#### To determine a segment of a parabola.

The vertex <term>vertex|the highest or peak point of a curve</term> of the parabolic mirror should be the same point B, and the focus should be point A, with the same interval AB, as well as the angle BAC. In this way, the comparison between both types of mirrors will be made more evident. It has been demonstrated by Marino Ghetaldus <note>Marino Ghetaldi (1568–1626) was a Ragusan mathematician and physicist who studied under Clavius and was a friend of Galileo; he wrote extensively on the geometry of parabolas.</note> in his propositions concerning the Parabola, that the *latus rectum* <term>latus rectum|literally "straight side"; the chord through the focus of a conic section perpendicular to the major axis</term> of a parabola is four times the interval AB—which is understood here to be the length BG, even if the whole length is not illustrated. However, it is established from the work of Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Perga (c. 240 – c. 190 BC) was a Greek geometer known as "The Great Geometer" whose work *Conics* defined the study of parabolas, ellipses, and hyperbolas.</note> that the square of the ordinate <note>original: *ordinatim applicata*; in classical geometry, this refers to a line drawn from a point on the curve perpendicular to the axis.</note>, for example the straight line CD, is equal to the rectangle formed by the *latus rectum* and the sagitta <term>sagitta|literally "arrow"; the distance from the center of an arc to the center of its base line, representing the depth of the curve.</term> BD. Finally, because in the right-angled triangle ADC, the angle A is 30 degrees, it is necessary that the square of line AD be three times the square of line CD—that is, three times the rectangle DBG.

If, therefore, the line AB is divided at point D in such a way that the square of AD is three times the rectangle formed by the remaining segment DB and four times AB, the depth of the mirror BD will have been found; and the square root of the rectangle DBG will give the semi-diameter of the same mirror, namely the straight line CD. We have shown elsewhere how the aforementioned division is performed, not only in a triple proportion, but in any others as well. For when two lines are given—as here we have AB, which is to be divided, and its quadruple, which is not divided—one must distribute the line to be divided into two segments so that the square of one has the given proportion to the rectangle formed by the other and the undivided line. Thus, in this particular case, the line AD is obtained if the square of AB is multiplied by 48, and six times AB is subtracted from the resulting square root.

In place of the upper segment BCD, let another more detailed one be taken here in the lower figure, and in it let the chord *bc* be drawn, along with another line *h i k* parallel to *bd*, and *im* parallel to *Cb*.

# The Great Art [of Light and Shadow], Book 10. Magic, Part 3.

From point V, an equal number of perpendicular lines have been raised, the first of which, for example, contains 2,500 parts out of the 10,000 parts into which the straight line TV is understood to be divided. The perpendicular, however, contains those same 10,000 parts, by the benefit of which points 1, 2, 3, 4, etc., are found on the arc CT. These points, when continued with due diligence and industry, exhibit the half of the <term>template<note>original: "norma"; a physical guide or pattern used by craftsmen to ensure correct curvature</note></term> according to which the <term>burning mirror<note>original: "speculum ustorium"; a concave mirror designed to focus sunlight to a point to generate intense heat or fire</note></term> is to be excavated.

If the final digits are omitted—and whenever they are greater than five, one unit should be added to the next figure—the remaining numbers will count the thousandth parts of the line VT. These are most conveniently taken from a measurement instrument divided into a hundred parts, in this manner described through the points. The template differs little from the curvature of a circle whose semidiameter is 2 and 1/12 feet, or 2 and 1/13 feet. Indeed, in this circle, the perpendiculars are almost the same as those we previously computed for the ellipse, as is clearly gathered from the second set of numbers assigned to those same perpendiculars, which differ from the former at most by 1/10,000 of a foot, or 1/1,000, or 1/2,130 of the same. But he would do more correctly who diligently describes the same curvature through elliptical points, or certainly through the arcs of several circles: by first finding a center on the extended line CV for a circle that passes through point C and point 5; then another center on the same CV for another circle that passes through points 5 and 10; again another for points 10 and 15; and finally another for points 15 and T. By this method, the difference of all four arcs from the elliptical arc will be much smaller than if a circle were described through points C and T with only a single interval and from only one center. The construction of the mold must be sought from those skilled in the art of casting; it is necessary that its material be of such a kind that it does not easily lose the curvature entrusted to it while it is dried or fired. <note>Giovanni Antonio Magini (1555–1617) was an influential Italian astronomer, cartographer, and mathematician.</note> Joannes Antonius Maginus is said to have used a certain kind of stone. However, we have prescribed the material of the mirror above.

But since the description of the figures of conic sections by points is fallacious unless a very great multitude of them are assumed, we shall subjoin here another new instrument by which any given conic section can be described with a single and continuous stroke.

# A new instrument for describing conic sections.

**I**t is composed of 9 rulers: four form the rectangle ABCH, two form a <term>gnomon<note>original: "gnomonem"; an L-shaped tool or carpenter's square</note></term> EFG, two others form a semi-gnomon HIK, and one is the ruler LM, which is called the <term>Rector<note>original: "Rector"; literally "the guider" or "ruler," referring to the guiding bar of the mechanism</note></term>.

The ruler AB has a slider O, and to it are attached two others for the rulers KI and EF.

Three other sliders at I, F, and Q have small axles around which the rulers can be moved. Finally, at N, there is another doubled slider. The rest is evident in the figure.

## The Parabola.

**L**et the axis of the parabola be AB, the slider A, the <term>upright side<note>original: "latus rectum"; a technical term in geometry referring to the chord through the focus of a conic section parallel to the directrix, which defines the "spread" of the curve</note></term> AC, and the guider M, K. Let it be applied to C itself, and let it be parallel to the axis AB, to which the side of the rectangle MO also adheres; and while these remain, the instrument is moved, and the stylus G describes the parabola.

For since MGA is always a right angle, and OLM a semi-right angle, the square of the <term>ordinate<note>original: "ordinatæ"; the vertical coordinate (y-axis) in a geometric construction</note></term> OG is always equal to the rectangle AOM—that is, AOL or OAC—as the parabola requires.

# CHAPTER I.

## Distinction III.

### On burning mirrors, or mirrors of fire, their effects and use.

### Section I.

## Whether the mirrors of Archimedes and Proclus set ships on fire at such a distance as authors describe?

<margin>The wonderful effects of burning mirrors.</margin>
**If what is passed down by authors concerning the mirrors of Archimedes is true, then surely <term>burning catoptrics<note>original: "καυσικὴ κατοπτρική" (kaustikē katoptrikē); the science of using mirrors to focus light and generate intense heat.</note></term>, as it deservedly surpasses all limits of human ingenuity, so it ought to be considered the greatest and most prodigious of the secrets of natural magic. For I know not what wonder and prodigy this catoptric fire claims for itself: who does not know that it possesses a power of burning much more subtle, sharp, pure, and effective than our ordinary kitchen fire? It also possesses other powers in no way shared by our common fire; for it liquefies lead and tin; gold and other metals are also turned to fire by it; and even the most delicate woods**

> When Marcellus had moved those [ships] a bowshot away,
> the old man constructed a certain hexagonal mirror;
> and from a distance proportionate to the mirror,
> having placed such small mirrors fourfold at the corners,
> to be moved by strips and certain hinges,
> he placed that [machine] in the middle of the rays of the sun,
> at midday, in summer, and in the depth of winter:
> the rays thereafter being reflected into this,
> a fearful fiery ignition appeared to the ships,
> and it reduced them to ashes from the distance of a bowshot.
> <note>This quote is a translation of the Greek verses from Tzetzes describing Archimedes' defense of Syracuse against the Roman general Marcellus.</note>

<margin>Proclus's machine.</margin>
The other was Proclus, of whom the Greek Zonaras writes in the third volume of his histories, that when Anastasius was raising a rebellion against Vitalian the Thracian (who was winning over the Mysians and Scythians) and was taking plunder in the Byzantine territory and besieging the city with a fleet, he resisted through the Prefect Marcian. A naval battle having been joined, the enemy fleet was defeated by a certain machine made by Proclus, a most excellent man (for he flourished then in Philosophy and Mechanics, and not only knew all the works of the most celebrated craftsman Archimedes, but had also invented some new things himself).

<margin>Proclus's projection of fire through mirrors.</margin>

It is said that Archimedes set fire to the enemy's triremes <note>Ancient warships with three banks of oars.</note> using burning mirrors; for wool, tow, wicks, silk, and anything similarly dry and porous are easily ignited by a burning mirror. Here I wonder what possessed Thomas Linacre <note>A famous 16th-century English humanist and physician.</note> when, commenting on Galen, he interpreted the word <term>pyreia</term> <note>original: πυρεία; typically meaning fire-making tools or mirrors</note> in this passage as "flint stones." Or by what reasoning he thought Archimedes could have stirred up such great fires on the ships of the Roman enemies that he burned them using stones that perhaps caught sparks. This is certainly an error; for by <margin>What is <italic>pyreia</italic>?</margin> <margin>On Burning Mirrors</margin> **pyreia** nothing else is understood here but caustic <note>burning</note> mirrors. Rivaldus, in his *Life of Archimedes*, records that Archimedes wrote a book about them titled <term>On Burning Mirrors</term> <note>original: περὶ πυρείων</note>, which is circulated under the name of a certain translator named Gogava. But having prefaced these things, we must first see at what distance Archimedes and Proclus <note>A 5th-century mathematician said to have used similar mirrors to defend Constantinople.</note> ignited the ships of the enemies.

### §. II.
### The distance, or the sphere of caustic power, in the mirrors of Archimedes.

Diodorus says the distance of the ships of Marcellus <note>The Roman general besieging Syracuse.</note> burned by Archimedes was three stadia <note>A stadium was roughly 600 feet; three stadia is about 550 meters.</note>; others, such as Cluverius in his *Sicily*, say three miles. Yet, above all others, Tzetzes <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar.</note> seems to have touched upon it more exactly, determining the distance to be a "bowshot." However, a bowshot varies greatly according to the variety of bows; stronger bows usually project an arrow to 200 paces, others to a greater or lesser space. In such uncertainty, while I was passing through Syracuse in the year 1636, I diligently examined the place from which Archimedes is said to have burned the ships with the help of mirrors. I found the space to be much smaller than authors report—namely, immediately at the walls of that part of the city they called Acradina in ancient times. From this, I concluded that such a combustion was possible, and that the "caustic line" <note>the focal length or range of the burning effect</note> was about 30 paces; for those who wish the ships to have stood further off can be entirely convinced of the <term>lack of power</term> <note>original: ἀδυναμία</note> of the caustic virtue, as will be shown in what follows.

### §. III.
### Whether a burning mirror can burn at an infinite distance?

Many have reached such a point of either arrogance or ignorance that they think a mirror can be given which burns at an almost infinite distance. Among others, Porta <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), an Italian scholar of "natural magic."</note> promises such a machine; so that you may better perceive it, I have decided to cite his words. "We shall deliver," he says, "a method far more excellent than that of Archimedes, handed down by no one (as far as I know), surpassing the invention of all ancients and moderns, nor do I think human genius could have devised anything greater. This mirror does not burn at 10, 20, 100, or 1,000 paces, or at a determined distance; but unto infinity. Nor does it ignite in a cone, where the rays meet, but from the center of the mirror a burning line proceeds of any length, which burns everything in its way." <margin>The vain promises of Porta.</margin> "Furthermore, it ignites behind, in front, and on every side. But I truly consider it an unworthy deed to broadcast this to the ignorant masses. Let it, therefore, come to light so that the immense goodness of the most high God may be praised. Through a larger section, by which the proportioned ray progresses, the greater is made from the lesser: avoiding these things, let it be made of a cylindrical section; for it is middle-sized and small, and let the axis of the larger division be established, which passes through the middle parallels. This, placed opposite the Sun, refracts the rays far away, and perpendicularly to the center of the cylindrical section; nor can a reason be found in this art for the meeting rays to be separated again. It therefore receives directly those rays which it transmits obliquely into rays far from its surface: for rays passing through the narrow opening of a window are immediately dilated, nor is their proportion preserved through their elongation. It will therefore reverberate and burn where the cone appears brighter; which will be near the center, nor will it be much elongated from the point of the meeting rays, but the ray exiting from that point from the mirror's surface is called parabolic, which remains firm in that place we have mentioned. Let its power be tested with iron or silk strings exiting from the sun's center; nor does it matter if it is a parabola, or spherical, or another section of the same order: then let it be fitted optimally above the center of said section. He who has ears to hear, let him hear; we have not spoken like a barbarian, nor could we have spoken more briefly or clearly." And this is the invention which Porta boasts of so much. But that he himself never made the machine, much less tested it, and that it is a mockery of his own imagination, can be proved from this: that in constructing it, he seems to have imitated those who, while trying to impose upon the world with a false invention to gain some fame, first make the work seem <margin>Deceptions and impostures.</margin> impressive with obscure veils of words and terms sought from the workshops of the Hebrews, Arabs, and Syrians. Then they command that ingredients first be brought from India and other remote regions of the world, so that having covered their trick with this art, they may snatch away all hope of the craftsman trying it—with no other purpose than that vain reputation for knowledge of the most secret things which they desire to have among the curious and those unskilled in affairs...

# Catoptric Magic.

...leaving [the truth] to their minds. Thus Porta, in this passage, describes that false mechanism of catoptric <note>The study of reflection and mirrors.</note> combustion with such obscurity that it could more truly be called a riddle than a **proof** <note>original: ἔλεγχον</note>. Indeed, one can gather even from his own words that he clearly contradicts himself in many places. For at one moment he claims to burn with lines that do not meet at the vertex of a cone, but through the parallelism of rays; at another, he asserts the opposite. Now he assumes a cylindrical section, then a parabolic one, and then a spherical one; at one point he prescribes straight rays, and a little later, oblique ones. Porta might indeed persuade those unskilled in such matters with fabrications of this kind; but as for persuading those who intimately know the nature and behavior of both light and the mirrors from whose surface it is reflected—"here is Rhodes, here is the leap" <note>A Latin proverb (Hic Rhodus, hic salta) challenging someone to prove their claims with immediate action rather than words.</note>. For he could more easily teach that white is black than persuade clever minds of the truth of this mechanism of his. Hence, I assert that it is not only improbable, but utterly **impossible** <note>original: ἀδύνατον</note>, and indeed openly repugnant to the principles of nature; and I demonstrate the matter by this reasoning.

First, if this mirror acts by combustion at the greatest possible distance, it acts either through a burning cylinder or through a burning cone. It cannot be the former, since we have demonstrated in the preceding pages that parallel rays in a burning cylinder, being dispersed, possess no power to burn, and that burning cannot happen by any reasoning unless the rays are united in a single point. Nor can it be the latter, since no infinite burning cone can exist that is not necessarily determined by its own vertex and, consequently, by a specific distance. 

Furthermore, since light acts "uniformly-difformly" <note>A scholastic term meaning a rate of change that is itself changing at a constant rate; here referring to the dissipation of intensity over distance.</note> both in illuminating and in burning—a privilege granted by nature to all qualities, whether primary, secondary, or specific—it is certain that the Sun's rays lose much of their vigor upon their first strike against the mirror. For once the reflection is made, they are weakened little by little, as if by the impact of the blow, and the further they travel, the more they lose of their efficacy in caustic <note>burning</note> power, just as they do in light. That is, the sharper the burning cone is, the more ineffective the future burning will always be, so much so that at a very great distance the rays no longer maintain a conical shape, but rather something of a cylindrical nature because of the very oblique intersection of the rays. If the distance is excessive, all those rays no longer act as a multitude, but as a single line, which physicists know is endowed with no power. In the same way, light entering through a hole in a house always appears darker the further it recedes from the hole, until it finally vanishes into nothing. Therefore, just as sight relates to its object, so does light struck by a mirror relate to the vertex of the burning cone; but vision cannot reach any object at too great a distance because of the weakness of the vanishing "species" <note>In older physics, "species" were the sensible forms or images emitted by objects that allowed them to be perceived.</note>; likewise, a burning mirror can produce no effect of combustion at too great a distance, as the light and heat vanish.

<margin>What could a mirror the size of St. Peter’s Dome achieve?</margin>
For let us suppose a segment of a parabolic mirror were assigned, as large as the Dome of Saint Peter. I say it would produce no effect at a distance of 1,200 paces, which is the distance from the Roman College to the Temple of Saint Peter <note>St. Peter's Basilica.</note>. For if the width of the said Dome is measured with a Ptolemaic dioptra <note>An ancient astronomical and surveying instrument.</note> from the Roman College, we will find that the base of the burning cone has a width of only an inch and a half of a Roman foot. Who would now believe that the burning cone of the said mirror could achieve anything at the given distance, when all the rays—besides the fact that they converge nearly to parallelism—are so gradually weakened that they utterly vanish at the said location? 

Furthermore, let a three-foot segment be made from that same giant segment. The ratio will be as the diameter of the larger (100 feet) is to the distance of 1,200 paces; so is the diameter of the three-foot specular segment to another; the result is 36 paces. From this proportion, it is clearly evident that just as experience teaches that a three-foot parabolic mirror possesses no power to burn at 36 paces (even three-palm mirrors only burn at an interval of one Roman foot), so much less should that giant mirror be judged to have any power to burn at an interval of 1,200 paces. If, therefore, a mirror of such unusual magnitude can have no effect at a space of 1,200 paces, how much less effect will it have at a distance of many miles?

<margin>The burning line.</margin>
But some will say at this point that it is true Archimedes did not accomplish the burning of the ships with a parabolic mirror reaching the ships with its burning cone, but with a burning cylinder; or, what is the same thing, not by conical radiation, but by cylindrical radiation, which can possess the power to burn unto infinity. They claim there is a certain power in parabolic mirrors by which they burn not only conically through rays meeting in a focus, but also through reflected parallel rays; and that this cylindrical radiation has the power of burning at any distance whatsoever; and that by this kind of caustic **ray-projection** <note>original: actinobolismo</note>, Archimedes could have burned ships at any distance.

<margin>The "burning line" invented by certain authors is false and achieves nothing.</margin>

If, therefore, you receive the rays in an opposite position with another parabolic tube B very close to point D, or the focus, those rays falling from the focus D onto the interior surface of tube B will be reflected into a radiation...

mirror B, applied at that same spot, will reflect the incoming conical <term>radiation</term> <note>original: *actinobolismum*; from the Greek *aktis* (ray) and *ballo* (to throw). It refers to the emission or projection of light rays</note> DB into a cylindrical <term>radiation</term> BE, which is entirely fiery. Because these fiery rays can be propagated across a very large space, there should be no doubt that they could have the power of ignition at a very great distance—indeed, at an almost infinite distance. And this is the objection which the simpler mathematicians raise against us. I concede that a parabolic mirror can both receive and reflect rays not only conically but also cylindrically; I know that <term>ignition</term> can occur along a line, and this is known even to children. However, I utterly deny that this cylindrical ignition maintains its force over a greater space than conical ignition.

<margin>Illustration 30.</margin>
For let there be (as the first figure of Illustration 30 shows) the Sun's rays GHI falling upon a parabolic or elliptical mirror NRM: it is certain that they will meet at a point. Here it must be noted that we must account not only for the rays HVR emanating from the center of the Sun, but also for the others, which have less power than those from the center. Thus, the intensity of the heat must be estimated from the size of the glass or mirror that collects them, compared with the size of the space in which they are gathered. For example, as <term>Descartes</term> <note>René Descartes (1596–1650), the famous philosopher and mathematician who wrote extensively on optics in his *Dioptrics*</note> also rightly notes: if the diameter of the glass NRM is four times greater than the distance between points ON, the rays collected by its aid will have sixteen times as much power as those passing through a flat glass (which would not bend them at all). And since the interval between VQ is greater or

lesser in proportion to the interval between those rays and the glass NRM (or any other similar body forcing the rays together), it is certain that neither the size of the diameter of this body nor its particular shape can increase that distance—except perhaps by a quarter at most. From this, the vanity of the idea of a "line that burns to infinity" can be most clearly concluded.

Furthermore, if we take two <term>burning mirrors</term> <note>original: *specula caustica*; mirrors designed to concentrate sunlight to create fire</note>, one larger than the other, regardless of what kind they are (provided they have similar shapes), the larger one will indeed collect the Sun's rays in a larger space and project them further than the smaller one. Nevertheless, in any single part of this space, these rays have no more power than in the other mirror. The largest mirrors, which have shapes similar to the small ones, gather just as many rays for burning in an equal space. Thus, very small pieces of glass and mirrors can be made that possess a <term>burning power</term> just as vehement as the largest ones. From this, I conclude that a burning mirror whose diameter is only 1/100th of the distance between the focus and the mirror can in no way make the captured rays burn or heat more effectively than those proceeding directly from the Sun. I wish for mathematicians to observe this matter seriously; for if they look into this more deeply, they will voluntarily agree with me and be forced to confess that conical or cylindrical ignition is entirely ineffective and weak over any great distance. From this, they will be forced to conclude again that a mirror of 100 geometric feet in diameter [has] no...
