->### Oooo 3<-

...to possess the power of burning for three miles. And this is exactly what we concluded a little while ago regarding the Dome of St. Peter’s, if it were a mirror; since rays that degenerate into a completely parallel state are deprived of all their power. If this is true—as no one who thinks correctly about geometry and <term>catoptrics</term> <note>original: *catoptrica*; the study of light reflection and mirrors</note> ought to doubt—I do not see why some try to sell us on a "cylindrical burning" of such great power. Let certain impostors, ignorant of reality, cease their attempts to enchant us with their fables while they boast that they can construct a mirror that burns at an infinite distance. 

But they will say that a segment of 100 or 200 paces, or a mirror segment with a diameter of 12 miles, is of such efficacy that it projects rays to a most remote and even infinite distance. This is absolute nonsense; for if a fragment of 200 feet were cut from a specular sphere whose diameter was 12 miles, who does not see that this segment, because of its overly obtuse arc, would nearly coincide with the flat surface of a mirror? Consequently, it would be entirely unfit for collecting rays and unsuitable for establishing a path <term>in a straight line</term> <note>original: *$\kappa\alpha\tau'\ \epsilon\hat{\upsilon}\theta\epsilon\tilde{\iota}\alpha\nu$* (kat' eutheian)</note>. 

What I say about parabolic concave mirrors must also be said about parabolic tubes, crowns, rings, and siphons. For the more obtuse the segments are, the more the diverging rays will approach parallelism due to the oblique intersections of the <term>burning rays</term> <note>original: *radiorum causticorum*; rays concentrated at a focal point to generate heat</note>, and consequently, they will gradually lose all power as their union dissolves. Therefore, let many people at this time stop boasting of parabolic, elliptical, and hyperbolic tubes that drive a burning parallelism across enormous distances. Anyone endowed with any sense and experience will easily see that these things cannot possibly hold true.

### Corollary I.

#### *Cardano’s Mirror, said to burn at a thousand paces.*

**FROM** these points it is clear that Cardano <note>Gerolamo Cardano (1501–1576), a famous Italian polymath</note> errs most shamefully when he boasts that he will construct a mirror with which he may ignite a fire at a thousand paces. I cite his own words so that the vanity and thoughtlessness of the man may be more widely known. *If we wish to ignite a fire at a thousand paces,* he says, *we shall describe a circle whose diameter is two thousand paces; of this we shall take a portion large enough that the curvature is visible—specifically a sixtieth part—to which we shall add the diameter for height at one end, and with the diameter fixed, we shall rotate the part of the circle, which will describe for us a portion of a sphere; when we have polished this, it will ignite a very powerful fire at 1,000 paces when exposed to the Sun at a distance.* 

Good heavens! What absurdities this otherwise most learned man babbles in these few words. First, he promises a mirror burning at a thousand paces, which we have demonstrated to be nearly impossible even at fifty paces. Second, he instructs a segment of 60 degrees to be polished; but who does not know that since a mirror of this kind would have a diameter of 2,000 paces, no power and no riches could suffice to cast a mirror of such unusual mass? Furthermore, with what compass, on what plain, or with what motors would he describe that immense circle from which the segment is to be cut? I do not see how anything more thoughtless could be said. If he had handed the matter over to be investigated by numbers, he might be excused in some way; but when he presumes to settle the matter with a machine, what else does he achieve but to expose himself to be laughed at and refuted even by children? You see therefore, curious Reader, how often unworthy things are proposed even by authors of no small rank; since their truth is not examined, it is no wonder that many even philosophical men collide in this precipice of errors, and shameful errors gradually creeping into the schools give birth to innumerable monsters in Philosophy.

### Corollary II.

#### *On the Mirror of Archimedes.*

**FROM** this it is also clear that Archimedes could by no means have burned the ships of Marcellus <note>Marcus Claudius Marcellus, the Roman general who besieged Syracuse in 214–212 BCE</note> with a parabolic mirror at a distance of three miles, nor even three <term>stadia</term> <note>A Greek unit of distance, roughly 185 meters</note>, but only in the closest proximity. This is true regardless of what historians say, whose habit it is to describe the portentous deeds of Heroes <term>rather hyperbolically</term> <note>original: *$\hat{\upsilon}\pi\epsilon\rho\beta\text{o}\lambda\iota\kappa\omega\tau\epsilon\rho\tilde{\omega}\varsigma$* (hyperbolikōterōs)</note>, both to win admiration in the minds of their listeners and to commend the specimen of Archimedean art to posterity as if it were inimitable. 

It also happens that since at that same time Archimedes alone was on everyone's lips and in everyone's eyes because of the miracles of his inventions, nothing was easier than to preach the inventions of Archimedean art as certain paradoxes to the world—especially a world still ignorant of said arts. Thus it happened that as the fame of his name resounded and grew throughout every land, the report grew even beyond the truth of the deeds performed by Archimedes. 

Indeed, Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian</note> seems to imply that this burning of the ships occurred only at a nearby station, namely at the wall of Acradina <note>A fortified quarter of the ancient city of Syracuse</note>, when he describes the machines prepared by Archimedes against Marcellus in these words: *When an iron hand, attached to a firm chain, was hung from a crane projecting over the wall and had been cast upon a prow, and with a heavy counterweight...*

### Book X of the Great Art. Part III: Magic.

<margin>Archimedes' Machine.</margin>
...lifting the lead weight, it would tear the ship from the ground; suspended from the prow to the stern, he would set it upright, then suddenly release it like a falling stone from a wall. This would strike the ship against the waves with such great terror for the sailors that, even if it fell straight back, it would take on a considerable amount of water. Plutarch agrees with this, stating that when the ships were suddenly lifted from the walls by the ends of the yardarms, some were weighed down from above by a heavy counterweight and submerged; others were caught by an iron hand or the beaks of cranes <gloss>but some [were caught] by iron hands or the beaks of cranes</gloss>. When they had been suspended, he says, and set upright from prow to stern, they were either submerged or pulled in and rotated in opposite directions, then dashed against the sharp rocks that protruded beneath the walls, resulting in the total destruction of the crews. Indeed, it was sometimes a horrific sight to see a ship <term>spinning</term> <note>original Greek: eilingiodi, referring to a dizzying or whirling motion</note> revolved here and there and suspended, until the sailors were thrown out or fixed against the wall, and the empty hull was dashed to pieces or fell back when released.

Polybius, who was nearly a <term>contemporary</term> <note>original Greek: synchronos</note> of Archimedes, confirms the same things, so that anyone who notes his words could easily reconstruct Archimedes' machine. For it had no other shape than that used by our architects today, consisting of two parts: the <term>yardarm</term> <note>original Greek: keraian</note> and the <term>mast-head</term> <note>original Greek: karchesion</note>. For the "mast-head" refers to that very high timber, which stood perpendicularly at the height of a "tollenon" <note>a "tollenon" was a type of ancient crane or sweep used to lift buckets of water or heavy loads</note>, and at its peak a transverse yardarm was moved, representing the beak of a crane raised on one side or the other, and moved crosswise in a circle both below and above. In the forward part, it carried long chains ending in the form of an iron hand, by which, through certain small chains and the service of the "Schasterian" art <note>the art of releasing or lowering mechanisms</note> and extensions, ships and any other engines were snatched away and carried on high, no matter how great their mass, by the help of a very heavy counterweight made of lead and iron, or some other massive weight. These were balanced internally like a giant <term>scale-weight</term> <note>original: sacomate</note>, and could be extended wherever the Syracusans wished. Polybius uses the word <term>machine</term> <note>original Greek: mechane</note> here, although that refers to the topmost part of the mast, because he only notes the part protruding above the walls, even though the "pterna" and "trachylus" <note>the "heel" and "neck," or the base and the swivel-joint of the mast</note>—both parts of the mast—were hidden near the fortifications. For the whole machine and the massive yardarm could not have been supported without a very strong mast, or rather, the sturdiest beams and braces. Furthermore, the word <term>mast-head</term> <note>karchesion</note> used by Polybius designates the ropes, pulleys, and finally the instruments by which both the yardarm and the iron hand were either lowered, loosened, tightened, or released according to the work and intention of the craftsman. It also signifies the art by which the entire operation of such stupendous sinking of ships and their crushing against nearby rocks was directed. But concerning these, see *Illustration 30.*

<margin>At what distance Archimedes' mirrors burned.</margin>
From all of this, it is very clearly evident that the station of the ships of Marcellus <note>Marcus Claudius Marcellus, the Roman general who besieged Syracuse in 213–212 BCE</note> when he was attacking Syracuse was almost at the very walls of *Acradina*. For *Acradina*, as I have explored myself with the greatest diligence, and as Mirabella clearly teaches in his *Ichnography* <note>a ground plan or map</note>, is washed by the sea on all sides at that place where fame says Archimedes so greatly afflicted the ships of Marcellus with his war engines. That Marcellus's ships stood in this place is sufficiently shown by Archimedes' machines; for with the crane, as was said shortly before, he would seize the enemy ships with an iron hand, pull them back, and dash them against the land, breaking them into tiny pieces along with everyone on board.

Now, the aforementioned mechanical operation could by no means be done at a remote distance, as is known to those who have even the slightest knowledge of mechanics—unless we wish to grant the use of "war-tubes" <note>cannons or firearms</note> in those times, which no historian of sound mind would easily concede. To seize the ships, the arm of the crane necessarily had to be as long as the interval between the ships and the walls of *Acradina*. It is likely, therefore, that from the same place, Archimedes could set the stationary ships on fire with his concave mirrors at a distance of 25 or at most 30 common paces; by no means beyond that, for the reasons suggested in the preceding pages. I have chosen to deduce all of this here from its very foundations to abolish that false opinion hitherto planted in men's minds—the belief that Archimedes' mirrors reduced ships to ashes while they were floating in the middle of the sea. But who is so unskilled in catoptrics <note>the study of mirrors and reflected light</note> that they do not see this is impossible with moving and floating ships?

However, so that with all deception uncovered, the truth alone may triumph, I demonstrate the matter thus. For catoptric combustion through concave and parabolic mirrors, three necessary things are required; if any one of these is missing, it is impossible for the burning effect to follow. <margin>Three things necessary for catoptric burning.</margin> First, both the burning source and the combustible object must be in a completely firm and unmoved state. Second, there must be a certain distance between the burner and the combustible—that is, the distance between the burning mirror and the thing to be ignited must be neither greater nor less, but such that the burning focus (the union of the rays) precisely reaches the object to be ignited. Third, the material must be suitable for catching fire. I show that all these conditions were present in the burning of the ships reported by Polybius. First—

# Catoptric Magic

<note>Catoptrics is the branch of optics dealing with the reflection of light by mirrors.</note>

First, that ships on the high sea can in no way be kept so steady as to not fluctuate at least a little is something only a person with no knowledge of maritime affairs could fail to know. Indeed, such fluctuation is the greatest enemy to **Catoptric burning**. Therefore, by reason of this movement, the ship must necessarily have been deprived of the intended burning effect. Second, the mirror could have had no effect due to the distance of the ship; for a ship must be so aligned and measured to the <term>caustic cone</term> <note>The cone-shaped path of light rays concentrated by a curved mirror toward a single point.</note> of Archimedes’ mirror that the focus, or vertex, ends precisely upon the ship itself. For this to happen, if the interval were longer than it should be, either the ship or the mirror would have to move closer; or if it were too short, they would have to move back to reach the middle point of focus. It is clear, however, that Archimedes did not go outside the city walls, nor could he have gone out if he had wanted to due to great obstacles and dangers; nor is it likely that the ship would have stationed itself there voluntarily. We would have to claim that the ships, by mere chance at that time, occupied the exact and precisely required distance—which we would be <term>assuming without proof</term>, just as one could use such logic to explain away any miraculous effect.

Certainly, anyone who examines this reasoning more deeply will be forced to assert that the credibility of the Histories in this matter cannot be supported. For if, even at the smallest distance, we must labor so much with our usual burning mirrors to determine and fix the caustic focus upon both the mirror and the <term>tinder</term> <note>The flammable material intended to be ignited.</note>, how much diligence and labor do we think would be required to produce an effect at such an enormous distance? Even if we grant—though do not concede—that a ship at that time accidentally held the required distance, I nevertheless say that the rays, weakened and scattered across such a distance, would have had scarcely any strength to produce the said effect. To all this, we must add the condition of the tinder: specifically, the ship was coated in pitch, and neither the wood nor the pitch is naturally suited to catch fire from Catoptric burning. Unless a flame is actually introduced, we wear down the ship with heatings in vain; pitch is indeed liquefied by a burning mirror, but it does not burst into flame by any means, unless we say the ship was by chance loaded with other combustible tinder and material fit for catching fire, which is likewise a groundless invention. In whatever way we combine the facts, we will always find them to be <gloss>impossible things</gloss> <note>original Greek: adynatois</note>. Therefore, lest the entire credibility of history perish, and lest we seem to have stripped such a famous Architect of the knowledge of such remarkable secrets, we must at the very least say that these stationary ships were not in the middle of the sea, but were standing at the shore of **Acradina** <note>A fortified district of the ancient city of Syracuse.</note> when they were set on fire by catoptric flame.

<margin>False report of Archimedes’ mirrors burning at a distance of 3 miles.</margin>
I marvel here that certain Mathematicians have reached such a peak of audacity that, whether out of ignorance of Catoptrics or to extol the excellence of Mathematics, they are not ashamed to say Archimedes burned ships at a distance of several thousand paces. Thus, thrusting a hand over the eyes of truth <note>An idiom for blinding someone to the truth.</note> and painting a false face on things, they seek patronage for themselves through lies and <gloss>impossible</gloss> fictions. He who possesses a deeper knowledge of the nature and properties of mirrors and reflected light will surely judge this prodigious feat differently. He will candidly admit with me that no human genius can construct a mirror, whether concave or parabolic, that could exert a burning force at a distance of three miles. Let this preconceived and false opinion—that a burning mirror can burn at a vast, let alone infinite, distance—now cease. Let Mathematicians not boast of more than they are able to demonstrate, lest they expose themselves and this most noble art to the mockery and derision of men. I would not deny, however, that if a parabolic mirror were made the size of a mountain, it could have its effect at a proportionate distance according to its caustic cone.

<margin>The mirror of Septala, burning at 15 cubits.</margin>
But who will build a mass of such portentous size for us? Truly, to arrive at some truth in this matter, I have applied myself with all zeal to find a parabolic mirror that could start a fire at 20 or 30 paces. Traveling through Germany, France, and Italy, I met with distinguished craftsmen to see if they had anything similar to show; but nowhere did anything appear such as I required. Our fellow Jesuit **Grinbergerus** had constructed one that burned at 3 or 4 paces. I also tested a mirror constructed by **Ghetaldo**, which is kept here in the <term>Barberini Gallery</term> <note>The private museum/collection of the powerful Barberini family in Rome.</note>, but I did not find it to work at the distance I had previously heard rumored. Finally, I encountered the distinguished mechanic **Manfredo Settala**, a singular friend and the worthy son of the famous physician Settala. He asserted that he had fashioned a mirror 5 <term>palms</term> <note>A "palm" was roughly 9 inches or 22 cm.</note> in diameter which exerted its force at 15 paces; about which a man named **Chappujus** wrote to me in a certain letter:

*I, the undersigned Burgundian Priest living in Milan with the most illustrious Gentlemen of the Settala family, bear witness and attest that the mirror of the most illustrious Lord Manfredo Settala, made of metal, ignites fire in the targeted material at a distance of fifteen paces by the reflection of solar rays gathering into the shape of a cone, and this occurs in the thinner part or point of the cone itself, indifferently between the fifteenth and sixteenth pace. Regarding which matter...*

<summary>The author argues against the historical legend that Archimedes used mirrors to burn ships at a great distance, citing physical limitations like ship movement and focal precision. He highlights contemporary efforts to create burning mirrors, noting a successful example by Manfredo Settala that works at 15 paces.</summary>

## Its True and Original Form

### THE ELLIPSE
> In which the Sun, occupying one of the foci, exerts a most powerful burning force toward the other <note>An ellipse has two focal points; light originating at one point reflects perfectly to the other.</note> through 48 straight lines.

### THE PARABOLA
> In which rays parallel to the axis are all effectively reflected to a single point, as the curvature of the mirror is very close to the true and original form.

### THE CIRCLE
> In which the reflected rays seek different points, specifically around the fourth part of the diameter; for a mirror is more fit for burning the more it resembles the original form <note>Kircher suggests the parabolic shape is the "original" or ideal form for a burning mirror, while circular mirrors are less precise because they suffer from "spherical aberration," where rays do not meet at a single point.</note>.

When I moved the board toward the narrower part of the reflected rays—that is, at a distance of fifteen to sixteen paces from the mirror itself—it caught fire with little effort, so that the wood itself burned and was reduced to a glowing coal. In witness of this fact, I have willingly signed this testimony, written with my own hand, on the fifteenth day of February in the year 1645.

From which it is plainly evident how much more weakly mirrors burn when the burning cone <note>The focal length or the convergence of rays.</note> is longer, and how much more effectively when it is shorter. It is also evident that when burning mirrors decline toward parallelism <note>When the reflected rays become parallel instead of converging to a point.</note>, they lose all their power at once.

<margin>The difficulty in preparing a parabolic mirror.</margin>
Finally, I myself saw to it that a parabolic mirror was made by a most skilled craftsman. We constructed the mold from steel with all possible diligence; but we found eventually that the mold, even with the slightest wear, caused the mirror to degenerate into a spherical surface. We tested this with various types of metals, but in vain; for we found that it always tended toward something spherical, about which I remember other craftsmen have also complained. So difficult and full of risk is the work of establishing a perfect parabolic surface; a diamond-hard parabola would be needed to produce the desired effect. I have seen many mirrors called "parabolic," but which, when brought to the <term>Lydian stone</term> <note>A touchstone used to test the purity of gold; here used metaphorically to mean a rigorous test of quality.</note>, were found to be purely spherical. From this, it is clear that a parabolic mirror can hardly be made by human industry that exerts a burning force beyond 30 paces. And, so that we may attribute to Archimedes something to be wondered at above others—as we said before and repeat here—his mirror could have reached the ships at the shore of Achradina <note>A district of ancient Syracuse.</note> at a distance of 30 paces by the multiplication of other mirrors, reaching them with a caustic cone. ### §. IV.
## On Burning Mirrors, Flat and Spherical.

**A** matter has long been controversial among students of <term>catoptrics</term> <note>The science of reflected light.</note>: whether a burning power can be induced in flat mirrors? Certainly, <term>Zetzes</term> <note>Joannes Tzetzes, a 12th-century historian who described Archimedes' mirrors as being composed of smaller flat mirrors.</note> indicates that the engine of <term>Proclus</term> <note>A Late Antique mathematician said to have used mirrors to burn the fleet of Vitalian in 514 AD.</note> was constructed with flat mirrors. Let us therefore elucidate the matter with a few propositions.

### Proposition I.

*If flat polygonal mirrors of any number of sides are fashioned in the shape of a pyramid, they will burn more effectively the more sides they consist of; moreover, the burning will occur on the very axis of the polyhedral pyramid.*

LET there be a mirror A, B, C, F, in the form of a triangular pyramid, whose axis is D, F. I say that if its opening is turned directly toward the Sun, it will unite only a triple radiation at point E of the axis, reflected from the sides CB, BA, and AC. For since the base of the pyramid ABC is [turned] directly

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a triangular pyramid (pyramis trigona). The base is labeled with vertices A, B, and C. A central axis line extends from the apex F through point E and point D (at the center of the base). Reflection lines are drawn from the interior surfaces of the pyramid's sides, converging at point E on the central axis. The diagram is labeled with letters A, B, C, D, E, F.</image-desc>

to the Sun, the principal ray of the Sun will necessarily—according to Book 1, Theorem 14 of <term>Vitello</term> <note>Erasmus Witelo, a 13th-century authority on optics.</note>—fall along the axis of the pyramid DF: therefore the Sun's rays will be equidistant from the sides. Since, furthermore, according to the first definition of our <term>Anaclastic Art</term> <note>Refraction and the behavior of light; Kircher's term for his optical studies.</note>, the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, the Sun's rays falling on the sides at an equal distance from the principal ray will make equal angles of reflection: therefore they converge at a single point; but this is only at point E of the axis DF, which I prove as follows: if it were not at a point on the axis...

<summary>Kircher discusses the practical difficulties of manufacturing perfect parabolic mirrors and suggests that Archimedes likely used an array of mirrors rather than a single large one. He begins a geometric proof showing how multiple flat mirrors arranged as a pyramid can focus light to a single burning point.</summary>

E; it therefore happens in S, and thus the angles of reflection and incidence would be equal and unequal at the same time, which is a contradiction. Therefore, they do not converge unless they are in the axis, which was to be demonstrated. The reason we assume a pyramidal polygonal mirror rather than a columnar polygonal mirror is the <term>parallelism<note>original Greek: $\pi\alpha\rho\alpha\lambda\lambda\eta\lambda\iota\sigma\mu\hat{o}\varsigma$</note></term> of the Solar rays; just as they cannot illuminate the inner surface of a columnar mirror, they likewise cannot produce any reflected rays.

### Corollary I.

From this it is clear that if a light were placed in the axis of a mirror-prism, the light would be reflected back into itself—namely into D; likewise, an eye placed at D would see itself as a third party.

### Corollary II.

<margin>A polygonal circle consists of infinite sides.</margin>
From this it is also clear that a four-sided pyramidal mirror exposed directly to the Sun contains, as it were, certain "seeds" of mirror-burning, as four surfaces terminate their reflection in its axis. Likewise, a five-sided mirror unites 5, a six-sided unites 6, and a seven-sided unites 7 <term>ray-focuses<note>original Greek: actinobolismos; refers to the convergence of light rays</note></term> in the axis. Thus, a mirror composed of 1,000 sides and placed directly facing the Sun would unite a thousand reflected rays in the axis, and so on into infinity. Consequently, the more sides a mirror consists of, the greater the evidence of <term>burning<note>Latin: ustio</note></term> it will provide, until it results in a circle, in which the most perfect <term>combustion<note>original Greek: $\kappa\alpha\hat{v}\sigma\iota\varsigma$</note></term> or burning is achieved. Just as the triangle is the first of all polygonal figures, so the circle is the last of all polygons; hence a Mathematical circle is rightly described as a polygonal figure of infinite sides. Bodies described from these figures behave in the same way: just as the pyramid is the first of bodies, the last is the cone, a figure of infinite triangular sides. From this it is necessarily concluded that no plane mirror, however skillfully arranged, can produce a significant burning effect, since to achieve perfect burning, innumerable rays must necessarily converge; this only takes place in circular concaves, not in polygonal concaves, which (as was demonstrated just before) unite reflected rays in the axis according to the number of their sides. As for the type of machine constructed of plane mirrors by <note>Proclus was a 5th-century mathematician; Zonaras was a 12th-century chronicler. Both recorded legends of Archimedes or Proclus using mirrors to burn enemy fleets.</note> Proclus, of which Zonaras speaks, it will be discussed below.

---

## Proposition II.

> *It is impossible to ignite a fire from the surface of a single convex spherical mirror; however, it could be done from a composition of several.*

Since, as shown in the preceding sections, the lines of reflection of the same point's form from different points of the same convex spherical mirror are not parallel and do not converge in the center of a single view: therefore, neither the solar rays, nor others incident upon the surface of this mirror, can ever converge at any point, but are dispersed in the medium itself. Therefore, burning can by no means occur in a convex mirror. But if a polygon were made, composed of innumerable specular half-circles—

<image-desc>A circular diagram illustrating a focal point F on a central vertical axis. Five arc-shaped mirror segments, labeled A, B, C, D, and E, are positioned around the circumference. Straight lines representing light rays originate from each mirror segment and converge at the central point F.</image-desc>

<margin>How convex mirrors can burn.</margin>
—I say that if it is placed directly opposite the Sun, it will unite all reflected rays in the axis, just as we said regarding plane mirrors. This is clear from the following pentagonal figure, in which the specular half-circles are A, B, C, D, and E, all being equal. If this is placed <term>symmetrically<note>original Greek: $\iota\sigma o\mu\epsilon\tau\rho\omega\varsigma$</note></term> toward the Sun, so that the principal ray of the Sun aligns with the axis, I say that the rays of the Sun incident upon the equal half-circles A, B, C, D, and E will be reflected from the points of the mirrors into point F of the axis and united there. The demonstration is exactly the same as in the first proposition. But since mirrors of this kind act only through single rays and are ineffective at carrying out combustion—indeed, they bring more difficulty than benefit—we shall set them aside and finally turn to declaring the use of concave mirrors, which we have described extensively in the preceding pages.

### Problem I.

*To construct a still with such art that, solely by the aid of burning mirrors, it achieves greater efficiency in distillation than a strong fire.*

The use of the crystalline lens described in the preceding sections is as follows. A convex lens kindles fire most violently—indeed, more quickly and vehemently than a concave mirror—so much so that I am certain it not only ignites and sets fire to wood and other materials, but even melts lead. A crystalline sphere <note>Latin: *pila crystallina*; likely a solid glass ball used as a lens</note> also follows these same laws. Therefore, if a very strong fire is needed, let the belly of the still <term>alembic<note>A historical chemical apparatus used for distillation, consisting of a boiling vessel and a cooling cap.</note></term> be made in a spherical shape from copper, lead, or glass. Around this, lenses or spherical glass balls should be arranged so that at any time of day, the Sun always radiates the surface of the still's belly at the burning focus, and you will see a marvelous effect: for throughout the entire day, it will heat the belly of the still so powerfully that the heat will be sufficient for extracting any oil or <term>quintessence<note>In alchemy, the "fifth essence" or the most concentrated and purified form of a substance.</note></term>. If anyone desires to distill things with even greater efficiency, he may accomplish it through our "conch" and the vial described previously—namely, by arranging glass stills in a row along the line of burning produced by both vessels.

### Problem II.

*To construct a machine which, at any given hour, raises a fire on an altar, lights candles, and, once the sacrifice is completed, activates a fountain that extinguishes the kindled fire. See figure 11, Illustration 31.*

<margin>Illustration 31.</margin>
First, a horizontal circle CMB should be prepared, equipped with its own foot CVBD. To this, at points D and A, you should attach another semicircle DMA in such a way that it can be raised or lowered above the quadrant MB. The arc MC represents the meridian quadrant, on which the degrees of the Sun's <term>declination<note>The angular distance of the sun north or south of the celestial equator; this adjustment accounts for the changing seasons.</note></term> are marked. The movable semicircle DMA represents the <term>equinoctial<note>The celestial equator; here, a ring aligned with the path of the sun.</note></term> circle, adjustable to any region, and thus you will have the completed machine.

<margin>A wonderful mechanical device.</margin>
Into this equinoctial semicircle, you will insert 12 spheres or crystalline balls at the 12-hour points, so that the hour points correspond exactly to the center of the balls. Each individual vial should be covered with thin paper so that you can cover or uncover them at will. Let circles also be made in such proportion to the glass balls that the focal point of burning corresponds perfectly to the center of said circles. When all these things are properly performed, let the movable equinoctial circle be raised to the degree of declination that the Sun occupies at that time. Once it is fixed to the meridian quadrant along with its lenses, let the sphere be positioned according to a magnetic compass. Next, having placed <term>tinder<note>Latin: *fomite*; combustible material used to start a fire.</note></term> in the center, let sulfur-tipped threads be attached to the candles. Cover each lens with paper except for the one representing the hour at which you wish to display the spectacle. It will happen that as soon as the Sun reaches the given hour, the focus of the burning ball will ignite the combustible material in the center into a flame and also light the sulfurous threads of the candles. Thus, wonderful to say, everything will happen at the given hour just as was predicted. 

If, moreover, you place a glass vial filled with water in the center, the trapped air, once heated and expanded, will expel the water through a small tube and extinguish the underlying flame. The glass vial should be made with this art: In a glass globe X, let another small tube XA be inserted all the way to the bottom, equipped with its own rim. Let the opening of globe X be sealed around the tube so that no air can escape. The vial will then be perfect: for when the focus of the balls strikes globe X, the air inside is thinned by the heat and expels the water (which should fill about a third of the globe) through the tube AX. This water, falling down through the holes in the rim, will extinguish the flame below. Furthermore, since there are 12 balls whose burning cones all terminate in the center, they will perform their operation in said center every single hour. If someone does not wish to set the matter up with so many balls, he could easily perform the operation with a single crystalline ball, provided he positions the ball centrally at the point of the given hour. Furthermore, if one wishes to perform this operation outside the center rather than in it, he may draw a concentric circle from the center of circle DMA through the burning focuses of the balls, and place the combustible material assigned for each hour there; he will achieve the same effect. The demonstration of all these things depends on Problem 26 concerning the "Burning Clock," where you will find many other curious things regarding this type of mechanical device.

### Corollary.

<margin>A wonderful hydraulic clock.</margin>
From these things, it is also clear by what means a clock can be made that displays a fountain every hour, leading out streams according to the number of the given hour: namely, if every hour you apply the vials proposed just above to tubes arranged according to the number of the hours.

### Problem IV.

*On the construction of the Magic or Wonder-Working Lantern.*

Although we made mention of this kind of lantern on page 767 of *The Great Art of Light and Shadow*, and on page 793 we provided the method for transmitting images <term>simulacra<gloss>projected figures or likenesses</gloss></term> into a dark place by means of the sun, along with the colors required for painting them: nonetheless, because in those cited places we left this truly remarkable invention to be refined alongside other greater inventions, it happened that many people, enticed by the novelty of the thing, applied their minds to perfecting it.

**A large, detailed woodcut engraving illustrating the "Magic Lantern" (Lucerna Magica). In a dark room with a checkered floor, an oil lamp (K) is set upon a block. Chief among these was Thomas Walgensten, a Dane and a mathematician of no small reputation, who, reflecting on my descriptions of these inventions and the lantern described by us on page 767, brought it into a better form; he afterwards sold it to various princes in Italy to his great profit.

### Catoptric Magic
<note>original: "Magia Catoptrica"; refers to magic or illusions created using mirrors and reflected light.</note>

...so much so that it has now become almost a common thing in Rome. There is no other difference between that lantern and the one we have described, except that the aforementioned **Walgenstenius** <note>Thomas Walgensten (1628–1682), a Danish mathematician and physicist credited with refining and naming the "Laterna Magica."</note> displays various types of images in a darkened room quite neatly and elegantly, and to the great wonder of the spectators. In our College <note>The Collegio Romano, where Kircher taught.</note>, in a darkened room, we are accustomed to exhibiting the "Four Last Things" <note>original: "4. novissima"; the Catholic theological concepts of Death, Judgment, Heaven, and Hell.</note> to the utter amazement of the onlookers. It is truly a sight worth seeing, since with its help, one can realistically present entire satyric, tragic, or theatrical scenes and similar things in sequence.

This **Catoptric** artifice, which we taught on page 793 of *The Great Art of Light and Shadow*, does not differ from this new lantern, except that the former uses a mobile lantern, while we use the rays of the sun reflecting into a mirror on which the likenesses of things have been drawn, projecting them realistically and in color onto the immobile wall of some inner house or room—displaying all the same things that are usually shown by a mobile lantern. However, in that same place, we also teach a way to represent things without the sun's rays, using a concave mirror or a transparent lens. I have discussed all of this here more extensively so that the reader might know where these new secrets of the lantern (which we have called, not without merit, **Magic and Wonder-Working** <note>original: "Magicam & Thaumaturgam"</note>, because of the marvelous representation of any things whatsoever in a darkened room or in the silence of the dead of night) take their origin. With these things established, nothing now remains but for us to explain its construction in a few words.

### Problem V.

## On the Small Representative Viewer,
<note>original: "Smicroscopio Parastatico." A "parastatic" device is one used for display or demonstration, while "smicroscope" refers to a small viewing instrument.</note>

*By which all those things we mentioned in the previous arrangement of the Lamp regarding the exhibition of things can be viewed in the same way through this small viewer.*

**W**e shall briefly explain this entire small machine divided into four parts, because the logic of the whole construction can be easily understood by the reader from the arrangement of the parts themselves. **AB** represents the front part; **EF** the back part with an opening. **GH** shows the exterior structure, which displays the picture on the glass. **KL** shows the interior arrangement of the pictures.

Therefore, first let two small discs be made of solid wood, worked on a lathe, which are joined together in such a way that they can be easily rotated around a central axis **D**, as appears in Figure **E. F.** Then, using a compass, let two circles divided into eight parts be drawn on the interior part **KL**. Afterward, place a flat mirror <note>The author likely means a piece of clear glass here, given the context of painting on it</note> of such a size as the capacity of the interior disc, so that it can be firmly fixed within the hollow **KL**. Once this is done, let eight images—whatever you wish—be painted on the flat glass with transparent water-based colors, according to the arrangement of the eight parts already drawn on the bottom of the disc, as appears in figure **KL**. Now you will have everything pertaining to the machine completed. What remains is the tube **CV** of figure **AB**; this should be equipped with a lens of superior quality, in such a proportion that the images painted on the bottom **KL** appear beautifully and as clearly as possible through it. Once you have achieved this, insert the tube of the <term>Small Viewer; original: "Smicroscopium"</term> **CV** according to the position shown in the Figure with such care that the looking eye **O** reaches the image precisely. Due to the refraction of the lens, the image will appear larger. Then, move the mobile disc, which turns on its axis **D**, to another image, and all things will be seen in order through the small tube, expressed as clearly as possible. In this way, I am accustomed to showing the Passion of the Lord <note>The series of events leading to the crucifixion of Jesus</note>, as appears in figure **KL**. By this same practice, it will be possible to show any history portrayed in parts on a flat glass surface. I could say countless things in this place concerning the use of this Small Viewer, which would be wonderfully useful for the delight of Princes; but the wise reader will easily perceive my intention from what has been said.

### Problem VI.

*To construct a machine from flat mirrors that burns at a hundred feet and beyond. See figure 1, Illustration 31.*

**I** suppose first, then, that a flat mirror reflects a light into some plane opposite it that is greater in proportion to how large the mirror itself is. Thus, I have found by experience that a mirror of one foot projects a foot of light on a nearby wall, but at a distance of a hundred feet, it projects light only about a quarter of a foot in size. Second, it must be supposed that infinite rays reflected from individual points of the mirror constitute this light. If, therefore, you set up another flat mirror so that the reflected light of the first mirror matches the reflected light of the second, I say that both the light and the heat will be doubled. And if you set up a third mirror so that its reflected light matches the light just doubled, I say that both the light and the heat will be tripled, and so on by proceeding to infinity. Third, it must be supposed that the light and heat of this kind of reflection from mirrors into a single space is multiplied according to the number of mirrors, as we have shown at length in Book 2 on the <term>Emission of Rays; original: "Actinobolismis," from the Greek "aktis" (ray) and "ballo" (to throw)</term>, part 1, page 93.

<margin>A Mirror Experiment.</margin>
I have certainly conducted an experiment of this matter with five mirrors: and the first light indeed had a different heat than direct light; the doubled light already received a notable increase in heat; the tripled light offered the heat of a fire; the quadrupled light provided a heat that was still somewhat tolerable; the quintupled light was almost intolerable. From this, I concluded certainly and beyond doubt that with flat mirrors multiplied and placed in such a way that they all force the reflected light of the Sun into one space, it would happen that they would provide not only a greater burning effect than any parabolic, hyperbolic, or elliptical burning mirrors, but would also reflect the radiant light into a much greater space. Experience taught me this with five mirrors at a distance of a hundred feet and more. Moreover, I show that mirrors arranged this way can produce a greater effect than parabolic burning mirrors: Parabolic burning mirrors perform their action only by lines forced into a single point. But flat mirrors constitute their action by <term>ray-emissions; original: "actinobolismis"</term>, or by entire luminous surfaces, each of which acts with infinite rays. Second, parabolic mirrors, when projected to a great distance, intersect each other too obliquely and degenerate almost into parallelism, losing all power of burning; for in this state, they are surpassed even by a single flat mirror or the direct heat of the Sun, as in the preceding—

# Catoptric Magic

<note>original: "Magia Catoptrica"</note>
<note>"Catoptrics" is the branch of optics dealing with the reflection of light by mirrors.</note>

It has already been declared in <term>Anacamptics</term> <note>From the Greek word for "bending back," this refers to the science of reflected light or sound.</note> (where we teach how to hurl the light of the Sun from any position through a flat mirror onto any determined point), that there is no doubt that such a dense collection of shining surfaces would achieve the same result—and much more effectively—than the parabolic concentration of rays near a focal point. From this, I entirely believe that the machine of Proclus <note>Proclus (c. 412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and mathematician; tradition claims he used mirrors to burn the ships of Vitalian during the siege of Constantinople.</note>, with which Zonaras <note>Joannes Zonaras, a 12th-century Byzantine chronicler.</note> records he burned the Byzantine ships, was effected by this kind of arrangement of mirrors.

<margin>What kind of mirrors Proclus used.</margin>
For let there be flat mirrors **A, B, C, D, E**, the Sun **G**, and a wall **F**, which are so arranged that the rays of the Sun reflected from each individual mirror meet at point **F**. It is therefore certain, and established by experience, that just as the light is gathered at **F**, so too is the heat five times greater and more intense than the light and heat reflected there by a single mirror; so much so that at **F**, a hand can scarcely be held firm due to the intense heat. If, therefore, five mirrors can do so much, what could a hundred or a thousand mirrors arranged by this ingenuity not do? It is certain that the heat would be so intense that it could burn all things and reduce them to ashes, since this focal point would be larger and more packed with light than in any other parabolic mirrors. I here earnestly ask mathematical catoptricians to undertake an experiment of this matter with the greatest diligence; they will find what I also suggested above: that there is no other catoptric machine that obtains both a greater power for burning and a greater distance.

### Problem VII.

->*To construct a statue which, at the rising of the Sun and at each following hour when struck by the Sun, produces a prodigious sound. See figure 3 of Illustration 31.*<-

These statues will be treated at length in our *Hieroglyphic Mechanics*; therefore, in this place, we shall describe the construction of the statue only in passing and in a few words, lest we seem to have omitted anything of curious matters in this our "Great Art."

Let a certain chest be made of lead or any other metal, marked with the letters **A, B, C, D, E, F**, as Figure 3 shows, four palms in length, and one palm in width and height.

<margin>The Memnon Statue producing various sounds at the rays of the Sun.</margin>
In this chest, the half-part **BEFL** is divided by a diaphragm <note>A dividing plate or partition.</note> **ELB**, through which a bent <term>syphon</term> **ELB** <note>A tube or pipe used to move liquid.</note> is led. Upon this vessel, the Memnon Statue <note>The "Colossi of Memnon" in Egypt were famous in antiquity for producing a sound like a harp string breaking at dawn, caused by the heating of the stone.</note> is placed in the posture and position shown by figure **MP**. Furthermore, from the inner surface of the upper side of this vessel, three syphons are led out; the first of which represents the body of a bird **Z**, the second a pipe **MN**. Let the third syphon be **OP**, which is led through the body of the statue into the mouth and eyes.

Now, let the vessel **ADLE** be equipped with its own intake-valve <note>original: "assario platismatoque"</note>, the foot of which is led through the bottom of the vessel into "living" <note>i.e., flowing or fresh</note> water. Let the vessel be so closed on all sides that not even the smallest bit of air can escape. On the upper side of the vessel, let two hemispheres **G** and **H** be placed, the hollows of which are continuous with the hollow of the vessel **ABKL**. With these things rightly performed, you will "animate" the machine thus: you expose the machine, previously filled to one-third with liquid, to the Sun. As soon as it feels the rays falling into the hemispheres **G** and **H**, it will violently rarefy the internal air. This, consequently, will press upon the water, which, being pressed and having no other way out, will work its way through the bent syphon into vessel **N**. There it will expel the latent air with great force through the syphons **B, O, N**, and will produce a bird's whistle in **Z**, the sound of an animal in **M**, and in **P** it will move artificial eyes—ingeniously inserted and fit for nodding—and it will also push an inflated tongue out of the mouth: a spectacle wonderful to tell. Furthermore, as the Sun recedes, the air condensed in vessel **AB**, requiring less space, will call for new water drawn in through the intake-valve **I** to replace what has receded. Then, the water of vessel **N** having been emptied through the stopcock **L**, it will prepare for new spectacles.

If, therefore, you wish to exhibit this kind of prodigious sound at every hour: the machine will be applied to the center **X** of figure 11 in such a way that either hemisphere **G** or **H** corresponds to the center **X**. The Sun, passing through the crystalline hourly globes <note>Glass spheres acting as lenses.</note>, will in a moment heat **G** or **H** with its burning focus at each hour; the intended effect of the sounding statue will necessarily follow this heating. When the Sun recedes from the crystalline globe and the heat ceases, the mentioned effects will also cease until the Sun illuminates another globe. And thus the statue will sound twelve times a day, acting as if it were an hourly herald, to the greatest admiration of the listeners; and this spectacle will be perpetual. Truly, by what method we can grant a voice closest to the human one to this machine shall be declared more fully elsewhere; hence, it suffices to have suggested here only in passing by what means this machine can be animated by the light of the Sun.

# Demonstration 1 <note>original: "Parastasis I"</note>

## Flat mirrors are multipliers of the forms of a single object. See figure 1 of Illustration 32.

<margin>Illustration 32.</margin>
<margin>A wonderful property of two flat mirrors.</margin>
A certain wonderful property, and one observed by no one else as far as I know, shines forth in two mirrors constructed in such a way that they can be opened and closed like a book. Let these be placed on a flat surface upon which you have drawn a semicircle divided into degrees. For if you place the point where the mirrors meet at the center of the semicircle, so that each side of the mirror rests upon the diameter, the image of the object will be seen only once; two things will appear, one real thing outside the mirror and another "phantom" <note>Kircher uses "phantastica" to describe the virtual image seen inside the mirror</note> inside.

If, however, you position the mirrors so that the opening of the sides intercepts 120 degrees, you will see the image of the object placed between the sides twice—that is, together with the real image, you will see it a third time. The reason for this is that the angle of reflection and incidence is as great as the angle intercepted by the sides, namely 120 degrees; since this is an obtuse angle, it can only cause a double image, as was shown in Proposition 5 on page 739.

But if the mirrors intercept an angle of 90 degrees, you will see a circle divided into four parts on the plane, in which four likenesses of the placed object will appear together: three phantom images and one real one. Since the reflection occurs at right angles, each reflecting side will cause two other forms within itself; consequently, the forms will be multiplied according to the multiplication of the sides, which will maintain the rule of the reflection of the sides, as we showed in Proposition 5 on page 739.

Furthermore, if the sides of the mirrors intercept an angle of 72 degrees, you will see a perfect and regular pentagon formed on the horizontal plane, in which the same number of forms will appear. Likewise, if they intercept an angle of sixty degrees, you will see a hexagon and the same number of forms: specifically five phantoms and one real. Thus, if the angle of the mirrors intercepts 51 and 3/7 degrees, a perfect heptagon <note>a seven-sided polygon</note> will appear, with the same number of forms of the object placed between the mirrors; likewise, an angle of the mirrors of 45 degrees will give an octagon; 40 degrees will give an enneagon <note>a nine-sided polygon</note>; 36 degrees a decagon; an angle of 32 and 8/11 degrees will give a hendecagon <note>an eleven-sided polygon</note>; and finally, an angle of 30 degrees will return a dodecagon with the same number of forms, and so on to infinity. Thus, the resulting reflective polygon <term>polygonum anacampticum</term> <note>anacamptic: a technical term from the Greek "anakamptein," meaning to bend back or reflect</note> and the number of forms will always have as many sides as the polygon whose side is intercepted by the opening of the mirrors. The reasons for all these depend on Proposition 5 of the preceding Distinction.

---

# Demonstration 2 <note>original: "Parastasis II"</note>

## To exhibit a dragon with as many heads as you like, each of which breathes fire, using two mirrors. See figure 2 of Illustration 32.

In the center of the circle, where we said the mirror ought to be fixed in the preceding problem, let the figure of a dragon be placed. It should be made with such a device that it breathes fire; this will be easily done if you fill a tube, led through the body of the dragon, with moistened gunpowder <note>original: "pulvere pyrio madefacto"</note> and the opening emerges out through the lower bottom. 

When this is completed, if the two mirrors are stood at right angles, four dragons will immediately present themselves. If they make an angle of 72 degrees, it will appear as a beast with five heads. If, however, the two mirrors are set at an angle of 60 degrees, behold, six heads of the dragon will appear from one trunk, all spitting fire. These heads will be multiplied more and more the more you contract the mirrors. It seems a wonder to those watching, for while they do not see the movement of the mirror, they nevertheless see the sudden multiplication of the heads.

# Corollary 1

## The multi-lamped candlestick <note>original: "Candelabrum polylychnium"</note>, fig. 1.

<margin>The sudden multiplication of the arms of the candlesticks.</margin>
From this it is clear by what means candlesticks of 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, or 12 arms may be represented: namely, if one arm, led out from the center of the mirrors' junction, is equipped with its candle and lit. For at an angle of 120 degrees you will see a three-lamped candle; at 45 degrees an eight-lamped one; at 72 degrees a five-lamped candlestick, with no less pleasure than admiration. If you place a small altar beneath this, a vast church will seem full of candlesticks; the spectacle will be more pleasant the larger the machine is.

Furthermore, you will display spectacles worthy of greater admiration if four boards are made like a book, opening and closing themselves as Figure 2 shows, each of which is covered with a mirror on both sides. Even though they are joined together, they can be positioned to form the desired angles as we taught in the preceding section. In this, it will be seen with no small delight that as much as the species of things increase in one part, they decrease in the other, so that they perfectly express arithmetical subtraction and addition.

# Mirror Magic <note>original: "Magia Catoptrica"</note>

## Corollary II.

### The Multi-Headed Statue.

<margin>The Multi-Headed Man.</margin>
**H**ence, if you wish to display a man with as many heads as you please, you will be able to perform it by this same industrious method: and likewise for showing countless other things, which we leave to your own ingenuity.

## Demonstration III <note>original: "Parastasis III"</note>

> *If mirrors are arranged into an equilateral prism, and any object is placed in the middle of the base, it will be multiplied according to the proportion that the root has to the cube.*

<margin>A new observation of the wonderful proportion of reflection <note>original: "anacampticæ"</note> to arithmetic.</margin>
**I**f mirrors are formed into prisms of any number of sides, the relationship of the form to its multiplication will be as 1 is to the cube of the sides of the polygon. Since this matter is new and, as far as I know, noted by no one until now, I am the first to bring it to light here, so that the curious reader may see that Nature has looked toward multiple proportions in all things. Therefore, if the prism is equilateral <note>three-sided</note>, the form placed at the bottom of the mirror will be multiplied twenty-seven times, which is the cube of three. Thus, a four-sided prism will multiply the object sixty-four times; a five-sided prism 125 times, and so on for the rest. I would demonstrate all these things more extensively here, had I not reserved them for our *Combinatory Art* <note>Referring to Kircher’s work on permutations and combinations</note>; for there, the proportion of catoptric multiplication will be treated professionally, where we trust we shall solve many problems from Algebra concerning multiple reflection—things which I am truly surprised never even entered the minds of any mathematicians.

---

## Demonstration IV <note>original: "Parastasis IV"</note>

> *To construct a Catoptric, Polydictic <term>Theater</term> <note>From Greek "poly" (many) and "deiktikon" (showing); a multi-display device</note>, in which whatever you wish may be displayed according to the model of nature. See figure 6 of Illustration 32.*

<margin>The mirror chest in the Villa Borghese in Rome.</margin>
**I**t is the property of flat mirrors to multiply the image of a seen object in a wonderful way by a certain arrangement, which I am about to describe. Since we have provided the demonstration of this matter in the preceding pages, we will now attempt to apply the same to various and pleasant uses. There is here in Rome, in the Villa Borghese outside the Pincian Gate, a certain mirror chest which displays wonderful phantasms of things: now forests drawn out in a long row of trees; now cities most well-equipped with houses and palaces; a little later, most crowded marketplaces; also a library equipped with a great abundance of books. It shows these and very different similar things at different times so vividly that the deception of the displays seemed to have imposed itself even upon the eyes of those otherwise not unskilled in the art of mirrors. Many of the more unrefined people, deluded by this catoptric phantasm, being unable to grasp with their eyes the types of things represented, are seen trying to explore them by felling with their hands—not without the laughter of the bystanders—so miraculously does the mirror-work mock the eyes of the spectators. Since many people wondered at this machine and could not understand it, they pleaded with me with the greatest prayers to open up the logic and causes of such an unusual machine. I have seen fit to perform this in this place with what diligence I could. And so, I have built another machine much more wonderful than the Borghese one, whether you look at the multiplication of images or the preparation of the scenic phantasms; and I offer it in my Museum for all to see. This is made with such artifice that it can be arranged into any scenic projection; so that if anyone looks into it, they think they see most ornate chambers, infinite rows of extended columns, and various diversions of walkways gleaming with gold, silver, and every kind of treasure <note>original: "cimeliorum"</note>. In this you will see gardens most well-provided with every kind of flower and plant; tables most full of every kind of delicacy <note>original: "cupediarum"</note>; inexhaustible treasures—the greatest torment of the greedy, some of whom, having greedily gazed upon an innumerable force of money before them, when they tried to stroke it with their hands, were seen to draw back with a groan and indignation, deluded by the empty appearance of the phantom. This machine contains many other things most worthy of knowing, all of which will be explained a little later more fully, after we have first handed down the construction and manufacture of the machine.

But on the arched surface I, they should also be so arranged that one does not stand out more than another; the external sides of the mirrors, however, must be joined with the greatest diligence with leaden or other wooden retainers. Once this is done, let a central body RM be made in the form...

If you desire to see gardens, you will fashion small flowerbeds out of paper or wax, adorned with every kind of plant and flower, which you will attach to the second side of the parallelogram body. If, however, you wish to show treasures and a various supply of precious things, you will tie crowns woven with coral, silver, and gold beads to the third face of the parallelogram body. If you wish to see a library, you will arrange little books made of gilded paper in order on the fourth face of the parallelogram body; and so you will proceed with exhibiting other things, if there are more than four sides.

## The Use of the Catoptric Machine.

IF, therefore, you wish to represent infinite forests to the spectators, by the turning of the handle, the side of the polyhedral body in which we just now arranged the trees is positioned within the mirror parallel to the horizon; and behold, once the curtain is removed, a most pleasant theater of forests stretched out into infinite space will immediately offer itself. You will be able to arrange this spectacle into any position and optical projection according to the placement of the doors. If the doors are parallel to each other, we will see the things projected in a straight order on both sides to infinity. If, however, one inclines toward the other, the <term>catoptric<gloss>relating to mirrors or reflected light</gloss></term> walkways will recede to the sides. Experience will teach all these things better. If you suddenly desire to transform this "Satiric" <note>In classical theater, a "Satiric" scene referred to a wild, woodland setting</note> scene into a garden scene, by the turning of the handle **T**, <margin>The catoptric apparatus for the treasury of gardens and forests.</margin> you will gaze with the greatest amazement at that side of the polyhedral body which was planted with gardens, stretched out into infinity in every perspective according to the arrangement of the doors. Likewise, when the side of the polyhedral body marked with treasures is turned and the curtain removed, treasures of inexhaustible riches will soon present themselves; if such things were real, no King in the world would have greater. Here there is no number of emeralds, pearls <note>original: "unionum"; refers to large, high-quality pearls</note>, and turquoises; no end of <term>pyropes<gloss>a fire-red gemstone, likely a garnet</gloss></term>, diamonds, and beryls. Finally, if you exhibit the fourth side, rows of palaces beautifully arranged according to all the rules of the architectural art, elegant divisions of streets, and series of obelisks and columns running forward into infinity will be revealed.

### Corollary I.

<margin>A luminous scene.</margin>
From these things it is clear: if you place a <term>dodecahedron<gloss>a twelve-sided solid</gloss></term> as the rotating body—that is, if the solid parallelogram had twelve sides—twelve different spectacles could be exhibited. If, therefore, you wish to exhibit a luminous scene, you will arrange candelabras on one of the said faces, set in order according to the proportion of the machine and equipped with their little wax candles; when these are lit, it can hardly be said how great a variety of light and shadow, how great a magnitude of candles, and in what varied positions they are seen exhibited, especially if the arrangement of the doors is straight.

<margin>A catoptric battle.</margin>
If, however, you desire to see a battle, on one of the twelve faces, little figures or statuettes of soldiers equipped with arms are to be arranged so that their flexible limbs can be moved by sinews and threads; then, by the opposing pulls of the threads, they are to be engaged in battle. You will see a remarkable spectacle. For if the whole world were gathered into an army, I hardly think so many ranks of combatants could be established.

<margin>A cat represented catoptrically.</margin>
The spectacle of a live cat placed on one of the said planes surpasses the entertainment of everything mentioned so far. For while it sees itself surrounded on all sides by an innumerable multitude of cats, and thinks they are real, it can hardly be said how many jests the cat performs in this theater; while it tries now to reach them, now fawns with its tail, now fixes kisses upon its own image, now tries to break through the obstacles in every way, now attacks with its claws; with how much longing, finally, it desires to be joined to them, [expressing itself] with a varied voice and a miserable groan of various emotions: indignation, rage, jealousy, longing, and love...

## Corollary II.

<margin>The Catoptric Amphitheater</margin>
**IF** you place the two sides, M and N, so they face each other not in a parallel position but at a slight slant: behold, the entire theater will pass into a circular form, or a perfect amphitheater; and if you attach folding doors to these, the various forms of the amphitheaters will be multiplied a hundredfold into innumerable spectacles.

## Corollary III.

<margin>Anoptic and Catoptric appearances.</margin>
**IF** you wish to display the said spectacles in the heights and the depths <note>"Anoptic" refers to illusions seen by looking upward, while "Catoptric" refers to those seen via reflection.</note>: Take the shutters of the upper chest XY and AS, attached to the sides. If you set them parallel to one another and place aerial spectacles—such as birds or weather effects—between both mirrors with such industry that they appear to hang in the air, you will see everything in the upper mirror displayed so naturally as if they were being viewed in the sky itself. In the lower mirror, however, it will appear as if you were looking down upon the said spectacles from a very high place. Thus, the upper mirrored shutter shows things on high, or in the sky as viewed from the earth; but the lower mirrored shutter displays the lowest things as if elevated above the earth from a very high place.

## Corollary IV.

**IT** is evident from all these things—narrated perhaps more extensively than was necessary—how a certain room in some Prince’s palace might be constructed according to the given proportion of the catoptric <note>Relating to mirrors and the laws of reflection.</note> chest, which would display all the mentioned things to the point of a miracle <term>high above</term> <note>original: ὑπεράνω</note>. This is how one must proceed: Let a small room be made 20 feet long and 15 feet high, arched in the manner of our chest. Let it have double shutters, both for varying the catoptric scene and for letting in opportune light, left in opposite places of the room. Let all the walls of this room, together with the floor, the ceiling, and the shutters, be dressed with their own mirrors, and let the mirrors be as large as possible. Whoever enters a room constructed this way:

1. Will see himself multiplied almost infinitely; now he will find himself walking in the air, now stationed in the deepest places. Frequently he will see himself with two, three, four, or five heads; sometimes he will behold himself crippled and mutilated in all his limbs. In a word, no <note>Proteus was a Greek sea-god capable of assuming any shape; a "Proteus Theater" refers to a place of constant transformation.</note>Proteus’s Theater can show such great metamorphoses as this mirrored room. For so many different streets will offer themselves that you will think yourself to be in some city.
<margin>A Catoptric City.</margin>
2. You will observe yourself hanging in the air with your feet resting on the ceiling and your head turned downward.
3. You will marvel at yourself flying through the air and standing on the very floor without feet.
4. You will see yourself now fleeing while approaching, and now approaching while fleeing, in a truly wondrous spectacle.
5. Stationed in the mirrored corners, you will now see yourself without eyes, now without ears; now transformed into no certain shape.
6. By walking through the room, you will seem to ascend and descend a mountain at the same time.
7. In this theater, you will behold your face in one place colored yellow like someone with jaundice, in another smeared with red as if with cinnabar, and soon tinted with a green color. The said room will exhibit to you countless other <term>bright</term> <note>original: φανὰ</note> and <term>unspeakable</term> <note>original: ἀνεκφώνηta</note> phantasms, which you, taught by experience alone, will find to be true. In this single machine, you will see whatever has been said dispersedly in the whole of Catoptric Magic, as if gathered in a certain epitome and <term>recapitulation</term> <note>original: ἀνακεφαλαίωσις</note>. But leaving these things aside for now, let us enter upon others.

## To construct another Catoptric Machine. See figure 3 of Plate 32.

**WHILE** I am treating these matters, through continuous combinations of mirrored bodies with one another, I have found a certain body—an irregular one, to be sure—but one which yields to no other in displaying catoptric miracles. Let it be made thus: let the mirrored glass be cut into the form shown to us in figure 7 of the present Plate. For this plane, composed of squares and triangles so that the mirrors turn inward, will show us a polyhedral <note>A solid geometric figure with many plane faces.</note> body, such as figure 3 in the Plate demonstrates. Let the upper plane be open to light, and from the side, through any of the squares (for example, A), let a place be given for the eye. Inside, in the middle, let a column be placed on which the thing to be represented is situated. Once these things are done, you will see such great spectacles in this body as in no other; for besides the innumerable multiplication of the image, you will find yourself as if stationed in the vast theater of <note>Morpheus is the Greek god of dreams.</note>Morpheus, with an incredible variety of metamorphoses. I say no more: the wise reader will find more by experience itself than I could explain even with many words.

# Catoptric Magic.

### CHAPTER III.

->On the emergence of the phantom outside the mirror, or on the representation of things in the air outside the mirror.<-

**M**ANY among the Catoptricians <note>Scholars who study the science of mirrors and reflection.</note> have mentioned this appearance of a phantom outside the mirror. The first was Vitellio <note>Erazmus Ciołek Witelo (c. 1230–1280/1300), a Polish friar and a major authority on optics in the Middle Ages.</note>, who maintained that if a convex cylindrical mirror is placed inside a dark room, and the likeness of an object situated outside the room is transmitted through a narrow slit, the image will appear to hang in the middle of the air between the wall and the surface of the mirror.

<margin>Vitellio's Error.</margin>
But I find the greatest difficulties in accepting this experiment. First, because it seems to me that a convex surface of a cylindrical mirror is <gloss>in my experience</gloss> incompatible with this; for as was said in the preceding sections, a cylindrical mirror has this specific property: it does not show the forms of things in their natural shape, but exhibits them contracted and compressed along their entire vertical length, as has been treated at length in the Anaclastic Art <note>The study of refracted light and distorted images (anamorphosis).</note>. Therefore, unless the form outside the room is first distorted—as taught by the transformation in the second book—it could never show an image in a natural form on the cylinder. This is the first point. Secondly, since images are scattered by any convex surface—because reflected rays never converge back to a single point, but rather the projection of the rays or forms is cast from every part of the convex surface toward opposite directions, and consequently no union of the rays occurs—it is brilliantly clear that an image cannot be seen in the air between the wall and the surface of a cylindrical mirror. Furthermore, although I have performed this very experiment above with the utmost diligence according to all the rules, I have never found even a trace of truth in it; hence I do not know what came into Vitellio’s mind that he dared to assert an experiment so contrary to the truth. I am not unaware that the reflection of a straight line parallel to the axis of a columnar convex mirror is made from the line of the mirror’s length to the sight, as Alhazen <note>Ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–1040), the "father of optics," whose work was central to European science.</note> proves at length in Proposition 26, number 2; but that does not effect the emergence of a phantom, since this is a property of concave mirrors, as we shall see shortly. However, so that I do not seem to do an injustice to such a great man and my fellow countryman, the curious reader may read Theorem 60 (or the last of the eighth book) for himself. The proposition of the theorem begins thus: *It is possible for a cylindrical mirror to be so positioned that an observer may see in the air, outside the mirror, the image of another object not otherwise seen.*

<margin>Porta’s Error.</margin>
Porta <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), an Italian scholar and polymath famous for his work on "Natural Magic."</note> cites this theorem quite differently in his catoptric experiments, and it has earned such applause among many that they have peddled the idea that wonderful things can be displayed by its power. Yet if they had undertaken the experiment as we have, and recognized the reasons that contradict the truth, they would not have so rashly given their assent to the matter. For there are many things smeared with cosmetic deception <note>original: "fucis illita"</note> which are only cleansed by their own light; many things promise wonders at first glance which, once the experiment is undertaken, are convicted of manifest falsehood. Diligent experience and tireless labor are the Lydian stone <note>A touchstone used to test the purity of gold.</note> by which we are taught what should be believed, without which nothing can ever be certain to us. Relying on this false phantom of Vitellio, Risnerus <note>Friedrich Risner (c. 1533–1580), a German mathematician who edited the works of Alhazen and Vitellio.</note> also devises various things in his *Introduction on the Use of Optics* which, as they stand on a false foundation, collapse of their own accord. But so that the reader may see many absurdities grasped together, I bring forward his words and his catoptric artifice as one.

> *Catoptrics teaches,* he says, *how to compose a mirror that does not retain the objects cast upon it within itself, but throws them back into the air; Vitellio wrote of its composition, and we shall say something as well. What, then, prevents cunning women from playing with the eyes of men with this mirror, so that they believe they see the ghosts <note>original: "Manes," the spirits of the dead.</note> of the deceased called forth, when in truth they see in the air outside the mirror the likeness of either a boy or a hidden statue? For while this is indeed most certain, it nonetheless seems to exceed all belief. If a cylindrical mirror is placed in a room closed on all sides, and a mask, or a statue, or something else is placed outside the room—in such a way, however, that there is some small crack in the window or the door of the room through which the rays from the mask may break forth onto the mirror—the image of the mask placed outside the room will be discerned inside the room, hanging in the air. And since the reflections from those mirrors are somewhat distorted, showing a deformed image of a beautiful thing, how foul and horrible must the image of a mask appear when it is designed for horror and consternation? Thus the <term>striges</term> <note>Witches or owl-like spirits from Roman folklore.</note> hang that mirror in the room, and that by a very thin thread; they command a fast and the other things which are thought to contribute to these mysteries. An unskilled and trembling consultant is led into these sacred rites, suspecting nothing of such wicked cleverness; meanwhile, the <term>venefica</term> <note>A sorceress or poisoner.</note> pours out exorcisms and adjurations by which the ghosts may be recalled from the underworld as if revived. So that the whole matter appears more divine, the consultant is placed in that spot where the ray reflected from the mirror tends. He sees, therefore, not in the mirror, but in the air outside the mirror, a trembling specter—trembling because the mirror, hanging by a thin thread, shakes slightly. He sees a hollow and bloodless image hanging in the air, horrific, even approaching him if the mask is moved closer to the crack. Stunned by this consternation, he does not think to investigate the trick, but only of his exit and flight*

He quotes Friedrich Risner to illustrate how such "magic" mirrors were allegedly used by sorceresses to trick people into seeing ghosts.</summary>
