# The Great Art, Book 10. Magic Part III.

He meditates on flight, which he easily obtains from that wicked woman. Then, as if snatched from the very jaws of <term>Orcus<gloss>A Roman name for the underworld or the god of the dead</gloss></term>, he openly proclaims that he has seen the ghosts of the dead, and that souls have been revived and raised from the underworld. Who would not be captivated by such wonders? Indeed, no one could escape these more-than-Pythian <note>original: "Pythonicas præstigias"; a reference to the Pythia, the priestess of the Delphic Oracle, implying deceptive or demonic delusions</note> tricks unless they were equipped with the aid of optics. Therefore, optics, the light of things, sufficiently shows that most ghosts do not have physical causes, but are artificial and proceed from imposture. 

Behold, these are the deceptions which the "Optician"—though hardly an expert in the light itself—sells to the world as paradoxes. For first, he thrusts forward a false experiment as a true one. Even though I have performed his experiments more than a hundred times, it never happened that I saw any of those things which the Author recklessly asserts. I will not say I saw an image visible outside the mirror or hanging in the air; I did not even happen to see a trace of any image hanging in the air outside the mirror. In the mirror, however, nothing appeared except a bright line. Behold, these are the "great wonders" which <term>Risnerus<gloss>Friedrich Risner (c. 1533–1580), a German mathematician known for his work on optics</gloss></term> boasts can be exhibited with the help of a convex cylindrical mirror; the wise reader will find all of these to be false and futile through his own experience. 

Furthermore, who does not see that Risner now requires witches, sorceresses, and hags to possess mathematical knowledge so they may perform their deceptions? For without the <term>catoptric art<gloss>The science of mirrors and reflection</gloss></term>, they would be unable to exhibit said phantoms by any other means. He who knows the fallacies and the thousand ways the devil has of deceiving will notice that these poor women are taught many other things by him besides catoptrics. 

<margin>The impiety of atheists.</margin> Among other things, it is also most wretched that he ascribes the appearances of specters not to divine permission, but to the cleverness of men mocking others with catoptric experiments. In this, he seems to support the atheists of our time, who—in order to abolish not only all sacred history but also profane history, along with God and all religion—affirm that these appearances proceed from the forces of nature and from clever men and deceptive philosophers. Since the most learned <term>Mersennus<gloss>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), a French polymath and priest who defended religion against atheism and magic</gloss></term> has refuted this impiety in an entire work, I do not wish to be longer here. 

I add only this: whoever knows how weak the light is with which specters appear, how accurately the eye must be positioned at the mirror, what a tiny proportion of distance must be kept to the object, how small and mutilated the phantom <note>original: "idolum"; used here in the optical sense of a reflected image</note> appears, and finally, what an exact proportion of darkness to light must be maintained so they can be represented—that person will easily notice the fraud. For if you make the opening a little wider, the incoming light will immediately abolish and scatter all the images in the middle. If, however, the opening is smaller, it will show nothing in the middle but darkness. From this, one will clearly see that no apparition can be ascribed to catoptric experiments. 

Of this same sort is the experiment which <term>Porta<gloss>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), an Italian scholar famous for his work "Natural Magic"</gloss></term> brings forward in Chapter 7 of his *Catoptric Experiments*. <margin>Another imposture of Porta.</margin> "In the dead of night," he says, "an image of any likeness will be seen hanging in the middle of a room, not without the terror of the beholders. Let the image we seek to represent as hanging in the middle of another dark room be placed before the opening of the room, and let many torches be lit around it. In the middle of the dark room, let a white linen cloth be placed, or some solid thing that can receive the admitted image; for the spectators, since they do not see the cloth, will see the image hanging and luminous in the middle of the air, not without fear and horror." 

These are beautiful allurements for the unskilled common folk. For whoever operates according to the stated method will indeed see the cloth, and on it the image of the likeness placed outside the room; however, he will see the image hanging in the air in the same way we see images brought inside the walls of a room—namely, inverted and expressed on the cloth—and not at all "hanging in the air," which Porta nevertheless sells as a great catoptric miracle.

<margin>The wonderful deed of Roger Bacon.</margin> Many have doubted whether it is possible for someone to project their shadow to a great distance by the help of mirrors (as it is rumored <term>Roger Bacon<gloss>The 13th-century English philosopher and friar often associated with early experimental science and legends of magic</gloss></term> once did, who is read to have shown himself from a tower to be seen on a distant walkway). We shall show a little later that this is entirely possible. 

That someone can also be seen hanging in the air by the benefit of thicker air reflecting the image alone was discussed at length in the second distinction of this work regarding the "aerial parastatic mirror," and the example of <term>Witelo<gloss>Vitellio (c. 1230–1280), a Polish friar and physicist whose work on optics was standard for centuries</gloss></term> clearly teaches this. <margin>The marvelous effect of an aerial mirror.</margin> Witelo had a studious and vigilant companion who, after staying awake for several nights without sleep and having become weaker, decided to set out on a journey at night. While riding near a river bank where the air was thicker and mistier, he saw another horseman preceding him and doing everything that he himself did. Astonished by this miracle, when he finally returned to Witelo and told of the omen, he learned from him that he had been a terror to himself, and had seen nothing other than his own image reflected by the thick and dewy air.

Therefore, these things having been duly set forth, we must now finally discuss the method by which we can view images as if hanging in the middle of the air. While we provide this, we will strive to hand down to the curious reader things discovered through our own experiments that everyone can trust, rather than false documents, so that once false teachings are outlawed, the truth we love may shine upon everyone.

## Catoptric Feat I.
### To represent the image of an object in the middle of the air.

<margin>A thing hanging in the air by means of a mirror.</margin>
The emergence of an <term>image<gloss>original: "idoli"; in early optics, this refers to the visual phantom or likeness produced by light rays</gloss></term> outside the mirror is the specific work of concave surfaces, although it could also be drawn out from a flat mirror by this art. First, take a glass plate suitable for making a mirror and hollow it out slightly on one side; then, by applying a sheet of tin-foil, you will have a mirror that projects your likeness outside the mirror so that it seems as if it can be touched. Moreover, the larger the cavity, the better the effect will be. It is a nearly common thing for "species" <note>Images or visual forms</note> to exit from a concave mirror, so much so that it has passed into a proverb; when people speak of something that appears serious at first glance but whose outcome reveals some hidden collusion, they are accustomed to saying it was "contested in a mirror-combat." For a man equipped with a drawn sword seems to provoke another latent figure in the mirror to burst forth with a sword. From this, at a certain and determined position—which occurs immediately after the <term>point of inversion<gloss>the focal point where an image flips</gloss></term>—the image is seen to exit and clash with the other, though in an inverted position. While many wish to apply a remedy for this defect <note>the upside-down nature of the image</note> using other mirrors, they destroy the whole mechanism; we, with almost no effort, both call the image out of the mirror and observe it standing upright in the air in this manner: We take a spherical concave mirror of any size and place it so that its position is parallel to the horizon. Then, let a visible object be placed somewhere opposite the mirror, which our eye, positioned in the line of reflection, will see standing completely upright in the air. By this industry, we draw out images of things to a distance of a palm and a half <note>about 4 to 6 inches</note> using a hand-sized mirror. If you hide the object with such skill that it cannot possibly be seen by the eyes of those present, the thing will appear all the more prodigious; and this is the most efficient way of all to exhibit things in the middle of the air by the help of a spherical concave mirror.

## Feat II.
### To draw out the images or phantoms of things outside a concave cylindrical mirror. See fig. 1 of Illustration 33.

<margin>An image hanging in the air. Illustration 33.</margin>
Let a concave cylindrical mirror be made, which you will obtain with easy effort if you coat a sheet of <term>selenite<gloss>a transparent, crystalline variety of gypsum used as a substitute for glass</gloss></term> with quicksilver to make a mirror, and fit it inside a crystalline cylinder so that it adheres perfectly to the cylindrical surface. You will then have a prepared mirror; the larger and more spacious it is, the more numerous and wonderful things it will exhibit. It is sufficient, however, for only half of the cylinder to be mirrored; the remaining part can easily be made opaque by any other substance. If you place any image in the bottom of this mirror so that it lies in an inverted position relative to you, and let it be perfectly illuminated: behold, wonderful to say, the image placed in the bottom—which previously seemed to appear nowhere—will now be seen outside the mirror, hovering in the free air above the very mouth of the mirror so naturally that when I showed this <term>phantom<gloss>original: "phantasma"</gloss></term> to many people, they could not be convinced it was incorporeal until they learned by their own experience, by moving their fingers through it, that it was truly a phantom that could not be felt. By this artifice, I exhibited the **Ascension of the Lord** so vividly that all the figures seemed to hang in the middle of the air. Innumerable other things can be exhibited by the aid of this mirror, which might not undeservedly seem like miracles, but we leave those to the industry of each individual. If the image in the bottom of the mirror is arranged so that it can be moved at the will of the operator, you will exhibit even more rare spectacles; for the figures will be seen moving here and there in the air with various gestures, not without causing astonishment. If such a mirror were three paces in width, and a man lay flat on his back on the floor and simulated various movements and gestures, all those things would present the portent of a man walking in the air. See the cited figure, where image **B** at the bottom, reflected in mirror **GFE**, appears at **A** above the mirror.

## Corollary.
### So that you may seem to handle a flame with your finger without injury. See fig. 2 of Illustration 33.

<margin>A harmless flame.</margin>
If you place a lit candle in the bottom of the aforementioned concave cylindrical mirror, behold, 그 flame will be projected into the middle of the air outside the mirror; and since that is not a true flame, but only its <term>image<gloss>original: "idolum"</gloss></term>, you will be able to handle it without harm. When I exhibited this spectacle to some friends, and they saw my hand moving through the middle of the flame with impunity, they were struck with terror; fearing that I would bring harm upon myself by such a long burning, they tried by every means to pull my hand away. While they were doing this, it would simultaneously appear that the hand was so far removed from the true flame that there could be no danger of burning. And I have found these two modes to be the true ones, surpassing all the other false ones cited everywhere by authors; therefore, I advise you to use them. In the same way, using an optical tube adapted in a certain manner, figures are represented in the middle of the air—

# The Great Art of Light and Shadow, Book 10. Magic, Part III.

### Trick III.

->*To represent any figures in the air.*<-

<margin>The visual forms of things cannot be represented in the air.</margin>
In the preceding two propositions, we discussed the images of things to be represented in the air by means of mirrors; now we must also consider whether the images of things can be cast into the air itself without a mirror. I answer that since pure air, uncontaminated by any stain of vapor, is incapable of receiving any impression due to its excessive <term>transparency<gloss>original Greek: ἀδιαφάνειαν, meaning a lack of opacity</gloss></term>, it is impossible by any means for a figure to be represented as if impressed upon it. This is because all visual forms, in order to appear, require a denser medium to terminate or "stop" them, as can be seen when images are projected into a <term>darkened room<gloss>a camera obscura</gloss></term>. This is also why the forms of things do not appear in open air, as they find no obstacle there by which they might be halted. However, if some obstacle occurs that stops the diffusion of these forms, they immediately begin to appear, as seen in the rainbows of a dewy cloud, <term>parhelia<gloss>sun dogs or "mock suns"</gloss></term>, various colors of clouds, and many other things of this kind. But if a denser medium is so prepared that it perfectly imitates a mirror, it will then reflect not only light, but also the colors and images of individual things, just as we treated at length in the second section regarding the "aerial mirror." Therefore, certain impostors and vain showmen are to be laughed at when they claim that, by the help of mirrors, any written letters or shapes can be painted and formed in the middle of the open air. We have already explained in the second section of this part how we can exhibit images of things within an artificial vapor. Furthermore, we showed in the final Problem of the second part how to represent this same thing in open air that is free of all vapor.

### Trick IV.

->*Forms of things are displayed in the air by means of a magnet used together with a mirror.*<-

Let the mirrors be arranged in such a way that the primary image hangs in the air, yet remains unseen, as if attracted by a magnet—much like what was handed down regarding the <term>Dove of Archytas<gloss>A famous mechanical wooden dove from antiquity said to be able to fly</gloss></term> in my work *The Magnetic Art*. For if you place another mirror opposite this, the reflected form will appear to hang in the middle of the air within it, to the great admiration of onlookers; yet no trace of any object to which the reflected image could belong will be found. I am accustomed to exhibiting a machine of this kind in my <term>Museum<gloss>Kircher’s famous "Wunderkammer" or gallery of curiosities in Rome</gloss></term>. Everyone marvels at it, yet no one perceives the hidden logic of its arrangement. More on this can be found in our work, *The Mechanical Wonder-Worker*.

---

## CHAPTER VI.

->*On Metamorphosis, or transformation by mirrors.*<-

Not long ago, a certain acquaintance reported that he had seen a book attributed to Johannes Trithemius <note>A famous 15th-century abbot and polymath often accused of practicing "black magic," whom Kircher here defends as a natural scientist.</note>, in which the author promised the transformation of men into any animal whatsoever. However, no one was able to grasp the reasoning behind this assertion; hence, most people reckoned that it could only be done by diabolical arts. Whatever the truth may be regarding the method of metamorphosis exhibited there, I do not wish to argue here. I only say that there are many things in the nature of reality that are <term>infinite and paradoxical<gloss>original Greek: ἄπειρα καὶ παράδοξα</gloss></term>, which can nevertheless be easily put into effect by those who are privy to the secrets of nature. I know that many impious things are falsely attributed to Trithemius, which are so far from being suspicious that nothing seems more consistent with nature, as we shall most clearly demonstrate—God willing—in our *Art of Combinations*. I believe Trithemius's promise can be fulfilled in two ways: either by the <term>catoptric art<gloss>the science of mirrors</gloss></term>, or by a more secret application of things through which a man might think himself turned into an animal. We shall attempt to carry out both according to the truth that experience, the mistress of things, has taught us.

<margin>How a man can be transformed into any animal.</margin>

### Metamorphosis I.

> To set up a mirror machine using flat mirrors so that a man looking into the mirror sees the face of a donkey, an ox, a deer, a hawk, or similar animals, instead of a human face.

First, let an octagonal wheel **HGFD** be made; that is, one which has eight seats or positions around its circumference, of the same size as a human head, as you see here. On each side, let the heads of various animals be painted, joined to a human neck. Let the rotating machine be enclosed on all sides so that none of the pictures can be seen, except for the one which is placed opposite the mirror and marked with the letters **DT**. This being done, let a wooden post **MV** be erected opposite the machine, at the end of which (**M**) there is a pulley (**M**); at **Q**, it is equipped with a joint, so that by a cord **NMOP**, the mirror...

...a goat’s head, and a little after a bear’s head, and so on, will appear; all these will be displayed according to the principles of <term>physiognomy<note>The practice of judging character or type from facial features; here used to mean the realistic appearance of different species.</note></term> <note>original: φυσιογνωμικὰ</note>, provided you place a human neck beneath them. If, however, you desire to see your own image by pulling the cord **MOP**, let the mirror be placed perpendicular to the horizon, and you will have what you seek. Note that the entire chest, within which the octagonal wheel is secretly turned, must be arranged so that no light is admitted except for the light **S** from **B**, which first enters the window toward mirror **C**, and from there is reflected through the opening **RSDV** onto the side of the octagonal wheel. For since this light illuminates the hidden images, it will also clearly carry the illuminated image from the mirror to the eye of the spectator **Z**. All of this will come close to being a magician’s trick if you create a solid head of some animal covered with natural fur, whose eyes, fashioned from glass enamel, are moved by small strings or some other artifice; let the mouth also be opened and closed by a secret thread. I say that if you enclose this simulacrum within the described machine so that it cannot be seen from any other place except where the light falls upon it, and if the opening is placed so high that a human of normal stature cannot reach it, you will perform things that will scarcely be believed possible by human ingenuity. I possess a machine of this kind which strikes everyone with great wonder, for as they look in, instead of a natural face, they see now a wolf's face, now a dog's, and then the face of another animal. If, furthermore, someone were to fashion a skull out of any material, hollow inside, and cover the bored-out eyes, nose, and the gap of the mouth with thin paper soaked in oil, and then hide a lamp in the designated place inside, he would undoubtedly see a spectacle more terrifying than words can describe.

## Metamorphosis II.
### *To exhibit various spectacles of things in the midst of darkness.*

If the theater of spectators were at **Z**, and larger mirrors were fixed at **NM** to receive their light from window **A**, any spectacles could be exhibited from the position of the wheel **HGFD**, which the spectators at **Z**, sitting in darkness, would see alone. For we assume that window **A** is placed in such a location that it can communicate none of its light to location **Z**. I performed an experiment of this thing before I committed these words to the press: and indeed, it can hardly be said how much admiration such a phantom excites in the spectator, who cannot conceive from where the light shines upon the represented objects when all cracks are most tightly sealed, since neither the pouring in of light nor the spectator can be noticed by any means. The spectacle will be increased by two or more mirrors attached like wings to a larger mirror, so that they form an obtuse angle with it. Once this is done, the <term>optical projection<note>The way images are cast or reflected into space.</note></term> of the forms from both sides will seem to stretch into infinite space, and a theater will appear filled with an infinite multitude of Actors, with a long order of columns produced over a very great distance according to the rules of <term>scenography<note>The art of perspective representation in theatrical scenery.</note></term>: but practice itself will instruct you better in all things. I read in the History of the Arabs, which is titled *Dakerellschriphin* <note>Likely *Dhakhirat al-Shurafa* (The Treasure of Nobles).</note>, that a certain King of Baghdad, a philosopher, performed such admirable things with the aid of a machine of this kind that he extorted whatever he wished from his subjects by means of such deceptive portents and apparitions; they believed these things happened by heavenly grace all the more easily because they were simple-minded.

### *By what means products can also be made through Epharmosis, or sciagraphic transformation.*

In a flat mirror, however, the said Metamorphosis can be displayed differently: and indeed by a most secret method, if you paint the said images on threads stretched over the image on the sides of the octagonal wheel, as we showed above in *Parastatic Magic* <note>The branch of magic dealing with appearing and disappearing images.</note> on page 811. For an image painted on threads and directed very obliquely toward the mirror will reflect one image when falling directly on the mirror, and another when reflected obliquely. The same will happen if you attach triangular tiles to the sides of the octagon and paint images on their sides: for in this way, the method of the appearance in the mirror is rendered so hidden that it can scarcely be investigated. As to how the said images ought to be painted on threads and tiles, see *Parastatic Magic*, on the cited page.

## Corollary.
### *To construct a Catoptric Clock.*

From these things, it is clear how a clock can be constructed in which the hour that is currently passing always appears to the viewer. For if you make a wheel consisting of 24 flat sides or seats, and paint the individual hours in order on each side, and assign a movement of twenty-four hours to the wheel by means of weights: you will have what you sought. By this industry, the governance of the seven Planets attributed to the individual hours could also be displayed: in a word, there is nothing so exotic that it cannot be represented to a person by this art. The demonstration depends on Proposition IV of this book.

->Catoptric Magic.<-

# Transformation III.

## Through convex cylindrical and conical mirrors.

*How to construct a cylindrical or conical mirror in which all the previously mentioned effects may appear. See Figure 4, Illustration 33.*

**F**irst, let a cylindrical mirror **O** be made of any size. Depending on its size, let the figure of any animal be painted—distorted according to the rules of the <term>Sciographic Art<note>The study of projecting shadows and perspective; here specifically referring to anamorphosis, where a drawing is stretched so it only looks normal when viewed in a specific mirror.</note></term> provided in the second book—onto the sides of the recently mentioned octagonal wheel. In the cylinder or cone, these will display the desired figure, so that the person looking into the mirror sees nothing except the figure depicted on the plane. If, however, you transform or distort any figure on the vertical plane **CDEF** into a conical shape according to the rules of the Sciographic Art, and you look at a cone fixed perpendicularly to a wall so that your lines of sight correspond perfectly to the axis of the cone: that image (of which scarcely a trace is found outside the mirror due to the excessive distortion of its outlines) will appear on the surface of the conical mirror. This effect is both beautiful and praiseworthy, especially if many conical mirrors are fixed perpendicularly here and there on the walls of a museum alongside these transformed figures, as shown in figure **B**. But leaving these things aside as they are commonly known, let us move on to others.

***

# Another method for this Transformation.

<margin>An image that is seen in the mirror without the spectator appearing.</margin>
I. **F**rom these things, it is clear that images can be so arranged toward a mirror that, depending on the tilt or reclining of the mirror, now a man, now a woman, now Peter, then Paul, now a human, then a donkey, presents itself to the view of the spectator **Z**. This is done if the images of said things are painted in pieces upon the sides of "scalar" <note>stepped or corrugated</note> wooden slats. For the hidden figures, when gathered back together in the mirror, will meet the eyes of the spectator as whole images. All these effects will be multiplied infinitely if you add mirror "wings" <note>side mirrors</note> to the mirror, as was demonstrated in the catoptric machine of the preceding illustration. To ensure that a specific image of a Prince always appears in the mirror and nothing else besides it (such as the portrait of Cosimo, Great Duke of Tuscany, which appears here in the Medici-Salustian Palace), this is easily achieved through "scalar" woods, as has been said. For the image, inscribed in pieces on the hidden sides of wooden triangles, is gathered in the mirror and carries the image to the eyes of the spectator. Or it may glide into the mirror from some other hidden place and be carried from there to the eyes.

We read that the Great Duke of Tuscany sent a mirror to Henry II, King of France, in which nothing could be seen except the perpetually visible portrait of the Great Duke. It is asked how this was done. I respond that it could have been done in various ways: first, with the image secretly distorted on the sides that held the mirror in place as an ornament, which were then gathered in the mirror to present the image to the spectator.
<margin>A heterodictic <note>showing something other than what is in front of it</note> mirror.</margin>
Furthermore, the mirror was tilted in such a way that the person looking in never saw themselves, but only the appearance of the distorted image, all of which is clear from the preceding sections. Secondly, if a painter were to etch an image with a fine stylus into the foil <note>original: "folio"</note> by which the mirror is backed with the help of quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, and then tilt the mirror slightly, it is certain that nothing would be seen in the mirror except the etched image.

<margin>What are "scalar" woods?</margin>
So that the reader may know what we mean by "scalar" woods: we say they are oblong pieces of wood fashioned in the manner of a prism and arranged in order, exactly in the manner shown by the figure of the glass prisms in Illustration 29 on page 818. These, glued onto a board at a slight distance from one another, will provide three spaces in which images may be dispersed. The first space is the background of the board; the second space is the right face of the prisms; and finally, the third space is provided by the left face of the prisms. If you paint different images on these three and place two mirrors on the right and left, different images will appear in the mirrors; and someone looking directly at the "scalar" board will find yet another different image. However, we have described this device somewhat more ingeniously using certain threads to grid the board in the second scenographic presentation of "Parastatic Magic," which the curious reader may consult.

II. From what has been said, it is also clear by what method letters can be represented in a mirror in a different language than they appear outside of it. Since everything in a mirror appears reversed, take different words which, when read backward, have a meaning in another language; move them toward the mirror so they can be read both outside and inside the mirror, and you will have what you seek. Thus the word **AVE** <note>Latin: "Hail"</note> will be read in the mirror as **EVA** <note>Latin: "Eve"</note>; the Greek **OTI** <note>original: "OTI", meaning "that"</note> as **ITO** <note>original: "ITO", meaning "go"</note>; **MARE** <note>Latin: "Sea"</note> as **ERAM** <note>Latin: "I was"</note>. In this way, this half-line of verse, when written outside and represented inside the mirror, will complete a full couplet.

# The Great Art, Book 10. Magic Part III.

->SIGN YOURSELF, YOU SIGN YOURSELF RASHLY<-

Countless other things could be said in this place: but since all these flow from one principle, I leave them to be unearthed by others.

### Metamorphosis IV.

->*To transform the face into various colors.*<-

Let an octagonal body or prism be made, onto each of whose sides mirrors of different colors are attached. For if you darken a green crystal into a mirror, men will appear conspicuous with green faces; if you darken red, blue, yellow, purple, or black crystal into mirrors, you will have mirrors in which you may behold men now red like <term>Satyrs</term><note>Wild woodland deities from Greek mythology, often depicted with red or ruddy skin.</note>, now yellow, as if they have jaundice; or perhaps blue, and black like <term>Ethiopians</term><note>A common early modern term for people from sub-Saharan Africa.</note>. Furthermore, if the glass is somewhat wrinkled, it will show premature old age—that is, a wrinkled face—but the clearest mirrors, stretched most evenly, will show a beautiful, bright, and clear face. If, therefore, as I said, you attach these said mirrors to the individual sides of an octagonal body and hide the body so that only one mirror appears through a certain opening, the sides of the different mirrors, applied to the opening with versatile skill, will show different effects in the representation of faces; which is what we intended to do.

### Metamorphosis V.

->*To deform a human face in a thousand ways.*<-

Let a segment of an elliptical mirror be made, or if you cannot have that, let a segment be formed out of thick paper; for if you apply a sheet of <term>selenite</term><note>A transparent variety of gypsum or mica that was often used for optical experiments before high-quality glass was widely available.</note> (previously made into a mirror) over this so that it adheres to the paper without a wrinkle or fold, you will have a mirror that transforms the human face into a thousand forms. For if you look into it lengthwise, the head will seem to gradually taper into a cone; soon it will sprout into 3, 4, 5, 6, or 8 eyes; and now the mouth, like a certain cave or a steep crag, will be made rough with sharp teeth.
<margin>The all-shaped face.</margin>
If you look into this mirror widthwise, it will first render you visible without a forehead, then with donkey ears: nothing can be more deformed than the nose and mouth, for they will be produced so sinuously—especially if you show a bared grin of teeth—that it might seem like a rocky sea coast; immediately it will give you a double or triple head: in a word, the monstrous variety of the appearance can scarcely be explained in words. You will produce the same monsters if you reduce wavy glass into a mirror by applying a leaf of tin.

### Metamorphosis VI.

->*To monstrously transform a human face into various animals.*<-

<margin>Face of a Stork.</margin>
If you desire to see yourself with the neck of a stork, let the plane of the mirror bulge out somewhere on the side into a boss, then downward from the boss into a cylindrical swelling; this will be easily done if you first make a mold and stretch a sheet of <term>selenite</term> mirror over it. If you look at this mirror straight on, you will see your face changed into the head of a Crane with a very long neck; if you look at it obliquely, it will be defiled into a river with a bank, or even a face with a rhinoceros horn growing out of the forehead. If you desire to exhibit a goat-like face, the mirror will bulge into two bosses from a somewhat wavy plane, and one will look at oneself under the form of a Satyr—foul, horned, wrinkled, and ridiculous with a wide-gaping mouth. It will also exhibit a ruddy and inflamed face of a drunkard if you line it with a red leaf. You will see a deer's head if you form the mirror with branching bosses. In a word, there is no monster so foul that you cannot see yourself under its form in a mirror prepared with similar industry: the reason for all of which is the mixing of the mirror plane with curved lines.

### Metamorphosis VII.

->*To show a human face in various ways with two flat mirrors.*<-

Let two flat mirrors be adapted in the manner of a book by a certain small box, so that they may be hidden, closed, and opened into the shape under which one intends to represent someone. This having been done, set up the machine so that one mirror is parallel to the horizon, but the other stands almost perpendicularly upon the first; and you will see, under this positioning, your face without eyes, ears, or nose—only the forehead and mouth protruding. If you incline it a little more, you will now behold the forehead, mouth, and nose, but without any eyes. If you incline it a little more, behold, he who a little before was destitute of eyes will now appear <term>tetrephthalmos</term><note>Greek: "four-eyed".</note>, that is, conspicuous with four eyes. Furthermore, if you incline the mirror to about the eightieth degree, you will now be gifted with a double head; and up to this point, all the said phantoms will maintain their position. From the 60th to the 45th degree of inclination, however, you will see yourself in a straight and natural form; thereafter, with the mirror always inclined more and more, you will appear <term>diphthalmos</term><note>Greek: "two-eyed".</note>, now <term>triophthalmos</term><note>Original Greek text says "πριέφθαλμος", likely a typo for "τριέφθαλμος" (three-eyed).</note>, now with two wh—

...indeed, with the heads [of the images] separated, but the vertices joined, you will witness a ridiculous sight, and in this way more and more different faces will constantly come forth until no more images appear in the mirror. But if you change the position of both mirrors so that both are in a vertical position, you will soon multiply yourself according to the degree of the opening: occasionally appearing with three eyes in two heads—in the same manner that they are accustomed to depicting the **Most Holy Trinity**<note>original: "Sanctissimam Trinitatem" — Kircher refers to a specific iconographic tradition, sometimes called the "Trifacial Trinity," where a single head was shown with three faces or overlapping features to represent the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Truly, all these things will be better seen by the experimenter. The reason for all this has been assigned at length in the preceding pages.

## Metamorphosis VIII.

->*To represent the same through concave-convex mirrors. See fig. 3. Icon. 33.*<-

Let two mirrors be made, of which one has a concave segment of 72 degrees—that is, the side of a **pentagon**<note>In geometry, the side of a regular pentagon subtends an angle of 72 degrees at the center of its circumscribed circle.</note>—while the other consists of a convex segment of 60 degrees; let these be joined together so that they appear as one mirror, as shown here in the figure. This mirror produces wondrous **illusions**<note>original: "phasmata" — ghostly appearances, specters, or optical phantasms.</note>; for to one standing two cubits away, the image will appear proportionate and similar to the true form; but to one standing further away, the image is stretched forward; yet to one approaching closer to the convex surface of the mirror, the image turns into a notable deformity, which will always be rendered more shapeless the more you approach. Now it looks like a long, drawn-out mass, now like a curved boss, now like a beaked likeness; now you will see a split face, so that the middle part turns upward and the other downward. Indeed, **Proteus**<note>A sea god in Greek mythology capable of changing his shape to any form.</note> himself did not transform into so many figures but that this fantastic mirror will transform you into even more. Countless things could be said here about the wondrous spectacles in spherical-convex, concave-convex, spherical-cylindrical, and cylindrical-conical mirrors which, as they are essentially distinct, also produce diverse and utterly marvelous transformations; but since anyone can more easily experience these for themselves than I can describe in even many words, we have decided to deliberately omit them, lest the work grow beyond measure. Contenting ourselves for now with this small collection of **Catoptric**<note>The branch of optics dealing with reflections and mirrors.</note> equipment, we trust the curious reader will derive countless other things from it.

## Metamorphosis IX.

->*To transform a human being through natural things.*<-

In the beginning of this book, we said that a human being could be transformed into any shape. Know, therefore, that there are certain natural things which, as soon as they are taken by mouth, exercise power over the **imagination**<note>original: "phantasia" — in early modern science, this was the mental faculty that processed sensory images; Kircher suggests that certain substances can chemically alter how we perceive ourselves.</note>, transforming the person into that toward which they are most inclined. Thus, I know of a root which, when eaten in food, soon transforms men into geese and ducks—not according to their outward appearance, but their internal sight; so that those who have taken it believe themselves to be geese. There are also other things which, when taken in food, transform and change one into cats, dogs, or wolves in the same manner. But since these things are established outside the limits of our art, and are such that, because of the many evils that could emerge from them, they neither should nor can be made public, we only venerate in them that supreme and admirable majesty of nature; we consecrate them to the highest and perpetual silence.

### PREFACE.

<image-desc>Woodcut decorative initial 'I' featuring floral and leaf patterns within a square border.</image-desc>

IT IS so ingrained in the human mind that it strives by every means—with a truly bold and utterly Titanic <note>original: "Giganteo." The author compares human ambition to the Giants of Greek mythology who attempted to scale the heavens.</note> daring—to reach those things that are the province of the Divine Power. These are, specifically, to know the future and to reveal the thoughts of the mind to those who are far away. Although both of these seem at first glance to far exceed the limits of human intelligence, they rightfully hold the chief place among the most hidden secrets. To say nothing of the secrets of astrology: certainly <term>Steganography</term> <note>The art of secret writing or "covered" communication.</note>, or that more hidden method of speaking at a distance, has at all times appeared so marvelous to mortals that even the Monarchs of the world themselves, struck by its rarity and excellence, have felt they possessed nothing so worthy of Royal Majesty as this supreme secret of curiosity. They consider that they alone are blessed by this secret—fortunate in seizing opportunities for counsel and able to complete matters of great importance with the highest speed through this means alone. How much the Emperor Maximilian <note>Maximilian I (1459–1519), Holy Roman Emperor.</note> loved the Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a monk and famous cryptographer whose "Steganographia" was legendary.</note>—who was at that time the only one particularly distinguished in the knowledge of this art—and how much the Emperor himself profited under him, the introduction to his <term>Polygraphy</term> <note>Trithemius's 1518 book on complex cipher systems.</note> sufficiently demonstrates. Concerning this Steganography, since we have discussed it at length in our <term>Magnetic Art</term> <note>Likely referring to the author's work "Magnes" or "Ars Magnetica."</note> and are to deal with it specifically in our <term>Combinatorial Art</term>, we have decided to remain silent in this place.

Therefore, nothing remains here except to reveal that greatest <term>catoptric</term> <note>The branch of optics dealing with reflections and mirrors.</note> secret, by which two friends can communicate with each other safely and securely with almost no effort, even at a distance of three miles. This invention is properly our own, since I do not remember reading anything similar in any author, so far as I know. It is an utterly admirable invention, worthy only of Royal curiosity, since by this single means one can transmit not only the hidden concepts of his mind, but even entire letters, and can write them upon walls; indeed, one can present his own ghostly image, or any other image, with the greatest ease at a very great distance, appearing to his friend in a size larger than a Giant. But leaving behind these wordy detours, let us approach the matter itself, lest we seem to be charming the Reader with words alone.

## PART ONE,
# ON THE PROJECTION
# OF FIGURES
## AT ANY DISTANCE
### BY MEANS OF THE SUN.

---

### CHAPTER I.

*Whether anything can be displayed to be read on the Lunar disk.*

**T**he presumptuous audacity of human madness has progressed so far that it is not content with transmitting characters of letters and forms to be read by friends in a nearby space; it even proposes that these letters be inscribed on the disk of the Moon to be viewed through the <term>catoptric art</term> <note>The science of reflected light and mirrors.</note>. I do not see what could be more foolish or stupid than such a mechanism. They take a mirror—yet they remain silent about its specific shape, out of a desire not to be convicted of insanity, or they describe it with such obscure verbal ambiguities that they themselves do not seem to understand what they mean. <note>Giambattista della Porta (1535–1615), an Italian scholar and polymath known for his work on optics and "natural magic."</note> Porta describes it in these words:

> The mirror is not made of steel, but of glass, a finger’s width in thickness. Let a tin foil be made from purified antimony and lead, such as is usually made in Germany. Let a mold be made of clay; let the glass be placed beneath it and melted in a glassmaker’s furnace so that it takes the shape of the mold. We shall be able to use this artifice in great and marvelous things, and especially for describing letters on the disk of the Moon; for whatever we have engraved on this mirror, we shall be able to send the letters very far away. And since we have said "to infinity," they will easily be sent as far as the Moon, especially since they are aided by its own light.

This is truly a remarkable piece of nonsense. <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous German polymath, physician, and occult writer.</note> Cornelius Agrippa asserts the following in his *Occult Philosophy*:

> If, he says, you inscribe letters on a parabolic mirror and expose it to the Moon at the time of the full moon, those letters—impressed and reflected as if in some vast mirror—can be read anywhere in the world. They say Pythagoras did this while staying at <note>The modern city of Otranto in Italy.</note> Hydruntum; he gave letters inscribed on the Moon to be read by friends at Constantinople.

O, what an impudent lie! Do these <note>original: "Nycticoraces" - literally "night-ravens," here used as a derogatory term for those who operate in intellectual darkness or secrecy.</note> Night-owls think there is no one who knows what a parabolic, or elliptical, or similar mirror is—things which they themselves undoubtedly do not even know by name—or what properties they possess? Is it possible that these manufacturers of lies are not ashamed to philosophize so impudently against all the principles of Catoptrics? For how is it possible for the figures of such tiny letters to be represented when projected across such an immense space? For if they can barely project the figures of letters to a distance of 50 paces, how much less across an infinite and utterly disproportionate space? For what else would a mirror be in relation to the Moon—I do not say a mirror three, four, or five paces long, but even 300, 400, or 500 paces long—if not an imperceptible point? And who could inscribe anything on an imperceptible point? Do these ignorant charlatans think that mathematicians are so unskilled that they do not know the qualities, conditions, and properties of a parabolic mirror? For if we can barely transmit letters fixed in wax to a distance of 20 paces using a parabolic mirror even three palms in diameter—as experience has often taught me—how much less can we do so to the Moon?

<margin>Letters cannot be written on the Moon by any power.</margin>
Even if it were granted (though it is not) that the Moon is like a mirror, there is no way human ingenuity on Earth could make a mirror that would project inscribed things onto the Moon and reflect them back to us from there—unless perhaps someone made a mirror as large as the surface of a quarter of the entire terrestrial sphere. But <note>A Latin idiom meaning "Here is the challenge, now prove yourself."</note> "Here is Rhodes, here is the leap"; for it would be necessary for each individual letter, in order to be represented on the Moon, to occupy twenty degrees, which constitutes 1,200 Italian miles. You see, therefore, curious Reader, what monstrous and absurd things result from such stupid and fanatical opinions, and how the principles of such ignorant men are devoid of all reason. I add: if the Moon were a mirror, it would be of the convex type; and who does not know that a convex...

...by itself, and by its own nature, it is so far from making objects larger that it instead makes them much smaller than their true size, as has been shown in the preceding pages. Therefore, let these "old wives' tales" and the ravings of idle men depart; let sensible Philosophers learn not to rashly trust everything, unless they have first explored every circumstance according to the principles of nature, or by the <term>Lydian stone</term><note>A touchstone used to test the purity of gold, here meaning a standard of truth.</note> of reason. As I have often said, many things are written, spoken, and even pervade the schools which, although they are utterly false and entirely foreign to the principles of nature, are nonetheless held as true everywhere under the pretext of "sympathy" or covered by the cloak of "occult qualities." Thus, I do not wonder that such absurdities are often admitted even in the more sophisticated schools. 

A certain Philosophy was published not long ago in which the Author, when dealing with various illusions, discusses mirrors of this kind among other things. <note>Kircher is likely referring to the works of Cornelius Agrippa or Johannes Trithemius, whose "Steganographia" was often controversial.</note> *There is also another admirable trick: for if someone on a clear night, by some artifice, places an image or written letters against the rays of the full Moon, anyone aware of the matter will be able to read them, and this from any distance, the images being multiplied in the air, carried upward, and reflected back to the earth together with the rays of the Moon. This can also happen with hearing, as sounds are reflected just as it is seen in an Echo, so that someone even at a great distance can hear and understand what another whispers in secret. From this he concludes that it is naturally possible, and without superstition—with no other spirit mediating—for one man to announce the concept of his mind to another at any vast, even unknown distance in a very short time. Although that time cannot be precisely measured, it must happen within 24 hours. He says that Cornelius Agrippa knew how to do this and did it, just as he sufficiently implies that Trithemius did it as well.* 

And although I do not deny that it is possible by human power to transmit the hidden concepts of the mind over a vast space in a short amount of time, we utterly deny that it happens via letters imprinted on a Lunar mirror, for the reasons indicated just before. I am also aware that "magic mirrors" are made in which images of absent things are exhibited as if present, of which kind was undoubtedly that which Agrippa said he used. 

<margin>Magic mirrors.</margin>
But since all these things occur through diabolical illusions, we, shunning them with all our might <note>original: "remis velisque fugientes," literally "with oars and sails."</note>, rightly condemn and execrate them along with the Holy Mother Church. Of this kind, if the things noted by Historians are true, was that mirror which King Ptolemy Euergetes is read to have constructed in the Tower of Pharos, in which the ships of enemies and whatever happened on land and sea, and even in all of Egypt, was represented. 

To all of these, since they exceed the limits of nature, no faith should be given.

## CHAPTER II.
## Regarding the Mirrors Necessary for Catoptric Steganography.

<margin>Glass mirror.</margin>
**F**or Catoptric Steganography <note>The art of projecting secret messages using reflected light.</note>, three things are required: a mirror, a <term>mesoptic glass</term><note>A lens placed in the middle of the optical path to focus the light.</note>, and a support. The mirror must be flat and not made of glass or steel, but cast from a metallic material. First, it cannot be glass or crystal because of the depth of the material that makes the mirror opaque; this causes the reflected ray, refracted in the denser medium, to return to the wall doubled. This makes the characters unsightly and causes the greatest confusion.

<margin>Steel.</margin>
It also cannot be made of steel, because steel is intolerant of all moisture <note>It would rust and lose its reflective quality.</note>.

<margin>Metallic.</margin>
Since we must write the perceptions of our mind upon this mirror—as it is the base and foundation of the entire steganographic operation—and since it is easily infected and fouled by the corrosive juice of ink, catching rust, it cannot serve our purpose conveniently. Therefore, a flat mirror cast from metal <note>Likely a polished alloy like bell-metal or speculum metal.</note> will be most suitable for our operations; for this, above others, can be polished most easily and can sustain the ink without any damage.

<margin>The superiority of hyperbolic glass.</margin>
Secondly, a mesoptic glass of either a lenticular or <term>hyperbolic</term> shape is required, as much as possible with an obtuse section of a half-palm diameter. Blessed is he who reaches the hyperbolic glass according to the standard of the eye’s pupil; for he will see and marvel at an effect ten times that of a particular lens. We have discussed the method for both the lens and the hyperbola extensively in the preceding sections; the hyperbola will have its effect at the greatest distance, while the lens at a shorter distance. The greater the distance, the larger the hyperbola must be. And these things suffice regarding the glass; however, to perform the experiment of the art, a lenticular glass of a more obtuse convexity will suffice.

Thirdly, a support is required, which should be made as follows. Let there be an oblong piece of wood **CD**, which has a cleft **GH** in the middle, within which the mirror **A** can run. Let the glass **B**, as well as the mirror **A**, be equipped with their own pivots <note>original: "vertebris," joints or vertebrae.</note> so that they may be fixed in every direction and position with versatile industry. The foot supporting the machine will be a short one, **F**, so that it can be more easily placed on the sills of windows.

<summary>Kircher dismisses superstitious claims about moon-mirrors and magical divination, instead proposing a scientific system for "Catoptric Steganography." He details the necessary equipment: a polished metal mirror, a specialized lens (hyperbolic or lenticular), and a mechanical wooden support.</summary>

## On Concave Mirrors.

**Concave mirrors** can also serve this business very well, for they greatly enlarge the images of things and present them most clearly. However, since not everyone possesses mirrors of this kind, we use **flat mirrors**, which are more easily obtained. Indeed, mirrors crafted according to a section of 18 degrees <note>The "18 degrees" likely refers to the specific curvature or angle of the mirror's manufacture intended to optimize reflection.</note> perform truly prodigious operations in this work and project the shadows of things over a greater distance. For this reason, I thought this matter should be shared only with a few friends and experts.

---

### CHAPTER III.
### On the distance required for projecting the forms of things.

<margin>No natural agent can act into infinity.</margin>

Since no natural agent can act across an infinite distance, it must necessarily have a certain and determined **sphere of activity**. We call the radius of this sphere the distance between the **agent** <note>The active source, in this case, the light and mirror.</note> and the **patient** <note>The receiving surface or target.</note>. Within this distance, all perceptible actions of natural things are contained. Light establishes such a sphere more sensibly than all other agents; as it propagates through a medium, it spreads itself in a varying manner until, the sensible images of light being lost, it finally ends in shadow. This sphere extends further when an intervening body intensifies the light; light is intensified most effectively by a **lenticular glass** <note>A magnifying lens.</note>, hyperbolic shapes, and others of this kind—as was said previously—when placed at a location proportioned to the distance between the light and the boundary of the light. Reflected forms, which are our proper subject here, are granted a shorter distance than direct forms. These things being established:

It is asked how far reflected forms of things can be projected. The answer is that since light is manifold, it also obtains a manifold sphere of its reflected diffusion. The rays of the Sun diffuse reflected forms to the greatest distance of all; a candle does so to a lesser distance.

<margin>The Author’s Experience.</margin>

Led by experience, I found that a glass the size of a **half-palm** <note>A "palm" was a common unit of measurement, approximately 3-4 inches or 9-10 cm.</note> could project the forms of things up to 500 feet, so that those standing around in a dark place could read the projections most distinctly. The mirror was, as stated, a flat mirror of half-palm size, while the round lenticular glass had a diameter of one-third of a palm. Therefore, assuming a proportional increase in both the mirror and the glass, it will project the reflected images of things farther the larger each of them is. Thus, if the mirror and the glass were both **eight palms** wide, I say that it could again sensibly project images to a distance of 12,000 feet; there is no reason to doubt this. 

Having found this, I do not see what could be more divine: for it is a paradox, and by everyone’s opinion incredible, to speak with another by a mirror at a distance of **three leagues** <note>A league was roughly 3 miles (4.8 km), meaning Kircher is claiming a range of 9 miles.</note>, and to exhibit any figures, and even entire letters, to be read before them. Yet, that this is indeed the case is known only to him to whom alone on earth I have revealed the secret. The only inconvenience that arises is that the images of things are enlarged immensely; for example, a single letter might appear to grow progressively to the size of a tower. Another inconvenience is that the further the images of things are carried, the more weakly they appear, so that unless the entire room is dark, almost nothing will show. If, therefore, someone finds a way to reduce the figures of things at a great distance to a smaller proportion and show them clearly, he will rejoice in having found a secret he can boast of. Being lacking in both the leisure and the funds for conducting such experiments, I have not yet been able to grasp the solution. Yet let no one doubt that this can be done by the arrangement of intervening concave mirrors. I believe I have sufficiently revealed the secret in this place.

FIRST, we shall teach how to transmit letters. But before we do so, it must be noted: nothing can be written by this art of ours except upon the walls of some shaded and dark place. For just as no reflected ray is easily seen in manifest light, neither are the species of things inscribed on a mirror seen when reflected from it. The darker the place is, the more exquisitely and minutely the shadows of things will appear. Whoever desires to perform this practice, then, should first inscribe whatever he wishes with simple ink upon a flat mirror (A). But since letters [have] a right and natural position on the mir—

<margin>Practical steganography.</margin>
Once the letters are inscribed, turn the flat mirror until the reflected ray falls precisely into a dark place. If, however, the reflected ray cannot be seen due to the distance, a line of sight directed alongside the reflected ray will immediately reveal the line of the steganographic <note>Steganography here refers to the art of hidden or long-distance communication.</note> direction. This being done at a distance in proportion—which one must first find through observation, namely by moving the glass closer to or further from the mirror—the form of the things will appear as distinctly as possible within the room.

<margin>Types of letters and various colors.</margin>
For once this is completed, the entire message will be seen within the walls of the room, to the great wonder of the onlookers, with letters projected a foot and a half long, and thus the entire wall will be seen covered in writing. Moreover, the letters will appear larger the longer the distance is. It should also be noted here that the individual letters appear to be painted in every kind of color by some hidden artifice of "Painting Nature" <note>Kircher often personifies Nature as an artist ("Natura pictrix") to explain natural optical phenomena.</note>; since this effect is so unusual, it can hardly be put into words how much admiration it arouses in the spectators.

### CHAPTER V.
->On the projection of shadows, or of figures of any kind.<-

<margin>Solomon's magical representation.</margin>
**A**fter we have dealt with the projection of letters in the preceding sections, we must speak in this chapter about the projection of figures. It is written in the book on Magic that the most wise King Solomon, in order to strike terror of his majesty into his subjects, represented his own image in many places, even those far distant from him. Most people interpret this as a fabrication of the Rabbis, since they do not think it could be done except by the necromantic art. We, however, shall show in this place that similar things could have been done naturally by the wisest of mortals through the catoptric art <note>The science of mirrors and reflection.</note>. And first of all, it is certain that there is no figure or image that cannot be transmitted by the aforementioned method. Therefore, if you wish to represent yourself to your friend, you should first paint your likeness on the aforementioned mirror; however, the outer outline of the face is sufficient, which is commonly called a **profile** <term>praefilum</term> <note>Kircher uses the term "praefilum" to mean a preliminary sketch or outline used as a template.</note>. With the mirror arranged toward the Sun, I say that the reflected ray will perfectly demonstrate your shadow or likeness in a dark place. For the principle is the same for characters and for images; but experience will teach you all things better than I could show even with many words.

<margin>Why was Roger Bacon certainly considered a Mage?</margin>
By this art, we read of many things done in histories which, in the common opinion of many, were held to be diabolical operations. Certainly Roger Bacon, while he offered his shadow to be recognized by distant and remote friends in a dark place, has been held by almost everyone even until now as a Necromancer; yet he was a man of philosophy who could have performed all said things by this art, without any trace of a suspect craft.

### CHAPTER VI.
->On shadows, or colored images.<-

**T**his appears the most paradoxical among the rest: that not only can shadows be transmitted and represented on distant walls, but even images shaded with every kind of color. Indeed, it would be a difficult business if experience had not made us more certain of it. For if you paint an image on our metallic mirror with that kind of colors which we call **translucent** <term>pellucentes</term> <note>Transparent pigments that allow light to pass through them, essential for projection.</note>, not only the shadow of the object, but the colors of the shadow will also appear on the walls.

<margin>Wondrous exhibitions of things.</margin>
Here you may see the faces of men shining with natural color, a garment now glowing with a red color, now a yellow; turning from yellow into white, from red into crimson and gold, and from this into green, and finally ending from green into blue with a certain admirable variety. You will recognize here any likenesses of men naturally exhibited according to the condition of the original model. This matter has quite frequently provided such an admirable spectacle that, even among those who otherwise have the reputation of being sharp philosophers, it has more than once led the Author <note>Kircher refers to himself in the third person here.</note> into the suspicion of the necromantic art.

# CHAPTER VII.
### *Concerning the theatrical or historical representation of things.*

**I**t has become sufficiently clear from what has preceded, if I am not mistaken, by what method likenesses of men and animals can be projected to a distance by the <term>Catoptric art</term> <note>original: "Catoptrica"; the branch of optics dealing with reflections and mirrors</note>. It remains, therefore, for us to explain how motion can be introduced to them. This shall be done in the following manner. Let realistic figures of the things to be shown be made out of paper, designed according to their outer surface only—what is commonly called a <term>profile</term> <note>original: "profilum"</note>; let the feet and arms be movable at the joints, so that at the will of the artist they can be raised, spread, or joined, or now lifted, lowered, and finally placed in any position by hidden threads. When these have been glued to the surface of the mirror, operate as before by projecting the reflected light together with the shadows of the images into a dark place: and behold, a sight to inspire dread, the shadows will display every movement upon the wall, not without causing a tremor in those watching. If, however, you desire to exhibit living flies, let the edge of the mirror be smeared with honey, and behold, the shadows of the flies walking every which way across the surface of the mirror, when projected onto the wall, will represent living flies there, but of remarkable size. This same trick can be performed by means of a magnet; for flies, or any other things equipped with a needle, will follow the lead of a magnet applied to the back of the mirror wherever the artist wishes. Certainly, these representations are so mysterious that unless the method were expressly taught to the spectators, hardly anyone could escape the suspicion of the Magic art.

# CHAPTER VIII.
### *To describe a steganographic clock.*

**L**et a clock be painted on a mirror by the same practice you see used here, together with the numbers; then let it be projected by a reflected ray onto the dark walls of some room: and behold, a perfect clock will be seen delineated in an instant. The hours, moreover, will be shown thus: Let the exact hour be known from some other clock, and above the line of the hour found, apply to the mirror a fly, or a lizard, or some other thing fashioned from thin paper to take the place of a <term>gnomon</term> <note>original: "gnomonis"; the part of a sundial or clock that casts the shadow to indicate time</note>: and behold, the shadow of the animal in the projected clock will show the desired hour, wherever you turn the shadow of the clock. I could bring forward countless other things in this place, but I deliberately remain silent about them so that I may provide the curious reader with some opportunity for new inventions. For this is truly and properly <term>Parastatic Natural Magic</term> <note>original: "Magia naturalis Parastatica"; a term used by Kircher for the art of producing apparitions or representations that seem to appear out of nowhere</note>, by which a man can truly exhibit those things which surpass every sense and faculty of the mind.

# PART TWO.
## CONCERNING CATOPTRIC STEGANOGRAPHY BY THE LIGHT OF A CANDLE.

**S**ince in the preceding part the projection of images of things into distant places by solar light has been treated more than enough, nothing else remains except that we teach how all the aforesaid things can be exhibited at night in distant places with the aid of a single candle. I explain the method. Having discovered this new <term>Catoptric Steganography</term> <note>original: "Steganographia Catoptrica"; secret signaling or writing via mirrors</note> through the reflected projection of solar light, a great desire suddenly came over my mind to know some way by which it might be done at night by the light of a lamp. For since experience taught that a flat mirror could be least suited to this nocturnal <term>Cryptology</term> <note>original: "Cryptologæ"; secret communication</note>, and could not project the images of things by any method due to the weakness of the light, I attempted everything so that I might finally achieve the desired success: and not in vain: I discovered certain methods through a continuous combination of things, by which all those things which solar li-

We have taught that what can be achieved with the aid of sunlight can also be displayed by the benefit of a single candle. In this way, images of things can be projected onto the outer surfaces of windows so that there is not even a need for any opening of the window; instead, those situated inside the room can conveniently perceive the mutual thoughts of a friend from the shadows cast upon paper windows. The practice is indeed exactly the same as the preceding ones, but the mirror used is different.

### *The First Method.*

**L**et there be made, first, a <term>concave mirror</term> <note>original: "speculum concavum"; a mirror curved inward like a bowl to focus light</note> with a section as obtuse as possible; such as we indicated in the preceding sections, of 18 degrees; or if the craftsman is industrious, let it be made in a <term>parabolic shape</term> <note>original: "forma parabolica"; a specific geometric curve that perfectly focuses light to a single point</note>; together with a <term>hyperbolic lens tube</term> <note>original: "tubo lenticulari hyperboliformi"</note> proportioned to the hollow of the mirror. For when these are properly prepared and exposed to a candle—positioned so that the candle is placed between the mirror and the glass at such a distance until you see the candle illuminating the entire concave surface of the mirror—you will then receive the reflected images of things inscribed in the middle of the glass. These will finally exhibit the appearance of things on a shaded wall, just as previously occurred in the sun. Furthermore, the representation of images or shadows in dark rooms is much more fearsome than that representation which happens in the sun. By this art, the wicked could easily be restrained from the perpetration of crimes by having the form of a devil inscribed on the mirror and transmitted into a dark place. But we leave all these things to be further refined by the curious genius of the reader.

### *The Second Method.*

**S**ince, however, not everyone is equipped with an apparatus of such mirrors, these things can be accomplished by a more easily obtained machine using this invention. Let a glass sphere be taken—the larger it is, the more fit it is for executing the purpose. On its convex surface, if you wish to speak with a friend, you shall inscribe your thought through abbreviated words. If you wish to represent yourself or anything else, you shall paint an image of yourself or something similar. This being done, if you place a lit torch behind the glass sphere opposite the letters, and then receive the radiant projection with a lens glass in a determined spot (as was done in the previous mirrors), you will project the letters and figures inscribed on the sphere onto the interior of walls even at a great distance, to the great admiration of onlookers. This experiment is much easier and more certain, and will act at a greater distance than a concave mirror. Note, however, that the use of this is only possible at night by candle; it has no use in the sun, because the radiant projection of the sun cannot reach any intended place through this. Innumerable things could be said in this place regarding the application of this mechanism. But so that we may leave new material for discovering things to others as well, and lest the work grow to an immense size, we voluntarily break off the thread of these machinations, mindful of the words of <note>Menander (c. 342–291 BC), a Greek dramatist</note> Menander himself:

->*The wise man says much in few words.*<-
<note>original Greek: "Ὁ σοφὸς πολλὰ ὀλίγοις τοῖς λόγοις"</note>

# EPILOGUE,
# OR THE
# METAPHYSICS
## OF LIGHT AND SHADOW.

**M**artianus, that famous philosopher <note>Martianus Capella, a 5th-century writer whose work "The Marriage of Philology and Mercury" allegorically described the liberal arts</note>, records that once, while Philosophy was meditating on climbing to the summit of the Triple Unity, she vomited forth spheres and circles along with fire. Is it any wonder that we, upon whom all labor weighs in the sphere of the soul, have—by an ardent study of that Philosophy, turning step by step from the lowest things through middle degrees toward that unspeakable light of the Union and the Trinity—lifted up our eyes and hands in prayer?

<margin>*A Declaration*</margin>
> Grant pardon, You great Sower of the Gods and King of Men: for I have done these things not in a spirit of contention, nor out of a desire to scrutinize Your majesty, nor in hope of empty glory, but for the sake of the common good; and so far as You Yourself permit, I shall establish this as a hymn and a burnt offering in praise of Your name. Only You, Father of Eternal Wisdom, sign the light of Your countenance upon us, and let even a small spark of such great splendor grow warm in our hearts—
