# The Great Art, Book 10. Epilogue. #

...tiny spark, so that the works of your hands may be revealed to both the infant and the small child, and that your majesty may be blessed from the highest, middle, and lowest levels of the world for ages of ages. <note>This opening fragment concludes a prayer or dedication to God, typical of 17th-century scientific treatises.</note>

The Sun, the source of light for the universe, an admirable vessel, a work of the Most High, the bridal chamber of divinity, the smile of heaven, the grace and beauty of the world, was established with such an admirable workmanship that, by the common consensus of the ancient theologians, it was not without merit regarded and worshipped everywhere as the "soul of the world" <note>original: "anima mundi"</note> and the divinity of "inaccessible darkness." Anyone who looks a little more deeply into its inestimable virtues will be forced to confess that it does not only animate all bodies of the world by a vital heat and the pouring out of life-giving light, and preserve those animated things in their vigor; but—and this might rightly seem a paradox to some—it contains within itself the <term>architectural reasons</term> <note>These are the underlying structural blueprints or "blueprints of creation" that God used to build the universe.</note> of all things, all the seeds, I say, of divine and human wisdom. Thus, no question in Theology or Philosophy is so intricate that it cannot be illuminated by the likeness of this "shadowy light"; there is no question which does not receive the greatest light from the mirror of this worldly light. By this mirror, the intellect is illustrated and led through a certain analogous comparison of the knowledge of things, and is thus rescued from obscurity. It is this which we shall attempt to demonstrate in this Epilogue of Light and Shadow (which we have also named the *Metaphysics of Light and Shadow*), not at great length, but through a certain summary deduction made from the first "Triune Archetypal Sun" through each individual class of created things.

## Argument I. ##
## The Triple Light. ##

Just as there is light in this corporeal world, by whose help all things that exist are preserved and persist, so too in that invisible <term>Archetype</term> <note>The "Archetype" refers to the divine realm of pure ideas or the mind of God, which serves as the original model for the physical world.</note> and supracelestial world, there is a certain infinite, incorruptible light. From this light, as from a most fertile fountain, all things flow. We say this light is nothing other than God, the Best and Greatest, of whom this material light is a kind of symbol. Simplicius, quoting Proclus, calls this <note>original: "φῶτα πρῶτον, εἰκόνα πατρικοῦ βύθου, ὑπερκόσμιον"</note> **the first light, the image of the paternal depth, the supramundane.** <note>Proclus and Simplicius were Neoplatonist philosophers who saw light as a bridge between the divine and the physical.</note> Now, "supramundane" things are those which exceed and excel the worldly bodies by the excellence of their essence—that is, they are incorporeal. Therefore, if this light is "first" and "supramundane," it is also incorporeal; it must necessarily proceed either from its own supramundane essence (namely, the "fountain soul") or from some higher source through a middle soul. Above the soul, however, is the Second Mind; before the second is the First Mind; and before the first is the Father, whom the student of Plato calls the "Prince Essence" and "Infinite Light." By Him, that empyrean orb is perpetually illuminated, and from that, the celestial orb. According to Plato, therefore, that infinite light is the "ideal world," full of the lights of ideas, and therefore it is rightly called the "paternal depth."

<margin>What is the Ideal world?</margin>
According to the ancient theologians, the First Mind is infinite light, from which that first incorporeal light shines forth, which is the image of the "paternal depth," and which light is transmitted through all true substances. Christian theologians transfer all these concepts to the Mystery of the Sacred Trinity: so that the infinite and eternal light is the **Father**; the "light from light" is the **Son** (or a certain ray of the divine substance and the splendor of paternal glory); and from these proceeds the heat, which is the **Holy Spirit**, nourishing the entire Archetype and the whole universe with the fire of heat. To this First Mind, the ancient theologians subordinate a "Second Intellect" as a kind of species of the First Mind, in which they say that light descends from the First Light. So says **Zoroaster**. <note>Kircher often cites "Zoroaster" based on the "Chaldean Oracles," which were highly influential in Renaissance Neoplatonism.</note> In this Second Intellect, light exists having proceeded from the "root of the intellect," no differently than a ray reflected from the Sun in a crystal. In the first place, then, from the Infinite Light, its light—the shining image of that light—illuminates the substances contained within it. In the second place, it illuminates the Second Intellect. In the third place, he says that from this intellect, light descends more weakly into the "reasoning soul"; for he says its light is thin and very similar to the morning twilight. In the fourth place, he says that from the light of the reasoning soul flows the nature of the "sensing soul," in which there is less light than in the one above; and from the light of this fourth stage flows the nature of the soul that falls into plants, which, because it is far removed from the pure and perfect light, hardly retains a trace of light. All of these things **Plato** approves as if by his own vote in his work on the duty of the world, where he says that incorporeal and intelligible light was the pattern of the Sun, because it is beautiful above the world. For the "intelligible light" is as much more splendid and glowing than the visible light as the Sun is than darkness, and day than night. Furthermore, the Mind is the leader of the whole soul; but the invisible and intelligible Divine **Word** <note>The Logos.</note> he calls the "image of God," and the image of this image is that intelligible word which was made the image of the divine word. This word was the "craftsman of its generation," and is the supracelestial star, the source of the sensible stars, which he also calls <note>original: "παμφάεινον"</note> **all-shining**, from which the Sun, the Moon, and the rest of the planets—each according to the condition of its nature—obtain their fitting brightness. All of these things **Trismegistus** approves by his own vote in the *Poimandres*. <note>Hermes Trismegistus was the legendary author of the Hermetic corpus, which Kircher believed contained ancient Egyptian wisdom compatible with Christianity.</note>

# The Metaphysics of Light and Shadow #

<margin>Pimander: And I beheld an unseeable vision, and all things became light, sweet and joyful. <note>original: "Καὶ ἐγὼ θέαν ἀθεώρητον, φῶς δὲ πάντα γεγεννημένα, ἡδύ τε & ἱλαρόν." This is a quote from the Corpus Hermeticum, a collection of Greek texts attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus.</note></margin>
<margin>Image.</margin> *And I discern an immense spectacle, and a light that made all things sweet and joyful.* And a little later: *From the light, a certain Word was produced and brooded over nature, and a most pure fire leapt up from the watery nature into the heights.* Which he explains a little later in these words: *The light, he says, is God the Mind, who existed before the watery nature that appeared out of the darkness: and the shining Word, which comes from the Mind, is the Son of God.* With these words, he describes the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity so aptly that he seems to have alluded to it by divine inspiration and instinct. 

Therefore, just as all the lights of the lower world come from the celestial light, so in the teachings of Zoroaster they come from the <term>empyrean</term> <note>The highest, most "fiery" heaven in ancient and medieval cosmology, believed to be the dwelling place of God.</note>; according to Philo, from the all-shining Word; according to Hermes, from the Word of God, which itself comes from the first paternal light; and in the opinion of Plato, the light of the vegetative soul comes from the light of the sensitive soul, and its light from the light of the rational soul; the light of the rational comes from the light of the mind, and the light of the mind from the primary infinite light of the mind and the Word of God. 

Mercury <note>Another name for Hermes Trismegistus.</note> describes this utterly admirable speech and the order of observed things even more clearly in his book on power and wisdom. For in that place, he seems to refer Power chiefly to the person of the Father, to assign Wisdom to the Son, and Love and Will to the Spirit. And in the formation of the world, he first describes an immense spectacle: namely, all things suddenly turned into light, a stable form prevailing over an infinite empire. A little later, he describes a horrendous shadow, or a darkness gliding beneath in a crooked revolution, agitated by an ineffable countenance, from which the watery and undigested nature immediately flowed forth: to which, thirdly, the <term>craftsman Word</term> <note>original: "opifex verbum"</note> stood by and, from elements that were like confused seeds, formed the world—hitherto distinguished by its orders—through measure, number, and proportion. Thus, if you weigh each point deeply, it will seem that he hinted at the origin of darkness through the conversion of light into itself. From the light breaking forth outward, perhaps he also understood the propagation of form; and from the diffused appearance of darkness, the abyss or matter.

<margin>The production of the worldly system was made according to the pattern of light diffused spherically.</margin>
Similarly, by means of the idea of a triple motion—both in the active principle, the passive, and the middle proportion of both—you may in some way conceive of a triple difference in action, will, and power. Let the first be in stable rest, like a ray of divine virtue containing itself within its own limit. Let the second be like a ray of divine light led back and forth in a continuum, breaking out toward other things from itself through the surrounding cloud of its own darkness. Let the third be a certain determined kind of essence, rolled together as if into a spherical orb by the conversion of the shining ray; in whose full circuit is placed the full perfection of things to be generated. And so, from the essence simply existing and the stable virtue comparable to the center of a sphere, there is born the <term>archetype</term> <note>The original "blueprint" or master-concept in the mind of God.</note> of all things—the most pure, eternal, and stable "being" of things in the mind of the Craftsman. From the flowing out of essence in a straight line (which is comparable to a surface area), the progress of things in generation proceeded after their conception—that is, the principles themselves were as yet unconnected, from which comes both simple and determined "being," until gradually, as the rays gathered into the shape of a circle, the first steps of obscure composition began; yet these remained indefinite due to the nature of the surface; from which, by a simpler breath, the first elements of the world were propagated.

But from the flowing out of essence into a perfect and solid orb (comparable to a spherical circumference), a "being" that is composite and entirely determined flowed out through these lower things. You see, therefore, how this entire corporeal mass of the world was gradually unfolded according to the physical motion of light.

<margin>The Sun is a symbol of the Holy Trinity.</margin>
Furthermore, nothing is found in the world more similar to the divine Trinity than the Sun. For in the one substance of the Sun, three things are indeed distinct from one another, yet equally united. The first is a natural fertility, imperceptible to the senses. The second is its manifest light, flowing from that same fertility and equal to it. The third is the heating power from both, entirely equal to each. The fertility represents the Father; the Light, like the intelligence, represents the Son conceived through the intellect; the Heat represents the Spirit of love. He indicates all these things most beautifully with this truly divine <term>epiphonema</term> <note>A summarizing exclamation or a finishing touch to an argument.</note>.

But so that these levels of shining things may be better understood, I have decided to reason about them a little more at length, so that it may be known how much the knowledge of Light and Shadow opens up mysteries in the more secret Philosophy.

## Argument II. ##
### On the descent of eternal Light into creatures. ###

**T**here is nothing in this sensible circuit of things that does not participate in essence, life, and motion from that infinite fertility of Light; James the Apostle, the beloved disciple of God, declared this in a truly subtle and profound summary:

> Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow of turning. <note>James 1:17</note>

Since these words are like a certain epitome of all Theology, let us explain each part as much as the strength of our intellect permits.

# Book X of the Great Art. Epilogue.

Since, therefore, every creature is at its best, and the gift descending from the Father of Lights is at its best, it seems that the gift itself is God; for nothing can be given that is not subject to His infinite power, nor can anything be given that is not contained within that same power of God. Within the power of the good, there is good; but it is not "the best" unless it is one and simple in <gloss>actuality and potentiality <note>original: ἔνεργ. & δυν. (energeia and dynamis), fundamental Aristotelian concepts for being in action versus being in a state of possibility</note></gloss>. Thus, He does not communicate anything except Himself; and since He is, as it were, the Best, and the Best is diffusive of itself, He will necessarily communicate Himself. Therefore, God and the creature shall be one and the same: according to the manner of the Giver, He is the eternal, infinite, and incomprehensible God; but according to the nature of the gift, it is the temporal, finite, and comprehended creature. But let us examine so subtle 

<margin>**The form of things is not God.**</margin>

a matter by the touchstone <note>original: Lydium, referring to the Lydian stone used to test the purity of gold</note> of truth. The Philosopher <note>likely Aristotle</note> rightly defines form as that which gives "being" to a thing. This must be understood in such a way that no one thinks a thing takes its "being" from a form as if the thing existed before it had "being"—that would mean the thing existed before it existed! Rather, the form that gives being to a thing is the "being" itself in every existing thing; so that the "being" given to the thing is the very form that gives that being. Now, God is the one who gives being, life, and motion to all things; He is the absolute and universal form, which the Platonists signified through the "Soul of the World" and the Egyptians through the "Spirit" diffused into all things. But because form gives being to any particular thing, the form is the very "being" of that thing; hence, God is the Best and Greatest, giving being itself. Therefore, God is not the specific form of earth, water, air, or any other thing, but He is the absolute form of the forms of earth, air, and water. Thus, God is the universal form of things, giving to each individual the form through which they exist. For the form of any created thing is a "descent" from the universal form; so the form of earth is the form of *that* thing and no other. All these things are expressed to us with truly marvelous subtlety in the Apostolic exclamation <note>original: epiphonemate; referring to James 1:17: "Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights."</note>, as if to say: the "Best Gift" descends, and the <term>Colchodemam <note>a term likely derived from the Arabic "Alchochoden," meaning the "Giver of Life" or "Giver of Forms," used here to describe God's creative output</note></term>—that is, the Giver of Forms—does not give anything other than Himself. Since His gift is the Best, Absolute, Greatest, and Universal, the only obstacle is on the part of the receiver, which prevents it from being received exactly as it is given. The reception of the gift is "descensive," which means the infinite is received finitely, the universal is received particularly, and the absolute is received in a "contracted" or restricted way. Since such a reception falls away from the truth of the one communicating Himself, it must necessarily tend toward a "likeness" or "image." Thus, it is no longer the absolute truth of the Giver, but a certain likeness, which is necessarily followed by "otherness" and diversity. I shall clarify the obscurity of this matter by using 

<margin>**How God is the form of things is shown through the example of light.**</margin>

light to bring it into the light. Light is indeed the universal form of all visible "being"—that is, of all color. For color is nothing other than the "contracted" reception of light. Light does not mix with things, but it is received according to the mode and condition of the receiver through a certain descending expansion. The boundary of this reception is color itself within a transparent medium—red in one mode, blue or purple in another, and so on. Thus, all the "being" of color is given through descending light; and so, light is a kind of form for all colors, diffused into all things by its own goodness. And although this most pure light diffuses itself in communication, it happens that when mixed with shadowy and opaque things—due to the various "descensive" receptions and the variety of bodies upon which it is poured—a various variety and mixture of colors arises. Consequently, light received in this way is no longer called "light," but "color"—or rather, light received in a "contracted" state. Just as the form of light relates to the form of colors, so the infinite light and universal form of things relates to the forms of creatures. So too our soul, a universal power descending to judge, is one and simple, whole in the whole body and in all the organs; yet the eye, in order to see the soul, does not receive it as a universal discerning power, but receives it through a certain "descent" or in a "contracted" way, which is why it only deals with the specific objects of its own power. Thus, following the model of light, the substantial form universally gives substantial "being" insofar as the simple unity is received as if through nine diffused rays—that is, in nine "descensive" modes according to the categories of quantity, quality, relation, action, passion, position, place, time, and habit—so that all things are completed in the number ten <note>original: denario; referring to the ten Aristotelian categories (one substance plus nine accidents)</note>. But because quantity is not received as pure substance, but descensively with a certain contraction, quantity is not substance itself, even though all the "being" of quantity is given by substance, just as all the "being" of color is given by physical light. We must reason similarly regarding 

<margin>**Why God is called by the names of all things.**</margin>

the nature of angels, humans, and beasts. From this, it becomes clear why Hermes Trismegistus <note>a legendary Hellenistic figure associated with a body of esoteric philosophy (Hermeticism)</note> wished to call God by the names of all things, and all things by the name of God. For God is the form of His own work (since He worked all things for His own sake), and He gave Himself as the sensible world so that the sensible world might exist for His sake. In this way, His "descensive" reception—which turns from light toward shadow at the level of the senses—might reach His goodness in a sensible way. Infinite light shines as a "sensible ray" to sensible things, a "vital ray" to living things, a "rational ray" to rational beings, and finally an "intellectual ray" to those with intellect. From this, it also becomes clear how the creature has always existed from eternity, or rather, from the eternal light from which it descends; for when the eternal...

## Metaphysics of Light and Shadow

...eternity is received only in a limited way <note>original: "contractè," a central concept in late medieval philosophy meaning the narrowing or restricting of an infinite essence into a specific, finite form</note>; hence, eternity exists in the world without a beginning in its source, yet exists as something received through a "descent." But now that these things have been declared, let us return to the Father of Lights.

God is the Father of Lights, in whom there is no change, nor any shadow of variation <note>A reference to the Epistle of James 1:17</note>. He is the Father of Lights in whom there are no shadows at all; the fountain of lights from whom every light comes. All things that exist in the world are appearances and certain "lights" of the one God, who, though He is one, can only appear in His creatures in various ways—just as light appears in the colors of opaque bodies.

<margin>A manifold Unity is considered in God.</margin>
Therefore, various lights descend from the intellect of the Father of Lights; and just as He manifests Himself in this way, He is a simple and absolute Unity. He is the principle of Number—a power so great and incomprehensible that His appearance is only perceived in the variety of numbers. He is the Point—an ineffable power that is only made known in the quantities descending from that simplest point, acting as various lights. He is the Moment—a power most simple and incomprehensible, which can only be perceived in the successive flow of time. All things, however, exist according to number within the Unity; according to quantity within the Point; according to successive flow within the Moment; and all things exist—according to what they are, were, will be, or could be—within the infinite power of God’s omnipotence. For God, the Best and Greatest, is infinite power in action; while He wills to communicate Himself out of the nature of His goodness, He pours forth from Himself various lights, which Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, an influential early Christian theologian who wrote on the "Divine Names"</note> calls <term>theophanies<note>original: θεοφανείας (theophaneias), meaning "appearances of God" or divine manifestations</note></term>. In all these lights, He makes known the riches of the light of His glory. But this generation that occurs happens voluntarily, having no cause except His own goodness. It happens in the Word of Truth; for the Word of Truth is the absolute Art, which can be called the light of all reason, according to that saying:

> *I am the light of the world.* <note>original: "Ego lux mundi," from John 8:12</note>

In this light, which is the Word and the firstborn Son, is the supreme appearance, and the light and splendor of the Father. Therefore, the Father of Lights begat all descending appearances so that, through the highest power and the strength of union, all other appearing lights might be voluntarily blessed—in whatever way they can be explained. In this most universal Art, everything is explainable through any art; and in absolute Reason or discernment, every light is either discerning or discernible. Furthermore, He begat us in that Word of eternal Art and appearance, so that while we receive the light of His manifestation (which is the infinite Word) in a "descending" manner—the only way such things can be received by us—we might be a certain "beginning" of His creature.

Furthermore, since our intellect cannot find rest unless it grasps a thing through its intellectual nature—so that it may move from the power of its potential into actual realization—the perfecting Spirit provides many lights to it. For all things that have been created are certain lights for the intellect to activate its power, so that, by the light granted to it in this way, it may travel toward the Fountain of Lights. A human sees that there are various creatures, and is illuminated by that very variety to travel toward the essential light of those creatures. In this way, the servant of God *Benedict* <note>St. Benedict of Nursia; this refers to a famous vision described by St. Gregory where Benedict saw the whole world gathered into a single ray of sun</note> saw the whole world in a single ray. For while he saw that one creature is without vital movement, another lives, and another reasons, he was immediately illuminated; he saw and understood that none of these things grasped in the variety of creatures belong to the absolute Essence.

<margin>How God is all things.</margin>
Since, therefore, every creature is something "contracted" or limited, the Essence of all things is not any one of those things, but is the "nothingness" of all things in an unlimited state <note>This paradoxical language suggests that God is "nothing" of the specific things because He is the source of "everything" generally</note>. Thus, the essences of sensible things exist insensibly within their species; the specific essences exist without specification within their genera; and the generic essences exist without generality in the absolute Essence, which is God. There are also other lights, poured in through divine illumination, which lead the intellect toward perfection. Such is the light of faith, through which the intellect is illuminated so that it may ascend above reason to the apprehension of truth. Because the intellect is led by this light to believe it can reach a truth that it cannot grasp with the help of reason (which is merely its instrument), it leaves behind its weakness or blindness—on account of which it used to lean on the staff of reason. By a certain effort divinely bestowed upon it, and strengthened in the word of faith so that it may walk, it is led by a steady hope of attaining the promise. This leads from a stable faith toward what it grasps in a course of love. Whoever is imbued with this without hesitation will, through the promise of Christ, infallibly obtain all things asked of God. Therefore, our power of intellectual light possesses ineffable riches in potential; yet, while they are in potential, we do not know we have them until they are opened to us through an intellectual light existing in actuality, and the method for bringing them into action is shown.

<margin>An analogy explaining the aforementioned.</margin>
Just as in the field of a poor man there are many riches in potential, if someone knows they are there and seeks them in the proper way, he will find them. For there is bread, wine, meat, milk, honey, fruit, flax, and wool, and whatever else is necessary to sustain life. Although he may not see these with his eye, reason provides him with light so that he knows they truly lie hidden there. Provided with the help of the art of agriculture, he brings forth grass, and crops, and every kind of plant and tree, by which sheep are fed...

<meta>This page continues the epilogue of Book 10 of The Great Art, concluding a metaphorical discussion on the "intellectual field" and transitioning into a philosophical treatise on the hierarchy of light and knowledge among different classes of beings.</meta>

# The Great Art, Book 10. Epilogue.

...for the cow provides milk, the crops grain, and flax provides the necessary support for covering our bodies. In this way, the person who is illuminated proceeds by faith and obtains the fruit of a sensible life. By this same reasoning, in the intellectual potential of the "field," <note>The author uses the "field" as a metaphor for the human mind or soul that must be cultivated.</note> everything that leads to the attainment of the intellectual life is expressed through proper methods; let it be rightly cultivated, and let its virtues be expressed through the required exercises and modes. We arrive at this kind of knowledge through the illuminations of those who, filled with virtue and internal light, have spent much long-term effort in cultivating this field—those who, fleeing the shadowy face of this world, devote themselves with their whole soul to works of light: the Philosophers, Prophets, and Apostolic Men. Through these, the Giver of Lights <note>original: "Dator luminum," a traditional title for God.</note> has revealed to us the hidden treasure, the way to guard the field, and the laws and precepts by which we can uproot harmful, fruitless weeds and tares, and in their place plant and cultivate the Tree of Life.

### Proof III.

->*How eternal light exists in creatures, and how creatures know light within light. The effects of the Sun and Moon are symbols of all created wisdom.*<-

<margin>The order of the archetypal world.</margin>
The **Sun** is primarily the visible expression of the Angelic intellect and its object; the **Moon**, however, is the visible expression of the human intellect and its object. In the Sun, the light is clear, pure, without stain, without cloud, shadow, or gloom; in the Moon, however, the light is seen as shadowy and mixed with various elements. The Sun is without image or outward form; the Moon is defined by its own form and image. Therefore, the Sun and the Moon, those great lights of the world, suggest to us the nature of all created wisdom; they express every divine appearance. In God, there is the primary, substantial, and uncreated wisdom; after God, the Angel; after the Angel, Man—these are the partners of divine wisdom. The irrational creature, however, is deprived of all such light. Divine wisdom is immutable, persisting in wisdom, identity, goodness, power, beauty, light, and clarity, immune from all foolishness, "otherness," <note>original: "alteritate," referring to the state of being different or separated from the divine unity.</note> malice, dissimilarity, and the gloom of shadows and darkness. But the Angelic and human creatures are wandering things; they are indeed capable of wisdom and are natural mirrors of the divine image and light—or to put it better, they are secret storehouses of the divine splendor. Yet, because they are not eternal but come forth from "non-being," they eventually fell away from God and became subject to foolishness, inequality, dissimilarity, mixture, and passions. The irrational animals, however, being free from the burdens of deliberation <note>original: "liberi ex-fortia consilii," meaning they lack the capacity for rational choice and thus the responsibility for it.</note> as they are guided by the reins of man, did not fall from their order; for that which God did not make capable of wisdom could not be changed into foolishness.

### Proof IV.

->*All knowledge is light, proceeding from the infinite primordial light.*<-

<margin>How God is known by the Angel and by man is declared through light.</margin>
Furthermore, since God is the preeminent Sun of all nature and the supreme object of all knowledge, every cognitive power is connected (as much as possible) to God, as potential is connected to an act. This power is like a certain gaze of God himself, a receptacle of his brilliance, and a natural emanation. Just as this material light is the natural object of the eyes toward which they turn, so every cognitive power strives toward God as its proper subject, as its true Sun, as its end, and its ultimate sustainer. But this infinite light is not revealed to the intellect, the reason, and the senses in the same way, or with the same face and appearance: for to the **intellect**, it is revealed as <term>Lumen</term> <note>Lumen: In this context, the active, radiating "glow" or "beam" of light, as opposed to "Lux," which is the source itself.</note>; to **reason**, it appears in shadow; to **sense**, it appears in darkness. By the Angelic intellect, it is perceived clearly and nakedly; by man, it is perceived through the likenesses of shadows; by the irrational animal, it is perceived in darkness and the privation of all light. Light itself (*Lux*) is in God—and is God. The *Lumen*, however, is the first emanation of Light, a direct ray of Light. **Shadow** is either the refraction or reflection of *Lumen*. **Darkness**, meanwhile, is called the privation of *Lumen*. Light is in the Sun, being the Sun’s native clarity; *Lumen* is that which is derived by a direct and unrefracted ray from the Sun all the way to the elemental world; shadow is a certain diminution of the *Lumen* through refraction; darkness is the total privation of light.

<margin>By what means the Angel, man, and beast perceive.</margin>
Therefore, as long as a single, continuous, direct, and unbroken ray of light is carried through a similar medium, it is *Lumen*; but where it is broken and scattered in a denser transparent or opaque medium, it is considered shadow. But where the medium is a solid opaque object, such as when it hits the earth, there is the beginning of darkness; there the very appearance of all light sets and perishes. These grades of light and shadow set before our eyes the entire distribution of the Universe. God is in the region of **Light**; He dwells in "inaccessible light," as Saint John testifies. The Angel is in the region of **Lumen**; man is in the region of **Shadow**; the animal is in the region of **Darkness**. The primary Light is in itself; the direct *Lumen* is in the empyrean space; the shadow is in the sublunary world; the darkness is in the bowels of the earth. Therefore, God as pure Light is revealed one way in the Angel, another in man, and another in the animal. For the Divine form received in the Angelic intellect is an unfailing light...

It contrasts these rational beings with animals, who exist in a state of intellectual darkness but remain in their natural order because they lack the capacity for wisdom and thus the capacity to "fall."</summary>

# The Metaphysics of Light and Shadow.

...free from every spot and refraction; but the divine image <note>original: "species"</note> received in human reason is a shadow, while, hindered by the service of the senses, it gazes upon God only through the shadows of sensible forms and the effects of natural things, as if in a mirror. In the animal, however, there is the total extinction of all divine light. For just as we showed in the preceding sections that there are two types of Light, namely Radiant Light <note>original: "Lumen," referring to light as it travels or fills a space.</note> and Shadow; so also we establish a twofold created light, the Angelic and the human, for the sake of which all things in the world were founded.

### Logical Proof V. <note>original: "Epichirema," a technical term for a complex syllogism or a reasoned argument.</note>

#### God is the fountain of light, the Angel is the first mirror of light, and the second mirror is man.

In the preceding parts, we spoke of the order of the transfusion of infinite light into lower things; now we must discuss the manner in which the image of divine light is received in these lower realms. God, therefore, the inexhaustible fountain of all light, is received by the Angel immediately through a medium that is luminous, clear, proximate, and near to God, defiled by no imperfection of distortion or hindrance. Nor does anything intervene between God and the Angel that could impede the diffusion of divine light into the Angelic intellect, or place an obstacle before it; but the Angel reflects the received image of divine light—as if from a primary mirror of light—through a dissimilar medium subject to refractions and distortions, into the second created intellect, namely man. For the Angelic intermediary is like a shadow by which the irradiation of divine light is refracted between God and man. By this shadow, the heat of the divine Sun, which would be intolerable to human fragility, is in a certain way restrained by the rays of divine light. Consequently, a shadow of divine brilliance is caused between the cloud and the Sun, which our own shadowy and imperfect knowledge follows.

Since, moreover, man is material and composed of the dregs of the earth, Light—refracted as if in an opaque body—denies further diffusion of light. Therefore, just as the cause of human shadow is the interposition of the Angelic "little cloud" between God and man; so the interposition of the darkness between the Angelic light and the human body is the cause of darkness in living creatures. Again, God is knowable by the Angel as if in heaven, by man as if in the clouds, and by the animal as if on the earth.

<margin>How the order of knowledge is revealed through colors.</margin>
But so that these things may be more clearly revealed: It must be noted that every cognitive power—as we said a little before—is fourfold: uncreated, Angelic, human, and animal. These emerged from the divine eye at the time of creation and relate to one another as colors do to light. We may best call the divine eye Light, the Angelic Whiteness, the human Redness, and the animal Blackness. For just as Light is the fountain, beginning, and perfection of all colors, far surpassing all colors; so also the divine eye is the beginning and fountain of all eyes. And just as every color is expressed primarily by three things—the two extremes with a middle—so also the created intellect is threefold. Just as every color is a certain appearance <note>original: "species"</note> and emanation of light, so every created eye is an appearance and substantial emanation of the divine uncreated vision <note>original: "aciei," literally "sharpness of sight" or "power of the eye."</note>. Thus the divine eye is the cause and fountain of every color; the Angelic will be aptly compared to Whiteness (the first appearance of light), the human to Redness, and finally the animal to Blackness. So the Angelic relates to the divine eye as the brightness of the midday light; the human relates to this as reddish clouds or the crimson color of the dawn; the animal, however, is as the night, shadows, and gloom, denoted by the color black. All of these we have included in the following table.

| God | Angel | Human | Animal |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Mind | Intellect | Reason | Sense |
| Light | Radiant Light | Shadows | Darkness |
| Light | Whiteness | Redness | Blackness |
| Super-celestial | Heaven | Clouds | Earth |
| Perpetual Light | Midday | Twilight | Nightly Darkness |
| Fire | Air | Water | Earth |

You see, therefore, how the Angel and the Human, through the influence of divine light, result in union with God, each according to the condition of their contemplation or vision: The Angel, raised up to God as to a most simple, eternal, immense, best, and truest object, is made one with Him by the power of contemplation without need of images. But the object of the human mirror expresses the union of God and the Angel, insofar as man does not know God immediately, but as accessible and transparent beneath the Angelic cloud. God is seen by the Angel as a White and bright Sun, worn by no spot of cloud or appearance of color; by man, He is seen as the Moon, glowing red under a spotted face, as if reflected from the Angelic mirror of light and beneath cloud and gloom; by the animal, as the black earth, dark...

<page-num>802</page-num>
# Book X of the Great Art. Epilogue.

...seen as dense, opaque, impervious to bright rays, and inaccessible. Angels and humans are the "middle colors" that are born when the divine light stretches toward either a cloud or a solid body: **God** is like fire; **the Angel** like air; **man** like water; **the animal** like earth. **God** is like the mind; **the Angel** like a concept of the mind; **man** like the voice; **the animal** like writing. And these are the four primary beings of the universe; these are the true and substantial elements of the world; these are those living creatures "full of eyes," as <term>Scripture testifies</term><note>A reference to the "four living creatures" in Ezekiel 1:18 and Revelation 4:6-8, symbolizing all-encompassing divine watchfulness.</note>, both in front and behind. For their "eyes" are the cognitive faculties inherent in these four: the divine mind is the Eye; the Angelic vision is motion; human reason is the eye; and the two senses of animals are their eyes.

<margin>Different modes of cognition for Angels and humans.</margin>
From this, it is clear how the Angel understands without a <term>species</term><note>In medieval philosophy, a "species" is a mental image or representation of an object, not a biological category.</note> or image, while man understands through a species and image. For the Angel, as we have said, sees God as pure, simple, without any mixture, and without any species or image—just as we see the worldly and most brilliant Sun, in which we detect no shape, shadow, cloud, or darkness. However, since the Angel, by the power of its cognition, is the first to emerge into God and is received into God, it follows that God—through this Angelic grafting and union—is in some way said to be "shadowy," fashioned like a most polished mirror with an indwelling species and an overshadowing figure. This figure is the reception and grafting of the Angel into the divine mirror, like a power within its object. Therefore, under this Angelic figure, image, and shadow of the divine mirror, the human intellect emerges into God in the second place after the Angelic intellect. For the human intellect, which proceeded into God after the Angelic, gazes upon God through a species or Angelic image. It perceives God through the shadow of the Angelic species and image, through which God shines into our intellect no differently than a face is shown to our eyes through a lunar mirror, under the shadow and grafting of the spotted Moon.

Furthermore, it is clear from this why the visible Sun of this world, with its overwhelming rays, dulls and blunts the weak vision of our eyes to such an extent that we cannot endure looking at it with un-turned eyes; whereas the Moon, with its tempered fires and milder mirrors of light, offers itself to be gazed upon by us with a harmless look. For the Sun is the trace of the object of the Angelic intellect—that is, of a higher eye; but the Moon, which is presented and represented to our intellects by nature, is seen fittingly and without harm. The Sun is the visible sign of all Angelic knowledge and contemplation; the Moon, likewise, is the visible sign of human speculation and science. For the divine Sun—pure, a mirror without spot or image—is open to the Angelic intellect; but to the human intellect, it becomes known through the Moon, visible with its spotted image. Much more could be said in this place regarding the wonderful effects of this invisible Light in the threefold world—the <term>Archetypal</term><note>The world of divine ideas or original patterns.</note>, the intellectual, and the rational. But since we have reserved all these matters for our *Hieroglyphic Theology*, we can only investigate them here in passing.
<margin>Hieroglyphic Theology.</margin>

### Proof VI.

#### On intellectual light.

**In order** that you may see the mutual binding of all intellects, know first that it is one and the same thing which, from a super-abundant goodness, flowed outside itself into other kinds of natures. It glided down gradually, as if by steps, from the most perfect natures through the less perfect to the most imperfect, and finally vanished into "prime matter," which seems to be almost nothing. Hence, we gather that in God there is a certain absolute and supereminent state of things; in the intellect, there is the "intelligible"; and in the soul, there is the "natural." In the first, therefore, things are placed before their species in a way that is most unified. In the second, or the intellect, they are placed by way of many ideas in a kind of primary exemplary and intelligible world. Consequently, the lower the order that things occupy in the world, the more they fall away from that first "being" of the intellect; and having slipped from the One into the multitude, they also draw a mode of cognition that is more changeable and subject to division. 

<margin>An elegant comparison.</margin>
<term>Maximus Tyrius</term><note>A 2nd-century AD Greek philosopher and rhetorician who sought to bridge Platonic philosophy with everyday life.</note>, the philosopher, rightly compares the divine mind to the Sun, whose power is to look widely upon all the works of heaven and earth in a single glance; but the human mind, he says, is like travelers who can only traverse the regions of the universe with the longest delay and at different times. But that former one is what <term>Plato</term> calls the Parent and Maker of the world; yet he neither utters his name, which he does not know, nor reveals his color, which he has not seen, nor finally exhibits his magnitude, which he could never reach. The whole [light] glides from the source only into a mind that is empty and contracted into itself, which then finally perceives itself seeing that light and is reflected back into its own act. This happens when the mind is so upright and strong that it can direct its most sincere gaze into that light—a vision that never grows dim, nor is its virtue, weighed down by shackles, pulled back too much toward earthly things. Rather, according to the counsel of the Tyrian, the mind should immediately block its ears to earthly and sensible things and commend itself only to the truest influx of reason and the governance of divine love.

It emphasizes the emanation of divine light through different levels of perfection down to material existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the epilogue of Book X, transitioning from the angelic hierarchy described on page 802 to a detailed analysis of the three classes of intelligent beings—God, Angels, and the Human Soul—using the metaphor of Light and Shadow.</meta>

<page-num>803</page-num>
<header>The Metaphysics of Light and Shadow</header>

<margin>
Three classes of intelligent beings.
</margin>

There are, therefore, three primary classes of intelligent beings: God, the Angel, and the Soul. God understands without receiving anything from outside; rather, through his way of comprehending all things within himself, he distributes his most universal power into each lower thing. The middle order of Angels receives universal <term>ideas</term><note>In this context, "ideas" are the divine archetypes or blueprints of all created things.</note> from the higher Good and distributes them to lower beings; through the light of God, which brings all things into being, the Angel draws in and understands the <term>species</term><note>original: "species"; here meaning the mental forms or "blueprints" of things.</note> of those same things. Rational souls receive the species of things but do not distribute them to lower beings. We declare all these things through the principles of Light and Shadow. Therefore, keep these four points especially before your eyes: First, imagine a ray of divine Light spread out from the Mind above. Second, imagine the species or ideas—the blueprints of things to be created—existing within that ray like individual lights. Third, imagine the Minds which receive this ray as it flows in a continuous stream. Fourth and finally, imagine the powers and actions of those fruitful Minds produced by that fruitful ray. For first, that divine Ray, as it exists in the most simple unity of God, is entirely simple and uniform; for that reason, it offers only a single idea to the divine eye. Yet, meanwhile, that idea is communicable to things to be born through many intermediate levels of being. However, the more an idea recedes from the divine unity, the more it takes on a manifold form, ending in a mixture of colors; just as a line drawn from a center is a single point at the center itself, but as it moves further away, it is extended into many parts. Thus, the higher Minds receive the ray more simply, while the rest receive it more multifariously the further they decline from the source.

<margin>
What is the human mode of understanding?
</margin>

Regarding the mode of understanding, which is most hidden within human minds, Plotinus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 204–270 AD) who heavily influenced Christian mysticism.</note> established that it always dwells upon divine things in a certain indivisible way. To me, however, it seems that because of its distance from the First Intellect and its affection for lower powers, the human mind departs somewhat from the stability of the highest Good and takes on a "shadow of mutability." Nonetheless, within this shadow, a most beautiful image of a single and stable nature always shines out above the other faculties of the soul. For this reason, three particular functions of that active intellect are listed by most scholars as distinct types: **Infusion**, **Abstraction**, and **Procreation of the intelligible species**. Infusion happens from the first being to the last through <term>analysis</term><note>original: "ἀνάλυσις" (analysis); here meaning the resolution of a complex thing into its simple divine source.</note>. Abstraction happens from the lowest things to the highest through <term>synthesis</term><note>original: "σύνθεσιν" (synthesis); the process of gathering sensory data to form a universal concept.</note>. The production of the intelligible species happens according to the law of light and colors, as the Philosopher <note>Usually a reference to Aristotle.</note> testifies by this comparison: Just as light makes colors—which are hidden in the abyss and only visible by potential—actually visible, so the <term>active intellect</term><note>The part of the mind that processes raw sensory information into abstract thoughts.</note> makes those things which are inherently understandable to us only in potential, actually understood. And just as light makes colors actually visible without itself "seeing" them, so the active intellect makes things understandable without "understanding" them in the same way. Finally, just as light makes colors transition from being potentially visible to actually visible while also producing their likeness (or matter) in the medium and the organ of sight (the eye), so the active intellect makes all things actually understandable while producing images of the things to be understood in the "possible mind," removed from all "contagion" of matter. And just as light, in performing its function, uses no help from a bodily instrument but makes colors visible by its mere presence, so too does the intellect. It performs each of these tasks as if in a moment, and with such great speed that the excited mind, while racing through its thoughts, can hardly observe or follow its own tracks. Hence, Plotinus not inappropriately calls the intellect, when considered in this way, "a Light perpetually reflected into itself with wonderful dexterity."

### Logical Exercise VII.
### Rational and Fantastic Light.

**S**o much shadow and darkness exists in the imaginative faculty (the lower part of the soul) that it thinks itself free to dream up things that are not even granted to Nature itself. Truly, this would quickly cast us into the foulest errors if the light of Reason did not provide illumination. Reason, like a watchman on a lookout tower, sharply rebukes and restrains these erroneous impulses. By bringing these empty phantoms into a higher theater of reality, Reason compares them with innate principles. Then, imitating a good steward who brings out and stores away goods, it bestows whatever its sharp scrutiny has discovered through <gloss>interpretation</gloss>. Reason, or thought, is therefore a certain true intelligence explained more broadly. Sometimes it stoops down toward the imagination and, through it, derives universal characteristics down to the specific traits of an animal nature. <margin>The motion of Reason.</margin> At other times, it clearly composes these traits, discerning and judging where they disagree or agree. Indeed, even the Metaphysicians assert that its path is perfectly circular. Depending on the nature of this path, it receives various names: as long as it revolves around itself and looks at things reflected within itself, the goal of its entire conversion appears properly "rational." When it returns to its intellectual nature, it becomes "intellectual" itself, reaching the center of perfection. But when it turns toward the imagination, it becomes "animal" and "fantastic"...

<summary>This page defines the hierarchy of intelligence (God, Angels, and Humans) through the physics of light, explaining how the human "active intellect" functions like physical light to make abstract concepts visible to the mind. It also introduces the "circular" motion of Reason, which mediates between high intellectual truths and low sensory imagination.</summary>
<keywords>active intellect, hierarchy of being, Neoplatonism, Plotinus, theory of knowledge, divine ray, abstraction, reason vs imagination, metaphysics of light</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the epilogue of the tenth book, concluding the discussion on the "Great Art" (likely the *Ars Magna Sciendi* or a similar work by Athanasius Kircher) regarding the nature of the mind and its relationship to the divine.</meta>

### The Great Art, Book 10: Epilogue

...practical, so that it can be reasonably established from what has been said before that the true circles of mental discourse <note>discursiomun: the process of moving from one thought to another</note> are not to be placed in the imagination <note>original: "phantasia"</note>, nor in the intellect itself as if they were subjects there, but rather in **Middle Reason**. For since the Intellect is stable, it produces only a stable action, such as flows from the purest orb of the Sun when it sends down a ray of its light into these lower regions. For the Intellect shines through light and a life-giving quality; it pierces through the intermediate spheres of the heavens and, passing through the ethereal nature, finally permeates through the air and the other elements all the way to the center of the universe. Yet, it has no motion other than the celestial one, nor does it properly reach this corruptible region, but only touches it according to the continuous flowing forth of its rays. Therefore, in the Intellect, there are the most perfect and most stable ideas of all circles; but because the Intellect does not move itself, nor does it create a circle by moving through arguments, **Reason** itself is struck by the ray of the Intellect. From that ray—just as a line is born from a point, or a ray from a shining body—Reason draws the first path of ascent and descent. In this path appears the simple and primary beginning of the entire revolution, like a line reflected back into a circle. From this principle, the circuits of the first ascent and descent are made, as we have said, in length only, and according to a relationship that refers back to the same common point or principle. We call this a metaphysical revolution, dependent on the intellect, because although Reason is the immediate cause, we see that this is not perfected by Reason simply as reason, but insofar as it is formed by the action of the ray and the higher mind. In the

<margin>*The Motion of Phantasy*</margin>
sensory Phantasy <note>the faculty of the mind that creates and stores mental images</note>, I can perceive certain shadows and rough types of revolutions rather than solid circles. This is not because of too much stability, as happened in the intellect, but because of a **disorder of motion** <note>original Greek: "ἀταξίαν" (ataxia)</note>. For although the imagination ascends and descends, and variously composes and divides things into a circle, this never becomes continuous unless the intervening Reason binds and restrains the mobility of these "specters" by the stability of the mind infused from above. For Reason, possessing the formulas of things to be learned partly from itself and partly drawing them from on high, carries the light of intelligence into the phantasy, just as the body of the Moon carries the rays of the other planets and stars into this elementary world. From this, Reason both acts upon the Phantasy and is in turn affected by it according to the different appearances of objects. These objects are abstracted by the light of the intellect and raised higher by reason to be weighed, until all things are revolved into a circle, and:

> *It has removed the ingrained stain, and leaves pure*
> *The ethereal sense, and the fire of simple air.*
> <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid (6.746–7), describing the purification of the soul.</note>

Thus, that divine ray flowing from the eternal Sun into a continuous circle passes from the mind through the soul into nature and matter, clouded by the shadows of colors. In matter, it finally fashions certain foreign, shadow-like similarities, just as light represents the images of colors in a mirror. For from pure things they gradually become impure as they are defiled by opposites; and so, scattered from a state of unity, made singular from universals, and completely unstable and falling from stable beginnings, they seek their former purity. Snatched from the depths to the heights, they emerge again by the power of the "Great Spirit"—to speak in the manner of the Egyptians—which is to say, by **Love**, as much as is within their power. Therefore, the soul, a colonist of the lower world, because of its commerce and conversation with the higher intelligences, and partly because of the fleeting body—like a fugitive from fate, tossed on land and sea <note>A reference to the opening lines of Virgil's Aeneid, comparing the soul's journey to Aeneas's travels.</note>—takes up through the senses these similarities of things polluted by matter. Then, having collected them through the phantasy, it purges and strains them through the "sieve of rational power." Finally, it binds them with the universal idea of the mind. Now, the beautiful **Psyche** <note>the Soul personified</note> enjoys the embraces of her husband, the **Celestial Cupid**, where, having drunk nectar and being full of *nepenthe* <note>a mythical medicine for sorrow</note> and ambrosia, she gradually becomes accustomed to the heavenly tables.

<margin>*The Union of the soul with celestial things*</margin>
And so the human soul, through the reflected ray, is restored from its descent into the "many" back into the sublime, weakened circle. If you wish to see an obscure image of this revolution in sensible things, turn yourself again to the action of the Sun. Observe diligently how from its vast orb (or rather, its diameter), the Sun forms a pyramidal cone through a narrow hole onto a wall. In that very hole of the nearest wall, the rays are slanted and carried forward continuously so that, having crossed deep inside and being depressed in equal proportion, the rays which they recently gathered fall onto the opposite surface of another wall. There, they recreate a shining orb in the likeness of the Sun, as was shown extensively in the second book of this work. Indeed, the image is as much larger as the crossed rays are extended further from the hole, eventually equaling the size of the Solar globe if they fall at a distance equal to where they first flowed from the Sun. In the same way, the influx of **Ideas** derived from the supreme life into the lower life are reduced from the widest scope into a particular narrowness, until, reflected by matter and bodies, they are made universal again from singular things within human souls, possessing their former greatness.

It uses the metaphor of light passing through a pinhole (camera obscura) to illustrate how universal ideas become particularized and then restored to their original scale.</summary>

->The Metaphysics of Light and Shadow<-

## Argument VIII <term>Epichirema: a form of syllogism or dialectical argument where a proof is attached to one or both of the premises.</term>

### How the creature is perfectly united to the Creator by light.

**N**o mortal can endure the Sun as it is with unshrinking eyes, unless they find a medium through whose help they may enter that most luminous darkness. Truly, media of this sort are glass lenses tinted with various colors; for through these intermediaries, the supreme force of the brilliance is broken so that the eye can sustain the ray. Now, glass is brought to this quality first from ash and sand and other dregs of the earthly mixture, thoroughly purified by a most burning fire in a furnace over a long time; then, with various polishings applied, it finally rises into a most clear and limpid substance, most similar to the purest air. By a not dissimilar reasoning, a thoroughly purified soul arrives at the union of eternal light and enters the darkness—which, according to Saint Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian mystic who wrote about "Divine Darkness" as a state where God is so bright He seems dark to human senses.</note>, is nothing other than the inaccessible light of the Divinity. It is an uncircumscribed, utterly boundless, and most overflowing fullness; a most splendid beauty; and finally, the serenity and sweetness of the eternal light, by which the soul is united to the eternal light in the following manner. When the contemplative soul is admitted to the divine darkness, since there is within it both an intellective and an affective part, that part which is the **Intellect** gazes in a certain way through the mist at the Beloved. It tracks and admires Him as He lies hidden in the streets and squares—that is, in the individual orders of created things, which act as certain mirrors. Yet this intuition is so obscure that in gazing, the soul does not truly "see." Therefore, it is considered to lie before the door or the inner sanctuary of the dark dwelling. There, with crying, groaning, sighs, vows, and repeated supplication, it asks for that face so often desired to be manifested to itself. To more easily attain what it intends, the soul must strip away the love of earthly things and the fleeting pleasures of even lawful things. Through perfect renunciation and the suppression of the titillation of the flesh—by a continuous exercise of mortification and the chastisement of the body—the soul is "cooked" as if in a furnace by the most burning fire of divine love. Gradually and completely stripped of the dregs of earthly affection, it rises into the greatest clarity and makes itself a path for the divine rays. Gradually becoming like the Beloved, and having sent a messenger through the exact conformation of its will with the divine, the soul pants for Him. Then the affective part, which is the **Will**, is snatched away to a most familiar meeting with the One inhabiting the darkness, while the intellect remains standing outside.

<margin>How the transformation of the soul into God occurs.</margin>
For this reason, the soul is raised up through the "charitative elevation of God," as the Theologians say, above the intellect itself. Once the Will is established there, it begins by a certain new covenant to be carried into God through a most incited affection; to be loved by Him as a bride; to love Him as her only beloved; to be squeezed in the arms of His most tender affection; to press Him, as her only hope, most sweetly to her mouth; and finally, by an ineffable reasoning, to be most purely joined, tied, bound, transfused into, flowed into, and transformed into that eternal light. Thus the Will, united to God, perceives, tastes, and enjoys its Beloved. But then the Intellect, by a singular favor of the Divine Power, is itself called up to the higher sanctuaries and enters as if into the **Holy of Holies** <note>The innermost sanctum of the Tabernacle and later the Temple in Jerusalem, accessible only to the High Priest.</note> of the dark Temple. It struggles through the thickest cloud of incomprehensible darkness and is led to the very throne of eternal light—like a piece of clean glass, purged of all turbid dregs—and is there illustrated with new splendors. And since no one can endure that inaccessible and incomprehensible light, the soul, established in this state like a most luminous glass tinted with a most radiant color, acting as an intermediary between the Sun and the soul, is finally carried with an unshrinking eye into the infinite light.

<margin>The gift of contemplation.</margin>
And this is that contemplation of the highest grade, sought by the vows of so many ascetics, celebrated by so many praises, veiled by so many coverings of names, and designated by so many symbols of things. Just as it is the greatest benefit granted to the soul in this mortal life, so too it is communicated only to a very few, and to men who are altogether divine.

# THE MYSTIC SPHERE
## OR THE
# MORAL INTERPRETATION
## OF LIGHT AND SHADOW.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'Q' historiated with a scene of a garden or rural landscape under a sun or sky.</image-desc>

**B**y what means we are able to know God through the Intellect—that is, through light—has been discussed in the preceding sections; it remains for us to consider how we may take hold of Him through the Will—that is, through shadow—and, having attained Him, how we may rejoice eternally. Thus, our contemplation proceeds through the elements as if by certain steps toward the ethereal and divine sphere. In this sphere, having left behind the filth of corruptible motion and matter, we shall gaze only upon divine things, which are far more excellent and far more worthy than these. God, therefore, is light, eternal light; and in the mind of Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus was a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various mystical and philosophical works were attributed; he was highly regarded by Renaissance scholars as a source of ancient wisdom.</note>, He is a sphere circumscribed by no boundaries and defined by no measurements, inasmuch as His center is everywhere and His circumference is nowhere <note>original: "cujus centrum ubique, circumferentia nusquam"</note>. He is a sphere of infinite light, whose radius is the splendor of eternal glory (or the divine Word); a radius reflected back into itself, that Spirit of love proceeding by an eternal origin from the Father and the Son. His axis is eternal subsistence; the extension of His infinite magnitude is the Horizon; the diffusion of His infinite goodness is the Meridian; Justice is the Equator. The Zodiac, visible with its twelve signs, represents the twelve emanations of divine virtues—which theologians call "attributes"—flowing forth from the ineffable fountain of divine light like so many <term>actinobolismi</term> (effusions of rays).

<margin>Creatures are the shadows of God's garment.</margin>
The Firmament of all things, whether possible or impossible, consists of the ideas and patterns in the divine mind; finally, all creatures exist as certain shadows, serving as the "garment of God," as <term>Rambam</term> (Maimonides) <note>Rabbi Moshe ben Maimon, a preeminent medieval Jewish philosopher and astronomer.</note> teaches. According to this pattern, the mystic sphere is established with seven planets moving perpetually beneath the circle of the twelve signs. It is a configuration of wonderful arrangement which, by its fertile influence, bestows the fruit of eternal life upon the mystical world of souls. To understand these things, one must know that this sensible machine of the world consists of a triple space, distinguished as if by three zones: the first of these defines the world, or the sublunary space; the kingdom of shadows and fluctuations.

<margin>The mystical distribution of the world.</margin>
The second defines the world or sidereal space, the hiding place of light, clarity, and beauty. The third is the empyrean world, or the Firmament, gleaming with an innumerable multitude of lights. The first space, that of the sublunary world, represents the Church Militant <note>The "Church Militant" refers to the community of Christians on Earth who are currently engaged in a spiritual struggle against sin and evil.</note>, most constant in its extreme instability through various shifts of shadows, clouds, and eclipses: it is the kingdom of mourning, warfare, temptation, and trial, where good things are so mixed with the bad, joyful with the sad, and bitter with the sweet, that it allows its inhabitants nothing solid or stable. The sidereal world, however, denotes the region of the seven spiritual gifts—represented as the seven planets—which stabilize and strengthen this mystical world of the Church Militant.

<margin>The Moon.</margin>
And by the Moon, the queen of moisture, what else is denoted but the life-giving washing of Holy Baptism? By this, minds are cleansed of all pollution by the lustral waters and are directed through Faith into the true and eternal path of light.

<margin>Mercury.</margin>
What does Mercury—the force that strengthens things—designate, if not the mystery of the holy chrism <note>Consecrated oil used in religious rites such as Confirmation.</note>? Through this, the soul is regenerated by the water of life and anointed with the oil of salvation, being strengthened and fortified against all the machinations of opposing powers.

<margin>The Sun.</margin>
By the Sun, if by anything at all, the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist is certainly and brilliantly signified. It is the vein of life, the fountain of salvation, the strength, food, and nourishment of souls, a ray of eternal light, the most radiant Sun of the mental world, and the storehouse of all spiritual gifts and graces. By it, all things are animated and strengthened, provided they receive the ray of such immense light with a careful and diligent disposition. What else is indicated by the "uniformly multiform" <note>original: "uniformiter difformem." A philosophical concept where a single, simple cause (God/Sun) produces diverse effects in different subjects.</note> light of the Sun, if not the divine splendor of this Church Militant? In her, there are "divisions of graces"—behold the multiformity—so that the Church of God may stand at the right hand of God "clothed in variety." Yet, it is the "same spirit"—behold the uniformity. There are "divisions of ministries"—behold the diversity; but the "same Lord"—behold the identity. There are "divisions of operations"—behold the multitude; but the "same Sun" who "works all things in all"—behold the unity. Divine Charity is likewise uniform,

<summary>This page introduces the concept of the 'Mystic Sphere' as a metaphorical map of God's attributes and the sacraments. It uses the movements of the planets and the nature of light to explain the relationship between the divine and the 'Church Militant' on Earth.</summary>
<keywords>Mystic Sphere, Light and Shadow, Hermes Trismegistus, Maimonides, Church Militant, Baptism, Eucharist, Divine Attributes, Uniformity and Diversity</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the moral and symbolic mapping of the celestial sphere onto the Christian life, specifically linking the planets and signs of the zodiac to the sacraments and various "states" of the blessed in heaven.</meta>

-># The Moral Interpretation of Light and Shadow.<-

...it is, since it raises everyone to the same blessedness; yet it is diverse, as it makes some shine like Arcturus, Aldebaran, Regulus <note>original: "Basilisi," referring to the "Little King" star in Leo</note>, Spica, Castor, and Pollux—some as stars of the first magnitude, others of the second, third, fourth, or fifth. But the only Sun is Christ, and the only Moon is the Mother of God, the presiding rulers of this mystical world.

<margin>Mars.</margin>
Through Mars, the **Sacrament of Penance** is suggested to us, by which the soul, strengthened with a certain "Martial" fortitude, declares war on the world, the Devil, and its own flesh. It conquers the monsters of sin through true contrition of heart and subdues rebellious members through continual chastisement of the body; and thus at last, as a victor under the guidance of the light of Faith, it puts to flight all the devices of the Devil.

<margin>Jupiter.</margin>
Through Jupiter, the giver of dignity and power, the **Sacrament of Holy Orders** is beautifully indicated to us, by whose influence power, dominion, and perfect jurisdiction in the administration of souls are granted.

<margin>Saturn.</margin>
Finally, through Saturn, the symbol of Death, the mysteries of **Extreme Unction** <note>Now often called the Anointing of the Sick</note> are rightly denoted, through which, by the health-giving anointing of oil, a person close to dissolution is prepared for the soul's happy and blessed transition.

<margin>Venus.</margin>
Finally, what is noted through Venus but the **Sacrament of Matrimony**, through which grace is established for spouses joined in a perpetual and inseparable partnership of life for the sake of propagating offspring, seasoned with the grace of faith, love, piety, and marital honesty?

<margin>The mystical Zodiac.</margin>
We have seen the influence of the seven mystical planets upon the world below the moon; now let us also briefly consider the influence of the empyrean <note>the highest heaven</note> world. The firmament, visible with the Zodiac, aptly denotes for us the Church Triumphant—the kingdom of the Saints, the kingdom of grace and light; where there is no change or shadow of variation, where there is neither night nor day, but the Lamb is the lamp. Under this Zodiac, the "Sun of Justice" <note>Christ</note>, the lamp of Paradise, running its perpetual course, illuminates the various states of the Blessed, signified by the twelve signs of the Zodiac, into which it pours the lights of graces and spiritual gifts. 

Thus, through **Aries** (the Ram), a mild animal ready for slaughter, the state of the **Martyrs** is designated. 

Through **Taurus** (the Bull), the state of the **Patriarchs** and all those who tilled the Lord's vineyard with the greatest labors endured for the honor of God. 

Through **Gemini** (the Twins), the state of the **Doctors** <note>Theologians and great teachers of the Church</note>, who, burning with the two wings of Charity—toward God and neighbor—opened the way of eternal light to all believers through their voice and writings. 

From this emerges the state of **Converts**, noted by **Cancer** (the Crab). 

Through **Leo** (the Lion), the **Apostolic men**, who by the "roar" of the divine word roused the sluggish world from the winter of death to the light of faith and life. 

Through **Virgo** (the Virgin), what else is suggested but the immaculate state of **Virgins**, who, making themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, brought forth the fruits of eternal life through voluntary barrenness, and who, not defiled by women, follow the Lamb wherever He goes? 

Through **Libra** (the Scales), the state of **Blessed Kings and Princes** is chiefly understood, who, administering justice with piety in this world, promoted the worship of divine light with all zeal and care. 

Through **Scorpio** (the Scorpion), the state of **Penitents** is rightly understood, who in this world received the laurel of the light of life through voluntary chastisement of the body and members, and the most burning compunction of heart. 

Through **Sagittarius** (the Archer), what else is denoted but the state of **Preachers**, who, piercing the hearts of sinners with the arrows of the divine word, directed them into the path of light, and like the strongest hunters, having slain pestilential monsters, kept the Lord's vineyard immune from all contagion? 

Through **Capricorn**, the state of **Contemplatives** is denoted, who, ascending the rock of divine contemplation and absorbed by the sweetness of the divine word, appear with "horned" faces <note>original: "cornuta... facie," a reference to the radiance of Moses’ face after speaking with God, traditionally translated as "horned" in the Latin Vulgate</note> from the rays spread by their fellowship with the speech of the Lord. 

Through **Aquarius** (the Water-Bearer), the state of **Anchorites** <note>Hermits</note> is designated, who, distressed and afflicted in this world, wandering in deserts in sheepskins and goatskins, testified to the long duration of their sojourn with overflowing fountains of tears. 

Finally, through **Pisces** (the Fish), what else is signified but that **great multitude of the blessed** which no one can number, who, wandering in the ocean of divine contemplation, triumph with laurels and with lights communicated to each in proportion to their merits? 

And this is the mystical Zodiac indicated in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> under the twelve gates, with the twelve names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel; the tabernacle of God with men: whose lamp is the Lamb, that is, Christ the Sun of Justice. The Moon is the Mother of God crowned with twelve stars, that is, surrounded by the twelve signs. The stars are the Saints, who "will run like sparks through the stubble" <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 3:7</note>; divided as if on twelve seats, they will judge the nations and rule over the peoples, and their Lord shall reign forever. We have seen, therefore, the mystical Zodiac. Now nothing remains but to provide certain practical rules taken from Light and Shadow, by which we may emerge from the darkness into that wonderful light of the fellowship of the Saints.
