# Tropological Rules.

<note>original: "Regulæ Tropologicæ." Tropology is a method of interpretation that finds moral or spiritual lessons in text or nature.</note>

->*By which the Soul, emerging from shadow into light, may be perfectly joined to the eternal Light from which it flowed.*<-

## Rule I.

### *Contemplation of the sensible world.*

**D**IONYSIUS the Areopagite <note>A 5th-6th century Christian theologian and philosopher, also known as Pseudo-Dionysius, whose "Mystical Theology" deeply influenced medieval and Renaissance thought.</note>, that most acute Theologian, contemplating the eternal light, asks: how can we know God, who is neither intelligible, nor sensible, nor entirely anything among the things that can be understood? Perhaps we shall say truly that we do not know the eternal light from its own nature—seeing as it is hidden in inaccessible and incomprehensible darkness, above all reason and sense—but from the most orderly arrangement of all creatures. Because they are produced by Him, and bear certain images and likenesses of His divine exemplars, we stretch toward that which transcends all things, as if through certain pathways of light, into the most eminent privation of all things, and into the cause of all. Therefore, eternal light is known in all things, and separately from all things; indeed, through light and shadow, that is, knowledge and ignorance, God is known. He is intellect, reason, notion, touch, sense, opinion, imagination, name, and all other things; and yet He is neither understood, nor spoken of, nor named, nor is He any of those things that exist, nor is He known in any creature. And yet He is all things in all, and nothing in nothing; and from all things He is known to all, and from nothing to no one. For we rightly say these things about God the eternal light, and He is celebrated from all substances and praised according to the analogy and reason of all things of which He is the Author. He is also known through ignorance or darkness, according to that union which is above the intellect. When the intellect, acting as a "secondary light," recedes from all beings and then lets go of itself, it is united to the most brilliant rays. Whence it is illuminated there by the unfathomable depth of wisdom. I said above that it is known from all things: for the incomprehensible light itself is the effective cause of all things, the cause of the indissoluble concord and order of all; always connecting the ends of the first things with the principles of the second, and making one beautiful conspiracy <note>original: "conspiratio," used here in its literal Latin sense of "breathing together" or harmonious agreement.</note> and harmony of the universe. For since this world had to be beautiful, and its parts could not be pre-

<margin>How the soul ascends to God through the contemplation of sensible things.</margin>
cisely similar, but varied—so that immense beauty might shine back more perfectly in their variety—it pleased the Creator to co-create such an arrangement for variety so that order, which is absolute beauty itself, might shine back in all things at once. Through this order, the highest parts of the lowest things and the lowest parts of the highest things, harmoniously connected, might conspire into the one beauty of the world. Therefore, the proportion of any member to any other, and to the whole, was ordained by the Ordainer of all, creating man as both a major and a minor world <term>macrocosm and microcosm</term>; without whom nothing would be ordered, nothing disposed, and all things would exist discordantly. And the intellect, illuminated by this knowledge, approaches more closely to the light of that eternal wisdom, even to the point of wondering at it. Since this wisdom is a "vapor," as Ecclesiasticus says <note>A reference to the Book of Wisdom 7:25 or Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 24:3, describing Wisdom as a breath or vapor of the power of God.</note>, of the most sweet power of the Majesty of God, the soul wonders at its whole intellectual capacity receiving the scent, and is inflamed with an unspeakable desire to run toward that scent, so that it may grasp what it does not doubt is near. By this joyful hope, the course of the soul is comforted and increased. However, because of the weighing down of the body which it carries about, and because of the most swift wisdom which "reaches from end to end mightily," it cannot fully comprehend; it desires to be loosed from bodily bonds and renounces the carnal bonds of friendship; nor does it fear to die, provided it may grasp and taste the immortal fruit of divine Wisdom.

## Rule II.

### *Properties of light to be proposed for imitation.*

<margin>The triple ray—direct, reflected, and refracted—is compared to three states of men.</margin>
**I**t happens, moreover, that this light is perceived by the intellect by a triple ray: by the Blessed and by travelers <term>viatores</term> <note>A theological term for humans still on their earthly journey toward God.</note> united to God through contemplation by a **direct ray**; by the faithful through a **reflected ray**; and by the unfaithful through a **refracted ray**. The first, broken by no opacity of an intermediary, is absorbed into the Light of lights. The second exhibits the beauty of divine light through effects and creatures, which are the "hinder parts" of God <note>A biblical reference to Exodus 33:23, suggesting that in this life we see God's "back" or his effects, rather than his face.</note>, as if looking through the lattices of the soul. The third demonstrates it through false shadows of likenesses, as if in a thick and shadowy medium of ignorance. Therefore, the more the soul has been purified from all imperfection of shadows by the study of contemplation, the closer it becomes to the central union of divine light. And just as from ash and sand the most splendid and shining glass is made; so also the body, an obstacle to light, through the ash of penance and mortification...

<summary>This page presents "Tropological Rules" that use the physics of light as a metaphor for spiritual ascent, arguing that the beauty and order of the visible world lead the soul toward the incomprehensible "eternal light" of God. It categorizes spiritual perception into three types of rays: direct (for the blessed), reflected (for the faithful), and refracted (for the unfaithful).</summary>
<keywords>Dionysius the Areopagite, spiritual light, contemplation, microcosm, macrocosm, divine order, mystical theology, direct ray, reflected ray, refracted ray</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Tropological Rules" from page 808, where the author applies the physical laws of optics—discussed in the previous nine books—to the spiritual life of the soul. The focus remains on how divine light transforms the human spirit.</meta>

<page-num>809</page-num>
<header>Tropology of Light and Shadow.</header>

...refined in the furnace of divine love, it finally renders itself most similar to the divine light, and most fit for receiving the favors of that divine light. This light makes the subject in whom it dwells pleasing, beautiful, useful, and worthy of commendation—indeed, of admiration.

<margin>The properties of light are applied to the soul.</margin>
In the blessed, certainly, there is the light of glory; in travelers <note>original: "viatoribus." In theology, a "viator" is a person currently living on Earth, a "wayfarer" on the journey toward heaven.</note> there is the light of faith. If either of these is absent from the soul, no words suffice to describe the darkness and horrendous foulness that remain. For this light shines in the soul like the Sun with such beauty that the beauty of the whole world is nothing compared to it. For by what else are we made a spectacle to God and men, if not through a living faith, by which we daily build that heavenly **Jerusalem**?

<margin>The warming power of light.</margin>
The soul, warmed by this light, acquires the power of heating, which it communicates to its neighbor either by exhortation or by the shining example of its life. The just man, imbued with this light, acts no differently than light itself: he is unstainable by any filth of the medium, any stench, or any mud. Amidst the foul conversations of sinners, he always remains the same, his light in no way diminished or polluted. From this results another property of light: just as light is rich in all things and lacks nothing, so the just man lives blessed and content within himself, having repudiated the riches, pomp, and triumphs of the world. Again, as light is invincible and untamable, so is the light in the just man. For there is no darkness so great that he cannot dissipate it with light as his guide; no distance so great that he cannot overcome it; nor any created force that can destroy it, according to that saying of Saint Paul:

<margin>What shall separate us from the love of Christ, etc.? <note>A reference to Romans 8:35.</note></margin>
> Just as light diffuses itself in a moment, so the sinful soul is turned toward the eternal light: so swift is the flash of heavenly light by which the shadow and blindness of the mind are abolished.

Furthermore, because light is propagated in straight lines, is that not like the light that has risen for the just, and the joy that belongs to the upright of heart? Is it not like those who, urged on by the charity of faith while meditating on heavenly things, proceed from the creature in a straight course toward God? For **Dionysius** <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a favorite source for Kircher on mystical hierarchy and light.</note> asserts that the soul moves in a straight line. What else does the representation of images in a dark room <note>A reference to the *camera obscura*, a device Kircher discussed at length in previous books as a tool for art and science.</note> through a single ray of light denote, if not the power of contemplation in a soul irradiated by supernal light? By this <term>anakatharsei</term> <note>original: "ανακαθάρσει" — meaning purification or cleansing, specifically the purging of the soul to prepare it for divine vision.</note>, even those unrefined in any branch of literature or science, and holy men, are suddenly shown such force of divine light that they seem to excel all the Doctors of the world in subtlety and knowledge.

<margin>The philosophy of Saints Anthony and Benedict.</margin>
Imbued with this light, **Saint Anthony** <note>Saint Anthony the Great (c. 251–356), the "Father of All Monks," who found God in the wilderness.</note> philosophized among the trees. By this light, **Benedict** <note>Saint Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–547), who famously had a vision of the whole world gathered into a single ray of light.</note> saw and understood the entire universe in a single ray of divine light. For, as was said above, all creatures are like certain particles of divine light which, while they cast their rays through the senses as if through apertures, what else can they represent in the dark chamber of the heart, if not all things in all, and all things in God? Whoever, therefore, wishes to reach such a sublime level of contemplation, must withdraw into himself with all the windows of the soul closed. With the door of the soul shut, he must expose a clean heart, most purified from every stain of earthly contagion, like a chaste world to the ray of divine light. Then, in his own heart, he will perfectly contemplate whatever is in the world, as if in a mirror of divine light. To achieve all this, he should be carried by the ray of a right intention straight into God. He must place no obstacle to the divine light through passions or the shadows of imperfections. Instead, as much as he can, he should reflect the incoming divine light into himself by a perpendicular action—that is, by the conformity of our will with the Divine. This reflection will be more effective and direct the more it is elevated above the horizon of falling things and the closer it is to the "normal" line <note>In optics, the "normal" is the line perpendicular to a surface. Kircher uses this to symbolize a soul perfectly aligned with God's vertical grace.</note>. By the power of this reflected light, the hidden things of darkness or the smallest traces of heat will soon be manifested as colors—that is, the various interior affections of the soul and the foulness of earthly attachments will appear. Finally, the soul, purged by the help of light, will turn into a most clear crystalline mirror. The rays of divine favor, derived and united in this mirror, will cause an inflammation that finally consumes all earthly things. In this mirror will be seen that Apocalyptic book written inside and out and sealed with seals: its page is the Eternal Word, the hand writing is the Son, the pen is the divine decree, the ink is the blood of Christ, the names of the elect are predestination; those written inside are ordained for glory, those written outside are the reprobate. In this will appear the vanity of fleeting things, but the perpetuity and unspeakable joy of heavenly delights. Struck by these, the mind soon sends a repudiation to the old, weary mass of the world, and conceives at once a love and desire for the knowledge of such things. Hence, although before a mortal man—by his very descent and the garment of his earthly body—was sick, jagged, and squalid, and almost submerged in the whirlpool of sensible ghosts; through this ascent he raises his head again. Little by little, purged from the turbid dregs, he migrates as if from the region of the Cimmerians <note>A mythical people described by Homer as living in perpetual mist and darkness at the edge of the world.</note> into the clearest light of the ether. Finally, penetrating the vault of Heaven, now free from hardships and desires, he receives immortality itself, as if by right of return <note>original: "postliminio," a legal term for the restoration of rights to someone returning from exile or captivity.</note>, there—

<summary>Kircher uses optical metaphors—straight lines, reflection, and the camera obscura—to describe the soul's journey toward God. He argues that a pure soul acts as a mirror, reflecting divine light to gain knowledge far superior to academic study.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as the final epilogue to Athanasius Kircher’s monumental work on light and shadow, concluding the tenth book. It transitions from the physical and mathematical study of optics into a spiritual and moral meditation on the nature of God as the ultimate light.</meta>

<page-num>810</page-num>
# Book 10 of the Great Art. Epilogue: The Moral Interpretation of Light and Shadow.

...and there, passing the night with an innumerable offspring of light, the soul constantly contemplates the Light of lights. And these are the things which we thought should be briefly said concerning the Metaphysics of Light and Shadow. Whoever desires this <term>Mystical Theology</term> <note>a branch of theology focusing on the direct, subjective experience of the divine</note> in greater detail should consult the Hieroglyphic Treatise on the Theology of the Ancients in our *Egyptian Oedipus* <note>original: *Oedipus Ægyptiacus*; this was Kircher's massive three-volume work attempting to decipher Egyptian hieroglyphs and synthesize ancient wisdom</note>, where he will find everything pertaining to this matter treated explicitly. 

Meanwhile, let the most abundant fruits of this Metaphysics suffice for us, so that we may learn to know ourselves by a certain ascent of the mind, as if translated from shadow into eternal light; so that when we have perceived the complex cycle of human change, we may constantly reflect that evil is sown in every fleeting good, and good in every evil. Let us love all these things as if we were destined to hate them; let us hate them as if we were destined to love them; let us be joyful in adversity and anxious in successful outcomes. Let us never be carried away—as if our restraints were broken—by empty hope, excessive fear, or any crooked desire; this will be achieved if we entrust ourselves and all our affairs to God. Give us this mind, Father of Lights, from whom as from a perennial fountain of light all gifts and graces flow; direct toward us the ray of your divine goodness, so that the shadows of our souls being dissipated, we may persist in the love of your knowledge.

> ->*So may my every love, my life, and all my power*<-
> ->*Refer its beginning to you alone, and end in you alone.*<-
> ->*Disperse these shadows with the shining rays of the soul,*<-
> ->*So that your light may be my light, and my light may be your light.*<-

# Decorative Cover

->**Marbled Paper Endpaper**<-

This page features a beautiful example of a **marbled paper pattern**, a decorative technique that was highly popular in bookbinding between the 17th and 19th centuries. The pattern shown here is known as a **"combed"** or **"nonpareil"** design <note>The "nonpareil" (meaning "matchless" in French) pattern is created by using a fine-toothed comb to pull floating pigments into small, uniform scalloped waves before the paper is laid on top to absorb the ink.</note>.

The visual composition consists of dense, repeating rows of these multicolored waves. The palette is dominated by a warm **terracotta red**, which is highlighted by accents of **light blue**, **ochre yellow**, and **cream**. 

<margin>Visible fading and light discoloration along the left edge, consistent with the age of the manuscript and its handling over time.</margin>

<summary>This page serves as the decorative marbled endpaper of the manuscript, featuring a hand-crafted "nonpareil" pattern typical of historical bookbinding. It contains no written text but demonstrates the high quality of the volume's physical production.</summary>

# Decorative Endpaper

->**Marbled Paper Pattern**<-

This page is entirely covered with a decorative **marbled paper** pattern, a common feature in high-quality historical bookbinding. The design shown here is a **"nonpareil"** or **"comb"** pattern <note>From the French word for "matchless," the nonpareil pattern is created by drawing a fine-toothed comb through pigments floating on a liquid surface before transferring the design to paper.</note>. 

The visual composition consists of small, repeating semi-circular arches or "scales" arranged in tight horizontal rows. The color palette is rich and varied, including:
*   **Deep maroon-red**
*   **Slate blue**
*   **Muted green**
*   **Ochre yellow**

These colors are layered against a cream-colored background, creating a dense, rhythmic texture that covers the entire surface of the page. This type of decoration was traditionally used to protect the transition between the heavy book cover and the internal manuscript pages, while also providing an aesthetic flourish.

<summary>This page features a classic "nonpareil" marbled paper pattern, serving as a decorative endpaper for the manuscript. It contains no text, representing instead the artisanal craftsmanship of the volume's physical binding.</summary>

<keywords>marbled paper, nonpareil pattern, bookbinding, endpaper, decorative arts, 18th century style</keywords>
